Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.

p.seg: The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra
is, indeed, the profound hall of the Dharmakāya,
the true appellation of perfect enlightenment,
the deep mirror of all sūtras,
and the ultimate source of all streams.
As for its essence,
it wondrously exists beyond all phenomena,
and flows throughout the boundless interior.
It acts spontaneously,
and responds to circumstances as they arise.
When it acts spontaneously,
it rides the void and reflects light to govern phenomena,
conveying transformation through words and symbols.
When it responds to circumstances as they arise,
it assumes myriad forms to manifest images,
and establishes teachings according to the sentiments of all beings.
Thus, its form fills the ten directions, yet its mind does not change its thoughts;
its teaching permeates the world, yet its feelings are not self-centered.
It mingles with dust and ants, yet does not lower itself;
it covers all sages, yet does not exalt itself.
It benefits all transformations, yet does not rely on them;
its brightness surpasses myriad suns, yet it does not dwell there.
It is utterly one with the vast void in measure,
and completely merged with the Dharmatā as one.
Indeed, Dharmatā takes the ultimate as its essence,
and the ultimate returns to changelessness.
Therefore, birth and death cannot shift its permanence.
Since birth and death cannot shift its permanence,
its permanence is therefore unmoving.
Suffering cannot diminish its joy,
therefore its joy is endless.
As for the Self, it is born from erroneous perception;
the non-Self arises from temporary imputation.
Temporary imputation exists in names and numbers,
therefore the ultimate Self transcends names and numbers, yet is not non-existent.
Because it transcends names and numbers yet is not non-existent,
it can abide in the sacred position of self-mastery.
Furthermore, the non-Self cannot change,
and impurity is born from emptiness.
Thus, purity truly mirrors all phenomena like clear water.
Because it mirrors all phenomena,
impurity cannot defile it.
Therefore, this sūtra, in its profound chapters, elucidates the permanence, joy, Self, and purity as the forest of its principal doctrines,
and explores the profound principles as the fundamental application of Nirvāṇa.
It can reveal the secret treasury unheard of before,
and activate the spiritual conduit for universal illumination.
It rescues from the sores and ulcers of the four grave offenses,
and excises the growths and warts of Avīci Hell.
By revealing the secret treasury, it clarifies the emotions of all consciousnesses,
and ascertains the existence of the wondrous Self within oneself.
By activating the spiritual conduit, it awakens the hidden profound mystery,
and reflects the divine pearl within the body.
However, the four grave offenses and Avīci Hell are slanders against the Vaipulya Sūtras.
These are the most severe afflictions and
the worst of initial growths.
Therefore, Mahāparinirvāṇa takes "being without growths or warts" as its meaningful name,
and this sūtra takes Mahāparinirvāṇa as its principal title.
When the principal title is raised, it illuminates the comprehensive inclusion of all wonders,
with concise words and complete meaning.
When the meaningful name is established, it illuminates the superiority and inferiority of the three vehicles,
and the existence of the ultimate.
However, subtle transformation leaves no trace,
and wondrous accord is beyond words.
If one allows it to operate in its profound state, the principle will not function in vain.
Therefore, this sūtra establishes sincere words as the foundation of its teaching,
extensively uses metaphors to illustrate its meaning,
establishes the protection of the Dharma for beginners,
and by contemplating the secret treasury, thoroughly investigates the origin.
It removes the long-standing obstacles of a thousand years,
and dispels the remaining doubts from Gṛdhrakūṭa.
As for the subtle principles, intricately hidden and subtler than the subtle,
the Bodhisattvas extensively demonstrate the skill of master craftsmen,
and provide the vast assistance of boats and ships.
Their questions and difficulties are raised like clouds,
turning and overturning with thoroughness and precision,
thereby making the obscure path smooth and clear,
and the ultimate truth suddenly apparent.
Therefore, one recites its text without weariness,
speaks its meaning without exhaustion,
savors its taste without satiety,
and partakes of its sound without厌.
It can be truly said that subtle words resound in Zhēndān,
and profound rhymes are first sung in Chìxiàn.
The Brahmic sound vibrates among the deaf populace,
and the true visage shines grandly in this present day.
But those of limited hearing,
and those who cling to biased views,
without assessing their foolish opinions,
dare to criticize the boundless scripture of the Great Sage.
Consequently, right and wrong arise in disputes,
and ridicule and slander are born from malicious pleasure.
Even earlier enlightened ones cannot turn them from their delusion,
and all sages cannot change their will.
They are about to sink into the net of the eight邪 paths,
and long remain in the abyss of the nine streams.
Is this not lamentable?
Is this not lamentable?
The Indian Śramaṇa Tánwúchèn
was a native of Central India,
of the Brahmin caste.
His natural endowment was outstanding,
and his perception keen and profound.
His discernment and eloquence were clear and superior,
encompassing both inner and outer knowledge.
Intending to spread the Dharma,
he first arrived in Dūnhuáng,
and resided there for several years.
The Great Jǔqú, King of Hexī,
whose supreme virtue was subtly manifest,
established and prospered his royal enterprise.
Although he was engaged in myriad affairs of state,
he always thought of promoting the great Dharma,
serving as a bulwark for the Dharma.
It happened that he pacified Xīxià.
This sūtra and Chèn came from afar.
If not for a preordained profound connection,
how could such a meeting occur?
After Chèn had arrived here,
in the tenth year of Xuánshǐ, which was the year Dàliáng,
on the twenty-third day of the tenth month,
the King of Hexī urged him to translate it.
Chèn held the Sanskrit text in his hand,
and verbally rendered it into Qín speech.
His spirit and demeanor were sharp,
and he held the Dharma in profound reverence.
During the translation, he was respectful and cautious,
leaving almost nothing unrevealed.
He meticulously researched the original and corrected it,
striving to preserve the sūtra's meaning.
His only regret was that the Sanskrit text was fragmented and incomplete.
As for me, being mediocre and shallow,
I happened to encounter this opportunity.
Day and night I feel gratitude and awe,
deeply joyful for this good fortune.
I have merely attempted to mark its position
and narrate its main principles,
how could I claim to truly glimpse its profound essence?
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was in Kuśinagara, in the land of the Mallas, by the Hiraṇyavatī River, between the twin Sāla trees.
At that time, the World-Honored One was accompanied by eighty myriads of hundreds of thousands of great Bhikṣus,
surrounding him in front and behind.
On the fifteenth day of the second month, as he was about to enter Nirvāṇa,
by the Buddha's divine power, a great sound emanated,
its sound filling everything up to the highest heaven,
universally proclaiming to all sentient beings in their respective languages:
"Today, the Tathāgata,
Arhat,
Samyaksaṃbuddha,
out of compassion for sentient beings,
protects sentient beings,
regards sentient beings equally like Rahula,
and serves as a refuge, shelter, and abode for them.
The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One is about to enter Nirvāṇa.
If any sentient beings have any doubts,
they may now all ask,
this being the last opportunity to ask."
At that time, the World-Honored One, in the morning,
emitted various lights from his face,
their brilliance of mixed colors:
blue,
yellow,
red,
white,
crystal,
and agate.
The light universally illuminated this three-thousand great-thousand Buddha-world,
and likewise the ten directions.
All sentient beings in the six realms who encountered this light
had all their sinful defilements and afflictions eliminated.
When these sentient beings saw and heard this,
their hearts were greatly grieved,
and simultaneously they raised their voices, crying and wailing:
"Alas, merciful father!
How painful, how bitter!"
They raised their hands and beat their heads, pounded their chests, and cried out.
Among them, some trembled in their bodies,
wept,
and choked.
the great earth, all mountains, and great seas,
all trembled.
Then all sentient beings said to each other:
“Let us each restrain ourselves,
and not grieve excessively.
We should quickly go to Jūshī Nàchéng, the birthplace of the strong men,
to the Tathāgata's presence,
prostrate with our heads to the ground in reverence,
and implore the Tathāgata not to enter Parinirvāṇa,
but to remain in the world for one kalpa or for less than one kalpa.”
Holding each other's hands, they further said:
“The world is empty and void,
the merits of sentient beings are exhausted,
and all unwholesome karmas
are growing and emerging.
You all should now quickly go, quickly go!
The Tathāgata will soon certainly enter Nirvāṇa.”
They further said:
“The world is empty and void,
the world is empty and void!
From now on, we will have no savior or protector,
no one to rely upon or revere,
poor, orphaned, and exposed.
Once separated from the unsurpassed World-Honored One,
if doubts arise, whom shall we ask?”
At that time, there were immeasurable great disciples,
the Venerable Móhē Jiāzhānyán,
the Venerable Bó Jùluó,
the Venerable Yōupō Nántuó,
and others like these great Bǐqiū,
who encountered the Buddha's radiance,
their bodies trembled and shook,
even violently shaking, unable to control themselves,
their minds turbid and confused,
they cried out loudly,
experiencing such various kinds of suffering and distress.
At that time, there were also eight hundred thousand Bǐqiū and others,
all Āluóhàn,
whose minds had attained freedom,
their tasks accomplished,
free from all defilements,
their faculties disciplined,
like great dragon kings possessing great power and virtue,
having achieved wisdom of emptiness,
having attained their own benefit,
like a sandalwood forest surrounded by sandalwood,
like a lion king surrounded by lions,
having accomplished such immeasurable merits,
all of them were true sons of the Buddha.
In the early morning,
when the sun first rose,
having left their usual dwellings,
while chewing willow twigs,
they encountered the Buddha's radiance,
and said to each other:
“Friends,
quickly rinse your mouths and wash your hands.”
Having said this,
their body hairs stood on end,
their entire bodies became red with blood like the Bōluóshē flower,
tears filled their eyes, and they experienced great distress.
Desiring to benefit and bring peace to sentient beings,
to accomplish the Dàshèng and the supreme practice of emptiness,
to manifest the Tathāgata's expedient secret teachings,
and to prevent the discontinuation of various teachings,
for the sake of disciplining sentient beings due to their karmic conditions,
they quickly went to the Buddha's presence, prostrated at the Buddha's feet,
circumambulated hundreds of thousands of times,
put their palms together in reverence,
and sat down to one side.
At that time, there were also Jūtuóluónǚ,
Bǐqiūní Shànxián,
Bǐqiūní Yōupō Nántuó,
Bǐqiūní Hǎiyì,
together with sixty kotis of Bǐqiūní and others,
all of whom were also great Āluóhàn,
whose defilements were exhausted,
whose minds had attained freedom,
their tasks accomplished,
free from all defilements,
their faculties disciplined,
like great dragons possessing great power and virtue,
having achieved wisdom of emptiness.
Also in the early morning,
when the sun first rose,
their body hairs stood on end,
their entire bodies became red with blood like the Bōluóshē flower,
tears filled their eyes, and they experienced great distress.
Also desiring to benefit and bring peace to sentient beings,
to accomplish the Dàshèng and the supreme practice of emptiness,
to manifest the Tathāgata's expedient secret teachings,
and to prevent the discontinuation of various teachings,
for the sake of disciplining sentient beings due to their karmic conditions,
they quickly went to the Buddha's presence, prostrated at the Buddha's feet,
circumambulated hundreds of thousands of times,
put their palms together in reverence,
and sat down to one side.
Among the assembly of Bǐqiūní, there were also other Bǐqiūní,
all of whom were Púsà,
dragons among men,
having reached the ten stages and dwelling immovably,
who, in order to transform sentient beings, appeared in female bodies,
and constantly cultivated the four immeasurable minds,
having attained power and freedom,
able to manifest as Buddhas.
At that time, there were also as many Púsà Móhēsà as the sands of one Gānghé River,
dragons among men,
having reached the ten stages and dwelling immovably,
who expediently manifested bodies.
Their names were:
Púsà Hǎidé,
Púsà Wújìnyì,
and other Púsà Móhēsà who were the leaders.
All of them revered the Dàshèng,
dwelled in the Dàshèng,
deeply understood the Dàshèng,
delighted in the Dàshèng,
protected the Dàshèng,
were skilled at conforming to all worldly conditions,
and made this vow:
“Those who are not yet delivered
shall be delivered.”
They had already, in past lives, over countless kalpas,
cultivated pure precepts,
perfectly maintained their practices,
enlightened those not yet enlightened,
continued the lineage of the Sānbǎo so that it would not be interrupted,
and in future lives, they would turn the Dharma wheel,
adorned with great adornments, thereby adorning themselves,
having accomplished such immeasurable merits,
viewing all sentient beings equally as if they were their only child.
Also in the early morning,
when the sun first rose, they encountered the Buddha's radiance,
their body hairs stood on end,
their entire bodies became red with blood like the Bōluóshē flower,
tears filled their eyes, and they experienced great distress.
Also desiring to benefit and bring peace to sentient beings,
to accomplish the Dàshèng and the supreme practice of emptiness,
to manifest the Tathāgata's expedient secret teachings,
and to prevent the discontinuation of various teachings,
for the sake of disciplining sentient beings due to their karmic conditions,
they quickly went to the Buddha's presence, prostrated at the Buddha's feet,
circumambulated hundreds of thousands of times,
put their palms together in reverence,
and sat down to one side.
At that time, there were also as many Upāsakas as the sands of two Gaṅgās,
who upheld the Five Precepts
and possessed perfect deportment.
Their names were:
Wēidé Wúgòu Chēngwáng Upāsaka,
Shàndé Upāsaka, and others, who served as their leaders.
They profoundly delighted in observing the gates of various antidotes,
namely, suffering and happiness,
permanence and impermanence,
purity and impurity,
self and non-self,
reality and unreality,
refuge and non-refuge,
sentient beings and non-sentient beings,
constancy and inconstancy,
safety and unsafety,
conditioned and unconditioned,
cessation and non-cessation,
Nirvāṇa and non-Nirvāṇa,
superiority and non-superiority.
They constantly delighted in observing such gates of antidotes to these dharmas.
They also wished to delight in hearing the unsurpassable Mahāyāna,
and having heard it,
were able to expound it to others.
They upheld pure precepts well
and yearned for the Mahāyāna.
Having satisfied themselves,
they were also able to satisfy others who yearned.
They were good at acquiring unsurpassable wisdom,
loved and delighted in the Mahāyāna,
and protected the Mahāyāna.
They were good at adapting to all worldly conditions,
delivering those not yet delivered,
and enlightening those not yet enlightened.
They propagated the lineage of the Three Jewels so it would not be interrupted,
and in future ages, they would turn the Dharma wheel.
They adorned themselves with great adornments,
their minds always deeply relishing pure conduct in the precepts.
They were all able to achieve such merits,
and generated great compassion for all sentient beings,
treating them equally and without difference, as if they were a single child.
Also, at dawn, when the sun first rose,
desiring to cremate the Tathāgata’s body,
each person took ten thousand bundles of fragrant wood,
Candanā and Agarwood,
Niútóu Candanā,
and heavenly fragrant woods.
Each of these woods,
its grain and knots,
all possessed the subtle radiance of seven precious gems,
like various painted decorations.
By the Buddha's power, they had such wondrous colors,
blue, yellow, red, and white,
which all sentient beings delighted to see.
All the woods were smeared with various fragrances,
turmeric, agarwood, and various resins,
and adorned with scattered flowers:
Utpala flowers,
Kumuda flowers,
Padma flowers,
Puṇḍarīka flowers.
On all the fragrant woods, five-colored banners were hung,
soft and subtle, like heavenly garments,
Kāśeya silk and fine linen.
These fragrant woods were loaded onto jeweled carriages.
These jeweled carriages emitted various lights,
blue, yellow, red, and white.
Their shafts and axles were all inlaid with seven precious gems.
Each carriage was drawn by four horses.
Each of these horses was swift as the wind.
Before each carriage, fifty-seven subtle jeweled banners were erected,
covered above by nets of pure gold.
Each jeweled carriage also had fifty subtle jeweled canopies.
From each carriage hung various flower garlands:
Utpala flowers,
Kumuda flowers,
Padma flowers,
Puṇḍarīka flowers.
The flowers had pure gold leaves,
and diamond flower-stands.
In these flower-stands, there were many black bees,
gathering and enjoying themselves with delight.
They also emitted wondrous sounds,
namely, impermanence,
suffering,
emptiness,
and non-self.
Within these sounds,
the Bodhisattva’s original path was also expounded.
There were also various songs, dances, and musical instruments:
zithers,
konghous,
xiaos, sê,
drums and wind instruments.
Within these musical sounds, these words were also uttered:
"Alas,
alas,
the world is empty!"
Before each carriage,
there was an Upāsaka holding four jeweled trays.
On these trays were various flowers:
Utpala flowers,
Kumuda flowers,
Padma flowers,
Puṇḍarīka flowers,
turmeric and other incense,
all subtle and supreme.
The Upāsakas prepared various food offerings
for the Buddha and the Saṅgha,
all fully equipped.
All were made from Candanā and Agarwood,
and ripened by water of eight merits.
The food was sweet and delicious, with six flavors:
one, bitter;
two, sour;
three, sweet;
four, pungent;
five, salty;
six, bland.
There were also three merits:
one, light and soft;
two, pure and clean;
three, in accordance with Dharma.
They made various adornments such as these.
Arriving at the birthplace of the Mallas, between the twin Śāla trees,
they again spread golden sand over the ground,
and covered the sand with Kālindī garments,
Kambala garments, and silk garments,
completely filling an area of twelve yojanas.
They arranged seven-jeweled lion thrones for the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
These thrones were high and grand like Mount Suméru.
On all these thrones were jeweled canopies,
from which hung various garlands.
All the Śāla trees
were hung with various subtle banners and canopies,
their trunks smeared with various fine fragrances,
and various famous flowers scattered among the trees.
The Upāsakas each thought:
"If any sentient being is in need,
we will give food if they need food,
drink if they need drink,
our heads if they need heads,
our eyes if they need eyes.
Whatever sentient beings need,
we will all give it."
When making these offerings,
they were free from desire, anger,
defilement, and poisonous thoughts,
without any other thought of seeking worldly blessings and happiness,
only aspiring to unsurpassable pure Bodhi.
These Upāsakas
had all established themselves in the Bodhisattva path.
They further thought:
"Now, having accepted our food, the Tathāgata
will enter Nirvāṇa."
Having this thought,
their body hairs stood on end,
and their whole bodies appeared blood-red like Palāśa flowers.
Tears filled their eyes, giving rise to great suffering and distress.
Each carrying their offering implements,
loaded onto jeweled carriages,
fragrant wood,
banners,
jeweled canopies,
and food,
they swiftly reached the Buddha's abode and bowed at the Buddha's feet.
With the offering implements they carried,
they made offerings to the Tathāgata,
circling him hundreds of thousands of times.
They cried out loudly,
their sorrow moving heaven and earth,
beating their chests and wailing loudly,
tears falling like rain.
They further said to each other:
"Alas,
friends!
The world is empty,
the world is empty!"
Then, they cast their bodies
before the Tathāgata
and spoke to the Buddha, saying:
"We only pray, Tathāgata,
to compassionately accept our last offering."
The World-Honored One, knowing the time, remained silent and did not accept.
They requested three times in this manner,
but all were refused.
The Upāsakas, unable to fulfill their wish,
were filled with sorrow and distress,
and remained silent.
Just like a kind father who has only one child,
who suddenly falls ill and dies,
and he carries the corpse to the burial ground,
then returns feeling desolate
and deeply grieved.
The Upāsakas' sorrow and grief were also like this.
They placed all their offerings in one place,
stepped aside,
and sat in silence.
At that time, there were also as many Ùpóyí as three Gaṅgā rivers' sands,
who upheld the Five Precepts,
and whose deportment was complete.
Their names were:
Shòudé Ùpóyí,
Démàn Ùpóyí,
Píshèqū Ùpóyí, and so on, eighty-four thousand in number,
who were their leaders.
They were all capable of preserving the Right Dharma,
and for the sake of liberating immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings,
they manifested female bodies and denounced the household life.
They regarded their own bodies as four poisonous snakes,
that this body is constantly devoured by innumerable insects,
that this body is foul-smelling,
filled with greed and desire,
and bound for hell,
that this body is loathsome like a dead dog,
that this body is impure, with nine orifices constantly flowing.
This body is like a city,
covered with blood, flesh, sinews, bones, and skin,
with hands and feet serving as turrets and watchtowers to repel enemies,
eyes as apertures,
and the head as a palace hall,
with the mind-king residing within.
Such a body-city
is abandoned by all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones,
but ordinary fools constantly crave and cling to it,
with lust,
hatred,
and ignorance,
and rākṣasas dwelling therein.
This body is impermanent,
like reeds,
eranda trees,
water bubbles,
or banana trees.
This body is impermanent,
changing in every thought,
like lightning flashes,
raging waters,
or illusory flames,
also like drawing on water,
which immediately closes up as it is drawn.
This body is easily destroyed,
like a large tree on a steep riverbank.
This body will soon be devoured
by foxes, wolves,
owls,
vultures,
magpies,
and hungry dogs.
What wise person
would delight in this body?
It would be easier to fill the great ocean with a cow's hoof print
than to fully explain the impermanence,
impurity,
and foulness of this body.
It would be easier to roll the whole earth into something like a date,
gradually reducing it to a tiny speck like a tīnglì seed, down to a particle of dust,
than to fully explain the faults of this body.
Therefore, one should abandon it,
like discarding snot or spit.
For these reasons,
these Ùpóyí
constantly cultivated their minds
with the Dharma of emptiness,
signlessness,
and wishlessness.
They deeply delighted in consulting and receiving Mahāyāna sūtras,
and having heard them, they could also expound them to others,
protecting their original vows,
denouncing the female body as
extremely detestable and loathsome,
its nature not being firm or stable.
Their minds constantly cultivated such right contemplation,
breaking the endless cycle of birth and death.
They longed for the Mahāyāna,
and having satisfied themselves,
they could also satisfy others who longed for it.
They deeply delighted in the Mahāyāna,
and protected the Mahāyāna.
Although they manifested female bodies,
they were in reality Bodhisattvas,
who were skilled at adapting to all worldly conditions,
liberating those not yet liberated,
enlightening those not yet enlightened,
and continuing the lineage of the Three Jewels so that it would not be interrupted.
In future ages, they would turn the Dharma wheel,
adorning themselves with great adornments,
firmly upholding the precepts,
and all having achieved such merits.
They aroused great compassion for all sentient beings,
treating them equally without discrimination,
like looking upon their only child.
Also, in the morning,
at sunrise, they said to each other:
"Today, we should go to the Sūangshù Grove."
The offerings prepared by the Ùpóyí
were even more splendid than before,
and they brought them to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads to the Buddha's feet,
circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times,
and said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
We have now
prepared various offerings for the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
We only pray that the Tathāgata
will graciously accept our offerings."
The Tathāgata remained silent and did not give permission.
The Ùpóyí could not achieve their wish,
and feeling disappointed,
they sat down to one side.
At that time, there were also as many Licchavis of Viyālícity as four Gaṅgā rivers' sands,
men and women,
young and old,
with their wives and family members,
and the royal families of all the kings of Yánfúqí,
who, for the sake of seeking the Dharma,
had cultivated pure conduct,
whose deportment was complete,
who had subdued externalist schools and those who corrupted the Right Dharma.
They constantly said to each other:
"We shall use our treasuries of gold and silver
to ensure that the sweet dew,
the inexhaustible Right Dharma,
and its profound treasures remain long in the world.
May we always be able to study and practice it.
If anyone slanders the Buddha's Right Dharma,
we shall cut out their tongues."
They also made this vow:
"If there are renunciants who violate the precepts,
we shall dismiss them and make them return to lay life and serve us.
If anyone deeply delights in
and protects the Right Dharma,
we shall respect them as if serving our parents.
If there is a Saṅgha that cultivates the Right Dharma,
we shall rejoice and empower them.
We constantly desire to hear Mahāyāna sūtras,
and having heard them, we can also widely expound them to others."
They all had achieved such merits.
Their names were:
Jìngwúgòuzàng Líchēzǐ,
Jìngbùfàngyì Líchēzǐ,
Héngshuǐwúgòujìngdé Líchēzǐ,
and so on. They said to each other:
"Friends,
let us now quickly go to the Buddha's abode."
The offerings prepared
were various and complete.
Each Licchavi
had prepared eighty-four thousand great elephants,
eighty-four thousand four-horse jeweled carriages,
eighty-four thousand bright moon jewels,
celestial wood,
candana, agarwood,
and bundles of firewood,
each kind numbering eighty-four thousand.
Before each elephant,
there were jeweled banners and canopies,
the smallest of these canopies
measuring one yojana in circumference and area,
the shortest banner being thirty-two yojanas long,
and the lowest jeweled banner being one hundred yojanas high.
They carried such offerings
to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads to the Buddha's feet,
circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times,
and said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
We have now
prepared various offerings for the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
We only pray that the Tathāgata will graciously accept our offerings."
The Tathāgata remained silent and did not give permission.
The Licchavis and others
could not achieve their wish,
and their hearts were filled with sorrow and distress.
Through the Buddha's divine power,
they remained silent in the air,
seven tāla trees above the ground.
At that time, there were also five Gaṅgā-sand-like ministers and
elders,
who revered the Mahāyāna.
If there were heterodox scholars who slandered the Right Dharma,
these people were capable of vanquishing them,
just as a hailstorm crushes grass and trees.
Their names were:
Rìguāng 长者 (Elder Rìguāng),
Hùshì 长者 (Elder Hùshì),
Hùfǎ 长者 (Elder Hùfǎ),
and others like them were their leaders.
The offerings they prepared
were five times greater than the previous ones.
Together they proceeded to the Sāluó Twin Trees,
bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him a hundred thousand times,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We now
offer these provisions to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
We only pray that you, out of compassion,
accept our offerings."
The Tathāgata remained silent and did not accept them.
The elders and others,
unable to fulfill their wish,
were filled with sorrow and distress.
By the Buddha's divine power,
they stood silently in the empty space,
seven tāla trees above the ground.
At that time, there was also King Píshèlì,
and his harem, wives, and retinue,
all the kings within Jambudvīpa,
except for Āshéshì, and the people of his cities and villages.
Their names were Yuèwúgòu 王 (King Yuèwúgòu) and others.
Each prepared their four armies,
desiring to go to the Buddha.
Each of these kings
had one hundred eighty myriad crores of people in their retinue.
These chariots and soldiers
were drawn by elephants and horses.
The elephants had six tusks,
the horses were swift as wind.
The offerings they adorned were six times greater than the previous ones.
Among the jeweled canopies, the smallest
was eight yojanas in circumference, length, and width.
The shortest banners were sixteen yojanas.
The lowest jeweled banners were thirty-six yojanas.
These kings
were all firmly established in the Right Dharma,
despised heterodox teachings,
revered the Mahāyāna,
deeply delighted in the Mahāyāna,
and pitied all sentient beings,
treating them as their only child.
The food they offered
diffused a fragrance that filled four yojanas.
Also, at dawn, when the sun first rose,
they brought these various excellent and delicious meals
to the Twin Trees,
to the Tathāgata,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We offer these provisions to the Buddha and the Bhikṣu-Saṅgha.
We only pray that the Tathāgata,
out of compassion, accept our final offering."
The Tathāgata, knowing the time,
also did not permit it.
These kings,
unable to fulfill their wish,
were filled with sorrow and distress,
and retreated to one side.
At that time, there were also seven Gaṅgā-sand-like royal consorts,
except for King Āshéshì's consort,
who, to liberate sentient beings,
manifested in female form.
They constantly observed their bodily conduct,
cultivating their minds
with the dharma of emptiness,
signlessness,
and wishlessness.
Their names were:
Sānjièmiào Fūrén (Consort Sānjièmiào),
Àidé Fūrén (Consort Àidé).
These royal consorts,
all firmly established in the Right Dharma,
practiced the precepts,
were perfect in deportment,
pitied all sentient beings,
treating them as their only child.
They said to each other:
"We should now quickly go
to the World-Honored One."
The offerings prepared by the royal consorts
were seven times greater than the previous ones:
fragrant flowers,
jeweled banners,
silken streamers,
flags and canopies,
and excellent food.
The smallest jeweled canopies were sixteen yojanas in circumference, length, and width.
The shortest banners were thirty-six yojanas.
The lowest jeweled banners were sixty-eight yojanas.
The fragrance of the food
diffused and spread to fill eight yojanas.
They brought these
offerings
to the Tathāgata,
bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him a hundred thousand times,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We offer these provisions to the Buddha and the Bhikṣu-Saṅgha.
We only pray that the Tathāgata,
out of compassion, accept our final offering."
The Tathāgata, knowing the time,
remained silent and did not accept.
Then the consorts,
unable to fulfill their wish,
were filled with sorrow and distress,
tore out their hair,
beat their chests and wept loudly,
like one who has just lost a beloved child.
They retreated to one side,
and remained silent.
At that time, there were also eight Gaṅgā-river-sands of celestial maidens,
among whom Guǎngmù Tiānnǚ (廣目天女) was the foremost.
They spoke thus:
"Sisters!
Observe closely,
observe closely,
these human multitudes
who are preparing various excellent offerings
to present to the Tathāgata and the Bhikṣu Saṅgha.
We too should do likewise,
preparing subtle and wonderful offerings
to present to the Tathāgata.
After the Tathāgata has accepted them,
he will enter Nirvāṇa.
Sisters!
Tathāgatas appear in the world with great difficulty,
and the final offering is even more difficult.
If the Buddha enters Nirvāṇa,
the world will be empty.
These celestial maidens
loved and delighted in the Mahāyāna,
wished to hear the Mahāyāna,
and having heard it, could also expound it widely to others.
Having satiated their own longing for the Mahāyāna,
they could also satiate others who longed for it.
They guarded the Mahāyāna,
and if there were heretics
who envied the Mahāyāna,
they had the power to destroy them
like hail destroys grass.
They upheld the precepts,
were fully endowed with dignified deportment,
were skilled at adapting to all worldly conditions,
saving those not yet saved,
liberating those not yet liberated.
In future ages, they would turn the Dharma Wheel,
continue the lineage of the Three Jewels,
preventing its interruption.
They practiced and studied the Mahāyāna,
adorning themselves with great adornments,
achieving immeasurable merits such as these.
They regarded all sentient beings with equal compassion,
as if they were their only child.
Also, at dawn, when the sun first appeared,
each took various heavenly fragrant woods and the like,
exceeding all the fragrant woods found in the human realm.
The fragrance of these woods
could eliminate all kinds of foul odors among humans.
With white carriages and white canopies,
drawn by four white horses,
on each carriage
was spread a white tent.
From the four sides of the tent hung golden bells,
various fragrant flowers,
jeweled banners and canopies,
exquisite delicacies,
and various musical instruments.
They spread lion thrones,
the four legs of which were made entirely of dark blue lapis lazuli.
Behind each throne
was a jeweled reclining couch made of seven treasures.
In front of each throne
was a golden table,
and moreover, jewel-trees made of seven treasures served as lamps,
with various precious gems as their light.
Subtle heavenly flowers were scattered everywhere on the ground.
After these celestial maidens had prepared these offerings,
their hearts were filled with sorrow and emotion,
tears streamed down their faces,
and great distress arose.
Also, for the benefit
and happiness of sentient beings,
to achieve the foremost empty practice of the Mahāyāna,
to reveal the Tathāgata's expedient secret teachings,
and to ensure the continuous exposition of various Dharma teachings,
they went to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
circumambulated him a hundred thousand times,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We only wish that the Tathāgata
would mercifully accept our final offering."
The Tathāgata, knowing the time,
remained silent and did not accept.
The celestial maidens,
their wish unfulfilled,
were filled with worry and distress.
They withdrew to one side
and sat silently.
At that time, there were also nine Gaṅgā-river-sands of Dragon Kings,
dwelling in the four directions,
whose names were:
Wéixiūjí Lóngwáng (和修吉龍王),
Nántuó Lóngwáng (難陀龍王),
Pónántuó Lóngwáng (婆難陀龍王) as the foremost.
These Dragon Kings,
also at dawn, when the sun first appeared,
prepared various offerings,
exceeding those of humans and devas,
brought them to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
circumambulated him a hundred thousand times,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We only wish that the Tathāgata
would mercifully accept our final offering."
The Tathāgata, knowing the time,
remained silent and did not accept.
These Dragon Kings,
their wish unfulfilled,
were filled with sorrow and distress,
and withdrew to one side to sit.
At that time, there were also ten Gaṅgā-river-sands of Ghost Kings,
among whom Píshāmén Wáng (毘沙門王) was the foremost.
They said to each other:
"Sirs,
now let us quickly go to the Buddha's abode.
Let us prepare offerings, exceeding those of the Dragons,
bring them to the Buddha's abode,
bow our heads at the Buddha's feet,
circumambulate him a hundred thousand times,
and address the Buddha, saying:
"We only wish that the Tathāgata
would mercifully accept our final offering."
The Tathāgata, knowing the time,
remained silent and did not permit it.
These Ghost Kings,
their wish unfulfilled,
were filled with sorrow and distress,
and withdrew to one side to sit.
At that time, there were also twenty Gaṅgā-river-sands of Garuḍa Kings (Jīnchìniǎo Wáng, 金翅鳥王),
among whom Jiàngyuàn Niǎowáng (降怨鳥王) was the foremost.
There were also thirty Gaṅgā-river-sands of Gandharva Kings (Gāntápó Wáng, 乾闥婆王),
among whom Nàluódá Wáng (那羅達王) was the foremost.
There were also forty Gaṅgā-river-sands of Kinnara Kings (Jǐnnàluó Wáng, 緊那羅王),
among whom Shànjiàn Wáng (善見王) was the foremost.
There were also fifty Gaṅgā-river-sands of Mahoraga Kings (Móhóuluójiā Wáng, 摩睺羅伽王),
among whom Dàshànjiàn Wáng (大善見王) was the foremost.
There were also sixty Gaṅgā-river-sands of Asura Kings (Āxiūluó Wáng, 阿修羅王),
among whom Shǎnbólì Wáng (睒婆利王) was the foremost.
There were also seventy Gaṅgā-river-sands of Dānava Kings (Tuónàpó Wáng, 陀那婆王),
among whom Wúgòu Héshuǐ Wáng (無垢河水王)
and Bátídátuō Wáng (跋提達多王) were the foremost.
There were also eighty Gaṅgā-river-sands of Rākṣasa Kings (Luóchà Wáng, 羅剎王),
among whom Kěwèi Wáng (可畏王) was the foremost.
They had abandoned their evil minds,
no longer ate humans,
and had developed compassionate hearts towards their enemies and hated ones.
Their forms, which were ugly,
were all made beautiful by the Buddha's divine power.
There were also ninety Gaṅgā-river-sands of Tree Spirit Kings (Shùlín Shénwáng, 樹林神王),
among whom Lèxiāng Wáng (樂香王) was the foremost.
There were also a thousand Gaṅgā-river-sands of Mantra-holding Kings (Chízhòu Wáng, 持呪王),
among whom Dàhuàn Chízhòuwáng (大幻持呪王) was the foremost.
There were also a hundred million Gaṅgā-river-sands of color-craving evil spirits (tānsè guǐmèi, 貪色鬼魅),
among whom Shànjiàn Wáng (善見王) was the foremost.
There were also ten billion Gaṅgā-river-sands of celestial maidens (tiān zhū xíngnǚ, 天諸娙女),
among whom Lánpó Nǚ (藍婆女),
Yùpóshī Nǚ (欝婆尸女),
Dìlùzhān Nǚ (帝路沾女),
and Píshèqié Nǚ (毘舍佉女) were the foremost.
There were also a hundred billion Gaṅgā-river-sands of terrestrial Ghost Kings (dì zhū guǐwáng, 地諸鬼王),
among whom Báishī Wáng (白濕王) was the foremost.
There were also a hundred trillion Gaṅgā-river-sands of celestial sons and celestial kings,
including the Four Heavenly Kings (Sìtiānwáng, 四天王) and others.
There were also a hundred trillion Gaṅgā-river-sands of wind spirits from the four directions,
who blew timely and untimely flowers from the trees to scatter between the twin Sāla trees.
There were also a hundred trillion Gaṅgā-river-sands of cloud and rain gods,
all thinking:
"When the Tathāgata enters Nirvāṇa and his body is cremated,
I will pour down rain
to extinguish the fire in time,
and bring coolness to those in the assembly who are hot and agitated."
There were also twenty Gaṅgā-river-sands of great fragrant elephant kings,
among whom Luóhóu Xiàngwáng (羅睺象王),
Jīnsè Xiàngwáng (金色象王),
Gānwèi Xiàngwáng (甘味象王),
Gàn Yǎn Xiàngwáng (紺眼象王),
and Yùxiāng Xiàngwáng (欲香象王) were the foremost.
They revered the Mahāyāna,
loved and delighted in the Mahāyāna,
and knew that the Buddha would soon enter parinirvāṇa.
Each pulled up immeasurable and boundless wonderful lotus flowers,
came to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads and prostrated before the Buddha,
then withdrew to one side.
There were also twenty Gaṅgā-river-sands of lion beast kings,
among whom Shīzihǒu Wáng (師子吼王) was the foremost.
They bestowed fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
They brought various flowers and fruits,
came to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
then withdrew to one side.
Furthermore, there were twenty times the number of sands of the Ganges of bird kings,
ducks, geese,
mandarin ducks,
peacocks, and various other birds,
such as Gandharva birds,
Kalaviṅka birds,
mynas, parrots,
Kūcīla birds,
Vāhīgha birds,
Kalaviṅka birds,
Jīvajīvaka birds.
These and other birds
carried various flowers and fruits,
came to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
and withdrew to one side.
Furthermore, there were twenty times the number of sands of the Ganges of water buffalo, cattle, and sheep,
who went to the Buddha's abode,
produced wondrous fragrant milk,
and this milk filled all the ditches and pits in the city of Kuśinagara.
Its color, fragrance, and delicious taste were all complete.
Having accomplished this,
they withdrew to one side.
Furthermore, there were twenty times the number of sands of the Ganges of divine immortals from the four continents,
with the Endurance Immortal (Rěnrǔ Xiān) as their leader.
They carried various fragrant flowers and sweet fruits,
came to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
circuited the Buddha three times,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We only wish, World-Honored One,
that you would compassionately accept our final offering."
The Tathāgata, knowing the time, remained silent and did not consent.
At that time, the immortals,
their wish unfulfilled,
were filled with sorrow and distress,
and withdrew to one side.
All the bee kings in Jambudvīpa,
with the Wondrous Sound Bee King (Miàoyīn Fēngwáng) as their leader,
carried various flowers and came to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
circuited the Buddha once,
and withdrew to one side.
At that time, all the Bhikṣus
and Bhikṣuṇīs in Jambudvīpa gathered,
except for the Venerables Mahākāśyapa
and Ānanda.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable Asaṃkhyeya times the number of sands of the Ganges of mountains in the space between worlds
and in Jambudvīpa,
with Mount Sumeru (Xūmí Shān) as their leader.
These mountains were adorned,
their forests dense and lush,
their trees flourishing,
their branches spreading far and wide,
shading the sunlight.
Various wondrous flowers were found everywhere,
and dragon springs flowed with pure and fragrant waters.
Devas,
Nāgas,
spirits,
Gandharvas,
Asuras,
Garuḍas,
Kiṃnaras,
Mahoragas,
divine immortals with magical arts,
musicians and entertainers,
these and other beings,
filled them completely.
These mountain spirits
also came to the Buddha,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
and withdrew to one side.
Furthermore, there were Asaṃkhyeya times the number of sands of the Ganges of gods of the four great oceans and various river gods,
who possessed great power
and great supernatural abilities.
The offerings they presented
were far superior to the previous ones.
The divine beings' radiance, music, and lamp lights
eclipsed the sun and moon, making them no longer visible.
They scattered Campaka (Zhānpó) flowers upon the Hiraṇyavatī River (Xīlián Hé),
came to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
and withdrew to one side.
At that time, the Sāla (Suōluó) grove in the city of Kuśinagara (Jūshī Nàchéng)
changed to white,
like white cranes.
In the empty sky,
there naturally appeared a seven-jeweled palace,
carved and engraved,
richly adorned and clearly patterned,
with balustrades all around,
and various jewels interspersed.
Below the palace were many flowing springs and bathing pools,
with supreme wondrous lotuses filling them completely,
just like the country of Uttarakuru (Yùdān Yuè Guó) in the north,
and also like the Joyful Garden (Huānxǐ Zhī Yuán) of Trāyastriṃśa (Dāolì).
At that time, the Sāla grove,
with its various adornments,
was extremely lovely and delightful,
and it was likewise.
These Devas,
humans,
Asuras, and others,
all beheld the Tathāgata's parinirvāṇa,
and were all saddened and moved,
grieved and unhappy.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings (Sì Tiānwáng) and Śakra (Shì Tíhuányīn)
said to each other:
"You all observe
that the Devas,
people of the world, and Asuras
are making great offerings,
desiring to make a final offering to the Tathāgata.
We too should make such an offering.
If we can make the final offering,
then the perfection of generosity (dānboluómì) will be accomplished and fulfilled without difficulty."
At that time, the offerings presented by the Four Heavenly Kings
were even more splendid than before.
They carried Maṇḍārava (Mántuóluó) flowers,
Mahāmaṇḍārava (Móhē Mántuóluó) flowers,
Kākiloṇa (Jiājílóují) flowers,
Mahākākiloṇa (Móhē Jiājílóují) flowers,
Mañjuṣaka (Mánzhūshā) flowers,
Mahāmañjuṣaka (Móhē Mánzhūshā) flowers,
Santānika (Sàntuōníkā) flowers,
Mahāsantānika (Móhē Sàntuōníkā) flowers,
beloved flowers,
great beloved flowers,
Samantabhadra (Pǔxián) flowers,
great Samantabhadra flowers,
timely flowers,
great timely flowers,
fragrant city flowers,
great fragrant city flowers,
joyful flowers,
great joyful flowers,
desire-arousing flowers,
great desire-arousing flowers,
fragrant intoxicated flowers,
great fragrant intoxicated flowers,
universal fragrant flowers,
great universal fragrant flowers,
heavenly golden leaf flowers,
Nāga (Lóng) flowers,
Pāricchattra (Bōlìzhìduō) tree flowers,
Kubera (Jūpílō) tree flowers,
and also carried various supreme wondrous sweet delicacies.
They came to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet.
The radiance of these Devas and humans
was able to cover the sun and moon,
making them no longer visible.
With these offerings,
they wished to make offerings to the Buddha.
The Tathāgata, knowing the time,
remained silent and did not accept.
At that time, the Devas,
their wish unfulfilled,
were filled with sorrow and distress,
and withdrew to one side.
At that time, Śakra (Shì Tíhuányīn) and the gods of Trāyastriṃśa (Sānshí Sān Tiān)
also presented offerings that were twice as splendid as before,
and the flowers they carried were likewise.
Their fragrance was subtle and wondrous, extremely lovely and delightful.
They carried supreme victorious palaces and various small palaces,
came to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
we deeply love
and protect the Great Vehicle.
We only wish that the Tathāgata would compassionately accept our food."
The Tathāgata, knowing the time,
remained silent and did not accept.
At that time, the Śakra Devas,
their wish unfulfilled,
were filled with sorrow and distress,
and withdrew to one side.
Even up to the Sixth Heaven,
the offerings they presented progressively surpassed the previous ones,
with jeweled banners, streamers, and canopies.
The smallest jeweled canopies covered the four continents,
the shortest streamers encircled the four oceans,
and the lowest banners reached the Maheśvara (Zìzài Tiān).
A gentle breeze blew the streamers,
emitting wondrous sounds.
They carried supreme sweet delicacies,
came to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
we only wish that the Tathāgata would compassionately accept our final offering."
The Tathāgata, knowing the time, remained silent and did not accept.
These Devas and others,
their wish unfulfilled,
were filled with sorrow and distress,
and withdrew to one side.
up to the Ākāniṣṭha (Abode of Formless Heavens),
and the remaining multitude of Brahmā heavens,
all came and gathered.
At that time, Mahābrahmā-devarāja and the other Brahmā multitudes
emitted light from their bodies,
which illuminated the four continents.
The Kāmadhātu,
humans,
and devas,
along with the light of the sun and moon,
were all no longer visible.
Bearing various precious banners,
silk streamers,
and canopies—
the shortest banners were suspended from the Brahmā palace to the Sālara tree—
they came to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān!
We only wish that the Tathāgata
would mercifully accept our final offering."
The Tathāgata, knowing the time,
remained silent and did not accept.
At that time, the Brahmās, not having their wishes fulfilled,
felt sorrow and distress,
and withdrew to one side.
At that time, Vimalacitta Āsurarāja,
together with an immeasurable great retinue of Asuras,
whose bodily light
surpassed that of the Brahmā devas,
bearing various precious banners,
silk streamers,
and canopies—
the smallest of which covered a thousand worlds—
and superior delicious delicacies,
came to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We only wish that the Tathāgata
would mercifully accept our final offering."
The Tathāgata, knowing the time,
remained silent and did not accept.
The Asuras,
not having their wishes fulfilled,
felt sorrow and distress,
and withdrew to one side.
At that time, the Kāmadhātu Māra Pāpīyān, with his retinue,
and the devas' female attendants,
an immeasurable and boundless Asaṃkhyeya multitude,
opened the gates of hell,
provided clear, cool water,
and then announced:
"You all now
are powerless to do anything;
you should solely contemplate the Tathāgata,
Arhat,
Samyak-sambuddha,
and establish a final offering of rejoicing,
which will enable you all to attain peace for a long night."
Then Māra Pāpīyān, in hell,
removed all swords, spears, and immeasurable suffering and poison,
and extinguished the raging flames by showering them with rain.
By the Buddha's divine power,
he again conceived this thought:
to make all his retinue
abandon swords,
bows and arrows,
armor, weapons,
pikes and lances,
long hooks,
golden hammers,
battle-axes,
combat wheels,
and nooses.
The offerings they held
were many times superior to those presented by all humans and devas;
the smallest of their canopies covered a middle thousand-world system.
They came to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We now
love and delight in Mahāyāna,
and protect Mahāyāna.
Bhagavān!
If there are virtuous men and women
who, for the sake of offering,
for the sake of fear,
for the sake of deceiving others,
for the sake of profit,
or for the sake of following others, accept this Mahāyāna,
whether truly or falsely,
we at that time shall, for these people,
remove their fears,
and recite this dhāraṇī:
'Duōzhǐ zhāzhā luóduōzhǐ lúhēlí móhē lúhēlí āluó zhēluó duōluó suōhē'
"This dhāraṇī can enable all those who have lost their minds,
the fearful,
the dharma-speakers,
those who do not interrupt the True Dharma—
for the sake of subduing external paths,
protecting oneself,
protecting the True Dharma,
and protecting Mahāyāna—
to recite this dhāraṇī.
If anyone can uphold this dhāraṇī,
they will have no fear of evil elephants.
If they go to open wilderness,
empty marshes,
or dangerous places, they will not experience fear,
nor will there be danger from water, fire,
lions, tigers, wolves,
thieves, or kings.
Bhagavān!
If anyone can uphold this dhāraṇī,
they can eradicate all such fears.
Bhagavān!
Those who uphold this dhāraṇī,
I shall protect them,
like a tortoise retracting its six limbs.
Bhagavān!
We now
do not speak these words with flattery or deceit;
those who uphold this dhāraṇī,
we shall sincerely
increase their power.
We only wish that the Tathāgata
would mercifully accept our final offering."
At that time, the Buddha said to Māra Pāpīyān:
"I do not accept your food and drink offerings.
I have already accepted the divine dhāraṇī you recited,
for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings
and the fourfold assembly."
After the Buddha said this,
he remained silent and did not accept.
Thus, even after three requests,
he still did not accept.
Then Māra Pāpīyān,
not having his wishes fulfilled,
felt sorrow and distress,
and withdrew to one side.
At that time, Mahāīśvara-devarāja, with his immeasurable and boundless retinue,
and all the devas' multitudes,
prepared offerings
that completely overshadowed all the offerings
of Brahmā,
Śakra,
the Four Lokapālas,
humans and devas of the eight classes,
and non-human beings.
The offerings presented by Brahmā and Śakra
were like a lump of ink beside a conch shell, completely disappearing from view.
The smallest of their precious canopies could cover a Mahāsāhasra Lokadhātu.
Bearing such offerings,
they came to the Buddha's abode,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
circumambulated countless times,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān!
The minuscule offerings we have presented
are like a mosquito offering to me,
or like someone pouring a scoop of water into the great ocean,
or lighting a small lamp to aid hundreds of thousands of suns,
or in the spring and summer months when myriad flowers flourish,
someone bringing one flower to add to the myriad flowers,
or adding a tiny seed to Mount Meru.
How could these possibly benefit the great ocean,
the light of the sun,
the myriad flowers,
or Mount Meru?
Bhagavān!
The minuscule offerings I now present
are likewise.
Even if one were to fill a Mahāsāhasra Lokadhātu with incense, flowers,
music,
and banners,
to offer to the Tathāgata,
it would still be insufficient to speak of its merit.
Why?
Because the Tathāgata, for the sake of all sentient beings,
constantly endures all kinds of suffering and distress
in hell,
among hungry ghosts,
and among animals in all evil destinies.
Therefore, Bhagavān!
You should show compassion
and accept our offerings."
At that time, to the east, countless immeasurable *asáṅkhyeya* worlds, like the dust motes of the Ganges River sands, away from here,
there was a Buddha-land
named Yìlèměiyīn (意樂美音).
The Buddha's name was Xūkōngděng Rúlái (虛空等如來),
Arhat,
Samyaksaṃbuddha,
Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata,
Lokavid,
Anuttara,
Puruṣadamyasārathi,
Śāstādevamanuṣyāṇām,
Buddha,
Bhagavān.
At that time, that Buddha addressed his foremost great disciple, saying:
"Good man!
You should now go to the Western Suōpó (娑婆) world.
In that land there is a Buddha
named Shìjiāmóuní Rúlái (釋迦牟尼如來),
Arhat,
Samyaksaṃbuddha,
Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna,
Sugata,
Lokavid,
Anuttara,
Puruṣadamyasārathi,
Śāstādevamanuṣyāṇām,
Buddha,
Bhagavān.
That Buddha will soon enter *parnirvāṇa*.
Good man!
You may take this world's fragrant rice—its rice is fragrant and delicious,
and eating it brings peace and comfort—and with this food,
offer it to that Buddha, the Bhagavān.
After the Bhagavān eats,
he will enter *parnirvāṇa*.
Good man!
You may also pay homage
and ask to resolve your doubts."
At that time, Wúbiānshēn Púsà-móhēsà (無邊身菩薩摩訶薩) immediately received the Buddha's instruction,
rose from his seat,
bowed his head at the Buddha's feet,
circumambulated him three times to the right,
and together with countless *asáṅkhyeya* bodhisattvas,
departed from that land
and came to this Suōpó (娑婆) world.
Immediately, the great earth of this Three Thousand Great Thousand World
trembled in six ways.
Thereupon, among the assembly,
Brahma,
Śakra,
the Four Heavenly Kings,
Māra Pāxún (波旬),
Maheśvara,
such a great multitude,
seeing this earthquake,
their hairs stood on end all over their bodies,
their throats and tongues dried up,
they were terrified and trembled,
each wanting to scatter in all directions.
They saw their own bodies
had no more radiance,
and all their majestic power
was utterly extinguished.
At that time, Wénshūshīlì (文殊師利) Dharma-Prince
rose from his seat
and addressed the great assembly:
"Good men!
Do not fear,
do not fear!
Why is this?
To the east, countless immeasurable *asáṅkhyeya* worlds, like the dust motes of the Ganges River sands, away from here,
there is a world named Yìlèměiyīn (意樂美音).
The Buddha's name is Xūkōngděng Rúlái (虛空等如來),
Arhat,
Samyaksaṃbuddha,
with the ten titles complete.
There is a bodhisattva named Wúbiānshēn (無邊身),
who, with countless bodhisattvas,
is coming here to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
By the power of that bodhisattva's majestic virtue,
your bodily light has completely disappeared.
Therefore, you should be joyful,
and not harbor fear."
At that time, the great assembly
all saw that Buddha and his great assembly from afar,
just as one sees one's own reflection in a clear mirror.
Then Wénshūshīlì (文殊師利) again addressed the great assembly:
"The Buddha and his great assembly that you now see
are like seeing this Buddha.
By the Buddha's divine power,
you will similarly be able to see the boundless Buddhas in the nine directions."
At that time, the great assembly spoke to one another, saying:
"Alas,
alas!
The world is empty and void;
the Tathāgata will soon enter *parnirvāṇa*."
At that time, the entire great assembly saw Wúbiānshēn Púsà (無邊身菩薩) and his retinue.
On the body of this bodhisattva,
from each and every pore,
a great lotus flower emerged.
Each lotus flower contained seventy-eight thousand cities and towns,
equal in length and breadth to the city of Píyélí (毘耶離).
Their walls and moats were adorned with the seven treasures,
and *duōluó* (多羅) jewel trees were arrayed in seven rows.
The populace was thriving, peaceful, abundant, and joyful.
The battlements were made of *Yánfútánjīn* (閻浮檀金).
Each battlement
had various seven-jewel
forests, trees, flowers, and fruits, lush and flourishing.
When a gentle breeze blew, it emitted a subtle and wonderful sound,
whose melody was harmonious and elegant,
like heavenly music.
The people in the city,
hearing this sound,
immediately attained supreme and exquisite joy.
In these moats,
fine water was full,
pure, fragrant, and clean like true lapis lazuli.
In these waters were seven-jewel boats.
People rode them to play and bathe,
enjoying themselves together,
with boundless joy.
There were also immeasurable variegated lotus flowers:
*Uṭpala* flowers,
*Kumuda* flowers,
*Padma* flowers,
*Puṇḍarīka* flowers;
their flowers were as wide as carriage wheels.
On the banks of the moats,
there were many gardens.
Each garden had five springs and ponds.
In these ponds there were also various flowers:
*Uṭpala* flowers,
*Kumuda* flowers,
*Padma* flowers,
*Puṇḍarīka* flowers;
their flowers were also as wide as carriage wheels,
their fragrance was rich,
very lovely and delightful.
Their water was pure, soft, and of the highest quality.
Ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks played within them.
Each garden had palatial residences of various jewels.
Each palatial residence was four *yojana* in length and breadth.
All their walls were made of four treasures,
namely gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
True gold formed the sounding board,
and railings surrounded them.
The ground was made of rose quartz,
and golden sands were spread upon it.
In these palatial residences,
there were many seven-jewel flowing springs and bathing ponds.
By each pond,
there were eighteen golden steps.
*Yánfútánjīn* (閻浮檀金) formed the plantain trees,
like the Garden of Joy in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Each and every one of these cities
had eighty-four thousand kings.
Each and every one of these kings
had countless wives
and concubines,
enjoying themselves together,
joyfully receiving pleasure.
The other people
were also like this,
each in their dwelling,
enjoying themselves together.
The beings within this place
heard no other names,
but purely heard the sound of the unsurpassed Great Vehicle.
Among these flowers,
each had a lion's throne.
The four legs of the throne were all dark lapis lazuli.
Soft, plain cloth was laid upon the seat.
This cloth was exquisite, surpassing the Three Realms.
On each throne
sat a king,
who taught beings with the Great Vehicle Dharma.
Some beings copied, held,
read, and recited,
practicing as instructed,
thus propagating the Great Vehicle sūtras.
At that time, Wúbiānshēn Púsà (無邊身菩薩),
having settled these countless beings
on his own body and made them renounce worldly pleasures,
all said:
"Alas,
alas!
The world is empty and void;
the Tathāgata will soon enter *parnirvāṇa*."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Wúbiānshēn,
surrounded by innumerable bodhisattvas,
having manifested such supernatural powers,
held various immeasurable offerings,
and the most exquisite, fragrant, and delicious food and drink.
If any were to smell the fragrance of this food,
all their afflictions and impurities would vanish.
Due to the supernatural powers of this Bodhisattva,
all the great assembly were able to see such transformations.
Bodhisattva Wúbiānshēn's body was vast and boundless,
its measure like empty space.
Except for the Buddhas,
none other could see the full extent of this Bodhisattva's body.
At that time, Bodhisattva Wúbiānshēn and his retinue,
whose offerings were far superior to the previous ones,
came to where the Buddha was,
bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
clasped their palms in reverence, and said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
We only wish that you would compassionately
accept our food."
The Tathāgata knew the time,
and remained silent, not accepting.
Thus, they made three requests,
but still, he did not accept.
At that time, Bodhisattva Wúbiānshēn and his retinue
withdrew and stood aside.
From the Buddhalands in the south, west, and north,
there also came innumerable Bodhisattvas Wúbiānshēn,
whose offerings were far superior to the previous ones.
They came to where the Buddha was,
and likewise, they withdrew and stood aside;
all were thus.
At that time, the auspicious and blessed ground of the Sāluó Twin Trees,
thirty-two yóuxún in length and breadth,
was completely filled with the great assembly,
without any empty space.
At that time, the places where the Bodhisattvas Wúbiānshēn from the four directions and their retinues sat,
were like the tip of an awl,
a needle point,
or a speck of dust.
Great Bodhisattvas from Buddhalands in the ten directions, numerous as specks of dust,
all came to assemble,
and all the great assembly of Yánfútí
also came to gather—
except for the two venerable ones, Móhē Jiāyè and Ānán,
and King Āshéshì and his retinue—
even venomous snakes,
dung beetles, and vipers that could kill with a look,
and those who engaged in sixteen kinds of evil deeds,
all came to assemble.
Dānápo spirits,
Āxiūluó, and others,
all abandoned evil thoughts,
and all gave rise to compassionate minds,
like a father,
like a mother,
like a elder sister,
like a younger sister;
the sentient beings of the Three Thousand Great Thousand Worlds,
facing each other with compassionate minds,
were likewise,
except for the Icchantikas.
At that time, in the Three Thousand Great Thousand Worlds,
due to the Buddha's divine power,
the ground became soft,
without hills,
sand,
gravel,
thorns,
or poisonous weeds.
It was adorned with various treasures,
like the Sukhāvatī World of the Buddha Wúliángshòu in the west.
At this time, the great assembly all saw the Buddhalands in the ten directions, numerous as specks of dust,
as if seeing their own reflections in a bright mirror;
seeing the Buddhalands was likewise.
At that time, the five-colored light emitted from the Tathāgata's face
covered all the great assembly with its brilliant radiance,
causing their body lights
to no longer appear.
Having accomplished what needed to be done,
it returned and re-entered his mouth.
At that time, the devas, humans, and all the assembly,
Āxiūluó, and others,
seeing the Buddha's light
return and re-enter his mouth,
were all greatly terrified,
their hairs standing on end,
and they said:
"The Tathāgata's light, having emerged and returned,
is not without a cause;
surely, what was to be done in the ten directions has been completed,
and this will be the sign of the final Nirvāṇa.
How lamentable,
how lamentable!
How can it be
that the World-Honored One will suddenly abandon the four immeasurable minds,
no longer accept the offerings presented by humans and devas,
the holy sun of wisdom will henceforth be extinguished forever,
and the supreme Dharma boat will here sink?
Alas, how painful,
the great suffering of the world!"
They raised their hands and beat their chests,
weeping and wailing in sorrow,
their limbs trembling,
unable to control themselves;
blood flowed from their pores and sprinkled upon the ground.
At that time, among the assembly, there was a Upāsaka,
a son of a craftsman from Kushinagarā,
named Chúntuó,
who was with fifteen others of his kind.
To enable the world to obtain good fruits,
he set aside his bodily demeanor,
rose from his seat,
bared his right shoulder,
placed his right knee on the ground,
clasped his palms towards the Buddha,
weeping with tears falling,
bowed his head at the Buddha's feet,
and said to the Buddha:
"We only wish, World-Honored One, and the Bhikṣu Saṅgha,
would compassionately accept our final offering,
for the sake of liberating innumerable sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
From now on, we will be without a lord,
without kin,
without a savior,
without a protector,
without refuge,
without destination,
poor and distressed by hunger.
We wish to seek future food from the Tathāgata.
We only wish that you would compassionately
accept our humble offering,
and then enter into Parinirvāṇa.
World-Honored One!
For example, a Kṣatriya,
or a Brāhmaṇa,
or a Vaiśya,
or a Śūdra,
due to poverty,
travels far to another country,
to labor in farming,
obtains good trained oxen,
and fertile, level land,
free from sand, alkali,
weeds,
and stumps,
only hoping for heavenly rain.
The trained oxen
symbolize the seven [actions] of body and speech.
The fertile, level land
symbolizes wisdom.
Removing sand, alkali,
weeds,
and stumps
symbolizes the removal of afflictions.
World-Honored One!
Now I have trained oxen,
fertile land,
and removed stumps,
I only hope for the Tathāgata's ambrosial Dharma rain.
The poor four castes
are myself,
poor in the wealth of the supreme Dharma.
We only wish that you would compassionately
eliminate our poverty and suffering,
and rescue innumerable distressed sentient beings.
Though my present offering
is meager,
I hope it will suffice for the Tathāgata's great assembly.
Now I am without a lord,
without kin,
without refuge.
Please show pity and compassion,
as you did for Ráhóuluó."
At that time, the Bhagavān,
omniscient,
the supreme tamer of men,
addressed Chúntuó, saying:
“Excellent,
excellent!
I shall now remove your poverty,
and shower the supreme Dharma rain upon your field of body,
causing the sprouts of Dharma to grow.
If you now wish to seek from me
longevity,
physical strength and appearance,
peace,
and eloquence,
I will bestow upon you eternal life,
physical strength and appearance,
peace,
and unimpeded eloquence.
Why is this so?
Chúntuó,
there are two types of food offerings,
but their retributions are not different.
What are these two?
The first is when, after receiving it,
one attains Anòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí;
the second is when, after receiving it,
one enters Nirvāṇa.
I now accept your final offering,
which will enable you to perfect Dānbōluómì.”
At that time, Chúntuó immediately said to the Buddha:
“What the Buddha said,
that the retributions of the two offerings are not different,
this meaning is incorrect.
Why is this so?
The recipient of the earlier offering
had not yet exhausted afflictions,
had not yet achieved omniscience,
and was also unable to enable sentient beings to perfect Dānbōluómì;
the recipient of the later offering
had already exhausted afflictions,
had already achieved omniscience,
and was able to enable all sentient beings to perfect Dānbōluómì.
The recipient of the earlier offering
was merely a sentient being;
the recipient of the later offering
is the God of gods.
The recipient of the earlier offering
had a body of mixed food,
a body of afflictions,
a final body,
a impermanent body;
the recipient of the later offering
has a body free from afflictions,
a Vajra body,
a Dharma body,
an eternal body,
a boundless body.
How can it be said
that the retributions of the two offerings are equally without difference?
The recipient of the earlier offering
had not yet perfected Dānbōluómì, up to Bānruòbōluómì,
possessing only the physical eye,
and not yet having attained the Buddha eye, up to the wisdom eye;
the recipient of the later offering
has already perfected Dānbōluómì, up to Bānruòbōluómì,
and possesses the Buddha eye, up to the wisdom eye.
How can it be said that the retributions of the two offerings are equally without difference?
Bhagavān!
The recipient of the earlier offering,
after receiving and consuming the food,
it was digested in the stomach,
and thus gained life,
gained physical strength and appearance,
gained power,
gained peace,
gained unimpeded eloquence;
the recipient of the later offering
does not eat,
does not digest,
and there are no five fruits;
how can it be said that the retributions of the two offerings are equally without difference?”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
The Tathāgata has, over immeasurable, boundless Asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
been without a body that eats,
without a body of afflictions,
without a final body,
but possesses an eternal body,
a Dharma body,
a Vajra body.
Good man,
one who has not yet seen the Buddha-nature
is called a body of afflictions,
a body of mixed food,
a final body.
When the Bodhisattva at that time received food and drink,
he entered the Vajra Samādhi;
after this food was digested,
he immediately saw the Buddha-nature
and attained Anòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Therefore, I say
that the retributions of the two offerings are equally without difference.
The Bodhisattva at that time destroyed the four Māras;
now entering Nirvāṇa,
he also destroys the four Māras.
Therefore, I say that the retributions of the two offerings are equally without difference.
Although the Bodhisattva at that time did not extensively preach the twelve divisions of the Sūtras,
he had already understood them.
Now entering Nirvāṇa,
he extensively differentiates and expounds them for sentient beings.
Therefore, I say that the retributions of the two offerings are equally without difference.
Good man!
The Tathāgata's body
has not received food and drink for immeasurable Asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
For the Śrāvakas, I said
that I first received the milk porridge offered by the two cowherding girls,
Nánduó and Nánduóbōluó,
and then attained Anòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí;
in reality, I did not eat.
I now, for the sake of the assembly here,
therefore accept your final offering;
in reality, I also do not eat.”
At that time, the great assembly, hearing the Buddha Bhagavān
had accepted Chúntuó’s final offering for the benefit of the great assembly,
rejoiced and leaped up, praising him in unison, saying:
“Excellent,
excellent!
Rare, Chúntuó!
The name you bear now
is not in vain.
The meaning of the word Chúntuó
is 'one who understands subtle meanings'.
You now establish such a great meaning,
therefore, the name is given based on the reality and meaning,
hence the name Chúntuó.
You have now gained great fame and benefit in this present life,
and your virtues and vows are fulfilled.
How wonderful, Chúntuó!
Born among humans,
you have moreover attained the supreme and difficult-to-obtain benefit.
Excellent, Chúntuó!
Like the Udumbara flower, which is rare in the world,
the appearance of a Buddha in the world is also exceedingly difficult.
To encounter a Buddha, give rise to faith, and hear the Dharma is difficult,
and to make the final offering when the Buddha is approaching Nirvāṇa,
to be able to accomplish this deed is even more difficult than that.
Namo Chúntuó!
Namo Chúntuó!
You have now perfected Dānbōluómì,
like the autumn moon,
on the night of the fifteenth,
pure and full,
without any clouds or obscurations,
all sentient beings look up to it;
you are also like this,
looked up to by us.
The Buddha has accepted your final offering,
enabling you to perfect Dānbōluómì.
Namo Chúntuó!
Therefore, it is said that you are like the full moon,
all sentient beings look up to you.
Namo Chúntuó!
Although you have received a human body,
your mind is like the Buddha's mind.
You, Chúntuó,
are truly a son of the Buddha,
like Luóhóuluó,
there is no difference.
At that time, the great assembly immediately spoke verses, saying:
At that time, Chúntuó rejoiced and leaped up,
just as if someone whose
parents had suddenly died were to come back to life,
Chúntuó's joy was likewise.
He again rose and bowed to the Buddha,
and spoke verses, saying:
The Buddha said to Chúntuó:
“So it is, so it is,
as you have said.
The appearance of a Buddha in the world is difficult, like the Udumbara flower;
to encounter a Buddha and give rise to faith is also exceedingly difficult.
To offer food for the last time when the Buddha is approaching Nirvāṇa,
and to be able to perfect Dān [bōluómì] is doubly difficult.
You, Chúntuó,
should not be greatly sorrowful;
you should give rise to joy,
and congratulate yourself,
for having encountered the opportunity to make the final offering to the Tathāgata,
thereby accomplishing and perfecting Dānbōluómì.
You should not ask the Buddha to remain long in the world.
You should now observe the realm of all Buddhas,
all of which are impermanent,
and the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena
are likewise.
Then he spoke verses for Chúntuó, saying:
At that time, Chún-Tuó (純陀) addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is so, it is so,
truly as the Sage has taught.
My present wisdom is shallow and slight, like that of a mosquito or a gnat;
how can I contemplate the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s Nirvāṇa?
World-Honored One!
I am now with the great dragon-elephant Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas
who have eradicated all fetters and defilements, such as Wén-Shū-Shī-Lì (文殊師利), the Dharma Prince.
World-Honored One!
For example, a youth who has just left home to become a monastic,
though not yet fully ordained, is already counted among the Saṅgha.
I am also like this,
due to the Buddha-Bodhisattvas’ miraculous power,
I am counted among these great Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, I now
wish that the Tathāgata
would dwell long in the world
and not enter Nirvāṇa.
Just as a hungry person
would never vomit;
I wish the World-Honored One would also be like this,
dwelling eternally in the world,
and not enter Nirvāṇa.”
At that time, Wén-Shū-Shī-Lì (文殊師利), the Dharma Prince, said to Chún-Tuó (純陀):
“Chún-Tuó (純陀)!
You should not utter such words now,
wishing for the Tathāgata to dwell eternally in the world
and not enter Nirvāṇa,
like that hungry person who does not vomit.
You should now observe the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāras);
such observation and practice embody the samādhi of emptiness.
If you seek the true Dharma, you should learn in this way.”
Chún-Tuó (純陀) asked,
“Wén-Shū-Shī-Lì (文殊師利)!
The Tathāgata
is the most venerable and supreme among devas and humans.
How can such a Tathāgata
be a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskāra)?
If he were a conditioned phenomenon,
he would be subject to birth and cessation.
For example, a water bubble
arises quickly and perishes quickly,
coming and going, circulating
like a chariot wheel.
All conditioned phenomena are likewise.
I have heard that devas
have extremely long lifespans.
How can the World-Honored One, who is the Deva of Devas,
have a shorter lifespan, not even reaching a hundred years?
Like a village head,
who holds power and is self-reliant;
by his power and self-reliance,
he can control others.
When that person’s merit is exhausted,
he later becomes poor and lowly,
despised by others,
and forced to labor for them.
Why is this?
Because he lost his power and authority.
The World-Honored One is also like this,
similar to all conditioned phenomena;
if similar to all conditioned phenomena,
then he cannot be called the Deva of Devas.
Why?
Because conditioned phenomena are precisely the laws of birth and death.
Therefore, Wén-Shū (文殊)!
Do not view the Tathāgata as being similar to all conditioned phenomena.
Furthermore, Wén-Shū (文殊)!
Do you speak from knowledge,
or from ignorance,
when you say the Tathāgata is similar to all conditioned phenomena?
If the Tathāgata were similar to all conditioned phenomena,
then he could not be said to be, in the Three Realms,
the Deva of Devas,
the Self-Sufficient Dharma King.
For example, a human king
has a mighty warrior
whose strength is equal to a thousand men.
No one else can subdue him;
therefore, this person is called ‘one man equal to a thousand.’
Such a warrior
is cherished by the king,
especially bestowed with titles and emoluments,
and naturally rewarded with fiefs.
The reason he is called ‘equal to a thousand men’
is not necessarily because his physical strength rivals a thousand,
but because he can overcome a thousand with various skills and arts;
thus, he is called ‘equal to a thousand.’
The Tathāgata is also like this:
he subdues the demon of afflictions (kleśa-māra),
the demon of aggregates (skandha-māra),
the demon of devas (deva-māra),
and the demon of death (mṛtyu-māra).
Therefore, the Tathāgata is called the ‘Venerable One of the Three Realms,’
like that warrior, ‘one man equal to a thousand.’
For this reason,
he has perfected and fully achieved various immeasurable true merits;
thus, he is called ‘Tathāgata,’
‘Arhat,’
‘Samayak-saṃbuddha.’
Wén-Shū-Shī-Lì (文殊師利)!
You should not now imagine or discriminate,
equating the Tathāgata’s Dharma with all conditioned phenomena.
For example, if a very wealthy elder has a son,
and a physiognomist predicts he has signs of a short life.
When the parents hear this,
knowing he cannot inherit the family lineage,
they no longer cherish him,
viewing him like straw.
Indeed, those with short lifespans
are not revered or remembered by śramaṇas,
brāhmaṇas, or people, male or female, old or young.
If the Tathāgata were similar to all conditioned phenomena,
he would also not be revered and respected by all sentient beings in the human and celestial realms of the world,
and the Tathāgata’s teaching—which is unchangeable,
unvarying,
and the true Dharma—would also have no recipients.
Therefore, Wén-Shū (文殊)!
You should not say that the Tathāgata is similar to all conditioned phenomena.”
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
For example, a poor woman,
having no home or protector,
moreover afflicted by illness, hunger, and thirst,
wandered about begging,
stopping at another's guest-house,
where she gave birth to a son.
The owner of the guest-house drove her away.
Not long after giving birth,
carrying her child,
she wished to go to another country.
On the way,
she encountered a fierce wind and rain,
with cold and suffering arriving simultaneously.
She was greatly bitten and eaten by mosquitoes and gnats,
bees,
and poisonous insects.
Passing through the Gaṅgā River,
she carried her child across,
but the current was swift, and she would not let go,
so mother and son both drowned together.
Because of such a woman's meritorious deed of loving compassion,
after her death,
she was born in Brahmā Heaven.
Mañjuśrī!
If there are good men who wish to protect the True Dharma,
they should not say that the Tathāgata is the same as all conditioned phenomena,
nor different from all conditioned phenomena!
They should only blame themselves, saying,
'I am now ignorant,
and do not yet possess the eye of wisdom.
