The Tathāgata's True Dharma is inconceivable.'
Therefore, one should not declare
that the Tathāgata is definitely conditioned,
or definitely unconditioned.
If one has right view,
one should say that the Tathāgata is definitely unconditioned.
Why?
Because he enables sentient beings to generate wholesome dharmas,
and to generate compassion.
Just like that poor woman in the Gaṅgā River,
who gave up her life out of love for her child.
Good men!
Bodhisattvas who protect the Dharma should also be like this,
rather giving up their lives
than saying that the Tathāgata is the same as conditioned phenomena.
They should say that the Tathāgata is the same as unconditioned phenomena.
By saying that the Tathāgata is the same as unconditioned phenomena,
one attains Anuttarā Samyak Saṃbodhi,
just as that woman was born in Brahmā Heaven.
Why?
Because of protecting the Dharma.
How does one protect the Dharma?
That is, by saying that the Tathāgata is the same as unconditioned phenomena.
Good men!
Such a person, though not seeking liberation,
liberation will come to them naturally;
just like that poor woman,
who did not seek Brahmā Heaven,
yet Brahmā Heaven came to her naturally.
Mañjuśrī!
Just as a person traveling a long distance,
extremely tired midway,
stays overnight at another's house,
and while sleeping,
a great fire suddenly breaks out in the room,
immediately startling them awake.
They then reflect:
'I am now certain to die.'
Filled with shame and remorse,
they wrap their body in clothing,
and then pass away,
being born in Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
From then on,
for eighty cycles, they become a Great Brahmā King,
for a hundred thousand kalpas, they are born among humans as a Cakravartin King.
This person will no longer be born in the three evil destinies,
but will constantly be reborn in places of peace and happiness.
For this reason,
Mañjuśrī!
If good men have shame and remorse,
they should not view the Buddha as the same as all conditioned phenomena.
Mañjuśrī!
Heretics with wrong views may say that the Tathāgata is the same as conditioned phenomena,
but a monk who upholds the precepts should not be like this,
generating the thought of conditioned phenomena with regard to the Tathāgata.
If one says that the Tathāgata is conditioned,
that is a lie;
one should know that such a person will die and enter hell,
just as a person dwells in their own home.
Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgata is truly an unconditioned dharma;
one should not again say that he is conditioned.
From this day forth, in saṃsāra,
you should abandon ignorance
and seek right wisdom.
You should know that the Tathāgata is precisely unconditioned.
If one can thus view the Tathāgata,
one will fully attain the thirty-two marks,
and swiftly achieve Anuttarā Samyak Saṃbodhi."
At that time, Mañjuśrī Fǎwángzǐ praised Chúntuó, saying:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
You have now created the cause for longevity,
being able to know that the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma,
the unchanging Dharma,
the unconditioned Dharma.
You now thus well cover the Tathāgata's conditioned aspect,
just like that person in the fire,
who, out of shame and remorse, covered their body with clothing,
and with that good mind was born in Trāyastriṃśa Heaven,
and again became a Brahmā King,
and a Cakravartin King,
not reaching the evil destinies,
always receiving peace and happiness.
You are also like this;
by well covering the Tathāgata's conditioned aspect,
in future ages, you will certainly attain the thirty-two marks,
the eighty minor characteristics,
the eighteen uncommon dharmas,
immeasurable life,
not being in saṃsāra,
constantly receiving peace and happiness,
and will soon achieve Arhatship
and perfect enlightenment.
Chúntuó!
The Tathāgata himself will then extensively preach;
you and I
shall also together cover the Tathāgata's conditioned nature.
Let us set aside 'conditioned'
and 'unconditioned' for now.
You should swiftly provide the meal in due course;
such giving
is the foremost among all giving.
If a bhikṣu,
bhikṣuṇī,
upāsaka,
or upāsikā,
exhausted from long travel,
whatever they need,
should be pure
and given to them in due time.
Such swift giving
is the root seed for the complete Dānapāramitā.
Chúntuó!
If there is anyone who makes a final offering to the Buddha and the saṅgha,
whether much
or little,
whether sufficient
or insufficient,
it should be done quickly and in time,
as the Tathāgata is about to enter parinirvāṇa."
Chúntuó replied:
"Mañjuśrī!
Why are you now
greedy for this food,
speaking of much or little,
sufficient or insufficient,
asking me to provide it in time?
Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgata endured six years of ascetic practices in the past,
still sustaining himself;
how much more so for a brief moment today?
Mañjuśrī!
Do you truly believe that the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Enlightened One, receives this food?
Yet I certainly know
that the Tathāgata's body
is the Dharma-body,
not a body that partakes of food."
At that time, the Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"It is so, it is so,
as Chúntuó says.
Excellent,
Chúntuó!
You have already attained subtle and great wisdom,
and have well entered the profound Mahāyāna sūtras."
Mañjuśrī said to Chúntuó:
"If you believe the Tathāgata is unconditioned,
then the Tathāgata's body is indeed longevity;
if you understand this,
the Buddha will be pleased."
Chúntuó replied:
"The Tathāgata is pleased not only with me,
but also with all sentient beings."
Mañjuśrī said:
"The Tathāgata is pleased with you, and with me,
and with all sentient beings."
Chúntuó answered,
"You should not say that the Tathāgata delights.
To delight
is to have a deluded thought.
If there is a deluded thought,
then there is saṃsāra.
If there is saṃsāra,
then there are conditioned phenomena.
Therefore, Wénshū!
Do not say that the Tathāgata is conditioned.
If you say that the Tathāgata is conditioned,
then both you and I are acting in delusion.
Wénshū Shīlì!
The Tathāgata has no thoughts of love and attachment.
Love and attachment
are like a mother cow loving and being attached to her calf;
though she is hungry and thirsty, she seeks water and grass,
but whether she has enough
or not enough,
she suddenly returns.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have no such thoughts;
they regard all beings equally, like Ráhóuluó.
Such thoughts
are the realm of the Buddhas' wisdom.
Wénshū Shīlì!
For example, a king
trains and drives a four-horse chariot;
to expect a donkey cart to catch up with it
is impossible.
It is the same with you and me;
to want to exhaust the subtle and profound mysteries of the Tathāgata
is also impossible.
Wénshū Shīlì!
Like a Golden-winged bird flying into the sky for immeasurable yojanas,
looking down at the great ocean, it sees all the aquatic creatures: fish, turtles,
soft-shelled turtles, alligators,
turtles and dragons,
and also sees its own reflection,
like seeing various images in a bright mirror.
Ordinary beings with little wisdom
cannot measure such perceptions;
it is the same with you and me,
we cannot measure the Tathāgata's wisdom."
Wénshū Shīlì said to Chúntuó,
"So it is, so it is,
just as you have said.
Regarding this matter,
it is not that I do not understand;
I merely wanted to test you on the affairs of the Bodhisattvas."
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various lights from his face,
and their brilliance
illuminated Wénshū's body.
Wénshū Shīlì, having encountered this light,
immediately understood the matter
and quickly informed Chúntuó,
"The Tathāgata is now showing this auspicious sign;
he will certainly enter Nirvāṇa before long.
The final offering you prepared earlier
should be presented to the Buddha and the great assembly at the proper time.
Chúntuó, you should know that
the Tathāgata emitting these various lights
is not without cause or condition."
Chúntuó, having heard this,
was choked with emotion and remained silent.
The Buddha told Chúntuó,
"The offering you are making to the Buddha and the great assembly,
now is the time;
the Tathāgata will immediately enter Parinirvāṇa."
The second
and third times, it was also thus.
At that time, Chúntuó, having heard the Buddha's words,
cried aloud,
choked with sorrow, and said,
"Alas,
alas,
the world is empty and void!"
He then said to the great assembly,
"All of us now should prostrate with our five limbs to the ground
and together implore the Buddha not to enter Parinirvāṇa."
At that time, the World-Honored One again told Chúntuó,
"Do not cry so loudly,
making your heart withered.
You should contemplate this body
as being like a plantain tree,
a mirage in hot weather,
a water bubble,
an illusion,
a Gandharva city,
a broken vessel,
a flash of lightning.
It is also like drawing on water,
a prisoner about to die,
ripe fruit, a piece of meat.
Like a loom running out of thread,
like a pestle moving up and down,
you should contemplate all conditioned phenomena
as being like food mixed with poison.
Conditioned phenomena
have many faults."
Thereupon, Chúntuó again said to the Buddha,
"If the Tathāgata does not wish to remain in the world for long,
how can I not weep?
Alas,
alas,
the world is empty and void!
We only pray, World-Honored One,
have compassion on us and all sentient beings,
remain in the world for a long time,
do not enter Parinirvāṇa."
The Buddha told Chúntuó,
"You should not speak like this now,
saying, 'Out of compassion for me,
remain in the world for a long time.'
It is because I have compassion for you and for all beings
that I now wish to enter Nirvāṇa.
Why is this?
It is the natural way of the Buddhas,
and it is also so for conditioned phenomena.
Therefore, the Buddhas speak this gāthā:
'Chúntuó!
You should now contemplate all conditioned phenomena as being mixed with all dharmas,
without self,
impermanent,
and non-abiding.
This body has immeasurable faults,
like a water bubble.
Therefore, you should not weep now.'"
At that time, Chúntuó again said to the Buddha,
"So it is, so it is,
truly as the Venerable One teaches.
Although I know that the Tathāgata expediently manifests entering Nirvāṇa,
I cannot but feel distress;
yet upon reflection,
I again feel joy."
The Buddha praised Chúntuó,
"Excellent,
excellent!
You are able to know that the Tathāgata shows himself to be like sentient beings
by expediently entering Nirvāṇa.
Chúntuó!
Listen now:
just like Sarasa cranes,
in the spring month, all gather at Ánòu dá Chí.
The Buddhas are also like this,
all arriving at this place.
Chúntuó!
You should not now contemplate whether the Buddhas have long or short lifespans;
all phenomena are like illusory appearances,
and the Tathāgata, by the power of skillful means, is unattached to anything in them.
Why is this?
It is the natural way of the Buddhas.
Chúntuó!
I now accept the offering you have presented,
so that you may cross over the currents of saṃsāra and all existences.
If any humans
or devas make this final offering to me,
they will all attain the unmoving fruit of retribution
and constantly experience peace and joy.
Why is this?
Because I am a good field of merit for sentient beings.
If you also wish to be a field of merit for sentient beings,
quickly prepare the offering;
you should not delay."
At that time, Chúntuó,
for the sake of sentient beings attaining liberation,
bowed his head, drinking his tears, and said to the Buddha,
"Excellent,
World-Honored One!
If I am capable of being a field of merit,
then I will be able to clearly understand the Tathāgata's Nirvāṇa and non-Nirvāṇa.
As for us, and all the Śrāvakas
and Pratyekabuddhas, our wisdom is like that of mosquitoes and ants;
we truly cannot measure the Tathāgata's Nirvāṇa and non-Nirvāṇa."
At that time, Chúntuó and his retinue,
sorrowful and weeping,
surrounded the Rúlái,
burning incense and scattering flowers,
devotedly revered and served Him.
Soon after, he and Wénshū left their seats
to prepare food offerings.
Not long after their departure,
at that time, this earth underwent six types of shaking,
and even the Fàn Shì was likewise affected.
Earthquakes are of two kinds:
some are 'earthquakes' (dìdòng),
and some are 'great earthquakes' (dàdìdòng).
A small tremor is called a dìdòng;
a great tremor is called a dàdìdòng.
One with a small sound is called a dìdòng;
one with a great sound is called a dàdìdòng.
When only the earth shakes, it is called a dìdòng;
when mountains, rivers, trees, and all the great waters of the sea also shake,
it is called a dàdìdòng.
When it moves in one direction, it is called a dìdòng;
when it rotates in a circle, it is called a dàdìdòng.
A tremor is called a dìdòng;
when the tremor is such that it moves the hearts of sentient beings, it is called a dàdìdòng.
When the Púsà first descended from Dōulǜ Tiān to Yánfútí, it was called a dàdìdòng.
From His initial birth,
renunciation,
attainment of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and entering Bōnièpán are all called dàdìdòng.
Today the Rúlái is about to enter Nièpán,
therefore this earth so greatly shook.
At that time, all the Tiān,
Lóng,
Gāntàpó,
Āxiūluó,
Jiālóuluó,
Jǐnnàluó,
Móhóuluójiā,
humans and non-humans,
having heard these words,
their hair stood on end,
and they wept sorrowfully in unison,
and spoke these verses:
"Shìzūn!
For example, a king
who had many sons,
of handsome appearance,
whom he always loved and cherished.
He first taught them various arts,
ensuring they mastered all of them.
Then he handed them over to the chief executioner to be killed.
Shìzūn!
We today are like Dharma princes,
having received the Fó's teachings,
and thereby possess right view.
We pray that you do not abandon us;
if you abandon us,
then we shall be like those princes.
We only wish that you would long abide,
and not enter Nièpán.
Shìzūn!
For example, someone
who is skilled in studying various treatises,
yet regarding these treatises,
generates fear.
The Rúlái is also like this:
having understood all dharmas,
yet regarding these dharmas,
generates fear.
If the Rúlái were to long abide in the world,
expounding the taste of gānlù,
satisfying everyone,
then such sentient beings would no longer fear falling into hell.
Shìzūn!
For example, someone
who just began to learn a craft,
was arrested by officials,
and imprisoned.
Someone asked him:
'What are you suffering?'
He replied:
'I am now suffering great anxiety and pain.
If I can escape,
then I shall attain peace and happiness.'
The Shìzūn is also like this:
for our sake,
You have practiced various asceticisms.
We now,
have not yet escaped the suffering of shēngsǐ.
How then can the Rúlái attain peace and happiness?
Shìzūn!
For example, a yīwáng,
skilled in understanding prescriptions and medicines,
exclusively teaches secret formulas to his own son,
not teaching others who seek to learn from outside.
The Rúlái is also like this:
You alone, with Your extremely profound and secret treasury,
exclusively teach Wénshū,
abandoning us,
not looking upon us with compassion.
The Rúlái should not be stingy with the Dharma,
like that yīwáng who exclusively teaches his son,
not teaching other students from outside.
The reason that physician cannot universally teach
is that he harbors thoughts of superiority or inferiority,
hence he has secrets he cherishes.
The heart of the Rúlái
ultimately has no thought of superiority or inferiority.
Why then is it like this,
that we do not receive teachings?
We only wish that you would long abide,
and not enter Bōnièpán.
Shìzūn!
For example, old and young people,
or those afflicted by illness,
who have strayed from the good path,
and walk on a perilous road.
The road is dangerous, difficult, and rough,
causing much suffering.
Then another person,
seeing them, takes pity,
and immediately shows them a flat and good path.
Shìzūn!
We are also like this.
The 'young' refers to those whose Fǎshēn has not yet grown;
the 'old' refers to those burdened by heavy fánnǎo;
the 'sick' refers to those not yet liberated from shēngsǐ;
the 'perilous road' refers to the twenty-five existences.
We only wish that the Rúlái,
would show and guide us to the right path of gānlù,
long abide in the world,
and not enter Nièpán.
At that time, the Shìzūn addressed all the Bǐqiū:
"You, Bǐqiū,
should not be like fánfū,
and all the Tiānrén,
sorrowful and weeping.
You should diligently exert yourselves,
and fix your minds on right mindfulness."
At that time, all the Tiānrén,
Āxiūluó, etc.,
having heard what the Fó said,
stopped their weeping.
It was like someone
who, after burying their child, stopped weeping.
At that time, the Shìzūn, for the sake of the great assembly,
spoke these verses:
“Furthermore, bhikṣus,
if you have any doubts
now is the time to ask.
Whether empty
or not empty,
whether permanent
or impermanent,
whether suffering
or not suffering,
whether dependent
or independent,
whether going
or not going,
whether returning
or not returning,
whether constant
or not constant,
whether severed
or permanent,
whether a sentient being
or not a sentient being,
whether existent
or non-existent,
whether real
or unreal,
whether true
or untrue,
whether extinguished
or unextinguished,
whether secret
or not secret,
whether two
or not two—
if there is anything you doubt among these various dharmas,
you should now inquire.
I will comply and resolve them for you,
and I will also first preach the sweet dew for you,
and only then enter Nirvāṇa.
Bhikṣus!
The appearance of a Buddha in the world is difficult,
a human body is difficult to obtain,
to meet a Buddha and generate faith is also difficult,
to be able to endure the unendurable is also difficult,
to accomplish pure precepts completely and without flaw,
and to attain the fruit of Arhatship is also difficult,
like seeking gold dust or the udumbara flower.
All you bhikṣus!
It is difficult to be free from the eight adversities and obtain a human body,
you should not let your encounter with me pass in vain.
In the past, I practiced various asceticisms,
and now I have obtained such unsurpassed skillful means.
For your sake,
through countless kalpas, I have sacrificed my body,
hands and feet,
head and eyes,
marrow and brain.
Therefore, you should not be negligent.
You bhikṣus!
How do you adorn the precious city of the true Dharma,
complete with various merits and treasures,
with precepts,
meditation,
and wisdom
as its walls, moats, and battlements?
Now that you have encountered this precious city of the Buddha Dharma,
you should not take these false and illusory things,
just like a merchant who, having encountered a city of true treasures,
takes some tiles and bricks and returns home.
You are also like this,
meeting the precious city and taking illusory things.
All you bhikṣus!
Do not have a lowly mind
and become content.
Although you have now left home,
you do not covet this Mahāyāna.
All you bhikṣus!
Though your bodies wear the kaṣāya dyed robes,
your minds have not yet been dyed by the pure Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
All you bhikṣus!
Though you go begging for food,
traveling through many places,
you have never begged for the Dharma food of the Mahāyāna.
All you bhikṣus!
Though you have shaved your beards and hair,
you have not yet eliminated all kleshas for the sake of the true Dharma.
All you bhikṣus!
Now I will truly instruct you.
I am now present, the assembly is harmonious,
the Tathāgata's Dharma-nature is true and not inverted.
Therefore, you should be diligent,
concentrate your minds, and bravely destroy all kleshas.
Once the sun of the ten powers and wisdom has set,
you will be covered by ignorance.
“Bhikṣus!
Just as the great earth,
mountains,
and medicinal herbs are for the use of sentient beings,
so is my Dharma.
It gives rise to the subtle and good flavor of the sweet dew Dharma,
and is a good medicine for the various diseases of affliction of sentient beings.
I will now cause all sentient beings,
and my children, the fourfold assembly,
to all dwell in the secret treasury,
and I too will dwell therein
and enter Nirvāṇa.
What is called the secret treasury?
It is like the three dots of the character Yī (伊).
If placed horizontally, it does not form Yī,
and if placed vertically, it also does not form it.
Like the three eyes on the face of Máxīshǒuluó,
only then can the three dots form Yī;
if separated, it also cannot be formed.
I am also like this.
The Dharma of liberation is also not Nirvāṇa;
the body of the Tathāgata is also not Nirvāṇa;
Mahā Prajñā is also not Nirvāṇa.
If the three dharmas are separate, they are also not Nirvāṇa.
I now dwell in these three dharmas,
for the sake of sentient beings,
and this is called entering Nirvāṇa,
like the character Yī in the world.
At that time, the bhikṣus heard that the Buddha, the Bhagavat, was certainly going to enter Nirvāṇa.
They were all sorrowful,
their body hairs stood on end,
tears filled their eyes.
They bowed their heads at the Buddha's feet,
circled him countless times,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavat!
You have spoken wonderfully of impermanence (anitya),
suffering (duḥkha),
emptiness (śūnya),
and non-self (anātman).
Bhagavat!
Just as among all footprints of living beings,
the elephant's footprint is supreme,
so too is the perception of impermanence (anityasaṃjñā);
among all perceptions, it is the foremost.
If one diligently cultivates it,
one can eliminate all desire-realm (kāmadhātu) craving,
form-realm (rūpadhātu) and formless-realm (arūpadhātu) craving,
ignorance (avidyā), conceit (māna), and the perception of impermanence itself.
Bhagavat!
If the Tathāgata were free from the perception of impermanence,
then he should not enter Nirvāṇa now.
If he is not free from it,
how can it be said that by cultivating the perception of impermanence,
one is freed from the cravings of the three realms,
ignorance,
conceit, and the perception of impermanence itself?
Bhagavat!
Just as a farmer,
in the autumn month,
deeply plows his land,
and can remove weeds;
so too is the perception of impermanence,
it can eliminate all desire-realm craving,
form-realm and formless-realm craving,
ignorance, conceit, and the perception of impermanence itself.
Bhagavat!
Just as in farming,
autumn plowing is superior;
just as among all footprints,
the elephant's footprint is superior;
among all perceptions,
the perception of impermanence is superior.
Bhagavat!
Just as a monarch,
knowing his life is ending,
grants a general amnesty to the world,
releasing all prisoners and captives,
allowing them to be freed,
and only then passes away;
the Tathāgata now,
should also be like this,
liberating all sentient beings,
freeing them from all ignorance,
delusion,
and bondage,
allowing them all to be released,
and only then enter Parinirvāṇa.
We are all not yet liberated;
how can the Tathāgata wish to abandon us
and enter Nirvāṇa?
Bhagavat!
Just as a person,
possessed by a ghost,
meets a good spell-master,
and by the power of the spell,
is cured and recovered;
the Tathāgata is also like this,
removing the ghost of ignorance for the śrāvakas,
enabling them to abide in the Mahāprajñā and the dharma of liberation,
like the letter 'I' in the world.
Bhagavat!
Just as a fragrant elephant,
bound by a person,
even with a good trainer,
cannot be restrained,
and breaks its ropes and chains,
going off freely;
we have not yet thus escaped the fifty-seven bonds of defilements;
how can the Tathāgata wish to abandon us
and enter Nirvāṇa?
Bhagavat!
Just as a person suffering from malaria,
meets a good doctor,
and his suffering is removed;
we are also like this,
having many ailments and sufferings,
the fever of wrong livelihood;
although we have met the Tathāgata,
our illness is not yet cured,
we have not yet attained the supreme, peaceful, permanent joy.
How can the Tathāgata wish to abandon us
and enter Nirvāṇa?
Bhagavat!
Just as a drunken person,
unaware of himself,
not recognizing relatives or strangers,
mothers or daughters,
sisters,
confused and sexually promiscuous,
speaking wildly,
lying in filth;
then a good physician
gives him medicine to take;
after taking it, he vomits the alcohol,
regains his memory,
feels shame and remorse,
deeply reproaching himself,
realizing alcohol is the root of all unwholesome evils;
if one can eliminate and cut it off,
then one is far from all sins.
Bhagavat!
We are also like this,
from past times,
revolving in saṃsāra,
intoxicated by emotions and forms,
greedy for the five desires,
perceiving non-mothers as mothers,
non-sisters as sisters,
non-daughters as daughters,
generating the perception of living beings towards non-living beings;
therefore, we revolve and suffer the pains of saṃsāra,
like that drunken person lying in filth.
The Tathāgata should now give us the dharma-medicine,
to make us vomit the evil alcohol of defilements;
but we have not yet attained a waking mind.
How can the Tathāgata wish to abandon us
and enter Nirvāṇa?
Bhagavat!
Just as for someone
to praise a banana tree as firm and solid,
there is no such possibility.
Bhagavat!
Sentient beings are also like this;
if one praises the self (ātman),
person,
sentient being,
life-span,
nurturer,
knower,
doer,
or experiencer
as real,
there is also no such possibility.
We thus cultivate the perception of non-self.
Bhagavat!
Just as dregs,
are of no further use;
this body is also like this,
without self,
without master.
Bhagavat!
Just as a saptaparṇa flower has no fragrance;
this body is also like this,
without self,
without master.
We thus
constantly cultivate the perception of non-self in our minds.
As the Buddha said:
'All dharmas are without self
and without what belongs to self.
You bhikṣus should cultivate this.
Having cultivated it thus,
you will eliminate conceit,
and having abandoned conceit,
you will enter Nirvāṇa.'
Bhagavat!
Just as for a bird's tracks
to appear in the sky,
there is no such possibility;
for one who can cultivate the perception of non-self
to still have various views,
there is also no such possibility."
At that time, the Bhagavat praised the bhikṣus:
"Excellent,
excellent!
You are well able to cultivate the perception of non-self."
At that time, the Bhikkhus immediately said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
We not only cultivate the thought of non-self (anātman),
but also cultivate other thoughts,
namely, the thought of suffering (duḥkha),
the thought of impermanence (anitya),
and the thought of non-self (anātman).
World-Honored One!
For example, when a person is drunk,
their mind is dazed and dizzy,
seeing mountains and rivers,
stone walls,
grass and trees,
palaces,
houses,
sun, moon, and stars,
all spinning around.
World-Honored One!
If there is someone who does not cultivate the thoughts of suffering,
impermanence,
and non-self,
such a person is not called a noble one (ārya),
is prone to laxity,
and transmigrates through saṃsāra.
World-Honored One!
For this reason,
we diligently cultivate these thoughts."
Then the Buddha told the Bhikkhus:
"Listen carefully,
listen carefully.
The simile of the drunk person you just cited,
you only know the words,
but have not comprehended their meaning.
What is the meaning?
Just as that drunk person,
seeing the sun and moon above,
which are not actually spinning,
generates the thought of spinning.
Sentient beings are also like this;
covered by afflictions (kleśas) and ignorance (avidyā),
they generate deluded thoughts:
counting non-self as self,
counting impermanence as permanence,
counting impurity as purity,
counting happiness as suffering,
because they are covered by afflictions.
Although they generate these thoughts,
they do not comprehend their meaning,
just like that drunk person, in a place that is not spinning,
generates the thought of spinning.
'Self' (ātman) here means the meaning of the Buddha (Fó),
'permanence' (nitya) is the meaning of the Dharma-body (fǎshēn),
'happiness' (sukha) is the meaning of Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
'purity' (śuci) is the meaning of the Dharma (fǎ).
You Bhikkhus!
How can you say that one who has the thought of self
is arrogant, conceited, and transmigrates through saṃsāra?
If you say,
'I also cultivate the thoughts of impermanence,
suffering,
and non-self,'
these three kinds of cultivation
have no true meaning.
I will now speak of a superior method of three cultivations:
counting suffering as happiness,
and happiness as suffering,
this is a deluded dharma.
Counting impermanence as permanence,
and permanence as impermanence,
this is a deluded dharma.
Counting non-self as self,
and self as non-self,
this is a deluded dharma.
Counting impurity as purity,
and purity as impurity,
this is a deluded dharma.
There are these four kinds of deluded dharmas,
such people do not know the correct cultivation of dharmas.
"You Bhikkhus,
in the dharma of suffering, generate the thought of happiness;
in impermanence, generate the thought of permanence;
in non-self, generate the thought of self;
in impurity, generate the thought of purity.
In the mundane world (saṃsāra) there are also permanence, happiness, self, and purity;
in the transcendent world (Nirvāṇa) there are also permanence, happiness, self, and purity.
The dharmas of the mundane world have the words but no meaning;
those of the transcendent world have the words and also the meaning.
Why is this?
The dharmas of the mundane world have four kinds of delusion,
therefore their meaning is not known.
Why is this?
There are delusions of thought (saṃjñā-viparyāsa),
delusions of mind (citta-viparyāsa),
delusions of view (dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa).
Because of these three delusions,
people of the mundane world
see suffering in happiness,
see impermanence in permanence,
see non-self in self,
see impurity in purity;
this is called delusion.
Because of delusion,
the mundane world knows the words but does not know the meaning.
What is the meaning?
Non-self is called saṃsāra (shēngsǐ);
self is called the Tathāgata (Rúlái);
impermanence is the Śrāvakas (shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (yuánjué);
permanence is the Dharma-body (fǎshēn) of the Tathāgata;
suffering is all heterodox teachers (wàidào);
happiness is Nirvāṇa (Nièpán);
impurity is conditioned dharmas (yǒuwéifǎ);
purity is the righteous Dharma (zhèngfǎ) possessed by all Buddhas (Fó) and Bodhisattvas (Púsà);
this is called non-delusion.
Because of non-delusion,
one knows the words and knows the meaning.
If you wish to be free from the four delusions,
you should know these permanence,
happiness,
self,
and purity.
At that time, the Bhikkhus said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said, those who are free from the four delusions
will then comprehend permanence,
happiness,
self,
and purity.
The Tathāgata now, being eternally free from the four delusions,
has already comprehended permanence, happiness, self, and purity.
If you have already comprehended permanence, happiness, self, and purity,
why do you not remain for a kalpa or half a kalpa,
teaching and guiding us,
to free us from the four delusions,
but instead abandon us
and wish to enter Nirvāṇa?
If the Tathāgata were to show concern, remember us, and teach us,
we would sincerely and reverently accept and cultivate it.
If the Tathāgata enters Nirvāṇa,
how can we remain in this poisonous body,
cultivating pure conduct (brahmacarya)?
We too shall follow the World-Honored Buddha,
and enter Nirvāṇa."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should not utter such words:
‘All the unsurpassed Right Dharma that I possess
has now been entrusted to Mahākāśyapa.
This Kāśyapa
shall be a great refuge for you,
just as the Tathāgata is a refuge for all sentient beings.
Mahākāśyapa is likewise
to be a refuge for you.’
For example, a great king,
who governs many territories,
when on tour,
entrusts all state affairs to his chief minister.
The Tathāgata is also like this;
all the Right Dharma
has also been entrusted to Mahākāśyapa.
You should know that
the notions of impermanence (anitya),
suffering (duḥkha) that you previously cultivated
are not real.
For example, in springtime,
there were some people
bathing in a large pond and playing in boats.
They lost a lapis lazuli jewel,
which sank deep into the water.
At that time, these people
all entered the water together
to search for this jewel.
They eagerly grabbed tiles and stones,
grass and wood,
and sand and gravel,
each believing they had found the lapis lazuli jewel,
joyfully brought them out,
and then realized they were not real.
At that time, the jewel remained in the water,
and by its power,
the water became clear.
Then the multitude saw the jewel still at the bottom of the water,
like gazing up at the shape of the moon in the sky.
At that time, there was a wise person among the crowd,
who, by skillful means (upāya),
calmly entered the water,
and immediately obtained the jewel.
You bhikṣus
should not thus cultivate the notions of impermanence (anitya),
suffering (duḥkha),
no-self (anātman),
impurity (aśubha), etc.,
taking them as the true meaning,
like those people
who took tiles and stones,
grass and wood,
and sand and gravel as the precious jewel.
You should skillfully learn skillful means (upāya),
and constantly cultivate the notions of self (ātman),
permanence (nitya),
bliss (sukha),
and purity (śubha) everywhere.
Furthermore, you should know that
the four characteristics of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa) you previously cultivated
are all inverted views (viparyāsa).
If you wish to truly cultivate notions,
be like that wise person who skillfully retrieved the precious jewel,
namely:
the notion of self (ātman),
permanence (nitya),
bliss (sukha),
and purity (śubha).”
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha previously taught:
‘All phenomena are without self (anātman),
you should cultivate this!
Having cultivated this,
you will be free from the notion of self (ātman);
being free from the notion of self (ātman),
you will be free from conceit;
being free from conceit,
you will attain Nirvāṇa.’
What does this meaning imply?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Excellent,
excellent!
You are now well able to inquire about this matter,
to resolve your own doubts.
For example, there was a king,
dull and of little wisdom.
There was a physician,
whose nature was also stubborn and foolish.
The king did not distinguish this,
and bestowed lavish stipends upon him.
For curing all illnesses, he used only milk medicine.
He also did not know the root cause of the illnesses.
Even if he knew milk medicine, he did not understand it well.
Whether it was a wind illness,
a cold illness,
a heat illness,
or any other illness,
he taught them all to take milk.
The king did not distinguish,
whether this physician knew the good or bad,
the quality of milk.
Then there was an enlightened physician who understood the eight types of arts,
was skilled at curing all illnesses,
and knew all kinds of prescriptions.
He came from afar.
At that time, the old physician did not know to consult and learn,
but instead developed a mind of arrogance and disdain.
At that time, the enlightened physician
immediately sought him out,
requested to take him as a teacher,
and consulted him about the secret and profound methods of medical prescriptions.
He said to the old physician:
'I now request you, benevolent one, to be my teacher.
I only wish that you would expound and explain to me.'
The old physician replied:
'If you are now able to serve me for forty-eight years,
then I will teach you medical methods.'
At that time, the enlightened physician immediately accepted his instruction:
'I shall do so,
I shall do so.
As far as I am able,
I shall serve you.'
At that time, the old physician
then took the guest physician and together they went in to see the king.
At that time, the guest physician
then spoke to the king about various medical prescriptions and other skills:
'Great King should know,
one should distinguish well.
This method is like this,
it can govern the state;
this method is like this,
it can cure illness.'
At that time, the king, having heard these words,
then realized that the old physician was foolish and ignorant,
and immediately expelled him,
ordering him out of the kingdom's borders.
After that, he showed double respect to the guest physician.
At that time, the guest physician thought:
'If I wish to teach the king,
now is the right time.'
He then said to the king:
'Great King, if you truly cherish me,
you should grant me one wish.'
The king immediately replied:
'From this right arm and other parts of my body,
whatever you desire,
I will give everything to you.'
The guest physician said:
'Although Your Majesty has promised me all parts of your body,
I do not dare to ask for much.
What I ask for now
is that Your Majesty issue a decree,
throughout the entire kingdom,
from now on,
no one is allowed to take the old physician's milk medicine again.
Why is that?
This medicine is poisonous and harmful,
causing much damage.
If anyone deliberately takes it, their head shall be cut off.'
After cutting off the milk medicine,
there will ultimately be no more people dying untimely deaths.
They will always live in peace and happiness.
Therefore, I ask for this wish.'
At that time, the king replied:
'What you ask for
is indeed a small matter.'
He immediately issued a decree:
'Throughout the entire kingdom,
sick people
are all forbidden to use milk as medicine.
If anyone uses it as medicine,
their head shall be cut off.'
At that time, the guest physician combined various flavors and various medicines,
such as pungent,
bitter,
salty,
sweet,
sour, and other flavors,
to cure all illnesses,
and none were not cured.
Not long after,
the king became ill again.
He immediately summoned this physician:
'I am now gravely ill,
suffering and near death.
How should I be treated?'
The physician examined the king's illness,
and found that milk medicine should be used.
He immediately reported to the king:
'According to Your Majesty's ailment,
you should take milk.'
The milk medicine I previously forbade
was a great falsehood.
If you take it now,
it will be most effective in eliminating the illness.
Your Majesty now suffers from heat,
and should indeed take milk.'
At that time, the king said to the physician:
'Are you mad now?
Or is it a heat illness?
Yet you say taking milk
can cure this illness.
You previously called it poison,
now how can I take it?
Do you wish to deceive me?
What the former physician praised,
you called poison,
causing me to expel him.
Now you again say it is good,
and most able to cure illness.
According to what you say,
my former old physician
was definitely superior to you.'
At that time, the guest physician again said to the king:
'Your Majesty should not speak in such a way.
It is like an insect eating wood,
and forming characters.
This insect does not know whether it is a character or not a character;
a wise person seeing it
will never declare that the insect understands characters,
nor will they be surprised.
Great King should know,
the old physician was also like that.
He did not distinguish between illnesses,
and gave everyone milk medicine,
just like the path of that insect,
accidentally forming characters.
That former old physician
did not understand the good or bad,
the quality of milk medicine.'
At that time, the king asked:
'How did he not understand?'
The guest physician replied to the king:
'This milk medicine
is both poisonous and harmful,
and also a sweet dew.
How is milk also called sweet dew?
If it is a cow
that does not eat wine dregs,
slippery grass,
or wheat bran,
whose calf is well-behaved and docile,
whose grazing ground is not on a high plateau
nor in a low, wet place,
is watered with clear streams,
not allowed to run wild,
not kept in the same herd as bulls,
whose feeding and watering are appropriate,
and whose movement and rest are proper.
Such milk
can cure all illnesses;
this is then called the miraculous medicine of sweet dew.
Apart from this kind of milk,
all other milk is called poisonous and harmful.'
At that time, the Great King, having heard these words,
praised the great physician:
'Excellent,
excellent!
From today onwards,
I finally know the good and bad,
the quality of milk medicine.'
He then took it,
and his illness was cured.
He immediately issued a decree throughout the entire kingdom:
'From now on, milk medicine must be taken.'
The people of the kingdom, hearing this, all became angry,
and all said to each other:
'Is the Great King now possessed by a ghost,
or has he gone mad?
He is deceiving us,
and again making us take milk.'
All the people
harbored anger,
and all gathered at the king's place.
The king said:
'You should not harbor anger towards me,
for whether this milk medicine is taken or not,
it is all the physician's instruction,
It is not my fault.
At that time, the great king and all the people,
leapt up with joy,
and redoubled their reverence,
and offered homage to this physician.
All the sick people took the milk medicine,
and their illnesses were all cured.
"You bhikṣus!
You should know that the Tathāgata,
Arhat,
Samyak-saṃbuddha,
Vidyā-caraṇa-saṃpanna,
Sugata,
Lokavid,
Anuttara,
Puruṣa-damya-sārathi,
Śāstā-deva-manuṣyāṇām,
Buddha,
Bhagavān,
is also like this,
appearing in the world as a great physician king,
subduing all external heretical physicians,
and proclaiming in the midst of kings and assemblies:
'I am the physician king.'
Wishing to subdue the external heretics,
I therefore proclaim this saying:
'There is no self,
no person,
no sentient being,
no life span,
no nurturer,
no seer,
no doer,
no receiver.'
Bhikṣus, you should know that
the 'self' spoken of by these external heretics
is like a worm eating wood,
accidentally forming a character.
Therefore, the Tathāgata,
in the Buddhadharma,
proclaims 'no-self,'
for the sake of disciplining sentient beings,
and for the sake of knowing the proper time,
he preaches this 'no-self.'
For certain reasons,
he also preaches 'self.'
Just like that excellent physician
who skillfully knows whether milk is medicine or not medicine,
it is not like the 'self' that ordinary people conceive of.
The 'self' conceived of by foolish ordinary people
is sometimes said to be as big as a thumb,
or as a mustard seed,
or as a fine dust particle;
the Tathāgata says that the self is none of these.
Therefore, it is said that
all phenomena are 'no-self,'
but in reality, there is not no-self.
What is the self?
If a dharma is real,
is true,
is permanent,
is master,
is support,
and its nature is unchangeable,
that is called the self.
Just like that great physician who skillfully understands milk medicine,
the Tathāgata is also like this,
for the sake of sentient beings,
he preaches that there is truly a self in all phenomena.
You four assemblies
should cultivate this Dharma in this way."
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you have any doubts about the precepts,
you may now freely ask,
and I will explain,
to gladden your hearts.
I have already cultivated and understood the inherently empty and tranquil nature of all phenomena,
and have clearly and thoroughly comprehended it.
You bhikṣus,
do not think that the Tathāgata only cultivates the inherently empty and tranquil nature of all phenomena."
He again addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you have any doubts about the precepts,
you may now ask."
At that time, the bhikṣus immediately said to the Buddha:
"Bhagavān!
We have no wisdom
to question the Tathāgata,
Arhat,
Samyak-saṃbuddha.
Why is that?
The Tathāgata's realm is inconceivable,
all his samādhis are inconceivable,
the teachings he expounds are inconceivable,
therefore we have no wisdom
to question the Tathāgata.
Bhagavān!
For example, an old man,
one hundred and twenty years old,
suffering from a chronic illness,
lying on his bed,
unable to rise or move,
weak and frail,
with not long to live.
A rich man,
having a matter to attend to,
was about to travel to another region,
and entrusted one hundred catties of gold to this old man,
saying:
'I am now traveling afar.
I am entrusting this treasure to you.
Perhaps I will return in ten years,
or twenty years,
you must return it to me.'
At that time, the old man
immediately accepted it.
However, this old man had no heirs.
Not long after,
he became seriously ill and died,
and the entrusted items were all scattered and lost.
When the owner returned from his journey,
he demanded his property but found nothing.
Such a foolish person
does not know how to weigh whether something can be entrusted or not.
Therefore, upon his return from the journey,
he demanded his property but found nothing,
and for this reason lost his wealth.
Bhagavān!
We Śrāvakas are also like this;
although we hear the Tathāgata's earnest teachings,
we cannot uphold them
to make the Dharma long-lasting,
like that old man who received an entrustment from another.
We are now without wisdom regarding the precepts,
what can we ask?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you now ask me,
you will benefit all sentient beings.
Therefore, I tell you,
feel free to ask whatever doubts you have,
at will."
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"Bhagavān!
For example, there is a person,
twenty-five years old,
strong and handsome,
with much wealth in gold, silver, and lapis lazuli,
whose parents,
wife and children,
relatives,
and clan members
are all alive.
Someone also comes to entrust him with precious objects,
saying to him:
'I have a matter to attend to;
I wish to go elsewhere,
and will return when the matter is finished.
You must return it to me.'
At that time, the strong person
guarded these objects
as if they were his own.
When that person fell ill,
he immediately instructed his family:
'This gold and treasure were entrusted by someone else.
If he comes to claim them, return them all.'
A wise person is like this,
skillfully able to weigh and consider.
When the traveler returns and asks for the items,
he receives them all,
with nothing lost.
The Bhagavān is also like this;
if he entrusts the Dharma jewel to Ānán and the bhikṣus,
it will not last long.
Why?
All Śrāvakas and Mahākāśyapa
will all be impermanent,
like that old man who received entrusted items from another.
Therefore, the supreme Buddhadharma
should be entrusted to the bodhisattvas,
because the bodhisattvas are skillful at asking and answering about such Dharma jewels,
and thus it can endure for countless thousands of eons,
increasing and flourishing,
benefiting and bringing peace to sentient beings,
like that strong person who received entrusted items from another.
For this reason,
only the great bodhisattvas are capable of asking;
our wisdom is like that of mosquitoes and gnats,
how can we consult about the Tathāgata's profound Dharma?"
At that time, the Śrāvakas
remained silent.
Then the Buddha praised the bhikṣus, saying:
"Excellent,
excellent!
You have well attained the undefiled mind,
the mind of an Arhat.
I, too, once thought that for these two reasons,
the Mahāyāna should be entrusted to the bodhisattvas,
so that this wonderful Dharma might endure in the world."
At that time, the Buddha told all the great assembly:
"Good men,
good women!
My lifespan cannot be measured,
and the eloquence of my joyful teaching can also not be exhausted.
You should ask questions freely according to your wishes,
whether about precepts
or refuges.
The second
and the third times are also like this."
At that time, there was a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in the assembly,
who was originally a person from the village of Duōluó,
whose family name was Dà Jiāyè,
of the Brahmin lineage.
Though young in age,
by the spiritual power of the Buddha, he immediately rose from his seat,
uncovering his right arm,
circumnambulating a hundred thousand times,
placing his right knee on the ground,
joining his palms toward the Buddha,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I now wish to ask a few questions.
If the Buddha grants permission,
then I dare to speak."
The Buddha told Jiāyè:
"The Tathāgata,
Arhat,
SamyaKsaṃbuddha (Perfectly Enlightened One),
allows you to ask whatever you wish.
I will explain it to you,
resolve your doubts,
and cause you to rejoice."
At that time, Jiāyè Bodhisattva Mahāsattva said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
Since the Tathāgata, out of compassion,
has graciously granted permission to listen,
I shall now ask my questions.
However, the wisdom I possess
is slight, like a mosquito or a gadfly.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is supremely virtuous and majestic,
purely surrounded by Zhāntán,
unconquerable by lions,
with an indestructible assembly as his retinue.
The body of the Tathāgata
is like true diamond,
its color like Liúlí,
truly difficult to destroy,
and furthermore, He is surrounded by such a great ocean of wisdom.
In this assembly,
all the great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas,
have all achieved immeasurable, boundless, profound, and wondrous merits,
like fragrant elephants.
In the presence of such a great assembly,
how would I dare to speak?
It is only by relying on the Buddha's supernatural power and the majestic virtue of the great assembly's good roots
that I shall venture to ask a small question."
Then, in the presence of the Buddha, he spoke verses to ask his questions:
At that time, the Buddha praised Jiāyè Bodhisattva:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
You have not yet attained All-Knowledge,
but I have attained it.
Yet, the extremely profound and hidden meaning you inquire about,
is no different from what one possessing All-Knowledge would ask.
Good man!
When I first achieved perfect enlightenment while seated at the place of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree,
at that time, there were Bodhisattvas in the worlds of Buddhas equal to the sands of measureless *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges Rivers,
who also previously asked me this extremely profound meaning.
The wording, meaning, and merit of their questions were also exactly like this,
without any difference.
One who asks thus
is able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings."
At that time, Jiāyè Bodhisattva again said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
I do not have the power of wisdom to ask the Tathāgata such a profound meaning.
World-Honored One!
Just as a mosquito or gadfly cannot fly across the far shore of the great ocean
or encompass the entirety of space.
I am also like this;
I cannot inquire about the extremely profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s ocean of wisdom
and the emptiness of Fǎxìng.
World-Honored One!
Just as a king entrusts the bright jewel from his topknot
to the minister in charge of the treasury.
When the minister receives it,
he respectfully places it upon his head
and increases its protection.
I am also like this,
respectfully holding and guarding
the profound meaning of the Fāngděng teachings spoken by the Tathāgata.
Why is this?
Because it allows me to widely attain profound wisdom."
At that time, the Buddha told Jiāyè Bodhisattva:
"Good man!
Listen carefully,
listen carefully!
I shall now speak to you about the karma of longevity attained by the Tathāgata.
Bodhisattvas, due to the causes and conditions of this karma,
attain long life.
Therefore, you should sincerely listen and receive it.
If the karma is capable of being the cause for Pútí,
one should sincerely listen to and receive this meaning,
and having listened and received it, transmit it to others.
Good man!
Because I cultivated such karma,
I attained Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
and now I widely speak this meaning for the benefit of people.
Good man!
For instance, if a prince
commits a crime and is imprisoned,
the king, being deeply compassionate,
and loving his son,
personally turns his carriage to go to the place of imprisonment.
Bodhisattvas are also like this:
if they wish to attain long life,
they should guard and remember all sentient beings with the thought that they are like sons,
generating Dàcí, Dàbēi,
Dàxǐ, and Dàshě.
They should administer the precept of non-killing,
and teach the cultivation of good dharma.
They should also establish all sentient beings in the Five Precepts and the Ten Goods,
further entering into all destinies, such as the hells,
hungry ghosts,
animals,
and Āxiūluó,
to rescue and assist the suffering beings therein,
to release those who are unreleased,
to save those who are unsaved,
to enable those who have not attained Nièpán to attain it,
and to comfort all who are terrified.
Because of such causes and conditions of karma,
the Bodhisattva attains long life
and gains mastery over all wisdom,
and whenever that life ends, they are born in heaven."
At that time, Jiāyè Bodhisattva again said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
The meaning that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas regard sentient beings equally
with the thought that they are like sons
is profoundly hidden,
and I cannot yet fully understand it.
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata should not say that Bodhisattvas cultivate equal-mindedness towards all sentient beings,
regarding them as sons.
Why is that?
Among the Buddha's teachings, there are those who break the precepts,
those who commit heinous sins,
and those who slander the true Dharma.
How can one regard such people with the same thought as one's own sons?"
The Buddha told Jiāyè:
"It is so,
it is so.
I truly regard sentient beings with the thought of sons,
like Luóhóuluó."
Jiāyè Bodhisattva again said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
Previously, on the fifteenth day during the Saṅgha Bùsà,
in the pure assembly that had received the full precepts,
there was a young boy
who had not diligently cultivated the karma of body,
speech,
and mind,
and who secretly listened to the reciting of the precepts from a hidden corner.
The Mìjī Lìshì, relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power,
crushed him into dust with a Jīngāng chǔ.
World-Honored One!
This Vajra Spirit,
having become extremely violent and wicked,
was thus able to sever the life-root of this boy.
How can the Tathāgata regard all sentient beings with the thought of sons,
like Luóhóuluó?"
The Buddha told Kāshè:
"You should not speak such words now,
saying that this boy
is merely an illusionary manifestation,
not real,
intended to expel and drive out those who violate the precepts and destroy the Dharma;
that Jīngāng Mìjì is also merely an illusion.
Kāshè!
Regarding those who slander the Proper Dharma and the Icchantika (Yīchǎntí),
or those who commit killing, or even those holding wrong views, or those who deliberately violate prohibitions,
for all these kinds of beings,
I completely generate a compassionate mind,
thinking of them equally as my own sons,
just like Luóhóuluó.
Good man!
For example, a king,
when his various ministers violate the royal law,
he executes them according to their crimes and does not spare them.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is not like that;
for those who destroy the Dharma,
he administers the *karma* of expulsion (qūqiǎn jiémó),
the *karma* of severe reprimand (hēzé jiémó),
the *karma* of suspension (zhì jiémó),
the *karma* of announcing offenses (jǔzuì jiémó),
the *karma* of non-seeing (bùkějiàn jiémó),
the *karma* of suppression (miè jiémó),
and the *karma* of not abandoning wrong views (wèishě èjiàn jiémó).
Good man!
The reason the Tathāgata administers such methods of subjugation (*jiàngfú jiémó*) to those who slander the Dharma
is to show that those who commit evil deeds will face retribution.
Good man!
You should now know that
the Tathāgata is the one who bestows fearlessness upon wicked beings.
If he emits one ray of light,
or two,
or five,
should anyone encounter it,
it causes them to completely abandon all evils.
The Tathāgata now possesses such immeasurable power.
Good man,
the Dharma that is not yet visible,
if you wish to see it,
I shall now describe its appearance for you.
After my Nirvāṇa,
wherever there is a region
where there are Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū) who uphold the precepts,
whose deportment is complete,
who guard and uphold the Proper Dharma,
and who, upon seeing those who destroy the Dharma,
are able immediately to expel them,
reprimand them, and punish them,
know that such a person
gains immeasurable and incalculable merit.
Good man!
Suppose there is a king
who specializes in brutal wickedness.
He happens to fall gravely ill.
A king from a neighboring state,
having heard his reputation,
raises an army and comes,
planning to exterminate him.
At that time, the sick king,
because he lacks power and influence,
only then becomes afraid
and reforms his mind to practice goodness.
And that neighboring king
gains immeasurable merit.
A Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) who upholds the Dharma is also like this;
by expelling and reprimanding those who destroy the Dharma,
and causing them to practice good Dharma,
he gains immeasurable merit.
Good man!
For example, in the residence of an elder (*zhǎngzhě*),
poisonous trees grow on the fields, houses, and dwellings.
When the elder knows this,
he immediately cuts them down
and causes them to be permanently destroyed.
Similarly, a vigorous person,
when white hairs appear on his head,
is ashamed and plucks them out,
not allowing them to grow.
A Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) who upholds the Dharma is also like this;
seeing those who violate the precepts and destroy the Proper Dharma,
they should immediately expel them,
reprimand them, and report their transgression.
If a virtuous Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū), seeing those who destroy the Dharma,
allows them to remain without reprimanding, expelling, or reporting their transgression,
know that this person is an enemy of the Buddha Dharma.
If one is able to expel, reprimand, and report their transgression,
that person is my disciple,
a true Śrāvaka (Shēngwén)."
Kāshè Púsà (Bodhisattva) again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If it is as the Buddha says,
then you do not regard all beings equally, thinking of them as your sons,
like Luóhóuluó.
World-Honored One!
If one person harms the Buddha with a knife,
and another person applies sandalwood paste to the Buddha,
if the Buddha generates an equal mind towards these two,
how can you then say
that those who violate prohibitions should be punished?
If those who violate prohibitions are punished,
then this statement is lost."
The Buddha told Kāshè Púsà:
"Good man!
For example, a king,
a minister,
or a chancellor raises several sons.
They are handsome in appearance,
clever and wise.
Whether two,
three,
or four,
they are entrusted to a strict teacher,
and the father says:
'Sir, please instruct my sons
in deportment,
etiquette,
skills,
writing,
calculation,
and arithmetic,
ensuring they fully achieve competence.
I now have four sons;
they receive instruction from you.
Even if three sons die from sickness or beating,
the remaining one son must be severely disciplined
to ensure he achieves competence.
Although I lose three sons,
I will never resent it.'
Kāshè!
Does that father and teacher incur the sin of killing?"
"No,
World-Honored One!
Why?
Because of love and affection,
and the desire for their achievement,
there is no evil intention.
Such instruction
gains immeasurable merit."
"Good man!
The Tathāgata is also like this;
he regards those who destroy the Dharma equally as one son.
The Tathāgata now entrusts the unsurpassed Proper Dharma
to the various kings,
ministers,
chancellors,
Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū),
Bhikṣuṇīs (Bǐqiūní),
Upāsakas (Yōupósè),
and Upāsikās (Yōupóyí).
These kings and the four assemblies,
should encourage those who are learning
to attain the higher precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
If there are any who do not study these three categories of Dharma,
who are lazy,
who break the precepts,
or who destroy the Proper Dharma,
the kings,
ministers,
and the four assemblies should severely punish them.
Good man!
Will these kings and the four assemblies
incur guilt?"
"No,
World-Honored One!"
"Good man!
Since these kings and the four assemblies do not incur guilt,
how much less so the Tathāgata.
Good man!
The Tathāgata excellently practices this kind of equality,
regarding all beings equally as one son.
One who practices thus
is called a Púsà (Bodhisattva) who cultivates the mind of equality,
regarding all beings equally as one son.
Good man!
A Púsà who cultivates this practice in this manner
gains longevity,
and is also able to know well the affairs of past lives."
Kāshè Púsà again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Shìzūn!
As the Buddha has taught,
if a Bodhisattva cultivates the mind of equality,
and regards all sentient beings as identical to one’s own children,
they attain longevity.
The Rúlái should not make such a statement.
Why is this?
It is like a person who understands the Dharma,
who can speak of various laws of filial piety,
but when they return home,
they use tiles and stones to hit and throw at their parents.
Yet these parents are excellent fields of merit (fútián),
providing great benefit,
difficult to encounter and difficult to meet,
and should be well-provided for and nourished.
Instead, harm and distress are inflicted upon them.
Such a Dharma-knower’s words and actions contradict each other.
What the Rúlái says
is also like this:
If a Bodhisattva cultivates the equal mind,
regarding sentient beings as identical to their children,
they should attain long life,
clearly know past lives (sùmìng),
permanently dwell in the world,
and be without change.
But now, Shìzūn,
by what cause or condition
is your lifespan extremely short,
the same as human beings?
Does the Rúlái perhaps harbor thoughts of resentment toward sentient beings?
What evil karma did the Shìzūn commit in the past,
how many lives did you sever the root of,
to receive this short life, not exceeding a hundred years?”
The Buddha said to Kāshè:
“Shànnánzǐ!
For what reason are you now
uttering these coarse words
in the presence of the Rúlái?
The Rúlái’s longevity,
among all lifespans,
is the most supreme and most excellent.
The everlasting Dharma attained,
among all things that are everlasting,
is the foremost.”
Kāshè Púsà again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Shìzūn!
How does the Rúlái attain great longevity?”
The Buddha said to Kāshè:
“Shànnánzǐ!
Like the eight great rivers:
The first is named Gēnghé,
the second Yánmóluó,
the third Sàluó,
the fourth Ā Líluóbátí,
the fifth Móhē,
the sixth Xīndú,
the seventh Bóshā,
the eighth Xītuó.
These eight great rivers and all smaller rivers all flow into the Great Sea.
Kāshè!
In the same way, all
the great rivers of lifespan, in the human realm,
heavenly realms, earth, and empty space,
all flow into the Rúlái’s ocean of life,
which is why the Rúlái’s lifespan is immeasurable.
Furthermore, Kāshè!
Just as the Ānòudá Chí gives rise to the four great rivers;
the Rúlái is also like this,
giving rise to all life.
Kāshè!
Just as among all things that are everlasting,
empty space is the foremost;
the Rúlái is also like this,
among all things that are everlasting,
the foremost.
Kāshè!
Just as among all medicines,
Tígū is the foremost;
the Rúlái is also like this,
among sentient beings,
the foremost in longevity.”
Kāshè Púsà again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Shìzūn!
If the Rúlái’s lifespan is like this,
you should remain for one kalpa or slightly less than one kalpa,
constantly proclaiming the sublime Dharma,
like a heavy downpour.”
“Kāshè!
You should not, concerning the Rúlái,
give rise to the thought of extinction.
Kāshè!
If there is a Bhīkṣu,
Bhīkṣuṇī,
Upāsaka,
Upāsikā,
or even an external practitioner (wàidào),
a deity possessing the five supernatural powers (wǔtōng shénxiān),
who has attained mastery,
if they remain for one kalpa or slightly less than one kalpa,
walking in the sky,
sitting and sleeping freely,
emitting fire from the left side,
emitting water from the right side,
smoke and flames issuing from their body,
like a heap of fire,
if they wish to remain in life,
they can achieve their desire,
controlling the length
or shortness of their lifespan as they please.
Since such a wǔtōng deity
can still possess such divine power at will,
how much more so the Rúlái, who, regarding all phenomena,
has attained the power of mastery?
How could the Rúlái be incapable of abiding in life for half a kalpa,
or one kalpa,
or a hundred kalpas,
or a hundred thousand kalpas,
or immeasurable kalpas?
For this reason,
you should know that the Rúlái
is the everlasting Dharma,
the unchanging Dharma.
This present body of the Rúlái
is a transformed body (biànhuà shēn),
not a body fed by mixed foods.
In order to save sentient beings,
it is presented as similar to a poisonous tree,
and therefore appears to pass away and enter Níèpán.
Kāshè!
You should know that the Buddha is the everlasting Dharma,
the unchanging Dharma.
Regarding this ultimate truth (dìyī yì), you all
should diligently exert yourselves,
cultivate it with undivided mind,
and having cultivated it,
broadly preach it to people.”
At that time, Kāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
“Shìzūn!
What is the difference between the transcendent Dharma (chūshì zhī fǎ) and the worldly Dharma (shìjiān fǎ)?
As the Buddha says:
The Buddha is the everlasting Dharma,
the unchanging Dharma.’
The world also says:
‘Brahmā Heaven (Fàntiān) is everlasting,
Īśvara Deva (Zìzàitiān) is everlasting,
without change.
The Self (wǒ) is everlasting,
Nature (xìng) is everlasting,
and even subtle atoms (wēichén) are everlasting.’
If it is said that the Rúlái is the everlasting Dharma,
why does the Rúlái not constantly appear?
If he does not constantly appear,
what is the difference?
Why is this?
Because Fàntiān, down to wēichén,
and World-Nature (shì xìng) also do not constantly appear.”
The Fó told Kāyè:
“For example, an Elder (Chángzhě),
had many cattle.
Although their colors varied,
they belonged together in one herd.
He entrusted them to a herdsman,
ordering him to follow water and grass,
but only for the sake of Tíhú (ghee),
not seeking milk or curds (Rǔlào).
That herdsman,
milked them and ate it himself.
When the Elder died,
all his cattle were plundered and seized by a band of thieves.
When the thieves obtained the cattle,
they had no women (to process the milk).
They immediately milked them themselves,
and having obtained (the milk), they ate it.
At that time, the band of thieves said to each other:
‘That great Elder,
kept these cattle,
not expecting milk or curds,
but only for Tíhú.
How should we now,
devise a method to obtain it?
Now, Tíhú,
is known as the world's foremost excellent flavor.
We have no containers;
even if we obtain milk,
there is nowhere to place it.’
They further said to each other:
‘We only have leather bags;
we can use those to hold it.’
Although they had a place to hold it,
they did not know how to churn it,
so even the curds were difficult to obtain,
much less raw butter.
At that time, those thieves,
for the sake of Tíhú,
added water to it.
Because the water was excessive,
milk, curds, and Tíhú,
were all completely lost.
Ordinary people (Fánfū) are likewise.
Although they possess good dharmas,
they are all remnants of the Tathāgata’s (Rúlái) correct Dharma.
Why is this?
After the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One (Shìzūn), entered Nièpán (Nirvāṇa),
they stole the remaining good dharmas left by the Tathāgata—
namely, Jiè (precepts),
Dìng (concentration),
and Huì (wisdom)—
just like those thieves plundering the herd of cattle.
All ordinary people,
although they might obtain these Jiè,
Dìng,
and wisdom (Zhìhuì),
lack skillful means (Fāngbiàn),
and cannot explain them.
Because of this reason,
they cannot achieve permanent Jiè,
permanent Dìng,
permanent Huì,
or liberation (Jiětuō);
just like that band of thieves,
not knowing the skillful means,
and losing the Tíhú.
Also, like the band of thieves,
who, for the sake of Tíhú,
added water to it.
Ordinary people are likewise.
For the sake of liberation,
they speak of Wǒ (self),
Zhòngshēng (sentient beings),
Shòumìng (lifespan),
Shìfū (person),
Fàntiān (Brahmā),
Zìzàitiān (Īśvara),
the atom-nature of the world (Wéichén Shìxìng),
and Jiè, Dìng, and wisdom, and liberation,
claiming that the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (Fēixiǎngfēifēixiǎng Tiān) is Nièpán.
In reality, they do not obtain liberation or Nièpán,
just as that band of thieves did not obtain Tíhú.
These ordinary people,
possessing minor pure practices (Fànxíng),
and supporting their parents,
due to these causes,
are reborn in heaven,
and experience minor joy and comfort,
like the milk to which the band of thieves added water.
Yet these ordinary people,
truly do not know the cause (of being reborn in heaven) is cultivating minor pure practices,
and supporting their parents.
to be reborn in heaven.
Furthermore, they cannot know Jiè,
Dìng,
and wisdom,
or taking refuge in the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo).
Because they do not know,
they speak of permanence (Cháng),
bliss (Lè),
Self (Wǒ),
and purity (Jìng).
Although they speak of them,
they truly do not understand.
Therefore, after the Tathāgata appeared in the world,
he then taught and expounded permanence (Cháng),
bliss (Lè),
Self (Wǒ),
and purity (Jìng).
It is like when a Cakravartin King (Zhuǎnlúnwáng) appears in the world;
due to the power of his merit and virtue,
the band of thieves retreats and scatters,
and the cattle suffer no loss of life.
Then, the Zhuǎnlúnwáng,
immediately entrusts the cattle to a herdsman,
who possesses many skillful means.
This person, using skillful means,
immediately obtains the Tíhú.
Because of the Tíhú,
all sentient beings,
are free from suffering and distress.
When the Sacred King of the Dharma Wheel (Fǎlún Shèngwáng) appears in the world,
those ordinary people who cannot expound Jiè, Dìng, and Huì,
immediately retreat and scatter,
just as the thieves retreat and scatter.
At that time, the Tathāgata skillfully teaches worldly dharmas and transcendent dharmas,
and for the sake of sentient beings,
allows the Bodhisattvas (Púsà) to follow and expound them.
The Mahāsattva Bodhisattvas (Púsà Mòhēsà), having obtained the Tíhú,
further enable immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to obtain the supreme sweet dew of the Dharma-flavor,
which is the Tathāgata’s permanence (Cháng),
bliss (Lè),
Self (Wǒ),
and purity (Jìng).
Because of this reason,
O good man!
The Tathāgata is permanent (Cháng);
the Dharma that does not change.
He is not like the worldly,
ordinary people,
and fools,
who claim that Fàntiān (Brahmā) and others are the permanent Dharma.
This designation of permanent Dharma truly belongs to the Tathāgata,
and not to any other dharma.
Kāyè!
You ought to know the Tathāgata’s body in this manner.
Kāyè!
All good men
and good women,
should constantly focus their minds on cultivating these two words:
The Fó is eternally abiding (Chángzhù).
Kāyè!
If there are good men
or good women who cultivate these two words,
know that such a person,
follows the path I have taken,
and reaches the place I have reached.
O good man!
If someone cultivates these two words as an extinction characteristic (Mièxiàng),
know that the Tathāgata is, for that person, entering Parinirvāṇa (Bān Nièpán).
O good man!
The meaning of Nièpán,
is the Dharma-nature (Fǎxìng) of all Buddhas.
Kāyè Púsà said to the Fó:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
What is the meaning
of the Fó's Dharma-nature?
Shìzūn!
I now wish to understand the meaning of Dharma-nature.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will mercifully explain it fully.
If Dharma-nature means abandoning the body (shěshēn),
and abandoning the body means having nothing (Wúsuǒyǒu),
if there is nothing,
how can the body exist?
If the body exists,
how can it be said that the body possesses Dharma-nature?
If the body possesses Dharma-nature, how can it exist?
How should I now understand this meaning?”
Buddha addressed Jiāshè Púsà:
“Good man!
You should not make such a statement now,
that the Dharma-nature is extinguished.
Indeed, the Dharma-nature
has no extinguishing.
Good man!
For example, the beings in the Wúxiǎng Tiān,
achieve the form aggregate but lack the perception of form;
you should not ask,
‘How do these Devas
abide?
How do they enjoy pleasure and receive happiness?
How do the volitional formations and perceptions function?
How do they see and hear?’
Good man,
the realm of the Rúlái
is not known by the Shēngwén and Yuánjué.
Good man,
you should not say,
‘The body of the Rúlái is a destructible phenomenon.’
Good man,
such a destructible phenomenon is the realm of the Buddha,
not reached by the Shēngwén and Yuánjué.
Good man,
you should not now ponder where the Rúlái abides?
Where does he walk?
Where does he see?
Where does he find joy?
Good man,
such principles
are also not known or reached by you and your peers.
The Fǎshēn of all Buddhas,
and their various skillful means,
are inconceivable.
“Furthermore, good man!
You should cultivate the perception of permanence regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
These three principles
have no perception of difference,
no perception of impermanence,
and no perception of change.
If one cultivates the perception of difference regarding the three principles,
you should know that such persons
have no reliance for their pure Three Refuges,
all their precepts are incomplete,
and they ultimately cannot realize the fruit of Shēngwén or Yuánjué Bodhi.
If one can, regarding this inconceivable matter,
cultivate the perception of permanence,
then one has a place of refuge.
Good man!
Just as, depending on a tree,
there is a tree shadow.
The Rúlái is also like that;
because he possesses the constant Dharma,
then there is refuge,
he is not impermanent.
If one says that the Rúlái is impermanent,
the Rúlái would not be the refuge of Devas
or people of the world.”
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
“Shìzūn!
For example, in the darkness,
there is a tree but no shadow.”
“Jiāshè!
You should not say there is a tree without a shadow;
it is merely not seen by the physical eye.
Good man!
The Rúlái is also like that;
his nature is permanently abiding,
it is unchanging.
Those without the eye of wisdom,
cannot perceive him,
just like in that darkness,
one does not see the tree shadow.
Ordinary people,
after the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa,
who say that the Rúlái is an impermanent phenomenon,
are also like this.
If one says that the Rúlái is different from the Dharma
and the Saṅgha,
then one cannot establish the Three Refuges,
just as your father and mother are separate and distinct,
making them impermanent.”
Jiāshè Púsà again said to the Buddha:
“Shìzūn!
Starting from this day forward,
I shall teach my parents,
up to the seventh generation,
about the permanence of the three matters—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—
and guide them to uphold this faith.
How wonderful,
Shìzūn!
I shall now learn about the
inconceivable nature of the Rúlái,
the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha.
Having learned it myself,
I shall also widely preach this meaning for others.
If there are people who cannot believe and accept it,
you should know that these people have long cultivated impermanence.
For such people,
I shall act as frost and hail against them.”
At that time, the Buddha praised Jiāshè Púsà:
“Excellent,
excellent!
You are now skillfully able to protect and uphold the Zhèngfǎ.
Protecting the Dharma in this way
does not deceive others.
Due to the cause of the good karma of not deceiving others,
you shall obtain long life
and skillfully know past lives.”
Then the Shìzūn again addressed Jiāshè:
“Good man!
The body of the Rúlái
is the permanently abiding body,
the indestructible body,
the Jīngāng body,
not a body sustained by mixed food;
it is none other than the Fǎshēn.”
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
“Shìzūn!
As the Buddha has said,
such bodies,
I do not see at all.
I only see the impermanent,
the destroyed,
the dust-like,
and bodies sustained by mixed food.
Why is that?
Because the Rúlái is about to enter Nièpán.”
Fó said:
“Jiāshè!
Do not now say that the Tathāgata’s (Rúlái) body
is impermanent and perishable,
like the body of an ordinary person (fánfū).
Good man!
You ought now to know that
the Tathāgata’s body
is firm and difficult to destroy for measureless hundreds of millions of kalpas,
it is not the body of humans or gods,
not a body of fear,
not a body sustained by mixed foods.
The Tathāgata’s body is non-body;
this body is neither born nor destroyed,
neither practiced nor cultivated,
measureless and boundless,
without tracks,
without perception and without form,
ultimately pure and clean,
without movement or shaking,
without reception (feeling) and without formation (volition),
neither abiding nor acting,
without flavor and without impurity,
it is not conditioned (yǒuwéi),
not karma (yè),
not retribution (guǒ),
not action (xíng),
not extinction (miè),
not mind (xīn),
not number (shù),
inconceivable,
eternally inconceivable,
without consciousness (shí), detached from mind,
and yet not detached from mind;
its mind is equal and balanced (píngděng),
it is non-existent yet also existent,
it has no coming or going, yet also comes and goes,
it is not broken,
not ruined,
not severed,
not terminated,
not produced,
not extinguished,
not master yet also master,
neither existence nor non-existence,
neither realization nor contemplation,
neither word nor non-word,
neither concentration (dìng) nor non-concentration,
cannot be seen yet clearly seen,
placeless yet also place,
homeless yet also home,
without darkness, without brightness (míng),
without stillness (jìng) yet also still;
it is non-possession,
neither accepting nor giving,
pure and without stain (gòu),
without contention, severing contention,
dwelling in the non-dwelling place,
neither grasping nor falling,
neither teaching (fǎ) nor non-teaching,
neither field of merit (fútián) nor non-field of merit,
inexhaustible yet not inexhaustible, separated from all exhaustion,
it is emptiness (kōng) yet detached from emptiness;
although it does not abide constantly, it is not extinguished momentarily,
without defilement or turbidity,
without words, detached from words,
neither sound nor speech,
nor is it cultivation or practice (xiūxí),
neither weighed nor measured,
neither one nor different,
neither image nor characteristic (xiàng),
yet adorned with all characteristics (zhū xiàng),
neither brave nor fearful,
not tranquil yet also tranquil,
not hot yet also hot,
cannot be perceived or seen,
without form or appearance (xiàngmào).
The Tathāgata delivers all sentient beings,
yet fundamentally there is no deliverance;
He can enlighten sentient beings,
yet fundamentally there is no enlightenment;
He realizes sentient beings,
yet fundamentally there is no realization;
He speaks the Dharma truly,
yet fundamentally there are no two things.
It is immeasurable and unequaled.
Equal like the void (xūkōng),
without form or appearance,
identical to the nature of non-production (wú shēng xìng),
neither severed nor eternal.
He constantly practices the One Vehicle (Yī Chéng),
but sentient beings see three (vehicles).
It neither retreats nor turns,
it severs all fetters (jié).
It neither fights nor touches,
it is non-nature abiding in nature,
neither combination nor dispersion,
neither long nor short,
neither round nor square,
neither skandhas (yīn), āyatanas (rù), or dhātus (jiè) yet also skandhas, āyatanas, and dhātus,
neither increase nor decrease,
neither victory nor defeat.
The Tathāgata’s body is perfected with such measureless meritorious qualities (gōngdé).
There is no one who knows it,
and no one who does not know it;
There is no one who sees it,
and no one who does not see it;
It is neither conditioned (yǒuwéi) nor unconditioned (wúwéi),
neither mundane (shì) nor non-mundane,
neither action nor non-action,
neither dependence nor non-dependence,
neither the Four Great Elements (sì dà) nor not the Four Great Elements,
neither cause (yīn) nor non-cause,
neither sentient being (zhòngshēng) nor non-sentient being,
neither Shāmén nor Brahmin (Póluómén).
It is the Lion, the Great Lion (Shīzǐ Dàshīzǐ),
neither body nor non-body,
and cannot be fully described.
Excluding the mark of the One Dharma (Yīfǎ xiàng),
it is uncountable.
When entering Nirvāṇa (Bān Nièpán), it does not enter Nirvāṇa.
The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body (Fǎshēn) is completely perfected with such measureless subtle meritorious qualities.
“Jiāshè!
Only the Tathāgata
knows these characteristics;
they are not known by the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué).
Jiāshè!
Such meritorious qualities constitute the Tathāgata’s body;
it is not a body nourished and sustained by mixed foods.
Jiāshè!
Since the meritorious qualities of the Tathāgata’s true body (zhēnshēn) are like this,
