how could it again experience all diseases and suffering,
being frail and impermanent like a broken vessel?
Jiāshè!
The reason the Tathāgata manifests sickness and suffering
is for the sake of taming and subduing all sentient beings.
Good man!
You ought now to know that
the Tathāgata’s body is the Vajra body (Jīngāng shēn).
From today onward, you must constantly and diligently contemplate this meaning.
Do not think of the food-sustained body,
and you must also speak to others,
that the Tathāgata’s body is precisely the Dharma-body (Fǎshēn).
The Bodhisattva (Púsà) Jiāshè said to the Fó:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If the Tathāgata is perfected with such meritorious qualities,
how could his body experience sickness and suffering,
and be broken and destroyed by impermanence (wúcháng)?
From today onward, I shall constantly contemplate
that the Tathāgata’s body is the eternal Dharma-body (cháng Fǎshēn),
the body of peace and bliss (ānlè zhī shēn),
and I shall broadly preach this to others in the same way.
Indeed, Shìzūn!
The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is Vajra and indestructible,
but I still do not know what the specific cause (suǒ yīn) for this is.”
The Fó said:
“Jiāshè!
Because of the cause and condition of being able to uphold and protect the Correct Dharma (Zhèng Fǎ),
one achieves and perfects this Vajra body.
Jiāshè!
I, in former times, based on the cause and condition of protecting the Dharma,
have now achieved and perfected this Vajra body,
which abides eternally and is indestructible.
Good man!
He who upholds and protects the Correct Dharma
does not necessarily receive the Five Precepts (Wǔ Jiè),
nor cultivate proper deportment (wēiyí).
He should carry swords and spears,
bows and arrows,
pikes and lances,
to guard and protect the Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū) who maintain pure precepts.
The Bodhisattva Jiāshè said to the Fó:
“Shìzūn!
If there is a Bhikṣu who is detached from guards and protectors,
dwells alone in solitude,
in graveyards or beneath trees,
we should say that this person is a true Bhikṣu.
If there are those who follow the actions of guards and protectors,
we should know that such persons are shaved laymen (tū jūshì).”
The Buddha instructed Jiāyè:
“Do not speak such words,
calling him a ‘bald householder.’
If there is a Bhikṣu,
who provides sufficiently for his body wherever he goes,
recites and studies the Sūtras,
contemplates and practices seated meditation (zuòchán),
and when someone comes to ask about the Dharma,
immediately proclaims it for them,
namely Dāna (bùshī),
keeping the precepts (chíjiè),
merit and virtue (fúdé),
having few desires, and being content (shǎoyù zhīzú).
Although he is able to preach the Dharma in various ways like this,
yet he still cannot make the lion’s roar (shīzǐhǒu),
nor is he surrounded by lions,
nor can he subdue evil people who break the law.
Such a Bhikṣu cannot benefit himself or sentient beings;
you should know that this type of person
is lazy and indolent (xièdài lǎnduò).
Even though he can maintain the precepts
and guard his pure conduct,
you should know that this person is incapable of accomplishing anything great.
If there is a Bhikṣu whose bodily provisions are always abundant,
who, furthermore, guards and maintains the prohibitions he has received,
who can make the lion’s roar,
and extensively preach the subtle Dharma,
that is, Sūtra (xiūdūluó),
Geya (qíyè),
Vyākaraṇa (shòujì),
Gāthā (gātuó),
Udāna (yōutuónà),
Itivṛttaka (yīdìyuēduōjiā),
Jātaka (shétuójiā),
Vaipulya (pífúlüè),
Adbhutadharma (āfútuódámó).
Using these nine divisions of the scriptures
to extensively preach for others,
for the sake of benefiting and bringing joy to all sentient beings,
he utters these words:
‘In the Nirvāṇa Sūtra,
all Bhikṣus are prohibited
from keeping slaves,
cattle, sheep,
or unlawful possessions.
If any Bhikṣu
possesses such impure objects,
he should be punished.
The Tathāgata previously stated in other divisions of the Sūtras
that if a Bhikṣu possesses such unlawful objects,
a certain king (mǒujiǎ guówáng) should punish him according to the law
and expel him to return to lay life (huánsú).
If a Bhikṣu
is able to make such a lion’s roar,
those who have broken the precepts,
having heard these words,
will all become angry and enraged,
and kill this Dharma Master (fǎshī).
Even if this speaker of the Dharma
should subsequently die,
he is still called a keeper of the precepts (chíjiè),
benefiting himself and benefiting others.
For this reason,
I permit rulers,
ministers,
prime ministers,
and all Upāsakas (yōupósè)
to protect the preachers of the Dharma.
If there is anyone who wishes to protect the Right Dharma (zhèngfǎ),
they should learn in this manner.
Jiāyè!
Such a breaker of the precepts who does not protect the Dharma
is called a ‘bald householder’ (tū jūshì);
it is not the one who maintains the precepts
who receives this name.
Good man!
In the past, immeasurable, boundless Asaṃkhyeya Kalpas ago,
in this city of Kuśinagara (Kūshīnà Chéng),
a Buddha appeared in the world,
named Pramuditavṛddhi Tathāgata (Huānxǐ Zēngyì Rúlái),
Arhat (Yìng),
Samyak-sambuddha (Zhèngbiànzhī),
Vidyācaraṇa-sampanna (Míngxíngzú),
Sugata (Shànshì),
Lokavid (Shìjiānjiě),
Anuttara (Wúshàngshì),
Puruṣadamyasārathi (Tiáoyù Zhàngfū),
Śāstā Devamanuṣyānām (Tiānrénshī),
Buddha (Fó),
Bhagavān (Shìzūn).
At that time, the world was vast, pure, and solemn,
rich, joyful, and peaceful,
with flourishing populations,
and no starvation or thirst,
like the Bodhisattvas in the Land of Bliss (Ānlè Guó).
That Buddha Bhagavan lived in the world for an immeasurable time,
and after having transformed sentient beings,
he then entered Parinirvāṇa (Bō Nièpán) between the twin Sāla trees.
After the Buddha entered Nirvāṇa,
the Right Dharma remained in the world for immeasurable eons,
and for the remaining forty years, the Buddha Dharma was not yet extinguished.
At that time, there was a precept-keeping Bhikṣu
named Juédé,
who had many disciples
and attendants surrounding him,
who was able to make the lion’s roar,
proclaiming and extensively preaching the nine divisions of the scriptures,
and prohibiting all Bhikṣus from keeping slaves,
cattle, sheep,
or unlawful possessions.
At that time, there were many precept-breaking Bhikṣus
who, hearing this statement,
all gave rise to evil intentions,
wielded knives and staffs,
and pressed upon this Dharma Master.
At that time, the King,
named Yǒudé,
having heard of this matter,
for the sake of protecting the Dharma,
immediately went to the location of the Dharma speaker,
and engaged in fierce battle with those evil precept-breaking Bhikṣus,
allowing the Dharma speaker to escape harm.
The King at that time
had his body wounded by knives, swords,
arrows, and spears;
there was no intact spot on his body, not even the size of a mustard seed.
At that time, Juédé immediately praised the King, saying:
‘Excellent!
Excellent!
The King is now truly a protector of the Right Dharma.
In future generations,
this body will become an immeasurable vessel for the Dharma.’
The King at that time,
having heard the Dharma,
felt great joy in his heart,
and immediately passed away,
and was born in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha (Āchù Fó Guó),
becoming the first disciple of that Buddha.
The King’s retinue and accompanying common people,
those who fought
and those who rejoiced,
all did not retreat from the heart of Bodhi (Pútí),
and upon death, were all born in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha (Āchù Fó Guó).
After Bhikṣu Juédé reached the end of his lifespan,
he also attained rebirth in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha (Āchù Fó Guó),
becoming the second disciple among the assembly of Śrāvakas (shēngwén zhòng) for that Buddha.
If the Right Dharma is about to perish,
one should uphold and protect it in this manner.
Jiāyè!
The King at that time
was none other than my present self;
the Bhikṣu who spoke the Dharma
was Kāśyapa Buddha (Jiāshè Fó).
Jiāyè!
Those who protect the Right Dharma
obtain such immeasurable retribution and rewards.
Because of this cause and condition,
I today possess various auspicious marks
to adorn myself,
achieving the Dharma Body (fǎshēn)
and the indestructible body.”
Jiāshè Púsà further said to the Buddha:
“Bhagavān!
The Tathāgata’s permanent body
is like an engraving on stone.”
The Buddha told Jiāshè Púsà:
“Good man!
For this reason,
Bhikṣus (bǐqiū),
Bhikṣuṇīs (bǐqiūní),
Upāsakas (yōupósè),
and Upāsikās (yōupóyí)
should diligently protect and uphold the Right Dharma,
for the karmic reward of protecting the Dharma is vast and boundless.
Good man!
Therefore, Upāsakas who protect the Dharma
should wield knives and staffs
to defend such Bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma.
If one upholds the five precepts (wǔjiè),
he is not necessarily called a Mahāyāna (Dàchéng) person;
but if one ignores the five precepts for the sake of protecting the Right Dharma,
he is then called Mahāyāna (Dàchéng).
Those who protect the Right Dharma
should wield swords,
weapons, and armor
to attend the speaker of the Dharma.”
Jiāyè addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Bhagavān!
If the Bhikṣus
associate as companions with such Upāsakas who bear knives and staffs,
do they have a master?
Or are they without a master?
Are they precept-keepers?
Or are they precept-breakers?”
The Buddha told Kāshyè:
“Do not call these individuals ‘transgressors of the precepts’ (pòjiè rén).
Good man!
After my Nirvāṇa,
in the evil age of defilement (zhuó è zhī shì), lands will be desolate and disordered,
people will plunder one another,
and the populace will starve.
At that time, many will abandon home and become renunciants (chūjiā) due to starvation;
such individuals are called ‘bald people’ (tǔ rén).
These bald people,
seeing those who uphold the precepts (chí jiè),
possess complete solemn deportment (wēiyí jùzú),
and are pure Bhikṣus protecting the Right Dharma (Zhèng Fǎ),
will drive them out,
or murder and harm them.
Kāshyè Púsà again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
How should these upholders of the precepts and protectors of the Right Dharma
travel through villages
and cities to teach and transform others?
“Good man!
Therefore, I now permit those who uphold the precepts
to rely on white-clothed laypeople (báiyī) who carry knives and staves (dāo zhàng),
and take them as companions.
If kings (guówáng),
high ministers (dàchén), elders (zhǎngzhě),
and Upāsakas (Yōupósā)
carry knives and staves
for the sake of protecting the Dharma (hù Fǎ),
I call these individuals upholders of the precepts (chí jiè).
Although they carry knives and staves,
they must not take life.
If they can act in this way,
they are entitled to be called the foremost upholders of the precepts.
“Kāshyè!
Those spoken of as protectors of the Dharma
possess right view (zhèngjiàn),
can broadly proclaim the Mahāyāna Sūtras (Dàchéng Jīngdiǎn),
and absolutely do not hold the precious canopies of kings (wángzhě bǎogài),
oil bottles, grain, rice,
or various fruits.
They do not approach kings,
high ministers, or elders for the sake of gain and support (lìyǎng).
Towards all donors (tán yuè),
their hearts are without flattery or deceit,
they possess complete solemn deportment,
and they vanquish all evil persons who transgress the precepts.
These are called masters who uphold the precepts and protect the Dharma (chí jiè hù Fǎ zhī shī);
they can be true good spiritual advisors (zhēn shàn zhīshi) for sentient beings,
and their minds are vast and great, like the great ocean.
Kāshyè!
If there is a Bhikṣu
who teaches the Dharma to others for the sake of gain and support,
the disciples and retinue belonging to this person
will also imitate their teacher in greedily seeking gain and support.
Such a person
thereby ruins their own community (zhòng).
Kāshyè!
Communities are of three types:
First, the mixed Saṅgha (zàsēng) that violates the precepts (fànjiè);
second, the ignorant Saṅgha (yúchī sēng);
and third, the pure Saṅgha (qīngjìng sēng).
The mixed Saṅgha that violates the precepts is easy to destroy.
The pure Saṅgha that upholds the precepts
cannot be destroyed by the causes and conditions of gain and support.
What is the mixed Saṅgha that violates the precepts?
If there is a Bhikṣu
who, though observing the moral prohibitions (jìnjiè),
associates, sits, rises, and travels with those who transgress the precepts
for the sake of gain and support,
attaches closely to them,
and shares their activities,
this is called transgression of the precepts,
and is also called a mixed Saṅgha.
What is the ignorant Saṅgha?
If there is a Bhikṣu dwelling in an isolated, quiet place (ālánruò chù),
whose faculties (zhū gēn) are not keen,
who is dim-witted and dull,
practices few desires, and begs for food (qǐ shí),
yet, on the day of teaching the precepts (shuō jiè rì) and during the time of self-praise (zìzī shí),
teaches his own disciples to purely repent (qīngjìng chàn huǐ),
but seeing non-disciples who frequently violate the moral prohibitions,
cannot teach them to purely repent,
and instead recites the precepts and holds the self-praise ceremony together with them,
this is called the ignorant Saṅgha.
What is called the pure Saṅgha?
There is a Bhikṣu Saṅgha
that cannot be destroyed by hundreds, thousands, or billions of Māras.
This community of Púsàs (Púsà zhòng) is pure by nature;
they can tame the two groups mentioned above,
causing them all to dwell in the pure community.
This is called the supreme great master who protects the Dharma (hù Fǎ wúshàng dà shī).
A good upholder of the Vinaya (lǜ zhě),
in order to tame and benefit sentient beings,
knows the marks of all precepts, whether light or heavy.
What is not Vinaya, they do not attest to;
what is Vinaya, they attest to.
How is this ‘taming sentient beings’?
If various Púsàs,
in order to transform sentient beings,
constantly enter villages
without regard for time or season.
Or they go to the homes of widows
or sexually immoral women (yín nǚ shèzhái),
and dwell together with them,
for many years.
This is what the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) should not do,
but it is called taming and benefiting sentient beings.
How is ‘knowing the heavy precepts’?
If one sees that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) established precepts based on certain incidents,
saying, ‘From this day forward, you must diligently refrain from committing this again.’
Such as the Four Grave Prohibitions (sì zhòng jìn);
things that renunciants should not do,
yet they deliberately commit them,
they are neither Śrāmaṇas (Shāmén)
nor sons of the Śākya clan (Shì zhǒng zǐ);
this is called heavy.
What is ‘knowing the light precepts’?
If one commits a minor offense,
and after being admonished three times in this manner, is able to renounce it,
this is called light.
As for ‘not attesting to what is not Vinaya,’
if someone praises impure objects (bù qīngjìng wù) and says they should be used,
one does not dwell with them.
As for ‘attesting to what is Vinaya,’
one studies the precepts and Vinaya well,
does not approach those who transgress the precepts,
and seeing actions that accord with the precepts and Vinaya,
one's heart gives rise to joy.
One can understand in this way,
and clearly explain
what the Buddha's Dharma (Fófǎ) teaches.
This is called a Vinaya Master (lǜ shī).
One who correctly understands a single character
and correctly upholds the Sūtras (Qì Jīng),
is also like this.
In this way,
good man!
The Buddha's Dharma is immeasurable and inconceivable (bù kě yīyì),
and the Tathāgata is likewise inconceivable.
Kāshyè Púsà said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
It is so,
it is so!
It is truly as the sacred teaching states.
The Buddha's Dharma is immeasurable and inconceivable,
and the Tathāgata is likewise inconceivable.
Therefore, we know that the Tathāgata perpetually abides without destruction
and is without change or alteration.
I now study well,
and I shall also broadly proclaim this meaning for others.”
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāshyè Púsà:
“Excellent,
excellent!
The Tathāgata’s body
is truly Vajra (Jīngāng),
an indestructible body.
A Púsà should study well in this way,
with right view and right knowledge.
If one can clearly know and see this way,
that is seeing the Tathāgata’s Vajra body,
the indestructible body,
just like seeing images in a mirror.”
At that time, the Tathāgata again addressed Kāshyè:
“Good man!
You should now carefully uphold the words
and phrases
and all the merit (gōngdé) of this Sūtra.
If there are good men
or good women
who hear the name of this Sūtra,
it is impossible
for them to be reborn in the four lower destinies (sì qù).
Why is this?
This Sūtra
is cultivated by immeasurable and boundless Buddhas.
I shall now speak of the merit attained from it.”
Kāshyè Púsà said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
What should this Sūtra be named?
How should the Púsà Mahāsattvas uphold it?
The Buddha addressed Kàshè:
“This Sūtra is named 'Dàbān Nièpán'.
The opening words are excellent,
the middle words are excellent,
and the concluding words are excellent.
Its meaning and flavor are profoundly deep;
its text is also excellent,
purely complete, fully possessing the pure Brahmacārya,
a diamond jewel-treasury, full and without defect.
Listen well now,
I shall now speak.
Good man,
that which is called 'Great'
is named 'Permanence' (Cháng).
Just as the eight great rivers all return to the great ocean,
this Sūtra is like this:
it vanquishes all fetters,
kleshas, and demonic natures,
and then essentializes Dàbān Nièpán,
relinquishing body and life.
Therefore, it is named Dàbān Nièpán.
Good man!
Also, it is like a physician who possesses one secret prescription
that encompasses all other medical prescriptions.
Good man!
The Tathāgata is also like this:
the various marvelous Dharmas, secret, profound, and hidden treasury gates that he preaches,
all enter into Dàbān Nièpán.
Therefore, it is named Dàbān Nièpán.
Good man!
For instance, a farmer,
who sows seeds in the spring month,
always harbors hope;
once the fruit is harvested,
all hopes cease entirely.
Good man!
All sentient beings are also like this:
when cultivating and studying other Sūtras,
they constantly hope for flavor (zǐwèi);
if they hear this Dàbān Nièpán,
the hope for all the flavors contained in other Sūtras is eternally severed.
This Dà Nièpán
is capable of enabling sentient beings to cross over all streams of existence (yǒu liú).
Good man!
Among all tracks,
the elephant's track is the greatest.
This Sūtra is like this:
among all Sūtra Samādhis, it is the foremost.
Good man!
For instance, concerning plowing fields,
autumn plowing is superior.
This Sūtra is like this:
it is superior among Sūtras.
Good man!
Just as among all medicines,
Gāndào (ghī/clarified butter) is the first;
it excels at treating the burning afflictions and disturbed minds of sentient beings,
this Dà Nièpán is the foremost.
Good man!
For instance, sweet Sū (butter/cream)
possesses eight flavors in full measure.
Dàbān Nièpán is also like this:
it possesses eight flavors in full measure.
What are the eight?
First is Permanence (Cháng),
second is Constancy (Héng),
third is Peace (Ān),
fourth is Cooling (Qīngliáng),
fifth is Non-aging (Bùlǎo),
sixth is Deathless (Bùsǐ),
seventh is Stainless (Wúgòu),
eighth is Bliss (Kuàilè).
These constitute the eight flavors in full measure.
Because it possesses these eight flavors,
it is therefore named Dàbān Nièpán.
If the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas abide therein,
they are further capable of manifesting Nièpán everywhere.
Therefore, it is named Dàbān Nièpán.”
“Kàshè,
good men
and good women,
if they wish to attain Nièpán through this Dàbān Nièpán,
they should learn in this manner that the Tathāgata is Permanent (Cháng Zhù),
and the Dharma and Sangha are also thus.”
Kàshè Púsà again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Extremely marvelous,
World-Honored One!
The merits of the Tathāgata are inconceivable;
the Dharma and Sangha are also inconceivable;
this Dà Nièpán is also inconceivable.
If there is one who cultivates and studies this classic Sūtra,
he attains the gate of the Right Dharma
and can become a good physician.
If one has not studied it,
one should know that this person
is blind, lacking the eye of wisdom,
covered by ignorance.”
The Buddha again addressed Kàshè:
“Good man!
Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas, in differentiating and elucidating Dàbān Nièpán,
have four aspects of meaning.
What are these four?
First is Self-Rectification (Zì Zhèng),
second is Rectifying Others (Zhèng Tā),
third is Being Able to Follow Questions and Answer (Néng Suí Wèndá),
fourth is Good Understanding of the Meaning of Causes and Conditions (Shàn Jiě Yīnyuán Yì).
What is Self-Rectification?
If the Buddha Tathāgata,
seeing all causes and conditions, has preached something,
for example, a Bhikkhu seeing a great fire pit
then says this:
'I would rather embrace this blazing fire pit
than dare to slander the twelve-division Sūtras and secret treasuries spoken by the Tathāgata,
saying they are spoken by Bōxún (Māra),
or saying that the Tathāgata,
the Dharma,
and the Sangha are Impermanent (Wú Cháng).
One who speaks in this manner
is deceiving and cheating himself,
and also cheating others.
I would rather use a sharp knife
to cut out my own tongue
than ever say that
the Tathāgata,
the Dharma,
and the Sangha
are Impermanent.
If I hear others speak thus,
I also do not believe or accept it.
Towards those who speak this,
compassion should arise.
The Tathāgata,
the Dharma,
and the Sangha are inconceivable.
One should uphold it like this,
viewing one's own body as a fire pit.
This is named Self-Rectification.'
“What is Rectifying Others?
When the Buddha was preaching the Dharma,
a woman
who was nursing an infant
came to the Buddha's location,
paid obeisance at the Buddha's feet,
having something weighing on her mind,
she pondered to herself,
and then sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One knew, but deliberately asked:
“Out of love and affection, you have given the child too much Sū (ghee),
not knowing whether it can be digested or not?”
At that time, the woman immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Extremely marvelous,
World-Honored One!
You are well able to know what is in my heart.
I only wish the Tathāgata would teach me how much is appropriate.
World-Honored One!
I gave my child too much Sū this morning,
I fear he cannot digest it.
Might he suffer an early death?
I only wish the Tathāgata would explain this for me.”
The Buddha said:
“What your child has eaten
will immediately be digested
and increase his lifespan.”
When the woman heard this,
her heart greatly rejoiced,
and she spoke again, saying:
“The Tathāgata speaks truly,
therefore I am delighted.”
“The World-Honored One is like this.
In order to subdue and transform sentient beings,
He is well able to differentiate
and speak of digestion
and non-digestion.
He also speaks of all phenomena as having No Self (Wú Wǒ)
and being Impermanent (Wú Cháng).
If the Buddha World-Honored One were to first speak of Permanence (Cháng),
those who are to be transformed
would say that this Dharma is the same as that of external paths,
and would immediately abandon it.
He further addressed the woman:
"If the child grows up,
and is able to walk independently,
whatever food he eats,
whether easily digested or difficult to digest,
the *sū* (ghee) originally provided
will no longer be sufficient.
All my *Shēngwén* (Hearer) disciples
are also like this,
like your infant,
they cannot digest the Dharma of permanence (the enduring Dharma).
Therefore, I first taught suffering (*kǔ*),
and impermanence (*wúcháng*).
If my *Shēngwén* disciples and others,
have fully prepared their merit (*gōngdé*),
and are suitable to cultivate the Mahāyāna Sūtras (Great Vehicle scriptures),
in this Sūtra,
I teach them the six flavors.
What are the six flavors?
Teaching suffering (*kǔ*) as the sour flavor,
impermanence (*wúcháng*) as the salty flavor,
non-self (*wúwǒ*) as the bitter flavor,
bliss (*lè*) as the sweet flavor,
self (*wǒ*) as the pungent flavor,
and permanence (*cháng*) as the bland flavor.
In that worldly realm, there are three flavors,
namely, impermanence (*wúcháng*),
non-self (*wúwǒ*),
and non-bliss (*wúlè*).
With defilements (*fánnǎo*) as firewood,
and wisdom (*zhìhuì*) as fire,
by these conditions, the meal of Nirvāṇa (*Nièpán*) is prepared,
which consists of permanence (*cháng*),
bliss (*lè*),
and self (*wǒ*),
causing all the disciples to savor it sweetly.
He further addressed the woman:
"If you have reason to go elsewhere,
you should drive out the wicked son,
making him leave the house,
and entrust all the treasures to the good son.
The woman reported to the Buddha (*Fó*):
"Indeed, just as the sacred teaching says,
the treasury of precious jewels should be shown to the good son,
and not shown to the wicked son."
"Elder Sister!
I am also like this:
when I enter Parinirvāṇa (*Bānnièpán*),
the subtle and supreme Dharma treasury of the Tathāgata (*Rúlái*)
is not given to the *Shēngwén* disciples and others,
just as your treasure is not shown to the wicked son;
instead, it must be entrusted and bequeathed to the *Púsà* (Bodhisattva) and others,
just as you carefully entrust your treasure to the good son.
Why is this?
The *Shēngwén* disciples give rise to the idea of change and difference,
believing that the Buddha (*Fó*) Tathāgata (*Rúlái*) truly passes into extinction (*mièdù*),
yet in truth, I do not pass into extinction.
Just as when you travel far and have not yet returned,
your wicked son immediately says you are dead,
but you are truly not dead.
The *Púsà* and others
say that the Tathāgata (*Rúlái*) is permanent (*cháng*),
and unchanging;
like your good son,
they do not say you are dead.
For this reason,
I entrust the supreme secret treasury to the *Púsà*.
"Good man,
if there are sentient beings
who believe the Buddha (*Fó*) is permanently abiding
and unchanging,
you should know that house
then has the Buddha (*Fó*),
and this is called 'the correct other.'
"Regarding 'those who can answer questions as they are posed':
If someone comes and asks the Buddha (*Fó*), the World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*):
'How can I avoid giving up wealth
yet be named a great patron (*dān yuè*) of generosity (*shī*)?'
The Buddha (*Fó*) said:
'If there are *Shāmén* (śramaṇas),
*Póluómén* (brahmins), and others,
who have few desires and are content,
who do not accept,
nor accumulate impure objects,
you should give such people slaves and maidservants,
and servants.
To those who practice pure conduct (*Fànxíng*),
give women.
To those who abstain from wine and meat,
give wine and meat.
To those who do not eat past midday,
give food past midday.
To those who do not wear flowers or incense,
give flowers and incense.
He who gives in this manner,
his name for generosity will spread,
reaching other lands,
and the expenditure of wealth will not be lost by a hair's breadth.
This is then called 'being able to answer questions as they are posed.'"
At that time, *Jiāyè Púsà* (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva) reported to the Buddha (*Fó*), saying:
"World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*)!
Meat should not be given to those who eat meat.
Why is this?
I see that those who do not eat meat
possess great merit (*gōngdé*)."
The Buddha (*Fó*) praised *Jiāyè*:
"Excellent!
Excellent!
You are now able to understand my meaning well;
Dharma-protecting *Púsà* should be like this.
Good man!
Starting from today,
I do not permit *Shēngwén* disciples to eat meat.
When receiving faith-based offerings (*shī*) from patrons (*dānyuè*),
they should regard that food as if it were the flesh of their own child.
*Jiāyè Púsà* reported again to the Buddha (*Fó*), saying:
"World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*)!
Why does the Tathāgata (*Rúlái*) prohibit the eating of meat?"
"Good man!
Those who eat meat
sever the seed of great compassion (*dàcí*)."
*Jiāyè* further said:
"Why did the Tathāgata (*Rúlái*)
previously permit *Bǐqiū* (bhikṣus) to eat the three kinds of pure meat?"
"*Jiāyè*!
These three kinds of pure meat
were gradually regulated depending on the circumstance."
*Jiāyè Púsà* reported again to the Buddha (*Fó*), saying:
"World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*)!
For what reason
are the ten kinds of impure (meat), and even the nine kinds of pure (meat), now prohibited?"
The Buddha (*Fó*) informed *Jiāyè*:
"They were also regulated gradually due to circumstances;
you should know that this immediately means the current prohibition of meat."
*Jiāyè Púsà* reported again to the Buddha (*Fó*), saying:
"Why did the Tathāgata (*Rúlái*) praise fish and meat as delicious food?"
"Good man!
I did not say that fish and meat and such things are delicious food,
I said sugarcane,
polished rice,
rock candy (crystal sugar),
all grains and wheat, and black rock candy,
curdled milk (*rǔlào*),
and butter (*sūyóu*),
constitute delicious food.
Although I spoke of allowing the accumulation of various kinds of clothing,
what should be accumulated must be garments of stained color (somber/patchwork colors);
how much more should one avoid craving the flavor of fish and meat?
*Jiāyè* further said:
"If the Tathāgata (*Rúlái*) prohibits the eating of meat,
then the five flavors—
curdled milk (*rǔlào*),
buttermilk (*làojiāng*),
raw ghee (*shēngsū*),
refined ghee (*shúsū*),
sesame oil and the like—
as well as various garments,
*Jiāshēyē* silk clothing,
cowrie shells (*kēbèi*),
leather,
and gold and silver bowls and vessels,
such items also should not be accepted."
"Good man!
You should not adopt the views of those *Nígān* (Nirgranthas).
All the precepts and prohibitions established by the Tathāgata (*Rúlái*)
each have a different purpose (intention).
Due to a different purpose,
I permitted the eating of the three kinds of pure meat.
Due to a different concept,
I prohibited the ten kinds of meat.
Due to a different concept,
all meat is entirely prohibited,
including that which died naturally.
*Jiāyè*!
From today forward, I decree to all disciples
that they shall no longer eat any kind of meat.
*Jiāyè*!
As for those who eat meat,
whether walking,
abiding,
sitting,
or lying down,
all sentient beings, upon smelling the scent of their meat,
will all give rise to terror.
This is comparable to someone who has been near a lion (*shīzǐ*);
when others see him,
and smell the lion’s odor,
they also give rise to terror."
“Shànnánzǐ!
It is like a person eating garlic;
the foul odor is repulsive.
When others see him,
they smell the stench and leave.
Even those who see him from afar do not wish to look,
how much less approach him?
It is also like this for all those who eat meat.
All sentient beings, smelling the odor of the meat,
are entirely terrified,
generating the thought of fear and death.
Creatures that move in water, on land, or in the air, who possess life,
all abandon him and flee,
all saying, ‘This person
is our enemy.’
Therefore, a Púsa does not habitually eat meat.
To liberate sentient beings,
he may demonstrate eating meat,
but although he appears to eat it,
in reality, he does not eat it.
Shànnánzǐ!
If such a Púsa still does not eat pure food,
how much less would he eat meat?
Shànnánzǐ!
After my Nièpán,
for countless hundreds of years,
the Sages of the Four Paths will all again enter Nièpán.
After the extinction of the Proper Dharma (Zhèngfǎ),
during the period of the Semblance Dharma (Xiàngfǎ),
there will be Bhikṣus
who merely appear to maintain the Vinaya,
who seldom read or chant Sūtras,
who greedily crave food and drink to nourish their bodies.
The clothing covering their bodies will be coarse, crude, and ugly;
their appearance will be emaciated, lacking dignity and virtue.
They will raise cattle and sheep, and carry firewood and grass.
The hair on their heads, their beards, and their fingernails will all be long and sharp.
Though they wear the kāṣāya, they will resemble hunters,
looking closely and walking slowly, like a cat stalking a mouse.
They constantly proclaim this saying:
‘I have attained Luóhàn (Arhatship).’
They suffer many sicknesses and pains,
and sleep and lie among filth and ordure.
Outwardly, they appear worthy and good,
but inwardly, they harbor greed and jealousy,
like Brāhmaṇas who observe the silent vow (yǎfǎ Pólúomén).
They are truly not Śrāmaṇas, yet they display the appearance of Śrāmaṇas.
Wrong views proliferate intensely,
and they slander the Proper Dharma.
Such people
will destroy the precepts and rules established by the Tathāgata,
the dignified manner of proper conduct,
the teaching of the fruit of liberation,
and the practice of detachment from defiled dharmas,
and they will destroy the exceedingly profound and secret teachings.
Each will follow his own wishes, misinterpreting the Sūtras and Vinaya,
and making this assertion:
‘The Tathāgata permits us all to eat meat.’
They generate this argument themselves,
claiming it was spoken by the Buddha.
They mutually dispute and quarrel,
each claiming to be a Śrāmaṇa, a son of Śākyamuni (Shì Zǐ).
Shànnánzǐ!
At that time, there will also be Śrāmaṇas
who store up raw grain,
accept fish and meat,
cook food themselves,
hold oil bottles,
precious parasols,
and leather sandals.
They will associate closely with kings,
ministers, and elders (Zhǎngzhě).
They will practice divination based on heavenly bodies,
diligently study the medical path,
keep male and female servants,
gold and silver,
lapis lazuli (Liúlí),
Tridacna shells (Chēqú),
agate (Mǎnǎo),
crystal (Pōlí),
pearls (Zhēnzhū),
coral (Shānhú),
amber (Hǔpò),
bi-discs of jade (Bìyù),
and cowrie shells (Kēbèi),
and various fruits and melons.
They will study various crafts and arts:
painting and masonry,
writing books and teaching,
planting roots and sprouts,
sorcery (gǔdào), chanting incantations, and illusions (zhòu huàn),
compounding various medicines,
performing songs, dances, and music,
treating the body with fragrant flowers,
playing games like pitch-pot (chūpú) and Wéiqí (Go),
and studying various skilled trades.
If there is a Bhikṣu
who is able to abandon these evil activities,
then that person should be called my true disciple.”
At that time, Kāyè again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Shìzūn!
The Bhikṣus,
Bhikṣuṇīs,
Upāsakas,
and Upāsikās
live dependent upon others.
If, while begging for food,
they receive food mixed with meat,
how should they eat it in accordance with the pure Dharma?”
The Buddha said:
“Kāyè!
They should wash it with water,
causing it to be separated from the meat,
and only then eat it.
If their eating vessel
is stained by the meat,
as long as there is no taste remaining,
it is permitted to use it without transgression.
If they see that there is much meat in the food,
then they should not accept it.
All meat that is visible (present),
should not be eaten at all.
Those who eat it incur transgression.
I now proclaim this restriction on cutting off (eating) meat.
If I were to speak extensively on this,
it would be inexhaustible.
The time for Nièpán has arrived,
and thus I speak briefly.
This is what is called answering according to the question.”
"Kāshè!
How is the meaning of dependent arising (yīnyuán yì) well understood?
If the assembly of the Four Groups (sì bù zhī zhòng) comes and asks me, saying:
'Shìzūn! (World-Honored One!)
Regarding meanings such as these,
when the Rúlái first appeared,
why did he not preach to King Bōsīnì (Prasenajit),
teaching the profound and subtle meaning of this Dharma gate?
Sometimes you preach the profound,
sometimes you preach the shallow,
sometimes named as transgression,
or named as non-transgression?
What is named 'fall' (duò)?
What is named 'discipline' (lǜ)?
What is named the meaning of Bōluótímùchā (Pratimokṣa)?'
The Buddha said:
'Bōluótímùchā
is named 'contentment' (zhī zú);
perfecting demeanor,
not receiving or accumulating anything,
and is also named 'pure livelihood' (jìng mìng).
'Fall' (duò) is named the Four Evil Destinies (sì è qù).
Furthermore, 'fall'
is falling into the Hells (dìyù), down to Ābí (Avīci);
discussing its speed,
it surpasses a torrential rainstorm.
Those who hear it are alarmed and terrified,
firmly upholding the restrictive precepts,
not violating proper demeanor,
cultivating contentment,
and not accepting any impure things.
Furthermore, 'fall'
sustains and increases the Hells,
the Animal Realm (chùshēng),
and the Realm of Hungry Ghosts (ègui).
Based on these various meanings,
it is thus called 'fall' (duò).
Bōluótímùchā
is separation from physical,
verbal,
and mental unwholesome wrong karma.
Lǜ (Discipline/Vinaya)
involves entering the precepts and proper demeanor,
the profound meanings of the Sūtras,
prohibiting the acceptance of all impure things and impure circumstances,
and also prohibiting the Four Cardinal Offenses (sì zhòng),
the Thirteen Saṅghāvaśeṣa (shísān sēng cán),
the Two Aniyata Dharmas (èr bùdìng fǎ),
the Thirty Niḥsargika Prāyaścittika (sānshí shě duò),
the Ninety-One Prāyaścittika (jiǔshíyī duò),
the Four Pratideśanīya Dharmas (sì huǐ guò fǎ),
the Numerous Śaikṣa Dharmas (zhòngduō xuéfǎ),
and the Seven Adhikaraṇaśamatha (qī miè zhēng), and so forth.
Furthermore, there are people who completely destroy all the precepts.
What is meant by 'all'?
It refers to the Four Cardinal Offenses up to the Seven Adhikaraṇaśamatha Dharmas.
Furthermore, there are people who slander the true Dharma and the extremely profound scriptures,
and the Icchantika (yīchǎntí).
They perfectly accomplish the cessation of all characteristics without any cause or condition.
Such people,
declare themselves to be clever and sharp-witted;
they entirely conceal minor and major offenses,
concealing all their evil deeds like a tortoise hiding its six limbs.
Such numerous offenses,
they do not repent throughout the long night (of saṃsāra).
Because they do not repent,
they increase day and night.
These Bhikkhus,
the numerous offenses they commit,
they never reveal.
This causes the offenses they commit
to proliferate further.
Therefore, the Rúlái, knowing these matters,
established the rules gradually,
not all at once.'
At that time, there was a virtuous man (shàn nánzǐ)
and a virtuous woman (shàn nǚrén) who said to the Buddha:
'Shìzūn,
the Rúlái has long known of such matters;
why did you not establish the rules beforehand?
Is it possible that the Shìzūn wishes living beings to enter the Ābí Hell?
For example, when many people,
wanting to travel to another region,
lose the correct path,
and follow wrong ways.
These people, because they do not realize they are lost,
all assume it is the right path,
and furthermore see no one they can ask whether the path is right or wrong.
Living beings are likewise confused in the Buddha Dharma,
and cannot see the genuine truth.
The Rúlái should first preach the right path for them,
commanding the Bhikkhus,
'This is a transgression of the precepts,
this is maintaining the precepts.'
You should establish the rules in this manner.
Why?
Because the Rúlái, the Perfectly Enlightened One (zhèng jué), is the one who is truly real,
knows and sees the right path.
Only the Rúlái, the God above Gods (tiān zhōng zhī tiān),
is able to preach the increasing merits of the Ten Wholesome Deeds (shí shàn) and their deep meaning.
Therefore, we implore you: you should have established the precepts first.'
The Buddha said:
'Shàn nánzǐ,
if it is said that the Rúlái is able to proclaim the increasing merits of the Ten Wholesome Deeds for living beings,
then the Rúlái regards all living beings as Rōuhóuluó (Rāhula).
How can you question me, saying, 'Is it possible that the Shìzūn wishes living beings to enter the Hells?'
I see one person who has the causes and conditions for falling into the Ābí Hell,
and yet I would remain in the world for the sake of this person,
for one kalpa or slightly less than one kalpa.
I possess great compassion (dà cíbēi) for living beings.
For what reason would I deceive those whom I regard as my children,
causing them to enter the Hells?
Shàn nánzǐ!
Just as within a king's domain,
when someone wearing an inner garment
sees a hole in the garment, only then does he patch it.
The Rúlái is also like this:
seeing that living beings
have the causes and conditions for entering the Ābí Hell,
he immediately patches it up with the wholesome deeds of the precepts.
Shàn nánzǐ!
Just as a Wheel-Turning Holy King (zhuǎnlún shèng wáng)
first preaches the Ten Wholesome Dharmas to living beings,
but subsequently, gradually, there are those who perform evil deeds,
the king then gradually stops (or punishes) them according to the matter;
having stopped all evil deeds,
he then personally practices the Dharma of the Holy King.
Shàn nánzǐ!
I am also like this:
although I have preached,
I cannot establish the rules beforehand.
It must be dependent upon the Bhikkhus gradually engaging in unwholesome deeds,
and only then are the rules established according to the matter.
Living beings who delight in the Dharma,
who cultivate according to the teaching—
such assemblies—
are then able to perceive the Rúlái's Dharma Body (fǎ shēn).
Just as the Wheel-Turning King's
possession of the wheel treasure (lún bǎo) is inconceivable,
the Rúlái is also inconceivable,
the two treasures, Dharma and Saṅgha, are also inconceivable,
and both those who are able to preach the Dharma and those who hear the Dharma are inconceivable.
This is called the 'well-understanding of the meaning of dependent arising' (shàn jiě yīnyuán yì);
when a Púsà (Bodhisattva) thus distinguishes and reveals the meaning of these four characteristics,
this is named the meaning of dependent arising (yīnyuán yì) within the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa (Dàshèng Dà Nièpán).
"Furthermore, 'self-rectification' (zì zhèng)
is defined as attaining this Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Bān Nièpán).
'Rectifying others' (zhèng tā) means:
I teach the Bhikkhus, saying,
'The Rúlái exists eternally and is unchangeable.'
'Answering according to the question' (suí wèn dá zhě),
Kāshè!
Because of the question you asked,
I am able to widely preach this extremely profound and subtle doctrinal truth
for the Púsà Móhēsà (Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas),
Bhikkhus,
Bhikkhuṇīs (bǐqiūní),
Upāsakas (yōupósè),
and Upāsikās (yōupóyí).
Regarding the meaning of dependent arising (yīnyuán yì):
the Śrāvakā (shēngwén)
and Pratyekabuddhas (yuánjué) do not comprehend such extremely profound meaning.
They do not hear that the three dots of the letter 'I' (yī zì sān diǎn) constitute liberation (jiětuō),
Nirvāṇa,
and Mahāprajñā (Móhē Bōrě), forming the secret storehouse.
I now, in this place,
expound and distinguish these meanings,
in order to develop the wisdom eye
of the Śrāvakā.
Suppose there is a person who speaks thus:
'How are these four matters
considered one?
Is this not illusory (xū wàng)?'
One should immediately question in return:
'Is it that empty space is non-existent,
unmoving, and unimpeded?
What difference is there between these four matters,
so that they might be called illusory?'
'No,
Shìzūn!
These various phrases are immediately one meaning,
namely, the meaning of Emptiness (kōng yì).'
Self-rectification (zì zhèng),
rectifying others (zhèng tā),
being able to answer according to the question (suí wèn dá),
and understanding the meaning of dependent arising (jiě yīnyuán yì)—
are also like this;
they are identical to Dà Nièpán and are without difference.
The Buddha told Jiāshè:
“If there are good men,
or good women who speak thus:
‘The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is impermanent.
How should we know that this is impermanent?
As the Buddha has said:
“The extinction of all afflictions (fánnǎo) is called Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
just like a fire going out,
there being utterly nothing left.
The extinction of all afflictions
is also like this,
therefore it is called Nirvāṇa.”
How can the Tathāgata be an eternally abiding Dharma (fǎ),
not subject to change?
As the Buddha says:
“Leaving all existence (yǒu)
is then called Nirvāṇa;
in this Nirvāṇa,
there is no existence.”
How can the Tathāgata be an eternally abiding Dharma,
not subject to change?
“Just as a worn-out garment,
is not called an object [of value],
Nirvāṇa is also like this;
the extinction of all afflictions is not called an object [of value].”
How can the Tathāgata be an eternally abiding Dharma,
not subject to change?
As the Buddha says:
“Leaving desire and attaining tranquil extinction (jìmie),
is called Nirvāṇa.
Just as a person whose head is severed
then has no head;
leaving desire and attaining tranquil extinction
is also like this,
empty and without anything existing,
therefore it is called Nirvāṇa.”
How can the Tathāgata be an eternally abiding Dharma,
not subject to change?’
As the Buddha says:
“ ‘How can the Tathāgata be an eternally abiding Dharma, not subject to change?
Jiāshè!
If there is someone who raises such a difficulty,
it is called a perverse difficulty.
Jiāshè!
You also should not hold this thought,
that the nature of the Tathāgata is utterly extinguished.
Jiāshè!
That which extinguishes afflictions,
is not called an object.
Why is this?
Because it is eternally ultimate;
therefore it is called permanent (cháng).
This phrase [or state] is tranquil and quiet,
and has nothing superior.
It extinguishes all characteristics,
leaving nothing behind;
this phrase is pure and bright,
eternally abiding and irreversible.
Therefore Nirvāṇa
is called eternal abiding.
The Tathāgata is also like this,
eternally abiding and unchanging.
The saying 'falling stars'
refers to afflictions.
The saying 'scattered, they immediately extinguish, their location unknown'
means that when the afflictions of the Tathāgata are extinguished,
he is not located in the five destinies.
Therefore the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma,
without change or alteration.
Furthermore, Jiāshè!
What all Buddhas take as their teacher,
is the Dharma.
Therefore the Tathāgata reveres and makes offerings;
because the Dharma is permanent,
the Buddhas are also permanent.”
The Bodhisattva Jiāshè again said to the Buddha:
“If the fire of afflictions is extinguished,
the Tathāgata is also extinguished.
In that case, the Tathāgata
has no permanent dwelling place.
It is like when molten iron spurts out,
once the red color is extinguished,
its destination is unknown.
The afflictions of the Tathāgata
are also like this—
extinguished and without destination.
And like that iron,
whose heat and red color
disappear when extinguished.
The Tathāgata is also like this;
when extinguished, he is impermanent.
When the fire of afflictions is extinguished,
he then enters Nirvāṇa.
It should be known that the Tathāgata is therefore impermanent.”
“Good man!
That which is called ‘iron’
refers to all ordinary beings (fánfū).
Ordinary people,
even if they extinguish afflictions,
after extinction, they arise again;
therefore they are called impermanent.
The Tathāgata is not like this;
having extinguished, he does not arise again;
therefore he is called permanent.”
Jiāshè replied again:
“Just as when the red color of iron is extinguished,
if it is placed back in the fire, the red color arises again.
If the Tathāgata is like this,
he should develop renewed fetters (jié).
If fetters arise again,
then he is impermanent.”
The Buddha said:
“Jiāshè!
You should not now say such a thing—that the Tathāgata is impermanent.
Why is this?
The Tathāgata is permanent.
Good man!
It is like burning wood;
when extinguished, there is ash.
When afflictions are extinguished,
there is Nirvāṇa.
The similes of the ruined garment,
the severed head,
the broken jar, and so on,
are also like this.
Objects such as these,
each have their own names,
being called ‘ruined garment,’
‘severed head,’
and ‘broken jar.’
Jiāshè!
When iron has cooled,
it can be made hot again.
The Tathāgata is not like this;
having severed afflictions,
he is ultimately cooled and tranquil.
The blazing fire of afflictions
will never arise again.
Jiāshè!
You should know that immeasurable sentient beings are like that iron.
I use the blazing fire of stainless wisdom
to burn the fetters of affliction of those sentient beings.”
Jiāshè replied again:
“Excellent,
excellent!
I now clearly know what the Tathāgata has said:
The Buddhas are permanent.”
The Buddha said:
“Jiāshè!
For example, a Sage King (Shèngwáng) normally stays in the rear palace,
or sometimes wanders in the rear garden for viewing.
Although the King is not among the court ladies,
it cannot be said that the Sage King has died.
Good man!
The Tathāgata is also like this;
although he does not appear in the continent of Yánfú Tí,
having entered Nirvāṇa,
he is not called impermanent.
The Tathāgata departed from immeasurable afflictions,
entered the blissful realm of Nirvāṇa,
wanders among the flowers of awakening,
and enjoys happiness and pleasure.”
Jiāshè asked again:
“As the Buddha says,
‘I have long ago crossed the great ocean of afflictions.’
If the Buddha has already crossed the ocean of afflictions,
for what reason did he again, together with Yēshūtuóluó,
give birth to Luóhóuluó?
Based on this cause and condition,
it must be known that the Tathāgata has not yet crossed the great ocean of afflictions and fetters.
I only wish that the Tathāgata would explain the reason for this.”
The Buddha told Kāshyè:
“You should not say,
‘The Tathāgata long ago crossed the great ocean of afflictions (kleshá).
For what reason did he then join with Yēshūtuóluó to give birth to Luóhóuluó?’
Due to this causality,
you should know that the Tathāgata has not yet crossed the great ocean of afflictions and all bonds (saṃyojanā).
Good man!
This Great Nirvāṇa is able to establish great meaning.
You should now listen with sincere hearts
and broadly speak of it to others.
Do not give rise to astonishment or doubt.
If there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abiding in the Great Nirvāṇa,
the Sūmí Mountain King, being so high and vast,
he is entirely able to make it enter a grain of tǐnglì seed husks.
The sentient beings who rely on Sūmí
are neither pressed nor confined,
and have no thought of coming or going;
they are not different from how they originally were.
Only those who are to be saved
see this Bodhisattva putting Sūmí Mountain into the tǐnglì husk,
and then bringing it back to rest in its original dwelling place.
Good man!
Furthermore, there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abiding in the Great Nirvāṇa
who can place the three thousand great-thousand world system (sāhà) into a tǐnglì husk.
The sentient beings within it
are also without pressure or confinement, or the thought of coming or going;
they are not different from how they originally were.
Only those who are to be saved
see this Bodhisattva placing this three thousand great-thousand world system into a tǐnglì husk,
and then bringing it back to rest in its original dwelling place.
Good man!
Furthermore, there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abiding in the Great Nirvāṇa
who can put the three thousand great-thousand world system inside a single hair pore,
and even returning it to its original place is also like this.
Good man!
Furthermore, there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abiding in the Great Nirvāṇa
who cuts off and takes the worlds of all Buddhas in the ten directions and the three thousand great-thousand systems,
places them upon a needle point,
like threading a jujube leaf,
and throws them into another Buddha’s world in a different direction.
All the sentient beings within them
do not perceive whether they are coming or going, or where they are situated.
Only those who are to be saved can see it,
and returning them to their original place is also like this.
Good man!
Furthermore, there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abiding in the Great Nirvāṇa
who cuts off and takes the worlds of all Buddhas in the ten directions and the three thousand great-thousand systems,
places them on his right palm like a potter’s wheel,
and throws them into a dust-mote world in a different direction.
Not a single sentient being has the thought of coming or going.
Only those who are to be saved can see it,
and returning them to their original place is also like this.
Good man!
Furthermore, there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abiding in the Great Nirvāṇa
who cuts off and takes all the immeasurable worlds of all Buddhas in the ten directions
and entirely places them within his own body.
The sentient beings within them are entirely without pressure or confinement,
and are also without the thought of coming or going, or of dwelling place.
Only those who are to be saved can see it,
and returning them to their original place is also like this.
Good man!
Furthermore, there is a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abiding in the Great Nirvāṇa
who puts the worlds of the ten directions within a single dust mote.
The sentient beings within them are also without the thought of pressure, confinement, or coming and going.
Only those who are to be saved can see it,
and returning them to their original place is also like this.
Good man,
this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, abiding in the Great Nirvāṇa,
is thus able to manifest various immeasurable spiritual powers and transformations.
Therefore, it is called the Great Pārinirvāṇa.
The immeasurable spiritual powers and transformations that this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva can manifest
cannot be measured by any sentient being.
How can you now know
that the Tathāgata practiced closeness to lust
to give birth to Luóhóuluó?”
"Good man!
I have long dwelt in this great Nièpán,
manifesting various supernatural transformations,
within these three thousand great thousand worlds (Sānqiān Dàqiān Shìjiè), a billion suns and moons,
and a billion Yánfú Tí, showing various manifestations,
as is extensively taught in the *Shǒuléngyán Jīng*.
In the Sānqiān Dàqiān Shìjiè, or in Yánfú Tí, I manifest Nièpán,
yet I do not ultimately enter into Nièpán.
Or, in Yánfú Tí, I manifest entering a mother’s womb,
causing the parents
to conceive the thought that I am their son;
but this body of mine
is ultimately not born through the union and harmony of sexual desire.
I have long, since immeasurable kalpas (jié), been separated from sexual desire.
This body of mine now
is the Dhármakāya (Fǎshēn),
yet conforming to the world,
I manifest entering the womb.
Good man!
Here in Yánfú Tí, in Línwēiní Yuán,
I manifest being born from my mother Móyē;
having been born, I was immediately able to walk seven steps to the east,
proclaiming these words:
'Among humans,
deities (tiān),
and Āxiūluó,
I am the most honored and supreme.'
Parents,
humans,
and deities, having seen this, were startled and delighted,
generating a sense of rarity and wonder.
Yet, these people said I was an infant.
However, this body of mine,
since immeasurable kalpas,
has long been separated from this phenomenon (of infancy).
The body of the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is the Dhármakāya,
not formed by flesh and blood,
sinews and veins,
or bones and marrow.
Because I conform to the doctrines of sentient beings in the world,
I manifest as an infant.
Walking seven steps to the south,
I manifest the intention to act as the supreme field of merit (Fútián) for immeasurable sentient beings.
Walking seven steps to the west,
I manifest the exhaustion of birth,
forever severing aging and death,
this is the last body.
Walking seven steps to the north,
I manifest having already crossed over all realms of existence and rebirth (shēngsǐ).
Walking seven steps to the east,
I manifest acting as the leader and guide for sentient beings.
Seven steps in the four intermediate directions,
I manifest the cessation and extinguishing of various afflictions (fánnǎo),
and the lineage/seeds of the Four Māras (Sì Mó),
achieving the state of Tathāgata,
Arhat (Yìng),
Samyaksaṃbuddha (Zhèngbiànzhī).
Walking seven steps upward,
I manifest not being defiled by impure things,
just like empty space.
Walking seven steps downward,
I manifest the Dharma rain (Fǎ Yǔ),
extinguishing the fires of the hells (Dìyù),
causing those sentient beings
to receive peaceful and hidden happiness,
and for those who destroy the prohibitions and precepts, manifesting as frost and hail.
Having been born in Yánfú Tí for seven days,
I again manifested shaving my hair.
All people say I am an infant
who is initially having his head shaved.
All humans,
deities,
Māra Pāpīyas (Mówáng Bōxún),
Śramaṇas (Shāmén),
and Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén),
none are able to see the top-knot characteristic (dǐngxiàng) of my head;
much less could someone approach with a knife to shave my hair.
If someone were to hold a knife to my head,
it would be impossible.
I have long since, throughout immeasurable kalpas,
shaved off my beard and hair.
In order to conform to the doctrines of the world,
I manifest the shaving of hair.
After I was born,
my parents took me and entered the temple of the gods (tiān cí),
presenting me to Máxīshǒuluó (Maheśvara).
When Máxīshǒuluó saw me,
he joined his palms in reverence and stood aside.
I have long since, throughout immeasurable kalpas,
abandoned the practice of entering temples of the gods like this.
In order to conform to the doctrines of the world,
I manifest in this way.
In Yánfú Tí, I manifest having my ears pierced.
In reality, none of the sentient beings are capable of piercing my ears.
Because I conform to the doctrines of sentient beings in the world,
I manifest in this way.
Furthermore, I use various treasures to create lion ear pendants,
with which to adorn my ears;
however, I have long since, throughout immeasurable kalpas,
abandoned adornments.
In order to conform to the doctrines of the world,
I manifest this.
I manifest entering a school,
and studying writing and documentation;
however, I have long since, throughout immeasurable kalpas,
achieved full accomplishment.
Surveying all sentient beings in the Three Realms (Sān Jiè),
there is none suitable to be my teacher.
In order to conform to the doctrines of the world,
I manifest entering a school.
Thus I am called Tathāgata,
Arhat,
Samyaksaṃbuddha.
I learn to ride elephants,
break horses,
compete in strength, and various other skills (jìyì);
this is also the case.
In Yánfú Tí, I again manifest as the Crown Prince (Wáng Tàizǐ),
and all sentient beings see me as the Prince,
indulging in pleasure and receiving happiness among the Five Desires (Wǔ Yù);
however, I have long since, throughout immeasurable kalpas,
abandoned such pleasures of the Five Desires.
In order to conform to the doctrines of the world,
I manifest this appearance.
The physiognomists predicted that if I did not renounce home life (chūjiā),
I would become a Cakravartin (Zhuǎnlún Shèng Wáng),
ruling over Yánfú Tí,
and all sentient beings believed this saying;
however, I have long since, throughout immeasurable kalpas,
abandoned the throne of a Cakravartin,
becoming a Dharma King (Fǎlún Wáng).
In Yánfú Tí, I manifest abandoning the pleasures of the Five Desires and the palace maidens,
and having seen old age, sickness, death, and a Śramaṇa,
I renounce home life and cultivate the path (xiūdào).
All sentient beings say that Prince Xīdá (Siddhārtha) is initially renouncing home life;
however, I have long since, throughout immeasurable kalpas,
renounced home life and studied the path.
Therefore, conforming to worldly doctrines,
I manifest in this way.
In Yánfú Tí, I manifest renouncing home life,
receiving the full precepts (jùzú jiè),
diligently cultivating the path,
obtaining the fruition of Srotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán Guǒ),
the fruition of Sakṛdāgāmin (Sītuóhán Guǒ),
the fruition of Anāgāmin (Ānàhán Guǒ),
and the fruition of Arhat (Āluóhàn Guǒ).
Everyone says that this fruition of Arhat is easily obtained and not difficult;
however, I have already achieved the fruition of Arhat throughout immeasurable kalpas.
In order to save and liberate sentient beings,
I sit in the place of enlightenment (Dàochǎng) beneath the Bodhi tree (Pútí Shù),
using grass as a cushion,
crushing and subduing the hosts of Māras.
Everyone says that I
am only now, at the place of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, subduing the retinues of Māra (Mó Guān);
however, I have long since subdued them throughout immeasurable kalpas.
In order to subdue those stubborn and difficult sentient beings,
I therefore manifest this transformation.
I also manifest passing large and small waste (defecation and urination),
exhaling and inhaling breaths.
Everyone says that I have large and small waste,
and exhaling and inhaling breaths;
however, the karmic reward (guǒbào) attained by this body of mine
is entirely without such large and small waste,
or in-and-out breaths, and so forth.
Conforming to the world, I manifest in this way.
I also manifest receiving charitable offerings (xìn shī) from people;
however, this body of mine is entirely without hunger or thirst.
Conforming to worldly doctrines,
I therefore manifest in this way.
I also manifest having sleep, in order to appear the same as all sentient beings;
manifesting having sleep;
however, I have long since, throughout immeasurable kalpas,
possessed complete, unsurpassed, profound, and subtle wisdom.
I am far removed from the Three Existences (Sān Yǒu),
in my advancing, stopping, and dignified deportment.
Headaches,
stomach aches,
back aches,
splinters (mù qiāng),
washing the feet,
washing the hands,
washing the face,
rinsing the mouth, chewing willow branches, and so forth—
everyone says that I have such things;
however, this body of mine is entirely without these things.
My feet are pure, like lotus flowers.
My breath is pure and clean, like the fragrance of the Utpala (Yōubōluó) flower.
All sentient beings say that I am human,
but I am truly not human.
I also manifest receiving rags taken from a dust heap (fèn sǎo yī),
washing, cleaning, sewing, and beating them;
however, I have long since had no need for such clothing.
Everyone says that Luóhóuluó (Rāhula) is my son,
that King Shūtóután (Śuddhodana) is my father,
and that Lady Móyē (Māyā) is my mother,
dwelling in the world and receiving all kinds of pleasure,
and then, separated from such matters, renouncing home life and studying the path.
People further say:
'This Crown Prince of the great clan Gautama (Qútán Dà Xìng),
abandoned worldly pleasures,
seek transcendent *dharmas*.
However, I have long been separated from worldly sexual desires,
and all such matters
are entirely manifestations.
All sentient beings universally say that this is a person,
but I am truly not.
"Good man!
Although I am in this Yánfútí,
repeatedly manifesting entering Nièpán,
I truly do not ultimately enter Nièpán.
Yet all sentient beings all say that the Rúlái is truly extinguished,
but the nature of the Rúlái is truly not eternally extinguished.
Therefore, you should know that this is the permanent *dharma* (Chángzhùfǎ),
the unchangeable *dharma* (Bùbiànyìfǎ).
Good man!
Dà Nièpán
is precisely the realm (Fǎjiè) of all Buddhas and Rúláis.
I also manifest emerging into the world in Yánfútí;
sentient beings all say that I have just attained Buddhahood;
but I have already completed what was to be done over immeasurable *kalpas*.
In accordance with worldly *dharma*,
I again manifest in Yánfútí by initially emerging and attaining Buddhahood.
I also manifest in Yánfútí by not upholding the precepts
and violating the four major offenses.
Everyone sees this and says I truly committed them;
but I have already, over immeasurable *kalpas*,
firmly maintained the precepts without leakage or defect.
I also manifest in Yánfútí as an Yīchǎntí (icchantika).
Everyone sees this and considers me an Yīchǎntí;
but I am truly not an Yīchǎntí.
How could an Yīchǎntí possibly attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi)?
I also manifest in Yánfútí by breaking the harmony of the Sangha.
Sentient beings all say that I am a breaker of the Sangha;
when I observe humans and *devas*,
there is no one who can break the harmony of the Sangha.
I also manifest in Yánfútí by protecting and upholding the orthodox *Dharma*.
Everyone says that I am a protector of the *Dharma*
and are all astonished and surprised;
this is the nature of all Buddhas' *Dharma* (Fǎ'ěr),
and should not cause astonishment.
I also manifest in Yánfútí as Mó Bōxún.
Everyone says that I am Bōxún;
but I have long been separated from the affairs of Māra over immeasurable *kalpas*.
I am pure and untainted, like a lotus flower.
I also manifest in Yánfútí attaining Buddhahood in a female body.
Everyone says:
'How remarkable!
A woman is able to attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.'
The Rúlái ultimately does not receive a female body,
but in order to subdue immeasurable sentient beings, I manifest a female image.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings,
I again manifest various forms.
I also manifest in Yánfútí by being born into the four destinies (Qù);
but I have long severed the causes for rebirth in those destinies.
Although (people think) I fall into the four destinies due to the cause of *karma*,
I am born therein for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
I also manifest in Yánfútí
as the Fàntiān Wáng,
causing those who worship Brahmā
to abide in the orthodox *Dharma*.
However, I am truly not (Brahmā),
yet all sentient beings universally regard me as the true Brahmā Heaven.
Manifesting the image of a *deva*
throughout all the *deva* temples
is also like this.
I also manifest in Yánfútí by entering the house of a courtesan.
However, I truly have no thought of greedy desire or lust;
I am pure and undefiled, like a lotus flower.
For those sentient beings who crave lust and desire beauty,
I proclaim the subtle *Dharma* at the crossroads.
However, I truly have no mind of defiled desire,
yet people say that I protect women.
I also manifest in Yánfútí by entering the houses of the servants (Qīngyī Shě),
in order to instruct the maids to abide in the orthodox *Dharma*.
However, I truly have no such evil *karma*
that would cause me to fall into the status of a servant (Qīngyī).
I also manifest in Yánfútí as a scholar (Bóshì),
in order to teach the ignorant children
and cause them to abide in the orthodox *Dharma*.
I also manifest in Yánfútí
by entering places of wine gatherings
and gambling (Bóyì) places.
I manifest experiencing various contests of winning, losing, fighting, and arguing,
in order to rescue and deliver those sentient beings;
yet I truly have no such evil *karma*.
However, sentient beings all say that I perform such *karma*.
I also manifest residing long in burial grounds
and assuming the body of a great vulture (Dàjiùshēn),
delivering all flying birds.
Yet sentient beings all say that I am a real vulture body;
but I have long since departed from that *karma*.
In order to deliver those birds and vultures,
I manifest such a body.
I also manifest in Yánfútí as a great elder (Dà Zhǎngzhě),
in order to establish immeasurable sentient beings in the orthodox *Dharma*.
Moreover, I manifest as various kings, great ministers,
princes, and chief counselors.
Among these multitudes, I am foremost in each capacity,
and I reside in the royal position for the sake of cultivating the orthodox *Dharma*.
I also manifest in Yánfútí when the *kalpa* of plagues arises.
Many sentient beings are troubled by disease.
First, I dispense medicine,
and then I proclaim the subtle orthodox *Dharma* for them,
causing them to abide in unsurpassed Bódí;
everyone says that the plague *kalpa* has arisen.
Moreover, I manifest in Yánfútí when the *kalpa* of famine arises.
I supply food and drink according to their needs,
and then I proclaim the subtle orthodox *Dharma* for them,
causing them to abide in unsurpassed Bódí.
Moreover, I manifest in Yánfútí when the *kalpa* of warfare arises.
I immediately proclaim the *Dharma* for them, causing them to abandon enmity and harm,
enabling them to abide in unsurpassed Bódí.
Moreover, I manifest speaking of the concept of impermanence (Wúcháng Xiǎng) for those who hold the concept of permanence.
For those who hold the concept of pleasure, I speak of the concept of suffering.
For those who hold the concept of self, I speak of the concept of no-self (Wú Wǒ Xiǎng).
For those who hold the concept of purity, I speak of the concept of impurity.
If there are sentient beings attached to the Three Realms (Sān Jiè),
I immediately proclaim the *Dharma* for them,
causing them to depart from these places.
For the sake of delivering sentient beings,
I proclaim the unsurpassed, subtle *Dharma* medicine.
In order to sever the tree of all afflictions (Fánnǎo),
I plant the tree of unsurpassed *Dharma* medicine.
In order to rescue and deliver all external adherents (Wàidào),
I proclaim the orthodox *Dharma*.
Although I manifest as the teacher of sentient beings,
my mind fundamentally holds no concept of being a teacher of sentient beings.
In order to rescue and deliver the lowly and humble,
I manifest entering among them and proclaiming the *Dharma* for them.
It is not due to evil *karma* that I receive this body.
The Rúlái, the Rightly Enlightened One (Zhèngjué), thus abides in Dà Nièpán.
Therefore, this is called permanent residence (Chángzhù) without change.
Just as in Yánfútí,
Dōngfúyú Dài (Pūrvavideha),
Xīqúyéní (Aparagodānīya),
and Běiyùdānyuè (Uttarakuru) are also like this.
As with the Four Continents (Sì Tiānxià),
the Three Thousand Great Thousand Worlds (Sānqiān Dàqiān Shìjiè) are also the same.
The Twenty-five Forms of Existence (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu)
are widely explained in the *Shǒuléngyán Jīng* (Śūraṅgama Sūtra).
For this reason, it is called Dà Bōnièpán.
If there is a Bódhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) who abides in such Dà Bōnièpán,
they can manifest such spiritual powers (Shéntōng) and transformations without fear.
"Jiāyè!
Because of this reason,
you should not say that Luóhóuluó is the son of the Buddha.
Why is this?
I, in the past, over immeasurable *kalpas*, have already left the existence of desire.
Therefore, the Rúlái is called Chángzhù (Permanently Abiding),
without change or variation."
Jiāyè spoke again:
"How is the Rúlái called Chángzhù?
Just as the Buddha said:
'When a lamp is extinguished,
there is no location (where it went).
The Rúlái is also like this;
having entered extinction (Mièdù),
there is also no location.'"
The Buddha said to Jiāyè:
"Good man!
You should not speak in this way:
'When the lamp is completely extinguished,
there is no location (where it went).
The Rúlái is also like this;
having entered extinction,
there is no location.'
Good man!
For example, when a man or woman lights a lamp,
the lamp vessel, large or small, is full of oil.
As long as there is oil remaining,
its light persists.
If the oil is exhausted,
the light is extinguished along with it.
The extinguishing of the light
symbolizes the extinguishing of afflictions (Fánnǎo).
Although the light is completely extinguished,
the lamp vessel still remains.
The Rúlái is also like this:
although afflictions are extinguished,
the *Dharma*-body (Fǎshēn) permanently exists.
Good man!
What do you think?
Are the light and the lamp vessel extinguished simultaneously or not?"
Jiāyè answered:
"No.
Shìzūn!
Although they are not extinguished simultaneously,
the vessel is nevertheless impermanent (Wúcháng).
If the Fǎshēn is likened to the lamp vessel,
the lamp vessel is impermanent.
The Fǎshēn is also like this,
and should therefore be impermanent."
“Good man!
You should not now raise a difficulty like this.
Just as in the world we speak of a vessel (器, *qì*),
the Tathāgata, the Bhagavān, is the Supreme Dharma-vessel (*fǎqì*),
but the vessel is impermanent (*wúcháng*),
not the Tathāgata.
Among all phenomena (*fǎ*), Nirvāṇa is permanent (*cháng*).
Since the Tathāgata embodies this, he is called Permanent.
Furthermore, good man,
the phrase ‘the lamp is extinguished’
refers to the Nirvāṇa realized by the Arhat (*Luóhàn*),
because greed and attachment (*tān’ài*) are extinguished,
and all vexations (*fánnǎo*) are extinguished,
it is likened to the extinguishing of a lamp.
The Anāgāmin (*Ānàhán*)
is called ‘having greed’ (*yǒutān*),
and because he has greed,
it cannot be said that he is the same as the extinguishing of a lamp.
Therefore, in the past, I
spoke using concealed characteristics,
likening it to the extinguishing of a lamp,
but the Mahāparinirvāṇa (*Dànièpán*) is not the same as the extinguishing of a lamp.
The Anāgāmin is not one who comes repeatedly,
nor does he return to the twenty-five existences (*èrshíwǔ yǒu*).
He will not again receive a foul body (*chòushēn*),
a worm body (*chóngshēn*),
a food body (*shíshēn*),
or a poison body (*dúshēn*).
This is called the Anāgāmin (*Ānàhán*).
If he were to receive a body again, he would be called a Nāgāmin (*Nàhán*).
If he does not receive a body, he is called an Anāgāmin.
If there is coming and going, he is called a Nāgāmin;
if there is no coming and going, he is called an Anāgāmin.
At that time, Kāśyapa (*Jiāyè*) Bodhisattva said to the Buddha:
“Bhagavān!
As the Buddha has stated,
the Buddhas, the Bhagavāns, possess a secret treasury (*mìmìzàng*).
This meaning is incorrect.
Why?
The Buddhas, the Bhagavāns, only possess secret words (*mìyǔ*),
they do not possess a secret treasury.
For example, a master puppeteer
uses mechanisms
and wooden figures;
although people see them bending, stretching, stooping, and raising,
they do not know the internal workings that make them so.
The Buddha’s Dharma is not like this.
It allows all sentient beings to fully know and see it.
How then can one say that the Buddhas, the Bhagavāns, possess a secret treasury?”
The Buddha praised Kāśyapa:
“Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
As you have said,
the Tathāgata truly has no secret treasury.
Why?
Just like the full moon in autumn,
clearly exposed in the sky,
pure and without blemish (*yì*),
everyone sees it.
The words of the Tathāgata
are also like this:
unveiled and clearly exposed,
pure and without blemish.
Fools do not understand,
and call it a secret treasury,
but the wise understand it completely,
and thus do not call it a treasury.
Good man!
For example, there is a person
who accumulates gold and silver up to measureless billions,
but his mind is stingy and avaricious (*qiānlìn*).
He is unwilling to bestow it in charity to save the poor.
Such an accumulation is called a secret treasury.
The Tathāgata is not like this.
Over measureless kalpas (*jié*) he has accumulated measureless wondrous Dharma treasures (*miàofǎ zhēnbǎo*),
but his mind is without stinginess or avarice.
He constantly bestows them in charity upon all sentient beings.
How can one say the Tathāgata possesses a secret treasury?
Good man!
For example, there is a person whose body faculties (*shēngēn*) are incomplete,
perhaps lacking one eye,
one hand,
or one foot.
Due to shame,
he does not let others see it.
Because others do not see it,
it is called a secret treasury.
The Tathāgata is not like this.
All the True Dharma (*zhèngfǎ*) he possesses
is complete and flawless.
He lets people see it.
How can one say the Tathāgata possesses a secret treasury?
Good man!
For example, a poor person
who owes much money to others,
fearing the creditors,
hides and does not wish to appear.
Therefore, it is called a treasury.
The Tathāgata is not like this.
He does not owe any worldly Dharma (*shìfǎ*) to any sentient being.
Although he owes the transcendental Dharma (*chūshì zhī fǎ*) to sentient beings, he does not conceal it either.
Why?
Because he constantly regards sentient beings
with the thought of ‘only son’ (*yīzǐ xiǎng*),
and expounds the Supreme Dharma for them.
Good man!
For example, a householder (*zhǎngzhě*)
who possesses much wealth,
has only one son.
He loves and cherishes him deeply,
and his affection is inseparable.
He uses all his treasures to show them to the son.
The Tathāgata is also like this.
He views all sentient beings as identical to his only son.
Good man!
Just as worldly people,
whose male and female organs are ugly
and repulsive (*bǐ’è*),
cover and conceal them with clothing.
Therefore, this is called a treasury.
The Tathāgata is not like this.
He has permanently severed these organs.
Since he has no organs,
there is nothing to cover or conceal.
Good man!
Just as the treatises (*yǔlùn*) possessed by the Brahmins (*Póluómén*)
are ultimately not desired to be heard by the Kṣatriyas (*Chàlì*),
Vaiśyas (*Píshè*),
Śūdras (*Shǒutuó*), and others.
Why?
Because there are flaws and evils within these treatises.
The Tathāgata’s True Dharma
is not like this.
It is good in the beginning,
middle,
and end.
Therefore, it cannot be called a secret treasury.
Good man!
For example, a householder
has only one son.
He constantly thinks of him
and loves him endlessly.
He takes him to a teacher’s place,
wishing him to study,
but fears he will not quickly succeed,
and soon takes him back.
Out of love and affection,
he diligently teaches him, day and night,
half a letter (*bànzì*),
but does not teach him the Vyākaraṇa treatise (*Pígāluólùn*).
Why?
Because he is young,
and his capacity is not yet ready.
Good man!
If the householder teaches half a letter,
can the child immediately fully understand the Vyākaraṇa treatise?”
“No,
Bhagavān!”
“Does this householder,
regarding this son,
have a secret treasury?”
“No,
Bhagavān!
Why?
Because the son is young,
he does not explain it to him;
it is not because it is a secret,
which he stingily withholds from speaking.
Why is this?
If there is a jealous and secretly stingy mind,
then it is called a treasury.
The Tathāgata is not like this.
How can one say the Tathāgata possesses a secret treasury?”
The Fó said:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
It is as you say.
If one possesses an angry mind,
jealousy, stinginess, and meanness,
then it may be called a store (zàng);
The Rúlái is free of the angry mind
and jealousy,
how then can it be called a store (zàng)?
Good man!
That great elder refers to the Rúlái,
the one son spoken of
refers to all sentient beings (zhòngshēng).
The Rúlái regards all sentient beings as an only son.
Teaching the one son refers to the Shēngwén (Śrāvaka) disciples;
the half-letters (bànzì) refer to the Nine Divisions of Scriptures (Jiǔbù Jīng).
The Píjiāluó (Viyākaraṇa) treatises are the so-called Fāngděng (Vaipulya) Mahāyāna Sūtras (Dàchéng Jīngdiǎn).
Since the Shēngwén lack the power of wisdom (huìlì),
therefore the Rúlái speaks for them the half-letters and the Nine Divisions of Scriptures,
but does not speak for them the Píjiāluó treatises or the Fāngděng Dàchéng.
Good man!
Just like that elder,
once the son has grown up
and is capable of study and learning,
if the elder does not speak for him the Píjiāluó treatises,
then it could be called a store (zàng).
If the Shēngwén possess the capability
to receive the Dàchéng Píjiāluó treatises,
and the Rúlái secretly withholds them and does not speak them,
then one could say the Rúlái has a secret store (mìmì zàng).
The Rúlái is not like this.
Therefore, the Rúlái has no secret store (mìzàng).
Just as that elder, having taught the half-letters,
subsequently expounded the Píjiāluó treatises;
I am now also like this:
having spoken the half-letters and the Nine Divisions of Sūtras for my disciples,
I subsequently expound the Píjiāluó treatises,
that is, that the Rúlái exists eternally and does not change (chángcún bùbiàn).
"Furthermore, good man!
Suppose that in the summer month,
great clouds and thunder arise
and pour down great rain,
causing those farmers who have sown seeds to obtain abundant fruit.
Those who have not sown seeds
will achieve nothing;
that they achieve nothing
is not the fault of the Dragon King (Lóngwáng).
Furthermore, this Dragon King conceals nothing.
I, the Rúlái, now
am also like this:
I pour down the great Dharma rain, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Nièpán Jīng).
If sentient beings
sow the seeds of goodness,
they obtain the fruit of the sprout of wisdom (huìyá guǒ).
Those without the seeds of goodness
will achieve nothing.
That they achieve nothing
is not the fault of the Rúlái;
truly, the Fó Rúlái
conceals nothing.
Jiāshè (Kāśyapa) spoke again:
"I now definitively know that the Rúlái,
the Shìzūn (World-Honored One), conceals nothing secretly.
However, concerning the Píjiāluó treatises spoken by the Fó,
stating that the Fó Rúlái exists eternally and does not change,
this doctrine is incorrect (bùrán).
Why is this?
The Fó previously spoke verses (gè) [indicating impermanence].
Now you speak:
'Exists eternally and does not change.'
What is the meaning of this doctrine?"
The Fó said:
"Good man!
I spoke those verses
for the sake of instructing all the Shēngwén disciples in the half-letters.
