Good man!
Bōsīnì Wáng (King Prasenajit), when his mother passed away,
wept and longed for her, unable to control himself.
He came to my place,
and I immediately asked him:
'Great King!
Why is your sorrow, bitterness, and vexation this extreme?'
The King said:
'Shìzūn!
The great lady of the country
passed away today.
Suppose there were someone capable of restoring my mother's life to what it was before.
I would give up my kingdom,
elephants, horses,
the seven treasures, and even my body and life,
and bestow them all upon him as a reward.'
I then spoke to him:
'Great King!
Do not fret,
mourn, grieve, or weep.
When the life of any sentient being is exhausted,
this is called death.
Even the Zhū Fó (Buddhas), Yuánjué (Pratyekabuddhas),
and Shēngwén disciples
still relinquish this body,
how much more so ordinary beings (fánfū)?
Good man!
It was for the sake of teaching the half-letters to Bōsīnì Wáng
that I spoke those verses.
Now, I speak the Píjiāluó treatises for the Shēngwén disciples,
declaring that the Rúlái exists eternally,
without change or alteration.
If there is someone who says the Rúlái is impermanent (wúcháng),
how is it that this person's tongue does not fall out?"
Jiāshè spoke again:
"Regarding what the Fó has said:
'What is the meaning of this doctrine?
Shìzūn!
Among this assembly,
who can be called one who has accumulated nothing (wú suǒ jījù)?
Who can furthermore be called one who is content with food (yú shí zhīzú)?
Who walks in emptiness (kōng) such that their tracks cannot be traced?
And where does this person who departs go?"
The Fó said:
"Jiāshè!
Accumulation
is named wealth and treasure.
Good man!
Accumulation has two types:
first, conditioned (yǒuwéi);
second, unconditioned (wúwéi).
Conditioned accumulation refers to the practices of the Shēngwén;
unconditioned accumulation refers to the practices of the Rúlái.
Good man!
The Saṅgha (sēng) also has two types:
conditioned,
and unconditioned.
The conditioned Saṅgha is called the Shēngwén.
The Shēngwén Saṅgha possesses no accumulation:
that is, slaves and maids, unlawful possessions,
stored grain and rice,
salted beans, sesame seeds (húmá),
and large and small varieties of beans.
If there is someone who says the Rúlái permits the keeping of slaves,
servants, or such possessions,
their tongue will shrivel up.
All my Shēngwén disciples
are called those who have accumulated nothing,
and are also called those who are content with food.
If one is greedy for food,
they are called discontented.
Those not greedy for food
are called contented.
He whose tracks are difficult to trace
is close to the supreme path of Pútí (Bodhi).
I say that although this person departs, they arrive nowhere.
Jiāshè spoke again:
"If the conditioned Saṅgha
still has no accumulation,
how much less the unconditioned Saṅgha?
The unconditioned Saṅgha
is precisely the Rúlái.
How then could the Rúlái have accumulation?
Accumulation
is called hiding and concealing.
Therefore, whatever the Rúlái speaks,
he holds nothing back stingily.
How can he be called a store (zàng)?
He whose tracks cannot be traced is what is called Nièpán (Nirvāṇa).
Within Nièpán there are no sun, moon,
stars,
constellations,
cold, heat, wind, or rain,
birth, old age, sickness, or death (shēnglǎo bìngsǐ),
the Twenty-Five Realms of Existence (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu).
It is free from all worry and suffering, and all afflictions (fánnǎo).
Such Nièpán,
the dwelling place of the Rúlái,
is eternal and unchanging.
For this reason,
the Rúlái has arrived at this location beneath the Suōluó (Sāla) trees
and entered Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán) in Nièpán (Parinirvāṇa).
Fó told Jiāyè:
"What is spoken of as 'Great,'
its nature is vast and expansive.
It is like a person whose lifespan is immeasurable,
who is called a Great Man (Dàzhàngfū).
If this person is able to abide peacefully in the True Dharma,
they are called the most excellent among men.
Regarding the Eight Great Awakenings (Bā Dàrén Jué) which I have taught,
are they possessed by one person?
Or are they possessed by many people?
If one person possesses all eight,
then that is the most excellent.
What is spoken of as Nièpán (Nirvāṇa),
is without all blemishes or afflictions.
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
For example, if a person is shot by a poisoned arrow,
and suffers great pain;
upon meeting a skilled physician,
who extracts the poisoned arrow,
applies wondrous medicine,
and enables him to leave suffering,
and obtain peace and joy.
This physician then travels through cities and various villages,
wherever there is suffering from sickness
or wounds and blemishes,
he immediately goes there,
to treat the numerous sufferings.
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The Rúlái (Tathāgata) is also like this,
having achieved complete perfect enlightenment (zhèngjué),
He is the Great King of Physicians (Dàyīwáng),
seeing sentient beings in Yánfútí (Jambudvīpa) who are afflicted by suffering,
who throughout immeasurable kalpas have been struck by the poisoned arrows of Yín (lust),
nù (anger),
chī (delusion),
and the kleśas (fánnǎo, afflictions),
and suffer extreme bitterness.
For these beings,
He preaches the Gānlù Fǎyào (Amṛta Dharma medicine) of the Dàchéng Jīng (Mahāyāna Sūtra),
and having treated them,
He again goes to other regions where there are poisoned arrows of afflictions,
manifesting as a Fó,
to treat them.
Therefore, this is named Dàbān Nièpán (Mahāparinirvāṇa).
Dàbān Nièpán is named the place of liberation.
Wherever there are sentient beings to be subdued and disciplined,
the Rúlái manifests there.
Because of this true and extremely profound meaning,
it is called Dà Nièpán.
Jiāyè Púsà (Bodhisattva) again spoke to the Fó, saying:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
Can worldly physicians
completely cure all sentient beings of their wounds, blemishes, and sicknesses?"
"Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Worldly wounds and blemishes
generally fall into two types:
First, those that can be cured;
Second, those that cannot be cured.
Those that can be cured,
the physician is able to treat.
Those that cannot be cured,
he cannot treat."
Jiāyè again said:
"If it is as the Fó says,
then the Rúlái has already treated the sentient beings in Yánfútí.
If you say they are already treated,
then among these sentient beings,
how is it that there are still those who have not yet attained Nièpán?
If they have not all attained it,
how can the Rúlái say that the treatment is complete
and wish to go to other regions?"
"Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The sentient beings within Yánfútí are of two types:
First, those who have faith;
Second, those who have no faith.
The people who have faith
are called curable.
Why is this?
They are certain to attain Nièpán,
and thus are without blemishes.
Therefore, I say that the sentient beings in Yánfútí have been treated.
The people without faith
are named Yīchǎntí (Icchantika).
The Yīchǎntí
are named incurable.
Excluding the Yīchǎntí,
the rest have all been treated.
Therefore, Nièpán
is named 'without blemishes'."
"Shìzūn,
what is named Nièpán?"
"Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Indeed, Nièpán
is named Liberation."
Jiāyè again said:
"What is spoken of as Liberation,
is it form (rùpa)?
Or is it non-form?"
Fó said:
"Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Sometimes it is form;
sometimes it is non-form.
What is meant by non-form
is the liberation of the Shēngwén (Śrāvakas) and Yuánjué (Pratyekabuddhas).
What is meant by form
is the liberation of all Fós and Rúlái.
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Therefore, liberation is also form
and non-form.
The Rúlái teaches it as non-form for the benefit of the Shēngwén disciples."
"Shìzūn!
If the Shēngwén and Yuánjué attain non-form,
how are they able to dwell (exist)?"
"Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Just as the Fēixiǎng Fēifēixiǎng Tiān (Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception)
is also form and non-form,
yet I also speak of it as non-form.
If a person raises the difficulty, saying:
'If the Fēixiǎng Fēifēixiǎng Tiān is non-form,
how can it dwell,
come and go,
advance and halt?'
Such a meaning,
is the realm of the Fós,
it is not known by the Shēngwén or Yuánjué.
Liberation is also like this:
though it is both form and non-form, it is spoken of as non-form.
Though it is both perception and non-perception, it is spoken of as non-perception.
Such a meaning is the realm of the Fós,
it is not known by the Shēngwén or Yuánjué."
At that time, Jiāyè Púsà again spoke to the Fó, saying:
"Shìzūn!
We sincerely pray for your pity and compassion,
and that you may again extensively preach
the meaning of liberation that characterizes the practice of Dà Nièpán."
The Buddha praised Jiāshè:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
True liberation
is named the far removal from all fetters.
If true liberation removes all fetters,
then there is no birth,
nor is there combination.
Just as parents combine to produce a child,
true liberation is not like this.
Therefore, liberation is named non-birth.
Jiāshè!
For example, Tíhú is pure in nature.
The Tathāgata is also like this,
not born through the combination of parents,
His nature is pure.
The reason He manifests having parents
is for the purpose of transforming and saving sentient beings.
True liberation is the Tathāgata,
The Tathāgata's liberation is non-dual and non-separate.
For example, when various seeds are sown in the spring month,
having received warm energy, they immediately spring forth;
true liberation is not like this.
Furthermore, liberation is named Emptiness (Xūwú).
Emptiness is liberation,
liberation is the Tathāgata,
the Tathāgata is Emptiness,
not that which is created or done.
All that is created
is like city walls,
towers,
and defenses;
true liberation is not like this.
Therefore, liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is the Unconditioned Dharma (Wúwéi Fǎ).
For example, a potter,
creates but then destroys;
liberation is not so.
True liberation is neither born nor destroyed,
therefore liberation is the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is also like this:
not born and not destroyed,
not aging and not dying,
not broken and not ruined,
not a conditioned dharma (Yǒuwéi Fǎ).
Because of this meaning,
He is named the Tathāgata entering Mahāparinirvāṇa.
What is the meaning of not aging and not dying?
Aging is named change and transformation,
hair turning white and face wrinkling;
dying is the destruction of the body and the end of life.
Such things
do not exist in liberation;
since these things do not exist,
it is named liberation.
The Tathāgata likewise does not have white hair,
wrinkled face,
or conditioned dharmas.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has no aging;
since there is no aging,
there is no dying.
Furthermore, liberation is named freedom from sickness.
What is meant by sickness
are the four hundred and four diseases and other external factors that damage the body.
Since these things do not exist in that state,
it is named liberation.
Freedom from sickness
is true liberation,
true liberation is the Tathāgata,
the Tathāgata is without sickness,
therefore the Dharma-body (Fǎshēn) is also without sickness.
Such freedom from sickness
is the Tathāgata.
Dying is named the destruction of the body and the end of life;
where there is no death
is Amṛta (Gānlù).
This Amṛta is true liberation,
true liberation is the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata accomplishes such merits;
how can it be said that the Tathāgata is impermanent?
If one says He is impermanent,
there is no such possibility.
This Vajra-body (Jīngāng Shēn),
how can it be impermanent?
Therefore, the Tathāgata is not named 'having ended life.'
The Tathāgata is pure,
without defilement or impurity.
The body of the Tathāgata is not defiled by the womb,
like the puṇḍarīka (Fèntuólì),
whose fundamental nature is pure.
The Tathāgata's liberation is also like this:
such liberation
is the Tathāgata,
therefore the Tathāgata is pure and undefiled.
Furthermore, liberation is where
all outflowing (lòu) sores and swellings are permanently eliminated without residue.
The Tathāgata is also like this,
without all outflowing sores and swellings.
Furthermore, liberation is without conflict or contention.
For example, a hungry person,
seeing others' food and drink,
gives rise to the thought of greedy seizure.
Liberation is not so.
Furthermore, liberation is named Calmness (Ānjìng).
Ordinary people say,
that calmness refers to Móxīshǒuluó.
Such a statement is false.
True calmness is ultimate liberation,
ultimate liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is named Peacefulness (Ānyǐn).
Just as a place with many thieves is not named peaceful,
only a place that is clear and tranquil is named peaceful.
In this liberation, there is no fear,
therefore it is named Peacefulness.
Therefore, Peacefulness is true liberation,
true liberation is the Tathāgata,
and the Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation
has no equal companion.
Having an equal companion
is like a king having neighboring kingdoms that are his equal.
Liberation is not like this.
That which has no equal companion is the Cakravartin (Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng),
there is none who can be made equal to him.
Liberation is also like this,
having no equal companion.
Having no equal companion is true liberation,
true liberation is the Tathāgata,
the King who Turns the Dharma Wheel.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has no equal companion.
That He has an equal companion is impossible.
Furthermore, liberation is named Freedom from Sorrow (Wú Yōuchóu).
Having sorrow is like a king fearing powerful neighbors,
and thereby giving rise to sorrow.
Liberation does not have such things.
For example, having destroyed enemies,
then there is no worry or anxiety.
Liberation is also like this,
It is freedom from worry and fear.
That which is freedom from worry and fear
is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation
is named Freedom from Sorrow and Joy (Wú Yōuxǐ).
For example, a woman,
who has only one son,
goes on a far journey for service.
Suddenly she receives bad news,
and hearing it, she suffers sorrow.
Later, she hears he is alive,
and immediately gives rise to joy.
In liberation,
there are no such things.
Freedom from sorrow and joy is true liberation,
true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is without dust or dirt.
For example, in the spring month,
after sunset,
the wind raises dust and haze.
In liberation, there are no such things.
Freedom from dust and haze illustrates true liberation,
true liberation is the Tathāgata.
For example, the bright jewel in the topknot of a holy king
is without defilement or impurity.
The nature of liberation is also like this,
without defilement or impurity.
Freedom from defilement and impurity illustrates true liberation,
true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Just as the nature of pure gold
is not mixed with sand or stone,
and is then named true treasure.
When someone obtains it, they give rise to the thought of wealth.
The nature of liberation,
is also like this,
like that true treasure.
That true treasure illustrates true liberation,
true liberation is the Tathāgata.
For example, a clay pot,
breaks and makes a cracking sound.
A Vajra jewel bottle
is not like this.
Liberation likewise has no shattering or breakage.
The Vajra jewel bottle illustrates true liberation,
true liberation is the Tathāgata,
therefore the body of the Tathāgata is indestructible.
The sound of shattering
is like castor seeds,
when the heat is intense,
and they are placed out in the sun,
they let out a cracking sound and burst.
Liberation has no such things.
It is like that Vajra true jewel bottle,
having no shattering or cracking sound.
Even if immeasurable hundreds and thousands of people all shoot arrows at it,
none can destroy it.
The absence of shattering or cracking sounds illustrates true liberation,
true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Just as a poor person, because he owes others property,
is bound by them,
with cangue, shackles, and whipping,
enduring all sufferings and poisons.
Now, in liberation (jiětuō), there are no such matters.
There is no burden of debt,
just like a wealthy elder (zhǎngzhě) who possesses immeasurable hundreds of millions of treasures,
having power and self-mastery,
owing nothing to others.
Now, the liberated one (jiětuō zhě) is also like this,
possessing boundless treasures of Dharma wealth (fǎcái),
having power and self-mastery,
owing nothing.
The one who owes nothing symbolizes true liberation (zhēn jiětuō).
True liberation is precisely the Táthāgata (Rúlái).
Furthermore, liberation is named "without oppression or duress" (wú bīqiē).
[It is] like experiencing heat in spring,
eating sweet things on a summer day,
or feeling the cold touch in winter.
In true liberation, there are no such undesirable matters.
Being without oppression or duress symbolizes true liberation.
True liberation is precisely the Táthāgata.
"Furthermore, the one without oppression or duress,
for example, is like a person who has eaten their fill of fish and meat,
and then drinks milk.
This person will soon approach death.
In true liberation, there are no such matters.
If this person obtains the sweet dew (gānlù) of good medicine,
their ailment will be eliminated.
True liberation is also like this.
The sweet dew of good medicine symbolizes true liberation.
True liberation is precisely the Táthāgata.
What is oppression (bīqiē)
and non-oppression (bù bīqiē)?
For example, the ordinary being (fánfū),
being arrogant and self-exalting,
creates this thought:
'Among all beings, who can harm me?'
[He] immediately carries and holds snakes, tigers, and poisonous insects.
Know that this person will not complete their lifespan;
they will suffer an untimely death (héngsǐ).
In true liberation, there are no such matters.
The one without oppression is like the Wheel-Turning King (Zhuǎnlúnwáng).
The spiritual pearl (shénzhū) he possesses can subdue dung beetles,
and ninety-six types of poisonous insects.
If anyone smells the fragrance of this spiritual pearl,
all poisons vanish.
True liberation is also like this;
it completely moves far away from the Twenty-Five Forms of Existence (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu).
The vanishing of poisons symbolizes true liberation.
True liberation is precisely the Táthāgata.
Furthermore, the one without oppression
is analogous to empty space (xūkōng).
Liberation is likewise.
That empty space
symbolizes true liberation.
True liberation is precisely the Táthāgata.
Furthermore, oppression is like approaching dry grass
and lighting oil lamps (dēnghuǒ).
When near, it blazes intensely.
In true liberation, there are no such matters.
Furthermore, the one without oppression
is analogous to the sun and the moon (rìyuè),
which do not oppress sentient beings (zhòngshēng).
Liberation is likewise;
toward all sentient beings, there is no oppression.
Being without oppression symbolizes true liberation.
True liberation is precisely the Táthāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is named the "unmoving Dharma" (wú dòng fǎ).
[It is unlike] enemies and relatives (yuān qīn).
In true liberation, there are no such matters.
Furthermore, the unmoving one is like the Wheel-Turning King (Zhuǎnlúnwáng).
There is no other holy king (shèng wáng) who takes him as a close friend.
If there were another close friend,
that would be impossible.
Liberation is likewise.
There is no other close friend.
If there were a close friend, that would also be impossible.
That king having no close friend symbolizes true liberation.
True liberation is precisely the Táthāgata.
The Táthāgata is precisely the Dharma (Fǎ).
Furthermore, the unmoving one is analogous to plain cloth (sù yī),
which is easily dyed with color.
Liberation is not like this.
Furthermore, the unmoving one is like the Vāśī flower (Póshī huā).
If one wished it to have a foul smell or a blue color,
that would be impossible.
Liberation is likewise.
If one wished it to have a foul smell or various colors,
that would also be impossible.
Therefore, liberation is precisely the Táthāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is named "rare" (xīyǒu).
For example, a lotus flower (liánhuā) growing in water
is not rare.
If it grows in fire,
that is indeed rare.
When people see it, they immediately give rise to joy.
True liberation is also like this.
Those who see it
generate joy in their hearts.
That rare phenomenon
symbolizes true liberation.
True liberation is precisely the Táthāgata.
That Táthāgata is precisely the Dharma Body (fǎshēn).
Furthermore, the rare one
is analogous to an infant (yīng'ér)
whose teeth have not yet grown.
[The teeth] gradually grow after the child gets older.
Liberation is not like this.
There is no existence of growing or not growing.
"Furthermore, regarding Jiětuō (liberation),
it is named Xūjì (Void and Tranquil),
having no uncertainty.
Uncertainty means,
for example, that an Yīchǎntí permanently cannot change,
or that one who commits grievous transgressions cannot attain the path of a Fó—
such a premise does not exist.
Why is this?
If such a person, within the Fó Zhèngfǎ (True Dharma of the Buddha),
attains pure faith in their mind,
at that time they immediately eliminate the Yīchǎntí state.
If they are further able to become an Yōupósāi (lay devotee),
they also attain the severing and extinguishing of the Yīchǎntí state.
One who commits grievous transgressions, having extinguished this sin,
then attains becoming a Fó.
Therefore, if it is said
that they are ultimately fixed and cannot change,
and cannot attain the Fó path,
such a premise does not exist.
Within True Jiětuō, there is entirely no such thing as perishing or exhaustion.
Furthermore, Xūjì falls within the Fǎjiè (Dharma Realm).
Just as the nature of the Fǎjiè is True Jiětuō,
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái (Tathāgata).
Furthermore, if the Yīchǎntí state is completely extinguished,
then one should not be called an Yīchǎntí.
What is referred to as an Yīchǎntí?
An Yīchǎntí is one
who has severed and extinguished all roots of goodness,
whose fundamental mind does not cling to any good Dharma,
and who does not even produce a single thought of good.
Within True Jiětuō, there are entirely none of these matters.
Because there are none of these matters,
it is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Immeasurable.
For example, a pile of grain—
its measure can be known.
True Jiětuō is not like this.
For example, the great ocean cannot be measured.
Jiětuō is also like this; it cannot be measured.
That which is immeasurable is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named the Boundless Dharma.
Just as a single sentient being has many karmic retributions,
Jiětuō is also like this:
it has boundless retribution.
That which has boundless retribution is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Vast and Great.
For example, the great ocean—nothing is equal to it.
Jiětuō is also like this; nothing can be equal to it.
That which has no equal is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Supreme.
For example, the empty sky is the highest and has no peer.
Jiětuō is also like this: the highest and without peer.
That which is high and peerless is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named That Which Cannot Be Surpassed.
For example, where a lion dwells,
all hundred beasts cannot surpass it.
Jiětuō is also like this; there is nothing that can surpass it.
That which cannot be surpassed is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Unexcelled.
For example, the Northern Quarter
is supreme among the quarters.
Jiětuō is also like this:
it is without anything above it.
That which has nothing above it is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Supreme Above the Supreme.
For example, the Northern Quarter compared to the Eastern Quarter
is Supreme Above the Supreme.
Jiětuō is also like this; it has nothing Supreme Above the Supreme.
That which is without Supreme Above the Supreme is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Constant Dharma.
For example, when humans and heavenly beings die and their bodies perish,
this is named Constant,
not non-Constant.
Jiětuō is also like this; it is not non-Constant.
That which is not non-Constant is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Solid and Real.
Just as Qiétuóluó (Khadira), Zhāntán (sandalwood), and Chénshuǐ (agarwood),
their nature is solid and real.
Jiětuō is also like this; its nature is solid and real.
That whose nature is solid and real is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Non-Hollow.
For example, bamboo and reeds—their substance is empty and sparse;
Jiětuō is not like this.
One should know that Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Unstainable.
For example, a wall that has not yet been plastered or painted,
mosquitoes and gnats land on it, dwell there, and play.
If it is plastered, painted with colors, or sculpted and decorated,
the insects, upon smelling the fragrance of the colors, immediately do not dwell there.
This not dwelling is compared to True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Boundless.
For example, a village
always has boundaries and markers.
Jiětuō is not like this.
For example, the empty sky has no borders or limits.
Jiětuō is also like this; it has no borders or limits.
Such Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Invisible.
For example, the tracks of a bird in the sky are hard to see.
This difficulty in seeing
is compared to True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Profound.
Why is this?
Shēngwén (Hearers) and Yuánjué (Solitary Realizers) cannot enter it.
That which cannot be entered is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, that which is Profound is revered by all Fó (Buddhas) and Púsà (Bodhisattvas).
For example, the merit of a filial child supporting their parents is extremely profound.
This extremely profound merit is compared to True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Invisible (or Unperceivable).
For example, a person cannot see the crown of their own head.
Jiětuō is also like this.
Shēngwén and Yuánjué cannot perceive it.
That which cannot be perceived is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Having No Dwelling.
For example, the empty sky has no dwelling.
Jiětuō is also like this.
The term "dwelling"
is compared to the Èrshíwǔ Yǒu (Twenty-five Forms of Existence).
That which has no dwelling
is compared to True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Untakeable.
Just as the Āmólègǔo fruit,
can be taken and held by people.
Jiětuō is not like this.
It cannot be taken and held.
That which cannot be taken and held is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Ungraspable.
For example, illusory objects cannot be grasped or held.
Jiětuō is also like this; it cannot be grasped or held.
That which cannot be grasped or held is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō has no physical body.
For example, a person whose body develops sores, warts, boils, or carbuncles,
madness, or wasting diseases.
Within True Jiětuō, there are no such illnesses.
Having no such illnesses is compared to True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Having a Single Flavor.
Just as milk has a single flavor,
Jiětuō is also like this.
It has only a single flavor.
This single flavor is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Pure.
Just as water without mud
is clear, still, and pure.
Jiětuō is also like this: clear, still, and pure.
That which is clear, still, and pure is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Having a Single Flavor.
Just as the rain in the sky
has a single flavor and is pure.
This single flavor and purity is compared to True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Removal.
For example, the full moon
has no clouds or shadows.
Jiětuō is also like this; it has no clouds or shadows.
Having no clouds or shadows is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Tranquil Stillness.
For example, a person whose fever is cured,
whose body attains tranquil stillness.
Jiětuō is also like this:
the body attains tranquil stillness.
The body attaining tranquil stillness is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is Equality.
For example, in a wild field, venomous snakes
and weasels both have the intention to kill.
Jiětuō is not like this.
It has no intention to kill.
That which has no intention to kill is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, regarding Equality,
for example, parents treat their children with equal mind.
Jiětuō is also like this; its mind is equal.
That whose mind is equal is True Jiětuō.
True Jiětuō is the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Jiětuō is named Having No Other Place.
For example, a person dwells only in a superior, wondrous, pure dwelling,
and has no other place.
Jiětuō is also like this."
There is no different place.
That which is without a different place is true liberation.
That which is true liberation is the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Furthermore, liberation is called contentment.
For example, a hungry person encounters sweet delicacies,
and eats them without satiety.
Liberation is not like this.
It is like eating milk gruel (rǔmí),
there is nothing further one needs.
Having nothing further one needs compares to true liberation.
That which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called severance.
For example, a person is bound,
and by severing the bonds gains release.
Liberation is also like this:
it severs and breaks all fetters of doubt.
Such severance of doubt is true liberation.
That which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called reaching the other shore (bǐ'àn).
For example, a great river has this shore (cǐ'àn)
and the other shore.
Liberation is not like this:
although there is no this shore, there is the other shore.
That which has the other shore is true liberation.
That which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called silence (mòrán).
For example, the water of the great ocean surges and overflows,
producing many sounds.
Liberation is not like this.
Such liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called wondrous beauty (měimiào).
For example, various medicines,
when mixed with harītaki (hēlílè),
have a bitter taste.
Liberation is not like this.
Its taste is like sweet dew (gānlù).
Its taste being like sweet dew compares to true liberation.
That which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation removes all afflictions (fánnǎo).
For example, a good physician mixes various medicines,
and skillfully cures all diseases.
Liberation is also like this; it can eliminate afflictions.
That which eliminates afflictions is true liberation.
That which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is called non-constriction (wú zé).
For example, a small house
cannot accommodate many people.
Liberation is not like this;
it accommodates many.
That which accommodates many is true liberation.
That which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation
is called the extinction of all cravings (ài),
and is unmixed with sexual desire (yínyù).
For example, women
have many loves and desires.
Liberation is not like this.
Such liberation is the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is like this, without the fetters of greed (tānyù),
hatred (chēnhuì),
delusion (yúchī),
and arrogance (jiāomàn).
Furthermore, liberation is called lack of craving (wú ài).
Craving has two types:
first, the craving of the hungry ghosts (èguǐ ài),
and second, the craving for the Dharma (fǎ ài).
True liberation is separate from the craving of the hungry ghosts.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, there is craving for the Dharma.
Such craving for the Dharma is true liberation.
That which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is separation from I (wǒ)
and mine (wǒ suǒ).
Such liberation is the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is the Dharma (Fǎ).
Furthermore, liberation is extinction (mièjìn),
separation from all existence-craving (yǒu tān).
Such liberation is the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation is rescue and protection (jiùhù).
It can rescue and protect all those who are fearful.
Such liberation is the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation is a place of refuge (guīchù).
If one takes refuge in such liberation,
one does not seek other refuges.
For example, a person
relies upon a king,
and does not seek other reliance.
Although relying upon a king,
there is still instability and movement.
Relying on liberation,
there is no instability or movement.
That which is without instability is true liberation.
That which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation is called a dwelling house (wūzhái).
For example, a person traveling in the wilderness
encounters dangers and difficulties.
Liberation is not like this;
there are no dangers or difficulties.
That which is without dangers or difficulties is true liberation.
That which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is fearlessness (wú suǒ wèi).
Like the Lion King (Shīzi Wáng),
it does not generate fear towards the hundreds of beasts.
Liberation is also like this;
it does not generate fear towards all hosts of Māra (Mózòng).
That which is without fear is true liberation.
That which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation is without tightness or narrowness (wú yǒu zéxiá).
For example, a narrow path cannot even accommodate two people walking abreast.
Liberation is not like this.
Such liberation
is the Tathāgata.
Also, [it means] not constricted.
For example, a person
fearing a tiger falls into a well.
Liberation is not like this.
Such liberation is the Tathāgata.
Also, [it means] not constricted.
It is like being in the great ocean:
abandoning a damaged small boat and obtaining a solid boat,
riding it across the ocean to a place of safety and tranquility,
the mind attains happiness.
Liberation is also like this;
the mind attains happiness.
That which attains happiness is true liberation.
That which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation eradicates all causes and conditions (yīnyuán).
For example, dependent on milk, one gets curds (lào);
dependent on curds, one gets clarified butter (sū);
dependent on clarified butter, one gets ghṛta (tíhú).
In true liberation, none of these causes exist.
That which is without these causes is true liberation.
That which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, liberation can subdue arrogance.
For example, a great king is arrogant toward a small king.
Liberation is not like this.
Such liberation is the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is the Dharma.
Furthermore, liberation subdues all heedlessness (fàngyì).
Those who are heedless generally have much greed and desire.
In true liberation, this name (heedlessness) does not exist.
That which is without this name is true liberation.
That which is true liberation is the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, *jiětuō* is that which can eliminate *wúmíng* (ignorance),
just like the finest quality butter,
removing all impurities and dross,
is then called *tíhú*.
*Jiětuō* is also like this:
it removes the dross of *wúmíng*,
and produces true clarity.
Such true clarity is true *jiětuō*,
and true *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* is called quiescence,
pure, single, and non-dual,
like a solitary wild elephant,
alone and without companion.
*Jiětuō* is also like this:
solitary and non-dual.
The solitary and non-dual is true *jiětuō*,
and true *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* is called substantiality,
just as bamboo and reeds,
or the castor plant,
have hollow stems and stalks,
but their seeds are substantial.
Excluding the Buddha *Rúlái*,
all other humans and devas are insubstantial.
True *jiětuō* is far removed from all outflows of existence,
such *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* is called the ability to awaken and understand,
and to increase the self.
True *jiětuō* is also like this;
such *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* is called abandoning all existences,
for example, like a person who eats and then vomits.
*Jiětuō* is also like this:
abandoning all existences.
That which abandons all existences is true *jiětuō*,
and true *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* is called certainty,
just as the fragrance of the *Póshī Huā*
is not found among the seven-leaved plants.
*Jiětuō* is also like this;
such *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* is called the *shuǐ dà* (Water Element),
just as the Water Element,
excels among all great elements,
and can moisten all grass, wood, and grains.
*Jiětuō* is also like this:
it can moisten all kinds of sentient beings.
Such *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* is called the entering,
just as if there is a gateway,
it opens the path to the place of the gold nature,
and the gold can then be obtained.
*Jiětuō* is also like this:
it is like that gateway.
Those who practice non-self (anātman),
can then enter it.
Such *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* is called the good,
just as a disciple who follows his master,
and faithfully obeys the instructions,
is thereby called good.
*Jiětuō* is also like this;
such *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
"Furthermore, *jiětuō* is called the Transcendent Dharma,
surpassing all other phenomena,
just as clarified butter and milk are supreme among all tastes.
*Jiětuō* is also like this;
such *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* is called immovability,
just as a door sill cannot be moved by the wind.
True *jiětuō* is also like this;
such *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* is called having no surging waves,
unlike the great ocean whose water has surging waves;
*jiětuō* is not like that.
Such *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* is compared to a palace;
*jiětuō* is also like this.
Know that *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* is called usefulness,
just as *Yánfúdántán Jīn* (Jāmbūnada gold),
is suitable for many tasks,
and no one can speak of defects in this gold.
*Jiětuō* is also like this:
it has no defects.
That which has no defects is true *jiětuō*,
and true *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* abandons the conduct of an infant,
just as an adult
abandons the behavior of a small child.
*Jiětuō* is also like this:
it eliminates and abandons the *wǔ yīn* (Five Aggregates).
Eliminating and abandoning the *wǔ yīn* is true *jiětuō*,
and true *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* is called ultimate attainment,
just as one who was bound,
is released from the bondage,
is cleansed by bathing,
and then returns home.
*Jiětuō* is also like this:
it is ultimately pure.
Ultimate purity is true *jiětuō*,
and true *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* is called *wúzuò lè* (unconditioned joy).
This *wúzuò lè* arises because
desire,
hatred,
and delusion are expelled (vomited forth);
it is likened to a person who accidentally drank snake venom.
In order to eliminate the poison,
he immediately takes an emetic.
Having successfully vomited,
the poison is eliminated and healed,
and the body attains peace and joy.
*Jiětuō* is also like this:
it expels *fánnǎo* (afflictions),
all bonds,
and the poison of fetters.
The body attains peace and joy,
which is called *wúzuò lè*.
*Wúzuò lè* is true *jiětuō*,
and true *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, *jiětuō* is called cutting off the *fánnǎo* (afflictions) that are like four types of poisonous snakes.
That which cuts off *fánnǎo* is true *jiětuō*,
and true *jiětuō* is the *Rúlái*.
“Furthermore, what is called liberation (jiětuō) means departing from all forms of existence (yǒu),
extinguishing all suffering (kǔ), and attaining all bliss (lè).
It means eternally severing greed (tānyù),
anger (chēnhuì),
and delusion (yúchī).
It means rooting out the origin of all afflictions (fánnǎo).
To root out the origin is precisely true liberation,
and true liberation is precisely the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Furthermore, what is called liberation means severing all conditioned phenomena (yǒuwéi zhī fǎ),
giving rise to all undefiled good dharmas (wúlòu shàn fǎ),
and blocking off all paths,
such as 'I' (wǒ),
'non-I' (wú wǒ),
'neither I' (fēi wǒ),
and 'neither non-I' (fēi wú wǒ).
It involves only cutting off grasping and attachment (qǔ zhuó),
but not cutting off the view of 'I' (wǒjiàn).
The view of 'I' is called the Buddha-nature (fóxìng),
and the Buddha-nature is precisely true liberation.
True liberation is precisely the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, what is called liberation
is defined as 'not-empty emptiness' (bù kōng kōng).
'Empty emptiness' (kōng kōng) means having nothing whatsoever (wú suǒ yǒu).
Having nothing whatsoever
is the liberation conceived of by externalists (wàidào) like the Nirgrantha (Níjiànzǐ) and others.
But this Nirgrantha truly has no liberation;
hence it is called 'empty emptiness.'
True liberation is not like this;
therefore it is 'not-empty emptiness.'
'Not-empty emptiness' is precisely true liberation,
and true liberation is precisely the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, what is called liberation
is defined as 'empty yet not empty' (kōng bù kōng).
Consider a jar
meant for water,
wine,
curd,
clarified butter (sū), honey (mì), and so on.
Although there are times when it contains no water, wine, curd, clarified butter, or honey,
it is still called a jar for water, and so on.
But regarding these jars,
one cannot speak of them as empty or as not empty.
If one says they are empty,
then they should not possess form (sè),
smell (xiāng),
taste (wèi),
or touch (chù).
If one says they are not empty,
yet there is truly no water,
wine, etc., within them.
Liberation is likewise:
one cannot speak of it as form or as non-form,
and one cannot speak of it as empty or as not empty.
If one says it is empty,
then it should not possess permanence (cháng), bliss (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng).
If one says it is not empty,
then who is the recipient of this permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
For this reason,
one cannot speak of it as empty or as not empty.
'Empty' refers to the non-existence of the twenty-five forms of existence (èrshíwǔ yǒu), along with all afflictions,
all suffering,
all characteristics (xiàng),
and all conditioned activities (yǒuwéi xíng).
Just as a jar without curd
is called empty.
'Not empty'
refers to the true good qualities: form,
permanence, bliss, self, and purity,
which are immovable and unchangeable.
Just like that jar,
which possesses form, smell, taste, and touch;
thus it is called 'not empty.'
Therefore, liberation is compared to that jar.
That jar, when encountering conditions, is liable to be broken;
liberation is not like that;
it is not subject to destruction.
That which is not subject to destruction is precisely true liberation,
and true liberation is precisely the Tathāgata.
“Furthermore, what is called liberation is defined as departing from love (ài).
For example, there are people
who, with hearts full of love, hope for Śakrā Devanām Indra (Shìtí Huányīn),
the Great Brahmā Heaven King (Dà Fàntiānwáng),
or the Īśvara Heaven King (Zìzàitiānwáng).
Liberation is not like that.
Once one has achieved Anuttara Samyak Saṃbodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
there is no love and no doubt.
No love and no doubt is precisely true liberation,
and true liberation is precisely the Tathāgata.
To say that liberation contains love or doubt
is absolutely impossible.
Furthermore, liberation severs the greed for all forms of existence,
severs all characteristics,
all bindings (xìfù),
all afflictions,
all birth and death (shēngsǐ),
all causes and conditions (yīnyuán),
and all consequences and retributions (guǒbào).
Such liberation is precisely the Tathāgata,
and the Tathāgata is precisely Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
All sentient beings, because they are terrified of birth, death, and all afflictions,
therefore take the Three Refuges (Sān Guī).
For instance, a herd of deer,
terrified of the hunter,
having managed to escape,
if they take one leap,
that is compared to one refuge.
Thus, three leaps are compared to the Three Refuges.
By means of the three leaps,
they attain and experience peace and bliss (ānlè).
Sentient beings are likewise:
terrified of the Four Māras (Sì Mó),
the wicked hunters,
they take refuge in the Three Refuges.
Because of the Three Refuges, they attain peace and bliss.
Attaining peace and bliss is precisely true liberation,
and true liberation is precisely the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is precisely Nirvāṇa,
Nirvāṇa is precisely the inexhaustible (wújìn),
the inexhaustible is precisely the Buddha-nature,
the Buddha-nature is precisely certainty (juédìng),
and certainty is precisely Anuttara Samyak Saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa (Jiāshè) Bodhisattva (Púsà) said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If Nirvāṇa,
Buddha-nature,
certainty,
and the Tathāgata
are one meaning,
why do you speak of there being Three Refuges?”
The Buddha addressed Kāśyapa:
“Good man!
All sentient beings are terrified of birth and death;
therefore they seek the Three Refuges.
By means of the Three Refuges,
they then know the Buddha-nature,
certainty,
and Nirvāṇa.
Good man!
There are dharmas that are one in name but different in meaning,
and there are dharmas that are different in both name and meaning.
Those that are one in name but different in meaning are:
the permanence of the Buddha (Fó cháng),
the permanence of the Dharma (Fǎ cháng),
the permanence of the Bhikṣu Saṅgha (Bǐqiū Sēng cháng),
and Nirvāṇa and space (xūkōng) are all also permanent.
This is what is meant by one in name but different in meaning.
Those that are different in both name and meaning are:
the Buddha is named 'Enlightenment' (jué),
the Dharma is named 'Non-enlightenment' (bù jué),
the Saṅgha is named 'Harmony and Union' (héhé),
Nirvāṇa is named 'Liberation,'
and space is named 'Neither good nor bad' and also named 'Unobstructed' (wú ài).
This is what is meant by different in both name and meaning.
Good man!
The Three Refuges are also like this:
they are different in both name and meaning.
How could they be one?
That is why I told Mahāprajāpatī (Móhē Bōshé Bōtí):
‘Gautamī (Qiáotánmí)!
Do not make offerings to me;
you should make offerings to the Saṅgha.
If you make offerings to the Saṅgha,
then you will completely make offerings to the Three Refuges.’
Mahāprajāpatī immediately replied to me:
‘Among the Saṅgha,
there is neither Buddha nor Dharma.
How can you say that making offerings to the Saṅgha
completely fulfills the offering to the Three Refuges?’
I replied to her again:
‘By following my instructions,
you are offering to the Buddha;
for the sake of liberation,
you are offering to the Dharma;
and by the Saṅgha accepting the offerings,
you are offering to the Saṅgha.’
Good man!
For this reason, the Three Refuges cannot be considered one.
Good man!
The Tathāgata sometimes speaks of one as three,
and speaks of three as one.
Meanings such as these
are the realm of the Buddhas,
not knowable by Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) or Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué).
Kāśyapa responded again:
“As the Buddha says,
that ultimate peace and bliss is called Nirvāṇa—
what does this meaning imply?
Now, Nirvāṇa involves abandoning the body and abandoning consciousness (zhì).
If the body and consciousness are abandoned,
who will then experience bliss?”
Fó said:
"Good man!
Suppose there is a person,
whose heart is distressed after eating,
who goes outside wanting to vomit.
After having vomited,
he then returns.
His companion asks him:
'Are the troubles you suffered now actually better or not?
Why have you already returned?'
He replies:
'I am already better,
and my body has attained peace and joy.'
The Rúlái is also like this:
ultimately abandoning the twenty-five existences (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu),
eternally attaining the place of Níèpán and peace and joy,
immovable,
without exhaustion or destruction,
cutting off all sensation,
this is called the Joy of Non-Sensation (Wúshòulè).
Such non-sensation
is called Eternal Joy (Chánglè).
If one says the Rúlái possesses sensation-joy,
there is no such possibility.
Therefore, ultimate joy
is identical to Níèpán.
Níèpán is identical to true liberation,
and true liberation is identical to the Rúlái."
Jiāshè replied again:
"Is non-arising and non-ceasing liberation?"
"It is so,
it is so.
Good man!
Non-arising and non-ceasing is identical to liberation,
and such liberation is identical to the Rúlái."
Jiāshè replied again:
"If non-arising and non-ceasing is liberation,
the nature of emptiness (xūkōng) also has no arising or ceasing,
so it should be the Rúlái.
Just as the Rúlái's nature
is identical to liberation."
The Fó told Jiāshè:
"Good man!
This matter is not so."
"Shìzūn!
Why is it not so?"
"Good man!
Take the example of the Jiālánjiā bird and the Mìngmìng bird;
their sounds are clear and marvelous.
Can they possibly be the same as the sound of the crow or magpie?"
"No,
Shìzūn!
The sound of the crow and magpie, when compared to the Mìngmìng and others,
cannot be compared even by a hundred thousand myriad times."
Jiāshè replied again:
"The sound of the Jiālánjiā and others is subtle and marvelous,
and their bodies are also different.
How can the Rúlái be compared to the crow or magpie?
It is no different from comparing the dìnglì (pepperwort) to Mount Xūmí.
The Fó and xūkōng are also like this.
The sound of the Jiālánjiā can be used to compare to the Fó’s sound,
but the sound of the crow or magpie cannot be used as an analogy."
At that time, the Fó praised the Bodhisattva Jiāshè, saying:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
You have now grasped well what is profoundly difficult to grasp.
Sometimes the Rúlái, due to certain circumstances,
brings in that xūkōng,
using it as an analogy for liberation.
Such liberation
is identical to the Rúlái.
True liberation
has nothing among all humans and devas that can be compared to it,
and yet this xūkōng is actually not its analogy.
In order to transform sentient beings,
we take xūkōng, which is not an analogy, as an analogy.
You should know that liberation is identical to the Rúlái,
the nature of the Rúlái is identical to liberation.
Liberation
and the Rúlái
are non-dual and non-separate.
Good man!
That which is not an analogy
is like that which has nothing comparable and cannot be used for analogy,
but due to certain circumstances, it can be brought in as an analogy.
Just as it is said in the Sūtras:
'A beautiful countenance is like the full, bright moon.'
'A white elephant is pure and clean,
like a snow mountain.'
The full moon cannot be identical to the face,
and the snow mountain cannot be identical to the white elephant.
Good man!
One cannot use analogies
to illustrate true liberation;
analogies are made merely for the purpose of transforming sentient beings.
Based on various analogies,
one knows that the nature of all phenomena
is also like this."
Jiāshè replied again:
"Why does the Rúlái speak in two ways?"
The Fó said:
"Good man!
Suppose there is a person
holding a sword,
with an angry mind,
who wishes to harm the Rúlái.
The Rúlái is peaceful and joyful,
without any expression of anger or hatred.
Would this person succeed in destroying the Rúlái's body and thereby commit an unpardonable sin?"
"No,
Shìzūn!
Why?
Because the realm of the Rúlái's body
cannot be destroyed.
Why is this?
Because there is no aggregate of body,
only the Dharma nature (Fǎxìng).
The nature of the Fǎxìng
fundamentally cannot be destroyed.
How can this person destroy the Fó's body?
Merely because of the malicious intent,
he therefore achieves the Avīci hell sin.
Due to these circumstances,
various analogies are introduced
to understand the true Dharma."
At that time, the Fó praised Bodhisattva Jiāshè:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
What I intended to say,
you have now already said.
Furthermore, good man!
Suppose a wicked person wishes to kill his mother.
He stands in a wild field beneath a stack of grain.
His mother brings him food.
When the person sees her,
he immediately gives rise to the intent to kill,
and proceeds to sharpen his knife.
The mother, realizing this,
flees into the grain stack.
The person, holding the knife,
chops all around the grain stack.
Having chopped, he rejoices,
generating the thought that he has successfully killed her.
His mother subsequently emerges from the grain stack,
and returns home.
What do you think?
Has this person achieved the Avīci sin?"
"No,
Shìzūn!
It cannot be definitively said.
Why?
If we say there is a sin,
the mother's body ought to have been destroyed.
If the body is not destroyed,
how can we say the sin exists?
If we say there is no sin,
he generated the thought of having killed her,
and rejoiced in his heart.
How can we say the sin is non-existent?
Although this person did not completely fulfill the unpardonable sin,
it is still considered unpardonable intent.
Due to these circumstances,
various analogies are introduced
to understand the true Dharma."
The Fó praised Jiāshè:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
Because of these circumstances,
I speak of various skillful analogies
to illustrate liberation.
Although I use immeasurable Asaṃkhyeya analogies,
in reality, analogies cannot be used for comparison.
In some cases, due to circumstances, it can be expressed through analogy;
in other cases, due to circumstances, it cannot be expressed through analogy.
Therefore, liberation achieves such immeasurable merit and virtue.
Those who approach Níèpán,
Níèpán,
and the Rúlái
also possess such immeasurable merit and virtue.
Because such immeasurable merit and virtue
is fully realized,
it is called the Great Níèpán."
Bodhisattva Jiāshè said to the Fó:
"Shìzūn!
Now I finally know
that the place to which the Rúlái attains
is inexhaustible.
If the place is inexhaustible,
then one should know that his lifespan must also be inexhaustible."
The Fó said:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
You are now well able to guard and uphold the True Dharma.
If there are good men
or good women who wish to sever the vexations and all bonds,
they should guard and uphold the True Dharma in this way.
"Good men!
In this profound scripture, the Dà Nièpán Wēimiào Jīng,
there are four types of people
who can protect the Right Dharma (Zhèng Fǎ),
establish the Right Dharma,
remember the Right Dharma,
and greatly benefit and pity the world,
serving as the reliance for the world and bringing peace and happiness to humans and devas.
What are these four?
The person who appears in the world possessing the nature of afflictions is named the first;
the Xu-tuó-yuán (Śrotaāpanna) person
and the Sī-tuó-hán (Sakṛdāgāmin) person are named the second;
the Ā-nà-hán (Anāgāmin) person is named the third;
the Ā-luó-hàn (Arhat) person is named the fourth.
When these four types of people appear in the world,
they can greatly benefit and pity the world,
serving as the reliance for the world and bringing peace and happiness to humans and devas.
"What is meant by possessing the nature of afflictions?
If there is a person who can observe the precepts,
whose demeanor is complete,
who establishes the Right Dharma,
having heard it from the Buddha,
understands its words and meaning,
and proclaims and explains it to others,
stating that having few desires is the Way,
and having many desires is not the Way,
extensively explaining the Eight Realizations of Great Beings (Bā Dàrén Jué) thus,
and instructing those who have transgressed to confess,
repent and eliminate their faults,
and who is skilled in knowing the secret methods practiced by Bodhisattvas (Púsà)—
this is called a common mortal (Fánfū),
not the eighth person (Bā Dì Rén).
That eighth person,
is not called a common mortal,
but is called a Bodhisattva,
and is not called a Buddha.
"The second type of person is named Xu-tuó-yuán
and Sī-tuó-hán.
If they attain the Right Dharma,
uphold the Right Dharma,
hear the Dharma from the Buddha,
in accordance with what they heard,
write it down after hearing it,
receive, uphold, read, and recite it,
and transmit it to others.
If, having heard the Dharma,
they do not write it down or receive it,
do not uphold it or speak it,
and yet say that it is permissible for the Buddha to keep slaves, maids, or impure things—
there is no such case.
This is called the second person.
Such a person, though having not attained the second
or third stage (zhùchù),
is called a Bodhisattva,
and has already received a prediction (shòujì).
"The third type of person is named Ā-nà-hán.
The Ā-nà-hán
slanders the Right Dharma if they say it is permissible to keep slaves,
servants,
impure things,
or if they receive and uphold heterodox (wàidào) scriptures
and treatises,
or are hindered by adventitious defilements (kèchén fánnǎo),
or are covered by all former afflictions,
or if they hide the Tathāgata's (Rúlái) true relics (shèlì),
or are harmed by external diseases,
or are attacked by the four great poisonous snakes (sì dà dú shé),
or discuss and assert the existence of self (wǒ)—
none of these cases exist;
but if they speak of non-self (wú wǒ),
this case exists.
If they speak of attachment to worldly dharmas,
there is no such case;
but if they speak of the uninterrupted continuity of the Great Vehicle (Dàchéng),
this case exists.
If they say that the body they have received contains eighty thousand worms,
there is no such case;
if they permanently depart from sexual desire, so that even in dreams they do not lose purity,
this case exists.
If they experience fear on the day of death,
there is no such case.
What is meant by Ā-nà-hán?
This person does not return (bù hái).
All the faults and failings mentioned above
can never defile his going forth and circling about.
They are called a Bodhisattva,
having already received a prediction,
and will soon achieve Anouduoluò Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi).
This is therefore called the third person.
"The fourth person is named Ā-luó-hàn.
The Ā-luó-hàn
cuts off all afflictions,
abandons the heavy burden,
attains their own benefit,
what was to be done is already accomplished (suǒ zuò yǐ bàn),
dwells on the Tenth Stage (Dì shí Dì),
and attains the Wisdom of Sovereignty (zìzài zhì);
according to what people desire, various forms and appearances
can all be manifested;
having adorned himself thus, wishing to accomplish the path to Buddhahood,
he is immediately able to accomplish it.
One who can accomplish such immeasurable merits
is named an Ā-luó-hàn.
These four are named the people who appear in the world,
who can greatly benefit and pity the world,
serving as the reliance for the world and bringing peace and happiness to humans and devas,
being the most venerable and supreme among humans and devas,
just like the Tathāgata,
named the Supreme One among men,
serving as a place of refuge (guīyī chù)."
Kāyè (Kāśyapa) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
I now do not rely upon these four types of people.
Why is this?
Just as in the Qúshīluó Jīng,
the Buddha spoke to Qúshīluó, saying:
'If the heavenly Māra (Mó), or Brahmā (Fàn), wishing to cause destruction,
transform into the image of a Buddha,
fully adorned with the thirty-two major marks (sānshí'èr xiàng)
and the eighty minor characteristics (bāshí zhǒng hǎo),
with a halo spanning one fathom,
and a face round and bright like the full moon,
the white hair mark (háo xiāng) between the eyebrows whiter than shell and snow—
if such an adorned figure approaches you,
you must examine and ascertain whether it is real or false.
Once you have become aware,
you should subjugate them.'
World-Honored One!
If Māra and others can still transform into the body of a Buddha,
how much more easily can they create the bodies of the four types of beings, such as the Arhats (Luóhàn),
sitting or lying down in the sky,
emitting water from the left side,
emitting fire from the right side,
smoke and flames coming from the body,
like a mass of fire?
For this reason,
my mind
does not give rise to faith in them.
Even if they speak something,
I cannot accept it,
nor do I hold them in reverence,
or take them as a place of reliance."
The Buddha said:
"Good men!
If you entertain doubt regarding what I have taught,
you still should not accept it,
much less things such as these.
Therefore, you should skillfully distinguish and know
what is good
and what is not good,
what is permissible to do
and what is impermissible to do.
Having acted in this way,
you will receive happiness throughout the long night (cháng yè).
Good men!
Just as a thieving dog
enters a person's house at night,
if the servants or maids of the household realize it,
they should immediately drive it out and scold it:
'You quickly get out!
If you do not get out,
we shall take your life.'
The thieving dog hears this
and leaves immediately, never returning.
You, from now on,
should also subjugate Poxún (Pāpīyān) in this manner,
and you should say this:
'Poxún!
You should not create such an image now.
If you persist in doing so,
we shall bind you
with the Five Bonds (wǔ jì).'
When Māra hears this,
he will return and leave,
just like that thieving dog,
and will not return again."
Kāyè addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha spoke to the elder Qúshīluó,
if one can thus subjugate Māra,
one can also approach the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Bō Nièpán).
Why does the Tathāgata necessarily say that these four people are places of reliance?
The words spoken
by these four people
are not necessarily reliable."
Jiāshè (Kāśyapa):
"Good man!
What I have taught
is indeed
just so, and is not otherwise.
Good man!
I stated that one must subdue Māra
for the Śrāvakas
and those with the flesh eye,
but I did not say this for those who practice the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).
Although the Śrāvakas
possess the heavenly eye, they are still called those with the flesh eye.
Those who study the Great Vehicle,
even if they only have the flesh eye, are called those with the Buddha eye.
Why is this?
This Mahāyāna Sūtra is called the Buddha Vehicle,
and this Buddha Vehicle is the most supreme and excellent.
Good man!
For instance, if there is a person who is brave, strong, and formidable,
weak-willed individuals constantly come to rely upon him.
The brave and strong person always instructs the weak ones:
'You should hold the bow and grip the arrows in this manner,
and study the ways of the spear,
the long hook,
and the snare.'
Moreover, he tells them:
'When fighting a battle,
even if it is like treading on a blade,
you should not give rise to thoughts of fear and dread.
You should regard humans and gods as weak and trivial,
and you should internally cultivate thoughts of bravery and strength.
Sometimes, there are people
who naturally lack courage, but falsely display signs of strength,
holding bows and swords
and various weapons,
adorning themselves,
coming into the formation,
shouting and yelling loudly.
Regarding these people,
you also should not give rise to worry or fear.
When such people,
if they see you and are not afraid,
you should know that they will soon collapse and be scattered,
like a thieving dog.
Good man!
The Tathāgata is also like this,
instructing the Śrāvakas:
'You should not fear Māra Bōxún.
If Māra Bōxún transforms himself into the body of a Buddha
and comes to you,
you must diligently strengthen your mind
and subdue Māra.'
At that time, Māra will immediately become distressed
and unhappy, and will return the way he came and depart.
Good man!
Just as that strong person does not learn from others,
those who study the Great Vehicle are also like this;
upon hearing various profound and secret sūtras,
their hearts rejoice and they are not struck by fear.
Why is this?
Because such people who practice the Great Vehicle
have previously made offerings to,
respected,
and bowed before immeasurable billions of Buddhas of the past;
thus, even if immeasurable billions of thousands of Māra hosts wish to come and harass them,
in this matter, they will ultimately not be alarmed or afraid.
Good man!
For instance, if a person obtains the Ājiétuó (Agada) medicine,
they fear nothing.
Poisonous snakes and the like fear the power of this medicine,
which can also neutralize all poisons and the like.
This Mahāyāna Sūtra is also like this;
like the power of that medicine, it fears no poisons of Māra,
and can also subdue them so they do not arise again.
"Furthermore, good man!
For example, there is a nāga (dragon)
whose nature is extremely jealous and ill-tempered.
When it wishes to harm someone,
it either looks at them with its eyes
or exhales its breath.
Therefore, all lions,
tigers and leopards,
jackals and wolves,
dogs and hounds
all become terrified. These evil beasts,
whether they hear its sound or see its form,
or touch its body,
none fail to lose their lives.
A skilled incantation master, by the power of his incantation,
can make all such evil poisonous nāgas,
Garuḍas (Jīnchìniǎo) and the like,
vicious elephants and lions,
tigers, leopards, and jackals
all well-tamed and docile,
suitable for riding and driving.
Such beasts
are immediately subdued
upon seeing that skilled incantation master.
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas
are also like this: seeing Māra Bōxún, they all give rise to fear,
but Māra Bōxún, in turn, does not give rise to a mind of fear,
and continues performing his Māra deeds.
Those who study the Great Vehicle
are also like this: seeing all the Śrāvakas fearing the deeds of Māra,
and not giving rise to faith and joy in this Great Vehicle,
they first use skillful means to subdue all the Māras,
making them all well-tamed and suitable for riding,
and thus extensively preach various wonderful Dharma.
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
having seen the Māras tamed, are no longer afraid,
and only then give rise to faith and joy
in this unsurpassed true Dharma of the Great Vehicle,
speaking thus:
'From now on, we should not create obstacles
within this true Dharma.'
"Furthermore, good man! Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas
give rise to fear toward all afflictions,
but those who study the Great Vehicle have no fear at all; practicing the Great Vehicle possesses such power.
For this reason, what was stated earlier
was intended to make those Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas subdue all Māras,
and was not for the Great Vehicle itself.
This subtle Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa
cannot be dissolved or subdued;
it is extremely wondrous and extraordinary.
If there is someone who hears it,
and having heard it, believes and accepts it,
and can believe that the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma,
such a person is extremely rare,
like the Udumbara (Yōután) flower.
After my Nirvāṇa,
if there is someone who manages to hear such a subtle Sūtra of the Great Vehicle
and gives rise to faith and reverence,
you should know that these people, in future ages of hundreds of thousands of koṭis (billions) of kalpas,
will not fall into evil paths.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Bodhisattva Jiāshè:
"Good man!
After my Nirvāṇa, there will be hundreds of thousands of immeasurable sentient beings
who slander and disbelieve
this subtle Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa." Bodhisattva Jiāshè
again said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One! How long after the Buddha’s passing
will these beings begin to slander this Sūtra?
World-Honored One!
What kind of purely virtuous sentient beings
will then be able to rescue these slanderers of the Dharma?"
The Buddha addressed Jiāshè:
"Good man!
For forty years after my Parinirvāṇa,
this Sūtra will widely circulate in Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí),
and only then will it gradually vanish into the ground.
Good man!
For instance, wherever
sugarcane,
rice,
rock candy,
milk-curd (sū), or clarified butter (tíhú) exists,
the people of that land
all say that this flavor
is the finest
among flavors.
Or, there might be people who subsist purely on millet and wild grain (bàizi);
these people also say that what they eat
is the finest.
This is because these people of meager merit are receiving karmic retribution.
But if they are people of great merit,
their ears have never heard the names of millet or wild grain;
what they eat consists solely of fine grain (jīngliáng),
sugarcane,
rock candy,
and clarified butter.
This subtle Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa
is also like this: those with dull faculties and meager merit do not enjoy hearing it,
just like those people of meager merit
who despise fine grain and rock candy and the like.
People of the Two Vehicles
are also like this: they despise the unsurpassed Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra.
However, there are sentient beings whose hearts happily desire to hear and receive this Sūtra;
having heard it, they rejoice
and do not give rise to slander,
just like those people of great merit
who eat fine rice and grain."
"Good man!
For example, there is a king,
who lives in the mountains, in a place of danger, difficulty, and evil (harsh environment).
Although he possesses sugarcane,
rice provisions (*dàoliáng*),
and rock candy (*shímì*),
because they are hard to obtain,
he covetously treasures and accumulates them,
daring not to consume them,
fearing that they might run out,
and only eats millet and weeds.
Another king from a different country hears of this and pities him and laughs.
He immediately loads rice provisions (*dàoliáng*) onto carts,
along with sugarcane, and sends them to him.
When that king receives them,
he immediately distributes them,
and the entire country eats together.
Once the people have eaten,
they all generate joy,
and universally say this:
'Because of that king,
we were allowed to obtain this rare food.'
Good man!
These four types of people are also like this.
Being the general (leader) of this unsurpassed great Dharma,
among these four types, there may be one person,
who sees immeasurable *Púsà* (Bodhisattvas) in other directions (lands).
Although they study such great *Mahāyāna* scriptures,
whether they transcribe them themselves,
or have others transcribe them,
for the sake of material gain,
for the sake of fame and praise,
for the sake of discerning the Dharma,
for the sake of reliance,
or for the sake of exchanging them for other scriptures,
they cannot widely proclaim them for others.
Therefore, [this person] takes these subtle scriptures,
sends them to that direction and gives them to those *Púsà*,
causing them to generate the mind of unsurpassed *Pútí* (Bodhi),
and abide in *Pútí*.
When those *Púsà* have obtained these scriptures,
they immediately widely expound them for others,
causing immeasurable multitudes to receive the flavor of this great *Mahāyāna* Dharma.
This is all due to the power of that one *Púsà*,
causing scriptures previously unheard to be heard by all,
just like those people,
who obtained rare food due to the power of the king.
Furthermore, good man!
Where this subtle scripture, the Great *Nièpán* Classic (*Dà Nièpán Wēimiào Jīngdiǎn*), is circulated and spread,
know that the ground there is *Jīngāng* (Vajra/Diamond),
and the people therein are also like *Jīngāng*.
If there is anyone who can listen to such a scripture,
they immediately attain non-retrogression toward *Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí* (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi).
All their wishes will be fulfilled,
just as I proclaim today.
You *Bǐqiū* (monks) should receive and uphold [this Dharma] well.
If there are sentient beings who cannot hear such a scripture,
know that such people are truly pitiable.
Why is that?
Because these people cannot receive and uphold the extremely profound meaning of this great *Mahāyāna* scripture."
*Jiāyè Púsà* (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva) said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*)!
During the forty years following the *Rúlái's* (Tathāgata's) passing,
this great *Mahāyāna* classic, the Great *Nièpán* Sūtra (*Dà Nièpán Jīng*), will be widely practiced and circulated throughout *Yánfútí* (Jambudvīpa).
After this time, [when the sūtra] sinks into the ground,
how long until it reappears?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
When eighty years remain of My True Dharma (*Zhèngfǎ*),
during the first forty years,
this sūtra will again, in *Yánfútí*,
rain the great Dharma rain."
*Jiāyè Púsà* (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva) again said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
When such a scripture,
when the True Dharma (*Zhèngfǎ*) is extinguished,
when the True Precepts (*Zhèngjiè*) are destroyed,
when non-Dharma increases,
when there are no beings suitable for the Dharma,
who will be able to listen and receive,
devoutly uphold,
read and chant it,
making it proficiently understood,
make offerings and show reverence,
transcribe and explain it?
We only wish that the *Rúlái* (Tathāgata),
out of compassion for sentient beings,
clearly distinguishes and extensively explains,
causing all *Púsà* (Bodhisattvas), having heard it, to receive and uphold it,
and having upheld it, immediately attain the non-retrogressing mind of *Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*."
At that time, the Buddha praised *Jiāyè* (Kāśyapa):
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
You are now very capable of asking about this meaning.
Good man!
If there are sentient beings who,
generated the *Pútí* mind before as many Buddhas as the sands of the *Xīlián Hé* (Hiraṇyavatī River),
then they will be able, in this evil age, to receive and uphold such a scripture,
and not generate slander.
Good man!
If there is one who can generate the *Pútí* mind before as many *Fó Shìzūn* (Buddha World-Honored Ones) as the sands of one *Hénghé Shā* (Ganges River),
only then will they be able, in the evil age,
not to slander this Dharma,
and to love and delight in this classic,
but they will not be able to clearly distinguish and extensively explain it for others.
Good man!
If there are sentient beings who generated the *Pútí* mind before as many Buddhas as the sands of two *Hénghé Shā*,
only then will they be able, in the evil age, not to slander this Dharma,
understand it correctly, believe in it and delight in it,
receive, uphold, read, and chant it,
but also cannot extensively explain it for others.
If there are sentient beings who generated the *Pútí* mind before as many Buddhas as the sands of three *Hénghé Shā*,
only then will they be able, in the evil age, not to slander this Dharma,
receive, uphold, read, chant, and transcribe the scripture scrolls,
though they speak it for others,
they have not understood the profound meaning.
If there are sentient beings who generated the *Pútí* mind before as many Buddhas as the sands of four *Hénghé Shā*,
only then will they be able, in the evil age, not to slander this Dharma,
receive, uphold, read, chant, and transcribe the scripture scrolls,
and extensively speak for others one part of the meaning out of sixteen parts,
although they expound it, it is still not complete.
If there are sentient beings who generated the *Pútí* mind before as many Buddhas as the sands of five *Hénghé Shā*,
only then will they be able, in the evil age, not to slander this Dharma,
receive, uphold, read, chant, and transcribe the scripture scrolls,
and extensively speak for others eight parts of the meaning out of sixteen parts.
If there are sentient beings who generated the *Pútí* mind before as many Buddhas as the sands of six *Hénghé Shā*,
only then will they be able, in the evil age, not to slander this Dharma,
receive, uphold, read, chant, and transcribe the scripture scrolls,
and extensively speak for others twelve parts of the meaning out of sixteen parts.
If there are sentient beings who generated the *Pútí* mind before as many Buddhas as the sands of seven *Hénghé Shā*,
only then will they be able, in the evil age, not to slander this Dharma,
receive, uphold, read, chant, and transcribe the scripture scrolls,
and extensively speak for others fourteen parts of the meaning out of sixteen parts.
If there are sentient beings who generated the *Pútí* mind before as many Buddhas as the sands of eight *Hénghé Shā*,
only then will they be able, in the evil age, not to slander this Dharma,
receive, uphold, read, chant, and transcribe the scripture scrolls,
and also encourage others to transcribe them,
personally being able to listen and receive it,
and further encouraging others to listen and receive it,
and read and chant it proficiently,
protecting and steadfastly maintaining it out of compassion for all sentient beings in the world.
They make offerings to this sūtra,
and also encourage others to make offerings, be reverent, respect, read, chant, and prostrate before it.
Moreover, they are like this:
they are completely able to understand,
exhausting its flavor and meaning,
which is to say that the *Rúlái* (Tathāgata) is eternally abiding and unchanging,
and ultimately tranquil and blissful.
They widely proclaim that all sentient beings completely possess *Fóxìng* (Buddha Nature),
and skillfully know all the Dharma Treasury (*Fǎzàng*) of the *Rúlái*.
Having made offerings to all such Buddhas,
they establish such unsurpassed True Dharma,
receiving, upholding, and protecting it.
If there is one who initially generates the mind of *Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*,
know that this person, in future ages,
will certainly be able to establish such True Dharma,
receiving, upholding, and protecting it.
Therefore, you should not be ignorant now [as to]
who the protector of the Dharma will be in future ages.
Why is that?
The one who generates the initial mind, in the future age,
will certainly be able to protect and uphold the unsurpassed True Dharma."
"Good son!
There are evil Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū),
who, hearing of my Nirvāṇa (Nièpán), feel no sorrow:
'Today the Tathāgata (Rúlái) enters Parinirvāṇa (Bōnnirèpán).
How timely and delightful!
While the Tathāgata was in the world,
he obstructed our gains.
Now that he enters Nirvāṇa,
who will again be there to obstruct and take them away from us?
If there is no one to obstruct and take them,
we shall regain the offerings and gains we originally had.
While the Tathāgata was in the world, the prohibitions (Jìnjiè) were strict.
Now that he enters Nirvāṇa,
we can totally disregard them.
The kaṣāya (jiāshā) robes received were originally meant for the Dharma standard,
but now they should be discarded and ruined, like wooden banners.'
Such people slander
and defy these Mahāyāna (Dàshèng) sūtras.
Good son!
You should now remember this:
if there are sentient beings who achieve and fulfill measureless merit (gōngdé),
only then can they believe in these Mahāyāna classics,
and having believed, accept and uphold them.
As for other sentient beings who delight in the Dharma,
if one can extensively explain and teach this Sūtra for them,
once those people hear it,
the evil karma (èyè) they created throughout measureless Asaṃkhyeya (Āsēngqí) kalpas (jié) in the past,
will all be eliminated and destroyed.
If there are those who do not believe in this Sūtra,
in their present life they will be afflicted and harmed by measureless sickness and suffering,
often insulted and reviled by the multitude,
after death they will be despised and held cheap by others,
their appearance will be ugly,
their means of livelihood will be difficult,
they will constantly lack sufficiency.
Even if they obtain a little, it will be coarse, rough, worn out, and poor.
Life after life they will constantly dwell among poverty,
meanness,
slandering the Correct Dharma (Zhèngfǎ),
or in families holding wicked views (xiéjiàn).
If, when approaching death,
they encounter famine and chaos,
where weapons and war arise,
where emperors (dìwáng) are tyrannical,
or are persecuted and oppressed by enemies (yuānjiā) and adversaries,
although they have good friends,
they will not encounter them.
What they require for livelihood they seek but cannot obtain.
Though they may obtain minor gains,
they constantly suffer from hunger and thirst.
They are only recognized and regarded by common and lowly people.
Kings (guówáng) and great ministers (dàchén) will not acknowledge them at all.
Even if they hear what such a person proclaims or explains,
even if it is reasonable,
they will ultimately not believe or accept it.
Such a person will not reach a good destination.
Just like a broken-winged bird cannot fly,
