this person is also like that in future lives;
they cannot attain the good destinations of humans or devas (tiān).
Furthermore, if there is a person who can believe in such Mahāyāna classics,
although the form they originally received was coarse and ugly,
by the merit of the Sūtra, they immediately become upright and handsome.
Their majestic color and strength
daily increases even more.
They are constantly sought out and happily seen by humans and devas,
reverenced and loved,
with hearts unwilling to abandon them.
Kings, great ministers, and their household relatives, upon hearing what they say,
all respectfully believe.
Among my Śrāvaka (Shēngwén) disciples,
whoever wishes to perform the foremost, rare deed,
ought to widely proclaim these Mahāyāna classics for the world.
"Good son!
Just as mist and dew,
though they seem inclined to stay,
cannot last beyond the sunrise.
Once the sun has risen,
they vanish without a trace.
Good son!
The evil karma possessed by all these sentient beings,
is also like this.
The power by which they persist in the world
cannot last beyond seeing the sun of the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
Once this sun has risen,
it can eliminate and destroy all evil karma.
"Furthermore, good son!
For instance, if a person leaves home and shaves their head,
although they wear the kaṣāya,
they have not yet received the ten precepts of a Śrāmaṇera (Shāmí).
If a householder (zhǎngzhě) comes to invite the Saṅgha (Sēng),
the one who has not yet received the precepts
immediately accepts the invitation together with the assembly.
Although they have not yet received the precepts,
they are already counted as part of the Saṅgha.
Good son!
If there are sentient beings
who initially arouse the mind to study this Mahāyāna text, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Nièpán Jīng),
writing it down, upholding it, reading and reciting it, it is also like this.
Although they have not fully attained the stage of the Ten Abodes (Shízhù),
they are already counted among the Ten Abodes.
Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who are disciples of the Buddha or not disciples,
whether due to greed or fear,
or for the sake of offerings and gain,
listen to and accept this Sūtra, even a single verse,
and having heard it, do not slander it—
know that this person is already close to Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).
Good son!
Due to these causes and conditions,
I say that four people are the reliance of the world.
Good son!
Concerning these four people,
to take what the Buddha spoke
and say it was not spoken by the Buddha,
there is no such possibility.
Therefore, I say that these four people are the reliance of the world.
Good son!
You should make offerings to these four people."
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
How shall I recognize these people
and make offerings to them?"
The Buddha (Fó) told Kāśyapa (Jiāyè):
"If there is one who establishes
and protects and upholds the Correct Dharma,
such a person should be sought out and invited.
You should make offerings to them, even at the cost of your body and life,
just as I have explained in this Mahāyāna Sūtra."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva (Jiāyè Púsà) said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has stated,
making offerings to teachers and elders should indeed be like this.
Now I have some doubts, and I only wish you would elaborate.
If there is a long-standing practitioner who protects and upholds the prohibitions,
and consults a young practitioner to receive teachings he has not heard,
should this elder person pay respects and venerate him or not?
If he pays respects and venerates him,
then he cannot be called an upholder of the precepts (Chíjiè).
If a young person protects and upholds the prohibitions,
and consults long-standing practitioners who have broken the precepts (Pòjiè) to receive teachings he has not heard,
should he again pay respects or not?
If a person who has left home (Chūjiārén)
consults a lay person (Zàijiārén) to receive teachings he has not heard,
should he again pay respects or not?
However, those who have left home should not pay respects and venerate lay people.
Nevertheless, in the Buddha’s Dharma, the young and junior practitioners ought to respect the elderly and long-standing practitioners,
because these long-standing practitioners received the full precepts (Jùjiè) earlier,
and accomplished dignified conduct.
Therefore, they ought to be offered to and venerated.
Moreover, the Buddha said:
'Those who have broken the precepts
are not tolerated within the Buddha's Dharma,
just like a good field filled with weeds and tares.'
Furthermore, the Buddha also said:
'Whoever knows the Dharma,
whether old or young,
should be offered to as if serving Śakra (Dìshì).'
What is the meaning
of these two statements?
Could it be that the Tathāgata spoke falsely?
Also, the Buddha said:
'A Bhikṣu who upholds the precepts also commits minor offenses.'
Why did the Tathāgata make this statement?
The World-Honored One also said in other sūtras that one is permitted to expel those who break the precepts.
Such statements,
their meaning is not yet clear."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son!
I spoke such verses for the sake of future Bodhisattvas and those who study the Mahāyāna,
not for the sake of Śrāvaka disciples.
Good son!
As I previously stated,
when the Correct Dharma is extinguished,
and the correct precepts are destroyed,
the breaking of precepts will increase.
When incorrect Dharma flourishes,
when all noble ones (shèngrén) are hidden and do not appear,
and when Bhikṣus keep slaves, maidservants, and impure possessions,
among these four people,
there will be one person appearing in the world,
shaving beard and hair,
leaving home to cultivate the Dao (Dào).
He sees that the various Bhikṣus each keep and raise slaves,
servants,
and impure possessions.
They know nothing of what is pure or impure.
They likewise do not recognize what is Vinaya (Lǜ) and what is not Vinaya.
This person, wanting to tame and subdue these Bhikṣus,
shares the same light with them,
but does not mingle with their dust (impurity).
He is well able to distinguish his own practice
and the practice of the Buddha.
Although he sees that these people commit Pārājika (Bōluóyí) offenses,
he remains silent and does not expose them.
Why is that?
I appeared in the world
to establish and protect and uphold the Correct Dharma.
Therefore, he remains silent and does not expose their faults.
Good son!
Such a person, for the sake of protecting the Dharma,
although he commits minor offenses,
is not called one who has broken the precepts."
"Shànnánzǐ!
If there is a king who dies of illness,
and the crown prince is young,
not yet able to succeed the throne.
There is a Caṇḍāla (Zhāntuóluó),
abundant in wealth and treasures,
immeasurably rich,
with many dependents,
who, relying on his own strength,
takes advantage of the country's weakness and usurps the royal position.
Not long after he begins to rule,
the people of the country,
the householders (Jūshì),
the Brahmins (Póluómén), and others,
flee and desert,
running far away to other countries.
Although some remain,
they do not even wish to look upon this king.
Or there are elders (Zhǎngzhě),
Brahmins, and others who do not leave their native land,
just like trees that, wherever they grow,
die right there.
The Caṇḍāla King,
knowing that many of his countrymen have fled and deserted,
immediately sends back his Caṇḍālas to guard and patrol the various roads.
Furthermore, for seven days,
he beats the drum and proclaims:
'All you Brahmins,
if there is anyone who can serve me as an abhiseka (guàndǐng) master,
I shall reward him with half of the kingdom as a noble rank.'
When the Brahmins heard this proclamation,
none came,
each saying:
'Where would one find a Brahmin descendant
to perform such a task?'
The Caṇḍāla King said again:
'If there is not a single person among the Brahmins to be my master,
I will surely make all Brahmins
live and dine together with the Caṇḍālas,
sharing their tasks;
but if someone can come and consecrate my crown,
the enfeoffment of half the kingdom—
this promise is not false.
The supreme sweet dew (gānlù) of the Trayastriṃśa heaven (Sānshísāntiān) achieved by magic spells (zhùshù),
the medicine of immortality,
shall also be shared and consumed together.'
"At that time, there was a son of a Brahmin,
young in age (at twenty),
cultivating pure conduct,
with long hair as his mark,
skilled in magic spells,
who went to the king's residence
and said:
'Great King!
The tasks you have commanded
I am fully capable of performing.'
At that time, the great king's heart was filled with joy,
and he accepted this youth as his abhiseka master.
When the Brahmins heard of this matter,
they were all enraged,
blaming the youth:
'You Brahmin,
how can you act as a Caṇḍāla's master?'
At that time, the king,
immediately divided half the kingdom and gave it to the youth,
and consequently ruled the country together
for a long period.
At that time, the youth said to the king:
'I abandoned the traditions of my family
to come and be the king's master,
and furthermore, I taught the Great King subtle and secret magic spells (zhùshù).
Yet now, Great King,
you still do not treat me as an intimate.'
Then the king replied:
'How is it that I do not treat you as an intimate?'
The youth replied:
'The medicine of immortality possessed by the former king
has not yet been shared and consumed.'
The king said:
'Excellent!
Excellent!
Great Master!
I truly did not know this.
If the Master requires it,
please take it away.'
At this time, the youth,
having heard the king's words,
immediately took it and returned home,
inviting the various ministers to consume it together.
After the ministers had consumed it,
they all reported to the king:
'How wonderful!
The Great Master
possesses this sweet dew (gānlù), the medicine of immortality!'
When the king knew this,
he spoke to his master:
'How is it, Great Master, that you alone consumed the sweet dew (gānlù) with the ministers,
without giving me a share?'
At that time, the youth,
then took the remaining poisoned medicine
and gave it to the king to take.
Once the king had taken it,
the poison immediately took effect,
causing him to become delirious, fall down,
losing all consciousness,
just like a dead person.
At that time, the youth installed the original crown prince,
returning him to the position of king,
and said thus:
'The lion seat (Shīzǐ Guòzuò)
should not rightfully be ascended by a Caṇḍāla (Zhāntuóluó).
Since ancient times,
I have never heard or seen a Caṇḍāla descendant become a king;
for a Caṇḍāla to govern the country and rule the people
is simply not right.
You should now return,
succeed the former king,
and govern the country with the True Dharma (Zhèngfǎ).'
At that time, the youth, having managed this situation,
then gave the antidote to the Caṇḍāla,
causing him to wake up.
Once he was awake,
he drove him out of the country.
Although the youth had performed this deed,
he still did not lose the traditions of the Brahmins (Póluómén Fǎ).
The remaining householders (Jūshì),
Brahmins, and others,
hearing what he had done, praised it as unprecedented,
saying in praise:
'Excellent!
Excellent!
Benevolent one!
You skillfully drove away the Caṇḍāla King.'
"Shànnánzǐ!
After my Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
the Bodhisattvas (Púsàs) who uphold the True Dharma (Zhèngfǎ),
will also act in the same way.
Using the power of skillful means (fāngbiàn),
they will associate in their undertakings
with monks who violate the precepts, falsely named, and accept and keep all impure objects.
At that time, if a Bodhisattva sees someone who, although having violated many precepts,
can discipline those wicked Bhikṣus (Bǐqiūs) who destroy the prohibitions,
he will immediately go to that person,
respectfully worship him,
offer him the four necessities (sì shì gòngyǎng),
and present him with all scriptures and material possessions;
if he himself lacks them,
he must use skillful means
to seek them from various donors (tányuès) and give them to that person.
Because of this task,
he should accept and keep the eight kinds of impure objects.
Why is this?
This person disciplines the wicked Bhikṣus,
just as that youth drove away the Caṇḍāla.
At that time, although the Bodhisattva respectfully worships this person,
and accepts and keeps the eight kinds of impure objects,
he is entirely without sin.
Why is this?
Because this Bodhisattva seeks to expel and discipline the wicked Bhikṣus,
allowing the pure saṅgha (sēng) to dwell in peace and security,
propagating the Vaipulya (Fāngděng) Mahāyāna (Dàshèng) Sūtras,
and benefiting all devas (tiān) and humans.
Shànnánzǐ!
Due to this reason,
I spoke these two verses (jì) in the Sūtra,
causing all Bodhisattvas to praise the upholders of the Dharma,
just as the householders (Jūshì) and Brahmins praised the youth:
'Excellent!
Excellent!'
The Bodhisattvas who uphold the Dharma should indeed act in this manner.
If anyone sees an upholder of the Dharma
engaging in the same tasks as a violator of the precepts,
and says that person is guilty,
know that this person will suffer the consequences himself.
That upholder of the Dharma truly has no sin.
Shànnánzǐ!
If a Bhikṣu violates the prohibitions and precepts,
and due to arrogance (jiāomàn),
conceals and does not repent,
know that this person is called a true violator of the precepts.
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà), for the sake of upholding the Dharma,
although having committed an offense, is not called a violator of the precepts.
Why is this?
Because he lacks arrogance,
confesses, and repents.
Shànnánzǐ!
Therefore, I concealed the meaning in the Sūtra
and spoke such verses (jì):
"For this reason,
I did not speak these verses
for those who study the Śrāvaka (Shēngwén) path, but only for the Bodhisattvas."
The Bodhisattva Kāyè (Jiāyè) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
These kinds of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas,
being extremely lax concerning the precepts,
do their originally received precepts remain completely intact?"
The Fó said:
“Good man!
You should not speak in this manner now.
Why is this?
The precepts originally received
are not fundamentally lost;
if there is any offense committed,
one should immediately repent,
and having repented, be pure.
Good man!
It is like an old embankment,
if holes are punctured through it,
water will leak out.
Why is this?
Because no one repairs it.
If someone repairs it,
the water will not escape.
Púsas are also like this;
though they perform Bùsà together with those who have broken the precepts,
receive precepts, Zìzī,
and participate in their Saṅgha affairs.
All their precepts
are not like the leakage from holes punctured in an embankment.
Why is this?
If there are no pure precept-holders,
the Saṅgha will decline,
and pride, negligence, and laziness will grow daily.
If there are pure precept-holders,
they are then able to perfectly maintain the original precepts without losing them.
Good man!
One who is negligent concerning the Vehicle is called negligent;
one who is negligent concerning the precepts is not called negligent.
The Púsa Móhēsà, concerning this Great Vehicle,
whose mind is neither lax nor arrogant,
this is called maintaining the original precepts.
In order to protect the True Dharma,
they bathe themselves with the water of the Great Vehicle.
Therefore, even if a Púsa appears to have broken precepts,
they are not called negligent.
Jiāshè Púsa said to the Fó:
“Among the members of the Saṅgha, there are four kinds of people,
like the Ānluó guǒ (mango) fruit,
whose ripeness is difficult to ascertain.
How can one identify
the precept-breaker and the precept-holder?”
The Fó said:
“Good man!
Through the subtle scripture of the Dà Nièpán,
it is then easily known.
How can this be known through this Dà Nièpán Jīng?
For example, a farmer,
sowing rice and grains,
weeds out the Bàiyòu (tares/weeds).
When observed with the physical eye,
it is called a pure field,
but when they come to fruition,
the grass and grain are distinct.
Similarly, these eight things
can pollute the Saṅgha;
if one is able to eliminate them,
when observed with the physical eye, they are known to be pure.
If there are precept-holders
and precept-breakers,
when they are not committing evil,
it is difficult to distinguish them through the physical eye;
but if the evil is revealed,
it is then easily known,
like those Bàiyòu,
easily distinguished.
It is the same within the Saṅgha:
if one is able to distance themselves from the eight impure, poisonous-snake dharmas,
this is called the pure Field of Merit of the Noble Assembly,
who should be offered to and supported by humans and devas.
The pure retribution
cannot be distinguished by the physical eye.
Furthermore, good man!
It is like the Jiāluókā Lín,
where there are many trees.
In this forest, there is only one tree
named Zhèntóujiā.
The fruit of the Jiāluókā tree
and the fruit of the Zhèntóujiā tree
are similar
and cannot be distinguished.
When the fruit ripened,
a woman
picked all of them up.
The Zhèntóujiā fruit amounted to only one portion,
while the Jiāluókā fruit amounted to ten portions.
The woman did not recognize them,
so she carried them to the market and offered them for sale.
Common, foolish children,
since they could not distinguish them,
bought the Jiāluókā fruit
and died after eating it.
When wise people
heard this matter,
they immediately asked the woman:
‘Sister, from where did you bring these fruits?’
Thereupon, the woman immediately showed them the location,
and the people immediately said:
‘In this location,
there are countless Jiāluókā trees,
but only one root of the Zhèntóujiā tree.’
Having understood this, the people
smiled and departed.
“Good man!
Among the great assembly,
the eight impure dharmas are also like this.
In this assembly, many accept and utilize these eight dharmas,
but only one person is purely holding the precepts,
not accepting these eight impure dharmas,
and knows that these people accept and keep illicit things.
Yet, they work with them and do not separate,
like the one Zhèntóujiā tree in that forest.
If there is an Yōupósè,
seeing that these people possess many illicit things,
they should not respectfully make offerings to them.
If they wish to make offerings,
they should first ask:
‘Venerable Sirs,
as for these eight matters,
do you accept and keep them?
Did the Fó permit them?’
If they say the Fó permitted them,
should such people be allowed to participate in Bùsà and Jiémó Zìzī together?
When this Yōupósè has thus asked,
the assembly all reply:
‘These eight matters,
the Tathāgata, out of compassion,
all permitted us to keep.’
The Yōupósè says:
‘There are Bhikṣus in Qíhuán Jīngshè
who say that the Fó permitted the keeping of gold and silver,
and others who say it was not permitted.
Those who say it is permitted,
those who say it is not permitted will not live together with them,
nor perform the precept recitation or Zìzī,
and they will not even drink water from the same river,
nor share any objects of gain and support.
How can you say that the Fó permitted it?
The Fó,
the God among Gods,
even if he accepts it,
you members of the Saṅgha should still not keep it.
If there is anyone who accepts it,
they should not even perform the precept recitation with them,
nor the Zìzī Jiémó,
nor participate in their Saṅgha affairs.
If they participate in the precept recitation together,
the Zìzī Jiémó,
or the Saṅgha affairs,
upon the end of life they will immediately fall into hell,
just like those people who died
after having eaten the Kālaka fruit.
“Furthermore, good man!
For example, in a city, there is a vendor of medicine.
He has excellent, sweet medicine that comes from Xuě Shān,
but he also sells many other miscellaneous medicines,
the taste of which is similarly sweet.
At that time, various people all wished to buy it,
but could not distinguish them.
They went to the vendor and asked:
‘Do you have Xuě Shān medicine?’
The vendor
immediately replied that he did.
This person was deceitful,
and using other miscellaneous medicines,
he told the buyer:
‘This is the sweet, fine, wonderful Xuě Shān medicine.’
The buyer,
because of their physical eyes, was unable to distinguish them well,
so they bought it and took it away,
and further thought:
‘I have now obtained the sweet Xuě Shān medicine.’
Jiāshè!
If within the Shēngwén Saṅgha,
there are nominal Saṅgha members,
there are true Saṅgha members,
and there are harmonious Saṅgha members,
whether precept-holders
or precept-breakers,
this assembly should be equally offered to,
reverenced, and paid homage to.
The Yōupósè, due to their physical eyes,
cannot distinguish them.
It is analogous to that person
who could not distinguish the sweet Xuě Shān medicine.
Who is a precept-holder?
Who is a precept-breaker?
Who is a true Saṅgha member?
Who is a nominal Saṅgha member?
Only those possessing the celestial eye can distinguish them.
Jiāshè!
If an Yōupósè knows that a certain Bhikṣu is a precept-breaker,
they should not give assistance, pay homage, or make offerings.
If they know that person accepts and keeps the eight dharmas,
they likewise should not give necessary aid, pay homage, or make offerings.
If there are precept-breakers within the Saṅgha,
one should not respectfully pay homage due to the cause of merely wearing the *jiāshā*.
Bodhisattva Jiāyè (Kāśyapa) again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Excellent,
excellent.
What the Rúlái has spoken is true and not false;
I shall receive it upon my head.
It is like a diamond,
a jewel or rare object.
As the Buddha has taught,
these bhikṣus should rely upon the Four Reliances (Sì Fǎ).
What are the four?
Rely on the Dharma, not on the person;
Rely on the meaning, not on the words;
Rely on wisdom, not on consciousness;
Rely on the sūtras of definitive meaning (liǎo yì jīng), not on the sūtras of non-definitive meaning (bù liǎo yì jīng).
Such are the Four Reliances.
One should realize and know them, not relying on four kinds of people."
The Buddha said:
"Good son!
Relying on the Dharma
means the great Mahāparinirvāṇa of the Rúlái.
All Buddhadharma is the nature of the Dharma (fǎxìng);
this nature of the Dharma is the Rúlái.
Therefore, the Rúlái is eternal and immutable.
If anyone says the Rúlái is impermanent,
that person neither knows
nor sees the nature of the Dharma.
If one neither knows nor sees this nature of the Dharma,
one should not rely upon them.
As stated above,
the four kinds of people who appear in the world protecting and upholding the Dharma
should be realized, known, and relied upon.
Why is that?
Because these people skillfully understand the Rúlái's subtle, secret, and profound treasury;
they know that the Rúlái is eternal and immutable.
If one were to say the Rúlái is impermanent and changing,
there would be no such instance.
These four kinds of people are thus named the Rúlái.
Why is that?
Because these people can comprehend the Rúlái's secret language and can articulate it.
If a person can understand the Rúlái's extremely profound secret treasury,
and knows that the Rúlái is eternal and immutable,
it is impossible
for such a person to assert, for the sake of gain and support, that the Rúlái is impermanent.
There is no such instance.
Such a person is still worthy of reliance;
how much more should one rely on these four people?
Relying on the Dharma means the nature of the Dharma (fǎxìng);
not relying on the person means the śrāvakas.
The nature of the Dharma is the Rúlái;
the śrāvakas are conditioned (yǒuwéi).
The Rúlái
is the eternal abiding;
the conditioned is the impermanent.
Good son!
If a person, having broken the precepts, says for the sake of gain and support
that the Rúlái is impermanent and changing,
such a person should not be relied upon.
Good son!
This is called definitive meaning.
"Relying on the meaning (yì) and not on the words (yǔ) means:
Meaning is named Enlightenment and Understanding (juéliǎo);
the meaning of Enlightenment and Understanding is named Non-Weakness or Non-Inferiority (bù léi liè);
Non-Weakness is named Fulfillment (mǎnzú);
the meaning of Fulfillment is the Rúlái's eternal and immutable abiding;
the meaning of the Rúlái's eternal and immutable abiding is the eternity of the Dharma;
the meaning of the eternity of the Dharma is the eternity of the Saṅgha.
This is called relying on the meaning, not on the words.
What kinds of words should not be relied upon?
Namely, various treatises
and ornate literary phrases.
[One should not rely upon words spoken by those who,] even when reciting the countless sūtras spoken by the Buddha,
seek gains insatiably,
are often treacherous, flattering, and deceitful,
falsely pretending to be devoted,
displaying their form to seek benefits,
managing lay people (báiyī) to work for them.
Furthermore, they proclaim:
'The Buddha permits bhikṣus to keep servants and maids,
unclean objects,
gold, silver, jewels,
grain, rice, and storage facilities,
oxen, sheep, elephants, and horses,
and to trade for profit.'
'[They say that] in times of famine, out of compassion for their sons,
the Buddha permits bhikṣus to store up old provisions,
make their own food by hand,
and eat without having received alms.'
Such words should not be relied upon.
"Relying on wisdom (zhì) and not on consciousness (shí) means:
The wisdom spoken of is the Rúlái.
If there are śrāvakas
who cannot skillfully know the Rúlái's merits,
such consciousness should not be relied upon.
If one knows the Rúlái is the Dharma Body (fǎshēn),
such true wisdom should be relied upon.
If one sees the Rúlái's expedient body
and says it is subsumed by the skandhas, dhātus, and āyatanas (yīn jiè zhū rù),
and sustained by food,
one should also not rely on this.
Therefore, consciousness should not be relied upon.
Moreover, if anyone makes such assertions,
their sūtras and writings should also not be relied upon.
"Rely on the sūtras of definitive meaning,
not on the sūtras of non-definitive meaning.
Sūtras of non-definitive meaning
refer to the Śrāvakayāna (shēngwén chéng).
When hearing about the Rúlái Buddha's location of profound secret treasury,
they all give rise to doubts and astonishment,
unaware that this treasury gives rise to the great ocean of wisdom.
This is like an infant who knows nothing distinctly.
This is therefore named non-definitive meaning.
"Definitive meaning is named the Bodhisattva,
whose true wisdom follows their own mind,
possessing unobstructed great wisdom,
like an adult who knows everything.
This is named definitive meaning.
Furthermore, the Śrāvakayāna is named non-definitive meaning;
the unsurpassed Mahāyāna (dàchéng) is named definitive meaning.
If one says the Rúlái is impermanent and changing, it is named non-definitive meaning;
if one says the Rúlái is eternal and immutable, this is named definitive meaning.
What the śrāvakas teach that should be realized and known is named non-definitive meaning;
what the Bodhisattvas teach that should be realized and known is named definitive meaning.
If one says the Rúlái is sustained by food,
this is non-definitive meaning;
if one says the Rúlái is eternal and immutable,
this is named definitive meaning.
If one says the Rúlái enters Nirvāṇa
like a fire being extinguished when the fuel is consumed,
it is named non-definitive meaning;
if one says the Rúlái enters the nature of the Dharma,
this is named definitive meaning.
The teaching of the Śrāvakayāna should not be relied upon.
Why is that?
Because the Rúlái, desiring to liberate sentient beings,
spoke the Śrāvakayāna by the power of skillful means (fāngbiàn lì),
just as an elder teaches his son half a character.
Good son!
The Śrāvakayāna is like the first plowing—
no fruit has yet been obtained.
This is named non-definitive meaning;
therefore, one should not rely on the Śrāvakayāna.
The teaching of the Mahāyāna should be relied upon.
Why is that?
Because the Rúlái, desiring to liberate sentient beings,
spoke the Mahāyāna by the power of skillful means.
Therefore, it should be relied upon;
this is named definitive meaning.
These Four Reliances should be realized and known.
"Furthermore, relying on meaning:
Meaning is named Honesty and Uprightness (zhì zhí);
Honesty and Uprightness is named Light (guāngmíng);
Light is named Non-Weakness;
Non-Weakness is named the Rúlái.
Furthermore, Light is named Wisdom (zhìhuì);
Honesty and Uprightness is named Eternal Abiding.
The eternity of the Rúlái is named reliance on the Dharma.
The Dharma is named Eternal,
and is also named Boundless,
Inconceivable,
Unable to be grasped,
Unable to be fettered, and yet Visible.
If anyone says it is invisible,
such a person should not be relied upon.
Therefore, rely on the Dharma, not on the person.
If a person uses subtle language
to proclaim impermanence,
such words should not be relied upon.
Therefore, rely on the meaning, not on the words.
Relying on wisdom means
that the Saṅgha (zhòng sēng) is eternal,
unconditioned (wúwéi), and immutable,
and does not accumulate the eight kinds of unclean objects.
Therefore, rely on wisdom, not on consciousness.
If one says,
'Consciousness creates and consciousness receives,'
there is no harmoniously united Saṅgha (héhé sēng).
Why is that?
Because harmony is named Non-Existence (wú suǒ yǒu);
if it is Non-Existence, how can it be called Eternal?
Therefore, this consciousness cannot be relied upon.
Relying on definitive meaning means:
Definitive meaning is named Contentment (zhī zú).
One will never falsely display pure deportment,
be arrogant and self-exalting,
or covet gain and support.
Moreover, one does not cling to the teachings spoken by the Rúlái through expedient means (suí yí fāngbiàn).
This is named definitive meaning.
If anyone can abide in these things,
know that this person
has attained abiding in the Ultimate Truth (dì yī yì).
Therefore, this is named reliance on the sūtras of definitive meaning.
"Do not rely on the non-definitive teaching (Bùliǎo Yì).
The non-definitive teaching (Bùliǎo Yì) is that which is stated in the Sūtras (Jīng), such as:
'Everything is burning,'
'Everything is impermanent (wúcháng),'
'Everything is suffering (jiēkǔ),'
'Everything is empty (jiēkōng),'
'Everything is without self (wúwǒ).'
This is named the non-definitive teaching (Bùliǎo Yì).
Why is this?
Because if one cannot fully understand this meaning,
it causes living beings (zhòngshēng) to fall into the Ābǐ Hell (Ābí Yù).
For what reason?
Because they grasp and cling (qǔzhuó),
they do not understand the true meaning.
Regarding 'Everything is burning':
It means that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) says Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) is also burning;
regarding 'Everything is impermanent (wúcháng)':
Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) is also impermanent (wúcháng);
suffering, emptiness, and no-self
are also like this.
Therefore, these are named Sūtras (Jīng) of Non-Definitive Teaching (Bùliǎo Yì),
and should not be relied upon.
Good man (Shàn Nánzǐ)!
If someone says that the Tathāgata (Rúlái), out of compassion for all living beings (yīqiè zhòngshēng),
skillfully knows the right circumstances (shíyí),
and because he knows the circumstances,
he speaks of the light as heavy,
and speaks of the heavy as light.
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) observes and knows which disciples
have various donors (dányuè) who supply their needs
so that they lack nothing.
For such persons,
the Buddha (Fó) does not permit them to accept or keep servants or slaves (núbì),
gold, silver, or treasures (cáibǎo),
or to engage in buying, selling, or trade (fànmài shìyì),
or other impure items (bùjìng wù).
If the disciples have no donors (dányuè) to supply their needs,
and the current age suffers famine (jījǐn),
making food and drink difficult to obtain,
for the purpose of establishing and upholding the True Dharma (Zhèng Fǎ),
I permit the disciples to accept and keep servants or slaves (núbì),
gold, silver, carriages (chēchéng),
fields, houses, grain, and rice (gǔmǐ),
and necessities acquired through trade.
Although permitted to accept and keep such items,
they must ultimately offer them purely as gifts (jìng shī) to deeply faithful donors (dányuè).
These Four Dharmas (Sì Fǎ) should be relied upon.
If there are Vinayas (Jièlǜ),
Abhidharmas (Āpítán),
or Sūtras (Xiūduōluó) that do not contradict these four,
they should also be relied upon.
If there is a teaching that says:
regardless of the time or lack thereof,
and regardless of whether one can protect the Dharma or cannot protect the Dharma,
the Tathāgata (Rúlái) permits all Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū)
to accept and keep such impure items (bùjìng wù)—
such a statement should not be relied upon.
If, within the Vinayas (Jièlǜ),
Abhidharmas (Āpítán),
or Sūtras (Xiūduōluó),
there is a corresponding statement,
these three sections (sān fēn) should likewise not be relied upon.
I speak of these Four Reliances (Sì Yī)
for the benefit of those living beings (zhòngshēng) who possess only the flesh eye (ròuyǎn);
I certainly do not speak them for those who possess the wisdom eye (huìyǎn).
Therefore, I now speak of these Four Reliances (Sì Yī):
Dharma (Fǎ) means the Dharma Nature (Fǎ Xìng);
Meaning (Yì) means the eternal and unchanging permanence of the Tathāgata (Rúlái);
Wisdom (Zhì) means understanding that all living beings (yīqiè zhòngshēng) fully possess the Buddha Nature (Fó Xìng);
Definitive Teaching (Liǎo Yì) means thoroughly comprehending all Mahāyāna Sūtras (Dàshèng Jīngdiǎn).
At that time, Kāśyapa (Jiāshè) addressed the Buddha (Fó), saying:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
Should the four types of people mentioned above
be relied upon?"
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"So it is,
so it is.
Good man (Shàn Nánzǐ)!
You should rely upon what I have spoken.
Why?
Because there are Four Māras (Sì Mó).
What are the four?
Those who are able to receive and uphold the various other Sūtras and Vinayas (Jīnglǜ) spoken by Māra (Mó)."
Bodhisattva Kāśyepa (Jiāshè Púsà) addressed the Buddha (Fó), saying:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
Since the Buddha (Fó) has spoken of the Four Māras (Sì Zhǒng Mó),
how am I to distinguish
between what Māra (Mó) speaks and what the Buddha (Fó) speaks?
Some living beings (zhòngshēng) follow and pursue the practice of Māra (Mó),
and others follow the teachings of the Buddha (Fó).
How are we to recognize these different groups?"
The Buddha (Fó) told Kāśyapa (Jiāshè):
"Seven hundred years after my complete Nirvāṇa (Bō Nièpán),
this Māra Pāpīyas (Mó Bōxún)
will gradually corrupt and destroy my True Dharma (Zhèng Fǎ).
Just as a hunter dresses himself in monastic robes,
King Māra Pāpīyas (Mó Wáng Bōxún) is also like this:
he takes the form of a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū Xiàng),
the form of a Bhikṣuṇī (Bǐqiūní Xiàng),
the form of an Upāsaka (Yōupósè Xiàng),
the form of an Upāsikā (Yōupóyí Xiàng).
He also transforms himself into the body of a Srotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán Shēn),
and even transforms himself into the body of an Arhat (Āluóhàn Shēn) and the physical body of a Buddha (Fó Sèshēn).
King Māra (Mó Wáng) uses these contaminated forms (yǒulòu zhī xíng)
to imitate uncontaminated bodies (wúlòu shēn),
thus destroying my True Dharma (Zhèng Fǎ).
When this Māra Pāpīyas (Mó Bōxún) destroys the True Dharma (Zhèng Fǎ),
he will make the following statements:
'The Bodhisattva (Púsà) formerly departed from Tuṣita Heaven (Dōushuài Tiān Shàng),
came to this Kapilavastu City (Jiāpíluó Chéng) in the palace of King Śuddhodana (Báijìng Wáng Gōng),
and relied upon the union of parents' desires and affection
to give birth to this body.'
If one were to say that a person born among humans,
is revered by the gods and humans (tiānrén) of all the worlds
and by the great assembly (dàzhòng)—
there is no such possibility.
Furthermore, he will say:
'In past lives, through ascetic practices (kǔxíng),
and various acts of generosity (bùshī) of his head, eyes,
marrow, brain,
city, nation,
wife, and children,
he therefore achieved the path to Buddhahood (Fódào) today.
Because of this condition,
he is revered by humans and gods (rén tiān),
Gandharvas (Gāntápó),
Asuras (Āxiūluó),
Garuḍas (Jiālóuluó),
Kiṃnaras (Jǐnnàluó),
and Mahoragas (Móhóuluójiā).
If there are Sūtras or Vinayas (Jīnglǜ) that state this,
you should know that they are entirely spoken by Māra (Mó)."
"Good man (Shàn Nánzǐ)!
If there are Sūtras or Vinayas (Jīnglǜ) that state this:
'The Tathāgata (Rúlái), the Rightly Enlightened One (Zhèng Jué), has long ago accomplished Buddhahood (Chéng Fó),
and now merely displays the appearance of attaining the path to Buddhahood (Fódào),
doing so in order to deliver all living beings (zhòngshēng).
He displays having parents and being born through the union of desire and affection,
making this manifestation in accordance with the ways of the world.'
Such Sūtras or Vinayas (Jīnglǜ),
you should know, are truly spoken by the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Those who follow what Māra (Mó) speaks
are the dependents of Māra (Mó Juànshǔ);
those who can follow the Sūtras and Vinayas (Jīnglǜ) spoken by the Buddha (Fó)
are Bodhisattvas (Púsà)."
"If there is a statement that says:
'When the Tathāgata (Rúlái) was born,
he walked seven steps in each of the ten directions,'
and claims this is unbelievable (bù kě xìn),
then
this is spoken by Māra (Mó)."
"If, conversely, there is a statement:
'When the Tathāgata (Rúlái) appeared in the world, in the ten directions
he walked seven steps in each,
this was the skillful manifestation (fāngbiàn shìxiàn) of the Tathāgata (Rúlái).'
This is named the Sūtra and Vinaya (Jīnglǜ) spoken by the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Those who follow what Māra (Mó) speaks
are the dependents of Māra (Mó Juànshǔ);
those who can follow what the Buddha (Fó) speaks
are Bodhisattvas (Púsà)."
"If there is a statement that says:
'After the Bodhisattva (Púsà) was born,
the royal father sent men to take him to the celestial temple (tiāncí).
When the Devas (zhū tiān) saw him, they all descended to pay homage.
Therefore, he is named the Buddha (Fó).'
And if someone raises a difficulty (nán) by saying:
'Devas (Tiān) appeared first,
the Buddha (Fó) appeared later,
how is it that the Devas (zhū tiān) pay homage to the Buddha (Fó)?'
He who raises this difficulty (nán),
you should know, is immediately speaking what Pāpīyas (Bōxún) speaks.
If there is a Sūtra (Jīng) that says:
'When the Buddha (Fó) arrived at the celestial temple (tiāncí),
these various Devas (zhū tiān),
Maheśvara (Móxīshǒuluó),
the Great Brahmā King (Dà Fàntiān Wáng),
and Śakra Devānām Indra (Shìtí Huányīn),
all pressed their palms together (hézhǎng) and paid homage to his feet.'
Such Sūtras and Vinayas (Jīnglǜ) are spoken by the Buddha (Fó).
Those who follow what Māra (Mó) speaks
are the dependents of Māra (Mó Juànshǔ);
those who can follow what the Buddha (Fó) speaks
are Bodhisattvas (Púsà)."
"If there are Sūtras or Vinayas (Jīnglǜ) that say:
'When the Bodhisattva (Púsà) was a crown prince (tàizǐ),
due to a mind of greed,
he took wives from the four directions,
dwelling in the deep palace,
entertaining himself with the five desires (wǔ yù),
happily enjoying pleasure.'
Such Sūtras and Vinayas (Jīnglǜ) are spoken by Pāpīyas (Bōxún)."
"If there are those who say:
'The Bodhisattva long ago abandoned greedy desire,
things pertaining to wives and children,
and furthermore, does not accept the superior subtle five desires of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Sānshí Sān Tiān),
regarding them as discarded snot and spit,
how much less human desires?
He shaves his beard and hair,
leaves home, and cultivates the Way.
Such sūtras and vinayas are spoken by the Buddha.
If one follows the sūtras and vinayas of the Māra,
one is a dependent of Māra;
if one follows the sūtras and vinayas of the Buddha,
one is a Bodhisattva.'
"If there are those who say:
'The Buddha, while in the Jītuó monastery (Jīngshè) in Shèwèi,
permitted all Bhikṣus to receive and possess male and female slaves (núbì),
servants (púshǐ),
cattle, sheep, elephants, horses, donkeys, mules,
chickens, pigs, cats, and dogs,
gold, silver, lapis lazuli (liúlí),
pearls, crystal (pōlí),
giant clam shells (jūqū), agate (mǎnǎo),
coral, amber (hǔpò),
seashell ornaments (kēbèi), jade disks (bìyù),
copper and iron pots and kettles (fǔfù),
and large and small copper basins—all necessary items.
He permitted plowing fields and planting,
trading and market exchange,
and storing grain and rice, and such various activities.
Because of the Buddha’s great compassion,
pitying sentient beings, he permitted them all to possess these things.
Such sūtras and vinayas,
are entirely spoken by Māra.'
"If there are those who say:
'The Buddha, while in the Jītuó monastery (Jīngshè) in Shèwèi, at the dwelling place of the ghost Nàlílóu,
at that time, the Tathāgata, prompted by the Brāhmaṇa named Gǔdīdē,
and King Pōxīní Wáng, said that
Bhikṣus should not receive or possess gold, silver, lapis lazuli (liúlí),
crystal (pōlí), pearls,
giant clam shells (jūqū), agate (mǎnǎo),
coral, amber (hǔpò),
seashell ornaments (kējù), jade disks (bìyù),
male and female slaves (núbì), servants (púshǐ),
young boys and girls,
cattle, sheep, elephants, horses,
donkeys, mules, chickens, pigs,
cats, dogs, and other such beasts,
copper and iron pots and kettles (fǔfù),
large and small copper basins,
various colored bedding and sleeping mats,
nor things necessary for earning a livelihood,
such as houses and dwellings,
plowing fields and planting,
trading and market exchange,
personally cooking food,
personally grinding and pounding (grain),
incantations for curing the body (zhìshēn zhòushù),
methods for training falcons,
gazing up at the constellations (xīngxiù),
calculating the waxing and waning (of the moon/stars),
physiognomy of men and women,
interpreting the auspiciousness or misfortune of dreams,
determining if one is male or female,
or neither male nor female,
the sixty-four skills (liùshísì néng),
or the eighteen methods of deceiving people through incantations,
various crafts and skills,
or speaking about countless worldly mundane affairs,
scattered incense, powdered incense,
anointing perfume, smoking incense,
various flower garlands,
techniques for treating hair (zhìfà fāngshù),
fraud, falsehood, and flattery,
insatiable greed for profit,
delighting in uproar and clamor,
joking, laughing, and conversing,
craving and consuming fish and meat, compounding poisonous drugs,
preparing pressed perfumed oils,
holding jewel-studded canopies and leather sandals,
making fans, chests, and boxes,
various paintings and images,
accumulating grain and rice,
wheat, barley, beans, and various fruits and melons.
Associating intimately with kings, princes, ministers, and various women,
laughing loudly or alternatively remaining silent,
generating many doubts concerning the various dharmas,
speaking excessively and falsely,
discussing merits and faults, beauty and ugliness, or good and bad (actions),
fond of wearing fine clothes,
and all such various impure items.
Personally praising oneself before donors,
going in and out of impure places,
such as selling wine (gūjiǔ),
prostitutes (yínnǚ),
and gambling (bóyì).
I now forbid such people from remaining among the Bhikṣus;
they should cease their practice of the Way,
return to secular life, and become laborers.
Just as weeds (bài) and darnel (shòu)
are completely eradicated without residue.
You should know that the prohibitions mandated by these sūtras and vinayas
are entirely spoken by the Tathāgata.
If one follows what Māra has spoken,
one is a dependent of Māra;
if one follows what the Buddha has spoken,
one is a Bodhisattva.'
"If there are those who say:
'The Bodhisattva, desiring to make offerings to heavenly spirits,
therefore enters the Heavenly Temples (tiāncí),
namely, Brahmā (Fàntiān),
Maheśvara (Dàzìzài Tiān),
Veda (Wéituó Tiān),
and Kātyāyana (Jiāzhānyán Tiān).
The reason for entering
is to tame and subdue the various gods and humans.
If one says otherwise,
there is no such possibility.
If one says that the Bodhisattva cannot enter into the heterodox doctrines of external paths,
know their demeanor,
literature, and skills,
cannot reconcile disputes among servants,
is not respected by men, women, kings, or ministers,
and furthermore does not know how to compound various medicines—
based on this lack of knowledge, he is then called the Tathāgata.
If he does know these things, then he belongs to the group holding false views.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata's mind is equal toward enemies and relatives,
just as if his body were cut with a knife or smeared with perfume;
towards these two types of people, he does not generate the mind of increasing benefit
or decreasing harm.
He is only able to maintain the middle way,
hence he is called the Tathāgata.
Such sūtras and vinayas,
you should know, are spoken by Māra.'
"If there are those who say:
'The Bodhisattva thus appears to enter the Heavenly Temples (tiāncí),
leaves home and cultivates the Way within the doctrines of external paths (Wàixué Fǎ),
demonstrates knowledge of their demeanor and rituals,
can comprehend all literature and skills,
appears to enter schools and places of craftsmanship,
is skilled at reconciling disputes among servants,
and among the great multitude,
young boys and girls,
concubines and queens in the inner palace,
elders among the people,
Brāhmaṇas, and others,
kings and ministers,
and the poor—is the most honored and supreme;
and furthermore, is revered by these same people,
and can manifest such deeds.
Although dwelling amidst various views,
he does not generate attachment,
just as a lotus flower is unstained by dust.
Because he seeks to save all sentient beings,
he skillfully practices such various expedients,
conforming to worldly dharma.
Such sūtras and vinayas, you should know, are immediately spoken by the Tathāgata.
If one follows what Māra has spoken,
one is a dependent of Māra;
if one can follow what the Buddha has spoken,
one is a Great Bodhisattva.'
"If there is someone who says:
'The Tàrúlái explained the Sūtras (Jīng) and Vinaya (Lǜ) for me,
concerning minor and major offenses (zuì) among evil dharmas, including Sūluánzhē,
all of which are heavy in nature.
We in our Lǜ will certainly not commit them.
I have long endured and accepted dharmas such as these.
If you do not believe [us],
how can I abandon my own Lǜ
and follow yours?
The Lǜ you possess was spoken by Māra,
while our Jīng and Lǜ were instituted by the Fó.
The Tàrúlái first spoke the nine divisions of the Dharma seals (Fǎyìn),
and these nine seals validate my Jīng and Lǜ.
I have never heard of the Fāngděng (Vaipulya) scriptures (Jīngdiǎn) before,
claiming that every phrase and every word was spoken by the Tàrúlái.
In which place among the infinite Jīng and Lǜ does it speak of the Fāngděng Jīng?
Among scriptures such as these,
I have never heard of the names of the ten divisions of Jīng.
If they exist,
know that they must certainly have been made by Tiáodá (Devadatta).
Tiáodá, the wicked person, extinguished good dharmas
and fabricated the Fāngděng Jīng.
We do not believe [them].
Jīng such as these are spoken by Māra.
Why is this?
Because they destroy the Fó Fǎ and hold contradictory views.'
'Words such as these:
"They are in your scripture (Jīng),
they are not in mine."
In my Jīng and Lǜ, the Tàrúlái said:
"After my Nièpán,
in the evil age, there will be incorrect Jīng and Lǜ,
namely, the Dàshèng Fāngděng scriptures (Jīngdiǎn).
In future ages, there will be evil Bhikkhus (Bǐqiū) like these."
I also said:
"Beyond the nine divisions of Jīng, there is the Fāngděng canon (Diǎn).
If there is someone who can fully understand its meaning (yì),
know that this person correctly understands the Jīng and Lǜ,
is far removed from all impure things,
subtly pure, like the full moon."
If there is someone who says:
'Although the Tàrúlái explained meanings and flavors (yìwèi) in each Jīng and Lǜ as numerous as the sands of the Hènghé (Ganges) River,
they are not in my Lǜ.
Therefore, they must be nonexistent.
If they did exist,
why did the Tàrúlái not explain them in my Lǜ?
Therefore, I cannot now believe and accept them.'
Know that this person incurs an offense (zuì).
This person further says:
'I must accept and uphold Jīng and Lǜ such as these.
Why is this?
Because they enable me to achieve contentment (zhīzú) and few desires (shǎoyù),
severing affliction (fánnǎo),
attaining wisdom and Nièpán,
and serve as the cause for good dharmas (shànfǎ).'
He who speaks thus
is not my disciple (Dìzǐ)."
"If there is someone who says:
'The Tàrúlái, desiring to deliver sentient beings (zhòngshēng),
spoke the Fāngděng Jīng.'
Know that this person is truly my Dìzǐ.
If there is someone who does not accept the Fāngděng Jīng,
know that this person is not my Dìzǐ,
did not leave home (chūjiā) for the Fó Fǎ,
but is rather a disciple of heterodox views (xiéjiàn) and external paths (wàidào).
'Jīng and Lǜ such as these were spoken by the Fó,
but if they are not like this, they were spoken by Māra.
If there is someone who complies with what Māra spoke,
he is a relative (juànshǔ) of Māra;
if there is someone who complies with what the Fó spoke,
he is a Bodhisattva (Púsà)."
"Furthermore, O good man (shànnánzǐ)!
If there is someone who says:
'The Tàrúlái was not perfected by immeasurable merits (gōngdé),
is impermanent (wúcháng), and subject to change (biànyì).
Having realized the dharma of emptiness (kōngfǎ),
he proclaimed non-self (wúwǒ),
and does not conform to the world (shìjiān).'
Jīng and Lǜ such as these are called those spoken by Māra."
"If there is someone who says:
'The Tàrúlái's Perfect Enlightenment (Zhèngjué) is inconceivable,
and was perfected by merits (gōngdé) equal to countless Asámkhyeyas (Āsēngqí).
Therefore, he dwells permanently (chángzhù)
and is without change (biànyì).'
Jīng and Lǜ such as these were spoken by the Fó.
If there is someone who complies with what Māra spoke,
he is a relative (juànshǔ) of Māra;
if there is someone who complies with what the Fó spoke,
he is a Púsà."
"Furthermore, there are those who say:
'There might be a Bhikkhu (Bǐqiū) who truly did not violate the Bōluóyí (Pārājika) offense (zuì),
yet everyone thinks he committed a Bōluóyí,
like cutting down a Tāluó (Tāla) tree.
But this Bhikkhu truly committed nothing.
Why is this?
I constantly say:
"The four Bōluóyí,
if one transgresses one of them,
it is like splitting a stone,
impossible to join back together."
If one claims to have attained a supra-human dharma (guòrén fǎ),
this is called committing a Bōluóyí.
Why is this?
Because having truly attained nothing,
he falsely displays the appearance of having attained it.
A person such as this loses the human dharma,
which is called Bōluóyí.
Suppose there is a Bhikkhu who has few desires (shǎoyù) and is content (zhīzú),
maintains pure precepts (chíjiè),
and dwells in a quiet, secluded place (kōngxián chù).
If a king (wáng) or minister (dàchén) sees this Bhikkhu,
they conceive the thought that he has attained Arhatship (Luóhàn),
and immediately approach, praising him, revering him, and bowing to him.
They further say:
"Such a Great Master (Dàshī),
having abandoned this body,
will attain the utmost, right, and perfect awakening (Ānòu Duōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí)."
The Bhikkhu, having heard this, immediately answers the king, saying:
"I have truly not yet attained the fruition of the Śramana (Shāmén) path.
O King, do not claim that I have already attained the fruition of the path.
I only wish, Great King (Dàwáng)!
Do not speak to me of the dharma of discontent (bù zhīzú).
Those who are discontent,
even if they are claimed to have attained Ānòu Duōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
all accept this silently.
If I were now to accept this silently,
I would be blamed by all the Fó.
The conduct of contentment (zhīzú)
is praised by the Fó.
Therefore, I wish to rejoice throughout my life
and practice contentment (zhīzú).
Moreover, due to contentment (zhīzú),
I definitely know myself that I have not attained the fruition of the path.
The King claims I have attained it,
but I do not accept it now,
hence it is called contentment (zhīzú)."
At that time, the King replied:
'The Great Master (Dàshī) truly attained the fruit of Arhatship (Āluóhànguǒ),
no different from the Fó.'
Thereupon, the King universally proclaimed to the people (rénmín) both inside and outside [the palace],
and to the empresses and consorts in the inner palace (zhōnggōng),
causing all of them to know that [the Bhikkhu] had attained the fruition of Śramana (Shāmén).
Therefore, all who heard this were caused
to generate reverence and faith (jìngxìn) in their hearts,
and offer veneration (gōngyǎng) and respect.
A Bhikkhu such as this is truly a pure person of Brahman conduct (fànháng),
and by this cause and condition,
he causes all people to attain great merit (fúdé).'
But this Bhikkhu truly did not violate the Bōluóyí offense.
Why is this?
Because the first person spontaneously generated a heart of joy,
praising and venerating [him].
What offense could a Bhikkhu such as this incur?
If there is someone who says that this person incurs an offense (zuì),
know that this Jīng was spoken by Māra."
"Furthermore, there are Bhikṣus who say:
'The Buddha's secret treasury of profound Sūtras teaches that
all sentient beings possess Fóxìng (Buddha nature).
Because of this nature,
when they sever immeasurably numerous kōṭis of vexations (fánnǎo) and bonds (jié),
they immediately achieve Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi),
excluding the Icchantika (Yīchǎntí).
If a king or high minister speaks thus:
'Bhikṣu, will you achieve Buddhahood
or not achieve Buddhahood?
Do you possess Fóxìng or not?'
The Bhikṣu replies:
'In my present body, I definitely possess Fóxìng,
but whether I will achieve it or not, I cannot yet be sure.'
The king says:
'Venerable Sir (Dàdé)!
If you are not an Yīchǎntí,
you will certainly achieve it without doubt.'
The Bhikṣu says:
'Yes,
it is truly as the king says.'
Although this person says they definitely possess Fóxìng,
they still do not commit a Pōluóyí (Pārājika) offense.
Furthermore, there are Bhikṣus
who, immediately upon renouncing home life, contemplate thus:
'I will definitely achieve Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí now.'
A person like this,
even though they have not yet attained the fruit of the unexcelled path,
has already acquired immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable merit.
Suppose someone were to say that this person commits a Pōluóyí;
then there would be no Bhikṣu who had not committed it.
Why is that?
I, throughout eighty kōṭis of kalpas in the past,
always kept away from all impure things,
had few desires and was content (shǎoyù zhīzú),
perfected my deportment (wēiyí chéngjiù),
and diligently cultivated the Tathāgata's unexcelled Dharma Treasury.
I also definitely know that my body possesses Fóxìng,
and for this reason, I now achieve Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
and attain the title of Buddha,
possessing great compassion (dàcí bēi).'
Sūtras and Vinayas such as these are spoken by the Buddha.
If there is anyone who cannot follow and comply with this,
they are dependents of Māra (mó juànshǔ);
if they can follow and comply,
they are Great Bodhisattvas (Dà Púsà).
"Furthermore, there are those who say:
'There are no Four Pōluóyí (Pārājika),
Thirteen Saṅghāvaśeṣa (Sēngcán),
Two Aniyata (Bùdìng Fǎ),
Thirty Niḥsargika Pācittiya (Shě Duò),
Ninety-one Pācittiya (Duò),
Four Pratideśanīya (Chànhuǐ Fǎ),
Numerous Śaikṣa (Xuéfǎ),
Seven Adhikaraṇaśamatha (Miè Zhēng), and so forth.
There are no Sthūlātyaya (Tōulánzhē),
Five Heinous Crimes (Wǔ Nì), and so forth,
nor Yīchǎntí.
If Bhikṣus who commit such offenses fall into Avīci Hell (dìyù),
then practitioners of external paths (wàidào) should all be reborn in heaven.
Why is that?
Because those of external paths have no precepts to violate.
Therefore, the Tathāgata demonstrated fear to people,
and hence taught these precepts.
If someone says the Buddha taught:
'If my Bhikṣus desire to engage in sexual conduct (yín),
they should relinquish the dharma robes and wear secular clothes,
and only then engage in sexual conduct.
They should also generate the thought:
"The condition of sexual desire
is not my fault;
when the Tathāgata was in the world,
there were also Bhikṣus
who practiced sexual conduct and attained true liberation (zhèng jiětuō),
or who, after death, were reborn in heaven.
This has happened throughout history,
not only performed by me alone."
Or those who violate the four heavy precepts (sì chóng),
or violate the Five Precepts (Wǔ Jiè),
or practice all impure vinaya disciplines,
can still attain true and genuine liberation.
Although the Tathāgata said that those who commit Duṣkṛta (Tújíluó) offenses,
must endure a lifespan equivalent to the lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven (Dāolì Tiān),
measured by suns, moons, and years,
eight million years,
falling into Avīci Hell,
this too was the Tathāgata demonstrating fear to people.
To say that Pōluóyí down to Tújíluó are indistinguishable in gravity,
is the baseless fabrication of certain Vinaya Masters (Lǜshī),
who falsely make this statement
and claim it is established by the Buddha.
One must definitively know that this was not spoken by the Buddha.
Such speech and teachings are Māra's Sūtras and Vinayas (mó jīnglǜ).
"If someone further says:
'Among the precepts, if one violates a minor precept,
even if it is extremely subtle,
one will endure suffering retribution
without limit.
Having known this,
one protects one's own body,
like a tortoise retracting its six limbs.'
If a Vinaya Master further makes this statement:
'Any violation of the precepts incurs no retribution of guilt (zuì bào) at all,'
a person like this should not be approached.
As the Buddha taught:
'Therefore, one should not associate closely with such a person.'
My Buddha Dharma is pure in this way.
How much more so if someone commits the offense of Tōulánzhē,
or violates Saṅghāvaśeṣa, or Pōluóyí—
could they possibly be guiltless?
Therefore, one should deeply guard and protect oneself regarding these kinds of teachings;
if one does not protect them,
by what Dharma should one be called a prohibited precept (jìnjiè)?
I also said in the Sūtras
that those who commit the Four Pōluóyí down to the minute Tújíluó, and so on,
should be severely punished.
If sentient beings do not guard and uphold the prohibited precepts,
how can they achieve the vision of Fóxìng?
'Although all sentient beings possess Fóxìng,
it is only by upholding the precepts that they can see it;
by seeing Fóxìng, they attain Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Among the Ninefold Scriptures (Jiǔ Bù Jīng), there are no Vaipulya Sūtras (Fāngděng Jīng);
therefore, they do not speak of the existence of Fóxìng.
Although the Sūtras do not speak of it,
you should know it truly exists.
If someone makes this statement,
you should know that this person is truly my disciple.'
Kāshè (Kāśyapa) Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
As stated above,
the idea that all sentient beings possess Fóxìng
has never been heard in the Ninefold Scriptures.
If one asserts its existence,
how is this not a violation of Pōluóyí?"
The Buddha said:
"Good son (Shàn Nánzǐ)!
As you have stated,
it truly does not violate Pōluóyí.
Good son!
For example, there is a person
who says that the great ocean
contains only seven treasures and not eight kinds;
that person has no fault.
If someone says that Fóxìng does not exist in the Ninefold Scriptures,
they are also guiltless.
Why is that?
I taught the existence of Fóxìng within the Great Wisdom Ocean of the Mahāyāna (Dàchéng Dàzhì Hǎi).
It is not known or seen by those of the Two Vehicles (Èr Chéng),
therefore, saying that it does not exist
does not constitute an offense.
A realm such as this
is known by all Buddhas,
and is not reached by the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) or Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué).
Good son!
If a person has not heard of the Tathāgata's extremely profound secret treasury,
how can they know that Fóxìng exists?
What is called the secret treasury?
It is the Vaipulya (Fāngděng) Mahāyāna Sūtras.
Good son!
There are external path practitioners
who claim the self (wǒ) is eternal,
or who claim the self is annihilated.
The Tathāgata is not like that;
he speaks both of the existence of the self
and of the non-existence of the self;
this is called the Middle Way (Zhōngdào).
If someone says:
'The Buddha taught the Middle Way,
and all sentient beings fully possess Fóxìng.
Because it is covered by vexations (fánnǎo),
it is unknown and unseen.
Therefore, one should diligently cultivate skillful means (fāngbiàn)
to sever and destroy vexations.'
If anyone can speak in this manner,
know that this person does not violate the Four Heavy Precepts (Sì Chóng).
If one cannot speak in this manner,
that is then called violating Pōluóyí.
If someone says:
'I have already attained Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Why is that?
Because Fóxìng exists.
Those who possess Fóxìng will definitely achieve Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
and for this reason,
I have now already achieved Bodhi (Pútí).'
Know that this person is then called having committed the offense of Pōluóyí.
Why is that?
Although Fóxìng exists,
because they have not yet cultivated various skillful means,
they have not yet seen it.
Because they have not yet seen it, they cannot achieve Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Good son!
For this reason,
the Buddha Dharma is extremely profound and inconceivable.
Kāshè Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If a king were to ask,
in what way does a Bhikṣu fall into the Transcendent Human Dharma (Guò Rén Fǎ)?"
The Fó instructed Jiāshè:
"If there are Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū),
who, for the sake of profit and sustenance,
for the sake of food and drink,
engage in flattery,
deceit, hypocrisy, and fraud, saying:
'How can I ensure that the people of the world
definitively and truly recognize me as a mendicant (qǐshì)?
By this means,
I will gain great profit, sustenance, and fame.'
Such a Bǐqiū,
because of great ignorance,
constantly thinks, night and day:
'I have not actually attained the Four Fruits of the Śramaṇa (Shāménguǒ),
how can I make the people of the world believe I have attained them?
Furthermore, how can I cause all the Upāsakas (Yōupósè) and Upāsikās (Yōupóyí)
to point to me and all together say:
"This person possesses merit and virtue;
truly, he is an awakened being (Shèngrén)."
Such contemplation
is solely for seeking profit,
not for seeking the Dharma.
In walking, coming, going, and entering,
in moving and resting, he is composed and serene.
He holds his robes and bowl,
not losing proper deportment (wēiyí).
He sits alone in an empty place like an Arhat (Āluóhàn),
causing the people of the world all to say:
"This Bǐqiū is excellent and foremost;
he diligently practices asceticism and cultivates the Dharma of Nirvāṇa (jìmièfǎ)."
By this means,
I will gain a great number of followers and disciples.
People will also offer abundant offerings,
robes, food, and drink,
bedding, and medicine,
and cause many women to respect, contemplate, love, and esteem me.'
If there are Bhikṣus or Bhikṣuṇīs (Bǐqiūní) who act in this way,
they fall into a transgression concerning superhuman attainments (guòrénfǎ).
Furthermore, there are Bǐqiūs who, wishing to establish the unsurpassed Right Dharma (Zhèngfǎ),
dwell in a silent, empty place.
Although they are not Āluóhàn,
they desire that people consider them to be Āluóhàn,
to be good Bǐqiūs,
to be virtuous Bǐqiūs,
and tranquil Bǐqiūs,
thus causing immeasurable sentient beings to generate faith.
'By this means,
I will gain immeasurable Bǐqiūs and others as my retinue.
Because of this, I can instruct the vow-breaking Bǐqiūs and Yōupósè, causing them all to uphold the precepts.
By this means, I will establish the Right Dharma,
illuminating and promoting the unsurpassed great matter of the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
manifesting and revealing the Vāipulya (fāngděng) Mahāyāna (Dàchéng) Dharma transformation,
delivering and liberating all immeasurable sentient beings.'
[He] also skillfully understands the meaning of the light and heavy matters within the Sūtras and Vinayas spoken by the Rúlái.
Furthermore, [he] says:
'I now also possess the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng).
There is a Sūtra called the Tathāgata's Secret Treasury (Rúlái Mìzàng).
In this Sūtra,
I will certainly attain the path to Buddhahood (Fódào),
and be able to exhaust immeasurable hundreds of millions of afflictive bonds (fánnǎojié);
I will extensively proclaim to immeasurable Yōupósè,
saying that all of you possess the Fóxìng.
I and you shall both abide in the ground of the Rúlái path,
and realize Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
exhausting immeasurable hundreds of millions of afflictive bonds.'
One who speaks thus,
this person is not said to fall into a transgression concerning superhuman attainments;
he is called a Bodhisattva (Púsà).
"If someone says:
'One who commits a minor offense (Tújíluó)
will fall into the hells and receive retribution for his crimes
for eight million years measured by the suns, moons, and years of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Dāolì Tiān),
how much more so if one intentionally commits a major offense (Tōulánzhē)?
If, within this Dàchéng, there is a Bǐqiū who commits a Tōulánzhē,
one should not associate closely with him.'
What is called the offense of Tōulánzhē within the Mahāyāna Sūtras?
If a wealthy householder (zhǎngzhě) erects a Buddhist temple (Fósì),
and uses various flower garlands to make offerings to the Fó,
and a Bǐqiū sees the thread stringing the flowers,
and takes it without asking,
he commits the Tōulánzhē offense.
Whether he knows or does not know, the offense is the same.
If, through greed, he destroys a Stūpa (Fótǎ),
he commits Tōulánzhē.
One should not associate closely with such a person.
If a king or minister sees an old and ruined Stūpa,
and wishes to repair it and make offerings to the relics (shèlì),
and perchance obtains rare treasures from within that Stūpa,
and entrusts them to a Bǐqiū,
and the Bǐqiū, having received them, uses them freely for himself,
such a Bǐqiū is called impure (bùjìng),
frequently giving rise to disputes.
Good Yōupósè should not associate closely with him,
or offer him reverence and respect.
Such a Bǐqiū is called one without faculty (wúgēn),
called one with dual faculties (èrgēn),
and called one with indeterminate faculties (bùdìnggēn).
One with indeterminate faculties, when desiring and craving women, immediately transforms into a woman;
when desiring and craving men, immediately transforms into a man.
Such a Bǐqiū is called one with evil faculties (ègēn);
he is not considered a man,
nor considered a woman,
nor considered one who has left home (chūjiā),
nor considered a layperson (zàijiā).
One should not associate closely with, offer reverence to, or respect such a Bǐqiū.
In the Buddhadharma (Fófǎ),
the Dharma of the Śramaṇa (Shāméngfǎ)
is to generate compassionate thoughts (bēixīn),
to protect and nurture sentient beings,
and to grant fearlessness (wúwèi) even to ants.
This is the Shāméngfǎ.
To avoid drinking alcohol, even to smelling its fragrance,
this is the Shāméngfǎ.
Not to engage in false speech (wàngyǔ), even in dreams not to contemplate false speech,
this is the Shāméngfǎ.
Not to generate lustful thoughts (yùxīn), and even in dreams it is likewise,
this is the Shāméngfǎ."
The Bodhisattva Jiāshè said to the Fó:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If there is a Bǐqiū who engages in sexual desire (yínyù) in a dream,
does this constitute a breach of the precepts?"
The Fó said:
"No.
One should generate the notion of foul impurity (chòuhuì xiǎng) regarding sexual desire,
and not generate even a single thought of purity
concerning it, thereby abandoning the afflictive attachment to women.
If one engages in sexual acts in a dream,
upon waking, one should generate remorse.
When a Bǐqiū goes begging for food and accepts offerings,
he should contemplate it as eating the flesh of one's own child during a famine,
and if lustful thoughts arise, they should be swiftly discarded.
Such Dharma gates (fǎmén),
you should know, are Sūtras and Vinayas spoken by the Fó.
If there are those who follow what Māra (Mó) preaches,
they are Māra's retinue;
if they are able to follow what the Fó preaches,
they are called Púsà.
"If there are those who say:
'The Fó permitted Bǐqiūs always to stand on one leg,
to remain silent and not speak,
to throw themselves into abysses, run toward fire,
and drop themselves from high cliffs without avoiding danger and difficulty,
to consume poison and stop eating,
to sleep upon ashes and dirt,
to bind their own hands and feet,
to kill sentient beings,
or to practice local divinations and spells,
and that children of the Caṇḍāla (Zhāntuóluó),
those without faculties (wúgēn),
those with dual faculties (èrgēn), and those with indeterminate faculties (bùdìnggēn),
and those with incomplete physical faculties—all such individuals—
the Rúlái permitted them all to leave home and seek the path.'
This is called Māra's teaching (Móshuō).
'The Fó previously permitted the eating of the five types of cow products (wǔzhǒng niúwèi), as well as oil and honey,
Kauśeya (jiāoshēyé) garments,
and leather sandals (gěxǐ) and other items.
Apart from these,
if there is anyone who says the Fó permitted the wearing of the Mahālaṃkā (Móhēlèngqié) garment,
and permitted the storage of all kinds of seeds,
and that things like grass and trees all possess life,
and that the Fó said this
just before entering Nirvāṇa (Nièpán]:
If there are Sūtras or Vinayas that make such a claim,
you should know that this is precisely what Māra has taught.
I do not permit standing constantly on one leg;
if it is for the sake of the Dharma, movement, dwelling, sitting, and lying down are permitted.
Furthermore, I do not permit consuming poison and stopping eating,
burning the body with five heats (wǔrè zhìshēn),
binding the hands and feet,
killing sentient beings,
local divinations and spells,
using cowrie shells, conch shells, or ivory as leather sandals (gěxǐ),
storing seeds,
or claiming that grass and wood possess life,
or wearing the Móhēlèngqié garment.
If one claims that the Shìzūn spoke thus,
you should know that this is the retinue of external paths (wàidào),
not my disciples.
'I only permit the eating of the five types of cow products and oil and honey, etc.,
and permit the wearing of leather sandals and Kauśeya (jiāoshēyé) garments.
I state that the Four Great Elements (Sìdà) do not possess life.
If there are Sūtras or Vinayas that speak thus,
this is called the Fó's teaching.
If there are those who follow what the Fó preaches,
you should know that they are truly my disciples.
If there are those who do not follow what the Fó preaches,
they are Māra's retinue.
If there are those who follow the Fó's Sūtras and Vinayas,
you should know that such a person is a Great Púsà.
"Good man!
The distinguishing characteristics between Māra's teaching (Móshuō) and the Fó's teaching (Fóshuō)
have now been extensively declared and discriminated for you."
Jiāshè said to the Fó:
"Shìzūn!
Only now do I begin to understand the distinguishing characteristics of the Móshuō
and the Fóshuō,
and through this, I am able to enter the profound meaning of the Buddhadharma (Fófǎ)."
Jiāyè:
“Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
Your ability to thus clearly distinguish and differentiate
is called wisdom.
Good man!
That which is spoken of as suffering (kǔ) is not called an Ārya Satya (Holy Truth).
Why is this?
If it were said that suffering (kǔ) is the Ārya Satya of Suffering,
then all oxen and sheep,
donkeys, horses, and beings in the hells
should possess the Ārya Satya.
Good man!
If there is someone who does not know the extremely profound realm of the Rúlái,
the eternal, unchanging, subtle, and mysterious Dharmakāya (Fǎshēn),
and maintains that this is a physical body sustained by food (shí shēn),
and not the Dharmakāya (Fǎshēn);
who does not know the Rúlái’s virtuous power and might—
this is called suffering (kǔ).
Why is this?
Because of not knowing,
they see the Dhárma (Fǎ) as non-Dhārma (Fēi Fǎ),
and non-Dhārma (Fēi Fǎ) as the Dhárma (Fǎ).
Know that such a person will surely fall into the evil destinies,
rotate through saṁsāra (shēngsǐ),
increase all attachments,
and undergo much suffering and distress.
If one is able to know that the Rúlái is eternal
and without change,
or hears the sound of the two words ‘eternal existence’ (cháng zhù),
if it passes through the ear once, they are born in the heavens.
Only upon subsequent liberation will they be able to verify and know
that the Rúlái is eternally existent and without change.
Having already verified and known this, they speak thus:
‘In the past, I once heard this meaning,
but only having attained liberation today do I verify and know it.
In fundamental reality (běn jì), because I did not know it,
I rotated through saṁsāra (shēngsǐ) boundlessly and eternally.
Beginning today, I have finally attained true knowledge (zhēn zhì).’
If one knows thus,
this is truly cultivating suffering,
and brings much benefit.
If one does not know this,
even if they diligently cultivate, there is no benefit.
This is called knowing suffering (zhī kǔ),
and is called the Ārya Satya of Suffering (Kǔ Shèngdì).
If a person cannot cultivate in this way,
this is called suffering,
but not the Ārya Satya of Suffering.
“Regarding the Satya of the Origin of Suffering (Kǔ Jí Dì):
It is failing to generate true knowledge (zhēn zhì) concerning the true Dhárma (zhēn fǎ),
accepting impure things,
such as slaves and maidservants.
Being able to take non-Dhārma (Fēi Fǎ)
and say it is the Right Dhárma (Zhèng Fǎ),
destroying and extinguishing the Right Dhárma,
and preventing it from lasting long.
Due to this cause and condition,
they do not know the nature of the Dhárma (Fǎ Xìng).
Because they do not know,
they rotate through saṁsāra (shēngsǐ) and receive much suffering and distress,
failing to be born in the heavens or attain true liberation (zhèng jiětuō).
If one has profound wisdom (shēn zhì) and does not destroy the Right Dhárma,
due to this cause and condition, they attain birth in the heavens and true liberation.
If there are those who do not know the locus of the Satya of the Origin of Suffering,
and say that the Right Dhárma is not eternally existent,
and that all are perishing dhármas;
due to this cause and condition,
throughout immeasurable kalpas,
they drift through saṁsāra (shēngsǐ) and suffer various distresses.
If one is able to know that the Dhárma is eternally existent and unchanging,
this is called knowing the Origin,
and is called the Ārya Satya of Origin (Jí Shèngdì).
If a person cannot cultivate in this way,
this is called the Origin,
but not the Ārya Satya of Origin.
“Regarding the Satya of the Cessation of Suffering (Kǔ Miè Dì):
If there are those who extensively cultivate and study the dhárma of emptiness (kōng fǎ),
this is unwholesome.
Why is this?
Because they annihilate all dhármas,
thereby destroying the Rúlái’s true Dhárma treasury (zhēn fǎzàng).
Performing such study and cultivation,
this is called cultivating emptiness (xiū kōng).
Those who cultivate the cessation of suffering (kǔ miè)
act contrary to all external paths (wàidào) and the like.
If it is said that cultivating emptiness is the Satya of Cessation,
then all followers of external paths also cultivate the dhárma of emptiness,
and should therefore possess the Satya of Cessation.
If someone says:
‘There is the Rúlái Zàng (Tathāgatagarbha),
although invisible,
if one can eliminate all afflictions (fánnǎo),
then one can enter it.’
If one generates this mind for a single thought’s duration as a cause and condition,
one attains sovereignty over all dhármas.
If one cultivates the secret treasury of the Rúlái (Rúlái Mìzàng)
[as] non-self (wú wǒ),
empty, and tranquil,
such a person, throughout immeasurable ages,
drifts through saṁsāra (shēngsǐ) enduring suffering.
If there are those who do not practice cultivation in this way,
although they possess afflictions,
they can quickly eliminate them.
Why is this?
Because they know the secret treasury of the Rúlái (Rúlái Mìzàng).
This is called the Ārya Satya of the Cessation of Suffering (Kǔ Miè Shèngdì).
If one is able to cultivate cessation (miè) in this way,
they are my disciple.
If one cannot practice cultivation in this way,
this is called cultivating emptiness (xiū kōng),
not the Satya of Cessation.
“Regarding the Satya of the Path (Dào Shèngdì):
This is the Buddha (Fó),
the Dhárma (Fǎ),
the Saṅgha jewel (Sēng Bǎo), and true liberation.
There are sentient beings whose deluded minds say:
‘There is no Buddha,
Dhárma,
Saṅgha, or true liberation,
and the cycle of saṁsāra (shēngsǐ) is merely like an illusion or transformation.’
Cultivating this view,
due to this cause and condition,
they rotate through the Three Realms of Existence (Sān Yǒu),
and endure great suffering for a long time.
If one can generate the mind to see the Rúlái as eternally existent and unchanging,
the Dhárma,
the Saṅgha, and liberation are also like this.
Relying on this single thought,
throughout immeasurable ages,
the retributions of mastery are obtained according to one's will.
Why is this?
In the past, I,
due to the four perversions (sì dǎo),
reckoned non-Dhārma (Fēi Fǎ) as Dhárma (Fǎ),
and received the retributions of immeasurable evil karma.
Since I have now eliminated such views,
I have attained Buddhahood (Fó) and Right Enlightenment (Zhèng Jué).
This is called the Ārya Satya of the Path (Dào Shèngdì).
If there is a person who says the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo) are impermanent,
and cultivates this view,
this is false cultivation,
not the Ārya Satya of the Path.
If one cultivates this Dhárma
as eternally existent,
they are my disciple.
Truly seeing and cultivating the Dhármas of the Four Ārya Satyas,
this is called the Four Ārya Satyas (Sì Shèngdì).”
Jiāyè Púsà (Bodhisattva) again spoke to the Buddha (Fó), saying:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
I now first realize
how to cultivate the extremely profound Dhármas of the Four Ārya Satyas.”
The Buddha (Fó) told Jiāyè:
“Good man!
The so-called four perversions (sì dǎo) are:
Generating the perception of suffering (kǔ xiǎng) concerning what is non-suffering (fēi kǔ);
this is called perversion (diāndǎo).
That which is non-suffering is called the Rúlái.
Generating the perception of suffering
means seeing the Rúlái as impermanent and changing.
If one says that the Rúlái is impermanent (wú cháng),
this is called the suffering of great sin.
If one says the Rúlái relinquished this suffering body
and entered Nièpán (Nirvāṇa),
like fire ceasing when the fuel is exhausted,
this is called generating the perception of suffering concerning what is non-suffering,
and this is called perversion.
‘If I say that the Rúlái is permanent (cháng), this is grasping to self (wǒ jiàn, ego-view).
Because of grasping to self, there are immeasurable sins.
Therefore, one should say the Rúlái is impermanent,
and by speaking thus, I will receive happiness (lè).’
The impermanence of the Rúlái is precisely suffering.
If it is suffering,
how can happiness be generated?
Because generating the perception of happiness concerning suffering,
is called perversion.
Generating the perception of suffering concerning happiness
is called perversion.
Happiness (lè) is precisely the Rúlái;
suffering (kǔ) is the Rúlái’s impermanence.
If one says the Rúlái is impermanent,
this is called generating the perception of suffering concerning happiness.
The Rúlái’s eternal existence
is called happiness.
“If I say:
‘The Rúlái is permanent,
how then does he enter Nièpán (Nirvāṇa)?
If it is said that the Rúlái is non-suffering,
how does he abandon the body and attain extinction (miè dù)?’
Because this is generating the perception of suffering concerning happiness.
This is called perversion,
and this is called the first perversion.”
"[Taking] the impermanent [as]
the thought of permanence,
or the permanent [as]
the thought of impermanence,
this is called perversion (diāndǎo).
Impermanence means not cultivating emptiness (kōng),
because emptiness is not cultivated,
lifespan is short.
If anyone says that one who does not cultivate quiescent emptiness (kōngjí) attains longevity,
