this is called perversion (diāndǎo),
this is called the second perversion (diāndǎo).
"Taking the non-self (wúwǒ) [as]
the thought of self (wǒxiǎng),
or the self (wǒ) [as]
the thought of non-self (wúwǒxiǎng),
this is called perversion (diāndǎo).
People of the world
also speak of having a self (wǒ);
within the Buddhadharma (Fófǎ),
it is also said there is a self (wǒ);
although people of the world speak of having a self (wǒ),
they lack the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng);
this is then called generating the thought of self (wǒxiǎng) within the non-self (wúwǒ),
this is called perversion (diāndǎo).
The self (wǒ) in the Buddhadharma (Fófǎ)
is the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng);
when people of the world say that the Buddhadharma (Fófǎ) is non-self (wúwǒ),
this is called generating the thought of non-self (wúwǒxiǎng) within the self (wǒ).
If one says that the Buddhadharma (Fófǎ) is absolutely non-self (wúwǒ),
and therefore the Tathāgata (Rúlái) instructs all his disciples
to cultivate non-self (wúwǒ),
this is called perversion (diāndǎo),
this is called the third perversion (diāndǎo).
"Taking the pure [as] the thought of impure,
or the impure [as] the thought of pure,
this is called perversion (diāndǎo).
Purity means the eternal existence of the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
not a body of mixed foods (zāshí shēn),
not a body of affliction (fánnǎo shēn),
not a body of flesh,
and not a body bound by sinews and bones.
If anyone says:
'The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is impermanent,
is a body of mixed foods,
and even a body bound by sinews and bones.
The Dharma (Fǎ),
the Saṅgha (Sēng),
and liberation (jiětuō) are utterly extinguished.'
This is called perversion (diāndǎo).
Taking the impure [as] the thought of pure, which is called perversion (diāndǎo),
is when someone says:
'In this body of mine, there is nothing that is impure,
since there is no impurity,
one will certainly attain entry into the place of purity.
The Tathāgata's (Rúlái) instruction to cultivate the contemplation of impurity (bùjìng guān),
such words are false assertions.'
This is called perversion (diāndǎo),
this is then called the fourth perversion (diāndǎo).
Bódhisattva Jiāshè (Kāśyapa) addressed the Buddha (Fó), saying:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
Starting today, I have only just attained right view (zhèngjiàn).
World-Honored One!
Before this time,
all of us were called people of wrong view (xiéjiàn).
World-Honored One!
In the twenty-five realms of existence (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu),
is there a self (wǒ) or not?"
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"Good son!
The self (wǒ) is precisely the meaning of the Tathāgata Store (Rúláizàng).
All sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
which is the meaning of the self (wǒ).
This meaning of the self (wǒ),
since primordial time,
has constantly been covered by measureless afflictions (fánnǎo),
therefore sentient beings cannot perceive it.
Good son!
Just like a poor woman whose house
contains many deposits of true gold,
but none of her household, great or small, knows about it.
At that time, there was another person,
skilled in skillful means (fāngbiàn),
who said to the poor woman:
'I will now employ you;
you can weed and remove the rubbish for me.'
The woman immediately replied:
'I cannot,
but if you can show my son the gold deposits,
then I will quickly work for you.'
That person replied again:
'I know the skillful means (fāngbiàn),
and I can show your son.'
The woman replied:
'My whole family, great and small, do not even know it themselves,
how much less could you know it?'
That person replied again:
'I am certain that I can now.'
The woman replied:
'I also wish to see it,
please show it to me as well.'
That person then dug up the deposits of true gold in her house.
When the woman saw it,
joy arose in her heart,
she conceived a marvelous thought,
and revered that person.
Good son!
The Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) of sentient beings is also like this;
all sentient beings cannot perceive it,
just like the poor person who did not know of the treasure deposit.
Good son!
I now universally demonstrate
that all sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
which is covered and obscured by all afflictions (fánnǎo),
just like that poor person who had a deposit of true gold
but could not perceive it.
Today, the Tathāgata (Rúlái) universally demonstrates the treasure deposit of enlightenment to all sentient beings,
that is, the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
and when these sentient beings see this matter,
joy arises in their hearts,
and they take refuge in and revere the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
The skilled practitioner of skillful means (shàn fāngbiàn) is the Tathāgata (Rúlái);
the poor woman is all measureless sentient beings;
the deposit of true gold is the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
"Furthermore, good son!
Suppose a woman gives birth to a son,
and the infant becomes ill.
The woman is worried and distressed,
and seeks out a physician.
When the physician arrives,
he compounds three kinds of medicine—
ghee (sū),
milk (rǔ),
and rock candy (shímì)—
and gives it to the child to take.
He then tells the woman:
'After the child has taken the medicine,
do not give him milk (rǔ) for now;
wait until the medicine has been digested,
then you may give it to him.'
At that time, the woman
immediately used a bitter substance to smear her breast,
and the mother told her son:
'My milk has been smeared with poison (dú), you must not touch it again.'
The infant, thirsty and weak,
wanted his mother's milk,
but smelling the poison (dú) on the milk,
he immediately went far away and abandoned it.
When the medicine was finally digested,
the mother cleansed her breast thoroughly with water,
and called her son, saying:
'Come, I will give you milk.'
At that time, although the infant was hungry and thirsty,
he had previously smelled the poisonous odor,
and therefore he did not come.
The mother spoke to him again:
'It was because you took medicine that I smeared it with poison (dú);
your medicine is digested, and I have finished washing it.
You may come now and drink the milk without harm.'
When the child heard this,
he gradually returned and drank.
Good son!
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is also like this.
In order to save all beings,
he taught all sentient beings to cultivate the Dharma of Non-Self (wúwǒ fǎ).
Having cultivated this way,
they eternally sever the concept of self (wǒ xīn),
and enter Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
This was done to eliminate all the false views of the world,
and to demonstrate the transcendence of worldly dharmas.
Furthermore, he demonstrated to the world
that the attachment to self (wǒ) is illusory
and not real;
thus, cultivate the Dharma of Non-Self (wúwǒ fǎ),
for the sake of attaining the purified body.
This is analogous to the woman who, for the sake of her son,
smeared her milk with a bitter taste.
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is also like this:
for the sake of cultivating emptiness (kōng),
he preached that all phenomena (zhūfǎ) are entirely without self (wǒ).
Just like that woman, having thoroughly washed the milk,
called her son,
wishing him to return and take it.
I am also like this now,
preaching the Tathāgata Store (Rúláizàng).
Therefore, bhikṣus (bǐqiū) should not generate fear,
just like that infant,
upon hearing his mother call, gradually returned and drank the milk.
Bhikṣus (bǐqiū) should also
discriminate for themselves:
the Tathāgata's (Rúlái) secret store must certainly exist.
Kǎyè Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Shìzūn!
Truly, there is no self (ātman).
Why is this?
When an infant is born, they know nothing.
If there were a self,
then on the day of birth,
immediately there should be knowledge;
based on this reasoning,
we definitively know there is no self.
If there were definitively a self,
after receiving birth,
there should be no final cessation (death).
If all beings possess Fóxìng (Buddha Nature),
and if this permanent nature were eternal, there should be no appearance of decay or ruin.
If there is no appearance of decay,
how can there be the differences of Kèlì (Kṣatriya),
Póluómén (Brāhmaṇa),
Píshè (Vaiśya),
Shǒutuó (Śūdra), and Chāntuólúo (Caṇḍāla),
and the distinction of animals?
Now we see the various differences arising from karmic conditions,
and the different destinies (gati).
If there were definitively a self,
all sentient beings should have neither superiority nor inferiority;
based on this reasoning,
we definitively know that Fóxìng is not an eternal dharma.
If you say that Fóxìng is definitively eternal,
for what reason are killing, stealing, sexual misconduct,
double-tongued speech, harsh speech,
false speech, frivolous speech,
greed, hatred, and wrong views still mentioned?
If the nature of the self were eternal,
why, after drinking wine, does one become confused, reckless, drunk, and disorderly?
If the nature of the self were eternal,
the blind should see forms,
the deaf should hear sounds,
the mute should be able to speak,
and the crippled should be able to walk.
If the nature of the self were eternal,
one should not avoid fire pits and great floods,
poisons, swords,
evil people, or wild beasts.
If the self were eternal,
things previously experienced should not be forgotten;
if they are not forgotten,
for what reason would one then say, 'Where did I previously see this person?'
If the self were eternal,
then there should be no decline or prosperity in youth,
prime,
or old age, regarding strength and power,
nor in recalling past events.
If the self were eternal,
where does it reside?
Is it in mucus and saliva,
or among the colors blue, yellow, red, and white?
If the self were eternal,
it should permeate the entire body like sesame oil,
without any empty space in between.
If the body is cut,
the self should also be cut."
The Buddha addressed Kǎyè:
"Good son!
For example, there was a great strong man in a royal household.
This man had a diamond bead between his eyebrows.
He wrestled and competed in strength with another strong man,
and that strong man struck his forehead with his head.
The bead immediately sank into the skin,
and he did not know where the bead was.
There was a sore in that place,
so he summoned a good physician, wishing to treat himself.
At that time, an insightful doctor, skilled in prescriptions and medicines,
immediately knew that the sore was caused by the bead having entered the body,
and that the bead had entered the skin
and settled there.
At that moment, the good physician quickly asked the strong man:
'Where is the bead on your forehead?'
The strong man replied in astonishment:
'Great Master, King of Physicians,
has the bead on my forehead truly disappeared?
Where is this bead now?
Was it perhaps illusory?'
He grieved, worried, wept, and cried.
At that moment, the good physician consoled the strong man:
'You should not harbor such great grief and distress.
Because during your fight,
the precious bead entered your body.
It is now inside the skin,
its image appearing externally.
When you were fighting,
the poison of hatred was intense,
so the bead sank into the body,
and thus you did not know it yourself.'
At that time, the strong man did not believe the physician's words:
'If it is inside the skin,
why does it not come out with the pus and blood (impurities)?
Why does it not come out?
If it is inside the sinews,
it should not be visible.
How are you deceiving me now?'
The physician then held up a mirror,
and reflected his face.
The bead was in the mirror,
clearly and brightly manifest.
When the strong man saw this,
his heart was filled with astonishment,
and he conceived a thought of wonder and rarity.
Good son!
All sentient beings are also like this:
Because they cannot draw near to a shàn zhīshì (spiritual friend),
although they possess Fóxìng, they are all unable to perceive it.
Instead, because they are obscured by greed, lust (tān'yín),
hatred (chēnhuì), and ignorance (yúchī),
they fall into the Dìyù (Hells),
animals (Chùshēng),
hungry ghosts (Èguǐ),
Āxiūluó (Asuras),
Chāntuólúo,
Kèlì,
Póluómén,
Píshè,
Shǒutuó;
they are born into these various kinds of families.
Due to the various karmic conditions arising from the mind,
although they receive a human body,
they are deaf and blind,
mute,
crippled (jūbì), lame (lóngbǒ),
and endure various retributions in the Twenty-Five Realms of Existence (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu).
Greed, lust, hatred, and ignorance cover their hearts,
and they do not know Fóxìng.
Just like that strong man,
whose precious bead was in his body,
yet he proclaimed it lost.
Sentient beings are also like this:
Because they do not know how to draw near to a shàn zhīshì,
they do not recognize the subtle, secret treasure of the Rúlái (Tathāgata).
They cultivate and study non-self (anātman),
like those who are not sages.
Although they speak of having a self,
they also do not know the true nature of the self.
My disciples are also like this:
Because they do not know how to draw near to a shàn zhīshì,
they cultivate and study non-self,
yet they also do not know the place where non-self truly applies.
Since they themselves do not know the true nature of non-self,
how much less can they know the true nature of the self that exists?
Good son!
The Rúlái proclaims that all sentient beings possess Fóxìng,
just as the good physician
showed the strong man the diamond precious bead.
These sentient beings are obscured by countless millions of afflictions (fánnǎo) and the like,
and thus do not recognize Fóxìng.
If they exhaust these afflictions,
then they can attain clear realization and knowledge,
just like that strong man, who saw his precious bead
in the bright mirror.
Good son!
The secret storehouse of the Rúlái is immeasurable and inconceivable like this."
"Furthermore, good man!
For example, on the Snow Mountain (Xuěshān) there is a single-flavored medicinal herb,
named Happy Flavor (Lèwèi).
Its taste is exceedingly sweet,
dwelling beneath dense thickets,
which people cannot see.
If a person smells its fragrance,
they immediately know that the ground must contain this medicine.
In past ages, there was a Wheel-Turning King (Zhuanlúnwáng),
who, for the sake of this medicine on this Xuěshān,
built wooden tubes everywhere,
to collect this medicine.
When the medicine matured,
it flowed out from the ground,
collecting in the wooden tubes.
Its flavor was genuine.
After the King died,
this medicine subsequently
became sour,
or salty,
or sweet,
or bitter,
or pungent,
or bland.
Although it is one flavor,
wherever it flows, it has various differences.
The true flavor of this medicine remains on the mountain,
like the full moon.
Ordinary people, having meager fortune,
although they labor and toil, digging with mattocks,
cannot obtain it.
Furthermore, there is a Sage King (Shèngwáng),
who appears in the world,
and by reason of his fortune,
immediately obtains the true flavor of this medicine.
Good man!
The Tathāgata's (Rúlái) Secret Store (Mìzàng)
is likewise of that flavor,
covered by the thicket-forest of various afflictions (fánnǎo),
so ignorant sentient beings cannot see it.
The single flavor is likened to the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
Due to afflictions, it manifests various flavors,
namely, hells (dìyù),
animals (chùshēng),
hungry ghosts (èguǐ),
celestial beings (tiānrén),
male, female,
neither male nor female,
Kṣatriya (Chàlì),
Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén),
Vaiśya (Píshě),
Śūdra (Shǒutuó).
The Fóxìng is valiant and difficult to crush or destroy,
therefore there is no one who can kill it.
If there were a killer, they would sever the Fóxìng.
Such a Fóxìng can ultimately never be severed.
If the nature were severable,
that would be impossible.
That which is my self-nature
is precisely the Tathāgata's Secret Store (Rúlái Mìmì zhī Zàng).
Such a Mìzàng
cannot be crushed, destroyed, or burned up by anything.
Although it cannot be destroyed,
it cannot yet be seen.
Only upon achieving Anuttarasamyaksambodhi (Ānòu duō luō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí)
is it certified and known.
For this reason,
there is no one who can kill it."
The Bodhisattva Kāshyapa (Jiāshè Púsà) again addressed the Buddha (Fó), saying:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If there is no killer,
then there should be no unwholesome karma (yè)."
The Fó addressed Jiāshè:
"There truly is the killing of life (shāshēng).
Why?
Good man!
The Fóxìng of sentient beings resides within the five aggregates (wǔyīn).
If one destroys the wǔyīn,
that is called shāshēng.
If there is shāshēng,
one immediately falls into the evil destinies (èqù).
Due to the karmic condition,
there arise Kṣatriya (Chàlì),
Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén), and the like,
Vaiśya (Píshě),
Śūdra (Shǒutuó), and Caṇḍāla (Zhāntuóluó),
whether male,
or female,
or neither male nor female—
the differentiating marks of the Twenty-Five Existences (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu)—
revolving through saṃsāra (shēngsǐ).
Unholy people
falsely calculate the self (wǒ) having various large and small marks,
like barnyard grass seeds,
or like grains of rice or beans,
or even up to the size of a thumb.
In these various ways, they generate delusional recollections and imaginings.
The thought based on delusion
has no reality.
The supramundane self-mark (chūshì wǒ xiàng) is called Fóxìng.
To calculate the self (wǒ) in this manner
is called the greatest goodness.
"Furthermore, good man!
For example, a person who knows well how to find hidden treasures
takes a sharp mattock and digs straight down into the earth.
He passes through bedrock, sand, and gravel without difficulty,
but when he reaches the Vajra (Jīngāng), he cannot penetrate it.
Now, Jīngāng
cannot be crushed or destroyed
by any swords or axes.
Good man!
The Fóxìng of sentient beings is also like this:
all debaters (lùnzhě),
Devamāra Pāpīyān (Tiānmó Bōxún), and all humans and celestials (rén tiān)
cannot destroy it.
The marks of the wǔyīn
are formations (qǐzuò).
The marks of formations
are likened to rock and sand,
which can be penetrated and destroyed.
Fóxìng is likened to Jīngāng (Vajra),
which cannot be crushed or destroyed.
For this reason,
destroying the wǔyīn is called shāshēng (killing of life).
Good man!
You must certainly know that the Buddha Dharma (Fófǎ) is thus inconceivable.
" 'Lying down upon ash and dirt,
throwing oneself from high cliffs,
leaping into abysses or rushing into fire,
roasting the body with five heats,
lying upon thorny bushes,
washing chaff to drink the liquid,
taking poison or stopping eating,
killing sentient beings,
intentionally training lions,
or using spells and techniques.
Allowing the Caṇḍāla (Zhāntuóluó) caste,
those with two sexual organs,
those with no sexual organs,
or those whose two organs are unified,
all to enter the path.
Forbidding the five kinds of flavors:
curd,
buttermilk,
fresh ghee,
refined ghee,
oil,
and honey, and the like.
Allowing the wearing of silk and colorful fabrics, and using carts (kē) as footwear (bá).
Declaring that all grains
and types of grasses and trees
possess life-span.
The Fó, having said this, then entered Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).'
Whoever makes such statements, that is Māra's (Mó) discourse.
If one says:
'The Tathāgata (Rúlái) does not permit Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū) to constantly stand on one leg,
to remain silent and speak not,
to lie down upon ash and dirt,
to throw oneself from high cliffs,
to leap into abysses or rush into fire,
to roast the body with five heats,
to lie upon thorny bushes,
to wash chaff to drink the liquid,
to take poison or stop eating,
to kill sentient beings,
to intentionally train lions,
or to use spells and techniques.
The Zhāntuóluó caste,
those with two sexual organs,
those with no sexual organs,
or those whose two organs are unified,
are not permitted to enter the path.
He permits the taking of five items:
curd,
buttermilk,
ghee,
oil,
and honey, and the like.
He does not permit the acceptance and wearing of silk and colorful clothing,
or using carts as footwear.
Grains,
grasses, and trees
have no life and no self (wú wǒ),
and are not counted among sentient beings.
If there is anyone who can speak thus,
they are my disciple.
If they cannot,
you should know they are disciples of external paths (wàidào).'
Such sūtras and monastic rules are spoken by the Fó.
If anyone follows and accords with what Mó has spoken,
they are Māra's dependents;
if they can follow and accord with what the Fó has spoken,
they are called a Bodhisattva (Púsà).
"Good man!
The Vaipulya sūtras (Fāngděng jīng)
are like sweet dew (gānlù),
and also like poison."
Jiāshè Púsà again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason does the Rúlái speak the Fāngděng Sūtras,
comparing them to sweet dew (gānlù),
and also to poison?
The Buddha said:
"Good man,
do you now wish to know the true meaning of the Rúlái's secret treasury (mìzàng)?
Jiāshè replied, 'Yes,
I truly wish to know the meaning of the Rúlái's secret treasury.'
At that time, the Shìzūn spoke a verse, saying:
At that time, Jiāshè again spoke a verse, saying:
At that time, the Buddha instructed Jiāshè Púsà:
"Good man!
You should not now, like the various Shēngwén
and common people (fánfū),
make distinctions regarding the Sānbǎo (Three Jewels);
in this Dàchéng (Mahāyāna) there is no distinguishing characteristic of the Three Refuges (Sān Guī).
Why is this?
Within Fóxìng (Buddha-Nature),
there are simultaneously Fǎ (Dharma)
and Sēng (Saṅgha).
It is for the purpose of transforming and guiding the Shēngwén and common people
that the different characteristics of the Three Refuges are taught separately.
Good man!
If one wishes to comply with worldly laws,
then one should distinguish the Three Refuges.
Good man!
A Púsà should practice such contemplation:
'I now take refuge in the Buddha with this body.
If, with this very body, I attain the path to Buddhahood (Fódào),
having already attained Buddhahood,
I should not respectfully worship,
prostrate,
or make offerings to the various Shìzūn (World-Honored Ones).
Why is this?
The Buddhas are all equal,
and equally serve as refuge for sentient beings.
If I wish to revere the shèlì (relics) of the Fǎshēn (Dharma Body),
then I should bow in reverence to the stūpas and shrines of the Buddhas.
Why is this?
It is for the purpose of transforming and guiding all sentient beings.
I also cause sentient beings
to conceive of my body as a stūpa or shrine,
bowing and making offerings.
Such sentient beings take my Fǎshēn as their place of refuge.
All sentient beings rely on non-genuine, heretical, and false teachings (fǎ).
I shall sequentially speak the true teachings for them.
Furthermore, for those who take refuge in the non-genuine Sēng,
I shall establish the true Sēng as their refuge.
If there are those who distinguish the Three Refuges,
I shall establish the Single Refuge for them,
without the difference of three.
For the multitude born blind,
I serve as their eyes.
Furthermore, I shall serve as the true place of refuge for the various Shēngwén
and Yuánjué (Pratyekabuddhas).
Good man!
Such a Púsà
performs the work of a Buddha (Fóshì) for measureless evil sentient beings and for the wise.
"Good man!
For example, when a man
is approaching a battle line,
he immediately gives rise to the thought:
'I am the foremost among them;
the entire army
depends entirely upon me.'
Similarly, a prince contemplates thus:
'I shall discipline the other princes,
succeeding to the vast enterprise of the Great King,
and thereby gain sovereignty (zìzài).
I shall cause all the princes to take refuge in me.
Therefore, one should not generate an inferior mindset.'
Just as the prince of a king,
so too are the great ministers.
Good man!
A Púsà Móhēsà is also like this;
he contemplates thus:
'How are these three things a single entity with me?'
Good man!
The three things that I demonstrate
are Níhpán (Nirvāṇa).
The Rúlái is called the peerless one (Wúshàng Shì).
Just as the head is the uppermost part of the human body,
not the other limbs
like the hands and feet.
The Buddha is also like this, the most highly revered;
not the Fǎ
nor the Sēng.
It is because of the desire to transform and guide the world
that various manifestations of difference are shown,
like steps on a ladder.
Therefore, you now
should not uphold the distinguishing characteristic of the Three Refuges
as understood by common, foolish people.
Your keen resolution regarding the Dàchéng
should be like a strong sword."
Jiāshè Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Shìzūn!
I asked because I knew,
not because I did not know.
Being a great valiant Púsà,
I asked about the stainless and pure domain of practice (xíngchù),
wishing the Rúlái to extensively proclaim and distinguish the wondrous matters
for the various Púsàs,
and to extol the Dàchéng Fāngděng Sūtras.
The Rúlái, through great compassion, has now spoken well.
I, too, shall abide in this way within it.
The pure domain of practice of the Púsà that has been spoken of
is precisely the proclamation of the Dà Nièpán Jīng (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra).
Shìzūn!
I shall now also extensively proclaim and extol such a Rúlái secret treasury for sentient beings,
and shall also realize and know the true place of the Three Refuges.
If any sentient being can believe in such a Dà Nièpán Jīng,
that person will naturally comprehend the place of the Three Refuges.
Why is this?
Because the Rúlái secret treasury contains the Fóxìng.
He who proclaims this Sūtra
says that within the body, all possess the Fóxìng.
Such a person will not seek the place of the Three Refuges far away.
Why is this?
Because in future ages,
my body shall forthwith realize the Sānbǎo.
Therefore, the Shēngwén, the Yuánjué, and other sentient beings
will all depend upon me,
respectfully bowing and worshipping."
"Good man!
Based on this meaning,
you ought to truly study the Dàchéng Sūtras."
Jiāshè replied again:
"The Fóxìng is thus inconceivable.
The Sānshí'èr Xiàng (Thirty-Two Marks)
and the Bāshí Zhǒng Hǎo (Eighty Minor Characteristics) are also inconceivable."
At that time, the Buddha praised Jiāyè Púsà (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva), saying:
“Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
You have already achieved profound and keen wisdom.
I shall now speak well for you further,
concerning entering the Rúlái Zàng (Tathāgata Store).
If the self exists, this is the doctrine of permanence (eternalism),
which is not separate from suffering;
if the self does not exist,
cultivating pure conduct
is without benefit.
If one says that all phenomena are without self,
this is the view of annihilation (nihilism);
if one says the self exists, this is the view of permanence.
If one says that all formations are impermanent,
this is the view of annihilation;
if formations are permanent, this is again the view of permanence.
If one speaks of suffering, this is the view of annihilation;
if one speaks of pleasure, this is again the view of permanence.
One who cultivates the permanence of all phenomena falls into the view of annihilation,
and one who cultivates the annihilation of all phenomena falls into the view of permanence.
Just as the measuring worm
must rely on its front feet to move its hind feet,
the cultivators of permanence and annihilation
are also like this,
they must rely on annihilation and permanence.
For this reason,
those who cultivate the suffering of other doctrines
are all called unskillful;
those who cultivate the pleasure of other doctrines
are called skillful.
Cultivating the non-self of other doctrines belongs to the realm of afflictions (fánnǎo);
cultivating the permanence of other doctrines is called the Rúlái Mìzàng (Tathāgata Secret Store),
which is called Nièpán (Nirvāṇa),
having no dwelling place.
Cultivating other impermanent doctrines
is wealth and material things;
cultivating other permanent doctrines
refers to the Fó (Buddha),
Fǎ (Dharma),
Sēng (Saṅgha), and genuine liberation.
One should know that the Buddhist Middle Way (Zhōngdào)
avoids the two extremes and speaks the true Fǎ.
Ordinary foolish people harbor no doubt concerning it,
just as a weak, sick person, having consumed clarified butter (sū),
becomes buoyant and energetic.
The doctrines of existence and non-existence
have natures that are not fixed,
just like the Four Great Elements (Sìdà);
their natures are different,
and they mutually contradict each other.
A good physician knows well
how to regulate them according to which is excessively manifesting.
Good man!
The Rúlái (Tathāgata) is also like this,
acting as a good physician toward all sentient beings.
He knows the differences in the substance and characteristics of the afflictions and removes and severs them,
revealing the Rúlái's Secret Store,
the pure Fóxìng (Buddha Nature), which is permanent and unchanging.
If one speaks of existence,
wisdom should not be defiled;
if one speaks of non-existence,
this is false speech.
If one speaks of existence,
one should not remain silent,
nor should one engage in playful debates or disputes;
one should only seek to fully know the true nature of all phenomena.
Ordinary people engage in playful debates and disputes,
because they do not understand the subtle and secret Store of the Rúlái.
If suffering is taught,
the fool immediately believes the body is impermanent.
When all suffering is taught,
they fail to know that the body has the nature of pleasure.
If impermanence is taught,
ordinary people calculate that all bodies are impermanent,
like a piece of earthenware;
the wise person
ought to distinguish,
and should not say that absolutely everything is impermanent.
Why is this?
Because my body contains the seed of Fóxìng.
If non-self is taught,
ordinary people immediately believe that all Buddhist doctrines are utterly without self;
the wise person ought to distinguish that non-self is merely a false name and not ultimately real.
Having known this,
one should not give rise to doubt.
If it is said that the Rúlái Mìzàng is void (kōng) and quiescent (jí),
ordinary people, upon hearing it,
give rise to the view of annihilation;
the wise person ought to distinguish that
the Rúlái is permanent
and without change.
If it is said that liberation is comparable to magical illusion,
ordinary people immediately believe that one who attains liberation is utterly extinguished;
the wise person ought to distinguish that
the Lion among Men (rénzhōng shīzǐ), though coming and going,
is permanently abiding and unchanging.
If it is said that formations (xíng) arise due to the condition of ignorance (wúmíng),
ordinary people, having heard it, distinguish
and produce the concept of duality,
illumination (míng) and ignorance;
the wise person understands that their nature is non-dual,
and the nature of non-duality is the true nature (shíxìng).
If it is said that consciousness (shì) arises due to the condition of formations,
ordinary people believe in duality,
formations and consciousness;
the wise person understands that their nature is non-dual,
and the nature of non-duality is the true nature.
If the ten virtues (shíshàn) and ten evils (shí'è),
the doable and the undoable,
the wholesome path and the unwholesome path,
white doctrines and black doctrines are discussed,
ordinary people believe in duality;
the wise person understands that
their nature is non-dual,
and the nature of non-duality is the true nature.
If it is said that one should cultivate the suffering of all phenomena,
ordinary people believe in duality;
the wise person understands that
their nature is non-dual,
and the nature of non-duality is the true nature.
If it is said that all formations are impermanent,
and that the Rúlái Mìzàng is also impermanent,
ordinary people believe in duality;
the wise person understands that
their nature is non-dual,
and the nature of non-duality is the true nature.
If it is said that all phenomena are without self,
and that the Rúlái Mìzàng is also without self,
ordinary people believe in duality;
the wise person understands that their nature is non-dual,
and the nature of non-duality is the true nature.
Self and non-self
are not two in nature.
The meaning of the Rúlái Mìzàng is thus,
praised by immeasurable and boundless Fó, beyond calculation or description.
I have now completely spoken of
all the merits achieved in this Sūtra.
“Good man!
Self and non-self are non-dual in nature and characteristics.
You should thus receive, maintain, and bear this upon your head.
Good man!
You should also firmly maintain and remember this Sūtra,
just as I previously said in the Móhē Bōrě Bōluómì Jīng (Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra) that self
and non-self
do not have two characteristics.
For example, due to milk, curds (lào) are produced;
due to curds, fresh butter (shēngsū) is obtained;
due to fresh butter, ripened butter (shúsū) is obtained;
due to ripened butter, cream (tíhú) is obtained.
Is the nature of curds produced from milk?
Is it self-produced?
Is it produced from another?
Up to cream, it is also thus.
If it is produced from another,
it is made by that other,
and is not produced by milk;
if it is not produced by milk,
milk has no function;
if it is self-produced,
it should not arise in a continuous succession of similarity.
If it arises continuously,
then they are not generated simultaneously.
If they are not generated simultaneously,
the five tastes do not exist at one time.
Although they are not simultaneous,
it is certain that they do not come from elsewhere.
One should know that the characteristic of curds pre-exists in the milk,
but because of the abundance of sweetness, it cannot change by itself.
Up to the cream, it is also thus.
The cow, by the condition of feeding on water and grass,
has its blood vessels transform and thereby produce milk.
If it eats sweet grass, its milk is sweet;
if it eats bitter grass, the milk is bitter.
In Xuěshān (Snow Mountain) there is grass called Féinì (Fatty);
if a cow eats it, only cream is obtained.
The milk, due to the conditions of green, yellow, red, white, or black grains and grasses,
will have differences in color and taste.
These sentient beings, relying on the conditions of karma of illumination
and ignorance,
give rise to the two characteristics.
If ignorance transforms,
it turns into illumination.
All phenomena—wholesome
and unwholesome, and so forth—
are also like this, having no dual characteristics.”
Kǎyè Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Regarding what the Buddha has said,
that curds exist within milk—
what is the meaning of this doctrine?
World-Honored One!
If you say that the nature of curds definitely exists within milk,
but is invisible because it is subtle,
why then is it said that curds are produced due to the conditions relating to milk?
If a phenomenon fundamentally did not exist, it is called 'production' (or 'being born').
If it already exists, how can it be called 'production'?
If you say that the nature of curds definitely exists within milk,
then milk should also exist within all grasses,
and similarly, grass should exist within milk.
If you say that curds definitely do not exist within milk,
how is it that curds can be produced based on milk?
If a phenomenon fundamentally did not exist,
yet later comes to exist,
why is it that grass is not produced from milk?
"Good man!
One cannot definitively say that curds exist within milk,
or that curds do not exist within milk,
nor can one say that they are produced from another source.
If you say that curds definitely exist within milk,
how is it that their substance and flavor are different?
Therefore, one cannot say that the nature of curds definitely exists within milk.
If you say that curds definitely do not exist within milk,
why is it that rabbit horns are not produced from milk?
If poison is placed in milk,
the curds produced will then kill people.
Therefore, one cannot say that the nature of curds definitely does not exist within milk.
If you say that these curds are produced from another source,
why is it that curds are not produced from water?
Therefore, one cannot say that curds are produced from another source.
Good man!
When cows eat and chew grass, due to these conditions,
the blood changes and becomes white.
Once the grass and blood are extinguished,
the power of living beings’ merit transforms it and forms milk.
Although this milk is produced from grass and blood,
one cannot say they are two (separate entities).
It can only be named 'produced from conditions.'
Curds up to refined cream (tíhú) are also like this.
Because of this meaning,
it is named the 'flavor of the cow.'
Once the milk is extinguished,
conditions form the curds.
What are these conditions?
It is either sourness (vinegar)
or warmth.
Therefore, it is named
'existence arising from conditions.'
Even up to refined cream (tíhú), it is also like this.
Therefore, one cannot definitively say that the nature of curds does not exist within milk.
As for 'being produced from another source,'
existing separate from milk—
there is no such possibility.
Good man!
Illumination (míng) and ignorance (wúmíng) are also like this.
If it is joined with afflictions and fetters,
it is called ignorance (wúmíng).
If it is joined with all good phenomena,
it is named illumination (míng).
Therefore, I say there are not two natures.
Because of this cause and condition, I previously spoke, saying:
On Xuěshān (Snowy Mountain), there is grass named Féi'nì (Fatty and Oily).
If cows eat it, it immediately becomes refined cream (tíhú).
The Buddhanature (Fóxìng) is also like this.
"Good man!
Living beings with little merit cannot see this grass.
The Buddhanature (Fóxìng) is also like this;
because it is covered by afflictions,
living beings cannot see it.
For example, the great ocean,
although uniformly salty,
contains within it supreme and wonderful water,
whose flavor resembles milk.
Just like Xuěshān (Snowy Mountain),
although it possesses various merits
and produces many medicines,
it also has poisonous grasses.
The bodies of all living beings are also like this:
although they contain the seeds of the four great poisonous snakes (the four elements),
they also contain the Great King of Wonderful Medicine,
which is called the Buddhanature (Fóxìng).
It is not a conditioned phenomenon;
it is merely covered by afflictions, which are like transient dust.
If Kṣatriyas (Chàlì),
Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén),
Vaiśyas (Píshě),
or Śūdras (Shǒutuó),
are able to cut them off,
they immediately see the Buddhanature (Fóxìng) and achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
For example, when thunder shakes the empty sky and clouds arise,
flowers grow upon all elephant tusks.
If there is no thunder shaking,
the flowers will not grow,
nor will they have a name.
The Buddhanature (Fóxìng) of living beings is also like this:
it is constantly covered by all afflictions and cannot be seen.
Therefore, I state that living beings are without self.
If they are able to hear this subtle and wonderful scripture, the Dà Bān Nièpán,
they will then see the Buddhanature (Fóxìng).
Just like the elephant tusk flowers.
Although one may hear the Sūtras (Qìjīng) and all samādhis,
if one does not hear this scripture,
one does not know the subtle nature of the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
It is like when there is no thunder:
the flowers on the elephant tusks cannot be seen.
Having heard this scripture,
one immediately knows that the secret storehouse Buddhanature (Fóxìng) is taught by all Tathāgatas (Rúlái).
This is compared to celestial thunder,
which allows the elephant tusk flowers to be seen.
Having heard this scripture,
one immediately knows that all immeasurable living beings possess the Buddhanature (Fóxìng).
Because of this meaning,
the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán) is spoken of,
and is named the secret storehouse of the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
which increases the Dharma Body (Fǎshēn),
just like the flowers on the elephant tusks when there is thunder.
Because it is able to foster and nourish this great meaning,
it is named the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Bān Nièpán).
If there are good men
or good women,
who are able to practice and study this subtle and wonderful scripture, the Dà Nièpán,
know that these people are able to repay the Buddha's kindness
and are true disciples of the Buddha."
Kǎyè Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Most wonderful,
World-Honored One!
The Buddhanature (Fóxìng) of which you speak
is exceedingly profound, exceedingly profound;
difficult to see, difficult to enter;
the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué) cannot comprehend it."
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
It is so,
it is so.
As you have praised it,
it does not contradict my teaching."
Kǎyè Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Regarding the Buddhanature (Fóxìng),
how is it that it is exceedingly profound, difficult to see, and difficult to enter?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Suppose a hundred blind people,
seeking to cure their eyes,
visit a good doctor.
At that time, the good doctor,
immediately uses a golden needle (pèi),
to pierce the cataract membrane.
He uses one finger to point,
and asks:
'Do you see it?'
The blind people answer:
'We still do not see.'
Again he uses two fingers,
and three fingers to point,
and then they say:
'We see a little.'
Good man!
When this subtle Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán jīng)
was not yet preached by the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
it was likewise.
Countless Bodhisattvas (Púsà),
although fully practicing all Pāramitās (Bōluómì),
reaching even the Ten Abodes (Shí zhù),
still could not perceive the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) that exists;
once the Tathāgata preached it,
they immediately saw a little.
These Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà), having attained this partial vision,
all speak thus:
'Most marvelous,
World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
We have been drifting through countless cycles of life and death,
constantly confused and misled by the concept of non-self.'
Good man!
Even such Bodhisattvas,
whose stage reaches the Ten Grounds (Shí dì),
still do not clearly and distinctly perceive the Buddha-nature,
how much less Śrāvakas (Shēngwén)
and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué),
could they attain vision of it?
Furthermore, good man!
For instance, looking up at wild geese (éyàn) in the sky,
is it the sky?
Or is it the wild geese?
By observing continuously and intently,
one faintly perceives them.
Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes (Shí zhù Púsà) regarding the Tathāgata-nature (Rúláixìng),
know and see a small portion,
and it is likewise,
how much less can Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas know and see it?
Good man!
For example, a drunken person,
wishing to traverse a long road,
sees the path dimly.
Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes regarding the Tathāgata-nature,
know and see a small portion,
and it is likewise.
Good man!
For example, a thirsty person,
traveling through a barren wilderness (kuàngyě),
this person is tormented by thirst,
traveling everywhere searching for water,
sees a clump of trees,
and white cranes (báihè) on the trees.
This person is confused and bewildered,
unable to distinguish whether it is trees or water,
By observing continuously and intently,
they finally perceive the white cranes and the clump of trees.
Good man!
Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes regarding the Tathāgata-nature,
know and see a small portion,
and it is likewise.
Good man!
For example, there is a person,
in the middle of the great sea, even at countless hundreds or thousands of yojanas (yóuxún) distant,
looking afar at a great ship with towers (lóulǔ) and palaces (tánggé),
immediately forms this thought:
'Are those towers?
Or are they empty space?'
After looking for a long time, the heart of certainty arises,
knowing them to be towers.
Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes seeing the Tathāgata-nature within their own bodies,
it is likewise.
Good man!
For example, a prince,
whose body is extremely weak,
plays throughout the night,
until the clear morning light,
and seeing everything with his eyes is not at all clear.
Although Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes see the Tathāgata-nature within themselves,
it is likewise not very clear.
"Furthermore, good man!
For example, a minister or official (chénlì),
constrained by royal affairs,
returns home late at night,
a flash of lightning momentarily appears,
and he sees a cluster of oxen (niújù).
He immediately forms this thought:
'Are these oxen?
Or a cluster of clouds or a house?'
Although this person looks for a long time,
and the notion of oxen arises,
he still cannot determine it clearly.
Although Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes see the Tathāgata-nature within themselves,
they cannot determine it clearly,
and it is likewise.
Furthermore, good man!
Like a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) maintaining the precepts,
who observes water without insects but perceives the appearance of insects,
he immediately forms this thought:
'What is moving in here,
is it insects?
Or is it dust?'
By observing continuously and intently,
although he knows it is dust,
it is still not clear.
Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes seeing the Tathāgata-nature within their own bodies,
it is likewise not very clear.
Furthermore, good man!
For example, a person,
in deep darkness, sees a small child from afar,
and immediately forms this thought:
'Is that an ox,
a vulture (jiù),
a bird,
or a person?'
After observing continuously and intently,
although he sees a small child, it is still not clear.
Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes seeing the Tathāgata-nature in their own person,
it is likewise not very clear.
Furthermore, good man!
For example, a person,
in the darkness of night, sees a painted image of a Bodhisattva (Púsà xiàng),
and immediately forms this thought:
'Is this a Bodhisattva image,
an image of Īśvara (Zìzàitiān xiàng),
an image of Mahābrahmā (Dà Fàntiān xiàng),
or merely dyed clothing?'
This person observes for a long time,
although he mentally concludes it is a Bodhisattva image,
it is still not clear.
Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes seeing the Tathāgata-nature in their own person,
it is likewise not very clear.
Good man!
The Buddha-nature is thus extremely profound,
difficult to know and see,
only the Buddha can know it,
it is not attainable by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Good man!
The wise should thus analyze and know the Tathāgata-nature.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa (Jiāshè Púsà) said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha-nature is thus subtle and difficult to know,
how can the physical eye be able to see it?"
The Buddha said:
"Kāśyapa!
Good man!
Just as the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (Fēixiǎngfēifēixiǎng tiān),
it is also not something that the Two Vehicles (Èr Chéng) are able to know,
but by relying on and following the Sūtras (Qìjīng),
one knows it through faith.
Good man!
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas faithfully follow this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Nièpán jīng),
and know that their own bodies possess the Tathāgata-nature,
it is likewise.
Good man!
Therefore, one should diligently cultivate and practice the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
Good man!
Such is the Buddha-nature;
only the Buddha can know it,
it is not attainable by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
Ordinary beings who are not Noble Ones (Fánfū) possess the nature of sentient beings (zhòngshēngxìng),
and all proclaim the existence of the self (wǒ).
The Fó said:
“For example, two people were close friends,
one was a prince (wángzǐ),
the other was poor and lowly.
These two people frequently visited each other.
At that time, the poor man saw that the prince (wángzǐ) had a fine sword,
pure, excellent, and foremost,
and his heart became attached to it with greed.
Later, the prince (wángzǐ), taking this sword, fled to another country.
Thereupon, the poor man,
later lodged and slept temporarily at another person’s house.
While sleeping,
he muttered ‘sword, sword’ in his sleep.
People nearby heard this
and seized him and brought him to the king (wáng).
The king (wáng) then asked:
‘This sword you speak of,
where did you get it?’
This man fully answered the king (wáng) with the aforementioned facts:
‘Even if the king (wáng) were now to slaughter and cut my body,
and tear apart my hands and feet,
it would be truly impossible
to obtain the sword you seek.
I have always been close friends with the prince (wángzǐ),
and formerly resided in the same place.
Although I once saw it with my own eyes,
I did not even dare to brush it with my hand,
much less deliberately take it?
The king (wáng) further asked:
‘When you saw the sword,
what did its appearance resemble?’
He replied:
‘Great King (dàwáng)!
What I saw
was like a ram’s horn.’
When the king (wáng) heard this,
he smiled happily and said:
‘You may now go wherever you please;
do not harbor worry or fear.
In my treasury, there is no such sword at all,
much less would you see it near the prince (wángzǐ)?’
The king (wáng) then asked his assembled officials:
‘Have you ever seen a sword like this?’
Having spoken, he passed away (bēngbèi).
Another son was immediately established to succeed to the throne (wángwèi).
He again asked the assisting officials:
‘Have you ever seen this sword in the royal treasury (guānzàng)?’
The officials replied:
‘We have seen it.’
He asked again:
‘What was its shape like?’
They replied:
‘Great King (dàwáng)!
Like a ram’s horn.’
The king (wáng) said:
‘In my royal treasury (guānzàng),
where could there possibly be a sword with such a shape?’
Subsequently, four kings (wáng)
all inspected (the treasury),
but could not find it.
A certain time having elapsed,
the prince (wángzǐ) who had previously fled,
returned from the other country,
came to his native land,
and regained the position of king (wáng).
Once he ascended the throne (wángwèi),
he again asked the officials:
‘Have you seen the sword?’
They replied:
‘Great King (dàwáng)!
We have all seen it.’
He asked again:
‘What was its shape like?’
They replied:
‘Great King (dàwáng)!
Its color was pure and clean,
like an Utpala (yōubōluó) flower.’
Others replied:
‘Its shape was like a sheep’s horn.’
Others spoke, saying:
‘Its color was bright red,
like a heap of fire.’
Others replied:
‘It was like a black snake.’
The king (wáng) laughed loudly:
‘None of you have seen the true form of my sword.’
“Good men (shànnánzǐ)!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) is also like this:
He appears in the world and speaks of the true characteristic of the self,
and having spoken, departs,
like the prince (wángzǐ) taking the pure and marvelous sword and fleeing to another country.
Ordinary, foolish people speak, saying, ‘Everything possesses a self,’
and ‘there is a self,’
like that poor man,
lodging in another’s house,
and muttering ‘sword, sword’ in his sleep.
The Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué) ask all sentient beings:
‘What is the characteristic of the self?’
They reply:
‘I see the self-characteristic
as large as a thumb.’
Some say:
‘Like a grain of rice,’
or ‘like a grain of millet.’
Some say:
‘The self-characteristic resides in the heart,
burning brightly like the sun.’
Such sentient beings do not know the self-characteristic,
just as the officials did not know the characteristics of the sword.
The Bodhisattva (Púsà) thus speaks of the Dharma of the self (wǒfǎ),
but ordinary people do not understand the various discriminations
and mistakenly create characteristics of the self;
just as when asked about the sword's characteristic,
they answered that it resembled a ram's horn.
These ordinary people successively and continuously give rise to wrong views (xiéjiàn).
In order to cut off these wrong views (xiéjiàn),
the Tathāgata (Rúlái) manifests and speaks of non-self (wúwǒ).
This is analogous to the prince (wángzǐ) telling the officials,
‘There is no such sword in my treasury.’
Good men (shànnánzǐ)!
The true self spoken of by the Tathāgata (Rúlái) today
is named the Buddha-Nature (Fóxìng).
This Buddha-Nature (Fóxìng),
in My Buddha-Dharma (Fófǎ), is likened to the pure sword.
Good men (shànnánzǐ)!
If there are ordinary people who can speak well of it,
this is conformity with the unsurpassed Buddha-Dharma (Fófǎ).
If one is skilled at discriminating and conforming to this declaration,
you should know that this is the appearance of a Bodhisattva (Púsà).
Good men (shànnánzǐ)!
All the various differing doctrines,
incantations (zhùshù),
languages,
and writings,
are all spoken by the Buddha (Fó),
not by external paths (wàidào).
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva (Jiāshè Púsà) said to the Buddha (Fó):
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
How does the Tathāgata (Rúlái) speak of the foundation of characters (zìběn)?”
The Buddha (Fó) said:
“Good men (shànnánzǐ)!
Speaking of the initial half-characters,
which are taken as the foundation,
they support all records and treatises,
incantations (zhùshù) and literature,
and the substantial Dharmas of the Skandhas (yīn shífǎ).
Ordinary people study this character foundation (zìběn),
and only then can they know what is Dharma (fǎ)
and what is non-Dharma (fēifǎ).
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva (Jiāshè Púsà) further said to the Buddha (Fó):
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
What is the meaning
of the word ‘character’ (zì)?”
“Good men (shànnánzǐ)!
There are fourteen sounds (yīn) that are called the meaning of the character (zìyì).
The word ‘character’ (zì)
is named Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
Because it is permanent (cháng), it does not flow (bùliú).
If it does not flow,
then it is inexhaustible (wújìn).
Now, the inexhaustible (wújìn)
is the Vajra Body (Jīngāng zhī Shēn) of the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
These fourteen sounds (shísì yīn)
are named the character foundation (zìběn).
means non-destruction (bù pòhuài).
Non-destruction (bù pòhuài)
is named the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo),
likened to the Vajra (Jīngāng).
Furthermore, ‘Ē (Ě)’
is named non-flowing (bùliú).
Non-flowing is the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
because the nine apertures of the Tathāgata (Rúlái) have nothing flowing out,
therefore it does not flow.
Also, lacking the nine apertures, therefore it does not flow.
Non-flowing is permanence (cháng).
Permanence (cháng) is the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) has no action, therefore it does not flow.
Furthermore, ‘Ē (Ě)’ is named merit (gōngdé).
Merit (gōngdé) is the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo).
Therefore, it is named ‘Ē (Ě).’”
"The character Ā (阿)
is named Āshélí (Āchálí).
What is the meaning
of Āshélí?
Among the world's people,
one is entitled Sage (Shèngzhě).
What is meant by Sage?
Sage means non-attachment (wúzhuó).
Having few desires and knowing contentment is also named purity (qīngjìng).
They are able to cross sentient beings over the great ocean of saṃsāra (birth and death) in the current of the three existences.
This is named a Sage.
Furthermore, Ā also means system and regulation (zhìdù).
Cultivating and upholding pure precepts and conforming to dignified conduct (wēiyí).
Furthermore, Ā means relying on the Sage.
One should learn the dignified conduct (wēiyí) of advancing, stopping, raising, and moving;
offering, respecting, and bowing to the Three Venerable Ones (Sānzūn);
showing filial piety to parents, and studying the Mahāyāna (Dàshèng).
Good men and women, etc., who fully uphold the prohibitions and precepts,
and all Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà), etc.
These are named Sages.
Furthermore, Ā means teaching and instruction (jiàohuì).
Such as saying, "You come,"
"You should act like this,"
"Do not act like this."
If one is able to prevent improper conduct (fēi wēiyí fǎ),
this is named a Sage.
Therefore, it is named Ā.
"The character Yì (億)
is the Buddha Dharma (Fófǎ).
The pure practice (fànhéng) is vast and great,
pure and stainless,
likened to the full moon.
You should understand what
should be done
and what should not be done,
what is right meaning
and what is wrong meaning,
what is spoken by the Buddha,
and what is spoken by Māra (Mó).
Therefore, it is named Yì.
"The character Yī (伊)
refers to the subtle, profound, and difficult-to-obtain Buddha Dharma.
Like Zìzàitiān and the Dà Fàntiānwáng,
the Dharma is named Sovereignty (Zìzài).
If one is able to uphold it,
then one is named a Dharma protector (hùfǎ).
Furthermore, Sovereignty
is named the Four Guardian Kings (Sì Hùshì).
These four Sovereigns
are thus able to gather and protect the Mòhē Bōnièpán Jīng (Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra),
and are also able to freely expound and proclaim it.
Furthermore, Yī
is able to freely preach the Dharma for sentient beings.
Moreover, Yī, for the sake of sovereignty,
speaks of what practice?
Namely, cultivating the Vaipulya Sūtras (Fāngděng Jīngdiǎn).
Moreover, Yī
is for cutting off jealousy (jídù),
like removing tares and weeds.
All are capable of being transformed into auspiciousness (jíxiáng).
Therefore, it is named Yī.
"The character Yù (郁)
is the most supreme and most excellent among all sūtras,
increasing the supreme of the supreme, namely the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
Furthermore, Yù refers to the nature of the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
which the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué) have never heard.
Just as among all places,
Uttarakuru (Běi Yùdānyuè) is the most exceptional;
if a Bodhisattva (Púsà) is able to hear and receive this sūtra,
they are the most exceptional among all beings.
For this reason,
this sūtra is entitled the most supreme and most excellent.
Therefore, it is named Yù.
"The character Yōu (優)
is likened to cow's milk,
the finest among all flavors.
The nature of the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is also like this,
the most venerable and most supreme among all sūtras.
If there is anyone who slanders it,
know that this person is no different from a cow.
Furthermore, Yōu
means that this person is named lacking wisdom (wú huì)
and right mindfulness (zhèng niàn).
Slandering the subtle, secret treasury of the Tathāgata,
know that this person is greatly to be pitied,
being far removed from the Tathāgata's secret treasury,
speaking of the doctrine of non-self (wú wǒ fǎ).
Therefore, it is named Yōu.
"The character 󱶐 (Ǎi)
is all Buddhas,
Dharma-nature (Fǎxìng),
and Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
Therefore, it is named 󱶐.
"The character Yě (嘢)
means the meaning of the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Furthermore, Yě refers to how
the Tathāgata's advancing and stopping,
bending and stretching,
raising and moving,
nothing fails to benefit all sentient beings.
Therefore, it is named Yě.
"The character Wū (烏)
means defilement (fánnǎo).
Defilements are named all outflows (zhū lòu).
The Tathāgata has eternally cut off all defilements.
Therefore, it is named Wū.
"The character Pào (炮)
means the meaning of the Mahāyāna (Dàshèng).
Among the fourteen sounds (shísì yīn), it is the meaning of ultimate realization (jiūjìng).
The Mahāyāna Sūtras are also like this,
being the ultimate realization among all sūtras and treatises.
Therefore, it is named Pào.
"The character Ān (菴)
is able to stop all impure objects.
Within the Buddha Dharma (Fófǎ), it is able to renounce all gold, silver, and precious objects.
Therefore, it is named Ān.
"The character Ā (阿)
means the superior vehicle (shèng chèng).
Why is this?
This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mòhē Bōnièpán Jīng (Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra),
is the most exceptional among all sūtras.
Therefore, it is named Ā.
"The character Jiā (迦)
means giving rise to great compassion (dà cíběi) toward all sentient beings,
generating the thought of them as one's children,
like Luóhóuluó (Rāhula),
accomplishing the meaning of subtle and supreme goodness.
Therefore, it is named Jiā.
"The character Qū (佉)
means non-good friends (fēi shànyǒu).
Non-good friends
are named mixed defilements (záhuì).
They do not believe in the Tathāgata's secret treasury.
Therefore, it is named Qū.
"The character Gā (伽)
means treasury (zàng).
The treasury is precisely the Tathāgata's secret treasury.
All sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng).
Therefore, it is named Gā.
"The character 𠷐 (Ngā)
means the Tathāgata's eternal sound (chángyīn).
What is named the Tathāgata's eternal sound?
Namely, the Tathāgata permanently dwells and is unchanging.
Therefore, it is named 𠷐.
"The character É (俄)
means the characteristic of destruction for all composite phenomena (zhū xíng).
Therefore, it is named É.
"The character Zhē (遮)
is the meaning of cultivation (xiū).
Because it tames and subdues all sentient beings,
it is named the meaning of cultivation.
Therefore, it is named Zhē.
"The character Chē (車)
means the Tathāgata sheltering and protecting all sentient beings,
likened to a great canopy.
Therefore, it is named Chē.
"The character Shé (闍)
means true liberation (zhèng jiětuō),
being free of the characteristic of aging.
Therefore, it is named Shé.
"The character Shàn (膳)
means luxuriant defilements,
likened to a dense forest.
Therefore, it is named Shàn.
"The character Ruò (喏)
is the meaning of wisdom (zhìhuì).
Knowing the true Dharma-nature (fǎxìng).
Therefore, it is named Ruò.
"The character Zhà (吒)
means manifesting half the body in Yánfú Tí (Jambudvīpa) while expounding the Dharma,
likened to the half moon.
Therefore, it is named Zhà.
"The character Chà (侘)
means the Dharma-body (fǎshēn) is complete,
likened to the full moon.
Therefore, it is named Chà.
"The character Tú (荼)
means ignorant monks (yúchī sēng),
who do not know the eternal versus the impermanent,
likened to a small child.
Therefore, it is named Tú.
"The character Zǔ (祖)
means not knowing the teacher's kindness,
likened to a ram.
Therefore, it is named Zǔ.
"The character Nú (拏)
means not the meaning of the Sage,
likened to outside paths (wàidào).
Therefore, it is named Nú.
"The character Duō (多)
means the Tathāgata informing the bhikṣus (bǐqiū) there,
that they should abandon alarm and fear,
for He shall now preach the subtle and wonderful Dharma for them.
Therefore, it is named Duō.
"The character Tā (他)
means the meaning of ignorance (yúchī).
Sentient beings revolve through saṃsāra,
wrapped up like silkworms or dung beetles (qiāngláng).
Therefore, it is named Tā.
"Tuó
means 'Great Giving' (Dà Shī),
which is the so-called Great Vehicle (Dàchéng).
Therefore, it is called Tuó.
"Tán
means praising merits and virtues,
which are the so-called Three Jewels (Sānbǎo),
like Mount Xūmí,
high, steep, vast, and great,
incapable of falling over.
Therefore, it is called Tán.
"Nà
means the Sānbǎo are firmly established,
without shaking or moving,
likened to a door sill.
Therefore, it is called Nà.
"Bō
means the meaning of inversion or perversity.
If someone says that the Sānbǎo are completely extinguished,
you should know that this person harbors self-doubt.
Therefore, it is called Bō.
"Pǒ
refers to worldly calamities.
If someone says that when worldly calamities arise, the Sānbǎo are also exhausted,
you should know that this person
is foolish and ignorant, having violated and lost the sacred decree.
Therefore, it is called Pǒ.
"Pó
means the Ten Powers of the Buddha (Fó Shí Lì).
Therefore, it is called Pó.
"Màn
means 'heavy burden,'
being capable of bearing the unsurpassed True Dharma (zhèngfǎ).
You should know that this person is a Great Bodhisattva (Dà Púsà).
Therefore, it is called Màn.
"Mó
refers to the strict rules and disciplines of all the Púsàs,
which is the so-called Great Vehicle Great Parinirvāṇa (Dàchéng Dà Bān Nièpán).
Therefore, it is called Mó.
"Shé
refers to all the Púsàs,
who, everywhere they go, preach the Dàchéng Dharma for the sake of living beings.
Therefore, it is called Shé.
"Luō
means being able to destroy greed,
hatred,
and delusion,
preaching the true Dharma.
Therefore, it is called Luō.
"Luó
means the Sound Hearer Vehicle (Shēngwén Chéng),
which moves and does not abide.
The Dàchéng is stable and firm, without moving or shaking.
[It means] abandoning the Shēngwén Chéng,
diligently cultivating and practicing the unsurpassed Dàchéng.
Therefore, it is called Luó.
"Hé
means that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One (Rúlái Shìzūn),
rains down the Great Dharma rain for all living beings,
which refers to worldly charms and scriptures.
Therefore, it is called Hé.
"Shē means departing far from the three arrows.
Therefore, it is called Shē.
"Shā
means the definition of completion or fullness.
If one can listen to this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Nièpán Jīng),
they will have attained the faculty of hearing and retaining all Dàchéng Sūtras.
Therefore, it is called Shā.
"Suō
means expounding the True Dharma for living beings,
causing their hearts to rejoice.
Therefore, it is called Suō.
"Hē
means the heart rejoicing:
'Wonderful is the Shìzūn,
who is far removed from all conditioned actions!'
'How marvelous is the Rúlái,
who enters Parinirvāṇa!'
Therefore, it is called Hē.
"Zhā
means the meaning of Māra (Mó yì).
The measureless Māras cannot destroy the secret treasury of the Rúlái.
Therefore, it is called Zhā.
Furthermore, Zhā
also refers to manifesting accordance with the world,
having parents, wife, and children.
Therefore, it is called Zhā.
"Lǔ,
Liú,
Lú,
Lóu—
these four characters
express four meanings:
namely, the Buddha (Fó),
the Dharma (Fǎ),
the Saṅgha (Sēng), and the Dui Fǎ (Abhidharma or Counter-Dharma).
The term 'Duì Fǎ' means conforming to the world,
such as Tiáo Pódá (Devadatta) manifesting the destruction of the Saṅgha,
transforming into various forms, appearances, and images.
This is done for the sake of establishing precepts.
The wise understand this fully
and should not give rise to fear
regarding this. This is called the conduct of conforming to the world.
Because of this, they are named Lǔ,
Liú,
Lú,
Lóu.
"The root of the tongue sucking air,
the sound following the nose,
the long and short exceeding sounds,
and understanding meaning based on sound—
all these have distinctions because of the tongue and teeth.
The meaning of these characters
is able to purify the verbal karma of living beings.
The Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) of living beings is not like this, dependent on characters and then becoming pure.
Why is this?
Because the nature is fundamentally pure.
Although it resides among the skandhas, dhātus, and āyatanas,
it is not the same as the skandhas, āyatanas, and dhātus.
Therefore, living beings should entirely take refuge in the Púsàs and others,
because of the Fóxìng, they regard all living beings equally, without differentiation.
Therefore, the Half-Character (Bàn Zì)
is the foundation
of all sūtras, commentaries, and writings.
Moreover, the meaning of the Half-Character
is the root of all discourse concerning afflictions.
Hence, it is called the Half-Character.
The Full-Character (Mǎn Zì), however, is the root of all discourse concerning good Dharmas.
For example, in the world,
those who practice evil are called Half-Men,
and those who cultivate goodness are called Full-Men.
In the same way, all sūtras, scriptures, and commentaries
take the Half-Character as their root.
If one says that the Rúlái and true liberation
enter into the Half-Character,
this statement is false.
Why is this?
Because they are divorced from written characters.
Therefore, the Rúlái, regarding all Dharmas,
is unimpeded and unattached, truly attaining liberation.
What is meant by understanding the meaning of characters?
It is knowing that when the Rúlái appears in the world,
he is able to extinguish the Half-Character.
Therefore, this is called understanding the meaning of characters.
If there is someone who chases after the meaning of the Half-Character,
this person does not know the nature of the Rúlái.
What is meant by the meaning of the Non-Character (Wú Zì yì)?
Those who draw near and practice unwholesome Dharmas,
this is called the Wú Zì.
Furthermore, the Wú Zì refers to those who, although able to draw near and practice wholesome Dharmas,
do not understand the Rúlái’s Eternal and Impermanent,
the Constant and Non-Constant,
and the two Jewels of the Dharma and the Saṅgha,
the Vinaya (Lǜ) and Non-Vinaya,
the Sūtra (Jīng) and Non-Sūtra,
Māra’s teachings and the Buddha’s teachings.
If one is unable to make such distinctions,
this is called chasing after the meaning of the Wú Zì.
I have now spoken of the meaning of thus chasing after the Wú Zì.
Good man!
Therefore, you should now abandon the Half-Character
and skillfully understand the Full-Character.
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"Shìzūn!
We should skillfully study the number of characters.
Now we have encountered the unsurpassed teacher,
and have already received the earnest instructions of the Rúlái."
The Buddha praised Jiāshè:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Those who delight in the True Dharma
should learn in this manner."
Thereupon, the Buddha informed Jiāshè Púsà:
"Good man!
There are two types of birds:
one is named Jiālín tí,
the second is the Yuānyang (Mandarin duck).
They dwell and rest together,
never separating from each other.
The Dharmas of suffering,
impermanence,
and non-self
are also like this;
they cannot be separated from each other."
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"Shìzūn!
How are suffering,
impermanence,
and non-self
like that Yuānyang
and the Jiālín tí bird?"
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
One dharma is suffering,
another dharma is joy;
one dharma is permanent,
another dharma is impermanent;
one dharma is Self,
another dharma is non-Self;
For example, rice is different from hemp and wheat,
and hemp and wheat, in turn, are different from beans, millet, and sugarcane.
In the case of all such seeds,
from their budding and sprouting up to their leaves and flowers,
all are impermanent;
when the fruits ripen,
and people make use of them,
then they are named permanence.
Why is this?
Because their nature is true reality.”
Jiāyè addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If objects like these,
are permanent,
are they the same as the Rúlái?”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
You should not speak in this way now.
Why is this?
If you say the Rúlái is like Mount Xūmí,
when the kalpa ends and Xūmí collapses,
would the Rúlái also collapse at that time?
Good man!
You should not accept or maintain this meaning now.
Good man!
Among all dharmas, apart from Nièpán,
there is no other dharma that is permanent;
it is merely by the mundane truth that we say the fruits are permanent.”
Jiāyè Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Excellent,
excellent!
It is just as the Buddha has said.”
The Buddha told Jiāyè:
“It is so,
it is so.
Good man!
Although one cultivates all the canonical scriptures and various samādhis,
as long as one has not heard the Dà Bān Nièpán,
they all say that everything is impermanent.
Having heard this sūtra,
although one still has afflictions, it is as if one has none,
and one can immediately benefit all humans and devas.
Why is this?
Because one clearly understands that one's own body possesses Fóxìng,
which is named permanence.
Furthermore, good man!
For example, take the Ànluó shù;
when its flowers first blossom, they are called the characteristic of impermanence,
but when they bear fruit,
which yields much benefit, they are named permanence.
Likewise,
good man!
Although one cultivates all the canonical scriptures and various samādhis,
as long as one has not heard this great Dà Nièpán teaching,
they all unanimously say that everything is impermanent;
Having heard this sūtra,
although one still has afflictions, it is as if one has none,
and one can immediately benefit all humans and devas.
Why is this?
Because one clearly understands that one's own body possesses Fóxìng,
which is named permanence.
Furthermore, good man!
For example, take gold ore;
when it is being smelted,
this is the characteristic of impermanence,
but once smelted and made into gold,
which yields much benefit,
then it is named permanence.
Likewise,
good man!
Although one cultivates all the canonical scriptures and various samādhis,
as long as one has not heard this great Dà Nièpán teaching,
they all unanimously say that everything is impermanent;
Having heard this sūtra,
although one still has afflictions, it is as if one has none,
and one can immediately benefit all humans and devas.
Why is this?
Because one clearly understands that one's own body possesses Fóxìng,
which is named permanence.
Furthermore, good man!
For example, take húmá;
when it has not yet been pressed, it is called impermanent,
but once pressed and made into oil, which yields much benefit,
then it is named permanence.
Good man!
Although one cultivates all the canonical scriptures and various samādhis,
as long as one has not heard this great Dà Nièpán Jīng,
they all unanimously say that everything is impermanent;
Having heard this sūtra,
although one still has afflictions, it is as if one has none,
and one can immediately benefit all humans and devas.
Why is this?
Because one clearly understands that one's own body possesses Fóxìng,
which is named permanence.
Furthermore, good man!
For example, just as all streams
flow toward the ocean,
all canonical scriptures, various meditations, and Sānmèi,
all flow toward the Dàshèng Dà Nièpán Jīng.
Why is this?
Because it ultimately and expertly proclaims the existence of Fóxìng.
Good man!
Therefore I say one dharma is permanent,
and another dharma is impermanent,
and likewise for non-Self.”
Jiāyè Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Rúlái is already far from the poisonous arrow of sadness and grief.
Now, sadness and grief characterize Tiān,
but the Rúlái is not a Tiān.
Sadness and grief characterize Rén,
but the Rúlái is not a Rén.
Sadness and grief characterize the Èrshíwǔ Yǒu,
but the Rúlái is not in the Èrshíwǔ Yǒu.
Therefore, the Rúlái has no sadness or grief.
Why do you speak of the Rúlái as being sad and grieving?
“Good man!
The Wúxiǎng Tiān,
is named Non-Thought.
If there is Non-Thought, there is no lifespan.
If there is no lifespan,
how can there be skandhas, dhātus, or āyatanas?
For this reason,
the lifespan of the Wúxiǎng Tiān,
cannot be definitively said to have a fixed dwelling place.
Good man!
For example, just as a Shù Shén dwells dependent on a tree,
one cannot definitively say it relies on the branches,
the joints,
the trunk,
or the leaves.
Although there is no fixed place,
it cannot be said not to exist;
the lifespan of the Wúxiǎng Tiān is likewise.
Good man!
Fóxìng is also like this—
profound and difficult to understand.
The Rúlái truly has no sadness, grief, suffering, or distress,
but towards sentient beings, he arouses Dà Cíbēi,
manifesting sadness and grief,
regarding all sentient beings as Luóhóuluó.
Furthermore, good man!
The lifespan that exists in the Wúxiǎng Tiān,
only the Buddha can know;
it is beyond the reach of others,
and the same applies even to the Fēixiǎng Fēifēixiǎng Chǔ.
Jiāyè!
The Rúlái’s nature is pure and undefiled,
like a Huàshēn;
where would there be sadness, grief, suffering, or distress?
If you say the Rúlái is without sadness and grief,
how can he benefit all sentient beings,
and greatly propagate the Fófǎ?
If you say he is without it,
how can it be said that he equally regards all sentient beings like Luóhóuluó?
If he does not equally regard them like Luóhóuluó,
then such words are false.
For this reason,
good man!
The Buddha is Bùkě Sīyì,
the Dharma is Bùkě Sīyì,
the Fóxìng of sentient beings is Bùkě Sīyì,
and the lifespan of the Wúxiǎng Tiān is Bùkě Sīyì.
Whether the Rúlái has sadness or is without sadness,
this is the realm of the Buddha,
and cannot be known by the Shēngwén and Yuánjué.”
“O good man!
For example, in the atmosphere,
dwelling places and fine dust cannot stand still.
If one says that dwelling places do not rely on the atmosphere to exist, that is impossible.
Based on this principle,
one cannot say that the dwelling place resides in the empty space,
nor that it does not reside in the empty space.
Ordinary people,
although they say that the dwelling place resides in the empty space,
yet this empty space truly has nothing that resides in it.
Why is this?
Because its nature is without dwelling.
O good man!
The mind is also like this;
one cannot say that it resides in the skandhas, dhātus, and āyatanas, nor that it does not reside there.
The lifespan of the Non-Ideational Heaven (Wúxiǎng Tiān) is also like this.
The Tathāgata’s (Rúlái) sorrow and compassion are also like this.
If there were no sorrow or compassion,
how could it be said that he views sentient beings equally, like Rāhula (Luóhóuluó)?
If one says that they exist,
then how can it be said that their nature is identical to empty space?
O good man!
For example, a magician (huànshī),
although they conjure various palaces,
killing, nurturing, binding, and releasing living beings,
and creating gold, silver,
lapis lazuli treasures,
groves, and trees,
none of them have actual reality.
The Tathāgata is also like this.
Following the ways of the world,
he manifests sorrow and compassion,
but they are not real.
O good man!
The Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa (bānnipán);
how could there then be sorrow, compassion, suffering, or affliction?
If one believes that the Tathāgata entering nirvāṇa (nièpán) is impermanent,
you should know that such a person then has sorrow and compassion.
If one believes that the Tathāgata does not enter nirvāṇa, but is permanent and unchanging,
you should know that such a person is without sorrow and compassion.
Whether the Tathāgata has sorrow or is without sorrow,
no one is capable of knowing.
“Furthermore, O good man!
For example, a lower-level person
can understand lower-level phenomena,
but does not understand middle or higher ones;
a middle-level person understands middle ones,
but does not understand the higher ones;
a higher-level person understands the higher ones,
and also understands the middle and lower ones.
The Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué) are also like this;
they only know their own stage (bhūmi).
The Tathāgata is not so;
he fully knows his own stage and those of others.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is named ‘Unimpeded Wisdom’ (Wú'ài Zhì).
He manifests illusory transformations,
following the ways of the world.
The flesh eyes of ordinary people consider them real.
But to desire to completely know the Tathāgata’s unimpeded, supreme wisdom
is impossible.
Whether there is sorrow or no sorrow,
only the Buddha (Fó) can know.
For this reason,
in some teachings there is a self (wǒ),
and in some teachings there is no self (wúwǒ).
This is called the nature of the Mandarin Duck (Yuānyāng)
and the Kalavinka Bird (Jiālín Tíniǎo).
“Furthermore, O good man!
The Buddha’s Dharma (Fófǎ) is like the Mandarin Ducks walking together.
These Kalavinka and Mandarin Ducks,
when the water rises in the height of summer,
choose a high plateau,
settle their young there,
for the sake of their nurturing,
and then follow their original course,
wandering in peace.
The Tathāgata appearing in the world is also like this;
he transforms countless multitudes, causing them to dwell in the Right Dharma (Zhèngfǎ),
just like those Mandarin Ducks and Kalavinka Birds,
choosing a high plateau and settling their young.
The Tathāgata is also like this:
after causing all sentient beings to complete what they had to do,
he then enters the Great Parinirvāṇa (Dàbānnipán).
O good man!
This is called ‘in some teachings there is suffering (kǔ),’
‘in some teachings there is joy (lè),’
‘all formations (zhūxíng) are suffering,’
and ‘nirvāṇa is joy,’
because it is the supreme subtlety that destroys all formations.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva (Jiāshè Púsà) addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
How is it that sentient beings who attain nirvāṇa are called having ‘supreme joy’?
The Buddha said:
“O good man!
As I have said,
the combination of formations
is called old age and death.
“The one who is negligent (fàngyì) is called being subject to conditioned phenomena (yǒuwéifǎ).
These conditioned phenomena are the supreme suffering.
The one who is not negligent is then called nirvāṇa.
That nirvāṇa is called ‘sweet dew’ (gānlù),
the supreme joy.
If one follows the formations,
this is called the place of death,
suffering the supreme suffering;
if one reaches nirvāṇa,
this is called the imperishable,
receiving the most excellent joy.
If one is not negligent,
although they accumulate formations,
this is also called permanence and joy,
imperishability,
and the body that is not destroyed.
What is negligence?
What is non-negligence?
Non-holy ordinary people are called negligence, the phenomenon of constant death.
Transcendent holy people are non-negligent and have no old age or death.
Why is this?
Because they have entered the supreme, permanent, and joyful nirvāṇa.
Based on this principle,
in some teachings there is suffering,
in some teachings there is joy,
in some teachings there is self,
and in some teachings there is no self.
It is like a person on the ground,
looking up at the empty sky,
who does not see the tracks of a bird.
