O good man!
Sentient beings are also like this:
without the Heavenly Eye (Tiānyǎn),
dwelling amidst the afflictions (fánnǎo), they do not see the Tathāgata-Nature (Rúláixìng) within themselves.
Therefore, I taught the secret teaching of ‘no self.’
Why is this?
Those without the Heavenly Eye
do not know the true self
and wrongly conceive of a self.
Because of the afflictions, the conditioned phenomena that are created
are immediately impermanent.
Therefore, I taught that in some teachings there is permanence (cháng),
and in some teachings there is impermanence (wúcháng).
“The Tathāgata has severed all immeasurable afflictions,
dwelling on the mountain of wisdom,
and sees all sentient beings constantly dwelling amidst immeasurable billions of afflictions.”
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is said in the verse
is not correct in principle.
Why is this?
One who enters nirvāṇa is without sorrow
and without joy;
how can he ascend the high palace of wisdom?
Furthermore, how can he dwell on the mountaintop and see sentient beings?
The Buddha said:
“O good man!
The palace of wisdom
is named nirvāṇa.
The one without sorrow or affliction is the Tathāgata.
The one with sorrow and affliction is named the ordinary person.
Because of the sorrow of ordinary people,
the Tathāgata is without sorrow.
The summit of Mount Sumeru (Xūmíshān) is named Right Liberation (Zhèng Jiětuō).
Diligent exertion (qín jīngjìn) is likened to Mount Sumeru, which does not move.
‘Ground’ refers to the conditioned formations.
These ordinary people dwell on this ground
and create formations.
Wisdom is named Right Enlightenment (Zhèngjué),
departing from conditioned existence and dwelling permanently;
therefore, it is named the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata compassionately remembers immeasurable sentient beings who are constantly struck by the poisoned arrows of existence.
Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata has sorrow.”
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgata has sorrow and affliction,
then he should not be called the Perfectly Enlightened One (Děng Zhèngjué).”
The Buddha said:
“Kāśyapa!
All things have causes and conditions.
Depending on the place where sentient beings are to be transformed,
the Tathāgata manifests taking birth in it.
Although he manifests taking birth,
in reality, there is no birth.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is named the ‘Permanently Dwelling Dharma’ (Cháng Zhùfǎ),
like the Kalavinka
and the Mandarin Duck and other birds.
"Furthermore, good man!
For example, there is a person
who sees the moon disappear
and everyone says the moon has set
and forms the idea of setting,
yet the nature of this moon
truly does not set;
it turns and appears in another direction,
and the sentient beings in that place
then say the moon has risen.
Yet the nature of this moon
truly does not rise.
Why is this?
Because it is obstructed by Mt. Xūmí Shān, it does not appear,
but the moon perpetually exists,
its nature being neither rising nor setting.
The Rúlái,
Yìng,
and Zhèngbiànzhī are also like this,
appearing throughout the Three Thousand Great-Thousand Worlds (Sānqiān Dàqiān Shìjiè).
Sometimes in Yánfútí he indicates having parents,
and all sentient beings believe the Rúlái was born within Yánfútí.
Sometimes in Yánfútí he manifests Nièpán,
yet the nature of the Rúlái truly has no Nièpán,
but the sentient beings all believe the Rúlái truly entered Pānnièpán,
just like the setting moon.
Good man!
The nature of the Rúlái truly has no generation or extinction;
in order to transform sentient beings, he manifests generation and extinction.
Good man!
Just as a full moon here,
is seen as a half moon elsewhere;
and a half moon here,
is seen as a full moon elsewhere.
If the people of Yánfútí see the moon begin to appear,
they all say it is the first day
and form the idea of the new moon.
If they see the moon at its peak fullness,
they say it is the fifteenth day
and generate the idea of peak fullness.
Yet the nature of this moon
truly has no waning or waxing;
it is because of Mt. Xūmí Shān that it appears to increase and decrease.
Good man!
The Rúlái is also like this,
sometimes manifesting initial birth in Yánfútí,
and sometimes manifesting Nièpán.
When manifesting initial birth,
he is like the new moon;
everyone says the child has just been born.
Walking seven steps is like the moon of the second day;
sometimes he manifests entering the schoolhouse,
like the moon of the third day;
manifesting leaving home (Chūjiā)
is like the moon of the eighth day.
Emitting great wisdom and subtle brilliant light,
able to destroy the demonic hosts (mó zhòng) of countless sentient beings,
is like the full moon of the fifteenth day.
Sometimes he manifests the Thirty-Two Marks (Sānshí'èr Xiàng)
and the Eighty Minor Characteristics (Bāshí Zhǒng Hǎo),
adorning himself and manifesting Nièpán,
likened to a lunar eclipse.
Thus, the appearances seen by sentient beings differ:
some see a half moon,
some see a full moon,
some see a lunar eclipse,
yet the nature of this moon truly has no increase or decrease,
nor is it eaten away;
it is always a full moon.
The body of the Rúlái is also like this,
hence it is called permanent and unchanging (Chángzhù Bùbiàn).
"Furthermore, good man!
For example, a full moon appears everywhere:
in every place,
cities and villages,
mountains, marshes, and water,
whether in wells or pools,
pots or kettles,
it appears in all of them.
There are sentient beings
who travel a hundred Yóuxún,
or a hundred thousand Yóuxún, and see the moon constantly follow them.
Ordinary foolish people wrongly generate recollection and thought,
saying:
'I formerly saw this moon
in the city or dwelling;
now I see it again in this open marsh.
Is this the original moon,
or is it different from the original?'
They each generate such thoughts.
The size of the moon’s shape is sometimes like the mouth of a kettle,
or sometimes they say it is as large as a carriage wheel,
or they say it is like forty-nine Yóuxún.
Everyone sees the moon's light,
and some see it round, likened to a golden plate.
The nature of this moon is singular,
but various sentient beings
each see different appearances.
Good man!
The Rúlái is also like this.
Appearing in the world,
some humans or deities generate this thought:
'The Rúlái is now dwelling before me.'
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who also generate this thought:
'The Rúlái is now dwelling before me.'
Some who are deaf and mute
also see the Rúlái manifesting the appearance of being deaf and mute.
Sentient beings are of mixed types,
their speech and sounds differing;
they all believe the Rúlái speaks exactly like them,
and each generates the thought:
'He is in my house receiving my offerings.'
Some sentient beings
see the Rúlái’s body as vast and measureless.
Some see it as minuscule.
Some see the Fó as a Shēngwén figure,
and others see him as a Yuánjué figure.
Various external followers (Wàidào) each generate the thought:
'The Rúlái is now
practicing the path and leaving home (Chūjiā Xuédào) within my Dharma.'
Some sentient beings further generate the thought:
'The Rúlái is now appearing in the world solely for my sake.'
The true nature of the Rúlái is likened to that moon;
this is the Dhārmakāya (Fǎshēn),
the body that is unproduced.
The body of expedient means (Fāngbiàn zhī shēn) adapts to the world,
manifesting measureless former karmic causes and conditions,
appearing to be born everywhere,
just like that moon.
For this reason,
the Rúlái is permanently dwelling and undergoes no change.
"Furthermore, good man!
Just as Rāhula the Āxiūluó King (Āxiūluó Wáng) covers the moon with his hand,
and all people in the world say it is a lunar eclipse,
the Āxiūluó King truly cannot eclipse (devour) it.
It is because the Āxiūluó obstructs its brightness;
the moon remains round and without damage,
but because of the hand's obstruction,
it causes it not to be seen.
When he withdraws his hand,
the world all says the moon has been restored (Hái Shēng),
and everyone says the moon suffered much distress.
Even if there were hundreds and thousands of Āxiūluó Kings,
they could not distress it.
The Rúlái is also like this:
he manifests that some sentient beings, directed toward the Rúlái,
generate coarse, evil minds,
shed the Fó’s blood (Chū Fó Shēn Xuè),
commit the Five Heinous Crimes (Wǔ Nì Zuì),
and even become an Icchantika (Yīchǎntí).
For the sake of sentient beings in future ages,
he thus manifests destroying the Saṅgha (Huài Sēng), cutting off the Dharma (Duàn Fǎ), and causing obstruction.
Even if hundreds, thousands, or measureless Māras (Mó) exist,
they cannot invade or draw the Rúlái’s blood.
Why is this?
The body of the Rúlái has no flesh, blood,
tendons, veins,
or bone marrow.
The Rúlái’s true reality is truly incapable of suffering distress or harm,
but sentient beings all believe the Dharma
and Saṅgha are destroyed,
and the Rúlái is extinguished.
Yet the nature of the Rúlái truly does not change,
nor is it destroyed;
conforming to the world,
he manifests thus.
Furthermore, good man!
If two people fight,
and one uses a sword or staff to wound the body and draw blood,
even if it leads to death,
one does not generate the idea of murder.
Such a karmic characteristic
is light, not heavy.
Directed toward the Rúlái,
if the original intention was not to kill,
although blood is shed,
this karma is also like that:
light and not heavy.
The Rúlái is thus:
for the sake of transforming sentient beings in future ages, he manifests karmic retribution (Yèbào).
"Furthermore, good man!
Just like a skilled physician
diligently teaches his son
the fundamentals of medical prescriptions:
'This is a root medicine,
this is a stem medicine,
this is a coloring medicine.
You must thoroughly understand these various characteristics.'
The son respectfully adheres to his father’s instructions,
studiously practices and learns,
and skillfully understands all the medicines.
When the physician later reaches the end of his lifespan and passes away,
his son weeps and says this:
'My father originally taught me:
root medicines are like this,
stem medicines are like this,
flower medicines are like this,
and the colors and characteristics are like this.'
The Rúlái is also like this.
To transform sentient beings, he manifests the establishment of precepts:
'It should be like this:
maintain and uphold them, and do not commit the Five Heinous Crimes (Wǔ Nì Zuì),
slander the Right Dharma (Zhèng Fǎ), or be an Yīchǎntí.'
He manifests these things
for the sake of those who will arise in future ages,
desiring that the Bǐqiū,
after the Buddha's passing, understand this:
'This is the profoundly deep meaning of the Sūtras (Jīng),
this is the nature of the light and heavy transgressions in the Vinaya (Jìe Lǜ),
this is the separate Dharma phrases of the Āpítán (Abhidharma),'
just like that physician's son.
"Furthermore, good man!
Just as people know the moon
is eclipsed once every six months,
yet the various celestial beings above
have already seen the moon eclipsed within a mere instant.
Why is this?
Because the celestial day is long,
while the human day is short.
Good man!
The Rúlái is also like this.
Devas and humans all claim the Rúlái's lifespan is short,
just as those celestial beings
frequently see the moon eclipsed within a mere instant.
The Rúlái, furthermore, within a mere instant,
manifests hundreds of thousands of millions of instances of Nièpán,
severing the demon of affliction (fán nǎo mó),
the demon of aggregates (yīn mó),
and the demon of death (sǐ mó).
Therefore, hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial demons
all know that the Rúlái enters Bōnièpán.
Moreover, he manifests countless hundreds of thousands of past karmic conditions.
Because he accords with the various natures of the mundane world,
he manifests such immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable phenomena.
Therefore, the Rúlái abides eternally and is unchangeable.
Furthermore, good man!
Just like the bright moon
is happily viewed by sentient beings,
therefore the moon is called 'Happily Viewed' (Lè Jiàn).
If sentient beings possess greed, hatred, and delusion,
then they cannot be called 'Happily Viewed.'
The Rúlái is like this:
his nature is purely good,
clean, pure, and stainless.
He is the one who can truly be called 'Happily Viewed.'
Sentient beings who delight in the Dharma
gaze upon him without weariness,
while those with wicked minds
dislike looking upon him.
Because of this meaning,
we say the Rúlái is likened to the bright moon.
"Furthermore, good man,
just as the daylight differs in three seasons,
namely spring, summer, and winter:
the winter day is short,
the spring day is moderate,
and the summer day is extremely long.
The Rúlái is also like this.
For those with short lifespans in this three-thousand great-thousand world system
and for the various Shēngwén, he manifests a short lifespan.
When these beings see this,
they all say the Rúlái's lifespan is brief,
likened to a winter day.
For the various Púsà, he manifests a medium lifespan,
whether it reaches one Kalpa (Jié) or is slightly less than one Kalpa,
likened to a spring day.
Only Buddhas perceive Buddhas:
their lifespan is immeasurable,
likened to a summer day.
Good man!
The Rúlái's teaching—the subtle and profound doctrine of the Fāngděng Dàchéng—
is manifested in the world,
raining the great Dharma rain.
In future ages,
if there is anyone who can uphold this scripture,
elucidate and explain it to benefit sentient beings,
you should know that these people are truly Púsà,
likened to a glorious summer
when heaven sends down sweet rain.
If there are Shēngwén or Yuánjué persons
who hear the Rúlái Buddha's subtle and profound teaching,
they are likened to suffering frequently from the cold of a winter day.
As for Púsà persons,
if they hear such subtle and profound instruction,
that the Rúlái abides eternally and his nature is unchangeable,
they are likened to a spring day
when sprouts and buds burst forth.
However, the nature of the Rúlái
truly has neither long nor short measure.
Because of the worldly realm,
he manifests it in this way,
which is the true Dharma nature of all Buddhas.
"Furthermore, good man!
Just as the multitude of stars
do not appear during the daytime,
and people all assume that the daytime stars have vanished,
in reality, they have not vanished.
The reason they do not appear
is because they are overshadowed by sunlight.
The Rúlái is also like this:
Shēngwén and Yuánjué cannot perceive him,
likened to worldly people not seeing the daytime stars.
Furthermore, good man!
Just as in the gloom and darkness,
the sun and moon do not appear,
and foolish people say that the sun and moon have been lost or have vanished,
yet the sun and moon have truly not been lost or vanished.
When the Rúlái's Zhèng Fǎ is extinguished and exhausted,
the apparent vanishing of the Sānbǎo is also like this.
It is not eternal extinction.
Therefore, you should know that the Rúlái abides eternally and is without change.
Why is this?
Because the true nature of the Sānbǎo
is not defiled by any impurities.
"Furthermore, good man!
Just as during the black moon (dark phase),
a comet appears at night;
its brilliant, blazing light appears for a moment and then vanishes.
When sentient beings see it,
they conceive notions of inauspiciousness.
The various Pìzhīfó are also like this:
they appear in an age without a Buddha.
When sentient beings see them,
they all assume the Rúlái has truly entered extinction (Nièpán)
and give rise to thoughts of sorrow and grief.
Yet, the body of the Rúlái truly does not perish or reach extinction,
just as the sun and moon are never lost or vanished.
"Furthermore, good man!
Just as when the sun rises,
all the mists are completely dispersed.
This profound and subtle scripture, the Dà Nièpán, is also like this:
when it arises and flourishes in the world,
if there are sentient beings who hear it just once,
they are all able to eradicate all evil deeds
and the karma leading to the continuous hell (Wújiàn).
The profoundly deep state of the Dà Nièpán is inconceivable.
It skillfully explains the subtle and secret nature of the Rúlái.
Because of this meaning,
all good men
and good women
should conceive the idea of the Rúlái's eternal abiding
and unchangeable nature,
that the Zhèng Fǎ is not cut off,
and the Sēngbǎo does not perish.
Therefore, one should frequently cultivate skillful means
and diligently study this scripture.
These persons will soon attain Ānǔduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Therefore, this scripture is called 'Accomplished by Immeasurable Merits.'
It is also called 'Pútí is inexhaustible.'
Because it is inexhaustible,
it is called the Dà Bōnièpán.
Because it possesses good radiance,
it is like the summer sun.
Because the body is boundless,
it is named Dà Nièpán.
"Furthermore, good man!
The light of the sun and moon
is the foremost among all lights;
all other lights
cannot equal it.
The light of Dà Nièpán
is also like this:
among all the Sūtras (Jīng),
its samādhi light is the most exceptional and supreme.
The lights produced by the samādhi of other scriptures
cannot equal it.
Why is this?
Because the light of Dà Nièpán
can enter all the pores of sentient beings.
Although sentient beings may not possess the mind of Pútí,
it can create the conditions for Pútí for them.
For this reason, it is again named Dà Bōnièpán."
Jiāyè Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Shìzūn!
As the Buddha has stated,
the light of the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán) enters the pores of all sentient beings.
Although these sentient beings do not possess the mind of Pútí,
they are still able to create the cause for Pútí.
This principle is incorrect.
Why is this?
Shìzūn!
Those who commit the four major prohibitions,
those who commit the five heinous acts, and the Yīchǎntí—
if the light enters their bodies and creates the cause for Pútí,
what difference is there between such people
and those who purely uphold the precepts
and cultivate all virtues?
If there is no difference,
why did the Tathāgata (Rúlái) preach the meaning of the Four Dependences (Sìyī)?
Shìzūn!
Furthermore, concerning what the Buddha said:
If there are sentient beings who hear the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán) even once,
they attain the severance of all afflictions (fánnǎo).
If so, why did the Tathāgata previously state
that there are people who, having generated the Pútí mind before Buddhas numerous as the sands of the Hénghéshā (Ganges),
heard the Mahāparinirvāṇa but did not comprehend its meaning?
If they do not comprehend the meaning,
how can they sever all afflictions?"
The Buddha said:
"Good son!
Excluding the Yīchǎntí,
the remaining sentient beings, having heard this Sūtra,
are all able to create the condition for Pútí.
Those into whose pores the light of the Dharma sound enters
shall certainly attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Why is this?
Only if one has made offerings and shown reverence to countless Buddhas
can one then hear the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Nièpán Jīng);
those with meager fortune cannot hear it.
Why is that?
Only persons of great virtue can hear of such a great matter;
lowly and insignificant people cannot hear it.
What is meant by 'great'?
It refers to the profoundly deep secret treasury of the Buddhas,
which is the Buddha-nature (fóxìng).
For this reason,
it is called a great matter."
Jiāyè Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Shìzūn!
How is it that those who have not yet generated the Pútí mind
obtain the cause for Pútí?"
The Buddha told Jiāyè:
"If there is someone who hears this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Nièpán Jīng),
and says, 'I do not need to generate the Pútí mind,'
thereby slandering the Correct Dharma (Zhèngfǎ),
that person immediately sees the image of a Rākṣasa (Luóchà) in a dream,
and fear arises in his heart.
The Rākṣasa says to him:
'Halt!
Good son!
If you do not now generate the Pútí mind,
I shall sever your life.'
That person is terrified,
and upon waking, immediately generates the Pútí mind.
When this person dies,
whether reborn in the three evil paths or among humans and devas,
he continually recalls the Pútí mind.
Know that this person is a great Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Dà Púsà Móhēsà).
For this reason,
due to the majestic spiritual power of the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán),
it is able to make those who have not yet generated the Pútí mind create the Pútí cause.
Good son!
This is called the condition for a Bodhisattva generating the Pútí mind;
it is not without condition.
For this reason,
the wondrous canon of the Mahāyāna (Dàchéng) is truly spoken by the Buddha.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a great rain cloud arising in the sky,
pouring down upon the earth.
Dead trees,
stone mountains,
high plains,
and hillocks
cannot retain the water,
which flows down to the lower fields,
filling all the reservoirs and pools,
benefiting countless sentient beings.
This wondrous Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán) is also like this:
it pours the great Dharma rain,
universally moistening sentient beings.
However, that an Yīchǎntí should generate the Pútí mind is utterly impossible.
Furthermore, good son!
Just as a scorched seed,
even if it encounters sweet rain,
for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas,
will ultimately not sprout a shoot;
that a shoot should grow is impossible.
The class of Yīchǎntí is also like this.
Even though they hear this Great Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Bān Nièpán) wondrous Sūtra,
they ultimately cannot sprout the seed of the Pútí mind;
that they should be able to sprout it is impossible.
Why is this?
These people have severed and extinguished all roots of virtue,
like that scorched seed,
unable to reproduce the root-sprout of Pútí.
Furthermore, good son!
For example, if a luminous pearl is placed in turbid water,
by the majestic power of the pearl, the water immediately becomes clear.
If it is thrown into mud, it cannot make the mud clear.
This wondrous Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán) is also like this.
When placed among the turbid waters of the five uninterrupted offenses (wǔ wújiàn zuì)
and the four heavy prohibitions (sì zhòng jìn fǎ) committed by other sentient beings,
it can still clarify them
and cause them to generate the Pútí mind.
But when thrown into the mud of the Yīchǎntí,
for hundreds of thousands of millions of years,
it cannot clarify them
or cause the Pútí mind to arise.
Why is this?
Because the Yīchǎntí
has extinguished all roots of virtue,
and is thus not a suitable vessel.
Even if this person
listens to and receives this great Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Nièpán Jīng)
for hundreds of thousands of millions of years,
he ultimately cannot generate the Pútí mind.
Why is that?
Because he possesses no virtuous mind.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a medicinal tree
named King of Medicine (Yàowáng),
which is the most supreme among all medicines.
Whether mixed with buttermilk,
or honey,
or clarified butter (sū),
or water,
or milk;
whether ground into powder,
or rolled into a pill;
or used to smear a wound,
or to fumigate the body,
or to anoint the eyes,
or merely seen,
or merely smelled—
it can eradicate all the diseases of sentient beings.
This medicinal tree does not produce the thought:
'Among all sentient beings,
if someone takes my root, they should not take my leaves;
if they take my leaves, they should not take my root;
if they take my wood, they should not take my bark;
if they take my bark, they should not take my wood.'
Although this tree does not generate such a thought,
it is still able to eliminate all suffering from sickness.
Good son!
This wondrous Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán) is also like this:
it can eliminate all evil karma of sentient beings,
the four Pārājika (Sì Bōluóyí),
and the five uninterrupted offenses (wǔ wújiàn zuì);
it eradicates all internal
and external evil.
All those who have not yet generated the Pútí mind
can, based on this, generate the Pútí mind.
Why is this?
This wondrous Sūtra
is the King among Sūtras,
just as that medicinal tree
is the King among medicines.
Whether one cultivates this Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán) or not,
if one hears the name of this Sūtra,
and having heard it, reverently believes,
all heavy afflictions and diseases are entirely eliminated,
except that it cannot settle and establish the class of Yīchǎntí in Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
It is like that wondrous medicine:
though it can cure various severe diseases,
it cannot heal a person who is certain to die.
"Furthermore, good son!
If a person has a wound on his hand
and grasps poison,
the poison immediately enters.
If there is no wound,
the poison does not enter.
The class of Yīchǎntí is also like this:
they have no Pútí cause.
Just as one without a wound,
the poison cannot enter.
The 'wound' refers
to the condition for unsurpassed Pútí;
the 'poison' refers to the foremost wondrous medicine;
and the one perfectly without a wound is called the Yīchǎntí.
Furthermore, good son!
For example, the Vajra (Jīngāng)
cannot be destroyed by anything,
yet it can shatter all things,
with the exception of the tortoise shell and the white sheep's horn.
This wondrous Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán)
is also like this:
it can entirely settle and establish countless sentient beings on the Pútí path,
but it cannot cause the class of Yīchǎntí to establish the Pútí cause."
“Furthermore, good man!
Just like the Mǎchǐcǎo,
the Suōluóchì Shù,
and the Níjiāluó Shù,
even if their branches and stems are cut off,
they continue to grow as before;
unlike the Duōluó,
which, once cut, does not regrow.
All sentient beings are likewise,
if they manage to hear this Dà Nièpán Jīng,
even if they have violated the Four Prohibitions and the Five Anantarya Karmas (Five Heinous Crimes),
they can still give rise to the causes and conditions for Pútí;
however, the Yīchǎntí group is not like this.
Although they hear and receive this marvelous sūtra,
they cannot give rise to the causes of the Pútí path.
Furthermore, good man!
Just like the Qūtuóluó Shù
and the Zhèntóujiā Shù,
which, once cut, do not regrow,
and like scorched seeds.
The Yīchǎntí group
is also like this.
Although they hear this Dà Nièpán Jīng,
they cannot initiate the causes and conditions for Pútí,
just like scorched seeds.
Furthermore, good man!
For example, great rain
ultimately does not linger in the sky.
This profound and subtle Dà Nièpán classic is also like this;
though it showers the Dharma Rain universally,
it cannot settle upon the Yīchǎntí.
The Yīchǎntí's entire being is densely compact,
like a diamond,
incapable of admitting external objects.”
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"Shìzūn!
Regarding the verse the Buddha spoke:
'Shìzūn!'
What meaning
does this teaching contain?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
'Not seeing'
means not seeing the Buddha Nature.
'Good'
refers to Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
'Not acting'
means being unable to draw near to good friends.
'Seeing only'
means seeing that there are no causes and results.
'Evil'
means slandering the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras.
'Can be acted upon'
means the Yīchǎntí saying there is no Vaipulya Dharma.
For this reason,
the Yīchǎntí group
has no mind to approach pure good Dharma.
What is this good Dharma?
It is Nièpán.
Those who approach Nièpán
are those who can cultivate virtuous and good conduct;
but the Yīchǎntí has no virtuous and good conduct,
therefore they cannot approach Nièpán.
'That place is dreadful'
means slandering the True Dharma.
Who should be afraid?
Namely, the wise ones.
Why is this?
Because those who slander the Dharma
have no good mind or skillful means (upāya).
'The dangerous and evil path' refers to all karmic activities."
Jiāshè repeated:
"Regarding what the Buddha said:
'What does this meaning imply?'"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
'Seeing what is acted upon'
means confessing all evils;
all evils committed since the beginning of saṃsāra are entirely confessed,
reaching the place where there is no reaching (the state of ultimate freedom).
For this reason,
that place is without fear.
It is like a human king
traveling upon the main road,
and the thieves within it
all flee.
Similarly, confessing all evils
eliminates them completely without remainder.
Furthermore, 'not seeing what is acted upon'
refers to the Yīchǎntí,
who does not see the many evils he has committed.
Because the Yīchǎntí has a mind of arrogance,
although he commits many evils,
he is never afraid of these deeds.
For this reason, he cannot attain Nièpán,
like a monkey grasping at the moon in the water.
Good man!
Suppose all immeasurable sentient beings
simultaneously achieve Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
these Tathāgatas still would not see that Yīchǎntí achieving Pútí.
For this reason, it is called 'not seeing what is acted upon.'
Moreover, 'not seeing whose actions'
means not seeing the actions of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha teaches sentient beings that they possess Buddha Nature,
but the Yīchǎntí group, migrating through saṃsāra,
cannot know or see it.
For this reason,
it is called 'not seeing the actions of the Tathāgata.'
Furthermore, when the Yīchǎntí sees the Tathāgata’s final Nièpán,
he considers it truly impermanent,
like a lamp being extinguished,
the wick and oil both depleted.
Why is this?
Because this person’s evil karma is not diminished.
If the good deeds performed by a Bodhisattva
are dedicated toward Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
even if the Yīchǎntí group reviles,
destroys, and disbelieves,
those Bodhisattvas still grant them the merits,
wishing to jointly achieve the Supreme Path.
Why is this?
It is the nature of all Buddhas' Dharma.
“The Yīchǎntí is called 'one without eyes,'
thus he does not see the path of the Āluóhàn.
Just as the Āluóhàn does not walk the dangerous and evil path of saṃsāra,
the Yīchǎntí, being eyeless, slanders the Vaipulya Dharma
and is unwilling to practice it.
Just as the Āluóhàn diligently cultivates the mind of loving-kindness,
the Yīchǎntí group's failure to cultivate the Vaipulya Dharma
is also like this.
If a person says:
'I do not now believe the Śrāvaka scriptures,
but I believe and accept the Mahāyāna,
I read, recite, and explain it,
therefore I am now a Bodhisattva.
All sentient beings universally possess Buddha Nature,
and due to this Buddha Nature,
within the body of sentient beings there are immediately the Ten Powers,
the Thirty-two Marks,
and the Eighty Minor Characteristics.
What I say
is no different from what the Buddha says.
You and I shall now together destroy innumerable evil afflictions,
like breaking a water jar,
and by destroying the fetters,
we immediately attain the sight of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.'
Although this person speaks and teaches in this way,
his mind does not truly believe that Buddha Nature exists;
he speaks according to the text merely for gain and sustenance.
Such a speaker is called an evil person.
Such an evil person
does not receive retribution quickly,
like milk turning into curd.
For example, an envoy of the king,
skilled in rhetoric
and clever in using skillful means (upāya),
when sent on a mission to another country,
would rather lose his own life
than conceal the words and teachings spoken by the king.
The wise one is also like this;
among ordinary people, he does not spare his life,
but must proclaim the secret treasury of the Tathāgata—the Vaipulya Mahāyāna Dharma—
that all sentient beings possess Buddha Nature.
Good man!
There is a certain Yīchǎntí who assumes the appearance of an Āluóhàn,
dwelling in solitude,
and slandering the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras.
When ordinary people see him, they all suppose
that he is a true Āluóhàn or a great Bodhisattva Móhēsà.
This Yīchǎntí,
and others among the evil *bhikṣus*,
dwell in Ālánruò places
but destroy the Dharma of the Ālánruò (forest dwelling).
Seeing others gain benefits,
they become jealous in their hearts,
and speak thus:
'All the Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras were spoken by the celestial Māra Bōxún.'
They also say the Tathāgata is impermanent Dharma,
thereby destroying the True Dharma
and disrupting the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, they say:
'What Bōxún taught
was not good or compliant speech.'
When such a person proclaims this wicked, erroneous Dharma,
his performance of evil does not immediately receive retribution, just like milk turning into curd.
Like fire covered by ash,
the ignorant carelessly tread upon it.
Such a person refers to the Yīchǎntí.
Therefore, you should know that the subtle and profound Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtras
are definitively pure,
just like the Móní Zhū: when it is cast into turbid water,
the water immediately becomes clear.
The Mahāyāna sūtras are also like this.”
"Furthermore, good man!
Just as a lotus flower is illuminated by the sun,
there is none that does not blossom.
All sentient beings are also like this:
if they can see or hear the Sun of the Mahāparinirvāṇa,
those who have not yet generated the resolve will all generate the resolve, serving as the cause for Bodhi.
Therefore, I say that the light of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, entering the pores of the skin,
certainly becomes a subtle cause.
Although those Icchantika have the Buddha-nature,
they are entangled by innumerable sins and defilements,
unable to escape,
like a silkworm in its cocoon.
Due to these karmic conditions,
they cannot give rise to the subtle cause of Bodhi,
and they transmigrate through Saṃsāra without end.
"Furthermore, good man!
Just as the Utpalā flowers,
Puṇḍarīka flowers,
Kumuda flowers,
and Puṇḍarīka flowers
grow in muddy silt,
yet are never stained by that mud.
If there are sentient beings who cultivate the subtle Sūtra, the Mahāparinirvāṇa,
they are also like this:
although they possess afflictions (kleśa),
they are never stained by these afflictions.
Why is this?
Because they know the power of the Tathāgata's nature and characteristics.
Good man!
For example, there is a country
with much cool and clear wind.
If it touches the pores of the skin of sentient beings,
it can remove all the distress of stifling heat.
This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇajing, is also like this:
it pervades and enters the pores of all sentient beings,
creating the subtle conditions for Bodhi,
excluding the Icchantika.
Why?
Because they are not vessels for the Dharma.
"Furthermore, good man!
Just as a skillful physician,
understanding eight kinds of medicine,
eliminates all illnesses,
except for those that are certainly fatal.
All the sūtras (kèjīng), Dhyāna concentration (chándìng), and Samādhi
are also like this:
they can cure all illnesses of greed (tān), hatred (huì), and delusion (yúchī),
and various afflictions;
they can remove the poisonous darts, such as the thorn of affliction,
but they cannot cure those who have transgressed the four cardinal prohibitions (sìzhòngjìn)
or committed the five uninterrupted sins (wǔwújiànzuì).
Good man!
Furthermore, there is a skillful physician
who surpasses the eight medical arts
and can remove all sickness and suffering of sentient beings,
but cannot cure diseases that are certainly fatal.
This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇajing,
is also like this:
it can remove all afflictions of sentient beings,
causing them to abide in the pure, subtle cause of the Tathāgata,
and causing those who have not yet generated the resolve to generate the resolve,
excluding only those Icchantika who are certainly destined for death.
"Furthermore, good man!
Just as a skillful physician
can use subtle medicine to treat blind people,
enabling them to see the sun and moon,
the constellations,
and all bright and colorful forms;
but cannot cure those who are congenitally blind (shēngmáng).
This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇajing, is also like this:
it can develop the eye of wisdom for the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha,
enabling them to abide in the innumerable and boundless Mahāyāna scriptures.
As for those who have not yet generated the resolve,
meaning those who have transgressed the four prohibitions
and committed the five uninterrupted sins,
it can entirely cause them to generate the Bodhi resolve;
excluding only the congenitally blind Icchantika.
Furthermore, good man!
Just as a skillful physician,
who thoroughly understands the eight medical arts,
offers various prescriptions
to treat all illnesses and sufferings of sentient beings—
emetic and purgative medicines,
as well as ointments,
fumigant medicines,
nasal irrigation,
scattered powders,
and pills—
if the poor and ignorant person is unwilling to take them,
the skillful physician, pitying them,
immediately brings that person back to their dwelling,
compels them to take the medicine,
and due to the power of the medicine,
the ailment is removed.
When a woman is giving birth
and the afterbirth (ér yī) does not emerge,
giving her the medicine causes her to take it,
and after taking it, it immediately emerges,
and also causes the infant to be peaceful and free from trouble.
This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇajing, is also like this:
wherever it reaches, if it reaches a dwelling,
it can remove the innumerable afflictions of sentient beings.
Those who have transgressed the four cardinal prohibitions,
committed the five uninterrupted sins,
and have not yet generated the resolve,
are all caused to generate the resolve,
excluding the Icchantika."
Kāśyapa Púsà said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
Transgressing the four cardinal prohibitions and the five uninterrupted sins
is called an extremely grave evil,
like cutting off the top of a Tāluó tree (palmyra palm),
which can never grow again.
If these beings have not yet generated the Bodhi resolve,
how can it act as the Bodhi cause for them?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
If these sentient beings,
in a dream, dream of falling into hell,
and undergo various sufferings and distress,
they immediately generate a mind of repentance:
'Alas!
We have brought this sin upon ourselves.
If we can now escape from this sin,
we will definitely generate the Bodhi resolve.
What I see now is the greatest evil.'
When they awaken from this,
they immediately know that the True Dharma has great retribution.
Just like that infant, gradually growing up,
constantly thinks:
'This physician is the best,
skillfully understanding prescriptions and medicines.
When I was first in the womb,
he gave medicine to my mother,
and because of the medicine, my mother's
body attained peace and comfort.
Due to this cause and condition,
my life was preserved.
How wonderful!
My mother endured great suffering and distress,
carrying me in her womb for a full ten months.
After giving birth,
she pushed away the dry and removed the wet,
cleared away the unclean feces and urine,
nursed and raised me,
protecting and cherishing my body.
For this reason,
I should repay her kindness,
provide for her, attend to her, protect her,
and comply with her wishes in making offerings.'
Those who transgress the four cardinal prohibitions and commit the uninterrupted sins,
at the time of their imminent death,
recall this Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇajing.
Even if they fall into hell,
the animal realm,
the realm of hungry ghosts,
the heavens,
or the human realm,
such a scripture
still acts as the Bodhi cause for that person,
excluding the Icchantika.
"Furthermore, good man!
Just as a skillful physician and the son of a skillful physician,
whose profound knowledge surpasses all other physicians,
skillfully understand the supreme incantations (zhòushù) for neutralizing poison.
If it is a vicious, poisonous snake,
or a dragon,
or a viper,
by means of various incantations,
they consecrate the medicine to make it effective.
They further use this medicine to smear leather sandals.
With these leather sandals, they touch the various poisonous creatures,
and the poison is neutralized,
excluding only one poison, called the great dragon.
This Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇajing, is also like this:
if there are sentient beings who transgress the four cardinal prohibitions
or commit the five uninterrupted sins,
it can entirely eliminate [their transgressions]
and cause them to abide in Bodhi,
just as the medicated leather sandals can neutralize various poisons.
It can cause those who have not yet generated the resolve to generate the resolve
and cause them to abide firmly on the path of Bodhi.
This is due to the majestic and efficacious medicine of that Mahāyāna scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇajing,
causing all sentient beings
to attain peace and comfort,
excluding only the Icchantika, who are like the great dragon.
"Furthermore, good man!
For instance, if there were a person,
who took mixed poisonous drugs,
and smeared them upon a large drum.
When struck in the midst of a great assembly, it emits sound.
Although they have no desire to listen,
upon hearing it, all die,
save for one person who is not fated to die prematurely.
The Mahāyāna scripture, the Dà Nièpán Jīng (Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra), is also like this.
Wherever it is, among the multitude of sentient beings, those who hear its voice (sound),
their greed and desire,
anger and hatred (chēnhuì), and ignorance,
are all completely extinguished.
Even if some among them have no intention or thought (to listen),
by the power of the conditions of this Dà Nièpán,
it can eliminate afflictions (fánnǎo),
and the bonds (jié) naturally cease.
Those who have violated the four cardinal prohibitions (Sì Zhòng Jìn) and committed the five unforgivable sins (Wǔ Wújiàn),
upon hearing this sūtra,
also create the conditions for unexcelled Bodhi (Pútí).
They gradually sever their afflictions,
excluding the one Icchantika (Yīchǎntí) who is not fated to die prematurely.
"Furthermore, good man!
For instance, during the dark night,
all activities and undertakings cease.
If something is unfinished, one must wait for the bright daylight.
Those who study the Mahāyāna,
although they cultivate the Sūtras (Qìjīng) and all forms of concentration (samādhi),
must await the sun of the Mahāyāna Dà Nièpán,
and hear the subtle and profound teachings of the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Only then can they undertake the deeds of Bodhi,
and abide securely in the True Dharma (Zhèngfǎ).
It is like the rain from heaven,
moistening, benefiting, and causing all seeds to grow,
bringing forth fruit,
completely eliminating famine,
and providing abundant joy and happiness.
The immeasurable Dharma rain of the Tathāgata’s (Rúlái's) secret treasury is also like this.
It can completely eliminate the eight kinds of feverish diseases.
When this sūtra appears in the world,
it is like that abundant fruit,
bringing great benefit,
comforting and bringing joy to all,
and enabling sentient beings to see the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng).
Just as in the Fǎhuā (Lotus Sūtra),
eight thousand Śrāvakas (Shēngwén),
received predictions (vyākaraṇa) of future Buddhahood and achieved great fruit (result).
It is like harvesting in autumn and storing in winter,
with nothing further left to do.
The class of Icchantikas (Yīchǎntí),
are also like this;
concerning all wholesome Dharmas,
they undertake no action or cultivation.
"Furthermore, good man!
For instance, if a good doctor,
hears that another person's child is possessed by a non-human entity,
he immediately takes marvelous medicine,
and sends an envoy,
commanding the envoy, saying:
'You carry this medicine,
and quickly give it to that person.
If that person encounters evil ghosts or spirits,
by the power of the medicine,
they will all retreat far away.
If you are slow or delayed,
I myself will go,
and I will definitely not allow that person to die a wrongful or premature death.
If that patient is able to see the envoy or my majesty and virtue,
all suffering will be removed,
and they will attain peaceful comfort and joy.'
The Mahāyāna scripture, the Dà Nièpán Jīng, is also like this.
If a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū),
Bhikṣuṇī (Bǐqiūní),
Upāsaka (Yōupósè),
Upāsikā (Yōupóyí), or any external follower (wàidào),
is able to receive and uphold such a scripture,
read, recite, and master it,
or furthermore, analyze and widely explain it for others,
or write it out themselves,
or cause others to write it out—
these acts are all conditions for Bodhi.
Even if one has violated the four prohibitions (Sì Jìn) or committed the five heinous crimes (Wǔ Nì Zuì),
or is possessed by evil ghosts, poison, or wickedness,
upon hearing this scripture,
all their wickedness will be eradicated.
It is like the evil ghosts fleeing far away upon seeing the good doctor.
You should know that this person is a true Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà).
Why is this?
Because merely having heard the Dà Nièpán temporarily,
and having also generated the thought,
that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is eternal.
If those who merely hear it temporarily achieve such results,
how much more so for those who write it out,
receive, uphold, read, and recite it?
Excluding the Icchantika (Yīchǎntí),
all others are Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà).
"Furthermore, good man!
For instance, a deaf person,
does not hear sound.
The class of Icchantikas (Yīchǎntí) is also like this;
although they may desire to listen to this marvelous scripture,
they are unable to hear it.
Why is that?
Because they lack the necessary conditions (yīnyuán).
"Furthermore, good man!
For instance, a good doctor,
who has mastered all medical prescriptions,
and there is nothing he does not understand,
and furthermore, widely knows countless dhāraṇīs (zhòushù).
This doctor sees a king and speaks thus:
'Great King, you currently have a fatal disease.'
The king answers, saying:
'You have not seen what is inside my belly,
how can you say I have a fatal disease?'
The doctor immediately replies:
'If you do not trust me,
you should take a laxative medicine.
After it has acted,
the King may verify it himself.'
The King refused to take it.
At that time, the good doctor, using the power of dhāraṇī (zhòushù),
caused sores and boils to appear all over the King's anus (fèn mén),
and furthermore, he began to suffer diarrhea,
excreting worms mixed with blood.
When the King saw this,
he generated great fear and terror,
and praised that good doctor:
'Excellent,
excellent!
What you stated earlier,
I did not heed it.
Now I realize that you
have performed a great benefit for this body of mine.'
He honored this doctor as if he were his parents.
The Mahāyāna scripture, the Dà Nièpán Jīng, is also like this.
Regarding sentient beings,
whether they have desire or lack desire (i.e., whether willing or unwilling),
it is fully able to cause their afflictions to crumble and fall away.
As for these sentient beings,
even if they merely dream of this sūtra in their sleep,
and show reverence and make offerings to it—
it is comparable to the Great King
honoring the good doctor.
This good doctor,
knowing who is certainly going to die,
ultimately does not treat them.
The Mahāyāna scripture, the Dà Nièpán Jīng, is also like this;
it ultimately cannot cure the class of Icchantikas (Yīchǎntí)."
"Furthermore, good man!
For example, a skilled physician,
who masters the eight kinds,
can treat and cure all illnesses,
but cannot treat a person who is certain to die.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are also like this;
they can save and heal all those who have committed sins,
but cannot treat those who are certain to die, the Yīchǎntí types.
Furthermore, good man!
For example, a skilled physician,
who masters the eight kinds of subtle medical texts and methods,
and moreover, can comprehend broadly,
going beyond the eight kinds,
uses his knowledge,
first teaching his son,
whether aquatic,
or terrestrial,
or herbs from mountain ravines,
making sure he recognizes them all.
After thus gradually teaching the eight subjects,
he then teaches the remaining, supreme, subtle methods.
The Rúlái,
the Yìng,
and the Zhèngbiànzhī are also like this:
First they teach their sons, the various Bǐqiū and others,
skillful means to eliminate all afflictions (fánnǎo),
cultivating the visualization of the pure body's lack of permanence,
referring to the aquatic,
the terrestrial,
and the mountain ravine.
The aquatic symbolizes the suffering experienced by the body,
like a bubble on water.
The terrestrial symbolizes the body's lack of firmness,
like a plantain tree.
The mountain ravine symbolizes the midst of afflictions,
cultivating the visualization of non-self.
For this reason,
the body is named 'non-self.'
The Rúlái, in this manner, toward all disciples,
gradually teaches the nine divisions of scripture and doctrine,
enabling them to thoroughly understand and master them.
Following this, they are taught the Rúlái's secret storehouse (mìzàng),
and for the sake of his sons,
he speaks of the Rúlái's permanence.
The Rúlái thus preaches the great Mahāyāna classic, the Dà Nièpán Jīng,
for all sentient beings who have already generated the resolve and those who have not yet generated the resolve,
creating the cause for Pútí,
excluding the Yīchǎntí.
Thus,
good man!
This great Mahāyāna classic, the Dà Nièpán Jīng,
is immeasurable, numberless, inconceivable, and unprecedented.
Know that this is the unsurpassed skilled physician,
the most honored and most excellent,
the King among all Sūtras.
"Furthermore, good man!
For example, a great ship,
crosses from this shore of the ocean to the other shore,
and then returns from that shore back to this shore.
The Rúlái,
the Yìng,
and the Zhèngbiànzhī are also like this:
they ride the treasured vessel of the Mahāyāna, the Great Nirvāṇa,
traveling back and forth,
rescuing and transporting sentient beings.
Wherever there are those who ought to be saved,
they cause all of them to be able to see the Rúlái's body.
For this reason,
the Rúlái is called the Unsurpassed Helmsman.
Just as where there is a boat, there is a helmsman;
because there is a helmsman,
sentient beings cross the great ocean.
The Rúlái constantly abides, transforming and saving sentient beings,
is also like this.
Furthermore, good man,
for example, a person on a boat in the great ocean wishing to cross over,
if they obtain a favorable wind,
in an instant, can cross over immeasurable Yóuyán;
if they do not obtain it,
although they remain there for a long time,
passing countless years,
they do not leave the original place.
Sometimes the boat breaks,
and they sink in the water and die.
Sentient beings are like this:
existing in the great ocean of ignorant life and death,
riding the boat of various conditioned actions,
if they are able to encounter the strong and swift wind of Dà Bān Nièpán,
then they can quickly reach the shore of the unsurpassed Way,
if they do not encounter it,
they will long wander through immeasurable life and death,
or sometimes be destroyed,
falling into the hells (Dìyù),
the realm of beasts (Chùshēng),
or hungry ghosts (Èguǐ).
"Furthermore, good man!
For example, a person,
not meeting the King of Winds,
remaining long in the great ocean,
thinks thus:
'We are certainly going to die here now.'
As they think this,
suddenly they meet a favorable wind,
which aids them in crossing the ocean.
They then say this:
'Excellent!
This wind
is unprecedented!
It allows us,
in peace and safety, to overcome the difficulty of the great ocean.'
Sentient beings are like this:
having long dwelled in the great ocean of ignorant life and death,
distressed, suffering, and withered,
before encountering the wind of the Great Nièpán,
they should generate the thought:
'We will certainly fall into the hells,
the realm of beasts,
or hungry ghosts.'
When these sentient beings contemplate this,
they suddenly encounter the wind of the Dàchén Dà Nièpán,
which favorably blows them toward,
entering into Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Only then do they realize the truth,
generating a marvelous thought,
and exclaiming:
'Excellent!
Since ancient times,
I have never seen or heard
such a subtle and secret storehouse of the Rúlái.'
Then they generate pure faith in this Dà Nièpán Jīng.
[Continuation of 130]
"Furthermore, good man!
When a snake sheds its skin,
is it said to have died and ceased to exist?"
"No.
Shìzūn!
"Good man,
the Rúlái is also like this.
By skillful means, he manifests,
casting away the poisonous body.
Can it be said that the Rúlái is impermanent and extinguished?"
"No.
Shìzūn!
The Rúlái, using skillful means, abandons his body in this Yánfútí,
just like that poisonous snake
sheds its old skin.
Therefore, the Rúlái is named 'permanently dwelling.'
"Furthermore, good man!
For example, a goldsmith,
having obtained fine, genuine gold,
can manufacture various vessels according to his will.
The Rúlái is also like this:
within the twenty-five realms of existence,
he is able to manifest various physical bodies (sèshēn),
in order to transform sentient beings and rescue them from life and death.
Therefore, the Rúlái is named 'Boundless Body.'
Although he manifests various bodies,
he is also named 'permanently dwelling' and without change.
"Furthermore, good man!
Just as the Ānluó tree and the Yánfú tree change three times in a year:
sometimes they produce flowers,
whose colors radiate and flourish;
sometimes they produce leaves,
growing lush and dense;
sometimes they wither and fall,
appearing like they are dried up and dead.
Good man!
What do you think?
Is this tree truly dried up and extinguished?"
"No.
Shìzūn!
"Good man!
The Rúlái is also like this:
within the Three Realms, he manifests three kinds of bodies:
sometimes appearing at birth,
sometimes growing large,
sometimes entering Nièpán.
However, the Rúlái's body is truly not impermanent."
Jiāshè Púsà praised him, saying:
"Well said!
Truly, as the sacred teaching states,
the Rúlái permanently abides and has no change."
"Good man!
The Tathāgata's secret language is profound and difficult to understand.
It is like a great king addressing all his ministers:
'Bring the Sàntuópó!'
Sàntuópó,
one name, has four meanings:
The first is salt,
the second is a vessel,
the third is water,
the fourth is a horse.
These four things
all share this same name.
A wise minister who knows this name well,
if the king requests Sàntuópó when washing,
immediately offers water.
If the king requests Sàntuópó when eating,
immediately offers salt.
If the king has finished eating and is about to drink liquid, requesting Sàntuópó,
he immediately offers a vessel.
If the king wishes to travel, requesting Sàntuópó,
he immediately offers a horse.
Such a wise minister excels at interpreting the great king's four types of secret language.
This Mahāyāna Sūtra is also like this.
There are four types of impermanence,
which the wise ministers of the Mahāyāna
should know well.
If the Buddha appears in the world and speaks of the Tathāgata's Nirvāṇa for sentient beings,
the wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of the characteristic of impermanence for those who adhere to permanence,
wishing to cause the Bhikṣus to cultivate the notion of impermanence.
Or if he speaks, saying, 'The Right Dharma is about to perish,'
the wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of the characteristic of suffering for those who adhere to bliss,
wishing to cause the Bhikṣus to cultivate the notion of suffering frequently.
Or if he speaks, saying, 'I am now afflicted by sickness,
and the assembly of monks is divided,'
the wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of the characteristic of non-self for those who adhere to the self,
wishing to cause the Bhikṣus to cultivate the notion of non-self.
Or if he speaks, saying, 'What is called emptiness is the true liberation,'
the wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of true liberation being free from the twenty-five existences,
wishing to cause the Bhikṣus to cultivate and learn the notion of emptiness.
For this reason,
this true liberation is named emptiness,
and is also named immobility (Adola).
As for the term immobility,
it is because there is no suffering in this liberation,
therefore it is immobile.
This true liberation is without characteristics.
As for being without characteristics,
it is free from form,
sound,
smell,
taste,
and touch, etc.;
therefore it is named without characteristics.
This true liberation is eternal and unchanging.
It is because in this liberation there is no impermanence,
no affliction of heat, or change;
therefore liberation is named eternal abode (Chángzhù),
unchanging,
and cooling (Qīngliáng).
Or if he speaks, saying, 'All sentient beings possess the Tathāgata nature,'
the wise minister should know that this is the Tathāgata speaking of the eternal Dharma,
wishing to cause the Bhikṣus to cultivate the proper eternal Dharma.
If these Bhikṣus can thus accord with and study it,
you should know that these persons are truly my disciples,
who know well the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata,
just like that wise minister of the great king,
who knows the king's intention well.
Good man!
Even a great king has such a method of secret language,
how could the Tathāgata not have it?
Good man!
Therefore, the subtle and secret teaching of the Tathāgata
is difficult to know;
only the wise are capable of understanding my profound Buddha Dharma,
it is not something that common folk
can believe.
"Furthermore, good man!
Just like the Pāluóshé (Palāśa) tree,
the Jiāníjiā (Karnikāra) tree,
and the Āshújiā (Aśoka) tree,
when encountering severe drought,
do not produce flowers or fruits,
and other things born on water or land
all wither and perish,
without any moisture,
unable to grow,
and all medicines lose their efficacy.
Good man!
This Mahāyāna Canon, the Mahā Pārinirvāṇa Sūtra, is also like this:
After my extinction,
there will be sentient beings who cannot revere it,
and it will possess no prestige.
Why is this?
It is because these sentient beings do not know the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata.
Why is this so?
Because these sentient beings have meager merit and virtue.
Furthermore, good man!
When the Tathāgata's Right Dharma is about to perish entirely,
at that time there will be many evil Bhikṣus in practice,
who do not know the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata.
Lazy and negligent,
they are unable to recite,
propagate,
or distinguish the Tathāgata's Right Dharma.
They are like foolish thieves who discard genuine jewels but carry straw husks.
Because they do not understand the subtle and secret treasury of the Tathāgata,
they are negligent and not diligent regarding this Sūtra.
Alas, what great peril!
The future era
is truly frightening.
How painful for sentient beings
who are not diligent in listening to and receiving this Mahāyāna Canon, the Mahā Pārinirvāṇa Sūtra.
Only the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas,
can extract the true meaning from this Sūtra,
not adhering to the words but according with it without opposition,
and explaining it to sentient beings.
"Furthermore, good man!
Just like a milkmaid, wishing to sell milk,
and coveting greater profit,
adds two parts water,
and then sells it to another milkmaid.
When that woman obtains it, she adds another two parts,
and then sells it to a woman near the city.
When the woman obtains it, she adds another two parts,
and then sells it to a woman in the city.
When that woman obtains it, she adds another two parts,
and goes to the market to sell it.
At that time, there was a man,
who was taking a wife for his son,
and required good milk
to entertain the guests.
He went to the market intending to buy.
The seller of the milk
asked a high price.
The man replied:
'Your milk has too much water,
it is not worth that much.
It is precisely because I am now entertaining guests
that I shall take it.'
After taking it and returning home,
he boiled it to make gruel.
It had no milk flavor at all.
Although it had no flavor,
it was a thousand times superior to a bitter flavor.
Why is this?
The flavor of milk
is the most excellent among all flavors.
Good man!
After my Nirvāṇa,
when the Right Dharma has eighty remaining years before its extinction,
at that time this Sūtra will be widely circulated in Jambudvīpa.
At that time, there will be evil Bhikṣus
who plagiarize and abridge this Sūtra, dividing it into many parts,
thereby destroying the color, aroma, and delicious flavor of the Right Dharma.
Although these evil persons
recite such canonical texts,
they eradicate the deep and essential meanings of the Tathāgata,
and insert worldly, ornate, literary embellishments
and meaningless phrases.
They copy the beginning and place it at the end;
copy the end and place it at the beginning;
place the front and back parts in the middle;
and place the middle parts at the front and back.
You should know that such evil Bhikṣus
are companions of Māra,
who accept and keep all impure objects,
claiming that the Tathāgata permitted them to keep everything.
Just as the milkmaid added much water to the milk,
the evil Bhikṣus are also like this:
they mix in worldly speech
and wrongly edit this Sūtra,
causing many sentient beings not to be able to correctly speak it,
correctly transcribe it,
correctly grasp it,
respect it,
praise it,
offer to it, or revere it.
These evil Bhikṣus, for the sake of profit and offerings,
cannot widely preach and circulate this Sūtra.
The little that is circulated is insignificant,
just like that poor milkmaid
who successively sold the milk,
until it became gruel without the flavor of milk.
This Mahāyāna Canon, the Mahā Pārinirvāṇa Sūtra, is also like this:
successively diluted,
it loses its spirit and flavor.
Although it lacks spirit and flavor, it is still a full thousand times superior to other Sūtras,
just as that milk flavor is a thousand times superior to bitter flavors.
Why is this?
This Mahāyāna Canon, the Mahā Pārinirvāṇa Sūtra,
is the foremost among the Śrāvakayāna Sūtras.
It is comparable to cow's milk,
which is the most excellent among flavors.
For this reason,
it is named the Mahā Nirvāṇa."
"Furthermore, good man!
If good men,
and good women, and so forth,
there are none who do not seek the male body.
Why is this?
All women are the dwelling place of all evils.
Furthermore, good man!
Just as mosquito urine cannot moisten this great earth,
it is likewise difficult to satisfy the lustful desires of women.
For instance, if all the earth were made into pellets like *tínglìzǐ*,
and men equal in number to these were to engage in sexual acts with one woman, they still would not be enough.
Even if the number of men were like the sands of the Gangā,
and they were to engage in sexual acts with one woman, they still would not be enough.
Good man!
Just as the great ocean,
all the rains from heaven,
a hundred rivers,
and all streams completely pour into it,
yet that great ocean is never satisfied.
The nature of women is likewise thus;
even if all beings were men,
and they were to engage in sexual acts with one woman, she would still not be satisfied.
Furthermore, good man!
Just as the *Āshújiā* tree,
the *Bōzhāluó* tree,
and the *Jiānījiā* tree,
spring flowers bloom,
bees sip and take their colors, fragrances, and subtle flavors,
and are never tired or satisfied.
A woman desiring a man is likewise thus,
she knows no weariness or satisfaction.
Good man!
For this reason,
all good men,
and good women, and so forth,
upon hearing the *Dàchèng Dànièpán Jīng* (Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra),
should constantly denounce the characteristics of womanhood and seek those of manhood.
Why is this?
This great classic possesses the characteristic of the great man (hero),
which is called the Buddha-nature (*Fóxìng*).
If a person does not know this Buddha-nature,
then they lack the characteristics of a man.
Why is that?
Because they cannot realize that they possess the Buddha-nature.
If there is one who cannot know the Buddha-nature,
I say that such beings are called women.
If one can realize that they possess the Buddha-nature,
I say that this person has the characteristics of a great man.
If there is a woman who can know that her own body definitely possesses the Buddha-nature,
you should know that such a being is instantly a man.
Good man!
This great Mahāyāna classic, the *Dànièpán Jīng*,
is an immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable accumulation of merit.
Why is this?
Because it expounds the secret treasury (*mìzàng*) of the *Rúlái* (Tathāgata).
Therefore, good men,
and good women,
if you wish to quickly know the *Rúlái*'s secret treasury,
you should skillfully and diligently practice this Sūtra.
*Jiāshè Púsà* (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva) said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
It is so,
it is so.
As the Buddha has said,
I now already possess the characteristics of a great man,
because I have attained entrance into the subtle and secret treasury of the *Rúlái*.
The *Rúlái* has just awakened me today,
and because of this, I immediately attained decisive understanding."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
You now speak this way in accordance with the worldly Dharma."
*Jiāshè* replied again:
"I do not speak in accordance with the worldly Dharma."
The Buddha praised *Jiāshè*:
"Excellent,
excellent!
The supreme flavor of the Dharma which you now know,
though extremely profound and difficult to know, you have been able to know it.
Just as a bee gathers flavor,
you are also like this.
Furthermore, good man!
Just as a mosquito's moisture,
cannot soak this great earth,
in the future age,
the widespread propagation of this Sūtra will also be thus,
like that mosquito's moisture.
When the Right Dharma (*Zhèngfǎ*) is about to perish,
this Sūtra will first sink into this earth.
You should know that this is the sign of the decline of the Right Dharma.
Furthermore, good man!
For instance, after the summer has passed,
the first month is called autumn,
and the autumn rains pour continuously.
This great Mahāyāna classic, the *Dànièpán Jīng*, is also like this;
for the sake of the *púsàs* (Bodhisattvas) in the South,
it will be widely propagated,
raining down the Dharma-rain,
completely filling those places.
When the Right Dharma is about to perish, it will reach *Jìbīn* (Kashmir or Kapisa),
complete and unimpaired, and sink secretly into the earth.
Whether there are believers or non-believers,
the nectar flavor of the Dharma of this great Mahāyāna *Fāngděng* (Vaipulya) classic,
will all sink into the earth.
Once this Sūtra has sunk,
all other remaining Mahāyāna classics will also perish and sink.
If they attain this Sūtra, complete and unimpaired,
the king-elephants among men, the *púsàs* and so forth,
should know that the *Rúlái*'s supreme Right Dharma will soon perish.
At that time, *Wénshūshīlì* (Mañjuśrī) said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
This *Chúntuó* (Cunda) still has a doubting mind.
We only wish that the *Rúlái*
would explain further for his sake,
allowing him to eliminate and cease [his doubt]."
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
What is the doubting mind?
You should speak of it,
and I will eliminate and cease it for him."
*Wénshūshīlì* said:
"*Chúntuó* doubts in his mind about the *Rúlái*'s* eternal abiding (permanence).
Because of the power of having attained knowledge and vision of the Buddha-nature,
if seeing the Buddha-nature means it is permanent,
when it was originally unseen,
it should have been impermanent.
If it was originally impermanent,
afterwards, it should also be thus.
Why is this?
Just like worldly things,
they originally did not exist but now exist,
and having existed, they cease to exist again.
Things such as these are all impermanent.
For this reason,
the *Fós* (Buddhas),
*púsàs*,
*shēngwéns* (Hearers),
and *yuánjués* (Pratyekabuddhas) have no difference."
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately spoke in verse:
"Good man,
for this reason,
the *Fós*,
*púsàs*,
*shēngwéns*,
and *yuánjués*,
also have differences,
and also have no differences."
*Wénshūshīlì* praised him, saying:
"Excellent,
truly as the sacred teaching states!
I now begin to understand that the *Fós*,
*púsàs*,
*shēngwéns*,
and *yuánjués*,
also have differences,
and also have no differences."
*Jiāshè Púsà* said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
As the *Rúlái* has spoken,
the *Fós*,
*púsàs*,
*shēngwéns*,
and *yuánjués*,
their nature is without difference.
We only wish that the *Rúlái* would differentiate and widely explain this,
benefiting and bringing peace and joy to all sentient beings."
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Listen carefully,
listen carefully,
I shall now speak for you.
Good man!
For example, a respected elder [zhǎngzhě],
or the son of a respected elder,
kept many dairy cows,
having various colors,
and constantly instructed one person to guard and tend to them.
This person, sometimes for the sake of sacrificial offerings [císì gù],
milked all the cows and placed it into a single container.
Seeing that the color of the milk was uniformly white,
he immediately became surprised and perplexed,
saying: 'The cows are different colors,
how is it that their milk is all the same color?'
This person reflected:
'This is all
due to the causal conditions [yīnyuán] of the karmic retribution [yèbào] of sentient beings, causing the milk color to be one.'
Good man!
Śrāvakas [Shēngwén],
Pratyekabuddhas [Yuánjué],
and Bodhisattvas [Púsà] are also like this;
the single Buddha-nature [Fóxìng] is like that milk.
Why is this so?
Because they equally eliminate the influxes [lòu].
But sentient beings say:
'The Buddha [Fó],
Bodhisattvas,
Śrāvakas,
and Pratyekabuddhas
have differences.'
There are certain Śrāvakas,
and ordinary people [fánfū zhī rén],
who doubt the Three Vehicles [Sān Chéng],
asking: 'How can there be no difference?'
These sentient beings,
after a long time, will realize on their own
that all Three Vehicles share the single Buddha-nature;
just like that person
who understood the characteristic of the milk,
due to causal conditions of karma.
Furthermore, good man!
For example, a gold ore,
is refined and its dross and impurities are filtered out;
only then is it melted down.
After it becomes gold,
its value is immeasurable.
Good man!
Śrāvakas,
Pratyekabuddhas,
and Bodhisattvas are also like this;
they all achieve the single Buddha-nature.
Why is this?
Because they remove the afflictions [fánnǎo],
just like that gold ore
removing all the dross and impurities.
For this reason,
all sentient beings share the single Buddha-nature,
without any difference.
Because they first heard the Tathāgata's [Rúlái] secret treasury [mìzàng],
they will naturally know this when they later attain Buddhahood,
just like that respected elder knew the uniform characteristic of the milk.
Why is this?
Because they have severed measureless hundreds of millions of afflictions.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa [Jiāyè Púsà] addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One [Shìzūn]!
If all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature,
what difference is there between the Buddha and sentient beings?
To speak in this way leads to many faults.
If all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature,
for what causal reason
did Śāriputra [Shèlìfú] and others enter Nirvāṇa [bānnièpán] via the Lesser Nirvāṇa [Xiǎo Nièpán]?
Why do Pratyekabuddhas enter Nirvāṇa via the Intermediate Nirvāṇa [Zhōng Nièpán]?
Why do Bodhisattvas enter Nirvāṇa via the Great Nirvāṇa [Dà Nièpán]?
If these people share the Buddha-nature,
why do they not enter Nirvāṇa in the same way as the Tathāgata's Nirvāṇa?"
"Good man!
The Nirvāṇa achieved by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
is not achievable by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
For this reason,
the Mahāparinirvāṇa [Dà Bānnièpán] is called 'Good Existence' [shànyǒu].
Even if there is no Buddha in the world,
it is not impossible for the two vehicles [èr chéng] to attain the two types of Nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa [Jiāyè] further said:
"What does this mean?"
The Buddha said:
"After immeasurable, boundless Asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
a single Buddha appears in the world,
revealing the Three Vehicles.
Good man!
Regarding what you said,
that Bodhisattvas
and the two vehicles are without difference:
I have previously explained this meaning
within this Tathāgata’s Secret Treasury Mahāparinirvāṇa.
The Arhats [Āluóhàn] do not possess 'Good Existence' [shànyǒu].
Why is this?
Because all Arhats will eventually attain this Great Nirvāṇa.
For this reason,
the Mahāparinirvāṇa contains ultimate bliss [bìjìng lè],
and is therefore called the Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa said:
"According to what the Buddha has taught,
I now for the first time understand the meaning of difference
and the meaning of non-difference.
Why is this?
All Bodhisattvas,
Śrāvakas,
and Pratyekabuddhas
will, in future ages, all return to the Mahāparinirvāṇa,
just as all streams flow into the Great Ocean.
Therefore, the people of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha paths
are all designated as permanent [cháng],
not impermanent [wúcháng].
For this reason,
there are also differences,
and there is also no difference."
Kāśyapa said:
"How is the nature [xìng] differentiated?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
The Śrāvaka is like milk,
the Pratyekabuddha is like curds,
the Bodhisattva is like crude or refined butter [shēng shú sū],
and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like clarified butter [tíhú].
For this reason,
in the Mahāparinirvāṇa, four types of nature [sì zhǒngxìng] are spoken of,
and they are differentiated.
Kāśyapa further said:
"What are the characteristics of the nature of all sentient beings?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Just as when a calf is newly born,
the milk and blood are not yet separate,
the nature of ordinary people [fánfū zhī xìng],
mixed with all afflictions, is also like this.
Kāśyapa further said:
"In the city of Kuśīnagara [Jūshīnà Chéng], there is a caṇḍāla [zhāntuóluó],
named Huānxǐ (Joy).
The Buddha predicted this person,
due to a single initial aspiration [fāxīn],
will quickly attain the unsurpassed, genuine, and true path [wúshàng zhèngzhēn zhī dào]
within the time of a thousand Buddhas in this realm.
For what reason
does the Tathāgata not grant venerable Śāriputra [Shèlìfú],
Maudgalyāyana [Mùjiànlián], and others, the prediction [jì] of swiftly achieving the Buddha path?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
There are some Śrāvakas,
Pratyekabuddhas,
and Bodhisattvas who make a vow, saying:
'I shall protect and uphold the True Dharma [Zhèngfǎ] for a long time,
and only then attain the unsurpassed Buddha path.'
Since [Huānxǐ] made a rapid vow,
I therefore granted him a rapid prediction.
Furthermore, good man!
For example, a merchant has a priceless treasure [wújià bǎo],
and goes to the market to sell it.
When foolish people see it,
not recognizing it, they ridicule and laugh.
The owner of the treasure announces:
'This precious pearl of mine is worth countless sums.'
Hearing this, they laugh again,
and speak to each other, saying:
'This is not a real jewel;
it is a crystal [pōlí] bead.'
Good man,
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are also like this.
If they hear a rapid prediction,
they will become lazy [xièdài],
ridicule, laugh, and disparage it,
just like those foolish people who do not recognize the true treasure.
In future ages there will be certain monks [bǐqiū]
who are unable to diligently practice good dharmas,
are oppressed by poverty, hardship, and hunger,
and enter the monastic life because of this,
merely to sustain their bodies.
Their minds and wills are light and restless,
and they practice wrong livelihood [xiémìng] and flattery.
If they hear the Tathāgata granting Śrāvakas rapid predictions,
they will certainly laugh loudly,
show contempt, and slander them.
Know that these people are those who have broken the precepts [pòjiè],
and who falsely claim to have achieved superhuman dharmas [guòrén zhī fǎ].
For this reason,
although [Huānxǐ] made a rapid vow,
I therefore gave him a rapid prediction.
For those who protect the True Dharma,
I grant a distant prediction.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa [Jiāyè Púsà] again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How do Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas [Púsà Móhēsà] achieve an indestructible assembly [juànshǔ]?"
The Buddha instructed Kāśyapa [Jiāyè]:
"If the Bodhisattvas
diligently strive to protect the True Dharma,
by this causal condition,
the assembly they attain cannot be destroyed."
Jiāyè Púsà again spoke to the Buddha, saying:
"Shìzūn!
For what reason
do sentient beings acquire this dryness of the lips and mouth?"
The Buddha told Jiāyè:
"If there are those who do not recognize that the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo) eternally abide,
due to this cause and condition,
their lips and mouth are dry and scorched.
Just as a person whose mouth is spoiled
does not know the differences between the six flavors: sweet,
bitter,
pungent,
sour,
salty,
and bland.
All sentient beings,
being foolish and witless,
do not recognize that the Three Jewels are the eternally abiding Dharma (Law);
therefore, this is called the dryness of the lips and mouth.
"Furthermore, good man (shànnánzǐ)!
If there are sentient beings who do not know that the Rúlái (Tathāgata) eternally abides,
you should know that such persons are born blind.
If they know that the Rúlái eternally abides,
even if such persons only possess flesh eyes,
I say that they possess what is called the celestial eye (tiānyǎn).
"Furthermore, shànnánzǐ!
If there are those who can know that the Rúlái is eternal,
you should know that such a person
has long cultivated and practiced such sūtras;
I say that they, too, are called tiānyǎn.
Even if they possess the celestial eye,
yet cannot know that the Rúlái is eternal,
I say that they are called flesh eyes (ròuyǎn).
Such persons cannot even recognize their own hands and feet,
or joints,
nor can they cause others to know [this truth];
for this reason,
they are called ròuyǎn.
"Furthermore, shànnánzǐ!
The Rúlái constantly acts as the father and mother for all sentient beings.
Why is this so?
All sentient beings,
in various forms and categories—
two-footed,
four-footed,
many-footed,
or footless—
the Buddha teaches the Dharma with a single sound,
and those various different species each obtain understanding,
each exclaiming in praise:
'Today the Rúlái has taught the Dharma for me.'
For this reason,
He is called father and mother.
"Furthermore, shànnánzǐ!
Just as when a person gives birth to a child,
when it is about sixteen months old, although it speaks,
its words cannot yet be understood.
However, when the parents wish to teach it to speak,
they first mimic its sound,
gradually teaching it.
Is the speech of the parents
perhaps incorrect?"
"No,
Shìzūn!"
"Shànnánzǐ!
All Buddhas, the Rúlái, are also like this:
they teach the Dharma following the various sounds and voices of sentient beings,
in order to enable them to abide in the True Dharma,
and they manifest various forms, corresponding to what should be seen.
When the Rúlái thus uses the same language as them,
is it perhaps incorrect?"
"No,
Shìzūn!
Why?
Because what the Rúlái teaches is like the lion's roar,
conforming to the various sounds and voices of the world,
yet praising and expounding the marvelous Dharma for sentient beings.
At that time,
the Shìzūn emitted lights of various colors from His face—
azure,
yellow,
red,
white,
crimson,
and purple— illuminating the body of Chúntuó.
Chúntuó, having encountered this,
along with his family and dependents,
carrying various delicacies,
quickly went to the Buddha's place,
wishing to offer the Rúlái and the community of Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū) the final offering.
The various vessels and implements,
filled and complete,
were carried to the Buddha's presence.
At that time, there were Devas (Tiānrén) of great majesty and virtue,
who blocked his path,
surrounding him completely,
saying to Chúntuó:
"Stop for now,
Chúntuó!
Do not immediately make this offering."
Precisely at that time,
the Rúlái again emitted immeasurable and boundless lights of various kinds.
When the great assembly of Devas encountered this light,
they immediately allowed Chúntuó to proceed to the Buddha's place
and present his offering.
At that time, the Tiānrén and all other sentient beings,
each took the offerings they were holding,
approached the Buddha,
knelt respectfully, and addressed the Buddha:
"We only wish that the Rúlái allow the Bhikṣus to accept this food and drink."
Then the Bhikṣus,
knowing it was the proper time,
held their robes and bowls,
composed and tranquil in mind.
At that time, Chúntuó, for the sake of the Buddha and the Saṅgha,
