arranged various jewel thrones like lion seats (shīzǐ băozuò),
hung silks,
banners and canopies,
flowers and incense,
and jeweled necklaces (yīngluò).
At that moment, the trichiliocosm (sānqiān dàqiān shìjiè) was subtly adorned,
resembling the Western Land of Bliss (Ānlè Guótŭ).
At that time, Chúntuó stood before the Buddha,
sorrowful, grieving, and disappointed, and again spoke to the Buddha:
"We only wish that the Rúlái,
still showing compassion,
remains in the world for an eon (jié) or even slightly less than an eon."
The Buddha told Chúntuó:
"If you desire that I remain in the world for a long time,
you should promptly offer the final, complete Dāna-pāramitā (Dánbōluómì, perfection of giving)."
At that time, all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà),
Devas and various other beings,
spoke simultaneously with different mouths but a single voice, proclaiming:
"Marvelous,
Chúntuó!
You have achieved great blessed merit,
enabling the Rúlái to accept the ultimate, unsurpassed offering.
But we, due to our lack of merit,
have offered provisions that will therefore be in vain."
At that time, the Shìzūn,
wishing to satisfy the hopes of the entire assembly,
manifested innumerable Buddhas from every single pore on His body.
[Innumerable Buddhas were manifested.]
Each one of these Buddhas
had an infinite number of Bhikṣus in their Saṅgha.
These Shìzūns and the countless multitudes
all manifested accepting their offerings,
while Śākyamuni Rúlái (Shìjiā Rúlái) personally accepted that which Chúntuó had presented.
At that time, the perfectly cooked rice grain provisions that Chúntuó had brought,
measuring eight *hú* (bushels) according to the measure of Magadha (Mógātuó) country,
by the Buddha's spiritual power,
completely satisfied the entire great assembly.
When Chúntuó saw this event,
joy arose in his mind,
boundless delight,
and the entire great assembly was likewise filled with joy.
At that time, the great assembly, having received the Buddha's sacred intention,
each formed this thought:
"The Rúlái has now accepted our offerings;
before long, He will enter Nirvāṇa (Nièpán)."
Having formed this thought,
their hearts were filled with both sorrow and joy.
Although the area of the grove was narrow,
by the Buddha's spiritual power,
even in a space the size of a needlepoint, there were innumerable Buddhas, Shìzūns, and their attendants sitting and eating equally.
The food they ate was also identical.
At this time, the Tiānrén,
Asuras (Āxiūluó), and others
wept, lamented, and sighed, saying:
"Today the Rúlái has accepted our final offering.
Having accepted the offering, He will soon enter Parinirvāṇa (Bān Nièpán).
Whom shall we then offer to?
We are now eternally separated from the Unsurpassed Controller (Wúshàng Tiáoyù),
blind and without eyes."
At that time, the Shìzūn, wishing to comfort and soothe the entire great assembly,
spoke verses, saying:
"If there are Bhikṣus (Bīqiū),
Bhikṣuṇīs (Bīqiūní),
Upāsakas (Yōupósè),
Upāsikās (Yōupóyí),
who are able to make vows using the Tathāgata’s (Rúlái) highest pledges,
you should know that these people
are without ignorance,
and are worthy of receiving offerings.
Due to the power of these vows,
their meritorious rewards and retributions are supreme in the world,
like an Arhat (Āluóhàn).
If there are those who cannot thus contemplate and understand the permanence of the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo),
they are a Caṇḍāla (Zhāntuóluó).
If there are those who can know the real Dharma conditions of the permanence of the Three Jewels,
they depart from suffering and attain tranquility and bliss;
there is no harassment or obstacle that can hinder them."
At that time, the great assembly of humans and heavenly beings,
along with the Asuras (Āxiūluó) and others,
having heard this Dharma,
their minds arose in joy,
leaping limitlessly for happiness.
Their minds were subdued and gentle,
having successfully extinguished all obscurations,
their minds were without arrogance or lowliness,
their majesty and virtue were pure,
and their countenances were pleasant.
Knowing that the Buddha (Fó) abides permanently,
they thus arranged various heavenly offerings,
scattering various flowers,
powdered incense,
scented pastes,
and playing heavenly music,
therewith making offerings to the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha said to the Bodhisattva (Púsà) Kāyè (Jiāyè):
"Good man!
Do you see this assembly and these rare occurrences?"
Kāyè replied:
"I have seen them,
World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
I see all the Tathāgatas, immeasurable, boundless, and countless,
receiving the great assembly’s
food and meal offerings presented by humans and heavenly beings.
I also see that the bodies of all the Buddhas are exceedingly vast and beautiful,
yet the place where they sit is like the point of a single needle,
and the many surrounding multitudes do not hinder one another.
Furthermore, I see the great assembly all issuing solemn vows,
speaking thirteen verses.
I also know that the great assembly members are each thinking in their minds,
'The Tathāgata is now receiving my offering alone.'
Even if the meal offering presented by Chúntuó (Chúntuó) were crushed into fine dust,
one Buddha for every particle of dust,
they still would not be fully accommodated.
But by the Buddha’s spiritual power,
everyone in the entire great assembly is fully satisfied.
Only the Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) and the Dharma Prince Wénshū Shīlì and others,
are able to know these rare occurrences,
which are all expedient manifestations of the Tathāgata.
The great assembly of Hearers (Shēngwén) and the Asuras and others,
all know that the Tathāgata is the permanently abiding Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Chúntuó, saying:
"Are what you see now
rare and marvelous occurrences?"
"Indeed they are,
World-Honored One!
What I saw previously—
immeasurable Buddhas with the thirty-two marks
and the eighty subsidiary characteristics adorning their bodies—
I now see them all with the mighty and extraordinary physical appearance of Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas,
exceedingly vast, beautiful, and wonderful.
I only see the Buddha’s body likened to a medicinal tree,
surrounded by the Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas and others."
The Buddha said to Chúntuó:
"Those immeasurable Buddhas that you saw previously
were transformations created by me,
for the purpose of benefiting all sentient beings
and enabling them to attain joy.
Such Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas and others,
their practices
are inconceivable;
they are able to perform the deeds of immeasurable Buddhas.
Chúntuó!
You have now already completely accomplished the practices of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva,
attained and abide in the Ten Stages (Shí Dì),
and fully completed the practices performed by a Bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Kāyè said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
It is so,
it is so.
As the Buddha has stated,
the Bodhisattva practices accomplished by Chúntuó—
I also rejoice in them.
Now, the Tathāgata, wishing to create great illumination for the immeasurable sentient beings of the future,
speaks this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Chéng Dà Nièpán Jīng)."
"World-Honored One!
Do all canonical sūtras speak of remaining meaning and
non-remaining meaning?"
"Good man!
What I speak of
includes remaining meaning,
and also non-remaining meaning."
Chúntuó said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said:
World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of this?
What is the difference between upholding the precepts and destroying the precepts?"
The Buddha said:
"Except for one person,
all other giving is praiseworthy."
Chúntuó asked:
"Who is referred to as ‘except for one person’?"
The Buddha said:
"It is the one who
destroys the precepts spoken of in this Sūtra."
Chúntuó further said:
"I have not yet understood this;
I only wish that you would explain it."
The Buddha said:
"Chúntuó!
The one referred to as destroying the precepts is called an Icchantika (Yīchǎntí).
All other acts of giving, wherever they occur,
are praiseworthy and result in great rewards."
Chúntuó further asked:
"As for the Icchantika,
what is the meaning of this?"
The Buddha said:
"Chúntuó!
If there are Bhikṣus or Bhikṣuṇīs,
Upāsakas,
or Upāsikās,
who utter coarse and evil speech
and slander the Proper Dharma (Zhèng Fǎ),
having created such heavy karma,
and who never repent or feel shame or remorse in their minds—
such people are called those who proceed toward the path of the Icchantika.
If they violate the four fundamental prohibitions
or commit the five heinous crimes,
knowing certainly that they have committed such serious matters,
yet their minds initially have no fear, shame, or remorse,
and they are unwilling to reveal (their wrongdoing),
and forever lack the mind to protect, cherish, or establish the Buddha’s Proper Dharma,
but rather defame, despise, and scorn it, saying it contains many faults—
such people are also called those who proceed toward the path of the Icchantika.
Furthermore, if they say that there is no Buddha,
Dharma,
or Saṅgha (Sēng),
such people are also called those who proceed toward the path of the Icchantika.
Except for such Icchantikas,
giving to all others is entirely praiseworthy."
At that time, Chúntuó again spoke to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The term ‘destroying the precepts’ (pò jiè)
—what is its meaning?"
He replied:
"Chúntuó!
If one violates the four fundamental prohibitions, commits the five heinous crimes,
or slanders the Proper Dharma,
such people are called those who destroy the precepts."
Chúntuó further asked:
"Can those who thus destroy the precepts
be rescued?"
"Chúntuó!
If there are conditions,
then they can be rescued.
If they are wearing the Dharma robes and have not yet abandoned them,
and their minds constantly hold shame and fear,
and they reflectively condemn themselves, saying:
'Alas!
Why did I commit such a grave sin?
How strange it is
that I created this painful karma?'
If their minds reform and repent,
giving rise to the intention to protect the Dharma,
and they wish to establish the Proper Dharma.
'Those who protect the Dharma,
I shall make offerings to them.
If there are those who read and recite the Mahāyāna scriptures,
I shall consult them,
receive, uphold, read, and recite them.
Once I have mastered them,
I shall again, for the sake of others,
distinguish and broadly explain them.'
I say that such a person is not considered one who has violated the precepts.
Why is this?
Good man!
Just as the rising sun
can remove all dust, haze,
and darkness.
The subtle scripture of the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán), appearing and flourishing in the world,
is also like this:
it can eliminate the multitudes of sins committed by sentient beings throughout countless kalpas.
Therefore, this sūtra
speaks of attaining great karmic reward by protecting the Proper Dharma,
thus rescuing those who have violated the precepts.
If there is anyone who slanders this Proper Dharma,
but is able to reform themselves and return to the Dharma,
contemplating all the non-virtuous deeds they have committed,
feeling as if they have harmed themselves,
giving rise to terror in their minds,
shock, fear, and shame,
knowing that apart from this Proper Dharma
there is no further rescue or protection,
therefore they should return to the Proper Dharma.
If they are able to take refuge in this way, as taught,
then offering gifts to such a person garners boundless blessings.
They are also called those in the world who should receive offerings.
If one commits the above-mentioned sins of evil karma,
and after a month or fifteen days
does not give rise to the mind of taking refuge and confessing openly,
then if gifts are given to such a person, the karmic reward is extremely small.
Those who commit the Five Heinous Crimes (wǔ nì) are also like this:
if they can generate a mind of repentance,
internally harboring shame and remorse, thinking:
'The non-virtuous karma I have committed today
is truly a great suffering.
I must establish
and uphold the Proper Dharma.'
Then this is not called the sin of the Five Heinous Crimes (wǔ nì zuì),
and if gifts are offered to this person, boundless blessings are gained.
Having committed the heinous crime,
if one does not give rise to the intention of protecting the Dharma and taking refuge,
then the blessings gained from making offerings to them are not worth mentioning.
Furthermore, good man!
Regarding those who commit grave sins,
you should now listen attentively.
I shall distinguish and broadly explain it for you:
one should generate this intention.
That is, the Proper Dharma
is the subtle secret treasury of the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Therefore, I must protect, uphold, and establish it.
One who offers gifts to such a person attains superior karmic reward.
Good man!
For example, a woman,
pregnant and about to give birth,
encountered a chaotic and desolate state,
and fled to another land.
She gave birth immediately in a celestial temple.
Hearing that her former homeland was safe, secure, and prosperous,
she carried her child, wishing to return to her native land.
Midway, she encountered a river whose waters were surging and violently swift.
Carrying the child, she could not cross.
She immediately thought to herself:
'I would rather die together with my child in one place
than abandon him and cross alone.'
Having thought this, mother and child both perished together.
After death, they immediately attained birth in the heavens,
due to her loving thought for her child, wishing him to cross.
Although this woman’s nature was originally harsh and evil,
because of her love for her child,
she was able to be born in the heavens.
Committing the four cardinal prohibitions (sì zhòng jìn)
or the five Anantarīya sins (wǔ wú jiàn zuì),
but generating the intention to protect the Dharma, is also like this.
Although they previously performed non-virtuous karma,
because of protecting the Dharma,
they are able to become the supreme field of merit for the world.
Those who protect the Dharma have immeasurable karmic rewards such as these.
Chúntuó spoke again:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If an Icchantika (yīchǎntí) is able to reform themselves and repent,
respectfully making offerings,
praising the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo),
does offering gifts to such a person yield great karmic reward?"
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"Good man!
You should not speak in this way now.
Good man!
For example, a person eats an Amra fruit (ānmó guǒ),
spits the seed out onto the ground,
and then thinks:
'There should be sweetness within this seed.'
He immediately takes it back,
breaks it open and tastes it.
Its flavor is extremely bitter,
and his mind generates regret.
Fearing the loss of the fruit species,
he gathers it back up
and plants it in the earth, diligently tending and caring for it,
irrigating it at the proper time with ghī (sū), oil, and milk.
What do you think?
Can it possibly grow?
"No,
World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
Even if the heavens were to send down the supreme sweet rain,
it still would not grow."
"Good man!
That Icchantika (yīchǎntí) is also like this.
Having burned up the roots of goodness,
where can they possibly find a place to eliminate their sins?
Good man!
If they generate a good intention,
then they are no longer called an Icchantika (yīchǎntí).
Good man!
For this reason,
the karmic rewards gained from all offerings
are not without distinction.
Why is this?
The reward gained from offering gifts to Śrāvakas (shēngwén) is different.
The reward gained from offering gifts to Pratyekabuddhas (Pìzhīfó) is also different.
Only by offering gifts to the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is the supreme fruit obtained.
Therefore, it is said that the rewards from all offerings are not without distinction.
Chúntuó spoke again:
"Why did the Tathāgata (Rúlái) speak this verse?"
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"Chúntuó!
Due to a certain condition,
I spoke this verse.
In the city of Rājagṛha (Wángshě Chéng), there was an Upāsaka (Yōupósāi)
who lacked pure faith
and served the Nirgranthas (Níjiān).
He came and asked me the meaning of giving (dāna).
Because of this condition, I spoke this verse,
and also explained the meaning of the secret treasury for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) and others.
What is the meaning of this verse?
'All' means a partial 'all'.
You should know that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) are the heroes among men:
they gather those who uphold the precepts
and offer them what they need,
while they abandon those who violate the precepts, just as one removes tares and weeds.
"Furthermore, good man,
as for the verse I previously spoke:
At that time, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Wénshū Shīlì Púsà Móhēsà)
immediately rose from his seat,
baring his right shoulder,
placing his right knee on the ground,
bowed before the feet of the Buddha (Fó),
and spoke this verse:
"The verses spoken by the Buddha,
their meaning is incomplete (or 'has a remainder').
We only ask that you extend your compassionate pity
and explain the underlying causes and conditions.
Why is this?
O Bhagavān (World-Honored One)!
Within this Great Trichiliocosm (Sānqiān Dàqiān Shìjiè),
there is an isle named Jūyení.
On that isle is a river,
perfectly straight, not bending, named Suōpóyē,
likened to an inked string (carpenter's line),
flowing straight into the Western Sea.
Such a characteristic of a river
the Buddha has never spoken of in other sūtras.
We only wish that the Tathāgata,
through the content of this Vaipulya Āgama Sūtra (Fāngděng Āhán Jīng),
will speak of the meaning that was previously incomplete,
enabling the Bodhisattvas to deeply understand this meaning.
O Bhagavān!
It is like a person who first recognizes the gold ore,
but later does not recognize the gold.
The Tathāgata is also like this:
having fully known all Dharmas,
yet what is expounded remains incomplete and not exhaustive.
Although the Tathāgata makes such incomplete statements,
one ought to skillfully understand their underlying intention.
If one says that every thicket must be composed of trees,
this is also incomplete.
Why is this?
Various trees made of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli treasures
are also called groves.
If one says that all women are inevitably deceitful and perverse,
this is also incomplete.
Why is this?
There are also women who observe the precepts well,
who have accomplished meritorious virtues and possess great compassion.
If one says that all those who are sovereign must enjoy pleasure,
this is also incomplete.
Why is this?
Those who are sovereign,
such as the Wheel-Turning Sacred King (Zhǎnlún Shèngdì)
and the Tathāgata, the Dharma King,
do not belong to the Māra of Death
and cannot be extinguished.
Brahmā, Śakra, and the various Devās,
although they achieve sovereignty,
are all impermanent.
Only those who achieve permanence and immutability
are truly called sovereign,
which is the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) Great Paranirvāṇa (Dàbān Nièpán).
The Buddha said:
'Good man!
You have now skillfully attained the eloquence of delight in speaking.
Stop now,
and listen carefully.
O Wénshūshīlì (Mañjuśrī)!
It is like a householder whose body is afflicted with sickness.
A good physician diagnoses him
and prepares a medicated paste (ointment).
At that time, the sick person
greedily desires to take too much.
The physician says to him:
"If you are able to digest it,
then you may take much.
But your body is now weak,
and you should not take too much.
You should know that this paste
is also called amrita (sweet dew),
and is also called poison.
If you take too much and cannot digest it,
then it is called poison.
Good man!
You must not now assume that what the physician says
violates the principles of meaning
and destroys the potency of the paste.
Good man!
The Tathāgata is also like this.
For the sake of the kings,
queens,
crown princes,
princes,
and ministers,
due to the arrogance of King Bōsīní (Prasenajit),
the prince,
and the queen,
desiring to tame and subdue them,
I demonstrated fear,
just like that good physician,
and thus spoke the verses.
O Wénshūshīlì!
You must now know
that what the Tathāgata speaks contains no error (or 'leakage').
Even if this great earth were to be overturned,
the words of the Tathāgata would never have any error.
For this reason,
all that the Tathāgata speaks is complete."
Thereupon the Buddha praised Wénshūshīlì:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
You have long known this meaning,
and out of compassion for all,
desiring to enable sentient beings to attain wisdom,
you have widely questioned the Tathāgata concerning the meaning of these verses.'
Thereupon Wénshūshīlì, the son of the Dharma King,
again spoke verses before the Buddha:
'Bhagavān, speaking this Dharma medicine in this way
is not the precise teaching.
You conform to the speech of others and do not oppose it.
We only wish that the Tathāgata would extend pity and speak the precise teaching.
Why is this?
The Bhagavān constantly says that all external schools (or heterodox paths),
ninety-five kinds,
all proceed toward evil paths;
while the Śrāvaka disciples all proceed toward the correct path.
Those who protect the precepts,
maintain proper deportment,
and carefully guard their faculties
are people who deeply delight in the Great Dharma
and proceed toward the good path.
Why does the Tathāgata, among the nine divisions (of scripture),
upon seeing someone slander another, then rebuke them?
What is the intention
of the meaning of these verses?'
The Buddha instructed Wénshūshīlì:
'Good man!
I spoke these verses
not entirely for the sake of all sentient beings.
At that time, it was solely for King Āshéshì (Ajātaśatru).
If there are no underlying causes and conditions, the Buddhas, the Bhagavāns, never speak contrary teachings.
Only when there are causes and conditions do they speak.
Good man!
King Āshéshì, having murdered his father,
came to my place,
desiring to challenge and defeat me,
and asked the following question:
"How can the Bhagavān possess omniscience
yet not possess omniscience?
If you are omniscient,
Tiáodá (Devadatta), throughout measureless past ages,
constantly harbored wicked intentions,
following the Tathāgata,
and seeking to kill him.
Why did the Tathāgata allow him to renounce home life?"
Good man!
Due to these causes and conditions,
I spoke these verses for that king:
"The Buddha told the Great King:
'You have now murdered your father
and committed the terrible offense (ānantarya-karma),
the heaviest sin leading to Avīci (Wújiān) Hell.
You ought to confess and reveal it
in order to seek purity.
Why then do you seek to perceive the faults of others?'"
Good man!
For this reason,
I spoke those verses for that king.
Furthermore, good man!
Also, for the protection of those who observe the precepts without violation and achieve proper deportment,
I spoke these verses to those who perceive the faults of others.
Moreover, if there is a person who receives instruction from others and keeps far away from all evils,
and furthermore instructs others to keep far away from all evils,
such a person is my disciple.'
Thereupon the Bhagavān
spoke verses for Wénshūshīlì:
Thereupon Wénshūshīlì
again spoke verses before the Buddha:
'The meaning of this Dharma phrase spoken by the Tathāgata
is also not exhaustive.
Why is this?
For example, an Arhat (Āluóhàn),
a Wheel-Turning Sacred King (Zhǎnlún Shèng Wáng),
the Jewel Woman, Elephant, and Horse,
and the Chief Treasurer Minister,
or the various Devās and humans, and Asuras (Āxiūluó)—
for anyone holding a sharp sword to be able to harm them,
there is no such possibility.
Brave warriors and virtuous women,
King of Horses and King of Beasts,
and Bhikṣus who hold the precepts—
even if they confront danger, they are not afraid.
For this reason,
the verses spoken by the Tathāgata
are also incomplete.
If one says that forgiveness towards oneself can be used as a metaphor,
this is also incomplete.
Why is this?
If an Arhat (Luóhàn) uses himself as a metaphor for others,
then there would be the perception of self (Wǒxiǎng) and the perception of life (Mìngxiǎng).
If there is the perception of self and the perception of life,
then he should protect ordinary beings,
and he should also see all Arhats (Āluóhàn) as merely practitioners.
If this is the case,
then it is wrong view (evil view).
If there is wrong view,
at the time of death,
one should immediately be reborn in Avīci Hell (Ābí Dìyù).
Furthermore, for an Arhat (Luóhàn) to generate a mind of harm towards sentient beings,
there is no such possibility.
Similarly, measureless sentient beings are also incapable of harming an Arhat.'
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
What is meant by the 'self-thought' (wǒ xiǎng)?
It means generating great compassion towards sentient beings
and having no thought of killing or harming.
It refers to the impartial mind of an Arhat (Āluóhàn).
Do not say that the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) speaks in contradiction without cause or condition.
In the past, in this city of Rājagṛha (Wángshě chéng),
there was a great hunter
who killed many herds of deer.
He invited me to eat the meat.
Although I accepted his invitation at that time,
I generated a compassionate mind toward all sentient beings, like toward Rāhula (Luóhóuluó),
and I spoke a verse, saying:
Therefore, I spoke this verse:
The Buddha said:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Mañjuśrī (Wénshū Shīlì)!
For the sake of the Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà),
you inquire about such secret teachings (mì jiào) of the Tathāgata (Rúlái)."
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke this verse again:
Thereupon, the Tathāgata
again answered Mañjuśrī with a verse:
At that time, the Tathāgata
spoke a verse again for the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What the Tathāgata has said
is also incomplete.
We only pray that the Tathāgata will again bestow compassion
and speak of the cause and condition.
Why?
For example, when a long-term student (zhǎng zhě zǐ)
is learning from a master (shī),
does he belong to the master or not?
If he belongs to the master, the meaning is not complete (yì bù chéngjiù).
If he does not belong to the master, it is also not complete.
If he gains freedom, it is also not complete.
Therefore, what the Tathāgata has said has a remainder (yǒu yú).
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
Just as a prince
who practices nothing,
fails in everything he touches;
this freedom (zìzài) is also constant suffering in ignorance and darkness (yú àn cháng kǔ).
If one says such a prince
is 'free' (zìzài), the meaning is also not complete.
If one says he 'belongs to others' (shǔ tā), the meaning is also not complete.
For this reason,
the meaning spoken by the Buddha is called having a remainder.
Therefore, not all who belong to others necessarily suffer,
and not all who are free necessarily experience joy.
All arrogance (jiāomàn), power, extreme violence, and wickedness also have a remainder.
World-Honored One!
Just as fierce women (liè nǚ)
leave home and study the Dao due to an arrogant mind,
upholding the precepts (jìn jiè)
and accomplishing perfect deportment (wēiyí chéngjiù),
controlling and gathering the senses (zhū gēn) so they do not scatter—
therefore, the fetter (jié) of all arrogance is not necessarily violent and wicked.
That all virtuous and good people are loved by everyone also has a remainder.
For example, a person who secretly violates the four grave prohibitions (sì chóng jìn)
but does not discard the Dharma robes and firmly maintains deportment—
those who protect the Dharma (hù chí fǎ zhě) see them and do not love them.
This person will certainly fall into hell upon death.
If there is a virtuous person who violates a grave prohibition,
the protectors of the Dharma see them and immediately drive them out, dismissing them from the path and returning them to secular life.
For this reason,
why must all virtuous and good people be universally loved?
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Due to cause and condition,
the Tathāgata speaks here of the meaning of 'having a remainder.'
Also due to cause and condition,
the Buddhas-Tathāgatas speak this Dharma.
At that time, there was a woman in Rājagṛha (Wángshě chéng),
named Shànxián,
who returned to her parents' home.
She came to my place
and took refuge in me, the Dharma, and the Sangha (zhòng sēng),
and made this statement:
'All women are not free in their power (shì bù zìyóu),
while all men are free and unobstructed.'
At that time,
knowing the mind of this woman,
I immediately proclaimed this verse for her.
Mañjuśrī!
Excellent,
excellent!
You are now able to ask the Tathāgata
such secret words for the sake of all sentient beings."
Mañjuśrī spoke a verse again:
"Thus,
World-Honored One!
Now receiving food and offerings from Cunda (Chúntuó),
is it not possible that the Tathāgata has fear?"
At that time, the World-Honored One
spoke a verse again for Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Mañjuśrī!
If you were to become sick,
I would likewise suffer illness.
Why?
Arhats (Āluóhàn), Pratyekabuddhas (Pìzhīfó),
Bodhisattvas,
and Tathāgatas
do not truly eat anything.
They only wish to transform others
by manifesting the reception and use of offerings provided by innumerable sentient beings,
enabling them to perfect Dāna Pāramitā (Dàna bōluómì)
and rescue those in hell,
animal realms,
and hungry ghosts (è guǐ).
To say that the Tathāgata, due to six years of arduous practices (kǔ xíng), had a frail and thin body
—there is no such possibility.
The Buddhas-World-Honored Ones are uniquely distinguished from all existences (zhū yǒu)
and are not like ordinary beings (fánfū).
How could they have a weak and inferior body?
The Buddhas-World-Honored Ones diligently cultivate practice
and obtain a vajra body (jīngāng shēn),
not like the frail bodies of worldly people.
My disciples are also like this;
they are inconceivable
and do not rely on food.
The statement that all powerful beings (dà lì) are without jealousy (jí dù) also has a remainder.
Just as worldly people
may be permanently without a jealous mind throughout their lives,
yet they are also without power.
The statement that all diseases and sufferings arise due to food
also has a remainder.
We also see people who suffer from external diseases (kè bìng),
such as being stabbed by a thorn,
or by swords, spears, or lances (dāo jiàn hóu shuò).
The statement that all those who practice purity (jìng xíng) receive peace and joy
is also incomplete.
There are also external practitioners (wàidào) in the world
who cultivate Brahma practice (Fàn xíng) but experience much suffering and affliction.
For this reason,
everything spoken by the Tathāgata has a remainder.
Therefore, the Tathāgata did not speak this verse without cause and condition;
it was spoken due to a cause.
In the past, in this country of Ujjayinī (Yōuchánní guó),
there was a Brahmin (Póluómén) named Gǔdí Dé,
who came to my place,
wishing to receive the fourth set of eight precepts (bā jiè zhāi fǎ).
At that time, I spoke this verse for him."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa (Jiāyè Púsà) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What is called the meaning of 'without remainder' (wú yú yì)?
And what is called 'all meanings' (yīqiè yì)?"
"Good man!
What is meant by 'all'
is only excluding the auxiliary practices (zhù dào) of permanent joy and wholesome Dharma (cháng lè shàn fǎ).
This is called 'all,'
and is also called 'without remainder.'
All other Dharmas
are also called 'having a remainder'
and also called 'without remainder.'
I wish to enable good men who delight in the Dharma
to know the meaning of 'having a remainder' and 'without remainder'."
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa's heart was greatly joyful,
leaping up boundlessly.
He stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How wonderful,
World-Honored One!
You regard sentient beings equally, like Rāhula (Luóhóuluó)."
At that time, the Buddha praised the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa:
"Excellent,
excellent!
What you now perceive is subtle, marvelous, and profoundly deep."
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We only pray that the Tathāgata will speak of the merits attained from the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dàshèng Dà Nièpán Jīng)."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good man!
If someone hears the name of this Sūtra,
the merits they attain
cannot be proclaimed by Śrāvakas (Shēngwén), Pratyekabuddhas (Pìzhīfó), and others;
only the Buddha can know it.
Why?
It is inconceivable and belongs to the realm of the Buddha (Fó jìngjiè).
How much more so for those who uphold,
read, recite, master,
or copy the Sūtra scroll!"
At that time, the Devas (Zhū tiān),
humans, and Asuras (Āxiūluó),
before the Buddha, spoke a verse with one voice, though from different mouths, saying:
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke a verse for the great assembly, saying:
Having made offerings to the Fó,
they immediately generated the mind of Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi),
and immeasurable, boundless multitudes of Bódísattvas, numerous as the sands of the Ganges, attained the dwelling of the First Stage (Bhūmi).
At that time, the Shìzūn,
together with Wénshū Shīlì,
Jiāyè (Kāśyapa) Púsà, and Chúntuó,
bestowed prophecies (vyākaraṇa).
Having bestowed the prophecies,
he spoke these words:
"All good men!
Cultivate your minds diligently;
beware of negligence.
I now have a back illness;
my entire body aches.
I now wish to lie down,
like a young child or one who is constantly afflicted.
You, Wénshū,
should extensively preach the great Dharma for the four assemblies.
I now entrust this Dharma to you.
Wait until Jiāyè
and Ānán (Ānanda) arrive;
then this true Dharma shall again be entrusted [to them]."
At that time, the Rúlái, having spoken these words,
desiring to subdue and guide all sentient beings,
manifested a physical illness
and lay down on his right side,
just like a sick person.
At that time, Jiāyè Púsà said to the Fó:
"Shìzūn!
The Rúlái is already free from all illnesses;
suffering and distress are completely eliminated,
and there is no longer any fear.
Shìzūn!
All sentient beings have four poisoned arrows,
which serve as the causes of illness.
What are these four?
They are covetousness (tānyù),
anger (chēnhuì),
delusion (yúchī),
and arrogance (jiāomàn).
If there are causes of illness,
then diseases arise,
namely: consumption,
rising qi (dyspnea) and vomiting,
emaciation of the skin and body,
anguish and confusion in the mind,
diarrhea, hiccoughing, and choking,
dripping and trickling urination,
pain in the eyes and ears,
fullness in the back and swelling of the abdomen,
madness, wasting disease, and possession by demons.
All such various physical and mental diseases,
the Fó Shìzūn have entirely eliminated.
For what reason today does the Rúlái look towards and instruct Wénshū Shīlì,
and speak these words:
'I now have a backache;
you should preach the Dharma for the great assembly'?
There are two reasons [for having done meritorious deeds]
which result in freedom from the suffering of illness.
What are the two?
The first is pity and compassion for all sentient beings,
and the second is providing medical treatment to the sick.
The Rúlái, in the past, cultivated the path of the Púsà throughout immeasurable billions of eons;
he constantly practiced kind speech,
benefiting sentient beings so they would not suffer distress,
and provided various medicines to the diseased and sick.
For what reason, then, does he now declare himself to be ill?
Shìzūn!
When a person in the world is ill,
they may sit or lie down restlessly,
or demand food and drink,
or instruct and admonish their family members
to manage their property and affairs.
Why does the Rúlái lie down silently
and not instruct his disciples, the Śrāvakās,
regarding Śīlapāramì (perfection of morality),
various Dhyānas (meditations) and Vimokṣas (liberations),
Sāmāpátí (Samāpatti, attainments),
and the cultivation of the right efforts (samyak-pradhāna)?
For what reason does he not speak of such profoundly deep Mahāyāna Sūtras?
Why does the Rúlái not use immeasurable skillful means (upāya)
to instruct Dà Jiāyè (Mahā Kāśyapa),
the King Elephant among men,
and other great persons,
so that they do not regress from Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí?
Why does he not chastise the evil Bhikṣus who accept and store all impure objects?
Shìzūn is truly without illness;
how can he silently
lie down on his right side?
All the Púsàs,
whenever they provide medical treatment to the sick,
dedicate all the accumulated roots of goodness (śubha-mūla) to sentient beings
and together dedicate them towards omniscience (sarvajñatā),
for the elimination of the obscurations of affliction (kleśa-āvaraṇa),
the obscurations of karma (karma-āvaraṇa),
and the obscurations of retribution (vipāka-āvaraṇa) for sentient beings.
The obscurations of affliction (Fánnǎo Zhàng) are:
covetousness (tānyù),
anger (chēnhuì),
delusion (yúchī),
resentment,
bondage and covering,
distress and anxiety,
jealousy,
stinginess and avarice,
deceit and fraudulence,
flattery and obsequiousness,
lack of shame and lack of remorse,
arrogance compounded by arrogance (mànmàn),
false arrogance (bù rú màn),
false pretense of attainment (zēngshàng màn),
ego arrogance (wǒ màn),
deviant arrogance (xié màn),
haughty arrogance (jiāomàn),
negligence and pride,
harboring resentment and engaging in disputes and lawsuits,
wrong livelihood and flattery,
falsely manifesting unusual characteristics,
seeking gain through gain,
improper seeking and excessive seeking,
lacking reverence,
not following instructions and admonishments,
associating closely with evil friends,
being greedy for gain without satisfaction,
difficult bondage and entanglement that is hard to undo,
desiring evil desires,
being greedy for evil greed,
self-view (kāya-dṛṣṭi), eternalism (bhavadṛṣṭi), and nihilism (vibhavadṛṣṭi),
constant yawning and habitual sleepiness,
restlessness and discontentment,
gluttony for food and drink,
a dull and hazy mind,
the mind dwelling on different thoughts,
unwholesome reflection,
frequent evil deeds of body and speech,
being fond of excessive speech,
dullness and darkness of the faculties,
speaking many falsehoods,
constantly covered by thoughts of desire (kāma-vitarka),
thoughts of malice (vyāpāda-vitarka),
and thoughts of harm (vihiṁsā-vitarka).
These are called the obscurations of affliction (Fánnǎo Zhàng).
The obscurations of karma (Yè Zhàng) are:
the Five Anantarya (Irremediable) Sins,
the sickness of heavy evil.
The obscurations of retribution (Bào Zhàng) are:
rebirth in the hells (dìyù),
as animals (chùshēng),
or as hungry ghosts (èguǐ),
slander of the True Dharma, and being an Icchantika.
These are called the obscurations of retribution (Bào Zhàng).
These three obscurations are termed the Great Sickness.
And when the Púsàs cultivated Bodhi throughout immeasurable eons,
they provided medical treatment for all sicknesses and diseases,
constantly making this vow:
that all sentient beings may forever eliminate the grave sickness of these three obscurations.
"Furthermore, Shìzūn!
When the Púsà Mahāsattvas cultivated Bodhi,
they provided medical treatment to all sick people,
constantly making this vow:
May sentient beings forever cut off all illnesses
and attain the Vajra body of the Rúlái.
They also vowed that all immeasurable sentient beings would become the wondrous King of Medicines,
cutting off all grave and evil diseases.
They vowed that all sentient beings would obtain the Agada medicine,
by the power of which they could eliminate all immeasurable evil poisons.
They also vowed that sentient beings would never regress from Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
and would quickly achieve the unsurpassed Fó medicine
to eradicate all poisoned arrows of affliction.
They also vowed that sentient beings would diligently cultivate vigor
and achieve the Vajra mind of the Rúlái,
creating subtle and wondrous medicine to cure all diseases,
and preventing anyone from generating thoughts of conflict or dispute.
They also vowed that sentient beings would become the Great Medicine Tree,
healing all grave and evil diseases.
They also vowed that sentient beings would pull out the poisoned arrows
and achieve the unsurpassed brightness of the Rúlái.
They also vowed that sentient beings would gain entry into the Rúlái’s great wisdom medicine, the subtle and secret Dharma treasury.
Shìzūn!
The Púsàs, in this way,
have made these great vows throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of eons,
aiming for all sentient beings to be entirely free of sickness.
For what reason, then, does the Rúlái today declare himself to be sick?"
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
There is a sick person in the world
unable to sit up,
bend forward or backward,
advance or halt;
food and drink cannot be consumed,
liquids cannot be swallowed,
nor can he teach and admonish his children
or manage the family affairs.
At that time, his parents,
wife and children,
brothers,
relatives,
and acquaintances,
each assume that this person is certain to die.
World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata today is also like this,
lying on his right side,
speaking nothing,
causing various ignorant people in this Yánfútí
to think this thought:
'The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Enlightened One, must certainly enter Nirvāṇa.'
They give rise to the thought of extinction and cessation.
However, the nature of the Tathāgata truly does not ultimately enter Nirvāṇa.
Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and changeless.
For this reason,
one should not say, 'My back hurts now.'
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
There is a sick person in the world,
whose body is wasted and damaged.
Whether lying flat or lying on his side,
he lies upon the bed covering.
At that time, his family harbors contempt and disgust,
giving rise to the thought of certain death.
The Tathāgata now is also like this,
about to be scorned and slighted by the ninety-five kinds of externalists (wàidào),
who give rise to the thought of impermanence.
Those externalists will make this statement:
'He is not equal to us,
because our nature is eternal.
Concepts like Īśvara (zìzài), Kāla (shíjié),
and atoms (wéichén), and other such principles, are eternally abiding
and without change.
Śramaṇa Gùtán (Gautama) is moved by impermanence;
he is a changing principle.
For this reason,
World-Honored One!
Today you should not remain silent
and lie upon your right side.'
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
There is a sick person in the world,
whose four great elements (sì dà) increase or decrease,
and are mutually unharmonious.
He is emaciated, weak, and utterly exhausted,
and therefore cannot sit up or rise as he wishes,
lying upon the bed covering.
The Tathāgata's four great elements are perfectly harmonious,
his bodily strength is complete, and there is no emaciation or damage.
World-Honored One!
Just as the strength of ten small oxen is not equal to the strength of one great ox,
the strength of ten great oxen is not equal to the strength of one dark ox,
the strength of ten dark oxen is not equal to the strength of one ordinary elephant,
the strength of ten ordinary elephants is not equal to the strength of one wild elephant,
the strength of ten wild elephants is not equal to the strength of one two-tusked elephant,
the strength of ten two-tusked elephants is not equal to the strength of one four-tusked elephant,
the strength of ten four-tusked elephants is not equal to the strength of one white elephant from the Snow Mountain (Xuěshān),
the strength of ten white elephants from Xuěshān is not equal to the strength of one Kṣemāṅga (Xiāngxiàng) elephant,
the strength of ten Kṣemāṅga elephants is not equal to the strength of one blue elephant,
the strength of ten blue elephants is not equal to the strength of one yellow elephant,
the strength of ten yellow elephants is not equal to the strength of one red elephant,
the strength of ten red elephants is not equal to the strength of one pure white elephant (Báixiàng),
the strength of ten pure white elephants is not equal to the strength of one mountain elephant (Shānxiàng),
the strength of ten mountain elephants is not equal to the strength of one Utpala (Yōubōluó) elephant,
the strength of ten Yōubōluó elephants is not equal to the strength of one Kumuda (Jūwùtóu) elephant,
the strength of ten Jūwùtóu elephants is not equal to the strength of one Puṇḍarīka (Fēntuólì) elephant,
the strength of ten Fēntuólì elephants is not equal to the strength of one human strongman (lìshì),
the strength of ten human lìshì is not equal to the strength of one Bhadraka (Bōjiàntí),
the strength of ten Bōjiàntí is not equal to the strength of one eight-armed Nārāyaṇa (Nàluóyán),
and the strength of ten Nàluóyán is not equal to the strength of one joint of a Ten-Dwelling Bodhisattva (Shí Zhù Púsà).
Regarding all common beings (fánfū),
the various joints in their bodies
do not touch each other at the ends.
In human strongmen (lìshì),
the ends of the joints meet.
In the body of a Bōjiàntí,
the various joints are connected.
In the body of a Nàluóyán,
the ends of the joints are locked together.
In the various joints and bones of a Shí Zhù Púsà,
they are bound together like coiling dragons;
therefore, the Bodhisattva's strength is the greatest.
When the world is formed,
the Vajra Seat (Jīngāng Zuò) arises from the boundaries of the vajra realm,
reaching up to the place of enlightenment (Dàochăng), beneath the Bodhi Tree (Pútí Shù).
Once the Bodhisattva sits there,
his mind immediately attains the Ten Powers (Shí Lì).
The Tathāgata today should not be like a baby or small child.
Babies and small children are foolish and ignorant,
unable to speak anything.
For this reason,
they can lie flat or on their side as they please,
and no one criticizes them.
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses great wisdom,
illuminating everything;
the Dragon among Men (Rén Zhōng zhī Lóng),
possessing great majesty and virtue;
the unsurpassed immortal (xiānrén) who has achieved spiritual powers (shéntōng);
who has eternally severed the net of doubt,
already extracted the poisoned arrow,
whose movements and stillness are serene and dignified,
whose deportment is complete,
and who has attained fearlessness.
Why now does he lie upon his right side,
causing all humans (rén) and devas (tiān) sorrow, grief, and distress?"
At that time, Kāshè Púsà (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva) immediately spoke verses before the Buddha:
At that time, the Shìzūn,
whose heart was imbued with great compassion,
knowing what all living beings were thinking,
was about to follow them and confer ultimate benefits.
He immediately rose from lying down
and sat cross-legged (in the *jiāfū zuò* posture).
His countenance was bright and joyful,
like a mass of molten gold.
His face and features were dignified and solemn,
like the full, flourishing moon.
His form was pure and clean,
free from all defilements.
He emitted a great brilliant light that filled the emptiness of space.
That light was immensely bright,
surpassing a hundred thousand suns.
It illuminated the east,
south, west, and north,
the four cardinal points, and up and down throughout the worlds of all Buddhas,
bestowing upon living beings the torch of great wisdom,
completely extinguishing the darkness of ignorance,
and causing hundreds of thousands of millions of *nàyóutuō* living beings
to settle their minds firmly in irreversible *Pútí*.
At that time, the Shìzūn,
with a mind free of doubt or worry,
like a king of lions,
adorned his body with the thirty-two marks of a great man
and the eighty minor characteristics.
From every pore on his body,
each single pore emitted a lotus flower.
These flowers were subtle and marvelous, each possessing a thousand petals.
They were of pure, true golden color,
with *liúlí* for stems,
*jīngāng* for filaments,
and rose quartz for the calyx.
Their form was large and round like a carriage wheel.
These various lotus flowers
each emitted various colored lights:
blue, yellow, red, white, purple, and crystal color.
These lights all completely reached the *Ābí Dìyù*,
the Thought Hells (*Xiǎng Dìyù*),
the Black Rope Hells (*Hēishéng Dìyù*),
the Multitude Gathering Hells (*Zhònghé Dìyù*),
the Howling Hells (*Jiàohuàn Dìyù*),
the Great Howling Hells (*Dà Jiàohuàn Dìyù*),
the Scorching Hot Hells (*Jiāorè Dìyù*),
and the Great Scorching Hot Hells (*Dà Jiāorè Dìyù*).
The living beings in these eight hells
were constantly tormented by various sufferings,
namely, burning and boiling,
roasting by fire,
hacking and stabbing,
and flaying and peeling.
Upon encountering this light,
all these sufferings were completely extinguished without remainder.
They found peace and coolness,
and limitless joy.
Within this light, the Rúlái's secret treasury was proclaimed,
stating that all living beings possess the Buddha Nature (*Fóxìng*).
When the beings heard this,
they immediately died and were reborn among humans and devas.
Furthermore, concerning the eight types of Cold Ice Hells:
namely, the *Ābōbō Dìyù*,
the *Āzhāzhā Dìyù*,
the *Āluóluó Dìyù*,
the *Āpópó Dìyù*,
the *Yōubōluó Dìyù*,
the *Bōtóumó Dìyù*,
the *Jūwùtóu Dìyù*,
and the *Fēntuólì Dìyù*.
The beings in these places were constantly afflicted by the suffering of cold,
namely, splitting open,
shattering of the body,
and mutual violence.
Upon encountering this light,
such sufferings were also extinguished without remainder,
and they immediately attained harmonious warmth that was comfortable for the body.
Within this light, the Rúlái's secret treasury was also proclaimed,
stating that all living beings possess the Buddha Nature (*Fóxìng*).
When the beings heard this,
they immediately died and were reborn among humans and devas.
At that time, in this *Yánfútí* realm and the other worlds,
all the hells were completely emptied;
there were no beings undergoing punishment,
except for the *Yīchǎntí*.
The hungry ghost (*Èguǐ*) beings, afflicted by hunger and thirst,
with hair wrapped around their bodies,
had not heard the name of thin gruel or water for hundreds of thousands of years.
Upon encountering this light,
their hunger and thirst were immediately removed.
Within this light, the Rúlái’s subtle and secret treasury was also proclaimed,
stating that all living beings possess the Buddha Nature (*Fóxìng*).
When the beings heard this,
they immediately died and were reborn among humans and devas,
causing all hungry ghosts to also be completely emptied,
except for those who slandered the *Dàshèng Fāngděng* true scriptures.
The animal (*Chùshēng*) beings,
killing each other
and feeding on each other,
upon encountering this light,
their feelings of hatred were all extinguished.
Within this light, the Rúlái’s secret treasury was also proclaimed,
stating that all living beings possess the Buddha Nature (*Fóxìng*).
When the beings heard this,
they immediately died and were reborn among humans and devas.
At that very time, the animal realm was also exhausted,
except for those who slandered the True Dharma.
On each and every one of these flowers resided a Buddha,
whose halo measured one *xún*.
They shone brightly with golden light,
subtle, dignified, solemn, unsurpassed, and incomparable,
with the thirty-two marks
and eighty minor characteristics adorning their bodies.
These various Shìzūn,
some were sitting,
some were walking,
some were lying down,
some were standing still.
Some caused the sound of thunder to shake,
some poured down rain,
some emitted lightning flashes,
some raised up wind,
some emitted smoke and flame, their bodies like masses of fire,
some manifested seven precious mountains,
ponds, springs, and rivers,
mountains, forests, and trees,
some manifested seven-jeweled lands,
cities and settlements,
palaces, houses, and dwellings,
some manifested elephants, horses, and lions,
tigers, wolves, peacocks,
phoenixes, and various birds,
some manifested scenes enabling all living beings in *Yánfútí*
to see the hells,
the animal realm (*Chùshēng*),
and the hungry ghost realm (*Èguǐ*),
and some manifested the six heavens of the Desire Realm.
Furthermore, there were Shìzūn
who spoke of the various faults of the *yīn*, *jiè*, and *rù* (aggregates, elements, and entrances),
some who spoke of the four noble truths (*Sì Shèng Dì* Dharma),
some who spoke of the causes and conditions of all phenomena,
some who spoke that all karma and afflictions arise from causes and conditions,
some who spoke of the self and non-self,
some who spoke of the two dharmas of suffering and happiness,
some who spoke of permanence, impermanence, and so forth,
and some who spoke of purity and impurity.
Furthermore, there were Shìzūn who, for the *Púsàs*, expounded the practice of the six *Bōluómì*,
some who spoke of the merits attained by the great *Púsàs*,
some who spoke of the merits attained by all Buddhas and Shìzūn,
some who spoke of the merits attained by the *Shēngwén* individuals,
some who spoke of adhering to the One Vehicle,
and some who spoke of the Three Vehicles achieving the Way.
Some Shìzūn emitted water from their left side
and fire from their right side.
Some manifested their initial birth and renunciation,
sitting at the *Dàochǎng* beneath the *Pútí* tree,
turning the wonderful Dharma wheel,
and entering *Nièpán*.
Some Shìzūn let forth a lion's roar,
causing those in the assembly to attain the first fruition,
the second fruition,
the third fruition,
up to the fourth fruition.
Others spoke of escaping *Shēngsǐ* (birth and death),
due to countless causes and conditions.
At that time, in this *Yánfútí*,
all living beings who encountered this light:
the blind gained sight of forms,
the deaf heard sounds,
the mute could speak,
the lame could walk,
the poor gained wealth,
the stingy became able to give,
the hateful gained compassion,
and the faithless gained faith.
In this world,
there was not a single living being practicing evil ways,
except for the *Yīchǎntí*.
At that time, all the Devas
, Nāgas
, Guǐshén
, Gandharvas (Qiántàpó)
, Asuras (Āxiūluó)
, Garuḍas (Jiālóuluó)
, Kiṃnaras (Jǐnnàluó)
, Mahuoragas (Móhóuluójiā)
, Rākṣasas (Luóchà)
, Jiàntuó
, Yōumótuó
, Āpó Móluó
, humans and non-humans, and so forth,
all spoke with a common voice, proclaiming these words:
“Excellent,
excellent!
O Unsurpassed Heavenly Venerable One (Wúshàng Tiānzūn)
, great is the benefit (you provide).”
Having spoken these words,
they leaped with joy and delight,
some singing, some dancing,
or shaking their bodies.
They scattered various flowers upon the Fó (Buddha) and the Saṅgha (Sēng)
, namely, Heavenly Utpalas (Yōubōluóhuā)
, Kumudas (Jūwùtóuhuā)
, Padmas (Pōtóumóhuā)
, Puṇḍarīkas (Fēntuólìhuā)
, Maṇḍāras (Màntuóluóhuā)
, Great Maṇḍāras (Móhē Màntuóluóhuā)
, Mañjūṣakas (Mànzhūshāhuā)
, Great Mañjūṣakas (Móhē Mànzhūshāhuā)
, Sandanas (Sàntuónàhuā)
, Great Sandanas (Móhē Sàntuónàhuā)
, Lúzhīnà flowers
, Great Lúzhīnà flowers
, fragrant flowers
, great fragrant flowers
, pleasing flowers
, great pleasing flowers
, beloved flowers
, great beloved flowers
, splendid flowers
, and foremost splendid flowers.
They further scattered various perfumes
, namely, aloeswood (Chénshuǐ)
, Tagara incense (Duōgēlóuxiāng)
, sandalwood (Zhāntán)
, turmeric (Yùjīn)
, mixed harmonious incense (Héhé záxiāng)
, and incense gathered from the seashore (Hǎi'àn jùxiāng).
Furthermore, they used heavenly jeweled banners
, pennants
, canopies
, and celestial music—
zithers and flutes
, reeds and lutes
, harps and wind instruments—
to make offerings to the Fó,
and they spoke verses (gè):
When these verses were spoken,
all the Fó in the Lotus Terrace (Liánhuātái)
, from Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí) up to the Pure Abodes (Jìngjū)
, all heard them.
At that time, the Fó addressed Kāshè Púsà (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva):
“Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
You have already fully attained such deep and subtle wisdom
, and you cannot be corrupted or destroyed by any Māras (mó) or heretics (wàidào).
Good man!
You are already firmly established
, and you cannot be shaken by any evil winds of falsehood.
Good man!
You have already perfected eloquence
, and have previously made offerings to countless past Fó Shìzūn (World-Honored Ones), equal to the sands of the Gaṅgā River
. Therefore, you are able to inquire about such meanings regarding the Tathāgata (Rúlái), the Perfectly Enlightened One (Zhèngjué).
Good man!
In my past
, during countless, limitless millions of nayuta (nàuyóu tā) hundreds of thousands of kalpas (jié)
, I have already eliminated the roots of sickness
and forever abandoned lying down or leaning.
Kāshè!
In countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas (ā sēng qí jié) in the past
, a Fó appeared in the world
, named Wúshàngshèng Rúlái (Unsurpassed Victorious Tathāgata)
, Arhat (Yìnggōng, Worthy of Offerings)
, Samyak-saṃbuddha (Zhèngbiànzhī, Perfectly and Universally Knowing)
, Vidyācaraṇa-saṃpanna (Míngxíngzú, Perfect in Understanding and Conduct)
, Sugata (Shànshì, Well-Gone)
, Lokavid (Shìjiānjiě, Knower of the World)
, Anuttara (Wúshàngshì, Unsurpassed Lord)
, Puruṣa-damya-sārathi (Tiáoyù Zhàngfū, Tamer of Men)
, Śāstā Devamanuṣyāṇām (Tiānrén Shī, Teacher of Devas and Humans)
, Fó
, Shìzūn (World-Honored One).
He taught the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Chéng Dà Nièpán Jīng) for the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén)
, illuminating and analyzing it
, revealing its meaning.
I
, at that time, was also a Śrāvaka of that Fó,
receiving and upholding that Great Nirvāṇa Canon,
reading it, reciting it fluently,
copying the sūtra scroll,
extensively illuminating and analyzing it for others,
and explaining its meaning;
with these roots of goodness (shàngēn)
, I dedicated them toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).
Good man!
Since then
, I have never been subject to the conditions of evil afflictions or karma,
falling into the evil realms (èdào)
, slandering the True Dharma (Zhèngfǎ)
, acting as an Icchantika (Yīchǎntí)
, receiving the body of a eunuch who lacks or possesses two sexual characteristics
, rebelling against and murdering my parents
, killing an Arhat (Āluóhàn)
, destroying stūpas or corrupting the Saṅgha
, causing the Fó's body to bleed
, or transgressing the four cardinal prohibitions (sì zhòng jìn).
Since that time
, my body and mind have been secure and peaceful
, free from all suffering and distress.
Kāshè!
I truly have no illness whatsoever now.
Why is this?
Because the Fó Shìzūn have long ago distanced themselves from all sickness.
“Kāshè!
These sentient beings, not knowing the profound teachings (mìjiào) of the Mahāyāna Vaipulya (Fāngděng)
, immediately assume that the Tathāgata truly suffers from sickness.
Kāshè!
For example, when it is said that the Tathāgata is a Lion among men
, yet the Tathāgata is truly not a lion
; such speech is the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
Kāshè!
For example, when it is said that the Tathāgata is a Great Dragon among men
, yet I have already abandoned this karma over countless kalpas.
Kāshè!
For example, when it is said that the Tathāgata is a human or a Deva
, yet I am truly neither human nor Deva
, nor Guǐshén
, Gandharva
, Asura
, Garuḍa
, Kiṃnara
, or Mahuoraga,
nor Self (wǒ)
, nor Life (mìng)
, nor capable of being fostered
, nor a true human being
, nor acting nor non-acting
, nor receiving nor non-receiving
, nor the Shìzūn nor a Śrāvaka
, nor speaking nor non-speaking.
Such statements
are all the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
“Kāshè!
For example, when it is said that the Tathāgata is like the great ocean
or Mount Sumeru (Xūmí Shānwáng)
, yet the Tathāgata is truly not salty in taste
or comparable to a stone mountain
; you should know that this speech is also the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
Kāshè!
For example, when it is said that the Tathāgata is like a Puṇḍarīka
, yet I am truly not a Puṇḍarīka
; such speech is the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
Kāshè!
For example, when it is said that the Tathāgata is like a father and mother
, yet the Tathāgata is truly not a father or mother
; such speech is also the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
Kāshè!
For example, when it is said that the Tathāgata is a great boatman
, yet the Tathāgata is truly not a boatman
; such speech is also the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
Kāshè!
For example, when it is said that the Tathāgata is like a caravan leader
, yet the Tathāgata is truly not a caravan leader
; such speech is also the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
Kāshè!
For example, when it is said that the Tathāgata can subdue the Māras
, yet the Tathāgata truly has no evil intention to make others submit
; such speech is all the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
Kāshè!
For example, when it is said that the Tathāgata can cure sores and abscesses
, yet I am truly not a master physician for sores
; such speech is also the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.”
“Kāśyapa!
As I previously stated:
‘If there is a good man
or good woman
who is skillful at cultivating the karma of the body,
speech,
and mind,
when they relinquish their life,
although relatives may take their corpse,
incinerate it with fire,
or cast it into a great water,
or abandon it in a burial ground
where foxes, wolves, and birds and beasts compete to eat it,
yet their mind-consciousness immediately arises in a good path.
But this dharma of the mind
truly has no going or coming,
nor does it reach any place.
It is truly a continuous succession, similar
in appearance, with no differences in form.
Such a statement
is precisely the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.’
Kāśyapa!
My statement now that I am ill
is also like this;
it is also the secret teaching of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, I instructed Mañjuśrī:
‘My back is now aching;
you all should teach the Dharma to the four assemblies.’
Kāśyapa!
The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, truly has no illness,
nor does lying on his right side
necessarily mean entering Nirvāṇa forever.
Kāśyapa!
This Great Nirvāṇa
is precisely the profound meditative concentration (Dhyāna) of all Buddhas.
Such meditative concentration
is not the domain for Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas to practice.
“Kāśyapa!
Regarding what you asked earlier,
why the Tathāgata is lying down and does not rise,
does not seek food or drink,
or instruct his family members to cultivate their livelihoods?
Kāśyapa!
The nature of empty space
likewise has no sitting or rising,
seeking food or drink,
or instructing family members to cultivate livelihoods,
nor has it going or coming,
arising, ceasing, aging, or robustness,
emergence, disappearance, injury, or damage,
liberation or bondage;
nor does it speak of itself,
nor speak of others,
nor liberate itself,
nor liberate others,
neither well nor sick.
Good man!
All Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are likewise like this,
like empty space.
How then could they have illnesses and suffering?
“Kāśyapa!
There are three types of people in the world
whose illnesses are difficult to cure:
First,
those who slander the Mahāyāna;
second,
those who commit the five heinous crimes (pāñcānantarya);
third,
Icchantikas.
These three types of illnesses are the gravest in the world,
and none of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas,
or Bodhisattvas are able to cure them.
Good man!
Suppose there is an illness that is definitely fatal and difficult to cure.
Whether someone attends to the sick and administers medicine as desired,
or whether no one attends to the sick or administers medicine as desired,
such an illness is definitely incurable.
Know that this person will undoubtedly die.
Good man!
These three types of people are also like this:
Whether there are Śrāvakas,
Pratyekabuddhas,
or Bodhisattvas,
whether they teach the Dharma
or do not teach the Dharma,
they cannot cause them to generate the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa!
Suppose a sick person,
if attended to and administered medicine as desired,
can then recover.
If these three (attendants, will, medicine) are absent, they cannot recover.
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are also like this:
Having heard the Dharma from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
they are then able to generate the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
but they cannot generate this mind without hearing the Dharma.
Kāśyapa!
Suppose a sick person, whether attended to and administered medicine as desired,
or whether no one attends to them or administers medicine as desired,
can still fully recover.
One type of person is also like this:
Whether they meet a Śrāvaka
or do not meet a Śrāvaka,
whether they meet a Pratyekabuddha
or do not meet a Pratyekabuddha,
whether they meet a Bodhisattva
or do not meet a Bodhisattva,
whether they meet a Tathāgata
or do not meet a Tathāgata,
whether they get to hear the Dharma
or do not hear the Dharma,
they naturally succeed in achieving Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This refers to people
who, whether for their own sake
or for the sake of others,
or out of fear,
or for gain and sustenance,
or for flattery and deceit,
or for deceiving others,
copy and write this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
uphold, read, and recite it,
make offerings and show reverence,
or teach it to others.
“Kāśyapa!
There are five types of people who, concerning this great Mahāyāna text of the Mahāparinirvāṇa,
have the practice domain of sickness;
they are not the Tathāgata.
What are these five?
First, having severed the three fetters,
they attain the fruit of a Srota-āpanna (Śu-tuóhán),
do not fall into hells,
animals,
or hungry ghosts,
return seven times to humans and devas,
permanently cut off all suffering,
and enter Nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa!
This is called the first person having the practice domain of sickness.
This person will, in the future, after passing 80,000 kalpas,
then succeed in achieving Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa!
The second person
severs the bond of the three fetters
and attenuates greed, hatred, and delusion,
attains the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin (Sī-tuóhán),
called ‘one return,’
permanently cuts off all suffering,
and enters Nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa!
This is called the second person having the practice domain of sickness.
This person will, in the future, after passing 60,000 kalpas,
then succeed in achieving Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa!
The third person
severs the five lower fetters,
attains the fruit of an Anāgāmin (Ānàhán),
will not come here again,
permanently cuts off all suffering, and enters Nirvāṇa.
This is called the third person having the practice domain of sickness.
This person will, in the future, after passing 40,000 kalpas,
then succeed in achieving Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa!
The fourth person
permanently severs greed,
hatred,
and delusion,
attains the fruit of an Arhat (Āluóhàn),
with afflictions extinguished without remainder,
enters Nirvāṇa,
and their practice is not the solitary practice of the Qílín (Kirin/rhinoceros).
This is called the fourth person having the practice domain of sickness.
This person will, in the future, after passing 20,000 kalpas,
then succeed in achieving Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa!
The fifth person
permanently severs greed,
hatred,
and delusion,
attains the path of a Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó),
with afflictions extinguished without remainder,
enters Nirvāṇa.
This is truly the solitary practice of the Qílín.
This is called the fifth person having the practice domain of sickness.
This person will, in the future, after passing 10,000 kalpas,
then succeed in achieving Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Kāśyapa!
This is called the fifth person having the practice domain of sickness;
they are not the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Fó told the Púsà Jiāshè:
“Good man!
A Púsà Móhēsà should, regarding this Dà Bān Nièpán Jīng,
concentrate their thoughts on five kinds of practice.
What are these five?
First is the Noble Practice (Shèngxíng),
second is the Pure Practice (Fànxíng),
third is the Heavenly Practice (Tiānxíng),
fourth is the Infant Practice (Yīng'érxíng),
and fifth is the Sick Practice (Bìngxíng).
Good man!
A Púsà Móhēsà must constantly cultivate these five kinds of practice.
Furthermore, there is one practice which is the Rúlái Practice,
which is the Mahāyāna Dà Nièpán Jīng.
Jiāshè!
How does a Púsà Móhēsà cultivate the Noble Practice (Shèngxíng)?
If a Púsà Móhēsà, whether from a Śrāmaṇa (Shēngwén)
or from a Rúlái,
hears this Dà Nièpán Jīng,
having heard it, faith arises.
Having faith, they should contemplate thus:
‘All the Fó Shìzūn have the unsurpassed path,
they possess the Great Right Dharma,
the great assembly follows the Right Practice,
and furthermore, there are the Vaipulya Mahāyāna Sūtras.
I should now, for the sake of loving, enjoying, and eagerly seeking the Mahāyāna sūtras,
abandon my beloved wives and children,
dependents,
dwelling houses,
gold, silver, and precious treasures,
subtle garlands,
incense, flowers, and music,
male and female slaves, servants,
young and old people,
elephants, horses, carriages,
cattle, sheep, chickens, and dogs,
and pigs and their kind.’
They further make this contemplation:
‘Householding is narrow and constrained,
like a prison;
all afflictions (fánnǎo) arise from it.
Leaving home is broad and expansive,
like empty space;
all wholesome Dharmas grow because of it.
If I remain a householder,
I cannot perfectly cultivate the pure Fànxíng throughout my life.
I should now shave off my beard and hair,
and leave home to learn the Way.’
Having made this contemplation,
‘I will now certainly leave home and cultivate the Way of the Unsurpassed Right and True Bodhi.’
When the Púsà thus wishes to leave home,
Tiān Mó Bōxún (the Heavenly Māra Papiyas) experiences great distress,
saying, ‘This Púsà is about to engage in a great struggle against me.’
Good man!
How could such a Púsà again engage in conflict with people?
At that time, the Púsà immediately goes to a monastery,
and if they see a Rúlái or a disciple of the Fó
whose deportment is perfect, whose senses are tranquil,
whose mind is gentle and harmonious,
pure, tranquil, and extinguished,
they go to that person and request to leave home,
shaving off their beard and hair,
and wearing the three Dharma robes.
Having left home,
they observe and uphold the precepts (jìnjiè);
their deportment is flawless;
their movements and stillness are composed
and they commit no offense.
Even regarding small offenses,
fear arises in their heart,
and their mind devoted to protecting the precepts
is like a diamond (jīngāng).
“Good man!
For example, if a person carries a flotation bag
and wishes to cross the great sea.
At that time, a Luóchà in the sea
immediately begs that person for the flotation bag.
Having heard this, the person immediately thinks:
‘If I give it now, I will certainly sink and die.’
They answer,
‘Luóchà!
You may kill me,
but the flotation bag cannot be taken.’
The Luóchà replies again,
‘If you cannot give it all to me,
please bestow half of it upon me.’
That person still refuses to give it.
The Luóchà replies again,
‘If you are unwilling to bestow half upon me,
I sincerely ask you to give me one-third.’
That person is unwilling.
The Luóchà replies again,
‘If you cannot do that,
then give me the amount of a handspan.’
That person is unwilling.
The Luóchà replies again,
‘If you still cannot give me the amount of a handspan,
I am now poor and starving,
oppressed by various sufferings;
I ask that you save me with an amount as small as a speck of dust.’
That person replies again,
‘What you now request
is truly not much;
however, I am currently attempting to cross the sea,
and I do not know how near or far the path ahead is.
If I give it to you,
the air will gradually leak out,
and how shall I overcome
the difficulties of the great sea?
I might sink into the water
and die midway.’
Good man!
The Púsà Móhēsà protecting and upholding the precepts
is also like this,
like that person crossing the sea guarding their flotation bag.
“When the Púsà thus protects the precepts,
the Fánnǎo (afflictions) and evil Luóchàs constantly
say to the Púsà:
‘You should trust me;
I will never deceive you.
Just break the four major prohibitions (sìjìn),
and uphold the remaining precepts.
By this condition,
you will be peaceful and safe,
and attain Nièpán.’
The Púsà at that time should say this:
‘I would rather uphold these precepts and fall into Ābí Yù (Avīci Hell),
than violate them and be born in heaven.’
The Fánnǎo Luóchà replies again,
‘If you cannot break the four major prohibitions,
then break the Sēngcán (secondary transgressions).
By this condition,
you will be peaceful and safe and attain Nièpán.’
The Púsà likewise should not follow that suggestion.
The Luóchà replies again,
‘If you cannot commit the Sēngcán,
you may deliberately commit the Tōulánzhē (grave offenses).
By this condition, you will be peaceful and safe and attain Nièpán.’
The Púsà at that time likewise does not follow.
The Luóchà replies again,
‘If you cannot commit the Tōulánzhē,
you may commit the Shěduò (offense requiring forfeiture).
By this condition, you can be peaceful and safe and enter Nièpán.’
The Púsà at that time also does not follow.
The Luóchà replies again,
‘If you cannot commit the Shěduò,
you may break the Bōyètí (minor offenses).
By this condition, you will be peaceful and safe and attain Nièpán.’
The Púsà at that time also does not follow.
The Luóchà replies again,
‘If you cannot commit the Bōyètí,
then hopefully you can violate the Tújíluó (least grave offenses) precept.
By this condition, you can be peaceful and safe and enter Nièpán.’
The Púsà at that time thinks to themselves:
‘If I now commit a Tújíluó offense
and do not confess it,
I will not be able to cross to the shore of Saṃsāra (shēngsǐ) and attain Nièpán.’
The Púsà Móhēsà, even regarding these minute precepts,
upholds them firmly, their mind like a diamond (jīngāng).
The Púsà Móhēsà holds the four grave prohibitions (sìzhòngjìn) and the Tújíluó
with equal reverence and firmness,
making no distinction.
If the Púsà can uphold them thus,
they fulfill the precepts that are the five roots (wǔgēn zhūjiè),
namely, the Precept of Pure Fundamental Karma of the Púsà,
the Precept of Pure Remaining Conduct of Former and Latter Dependents,
the Precept of Pure Awakening Without Evil Awakenings,
the Precept of Pure Mindfulness Upholding Right Mindfulness,
and the Precept of Dedication toward Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.”
"Jiāyè!
This Púsà Mòhēsà further possesses two kinds of precepts:
First, the precepts received from worldly instruction;
second, the precepts attained from the Right Dharma.
If the Púsà receives the precepts of the Right Dharma, they never commit evil.
Concerning those who receive the precepts of worldly instruction,
they only obtain them after the Four-Part Karma (White Ritual).
Furthermore, good man!
There are two kinds of precepts:
First, precepts of inherent gravity;
second, precepts that cease worldly reproach and suspicion.
The precepts of inherent gravity
are called the Four Prohibitions.
The precepts that cease worldly reproach and suspicion are:
not engaging in buying and selling;
using light scales and small bushels;
cheating and deceiving people;
exploiting the position or influence of others to seize property;
having malicious intent to bind (imprison) and destroy successful endeavors;
sleeping while a lamp is lit;
planting fields and homesteads;
maintaining household industries or sitting in a shop.
They do not keep elephants, horses, or carriages;
oxen, sheep, camels, or donkeys;
chickens, dogs, or monkeys;
peacocks or parrots;
*gòngmìng* birds (Jīvajīvaka) or Kūzhǐluó (Indian cuckoo);
jackals, wolves, tigers, or leopards;
cats, badgers, pigs, boars, or other vicious beasts;
young boys and young girls;
adult men and adult women;
slaves, maidservants, or attendants;
gold, silver, or lapis lazuli (liúlí);
crystal (pōlí) or pearls;
giant clams (chēqǔ) or agate (mǎnǎo);
coral or jade discs (bìyù);
cowrie shells (kēbèi) and various treasures;
red copper or white tin/brass (báilá);
brass (tōushí) or containers/bowls;
woolen blankets (qiūyú) or rugs;
heavy furs (jūzhí) or soft garments;
all kinds of grain;
wheat, barley, and beans;
millet (mé), common millet (sù), rice, and hemp;
raw or cooked food containers.
They constantly accept one meal and never eat a second time;
whether going out to beg for food or eating among the Sangha;
they constantly know contentment and do not accept private invitations;
they do not eat meat and do not drink alcohol;
the five pungent roots (wǔxīn) that cause odor are completely avoided.
Therefore, their body has no foul odor,
and they are constantly revered, offered to,
respected, and praised by all devas and worldly people.
They eat only enough to be satisfied and never receive long-term provisions.
The clothes they receive are just enough to cover the body.
When traveling or staying put, they constantly keep the three robes and the begging bowl apparatus,
and never abandon them,
like a bird's two wings.
They do not store seeds (for roots/tubers),
stem seeds,
joint/node seeds,
cutting/grafting seeds,
or fruit seeds.
They do not hoard treasures,
whether gold,
or silver.
Food, drink,
kitchens, or storerooms,
garments, clothing, and ornaments,
high, wide, and large couches,
ivory beds or gold beds,
or variously colored woven materials,
are all things they do not sit upon.
They do not keep any fine or soft mats;
they do not sit on elephant mats or horse mats;
they do not use fine, soft, and excellent garments to spread upon a couch for sleeping.
They do not place two pillows at the two ends of their couch;
nor do they accept or keep excellent red pillows,
but use simple yellow wooden pillows.
They never watch elephant fights,
horse fights,
chariot fights,
soldier fights,
men fighting,
women fighting,
ox fights,
sheep fights,
water buffalo, chicken, pheasant, parrot, and other such fights.
Nor do they intentionally go to observe military formations.
They should not intentionally listen to the sound of blowing conchs,
drums, or horns,
zithers (qín), lutes (sè), zithers (zhēng), or flutes (dí),
harps (kōnghóu), singing, or shouting,
or the sound of musical performance,
except when offering to the Buddha.
They do not watch the games of backgammon (chūpú), Go (wéiqí), or dice games (bōluósài xì),
lion fights or elephant fights,
board games (dánqí), or the six-stick dice game (liùbó),
kicking leather balls (pāijú) or throwing stones,
pitch-pot (tóuhú) or board path games (qiāndào),
Eight-Path game (bādào xíngchéng),
or any kind of games and humor, and they do not observe or participate in them.
They never look at hands, feet, or faces to perform physiognomy.
They do not use claw-marks on mirrors,
spirit mushrooms (zhīcǎo),
willow branches,
begging bowls (bōyú),
or skulls to perform divination or fortune-telling.
Nor do they look up at the void and constellations,
except when trying to overcome sleepiness.
They do not act as royal messengers going back and forth,
using this one’s words to speak to that one,
or using that one’s words to speak to this one.
They never flatter or fawn.
They do not live by means of wrong livelihood (xiémìng).
Nor do they discuss or proclaim matters of kings, ministers, thieves, fighting, or disputes,
food, drink, kingdoms, lands,
famine, fear,
or matters of abundance, joy, peace, and security.
Good man!
This is called the precepts of the Púsà Mòhēsà that cease worldly reproach and suspicion.
Good man!
The Púsà Mòhēsà who upholds such prohibitive precepts,
finds them to be non-different from the precepts of inherent gravity."
"Good men,
after the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has upheld such various prohibitory precepts,
he makes this vow, saying:
'I would rather cast this body into a deep pit of fiercely burning flames
than violate the prohibitory precepts established by the Buddhas
of the future
and the present,
and engage in impure conduct with Kṣatriya women,
Brāhmaṇa women,
or householder women.'
Furthermore, good men!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have hot iron wrapped all around my body
than dare to receive clothing from faithful Dàn’yuè
Furthermore, good men!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather swallow a hot iron ball with this mouth
than dare to consume food and drink from faithful Dàn’yuè
Furthermore, good men!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again makes this vow:
