'I would rather lie on a large hot iron plate with this body
than dare to receive bedding and sleeping mats from faithful Dàn’yuè
Furthermore, good men!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather endure three hundred spears piercing my body
than dare to receive medicine from faithful Dàn’yuè
Furthermore, good men!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather cast this body into a hot iron cauldron
than, through breaking the precepts,
Furthermore, good men!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have this body smashed with an iron hammer,
causing it to become like fine dust from head to foot,
than, through breaking the precepts,
receive respect and prostrations from all Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, and householders.'
Furthermore, good men!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have hot iron gouge out my two eyes
than look upon beautiful forms of others with a defiled mind.'
Furthermore, good men!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather be pierced all over my body with iron awls
than listen to beautiful sounds with a defiled mind.'
Furthermore, good men!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have my nose cut off with a sharp knife
than crave and smell various fragrances with a defiled mind.'
Furthermore, good men!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have my tongue cut and split with a sharp knife
than crave and be attached to delicious tastes with a defiled mind.'
Furthermore, good men!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again makes this vow:
'I would rather have my body chopped and cut with a sharp axe
than crave and be attached to various tactile sensations with a defiled mind.'
Why is this?
Because these causes and conditions
can cause the practitioner to fall into the Hells,
the animal realm,
and the realm of hungry ghosts.
Kāśyapa!
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva protecting and upholding the prohibitory precepts.
Having protected and upheld such various prohibitory precepts, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva
bestows them entirely upon all sentient beings.
Due to these causes and conditions,
he vows that sentient beings will protect and uphold the prohibitory precepts,
attaining the pure precepts,
the good precepts,
the unbroken precepts,
the undivided precepts,
the Mahāyāna precepts,
the non-retrogressing precepts,
the accordant precepts,
the ultimate precepts,
and fully achieving the Pāramitā precepts.
"Good men!
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices such pure precepts,
he immediately attains abiding in the First Immovable Stage (Ācāla-bhūmi).
What is meant by the Immovable Stage?
When the Bodhisattva dwells in this Immovable Stage,
he is neither moved,
nor falls,
nor retrogresses,
nor is scattered.
Good men!
It is like Mount Sūmí:
fierce winds swirling around it cannot cause it to move,
fall down, retrogress, or scatter.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in this stage
is also like this:
he is not moved by form, sound, smell, or taste;
he does not fall into the Hells,
the animal realm,
or the realm of hungry ghosts;
he does not retrogress to the stage of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
and he is not scattered by the evil winds of aberrant views to engage in wrongful livelihood.
Furthermore, good men!
Regarding being moved,
he is not moved by greed, hatred, and delusion;
Regarding falling,
he does not fall into the four heavy offenses;
Regarding retrogressing,
he does not regress from the precepts and return home;
Regarding scattering,
he is not scattered and destroyed by those who oppose the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Furthermore, good men!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also not swayed by the Māras of the afflictions,
nor cast down by the Māra of the aggregates.
Even when seated beneath the Bodhi tree at the place of enlightenment (Bodhimanda),
although there may be the Māra of the Heavens,
it cannot cause him to regress from Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi,
nor is he scattered by the Māra of Death.
Good men!
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivating the Noble Practice (Śānta-carya).
"Good men!
What is meant by the Noble Practice?
The Noble Practice
is so named because it is the practice of the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas.
Hence it is called the Noble Practice.
For what reasons
are the Buddha and Bodhisattvas called Noble Persons (Ārya)?
Such persons possess the noble Dharma,
and constantly contemplate that the nature of all phenomena is emptiness and tranquility.
Because of this meaning,
they are called Noble Persons.
Because they possess the noble precepts,
they are again called Noble Persons.
Because they possess the noble concentration and wisdom,
they are therefore called Noble Persons.
Because they possess the seven noble possessions—
namely, faith,
precepts,
shame (before oneself),
remorse (before others),
extensive learning,
wisdom,
and relinquishment—
they are called Noble Persons.
Because they possess the seven noble awakenings,
they are called Noble Persons.
Because of this meaning,
it is again called the Noble Practice.
“Furthermore, good man!
The holy practice of a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva
observes this body,
from head to foot,
that within it there are only hair and down,
nails and teeth,
foul filth and dirt,
skin, flesh, sinews, and bones,
spleen, kidneys, heart, and lungs,
liver, gallbladder, intestines, and stomach,
the two reservoirs of raw and digested food,
great and small discharges,
snot, spit, eye mucus, and tears,
fat, grease, brain membrane,
bone marrow, pus, and blood,
brain, marrow, and all the blood vessels.
When the Bodhisattva focuses his mind on this observation thus,
who is the ‘self’ here?
To whom does the ‘self’ belong?
Where does it reside?
Who belongs to the ‘self’?
He further makes this thought:
‘Are the bones the “self”?
Is that which is separate from the bones the “self”?’
The Bodhisattva at that time removes the skin and flesh,
observing only the white bones,
and further makes this thought:
‘The colors and forms of the bones differ,
namely blue, yellow,
red, white, and also dove-color.
Such bone forms are also not the “self.”
Why?
The “self” is also not blue, yellow,
red, white, or dove-color.’
When the Bodhisattva fastens his mind upon this observation,
he immediately obtains the severance of all desires for form (rūpa-kāma).
He further makes this thought:
‘These bones arise from causes and conditions,
relying on the foot bones to support the ankle bones,
relying on the ankle bones to support the shank bones,
relying on the shank bones to support the knee bones,
relying on the knee bones to support the thigh bones,
relying on the thigh bones to support the hip bones,
relying on the hip bones to support the waist bones,
relying on the waist bones to support the spine bones,
relying on the spine bones to support the rib bones,
and relying on the spine bones to support the neck bones,
relying on the neck bones to support the jaw bones,
relying on the jaw bones to support the teeth,
and above that, the skull.
Furthermore, relying on the neck bones to support the shoulder bones,
relying on the shoulder bones to support the arm bones,
relying on the arm bones to support the wrist bones,
relying on the wrist bones to support the palm bones,
relying on the palm bones to support the finger bones.’
When the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva observes thus,
all the bones the body possesses
are completely separated.
Having attained this observation, he immediately severs the three desires:
first, the desire for physical appearance (xíngmàoyù),
second, the desire for posture and manner (zītài yù),
and third, the desire for subtle touch (xìchù yù).
“When the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva observes the blue bones,
he sees this great earth—
East, West, South, and North,
the four intermediate directions, and above and below—all having the blue characteristic.
The observations of yellow, white, and dove-color,
like the observation of the blue color,
are also just like this.
When the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva makes this observation,
blue,
yellow,
red,
white,
and dove-colored light immediately issues forth from between his eyebrows.
In each of these lights, this Bodhisattva sees images of the Buddhas.
Having seen them, he immediately asks:
‘This body,
composed and achieved through the union of impure causes and conditions,
how is it able to sit up,
walk, stand,
bend, extend,
bow down, look up,
gaze, blink,
breathe,
weep,
and laugh?
There is no master within this;
who causes it to be so?’
Having made this inquiry,
the Buddhas in the light suddenly disappear.
He further makes this thought:
‘Perhaps consciousness is the “self,”
which is why the Buddhas did not speak for me.’
He then observes this consciousness,
which arises and ceases in sequence,
like flowing water.
It is also not the ‘self.’
He further makes this thought:
‘If consciousness is not the “self,”
perhaps exhalation and inhalation are the “self.”’
He further makes this thought:
‘This exhalation and inhalation
is merely the nature of wind.
And this nature of wind
is the Four Great Elements.
Among the Four Great Elements, which one is the “self”?
The nature of earth is not the “self”;
the natures of water, fire, and wind are also not the “self.”’
He further makes this thought:
‘In this entire body,
there is completely no “self.”
There is only the harmonious union of mind and wind through causes and conditions,
displaying various actions performed,
for example, like the power of a spell,
or that produced by magical illusion,
and also like a kōnghóu (harp),
producing sound according to one’s will.
Therefore, this body is impure in this way,
composed and achieved through the coalescence of many causes and conditions.
Where, then, does this craving (tānyù) arise?
If one is cursed or insulted,
where then does anger (chēnhuì) arise?
This body of mine,
consisting of thirty-six objects, is impure and foul-smelling.
Where can there be a recipient of the cursing or insulting?
If he hears the cursing,
he should immediately reflect:
“With what sound is one cursing me?”
Each sound individually cannot curse;
if one cannot,
then many also cannot.
Based on this principle,
one should not generate anger.
If others come and strike him,
he should also reflect:
“Whence does such striking arise?”
He further makes this thought:
‘Due to the hand, knife, or staff,
and also my body,
the name “striking” is obtained.
Why should I now wrongfully be angry at others?
It is my own body
that has brought this calamity upon itself,
because I accept this body of the Five Skandhas (Wǔyīn shēn).
Just as an arrow hits because there is a target,
my body is also like this:
where there is a body, there is striking.
If I am not patient, my mind becomes scattered.
If the mind is scattered, then right mindfulness is lost.
If right mindfulness is lost, then one cannot observe the meaning of good
and not-good.
If one cannot observe the meaning of good
and not-good, one practices evil dharmas.
Due to the causes and conditions of evil dharmas, one falls into the hells (dìyù),
the animal realm (chùshēng),
or the realm of hungry ghosts (èguǐ).’
When the Bodhisattva makes this observation at that time,
he attains the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Sì Niànchù).
Having attained the Four Foundations of Mindfulness,
he then attains dwelling in the stage of Endurance (kānrěn dì).
Having dwelt in this stage, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva
is then able to endure craving, anger, and delusion,
and is also able to endure cold, heat, hunger, and thirst,
mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, and lice,
violent winds and harsh contacts,
various diseases and epidemics,
abusive words and curses,
flogging, striking, and lashing.
All physical and mental suffering and distress he can endure.
Therefore, this is called dwelling in the Stage of Endurance.
Jiāshè (Kāśyapa) Bodhisattva-mahāsattva said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
When a Bodhisattva has not yet attained dwelling in the Immovable Stage (Bùdòng Dì),
while purely observing the precepts,
is there any condition
under which he may break the precepts?”
“Good man!
There are Bodhisattvas who have not yet attained dwelling in the Immovable Stage,
and due to certain conditions,
they may break the precepts.”
Jiāshè respectfully assented:
“What are they?”
The Buddha said:
"Kāyè!
If there is a Bodhisattva who knows that by reason of breaking precepts,
one can enable people to receive, uphold, and cherish the Mahāyāna Sūtras (Dàchén Jīngdiǎn),
and can enable them to read, recite, and fully understand them,
to copy the sūtra scrolls,
to widely preach them for others,
and not retreat from Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi),
for the sake of this,
it is permitted to break the precepts.
The Bodhisattva at that time should have this thought:
'I would rather fall into Ābǐ Dìyù (Avīci Hell) and suffer punishment
for one kalpa or less than one kalpa,
provided that I certainly enable such a person
not to retreat from Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Kāyè!
By reason of this cause,
a Púsà Móhēsà (Bodhisattva Mahāsattva) is permitted to violate the pure precepts."
At that time, Wénshū Shīlì Púsà Móhēsà (Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Shìzūn (World-Honored One)!
If there is a Bodhisattva
who embraces and protects such a person,
and enables them not to retreat from the heart of Bodhi,
for the sake of this breaking the precepts;
it is impossible
that they should fall into Ābǐ (Avīci)."
At that time, the Buddha praised Wénshū Shīlì:
"Excellent!
Excellent!
It is as you say.
I recall in the past,
in this Yánfú Tí (Jambudvīpa), I was a great king,
named Xiānyù.
I loved, remembered, respected, and highly valued the Mahāyāna Sūtras (Dàchén Jīngdiǎn).
My heart was purely good,
without crudeness, malice, envy, or stinginess.
My mouth constantly spoke loving words
and wholesome words.
My body constantly embraced and protected the poor
and the solitary.
My generosity (Bùshī) and vigorous effort (Jīngjìn) never ceased.
At that time, there were no Buddhas,
Śrāvakas (Shēngwén),
or Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué) in the world.
At that time, I loved and delighted in the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtras (Dàchén Fāngděng Jīngdiǎn).
For twelve years, I served the Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén),
supplying their needs.
After the twelve years, having completed the offering and sustenance,
I then said:
'You masters should now arouse the heart of Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.'
The Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén) said:
'Great King!
The nature of Bodhi is non-existent.
The Mahāyāna Sūtras (Dàchén Jīngdiǎn) are also like this.
Great King!
Why do you make beings and things equivalent to emptiness?'
Good man!
I, at that time, esteemed the Mahāyāna in my heart.
When I heard the Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén) slander the Vaipulya (Fāngděng),
having heard this, I immediately cut off their life force.
Good man!
By reason of this cause,
from that time onward, I have not fallen into the Hells (Dìyù).
Good man!
Embracing, protecting, and upholding the Mahāyāna Sūtras (Dàchén Jīngdiǎn)
has such immeasurable power.
"Furthermore, Kāyè!
There is also the noble practice,
which is the Four Noble Truths (Sì Shèngdì).
Suffering (Kǔ),
Arising (Jí),
Cessation (Miè),
and the Path (Dào),
these are called the Four Noble Truths (Sì Shèngdì).
Kāyè!
Suffering (Kǔ) is the characteristic of oppression.
Arising (Jí) is the characteristic of being able to engender and grow.
Cessation (Miè) is the characteristic of tranquil extinction.
The Path (Dào) is the characteristic of the Mahāyāna (Dàchén).
Furthermore, good man!
Suffering (Kǔ) is the characteristic of manifestation.
Arising (Jí) is the characteristic of transition.
Cessation (Miè) is the characteristic of removal.
The Path (Dào) is the characteristic of being able to remove.
Furthermore, good man!
Suffering (Kǔ) has three characteristics:
the characteristic of suffering upon suffering (kǔ kǔ xiàng),
the characteristic of suffering due to conditioned existence (xíng kǔ xiàng),
and the characteristic of suffering due to decay (huài kǔ xiàng).
Arising (Jí) is the twenty-five realms of existence (èrshíwǔ yǒu).
Cessation (Miè) is the extinction of the twenty-five realms of existence (èrshíwǔ yǒu).
The Path (Dào) is the cultivation of precepts (Jiè), concentration (Dìng), and wisdom (Huì).
Furthermore, good man!
The conditioned phenomena (yǒulòu fǎ) are of two kinds:
having cause,
and having effect.
The unconditioned phenomena (wúlòu fǎ) are also of two kinds:
having cause,
and having effect.
The conditioned effect (yǒulòu guǒ) is called Suffering (Kǔ).
The conditioned cause (yǒulòu yīn) is called Arising (Jí).
The unconditioned effect (wúlòu guǒ) is called Cessation (Miè).
The unconditioned cause (wúlòu yīn) is called the Path (Dào).
"Furthermore, good man!
Eight characteristics are called Suffering (Kǔ):
namely, the suffering of birth (shēng kǔ),
the suffering of old age (lǎo kǔ),
the suffering of sickness (bìng kǔ),
the suffering of death (sǐ kǔ),
the suffering of separation from the beloved (ài biélí kǔ),
the suffering of meeting with the hated (yuànzēng huì kǔ),
the suffering of not obtaining what is sought (qiú bùdé kǔ),
and the suffering of the five aggregates (wǔ shèng yīn kǔ).
That which can give rise to these eight phenomena of suffering
is called the Cause (Yīn).
The place where these eight phenomena do not exist
is called Cessation (Miè).
The Ten Powers (Shílì),
the Four Fearlessnesses (Sì Wúsuǒwèi),
the Three Stations of Mindfulness (Sān Niànchù),
and Great Compassion (Dàbēi),
these are called the Path (Dào)."
"O virtuous man,
'birth' is the manifestation of emergence,
which is categorized into five types:
first, initial emergence;
second, reaching the end;
third, growth;
fourth, emerging from the womb (out of the fetus);
fifth, species-based birth.
What is ‘aging’ (lǎo)?
Aging has two types:
first, aging moment by moment (niàn niàn lǎo);
second, aging over the entire lifespan (zhōng shēn lǎo).
Furthermore, there are two types:
first, growth-aging (zēng zhǎng lǎo);
second, decay-aging (miè huài lǎo).
This is what is called aging.
What is ‘sickness’ (bìng)?
Sickness means the four great poisonous snakes [the elements],
being mutually unbalanced and discordant.
There are also two types:
first, physical sickness (shēn bìng);
second, mental sickness (xīn bìng).
Physical sickness has five types:
first, caused by water;
second, caused by wind;
third, caused by heat;
fourth, combined sicknesses (zá bìng);
fifth, external sicknesses (kè bìng).
External sicknesses have four types:
first, excessively strenuous activity;
second, falling due to carelessness or error;
third, injury from knives, staffs, tiles, or stones;
fourth, possession by ghosts or demons (guǐ mèi suǒ zhù).
Mental sickness also has four types:
first, agitation (yǒng yuè);
second, terror (kǒng bù);
third, sorrow (yōu chóu);
fourth, ignorance (yú chī).
Furthermore, O virtuous man,
sicknesses of the body and mind generally fall into three types.
What are these three?
First, karmic retribution (yè bào);
second, inability to stay far away from evil enemies (è duì);
third, the transition of seasons and time (shí jié dài xiè).
Birth gives rise to such causes, conditions, and names [of ailments],
and manifests as differentiated sicknesses based on experience (shòu).
Causes and conditions (yīn yuán zhě) refer to
sicknesses like those caused by wind, etc.
Names (míng zì zhě) refer to
chest tightness and lung distension (xīn mèn fèi zhàng),
shortness of breath and coughing (shàng qì ké nì),
heart palpitations and diarrhea (xīn jīng xià lì).
Differentiated sicknesses based on experience (shòu fēn bié zhě) refer to
pain in the head or pain in the eyes,
pain in the hands or feet, and similar pains.
This is what is called sickness.
What is ‘death’ (sǐ)?
Death means abandoning the body that was received.
Abandoning the received body also has two types:
first, death when life span is exhausted (mìng jìn sǐ);
second, death by external cause (wài yuán sǐ).
Death when life span is exhausted also has three types:
first, life span is exhausted but merit is not exhausted;
second, merit is exhausted but life span is not exhausted;
third, both merit and life span are exhausted.
Death by external cause also has three types:
first, death by self-harm due to inappropriate action;
second, death violently caused by others;
third, simultaneous death [of life span and external cause].
There are also three other types of death:
first, death by negligence (fàng yì sǐ);
second, death by breaking precepts (pò jiè sǐ);
third, death by destroying the root of life (huài mìng gēn sǐ).
What is meant by death by negligence?
If someone slanders the Great Vehicle Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
this is called death by negligence.
What is meant by death by breaking precepts?
Violating the prohibitions and precepts established by
past,
future, and present Buddhas,
this is called death by breaking precepts.
What is meant by death by destroying the root of life?
Abandoning the body of the Five Aggregates (wǔ yīn shēn),
this is called death by destroying the root of life.
Thus, death is called great suffering.
"What is meant by the suffering of separation from the beloved (ài bié lí kǔ)?
It is the destruction and scattering separation of beloved objects.
The destruction and scattering separation of beloved objects
also has two types:
first, the destruction of the Five Aggregates among humans;
second, the destruction of the Five Aggregates among the deities.
Such beloved Five Aggregates of humans and deities,
when differentiated and analyzed, are of immeasurable kinds.
This is what is called the suffering of separation from the beloved.
What is meant by the suffering of encountering the hated (yuàn zēng huì kǔ)?
It is the gathering together of those whom one dislikes.
The gathering together of those whom one dislikes
also has three types:
namely, those in the Hells (dì yù),
the hungry ghosts (è guǐ),
and the animals (chù shēng).
Such beings in the three realms, when differentiated and analyzed, are of immeasurable kinds.
This is what is called the suffering of encountering the hated.
What is meant by the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks (qiú bù dé kǔ)?
The suffering of not obtaining what one seeks also has two types:
first, seeking something one hopes for but failing to obtain it;
second, expending much effort and energy but failing to receive the result (guǒ bào).
This is what is called the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
What is meant by the suffering of the flourishing Five Aggregates (wǔ shèng yīn kǔ)?
The suffering of the flourishing Five Aggregates encompasses
the suffering of birth (shēng kǔ),
the suffering of aging (lǎo kǔ),
the suffering of sickness (bìng kǔ),
the suffering of death (sǐ kǔ),
the suffering of separation from the beloved (ài bié lí kǔ),
the suffering of encountering the hated and greedy (yuàn zēng tān kǔ),
and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks (qiú bù dé kǔ).
Therefore, this is called the suffering of the flourishing Five Aggregates."
"Kāshè!
The root of existence,
contains these seven types of suffering,
from the suffering of old age up to the suffering of the five flourishing aggregates (wǔ shèng yīn kǔ).
Kāshè!
Indeed, decline and aging do not affect everything.
Buddhas and the various devas (tiān) certainly and uniformly lack them.
Among humans, it is uncertain; sometimes present, sometimes absent.
Kāshè!
When taking a body in the Three Realms (sān jiè),
none are without birth,
but aging is not necessarily fixed.
Therefore, existence (birth) is the fundamental root of everything.
Kāshè!
Sentient beings (zhòngshēng) in the world have confused and covered minds;
they crave the phenomenon of birth,
yet loathe and fear old age and death.
Kāshè!
A Púsà (Bodhisattva) is not like this;
observing their initial birth,
they immediately perceive its fault.
Kāshè!
It is like a woman entering another's house.
This woman is proper and upright,
her face and appearance are beautiful and magnificent,
and she adorns her body with fine necklaces (yīngluò).
The master of the house sees her and immediately asks,
'What is your name?
To whom are you related?'
The woman replies,
'I am the Great Goddess of Merit (Gōngdé Dà Tiān).'
The master asks,
'What do you do in the places you visit?'
The woman replies,
'Where I go,
I am able to give various types of gold, silver, lapis lazuli (liúlí),
crystal (pōlí), genuine pearls (zhēnzhū),
coral (shānhú), amber (hǔpò),
giant clam (chēqú), agate (mǎnão),
elephants, horses, and carriages,
as well as maidservants and servants.'
When the master hears this,
his heart is filled with joy,
leaping up without measure:
'My merit (fúdé) today
has caused you to come to my residence.'
He immediately burned incense and scattered flowers,
offering devotion, reverence, and prostration.
Again, outside the gate, he saw another woman.
Her figure was ugly,
her clothes were tattered and ruined,
she had much filth and grease,
her skin was chapped and cracked,
and her color was pale white (àibái).
Seeing her, he asked,
'What is your name?
To whose family are you related?'
The woman replied,
'My name is Darkness (Hēi'àn).'
He asked again,
'Why are you named Darkness?'
The woman replied,
'Where I travel,
I cause all the wealth and treasures of that household to decline and diminish completely.'
When the master heard this,
he immediately took a sharp knife
and said this:
'If you do not leave,
I will cut off your life.'
The woman replied,
'You are extremely foolish
and lack wisdom.'
The master asked,
'Why do you call me foolish and lacking wisdom?'
The woman replied,
'The one inside your house
is my elder sister.
I am always with my sister;
we move and rest together.
If you drive me away,
you must also drive her away.'
The master returned inside and asked the Goddess of Merit (Gōngdé Tiān):
'There is a woman outside
who says she is your younger sister.
Is this truly so?'
The Goddess of Merit (Gōngdé Tiān) said,
'She truly is my sister.
I and this sister
walk and dwell together,
never having separated from each other.
Wherever we reside,
I constantly create good things,
and she constantly creates bad things.
I constantly bring benefit,
and she constantly causes ruin.
If you love me,
you should also love her.
If you revere me,
you should also revere her.'
The master then said,
'If there are such good and bad affairs,
I desire neither of you.
Both of you may go as you wish.'
At that time, the two women
together accompanied each other back to where they lived.
At that time, the master saw them leaving and
his heart was filled with measureless joy and delight.
At that time, the two women traveled together again and came to a poor family.
The poor person saw them
and his heart was filled with joy.
He immediately invited them, saying:
'From now on,
I wish that you two
will always reside in my house.'
The Goddess of Merit (Gōngdé Tiān) said,
'We were previously driven away by someone else,
so for what reason do you invite us both to stay?'
The poor person replied,
'Since you now remember me,
because of you,
I must also revere her.
Therefore, I invite both of you to stay in my house.'
Kāshè!
A Púsà Mòhēsà (Bodhisattva Mahāsattva) is likewise:
they do not wish for birth in heaven (tiān),
because when there is birth, there must follow old age, sickness, and death.
Therefore, they reject both,
never having a mind of attachment.
Ordinary, foolish people (fánfū) do not know the faults of old age, sickness, and death;
therefore, they greedily accept the two principles of birth and death (shēngsǐ).
"Furthermore, Kāshè!
It is like a young Bōluómén (Brahmin) boy
who is tormented by hunger.
Seeing a mango (ānmó guǒ) in human excrement, he immediately takes it.
A wise person sees this
and rebukes him, saying:
'You Bōluómén,
of pure lineage,
why do you take this filthy fruit from the excrement?'
The boy hears this,
feels shame and embarrassment,
and immediately replies,
'I truly will not eat it;
I intend to wash it clean
and then discard it.'
The wise person says:
'You are utterly foolish and ignorant.
If you are going to discard it later,
you should not have taken it in the first place.'
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
A Púsà Mòhēsà is likewise:
regarding this portion of existence,
they neither accept nor reject it,
just as that wise man rebuked the boy.
Ordinary people rejoice in birth and detest death,
like that boy who took the fruit and then discarded it.
"Furthermore, Kāshè!
For example, at the head of a crossroads (sìqú dàotóu),
someone has vessels filled with food,
complete in color, aroma, and taste,
and intends to sell it.
A person comes from afar, hungry, weak, and exhausted.
Seeing the meal, complete in color, aroma, and taste,
he points to it and says:
'What is this thing?'
The food vendor replies:
'This is superior food,
complete in color, aroma, and taste.
If you eat this food,
you gain beauty and strength,
you can eliminate hunger and thirst,
and you can see the devas (tiān);
but there is only one fault (huàn),
namely, the end of life (mìngzhōng).'
When that person hears this,
he immediately thinks:
'I do not need beauty, strength, or seeing the devas (tiān),
nor do I need to die.'
He immediately says:
'If eating this food
results in the end of life,
why are you selling it here now?'
The food vendor replies:
'A wise person
will ultimately not buy it.
Only foolish people who do not know this fact
give me a high price
and eat it greedily.'
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
A Púsà Mòhēsà is likewise:
they do not wish for birth in heaven (tiān),
gaining beauty, gaining strength, or seeing the devas (tiān).
Why is this?
Because they cannot avoid all suffering and affliction.
Ordinary, foolish people (fánfū)
cherish and crave
whatever place of birth they find,
because they do not perceive the suffering of old age, sickness, and death.
"Furthermore, good man!
For example, like a poisonous tree,
the root can kill,
the stem can kill,
the bark, flowers, and fruits can all kill.
Good man!
The places where life is received in the twenty-five realms of existence (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu),
the Five Aggregates (Wǔ Yīn) that are received,
are also like this;
they can all kill.
Furthermore, Jiāshè!
For example, like filth and excrement,
whether abundant or meager, they both stink.
Good man!
Birth is also like this;
whether the lifespan is eighty thousand [years],
or as short as ten years,
all equally suffer pain.
Furthermore, Jiāshè!
For example, like a treacherous cliff,
covered above with grass,
on the edge of that cliff,
there is much sweet dew (gānlù).
If one eats it,
one lives for a thousand heavenly years,
eternally eradicating all illnesses,
peaceful, tranquil, and joyful.
Ordinary, ignorant people,
coveting its flavor,
unaware that beneath it lies a great, deep pit (shēnkēng),
immediately go forward intending to take it,
stumble unknowingly,
fall into the pit, and die.
The wise person, having known this,
abandons it and departs far away.
Good man!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) is also like this;
they still do not wish to partake of the sublime food of heaven,
much less that of the human realm?
How can an ordinary person, who in hell swallows iron balls,
much less [in the realms of] humans and gods,
not eat superior, exquisite food?
Jiāshè!
Based on such analogies,
and countless other boundless parables,
one should know that birth,
is truly great suffering.
Jiāshè!
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abiding in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dàchéng Dà Nièpán Jīng),
contemplating the suffering of birth.
"Jiāshè,
how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
in this Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, contemplate the suffering of old age?
Old age causes coughing, wheezing, and shortness of breath;
it destroys courage and strength,
memory and perseverance,
the joys of vigorous youth,
arrogance and haughtiness,
and peaceful freedom;
it causes hunchback,
laxity and laziness,
and being scorned by others.
Jiāshè!
For example, like a pond,
filled with lotus flowers,
opening, fresh, and glorious,
extremely lovely and desirable;
when it encounters hailstones falling from the sky,
they are all destroyed.
Good man!
Old age is also like this;
it is entirely able to destroy vigorous, strong, and beautiful appearance.
Furthermore, Jiāshè!
For example, like a king,
who has a wise minister skilled in the art of war.
When a rival king resists and is disobedient,
the king sends this minister to subdue and punish him,
and immediately captures him and brings him before the king.
Old age is also like this;
it captures vigor and beauty,
and delivers it to the King of Death (Sǐ Wáng).
Furthermore, Jiāshè!
For example, like a broken axle,
which is no longer of any use,
old age is also like this—of no further use.
Furthermore, Jiāshè!
Like a family of great wealth,
having many treasures and valuables:
gold, silver, lapis lazuli (liúlí),
coral, amber (hǔpò),
mother-of-pearl (chēqú), and agate (mǎnǎo).
If hostile thieves,
were to enter their house,
they immediately rob and plunder,
making everything completely empty.
Good man!
Vigorous youth and beautiful appearance are also like this;
they are constantly plundered and robbed by the thief of old age.
Furthermore, Jiāshè!
For example, like a poor person who covets superior food
and fine, soft clothing;
although he hopes for them, he cannot obtain them.
Good man!
Old age is also like this;
although one has a heart of craving,
desiring to receive wealth and happiness,
indulging in the five desires (Wǔ Yù),
one cannot obtain them.
Furthermore, Jiāshè!
Like a land tortoise,
whose heart constantly yearns for water.
Good man!
Humans are also like this;
since they have been dried out by decay and old age,
their hearts constantly recall the pleasures of the five desires experienced in their youth.
Furthermore, Jiāshè!
Just like the lotus flowers of the autumn month,
all of which are a joy for everyone to behold;
but when they wither and yellow,
they are hated and despised by people.
Good man!
Vigorous youth and strong appearance,
are also like this;
they are loved and cherished by everyone,
but when old age arrives,
they are hated and despised by the multitude.
Furthermore, Jiāshè!
For example, like sugarcane;
once it has been pressed,
the dregs no longer have any taste.
Good man!
Strong youth and vigorous appearance are also like this;
once crushed by old age,
they lose the three kinds of flavor (wèi):
the first, the flavor of renunciation (chūjiā);
the second, the flavor of recitation (dúsòng);
the third, the flavor of meditation (zuòchán).
Furthermore, Jiāshè!
For example, like a full moon;
at night it has abundant brightness,
but during the day it is not so.
Good man!
Humans are also like this;
when vigorous, they are dignified and severe,
their appearance is rare and extraordinary,
but when old, they are decayed and emaciated,
their body and spirit dried up and haggard.
“Furthermore, Káshèpù!
For instance, there was a king
who always governed his kingdom with the correct Dhárma,
being truthful and without distortion,
compassionate and fond of giving.
At that time, he was destroyed by an enemy kingdom,
scattered and fleeing,
eventually arriving in another land.
When the people of that land saw him,
a heart of pity and compassion arose in them,
and they all spoke, saying:
‘Great King!
In the past, you governed the country with the correct Dhárma;
you did not wrong the myriad common people.
How is it that suddenly you are fleeing here?’
Good man!
People are also like this:
once they have been ruined and defeated by decline and aging,
they constantly praise the deeds they accomplished during their strong youth.
Furthermore, Káshèpù!
For instance, a lamp wick
relies solely on oil;
when the oil is exhausted,
its condition cannot last long.
Good man!
People are also like this:
they rely solely on the oil of strength (youth).
When the oil of strength is exhausted,
how can the wick of decline and aging last long?
Furthermore, Káshèpù!
For instance, a dried-up river
cannot benefit humans, non-humans,
flying birds, or walking beasts.
Good man!
People are also like this:
withered by old age,
they cannot benefit all deeds (work).
Furthermore, Káshèpù!
For instance, a tree on the precipitous bank of a river,
if it encounters a fierce wind, is bound to fall and collapse.
Good man!
People are also like this:
standing on the perilous bank of old age,
when the wind of death arrives,
they cannot maintain their existence.
Furthermore, Káshèpù!
Just as an axle of a cart breaks,
it is no longer fit to bear a heavy load.
Good man!
Old age is also like this:
one cannot consult and receive all wholesome Dhármas.
Furthermore, Káshèpù!
For instance, an infant is looked down upon by people.
Good man!
Old age is also like this:
it is always disparaged and scorned by all.
Káshèpù!
Based on these comparisons,
and countless, boundless other analogies,
you should know that this aging
is truly a great suffering.
Káshèpù!
This is called the Bodhisáttva Máhāsàttva practicing the Mahāyāna Mahāpànípán Jīng,
contemplating the suffering of aging.
“Káshèpù!
How does the Bodhisáttva Máhāsàttva practice the Mahāyāna Mahāpànípán Jīng
by contemplating the suffering of sickness?
Sickness, as it is called,
can destroy all peaceful and joyful matters,
just like hail and rain damage grain seedlings.
Furthermore, Káshèpù!
If a person has an enemy,
their mind is constantly worried
and filled with terror.
Good man!
All sentient beings are also like this:
constantly fearing the suffering of sickness,
their minds are filled with sorrow and worry.
Furthermore, Káshèpù!
For instance, there was a man
of upright and handsome appearance,
desired by the king’s consort due to lustful intention.
She sent a messenger to compel him to come
and engage in intercourse.
When the king caught him,
he immediately ordered someone
to gouge out one of his eyes,
cut off one of his ears,
and sever one of his hands and feet.
At that time, this man’s appearance was utterly changed
and detested by people.
Good man!
People are also like this:
even though their bodies, ears, and eyes may be complete,
once they are entangled and afflicted by the suffering of sickness,
they are detested and despised by the multitude.
Furthermore, Káshèpù!
Just like the plantain tree,
bamboo, reeds, or a mule,
they die when they bear offspring.
Good man!
People are also like this:
they die when they have sickness.
Furthermore, Káshèpù!
Just like a Cakravarti-rája,
whose army general always leads the way,
while the king follows afterward.
Also, like the king of fish,
the king of ants,
the king of locusts (or wasps),
the king of cattle,
or the chief of merchants,
when they lead the way,
all these multitudes
follow them,
none abandoning them.
Good man!
The Cakravarti-rája of death is also like this:
constantly following the minister of sickness and never abandoning him.
The kings of fish,
ants,
locusts,
cattle,
and the chief of merchants,
the king of sickness, are also like this:
they are constantly followed by the multitude of death.
Káshèpù!
The causes and conditions of sickness
are what are called anguish,
sorrow, worry, sadness, and sighing,
and physical and mental disquiet.
Or it is being oppressed and harmed by enemies and thieves,
smashing the floating raft (of life),
pulling away the bridge,
and being able to rob and seize the root of correct mindfulness.
Furthermore, it can ruin flourishing health and beauty,
strength, power, and peace,
removing shame and conscience,
and causing the body and mind to burn intensely.
Based on these comparisons,
and countless, boundless other analogies,
you should know that the suffering of sickness is a great suffering.
Káshèpù!
This is called the Bodhisáttva Máhāsàttva practicing the Mahāyāna Mahāpànípán Jīng,
contemplating the suffering of sickness.
“Káshèpù!
How does the Bodhisáttva Máhāsàttva practice the Mahāyāna Mahāpànípán Jīng
by contemplating the suffering of death?
Death, as it is called,
is that which can burn and extinguish.
Káshèpù!
Just as a fire disaster arises,
it can burn everything,
except for the Second Jhāna,
because its power cannot reach it.
Good man!
The fire of death is also like this: it can burn everything,
except for the Bodhisáttva who abides in the Mahāyāna Mahāpànípán,
because its force cannot reach him.
Furthermore, Káshèpù!
Just as a water disaster arises,
everything is submerged,
except for the Third Jhāna,
because its power cannot reach it.
Good man!
The water of death is also like this:
it submerges everything,
except for the Bodhisáttva who abides in the Mahāyāna Mahāpànípán.
Furthermore, Káshèpù!
Just as a wind disaster arises,
it can blow everything away and cause it all to scatter and perish,
except for the Fourth Jhāna,
because its power cannot reach it.
Good man!
The wind of death is also like this:
it can blow away and extinguish all that exists,
except for the Bodhisáttva who abides in the Mahāyāna Mahāpànípán.”
Káshèpù Bodhisáttva said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
That Fourth Jhāna,
for what reason
can the wind not blow it,
the water not submerge it,
and the fire not burn it?
The Buddha addressed Kāshè:
“Good man!
That Fourth Dhyāna,
is entirely without the inner and outer drawbacks.
Good man!
The drawbacks of the First Dhyāna
are the inner arousal of thoughts and examination,
and the outer fire catastrophe.
The drawbacks of the Second Dhyāna
are the inner feeling of joy,
and the outer water catastrophe.
The drawbacks of the Third Dhyāna
are the inner presence of breathing,
and the outer wind catastrophe.
Good man!
That Fourth Dhyāna
is entirely without any inner or outer drawbacks,
therefore, all calamities cannot reach it.
Good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this;
dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa,
all inner and outer drawbacks are exhausted,
therefore, the King of Death cannot reach him.
“Furthermore, good man!
Just as the golden-winged bird (Garuda) can consume and digest all dragons, fish,
and treasures like gold and silver,
except for diamond (Vajra), which it cannot dissolve.
Good man!
Death, the golden-winged bird, is also like this;
it can consume and dissolve all sentient beings,
except it cannot dissolve the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who dwells in the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Kāshè!
Suppose all the grass and trees along a river bank,
when a great flood surges,
are all swept away and flow into the great ocean,
except for the willow tree, because of its softness.
Good man!
All sentient beings are also like this;
they are all swept away and flow into the Sea of Death,
except for the Bodhisattva who dwells in the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Kāshè!
Just as Nàluóyán
can subdue and crush all strongmen,
except for the great wind.
Why is this?
Because it has no obstruction.
Good man!
Death, the Nàluóyán, is also like this;
it can subdue and crush all sentient beings,
except for the Bodhisattva who dwells in the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa.
Why is this?
Because he has no obstruction.
Furthermore, Kāshè!
Suppose there is a person who, among his enemies,
falsely presents himself as a close friend,
constantly pursues them,
like a shadow following a form,
searching for an opportunity
to kill them;
but that enemy is careful,
firmly prepared,
and thus prevents that person from successfully killing them.
Good man!
Death, the enemy, is also like this;
it constantly watches sentient beings, wanting to kill them,
but it cannot kill the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who dwells in the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa.
Why is this?
Because this Bodhisattva is not negligent.
Furthermore, Kāshè!
Just as a sudden downpour of diamond (Vajra) rain
destroys medicinal herbs,
all trees, mountains, and forests,
earth, sand, tiles, and stones,
and all objects made of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli,
but cannot destroy the true diamond treasure.
Good man!
Death, the diamond rain, is also like this;
it can destroy all sentient beings,
except for the Diamond Bodhisattva who dwells in the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Kāshè!
Just as the golden-winged bird can consume all dragons,
except those who have taken refuge in the Three Jewels.
Good man!
Death, the golden-winged bird, is also like this;
it can consume all immeasurable sentient beings,
except for the Bodhisattva who dwells in the Three Concentrations.
What are the Three Concentrations?
Emptiness (Kōng),
Signlessness (Wúxiāng),
and Wishlessness (Wúyuàn).
Furthermore, Kāshè!
Just as the Mólúo venomous snake,
whomsoever it bites and stings,
even if there are excellent incantations
and superb, fine medicines,
nothing can be done about it;
only the Ājiéduō star incantation
can make it disappear and heal.
Good man!
Whoever is stung by the poison of Death
is also like this;
all medical formulas are helpless against it,
except for the incantation of the Bodhisattva who dwells in the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Kāshè!
Suppose there is a person who has incurred the king's wrath;
if that person is able to use gentle and kind words
and present treasures,
they may be able to escape.
Good man!
The King of Death is not like this;
even if one offers him
gentle words,
money, wealth, and treasures,
one still cannot escape.
Good man!
Death is a perilous place where there are no provisions;
the destination is remote,
and there is no companion.
It is a constant journey, day and night, whose boundary is unknown.
It is deep, dark, and without light.
One enters without a door but finds a place.
Though there is no painful spot, it cannot be cured.
Going forth cannot be prevented, but arriving there, one cannot escape.
It breaks nothing, yet those who see it are filled with sorrow and bitterness.
It is not an evil sight, yet it causes people fear.
It is spread out around the body but cannot be perceived.
Kāshè!
By these metaphors,
and other immeasurable and boundless analogies,
you should know that Death
is truly a great suffering.
Kāshè!
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivating the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa Sūtra
by contemplating the suffering of Death.
“Kāshè,
how does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwell in the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa Sūtra
and contemplate the suffering of separation from the beloved?
The suffering of separation from the beloved
is able to be the root of all sufferings,
as the verse says:
distress and suffering arise (zé shēng yōukǔ).
Because of distress and suffering (yǐ yōukǔ gù),
living beings are caused
to undergo decline and aging (shēng yú shuāilǎo),
and the suffering of separation from the beloved (ài biélí kǔ),
which is called the termination of life (suǒwèi mìng zhōng).
Virtuous man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Because of separation (yǐ biélí gù),
various subtle sufferings are produced (néng shēng zhǒngzhǒng wēixì zhū kǔ).
I will now differentiate and illustrate them for you (jīn dāng wèi rǔ fēnbié xiǎnshì).
Virtuous man (Shànnánzǐ)!
In ages past, the lifespan of humans was immeasurable (rénshòu wúliàng).
At that time there was a king,
named Shànzhù (Míng wéi Shànzhù).
That king, at that time, was a young boy (tóngzǐ shēn).
He governed affairs as the crown prince (tàizǐ zhì shì),
and ascended the throne,
each period lasting eighty-four thousand years.
At that time, a fleshy tumor (ròu pào) grew on the king's head.
This tumor was soft,
like fine cotton (dōu luó mián),
or soft, thin kapok (jiébèi).
It gradually grew
but was not considered a source of trouble.
After exactly ten months,
the tumor split open,
and a boy was born.
His appearance was correct and upright,
wondrous and rarely matched.
His complexion and form were clear and brilliant,
the foremost among men.
The father king rejoiced,
and named him Dǐngshēng.
At that time, King Shànzhù,
consequently entrusted the affairs of the kingdom to Dǐngshēng.
He abandoned the palace,
his wife and children (qīzǐ),
and his retinue (juànshǔ),
entered the mountains to study the Way (xué dào),
for a full eighty-four thousand years.
At that time, Dǐngshēng, on the fifteenth day,
dwelling in a high tower,
having bathed and received the precepts (shòu zhāi),
immediately there appeared from the east the precious Golden Wheel (Jīnlúnbǎo).
That wheel had a thousand spokes,
with the hub and rim fully complete.
It was not made by craftsmen,
but formed naturally,
and came to correspond with him.
King Dǐngshēng immediately had this thought:
'I once heard the Five-Abilities Sages (Wǔtōng Xiān) say
that if a Kṣatriya king (Chàlì Wáng), on the fifteenth day,
dwells in a high tower, having bathed and received the precepts,
and if there appears a Golden Wheel,
which lacks none of its thousand spokes, and has its hub and rim fully complete,
which was not made by craftsmen but formed naturally,
and which comes to correspond with him,
know that this king is immediately destined to become a Cakravartin Holy Emperor (Zhuǎnlún Shèngdì).'
He further had this thought:
'I must now test this.'
He immediately raised this precious wheel with his left hand,
held an incense burner in his right,
knelt his right knee to the ground and made this vow:
'If this precious Golden Wheel is truly real and not false,
it should travel the path taken by previous Cakravartin Holy Kings (Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng).'
Having made this vow,
this precious Golden Wheel flew up into the void, encompassed the ten directions,
and returned to rest in Dǐngshēng's left hand.
At that time, Dǐngshēng's heart was filled with joy,
leaping with boundless delight.
He further said:
'I am now definitely destined to be a Cakravartin King (Zhuǎnlún Wáng).'
Not long after this, there appeared the precious Elephant (Xiàngbǎo),
whose form and appearance were dignified and solemn,
like a white lotus flower,
supporting itself on seven limbs.
Having seen this, Dǐngshēng again had this thought:
'I once heard the Five-Abilities Sages say
that if a Cakravartin King, on the fifteenth day,
dwells in a high tower, having bathed and received the precepts,
and if there appears a precious Elephant,
whose form and appearance are dignified and solemn,
like a white lotus flower,
supporting itself on seven limbs,
and which comes to correspond with him,
know that this king is immediately a Holy King (Shèngwáng).'
He further had this thought:
'I must now test this.'
He immediately raised the incense burner,
knelt his right knee to the ground and made this vow:
'If this precious White Elephant (Bái Xiàngbǎo)
is truly real and not false,
it should travel the path taken by previous Cakravartin Holy Kings.'
Having made this vow,
this precious White Elephant,
from dawn till dusk, traversed the eight directions, reaching the edge of the great ocean,
and returned to rest in its original place.
At that time, Dǐngshēng's heart was greatly joyful,
leaping with boundless delight.
He further said:
'I am now definitively a Cakravartin Holy King.'
Not long after this, next came the precious Horse (Mǎbǎo),
whose color was dark blue and glowing (gàn yàn),
with a mane and tail of golden color.
Having seen this, Dǐngshēng again had this thought:
'I once heard the Five-Abilities Sages say
that if a Cakravartin King, on the fifteenth day,
dwells in a high tower, having bathed and received the precepts,
and if there appears a precious Horse,
whose color is dark blue and dazzling (gàn yàn),
with a mane and tail of golden color,
and which comes to correspond with him,
know that this king is immediately a Holy King.'
He further had this thought:
'I must now test this.'
He immediately held the incense burner, knelt his right knee to the ground and made this vow:
'If this precious Dark Blue Horse (Gànmǎbǎo)
is truly real and not false,
it should travel the path taken by previous Cakravartin Holy Kings.'
Having made this vow,
this precious Dark Blue Horse,
from dawn till dusk, traversed the eight directions, reaching the edge of the great ocean,
and returned to rest in its original place.
At that time, Dǐngshēng's heart was greatly joyful,
leaping with boundless delight.
He further said:
'I am now definitively a Cakravartin Holy King.'
Not long after this,
there appeared the precious Woman (Nǚbǎo),
whose appearance was correct and upright,
subtle and foremost.
She was neither tall nor short, neither white nor black.
Sandalwood fragrance (zhāntán xiāng) issued from all the pores of her body,
and her breath was fragrant and pure like a blue lotus flower.
Her eyes could see one Yojana (yóu xún) away;
and her ability to hear and smell was likewise.
Her tongue was broad and large,
and when extended could cover her face.
Its color was delicate and thin,
like a copper leaf.
Her mind was intelligent and sagacious,
possessing great wisdom.
Towards all living beings, she always spoke gentle words (ruǎnyǔ).
When this woman touched the king's clothes with her hand,
she instantly knew whether the king's body was at ease or suffering illness,
and also knew the object of the king's mind.
At that time, Dǐngshēng again had this thought:
'If there is a woman who can know the king's mind,
she is the precious Woman.'
Not long after this,
within the royal palace,
there naturally appeared a precious Mani Pearl (Bǎo Móní Zhū),
of pure blue lapis lazuli (liúlí),
as large as a human thigh (rén bàng).
It was able to illuminate one Yojana in the darkness.
If the sky sent down rain, with drops as thick as cart axles,
the power of this pearl could create a cover,
fully covering an area of one Yojana,
blocking this heavy rain,
and preventing it from falling through.
At that time, Dǐngshēng again had this thought:
'If a Cakravartin King obtains this precious pearl,
he is certainly a Holy King.'
Not long after this, the Minister of the Treasury (Zhǔzàng Chén) naturally appeared.
He possessed abundant treasures,
with immeasurable great wealth.
His storehouses were full to overflowing,
lacking nothing.
Through his karmic retribution, he had obtained the eye faculty (yǎngēn)
whose power enabled him to see completely all hidden treasures within the earth.
Whatever the King desired,
he was able to provide it.
At that time, Dǐngshēng wanted to test him.
He immediately sailed with him on a boat into the great ocean,
and addressed the Minister of the Treasury (Zàng Chén) saying:
'I now wish to obtain rare and exotic treasures.'
Having heard this, the Minister of the Treasury,
immediately stirred the great ocean water with both hands.
At that time, ten treasures emerged from the tips of his ten fingers.
He presented them to the Holy King (Shèngwáng) and said to the King:
'Great King (Dàwáng)!
Use what you require as you wish.
The remainder
should be cast into the great ocean.'
At that time, Dǐngshēng,
his heart greatly joyful and leaping with boundless delight,
further had this thought:
'I am now definitively a Cakravartin Holy King.'
Not long after this,
the Minister of the Army (Zhǔbīng Chén)
naturally appeared.
He was brave, strong, and fierce in strategy (měng lüè),
foremost in planning and tactics.
He excelled in the knowledge of the four armies (sì bīng).
If someone was suitable for combat, he presented them to the Holy King.
If someone was unsuitable, he retired them and did not allow them to appear.
Those not yet defeated, he was able to cause to be defeated.
Those already defeated, he had the power to protect and guard.
At that time, Dǐngshēng again had this thought:
If the Cakravartin obtains this Soldier Jewel,
one should know he is definitely a holy Cakravartin King.
“At that time, the holy Cakravartin Emperor Dǐngshēng,
addressed his ministers:
‘You all should know that this Yánfú Tí,
is peaceful, safe, and prosperous.
Now I have achieved the Seven Treasures,
and possess a thousand sons.
What more should I do?’
The ministers replied:
‘Yes,
Great King!
Dōng Fú Pó Tí,
has not yet submitted to your virtue.
The King should go and subdue it.’
At that time, the Holy King, along with his Seven Treasures and entire entourage,
flew through the sky and went to Dōng Fú Pó Tí.
The people of that land happily submitted to his rule.
He again addressed his ministers:
‘My Yánfú Tí and Fú Pó Tí,
are peaceful, safe, and prosperous,
the people are flourishing,
all have submitted to my rule,
the Seven Treasures are achieved,
and a thousand sons are complete.
What more should I do?’
The ministers replied:
‘Yes,
Great King!
Xī Qú Tuó Ní has not yet submitted to your virtue.’
At that time, the Holy King, again with his Seven Treasures and entire entourage,
flew through the sky and went to Xī Qú Tuó Ní.
When the King arrived there,
the people of that land also submitted to his rule.
He again addressed his ministers:
‘My Yánfú Tí, Fú Pó Tí,
and this Qú Tuó Ní,
are peaceful, safe, and prosperous,
the people are flourishing,
all have submitted to my rule,
the Seven Treasures are achieved,
and a thousand sons are complete.
What more should I do?’
The ministers replied:
‘Yes,
Great King!
Běi Yù Dān Yuè has not yet submitted to your rule.’
At that time, the Holy King, again with his Seven Treasures and entire entourage,
flew through the sky and went to Běi Yù Dān Yuè.
When the King arrived there,
the people of that land happily submitted to his virtue.
He again addressed his ministers:
‘My four great continents,
are peaceful, safe, and prosperous,
the people are flourishing,
all have submitted to my virtue.
The Seven Treasures are achieved,
and a thousand sons are complete.
What more should I do?’
The ministers replied:
‘Yes,
Holy King!
The Thirty-three Heavens,
their lifespans are extremely long,
they are peaceful and joyful.
The bodies of those devas,
are incomparable in grace and solemnity.
The palaces they dwell in,
their couches and bedding,
are all made of the Seven Treasures.
Relying on their celestial fortune,
they have not yet submitted to your rule.
You may now go and subdue them, causing them to submit.’
At that time, the Holy King, again with his Seven Treasures and entire entourage,
flew up into the void,
ascending to Dàolì Tiān.
He saw a tree,
whose color was bluish-green.
When the Holy King saw it,
he immediately asked his ministers:
‘What is this color?’
The ministers replied:
‘This is the Bōlìzhìduōluó Tree.
The devas of Dàolì
often enjoy themselves and take pleasure beneath it
during the three months of summer.
He again saw a white object, like a white cloud,
and again asked his ministers:
‘What is that color?’
The ministers replied:
‘That is the Shànfǎ Táng.
The devas of Dàolì
constantly gather inside it
to discuss matters concerning humans and devas.’
Thereupon, the Lord of Heaven, Shì Tí Huán Yīn,
knowing that King Dǐngshēng had arrived outside,
immediately went out to welcome him.
Seeing him, they joined hands and ascended the Shànfǎ Táng,
sitting side by side on separate seats.
At that time, the two kings
were completely identical in form and appearance,
only the winking of the eyes being the difference.
At this moment, the Holy King immediately conceived the thought:
‘Could I perhaps usurp his throne
and dwell here as the King of Heaven?’
Good man!
At that time, Dìshì upheld and recited the Mahāyāna Sūtras,
analyzed and distinguished them,
and expounded them to others,
but he had not yet completely attained penetrating insight into the profound meaning.
Due to the power of this reading and recitation,
upholding, distinguishing,
and widely speaking for others,
he possessed great majesty and virtue.
Good man!
But this Dǐngshēng, having conceived evil intent towards Dìshì,
immediately fell down,
returning to Yánfú Tí.
Separated from the humans and devas he loved and cherished,
he gave rise to great suffering and distress,
further encountered a grave illness,
and immediately reached the end of his life.
At that time, Dìshì
was Kèshè Fó.
The Holy Cakravartin King
was myself.
Good man!
You should know that such separation from what is loved
is extremely great suffering.
Good man!
If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva still recollects the suffering of separation from the loved ones of such people in the past,
how could a Bodhisattva, dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa Sūtra,
fail to observe the suffering of separation from the loved ones in the present world?
“Good man!
How does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practice the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa Sūtra
and contemplate the suffering of association with what is hated?
Good man!
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva observes that in the hells,
the animal realm,
the hungry ghost realm,
the human realm,
and the heavens,
there is all such suffering of association with what is hated.
For example, when a person regards incarceration,
confinement,
neck restraints,
and fetters as great suffering.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this,
observing all births in the Five Paths,
are entirely the great suffering of being joined with what is hated.
Furthermore, good man!
For example, there is a person
who constantly fears enemies,
neck restraints,
and fetters,
abandoning his parents,
wife, and children,
relatives,
and precious property,
and flees far away to avoid them.
Good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this,
fearing saṃsāra,
completely practicing the Six Pāramitās,
and entering Nirvāṇa.
Kèshè!
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa,
and contemplating the suffering of association with what is hated.
“Good man!
How does a Bodhisattva practice the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa
and contemplate the suffering of not obtaining what is sought?
‘Seeking’ means seeking everything completely.
‘Seeking everything completely’ has two types:
first, seeking wholesome dharmas;
second, seeking unwholesome dharmas.
The suffering of not yet obtaining wholesome dharmas,
and the suffering of not yet being separated from unwholesome dharmas—
this is a brief explanation of the suffering of the Five Flourishing Skandhas.
Kèshè!
This is called the Truth of Suffering.”
At that time, Kāyè Púsà Móhēsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
The statement made by the Buddha,
that the Five Aggregates of Attachment (Wǔ Shèng Yīn) are suffering (kǔ),
this meaning is incorrect.
Why is that?
Just as the Buddha previously told Shì Mó'nán:
'If form (sè) were suffering,
all sentient beings would not seek form;
if they do seek it,
then it should not be called suffering.'
Just as the Buddha told the various Bhīkṣus:
'There are three kinds of feeling (shòu):
feeling of suffering (kǔ shòu),
feeling of joy (lè shòu),
and feeling of neither suffering nor joy (bù kǔ bú lè shòu).'
Just as the Buddha previously taught the Bhīkṣus:
'If a person is able to cultivate wholesome Dharma (shàn fǎ),
then they will attain the feeling of joy.'
Furthermore, just as the Buddha taught:
'In the wholesome path, the six sense contacts (liù chù) result in the feeling of joy;
the eye seeing beautiful form is therefore joy;
the ear,
nose,
tongue,
body,
and mind perceiving wholesome Dharma (fǎ),
are likewise thus.'
Just as the Buddha spoke in a verse:
"World-Honored One!
The characteristics of joy (lè xiàng) spoken of in the various Sūtras,
their meaning is like this.
How can the meaning which the Buddha now speaks
correspond to this meaning?"
The Buddha told Kāyè:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
You are skillful in inquiring of the Tathāgata regarding this meaning.
Good man!
All sentient beings, within inferior suffering,
falsely generate the perception of joy (lè xiǎng).
Therefore, the characteristic of suffering (kǔ xiàng) which I now speak of
does not differ from the original (teaching)."
At that time, Kāyè Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As the Buddha has taught,
that the perception of joy arises within inferior suffering—
inferior birth (shēng),
inferior aging (lǎo),
inferior sickness (bìng),
inferior death (sǐ),
inferior separation from what is loved (ài bié lí),
inferior not obtaining what is sought (qiú bù dé),
inferior meeting with what is hateful (yuàn zēng huì),
inferior Five Aggregates of Attachment (Wǔ Shèng Yīn)—
suffering such as this should also contain joy.
World-Honored One!
The 'inferior birth'
refers to the three evil paths (sān è qù).
The 'intermediate birth'
refers to the human realm (rén zhōng).
The 'superior birth'
refers to the heavens (tiān shàng).
Now, if someone were to ask:
'If, regarding inferior joy (xià lè), the perception of suffering (kǔ xiǎng) arises;
regarding intermediate joy (zhōng lè), the perception of neither suffering nor joy (wú kǔ lè xiǎng) arises;
and regarding superior joy (shàng lè), the perception of joy (lè xiǎng) arises.'
How should we answer?
World-Honored One!
If the perception of joy arises within inferior suffering,
I have not seen anyone who, when about to receive a thousand strokes of punishment,
already generates the perception of joy upon receiving the very first stroke.
If it does not arise,
how can it be said that the perception of joy arises within inferior suffering?"
The Buddha told Kāyè:
"It is so,
it is so,
just as you have stated.
Because of this meaning,
there is no perception of joy (lè xiǎng).
Why is that?
It is like that person who is about to receive a thousand strokes,
but who, after receiving one stroke, immediately gains release (from the rest)—
that person then and there generates the perception of joy.
Therefore, you should know that the perception of joy is falsely generated in that which is not joy."
Kāyè said:
"World-Honored One!
That person does not generate the perception of joy because of the single stroke;
they generate the perception of joy because they gained release (from the rest)."
"Kāyè!
Therefore, when I previously taught Shì Mó'nán,
the joy within the Five Aggregates (Wǔ Yīn) was truly not false.
Kāyè!
There are three feelings (sān shòu) and three sufferings (sān kǔ).
The three feelings
are the feeling of joy (lè shòu),
the feeling of suffering (kǔ shòu),
and the feeling of neither suffering nor joy (bù kǔ bú lè shòu).
The three sufferings
are the suffering of suffering (kǔ kǔ),
the suffering of formation (xíng kǔ),
and the suffering of decay (huài kǔ).
Good man!
The feeling of suffering is called the three sufferings,
namely the suffering of suffering,
the suffering of formation,
and the suffering of decay.
The other two feelings,
are called the suffering of formation
and the suffering of decay.
Good man!
For this reason,
there truly exists the feeling of joy (lè shòu) within Saṃsāra (shēngsǐ).
A Púsà Móhēsà, seeing that the nature of suffering and joy do not abandon each other,
therefore states that all is suffering (kǔ).
Good man!
In truth, there is no joy within Saṃsāra;
but the various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, conforming to worldly convention, speak of there being joy."
Kāyè Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If the various Buddhas and Bodhisattvas conform to worldly convention and speak thus,
is this false speech (xū wàng)?
As the Buddha has said:
'Those who cultivate goodness then receive joyful retribution (lè bào)';
'Maintaining precepts (chí jiè) brings peace and joy, the body does not receive suffering';
and further, 'When all matters are accomplished, that is the ultimate joy (zuì lè)'—
in Sūtras such as these,
is the feeling of joy (lè shòu) spoken of
false speech (xū wàng)?
If it is false speech,
the various Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have long cultivated the Bodhi Path (Pútí Dào) for immeasurable hundreds, thousands, myriads, and millions of Asankyeya Kalpas (Āsēngqí Jié),
and have already abandoned false speech (wàng yǔ);
if they now make this statement, what is its meaning?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
The verses concerning the feeling of joy mentioned above,
are precisely the foundation of the Bodhi Path (Pútí Dào),
and can also nourish Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Because of this meaning,
I first spoke of these characteristics of joy (lè xiàng) in the Sūtras.
Good man!
For example, in the world,
the necessities of life (zī shēng) sought after are able to be causes of joy,
hence they are called joy.
Namely, feminine beauty (nǚ sè),
indulgence in wine and drink,
superior food and sweet flavors,
obtaining water when thirsty,
encountering fire when cold,
clothing and adornments (yīng luò),
elephants, horses, and carriages,
male and female servants and attendants,
gold, silver, Lǐulí,
coral, and genuine pearls,
granaries and grains—
objects such as these are what the world seeks,
are able to be the causes of joy,
and are called joy.
Good man!
Objects such as these are also able to generate suffering.
Because of women, the suffering of giving birth to males arises,
distress, sorrowful weeping, and even severance of life.
Because of wine, sweet flavors, and even granaries and grains,
people can also be caused to generate great worry and distress.
Because of this meaning,
all is suffering,
and there are no characteristics of joy.
Good man!
A Púsà Móhēsà, regarding these Eight Sufferings (bā kǔ),
understands suffering (kǔ),
and non-suffering (wú kǔ).
Good man!
All Śrāvakās (Shēngwén), Pratyekabuddhas (Pìzhīfó), and others,
do not know the cause of joy.
It is for people such as these
that I speak of the characteristics of joy (lè xiàng) within inferior suffering.
Only a Púsà who dwells in the Great Vehicle (Dà Chéng) and Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Bān Nièpán),
is then able to know the cause of suffering (kǔ yīn),
and the cause of joy (lè yīn)."
“O good man!
How does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa,
observe the Saṃudaya-satya (Truth of Origination)?
O good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva observes that this Saṃudaya-satya is the condition (yin yuán) for the aggregates (yīn),
meaning that origination (jí) is still the craving (ài) for existence (yǒu).
Craving (ài) has two types:
First, craving for one's own body (jǐ shēn).
Second, craving for what is needed (suǒ xū).
Furthermore, there are two types:
Not yet obtaining the five desires (wǔ yù),
one focuses the mind (xì xīn) and single-mindedly seeks them;
Having sought and obtained them,
one endures and single-mindedly clings (zhuó) to them.
Furthermore, there are three types:
Craving for desires (yù ài),
craving for form (sè ài),
and craving for formlessness (wú sè ài).
Furthermore, there are three types:
Craving conditioned by karma (yè yīn yuán ài),
craving conditioned by afflictions (fán nǎo yīn yuán ài),
and craving conditioned by suffering (kǔ yīn yuán ài).
A person who has left home (chū jiā zhī rén) has four types of craving:
What are the four?
Robes (yī fú),
food and drink (yǐn shí),
bedding (wò jù),
and medicine (tāng yào).
Furthermore, there are five types:
Greedily clinging to the five aggregates (wǔ yīn),
and clinging to all things needed (suǒ xū);
When distinguished, calculated, and analyzed, they are measureless and boundless.
O good man!
Craving (ài) has two types:
First, wholesome craving (shàn ài).
Second, unwholesome craving (bù shàn ài).
Unwholesome craving
is sought only by the foolish (yú).
Craving for wholesome Dharma (shàn fǎ ài)
is sought by the Bodhisattvas.
Craving for wholesome Dharma (shàn fǎ ài) again has two types:
Unwholesome and wholesome.
Seeking the two vehicles (èr chéng) is called unwholesome.
Seeking the Mahāyāna (dà chéng) is called wholesome.
O good man!
The craving of ordinary beings (fán fū ài) is named Origination (Jí),
it is not named Truth (Dì).
The craving of Bodhisattvas
is named ultimate Truth (shí Dì), it is not named Origination (Jí).
Why is this?
In order to save sentient beings (zhòng shēng),
they therefore undergo birth (shòu shēng);
they do not undergo birth due to craving.
Kāśyapa Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
As the World-Honored One, the Buddha (Fó Shìzūn), in other sūtras,
taught sentient beings that karma (yè) is the condition (yīn yuán),
or taught that arrogance (jiāo màn) is the condition,
or taught that the six contacts (liù chù) are the condition,
or taught that ignorance (wú míng)
serves as the condition for the five flourishing aggregates (wǔ shèng yīn),
what is the meaning now that, in speaking of the Four Noble Truths (Sì Shèng Dì),
You exclusively designate the nature of craving (ài xìng) as the cause (yīn) of the five aggregates (wǔ yīn)?”"
The Buddha praised Jiāshè Púsa:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
As you have said,
all conditions (yīnyuán) are not non-causes,
but the Wǔ Yīn must have craving (ài) as their condition.
Good man!
For example, when a great king goes out on an inspection tour,
ministers
and relatives all follow him.
Craving is also like this;
wherever craving goes,
those fetters also follow.
For example, like greasy clothes:
wherever dust adheres,
the adherence stays with it.
Craving is also like this;
wherever it is attached with love,
the karmic fetters also reside.
Furthermore, good man!
For example, wet ground can produce shoots (yá);
craving is also like this,
it can produce the shoots of all karma and defilements.
Good man!
The Púsa Móhēsà, dwelling in this Great Vehicle (Dà Chéng) Dà Bān Nièpán,
deeply observes this craving,
which generally has nine types:
One, like remaining debt;
two, like a Luóchà Nǚ wife;
three, like a stalk of wonderful flower wrapped by a poisonous snake;
four, like bad food that is inconvenient for one's nature but is forced down;
five, like a prostitute;
six, like the Mólóujiā Zǐ;
seven, like polyps within a sore;
eight, like a violent storm;
nine, like a comet.
What is called 'like remaining debt'?
Good man!
For example, a poor person
who owes money to others,
although repayment is nearly complete,
because a remainder is not yet finished,
he remains imprisoned in jail
and cannot be released.
The Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué) are also like this;
because there is a remnant of the habitual scent of craving,
they cannot achieve Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpú tí.
Good man!
This is called 'like remaining debt.'
Good man!
What is 'like a Luóchà Nǚ wife'?
Good man!
For example, if a man
takes a Luóchà Nǚ as a wife or concubine,
this Luóchà Nǚ, whatever children she gives birth to,
having given birth, immediately devours them.
When the children are all gone, she then devours her husband as well.
Good man!
The Luóchà Nǚ of craving is also like this;
following living beings,
she gives birth to the children of good roots;
as soon as they are born, she consumes them.
When the good children are all gone,
she then devours the living being,
causing them to fall into hells (dìyù),
the animal realm (chùshēng),
and the hungry ghost realm (èguǐ).
Only Púsa are excluded.
This is called 'like a Luóchà Nǚ wife.'
Good man!
What is 'like a stalk of wonderful flower wrapped by a poisonous snake'?
For example, if a person by nature loves beautiful flowers,
but does not see the danger of the poisonous snake on the flower stalk,
he immediately goes forward and grabs it.
Having grabbed it, the snake bites him;
having been bitten, his life ends.
All ordinary beings (fánfū) are also like this;
craving the flowers of the five desires (wǔ yù),
they do not see the danger of the poisonous snake of craving,
and thus receive and accept them.
They are then stung and bitten by the poison of craving,
and at the end of their lives, they fall into the Three Evil Paths (Sān È Dào).
Only Púsa are excluded.
This is called 'like a stalk of wonderful flower wrapped by a poisonous snake.'
Good man!
What is 'food that is inconvenient but is forced down'?
For example, if a person
eats food that is inconvenient for his system and forces it down,
after eating it, his stomach aches,
and suffering from diarrhea, he dies.
The food of craving is also like this;
living beings in the Five Paths (Wǔ Dào),
forcefully consume attachments.
For this reason, they fall into the Three Evil Paths.
Only Púsa are excluded.
This is called 'food that is inconvenient but is forced down.'
Good man!
What is 'the prostitute'?
For example, a foolish person has relations with a prostitute (yín nǚ);
and that prostitute cleverly uses various flatteries to feign intimacy,
completely seizing all of this person's money and possessions.
Once the money and possessions are exhausted, she then drives him away.
The prostitute of craving is also like this;
the ignorant foolish person has intercourse with her,
and this craving-woman seizes all his good dharmas (shàn fǎ).
Once the good dharmas are exhausted,
she drives him away, causing him to fall into the Three Evil Paths.
Only Púsa are excluded.
This is called 'the prostitute.'
Good man!
What is 'the Mólóujiā Zǐ'?
For example, the Mólóujiā Zǐ—
if a bird eats it,
it falls to the ground with the feces,
or perhaps it is blown by the wind,
arrives beneath a tree, and immediately grows,
winding and binding the Nígōutuó Shù,
causing it not to grow,
until it withers and dies.
The Mólóujiā Zǐ of craving is also like this;
it winds and binds all the good dharmas of ordinary beings,
preventing them from growing until they wither and vanish.
Once withered and vanished,
after the end of life, they fall into the Three Evil Paths.
Only Púsa are excluded.
This is called 'the Mólóujiā Zǐ.'
Good man!
What is 'polyps within a sore'?
Just as a person has an old sore
in which polyps grow,
that person must diligently treat and heal it,
and not give rise to an attitude of neglect.
If they give rise to neglect,
the polyps of the sore will grow,
and abscesses and ulcers will reappear.
For this reason, their life will immediately end.
The sores and wounds of the Wǔ Yīn of ordinary foolish beings are also like this;
craving acts as the polyp within them.
One should diligently treat and heal the polyp of craving.
If one does not treat it,
at the end of life, one will immediately fall into the Three Evil Paths.
Only Púsa are excluded.
This is called 'polyps within a sore.'
Good man!
What is 'a violent storm'?
For example, a violent storm
can flatten mountains and move peaks,
pulling up deeply rooted saplings.
The great violent storm of craving
is also like this;
in regard to parents, it gives rise to malicious thoughts,
and it can uproot the unparalleled, deep, and solid roots of Bodhi (Pútí) planted by great sages like Shèlìfú.
Only Púsa are excluded.
This is called 'a violent storm.'
Good man!
What is 'like a comet'?
For example, when a comet appears under heaven,
all the people suffer famine, sickness, emaciation,
and various afflictions.
The comet of craving
is also like this;
it can sever the seeds of all good roots,
causing ordinary beings (fánfū rén) to be isolated, destitute, and hungry,
generating the sickness of defilements,
and revolving through Saṃsāra (shēngsǐ), enduring various sufferings.
Only Púsa are excluded.
This is called 'a comet.'
Good man!
The Púsa Móhēsà, dwelling in the Great Vehicle Dà Bān Nièpán,
observe the fetter of craving
in these nine types."
"Good man!
For this reason,
all ordinary beings experience suffering but have no Truth (dì);
the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas experience suffering and have the Truth of Suffering, but lack ultimate reality (zhēnshí);
Púsa understand suffering
and are without suffering,
therefore, they are without suffering but possess ultimate reality.
All ordinary beings experience origination (jí) but have no Truth;
the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas experience origination and have the Truth of Origination;
Púsa understand origination and are without origination,
therefore, they are without origination but possess the true Truth.
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess cessation (miè), but it is not ultimate reality;
the Púsa Móhēsà possess cessation and possess the true Truth.
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas possess the path (dào), but it is not ultimate reality;
the Púsa Móhēsà possess the path and possess the true Truth."
"Good man!
How does a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà), dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dàbān Nièpán),
perceive extinction,
perceive the Truth of Extinction (Mìedì)?
It is defined as completely severing all defilements (fánnǎo).
If defilements are severed,
it is called permanence (cháng).
Extinguishing the fire of defilements
is called tranquil extinction (jìmìe).
Because defilements are extinguished, one receives bliss.
Because all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas seek the cause and conditions,
it is therefore called purity (jìng).
