Since one no longer experiences the twenty-five realms of existence (èrshíwǔ yǒu), it is called transcendence (chūshì).
Because of transcendence, it is called the Permanent Self (wǒ cháng).
With respect to form (sè),
sound (shēng),
smell (xiāng),
taste (wèi),
touch (chù),
male,
female,
origination (shēng),
abiding (zhù),
extinction (mìe),
suffering (kǔ),
bliss (lè),
neither suffering
nor bliss (bù kǔ bù lè)—
if one does not grasp characteristics,
it is called the Ultimate Truth of Tranquil Extinction (Bìjìng Jìmìe Zhēndì).
Good man!
The Bodhisattva, dwelling thus in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa,
contemplates the Noble Truth of Extinction (Mìe Shèngdì).
"Good man!
How does a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa,
contemplate the Noble Truth of the Path (Dào Shèngdì)?
Good man!
Just as in the darkness,
one sees coarse and subtle objects by means of a lamp.
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this,
dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa,
perceiving all phenomena (yīqiè fă) through the Eightfold Noble Path (Bā Shèngdào).
Namely: permanent (cháng),
impermanent (wúcháng);
conditioned (yǒuwéi),
unconditioned (wúwéi);
having sentient beings,
not having sentient beings;
thing,
not-thing;
suffering,
bliss;
self (wǒ),
non-self (wúwǒ);
pure,
impure;
defilement,
non-defilement;
karma (yè),
non-karma;
real,
unreal;
vehicle (chéng),
non-vehicle;
knowledge,
non-knowledge;
dravya (tuóluópìao),
non-dravya (fēi tuóluópìao);
guṇa (qíu nà),
non-guṇa (fēi qíu nà);
view,
non-view;
form,
non-form;
path (dào),
non-path;
release,
non-release.
Good man!
The Bodhisattva, dwelling thus in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa,
contemplates the Noble Truth of the Path.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa (Jiāshè Púsà) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If the Eightfold Noble Path is the Noble Truth of the Path,
the meaning does not accord [with other teachings].
Why is this?
The Tathāgata sometimes speaks of faith (xìnxīn) as the path,
which is able to overcome the outflows (zhū lòu).
Sometimes the path spoken of is diligence/non-negligence (bù fàngyì).
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, practiced non-negligence,
they attained Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
which is also the supporting Dharma for the Bodhisattvas' path.
Sometimes it is said that energetic effort (jīngjìn) is the path,
as when you informed Ānán:
'If there is a person who can diligently practice energetic effort,
they shall achieve Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.'
Sometimes it is said that contemplation of the body (guān shēn niànchù) is the path.
If one fixes the mind
and diligently practices this contemplation of the body,
they shall achieve Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.
Sometimes it is said that proper concentration (zhèngdìng) is the path,
as when you informed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa (Móhē Jiāshè):
'Indeed, proper concentration is truly the path,
and improper concentration is not the path.
If one enters proper concentration,
one is then able to contemplate the arising and cessation of the Five Aggregates (Wǔ Yīn shēng mìe);
one cannot contemplate if one does not enter concentration.'
Or [You] spoke of a single Dharma
which, if a person cultivates it,
can purify sentient beings,
eliminate all worries, sorrow, and suffering,
and attain the True Dharma—
namely, the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha (Niàn Fó Sānmèi).
Or again, You spoke of cultivating the perception of impermanence (wúcháng xiǎng),
and called this the path,
as when You informed the Bhikṣus (Bĭqiū):
'Whoever can frequently cultivate the perception of impermanence
can attain Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.'
Or [You] spoke of an empty and quiet Āraṇya (Ālánruò) place,
sitting alone and contemplating,
as being able to quickly achieve Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.
Sometimes it is said
that expounding the Dharma for others
is called the path.
If the web of doubt is immediately severed upon hearing the Dharma,
once the web of doubt is severed, one attains Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.
Sometimes it is said that upholding the precepts (chí jiè) is the path,
as when you informed Ānán:
'If one diligently cultivates and upholds the moral precepts,
that person overcomes the great suffering of transmigration (shēngsǐ).'
Sometimes it is said that associating closely with good friends (shàn yǒu) is called the path,
as when you informed Ānán:
'If one associates closely with good spiritual advisors (shàn zhīshì),
then one will possess pure precepts.
If there are sentient beings who can associate closely with Me,
they will give rise to the mind set on Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.'
Sometimes it is said
that cultivating loving-kindness (cí) is the path.
One who cultivates and learns loving-kindness
severs all defilements and attains the immovable state (bù dòng chù).
Sometimes it is said that wisdom (zhìhuì) is the path,
as when the Buddha previously spoke to the Bhikṣuṇī (Bĭqiūní) Prajāpati (Bōshé Bōtí):
'Sister!
Like the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén),
using the sword of wisdom,
they are able to sever all streams
and the outflows and defilements.'
Sometimes the Tathāgata spoke of giving (shī) as the path,
as when the Buddha previously informed King Prasenajit (Bōsíní Wáng):
'Great King!
You should know that in the past, I performed many acts of giving.
Due to these causes and conditions,
I have today achieved Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.'
World-Honored One,
if the Eightfold Noble Path is the Truth of the Path,
are not sūtras such as these
false?
If those sūtras are not false,
for what reason do they not speak of the Eight Paths as the Noble Truth of the Path?
If they do not speak of it,
why was the Tathāgata mistaken in the past?
However, I know for certain that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas
have long been free from error."
At that time, the Bhagavān (World-Honored One) praised Jiāyè Púsà:
“Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
You now desire to know the secrets contained within the subtle Sūtras (classics) of the Mahāyāna (Great Vehicle) for the Bodhisattvas (Púsàs),
which is why you pose this question.
Good man!
All such Sūtras
entirely enter into the truth of the path (Dàodì).
Good man!
As I have stated:
if one has faith in the path,
such faith in the path
is the root of faith,
it is that which can assist the path to Bodhi (Pútí);
therefore, what I speak contains no error.
Good man!
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is perfectly aware of countless skillful means (fāngbiàn);
desiring to transform sentient beings,
he therefore presents various types of Dharma (Fǎ) teachings.
Good man!
Just as a skillful physician
recognizes the various causes of sicknesses in all beings,
and according to the ailment they suffer, prepares the medicine,
along with what the medicine forbids,
only water is not included among the forbidden items.
Perhaps one takes ginger water,
or licorice water,
or wild ginger water,
or dark rock sugar water,
or Āmólè water,
or Nípóluó water,
or Bōzhòuluó water,
or takes cold water,
or takes hot water,
or grape water,
or pomegranate water.
Good man!
This skillful physician,
knowing well the various ailments of sentient beings,
though the medicines have many prohibitions,
water is not subject to exception.
The Tathāgata is also like this:
knowing skillful means perfectly,
regarding the reality of the one Dharma (Yī Fǎxiàng),
he speaks extensively,
distinguishing various names and forms according to sentient beings.
Those sentient beings accept what is taught,
and having accepted it, they cultivate practice,
eradicating and severing afflictions (fánnǎo),
just like those patients
who, following the instructions of the skillful physician,
have their ailments removed.
“Furthermore, good man!
Suppose there is a person
who is skilled in various languages.
When among a great assembly,
and this great assembly
is afflicted by heat and thirst,
they all cry out, saying:
‘I want to drink water!
I want to drink water!’
This person immediately takes clear, cool water
and, according to their dialects, says it is water,
perhaps calling it Bōní,
or calling it Yùchí,
or calling it Kèlìlán,
or calling it Kèlì,
or calling it Póyē,
or calling it Gānlù (Amrita),
or calling it milk.
Using these and other countless names for water,
he speaks to the great assembly.
Good man!
The Tathāgata is also like this:
using the one Holy Path (Yī Shèngdào),
he expounds various teachings for the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén),
ranging from the root of faith (Xìngen) up to the Eightfold Holy Path (Bā Shèngdào).
“Furthermore, good man!
Just as a goldsmith,
using one kind of gold, creates various ornaments (yīngluò) according to desire,
namely necklaces (qiánsuǒ),
bracelets (huánchuàn), hairpins (chāidāng),
celestial crowns (tiānguān), and arm seals (bìyìn);
although there are such differences and variations,
yet they never leave the gold.
Good man!
The Tathāgata is also like this:
using the one Buddha Path (Yī Fódào), he speaks,
making various distinctions according to sentient beings.
Sometimes he speaks of one kind,
which is that the paths of all Buddhas are one and without duality.
He also speaks of two kinds,
namely concentration (Dìng)
and wisdom (Huì).
He also speaks of three kinds,
namely viewing (Jiàn),
wisdom (Huì),
and knowledge (Zhì).
He also speaks of four kinds,
namely the Path of Viewing (Jiàndào),
the Path of Cultivation (Xiūdào),
the Path of No More Learning (Wúxuédào),
and the Buddha Path (Fódào).
He also speaks of five kinds,
namely the Path of Faith Practice (Xìnxíngdào),
the Path of Dharma Practice (Fǎxíngdào),
the Path of Faith Liberation (Xìnjiětuōdào),
the Path of Viewing Attainment (Jiàndàodào),
and the Path of Physical Realization (Shēnzhèngdào).
He also speaks of six kinds,
namely the Path of the Sūtuóhuán (Sotāpanna),
the Path of the Sītuóhán (Sakadāgāmin),
the Path of the Ānàhán (Anāgāmin),
the Path of the Āluóhàn (Arhat),
the Path of the Pìzhīfó (Pratyekabuddha),
and the Buddha Path (Fódào).
He also speaks of seven kinds,
namely the Limb of Enlightenment of Mindfulness (Niàn Juéfēn),
the Limb of Enlightenment of Investigation of Dharma (Zéfǎ Juéfēn),
the Limb of Enlightenment of Effort (Jīngjìn Juéfēn),
the Limb of Enlightenment of Joy (Xǐ Juéfēn),
the Limb of Enlightenment of Tranquilization/Relief (Chú Juéfēn),
the Limb of Enlightenment of Concentration (Dìng Juéfēn),
and the Limb of Enlightenment of Equanimity (Shě Juéfēn).
He also speaks of eight kinds,
namely Right View (Zhèngjiàn),
Right Thought (Zhèngsīwéi),
Right Speech (Zhèngyǔ),
Right Action (Zhèngyè),
Right Livelihood (Zhèngmìng),
Right Effort (Zhèngjīngjìn),
Right Mindfulness (Zhèngniàn),
and Right Concentration (Zhèngdìng).
He also speaks of nine kinds,
namely the Eightfold Holy Path (Bā Shèngdào) and faith (xìn).
He also speaks of ten kinds,
namely the Ten Powers (Shílì).
He also speaks of eleven kinds,
namely the Ten Powers
and Great Loving-Kindness (Dàcí).
He also speaks of twelve kinds,
namely the Ten Powers,
Great Loving-Kindness,
and Great Compassion (Dàbēi).
He also speaks of thirteen kinds,
namely the Ten Powers,
Great Loving-Kindness,
Great Compassion,
and the Samādhi (Sānmèi) of Recollection of the Buddha (Niànfó Sānmèi).
He also speaks of sixteen kinds,
namely the Ten Powers,
Great Loving-Kindness,
Great Compassion,
the Samādhi of Recollection of the Buddha, and the Three Foundations of Mindfulness (Sān Zhèngniànchù) attained by the Buddha.
He also speaks of twenty paths,
namely the Ten Powers,
the Four Fearlessnesses (Sì Wúsuǒwèi),
Great Loving-Kindness,
Great Compassion,
the Samādhi of Recollection of the Buddha,
and the Three Foundations of Mindfulness.
Good man!
This path is a single entity;
the Tathāgata in the past distinguished it in various ways for the sake of sentient beings.
“Furthermore, good man!
Just as a single fire,
due to what it burns,
obtains various names,
namely wood fire (mùhuǒ),
grass fire (cǎohuǒ),
chaff fire (kānghuǒ),
grain dust fire (sǔohuǒ),
or cow and horse dung fire (niúmǎfènhuǒ).
Good man!
The Buddha Path (Fódào) is also like this:
it is one and without duality,
but for the sake of sentient beings, it is variously distinguished.
“Furthermore, good man!
Just as a single consciousness (shì)
is distinguished and spoken of as six;
when pertaining to the eye, it is called eye-consciousness (yǎnshì),
and so too is the mind-consciousness (yìshì).
Good man!
The Path (Dào) is also like this:
it is one and without duality;
the Tathāgata distinguishes it in various ways in order to transform all sentient beings.”
“Furthermore, Sʰànnánzǐ!
For example, a single color,
when seen by the eyes,
is then called form (sè).
When heard by the ears,
is then called sound (shēng).
When smelled by the nose,
is then called fragrance (xiāng).
When tasted by the tongue,
is then called flavor (wèi).
When sensed by the body,
is then called touch (chù).
Sʰànnánzǐ!
The path (dào) is also like this,
it is one and not two.
The Tárulái makes various distinctions in order to transform sentient beings.
Sʰànnánzǐ!
For this reason,
the Eight Noble Path Components,
are named the Noble Truth of the Path (Dào Shèngdì).
Sʰànnánzǐ!
These Four Noble Truths (Sì Shèngdì),
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones (Shìzūn), teach them sequentially.
Due to these causes and conditions,
immeasurable sentient beings attain liberation from Sa¹ngsāra.
Jiāshè Púsa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Formerly, the Buddha was once on the bank of the Hénghé (Ganges) in the forest of corpses (Shīshǒu Lín),
at that time, the Tárulái picked up a leaf from the tree
and addressed the Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū):
‘Are the leaves I hold in my hand many,
or are the leaves of the grass and trees upon the whole earth many?’
The Bhikṣus replied:
‘World-Honored One!
The leaves of the grass and trees upon the whole earth are many,
incalculable.
What the Tárulái holds
is little and insignificant.’
‘Bhikṣus!
All the Dharmas that I have awakened to and understood
are like the grass and trees growing upon the earth;
those that I have preached for sentient beings
are like the leaves in my hand.’
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke such words:
‘Among the immeasurable Dharmas that the Tárulái has understood,
if they are included in the Four Truths,
then they have been preached;
if they are not included,
then there should be Five Truths.’
At that time, the Buddha praised Jiāshè Púsa:
“Excellent,
excellent!
Sʰànnánzǐ!
The question you now ask
will benefit, comfort, and bring happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
Sʰànnánzǐ!
Such Dharmas
are all already included within the Four Noble Truths.”
Jiāshè Púsa then spoke again:
“If such Dharmas
are within the Four Truths,
why did the Tárulái proclaim that they were not preached?”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
Even though it enters the scope,
it is still not called 'speaking' (of the full teaching).
Why is this?
Good man!
Knowing the Sìshèngdì (Four Noble Truths)
has two kinds of wisdom:
one is Intermediate,
and the second is Supreme.
Intermediate refers to the wisdom of the Shēngwén (Hearers) and Yuánjué (Pratyekabuddhas);
Supreme refers to the wisdom of the Zhūfó (Buddhas) and Púsà (Bodhisattvas).
Good man!
Knowing the suffering of the various Yīn (Skandhas)
is called Intermediate Wisdom;
discriminating the various Yīn as having immeasurable characteristics
and that all are instances of suffering,
which is not known by the various Shēngwén and Yuánjué,
is called Supreme Wisdom.
Good man!
Such meanings as these,
I did not speak of them in that Sūtra (scripture).
Good man!
To know the various Rù (Sense-bases)
is called the Gate,
and is also called suffering;
this is called Intermediate Wisdom;
discriminating the various Rù
as having immeasurable characteristics,
and that all are instances of suffering,
which is not known by the various Shēngwén and Yuánjué,
is called Supreme Wisdom.
Such meanings as these,
I also did not speak of them in that Sūtra.
Good man!
To know the various Jiè (Elements/Dhatus)
is called Division,
and is also called Nature,
and is also called suffering;
this is called Intermediate Wisdom;
discriminating the various Jiè
as having immeasurable characteristics,
and that all are instances of suffering,
which is not known by the various Shēngwén and Yuánjué,
is called Supreme Wisdom.
Good man!
Such meanings as these,
I also did not speak of them in that Sūtra.
Good man!
To know the characteristic of Rù (Form/Matter) as being perishable
is called Intermediate Wisdom;
discriminating the various Rù
as having immeasurable characteristics,
and that all are instances of suffering,
which is not known by the various Shēngwén and Yuánjué,
is called Supreme Wisdom.
Such meanings as these,
I also did not speak of them in that Sūtra.
Good man!
To know the characteristic of Shòu (Feeling) as sensation
is called Intermediate Wisdom;
discriminating the various Shòu
as having immeasurable characteristics of sensation,
which is not known by the various Shēngwén and Yuánjué,
is called Supreme Wisdom.
Good man!
Such meanings as these,
I also did not speak of them in that Sūtra.
Good man!
To know the characteristic of Xiǎng (Conception) as apprehension
is called Intermediate Wisdom;
discriminating this Xiǎng
as having immeasurable characteristics of apprehension,
which is not known by the various Shēngwén and Yuánjué,
is called Supreme Wisdom.
Such meanings as these,
I also did not speak of them in that Sūtra.
Good man!
To know the characteristic of Xíng (Volition) as action
is called Intermediate Wisdom;
discriminating this Xíng
as having immeasurable characteristics of action,
which is not known by the various Shēngwén and Yuánjué,
is called Supreme Wisdom.
Good man!
Such meanings as these,
I also did not speak of them in that Sūtra.
Good man!
To know the characteristic of Shí (Consciousness) as differentiation
is called Intermediate Wisdom;
discriminating this Shí
as having immeasurable characteristics of knowing,
which is not known by the various Shēngwén and Yuánjué,
is called Supreme Wisdom.
Good man!
Such meanings as these,
I also did not speak of them in that Sūtra.
Good man!
To know that Āi (Craving), as a cause and condition,
is able to generate the Five Yīn,
is called Intermediate Wisdom;
that one person arouses Āi immeasurably and boundlessly,
which the Shēngwén and Yuánjué are unable to know,
and being able to know the Āi that all sentient beings arouse—such is
called Supreme Wisdom.
Such meanings as these,
I also did not speak of them in that Sūtra.
Good man!
To know the cessation of Fánnǎo (Afflictions)
is called Intermediate Wisdom;
discriminating Fánnǎo
as unquantifiable and immeasurable;
the cessation is likewise
unquantifiable and immeasurable,
which is not known by the various Shēngwén and Yuánjué,
is called Supreme Wisdom.
Such meanings as these,
I also did not speak of them in that Sūtra.
Good man!
To know the characteristic of the Dào (Path)
that is able to depart from Fánnǎo
is called Intermediate Wisdom;
discriminating the characteristics of the Dào
as immeasurable and boundless,
and the Fánnǎo that are departed from
are also immeasurable and boundless,
which is not known by the various Shēngwén and Yuánjué,
is called Supreme Wisdom.
Such meanings as these,
I also did not speak of them in that Sūtra.
Good man!
To know the Shìdì (Mundane Truth)
is called Intermediate Wisdom;
discriminating the Shìdì
as immeasurable, boundless, and unquantifiable,
which is not known by the various Shēngwén and Yuánjué,
is called Supreme Wisdom.
Such meanings as these,
I also did not speak of them in that Sūtra.
Good man!
That all conditioned phenomena are impermanent,
that all Dharmas are without self (no-self),
and that Nièpán (Nirvana) is tranquil cessation, which is the Dìyīyì (Ultimate Truth),
is called Intermediate Wisdom;
to know the Dìyīyì as immeasurable, boundless, and unquantifiable,
which is not known by the various Shēngwén and Yuánjué,
is called Supreme Wisdom.
Such meanings as these,
I also did not speak of them in that Sūtra.”
At that time, Wénshū Shīlì Púsà Móhēsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Shìdì you spoke of
and the Dìyīyìdì (Ultimate Truth),
what do their meanings imply?
World-Honored One,
is there Shìdì within the Dìyīyì?
Is there Dìyīyì within the Shìdì?
If there is, then they are just one single truth;
if there is not, then is this not the Tathāgata speaking falsehood?”
“[Good man!
The Shìdì is precisely the Dìyīyìdì.”
“World-Honored One!
If that is the case,
then there are not two truths.
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
Using skillful means,
in accordance with sentient beings,
I speak of the existence of the two truths (Èrdì).
Good man!
If one follows the conventional discourse, there are two types:
First, mundane reality (Shìfǎ);
Second, supramundane reality (Chūshìfǎ).
Good man!
That which is known by the supramundane person,
is called the Ultimate Truth (Dìyīyìdì);
that which is known by the worldly person,
is called the Mundane Truth (Shìdì).
Good man!
When the Five Aggregates (Wǔyīn) combine,
they are called by names, such as ‘so-and-so,’
and ordinary sentient beings follow these appellations;
this is called the Mundane Truth (Shìdì);
to understand that the aggregates do not possess the name ‘so-and-so,’
and that separate from the aggregates there is also no name ‘so-and-so,’
the supramundane person, in accordance with the true nature (xìngxiàng),
is able to know this:
this is called the Ultimate Truth (Dìyīyìdì).
Furthermore, good man!
Furthermore, there are phenomena (fǎ) that have name and have reality,
and there are phenomena that have name but have no reality.
Good man!
That which has name but no reality is the Mundane Truth (Shìdì);
that which has name and has reality is the Ultimate Truth (Dìyīyìdì).
Good man!
Such as the self (wǒ),
sentient beings (zhòngshēng),
life span (shòumìng),
knowledge and views (zhījiàn),
nourishment (yǎngyù),
the hero/man (zhàngfū),
the actor/doer (zuòzhě),
the receiver/experiencer (shòuzhě),
the shimmering heat haze (yán) in summer,
a Gandhārvā city (Qiántàpó chéng),
tortoise hair and rabbit horns,
the wheel made by whirling fire,
and all the aggregates (yīn), elements (jiè), and sense bases (rù):
These are called the Mundane Truth (Shìdì);
The suffering, origin, cessation, and path (Kǔ Jí Miè Dào) are called the Ultimate Truth (Dìyīyìdì).
“Good man!
The mundane realities (Shìfǎ) are of five types:
First, the world of nomenclature (Míngshì),
Second, the world of phrases (Jùshì),
Third, the world of bindings (Fúshì),
Fourth, the world of rituals/dharma (Fǎshì),
Fifth, the world of attachment/clinging (Zhízhuóshì).
Good man!
What is the world of nomenclature (Míngshì)?
Man and woman,
jars and clothes,
carriages, vehicles, and houses;
objects such as these,
are called the world of nomenclature (Míngshì).
What is the world of phrases (Jùshì)?
Four phrases make one stanza (Jì),
stanzas such as these,
are called the world of phrases (Jùshì).
What is the world of bindings (Fúshì)?
Rolling up and joining together (juǎnhé),
tying knots (jìjié),
binding up (shùfù),
and joining palms (hézhǎng);
these are called the world of bindings (Fúshì).
What is the world of rituals/dharma (Fǎshì)?
Such as beating the mallet (míng chuí),
assembling the Saṅgha (jí sēng),
decorating the drum (yángǔ),
commanding soldiers (jiè bīng),
blowing the conch (chuī bèi),
and knowing the proper time (zhī shí);
these are called the world of rituals (Fǎshì).
What is the world of attachment/clinging (Zhízhuóshì)?
For example, when looking at a distant person,
if they wear dyed robes,
one forms a perception and clings to the idea,
saying, “This is a Śrāmaṇa (Shāmen), not a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén)”;
if one sees someone with a knotted cord carried across their body,
one immediately thinks and says, “This is a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén), not a Śrāmaṇa (Shāmen)”;
this is called the world of attachment/clinging (Zhízhuóshì).
Good man!
These are called the five types of mundane reality (Shìfǎ).
Good man!
If there is a sentient being who regards these five types of mundane reality,
whose mind is without delusion,
and who knows them as they truly are,
this is called the Ultimate Truth (Dìyīyìdì).
“Furthermore, good man!
To burn (ruò shāo),
to cut (ruò gē),
to die (ruò sǐ),
or to be destroyed (ruò huài),
this is called the Mundane Truth (Shìdì);
not to burn,
not to cut,
not to die,
not to be destroyed,
this is called the Ultimate Truth (Dìyīyìdì).
Furthermore, good man,
the characteristics of the eight sufferings (bā kǔ xiàng) exist,
this is called the Mundane Truth (Shìdì);
no birth (wú shēng),
no old age (wú lǎo),
no sickness (wú bìng),
no death (wú sǐ),
no separation from the beloved (wú ài biélí),
no meeting with the hated (wú yuānzēng huì),
no failure to obtain what is sought (wú qiú bùdé),
and no flourishing of the five aggregates (wú wǔ shèng yīn),
this is called the Ultimate Truth (Dìyīyìdì).
Furthermore, good man!
For example, one person may have many abilities;
when he runs, he is called a runner (zǒuzhě);
or when he harvests, he is called a harvester (yìzhě);
or when he prepares food and drink, he is called a food preparer (zuòshízhě);
when he works wood, he is called a craftsman (gōngjiàng);
when he forges gold and silver, he is called a gold and silver master (jīnyín shī);
in this way, one person has many names;
reality (fǎ) is also like this,
its reality is singular, yet it has many names.
To rely on the harmonious union of mother and father for birth is called the Mundane Truth (Shìdì);
to be born from the harmonious union of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yīnyuán) is called the Ultimate Truth (Dìyīyìdì).
Mánjúshīlì Púsà Móhēsà (Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Mahāsattva) addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
The truth (shídì) of which you speak,
what is its meaning?”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
That which is called the truth (Shídì) is named the genuine Dharma (Zhēnfǎ).
Good man!
If a Dharma is not genuine, it is not called the truth (Shídì).
Good man!
The truth (Shídì) is without confusion (diān) and without inversion (dǎo);
that which is without confusion or inversion is called the truth (Shídì).
Good man!
The truth (Shídì) is without falsehood or delusion (xūwàng);
if there is falsehood or delusion, it is not called the truth (Shídì).
Good man!
The truth (Shídì) is called the Mahāyāna (Dàshèng);
that which is not the Mahāyāna is not called the truth (Shídì).
Good man!
The truth (Shídì) is what the Buddha speaks, not what Māra (Mó) speaks;
if it is Māra’s (Mó) teaching and not the Buddha’s teaching,
it is not called the truth (Shídì).
Good man!
The truth (Shídì) is the single pure path (yīdào qīngjìng);
there is nothing dual about it.
Good man!
To possess permanence (yǒu cháng),
to possess bliss (yǒu lè),
to possess the self (yǒu wǒ),
and to possess purity (yǒu jìng):
this is called the meaning of the truth (Shídì).
Mánjúshīlì (Mañjuśrī) addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If genuine reality is taken as the truth (Shídì),
then the genuine reality (zhēnshí zhī fǎ) is the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
empty space (xūkōng),
and Buddha-Nature (Fóxìng).
If this is the case,
the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
empty space (xūkōng), and Buddha-Nature (Fóxìng) have no differences.
The *Fó* told *Wénshū Shīlì*:
“There is suffering (*kǔ*), there is the Truth (*dì*), there is the Reality (*shí*).
There is accumulation (*jí*), there is the Truth, there is the Reality.
There is extinction (*miè*), there is the Truth, there is the Reality.
There is the Path (*dào*), there is the Truth, there is the Reality.
Good man!
The *Rúlái* is neither suffering nor the Truth, but is Reality.
Empty space (*xūkōng*) is neither suffering nor the Truth, but is Reality.
*Fóxìng* (Buddha-nature) is neither suffering nor the Truth, but is Reality.
*Wénshū Shīlì*!
What is called suffering has the characteristic of impermanence (*wúcháng xiàng*),
it is a characteristic that can be severed,
this is called the True Reality (*shídì*).
The nature of the *Rúlái*
is not suffering,
is not impermanence,
is not a characteristic that can be severed,
therefore it is Reality.
Empty space,
*Fóxìng*,
are also like this.
Furthermore, good man!
What is called accumulation,
is what enables the five *yīn* (skandhas) to harmonize and arise,
it is also called suffering,
it is also called impermanence,
it is a characteristic that can be severed,
this is called the True Reality.
Good man!
The *Rúlái* is not the nature of accumulation,
is not the cause of the *yīn*,
is not a characteristic that can be severed,
therefore it is Reality.
Empty space,
*Fóxìng*,
are also like this.
Good man!
What is called extinction,
is named the extinction of afflictions (*fánnǎo miè*);
it is both permanence (*cháng*)
and impermanence.
What the Two Vehicles (*Èrshèng*) obtain is called impermanence;
what all *Fó* (Buddhas) obtain is then called permanence;
it is also called the verified *dharmas* (truths),
this is called the True Reality.
Good man!
The nature of the *Rúlái*
is not called extinction,
but it is able to extinguish afflictions.
It is neither permanence
nor impermanence,
it is not called verification and knowledge,
it resides permanently and is without change,
therefore it is Reality.
Empty space,
*Fóxìng*,
are also like this.
Good man!
The Path is able to sever afflictions;
it is both permanence
and impermanence,
it is a *dharma* that can be cultivated,
this is called the True Reality.
The *Rúlái* is not the Path,
but is able to sever afflictions;
it is neither permanence,
impermanence,
nor a *dharma* that can be cultivated,
it resides permanently and is unchanging,
therefore it is Reality.
Empty space,
*Fóxìng*,
are also like this.
“Furthermore, good man!
What is called True Reality (*zhēnshí*) is precisely the *Rúlái*;
the *Rúlái* is precisely True Reality.
True Reality is precisely empty space;
empty space is precisely True Reality.
True Reality is precisely *Fóxìng*;
*Fóxìng* is precisely True Reality.
*Wénshū Shīlì*!
There is suffering,
there is the cause of suffering,
there is the cessation of suffering,
there is the means to counter suffering.
The *Rúlái* is not suffering, nor is it the means to counter it;
therefore it is Reality, and is not called the Truth.
Empty space,
*Fóxìng*,
are also like this.
Suffering is conditioned (*yǒuwéi*),
contaminated (*yǒulòu*),
and without joy.
The *Rúlái* is not conditioned,
is not contaminated,
is clear and peaceful joy (*ānlè*);
it is Reality, not the Truth.
*Wénshū Shīlì* addressed the *Fó*, saying:
“World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*)!
According to what the *Fó* has said,
that which is not inverted is called the True Reality.
If so,
do the Four Truths (*sìdì*) contain the Four Inversions (*sìdǎo*) or not?
If they do,
how can it be said
that the absence of inversion is called the True Reality,
and that all inversions are not called Reality?”
The *Fó* told *Wénshū Shīlì*:
“All inversions
are included in the Truth of Suffering.
Just as when living beings
have an inverted mind,
this is called inversion.
Good man!
For example, if there is a person
who does not accept the instructions of their parents
or respected elders,
or who, though accepting them, cannot follow and practice them accordingly—
such people are called inverted.
Such inversion
is not non-suffering,
it is precisely suffering.
*Wénshū Shīlì* said:
“According to what the *Fó* has said,
that which is not false (*xūwàng*) is precisely the True Reality.
If so,
we should know that falsity is therefore not the True Reality.”
The *Fó* said:
“Good man!
All falsity is included in the Truth of Suffering.
Just as when a living being deceives others;
due to this condition and cause,
they fall into the hells (*dìyù*),
the animal realm (*chùshēng*),
or the hungry ghost realm (*ègǔi*).
Such *dharmas* are called falsity.
Such falsity
is not non-suffering,
it is precisely suffering.
The *Shēngwén* (Hearers), *Yuánjué* (Pratyekabuddhas),
and all *Fó*, the *Shìzūn*,
keep far away from and do not practice it,
hence it is called falsity.
Since such falsity
is what all *Fó* and the Two Vehicles sever and eliminate,
therefore the elimination is called the True Reality.”
*Wénshū Shīlì* said:
“According to what the *Fó* has said,
if the Great Vehicle (*Dàchéng*) is the True Reality,
we should know that the vehicle of the *Shēngwén*
and the *Pìzhīfó* (Pratyekabuddhas)
is then unreal.”
The *Fó* said:
“*Wénshū Shīlì*!
Those Two Vehicles
are both Reality
and unreality.
When the *Shēngwén* and *Yuánjué* sever all afflictions,
this is called Reality.
Impermanent,
non-abiding,
and being a *dharma* of transformation and change,
this is called unreality.”
*Wénshū Shīlì* said:
“According to what the *Fó* has said,
if what the *Fó* speaks is called Reality,
we should know that the speech of *Mó* (Māra) is then unreal.
*Shìzūn*!
Is what *Mó* speaks
included within the Noble Truths (*Shèngdì*) or not?”
The *Fó* said:
“*Wénshū Shīlì*!
What *Mó* speaks
is included in two Truths,
namely, Suffering and Accumulation.
In general, all non-*dharma*
and non-*vinaya* (precepts)
cannot enable people to obtain benefit.
Even if they proclaim it all day long,
there is no one
who sees suffering, severs accumulation,
verifies extinction, or cultivates the Path;
this is called falsity.
Such falsity
is called the speech of *Mó*.”
*Wénshū Shīlì* said:
“According to what the *Fó* has said,
there is one pure Path (*yīdào qīngjìng*),
without a second.
All the outside paths (*wàidào*) also say:
‘We have one path,
pure and without a second.’
If you say that the one Path is the True Reality,
what difference is there between it and those outside paths?
If there is no difference,
it should not be said that the one Path is pure.”
Fó said:
Noble son!
The various *wàidào* (external practitioners)
possess the truths of suffering (*Kǔ Dì*) and accumulation (*Jí Dì*),
but lack the truths of cessation (*Miè Dì*) and the path (*Dào Dì*).
In what is not cessation, they generate the thought of cessation,
in what is not the path, they generate the thought of the path,
in what is not the fruit, they generate the thought of the fruit,
in what is not the cause, they generate the thought of the cause,
for these reasons,
their path is neither pure, singular, nor non-dual.
said:
“As the Buddha has taught,
if permanence (cháng),
self (wǒ),
bliss (lè),
and purity (jìng) are the true meaning (ultimate reality),
then the various external paths (wai dòu) should possess true reality,
and the Dharma of the Buddha would not.
Why is this?
The followers of the various external paths also say:
'All formations (xíng) are permanent.
How are they permanent?
The desirable
and undesirable karmic retributions (yè bào),
etc., are received and not lost.
What is desirable is called the retribution for the Ten Virtues (shí shàn bào);
what is undesirable is the retribution for the Ten Non-Virtues (shí bù shàn bào).
If one says that all formations are entirely impermanent,
and the one who performs the action has already perished here,
who then receives the resulting retribution there?
Due to this meaning,
all formations are permanent.
Killing living beings (shā shēng) is called permanence due to its causal condition.
Bhagavān!
If one says that all formations are entirely impermanent,
the killer
and the killed
are both impermanent;
if they are impermanent,
who endures the sinful retribution in the hells (dì yù)?
If one definitely states that there is someone who receives retribution in hell,
then it should be known that all formations are truly not impermanent.
Bhagavān!
Focused and concentrated attention (xì xīn zhuān niàn) is also called permanence,
that which is contemplated for ten years, or even a hundred years, is not forgotten or lost;
therefore, it is permanent.
If it were impermanent,
who would remember or contemplate the things originally seen?
Due to this causal condition,
all formations are not impermanent.
Bhagavān!
All memory and thought (yì xiǎng) are also called permanence.
If someone first sees the physical features
of another person's hands,
feet,
head, neck, etc.,
and sees them again later,
they immediately recognize them.
If it were impermanent,
the original perception should have vanished.
Bhagavān!
Various undertakings,
when cultivated for a long time—
if one begins learning,
perhaps passing three years,
or perhaps passing five years—
and then becomes proficient,
this is called permanence.
Bhagavān!
The method of calculation (suàn shù zhī fă):
going from one to two,
from two to three, and extending up to hundreds or thousands.
If it were impermanent,
the initial 'one' should have vanished.
If the initial 'one' vanishes, who proceeds to two?
Thus, if the 'one' is permanent,
there is ultimately no 'two.'
Because the 'one' does not vanish,
one can proceed to two, and up to hundreds or thousands.
Therefore, it is permanent.
Bhagavān!
Like the method of recitation and reading:
reciting the first Āhán up to the second Āhán,
and extending to the third
and fourth Āhán.
If it were impermanent,
the recitation would ultimately not reach the fourth.
Because this reading and recitation
increase due to causal conditions,
it is called permanence.
Bhagavān!
Vases, clothing, carriages,
debt carried by a person,
the forms and features of the great earth,
mountains, rivers, trees, forests,
medicinal plants, wood, grass, and leaves,
and the healing of sicknesses for sentient beings—
all of these are permanent,
and likewise.
Bhagavān!
All external paths declare this:
'All formations are permanent,
and if they are permanent, then they are True Reality (shí dì).'
Bhagavān,
there are external paths that further state that there is bliss (lè).
How is this known?
Because the recipient definitely obtains desirable retribution.
Bhagavān!
Whoever receives bliss certainly obtains it—
namely, Dàfàntiānwáng (Mahābrahmā),
Dàzìzàitiān (Maheśvara),
Shìdì Huán Yīn (Sakra Devānām Indra),
Píniǔtiān (Viṣṇu), and all humans and devas.
Due to this meaning,
it is named 'definite existence of bliss.'
Bhagavān!
There are external paths that further state there is bliss,
because it enables sentient beings
to generate seeking and expectation.
The hungry seek food,
the thirsty seek drink,
the cold seek warmth,
the hot seek coolness,
the weary seek rest,
the sick seek recovery,
those desiring seek forms (sensuality).
If there were no bliss, why would they seek it?
Because there are seekers,
we know there is bliss.
Bhagavān!
There are external paths that further make this statement:
giving (shī) can obtain bliss.
People in the world
enjoy giving to śramanas,
various brāhmaṇas,
and the poor and suffering,
giving clothing,
food and drink,
bedding, medicine,
elephants, horses, carriages,
powdered incense, perfumed unguents,
various flowers, houses,
and providing lamps and light.
They perform various acts of generosity like these,
hoping to receive desirable retribution in a future life.
Therefore, it should be known that there is definitely bliss.
Bhagavān!
There are external paths that further make this statement:
it should be known there is bliss due to causal conditions.
That is, because the recipient of bliss has causal conditions,
it is called pleasurable contact (lè chù).
If there were no bliss,
how could its causal conditions arise?
Just as if there are no rabbit horns (tù jiǎo),
then there are no causal conditions for them.
Since there are causal conditions for bliss,
then we know there is bliss.
Bhagavān!
There are external paths that further make this statement:
it should be known there is bliss
because of the superior, middle, and inferior classifications.
The inferior recipient of bliss is Shìdì Huán Yīn;
the middle recipient of bliss is Dàfàntiānwáng;
the superior recipient of bliss is Dàzìzàitiān.
Since there are such superior, middle, and inferior degrees,
it should be known that there is bliss.
Bhagavān,
there are external paths that further state there is purity (jìng).
Why is this?
If there were no purity,
desire should not arise.
If desire arises,
then it should be known there is purity.
Furthermore, they state that
gold, silver, precious jewels,
lapis lazuli (liúlí), crystal (pōlí),
giant clamshell (chēqú), agate (mǎnǎo),
coral (shānhú), true pearls (zhēnzhū),
jades (bì yù), nacreous shells (kē bèi),
running springs, bathing ponds,
food, drink, clothing,
flowers, fragrance, powdered incense, perfumed unguents,
and the light of lamps and candles—
objects such as these are all Dharma of Purity (jìng fă).
Furthermore, there is purity,
which is said to be the Five Aggregates (wǔ yīn);
these are pure vessels containing various pure objects,
namely, humans and devas,
various immortals (xiān),
Arhats (Āluóhàn),
Pratyekabuddhas (Pìzhīfó),
Bodhisattvas (Púsà),
and all Buddhas.
Due to this meaning, it is called purity.
Bhagavān!
There are external paths that further state there is a self (wǒ),
because there is something that observes and is capable of action.
For example, when someone
enters a potter's house,
although they do not see the body of the potter,
by seeing the wheel and the cord, they definitely know
that the house must belong to a potter.
The self (wǒ) is also like this:
once the eye sees forms,
one must know that the self exists.
If there were no self,
who would be able to see forms,
hear
sounds, or even feel touch?
This is also the case for Dharma (mental objects).
Furthermore, there is a self (ātman).
How is this known?
It is known by means of signs.
What are these signs?
Breathing and blinking,
lifetime and the function of the mind,
experiencing all suffering and joy,
greed and seeking (tānqiú),
and hatred (chēnhuì).
Phenomena such as these,
are all signs of the self.
Therefore, one should know that the self definitely exists.
Furthermore, there is a self,
because it can distinguish tastes.
When a person eats a fruit,
they see and know its taste.
Therefore, one should know that the self definitely exists.
Furthermore, there is a self.
How is it known?
Because it holds and performs actions.
Holding a sickle allows cutting,
holding an axe allows chopping,
holding a vase allows water storage,
holding the reins (or the vehicle) allows driving.
Such activities as these,
the self holding (these implements) can perform.
One should know that the self definitely exists.
Furthermore, there is a self.
How is it known?
Immediately upon birth,
there is the desire to obtain milk (or nourishment),
relying on previous habits.
Therefore, one should know that the self definitely exists.
Furthermore, there is a self.
How is it known?
Because combination benefits other sentient beings.
For example, a vase or clothes,
chariots (vehicles), fields, and houses,
mountains, forests, and trees,
elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep:
If such things are combined,
they bring benefit.
These internal Five Skandhas (Wǔyīn) are also like this.
Because the organs, such as the eyes, are combined,
they benefit the self.
Therefore, one should know that the self definitely exists.
Furthermore, there is a self.
How is it known?
Because there is the phenomenon of obstruction.
If there is an object,
then there is obstruction and hindrance.
If the object is nonexistent,
then there is no obstruction.
If there is obstruction, then we know there is a self.
Therefore, one should know that the self definitely exists.
Furthermore, there is a self.
How is it known?
Because of companion and non-companion.
Relatives and non-relatives are not companions.
The True Dharma (Zhèngfǎ),
and the False Dharma (Xiéfǎ) are also not companions.
Wisdom and non-wisdom are also not companions.
A Śrāmaṇa (Shāmén),
and a non-Śrāmaṇa.
A Brāhmaṇa (Bóluómén),
and a non-Brāhmaṇa.
Son,
and non-son.
Day,
and non-day.
Night,
and non-night.
Self,
and non-self.
Phenomena such as these,
are companions and non-companions.
Therefore, one should know that the self definitely exists.
O Bhagavān (Shìzūn)!
The various external practitioners (wàidào) assert in many ways:
Existence of permanence (cháng),
joy (lè),
self (wǒ),
and purity (jìng).
One should know that permanence, joy, self, and purity definitely exist.
O Bhagavān!
Because of this principle,
these external practitioners can also say,
“I possess the ultimate truth (zhēndì).”
The Buddha (Fó) said:
“Good man!
If there is a Śrāmaṇa (Shāmén),
or a Brāhmaṇa (Bóluómén),
who holds permanence,
who holds joy,
who holds purity,
and who holds a self,
then they are not a Śrāmaṇa (Shāmén),
nor a Brāhmaṇa (Bóluómén).
Why is this?
They are deluded about life and death (saṃsāra),
because they are separated from the great guide who possesses all wisdom.
Such Śrāmaṇas (Shāmén),
and Brāhmaṇas (Bóluómén),
are submerged in all desires,
and virtuous dharmas (shànfǎ) are diminished and damaged.
These external practitioners (wàidào),
are bound in the prison of greed (tānyù),
hatred (chēnhuì),
and delusion (chīyù),
which they endure,
and enjoy.
Although these external practitioners know that they create and experience the results of their own karma (yèguǒ),
they still cannot keep away from evil dharmas (èfǎ).
These external practitioners,
do not live by the True Dharma (Zhèngfǎ),
or right livelihood (zhèngmìng).
Why is this?
Because they lack the fire of wisdom (zhìhuì) that can burn them away.
Although these external practitioners desire and cling to the supreme and wonderful five desires (wǔyù),
they are poor in virtuous dharmas (shànfǎ),
because they do not diligently cultivate them.
Although these external practitioners wish to attain genuine liberation (zhèngjiětuō),
their foundation of holding the precepts is incomplete.
Although these external practitioners seek joy,
they cannot seek the causes and conditions of joy.
Although these external practitioners hate and despise all suffering,
yet their actions,
cannot keep them away from the causes and conditions of suffering.
Although these external practitioners are entangled by the four great poisonous snakes (sìdà),
they still act recklessly,
and cannot be cautious.
These external practitioners are covered by ignorance (wúmíng),
are far from good friends (shànyǒu),
and delight in staying within the great, fiercely burning, impermanent fire of the three realms (sānjiè),
and cannot escape.
These external practitioners,
encounter the diseases of defilements (fánnǎo) that are difficult to cure,
yet they do not seek the great wise physician.
These external practitioners,
will in the future travel an endless, perilous, and distant road,
but they do not know how to practice the provisions of virtuous dharmas (shànfǎ) to adorn themselves.
These external practitioners are constantly harmed by the calamity and poison of lust (yínyù),
yet they cling to the frost-poison of the five desires (wǔyù).
These external practitioners have rampant hatred (chēnhuì),
yet they instead repeatedly approach evil friends (èyǒu).
These external practitioners are constantly obscured and covered by ignorance (wúmíng),
yet they instead seek after perverse and evil dharmas.
These external practitioners are constantly deceived and misled by wrong views (xiéjiàn),
yet they instead conceive friendly thoughts within them.
These external practitioners fear eating sweet fruit,
but sow bitter seeds.
These external practitioners are already residing in the dark room of defilements (fánnǎo),
yet they instead distance themselves from the illuminating torch of great wisdom.
These external practitioners suffer from the thirst of defilements (fánnǎo),
yet they repeatedly drink the salty water of various desires.
These external practitioners drift and sink in the boundless great river of life and death (saṃsāra),
yet they repeatedly distance themselves from the unsurpassed Boat Master.
These external practitioners are confused and deluded,
claiming that all conditioned things (xíng) are permanent.
If conditioned things were permanent,
this would be impossible.”
“Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
I observe that all conditioned phenomena (zhūxíng) are entirely impermanent (wúcháng).
How is this known
to be so?
Because of causes and conditions (yīnyuán).
If phenomena arise from conditions,
then they are known to be impermanent.
Among these external paths (wàidào), there is not a single phenomenon (fǎ) that does not arise from conditions.
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Buddhahood (Fóxìng) is without arising (wúshēng),
without cessation (wúmiè),
without going (wúqù),
without coming (wúlái),
is not past (fēiguòqù),
is not future (fēiwèilái),
is not present (fēixiànzài),
is not made by cause (fēiyīn suǒzuò),
is not made without cause (fēiwúyīnzuò),
is not action (fēizuò),
is not agent (fēizuòzhě),
is not mark (fēixiāng),
is not unmarked (fēiwúxiāng),
is not having name (fēiyǒumíng),
is not nameless (fēiwúmíng),
is not name (fēimíng),
is not form (fēisè),
is not long (fēicháng),
is not short (fēiduǎn),
is not contained and upheld by the aggregates (yīn), spheres (jiè), or bases (rù) (yīn jiè rù zhī suǒ shèchí).
Therefore, it is called permanence (cháng).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Buddhahood (Fóxìng) is precisely the Tathāgata (Rúlái);
the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is precisely the Dharma (Fǎ);
the Dharma (Fǎ) is precisely permanence (cháng).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Permanence (cháng) is precisely the Tathāgata (Rúlái);
the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is precisely the Saṅgha (Sēng);
the Saṅgha (Sēng) is precisely permanence (cháng).
Because of this meaning,
phenomena (fǎ) that arise from causes
are not called permanent.
Among these external paths (wàidào), there is not a single phenomenon
that does not arise from causes.
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
These external paths (wàidào) do not see Buddhahood (Fóxìng),
the Tathāgata (Rúlái), and the Dharma (Fǎ).
Therefore, the words spoken by the external paths (wàidào)
are entirely false speech (wàngyǔ),
and possess no ultimate truth (zhēndì).
All ordinary people (fánfú rén),
first seeing jars and clothes (píng yī),
carriages and vehicles (chēchéng), houses and dwellings (shèzhái),
cities and walls (chéngguō), rivers and water (héshuǐ),
mountains and forests (shānlín), men and women (nánnǚ),
elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep (xiàngmǎniúyáng),
and afterwards seeing similar things,
thereupon claim that they are permanent.
You should know that in reality,
they are not permanent.
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
All conditioned phenomena (yīqiè yǒu wéi)
are impermanent (wúcháng);
the unconditioned nature of space (xūkōng wú wéi) is therefore permanent (cháng);
the unconditioned nature of Buddhahood (Fóxìng wú wéi) is therefore permanent (cháng).
Space (xūkōng) is precisely Buddhahood (Fóxìng);
Buddhahood (Fóxìng) is precisely the Tathāgata (Rúlái);
the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is precisely the unconditioned (wúwéi);
the unconditioned (wúwéi) is precisely permanence (cháng).
Permanence (cháng) is precisely the Dharma (Fǎ);
the Dharma (Fǎ) is precisely the Saṅgha (Sēng);
the Saṅgha (Sēng) is precisely the unconditioned (wúwéi);
the unconditioned (wúwéi) is precisely permanence (cháng).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Conditioned phenomena (yǒuwéi zhī fǎ)
are generally of two kinds:
form-phenomena (sèfǎ)
and non-form-phenomena (fēisèfǎ).
Non-form-phenomena (fēisèfǎ)
are mind (xīn) and mental factors (xīn shù fǎ).
Form-phenomena (sèfǎ)
are earth (dì),
water (shuǐ),
fire (huǒ),
and wind (fēng).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Mind (xīn) is called impermanent (wúcháng).
Why is this?
Because its nature (xìng) is the characteristic of clinging and conditioning (pānyuán xiāng),
and thus it should be differentiated.
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The nature of eye-consciousness (yǎnshì) is different,
and similarly, the nature of mental consciousness (yìshì) is different;
therefore, they are impermanent (wúcháng).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The sphere of form (sè jìngjiè) is different,
and similarly, the sphere of phenomena (fǎ jìngjiè) is different;
therefore, they are impermanent (wúcháng).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The correlation of eye-consciousness (yǎnshì xiāngyīng) is different,
and similarly, the correlation of mental consciousness (yìshì xiāngyīng) is different;
therefore, they are impermanent (wúcháng).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
If the mind (xīn) were permanent (cháng),
then eye-consciousness (yǎnshì) alone ought to cognize all phenomena (fǎ).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
If eye-consciousness (yǎnshì) is different, and similarly, mental consciousness (yìshì) is different,
then it is known that they are impermanent (wúcháng).
Because the phenomena (fǎ) are similar,
arising and ceasing moment by moment (niàn niàn shēng miè),
when ordinary people (fánfū) see them,
they mistakenly take them for permanence (cháng).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The characteristics of causes and conditions (zhū yīnyuán xiāng),
since they can be destroyed,
are also called impermanent (wúcháng).
For example, relying on the eye (yīn yǎn),
relying on form (yīn sè),
relying on light (yīn míng),
and relying on thought (yīn sīwéi),
eye-consciousness (yǎnshì) arises.
When ear-consciousness (ěrshì) arises,
the causes relied upon are each different,
and are not the causes and conditions of eye-consciousness (yǎnshì yīnyuán).
Likewise, the difference in mental consciousness (yìshì) is also like this.
"Furthermore, good son!
Because the causes and conditions that destroy various formations are different,
the mind is called impermanent.
Specifically, the mind cultivating impermanence is distinct,
and the mind cultivating suffering,
emptiness,
and non-self is distinct.
If the mind were permanent,
it should always cultivate impermanence,
but it would not even be able to contemplate suffering,
emptiness,
or non-self,
much less be able to contemplate permanence,
joy,
self, and purity?
For this reason,
the doctrines of the Wàidào [Tīrthikas]
cannot embrace permanence, joy, self, and purity.
Good son!
You should know that the mental dharma is certainly impermanent.
Furthermore, good son!
Because the nature of the mind is diverse,
it is called impermanent.
Specifically, the mental nature of the Shēngwén [Śrāvakas] is distinct,
the mental nature of the Yuánjué [Pratyekabuddhas] is distinct,
and the mental nature of the various Fó is distinct.
The minds of all Wàidào have three types:
first, the mind of one who has left home (chūjiā xīn);
second, the mind of one who resides at home (zàijiā xīn);
third, the mind of one who is detached while residing at home (zàijiā yuǎnlí xīn).
The mind associated with joy is distinct,
the mind associated with suffering is distinct,
the mind associated with neither suffering nor joy is distinct,
the mind associated with greed is distinct,
the mind associated with hatred is distinct,
and the mind associated with delusion is distinct.
The mental characteristics of all Wàidào are also distinct,
specifically, the mind associated with delusion is distinct,
the mind associated with doubt is distinct,
the mind associated with wrong views is distinct,
and their minds are also distinct regarding their advancing, stopping, and deportment.
Good son!
If the mind were permanent,
it would also be unable to distinguish various colors,
namely, blue, yellow, red, white, and purple.
Good son!
If the mind were permanent,
the things one remembers should not be forgotten.
Good son!
If the mind were permanent,
whatever is read and recited should not increase.
Furthermore, good son!
If the mind were permanent,
one should not speak of 'already done,'
'doing now,'
or 'will do.'
If there are 'already done,'
'doing now,'
and 'will do,'
you should know that this mind is certainly impermanent.
Good son!
If the mind were permanent,
then there would be no enemies,
friends,
non-enemies,
or non-friends.
If the mind were permanent,
then one should not speak of 'my possessions,'
or 'his possessions,'
whether dead,
or alive.
If the mind were permanent,
although there are actions performed,
they should not increase.
Good son!
For this reason,
you should know that the nature of the mind is distinct in each case,
and because there are distinctions, you should know it is impermanent.
"Good son!
I have now explained impermanence
concerning these non-form dharmas,
and the meaning is already clear.
I shall now explain to you the impermanence of form (sè).
This form is impermanent,
originally non-existent before being born,
because having been born, it ceases.
When the internal body is in the womb during the Gēluólúo [Kālalā] stage,
it was originally unborn,
because having been born, it changes;
external sprouts and stems,
were also originally unborn,
because having been born, they change;
therefore, you should know that all dharmas of form,
are entirely impermanent.
Good son!
All internal forms
change according to the time:
the time of the Gēluólúo stage is distinct,
the time of the Ānfútuó stage is distinct,
the time of the Qié'nà stage is distinct,
the time of the Bìshǒu stage is distinct,
the time of the limbs (zhū pào) stage is distinct,
the time of initial birth is distinct,
the time of infancy is distinct,
the time of childhood is distinct,
and even up to the time of old age, they are all distinct and changing.
External forms are also like this:
the sprout is distinct,
the stem is distinct,
the branch is distinct,
the leaf is distinct,
the flower is distinct,
and the fruit is distinct.
Furthermore, good son!
The internal flavor is also distinct;
from the time of the Gēluólúo stage up to the time of old age,
they are all distinctly changing.
The external flavor is also like this:
the flavor of the sprout,
stem,
branch,
leaf,
flower,
and fruit is distinct.
The strength during the Gēluólúo stage is distinct,
and the strength up to the time of old age is distinct.
The appearance during the Gēluólúo stage is distinct,
and the appearance up to the time of old age is also distinct.
The karmic fruition (guǒbào) during the Gēluólúo stage is distinct,
and the guǒbào up to the time of old age is also distinct.
The name during the Gēluólúo stage is distinct,
and the name up to the time of old age is also distinct.
Specifically, internal forms,
having been destroyed, recombine,
thus we know they are impermanent.
External trees and wood
also, having been destroyed, recombine,
thus we know they are impermanent.
They arise gradually and successively,
thus we know they are impermanent.
Successive arising from the Gēluólúo stage up to the time of old age,
successive arising from the sprout up to the fruit,
thus we know they are impermanent.
All forms are capable of ceasing,
thus we know they are impermanent.
The time of cessation for the Gēluólúo stage is distinct,
and the time of cessation up to old age is distinct.
The time of cessation for the sprout is distinct up to the time of cessation for the fruit,
thus we know they are impermanent.
Ordinary unenlightened beings (fánfū) are ignorant;
seeing similar successive arising,
they reckon it to be permanent.
For this reason,
it is called impermanent.
If it is impermanent, it is suffering (kǔ);
if it is kǔ, it is impure.
"Good son!
Because Jiāshè previously inquired about this matter,
I have already replied to him about it."
“Furthermore, good man!
All conditioned phenomena are without self.
Good man!
To summarize all phenomena,
they are called form [sè]
and non-form [fēi sè].
Form is not the self.
Why is this?
Because it can be broken,
it can be destroyed,
it can be torn apart,
it can be struck,
and it undergoes generation and growth.
The self, however, cannot be broken, destroyed,
torn apart, or struck,
nor does it undergo generation and growth.
For this reason,
we know that form is not the self.
The phenomenon of non-form is likewise not the self.
Why is this?
Because it arises from causes and conditions.
Good man!
If the various external paths [wàidào] claim that by focused mindfulness [zhuānniàn],
they know the existence of the self,
the nature of focused mindfulness is actually not the self.
If focused mindfulness is taken as the nature of the self,
then past events would be subject to forgetfulness.
Since there is forgetfulness, we definitely know there is no self.
Good man!
If the various external paths know the existence of the self based on recollection and thought [yìxiǎng],
since there is non-recollection and non-thought, we definitely know there is no self.
Just as when seeing a person with six fingers on their hand,
one immediately asks them:
‘Where did I see you before?’
If there were a self,
one should not have to ask again.
Because one asks,
we definitely know there is no self.
Good man!
If the various external paths, based on having a negation [zhē],
know the existence of the self,
good man!
Because there is negation,
we definitely know there is no self.
For example, one says Dàidá [Dèvadatta],
and never declares 'non-Dàidá'.
The self is also like this:
if it were definitely the self,
it would never negate the self.
Because the self is negated,
we definitely know there is no self.
If, based on negation,
one knows the existence of the self,
since you do not negate now,
then there should definitely be no self.
Good man!
If the various external paths,
based on the concepts of companion [bàn] and non-companion [fēi bàn], know the existence of the self,
then, due to the absence of a companion,
there should be no self.
There are phenomena without companions,
such as the Tathāgata [Rúlái],
empty space [xūkōng],
and the Buddha-nature [Fóxìng].
The self is also like this; it truly has no companion.
For this reason,
we definitely know there is no self.
Furthermore, good man!
If the various external paths, based on a name [míngzi],
know the existence of the self,
even within phenomena that are without self,
there is the name 'self',
just as a poor and humble person is named 'Wealthy and Noble'.
For example, when one says 'I die',
if the self dies,
then the self kills the self.
But the self is truly unkillable;
it is falsely named 'killing the self'.
It is also like a short person [cuórén]
being named 'Elder' [zhǎngzhě].
For this reason,
we definitely know there is no self.
“Furthermore, good man!
If the various external paths,
based on the newborn seeking milk, know the existence of the self,
good man!
If there were a self,
all infants should not grasp at feces,
fire, snakes,
or poison.
For this reason,
we definitely know there is no self.
Furthermore, good man!
All sentient beings possess equal wisdom [děng zhì]
regarding three phenomena,
namely lust [yínyù],
eating and drinking, and fear [kǒngbù].
Therefore, there is no self.
Furthermore, good man!
If the various external paths, based on characteristics [xiàngmào],
know the existence of the self,
good man!
Based on characteristics, there is no self,
and based on non-characteristics, there is also no self.
When a person is asleep,
they cannot advance or stop,
bend down or look up or blink [shùn],
nor are they aware of suffering or happiness,
so there should be no self.
If, based on advancing and stopping,
bending down, looking up, and blinking,
one knows the existence of the self,
then a wooden mechanism [jīguān mùrén] should also possess a self.
Good man!
The Tathāgata is also like this:
neither advancing
nor stopping,
neither bending down
nor looking up,
neither looking
nor blinking,
neither suffering
nor happy,
neither greedy
nor hateful [huì],
neither deluded [chī],
nor acting [xíng].
The Tathāgata, being like this, truly has the self.
Furthermore, good man!
If the various external paths, based on seeing others eat fruit and saliva generating in one's mouth,
know the existence of the self,
good man!
It is due to recollection [yìniàn]
that seeing generates saliva,
and saliva is not the self.
The self is also not saliva,
not joy [xǐ] nor sorrow [bēi],
not yawning [qiàn] nor laughing [xiào],
not sleeping nor rising,
not hungry nor full.
For this reason,
we definitely know there is no self.
“Good man!
These external paths are foolish, like little children;
they lack wisdom and skillful means [fāngbiàn].
They cannot comprehend the permanent and the impermanent,
suffering and happiness,
the pure and the impure,
self and non-self,
life and non-life,
sentient being and non-sentient being,
real and non-real,
existent and non-existent.
They take a small portion of the Buddhadharma [Fófǎ],
and falsely assert the existence of the permanent,
joy,
self,
and purity,
yet they truly do not know the permanent, joy, self, or purity.
It is like a person born blind who does not recognize the color of milk.
He then asks others:
‘What is the color of milk like?’
Another person answers:
‘It is white, like a shell [bèi].’
The blind person asks again:
‘Is the color of milk like the sound of a shell?’
The answer is:
‘No.’
He asks again:
‘Then what is the color of a shell like?’
The answer is:
‘It is like rice flour [dàomǐ mò].’
The blind person asks again:
‘Is the color of milk soft like rice flour?
And what is rice flour like?’
The answer is:
‘It is like falling snow.’
The blind person asks again:
‘Is that rice flour cold like snow?
And what is snow like?’
The answer is:
‘It is like a white crane [báihè].’
Although this person born blind hears these four kinds of analogies,
he can ultimately never recognize the true color of milk.
These external paths are also like this;
they can ultimately never recognize the permanent, joy, self, or purity.
Good man!
For this reason,
in my Buddhadharma, there is true ultimate reality [zhēnshí dì],
not among the external paths.”
Wénshū Shīlì [Mañjuśrī] said to the Buddha:
“Rare is this, World-Honored One [Shìzūn]!
The Tathāgata, now facing parinirvāṇa [bōnièpán],
is instead setting in motion the unsurpassed Dharma Wheel [Fǎlún],
and thus performing such discrimination of ultimate reality [zhēndì].”
The Fó told Wénshūshīlì:
"Why is it that you now harbor the notion of Nirvāṇa concerning the Rúlái?
Good man!
The Rúlái is truly permanent, abiding, and unchanging,
and does not enter into parinirvāṇa.
Good man!
If there were one who calculated (thought): 'I am the Fó,'
'I achieved Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.'
'I am the Dharma,'
'The Dharma belongs to me.'
'I am the Way,'
'The Way belongs to me.'
'I am the Shìzūn,'
'The Shìzūn belongs to me.'
'I am the Shēngwén,'
'The Shēngwén belongs to me.'
'I am able to preach the Dharma,'
'Causing others to hear and receive it,'
'I turn the Dharma Wheel,'
'Others cannot.'
The Rúlái certainly does not make such calculations;
therefore, the Rúlái does not turn the Dharma Wheel.
Good man!
If there were one who made such a false calculation:
'I am the eye,'
'The eye belongs to me,'
the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also like this.
'I am form,'
'Form belongs to me,'
and even phenomena are also like this.
'I am earth,'
'Earth belongs to me,'
water, fire, wind, and so forth are also like this.
Good man!
If there were one who said:
'I am faith,'
'Faith belongs to me.'
'I am great learning,'
'Great learning belongs to me.'
'I am Dánbōluómì,'
'Dánbōluómì belongs to me.'
'I am Shīpōluómì,'
'Shīpōluómì belongs to me.'
'I am Chàntíbōluómì,'
'Chàntíbōluómì belongs to me.'
'I am Pílìyēbōluómì,'
'Pílìyēbōluómì belongs to me.'
'I am Chánbōluómì,'
'Chánbōluómì belongs to me.'
'I am Bōrěbōluómì,'
'Bōrěbōluómì belongs to me.'
'I am the Four Foundations of Mindfulness,'
'The Four Foundations of Mindfulness belong to me.'
The Four Proper Exertions,
the Four Bases of Supernatural Power,
the Five Faculties and Five Powers,
the Seven Factors of Enlightenment and the Eightfold Noble Path,
are also like this.
Good man!
The Rúlái certainly does not make such calculations;
therefore, the Rúlái does not turn the Dharma Wheel.
Good man!
If it is said that [the Rúlái] is permanent, abiding, and without change,
how can it be said that the Fó turns the Dharma Wheel?
Therefore, you should not now say
that the Rúlái is currently turning the Dharma Wheel.
"Good man!
For example, relying on the eye,
relying on form,
relying on light,
relying on deliberation,
when the conditions and causes harmonize and unite,
visual consciousness is produced.
Good man!
The eye does not think,
'I can produce consciousness';
form, down to deliberation,
certainly does not think, 'I produce visual consciousness,'
and visual consciousness likewise does not think,
'I can produce myself.'
Good man!
Such phenomena,
when causes and conditions harmonize and unite,
are called 'seeing.'
Good man!
The Rúlái is also like this:
relying on the Six Pāramitās,
and the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment,
awakening to and understanding all phenomena,
and further relying on the throat,
tongue, teeth, lips, and mouth,
speech and sound,
preached the Dharma initially for Jiāochénrú,
which is called turning the Dharma Wheel.
For this reason,
the Rúlái is not called the turner of the Dharma Wheel.
"Good man!
If it is not turned,
then it is called the Dharma,
and the Dharma is the Rúlái.
Good man!
For example, relying on the fire drill,
relying on the boring stick,
relying on the hand,
relying on dry cow dung,
fire is produced.
The fire drill does not say, 'I can produce fire,'
the boring stick, hand, and cow dung each do not think, 'I can produce fire,'
and the fire also does not say, 'I can produce myself.'
The Rúlái is also like this:
relying on the Six Pāramitās,
down to Jiāochénrú,
[the result] is called turning the Dharma Wheel.
The Rúlái also does not give rise to the thought,
'I turn the Dharma Wheel.'
"Good man!
If it does not arise,
this is called the turning of the True Dharma Wheel,
and this turning of the Dharma Wheel
is called the Rúlái.
Good man!
For example, relying on curds,
relying on water,
relying on churning,
relying on the jar,
relying on the rope,
relying on being held by a person's hand,
butter is produced.
The curds do not think, 'I can produce butter,'
down to the person's hand, which also does not think, 'I can produce butter,'
and the butter also does not say, 'I can produce myself.'
The assemblage of conditions harmonizes,
and thus butter is produced.
The Rúlái is also like this,
certainly not thinking, 'I turn the Dharma Wheel.'
"Good man!
If it is not produced,
this is called the turning of the True Dharma Wheel,
and this turning of the Dharma Wheel is the Rúlái.
Good man!
For example, relying on the seed,
relying on the earth,
relying on the water,
relying on the fire,
relying on the wind,
relying on the manure,
relying on the season,
relying on human labor,
a sprout is produced.
Good man!
The seed does not say, 'I can produce the sprout,'
down to the labor, which also does not think, 'I can produce the sprout,'
and the sprout also does not say, 'I can produce myself.'
The Rúlái is also like this,
certainly not thinking,
'I turn the Dharma Wheel.'
"Good man!
If there is no ability (agency),
this is called the turning of the True Dharma Wheel,
and this turning of the Dharma Wheel is the Rúlái.
Good man!
For example, relying on the drum,
relying on space,
relying on the skin,
relying on the person,
and relying on the drumstick harmonizing to produce sound,
the drum does not think, 'I can produce sound,'
down to the drumstick, which is also like this,
and the sound also does not say, 'I can produce myself.'
Good man!
The Rúlái is also like this,
certainly not thinking, 'I turn the Dharma Wheel.'
Good man!
The turning of the Dharma Wheel is called non-action,
and non-action is the turning of the Dharma Wheel.
The turning of the Dharma Wheel is the Rúlái.
Good man!
The turning of the Dharma Wheel is the realm of all Fós and Shìzūns,
and is not known by the Shēngwén or Yuánjué.
Good man!
Empty space is not born,
does not arise,
is not made,
is not created,
and is not conditioned phenomena.
The Rúlái is also like this:
not born,
does not arise,
is not made,
is not created,
and is not conditioned phenomena.
Just as the nature of the Rúlái is,
so too is the Fó-nature:
not born,
does not arise,
is not made,
is not created,
and is not conditioned phenomena.
"Good man!
The Bhagavāns (Shìzūn) have two kinds of discourses:
First, worldly discourse (shìyǔ);
Second, transcendental discourse (chūshìyǔ).
Good man!
The Rúlái speaks the worldly discourse for the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué),
and speaks the transcendental discourse for the Bodhisattvas (Púsà).
Good man!
Furthermore, these great assemblies have two kinds:
First, those who seek the Lesser Vehicle (Xiǎochéng);
Second, those who seek the Great Vehicle (Dàchéng).
In former days, in the city of Bōluónài (Vārāṇasī),
I turned the Dharma Wheel (fǎlún) for the Śrāvakas;
now I begin here in the city of Jūshīnà (Kuśinagara),
turning the Great Dharma Wheel (Dàfǎlún) for the Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, good man!
There are also two kinds of people:
those of middle capacity (zhōnggēn),
and those of superior capacity (shànggēn).
For those of middle capacity,
I turned the Dharma Wheel in Bōluónài;
For those of superior capacity,
the Elephant Kings among men,
such as Jiāshè Púsà (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva),
I am now here in the city of Jūshīnà,
turning the Great Dharma Wheel.
Good man!
The Rúlái never turns the Dharma Wheel for those of extremely low capacity (jí xiàgēn),
and those of extremely low capacity are the Icchantikas (Yīchǎntí).
Furthermore, good man!
There are also two kinds of seekers of the Buddha Way:
First, those of moderate exertion (zhōng jīngjìn),
second, those of superior exertion (shàng jīngjìn).
In Bōluónài,
I turned the Dharma Wheel for those of moderate exertion;
now here in the city of Jūshīnà,
I turn the Great Dharma Wheel for those of superior exertion.
Furthermore, good man!
When I first turned the Dharma Wheel in that city of Bōluónài in the past,
eighty thousand devas and humans attained the fruit of Sūtuóhuán (Sotāpanna);
now here in the city of Jūshīnà,
eighty myriad (800,000,000,000,000) people achieved non-retrogression from Anòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi).
Furthermore, good man!
In the city of Bōluónài,
the Great Brahmā King (Dà Fàntiānwáng) bowed his head and requested me to turn the Dharma Wheel;
now here in the city of Jūshīnà,
Jiāshè Púsà bows his head and requests me to turn the Great Dharma Wheel.
Furthermore, good man!
When I turned the Dharma Wheel in that city of Bōluónài in the past,
I taught impermanence (wúcháng),
suffering (kǔ),
emptiness (kōng),
and non-self (wúwǒ);
now, when turning the Dharma Wheel here in the city of Jūshīnà,
I teach permanence (cháng),
bliss (lè),
self (wǒ),
and purity (jìng).
"Furthermore, good man!
When I turned the Dharma Wheel in that city of Bōluónài in the past,
the sound produced reached the heavens of Fàntiān (Brahmā);
when the Rúlái now turns the Dharma Wheel in the city of Jūshīnà,
the sound produced
pervades the worlds of all Buddhas in the East equal to twenty times the sands of the Gangā River (Hénghéshā),
and in the South, West, and North,
the four intermediate directions, above and below,
it is likewise thus.
Furthermore, good man!
Everything that all Buddhas, the Bhagavāns, preach,
is entirely called the turning of the Dharma Wheel.
Good man!
For example, the Wheel Treasure (lúnbǎo) possessed by a Cakravartin King (Shèngwáng),
can subdue those who have not yet submitted,
and can bring peace to those who have already submitted.
Good man!
The Dharma preached by all Buddhas, the Bhagavāns,
is likewise thus:
those with immeasurable afflictions (fánnǎo) who have not yet been tamed,
are enabled to be tamed,
and those who have already been tamed are caused to generate wholesome roots (shàngēn).
Good man!
For example, the Wheel Treasure possessed by a Cakravartin King
is able to eliminate all enemies and robbers.
The Rúlái’s exposition of the Dharma is likewise thus;
it enables all thieves of affliction
to become completely tranquil.
Furthermore, good man!
For example, the Wheel Treasure possessed by a Cakravartin King
revolves both downward and upward.
The Rúlái’s teaching of the Dharma is likewise thus:
it enables all evil sentient beings in the lower destinies,
to ascend and be reborn among humans and devas, and even attain the Buddha Way (Fódào).
Good man!
Therefore, you should not now praise, saying,
'The Rúlái is turning the Dharma Wheel again here.'
At that time, Wénshū Shīlì (Mañjuśrī) said to the Buddha:
"Bhagavān!
It is not that I do not understand this meaning;
the reason I ask
is because I wish to benefit sentient beings.
Bhagavān!
I have long known that the turning of the Dharma Wheel
is truly the realm (jìngjiè) of the Buddhas and Rúláis,
and is not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed Jiāshè Púsà:
"Good man!
This is called the Holy Practice (Shèngxíng) performed by Bodhisattvas dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dàchéng Dà Nièpán Jīng)."
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"Bhagavān!
Furthermore, by what meaning is it named the Holy Practice?"
"Good man!
'Holy' refers to the Buddhas, the Bhagavāns;
based on this meaning,
it is named the Holy Practice.
"Bhagavān!
If this is what all Buddhas practice,
then it is not what Śrāvakas,
Pratyekabuddhas,
or Bodhisattvas are able to practice."
"Good man!
These Bhagavāns dwell securely in this Great Parinirvāṇa (Dà Bōnièpán),
and make such elucidations and distinctions,
expounding its meaning.
Based on this meaning,
it is called the Holy Practice.
When the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Bodhisattvas hear this,
they are then able to respectfully carry it out;
hence it is named the Holy Practice.
Good man!
When this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) obtains this practice,
he attains dwelling in the stage of fearlessness (wúsuǒwèidì).
Good man!
If a Bodhisattva attains dwelling in such a stage of fearlessness,
he no longer fears greed (tān), hatred (huì), and delusion (yúchī),
birth, aging, sickness, and death,
nor does he fear the evil destinies (èdào),
hells (dìyù),
hungry ghosts (èguǐ), and animals (chùshēng).
Good man!
There are two kinds of evil beings (è):
First, the Āsura (Āxiūluó),
second, those among humans.
Among humans, there are three kinds of evil beings:
First, the Yīchǎntí (Icchantika),
second, those who slander the Vaipulya Sūtras (Fāngděng jīngdiǎn),
third, those who violate the Four Cardinal Prohibitions (sìzhòng jìn).
Good man!
The Bodhisattvas dwelling in this stage
never fear falling into such evils;
nor do they fear Śramaṇas (shāmén),
Brāhmaṇas (póluómén),
externalists (wàidào) with wrong views (xiéjiàn),
or the Heavenly Māra Pāpīyas (Tiānmó Bōxún);
nor do they fear undergoing the Twenty-Five Forms of Existence (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu);
therefore this stage
is named Fearlessness (Wúsuǒwèi).
Good man!
The Púsà Móhēsà, dwelling in the Stage of Fearlessness,
attains the Twenty-Five Samādhis (sānmèi),
destroying the Twenty-Five Forms of Existence.
Good man!
Attaining the Samādhi of Immaculate (Wúgòu Sānmèi) can destroy the existence of the Hells (dìyù yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Non-Retrogression (Wútuì Sānmèi) can destroy the existence of Animals (chùshēng yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Mental Joy (Xīnlè Sānmèi) can destroy the existence of Hungry Ghosts (èguǐ yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Rejoicing (Huānxǐ Sānmèi) can destroy the existence of Āxiūluó (Āsura yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Sunlight (Rìguāng Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of Fú Pótí (Pūrvavideha yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Moonlight (Yuèguāng Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of Qúyēnī (Aparagodānīya yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Fiery Heat (Rèyán Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of Yùdānyuè (Uttarakuru yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Illusion-like (Rúhuàn Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of Yánfútí (Jambudvīpa yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Immovability in All Dharmas (Yīqiè Fǎ Bùdòng Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of the Place of the Four Devas (Sì Tiānchù yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Difficulty to Subdue (Nánfú Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of the Place of the Thirty-Three Devas (Sānshísān Tiānchù yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Pleasing Intent (Yuèyì Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of Yánmó Tiān (Yāma Heaven yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Blue Color (Qīngsè Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of Dōushuài Tiān (Tuṣita Heaven yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Yellow Color (Huángsè Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of Huàlè Tiān (Nirmāṇarati Heaven yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Red Color (Chìsè Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of Tāhuà Zìzài Tiān (Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven yǒu);
