attaining the Samādhi of White Color (Báisè Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of the First Dhyāna (Chūchán yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Various Kinds (Zhǒngzhǒng Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of the Great Brahmā Heaven (Dà Fàntiān yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of the Pair (Shuāng Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of the Second Dhyāna (Èrchán yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Thunder Sound (Léiyīn Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of the Third Dhyāna (Sānchán yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Downpour (Zhùyǔ Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of the Fourth Dhyāna (Sìchán yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Emptiness-like (Rú Xūkōng Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of Non-Ideation (Wúxiǎng yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Mirror Illumination (Zhàojìng Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of Pure Dwelling Anāgāmins (Jìngjū Ānàhán yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Unimpeded (Wúài Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of the Sphere of Infinite Space (Kōngchù yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Permanence (Cháng Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (Shíchù yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Bliss (Lè Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of the Sphere of Nothingness (Bùyòngchù yǒu);
attaining the Samādhi of Self (Wǒ Sānmèi) can cut off the existence of the Sphere of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception (Fēixiǎng Fēifēixiǎngchù yǒu).
Good man!
This is how the Bodhisattvas attain the Twenty-Five Samādhis,
cutting off the Twenty-Five Forms of Existence.
"O good men!
These twenty-five *sānmèi*
are called the Kings of all *Sānmèi*.
O good men!
When the *Púsà Mòhēsà* enters these Kings of *Sānmèi*,
if they wish to blow apart and destroy Mount *Xūmíshān* King, they can do so immediately as they wish.
If they wish to know the thoughts of all sentient beings in the Three Thousand Great Thousand Worlds, they can also know them all.
If they wish to place all sentient beings of the Three Thousand Great Thousand Worlds within a single pore of their own body, they can do so immediately as they wish.
They also ensure that the sentient beings have no feeling of being restricted or oppressed.
If they wish to manifest immeasurable sentient beings, filling the Three Thousand Great Thousand Worlds, they can also do so as they wish.
If they wish to divide one body into multiple bodies,
and then recombine the multiple bodies into a single body,
although performing thus,
their mind is unattached,
just like a lotus flower.
O good men!
After the *Púsà Mòhēsà* attains entry into these Kings of *Sānmèi*,
they immediately attain dwelling in the Stage of Sovereignty (*Zìzài*).
When the *Púsà* attains dwelling in this Stage of Sovereignty,
they obtain the power of sovereignty (*Zìzài lì*),
and wherever they wish to be born,
they immediately attain rebirth there.
O good men!
Just as a Sage King leads the Four Continents (*Sì Tiānxià*),
traveling wherever he wishes without impediment.
The *Púsà Mòhēsà* is also like this;
in all places of rebirth, if they wish to be born,
they go and are born there as they wish.
O good men!
If the *Púsà Mòhēsà* sees all sentient beings in the hells,
and there are those who can be transformed to abide in good roots,
the *Púsà* immediately goes and is born among them.
Although the *Púsà* is born there,
it is not the fruit of former karma.
Due to the power and condition of the *Púsà Mòhēsà* dwelling in the Stage of Sovereignty,
they are born among them.
O good men!
Although the *Púsà Mòhēsà* is in the hells,
they do not experience burning heat
or the suffering of being pulverized.
O good men!
The merits thus accomplished by the *Púsà Mòhēsà*
are immeasurable and boundless, hundreds of thousands of billions, and still cannot be fully spoken of.
How much less can the merits possessed by the *Zhūfó* (all Buddhas) be spoken of?
At that time, there was a *Púsà* in the assembly,
named *Zhù Wúgòu Zàngwáng* (Dwelling in the Stainless Treasury King),
who possessed great majesty and virtue,
had perfected spiritual powers,
and attained the Great *Dhāraṇī Sānmèi*.
He had fully attained fearlessness.
He immediately rose from his seat,
bared his right shoulder,
placed his right knee on the ground,
knelt, joined his palms, and spoke to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*)!
As the Buddha has stated,
the meritorious virtues and wisdom accomplished by the *Zhūfó* and *Púsàs* are immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of billions, and truly cannot be spoken of.
Yet in my mind, I still believe
that they are not equal to these *Dàchéng* Sūtras.
Why is this?
It is because of the power of these *Dàchéng Fāngdeng* Sūtras
that they are able to give rise to the *Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí* (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi) of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones."
At that time, the Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent!
Excellent!
O good men!
It is so!
It is so!
It is as you have said.
Although these *Dàchéng Fāngdeng* Sūtras
accomplish immeasurable merits,
when comparing them to this Sūtra, they cannot serve as a metaphor—
a hundred times,
a thousand times,
hundreds of thousands of billions of times—
even calculations and similes cannot reach it.
O good men!
For example, from the cow comes milk;
from milk comes curds;
from curds comes raw cream;
from raw cream comes refined cream;
and from refined cream comes *tíhú*.
*Tíhú* is the most supreme.
If one consumes it, all diseases are removed,
and all medicines
are contained within it.
O good men!
The Buddha is also like this:
From the Buddha come the Twelve Divisions of the Canon;
from the Twelve Divisions of the Canon comes the *Xiūduōluó* (Sūtras);
from the *Xiūduōluó* comes the *Fāngdeng* Sūtras;
from the *Fāngdeng* Sūtras comes the *Bōrě Bōluómì*;
and from the *Bōrě Bōluómì* comes the *Dà Nièpán*,
which is like *tíhú*.
What is meant by *tíhú*
is a metaphor for the Buddha-Nature (*Fóxìng*).
The Buddha-Nature is precisely the *Rúlái* (Tathāgata).
O good men!
For this reason,
it is said that the merits possessed by the *Rúlái* are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable."
The *Jiāshè Púsà* addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has praised,
the *Dà Nièpán* Sūtra is like *tíhú*, the most supreme and wondrous.
If there is one who can consume it,
all diseases are removed,
and all medicines are contained within it.
Having heard this,
I secretly thought further,
that if there is one who cannot hear and accept this Sūtra,
you should know that this person
is extremely ignorant and lacks a good heart.
World-Honored One!
As for me now,
I can truly endure stripping my skin for paper,
pricking my blood for ink,
using marrow for water,
and breaking my bones for brushes,
to write out this *Dà Nièpán* Sūtra.
After writing it, I will recite and chant it,
making it fluent and proficient,
and then broadly explain its meaning for others.
World-Honored One!
If there are sentient beings who are greedy and attached to wealth and possessions,
I shall first bestow wealth upon them,
and then use this *Dà Nièpán* Sūtra
to urge them to read it.
If they are lofty and honorable,
I will first use kind words and follow their intentions,
and then gradually urge them to read this *Dàchéng Dà Nièpán* Sūtra.
If they are ordinary common people,
I should use majesty and power
to compel them to read it.
If they are arrogant,
I shall become their servant,
comply with their intentions, and cause them joy,
and then instruct and guide them with the Great *Bō Nièpán*.
If there are those who slander the *Dàchéng* Sūtras,
I shall use force to crush and subdue them.
Once they have been crushed and subdued,
I will then urge them to read the *Dà Nièpán* Sūtra.
If there are those who love and delight in the *Dàchéng* Sūtras,
I shall personally go to them,
reverently offer them homage,
and respect and praise them."
At that time, the Buddha praised Jiāshè Púsà (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva), saying:
"Excellent,
excellent!
You greatly love and delight in the Mahāyāna Sūtras,
crave the Mahāyāna Sūtras,
cherish the Mahāyāna Sūtras,
savor the Mahāyāna Sūtras,
and believe in, respect, honor, and make offerings to the Mahāyāna.
Good man!
Through the causality of this virtuous mind,
you shall surpass measureless, boundless, great Bodhisattvas, numerous as the sands of the Gangā,
and first attain Anòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Saṃbodhi).
You, too, will shortly be like me,
extensively expounding to the great assembly this Great Pari-Nirvāṇa (Dà Bān Nièpán),
the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
the hidden treasury spoken of by all Buddhas.
Good man!
In ages past,
before the Sun of the Buddha had risen,
I was at that time
a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén),
practicing the Bodhisattva path,
capable of fully understanding all the Sūtras and śāstras of the external paths (non-Buddhist doctrines).
I cultivated tranquil practices,
possessed perfect deportment,
and my mind was pure,
not corrupted by external causes capable of generating lustful thoughts.
I extinguished the fire of hatred and anger,
upheld the doctrines of permanence (cháng),
bliss (lè),
self (wǒ),
and purity (jìng),
and extensively sought the Mahāyāna Sūtras,
but did not even hear the name of the Vaipulya (Fāngděng) teachings.
At that time, I lived upon Snow Mountain (Xuěshān).
That mountain was pure,
with flowing springs, bathing ponds,
forests, and medicinal herbs
covering the ground.
Clear water flowed between the rocks everywhere,
and it was universally adorned with many fragrant flowers.
The multitude of birds and animals was uncountable,
and the abundance of sweet fruits of various kinds was difficult to calculate.
Moreover, there were measureless lotus roots (ǒugēn),
sweet roots (gāngēn),
and costus roots (qīngmùxiānggēn).
At that time, I dwelt there alone,
eating only fruits.
After eating, I concentrated my mind on contemplation and seated meditation (zuòchán).
After immeasurable years,
I still had not heard the name of a Mahāyāna Sūtra delivered by a Tathāgata appearing in the world.
Good man!
While I was cultivating such difficult practices (nánxíng)
and ascetic practices (kǔxíng),
the minds of Śakra Devānām Indra (Shìtí Huányīn) and the other devas
were greatly astonished. They immediately assembled
and spoke to one another,
reciting verses, saying:
At that time, there was a Deva-son (Tiānzǐ) in the assembly
named Huānxǐ (Joy),
who recited further verses, saying:
At that time, there was another Immortal Deva-son (Xiān Tiānzǐ)
who recited verses for the benefit of the Lord Śakra (Dìshì), saying:
After reciting these verses, he spoke again, saying:
'Kāuśika (Jiāoshījiā)!
There are Great Beings (Dàshì) in the world
who, for the sake of sentient beings, do not cling to their own bodies.
Wishing to benefit all sentient beings,
they cultivate various measureless ascetic practices.
Such people,
seeing the faults and offenses within saṃsāra (shēngsǐ),
even if they saw treasures filling this great earth,
mountains,
and great seas,
would not generate attachment,
regarding them as snot or spittle.
Such Great Beings
renounce wealth and treasures,
beloved wives and children,
heads, eyes, marrow, and brains,
hands, feet, and limbs,
dwelling houses,
elephants, horses, and carriages,
male and female servants.
They do not seek rebirth in the heavens either;
they only seek to enable all sentient beings to experience bliss and joy.
According to my understanding,
such Great Beings are pure and undefiled,
having permanently exhausted all bonds (jié).
They only wish to seek Anòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.'
Śakra Devānām Indra (Shìtí Huányīn) spoke again, saying:
'If what you say is true,
then this person is embracing all sentient beings in the world.
Great Immortal (Dà Xiān)!
If there were a Buddha-Tree (Fóshù) in this world,
it would eliminate the poisonous snakes of affliction (fánnǎo) for all devas, worldly humans, and asuras (Āxiūluó).
If sentient beings dwell in the cool shade of this Buddha-Tree,
all poisons of affliction are completely extinguished.
Great Immortal!
If this person becomes a Sugata (Shànshì) in the future world,
we all shall be able to extinguish immeasurable blazing afflictions.
Such a matter is truly hard to believe.
Why is this?
Countless hundreds and thousands of sentient beings generate the mind seeking Anòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
but upon seeing even a minor cause for deviation from Anòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
they immediately waver.
It is like the moon in the water:
when the water moves, it moves.
It is like a painted image,
hard to complete but easy to ruin.
The mind of Bodhi is also like this:
hard to arouse but easy to destroy.
Great Immortal!
Just as many people
strongly arm themselves with armor and weapons
desiring to advance and fight bandits,
but are terrified when facing the battle line and immediately retreat and scatter.
Measureless sentient beings are also like this:
they generate the Bodhi mind,
strongly arming themselves,
but upon seeing the faults of transmigration,
fear arises in their minds,
and they immediately retreat and scatter.
Great Immortal!
I see that measureless sentient beings like these, after generating the Bodhi mind,
all experience wavering.
Therefore, although I now see this person cultivating ascetic practices,
without distress
or fever,
dwelling upon a perilous path,
I cannot yet trust that his practice is pure.
I must now go myself and test him,
to know if he is truly capable of bearing
the great heavy burden of Anòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Great Immortal!
Just as a carriage with two wheels
can be used for transport,
and a bird with two wings
is capable of flight,
this ascetic practitioner
is also like this.
Although I see him firmly upholding the precepts,
I do not know if this person possesses profound wisdom.
If he possesses profound wisdom,
then we should know he is capable of bearing the heavy burden of Anòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Great Immortal!
For example, a mother fish
has many fry,
but few reach maturity.
It is like the āmalaka tree (āmluóshù):
many flowers, but few fruits.
Sentient beings who generate the Bodhi mind are indeed measureless,
but those who achieve fruition
are too few to mention.
Great Immortal!
I will go with you both to test him.
Great Immortal!
Just as genuine gold must be subjected to three tests
before its genuineness is known—
namely, heating (shāo),
pounding (dǎ),
and grinding (mó) —
testing that ascetic practitioner
must be done likewise.'
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra (Shìtí Huányīn)
transformed his body into the appearance of a Rākṣasa (Luóchà),
terrifying in form.
He descended to Snow Mountain (Xuěshān),
and stood not far from him.
This Rākṣasa
had no fear in his heart,
was exceptionally brave and irresistible,
possessed sequential eloquence,
and his voice was clear and elegant.
He proclaimed half a verse spoken by a past Buddha:
"Having spoken half a verse,
he then stood before him.
The form he displayed was extremely terrifying.
He looked around everywhere,
observing the four directions.
This Kǔxíngzhě,
hearing this half verse,
felt joy in his heart.
Just like a merchant,
traveling alone at night in a dangerous place, having lost his companions,
terrified while seeking [them],
when he encounters his comrades again,
joy arises in his heart,
and his elation is measureless.
Also like someone long ill,
who has not yet met a good physician,
suddenly obtaining excellent medicine for observing his sickness.
Like a person submerged in the ocean,
suddenly encountering a ship.
Like a person afflicted by thirst,
encountering clear, cold water.
Like one pursued by an enemy,
suddenly gaining freedom.
Like one long imprisoned suddenly hearing he is released.
Also like a farmer finding rain during a scorching drought.
Also like a traveler returning home,
whose family, seeing him,
feels great joy.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
When I heard this half verse at that time,
the joy in my heart was also like this.
I immediately rose from my seat,
lifted my hair with my hand,
looked around in the four directions, and spoke these words:
'The verse just heard,
by whom was it spoken?'
At that time, I saw no other person,
only the Luóchà.
I then spoke these words:
'Who has opened such a gate of liberation?
Who can thunder forth the sounds of the Buddhas?
Who, amidst the slumber of birth and death,
has awakened alone to proclaim such words?
Who can, in this [world],
reveal the flavor of the unsurpassed Way to sentient beings starving in the famine of Samsāra (birth and death)?
Countless sentient beings are sinking in the ocean of birth and death;
who can act as the great shipmaster among them?
These sentient beings are constantly entangled by the heavy sickness of affliction;
who can act as the good physician among them?
The speaking of this half verse enlightened my mind,
just like the half-moon gradually opens the lotus flower.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
At that time, I saw nothing else,
only the Luóchà.
I further conceived this thought:
'Could it be this Luóchà who spoke this verse?'
Yet doubt arose again:
'Perhaps he did not speak it.
Why?
The appearance of this person is extremely terrifying.
If someone manages to hear these verse phrases,
all fear
and ugliness are instantly eliminated.
How can a person whose appearance is like this
be able to speak this verse?
It is not fitting that a lotus should emerge from fire,
nor that cold water should spring forth from sunlight.
Shàn Nánzǐ,
at that time I further conceived this thought:
'I am now unwise.
Perhaps this Luóchà has seen the Buddhas of the past
and heard this half verse from those Buddhas.
I must now ask him.'
I immediately went forward to the Luóchà's location
and spoke these words:
'Excellent,
Great Being (Dàshì)!
Where did you obtain this half verse spoken by the fearless ones of the past?
Dàshì!
Where else did you obtain such a half wish-fulfilling pearl?
Dàshì!
The meaning of this half verse
is truly the correct path
of the past,
future,
and present Buddhas, the Shìzūn.
Countless sentient beings in all worlds
are constantly covered by the net of various views,
and throughout their lives, amid these external teachings (non-Buddhist doctrines),
they have never heard
the meaning of emptiness,
"O good man!
When I had asked this,
he immediately answered me, saying:
'O great Brāhmaṇa!
You should not now ask me this meaning.
Why is this?
Many days have passed since I last ate,
I have sought everywhere,
but absolutely cannot find [food].
Tormented by hunger and thirst,
my mind is confused and I speak nonsense,
it is not what my original mind knows.
Even if I now had the power to fly through the void to Yùdānyuè,
or even to heaven,
I would still not be able to find food anywhere,
it is for this reason
that I speak these words.'
O good man!
I then immediately replied to the Luóchà, saying:
'O Great Being (Dàshì)!
If you can complete this verse (gè) for me,
I shall be your disciple for life.
Great Being!
What you have spoken
does not end in name,
nor is its meaning exhausted.
For what reason do you not wish to speak it?
Now, material giving (cáishī) is subject to exhaustion,
but the cause and condition of Dharma giving (fǎshī) cannot be exhausted.
Although it is inexhaustible,
it yields great benefit.
Now that I have heard this Dharma of the half-verse,
doubt and alarm have arisen in my mind.
I sincerely hope you can now remove and sever this doubt for me.
Complete this verse,
and I shall be your disciple for life.'
The Luóchà replied:
'Your wisdom is excessive;
you only worry about your own person,
and show no thought [for me].
I am now certainly oppressed by the suffering of hunger,
and truly cannot speak.'
I then asked him, saying:
'What
is it that you eat?'
The Luóchà replied:
'You should not ask.
If I were to tell you,
it would cause many people to be afraid.'
I asked again, saying:
'We are alone here;
there is no one else.
I do not fear you.
Why do you not speak?'
The Luóchà replied:
'What I eat
is only warm human flesh.
What I drink
is only hot human blood.
Because of my meager fortune (fú),
I only consume this food,
but although I seek everywhere, I am distressingly unable to obtain it.
Although there are many people in the world,
they all possess merit and virtue (fúdé),
and are moreover protected by the various devas (zhūtiān),
while I lack the power to kill them.'
O good man!
I spoke to him again, saying:
'Just fully
speak this half-verse.
After I have heard the verse,
I shall offer up and sacrifice this body to you.
Great Being!
If I were to die,
this body would be useless;
it would be consumed by tigers, wolves,
owls,
and eagles,
yet I would not obtain the slightest bit of merit (fú).
I now, seeking Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
give up this impermanent body
to exchange it for an enduring body.'
The Luóchà replied:
'Who would believe such words of yours,
that for the sake of eight syllables (zì),
you would abandon your beloved body?'
O good man!
I immediately replied:
'You are truly unwise.
For example, a person
gives away an ordinary vessel to another
and obtains a vessel of the Seven Jewels (qībǎo).
I am likewise:
I give up this impermanent body
to gain the Vajra body (Jīngāng shēn).
As for your question, 'Who would believe this?'
I now have witnesses:
Dà Fàntiān Wáng (Great Brahma King),
Shìtí Huányīn (Sakra Deva-Indra), and the Four Heavenly Kings (Sì Tiān Wáng)
can bear witness to this matter.
Furthermore, there are all the Bódàsàs (Bodhisattvas) possessing the heavenly eye,
who, desiring to benefit countless sentient beings (zhòngshēng),
practice the Mahāyāna (Dàshèng) and fulfill the Six Pāramitās (liùdù),
and they can also attest to this.
Furthermore, the Buddhas (Fó) and Bhagavāns (Shìzūn) of the ten directions, who benefit sentient beings,
can also bear witness that I,
for the sake of eight syllables,
abandon my body and life.'
The Luóchà spoke again:
'If you are truly able to abandon your body like this,
listen carefully, listen carefully!
I shall now speak for you
the remaining half-verse.'
"O good man!
When I heard this at that time,
joy arose in my heart.
I immediately untied the deerskin I was wearing
and laid it out as a Dharma seat (fǎzuò) for this Luóchà,
saying respectfully:
'O Teacher (Héshàng)!
Please be seated upon this seat.'
I then knelt down before him,
clasping my hands,
and spoke thus:
'I only pray, O Teacher,
that you kindly speak for me
the remaining half-verse,
so that it may be complete.'
The Luóchà then spoke:
"At that time, after the Luóchà had spoken the verse, he spoke again, saying:
'O Bódàsà Móhēsà (Bodhisattva Mahāsattva),
you have now heard the full meaning of the verse,
and your vow is completely fulfilled.
If you truly desire to benefit all sentient beings,
then give your body to me now.'
O good man!
I deeply contemplated this meaning at that time,
and then everywhere—
whether on stones,
on walls,
on trees,
or on pathways—
I inscribed this verse.
I immediately fastened the clothes I was wearing more tightly,
fearing that my body would be exposed after death,
and then climbed a tall tree.
At that time, the tree spirit (shùshén) asked me again, saying:
'Well done!
Virtuous one!
What are you intending to do?'
O good man!
I then replied:
'I wish to abandon my body
to repay the price of the verse.'
The tree spirit asked:
'This verse
— what benefit does it hold?'
I then replied:
'These lines of the verse
are the Dharma path (fǎdào) revealing emptiness, spoken by the Buddhas (Fó) of the past,
future,
and present.
For the sake of this Dharma,
I cast aside my body and life.
It is not for profit,
fame,
wealth,
Cakravarti Rāja (Zhuǎnlún Shèng Wáng),
the Four Heavenly Kings (Sìdà Tiān Wáng),
Shìtí Huányīn,
Dà Fàntiān Wáng,
or the joys among men and devas (tiān).
It is solely to benefit all sentient beings
that I abandon this body.'
O good man!
When I was about to abandon my body,
I spoke again, saying:
'May all stingy and grasping people
come and see me
abandoning this body.
If there are any who perform slight giving (shī) yet grow arrogant,
may they also witness
me abandoning this body and life for a single verse,
like discarding grass or wood.'
When I had spoken these words at that time,
I immediately released my body and threw myself down from the tree.
Before I reached the ground,
various sounds issued forth from the void,
reaching even the Ājiānítuó (Akaniṣṭha) Heaven.
At that moment, the Luóchà reverted back to the body of Shì,
and immediately caught my body in mid-air
and placed it safely on the ground."
"At that time, Śakrà Devānáyìndra and all the devas and humans,
the Mahābrahmā Rājā,
bowed their heads and paid homage beneath my feet,
praising me, saying:
'Excellent!
Excellent!
Truly you are a Bodhisattva,
capable of greatly benefiting immeasurable sentient beings,
intending to light the great Dharma torch amidst the darkness of ignorance.
Because I cherished and was reluctant to part with the Tathāgata’s great Dharma,
I thus caused you distress and vexation.
I only wish that you would allow me to repent my transgressions and faults.
In the future, you will certainly achieve Ānòu duōluó Sānmǐao Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi).
May you wish to save and deliver me.'
At that time, Śakrà Devānáyìndra and all the devas,
paid homage to my feet,
and then took their leave,
and suddenly vanished.
"Good son!
Because I formerly gave up this body for the sake of half a verse (gāthā),
I abandoned this body.
Due to this cause and condition,
I was able to transcend fully twelve kalpas,
and shall achieve Ānòu duōluó Sānmǐao Sānpútí before Mílè.
Good son!
The immeasurable merits I have attained in this way,
are all due to making offerings to the Tathāgata's true Dharma.
Good son!
You are now likewise;
having generated the resolve for Ānòu duōluó Sānmǐao Sānpútí,
you have already surpassed countless and boundless Bodhisattvas, numerous as the sands of the Gangā.
Good son!
This is called the Bodhisattva dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāpárìpán (Mahāparinirvāṇa) and cultivating the holy practice.
"Good son!
What is the Brahmacarya (pure conduct) of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva?
Good son!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāpárìpán,
dwells in seven wholesome Dharmas,
and thus fulfills Brahmacarya.
What are the seven?
First, knowing the Dharma (Dharma-jñāna);
second, knowing the meaning (Artha-jñāna);
third, knowing the time (Kāla-jñāna);
fourth, knowing contentment (Santuṣṭi-jñāna);
fifth, knowing oneself (Ātma-jñāna);
sixth, knowing the assembly (Pariṣad-jñāna);
seventh, knowing superiors and inferiors (Pudgala-jñāna).
Good son!
How does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva know the Dharma?
Good son!
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva knows the Twelve Divisions of the Scriptures (Dvādaśānga-Dharma-Pravacana),
namely Sūtra (Xiūdūoluó),
Geya (Qíyè),
Vyākaraṇa (Shòujì),
Gāthā (Qiétuó),
Udāna (Yōutuónà),
Nidāna (Níduōnà),
Avadāna (Ābōtuónà),
Itivṛttaka (Yīdì yuēduōjiā),
Jātaka (Shétuójiā),
Vaipulya (Pífúlüè),
Adbhutadharma (Āfútuódámó),
and Upadeśa (Yōupōtíshě).
"Good son!
What is called the Sūtra (Xiūdūoluó) division of scriptures?
From 'Thus have I heard' (Rúshì wǒ wén) up to 'Joyfully received and practiced' (Huānxǐ fèngxíng),
all such are called Xiūdūoluó.
"What is called the Geya (Qíyè) division of scriptures?
The Buddha told the Bhikṣus,
'Formerly, you and I were foolish and lacked wisdom,
unable to truly see the Four Noble Truths.
Therefore, we have transmigrated and dwelt long in Saṃsāra,
sinking in the great sea of suffering.'
What are the four?
Suffering (Duhkha),
Origin (Samudaya),
Cessation (Nirodha),
Path (Mārga).
For instance, when the Buddha formerly finished speaking a prose Sūtra (Kèjīng) for the Bhikṣus,
at that time, there were sentient beings of sharp faculties who,
for the sake of hearing the Dharma,
later arrived at the Buddha's location,
and immediately asked someone,
'What did the Tathāgata just speak about?'
The Buddha, knowing this at the time,
then based on the original scripture,
proclaimed it in verse (gāthā), saying:
"This is called the Qíyè scripture.
"What is called the Vyākaraṇa (Shòujì) division of scriptures?
For example, in the Sūtras or Vinayas,
when the Tathāgata speaks,
he bestows a prophecy upon great people,
giving them the Buddha's distinct prophecy:
'You, Āyìduō,
in the future, a King
named Rǎngqié,
will be born in that world,
and will achieve Buddhahood,
named Mílè.'
This is called the Shòujì scripture.
"What is called the Gāthā (Qiétuó) division of scriptures?
Excluding Xiūdūoluó and all the Vinaya (precepts),
all others which speak of verses of four lines,
such as:
"This is called the Qiétuó scripture.
"What is called the Udāna (Yōutuónà) division of scriptures?
For example, when the Buddha entered absorption (Dhyāna) in the late afternoon,
and extensively expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the assemblies of devas.
At that time, the Bhikṣus each thought:
'What is the Tathāgata doing now?'
When the Tathāgata arose from absorption the next morning,
though no one had asked him,
he spoke spontaneously using his knowledge of others' minds, saying:
'Bhikṣus, you should know,
all devas have extremely long lifespans.
You Bhikṣus!
It is excellent to act for others,
not seeking self-benefit.
It is excellent to have few desires.
It is excellent to know contentment.
It is excellent to be tranquil (Śamatha).'
All scriptures spoken thus spontaneously without being asked,
are called the Yōutuónà scripture.
"What is called the Nidāna (Níduōnà) division of scriptures?
Like the verses in various scriptures,
concerning the original cause and basis,
when they are expounded for others.
For instance, in Śèwèi Guó (Śrāvastī),
there was a man
who caught birds with a net,
and having caught them, caged them,
but then gave them water and grain and subsequently released them.
The World-Honored One, knowing the original causes and conditions,
spoke a verse, saying:
"This is called the Níduōnà scripture.
"What is called the Avadāna (Ābōtuónà) division of scriptures?
Like the parables spoken within the Vinaya (precepts),
this is called the Ābōtuónà scripture.
"What is called the Itivṛttaka (Yīdì yuēduōjiā) division of scriptures?
For instance, the Buddha said,
'Bhikṣus, you should know,
the things I am able to speak
when I appear in the world,
are named the Precepts Scripture (Jiè Jīng).
When Jìuliúqín Fó (Krakucchanda Buddha) appeared in the world,
it was named the Nectar Drum (Gānlù Gǔ).
During the time of Jūnàhánmóuní Fó (Kanakamuni Buddha),
it was named the Mirror of Dharma (Fǎ Jìng).
During the time of Jiāyè Fó (Kāśyapa Buddha),
it was named the Analysis of Emptiness (Fēnbíe Kōng).'
This is called the Yīdì yuēduōjiā scripture.
"What is called the Jātaka (Shétuójiā) division of scriptures?
For instance, the World-Honored Buddha,
originally as a Bodhisattva,
cultivated various ascetic practices.
He said, 'Bhikṣus, you should know,
in the past I was born as a deer,
born as a bear,
born as a roe deer,
born as a rabbit,
born as a Minor King (Sùsàn Wáng),
born as a Cakravarti Rājā (Zhǎnlún Shèng Wáng),
born as a Nāga,
born as a Garuḍa (Jīnchì Niǎo),
and all such beings;
the bodies I took on while practicing the Bodhisattva Path.'
This is called the Shétuójiā.
"What is called the Vaipulya (Pífúlüè) division of scriptures?
Namely, the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtras (Fāngděng jīngdiǎn),
whose meaning is vast and great, like space.
This is called the Pífúlüè.
"What is called the Adbhutadharma (Wèicéngyǒu) division of scriptures?
For instance, when that Bodhisattva
was first born,
without anyone supporting him,
he immediately walked seven steps,
emitted a great light,
and gazed throughout the ten directions.
Also, like the monkey that presented a honey pot,
offering it to the Tathāgata.
Like the white-collared dog
hearing the Dharma by the Buddha.
Like Māra Pāpīyan (Mó Bōxún) transforming into a blue ox,
moving between the clay bowls (alms bowls),
causing the clay bowls to knock against and touch each other,
yet suffering no damage.
For instance, when the Buddha was first born
and entered the temple of the devas,
he caused the divine statues
to rise up and bow in reverence.
Scriptures such as these,
are named Wèicéngyǒu scriptures.
"What is called the Upadeśa (Yōupōtíshě) division of scriptures?
When the scriptures spoken by the World-Honored Buddha
are analyzed and discussed,
differentiated and extensively expounded,
clarifying their characteristics,
this is called the Yōupōtíshě scripture.
If a Bodhisattva is able to thus understand the Twelve Divisions of the Scriptures,
this is called 'knowing the Dharma.'"
"How does the Púsà Mòhēsà know meaning?
If the Púsà Mòhēsà comprehensively
knows the meaning of all written characters and
speech,
this is called knowing meaning.
How does the Púsà Mòhēsà know timing?
Good man!
The Púsà skillfully knows
that in such a time, it is appropriate to cultivate stillness;
in such a time, it is appropriate to cultivate diligence;
in such a time, it is appropriate to cultivate concentration through relinquishment;
in such a time, it is appropriate to make offerings to the Buddha;
in such a time, it is appropriate to make offerings to the teacher;
in such a time, it is appropriate to cultivate dāna,
śīla,
kṣānti,
vīrya,
dhyāna,
and to perfect Bōrě Bōluómì (Prajñāpāramitā).
This is called knowing timing.
How does the Púsà Mòhēsà know contentment?
Good man!
The Púsà Mòhēsà knows
contentment regarding food, drink, clothing, medicine,
walking, standing, sitting, lying down,
sleeping, waking, speaking, and silence.
This is called knowing contentment.
Good man!
How does the Púsà Mòhēsà know himself?
This Púsà knows himself, saying:
'I possess such faith,
such morality,
such extensive hearing (learning),
such relinquishment,
such wisdom,
such going and coming,
such right mindfulness,
such good conduct,
such questioning,
such answering.'
This is called knowing oneself.
How does the Púsà Mòhēsà know the assembly?
Good man!
This Púsà knows such assemblies,
identifying: This is a Kṣàlì (Kshatriya) assembly,
a Póluómén (Brahman) assembly,
a layman assembly,
a Shāmén (Śramaṇa) assembly.
He knows how he should walk and approach such assemblies,
how he should sit and rise,
how he should teach the Dharma,
and how he should question and answer.
This is called knowing the assembly.
Good man!
How does the Púsà Mòhēsà know the noble and the base among people?
Good man!
People are of two kinds:
first, those who have faith;
second, those who lack faith.
The Púsà should know that those who have faith are good,
and those who lack faith are not called good.
Furthermore, faith has two kinds:
first, those who constantly go to the Saēngfāng (monastery);
second, those who do not go.
The Púsà should know that those who go are good,
and those who do not go are not called good.
Those who go to the Saēngfāng are also of two kinds:
first, those who bow (pay reverence);
second, those who do not bow.
The Púsà should know that those who bow are good,
and those who do not bow are not called good.
Those who bow are also of two kinds:
first, those who listen to the Dharma;
second, those who do not listen to the Dharma.
The Púsà should know that those who listen to the Dharma are good,
and those who do not listen to the Dharma are not called good.
Those who listen to the Dharma are also of two kinds:
first, those who listen attentively;
second, those who do not listen attentively.
The Púsà should know that those who listen attentively are called good,
and those who do not listen attentively are not called good.
Those who listen attentively to the Dharma are also of two kinds:
first, those who reflect on the meaning;
second, those who do not reflect on the meaning.
The Púsà should know that those who reflect on the meaning are good,
and those who do not reflect on the meaning are not called good.
Those who reflect on the meaning are also of two kinds:
first, those who practice according to what is taught;
second, those who do not practice according to what is taught.
Those who practice according to what is taught are called good,
and those who do not practice according to what is taught are not called good.
Those who practice according to what is taught are also of two kinds:
first, those who seek Shēngwén (Śrāvaka),
who are unable to bring benefit, peace, or extensive help to all suffering sentient beings;
second, those who dedicate themselves to the unsurpassed Mèihàchèng (Mahāyāna),
benefiting many people, allowing them to attain peace and joy.
The Púsà should know that those who are able to benefit many people and allow them to attain peace and joy
are the most excellent and the best.
Good man!
Just as among all jewels,
the Rúyì Bǎozhū (Wish-Fulfilling Pearl) is the most superior and wonderful;
just as among all flavors, sweet dew (amṛta) is the most excellent;
likewise, the Púsà is the most superior and excellent among humans and devas,
beyond comparison.
Good man!
This is called the Púsà Mòhēsà dwelling in the Dàchéng Dà Nièpán Jīng (Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra),
dwelling in the Seven Good Dharmas.
When the Púsà dwells in these Seven Good Dharmas,
he attains the complete Brahmacarya (pure conduct).
"Furthermore, good man!
There are also Brahmacaryas,
namely Cí (loving-kindness),
Bēi (compassion),
Xǐ (sympathetic joy),
and Shě (equanimity)."
Kāyè (Kāśyapa) Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If cultivating Cí extensively
can cut off hatred,
and cultivating the Bēi heart also cuts off hatred,
why are there said to be Four Immeasurable Minds?
Judging by the meaning,
there should only be three.
World-Honored One!
Cí has three bases:
First, basing on sentient beings;
second, basing on dharmas (phenomena);
third, having no basis.
The hearts of Bēi,
Xǐ,
and Shě are also like this.
If we follow this reasoning,
there should only be three,
not four.
Regarding the basis of sentient beings:
It is based on the Five Skandhas (Wǔyīn), wishing to give them joy.
This is called the basis of sentient beings.
Regarding the basis of dharmas:
It is based on the things that all sentient beings need, and giving them away.
This is called the basis of dharmas.
Regarding having no basis:
It is based on the Rúlái (Tathāgata).
This is called having no basis.
Cí mostly bases itself on poor sentient beings.
The Rúlái, the Great Teacher, has eternally departed from poverty and receives the highest joy.
If Cí bases itself on sentient beings,
then it does not base itself on the Buddha.
Dharma is also like this.
For this reason,
basing on the Rúlái
is called having no basis.
World-Honored One!
The object of Cí is all sentient beings,
just as when based on parents,
wife, children, and relatives.
For this reason,
it is called the basis of sentient beings.
Regarding the basis of dharmas:
One does not perceive parents,
wife, children, or relatives, but perceives
that all dharmas arise from conditions.
This is called the basis of dharmas.
Regarding having no basis:
One does not abide in the characteristics of dharmas
nor the characteristics of sentient beings. This is called having no basis.
The hearts of Bēi,
Xǐ,
and Shě are also like this.
Therefore, there should be three,
not four.
World-Honored One!
There are two kinds of people:
first, those whose practice is based on right view (dṛṣṭicārita);
second, those whose practice is based on craving (tṛṣṇācārita).
People whose practice is based on view mostly cultivate Cí and Bēi.
People whose practice is based on craving mostly cultivate Xǐ and Shě.
Therefore, there should be two,
not four.
World-Honored One!
That which is called immeasurable
means boundless.
Because boundaries cannot be obtained,
it is called immeasurable.
If it is immeasurable,
then it should be one,
and should not be spoken of as four.
If we speak of four,
how can they be immeasurable?
Therefore, there should be one,
not four."
The Buddha addressed
Kāshè: “Good man!
The essential teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgatas for all sentient beings
have cryptic statements,
and are difficult to fully understand.
Sometimes, for sentient beings, they speak of one cause and condition.
How are they said to speak of one cause and condition?
It refers to all compounded phenomena (yǒuwéi zhī fǎ).
Good man!
Sometimes they speak of two kinds:
cause and effect.
Sometimes they speak of three kinds:
afflictions (fánnǎo),
karma (yè),
and suffering (kǔ).
Sometimes they speak of four kinds:
ignorance (wúmíng),
formations (zhū xíng),
birth (shēng), and old age and death (lǎosǐ).
Sometimes they speak of five kinds:
namely, feeling (shòu),
craving (ài),
grasping (qǔ),
becoming (yǒu), and birth (shēng).
Sometimes they speak of six kinds:
cause and effect across the three times (sānshì yīnyuán).
Sometimes they speak of seven kinds:
namely, consciousness (shí),
name (míng),
form (sè),
six sense-bases (liù rù),
contact (chù),
feeling (shòu), and also craving and grasping (àiqǔ).
Sometimes they speak of eight kinds:
excluding ignorance (wúmíng),
formations (xíng), and birth, old age, and death (shēnglǎosǐ),
the remaining eight elements;
sometimes they speak of nine kinds,
as in the Chéng Jīng (City Sūtra),
excluding ignorance (wúmíng),
formations (xíng),
and consciousness (shí),
the remaining nine elements.
Sometimes they speak of eleven,
as when teaching Sàzhēnīqiánzi,
excluding the one factor of birth (shēng),
the remaining eleven.
Sometimes they fully speak of the twelve causes and conditions (shí'èr yīnyuán),
such as in Wangshě Chéng (Rājagṛha),
where for
Kāshè and others, they fully spoke of the twelve, from ignorance (wúmíng) up to birth, old age, sickness, and death (shēng lǎo bìng sǐ).
Good man!
Just as with one cause and condition,
for the sake of sentient beings,
manifold distinctions are made,
the immeasurable phenomena of the mind (wúliàng xīn fǎ) are also thus.
Good man!
For this reason,
you should not generate doubt
regarding the deeply secret conduct of the Tathāgatas.
Good man!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One (Shìzūn),
possesses great skillful means (fāngbiàn).
He speaks of permanence (cháng) regarding impermanence (wúcháng),
and speaks of impermanence regarding permanence;
He speaks of suffering (kǔ) regarding bliss (lè),
and speaks of bliss regarding suffering;
He speaks of purity (jìng) regarding impurity (bùjìng),
and speaks of impurity regarding purity;
He speaks of self (wǒ) regarding non-self (wúwǒ),
and speaks of non-self regarding self;
He speaks of non-sentient beings as sentient beings,
and speaks of genuine sentient beings as non-sentient beings;
He speaks of non-matter (fēiwù) as matter (wù),
and speaks of matter as non-matter;
He speaks of non-reality (fēishí) as reality (shí),
and speaks of reality as non-reality;
He speaks of non-objects (fēijìng) as objects (jìng),
and speaks of objects as non-objects;
He speaks of non-arising (fēishēng) as arising (shēng),
and speaks of arising as non-arising;
And even speaks of brightness (míng) regarding ignorance (wúmíng),
and speaks of ignorance regarding brightness;
He speaks of non-form (fēisè) regarding form (sè),
and speaks of form regarding non-form;
He speaks of the path (dào) regarding the non-path (fēidào),
and speaks of the non-path regarding the path.
Good man!
The Tathāgata uses these immeasurable skillful means
to tame sentient beings.
How can this be false speech (xūwàng)?
Good man!
If there are sentient beings who are greedy for wealth and goods,
I transform myself for that person into a cakravartin (zhuǎnlúnwáng),
for immeasurable years,
supplying them with all their needs,
and afterwards I teach and convert them,
causing them to abide in Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòu Duōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).
If there are sentient beings attached to the five desires (wǔ yù),
for immeasurable years,
I satisfy their wishes with wonderful five desires,
and afterwards exhort and convert them,
causing them to abide in Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.
If there are sentient beings who are honored and consider themselves noble,
I act as their servant for immeasurable years,
running about and attending to them.
After gaining their trust,
I then exhort and convert them, causing them to abide in Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.
If there are sentient beings who are inherently intractable and self-righteous,
and require reprimand and admonishment,
I spend immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years,
teaching, reprimanding, and guiding them through admonitions,
causing their minds to become tamed,
and afterwards I exhort them again,
causing them to abide in Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.
Good man!
The Tathāgata is like this;
for immeasurable years,
using various skillful means,
He causes all sentient beings to abide in Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.
How can this be false speech?
Though the Tathāgatas
dwell in all evils,
they are not polluted by them,
just like a lotus flower.
Good man!
You should understand the meaning of the Four Immeasurables (Sì Wúliàng Yì) in this way.”
“Good man!
These immeasurable minds
inherently possess four natures.
If one cultivates them,
they are born in the state of the Great Brahmā.
Good man!
These immeasurables
have four counterparts;
thus, they are named ‘four.’
Generally, one who cultivates loving-kindness (Cí) can cut off greed (tānyù).
One who cultivates compassion (Bēi) can cut off hatred (chēnhuì).
One who cultivates sympathetic joy (Xǐ) can cut off unhappiness (bùlè).
One who cultivates equanimity (Shě) can cut off living beings afflicted by greed and hatred.
Good man!
Based on this principle,
they are named ‘four,’
not one,
two,
or three.
Good man!
As you have said,
Cí can cut off hatred,
and Bēi is also like this—
suggesting they should be called ‘three.’
You should not raise such a difficulty now.
Why?
Good man,
hatred has two types:
one that takes life,
and one that whips and beats.
Cultivating Cí can cut off that which takes life.
Cultivating Bēi can remove that which whips and beats.
Good man!
Based on this principle,
are they not four?
Furthermore, hatred has two types:
one is hatred toward sentient beings,
and the second is hatred toward non-sentient beings.
The one who cultivates the mind of Cí cuts off hatred toward sentient beings.
The one who cultivates the mind of Bēi cuts off hatred toward non-sentient beings.
Furthermore, hatred has two types:
one has causes and conditions,
and the second has no causes and conditions.
The one who cultivates the mind of Cí cuts off that which has causes and conditions.
The one who cultivates the mind of Bēi cuts off that which has no causes and conditions.
Furthermore, hatred has two types:
one is cultivated over a long time in the past,
and the second is cultivated right now in the present.
The one who cultivates the mind of Cí can cut off the past one.
The one who cultivates the mind of Bēi cuts off the present one.
Furthermore, hatred has two types:
one is hatred toward noble persons (shèngrén),
and the second is hatred toward ordinary people (fánfū).
The one who cultivates the mind of Cí cuts off hatred toward noble persons.
The one who cultivates the mind of Bēi cuts off hatred toward ordinary people.
Furthermore, hatred has two types:
one is supreme,
and the second is middling.
Cultivating Cí cuts off the supreme one.
Cultivating Bēi cuts off the middling one.
Good man!
Based on this principle,
they are named ‘four.’
How can you raise the difficulty that they should be three, not four?
Therefore, Kèshè!
These immeasurable minds,
when mutually contrasted with their counterparts,
are distinguished as four.
Furthermore, based on the vessel,
they should be named ‘four.’
If the vessel possesses Cí,
it cannot possess the minds of Bēi,
Xǐ,
or Shě.
Based on this principle,
there should be four, without reduction.
Good man!
Based on the distinction in practice,
there should be four.
When one is practicing Cí,
there is no Bēi,
Xǐ,
or Shě.
Therefore, there are four.
“Good man!
Based on their being immeasurable,
they are also named ‘four.’
The immeasurable itself comprises four types:
the immeasurable mind
that has an object (yuán),
but is not sovereign (zìzài);
the immeasurable mind
that is sovereign,
but has no object;
the immeasurable mind
that has both an object
and is sovereign;
and the immeasurable mind
that has neither an object
nor is sovereign.
What is the immeasurable
that has an object,
but is not sovereign?
It is having immeasurable, boundless sentient beings as objects,
yet being unable to attain the sovereign Samādhi.
Although attained, it is unstable—
sometimes attained, sometimes lost.
What is the immeasurable
that is sovereign,
but has no object?
It is like having one’s parents,
brothers, and sisters as objects,
desiring their happiness and peace—
but they are not immeasurable objects.
What is the immeasurable
that has both an object
and is sovereign?
This refers to all the Fó and Púsà.
What is the immeasurable
that has neither an object
nor is sovereign?
The Shēngwén and Yuánjué,
who cannot widely take immeasurable sentient beings as objects,
and are also not sovereign.
Good man!
Based on this principle,
they are named the ‘Four Immeasurables.’
They are not known by the Shēngwén and Yuánjué,
but are the realm of the Fó Rúlái.
Good man!
Although these four matters
are named ‘immeasurable’ by the Shēngwén and Yuánjué,
they are little and insufficient to speak of.
For the Fó Púsà,
they are rightly named ‘immeasurable and boundless.’
Púsà Kèshè said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
It is so,
it is so.
It is truly as the holy teaching states:
the realm possessed by the Fó Rúlái
is not reached by the Shēngwén and Yuánjué.
World-Honored One!
Is it possible that a Púsà dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāpārinirvāṇa
attains the mind of Cí and Bēi,
yet it is not the mind of Great Cí and Great Bēi?”
The Buddha said, “There is:
“Good man!
If a Púsà discriminates among sentient beings into three classes:
first, relatives;
second, enemies and those disliked;
third, neutral persons.
Among relatives,
they further make three classes:
namely, supreme,
middling,
and inferior;
the same applies to enemies and those disliked.
This Púsà Mòhēsà grants supreme joy (zēngshàng lè) to the supreme relatives.
They likewise equally grant supreme joy to the middling and inferior relatives.
They grant a small portion of joy to the supreme enemies.
They grant middling joy to the middling enemies.
They grant supreme joy to the inferior enemies.
When the Púsà practices again and cultivates this,
they grant middling joy to the supreme enemies.
They equally grant supreme joy to the middling and inferior enemies.
When they practice again and cultivate this,
they equally grant supreme joy to the supreme, middling, and inferior.
If they grant supreme joy to the supreme enemies,
at that time, they are named ‘having accomplished the mind of Cí.’
At that time, the Púsà attains an equal mind toward their parents and the supreme enemies,
without difference.
Good man!
This is called the attainment of Cí,
but not Great Cí.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does the Púsà, having attained such Cí,
still not receive the name ‘Great Cí’?”
"Shànnánzǐ!
Because it is difficult to achieve,
it is not called Dàcí (Great Loving-kindness).
Why is this?
For a long time, throughout measureless kalpas in the past,
one has accumulated many afflictions (kleshas)
and has not cultivated wholesome dharmas (good methods).
Therefore, one cannot, in a single day,
subdue their mind.
Shànnánzǐ!
Just like digging out a pea [from a pod],
when dried, if pricked with an awl,
it ultimately cannot be attached.
Afflictions are hard and stiff;
they are likewise thus.
Even if day and night,
the mind is restrained and not scattered,
it is difficult to subdue.
Moreover, like a house dog
that is not afraid of people,
while a wild deer of the mountain forests
flees in terror upon seeing a person.
Anger (chēnhuì) is hard to remove,
like a dog guarding the house;
the mind of loving-kindness (cíxīn) is easily lost,
like that wild deer.
Therefore, this mind is difficult to subdue,
for this reason,
it is not called Dàcí.
Furthermore, Shànnánzǐ!
For example, drawing on stone—
the inscription remains permanently.
Drawing on water quickly vanishes;
the effect does not last long.
Anger is like drawing on stone;
all roots of goodness are like drawing on water.
Therefore, this mind is difficult to achieve and subdue.
Like a great pile of fire,
its light remains for a long time;
the light of lightning does not last even momentarily.
Anger is like a pile of fire;
Loving-kindness (cí) is like the light of lightning.
Therefore, this mind is difficult to achieve and subdue,
for this reason,
it is not called Dàcí.
"Shànnánzǐ!
A Púsà Mòhēsà (Bodhisattva Mahāsattva) who dwells on the first stage,
is called Dàcí.
Why is this?
Shànnánzǐ!
The extremely wicked are called Yīchǎntí (Icchantika).
When the Púsà dwelling in the first stage cultivates Dàcí,
their mind makes no distinction toward the Yīchǎntí,
they see no faults in them and therefore do not generate anger.
For this reason, they attain the name Dàcí.
Shànnánzǐ!
To remove non-beneficial things for all sentient beings,
this is called Dàcí (Great Loving-kindness);
to desire to grant measureless benefits and joy to sentient beings,
this is called Dàbēi (Great Compassion);
to generate joy in the mind toward all sentient beings,
this is called Dàxǐ (Great Joy);
to offer protection to none (i.e., treating all equally),
this is called Dàshě (Great Equanimity);
if one does not perceive the Wǒ (Self),
the Fǎxiàng (Characteristics of Phenomena),
or one's own body,
but sees all dharmas as equal and non-dual,
this is called Dàshě;
to relinquish one's own joy,
and bestow it upon others,
this is called Dàshě.
Shànnánzǐ!
Only the Four Immeasurable Minds
are able to make a Púsà increase and perfect the Liù Bōluómì (Six Pāramitās);
other practices are not necessarily able to do so.
Shànnánzǐ!
A Púsà Mòhēsà first achieves the mundane Four Immeasurable Minds,
and only then generates the mind of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi),
and subsequently achieves the supramundane ones.
Shànnánzǐ!
Dependent on the mundane Immeasurable Minds,
the supramundane Immeasurable Minds are achieved.
For this reason,
they are called the Great Immeasurable Minds.
Jiāshè Púsà (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva) said to the Buddha:
"Shìzūn (World-Honored One)!
Removing non-beneficial things
and granting benefits and joy is, in reality, accomplishing nothing.
Such contemplation
is merely an empty view,
possessing no real benefit.
Shìzūn!
For example, when a Bǐqiū (monk)
contemplates impurity,
he sees the robes he wears
as entirely having the characteristic of skin,
yet they are not actually skin.
What can be eaten
is all viewed as having the characteristic of insects,
yet they are not actually insects.
Contemplating thick bean soup,
he regards it as sewage,
yet it is not actually excrement.
Contemplating the yogurt he eats,
it seems like marrow and brains,
yet it is not actually brains.
Contemplating bone fragments,
they seem like sperm,
yet they are not actually sperm.
The Four Immeasurable Minds are likewise thus;
they cannot truly benefit sentient beings
and cause them to attain joy.
Although one speaks of granting joy to sentient beings,
they do not truly receive it.
Is such contemplation not illusory?
Shìzūn!
If it is not illusory
and truly grants joy,
then why do not all sentient beings,
by the majestic power of all Buddhas and Púsàs, attain joy?
If it is truly ineffective
in granting joy,
then regarding what the Buddha has said:
'I recall in the past,
I cultivated the mind of loving-kindness alone,
spanning seven cycles of formation and destruction (kalpas),
and did not return to this life.
When the world formed,
I was born in Fàntiān (Brahmaloka).
When the world was destroyed,
I was born in Guāngyīn Tiān (Abhasvara Heaven).
If born in Fàntiān,
one is powerful and self-mastered,
unable to be suppressed by anyone,
and is the most excellent and supreme among a thousand Brahmās,
named Dàfànwáng (Great Brahma King).'
There were sentient beings
who, regarding me,
generated the supreme perception.
Thirty-six times
I served as Dāolì Tiānwáng Shìtíhuányīn (Śakra, King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven),
and measureless hundreds and thousands of times
served as a Cakravartin King.
By cultivating the mind of loving-kindness alone,
I attained such rewards of humans and devas.
If it is not real,
how could this meaning correspond?"
The Buddha said:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Shànnánzǐ!
You are truly brave
and fearless.
He immediately spoke a verse to Jiāshè (Kāśyapa), saying:
"Shànnánzǐ!
As for the cultivation of loving-kindness,
it is truly not illusory thought;
it is certainly real.
If it is the loving-kindness of the Shēngwén Yuánjué (Hearers and Pratyekabuddhas),
that is called illusory.
The loving-kindness of all Buddhas and Púsàs is real and not illusory.
How is this known?
Shànnánzǐ!
A Púsà Mòhēsà who practices this great Dà Nièpán (Great Nirvana),
contemplates earth as gold,
contemplates gold as earth;
earth becomes the characteristic of water,
water becomes the characteristic of earth;
water becomes the characteristic of fire,
fire becomes the characteristic of water;
earth becomes the characteristic of wind,
wind becomes the characteristic of earth.
All are achieved according to intent and are not illusory.
They contemplate actual sentient beings as non-sentient beings,
and contemplate non-sentient beings as actual sentient beings.
All are achieved according to intent,
without illusion.
Shànnánzǐ!
You should know that the Four Immeasurable Minds of the Púsà
are real contemplation,
not untruthful.
Furthermore, Shànnánzǐ!
What is called real contemplation?
It is that which can cut off all afflictions.
Shànnánzǐ!
Cultivating loving-kindness can sever greed and desire (tānyù);
cultivating compassion (bēi) can sever anger (chēnhuì);
cultivating joy (xǐ) can sever dissatisfaction;
cultivating equanimity (shě) can sever greed, anger, and the characteristics of sentient beings.
For this reason, it is called real contemplation."
"Furthermore, good man!
The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva's Four Immeasurable Minds
can be the root of all good things.
Good man!
If the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva does not see poor sentient beings,
loving-kindness (cí) will not arise in relation to them.
If loving-kindness does not arise,
then the mind of charitable giving (huìshī) cannot be aroused.
Through the cause and condition of giving,
sentient beings are enabled to attain peaceful joy,
namely food and drink,
carriages and clothing,
flowers, incense, beds, and couches,
dwellings, and lamps.
When giving such things,
the mind is without attachment,
does not give rise to craving or clinging,
and is definitively dedicated (huíxiàng) to Anūttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, their mind
has no reliance,
false discrimination (wàngxiǎng) is forever severed,
they do not act out of fear,
fame, or profit,
they do not seek the joy received by humans and gods,
they do not give rise to arrogance,
they do not expect return recompense,
and they do not act to deceive others.
Therefore, they practice giving (bùshī) without seeking wealth or nobility.
Whenever they practice giving, they do not perceive the recipient,
whether they observe the precepts (chíjì)
or violate the precepts (pòjiè),
whether they are a field (tián)
or not a field,
'this is an acquaintance,'
'this is not an acquaintance.'
When giving, they do not perceive whether one is worthy (qì)
or unworthy,
they do not select the time
or the place,
or the inappropriateness of the place.
They also do not consider whether there is famine
or abundance and joy.
They do not perceive cause and effect,
'this is a sentient being,'
'this is not a sentient being,'
'this is merit (fú),'
'this is not merit.'
Although they do not perceive the giver,
the recipient,
or the property,
and furthermore do not perceive the cutting off (of self/attachments) and the karmic recompense (guǒbào),
they constantly practice giving without cessation.
Good man!
If the Bodhisattva perceives those who observe the precepts
or violate the precepts, or even the karmic recompense,
they ultimately cannot give.
If they do not practice giving,
they cannot fully realize Dānapāramitā.
If they do not fully realize Dānapāramitā,
they cannot attain Anūttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good man!
For example, there is a person
whose body is struck by a poisoned arrow.
That person's family and dependents,
wishing them peace and safety,
in order to remove the poison,
immediately summon a good doctor to extract the arrow.
That person then says:
'Wait a moment, do not touch it!
I must now observe:
From which direction did this poisoned arrow come?
Who shot it?
Was it a Kṣatriya,
a Brāhmaṇa,
a Vaiśya,
or a Śūdra?'
They further reflect:
'What kind of wood is this?
Bamboo?
Willow?'
'The iron arrowhead,
which smithy forged it?
Is it hard
or soft?'
'The feathers,
whose bird's wing are they from?
Crow, owl, or vulture?'
'The poison contained therein,
was it artificially made or did it naturally exist?
Is it human poison
or venomous snake poison?'
This foolish person,
before they can find out,
immediately dies.
Good man!
The Bodhisattva is also like this.
If, when practicing giving,
they discriminate the recipient,
observing the precepts,
violating the precepts,
or even the karmic recompense,
they ultimately cannot give.
If they cannot give,
they do not fully realize Dānapāramitā.
If they do not fully realize Dānapāramitā,
they cannot attain Anūttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Good man!
When the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices giving,
towards all sentient beings,
their mind of loving-kindness (cíxīn) is equal,
like thinking of one's own child.
Furthermore, when practicing giving,
towards all sentient beings,
they arouse the mind of compassion (bēimǐn xīn),
just like parents tending to a sick child.
When practicing giving,
their mind is joyful,
just like parents
seeing their child recover from illness.
After giving,
their mind is released (fàngshě),
just like parents
seeing their child grow up
and able to live independently.
This Bodhisattva-mahāsattva,
in their mind of loving-kindness,
when offering food,
constantly makes this vow:
'The merit of what I now offer
I fully share with all sentient beings.
By means of this cause and condition,
may all sentient beings attain the food of great wisdom (dàzhì shí),
diligently dedicating themselves to the unsurpassed Great Vehicle (Wúshàng Dàshèng).
May all sentient beings attain the food of good wisdom (shànzhì shí),
and not seek the food of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
May all sentient beings attain the food of Dharma-joy (fǎxǐ shí),
and not seek the food of craving (ài shí).
May all sentient beings fully attain the food of Prajñāpāramitā,
filling them completely,
gathering unimpeded supreme good roots.
May all sentient beings awaken to and understand the characteristics of emptiness (kōng xiàng),
and attain an unimpeded body
like space.
May all sentient beings constantly be recipients,
compassionate towards all,
and be fields of merit for the masses.
Good man!
When the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates the mind of loving-kindness,
whatever food they offer,
they should firmly make such vows.
"Furthermore, good man!
When the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in their mind of loving-kindness, offers beverages,
they should make this vow:
'The merit of what I now offer
I fully share with all sentient beings.
By means of this cause and condition,
may all sentient beings proceed to the river of the Great Vehicle,
drink the water of the eight flavors (bāwèi shuǐ),
and swiftly tread the path of unsurpassed Bodhi.
May they depart from the withered desiccation of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
and thirstily aspire to the unsurpassed Buddha Vehicle.
May they cut off the thirst of afflictions (fánnǎo kě),
and thirstily aspire to the flavor of the Dharma.
May they depart from the love of saṃsāra,
and delight in the Great Vehicle and Mahāparinirvāṇa,
fully realizing the Dharma-body (fǎshēn),
attaining all Samādhis,
and entering the deep ocean of wisdom.
May all sentient beings
attain the flavor of sweet dew (gānlù wèi),
the flavor of transcendental Bodhi,
and the flavor of departure from desire and stillness (líyù jìjìng)—such flavors.
May all sentient beings fully realize immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Dharma flavors (fǎwèi).
Having fully realized the Dharma flavors,
may they attain the vision of the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng).
Having seen the Buddha-nature,
may they be able to rain down the Dharma-rain.
Having rained down the Dharma-rain,
may the Buddha-nature universally cover,
like space.
Furthermore, may they cause other immeasurable sentient beings to attain the single flavor of the Dharma,
which is the Great Vehicle,
not the flavor of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
May all sentient beings attain the single sweet flavor,
without the six different flavors.
May all sentient beings only seek the Dharma flavor,
the flavor of the unimpeded Buddha-Dharma's practice,
and not seek other flavors.
Good man!
When the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in their mind of loving-kindness, offers beverages,
they should firmly make such vows."
"Furthermore, good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, acting out of a mind of compassion (cíxīn), gives the gift of vehicles (chēchéng),
he should make this vow:
'May the gifts I now bestow
be shared universally with all sentient beings (zhòngshēng).
Through this causality,
may all beings universally realize the Mahāyāna (Dàchéng),
abide in the Mahāyāna,
never retreat from the Vehicle,
realize the Unmoving Vehicle,
realize the Vajrāsana (Jīngāngzuò) Vehicle,
not seek the Śrāvakayāna (Shēngwén) or Pratyekabuddhayāna (Pìzhīfó),
proceed toward the Buddhayāna (Fóchěng),
realize the Unconquerable Vehicle,
realize the Vehicle without Weariness or Lack,
realize the Vehicle that does not Sink or Recede,
realize the Unexcelled Vehicle (Wúshàngchěng),
realize the Daśabala (Shílì) Vehicle,
realize the Vehicle of Great Merit (Dàgōngdé),
realize the Unprecedented Vehicle,
realize the Rare Vehicle,
realize the Hard-to-Obtain Vehicle,
realize the Boundless Vehicle,
realize the Vehicle that Knows Everything.'
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, acting out of a mind of compassion, gives the gift of vehicles,
he should always firmly make vows such as these.
"Furthermore, good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, acting out of a mind of compassion, gives the gift of clothes,
he should make this vow:
'May the gifts I now bestow
be shared universally with all sentient beings.
Through this causality,
may all beings obtain the Garment of Shame and Repentance (Cánkuì Yī),
covering their bodies with the Dharma Realm (Fǎjiè),
tearing apart the Garments of all Views (Jiàn Yī),
having their clothing suspended one foot six inches from their body,
obtaining a golden body,
experiencing all contacts as soft and unobstructed,
possessing radiant and moist complexions (guāngsè rùnzé),
having delicate and smooth skin,
possessing measureless perpetual light,
being formless and apart from form.
May all sentient beings universally obtain the body of formlessness,
surpassing all form,
and entering the Great Parinirvāṇa (Dà Bōnièpán) of Formlessness.'
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva gives the gift of clothes,
he should firmly make vows such as these.
"Furthermore, good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, cultivating compassion (xiū cí),
gives the gift of flowers, incense,
anointing perfumes (túxiāng),
powdered perfumes (mòxiāng),
and various mixed perfumes,
he should make this vow:
'May the gifts I now bestow
be shared universally with all sentient beings.
Through this causality,
may all sentient beings universally attain the Samādhi (Sānmèi) of the Buddha's Flowers,
binding the wonderful garland (miàomán) of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (Qījué) upon their heads.
May all beings be shaped like the full moon,
and may all colors they perceive be subtle and supreme.
May all beings realize the One Characteristic (Yī Xiàng),
adorned with a hundred merits.
May all beings, according to their wish, be able to perceive agreeable colors.
May all beings constantly meet good friends (shànyǒu),
obtain unimpeded fragrance (wú'ài xiāng),
and be separated from all stench and filth.
May all beings possess the unexcelled treasures of all wholesome roots.
May all beings regard each other with harmony and joy,
be free from sorrow and suffering,
be perfected in all wholesome qualities,
and not worry or be concerned about each other.
May all beings be complete in the fragrance of morality (jièxiāng).
May all beings maintain unimpeded morality (wú'ài jiè),
so that their sweet fragrance (xiāngqì fēnfù)
fills the ten directions.
May all beings obtain firm morality (jiānláo jiè),
morality without regret,
morality of omniscience (Yīqiè Zhì Jiè),
departing from all violations of morality,
and universally obtain Non-Morality (Wújiè),
unprecedented morality (wèicéngyǒu jiè),
morality without a teacher (wúshī jiè),
morality without fabrication (wúzuò jiè),
morality without wilderness/neglect (wúhuāng jiè),
morality without defilement (wúwūrǎn jiè),
morality that is finished,
ultimate morality (jiūjìng jiè),
and obtain equal morality (píngděng jiè).
Whether anointed with perfume or subjected to cutting and stabbing,
may they be equally free from hatred and love.
May all beings obtain the unexcelled morality,
the morality of the Mahāyāna, not the morality of the Hīnayāna (Xiǎochéng).
May all beings universally realize the perfection of Śīlapāramitā (Shī Bōluómì),
like the morality attained by all Buddhas.
May all beings be universally cultivated and perfumed by giving (bùshī),
morality (chíjiè),
patience (rěnrǔ),
effort (jīngjìn),
meditation, and wisdom (chán zhì).
May all beings universally realize the subtle lotus of the Great Parinirvāṇa,
the fragrance of which fills the ten directions.
May all beings purely consume the unexcelled fragrant sustenance (xiāngzhuàn) of the Mahāyāna Great Parinirvāṇa,
just as bees collect from flowers, taking only the fragrance and flavor.
May all beings universally achieve
the body perfumed by measureless merits (gōngdé).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, acting out of a mind of compassion, gives the gift of flowers and incense,
he should always firmly make vows such as these.
"Furthermore, good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, acting out of a mind of compassion, gives the gift of beds and furnishings (chuángfū),
he should make this vow:
'May the gifts I now bestow
be shared universally with all sentient beings.
Through this causality,
may all beings obtain the bed upon which the God of Gods (Tiānzhōngtiān) rests,
obtain great wisdom (dàzhìhuì),
and dwell in the abode of the Four Meditations (Sìchán);
sleeping on the bed upon which the Bodhisattvas sleep,
not sleeping on the beds of the Śrāvakayānas
or Pratyekabuddhayānas,
and leaving behind the sleeping on evil beds.
May all beings obtain peaceful and blissful rest (ānlè wò),
depart from the bed of transmigration (shēngsǐ),
and realize the Lion's Couch (Shīzǐ Wòchuáng) of Great Nirvāṇa.
May all beings, having sat upon this couch,
furthermore, for the sake of other measureless beings,
display the supernatural powers (shéntōng) of the Lion's Sport (Shīzǐ Yóuxì).
May all beings abide in this great palace (dàgōngdiàn) of the Mahāyāna,
and expound the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) for all beings.
May all beings sit upon the unexcelled couch (wúshàng chuáng),
and not be subdued by worldly dharmas (shìfǎ).
May all beings obtain the Couch of Patience (Rěnrǔ Chuáng),
departing from the hunger, famine, freezing, and starvation of transmigration.
May all beings obtain the Couch of Fearlessness (Wúwèi Chuáng),
forever separating from all afflictions (fánnǎo), enemies, and bandits.
May all beings obtain the Pure Couch (Qīngjìng Chuáng),
exclusively seeking the unexcelled true and proper path (zhèngzhēn zhī dào).
May all beings obtain the Couch of Wholesome Dharmas (Shàn Fǎ Chuáng),
and constantly be protected and guarded by good friends.
May all beings obtain the Couch of Right-Side Resting,
relying upon the Dharma practiced by all Buddhas.
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, acting out of a mind of compassion,
gives the gift of beds and furnishings,
he should firmly make vows such as these.
"Furthermore, good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, acting out of a mind of compassion,
gives the gift of houses and dwellings (shèzhái),
he should constantly make this vow:
'May the gifts I now bestow
be shared universally with all sentient beings.
Through this causality,
may all beings dwell in the Dwelling of the Mahāyāna (Dàchéng Shě),
practice the conduct practiced by good friends,
cultivate the conduct of great compassion (dàbēixíng),
the conduct of the Six Pāramitās (Liù Bōluómì),
the conduct of great proper enlightenment (dàzhèngjuéxíng),
the path-conduct practiced by all Bodhisattvas,
and conduct that is boundless and vast like the void (xūkōng).
May all beings universally attain right mindfulness (zhèngniàn),
and far depart from evil mindfulness (èniàn).
May all beings universally abide peacefully in permanence (cháng), bliss (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng),
forever departing from the Four Inversions (Sì Dǎo).
May all beings universally receive and maintain transcendent scriptures and texts (chūshì wénzì).
May all beings certainly become vessels for the unexcelled omniscience (Yīqiè Zhì).
May all beings universally enter the House of Amṛta (Gānlù Wūzhái).
May all beings, in their initial,
intermediate,
and final thoughts,
constantly enter the House of Nirvāṇa (Nièpán Wūzhái) of the Mahāyāna.
May all beings throughout future ages
constantly dwell in the palaces (gōngdiàn) inhabited by Bodhisattvas.
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, acting out of a mind of compassion,
gives the gift of houses and dwellings,
he should always firmly make vows such as these."
"Furthermore, good man!
When a Bódìsà Móhēsà, dwelling in the mind of Cí (loving-kindness/compassion),
bestows the light of lamps,
he constantly makes this vow:
'That which I now bestow,
I share completely with all sentient beings.
By means of this condition and cause,
may all sentient beings attain immeasurable radiance,
and peacefully abide in the Buddhadharma.
May all sentient beings constantly attain illumination.
May all sentient beings attain subtle and wonderful form,
and unsurpassed brilliance and luster.
May the eyes of all sentient beings be pure,
free from all cataracts and obstructions.
May all sentient beings attain the great torch of wisdom,
thoroughly understanding non-self,
the mark of non-sentient-being,
non-person, and non-life.
May all sentient beings behold the pure Buddha Nature,
like the empty space.
May the physical eyes of all sentient beings be pure,
penetratingly seeing the worlds of sands of the Ganges in the ten directions.
May all sentient beings attain the Buddha's radiance,
universally illuminating the ten directions.
May all sentient beings attain unobstructed clarity,
and fully behold the pure Buddha Nature.
May all sentient beings attain the clarity of great wisdom,
breaking through all darkness and even the *Yīchăntí*.
May all sentient beings attain immeasurable light,
universally illuminating immeasurable Buddha Worlds.
May all sentient beings light the lamp of the Great Vehicle,
departing from the lamps of the Two Vehicles.
May the radiance attained by all sentient beings
extinguish the darkness of ignorance,
surpassing the achievement of the universal illumination of a thousand suns.
May all sentient beings attain the clarity of the fire-pearl,
completely extinguishing all the darkness existing in the three thousand great-thousand worlds.
May all sentient beings be complete with the Five Eyes,
awakening to the marks of all phenomena,
achieving the realization that requires no teacher.
May all sentient beings be without views and without ignorance.
May all sentient beings attain the subtle and wonderful radiance of the Mahāyāna Great Parinirvāṇa,
demonstrating and awakening sentient beings to the true Buddha Nature.
Good man!
When a Bódìsà Móhēsà, dwelling in the mind of Cí, bestows the light of lamps,
he should constantly and diligently utter such solemn vows.
"Good man!
All Śrāvakas,
Pratyekabuddhas,
Bódìsàs,
and all Buddhas and Tathāgatas,
all have good roots,
Cí as their foundation.
Good man!
When a Bódìsà Móhēsà practices the mind of Cí,
he can generate such immeasurable good roots,
namely: impurity contemplation,
outgoing breath,
incoming breath,
impermanence,
arising and ceasing,
the Four Stations of Mindfulness,
the Seven Expedients,
the Three Contemplations,
the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination,
the contemplation of non-self and others,
the Warmth Dharma,
the Summit Dharma,
the Forbearance Dharma,
the World's Foremost Dharma,
the Path of Insight,
the Path of Cultivation,
the Right Efforts,
the Bases of Psychic Power,
the Faculties,
the Powers,
the Seven Constituents of Awakening,
the Eightfold Noble Path,
the Four Jhānas,
the Four Immeasurable Minds,
the Eight Liberations,
the Eight Superior Places,
All-pervasiveness,
Emptiness,
Signlessness,
the Samādhi of Non-contention,
the knowledge of others' minds,
and all the psychic penetrations,
the knowledge of the fundamental reality,
the wisdom of the Śrāvakas,
the wisdom of the Pratyekabuddhas,
the wisdom of the Bódìsàs,
and the wisdom of the Buddha.
Good man!
Such Dharmas as these,
have Cí as their foundation.
Good man!
By reason of this meaning,
Cí is true reality,
not falsehood.
If someone asks:
'Who is the foundation of all good roots?'
You should say, 'It is Cí.'
By reason of this meaning,
Cí is true reality,
not falsehood.
Good man!
That which can act as the root of goodness,
is called true contemplation.
True contemplation,
is immediately called Cí.
Cí is immediately the Tathāgata.
Cí is immediately the Mahāyāna.
The Mahāyāna is immediately Cí.
Cí is immediately the Tathāgata.
Good man!
Cí is immediately the path to Bodhi (Pútídào).
The path to Bodhi is immediately the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is immediately Cí.
Good man!
Cí is immediately the Great Brahmā (Dàfàn).
The Great Brahmā is immediately Cí.
Cí is immediately the Tathāgata.
Good man!
Cí is capable of being the mother and father to all sentient beings.
The mother and father are immediately Cí.
Cí is immediately the Tathāgata.
Good man!
Cí is truly inconceivable.
The realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable.
The realm of the Buddhas is immediately Cí.
You should know that Cí is immediately the Tathāgata.
Good man!
Cí is immediately the Buddha Nature of sentient beings.
Because this Buddha Nature
has long been obscured by the defilements,
it causes sentient beings not to behold it.
The Buddha Nature is immediately Cí.
Cí is immediately the Tathāgata.
Good man!
Cí is immediately the Great Emptiness.
The Great Emptiness is immediately Cí.
Cí is immediately the Tathāgata.
Good man!
Cí is immediately empty space.
Empty space is immediately Cí.
Cí is immediately the Tathāgata.
Good man!
Cí is immediately permanence.
Permanence is immediately the Dharma.
The Dharma is immediately the Saṅgha.
The Saṅgha is immediately Cí.
Cí is immediately the Tathāgata.
Good man!
Cí is immediately bliss.
Bliss is immediately the Dharma.
The Dharma is immediately the Saṅgha.
The Saṅgha is immediately Cí.
Cí is immediately the Tathāgata.
Good man!
Cí is immediately purity.
Purity is immediately the Dharma.
The Dharma is immediately the Saṅgha.
The Saṅgha is immediately Cí.
Cí is immediately the Tathāgata.
Good man!
Cí is immediately the Self.
The Self is immediately the Dharma.
The Dharma is immediately the Saṅgha.
The Saṅgha is immediately Cí.
Cí is immediately the Tathāgata.
Good man!
Cí is immediately sweet dew/nectar.
Sweet dew is immediately Cí.
Cí is immediately the Buddha Nature.
The Buddha Nature is immediately the Dharma.
The Dharma is immediately the Saṅgha.
The Saṅgha is immediately Cí.
Cí is immediately the Tathāgata.
Good man!
Cí is immediately the unsurpassed path of all Bódìsàs.
The path is immediately Cí.
