Cí is immediately the Tathāgata.
Good man!
Cí is immediately the immeasurable realm of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
The immeasurable realm is immediately Cí.
You should know that this Cí is immediately the Tathāgata."
"Good man,
if compassion (cí) is impermanent (wúcháng),
and impermanence is compassion,
know that this compassion
is the compassion of the Shēngwén.
Good man!
If compassion is suffering (kǔ),
and suffering is compassion,
know that this compassion is the compassion of the Shēngwén.
Good man!
If compassion is impure (bùjìng),
and impurity is compassion,
know that this compassion is the compassion of the Shēngwén.
Good man!
If compassion is non-self (wúwǒ),
and non-self is compassion,
know that this compassion is the compassion of the Shēngwén.
Good man!
If compassion is false imagination (wàngxiǎng),
and false imagination is compassion,
know that this compassion is the compassion of the Shēngwén.
Good man!
If compassion is not named Dán Bōluómì,
compassion which is not Dāna,
know that this compassion is the compassion of the Shēngwén;
up to and including Bānruò Bōluómì, it is likewise.
Good man!
If compassion cannot benefit sentient beings,
compassion of this kind is the compassion of the Shēngwén.
Good man!
If compassion does not enter the path of the Yīchèng,
know that this compassion is the compassion of the Shēngwén.
Good man!
If compassion cannot fully awaken to all phenomena,
know that this compassion is the compassion of the Shēngwén.
Good man!
If compassion cannot perceive the nature of the Rúlái,
know that this compassion is the compassion of the Shēngwén.
Good man!
If compassion, upon seeing phenomena,
takes them all to have characteristics (yǒu xiàng),
know that this compassion is the compassion of the Shēngwén.
Good man!
If compassion is associated with defilement (yǒulòu),
that defiled compassion is the compassion of the Shēngwén.
Good man!
If compassion is conditioned (yǒuwéi),
that conditioned compassion is the compassion of the Shēngwén.
Good man!
If compassion cannot abide in the Chūzhù (First Stage),
compassion which is not the Chūzhù compassion,
know that it is the compassion of the Shēngwén.
Good man!
If compassion cannot attain the Buddha’s ten powers,
and the four kinds of fearlessness,
know that this compassion is the compassion of the Shēngwén.
Good man!
If compassion is capable of attaining the four fruits of a śramaṇa,
know that this compassion is the compassion of the Shēngwén.
"Good man!
Compassion that is existence (yǒu),
non-existence (wú),
neither existence,
nor non-existence (fēi wú)—
such compassion
is not what Shēngwén,
Pìzhīfó, and others are able to conceive of.
Good man!
If compassion is inconceivable,
phenomena are inconceivable,
Buddha-nature is inconceivable,
and the Rúlái is also inconceivable.
Good man!
The Púsà Móhēsà, dwelling in the Great Vehicle of the Great Parinirvāṇa,
cultivates such compassion.
Although they rest in sleep,
they do not sleep,
because of their diligent exertion;
although they are constantly enlightened,
there is also no enlightenment,
because there is no sleep;
while they are sleeping,
although the devas protect them,
there is also no one who protects them,
because they commit no evil;
in sleep they have no bad dreams,
nor any unwholesomeness,
because they are free from sleep;
after the end of life,
although they may be born in Fàntiān,
they are also not born anywhere,
because they have attained sovereignty.
Good man!
One who cultivates compassion
can attain and accomplish such immeasurable and boundless merit and virtue.
Good man!
This subtle scripture of the Great Nirvāṇa
is also able to accomplish such immeasurable and boundless merit and virtue,
and all Buddhas and Rúlái also attain the accomplishment of such immeasurable and boundless merit and virtue.
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"Shìzūn!
The thoughts of the Púsà Móhēsà
are all true,
while those of the Shēngwén and Pratyekabuddhas are not true.
Why do not all sentient beings, by the mighty power of the Púsà,
equally receive happiness?
If sentient beings truly do not attain happiness,
know that the compassion cultivated by the Púsà is without benefit."
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
The compassion of the Púsà
is not without benefit.
Good man!
There are sentient beings
who are certain to receive suffering,
and others who are not certain to receive it.
If there are sentient beings certain to receive suffering,
the compassion of the Púsà is without benefit to them,
namely, the Yīchǎntí.
If there are those whose reception of suffering is not definite,
the compassion of the Púsà is indeed of benefit,
enabling those sentient beings all to receive happiness.
Good man!
For example, when a person
sees a lion,
a tiger or leopard,
a jackal or wolf,
or a Rákṣasa demon,
they naturally generate fear.
When walking at night and seeing a stump, they also generate fright.
Good man!
Such people naturally feel fright.
Sentient beings are like this:
upon seeing one who cultivates compassion, they naturally receive happiness.
Good man!
Based on this principle,
the Púsà's cultivation of compassion is true thinking,
and not without benefit.
"Good man!
I say that this compassion
has immeasurable doors,
namely, spiritual powers.
Good man!
For example, Tí Pódá
instructed Āshéshì
to try and harm the Rúlái.
At that time, I entered Wángshě Dàchéng
to beg for food in order.
King Āshéshì immediately released the mad and drunken elephant Hùcái,
intending for it to harm me and my disciples.
That elephant at that time
trampled and killed immeasurable hundreds and thousands of sentient beings.
Once the beings were dead,
there was much blood and scent.
When the elephant smelled this,
its frenzy and drunkenness doubled.
Seeing me and my attendants
wearing reddish robes,
it mistook them for blood
and rushed towards us again.
Among my disciples, those who had not yet eliminated desire
fled in all directions out of fear,
except for Ānán.
At that time, all the people in Wángshě Dàchéng
raised their voices simultaneously, wailing and weeping,
saying thus:
'Alas!
The Rúlái perishes today!
How can the Perfectly Enlightened One suddenly be destroyed?'
At that moment, Tiáodá
felt joy in his heart:
'It is excellent that Qú Tán Shāméng should perish!
From now onward, he truly will not appear.
Wonderful is this plan!
My wish has been fulfilled.'
Good man!
At that time,
in order to subdue the elephant Hùcái,
I immediately entered the concentration of compassion,
extended my hand and showed it,
and from the five fingers projected five lions.
When the elephant saw this,
its heart was struck with terror,
and it immediately voided its bowels,
cast its whole body to the ground,
and reverently worshipped my feet.
Good man!
At that time,
there were truly no lions on the tips of my five fingers;
it was merely the power of the roots of goodness cultivated through compassion
that caused the elephant to be subdued."
"Furthermore, good man!
When I was about to enter Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
just starting out toward the city of Jūshīnàchéng,
there were five hundred strong men (lìshì).
On that path,
leveling the ground and sweeping,
there was a stone in the middle.
The crowd wanted to lift and discard it,
but despite using all their strength, they could not.
I then took pity on them,
and immediately gave rise to a compassionate heart.
Those strong men,
immediately saw me,
lift this great stone with my big toe,
throw it up into the sky,
then catch it with my hand,
place it in my right palm,
blow it into fine dust,
and then reunite it again.
I made those strong men cease their arrogance,
and then briefly spoke various essential Dharma teachings to them,
causing them all to arouse the mind of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòuduōluósānmiǎosānpútíxīn).
Good man!
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) at that time,
truly did not use a toe to lift this great stone into the sky,
nor place it back in the right palm, blow it into dust, and reunite it as before.
Good man!
You should know that this was the power of the root of loving-kindness and compassion (císhàn gēnlì),
which caused the strong men to see such a thing.
"Furthermore, good man!
In Southern India (Nántiānzhú) there was a great city named Shǒubōluó.
In this city there was an elder,
named Lúzhì,
who was the leader and guide of the masses,
and who had already planted numerous roots of goodness
at the dwellings of immeasurable Buddhas in the past.
Good man!
All the people in that great city
believed and submitted to heterodox paths,
and served the Nirgranthas (Níjiān).
At that time, because I desired to deliver that elder,
I traveled from the city of Rājagṛha (Wángshěchéng) to that settlement.
The distance between them was sixty-five Yojanas (yóuxún).
I proceeded on foot,
for the purpose of transforming and delivering those people.
Those Nirgranthas (Níjiān),
hearing that I intended to arrive at Shǒubōluó City,
immediately thought:
‘If Śramaṇa Gautama (Shāmén Qútán) arrives here,
these people will abandon us,
and no longer provide us with supplies.
We will be distressed and impoverished;
how can we sustain ourselves?’
The Nirgranthas (Níjiān)
scattered and separately announced to the people of that city:
‘Śramaṇa Gautama (Shāmén Qútán) is now intending to come here.
However, that śramaṇa,
abandoned his parents,
and rushes about East and West.
Wherever he goes,
he causes the land’s grain and rice not to ripen,
the people suffer famine,
and the dead are numerous.
Illness and wasting follow one after another,
and there is no rescue or remedy.
Gautama (Qútán) is reckless,
leading only various evil beings,
Rākṣasas (Luóchà) and ghosts, as his attendants.
People who are parentless,
isolated, and destitute,
come seeking instruction,
and become his disciples.
The doctrines he teaches and instructs in
purely speak of emptiness (xūkōng).
Wherever he arrives,
there is never any peace or happiness.’
When those people heard this,
they immediately felt fear,
bowed their heads in reverence at the Nirgrantha’s (Níjiān) feet,
and said:
‘Great Master!
For us now,
what plan should we make?’
The Nirgrantha (Níjiān) replied:
‘Śramaṇa Gautama (Shāmén Qútán)
by nature loves groves,
flowing springs,
and clear water.
If any exist outside the city,
they should be destroyed.
You should go together out of the city,
chop down completely whatever is there,
and leave nothing remaining.
Into the flowing springs, wells, and ponds,
place manure and corpses.
Firmly close the city gates,
everyone prepare weapons,
guard along the walls,
and diligently secure your defenses.
If he attempts to approach,
do not let him advance.
If he does not advance,
you will be safe and peaceful.
We will also perform various magical spells,
to make that Gautama (Qútán)
turn around and go back the way he came.’
When those people heard these words,
they respectfully agreed and carried them out.
They chopped down trees,
polluted all the waters,
prepared their weapons,
and strongly protected themselves.
"Good man!
When I arrived at that city at that time,
I did not see any trees or groves,
I only saw the people preparing their weapons,
and guarding themselves along the walls.
Seeing this matter,
I immediately generated pity,
and directed a compassionate heart towards them.
All the trees instantly grew back to their original state,
and furthermore, immeasurable other trees grew;
rivers, ponds, wells, and springs,
their waters were pure and clean,
filling them up,
like sapphires (qīng liúlí);
various flowers blossomed,
covering the surface;
the city walls were transformed into dark blue lapis lazuli (gàn liúlí);
and the people inside the city were able to clearly see me and the great assembly.
The gates opened themselves,
no one being able to restrain them;
the weapons they had prepared,
transformed into various flowers.
The elder Lúzhì, acting as the leader,
together with his people,
followed one another to the dwelling of the Buddha.
I immediately spoke various essential Dharma teachings for them,
causing those people,
all of them, to arouse the mind of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòuduōluósānmiǎosānpútíxīn).
Good man!
At that time, I
truly did not miraculously create various trees,
pure flowing water,
or full rivers and ponds;
nor did I transform the original city into dark blue lapis lazuli (gàn liúlí),
causing those people to clearly see me,
open the city gates,
or turn their weapons into flowers.
Good man!
You should know that all of this was the power of the root of loving-kindness and compassion (císhàn gēnlì),
which enabled those people to see such things.
"Furthermore, good man!
In the city of Śrāvastī (Shěwèichéng) there was a Brahmin woman,
whose clan name was Póshītā.
She had only one son,
whom she loved deeply,
but he fell ill and died.
At that time, the woman,
with grief and anguish piercing her heart,
became distraught and lost her sanity,
stripping herself naked without shame,
wandering along the four crossroads,
weeping until she lost her voice,
crying out:
‘Son! Son!
Where did you go?’
She went all over the city and its environs,
without tiring.
But this woman
had already planted many roots of virtue under previous Buddhas.
Good man!
I conceived a heart of compassion and pity toward this woman.
At that moment, the woman immediately saw me,
and conceived the thought that I was her son.
She regained her original mind,
came forward and embraced my body,
and kissed my mouth.
I then immediately told my attendant Ānán (Ānanda):
‘You may take a robe and give it to this woman.’
After the robe had been given,
I spoke various essential Dharma teachings to her.
When the woman heard the Dharma,
she was overjoyed and ecstatic,
and aroused the mind of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòuduōluósānmiǎosānpútíxīn).
Good man!
At that time, I was truly not her son,
she was not my mother,
nor was there any embracing.
Good man!
You should know that all of this was the power of the root of loving-kindness and compassion (císhàn gēnlì),
which caused that woman to see such a thing."
"Furthermore, noble son!
In the city of Bōluónài chéng, there was a Upāsikā (laywoman),
named Móhēsīnàdádūo,
who had planted various good roots under countless Buddhas in the past.
This Upāsikā,
during the ninety days of summer,
invited the assembly of monks
and offered them medical treatment and medicine.
At that time, there was a Bhikṣu (monk) among the assembly
whose body was afflicted with a severe illness.
A good physician examined him,
and stated that medicine made from meat was required;
if meat could be obtained,
the illness could be removed;
if meat could not be obtained,
his life would not be preserved.
When the Upāsikā heard these words from the physician,
she immediately took gold,
traveled throughout the marketplace,
and announced thus:
'Who has meat for sale?
I will buy it with gold.
If there is meat,
I shall pay an equal amount of gold for it.'
Searching throughout the city,
she could not obtain it.
This Upāsikā then took a knife herself and cut the flesh from her thigh,
sliced it to make a broth,
added various spices,
and sent it to the sick Bhikṣu.
After the Bhikṣu consumed it,
the illness was immediately cured.
The Upāsikā suffered severe pain from the wound,
which she could not endure,
and immediately cried out, saying:
'Námó Fútuó! Námó Fútuó!' (Homage to the Buddha! Homage to the Buddha!)
I was dwelling in Shěwèichéng at that time,
and heard her voice,
whereupon I generated great compassion for this woman.
The woman immediately saw
me holding fine medicine,
which I applied to her wound,
and it healed, returning to its original state.
I then taught various aspects of the Dharma to her,
and hearing the Dharma, she rejoiced
and generated the resolve for Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Noble son!
At that time, I
truly did not go to Bōluónài chéng,
holding medicine to apply to the Upāsikā’s wound.
Noble son!
You should know that this was entirely the power of the roots of goodness and compassion,
which caused that woman to see such an event.
"Furthermore, noble son!
Dàodá, the wicked person,
was greedy and discontented,
and because he consumed too much butter/ghee,
he suffered from headaches and stomachaches,
undergoing great distress and pain,
which he could not endure,
and he cried out thus:
'Námó Fútuó! Námó Fútuó!'
I was residing in Yōuchánní chéng at the time,
and hearing his voice,
I immediately generated a compassionate mind.
At that time, Dàodá immediately saw me
going to his location,
rubbing his head and stomach with my hand,
and giving him salted soup
to consume.
After consuming it, he recovered and returned to normal.
Noble son!
I truly did not go to Dàopódá’s location,
rub his head and stomach, or give him soup to consume.
Noble son!
You should know that this was entirely the power of the roots of goodness and compassion,
which caused Dàopódá to see such an event.
"Furthermore, noble son!
In the kingdom of Jiāosàluó guó, there were groups of bandits,
five hundred in number,
who banded together to plunder and rob,
causing severe harm.
King Bōsīnì Wáng was troubled by their wild violence,
and sent troops to seek and capture them.
Having captured them, he gouged out their eyes
and cast them beneath a dense, dark forest.
These groups of bandits
had already planted various roots of virtue under previous Buddhas.
Having lost their eyes,
they suffered great distress,
and each one cried out, saying:
'Námó Fútuó! Námó Fútuó!
We now have no one to rescue and protect us.'
They wept and wailed.
I was residing in the Qíhuán Jīngshě at the time,
and heard their voices,
and immediately generated a compassionate mind.
At that time, a cool breeze arose,
blowing various fragrant medicines from the Fragrant Mountains (Xiāng shān),
filling their eye sockets.
Immediately, they recovered their sight,
no different from before.
The bandits opened their eyes
and immediately saw the Tathāgata
standing before them teaching the Dharma.
Having heard the Dharma, the bandits
generated the resolve for Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Noble son!
I truly did not, at that time, create the wind
to blow the various fragrant medicines from the Fragrant Mountains,
nor did I stand before those people teaching the Dharma.
Noble son!
You should know that this was entirely the power of the roots of goodness and compassion,
which caused those groups of bandits to see such an event.
"Furthermore, noble son!
Prince Liúlí Tàizǐ, due to his foolishness,
deposed his father, the king,
and established himself as ruler.
Furthermore, remembering an old grudge,
he harmed many of the Śākya clan,
taking twelve thousand women of the Śākya clan,
cutting off their ears and noses,
severing their hands and feet,
and casting them into pits and ditches.
At that time, all the women,
whose bodies were suffering distress,
cried out thus:
'Námó Fútuó! Námó Fútuó!
We now have no one to rescue and protect us.'
They wailed loudly again.
These women
had already planted various roots of goodness under previous Buddhas.
I was in the Bamboo Grove at that time,
and hearing their voices,
I immediately generated a compassionate mind.
At that time, the women
saw me arriving at Jiāpíluó chéng,
washing their wounds with water,
applying medicine to them.
Their pain was immediately removed,
and their ears, noses, hands, and feet
were restored to their original state.
I then briefly spoke the essentials of the Dharma to them,
causing all of them to jointly generate the resolve for Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
They then left home and received the complete precepts
from Dà Àidào Bǐqiūní.
Noble son!
The Tathāgata truly did not go to Jiāpíluó chéng at that time,
wash their wounds with water, or apply medicine to stop the suffering.
Noble son!
You should know that this was entirely the power of the roots of goodness and compassion,
which caused those women to experience such events.
The minds of pity and joy are also like this.
Noble son!
For this reason,
when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates the contemplation of loving-kindness,
it is genuine,
not false.
Noble son!
The immeasurable states are inconceivable.
The conduct of the Bodhisattvas is inconceivable.
The conduct of the Buddhas is also inconceivable.
This Great Vehicle scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, is likewise inconceivable."
"Furthermore, good man!
When a Púsà Móhēsà has practiced loving-kindness, compassion, and joy,
he attains dwelling in the stage (bhūmi) of Utmost Love and Only Son (Jí'ài Yīzǐ zhī Dì).
Good man!
How is this stage named Utmost Love (Jí'ài)?
And further, how is it named Only Son (Yīzǐ)?
Good man!
Just as parents,
seeing their child secure and peaceful,
feel great joy in their hearts.
A Púsà Móhēsà dwelling in this stage,
is likewise thus:
he regards all sentient beings as his only son,
and seeing those who cultivate goodness, he generates great joy.
Therefore, this stage is named Utmost Love (Jí'ài).
Good man!
Just as parents seeing their child afflicted by illness,
feel suffering and distress in their hearts,
and pity them with intense sorrow,
never abandoning them.
A Púsà Móhēsà dwelling in this stage is likewise thus:
seeing all sentient beings,
afflicted and bound by the sickness of defilements (fánnǎo),
his heart generates sorrow and distress;
he worries and contemplates them as his son,
and from the pores of his body,
blood all streams forth.
Therefore, this stage
is named Only Son (Yīzǐ).
Good man!
Just as when a person is young,
he picks up clumps of earth,
filth,
broken tiles and stones,
dead bones,
or wooden sticks,
and places them in his mouth.
When the parents see this,
fearing injury to him,
they hold his head with the left hand,
and pull it out with the right hand.
A Púsà Móhēsà dwelling in this stage,
is likewise thus:
seeing that the Dharma-body (fǎshēn) of sentient beings has not yet grown,
or that they commit unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind,
when the Púsà sees this,
he extracts them using the hand of wisdom,
not wishing them to continue revolving in saṃsāra and suffering distress.
Therefore, this stage
is further named Only Son (Yīzǐ).
Good man!
Just as parents,
when their beloved son departs and dies,
are full of sorrow and distress,
wishing to join him in death.
The Púsà is also like this:
seeing an icchantika (yīchǎntí) fall into the hells,
he also wishes to be born alongside them in the hells.
Why is this?
If this icchantika, when suffering torment,
should happen to generate a single thought of repentance,
I will immediately speak various Dharma teachings for them,
causing them to attain the generation of a single root of goodness.
Therefore, this stage
is further named Only Son (Yīzǐ).
Good man!
Just as parents,
who have only one son,
whether their son is waking or sleeping,
walking or standing,
sitting or lying down,
always keep him in mind.
If there is fault or transgression,
they guide and persuade him with kind words,
and do not inflict harm upon him.
A Púsà Móhēsà is likewise thus:
seeing all sentient beings, whether falling into the hells,
animal realm (chùshēng),
hungry ghost realm (ègǔi),
or among humans,
or among devas (tiān),
performing good or evil deeds,
he always keeps them in mind,
never abandoning them.
If they perform various evils,
he ultimately does not generate hatred,
nor inflict evil upon them.
Therefore, this stage
is further named Only Son (Yīzǐ).
Púsà Jiāyè addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Shìzūn!
As the Buddha has spoken,
those words are profound and secret.
My wisdom now is shallow;
how can I understand?
If all Púsàs dwelling in the Only Son stage
can act like this,
how is it that the Rúlái, when he was formerly a king practicing as a Púsà,
cut off the lives of so many Póluómén?
If he had attained this stage,
he should have protected and cherished them.
If he had not attained it,
then for what reason did he not fall into the hells?
If he equally regards all sentient beings,
thinking of them as his son, like Luóhóuluó,
why did he furthermore speak to Típódáduō with such words:
'Stupid man without shame,
eating the snot and spittle of others.'
Having heard this, he [Típódáduō]
generated hatred and resentment,
aroused unwholesome thoughts,
and shed the blood of the Buddha's body.
After Típódáduō committed this evil,
the Rúlái further predicted
that he would fall into the hells and suffer punishment for one kalpa.
Shìzūn!
How is it that these words do not contradict the meaning [of the teachings]?
Shìzūn!
Xūpútí, dwelling in the Xūkōng Dì (Emptiness Stage),
whenever he wishes to enter a city to seek food and drink by begging,
must first observe the people.
If anyone harbors feelings of dislike or jealousy toward him,
he stops and does not proceed.
Even if extremely hungry,
he still does not go begging.
Why is this?
This Xūpútí constantly holds this thought:
'I recall that in the past, I generated one evil thought toward a field of merit (fútián),
and because of this cause and condition, I fell into the great hells,
suffering various torments.
I would rather starve now,
going all day without eating,
than cause them to conceive aversion toward me
and fall into the hells to suffer distress.'
He further holds this thought:
'If there are sentient beings who dislike my standing,
I will remain seated upright the whole day without rising.
If there are sentient beings who dislike my sitting,
I will stand the whole day without moving my position,
and it is the same for walking and lying down.'
This Xūpútí,
because he protects sentient beings,
still generates such a mindset;
how much more so a Púsà?
If a Púsà attains the Only Son stage,
for what reason did the Rúlái utter such harsh words,
causing sentient beings to arouse severe evil thoughts?
"Good man!
You should not now make such a difficulty (nán),
saying that the Buddha Rúlái creates the causes and conditions for the defilements of sentient beings.
Good man!
Even if a gnat or mosquito (wénzhèn) could drain the bottom of the sea completely,
the Rúlái would ultimately not create the causes and conditions for the defilements of sentient beings.
Good man!
Even if the great earth were entirely non-material (fēi sè),
water were to possess the characteristic of hardness (jiān xiāng),
fire were to possess the characteristic of coldness (lěng xiāng),
and wind were to possess the characteristic of immobility (zhù xiāng);
or if the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo), Buddha-nature (fóxìng), and emptiness (xūkōng)
were to take on the characteristic of impermanence (wúcháng xiāng);
the Rúlái would ultimately not create the causes and conditions for the defilements of sentient beings.
Good man!
Even if those who violate the four major prohibitions (sìchóng jìn zuì) or are icchantikas (yīchǎntí),
or slander the Right Dharma (zhèngfǎ),
could in their present body attain the ten powers (shílì),
fearlessness (wúwèi),
thirty-two marks (sānshí'èr xiāng),
and eighty subsidiary characteristics (bāshí zhǒng hǎo),
the Rúlái would ultimately not create the causes and conditions for the defilements of sentient beings.
Good man!
Even if Śrāvakas (shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (pìzhīfó), etc., were eternally abiding and unchanging,
the Rúlái would ultimately not create the causes and conditions for the defilements of sentient beings.
Good man!
Even if Púsàs in the Ten Stages (shízhù zhū Púsà)
were to violate the four major prohibitions,
become icchantikas,
and slander the Right Dharma,
the Rúlái would ultimately not create the causes and conditions for the defilements of sentient beings.
Good man!
Even if all immeasurable sentient beings were to lose and destroy their Buddha-nature (fóxìng),
and the Rúlái ultimately entered Bān Nièpán,
the Rúlái would ultimately not create the causes and conditions for the defilements of sentient beings.
Good man!
Even if a snare thrown could bind the wind,
teeth could break iron,
and claws could destroy Xūmí (Mount Sumeru),
the Rúlái would ultimately not create the causes and conditions for the defilements of sentient beings.
I would rather stay in the same place as a poisonous snake,
put my hands into the mouth of a starving lion,
or wash my body with Quétuóluó charcoal,
than utter the statement
that the Rúlái Shìzūn creates the causes and conditions for the defilements of sentient beings.
Good man!
The Rúlái truly enables sentient beings to cut off their defilements,
and ultimately does not create the causes of defilement for them."
“Good son!
Regarding what you said,
that the Tathāgata in times past killed a Brāhmaṇa;
Good son!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva intentionally kills not even an ant,
how much less a Brāhmaṇa?
A Bodhisattva constantly employs various expedients,
bestowing immeasurable lifespan upon sentient beings.
Good son!
Indeed, one who bestows food thereby bestows life,
when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices Dānapāramì,
he constantly bestows immeasurable lifespan upon sentient beings.
Good son!
By cultivating the precept of non-killing, one attains longevity;
when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices Sīlapāramì,
he thereby bestows immeasurable lifespan upon all sentient beings.
Good son!
By guarding the mouth and avoiding transgressions, one attains longevity;
when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices Kshāntipāramì,
he constantly encourages sentient beings not to give rise to thoughts of resentment,
to attribute rectitude to others,
and to take the crookedness upon oneself,
and by having no disputes or contention, one attains longevity;
therefore, when the Bodhisattva practices Kshāntipāramì,
he has already bestowed immeasurable lifespan upon sentient beings.
Good son!
By diligently cultivating goodness, one attains longevity;
when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices Vīryapāramì,
he constantly encourages sentient beings to diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas;
when sentient beings practice this,
they attain immeasurable lifespan;
therefore, when the Bodhisattva practices Vīryapāramì,
he has already bestowed immeasurable lifespan upon sentient beings.
Good son!
By cultivating the restraint of mind, one attains longevity;
when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices Dhyānapāramì,
he encourages all sentient beings to cultivate an impartial mind,
when sentient beings practice this, they attain longevity,
therefore, when the Bodhisattva practices Dhyānapāramì,
he has already bestowed immeasurable lifespan upon sentient beings.
Good son!
By not being heedless regarding wholesome dharmas, one attains longevity;
when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices Prajñāpāramì,
he encourages all sentient beings not to give rise to heedlessness regarding wholesome dharmas,
when sentient beings practice this, due to this cause and condition, they attain longevity,
therefore, when the Bodhisattva practices Prajñāpāramì,
he has already bestowed immeasurable lifespan upon sentient beings.
Good son!
For this reason,
a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva never takes the life of any sentient being.
“Good son!
The question you previously asked,
did I attain this stage when I killed the Brāhmaṇa or not?
Good son!
At that time I had already attained it.
Due to love and concern,
I severed his life root,
it was not an evil intention.
Good son!
Suppose parents,
who have only one child,
love him very dearly,
and he violates the laws of the state;
at that time, the parents, out of fear,
either banish him or kill him,
and even though they banish or kill him,
they do not have an evil intention.
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva protecting the True Dharma is also like this;
if there are sentient beings who slander the Mahāyāna,
he immediately chastises them with whips,
inflicts severe punishment upon them,
or takes their lives,
wishing them to reform their ways,
and follow and cultivate wholesome dharmas.
The Bodhisattva should constantly think in this way:
‘By what cause and condition
can I enable sentient beings to generate faith?’
According to the expedient means available,
he must act for their sake.
When those Brāhmaṇa men died,
and were born in the Ābì Dìyù (Avīci Hell),
they necessarily had three thoughts:
First, they thought to themselves:
‘From where did I come to be born here?’
They immediately knew themselves
to have come from the human path.
Second, they thought to themselves:
‘Where is this place where I am now born?’
They immediately knew themselves to be in the Ābì Yù (Avīci Hell).
Third, they thought to themselves:
‘Riding on what karmic condition did I come to be born here?’
They immediately knew themselves to have been born here because they had slandered the Vaipulya Mahāyāna Sūtras,
had lacked faith in the cause and condition,
and had been killed by the ruler of the country.
After contemplating these matters,
they immediately generated faith and respect
towards the Vaipulya Mahāyāna Sūtras,
and swiftly died at that moment,
and were born in the world of the Tathāgata Gānlù Gǔ (Amṛtadundubhi),
where their lifespan was complete for ten kalpas.
Good son!
For this reason,
I formerly bestowed a ten-kalpa lifespan upon that person;
how can it be called killing?
Good son!
If a person digs the earth,
cuts grass, chops trees,
dismembers a dead body,
or reviles and whips,
due to these karmic conditions,
does he fall into hell or not?”
Kāshè Púsà (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva) said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has spoken,
he should fall into hell.
Why?
Just as the Buddha formerly taught the Śrāvakas:
‘You Bhikṣus,
do not give rise to evil intentions
towards even dry wood.
Why?
All sentient beings fall into hell due to evil intentions.”
At that time, the Buddha praised Gāyè Púsà:
“Excellent!
Excellent!
As you have said,
one should properly receive and uphold it.
Good man!
If one who falls into the hells is due to an evil mind,
then the Púsà at that time truly had no evil mind.
Why is this?
Because the Púsà Móhēsà, regarding all sentient beings down to insects and ants,
gives rise to minds of compassion and benefit.
Why is that?
Because they skillfully know the causes and conditions and all expedient means.
By the power of expedient means,
they desire to cause sentient beings to plant all good roots.
Good man!
For this reason,
I, at that time,
by skillful expedient means,
though I took their lives, it was not an evil mind.
Good man!
According to the law of the Brāhmaṇas (Pólúomén),
if one kills ant children
there is no karmic retribution (zuìbào).
Mosquitoes,
gnats, fleas, lice,
cats, badgers, lions (shīzi),
tigers, wolves, bears (xióngpī),
all evil insects and beasts,
and others that can harm sentient beings—
if killed, filling ten carts;
ghosts and spirits, Ràchàs,
Kūbănchá,
Jiāluó,
Fùdānnà,
and various insane and desiccated ghosts and spirits (guǐshén)
that can afflict and harm sentient beings—
if their lives are taken,
there is entirely no karmic retribution.
If one kills an evil person,
there is karmic retribution.
If, having killed, one does not repent,
one falls into the realm of hungry ghosts (èguǐ).
If one can repent,
and fast for three days,
the transgression is extinguished,
without any remainder.
If one kills an Upādhyāya (Héshàng),
harms their parents, a woman, or a cow,
one will remain in the hells for countless thousands of years.
Good man!
The Buddha and the Púsàs know there are three types of killing:
low, medium, and high.
The low is from ant children up to all animals,
except for those Púsàs who manifest their births.
Good man!
The Púsà Móhēsà, due to the causes and conditions of their vows,
manifests as accepting an animal birth.
This is named low killing.
Due to the causes and conditions of low killing,
one falls into the hells,
the animal realm (chùshēng),
or the realm of hungry ghosts,
and completely suffers low suffering.
Why is this?
Because these animals possess minute good roots,
therefore, the killer completely suffers the karmic retribution.
This is named low killing.
Medium killing
is from ordinary people (fánfū rén) up to an Anāgāmi (Ānàhán); this is named medium.
Due to this karma, one falls into the hells,
the animal realm,
or the realm of hungry ghosts,
and completely suffers medium suffering.
This is named medium killing.
High killing
is parents, up to an Arhat (Āluóhàn),
a Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó),
or a Definite Púsà (Bìdìng Púsà);
this is named high.
Due to the causes and conditions of this karma,
one falls into the Ābǐ Great Hell (Dàdìyù),
and completely suffers high suffering.
This is named high killing.
Good man!
If someone can kill an Iccantika (Yīchǎntí),
they do not fall into these three types of killing.
Good man!
Those Brāhmaṇas are all Iccantikas.
Just as digging the ground,
cutting grass, chopping down trees,
slicing and cutting corpses, or cursing and whipping,
has no karmic retribution,
killing an Iccantika is also like this;
there is no karmic retribution.
Why is this?
The Brāhmaṇas do not even possess the Five Roots (wǔ gēn) such as faith;
therefore, although one kills them, one does not fall into the hells.”
"Good man!
What you previously stated,
'Why did the Tathāgata curse Dìpó Dáduō as a fool who eats spittle?'
You should also not ask such a question.
Why?
All Buddhas, Bhagavāns,
whatever they speak,
is inconceivable.
Good man!
There might be true words,
loved by the world,
but if they are not timely, not lawful,
and do not bring benefit,
such words
I will never speak.
Good man!
Or there might be words
that are coarse, cruel, and false,
not timely, not lawful,
not loved by those who hear them,
and unable to benefit them;
I also do not speak these.
Good man!
If there are words,
even if they are coarse and cruel,
true and not false,
timely and lawful, able to benefit all sentient beings,
even if hearing them is displeasing,
I must speak them.
Why?
Because all Buddhas, Bhagavāns,
Arhats,
and Samyaksaṃbuddhas,
know the means (upāya).
Good man!
For instance, once,
when I was traveling in that wilderness (Kuàngyě),
near a village where trees gathered,
under the trees,
there was a ghost (guǐshén),
named Kuàngyě,
who subsisted solely on meat and blood, and killed many sentient beings.
Moreover, in that settlement,
he ate one person daily.
Good man!
At that time, I
broadly expounded the essential Dharma to that ghost;
however, he was savage and evil,
foolish, ignorant, and unwise,
and would not accept the teachings of the Dharma.
I immediately transformed my body into a ghost of great power,
shook his palace,
and made it unstable.
That ghost then led his retinue,
exited his palace,
intending to come and resist me.
When the ghost saw me,
he immediately lost his consciousness,
fell to the ground in terror,
fainted, utterly cut off,
just like a dead person.
I, out of compassion,
stroked his body with my hand.
He immediately stood up and sat down,
and spoke thus:
'How wonderful!
Today I have recovered my body and life.
This great Spirit King,
possessing great majesty and virtue,
has a compassionate heart
and has pardoned my faults and transgressions.'
Immediately, in my presence,
he gave rise to pure faith.
I then reverted back to the body of the Tathāgata,
and further spoke various essential Dharmas for him,
causing that ghost,
to accept the precept of non-killing.
On that very day,
in the village of Kuàngyě,
there was an elder (zhǎngzhě) who was next in line to die,
and the villagers had already delivered him to that ghost.
After the ghost received him,
he immediately offered him to me;
after I received him,
I then gave the elder
a new name,
calling him Shǒuzhǎngzhě.
At that time, that ghost immediately said to me:
'Bhagavān!
I and my retinue
depend solely on blood and meat
to sustain life.
Now, because of the precept,
how shall we live?'
I immediately replied:
'From now on, I shall instruct my Śrāvaka disciples
that wherever the Buddha Dharma is practiced,
they should all be made to offer you food and drink.'
Good man!
Due to this cause and condition,
I established this precept for all Bhikṣus (monks):
'From now on, you all
must constantly offer food to that Kuàngyě ghost.
If there is a dwelling place where this offering cannot be made,
you should know that those individuals
are not my disciples,
but are the followers and retinue of the Heavenly Māra.'
Good man!
The Tathāgata, in order to subdue sentient beings,
demonstrates various skillful means such as these,
not intentionally causing them to feel fear."
"Good man!
I also struck the guardian Dharma ghost with a piece of wood.
Furthermore, at another time,
while on a mountain,
I pushed the Yángtóu Guǐ (Sheep-Head Ghost),
causing him to fall down the mountain.
Again, from a treetop,
I knocked down the Hùmíhóu Guǐ (Guardian Monkey Ghost);
I made the Hùcái Xiàng (Treasure-Guarding Elephant)
see five lions;
I employed the Jīngāng Shén (Vajra Spirits) to terrify Sàzhē Níjiān;
I also pricked the body of the Jiànmáo Guǐ (Arrow-Haired Ghost) with a needle.
Although I acted like this,
I did not cause any of those ghosts or spirits to be destroyed or perish.
I simply intended for them
to dwell peacefully in the Correct Dharma;
therefore, I showed these various skillful means.
Good man!
At that time, I
truly did not curse or insult Dìpó Dáduō (Devadatta);
nor was Dìpó Dáduō foolish, eating human spittle,
nor was he born in the evil realms,
suffering punishment for one kalpa in the Ābí Dìyù (Avīci Hell),
nor did he shatter the Saṅgha or draw the Buddha's blood,
nor did he violate the four cardinal offenses,
slander the Correct Dharma, or the Mahāyāna Sūtras.
He is not an Icchantika,
nor is he a Śrāvaka (Sound-Hearer),
nor a Pratyekabuddha.
Good man!
The case of Dìpó Dáduō
is truly not the realm of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
it is only known and seen by all Buddhas.
Good man!
Therefore, you should not now raise the difficulty by saying:
'For what reason did the Tathāgata scold, curse, and insult Dìpó Dáduō?'
Regarding the realms of all Buddhas,
you should not give rise to such nets of doubt."
Kāshè Púsà (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva) said to the Buddha:
"Bhagavān!
Just as sugarcane,
repeatedly boiled and cooked,
obtains various tastes;
I am also like this,
repeatedly hearing from the Buddha,
I gain many tastes of the Dharma,
namely, the taste of renunciation,
the taste of detachment from desire,
the taste of stillness and extinction,
and the taste of the Path.
Bhagavān!
Just as true gold,
repeatedly heated and beaten,
melted, purified, refined, and processed,
becomes ever brighter and purer,
temperate and soft,
with exquisite luster and color,
its value is immeasurable,
and only then is it treasured by humans and devas.
Bhagavān!
The Tathāgata is also like this;
when solemnly questioned,
one obtains the hearing and seeing of extremely profound meanings,
allowing those who practice profoundly to receive, uphold, respect, and cultivate them,
causing immeasurable sentient beings to generate the aspiration for Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí Xīn (Anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi),
and only then is he revered by all humans and devas,
with respect and offerings."
At that time, the Buddha praised Kāshè Púsà:
"Excellent!
Excellent!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in order to benefit sentient beings,
inquires of the Tathāgata about such profound meanings.
Good man!
Because of this principle,
I will follow your intention
and speak the extremely profound and secret Dharma of the Fāngděng (Vaipulya) Mahāyāna,
namely, the stage of Jí'ài Rú Yīzǐ Dì (Utmost Love, like an Only Son)."
Kāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"Bhagavān!
If Bodhisattvas cultivate Maitrī (Cí),
Karuṇā (Bēi),
and Muditā (Xǐ),
and attain the stage of the Only Son,
when cultivating Upekṣā (Shě Xīn, equanimity),
what stage do they then attain?"
The Fó said:
“Excellent,
excellent!
Shànnánzǐ!
You know the time well;
knowing I wish to speak,
you then inquire.
When a Púsà Móhēsà cultivates the mind of abandonment,
he obtains dwelling in the ground of emptiness and equality,
like Xūpútí.
Shànnánzǐ!
When a Púsà Móhēsà dwells in the ground of emptiness and equality,
he does not see parents,
brothers,
sisters,
children,
relatives,
acquaintances,
or people who are enemies, hated, or neutral;
up to and including not seeing the aggregates, realms, and entrances [sense bases],
sentient beings,
or lifespan.
Shànnánzǐ!
Just as empty space
has no parents,
brothers,
or wife and children,
up to and including having no sentient beings
or lifespan.
All phenomena
are also like this,
having no parents up to and including lifespan.
A Púsà Móhēsà, seeing all phenomena
are also like this,
his mind is equanimous,
like that empty space.
Why is this?
Because he is skilled at cultivating and practicing the Dharma of emptiness.
Jiāyè Púsà addressed the Fó, saying:
“Shìzūn!
What is called emptiness?”
"Good son! (Shànnánzǐ!)
Emptiness (kōngzhě),
refers to inner emptiness (nèikōng),
outer emptiness (wàikōng),
inner and outer emptiness (nèiwàikōng),
conditioned emptiness (yǒuwéikōng),
unconditioned emptiness (wúwéikōng),
beginningless emptiness (wúshǐkōng),
nature emptiness (xìngkōng),
non-possession emptiness (wúsuǒyǒukōng),
ultimate truth emptiness (dìyīyìkōng),
emptiness of emptiness (kōngkōng),
and great emptiness (dàkōng).
How does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) contemplate inner emptiness (nèikōng)?
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates the emptiness of internal dharmas (nèifǎ).
This internal dharma emptiness
means the non-existence of parents (fùmǔ),
enemies, relatives, or neutral persons (yuànqīnzhōngrén),
sentient beings, lifespans,
permanence (cháng), joy (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng),
the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
the Dharma (Fǎ),
the Saṅgha (Sēng),
and all possessions (cáiwù).
Although within these internal dharmas
there exists the Buddha-nature (fóxìng),
yet this Buddha-nature
is neither internal nor external.
Why is this so?
Because the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) is permanent and abiding (chángzhù),
and is without change or alteration.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplating inner emptiness.
Outer emptiness (Wàikōng)
is likewise the same,
concerning the non-existence of internal dharmas (nèifǎ).
Inner and outer emptiness (Nèiwàikōng)
is likewise the same.
Good son! (Shànnánzǐ!)
Only the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
the Dharma (Fǎ),
the Saṅgha (Sēng),
and the Buddha-nature (fóxìng),
are not included in these two types of emptiness (kōng).
Why?
Because these four dharmas
are permanent (cháng),
joyful (lè),
self (wǒ),
and pure (jìng).
Therefore, these four dharmas
are not called emptiness.
This is called inner and outer dual emptiness (jùkōng).
Good son! (Shànnánzǐ!)
Conditioned emptiness (Yǒuwéikōng) means that
all conditioned dharmas (yǒuwéizhīfǎ) are entirely empty,
namely inner emptiness,
outer emptiness,
inner and outer emptiness,
the emptiness of permanence, joy, self, and purity (chánglèwǒjìng kōng),
and the ultimate truth emptiness (dìyīyìkōng) of sentient beings, lifespan, Tathāgata (Rúlái), Dharma (Fǎ), and Saṅgha (Sēng).
Within this, the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng)
is not a conditioned dharma (yǒuwéi fǎ),
thus the Buddha-nature is not the emptiness of conditioned dharmas.
This is called conditioned emptiness.
Good son! (Shànnánzǐ!)
How does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplate unconditioned emptiness (wúwéikōng)?
These unconditioned dharmas (wúwéi fǎ)
are all entirely empty,
namely impermanence (wúcháng),
suffering (kǔ),
impurity (bújìng),
non-self (wúwǒ),
Skandhas (yīn), Dhātus (jiè), and Āyatanas (rù),
sentient beings,
characteristics of lifespan,
conditioned existence (yǒuwéi),
defilements (yǒulòu),
internal dharmas,
and external dharmas.
Within unconditioned dharmas,
the four dharmas, starting with the Buddha (Fó),
are neither conditioned (yǒuwéi)
nor unconditioned (wúwéi).
Because their nature is good (shàn),
they are not unconditioned;
because their nature is permanent and abiding (chángzhù),
they are not conditioned.
This is called the Bodhisattva contemplating unconditioned emptiness.
How does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplate beginningless emptiness (wúshǐkōng)?
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sees that Saṃsāra (shēngsǐ) is beginningless
and is entirely empty and quiescent.
That which is called empty,
permanence, joy, self, and purity,
are all entirely empty and quiescent,
and without change or alteration.
Sentient beings, lifespan, the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo), Buddha-nature (fóxìng), and unconditioned dharmas (wúwéi fǎ),
this is called the Bodhisattva contemplating beginningless emptiness.
How does the Bodhisattva contemplate nature emptiness (xìngkōng)?
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates that all dharmas
are fundamentally empty in nature,
namely Skandhas (yīn), Dhātus (jiè), Āyatanas (rù),
permanence,
impermanence,
suffering,
joy,
purity,
impurity,
self,
and non-self.
Contemplating all such dharmas,
one does not perceive their fundamental nature.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplating nature emptiness.
How does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplate non-possession emptiness (wúsuǒyǒukōng)?
Just as a person without a son
says the house is empty,
ultimately contemplating emptiness,
being without attachment (qīn'ài).
Ignorant persons (yúchī zhī rén)
say that all directions are empty.
Impoverished persons (pínqióng zhī rén)
say that everything is empty.
The way these things are counted,
sometimes they are empty,
sometimes they are not empty.
When the Bodhisattva contemplates,
like the impoverished person,
everything is empty.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplating non-possession emptiness.
How does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplate ultimate truth emptiness (dìyīyìkōng)?
Good son! (Shànnánzǐ!)
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates the ultimate truth (dìyīyì),
when the eye arises,
it comes from nowhere,
and when it ceases,
it goes nowhere;
originally non-existent, it now exists;
having existed, it returns to non-existence;
examining its true nature,
there is no eye and no master.
Just as the eye has no inherent nature (wúxìng),
all dharmas (zhūfǎ) are likewise the same.
What is called ultimate truth emptiness?
There is karma (yè),
there is retribution (bào),
but the agent (zuòzhě) is not seen.
Such emptiness dharma (kōngfǎ)
is called ultimate truth emptiness.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplating ultimate truth emptiness.
How does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplate emptiness of emptiness (kōngkōng)?
This emptiness of emptiness
is precisely the place where Śrāvakās (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Pìzhīfó) are bewildered and submerged.
Good son! (Shànnánzǐ!)
To be existence (yǒu),
to be non-existence (wú),
this is called emptiness of emptiness;
to be what is (shì),
to be what is not what is (fēi shì shì),
this is called emptiness of emptiness.
Good son! (Shànnánzǐ!)
The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (Shízhù Púsà) still only penetrate a small fraction of this,
like a mere speck of dust,
how much less other people?
Good son! (Shànnánzǐ!)
This emptiness of emptiness
is also different from the emptiness of emptiness samādhi (kōngkōng sānmèi) attained by the Śrāvakās (Shēngwén).
This is called the Bodhisattva contemplating emptiness of emptiness.
Good son! (Shànnánzǐ!)
How does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplate great emptiness (dàkōng)?
Good son! (Shànnánzǐ!)
That which is called great emptiness
is Prajñāpāramitā (Bōrě Bōluómì).
This is called great emptiness.
Good son! (Shànnánzǐ!)
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains this Dharma Gate of Emptiness (kōngmén),
they attain dwelling on the ground of space (xūkōng děngdì).
"Good man!
When I now speak of the meanings of various kinds of emptiness (kōng yì) among this great assembly,
there are ten times the sands of the Gangā River (Hénghé Shā) worth of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas (Púsa Móhēsà),
who immediately attain dwelling in the Stage of Empty Space (Xūkōng Děng Dì).
Good man!
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsa Móhēsà) dwells in this Stage,
regarding all phenomena (fǎ),
there is no obstruction,
no bondage,
no grasping,
and the mind is without confusion or dullness.
For this reason,
it is named the Stage of Empty Space (Xūkōng Děng Dì).
Good man!
For example, empty space (xūkōng),
regarding pleasant forms,
does not generate greed or attachment;
regarding unpleasant forms,
does not generate anger or hatred.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsa Móhēsà) dwelling in this Stage
is also like this:
regarding good and bad forms,
the mind is without greed
and hatred.
Good man!
For example, empty space (xūkōng),
is vast and peerless,
and is entirely able to contain all phenomena (zhū fǎ).
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsa Móhēsà) dwelling in this Stage is also like this:
vast and peerless,
entirely able to contain all phenomena (zhū fǎ).
For this reason,
it is again named the Stage of Empty Space (Xūkōng Děng Dì).
"Good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsa Móhēsà) dwelling in this Stage,
regarding all phenomena, both sees
and knows.
Whether activity,
or condition,
or nature,
or characteristic,
or cause and condition,
or the minds of sentient beings,
or faculties,
or meditation (chán dìng),
or vehicle,
or virtuous friend (shàn zhī shí),
or upholding precepts,
or what is bestowed—
all such phenomena are completely known and seen.
Furthermore, good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsa Móhēsà) dwelling in this Stage,
knows but does not see.
What is meant by 'knows'?
Knowing the practice of self-starvation (zì è fǎ),
leaping into abysses or rushing into fire,
casting oneself down from high cliffs,
constantly standing on one leg,
burning the body with the five fires (wǔ rè zhì shēn),
constantly lying on ash and dirt,
on thorns woven into rafters,
or on tree leaves, noxious weeds, or cow dung,
wearing coarse hemp clothes,
ragged, discarded monastic robes from graves,
Kuśala (Qīnpóluó) robes,
the skins of roe deer and ordinary deer,
or garments made of straw and grass,
eating vegetables,
consuming grass,
lotus roots,
oil dregs,
cow dung, roots, and fruits.
If going out for alms,
limiting oneself to one household;
if the householder says there is none,
they immediately depart,
and even if called back,
they never look back.
Not eating salted meat or the five kinds of ox flavors,
constantly drinking husks juice and boiled water,
observing the Ox Vow (niú jiè),
or the Vows of the Dog, Chicken, or Pheasant,
smearing the body with ash,
taking long hair as a characteristic sign,
when sacrificing a sheep,
first chanting incantations, then slaughtering it.
Serving the fire for four months,
eating the wind for seven days,
using hundreds of thousands of millions of flowers,
to make offerings to the various Devas (zhū tiān).
Regarding all the wishes and desires
that are achieved through these practices,
regarding such practices,
that they can be the cause of unsurpassed liberation (jiě tuō),
there is no such possibility.
This is called 'knows.'
What is meant by 'does not see'?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsa Móhēsà) does not see anyone
who practices such methods
attain true liberation (zhèng jiě tuō).
This is called 'does not see.'
"Furthermore, good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsa Móhēsà) both sees
and knows.
What is meant by 'sees'?
Seeing that sentient beings
who practice these heterodox methods (xié fǎ),
will surely fall into the Hells (Dìyù).
This is called 'sees.'
What is meant by 'knows'?
Knowing that sentient beings,
having emerged from the Hells (Dìyù),
born into the human realm,
if they are able to cultivate Dānapāramitā (Tán Bōluómì),
and subsequently complete all Pāramitās (Bōluómì),
these people will surely attain entry into true liberation (zhèng jiě tuō).
This is called 'knows.'
Furthermore, good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsa Móhēsà) again has 'both sees'
and 'knows.'
What is meant by 'sees'?
Seeing permanence and impermanence (cháng wúcháng),
suffering and pleasure,
purity and impurity,
self and non-self.
This is called 'sees.'
What is meant by 'knows'?
Knowing that the Tathāgatas (Rúlái) definitely do not ultimately enter Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
knowing that the body of the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is adamantine (jīngāng) and indestructible,
it is not a body established by afflictions (fánnǎo),
nor is it a body that is foul, filthy, or subject to decay.
Moreover, being able to know that all sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature (Fó Xìng).
This is called 'knows.'
Furthermore, good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsa Móhēsà) again has 'both knows'
and 'sees.'
What is meant by 'knows'?
Knowing that this sentient being has accomplished faith,
knowing that this sentient being seeks the Great Vehicle (Dàchéng);
this person follows the stream,
this person goes against the stream,
this person abides correctly,
knowing that this sentient being has already reached the other shore.
Those who follow the stream are called common people (fán fú rén);
those who go against the stream are from Srotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán) up to Pratyekabuddha (Yuánjué);
those who abide correctly are the various Bodhisattvas (Púsa), and so forth;
those who have reached the other shore are the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
Arhat (Yīng),
and Samyaksaṃbuddha (Zhèng Biànzhī).
This is called 'knows.'
What is meant by 'sees'?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsa Móhēsà), dwelling in the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dàchéng Dà Nièpán Diǎn),
cultivating the mind of pure practice,
with the pure celestial eye,
sees sentient beings who commit unwholesome deeds
through body, speech,
and mind (the three karmas),
falling into the Hells (Dìyù),
the animal realm,
or the realm of hungry ghosts.
Seeing sentient beings who cultivate wholesome karma,
who, at the end of life, will be born in the heavens
or among humans.
Seeing sentient beings who proceed from darkness into darkness,
some sentient beings who proceed from darkness into light,
some sentient beings who proceed from light into darkness,
and some sentient beings who proceed from light into light.
This is called 'sees.'"
"Furthermore, noble son!
The Bódhisattva Móhāsàtva also possesses 'both knowledge'
and 'both vision'.
The Bódhisattva Móhāsàtva knows that certain sentient beings cultivate the body,
cultivate the precepts,
cultivate the mind,
and cultivate wisdom;
these people have accomplished bad karma in this current life,
perhaps due to greed (tānyù),
anger (chēnhuì),
or ignorance (yúchī).
This karma must result in retribution in Dìyù (hell);
yet, simply because these people cultivate the body,
cultivate the precepts,
cultivate the mind,
and cultivate wisdom,
they experience light retribution in the present world,
and do not fall into Dìyù.
How is it that this karma can result in present retribution?
They confess and reveal all their evils,
and having repented, they dare not commit them again.
Because shame and remorse (cánkuì) are accomplished,
because of making offerings to the Sānbǎo (Three Jewels),
and because of constantly reprimanding oneself,
these people, through the conditions of this good karma,
do not fall into Dìyù but receive retribution in the present world.
Namely, headaches,
eye pain,
stomach aches,
back pain,
encountering sudden misfortune leading to death,
being scolded and insulted,
being whipped, beaten, imprisoned,
and suffering the distress of hunger and starvation.
They receive such light retributions in the present world.
This is called 'knowledge'.
What is 'vision'?
The Bódhisattva Móhāsàtva sees people like this,
who are unable to cultivate the body,
precepts,
mind,
or wisdom,
but commit a small evil deed.
Due to the conditions of this karma,
they should receive retribution in the present life.
These people cannot repent of their minor evil,
do not reprimand themselves,
do not generate shame and remorse,
and have no fear or dread.
This karma grows,
resulting in retribution in Dìyù.
This is called 'vision'.
"Furthermore, there is 'knowledge without vision'.
How is it 'knowledge without vision'?
Knowing that all sentient beings possess Fóxìng (Buddha-nature),
but being covered and obscured by various afflictions (fánnǎo),
so they cannot attain vision.
This is called 'knowledge without vision'.
Furthermore, there is 'knowledge with little vision'.
The Bódhisattva Móhāsàtva of the Ten Abodes (Shízhù),
equally knows that all sentient beings possess Fóxìng,
but the vision is not clear and bright,
just as what is seen on a dark night is unclear.
Furthermore, there is 'both vision'
and 'both knowledge'.
This refers to the various Fó Rúlái (Tathāgatas),
who have both vision and knowledge.
Furthermore, there is 'both vision and knowledge',
and 'neither vision nor knowledge'.
Those who have both vision and knowledge [perceive]:
namely, worldly script and characters,
speech,
men and women,
carriages, carts, vases, and jars,
houses, cities, and towns,
clothing, food, and drink,
mountains, rivers, parks, and forests,
and the lifespan of sentient beings.
This is called 'both knowledge and vision'.
What is 'neither vision nor knowledge'?
The subtle and esoteric words possessed by the sages,
which contain neither men nor women, down to parks and forests.
This is called 'neither vision nor knowledge'.
Furthermore, there is 'knowledge without vision'.
Knowing what is bestowed (dāna),
knowing the recipient of offerings,
knowing the receiver,
and knowing the cause and effect retribution.
This is called 'knowledge'.
What is 'without vision'?
Not seeing what is bestowed,
the recipient of offerings, the receiver,
and the retribution.
This is called 'without vision'.
The Bódhisattva Móhāsàtva has eight types of knowledge,
which are known by the Wǔyǎn (Five Eyes) of the Rúlái.
Jiāyè Bódhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Shìzūn! (World-Honored One!)
If the Bódhisattva Móhāsàtva is able to know thus,
what benefit does he obtain?"
The Buddha said:
"Noble son!
If the Bódhisattva Móhāsàtva is able to know thus,
he obtains the Four Unimpeded Knowledges (Sì Wú'ài):
unimpeded dharma (fǎ wú'ài),
unimpeded meaning (yì wú'ài),
unimpeded language (cí wú'ài),
and unimpeded eloquence in preaching (lèshuō wú'ài).
Unimpeded dharma means
knowing all dharmas and the names of the dharmas.
Unimpeded meaning means
knowing all the meanings that all dharmas possess,
and being able to assign meaning based on the names established for the various dharmas.
Unimpeded language means
the doctrine of following characters (Suízì Lùn),
the doctrine of correct sound (Zhèngyīn Lùn),
the doctrine of metric forms (Chǎntuó Lùn),
and the doctrine of worldly debate (Shìbiàn Lùn).
Unimpeded eloquence in preaching means
that whatever the Bódhisattva Móhāsàtva expounds and explains,
there are no obstacles,
it cannot be shaken or altered,
he feels no hesitation or fear,
and it is difficult to defeat or subdue.
Noble son!
This is called the ability of the Bódhisattva to see and know thus,
immediately obtaining such Four Unimpeded Knowledges.
"Furthermore, noble son!
Regarding unimpeded dharma,
the Bódhisattva Móhāsàtva
comprehensively knows the dharmas of the Shēngwén (Hearers),
Yuánjué (Pratyekabuddhas),
Bódhisattvas,
and the various Buddhas.
Regarding unimpeded meaning,
although there are Three Vehicles,
he knows they return to the One,
and ultimately does not claim there are differentiating characteristics.
Regarding unimpeded language,
the Bódhisattva Móhāsàtva, concerning a single dharma,
creates various names,
and speaks for immeasurable kalpas,
explaining them inexhaustibly;
that the Shēngwén and Yuánjué could make such explanations
is impossible.
Regarding unimpeded eloquence in preaching,
the Bódhisattva Móhāsàtva, throughout immeasurable kalpas,
expounds the various dharmas for sentient beings,
whether names,
or meanings,
with various and distinct explanations,
which cannot be exhausted.
"Furthermore, noble son!
Regarding unimpeded dharma,
the Bódhisattva Móhāsàtva, although knowing the various dharmas,
does not grasp or cling to them.
Regarding unimpeded meaning,
the Bódhisattva Móhāsàtva, although knowing the various meanings,
likewise does not cling.
Regarding unimpeded language,
the Bódhisattva Móhāsàtva, although knowing the names,
likewise does not grasp or cling.
Regarding unimpeded eloquence in preaching,
the Bódhisattva Móhāsàtva, although knowing the eloquence in preaching,
which is supreme like this,
likewise does not cling.
Why is that?
Noble son,
if one grasps and clings,
one is not called a Bódhisattva."
Jiāyè Bódhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Shìzūn!
If one does not grasp or cling,
then one does not know the dharma;
if one knows the dharma,
then this is grasping and clinging.
If one knows without clinging,
then there is nothing known.
How is it that the Rúlái says one knows the dharma without grasping or clinging?"
The Bó (Fó) said:
“Shànnánzǐ!
Those who grasp and cling,
are not called unimpeded (Wú'ài);
those who have nothing to grasp or cling to,
are then called unimpeded (Wú'ài).
Shànnánzǐ!
Therefore, all the various Bódhisattvas (Púsà) and the like,
if they grasp and cling,
then they lack unimpededness (Wú'ài);
if they lack unimpededness,
they are not called Bódhisattvas (Púsà);
you should know that such persons are called Fánfū (ordinary beings/mortals).
Why is grasping and clinging called a Fánfū?
All Fánfū
grasp and cling to form (sè) up to consciousness (shì).
Because they cling to form (sè),
they give rise to the mind of greed (tānxīn);
because they give rise to the mind of greed,
they are bound by form (sè),
and likewise bound by consciousness (shì);
because of this bondage,
they cannot escape birth,
aging,
sickness,
death,
sorrow and grief (yōubēi),
great suffering, and all afflictions (fánnǎo).
Therefore, grasping and clinging is called Fánfū.
Because of this principle,
all Fánfū
lack the Four Unimpedednesses (Sì Wú Hé/Ài).
Shànnánzǐ!
Bódhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà), having, through countless Asámkhyeyakalpas (Āsēngqí Jié),
known and seen the characteristics of the Dhárma (Fǎ xiāng),
because they know and see,
they thus know its meaning (yì);
Because they see the characteristics of the Dhárma (Fǎ xiāng) and know the meaning,
they do not give rise to attachment in form (sè),
and likewise in consciousness (shì);
because they do not cling,
Bódhisattvas do not give rise to the mind of greed (tānxīn) regarding form (sè),
and likewise do not give rise to greed regarding consciousness (shì);
Because there is no greed,
they are not bound by form (sè),
and likewise are not bound by consciousness (shì);
because they are not bound,
they attain liberation from birth, aging, sickness, and death,
sorrow and grief (yōubēi), great suffering,
and all afflictions (fánnǎo).
Because of this principle,
all Bódhisattvas attain the Four Unimpedednesses (Sì Wú'ài).
Shànnánzǐ!
For this reason,
I speak among the Twelve Divisions (Shí'èr Bù) for my disciples: those who are bound and attached are called Mō (Mó) bondage,
but those who do not cling are freed from Mō (Mó) bondage.
Just as in the world, a person who has committed a crime
is bound by the king (wáng),
a person without crime cannot be bound by the king.
Bódhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) are also like this:
those who have attachments and bondage
are bound by Mō (Mó);
those who have no attachments and bondage cannot be bound by Mō (Mó).
Because of this principle,
Bódhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) have nothing they cling to.
“Furthermore, Shànnánzǐ!
Regarding the Unimpededness of the Dhárma (Fǎ Wú'ài):
The Bódhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) skillfully know the maintenance (dhāraṇī) of characters (zì chí),
and do not forget or lose them.
What is meant by 'maintenance' (chí)?
It is like the earth (dì),
like a mountain (shān),
like an eye (yǎn),
like a cloud (yún),
like a person (rén),
like a mother (mǔ).
All various Dhármas (Fǎ) are also like this.
Regarding the Unimpededness of Meaning (Yì Wú'ài):
A Bódhisattva may know the names of the various Dhármas (Fǎ míngzì) but not know the meaning;
when they attain the Unimpededness of Meaning (Yì Wú'ài),
they then know the meaning.
How do they know the meaning?
Regarding the maintenance of the earth (dì chí):
The earth universally maintains all sentient and non-sentient beings.
Because of this principle,
the earth is named 'maintenance' (chí).
Shànnánzǐ!
Regarding the maintenance of the mountain (shān chí):
The Bódhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) contemplate this:
‘Why is a mountain called maintenance (chí)?
A mountain can support the earth,
preventing it from tilting or moving.
Therefore, it is called maintenance.’
Why, furthermore, is the eye (yǎn) called maintenance (chí)?
The eye can contain light,
hence it is called maintenance.
Why, furthermore, is the cloud (yún) called maintenance (chí)?
A cloud is called the vital energy of the dragon (lóng qì);
the dragon’s vital energy holds water.
Therefore, it is called cloud maintenance (yún chí).
Why, furthermore, is a person (rén) called maintenance (chí)?
A person can uphold the Dhárma (Fǎ) and the non-Dhárma.
Therefore, it is called person maintenance (rén chí).
Why, furthermore, is a mother (mǔ) called maintenance (chí)?
A mother can bear her child.
Therefore, it is called mother maintenance (mǔ chí).
Bódhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) know the names
and the meaning of the phrases of all Dhármas (Fǎ),
which is also like this.
Regarding the Unimpededness of Eloquence/Speech (Cí Wú'ài):
Bódhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) use various forms of speech
to expound a single meaning,
or even a lack of meaning,
such as the names for male and female,
houses and carriages,
and sentient beings, etc.
Why is there no meaning?
Shànnánzǐ!
Meaning (yì),
is truly the realm of Bódhisattvas (Púsà) and all Buddhas (Fó);
while eloquence (cí) is the realm of Fánfū.
Because they know the meaning,
they attain the Unimpededness of Eloquence (Cí Wú'ài).
Regarding the Unimpededness of Delight in Preaching (Lè Shuō Wú'ài):
Bódhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà), because they know the eloquence
and know the meaning,
through countless Asámkhyeyakalpas (Āsēngqí Jié),
they speak the eloquence
and speak the meaning without exhaustion.
This is called the Unimpededness of Delight in Preaching (Lè Shuō Wú'ài).
“Shànnánzǐ!
Bódhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà), through measureless and boundless Asámkhyeyakalpas (Āsēngqí Jié),
cultivate the Mundane Truth (Shì Dì).
Because of this cultivation,
they attain the Unimpededness of the Dhárma (Fǎ Wú'ài).
Furthermore, through countless Asámkhyeyakalpas (Āsēngqí Jié),
they cultivate the Highest Meaning Truth (Dìyī Yì Dì).
Thus, they attain the Unimpededness of Meaning (Yì Wú'ài).
Likewise, through countless Asámkhyeyakalpas (Āsēngqí Jié),
they study the Vibhāṣā (Píjiāluōnà) treatise.
Thus, they attain the Unimpededness of Eloquence (Cí Wú'ài).
Likewise, through countless Asámkhyeyakalpas (Āsēngqí Jié),
they practice and study the treatises that expound the Mundane Truth (Shì Dì).
Thus, they attain the Unimpededness of Delight in Preaching (Lè Shuō Wú'ài).
“Good man!
For Śrāvakās and Pratyekabuddhas to obtain these Four Unobstructed Knowledges
is not possible.
Good man!
In the nine divisions of scripture, I speak of Śrāvakās and Pratyekabuddhas having Four Unobstructed Knowledges,
but Śrāvakās and Pratyekabuddhas truly do not possess them.
Why is that?
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, for the sake of liberating sentient beings,
cultivate such Four Unobstructed Knowledges.
Pratyekabuddhas cultivate the Dharma of tranquil extinction,
and delight in solitary dwelling.
If they transform sentient beings,
they only display supernatural powers,
remaining silent all day without uttering any words.
How then can they possess the Four Unobstructed Knowledges?
Why are they silent and say nothing?
Pratyekabuddhas cannot preach the Dharma to save people.
Even if they obtain the Nuǎn Fǎ (Warming Dharma),
Dǐng Fǎ (Crowning Dharma),
Rěn Fǎ (Forbearance Dharma),
Shì Dì Yī Fǎ (World's Foremost Dharma),
Śrotāpanna,
Sakṛdāgāmin,
Anāgāmin,
Arhat,
Pratyekabuddha,
or Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
they cannot inspire people to generate the mind of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.
Why is that?
Good man!
When a Pratyekabuddha appears in the world,
the world does not contain the nine divisions of scripture.
Therefore, Pratyekabuddhas have no unobstructed eloquence in phrasing (Cí Wú'ài),
nor unobstructed eloquence in delightful speech (Lè Shuō Wú'ài).
Good man!
Although Pratyekabuddhas know all Dharmas,
they lack unobstructed knowledge of the Dharma (Fǎ Wú'ài).
Why is that?
Unobstructed knowledge of the Dharma
is called knowing the written characters (Zì).
Although Pratyekabuddhas know written characters,
they lack unobstructed knowledge of characters (Zì Wú'ài).
Why is that?
Because they do not know the two characters 'Permanent Dwelling' (Cháng Zhù).
Therefore, Pratyekabuddhas do not attain unobstructed knowledge of the Dharma.
Although they know the meaning (Yì),
they lack unobstructed knowledge of the meaning (Yì Wú'ài).
True knowledge of the meaning
is knowing that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature.
The meaning of Buddha-nature
is called Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.
Due to this meaning,
Pratyekabuddhas do not attain unobstructed knowledge of the meaning.
Therefore, Pratyekabuddhas
completely lack the Four Unobstructed Knowledges.
How is it that Śrāvakās lack the Four Unobstructed Knowledges?
Śrāvakās lack three kinds of skillful means.
Which three?
First, they must use gentle language before they accept the Dharma.
Second, they must use harsh language before they accept transformation.
Third, they accept transformation without language being either gentle or harsh.
Because Śrāvakās lack these three,
they lack the Four Unobstructed Knowledges.
Furthermore, Śrāvakās and Pratyekabuddhas cannot ultimately know the phrasing (Cí)
and know the meaning (Yì);
they lack the wisdom of self-mastery
in knowing the realm.
They do not possess the Ten Powers (Shí Lì)
or the Four Fearlessnesses (Sì Wú Suǒ Wèi);
they cannot ultimately cross the great river of the Twelvefold Chain of Dependent Origination (Shí Èr Yīn Yuán);
they cannot skillfully know the distinctions between the sharp and dull faculties of sentient beings (Zhòng Shēng Zhū Gēn Lì Dùn Chā Bié);
they have not yet completely severed the doubts regarding the Two Truths (Èr Dì Yí Xīn);
they do not know the variety of realms (Suǒ Yuán Jìng Jiè) upon which the minds of sentient beings focus;
they cannot skillfully explain the Ultimate Meaning of Emptiness (Dì Yī Yì Kōng).
Therefore, the Two Vehicles lack the Four Unobstructed Knowledges.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
If all Śrāvakās and Pratyekabuddhas
completely lack the Four Unobstructed Knowledges,
why does the World-Honored One say that Śāriputra’s wisdom is foremost?
That Mahāmaudgalyāyana’s supernatural powers are foremost?
That Mahākauṣṭhila’s Four Unobstructed Knowledges are foremost?
If they do not possess them,
why did the Tathāgata say this?”
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Kāśyapa, saying:
“Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
For example, the Gaṅgā River has immeasurable water,
the Sindhu Great River also has immeasurable water,
the Vakṣu Great River also has immeasurable water,
the Sītā Great River also has immeasurable water,
Lake Anavatapta also has immeasurable water,
and the great ocean also has immeasurable water.
Although these waters are all equally immeasurable,
their quantity is in fact unequal.
The Four Unobstructed Knowledges of Śrāvakās, Pratyekabuddhas, and all Bodhisattvas
are likewise similar.
Good man!
To say they are equal
is not possible.
Good man!
I said, for the sake of ordinary people,
that Mahākauṣṭhila’s Four Unobstructed Knowledges are the most foremost.
The meaning of your question is thus.
Good man!
Among Śrāvakās,
some may attain one,
some may attain two;
but for them to be complete with all four
is not possible.”
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha previously said in the Chapter on Pure Conduct (Fàn Xíng Pǐn),
when a Bodhisattva’s insight and understanding attain the Four Unobstructed Knowledges,
the Bodhisattva’s insight and understanding are without attainment (Wú Suǒ Dé),
and there is no thought of saying ‘without attainment.’
World-Honored One!
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva truly has no attainment.
If the Bodhisattva’s mind had attainment,
then he would not be a Bodhisattva,
but would be called an ordinary person.
How does the Tathāgata speak of the Bodhisattva having attainment?”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
Excellent,
excellent!
I was about to speak,
and you have asked it again.
Good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is truly without attainment (Wú Suǒ Dé).
That which is without attainment is called the Four Unobstructed Knowledges.
Good man!
For what reason
is ‘without attainment’ called ‘unobstructed’?
If there were attainment, it would be called an obstruction (Ài).
That which has obstruction is called the Four Inversions (Sì Diān Dǎo).
Good man!
Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is without the Four Inversions,
he attains ‘unobstructed.’
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is called ‘without attainment.’
“Furthermore, good man!
‘Without attainment’ is called wisdom (Huì).
Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains this wisdom, he is called ‘without attainment.’
‘Having attainment’ is called ignorance (Wú Míng).
Because the Bodhisattva permanently severs the darkness of ignorance,
he is without attainment.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is called ‘without attainment.’
“Furthermore, good man!
‘Without attainment’ is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva abides in such Mahāparinirvāṇa,
he does not perceive the inherent characteristics of any Dharma.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is called ‘without attainment.’
‘Having attainment’ is called the Twenty-Five Existences (Èr Shí Wǔ Yǒu).
The Bodhisattva permanently severs the Twenty-Five Existences
and attains Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is called ‘without attainment.’
“Furthermore, good man!
‘Without attainment’ is called the Mahāyāna.
Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not dwell in any Dharma,
he attains the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is called ‘without attainment.’
‘Having attainment’ is called the path of Śrāvakās and Pratyekabuddhas.
Because the Bodhisattva permanently severs the path of the Two Vehicles
and attains the Buddha Path,
therefore, the Bodhisattva is called ‘without attainment.’
“Furthermore, good man!
‘Without attainment’ is called the Vaipulya Sūtras (Fāng Děng Jīng).
Because the Bodhisattva reads and recites such sūtras, he attains Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is called ‘without attainment.’
‘Having attainment’ is called the eleven divisions of sūtras.
The Bodhisattva does not cultivate them;
he purely preaches the Vaipulya Mahāyāna scriptures.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is called ‘without attainment.’
“Furthermore, good man!
‘Without attainment’ is called empty space (Xū Kōng).
In the world, having no thing is called empty space.
Because the Bodhisattva attains this Samādhi of Empty Space
and sees nothing,
therefore, the Bodhisattva is called ‘without attainment.’
‘Having attainment’ is called the wheel of Saṃsāra (Shēng Sǐ Lún).
All ordinary people revolve in Saṃsāra,
and thus have perceptions.
The Bodhisattva permanently severs all Saṃsāra.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is called ‘without attainment.’
“Furthermore, good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s ‘without attainment’
is called Permanence (Cháng), Bliss (Lè), Self (Wǒ), and Purity (Jìng).
Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perceives the Buddha-nature,
he attains Permanence, Bliss, Self, and Purity.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is called ‘without attainment.’
‘Having attainment’
is called impermanence (Wú Cháng),
non-bliss (Wú Lè),
non-self (Wú Wǒ),
and impurity (Wú Jìng).
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva severs this impermanence, non-bliss, non-self, and impurity.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is called ‘without attainment.’
"Furthermore, good man!
The state of having nothing to attain (Wúsuǒdé)
is called the foremost meaning of emptiness (Dìyī Yì Kōng).
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, observing the foremost meaning of emptiness (Dìyī Yì Kōng),
sees absolutely nothing.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is called Wúsuǒdé (having nothing to attain).
That which is attained is called the five views (wǔjiàn).
Because the Bodhisattva eternally severs these five views,
