he attains the foremost meaning of emptiness (Dìyī Yì Kōng).
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is called Wúsuǒdé.
"Furthermore, good man!
Wúsuǒdé is named Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi).
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí, he sees absolutely nothing,
therefore, the Bodhisattva is called Wúsuǒdé.
That which is attained
is named the Bodhi of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas (Shēngwén Yuánjué Pútí).
The Bodhisattva eternally severs the Bodhi of the two vehicles (Èr Chéng Pútí).
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is called Wúsuǒdé.
"Good man!
What you ask also has nothing to attain (Wúsuǒdé).
What I speak also has nothing to attain (Wúsuǒdé).
If there is something attained,
this is Māra's (Mó) retinue,
and not my disciple."
Kāyè Púsà (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva) said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, when you explained to me this concept of the Bodhisattva having nothing to attain (Wúsuǒdé),
immeasurable sentient beings severed the mind of existing characteristics.
Because of this matter,
I dare to consult and initiate this discussion
concerning the meaning of having nothing to attain (Wúsuǒdé Yì),
so that these immeasurable sentient beings,
may leave Māra's (Mó) retinue,
and become disciples of the Buddha."
Kāyè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata previously, between the pair of Sāluó trees,
spoke a verse for Chúntuó."
"World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of this?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
I spoke this
in order to transform and save all sentient beings.
I also spoke this for the sake of the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Pìzhīfó).
I spoke this
also for the sake of Wénshū Shīlì (Mañjuśrī), the Dharma Prince.
I spoke this;
it was not spoken solely for Chúntuó alone.
At that time, Wénshū Shīlì was about to question me.
I knew his mind,
and spoke for him.
After I had spoken,
Wénshū Shīlì immediately understood and apprehended it."
Kāyè Púsà said:
"World-Honored One!
How many people, like Wénshū,
are there
who can comprehend this meaning?
We only wish that the Tathāgata would extensively distinguish and explain it again for the great assembly."
"Good man!
Listen carefully,
listen carefully!
Now I shall expound it for you again.
Regarding the statement 'originally existing' (běn yǒu):
In the past, I originally had immeasurable afflictions (fánnǎo).
Because of afflictions,
there is presently no Great Pariṇirvāṇa (Dà Bān Nièpán).
Regarding the statement 'originally non-existing' (běn wú):
Originally, there was no Prajñāpāramitā (Bānruò Bōluómì).
Because there was no Prajñāpāramitā,
there are presently complete ties of affliction.
If there is any Śramaṇa (shāmén),
or Brāhmaṇa (póluómén),
or god (tiān),
or Māra (mó),
or Brahmā (fàn),
or human,
who says that the Tathāgata, in the past (qù),
future (lái),
or present, possesses afflictions (fánnǎo),
there is no such possibility.
"Furthermore, good man!
Regarding the statement 'originally existing' (běn yǒu):
I originally had a body formed by the union of father and mother.
Therefore, there is presently no subtle Adamantine Dharma-body (Jīngāng Miàowēi Fǎshēn).
Regarding the statement 'originally non-existing' (běn wú):
My body originally did not have the thirty-two marks (sānshí'èr xiàng)
or the eighty subsidiary characteristics (bāshí zhǒng hǎo).
Because it originally did not have the thirty-two marks
or the eighty subsidiary characteristics,
it presently possessed the four hundred and four diseases.
If there is any Śramaṇa (shāmén),
or Brāhmaṇa (póluómén),
or god (tiān),
or Māra (mó),
or Brahmā (fàn),
or human,
who says that the Tathāgata, in the past (qù),
future (lái),
or present, possesses the suffering of illness,
there is no such possibility.
"Furthermore, good man!
Regarding the statement 'originally existing' (běn yǒu):
In the past, I originally had impermanence (wúcháng),
non-self (wúwǒ),
non-joy (wúlè),
and impurity (wújìng).
Because there was impermanence,
non-self,
non-joy,
and impurity,
there is presently no Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Regarding the statement 'originally non-existing' (běn wú):
Originally, the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) was not seen.
Because it was not seen,
there was impermanence (wúcháng),
joy (lè),
self (wǒ),
and purity (jìng).
If there is any Śramaṇa (shāmén),
or Brāhmaṇa (póluómén),
or god (tiān),
or Māra (mó),
or Brahmā (fàn),
or human,
who says that the Tathāgata, in the past (qù),
future (lái),
or present, possesses impermanence (wúcháng),
joy (lè),
self (wǒ),
and purity (jìng),
there is no such possibility.
"Furthermore, good man!
Regarding the statement 'originally existing' (běn yǒu):
Originally, there was the mind of an ordinary person (fánfū) practicing asceticism (kǔxíng),
supposing that he would attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Because of this matter,
he is presently unable to destroy the four Māras (sì mó).
Regarding the statement 'originally non-existing' (běn wú):
I originally did not possess the six Pāramitās (Liù Bōluómì).
Because I originally did not possess the six Pāramitās,
I cultivated the mind of an ordinary person practicing asceticism,
supposing that I would attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
If there is any Śramaṇa (shāmén),
or Brāhmaṇa (póluómén),
or god (tiān),
or Māra (mó),
or Brahmā (fàn),
or human,
who says that the Tathāgata, in the past (qù),
future (lái),
or present, possesses ascetic practices (kǔxíng),
there is no such possibility.
"Furthermore, good man!
Regarding the statement 'originally existing' (běn yǒu):
In the past, I originally had a body of mixed food (záshí zhī shēn).
Because I had a body of food,
there is presently no boundless body (wúbiān zhī shēn).
Regarding the statement 'originally non-existing' (běn wú):
Originally, there were no thirty-seven factors contributing to the Path (Sānshíqī Zhùdào Fǎ).
Because there were no thirty-seven factors contributing to the Path,
there presently existed the body of mixed food.
If there is any Śramaṇa (shāmén),
or Brāhmaṇa (póluómén),
or god (tiān),
or Māra (mó),
or Brahmā (fàn),
or human,
who says that the Tathāgata, in the past (qù),
future (lái),
or present, possesses a body of mixed food,
there is no such possibility.
"Furthermore, good man!
Regarding the statement 'originally existing' (běn yǒu):
In the past, I originally had the mind of grasping and attachment (qǔ zhuó zhī xīn) toward all phenomena (yīqiè fǎ).
Because of this matter,
there is presently no ultimate emptiness samādhi (Bìjìng Kōng Dìng).
Regarding the statement 'originally non-existing' (běn wú):
I originally did not possess the true meaning of the Middle Way (Zhōngdào Shí Yì).
Because there was no true meaning of the Middle Way,
there was a mind of attachment toward all phenomena.
If there is any Śramaṇa (shāmén),
or Brāhmaṇa (póluómén),
or god (tiān),
or Māra (mó),
or Brahmā (fàn),
or human,
who says that the Tathāgata, in the past (qù),
future (lái),
or present, says that all phenomena (yīqiè fǎ) possess characteristics (yǒu xiàng),
there is no such possibility."
"Furthermore, good man!
Regarding the statement 'originally existent,'
when I first attained Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
there were disciples of the Śrāvaka path who had dull faculties.
Because of the existence of these Śrāvaka disciples with dull faculties,
I could not proclaim the truth of the One Vehicle (Yīchèng).
Regarding the statement 'originally nonexistent,'
originally there were no people of sharp faculties,
such as the elephant king among men, the Bodhisattva Jiāshè, and others.
Because there were no Jiāshè and others of sharp faculties,
I conveniently expounded the Three Vehicles (Sānchèng) according to the circumstances.
If there is any Śramaṇa,
or Brāhmaṇa,
or deity (tiān),
or demon (mó),
or Brahmā (Fàn),
or human,
who says that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) in the past,
present,
or future ultimately preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles,
there is no such possibility.
"Furthermore, good man!
Regarding the statement 'originally existent,'
I formerly declared that after three months,
I would enter Parinirvāṇa (Bān Nièpán) beneath the twin Sāla trees (Suōluó Shuāngshù).
Therefore, at present, I cannot preach the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra (Dà Fāngděng Diǎn) of the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Bān Nièpán).
Regarding the statement 'originally nonexistent,'
in the past, there was no great Bodhisattva Wénshū Shīlì and others.
Because they did not exist,
I presently declare that the Tathāgata is impermanent.
If there is any Śramaṇa,
or Brāhmaṇa,
or deity,
or demon,
or Brahmā,
or human,
who says that the Tathāgata in the past,
present,
or future is impermanent,
there is no such possibility.
"Good man!
The Tathāgata, universally for the sake of all sentient beings,
though knowing all dharmas,
says he does not know;
though seeing all dharmas,
says he does not see;
he says that conditioned dharmas are without characteristics,
and says that dharmas without characteristics have characteristics;
he says that what is truly impermanent is permanent,
and says that what is truly permanent is impermanent.
The declarations concerning the self (wǒ), bliss (lè), purity (jìng), and others are also like this.
The Dharma of the Three Vehicles is declared as the One Vehicle;
the Dharma of the One Vehicle is expediently taught as three.
Concise aspects are taught broadly;
broad aspects are taught concisely.
The law of the four cardinal offenses (Sìzhòng) is taught as Tōulánzhē;
the law of Tōulánzhē is taught as the four cardinal offenses.
Transgressions are said to be non-transgressions;
non-transgressions are said to be transgressions;
light offenses are taught as heavy;
heavy offenses are taught as light.
Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata clearly perceives the faculties of sentient beings.
Good man!
Although the Tathāgata speaks thus,
he is ultimately never deceitful.
Why is this?
False speech is precisely sin and transgression,
and the Tathāgata has severed all sins and transgressions.
How then could he utter false speech?
Good man!
Although the Tathāgata has no deceitful words,
if he knows that sentient beings can gain benefit from the Dharma through deceitful teaching,
he will expediently preach it accordingly.
Good man!
All worldly truths (Shìdì),
for the Tathāgata, are the Ultimate Truth (Dìyī Yìdì).
Why is this?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones (Shìzūn), for the sake of the Ultimate Meaning,
teach the worldly truths,
and also enable sentient beings to attain the Ultimate Truth.
If sentient beings could not attain this Ultimate Meaning,
the Buddhas would ultimately not proclaim the worldly truths.
Good man!
Sometimes the Tathāgata preaches the worldly truths,
and sentient beings suppose the Buddha is teaching the Ultimate Truth;
sometimes he preaches the Ultimate Truth,
and sentient beings suppose the Buddha is teaching the worldly truths.
This then is the profound realm (jìngjiè) of the Buddhas,
which is not understood by the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué).
Good man!
Therefore, you should not have previously posed the difficulty, saying:
'The Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà), have nothing to attain.'
Bodhisattvas constantly attain the Ultimate Truth.
Why do you pose the difficulty that there is nothing attained?
Jiāshè spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
The Ultimate Truth is also called the Path (Dào),
it is also called Bodhi (Pútí),
and it is also called Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
If any Bodhisattva says that the Path,
Bodhi,
or Nirvāṇa is attainable,
then it is impermanent.
Why is this?
If a dharma is permanent, then it cannot be attained,
just like empty space—who attains it?
World-Honored One!
Just like worldly objects:
originally nonexistent but now existent
is called impermanent.
The Path is also like this.
If the Path is attainable,
then it is called impermanent.
If a dharma is permanent,
there is neither attainment nor arising,
just like the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng),
which has neither attainment nor arising.
World-Honored One!
The Path, fundamentally,
is neither form (sè),
nor non-form.
It is not long,
not short,
not high,
not low,
not arising,
not ceasing,
not red,
not white,
not green,
not yellow,
not existent,
not nonexistent.
How can the Tathāgata say that it is attainable?
Bodhi and Nirvāṇa are likewise so."
The Buddha said:
“So it is,
so it is.
O good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The path (Dào) has two kinds:
the first is permanent (cháng),
the second is impermanent (wúcháng).
The characteristics of Enlightenment (Pútí) also have two kinds:
the first is permanent,
the second is impermanent,
Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) is also like this.
The path of externalists (wàidào)
is called impermanent;
the path of internalists (nèidào) is called permanent.
The Enlightenment possessed by Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué) is called impermanent;
the Enlightenment possessed by Bodhisattvas (Púsà) and all Buddhas (Fó) is called permanent.
External liberation (jiětuō) is called impermanent;
internal liberation is called permanent.
O Shànnánzǐ!
The path, Enlightenment, and Nièpán are all designated as permanent.
All sentient beings
are constantly covered by immeasurable afflictions (fánnǎo).
Because they lack the eye of wisdom (huìyǎn),
they cannot perceive (or attain sight of) them.
However, those sentient beings, desiring to see (them),
cultivate precepts (jiè),
meditation (dìng),
and wisdom (huì).
By means of this cultivation,
they perceive the path,
Enlightenment, and Nièpán.
This is called the Bodhisattva attaining the path,
Enlightenment, and Nièpán.
The nature and characteristics of the path
are truly neither born nor extinguished.
For this reason,
they cannot be grasped or held.
O Shànnánzǐ!
Although the path has no visible form
or measurable quantity that can be known,
it is truly beneficial (or existent/useful).
O Shànnánzǐ!
Just like the mind of sentient beings,
although it is not matter (sè),
not long,
not short,
not coarse,
not fine,
not bound,
not liberated,
and is not a visible phenomenon (jiànfǎ),
it nonetheless exists.
For this reason,
I instructed Sūdá (Xūdá) saying:
‘Elder (Zhǎngzhě)!
The mind is the lord of the city.
If the Elder does not guard the mind,
he will not guard the body
and speech.
If one guards the mind,
one guards the body
and speech.
By not properly guarding this body
and speech,
sentient beings are caused to reach the three evil destinies (sān'èqù).
Those who guard the body
and speech
cause sentient beings to attain human and heavenly realms (rén tiān)
and Nièpán,
and are called genuine (zhēnshí).
Those who do not attain this
are not called genuine.’
O Shànnánzǐ!
The path, Enlightenment, and Nièpán are also like this:
they exist,
and they are permanent.
If they did not exist,
how could one sever all afflictions?
Because they exist,
all Bodhisattvas clearly perceive and know them.
“O Shànnánzǐ!
Perception (jiàn) has two kinds:
the first is perception by characteristic (xiàngmào jiàn),
the second is clear perception (liǎoliǎo jiàn).
What is perception by characteristic?
For example, seeing smoke from afar
is called seeing fire,
though one does not truly see the fire;
although one does not see the fire,
it is also not false.
Seeing a crane (hè) in the sky
and then saying one sees water;
although one does not see the water,
it is also not false.
Just as seeing flowers and leaves
and then saying one sees the roots;
although one does not see the roots,
it is also not false.
Just as a person sees the horn of an ox between a fence from afar,
and then saying one sees the ox;
although one does not see the ox,
it is also not false.
Just as seeing a woman pregnant,
and then saying one sees desire (yù);
although one does not see desire,
it is also not false.
Just as seeing a tree growing leaves,
and then saying one sees water;
although one does not see the water,
it is also not false.
Furthermore, just as seeing clouds,
and then saying one sees rain;
although one does not see the rain,
it is also not false.
Just as seeing bodily karma (shēnyè) and verbal karma (kǒuyè),
and then saying one sees the mind;
although one does not see the mind,
it is also not false.
This is called perception by characteristic.
What is clear perception?
It is like the eye seeing form (sè).
O Shànnánzǐ!
It is like a person whose eye faculty (yǎngēn) is pure and undamaged,
personally observing the Āmālaka fruit (Āmólè Guǒ) in their palm.
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) clearly perceiving the path,
Enlightenment,
and Nièpán is also like this.
Although they see them thus,
they fundamentally have no characteristic of perception.
O Shànnánzǐ!
For this reason,
I previously told Śāriputra (Shèlìfú):
‘In all the world,
that which Śramaṇas (Shāmén),
Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén),
Devas (Tiān),
Māras (Mó),
Brahmā (Fàn),
or humans do not know,
do not see,
and do not perceive,
only the Tathāgata (Rúlái) fully knows,
sees,
and perceives.
All Bodhisattvas are also like this.
Shèlìfú!
If there is anything that all the world knows,
sees,
and perceives,
I and the Bodhisattvas also know, see, and perceive it.
That which sentient beings in the world do not know,
do not see,
and do not perceive,
they also do not know that they do not know,
see,
or perceive;
when worldly sentient beings know,
see,
and perceive something,
they immediately say of themselves, 'I know,
I see,
I perceive.'
Shèlìfú!
The Tathāgata fully knows, sees, and perceives everything,
yet does not speak of Himself saying, 'I know, I see, I perceive';
all Bodhisattvas are also like this.
Why is this?
If the Tathāgata were to entertain the characteristic of knowing, seeing, or perceiving,
one should know that this would not be the Buddha, the World-Honored One (Shìzūn),
but would be called an ordinary person (fánfū).
Bodhisattvas are also like this.”
Bodhisattva Jiāyè (Kāśyapa) said:
“The statement made by the Buddha, the Shìzūn, to Shèlìfú,
that which the world knows,
I also know;
that which the world does not know,
I also fully know—
what is the meaning of this?”
“O good man!
All worldly beings,
do not know,
do not see,
and do not awaken to the Buddha-nature;
if there are those who know,
see,
and awaken to the Buddha-nature,
they are not called worldly beings,
but are called Bodhisattvas.
Worldly people
also do not know, do not see, and do not awaken to the twelve divisions of the canon (shí’èr bù jīng),
the twelve links of dependent origination (shí’èr yīnyuán),
the four inversions (sì dǎo),
the four noble truths (sì dì),
the thirty-seven factors leading to enlightenment (sānshíqī pǐn),
Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
and the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Bān Nièpán);
if they know, see, and awaken to these things,
they are not called worldly beings,
but should be called Bodhisattvas.
O good man!
This is what is meant by worldly beings not knowing, seeing, and awakening.
What are the things that worldly beings know, see, and awaken to?
Namely, Brahmā Heaven (Fàntiān),
Īśvara Heaven (Zìzàitiān),
Aṣṭabhuja Heaven (Bābìtiān),
nature (xìng),
time (shí),
subtle dust (wéichén),
dharma and non-dharma,
that they are the creators who control the beginning and end of the world, and the two views of nihilism and eternalism (duàn cháng èr jiàn),
and they state that from the First Dhyāna (chū chán) up to the Sphere of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception (fēifēixiǎng),
is called Nirvāṇa.
O good man!
This is what is meant by worldly beings knowing, seeing, and awakening.
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva also knows, sees, and awakens to such matters,
but if the Bodhisattva, after knowing, seeing, and awakening in this way,
says that he does not know,
does not see,
or does not awaken,
this is falsehood.
The law of falsehood
is then sin,
and because of this sin,
they fall into the Avīci Hell (dìyù).
O good man!
If a man,
or a woman,
or a Śramaṇa (Shāméng),
or a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén),
speaks saying there is no Way,
no Bodhi,
and no Nirvāṇa,
you should know that these people
are called Icchantikas (Yīchǎntí),
kin of Māra (mó zhī juànshǔ),
and are called slanderers of the Dharma (bàng fǎ),
and such slander of the Dharma
is called slandering all Buddhas.
Such people
are not called worldly beings,
nor are they called non-worldly beings.
At that time, Kāśyapa (Jiāyè), having heard these matters,
immediately praised the Buddha with verses:
After Kāśyapa Bodhisattva recited these verses,
he immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said,
all worldly beings do not know,
see,
and awaken,
but Bodhisattvas are fully able to know,
see,
and awaken;
if the Bodhisattva were a worldly being,
it should not be said that worldly beings do not know,
do not see,
and do not awaken,
yet the Bodhisattva is able to know, see, and awaken.
If they are not worldly beings,
what distinctive characteristics do they possess?”
The Buddha said:
“O good man!
When speaking of Bodhisattvas,
they are both worldly beings
and non-worldly beings.
Those who do not know, see, or awaken
are called worldly beings;
those who know, see, and awaken
are not called worldly beings.
You ask what distinctive characteristics they possess?
I shall now explain.
O good man!
If a man,
or a woman,
upon first hearing this Nirvāṇa Sūtra,
immediately generates reverence and faith,
and gives rise to the mind of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí xīn),
this is then called a worldly being.
The Bodhisattva, just like all worldly beings, does not know,
see,
and awaken.
Such a Bodhisattva
is also the same as worldly beings in not knowing, seeing, and awakening.
The Bodhisattva, having heard this Nirvāṇa Sūtra,
knows that what worldly beings do not know, see, and awaken
should be known, seen, and awakened to by a Bodhisattva.
Having known this matter,
he immediately contemplates:
‘How should I skillfully cultivate
so that I may attain knowing, seeing, and awakening?’
He further reflects:
‘I must deeply and wholeheartedly cultivate and uphold the pure precepts.’
O good man!
The Bodhisattva, at that time, because of this cause,
in future lives,
wherever he is reborn,
his precepts are always pure.
O good man!
Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s precepts are pure,
wherever he is reborn,
he is always without arrogance,
false views, or nets of doubt,
and he will never say that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) finally entered Nirvāṇa.
This is called the Bodhisattva cultivating and upholding the pure precepts.
After the precepts are purified,
he next cultivates concentration (chándìng);
due to the cultivation of concentration,
wherever he is reborn, he maintains right mindfulness and does not forget,
namely that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature,
the twelve divisions of the canon,
and that the World-Honored Buddhas (Zhūfó Shìzūn) are permanent, joyful, self, and pure (cháng lè wǒ jìng).
All Bodhisattvas dwell in the Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Fāngděng Dà Bān Nièpán Jīng),
and fully see the Buddha-nature;
he remembers and does not forget
such matters.
Due to cultivating concentration, he attains the eleven kinds of emptiness (shíyī kōng);
this is called the Bodhisattva cultivating pure concentration.
When precepts and concentration are fully prepared,
he next cultivates pure wisdom;
due to cultivating wisdom,
he initially does not cling to the notion that there is a self within the body,
or a body within the self,
or that this body is the self,
or that what is not the body is the self.
This is called the Bodhisattva cultivating pure wisdom.
Due to cultivating wisdom,
the precepts he upholds become firm and unmoving.
O good man!
Just as Mount Meru (Xūmí) is not shaken by the four winds,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this,
not shaken by the four inversions.
O good man!
When the Bodhisattva himself knows and sees and awakens
that the precepts he upholds are unmoving,
this is called what the Bodhisattva knows, sees, and awakens to,
not a worldly being.
O good man!
When the Bodhisattva sees that the precepts he upholds are firm and unmoving,
his mind is without regret;
being without regret, his mind gains joy;
gaining joy, his mind gains delight;
gaining delight, his mind is peaceful and serene;
being peaceful and serene, he attains unmoving concentration (wú dòng dìng);
attaining unmoving concentration, he gains true knowledge and vision;
gaining true knowledge and vision, he grows weary of and separates from cyclic existence (shēngsǐ);
being weary of and separated from cyclic existence, he then attains liberation (jiětuō);
attaining liberation, he clearly sees the Buddha-nature.
This is called what the Bodhisattva knows, sees, and awakens to,
not a worldly being.
O good man!
This is what is meant by worldly beings not knowing, seeing, and awakening,
but what the Bodhisattva knows, sees, and awakens to.
Kāśyapa asked again:
“How does the Bodhisattva cultivate and uphold the pure precepts,
so that his mind is without regret,
and even clearly sees the Buddha-nature?
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
The precepts of the world
are not called pure (qīngjìng).
Why is that?
The precepts of the world,
because they are focused on existence (yǒu),
because their nature is indeterminate,
and because they are not ultimate,
cannot universally benefit all sentient beings.
For these reasons,
they are called impure.
Because of impurity, there arises a heart of regret (huǐhèn).
Because of regret, the heart lacks joy (huānxǐ).
Without joy, there is no delight (yuèlè).
Without delight, there is no peace and safety (ānwěn).
Without peace and safety, there is no unwavering concentration (búdòng dìng).
Without unwavering concentration, there is no true knowledge and vision (shí zhījiàn).
Without true knowledge and vision, there is no weariness and separation (yànlí).
Without weariness and separation, there is no liberation (jiětuō).
Without liberation, one does not see the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng).
Because one does not see the Buddha-nature,
one ultimately cannot attain the Great Parinirvāṇa (Dà Bānnipán).
This is why the worldly precepts are impure.
Good man!
The pure precepts of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà),
are because the precept is non-precept,
because they are not focused on existence,
because they are definitely ultimate,
and because they are for the sake of sentient beings.
This is called the purity of the Bodhisattva precepts.
“Good man!
Although the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not desire to give rise to a heart free of regret (wú huǐhèn xīn) through pure precepts,
the heart free of regret arises naturally.
Good man!
For instance, if a person holds a bright mirror,
they do not intend to see their face,
but the image of the face appears spontaneously.
It is also like a farmer
sowing in fertile fields;
they do not intend for sprouts to emerge,
yet the sprouts emerge spontaneously.
It is also like lighting a lamp;
one does not intend to extinguish the darkness,
yet the darkness extinguishes itself.
Good man!
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva strictly observes pure precepts,
the heart free of regret naturally arises,
and it is likewise so,
because of the pure precepts,
the mind attains joy.
Good man!
Just as a handsome person
sees their own appearance
and generates joy in their heart,
it is likewise so for the observer of pure precepts.
Good man!
A person who violates the precepts (pòjiè zhī rén),
seeing the impurity of their precepts,
has no joy in their heart.
Just as a physically deformed person
sees their own appearance
and does not generate happiness and delight,
it is likewise so for the person who violates the precepts.
Good man!
For instance, while herding cattle,
there were two women.
One carried a bottle of milk curds (lào píng),
and one carried a bottle of sour milk (jiāng píng).
They both went to the city together intending to sell them.
On the road, they stumbled,
and both bottles broke simultaneously.
One was joyful,
and the other was distressed and troubled.
It is likewise so for observing precepts (chíjiè)
and violating precepts (pòjiè).
The observer of pure precepts has a joyful heart.
Because the heart is joyful,
they then contemplate:
‘All Tathāgatas (Rúlái)
have taught in the Nirvāṇa (Nièpán)
that those who are able to uphold pure precepts attain Nirvāṇa.
Since I am now practicing such pure precepts,
I should also attain it.’
For this reason,
the heart is delighted and happy (yuèlè).”
Kāśyapa (Jiāshè) then spoke again:
“Joy (xǐ) and delight (lè),
what difference is there?”
“Good man!
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does no evil,
this is called joy (huānxǐ).
When the mind is pure and observes the precepts,
this is called delight (lè).
Good man!
When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva contemplates birth and death (shēngsǐ), this is called joy.
When they see the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán), this is called delight.
The lower is called joy.
The higher is called delight.
Separating from common worldly doctrines (shì gòngfǎ) is called joy.
Attaining uncommon doctrines (bù gòngfǎ) is called delight.
Because the precepts are pure,
the body is light and supple,
and the mouth has no coarse faults.
At that time, the Bodhisattva,
whether seeing,
hearing,
smelling,
tasting,
touching,
or knowing, is completely free of all evils.
Because there is no evil, the mind attains peace and safety (ānwěn).
Because of peace and safety, one attains tranquil concentration (jìngdìng).
Because of attaining tranquil concentration, one attains true knowledge and vision (shí zhījiàn).
Because of true knowledge and vision, one is weary of and separated from birth and death (shēngsǐ).
Because of weariness of birth and death, one attains liberation (jiětuō).
Because of attaining liberation, one attains sight of the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng).
Because of seeing the Buddha-nature, one attains the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
This is called the pure precept observance of the Bodhisattva,
not the worldly precepts.
Why is that?
Good man!
The pure precepts received by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva
are aided by five teachings/qualities.
What are the five?
First, faith (xìn);
second, shame (cán);
third, embarrassment (kuì);
fourth, good friends (shàn zhīshì);
fifth, honoring and respecting the precepts (zōng jìng jiè).
Because one is separated from the Five Hindrances (wǔ gài).
The views attained are pure,
because one is separated from the Five Views (wǔ jiàn).
The mind is free of the net of doubt (yí wǎng),
because one is separated from the Five Doubts (wǔ yí):
First, doubt concerning the Buddha (Fó);
second, doubt concerning the Dharma (Fǎ);
third, doubt concerning the Saṅgha (Sēng);
fourth, doubt concerning the precepts (jiè);
fifth, doubt concerning diligence (bù fàngyì).
At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately attains the Five Faculties (wǔ gēn):
namely, faith,
mindfulness (niàn),
effort (jīngjìn),
concentration (dìng),
and wisdom (huì).
Because of attaining the Five Faculties,
one attains five kinds of Nirvāṇa:
namely, liberation from form (sè jiětuō),
and extending up to liberation from consciousness (shí jiětuō).
This is called the pure precept observance of the Bodhisattva,
which is not worldly.
Good man!
This is what the world does not know,
does not see,
and does not perceive,
but is known,
seen,
and perceived by the Bodhisattva (Púsà).”
"Good man (*shànnánzǐ*)!
If my disciples receive, uphold, read, and recite,
copy, and expound the *Dà Nièpán Jīng* (Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra),
and there are those who violate the precepts (*pòjiè zhě*),
people will scold them,
despise them,
and insult them, saying:
'If the Buddha's Secret Treasury, the *Dà Nièpán Jīng*, possesses spiritual power (*wēilì*),
how could it allow you to destroy the precepts you received?
If a person upholds this *Nièpán Jīng* while destroying the restrictive precepts,
you should know that this Sūtra has no spiritual power.
If it lacks spiritual power,
although you read and recite it,
it brings no benefit.
Because of this belittling and slandering of the *Nièpán Jīng*,
it further causes countless, boundless sentient beings to fall into hell (*dìyù*).
Those who uphold this Sūtra yet destroy the precepts,
are truly the evil companions (*è zhīshì*) of sentient beings,
they are not my disciples,
but the retinue of Māra (*Mó*).
Such people,
I also do not permit to receive and uphold this canon.
I would rather they do not receive it,
do not uphold it,
and do not practice it,
than receive, uphold, and practice it while destroying the precepts.
Good man (*shànnánzǐ*)!
If my disciples receive, uphold, read, and recite,
copy, and expound the *Nièpán Jīng*,
they should correct their body and mind.
Carefully avoid frivolity (*tiáoxì*)
and light, restless actions (*qīngzào jǔdòng*).
The body engaging in frivolity
and the mind being lightly agitated.
The mind seeking existence (*qiú yǒu*),
is called light agitation;
the body creating various karma (*yè*),
is called frivolity.
If my disciples seek existence,
and create karma,
they should not receive and uphold this Great Vehicle (*Dàchéng*) canon, the *Dà Nièpán Jīng*.
If there are those who uphold the Sūtra in this manner,
people will belittle and scold them,
saying:
'If the Buddha's Secret Treasury, the *Dà Nièpán Jīng*,
possesses spiritual power,
how could it allow you to seek existence
and create karma?
If the one who upholds the Sūtra seeks existence
and creates karma,
you should know that this Sūtra has no spiritual power.
If it lacks spiritual power,
even if upheld,
it brings no benefit.
Because of this belittling and slandering of the *Nièpán Jīng*,
it further causes countless, boundless sentient beings to fall into hell (*dìyù*).
Those who uphold this Sūtra, seeking existence
and creating karma,
are truly the evil companions (*è zhīshì*) of sentient beings,
they are not my disciples,
but the retinue of Māra (*Mó*).
"Furthermore, good man (*shànnánzǐ*)!
If my disciples receive, uphold, read, and recite,
copy, and expound this *Nièpán Jīng*,
do not preach at the wrong time (*fēishí*),
do not preach in the wrong place (*fēiguó*),
do not preach without being invited (*bù qǐng shuō*),
do not preach with a frivolous mind (*qīngxīn*),
do not preach everywhere,
do not preach by praising oneself (*zìtàn*),
do not preach by belittling others,
do not preach extinguishing the Buddha Dharma (*Fófǎ*),
do not preach blazing up worldly doctrines (*shìfǎ*).
Good man (*shànnánzǐ*)!
If my disciples uphold this Sūtra,
and preach at the wrong time,
or even preach blazing up worldly doctrines,
people will belittle and scold them, saying:
'If the Buddha's Secret Treasury, the *Dà Nièpán Jīng*, possesses spiritual power,
how could it allow you to preach at the wrong time,
or even preach blazing up worldly doctrines?
If the one who upholds the Sūtra speaks in this manner,
you should know that this Sūtra has no spiritual power.
If it lacks spiritual power,
although upheld, it brings no benefit.
Because of this belittling and slandering of the *Nièpán Jīng*,
it causes countless sentient beings to fall into hell (*dìyù*).
Those who uphold this Sūtra,
preaching at the wrong time or even preaching blazing up worldly doctrines,
are truly the evil companions (*è zhīshì*) of sentient beings,
they are not my disciples,
but the retinue of Māra (*Mó*).
Good man (*shànnánzǐ*)!
If one wishes to uphold it,
to speak of the Great Nirvāṇa (*Dà Nièpán*),
to speak of the Buddha Nature (*Fóxìng*),
to speak of the Tathāgata's Secret Treasury (*Rúlái Bìzàng*),
to speak of the Great Vehicle (*Dàchéng*),
to speak of *Fāngděng Jīng* (Vaipulya Sūtras),
to speak of the *Shēngwén* Vehicle (Hearers' Vehicle),
to speak of the *Pìzhīfó* Vehicle (Pratyekabuddhas' Vehicle),
to speak of liberation (*jiětuō*),
or to see the Buddha Nature (*Fóxìng*),
they must first purify their body.
Because the body is pure, there is no scolding,
and because there is no scolding, countless people are caused to generate pure faith in the Great Nirvāṇa (*Dà Nièpán*).
Because faith arises, they venerate this Sūtra.
If they hear one verse (*jì*),
one sentence,
one character, or [respect] the Dharma teacher (*shuōfǎ zhě*),
they will attain the generation of the resolve for *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí* (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi).
You should know that such a person is the true good companion (*shàn zhīshì*) of sentient beings,
not an evil companion (*è zhīshì*).
They are my disciples,
not the retinue of Māra (*Mó*).
This is called a *Púsà* (Bodhisattva), not a worldly person.
Good man (*shànnánzǐ*)!
This is what the world does not know,
does not see,
and does not realize,
but which the *Púsà* knows, sees, and realizes.
"Furthermore, good man (*shànnánzǐ*)!
What else is called that which all the world does not know, see, or realize,
but which the *Púsà* knows, sees, and realizes?
Namely, the Six Recollections (*liù niànchù*).
What are the six?
Recollection of the Buddha (*niàn fó*),
Recollection of the Dharma (*niàn fǎ*),
Recollection of the Saṅgha (*niàn sēng*),
Recollection of the Precepts (*niàn jiè*),
Recollection of Giving (*niàn shī*),
and Recollection of Heaven (*niàn tiān*).
Good man (*shànnánzǐ*)!
How is the Buddha recollected?
The *Rúlái* (Tathāgata),
the *Yìng* (Arhat),
the *Zhèng Biànzhī* (Truly Universally Knowing),
the *Míng Xíng Zú* (Perfect in Clarity and Conduct),
the *Shànshì* (Well Gone),
the *Shìjiān Jiě* (Knower of the World),
the *Wú Shàng Shì* (Unsurpassed Man),
the *Tiáo Yù Zhàngfu* (Tamer of Men),
the *Tiān Rén Shī* (Teacher of Gods and Humans),
the *Fó* (Buddha),
the *Shìzūn* (World-Honored One)—
constantly immutable,
complete with the Ten Powers (*shílì*),
the Four Kinds of Fearlessness (*sì wúsuǒwèi*),
the Great Lion's Roar (*Dà Shīzǐ Hǒu*).
Called the Great Śramaṇa (*Dà Shāméng*),
the Great Brāhmaṇa (*Dà Póluómén*),
the Greatly Pure, ultimately arrived at the Other Shore,
the Unconquerable,
the One whose Crown is Unseen,
fearless, unafraid, unmoving,
unique and companionless,
self-awakened without a teacher,
possessing rapid wisdom (*zhì*),
great wisdom,
sharp wisdom,
profound wisdom,
liberated wisdom (*jiětuō zhì*),
non-shared wisdom (*bù gòng zhì*),
vast universal wisdom,
ultimate wisdom.
The attainment of the treasury of wisdom.
The King Elephant among men,
the King Ox among men,
the King Dragon among men,
the Great Man among men,
the Lotus Flower among men,
the Puṇḍarīka Flower (*Púntuólì Huā*),
the master tamer of humans,
the Great Benefactor and Master of the Great Dharma.
Because he knows the Dharma, he is called the Great Dharma Master (*Dà Fǎshī*);
because he knows the meaning, he is called the Great Dharma Master;
because he knows the timing, he is called the Great Dharma Master;
because he knows contentment (*zhī zú*), he is called the Great Dharma Master;
because he knows the self (*zhī wǒ*), he is called the Great Dharma Master;
because he knows the multitude, he is called the Great Dharma Master;
because he knows the various natures (*zhǒngzhǒngxìng*) of sentient beings, he is called the Great Dharma Master;
because he knows the sharp, dull, and average capacities of the faculties (*zhū gēn*), he is called the Great Dharma Master;
because he speaks of the Middle Way (*zhōngdào*), he is called the Great Dharma Master.
"Why is he called the *Rúlái*?
Because he is unchanging, just like the teachings of the past Buddhas (*Fó*).
How is he unchanging?
The past Buddhas,
in order to save sentient beings, preached the Twelve Divisions of the Canon (*shí'èr bù jīng*).
The *Rúlái* is also like this,
therefore he is called the *Rúlái*.
All the World-Honored Buddhas (*Fó Shìzūn*), from the Six Pāramitās (*liù bōluómì*),
the Thirty-seven Wings of Enlightenment (*sānshíqī pǐn*),
and the Elevenfold Emptiness (*shíyī kōng*) arrived at the Great Nirvāṇa (*Dà Nièpán*).
The *Rúlái* is also like this,
therefore the Buddha is called the *Rúlái*.
All the World-Honored Buddhas, for the sake of sentient beings,
expediently revealed and taught the Three Vehicles (*sānchéng*) according to circumstance.
Their lifespan is immeasurable and beyond calculation.
The *Rúlái* is also like this,
therefore the Buddha is called the *Rúlái*.
"What is meant by Yìng (應, Worthy)?
All dharmas of the world are called enemies,
because the Buddha should destroy them.
Therefore, the term is Yìng.
The Four Māras are the enemies of the Bodhisattvas.
When the Tathāgatas were Bodhisattvas,
they were able to destroy the Four Māras with wisdom.
Therefore, the term is Yìng.
Furthermore, Yìng means detachment/far-reaching.
When one is a Bodhisattva,
one should detach oneself from immeasurable afflictions (fánnǎo).
Therefore, the term is Yìng.
Furthermore, Yìng means joy.
When the Buddhas of the past were Bodhisattvas,
although they endured all sufferings and vexations for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable Asaṃkhyeya Kalpas,
they were never without joy,
but always found joy in it.
The Tathāgata is also like this.
Therefore, the term is Yìng.
Furthermore, regarding Yìng,
all humans and devas
should make offerings with various incense, flowers,
necklaces (yīngluò),
banners (chuángfān),
and music.
Therefore, the term is Yìng.
"What is meant by Zhèng Biàn Zhī (正遍知, Perfectly and Universally Knowing)?
Zhèng (Perfectly) means non-perversion,
and Biàn Zhī (Universally Knowing) means comprehending fully all four perversions.
Furthermore, Zhèng means ascetic practice (kǔxíng).
Biàn Zhī means
knowing that based on ascetic practice,
the result of suffering (kǔ guǒ) is inevitable.
Furthermore, Zhèng means being within the world (shìjiān zhōng).
Biàn Zhī means ultimately knowing with certainty
that cultivating the Middle Way (Zhōngdào) attains Anouduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Furthermore, Zhèng
means countable,
measurable,
and weighable.
Biàn Zhī means
uncountable,
immeasurable,
and unweighable.
Therefore, the Buddha is titled Zhèng Biàn Zhī.
Good man!
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas also have Biàn Zhī,
and also lack Biàn Zhī.
Why is this?
Biàn Zhī
refers to the Five Skandhas (wǔ yīn),
the Twelve Āyatanas (shí'èr rù),
and the Eighteen Dhātus (shíbā jiè).
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas also attain perfect knowledge of these;
this is called Biàn Zhī.
What is meant by lacking Biàn Zhī?
Good man!
Suppose the practitioners of the Two Vehicles (Èr Chéng) spend immeasurable Kalpas
observing just one Skandha of form (sè yīn).
They cannot know it completely.
For this reason,
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not possess Biàn Zhī.
"What is meant by Míng Xíng Zú (明行足, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct)?
Míng (Knowledge/Light) means attaining immeasurable good results.
Xíng Zú means feet/basis.
The good result is called Anouduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
The feet/basis are called Precepts (Jiè)
and Wisdom (Huì).
Riding upon the basis of Precepts and Wisdom,
one attains Anouduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Therefore, the term is Míng Xíng Zú.
Furthermore, Míng means incantation (zhòu).
Xíng means auspiciousness (jí).
Zú means result (guǒ).
Good man!
This is the worldly meaning (shìjiān yì);
incantation means liberation (jiětuō).
Auspiciousness means Anouduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Result means Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Bān Nièpán).
Therefore, the term is Míng Xíng Zú.
Furthermore, Míng means light (guāng).
Xíng means action/karma (yè).
Zú means result (guǒ).
Good man!
This is the worldly meaning;
light means non-negligence (bú fàngyì).
Action means the Six Pāramitās (Liù Bōluómì).
Result means Anouduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Furthermore, Míng means the Three Knowledges (Sān Míng):
First, the Bodhisattva Knowledge (Púsà Míng);
second, the Buddhas' Knowledge (Zhū Fó Míng);
third, the Knowledge of No Knowledge (Wú Míng Míng).
The Bodhisattva Knowledge is Prajñāpāramitā (Bōrě Bōluómì).
The Buddhas' Knowledge is the Buddha Eye (Fó Yǎn).
The Knowledge of No Knowledge is ultimate emptiness (bìjìng kōng).
Xíng (Conduct) means cultivating all good karma for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable Kalpas.
Zú (Perfect/Complete) means clearly seeing the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng).
For this reason, the term is Míng Xíng Zú.
"What is meant by Shàn Shì (善逝, Well Gone)?
Shàn means lofty/high (gāo).
Shì means not lofty (bù gāo).
Good man!
This is the worldly meaning;
lofty means Anouduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Not lofty is the mind of the Tathāgata.
Good man!
If the mind were lofty, he would not be called a Tathāgata.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is called Shàn Shì.
Furthermore, Shàn means good spiritual friend (shàn zhīshì).
Shì means the result of the good spiritual friend.
Good man!
This is the worldly meaning;
the good spiritual friend is the initial arising of the mind (chū fā xīn).
The result is called Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Bān Nièpán).
The Tathāgata did not abandon the initially arisen mind and attained Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is called Shàn Shì.
Furthermore, Shàn means good/excellent (hǎo).
Shì means existence/having (yǒu).
Good man!
This is the worldly meaning;
Good/Excellent means seeing the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng).
Existence means Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Good man!
The nature of Nirvāṇa is truly non-existent.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones (Shìzūn), because of the world,
state that it exists.
Good man!
For example, worldly people,
who truly have no son, say they have a son;
who truly have no path, say they have a path.
Nirvāṇa is also like this;
because of the world, it is said to exist.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, achieved Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
Therefore, the term is Shàn Shì.
"Good man!
What is meant by Shìjiān Jiě (世間解, Knower of the World)?
Good man!
The world (shìjiān) means the Five Skandhas (wǔ yīn).
Jiě means knowing.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, know the Five Skandhas well.
Therefore, the term is Shìjiān Jiě.
Furthermore, the world means the Five Desires (wǔ yù).
Jiě means non-attachment (bù zhuó).
Because of non-attachment to the Five Desires,
the term is Shìjiān Jiě.
Furthermore, regarding Shìjiān Jiě,
concerning the immeasurable Asaṃkhyeya worlds in the East,
all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas neither know,
nor see,
nor comprehend them.
The Buddhas completely know them,
completely see them,
and completely comprehend them.
The South, West, and North directions,
the four intermediate directions, and above and below,
are also like this.
Therefore, the Buddha is titled Shìjiān Jiě.
Furthermore, the world means all ordinary beings (fánfū).
Jiě means knowing the causes and results (yīn guǒ) of the good and bad deeds of all ordinary beings.
This is not known by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Only the Buddha can know this.
Therefore, the Buddha is titled Shìjiān Jiě.
Furthermore, the world is called the lotus flower (liánhuā).
Jiě means unstained (bù wū).
Good man!
This is the worldly meaning;
the lotus flower is the Tathāgata.
Unstained means
that the Tathāgata is not defiled by the Eight Worldly Dharmas (Shìjiān Bā Fǎ).
Therefore, the Buddha is titled Shìjiān Jiě.
Furthermore, regarding Shìjiān Jiě,
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called Shìjiān Jiě.
Why is this?
Because the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas see the world.
Therefore, the term is Shìjiān Jiě.
Good man!
Just as life is sustained by food,
and food is therefore called life;
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are also like this.
Because they see the world,
they are called Shìjiān Jiě.
"What is the title Wúshàngshì (Unsurpassed Guide)?
Shàngshì (Superior Guide) means that which is broken,
He who has nothing to break,
is called Wúshàngshì.
All the Fó Shìzūn (Buddhas, World-Honored Ones) have no *fánnǎo* (afflictions),
therefore there is nothing to break.
For this reason, the Fó is titled Wúshàngshì.
Furthermore, Shàngshì means contention or litigation.
Wúshàngshì means having no contention.
The Rúlái (Tathāgata) is without contention,
for this reason, the Fó is titled Wúshàngshì.
Furthermore, Shàngshì means speech that can be undermined.
Wúshàngshì means speech that cannot be undermined.
The words spoken by the Rúlái,
cannot be undermined by any sentient being.
For this reason, the Fó is titled Wúshàngshì.
Furthermore, Shàngshì means an honored seat (Shàngzuò).
Wúshàngshì means having no seat above.
Among the Fó of the three ages, there is none who surpasses him.
For this reason, the Fó is titled Wúshàngshì.
*Shàng* (Above/Superior) means new.
*Shì* (Guide/Person) means old.
All Fó Shìzūn embody the great Nièpán (Nirvāṇa).
They are neither new nor old.
For this reason, the Fó is titled Wúshàngshì.
"What is the title Tiáoyù Zhàngfū (Tamer of Men)?
He is himself a *zhàngfū* (great man),
and furthermore he disciplines *zhàngfū*.
Shànnánzǐ (Good man)!
When speaking of the Rúlái,
truly he is neither *zhàngfū* (masculine),
nor not *zhàngfū* (not masculine).
Because he disciplines *zhàngfū*,
therefore the Rúlái is called *zhàngfū*.
Shànnánzǐ!
All men and women,
if they possess four teachings (dharma),
are then called *zhàngfū*.
What are these four?
First, Shànzhīshì (Spiritual mentor);
second, being able to hear the Dharma;
third, contemplating the meaning;
fourth, practicing as taught.
Shànnánzǐ!
If a man or a woman possesses these four teachings,
then they are called *zhàngfū*.
Shànnánzǐ!
If there is a man
who lacks these four teachings,
then he should not be called *zhàngfū*.
Why is this?
Although the body is that of a *zhàngfū*,
the conduct is the same as an animal (*chùshēng*).
The Rúlái disciplines men and women alike,
therefore the Fó is titled Tiáoyù Zhàngfū.
Furthermore, Shànnánzǐ!
Like a charioteer who manages horses,
there are generally four types:
the first touches the hair,
the second touches the skin,
the third touches the flesh,
the fourth touches the bone.
According to where he touches,
it matches the intention of the charioteer.
The Rúlái is also like this;
using four types of Dharma,
he disciplines sentient beings:
The first is speaking of birth,
making them accept the words of the Fó,
like touching the hair,
matching the intention of the charioteer.
The second is speaking of birth and aging,
and they accept the words of the Fó,
like touching the hair and skin,
matching the intention of the charioteer.
The third is speaking of birth, as well as aging and sickness,
and they accept the words of the Fó,
like touching the hair, skin, and flesh,
matching the intention of the charioteer.
The fourth is speaking of birth, as well as aging, sickness, and death,
and they accept the words of the Fó,
like touching the hair, skin, flesh, and bone,
matching the intention of the charioteer.
Shànnánzǐ!
When the charioteer disciplines the horse,
it is not definitively successful.
When the Rúlái Shìzūn disciplines sentient beings,
it is certainly not in vain.
For this reason, the Fó is titled Tiáoyù Zhàngfū.
"What is the title Tiānrénshī (Teacher of Gods and Humans)?
Teachers are of two kinds:
the first teaches goodness,
the second teaches evil.
All Fó and Púsà (Bodhisattvas) constantly teach sentient beings with good Dharma.
What is this good Dharma?
Namely, goodness of body,
mouth,
and intention (mind).
Fó and Púsà instruct sentient beings,
saying thus:
'Shànnánzǐ,
you ought to completely avoid non-good *karmā* (karma) of the body.
Why is this?
Because evil *karmā* of the body,
is avoidable,
and thus one can gain liberation (*jiětuō*).
For this reason, I teach you with this Dharma.
If this evil *karmā* were unavoidable,
and one could gain liberation,
I would ultimately not teach you to avoid it.
If sentient beings, having left evil *karmā*,
were to fall into the three evil paths (sān'è), there is no such case.
Because of avoiding it,
one achieves Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi),
and obtains the great Nièpán.
For this reason, Fó and Púsà constantly instruct sentient beings with this Dharma.
The mouth,
and intention are also like this.
For this reason, the Fó is titled Wúshàngshī (Unsurpassed Teacher).
Furthermore, in the past, he had not attained the Way,
but now he has attained it,
and he speaks of the Way he has attained
for sentient beings.
Since the beginning, he had not practiced pure conduct (*fànxíng*),
but now he has completed the practice,
and he speaks of his own practice
for sentient beings.
He himself destroyed Wúmíng (Ignorance),
and furthermore, he destroys Wúmíng for sentient beings.
He himself gained pure sight,
and furthermore, for sentient beings, he breaks through blindness and darkness,
allowing them to gain pure eyes.
He himself knows the two Truths (*èrdì*),
and furthermore, he expounds the two Truths for sentient beings.
Having liberated himself,
he furthermore speaks the Dharma of liberation for sentient beings.
He himself crossed the boundless great river of life and death (*shēngsǐ*),
and furthermore, he enables all sentient beings to cross it.
He himself gained fearlessness (*wúwèi*),
and furthermore, he teaches sentient beings to be without terror or fear.
Having himself entered Nièpán,
he furthermore expounds the great Nièpán for sentient beings.
For this reason, the Fó is titled Wúshàngshī.
*Tiān* (Heaven/God) means daytime.
In the heavens, the day is long and the night is short,
this is why it is called *tiān*.
Furthermore, *tiān* means being without worry or distress,
constantly experiencing joy, this is why it is called *tiān*.
Furthermore, *tiān* means illumination,
being able to break through darkness and become a great light,
this is why it is called *tiān*.
Also, by being able to break through the darkness of evil *karmā*,
obtaining good *karmā*,
and being born into the heavens,
this is why it is called *tiān*.
Furthermore, *tiān* means auspicious (*jí*).
Because of auspiciousness,
it obtains the name *tiān*.
Furthermore, *tiān* means the sun (*rì*).
Because it possesses light,
it is called *tiān*.
Based on these meanings,
it is called *tiān*.
*Rén* (Human) means being capable of much kindness and righteousness (*ēnyì*).
Furthermore, *rén* means having a gentle body and mouth.
Furthermore, *rén* means possessing arrogance (*jiāomàn*).
Furthermore, *rén* means being able to destroy *jiāomàn*.
Shànnánzǐ!
Although all Fó are the Wúshàng Dàshī (Unsurpassed Great Teacher) for all sentient beings,
yet the Sūtras state they are the Tiānrénshī.
Why is this?
Shànnánzǐ!
Among sentient beings, only *tiān* and *rén* (gods and humans),
are able to arouse the mind of Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi),
are able to cultivate the path of the ten good *karmā* (*shí shàn yè dào*),
are able to attain the result of the Xūtuóhuán (Śrotāpanna),
the result of the Sītuóhán (Sakṛdāgāmin),
the result of the Ānàhán (Anāgāmin),
the result of the Āluóhàn (Arhat),
the path of the Pìzhīfó (Pratyekabuddha),
and obtain Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
For this reason, the Fó is titled Tiānrénshī.
"What is the meaning of Fó?
Fó means Jué (Enlightenment/Awakening).
Having awakened himself,
he is furthermore able to awaken others.
Shànnánzǐ!
For example, there is a person
who is aware of a thief,
and the thief is unable to act.
The Púsà Móhēsà (Bodhisattva Mahāsattva) is able to perceive all limitless *fánnǎo*,
having perceived and understood them,
he makes it so that the various *fánnǎo* are unable to act.
This is why he is called Fó.
Because of this awakening,
there is no birth,
no aging,
no sickness,
and no death.
This is why he is called Fó.
"Regarding Pójiāpó,
Bhaga means breaking,
vā means afflictions (Fánnǎo).
Because he can break afflictions,
he is named Pójiāpó.
Moreover, because he accomplishes all virtuous Dharmas,
moreover, because he expertly understands the meaning of all Dharmas,
because he possesses great merit (Gōngdé) that none can surpass,
because he has great renown that spreads throughout the ten directions,
moreover, because he bestows various great wisdom (Huì) gifts,
moreover, because he emitted the female root over measureless Āsēngqí jié.
"O Good Man!
If any man,
or any woman,
can contemplate the Buddha in this manner,
whether walking,
or standing,
or sitting,
or lying down,
whether by day,
or by night,
whether in light,
or in darkness,
they will constantly be able to see the World-Honored Buddha (Shìzūn) without separation.
"O Good Man!
Why is he named Rúlái,
Yīng,
Zhèngbiànzhī, and so forth, up to Pójiāpó,
possessing such measureless merit (Gōngdé) and great renown?
O Good Man!
The Púsà Móhēsà, in measureless past Āsēngqí jié,
respectfully served parents,
Héshàng,
all teachers,
elders (Shàngzuò),
and venerables (Zhǎnglǎo).
For measureless kalpas, they constantly practiced giving (Bùshī) for the sake of sentient beings,
firmly upholding the precepts (Jìnjiè),
cultivating patience (Rěnrù),
diligently practicing vigor (Jīngjìn),
meditation (Chándìng),
and wisdom (Zhìhuì),
great loving-kindness (Dàcí),
great compassion (Dàbēi),
great joy (Dàxǐ),
and great equanimity (Dàshě).
Therefore, they now possess the Thirty-two Marks,
the Eighty Minor Characteristics,
and a Vajra body (Jīngāng zhī shēn).
Furthermore, the Púsà, in measureless past Āsēngqí jié,
cultivated the roots of faith (Xìn),
mindfulness (Niàn),
vigor (Jìn),
concentration (Dìng),
and wisdom (Huìgēn).
Toward all teachers and elders,
they offered reverence and offerings,
always acting for the benefit of the Dharma (Fǎ lì),
and not for the benefit of food.
If the Púsà upholds the twelve divisions of the scriptures (Jīng),
whether reading,
or reciting,
they constantly do so to enable sentient beings to attain liberation (Jiětuō),
peace (Ānyǐn),
and happiness (Kuàilè),
never for themselves.
Why is this?
The Púsà constantly cultivates the mind of transcending the world (Chūshìjiān xīn), the mind of leaving home (chūjiā xīn),
the mind of non-action (Wúwéi),
the mind free of contention,
the mind free of defilement,
the mind free of bondage,
the mind free of grasping,
the mind free of obscuration,
the mind free of indeterminate states (Wú jì xīn),
the mind free of life and death (Shēngsǐ),
the mind free of the net of doubt,
the mind free of covetous desire (Tānyù),
the mind free of hatred (Chēnhuì),
the mind free of delusion (Yúchī),
the mind free of arrogance (Jiāomàn),
the mind free of filth and turbidity,
the mind free of afflictions (Fánnǎo),
the mind free of suffering,
the measureless mind,
the vast and great mind,
the empty space mind,
the non-mind,
the mind of non-non-mind,
the tamed mind,
the unprotected mind,
the mind free of concealment,
the mind free of worldly attachment (Shìjiān xīn),
the mind constantly in concentration (Dìng),
the mind constantly cultivated,
the mind constantly liberated (Jiětuō xīn),
the mind free of retribution (Bào xīn),
the mind free of specific vows,
the mind of virtuous vows,
the mind free of error,
the gentle mind,
the non-abiding mind,
the self-mastered mind (Zìzài xīn),
the undefiled mind (Wúlòu xīn),
the mind of the ultimate truth (Dìyī yì xīn),
the non-retrogressing mind,
the mind of impermanence (Wúcháng xīn),
the straightforward mind,
the mind free of flattery and deceit,
the purely virtuous mind,
the mind without smallness or greatness,
the mind without hardness or rigidity,
the mind free of common mortal thoughts (Fánfū xīn),
the mind free of Śrāvaka thoughts (Shēngwén xīn),
the mind free of Pratyekabuddha thoughts (Yuánjué xīn).
They expertly know the realm of the mind (Xīnjiè),
know the realm where the mind arises,
know the realm where the mind abides,
and know the mind's realm of self-mastery (Zìzài jiè xīn).
Therefore, they now attain the Ten Powers (Shí Lì),
the Four Fearlessnesses (Sì Wúsuǒwèi),
Great Compassion (Dàbēi),
the Three Stations of Mindfulness (Sān Niànchù),
permanence (cháng), bliss (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng).
Therefore, they are entitled to be called Rúlái and so forth, up to Pójiāpó.
This is known as the Púsà Móhēsà contemplating the Buddha.
"How does the Púsà Móhēsà contemplate the Dharma?
O Good Man!
The Púsà Móhēsà reflects that the Dharma spoken by all Buddhas is the most wondrous and supreme.
Because of this Dharma,
sentient beings are able to attain immediate results.
Truly, this True Dharma (Zhèngfǎ)
is timeless,
seen by the Dharma Eye (Fǎ Yǎn),
not seen by the physical eye.
Furthermore, it cannot be compared with analogies.
It does not arise,
does not emerge,
does not abide,
does not cease,
has no beginning,
has no end,
is unconditioned (Wúwéi),
is innumerable.
For those without refuge, it creates a refuge;
for those without reliance, it creates reliance;
for those without light (Wúmíng), it creates light;
it causes those who have not reached the Other Shore (Bǐ'àn) to reach the Other Shore.
For places without fragrance, it creates unobstructed fragrance.
It is seen by the unseen,
unmoving and unchanging,
neither long nor short.
It eternally severs all worldly pleasures, yet it is the bliss of tranquility.
It is ultimately subtle and wondrous.
It is not form (Sè), yet it severs form and is also form;
likewise, it is not consciousness (Shì), yet it severs consciousness and is also consciousness;
it is not karma (Yè), yet it severs karma;
it is not defilement, yet it severs defilement;
it is not substance (Wù), yet it severs substance and is also substance;
it is not realm (Jiè), yet it severs realm and is also realm;
it is not existence (Yǒu), yet it severs existence and is also existence;
it is not sense-base (Rù), yet it severs sense-base and is also sense-base;
it is not cause (Yīn), yet it severs cause and is also cause;
it is not effect (Guǒ), yet it severs effect and is also effect;
neither void nor real;
it severs all reality yet is also reality;
neither arising nor ceasing;
it eternally departs from arising and ceasing, yet it is also cessation;
neither characteristic (Xiàng) nor non-characteristic;
it severs all characteristics yet is also characteristic;
neither teaching nor non-teaching, yet it is also the Teacher (Shī);
neither fear nor peace (Ān);
it severs all fear yet is also peace;
neither patience (Rěn) nor non-patience;
it eternally severs non-patience yet is also patience;
neither stillness (Zhǐ) nor non-stillness;
it severs all stillness yet is also stillness.
The summit of all Dharmas (Fǎ),
entirely able to eternally sever all afflictions (Fánnǎo),
pure and signless,
eternally escaping all characteristics,
the ultimate dwelling place for measureless sentient beings,
capable of extinguishing the blazing fire of all cycles of life and death (Shēngsǐ),
it is truly the place where all Buddhas dwell and roam,
constantly immutable.
This is known as the Púsà contemplating the Dharma."
"How is the recollection of the Sáṅgha?
The noble Sáṅgha of all Buddhas,
who abide according to the Dhárma (Fǎ),
receive the upright Dhárma,
practice in compliance,
cannot be seen,
cannot be grasped,
cannot be destroyed,
cannot be harmed by anyone,
are inconceivable,
are the field of merit and excellent protector for all sentient beings.
Although they are a field of merit,
they take or receive nothing.
They are pure and undefiled,
without outflow (wú lòu),
unconditioned (wú wéi),
vast, universal, and boundless.
Their minds are gentle and pliant,
equal and non-dual,
without disturbance or impurity,
constantly unchanging.
This is called the recollection of the Sáṅgha (Niàn Sēng).
"How is the recollection of Precepts (Niàn Jiè)?
A Bódhisattva (Púsà) contemplates the existence of Precepts,
which are unbroken and without leakage,
undamaged and unmixed.
Although without form or appearance,
they can be upheld and protected.
Although without contact or opposition,
through the good cultivation of skillful means,
they can be perfectly attained.
They are without fault or blame,
praised by all Buddhas and Bódhisattvas.
This is the cause of the Great Vaipulya (Dà Fāngděng) Great Nírvaṇa (Dà Nièpán).
O good man!
For instance, like the great earth,
a boat or ship,
a necklace,
a great clan,
the great sea,
alkaline ash water,
a house or dwelling,
a sword or blade,
a bridge,
an excellent physician and wonderful medicine,
Āgàtuó medicine,
the wish-fulfilling jewel (Rúyì Bǎozhū),
feet, eyes, and sight,
the shade provided by parents.
None can rob them, nor can they be harmed;
fire cannot burn them,
water cannot wash them away.
They are like the steps of a great mountain,
the wonderful treasure and victorious banner of all Buddhas and Bódhisattvas.
If one abides in these Precepts,
one attains the fruit of Sūtuóhuán (Srotaāpanna).
I also have a share in this,
but I do not require it.
Why is this?
If I were to attain the fruit of Sūtuóhuán,
I would not be able to extensively save all sentient beings.
If one abides in these Precepts,
one attains Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambódhi).
I also have a share in this,
which is what I desire.
Why is this?
If I attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
I shall extensively expound the wonderful Dhárma for sentient beings and act as their protector.
This is called the recollection of Precepts by a Bódhisattva Mahāsáttva (Púsà Móhēsà).
"How is the recollection of Giving (Niàn Shī)?
The Bódhisattva Mahāsáttva profoundly observes that this giving
is indeed the cause of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
All Buddhas and Bódhisattvas draw near to and cultivate such giving;
I shall likewise draw near to and cultivate it.
If one does not bestow gifts,
one cannot adorn the assembly of the fourfold community.
Although giving cannot ultimately sever defilements,
it can eliminate and destroy present afflictions.
Because of the condition of giving,
one is constantly praised by sentient beings in worlds numerous as the sands of the Gánghé (Ganges) River, boundless and immeasurable, throughout the ten directions.
When a Bódhisattva Mahāsáttva gives food to sentient beings,
they bestow life upon them.
Due to this fruition,
when attaining Buddhahood,
they will constantly be unchanging.
Because they bestow happiness,
when attaining Buddhahood, they obtain peace and happiness.
When the Bódhisattva gives,
they seek wealth lawfully (according to the Dhárma),
they do not infringe upon others to achieve this giving.
Therefore, upon attaining Buddhahood, they obtain pure Nírvaṇa (Nièpán).
When the Bódhisattva gives,
they enable sentient beings to receive without asking;
therefore, upon attaining Buddhahood, they obtain sovereignty (mastery).
Due to the condition of my giving,
others gain power/strength.
Therefore, upon attaining Buddhahood, I acquire the Ten Powers (Shí Lì).
Due to the condition of giving, others gain speech.
Therefore, upon attaining Buddhahood, I acquire the Four Unimpeded Knowledges (Sì Wú Ài).
All Buddhas and Bódhisattvas cultivate and accumulate this giving,
making it the cause of Nírvaṇa.
I shall also cultivate and accumulate giving in this manner,
making it the cause of Nírvaṇa.
The extensive exposition is found in the *Záhuā*.
"How is the recollection of Devas (Niàn Tiān)?
There are the realms of the Four Heavenly Kings (Sì Tiānwáng Chù),
up to the realm of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception (Fēixiǎng Fēifēixiǎng Chù).
If one has faith,
one attains the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings;
I also have a share in this.
If through Precepts,
vast learning,
giving,
and wisdom,
one attains the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings,
or even attains the realm of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception,
I also have a share in this;
however, this is not what I desire.
Why is this?
The realms from the Four Heavenly Kings up to the realm of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception are all impermanent (wú cháng).
Because they are impermanent,
there is birth, aging, sickness, and death.
For this reason,
they are not what I desire.
They are like magical illusions,
deceiving foolish commoners;
but wise people
are not confused by or attached to them.
That which is like a magical illusion is precisely the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings,
up to the realm of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception.
The foolish are precisely all ordinary beings (fánfū).
I am different from foolish ordinary beings.
I have heard of the Heaven of the Highest Meaning (Dìyī Yì Tiān),
which means all Buddhas and Bódhisattvas who are constant and unchanging.
Because they constantly abide,
there is no birth,
no aging,
no sickness,
and no death.
For the sake of sentient beings, I diligently seek the Heaven of the Highest Meaning (Dìyī Yì Tiān).
Why is this?
The Heaven of the Highest Meaning can enable sentient beings to eliminate and sever their afflictions,
like the wish-fulfilling tree (Rúyì Shù).
If I possess faith, and even wisdom,
I will be able to attain this Heaven of the Highest Meaning,
and shall extensively analyze and explain the Heaven of the Highest Meaning for sentient beings.
This is called the recollection of Devas by a Bódhisattva Mahāsáttva.
"O good man!
This is called the Bódhisattva who is non-mundane.
This is what the world does not know, see, or realize,
but which the Bódhisattva knows, sees, and realizes.
O good man!
If my disciples
receive, uphold, read, and recite
the Twelve Divisions of the Scriptures (Shí'èr Bù Jīng),
and also receive, uphold, read, and recite,
transcribe, expound,
and explain the Great Nírvaṇa Sūtra (Dà Nièpán Jīng),
and maintain there is no difference between them—
this assertion is incorrect.
Why is this?
O good man!
The Great Nírvaṇa
is precisely the extremely profound secret treasury of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones (Shìzūn).
Because it is the extremely profound secret treasury of the Buddhas,
it is therefore superior.
O good man!
For this reason,
the Great Nírvaṇa Sūtra is extremely wondrous,
extremely singular,
and inconceivable.
Kèyè Púsà (Kāśyapa Bódhisattva) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I also know that the Great Nírvaṇa Sūtra
is extremely wondrous, extremely singular, and inconceivable.
The Buddha (Fó), the Dhárma, and the Sáṅgha (Sēng) are inconceivable.
The Bódhi (Pútí) of the Bódhisattvas,
and the Great Pārinirvāṇa (Dà Bōnièpán) are also inconceivable.
World-Honored One!
For what reason
is it further said that the Bódhisattva is inconceivable?"
“‘Good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not have a teacher,
yet is able to spontaneously arouse the Bodhi mind.
Having aroused this mind,
he diligently cultivates vigor.
Even if great fire burns his body and head,
he ultimately does not seek rescue
or abandon the mind that recollects the Dhamma.
Why is this?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva constantly thinks to himself:
“During measureless Asaṃkhyeya Kalpas,
whether in the hells,
among hungry ghosts,
as animals,
among humans,
or in the heavens,
I was burned by the fire of afflictions,
but never obtained a definitive Dhamma.
The definitive Dhamma
is none other than Anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi.
If it is for the sake of Anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi,
I will ultimately not spare my body, mind, or life.
For the sake of Anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi,
even if my body is ground into fine dust,
I will never abandon the cultivation of vigor.
Why is this?
The mind of diligence and vigor
is the cause of Anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi.”
Good man!
Such a Bodhisattva,
who has not yet seen Anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi,
is already able to be so unsparing of body and life;
how much more so after seeing it!
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is inconceivable.
Furthermore, the inconceivable thing is that
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva perceives measureless faults in Saṃsāra,
which are not reached by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Although he knows the measureless faults and evils of Saṃsāra,
for the sake of sentient beings,
he endures suffering within it,
without giving rise to weariness or aversion.
Therefore, he is again called inconceivable.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, for the sake of sentient beings,
though he is in the hells,
experiences all suffering and distress as the joy of the third Dhyāna.
Therefore, he is again called inconceivable.
Good man!
For example, a householder,
whose house catches fire.
The householder sees it and rushes out of the dwelling,
but his sons are left behind and have not escaped the fire peril.
The householder at that time definitely knows the danger of the fire;
yet, for the sake of his sons,
he turns back to rush in and rescue them,
disregarding his own danger.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this:
although he knows that Saṃsāra has many faults and evils,
for the sake of sentient beings,
he dwells within it without aversion.
Therefore, he is again called inconceivable.
Good man!
Measureless sentient beings arouse the Bodhi mind,
but when they see the many faults and evils in Saṃsāra,
their minds immediately regress and collapse,
becoming either Śrāvakas
or Pratyekabuddhas.
If there is a Bodhisattva who hears this Sūtra,
he will ultimately not regress from the Bodhi mind to become a Śrāvaka
or a Pratyekabuddha.
Although such a Bodhisattva has not yet attained the first Immovable Stage (Ācāla-bhūmi),
his mind is firm
and does not regress or collapse.
Therefore, he is again called inconceivable.
Good man!
If someone says,
“I can swim across the water of the great ocean,”
is this statement conceivable or not?
“No,
World-Honored One!
Such a statement
is sometimes conceivable
and sometimes inconceivable.
Why is this?
If a human crosses it,
then it is inconceivable.
If an Aśura crosses it,
then it is conceivable.
“Good man!
I am not speaking of Aśuras;
I am specifically speaking of humans.”
“World-Honored One!
Among humans, there are also those who are conceivable
and those who are inconceivable.
World-Honored One!
Humans are also of two kinds:
one is the noble person (Ārya),
the other is the ordinary person (Pṛthagjana).
The ordinary person is inconceivable,
but the wise and noble person is conceivable.”
“Good man!
I am speaking of the ordinary person;
I am not speaking of the noble person.”
“World-Honored One!
If it is an ordinary person,
it is truly inconceivable.”
“Good man!
An ordinary person
is truly unable to cross the water of the great ocean.
Similarly, this Bodhisattva
is truly able to cross the great ocean of Saṃsāra.
Therefore, he is again called inconceivable.
Good man!
If someone can suspend Mount Sumeru (Sūméixū) with a lotus root fiber,
is this conceivable or not?”
“No,
World-Honored One!”
“Good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in the space of a single thought,
is fully able to measure all of Saṃsāra.
Therefore, he is again called inconceivable.
Good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has already, during measureless Asaṃkhyeya Kalpas,
constantly contemplated Saṃsāra,
observing impermanence,
non-self,
non-bliss,
and impurity;
yet, for the sake of sentient beings, he analyzes and expounds upon permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Although he speaks this way,
it is nevertheless not erroneous view (Mithyādṛṣṭi).
Therefore, he is again called inconceivable.
Good man!
Just as a person entering water
cannot be swept away by the water,
or entering a great raging fire
cannot be burned by the fire—
such an occurrence is inconceivable.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this:
although he dwells in Saṃsāra,
he is not tormented or harmed by Saṃsāra.
Therefore, he is again called inconceivable.
Good man!
Humans have three grades,
namely upper, middle, and lower.
The person of the lower grade, upon first entering the womb,
has this thought:
‘I am now dwelling in a latrine,
a place where all filth converges,
like amidst corpses,
amidst masses of thorns,
in a place of great darkness.’
Upon first emerging from the womb, he again has this thought:
‘I am now emerging from the latrine,
emerging from the place of all filth,’
and so forth, emerging from the place of great darkness.
The person of the middle grade has this thought:
‘I am now entering among the multitudes of trees,
into a clean river,
a residence or dwelling.’
When emerging, it is also like this.
The person of the upper grade has this thought:
‘I am ascending a high hall,
dwelling among flower forests,
riding horses and elephants,
climbing and traversing high mountains.’
When emerging, it is also like this.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, upon first entering the womb, knows that he is entering the womb;
when dwelling, he knows that he is dwelling;
when emerging, he knows that he is emerging.
He ultimately does not give rise to the mind of greed or anger,
even though he has not yet attained the stage of the first Dwelling (Prathama-vihāra-bhūmi).
Therefore, he is again called inconceivable.”’
"O good man!
Anouduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí
truly cannot be compared by analogy or metaphor.
O good man!
The mind also cannot be compared by simile or metaphor,
yet all can be spoken of.
A Púsà Móhēsà has no place to consult a teacher and receive instruction,
yet is able to attain the Dharma of Anouduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Having attained this Dharma,
their mind is without stinginess or greed,
and they constantly expound it for sentient beings;
therefore, it is again named Inconceivable (Bùkě Sīyì).
O good man!
A Púsà Móhēsà has bodily detachment but not vocal detachment,
has vocal detachment but not bodily detachment,
and has detachment that is neither bodily nor vocal.
Bodily detachment
means refraining from killing,
stealing,
and sexual misconduct;
this is called bodily detachment.
Not vocal—
vocal detachment
means refraining from false speech,
double-tongued speech,
harsh speech,
and idle talk;
this is called vocal detachment.
Not bodily—
detachment that is neither bodily nor vocal
means refraining from covetousness and jealousy (tānjí),
anger and hatred (chēnhuì),
and wrong views (xiéjiàn).
O good man,
this is named detachment that is neither bodily nor vocal.
O good man!
A Púsà Móhēsà does not perceive any single phenomenon as body, as action (karma), or as the agent of detachment,
yet detachment still occurs;
therefore, it is again named Inconceivable (Bùkě Sīyì);
speech is also like this.
O good man!
Detachment from body arises from the body,
detachment from speech arises from speech,
and detachment that is neither bodily nor vocal arises from wisdom (huì).
O good man!
This wisdom truly exists,
yet it cannot cause the Púsà to attain detachment.
Why is this?
O good man!
There is no single phenomenon that can destroy
or create,
for the nature of conditioned phenomena (yǒuwéi fǎ) is that they arise and cease independently;
therefore, this wisdom cannot effect detachment.
O good man!
Wisdom cannot break,
fire cannot burn,
water cannot rot,
wind cannot move,
earth cannot hold,
birth cannot give birth,
aging cannot age,
abiding cannot abide,
decay cannot decay,
greed cannot covet,
hatred cannot hate,
delusion cannot delude,
because the nature of conditioned existence is independent arising and independent cessation.
A Púsà Móhēsà ultimately does not entertain the thought:
'I destroy all afflictions (fánnǎo) with this wisdom.'
Yet they declare:
'I have destroyed afflictions.'
Although they speak thus,
it is not false speech;
therefore, it is again named Inconceivable (Bùkě Sīyì).
Kāyè again spoke:
"World-Honored One!
I now finally know that Púsà Móhēsàs are inconceivable,
and that the Buddha (Fó),
the Dharma,
the Saṅgha (Zhòngsēng),
the Dà Nièpán Jīng (Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra), and those who uphold it,
Bodhi,
and Nirvāṇa (Nièpán)
are all inconceivable.
World-Honored One!
How long will the supreme Buddha Dharma remain in the world?
When will it perish?"
"O good man!
If, regarding the Dà Nièpán Jīng, these five practices (xíng) still exist,
namely, the Holy Practice (shèngxíng),
the Brahma Practice (fànxíng),
the Heavenly Practice (tiānxíng),
the Sick Practice (bìngxíng),
and the Infant Practice (yīng'érxíng);
and if my disciples
are able to uphold, study, recite,
copy, and expound its meaning,
and are revered,
respected,
praised,
and offered various offerings by all sentient beings,
know that at that time the Buddha Dharma has not yet perished.
O good man!
If the Dà Nièpán Jīng is widely circulated,
but at that time,
my disciples
frequently violate the precepts,
commit all manner of evils,
and are unable to revere and believe in this sūtra,
because of their lack of faith,
they cannot uphold, study, recite,
copy, or explain its meaning,
nor are they revered or offered offerings by the multitude;
they see those who do uphold it and lightly slander and defame them, saying:
'You belong to the Six Teachers (liùshī) and are not disciples of the Buddha.'
Know that the Buddha Dharma will soon perish.
Púsà Kāyè again addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
I personally heard this meaning from the Buddha:
the Dharma of Kāyè Fó remained in the world for seven days,
and then completely perished.
World-Honored One!
Did Kāyè Rúlái possess this sūtra?
If he possessed it,
