how can it be said that it perished?
If he did not possess it,
how can it be said that the Dà Nièpán Jīng is the secret treasury of all Tathāgatas (Rúlái)?"
The Buddha said:
"O good man!
I said previously
that only Wénshū understood this meaning.
I shall now explain it again;
listen attentively and earnestly.
O good man!
All Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have two kinds of Dharma:
first, the worldly Dharma (shìfǎ),
and second, the ultimate truth Dharma (dìyī yìfǎ).
The worldly Dharma is subject to decay and destruction;
the ultimate truth Dharma is not subject to decay and destruction.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, impermanence (wúcháng),
non-self (wúwǒ),
suffering (wúlè),
and impurity (wújìng);
second, permanence (cháng), joy (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng).
Impermanence,
non-self,
suffering,
and impurity
are subject to decay and destruction;
permanence, joy, self, and purity are not subject to decay and destruction.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, that upheld by the Two Vehicles (èrchen);
second, that upheld by the Púsàs.
That upheld by the Two Vehicles is subject to decay and destruction;
that upheld by the Púsàs is not subject to decay and destruction.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, external (wài);
second, internal (nèi).
The external Dharma is subject to decay and destruction;
the internal Dharma is not subject to decay and destruction.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, conditioned (yǒuwéi);
second, unconditioned (wúwéi).
Conditioned Dharma is subject to decay and destruction;
unconditioned Dharma has no decay or destruction.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, attainable (kědé);
second, unattainable (bùkědé).
Attainable Dharma is subject to decay and destruction;
the unattainable has no decay or destruction.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, shared Dharma (gòngfǎ);
second, unshared Dharma (bùgòngfǎ).
Shared Dharma is subject to decay and destruction;
unshared Dharma has no decay or destruction.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, in the realm of humans (rénzhōng);
second, in the realm of devas (tiānzhōng).
That in the realm of humans is subject to decay and destruction;
that in the realm of devas has no decay or destruction.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the eleven divisions of sūtras (shíyī bù jīng);
second, the Vaipulya sūtras (fāngděng jīng).
The eleven divisions of sūtras are subject to decay and destruction;
the Vaipulya sūtras have no decay or destruction.
O good man!
If my disciples uphold, study, recite,
copy, and explain the Vaipulya sūtras,
revere, make offerings,
respect, and praise them,
know that at that time the Buddha Dharma has not perished.
"Good man!
Regarding what you previously asked, whether *Jiāshè Rúlái* (Kāśyapa Tathāgata) possessed this scripture—
Good man!
The *Dà Nièpán Jīng* (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra) is entirely the secret treasury of all Buddhas.
Why is this?
Although the Buddhas possess eleven divisions of scriptures,
they do not speak of the Buddha-nature,
they do not speak of the *Rúlái* being permanence, bliss, self, and purity,
nor that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, never definitively enter *Nièpán* eternally.
Therefore, this scripture is called the secret treasury of the *Rúlái*.
Because it is not taught in the eleven divisions of scriptures,
therefore it is called a treasury.
Just as a person's seven treasures are not used externally,
they are called a treasury.
Good man!
The reason this person stores and accumulates these things
is for future needs.
What are these future needs?
They are: high grain prices,
bandits invading the country,
encountering evil kings,
being used to ransom life,
difficulties and obstacles on the road.
Only when wealth is hard to acquire should they be taken out and used.
Good man!
The secret treasury of the Buddhas and *Rúlái*s is also like this.
For the future age,
when evil *Bǐqiū*s (monks) keep impure possessions,
and tell the four assemblies that the *Rúlái* definitively enters *Nièpán*,
reading and reciting secular texts and not respecting the Buddhist scriptures—
when such evils appear in the world,
the *Rúlái*, desiring to eliminate these evils,
and cause them to attain separation from improper livelihood and gain,
the *Rúlái* then expounds this scripture.
If this classic, the secret treasury, were to disappear and not be manifest,
you should know that at that time, the Dharma of the Buddha would perish.
"Good man!
The *Dà Nièpán Jīng* is constantly unchanging.
Why do you question whether it existed during the time of *Jiāshè* Buddha?
Good man!
During the time of *Jiāshè* Buddha,
all sentient beings had weak greed and desire,
wisdom flourished greatly,
the *Púsà Móhēsà* (Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas) were tame, gentle, and easily transformed,
possessing great majesty and virtue,
retaining all (teachings) and forgetting nothing,
like a great elephant king—the world was pure.
All sentient beings completely knew that the *Rúlái* would never definitively enter *Nièpán*,
dwelling permanently without change.
Although this text existed,
there was no need to expound it.
Good man!
The sentient beings of the present age have many afflictions,
ignorance,
are prone to forgetting,
lack wisdom,
have many nets of doubt,
and the root of faith is not established.
The world is impure.
All sentient beings unanimously believe that the *Rúlái* is impermanent,
subject to change,
and definitively enters the Great *Bō Nièpán* (Parinirvāṇa).
Therefore, the *Rúlái* expounds this text.
Good man!
The Dharma of *Jiāshè* Buddha, in reality, also does not perish.
Why is this?
Because it is constantly unchanging.
Good man!
If there are sentient beings who see the self as non-self,
and the non-self as self;
who see permanence as impermanence,
and impermanence as permanence;
who see bliss as non-bliss,
and non-bliss as bliss;
who see purity as impurity,
and impurity as purity;
who see cessation as non-cessation,
and non-cessation as cessation;
who see sin as non-sin,
and non-sin as sin;
who see light sins as heavy,
and heavy sins as light;
who see the Vehicle as non-Vehicle,
and the non-Vehicle as Vehicle;
who see the Path as non-Path,
and the non-Path as Path;
who see what is truly *Pútí* (Bodhi) as non-*Pútí*,
and mistakenly see what is truly non-*Pútí* as *Pútí*;
who see suffering as non-suffering,
and accumulation as non-accumulation;
who see extinction as non-extinction,
and reality as non-reality;
who see what is truly conventional truth as the highest truth,
and the highest truth as conventional truth;
who see refuge as non-refuge,
and non-refuge as refuge;
who call the true words of the Buddha the words of a *mó* (demon),
and take the true words of a *mó* as the words of the Buddha—
at such a time,
the Buddhas then preach the *Dà Nièpán Jīng*.
Good man!
Rather say that mosquitoes and gnats can drink dry the bottom of the great ocean,
but you must not say that the *Rúlái*'s Dharma perishes.
Rather say that one can blow the *Xūmí* (Sumeru) mountain apart and destroy it,
but you must not say that the *Rúlái*'s Dharma perishes.
Rather say that one can bind a fierce wind with a rope,
but you must not say that the *Rúlái*'s Dharma perishes.
Rather say that a lotus flower can bloom in a *Qiétuóluó* (Khādira) fire,
but you must not say that the *Rúlái*'s Dharma perishes.
Rather say that the *Ējiātuó* (Agada) medicine can become poison,
but you must not say that the *Rúlái*'s Dharma perishes.
Rather say that the moon can be made hot,
and the sun can be made cold,
but you must not say that the *Rúlái*'s Dharma perishes.
Rather say that the four great elements (earth, water, fire, wind) can each abandon their own nature,
but you must not say that the *Rúlái*'s Dharma perishes.
"Good man!
If, when a Buddha first appears and has attained *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí* (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi),
there are yet no disciples who understand the extremely profound meaning,
and that Buddha, the World-Honored One, then enters *Nièpán*,
you should know that this Dharma will not long remain in the world.
Furthermore, good man!
If, when a Buddha first appears and has attained *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*,
there are disciples who understand the extremely profound meaning,
even if the Buddha enters *Nièpán*,
you should know that this Dharma will long remain in the world.
"Furthermore, good man!
If, when a Buddha first appears and has attained *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*,
although there are disciples who understand the extremely profound meaning,
but there are no sincerely believing lay *Dàn yuè* (Dānapati/donors) who respect and venerate the Buddha Dharma,
and the Buddha then enters *Nièpán*,
you should know that this Dharma will not long remain in the world.
Furthermore, good man!
If, when a Buddha first appears and has attained *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*,
there are many disciples who understand the extremely profound meaning,
and there are sincerely believing lay *Dàn yuè* who respect and venerate the Buddha Dharma,
even if the Buddha enters *Nièpán*,
you should know that the Buddha Dharma will long remain in the world.
"Furthermore, good man!
If, when a Buddha first appears and has attained *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*,
and there are disciples who understand the extremely profound meaning,
although there are sincerely believing lay *Dàn yuè* who respect and venerate the Buddha Dharma,
yet those disciples expound the scriptures and Dharma out of greed for gain and profit,
not for *Nièpán*,
and the Buddha subsequently passes into extinction,
you should know that this Dharma will not long remain in the world.
Furthermore, good man!
If, when a Buddha first appears and has attained *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*,
there are disciples who understand the extremely profound meaning,
and there are sincerely believing lay *Dàn yuè* who respect and venerate the Buddha Dharma,
and those disciples, in all that they expound, are not greedy for gain and profit, but seek *Nièpán*,
even if the Buddha passes into extinction,
you should know that this Dharma will long remain in the world.
"Furthermore, good man!
If, when a Buddha first appears and has attained *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*,
although there are disciples who understand the extremely profound meaning,
and there are sincerely believing lay *Dàn yuè* who respect and venerate the Buddha Dharma,
yet those disciples frequently engage in disputes,
mutually judging right and wrong,
and the Buddha subsequently enters *Nièpán*,
you should know that this Dharma will not long remain in the world.
Furthermore, good man!
If, when a Buddha first appears and has attained *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*,
there are disciples who understand the extremely profound meaning,
and there are sincerely believing lay *Dàn yuè* who respect and venerate the Buddha Dharma,
and those disciples practice the Dharma of harmony and respect,
not mutually judging right and wrong,
mutually respecting each other,
even if the Buddha enters *Nièpán*,
you should know that this Dharma will long remain and not perish.
"Furthermore, good man!
If, when a Buddha first appears and has attained *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*,
although there are disciples who understand the extremely profound meaning,
and there are sincerely believing lay *Dàn yuè* who respect and venerate the Buddha Dharma,
those disciples expound the Dharma for the sake of the Great *Nièpán*,
mutually venerating each other and not engaging in disputes,
however, they keep all manner of impure possessions,
and furthermore boast, saying:
'I have attained the *Xūtuóhuán Guǒ* (Srotāpanna fruit), and even the *Āluóhàn Guǒ* (Arhat fruit).'
And the Buddha subsequently enters *Nièpán*,
you should know that this Dharma will not long remain in the world.
Furthermore, good man!
If, when a Buddha first appears and has attained *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*,
there are disciples who understand the extremely profound meaning,
and there are sincerely believing lay *Dàn yuè* who respect and venerate the Buddha Dharma,
and those disciples expound the scriptures and Dharma for the sake of the Great *Nièpán*,
skillfully practicing harmony and respect and mutually venerating each other,
not keeping any impure possessions,
nor claiming themselves to have attained *Xūtuóhuán*, or even attained *Āluóhàn*,
then even though that Buddha, the World-Honored One, passes into extinction,
you should know that this Dharma will long remain in the world."
"Furthermore, good man!
If a Buddha first appears and attains Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
there are disciples,
who even refrain from hoarding unclean objects,
and who do not personally claim to have attained Xūtuóhuán or even Āluóhàn,
but each clings to his own view,
giving various differing explanations,
and they make this statement:
'Elder!
The Four Serious Precepts (Sì Zhòng zhī Fǎ) established by the Buddhas,
and even the Seven Methods for Quelling Disputes (Qī Miè Zhēng Fǎ),
are, for the sake of sentient beings,
sometimes prohibited and sometimes permitted.
The Twelve Divisions of the Scriptures (Shí'èr Bù Jīng) are also like this.
Why is this?
Because the Buddha knows that lands and times differ,
and sentient beings vary, being sharp or dull,
therefore, the Tathāgata either prohibits or permits,
having light and heavy (minor and major) teachings.
Good man!
Just like a skilled physician,
prescribes milk for a certain illness,
and prohibits milk for another illness;
for a fever, he allows its consumption,
but for a cold illness, he prohibits it.
The Tathāgata is also like this,
observing the root sicknesses (afflictions) of all sentient beings,
he both permits and prohibits.
Elder!
I personally heard this meaning from the Buddha.
Only I know the meaning,
you are unable to know it.
Only I understand the Vinaya,
you are unable to understand it.
I know the scriptures,
you are unable to know them.'
When that Buddha again enters parinirvāṇa,
you should know that this Dharma will not long remain in the world.
Furthermore, good man,
if a Buddha first appears and attains Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
there are disciples,
who do not even say, 'I have attained the fruition of Xūtuóhuán up to Āluóhàn,'
nor do they say:
'The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, prohibit or permit things for the sake of sentient beings.'
'Elder!
I personally heard this meaning from the Buddha,
this Dharma,
and this Vinaya.'
'Elder!
We must rely on the Tathāgata’s Twelve Divisions of the Scriptures (Shí'èr Bù Jīng).
If this meaning is correct,
I shall accept and uphold it.
If it is not correct,
I shall abandon it.'
Although that Buddha, the World-Honored One, may enter Nièpán,
you should know that this Dharma will long abide in the world.
"Good man!
When my Dharma perishes,
there will be Śrāvaka (Shēngwén) disciples,
some who say there is a soul (shén),
and some who say the soul is empty (shén kōng).
Some who say there is an intermediate state (Zhōngyīn),
and some who say there is no intermediate state.
Some who say there are Three Ages (Sānshì),
and some who say there are no Three Ages.
Some who say there are Three Vehicles (Sān Chéng),
and some who say there are no Three Vehicles.
Some who say everything exists,
and some who say everything is nonexistent.
Some who say sentient beings have a beginning and an end,
and some who say sentient beings have no beginning and no end.
Some who say the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yīnyuán) are conditioned phenomena (yǒu wéi fǎ),
and some who say dependent origination is unconditioned phenomena (wú wéi fǎ).
Some who say the Tathāgata experienced sickness and painful asceticism,
and some who say the Tathāgata did not experience sickness and painful asceticism.
Some who say the Tathāgata prohibits Bǐqiū from eating ten types of meat.
What are these ten?
Human,
snake,
elephant,
horse,
donkey,
dog,
lion (Shīzi),
pig-fox (Zhū Hú),
macaque (Míhóu).
All others are permitted;
or some say everything is prohibited.
Some who say a Bǐqiū does not engage in five activities.
What are these five?
Not selling living beings (shēng kǒu),
knives,
alcohol,
curds and sugar/sand (làoshā),
sesame oil (húmá yóu), and others.
All others are permitted.
Some who say entering five types of houses is prohibited.
What are these five?
Butcher's house,
prostitute's house (yín nǚ),
wine-seller's house (jiǔ jiā),
royal palace (wáng gōng),
and the house of a Zhāntuóluó (Caṇḍāla).
Other houses are permitted.
Some who say wearing Jiāoshēyē robes (silk robes) is prohibited,
and all others are permitted.
Some who say the Tathāgata permits Bǐqiū to receive and hoard robes, food, and bedding,
the value of which can reach 100,000 ounces of gold each;
and some who say it is prohibited.
Some who say Nièpán possesses Permanence (Cháng), Bliss (Lè), Self (Wǒ), and Purity (Jìng),
and some who say Nièpán is merely the exhaustion of the fetters,
and there is no separate entity called Nièpán,
just as woven threads are called a robe,
once the robe is destroyed,
it is called 'robe-less' (wú yī),
but there is truly no separate entity called 'robe-less.'
The essence of Nièpán is also like this.
Good man!
At that time,
among my disciples, those who preach the true Dharma will be few,
and those who preach the false Dharma will be many;
those who accept the true Dharma will be few,
those who accept the false Dharma will be many;
those who accept the Buddha's words will be few,
and those who accept Mó's (Mara's) words will be many."
"Good man!
At that time, in the country of Jūshǎn mí, there were two disciples:
one was an Arhat (Luóhàn),
and the second had violated the precepts (pòjiè).
The assembly of disciples who violated the precepts totaled five hundred,
and the assembly of the Arhat totaled one hundred.
The one who violated the precepts spoke:
'The Tathāgata (Rúlái) definitively entered Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
I personally heard this meaning from the Buddha (Fó).
Regarding the four fundamental precepts (sì zhòng zhī fǎ) laid down by the Tathāgata,
if one upholds them, it is permissible;
if one violates them, there is no offense.
I have now also attained the fruit of Arhatship (Āluóhànguǒ),
and the Four Unhindered Wisdoms (sì wú ài zhì).
Yet, the Arhats (Āluóhàn) also violate these four fundamental precepts.
If the four fundamental precepts constituted a real offense,
the Arhats should never violate them.
When the Tathāgata was alive, he commanded that they be upheld firmly,
but just before entering Nirvāṇa, he let them all go.'
The Arhat Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) said:
'Elder!
You should not say that the Tathāgata definitively entered Nirvāṇa.
I know that the Tathāgata is eternally constant and unchanging.
Whether the Tathāgata is alive or after his Nirvāṇa,
the offense of violating the Four Fundamental Prohibitions (sì zhòng jìn) is no different.
If you say that an Arhat violates the Four Fundamental Prohibitions,
this statement is incorrect.
Why?
Even a Srotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán) does not violate the prohibitions,
much less an Arhat?
If the Elder says,
"I am an Arhat,"
an Arhat
would never conceive the thought, "I have attained Arhatship."
Arhats
only speak of good Dharma (shàn fǎ),
they do not speak of the non-good.
What the Elder has spoken
is entirely non-Dharma (fēifǎ).
If one has seen the Twelve Divisions of the Sūtras (shí'èr bù jīng),
one would definitely know that the Elder is not an Arhat.'
"Good man!
At that time, the assembly of Bhikṣus who violated the precepts,
immediately conspired to take the life of that Arhat.
Good man!
At that time, the Demon King (Mówáng),
taking advantage of the furious and resentful minds of these two assemblies,
killed all six hundred of these Bhikṣus.
At that time, ordinary beings (fánfū) all spoke, saying:
'Alas for the Buddha Dharma!
It is now entirely extinguished.'
But my True Dharma (Zhèngfǎ) was truly not extinguished.
At that time, in that country, there were one hundred and twenty thousand Great Bodhisattvas (Dà Púsà),
who skillfully upheld my Dharma.
How then can it be said that my Dharma was extinguished?
Precisely at that time,
within Jambudvīpa (Yánfú tí), there was not a single Bhikṣu who was my disciple.
At that time, Pāpīyās (Bōxún) burned all existing scriptures (jīngdiǎn) with a great fire.
If there were any remnants left behind,
the various Brahmins (Pólúomén) immediately stole them,
gathering them everywhere and placing them in their own canons.
Due to this reason,
the Lesser Bodhisattvas,
before the Buddha appeared,
generally believed and accepted the words of the Brahmins.
Although the Brahmins said:
'We maintain purification and precepts (zhāijiè),'
the external paths (wàidào) truly did not possess them.
Although those on the external paths claimed:
'We possess the self, bliss, and purity (wǒ lè jìng),'
they truly did not understand the meaning of the self, bliss, and purity.
They merely took one character of the Buddha Dharma,
two characters,
one phrase,
two phrases,
and claimed that their own canons
held such meanings.
At that time, between the twin Sāla trees (Suōluó shuāng shù) in the city of Kuśinagara (Jūshīnàchéng),
measureless, boundless, and innumerable Asaṃkhyeya (Āsēngqí) beings, having heard this news,
all cried out together:
"The world is empty!
The world is empty!"
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva (Jiāshè Púsà) addressed the great multitude:
"You should all cease your worrying, sorrowing, and weeping.
The world is not empty.
The Tathāgata abides eternally,
without change or alteration.
The Dharma and the Saṅgha (Fǎ Sēng) are likewise."
At that time, the great multitude,
having heard this speech,
immediately stopped weeping,
and all generated the mind of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).
At that time, King Ajātaśatru (Āshéshì Wáng) of the great city of Rājagṛha (Wángshě Dàchéng),
whose nature was wicked and perverse,
who delighted in killing and slaughter,
who possessed the four verbal evils,
whose greed, hatred, and delusion (tān huì yú chī)
burned fiercely in his heart,
only saw the present,
and did not see the future.
He kept only evil people as his retinues,
and because he was deeply attached to the present worldly pleasure of the Five Desires (wǔ yù lè),
he wickedly and wrongfully killed his innocent father king.
After killing his father,
repentance and burning remorse arose in his heart.
He could no longer wear his various bodily ornaments (yīngluò) or enjoy music and entertainment (jì yuè).
Because of the burning remorse in his heart, sores broke out all over his body.
The sores were so putrid and foul that no one could approach him.
He immediately thought to himself:
"This body of mine is now receiving the preliminary retribution (huābào).
The karmic consequence of the hells (dìyù guǒ bào) is approaching and not far off."
At that time, his mother, named Vaidehī (Wéidéxī),
applied various medicines to him,
but his sores increased even further,
without any reduction or abatement.
The King then said to his mother:
"Such sores
originate from the mind,
and are not caused by the Four Great Elements (sì dà qǐ).
If it is said that any being can cure them,
there is no such possibility."
At that time, a great minister named Yuechēng (Moon-Praised)
went to the King's location,
and stood to one side,
reporting:
"Great King!
Why are you sorrowful and withered?
Why is your countenance displeased?
Is it pain of the body,
or pain of the mind?"
The King immediately replied:
"How can my body and mind
not be in pain now?
My father was innocent,
yet I wickedly and wrongfully killed him.
I once heard this meaning from the wise:
there are five people in the world
who cannot escape the hells—
namely, those who commit the Five Heinous Crimes (wǔ nì zuì).
I now possess measureless, boundless, Asaṃkhyeya sins.
How can my body and mind not be in pain?
Moreover, there is no good physician to treat my body and mind."
The minister said:
"Great King!
Do not sorrow greatly."
He immediately spoke a Gāthā (Jì) saying:
"As the King has said,
there are five people in the world
who cannot escape the hells;
who went to see this,
and came back to tell the King?
What is called the 'hells'
is merely the world itself,
as said by those with great wisdom.
As the King has said,
that there is no good physician in the world to treat the body and mind—
currently there is a great physician named Pūraṇa (Fùlánnà).
He possesses all knowledge and vision,
and has attained mastery in concentration (dìng).
He definitively cultivates the pure Brahma-practice (fànxíng),
and constantly explains the supreme path to Nirvāṇa
for measureless, boundless sentient beings.
He teaches his disciples this Dharma:
there is no dark karma (hēi yè),
and no retribution for dark karma;
there is no white karma (bái yè),
and no retribution for white karma;
there is no mixed dark and white karma,
and no retribution for mixed dark and white karma;
there is neither superior karma nor inferior karma.
This teacher is currently in Rājagṛha.
We only wish, Great King,
that you would condescend to go there.
This teacher should be able
to heal your body and mind."
The King then replied:
"If he can truly eliminate my sins in this manner,
I shall take refuge in him."
There was another minister named Zàngdé (Store of Virtue),
who again went to the King's location,
and spoke thus:
"Great King!
Why is your face withered and emaciated?
Your lips and mouth are dry and scorched,
and your voice is faint and low,
like a timid person seeing a great enemy.
Why is your complexion chapped and cracked?
What suffering affects you?
Is it pain of the body,
or pain of the mind?"
The King immediately replied:
"How can my body and mind
not be in pain?
I was blindly deluded,
without the eye of wisdom.
I befriended and drew near to evil companions,
following the words of the wicked person Devadatta (Diàopódá).
I wickedly and wrongfully killed the king of the True Dharma.
I once heard the wise speak a Gāthā (Jì):"
"Due to this matter,
my heart is filled with fear,
generating great suffering and distress,
and I have no skilled physician to offer me relief and healing."
The great minister replied again:
"We humbly request, Great King!
For now, cease your worry and fear.
There are two types of dharma (laws/practices):
The first is leaving the home life (renunciation),
the second is the Royal Dharma (the law of kingship).
Regarding the Royal Dharma:
it means that killing one's father allows one to rule the kingdom;
although it is called rebellious,
in reality, there is no offense.
Just like the jiāluóluó (迦羅羅) insect,
it must destroy its mother's belly,
and only then can it be born.
The law of birth is thus:
although it damages the mother's body,
in reality, there is also no offense.
Pregnancy in mules and the like is also similar.
The law for governing a nation,
the dharma ought to be thus:
although you kill your father or elder brother,
in reality, there is no offense.
Regarding the dharma of leaving the home life:
even killing a mosquito or an ant
constitutes a transgression.
We humbly request, Great King!
Ease your mind and do not worry.
Why is this?
"Concerning what the King has said,
that there is no skilled physician in the world to treat the body and mind,
there is now a Great Master,
named Mòjiālǐ Jūshělízǐ (末伽梨拘舍離子),
who knows and sees everything,
pitying sentient beings just like infants.
He has already separated from vexations,
and is able to pull out the sharp arrows of the three poisons from sentient beings.
All sentient beings lack the knowledge, vision, and enlightenment concerning all dharmas;
only this single person uniquely possesses the knowledge, vision, and enlightenment.
This Great Master,
constantly speaks the following dharma for his disciples:
'All sentient beings' bodies possess seven divisions.
What are these seven?
Earth,
water,
fire,
wind,
suffering,
joy,
and longevity.
These seven dharmas
are neither transformed nor created,
and cannot be destroyed or harmed.
Like the Yīshījiā (伊師迦) grass,
they abide peacefully without movement.
Like Mount Xūmí (須彌山),
they neither abandon nor create.
Like milk and curds,
they do not dispute with each other.
Whether suffering or joy,
whether good or non-good,
if one throws a sharp knife at it,
it cannot be harmed.
Why is this?
Because the seven divisions exist in space (emptiness) and have no hindrance.
Life is also unharmed.
Why is this?
Because there is no one who harms and no one who dies.
There is no action and no reception,
no speaking and no listening,
no one who remembers and no one who teaches.
He constantly preaches this dharma,
which enables sentient beings to eliminate all immeasurable heavy offenses.
This master is currently in the great city of Wángshě (王舍).
We humbly request, Great King!
Go visit him;
if the King sees him,
all offenses will vanish and be eliminated.'
The King then replied:
"If he is truly able to eliminate my offenses in this way,
I shall take refuge in him."
Furthermore, there was another minister,
named Shídé (實得),
who came again to the King's presence,
and immediately spoke a verse:
"Why is the King's countenance sorrowful and distressed now?
It is just like a farmer who has sown seeds,
but heaven does not send down rain,
causing such worry and suffering.
Is this pain in the heart,
or pain in the body?"
The King immediately replied:
"How can my body and mind not be in pain now?
My father, the former King,
was compassionate and full of sympathy,
showing special concern and care for me,
and was truly without fault or blame.
He went to consult a physiognomist,
and the physiognomist replied:
'This child, once born, is definitely fated to harm his father.'
Although he heard this statement,
he still cared for and raised me.
I once heard a wise person say this:
'If a person violates his mother or a bhikṣuṇī,
steals objects belonging to the Saṅgha,
kills one who has given rise to the unsurpassed Bodhicitta (Enlightenment Mind),
or harms his father,
such a person will surely fall into the Ābǐ Dìyù (阿鼻地獄).'
How can my body and mind not be in pain now?"
The great minister replied again:
"We humbly request, Great King!
For now, cease your worry and suffering.
If your father, the King,
were practicing liberation (Dharma),
then harming him would constitute a transgression;
but according to the law of governing the state,
killing him constitutes no offense.
Great King!
What is not the dharma is called 'not dharma,'
and what lacks the dharma is called 'lacking dharma.'
For example, lacking a son is called 'lacking a son,'
and likewise, a wicked son is called 'lacking a son';
although called 'lacking a son,' in reality, he does not lack a son.
Just as food without salt
is called 'saltless,'
food that has little salt is also called 'saltless.'
Just as a river without water
is called 'waterless,'
if there is little water, it is also called 'waterless.'
Just as momentary extinction
is also called 'impermanent,'
even abiding for a kalpa is also called 'impermanent.'
Just as a person experiencing suffering is called 'joyless,'
even experiencing minor joy is also called 'joyless.'
Just as not being self-governed
is called 'non-self' (anātman),
even having minor self-governance is also called 'non-self.'
Just as dark night is called 'sunless,'
a time of clouds and fog is also called 'sunless.'
Great King!
Although we speak of a minimal dharma,
it is called 'lacking dharma,'
but in reality, it is not lacking dharma.
May the King please pay attention and listen to what your minister says:
All sentient beings possess residual karma.
Because of karmic causes,
they repeatedly experience birth and death.
If the former King possessed residual karma,
and the King now kills him,
what offense could there possibly be?
We humbly request, Great King, ease your mind and do not worry.
Why is this?
"As the King has said,
there is no skilled physician in the world who can heal the body and mind.
Now there is a Great Master named Shānshéyé Píluōzhīzǐ.
He knows and sees everything;
his wisdom is profound, like the great ocean.
He possesses great awesome virtue,
and is endowed with great supernatural powers.
He can enable sentient beings to escape all nets of doubt.
All sentient beings do not know, see, or perceive,
only this one person alone knows, sees, and perceives.
Currently, he resides nearby in Wángshě Chéng (Rājagṛha),
teaching his disciples thus:
'Among all people,
if one is a King,
he is free and acts as he pleases,
creating good and evil deeds.
Even though he commits all manner of evil,
he is entirely without sin.
Just as fire burns things,
without distinction between clean and unclean,
the King is also like this,
sharing the same nature as fire.
For example, the great earth
carries both the pure and the defiled everywhere,
and although it does this,
it harbors neither anger nor joy.
The King is also like this,
sharing the same nature as the earth.
For example, the nature of water
washes both the pure and the defiled,
and although it does this,
it has neither sorrow nor joy.
The King is also like this,
sharing the same nature as water.
For example, the nature of wind
blows equally upon the pure and the defiled,
and although it does this,
it has neither sorrow nor joy.
The King is also like this,
sharing the same nature as the wind.
Like a tree stripped bare in autumn,
it grows again in spring;
although it is stripped and cut down,
there is truly no offense.
All sentient beings are also like this:
they die in this realm
and are born again in this realm.
Since they are born again,
what sin can there be?
The retribution of suffering and joy for all sentient beings
is entirely not determined by deeds done in the present age.
The cause lies in the past,
and the fruit is received in the present.
In the present there is no cause,
and in the future there is no fruit.
Because the fruit is manifest,
if sentient beings uphold the precepts and diligently cultivate exertion,
they block the manifest evil fruit.
Because of upholding the precepts,
they attain non-outflow (āsrava-free).
Because of attaining non-outflow,
they exhaust the outflowing karma.
Because the karma is exhausted,
all sufferings are ended.
Because all sufferings are ended,
they therefore attain liberation.'
We only wish, Great King,
that you quickly go to his place,
and let him treat the suffering and pain of your body and mind.
If the King sees him, all sins will be eradicated."
The King immediately replied:
"If there truly is such a Master who can eradicate my sins,
I will take refuge in him."
Furthermore, there was another minister named Xīzhīyì,
who immediately approached the King
and spoke thus:
"Why is the King's appearance today not majestic,
like one who has lost his kingdom,
like a dried up spring,
a pond without lotus flowers,
or a tree without flowers or leaves,
or a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts,
whose body lacks awesome virtue?
Is it physical pain?
Or is it mental pain?"
The King immediately replied:
"How can my body and mind not be in pain now?
My father, the former King,
was compassionate and constantly mindful [of me].
Yet I was unfilial
and did not know how to repay his kindness.
He constantly used peace and happiness
to bring me peace and happiness,
but I turned against his kindness,
and instead cut off his happiness.
The former King was innocent,
yet I arbitrarily carried out wicked harm.
I also once heard a wise person say:
'If one harms one's father,
one will suffer great pain and affliction throughout measureless Asaṃkhyeya kalpas.'
I will certainly soon fall into Avīci Hell,
and there is no skilled physician to cure my sin."
The minister immediately said:
"We only wish, Great King!
that you abandon your sorrow and suffering.
Have you not heard?
In the past, there was a king
named Luómó,
who, after harming his father,
succeeded to the throne.
King Bátí,
King Pílóuzhēn,
King Nàhóushā,
King Jiādìjiā,
King Píshèqié,
King Yuèguāngmíng,
King Rìguāngmíng,
King Ài,
King Chíduōrén,
Kings such as these
all harmed their fathers and succeeded to the throne,
yet not a single one of them entered Avīci Hell.
And now, currently, King Píliúlí,
King Yōutuónà,
King Èxìng,
King Shǔ,
King Liánhuā,
Kings such as these have all harmed their fathers,
yet not a single one of them has given rise to sorrow or affliction.
Although we speak of Avīci Hell,
the hungry ghosts (Pretas),
or the heavens (Devas),
who has ever seen them?
Great King!
There are only two existences:
first, the human realm,
second, the animal realm.
Although these two exist,
they are not born of causes and conditions,
nor do they die by causes and conditions.
If they are not based on causes and conditions,
how can there be good or evil?
We only wish, Great King!
Do not harbor sorrow or fear.
Why is this?
"As the King has said,
there is no skilled physician in the world who can heal the body and mind.
Now there is a Great Master
named Āqíduō Qìshě Qīnpóluó.
He knows and sees everything;
he views gold and earth as equal and non-dual.
If one person cuts his right flank with a knife,
and another smears sandalwood paste on his left,
in respect to these two people,
his mind makes no distinction.
He regards enemies and relatives equally;
his mind holds no differing perceptions.
This Master is truly a skilled physician of the world.
Whether walking,
standing,
sitting,
or lying down,
he is constantly in Samādhi;
his mind is not scattered.
He tells his disciples this:
'If one acts oneself,
or teaches others to act;
if one cuts oneself,
or teaches others to cut;
if one burns oneself,
or teaches others to burn;
if one harms oneself,
or teaches others to harm;
if one steals oneself,
or teaches others to steal;
if one commits sexual misconduct oneself,
or teaches others to commit sexual misconduct;
if one lies oneself,
or teaches others to lie;
if one drinks alcohol oneself,
or teaches others to drink alcohol;
if one kills an entire village, city, or country;
or if one uses a sharp wheel to kill all sentient beings;
or if one gives alms to beings south of the Hénghé (Ganges) River,
or kills beings north of the Hénghé River—
there is entirely no sin and no merit,
no giving,
no precepts,
and no concentration (samādhi).
He currently resides nearby in Wángshě Chéng.
We wish the King would quickly go there.
If the King sees him,
all sins will be eliminated."
The King said:
"Minister!
If he can truly eliminate my sins in this manner,
I will take refuge in him."
Furthermore, there was a great minister,
named Jídé,
who again went to the king's location,
and spoke these words:
“O King, why now is your face lacking luster,
like a lamp in the midday sun,
like the moon during the day,
like a ruler who has lost his state,
or like desolate and ruined land?
Great King!
Now the four directions are peaceful and calm,
devoid of all resentful enemies,
yet why now are you so worried and distressed?
Is it suffering of the body?
Or is it suffering of the mind?
All the princes constantly gave rise to this thought:
‘When will I now attain sovereignty?’
Great King!
Now that has been fulfilled,
your wish for sovereignty.
You govern the state of Mójiātuó,
and have fully obtained the treasures of the former king.
You should only seek pleasure,
indulge your emotions and receive joy.
Such worry and distress,
why do you hold it in your heart?”
The King immediately replied:
“How can I now avoid worry and anxiety?
O Minister!
For example, the foolish person
only covets the flavor,
but does not see the sharp knife,
like one who eats mixed poison
and does not perceive its fault.
I am also like this,
like a deer that sees the grass
but does not see the deep pitfall,
like a mouse that craves food
but does not see the cat or weasel.
I am also like this,
seeing present happiness
but not seeing the unwholesome bitter consequences in the future.
I once heard a wise person speak these words:
‘It is better to endure three hundred strikes
in one day than to generate a single evil thought toward one's parents.’
I am now already near the raging fires of the hells;
how can I possibly avoid worry and anxiety?”
The Minister replied again:
“Who came and deceived Your Majesty,
saying that there are hells?
Like the sharpness of thorns,
by whom was it created?
The different colors of flying birds,
by whom again were they produced?
The moistening nature of water,
the hard nature of stone,
like the nature of wind to move,
like the nature of fire to heat—
all myriad things die and are born by themselves;
who creates them?
The concept of ‘hell’ [Dìyù],
is merely a literary construction created by the wise.
What meaning does the word ‘hell’ have?
Your subject shall explain it.
‘Dì’ (earth) means land,
and ‘yù’ (prison) means destruction.
To destroy the earth-prison,
when there are no consequences for wrongdoing,
this is called Dìyù.
Furthermore, ‘Dì’ means humanity (rén),
and ‘yù’ means heaven (tiān).
Because you harmed your father,
you attained the realms of humanity and heaven (rén tiān).
Because of this meaning,
the immortal Póu Sù proclaimed,
‘By killing a sheep, one obtains the joys of humanity and heaven.’
This is called Dìyù.
Furthermore, ‘Dì’ means life (mìng),
and ‘yù’ means long (cháng).
Because of killing living beings,
one obtains long life;
thus it is called Dìyù.
Great King!
Therefore, you should know that truly there are no hells.
Great King!
Just as planting wheat yields wheat,
and planting rice yields rice;
if one kills a resident of hell,
one should return to hell;
if one kills a person,
one should return as a person.
Great King!
Now listen to what your subject says:
In truth, there is no killing or harming.
If there is a self [ātman],
truly there is no harm;
if there is no self,
then again, there is nothing to be harmed.
Why is this?
If there is a self,
it is constant and unchanging.
Because it is permanently abiding, it cannot be killed or harmed;
it is not fractured,
it is not destroyed,
it is not restrained,
it is not bound,
it does not hate,
it does not rejoice;
it is like empty space.
How then can there be the sin of killing and harming?
If there is no self,
all dharmas are impermanent.
Because they are impermanent, they perish and cease moment by moment.
Since they cease moment by moment,
both the killer and the killed cease moment by moment.
If they cease moment by moment, who then bears the sin?
Great King!
Just as fire burns wood,
the fire incurs no sin;
just as an axe cuts a tree,
the axe also incurs no sin;
just as a sickle reaps grass,
the sickle truly incurs no sin;
just as a knife kills a person,
the knife is truly not a person.
Since the knife incurs no sin,
how can the person incur sin?
Just as poison kills a person,
the poison is truly not a person.
The poison is not sinful;
how can the person be sinful?
All myriad things are likewise such.
Truly there is no killing or harming;
how can there be sin?
May it please the Great King!
Do not give rise to worry and distress.
Why is this?
“Regarding what the King said,
that there is no good physician in the world to cure the consequences of evil deeds:
Now there is a great master,
named Jiāluójiūtuó Jiāzhānyán,
who possesses universal knowledge and insight,
who clearly understands the three ages (past, present, future).
In a single instant of thought,
he can see immeasurable and boundless worlds,
and hearing sounds is also like this.
He can cause sentient beings to abandon faults and evils,
just as the Gaṅgā River [Hénghé],
whether internally
or externally,
completely purifies all sins.
This great good master is also like this,
able to eliminate the internal and external sins of sentient beings,
and preaches such Dharma for his disciples:
‘If a person kills all sentient beings
and their mind is without shame or remorse, they will ultimately not fall into evil [realms],
like empty space which is untouched by dust or water;
those who possess shame and remorse immediately enter the hells,
like great water soaking the earth.
All sentient beings are entirely the creations of Īśvara [Zìzàitiān].
If Īśvara is pleased,
sentient beings are peaceful and happy;
if Īśvara is angered,
sentient beings suffer distress.
Whether sentient beings experience sin or merit,
it is ultimately the action of Īśvara.
How can one say that people possess sin or merit?
For example, a craftsman
makes a mechanical wooden puppet,
which walks, stands, sits, and lies down,
but only cannot speak.
Sentient beings are also like this;
Īśvara is compared to the craftsman,
and the wooden puppet is compared to the body of sentient beings.
In such creation and transformation, who should incur sin?’
Such a great master
is now residing nearby in Wángshěchéng.
I only request that you quickly go to him;
if you can see him,
all your sins will be eliminated.”
The King immediately replied:
“If there is truly such a person who can eliminate my sins,
I shall take refuge in him.”
Again, there was a minister named Wúsuǒwèi,
who went to the king,
and spoke thus:
"Great King!
In the world, there are foolish people
who in one day experience a hundred joys and a hundred sorrows,
a hundred sleeps and a hundred awakenings,
a hundred frights and a hundred cries.
A person of wisdom does not experience these things.
Great King!
Why are you grieving thus?
Like a traveler who has lost his companion,
like one fallen into deep mud with no one to rescue him,
like a person dying of thirst who cannot get liquid,
like a lost person with no guide,
like a critically ill patient without a doctor to save and treat him,
or like a broken ship at sea with no one to rescue or receive them?
Great King!
Is it physical pain you suffer now?
Or is it mental pain?"
The King immediately replied:
"How can
my body and mind not be in pain now?
I associated with evil friends
and did not observe my faults in speech.
I wrongfully committed rebellious harm against the former king, who was innocent.
I now certainly know I must enter the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, there is no good doctor to save and relieve me."
The minister immediately spoke to him, saying:
"I earnestly wish, Great King!
Do not produce such harmful sorrow.
The Kṣatriya (Chàlì),
known as the royal lineage,
if they act for the sake of the nation,
or for the Śramaṇas (Shāmén) and Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén),
or for the peace of the populace,
even if they commit killing, they have no fault.
Although the former king respected the Śramaṇas,
he could not attend to the Brāhmaṇas.
His mind lacked impartiality,
and because his mind lacked impartiality, he was not a Kṣatriya.
Great King!
Now, for the sake of offering provisions to the Brāhmaṇas,
you killed the former king.
What fault can there be?
Great King!
In reality, there is no killing.
Killing, by definition,
is the destruction of the lifespan.
Life is named ‘wind energy’ (breath/vitality),
and the nature of wind energy
cannot be killed.
How can harming life result in fault?
I earnestly wish, Great King!
Do not grieve again.
Why?
"As the King has said,
there is no good doctor in the world to cure this disease.
But now there is a great master,
named Nígāntuò Ruòtízǐ,
who possesses all knowledge and vision,
and compassionately pities sentient beings.
He skillfully knows whether the faculties of sentient beings are sharp or dull,
and comprehends all skillful means according to necessity.
He cannot be defiled by the eight worldly dharmas,
is tranquil, and practices pure Brahmā-conduct (Fànxíng).
He speaks thus to his disciples:
‘There is no giving,
no goodness,
no father, no mother,
no present world or future world,
no Arhat (Āluóhàn),
no cultivation,
no path.
All sentient beings, after passing through eighty thousand kalpas,
will naturally achieve liberation from the cycle of birth and death.
Those with sin and those without sin will all be like this;
just like the four great rivers,
namely Xīndóu,
Hénghé,
Bózhā,
and Sītuó,
all enter the great ocean
without any distinction.
All sentient beings are likewise,
when they attain liberation,
there is no distinction whatsoever.
This master now resides in the city of Wángshěchéng.
I earnestly wish, Great King, that you quickly go to his place,
for if you meet him, your many faults will be eliminated."
The King immediately replied:
"If there is truly such a master who can eliminate my faults,
I shall take refuge in him."
At that time, the great physician,
named Jīpó,
went to the King and said:
"Great King!
Are you able to sleep peacefully?"
The King then answered him with a verse:
"Jīpó!
My sickness is now severe.
I inflicted wicked, rebellious harm
upon the King of Righteous Dharma (Zhèngfǎwáng).
All good doctors, marvelous medicines,
incantations,
or skillful means,
or nursing care cannot treat it.
Why?
My father, the King of Dharma, governed the nation according to the Dharma,
and was truly without fault or blame,
yet I wrongfully inflicted rebellious harm.
Like a fish on dry land,
what happiness can there be?
Like a deer caught in a snare (bèi),
there is utterly no joyful feeling;
like a person who knows he will not live past the day;
like a king who has lost his kingdom and fled to another territory;
like a person hearing of an incurable disease;
or like a transgressor hearing his faults being spoken of.
I once heard a wise person say:
‘If one’s deeds of body, speech, and mind are impure,
one should know that this person will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell.’
I am also like this.
How then can I sleep peacefully?
Now I lack the supreme great physician,
who expounds the Dharma medicine,
to eliminate my suffering from this illness."
replied, saying:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Although the King has committed an offense,
his heart has generated deep repentance,
and he harbors shame and remorse.
Great King!
All Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly speak this saying:
'There are two white teachings (dharmas)
that can save sentient beings:
first, shame (Hrí, 慚);
second, remorse (Apatrāpya, 愧).
Shame means not committing offenses oneself,
remorse means not teaching others to commit them;
shame means feeling embarrassed internally,
remorse means revealing the fault externally to others;
shame fears man,
remorse fears heaven;
this is called shame and remorse.
Those without shame and remorse are not called human beings,
they are called beasts.
Because one has shame and remorse,
one is then able to respectfully honor parents, teachers, and elders;
because one has shame and remorse,
it is said one has parents, brothers, and sisters.
Excellent, Great King!
You possess shame and remorse.
Great King, please listen!
Your servant heard the Buddha speak:
'There are two types of wise men:
first, those who do not commit any evils;
second, those who repent after committing them.
There are also two types of fools:
first, those who commit offenses;
second, those who conceal them.
Although one may have committed evil earlier, if one can later expose it,
and having repented with shame and remorse, dares not commit it again,
it is like placing a brilliant jewel into turbid water;
by the power of the jewel, the water immediately becomes clear.
It is like when smoke and clouds disperse,
the moon becomes pure and bright.
Being able to repent for committed evil
is also like this.
If the King repents and harbors shame and remorse,
the offenses will immediately be eliminated,
and you will be pure as you were originally.
Great King!
Wealth has two kinds:
first, elephants, horses,
and all kinds of livestock;
second, gold, silver,
and all kinds of precious jewels.
Though the elephants and horses are numerous,
they cannot compare to one jewel.
Great King!
Sentient beings are also like this:
first, the wealth of evil;
second, the wealth of goodness.
To commit many evils
is not as good as one single good deed.
Your servant heard the Buddha say that
cultivating one moment of good intention
can destroy a hundred kinds of evil.
Great King!
Just as a small amount of vajra can destroy Mount Xūmí,
and just as a small amount of fire can burn everything,
and just as a small amount of poison can harm sentient beings,
a small good deed is also like that, capable of destroying great evil.
Although it is called a small good,
in reality, it is great.
Why is this?
Because it destroys great evil.
Great King!
As the Buddha has taught, those who conceal their faults leak,
but those who do not conceal them have no leaks (āsravas);
revealing and confessing one's transgression is why there are no leaks.
If one commits offenses but does not cover them up or conceal them,
because they are not concealed, the offenses are attenuated;
if one harbors shame and remorse, the offenses are extinguished.
Great King!
Just as a drop of water, though tiny,
gradually fills a large vessel,
good intention is also like that;
each individual good intention can destroy great evil.
If one conceals offenses, the offenses grow;
if one reveals them with shame and remorse, the offenses are extinguished.
Therefore, all Buddhas teach that the wise do not conceal their offenses.
Excellent, Great King!
You are able to believe in cause and effect,
believe in karma,
and believe in retribution.
I only wish that the Great King may not harbor sorrow or fear.
If there are sentient beings who commit various offenses,
conceal them without repenting, have no shame or remorse in their hearts,
do not see cause and effect or karmic retribution,
are unable to consult wise people, and do not approach good friends—
such people cannot be cured by any good physician, even by someone attending to the sick.
It is like the Jiāmóluó disease, for which worldly doctors fold their hands [in helplessness];
those who conceal their offenses are also like this.
Who is meant by the 'offending person'?
It refers to the Yīchǎntí.
The Yīchǎntí
does not believe in cause and effect,
has no shame or remorse,
does not believe in karmic retribution,
does not see the present or future worlds,
does not associate closely with good friends,
and does not follow the teachings and precepts spoken by the Buddhas.
Such a person is called an Yīchǎntí,
whom the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, cannot cure.
Why?
Just as worldly doctors cannot cure
a corpse.
The Yīchǎntí is also like this;
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, cannot cure him.
Since the Great King is presently not an Yīchǎntí,
how can you say that you cannot be saved or cured?
"Regarding the King's statement that there is no one who can cure you,
Great King, you should know that
the Prince of Jìngfàn from Jiāpíluó Chéng,
whose clan name is Qúntán Shì [Gautama],
whose given name is Xīdáduō [Siddhārtha],
attained enlightenment without a teacher,
naturally achieved Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi).
He is adorned with the thirty-two marks
and the eighty subsidiary characteristics,
perfectly possessing the ten powers,
the four fearlessnesses,
all knowledge and insight,
and great loving-kindness and great compassion.
He has compassion for all beings just like for Luóhóuluó [Rāhula].
He follows good sentient beings like a calf follows its mother.
He speaks when the time is right,
and does not speak when the time is not right.
He speaks truth,
pure words,
wonderful words,
meaningful words,
Dharma words,
and singular words [perfect speech],
which can cause sentient beings to forever leave vexations.
He perfectly understands the roots and mental natures of sentient beings,
and uses appropriate skillful means (upāya) to achieve thorough comprehension in everything.
His wisdom is lofty and great, like Mount Xūmí,
deep, profound, vast, and boundless, like the great ocean.
This Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses Vajra Wisdom,
which can shatter all the evil offenses of sentient beings.
If you say he cannot,
there is no such possibility.
Presently, twelve yojanas from here,
in the city of Jūshīnà Chéng [Kuśinagara], between the Suōluó Shuāngshù (Sāla Twin Trees),
he is expounding various kinds of Dharma
for countless Āsēngqí Bodhisattvas and monks:
whether conditioned (saṃskṛta)
or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta),
whether created
or uncreated,
whether having outflows (sāsrava)
or without outflows (anāsrava),
whether the result of vexations
or the result of good dharmas,
whether material phenomena (rūpa-dharma)
or immaterial phenomena,
or neither immaterial nor non-immaterial phenomena,
whether self
or non-self,
or neither non-self nor non-non-self,
whether permanent
or impermanent,
or neither impermanent nor non-impermanent,
whether bliss
or non-bliss,
or neither non-bliss nor non-non-bliss,
whether characteristic
or non-characteristic,
or neither non-characteristic nor non-non-characteristic,
whether cut off
or not cut off,
or neither not cut off nor non-not cut off,
whether worldly
or transcendental (out-of-the-world),
or neither worldly nor transcendental,
whether vehicle
or non-vehicle,
or neither non-vehicle nor non-non-vehicle,
whether committed by oneself and received by oneself,
whether committed by oneself and received by others,
or whether neither committed nor received.
Great King!
If you go to the Buddha's presence
and hear the teaching of 'neither committed nor received,'
all your heavy offenses will immediately be eliminated."
Shìtí Huányīn's
life is about to end;
five signs have appeared:
First, his clothes are filthy and greasy;
second, the flowers on his head have withered;
third, his body is foul and impure;
fourth, sweat pours from his armpits;
fifth, he finds no joy in his original seat.
At that time, Dìshì (the Heavenly Emperor) was in a quiet place,
whether he saw a Śramaṇa
or a Brāhmaṇa,
he immediately went to their location,
and gave rise to the thought that they were the Buddha.
At that time, the Śramaṇas and Brāhmaṇas, seeing Dìshì approach,
felt deeply fortunate,
and immediately spoke these words:
'Lord of Heaven!
We now take refuge in you.'
Shì, having heard this,
then knew they were not the Buddha.
He further thought to himself:
'If they are not the Buddha,
they cannot cure my five signs of decline and demise.'
At that time, the charioteer minister, named Bānzhēshī,
said to Dìshì:
'Jiāoshījiā!
The Gandhārva King, named Dūnfúlóu,
that King has a daughter
named Xūbátuó.
If the King can give this daughter to me,
your servant will show the King the place to eliminate the signs of decline.'
Shì immediately replied:
'Good man!
Pímózhìduō Āxiūluó Wáng has a daughter, Shèzhī,
whom I revere.
If you can definitely show me the place to eliminate these evil signs,
I would still give you her,
let alone Xūbátuó?'
'[Jiāoshījiā!]
There is a Buddha, the World-Honored One, named Shìjiāmóuní,
who is now residing in Wángshě Dàchéng.
If you can go there and inquire about what you have not yet heard,
the signs of decline and demise will certainly be eliminated.'
'Good man!
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can truly eliminate them,
then turn the chariot and proceed to his dwelling.'
The charioteer minister accepted the command and immediately turned the chariot,
arriving at Qíshéjué Shān in Wángshě Chéng.
He reached the Buddha's location, bowed his head to the Buddha's feet,
sat back on one side,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!
Among devas and humans, who is subject to bondage?'
'Jiāoshījiā!
Stinginess,
greed,
and jealousy.'
He further asked:
'Stinginess, greed, and jealousy,
arise due to what cause?'
The answer was:
'They arise due to ignorance.'
He further asked:
'And ignorance, due to what does it arise?'
The answer was:
'It arises due to recklessness.'
He further asked:
'And recklessness, due to what does it arise?'
The answer was:
'It arises due to delusion.'
He further asked:
'And delusion, due to what does it arise?'
The answer was:
'It arises due to doubt.'
'World-Honored One!
That the dharma of delusion arises from doubt,
truly accords with the Sacred Teaching.
Why is this?
I had a doubtful mind,
and because of that doubtful mind,
delusion arose,
causing me to perceive as the World-Honored One
those who were not the World-Honored One.
Now that I see the Buddha,
the net of doubt is immediately removed.
Because the net of doubt is removed, delusion is also exhausted.
Because delusion is exhausted,
there is no mind of stinginess, nor even the mind of jealousy.'
The Buddha said:
'You say you have no mind of stinginess or jealousy;
have you now attained the level of Ānàhán?
One who is an Ānàhán has no mind of greed.
If you have no mind of greed,
why have you come to my presence seeking life?
An Ānàhán truly does not seek life.'
'World-Honored One!
He who has delusion seeks life;
he who has no delusion does not seek life.
I now truly do not seek life.
What I desire to seek
is only the Buddha's Dharmakāya and the Buddha's wisdom.'
'Jiāoshījiā!
Seeking the Buddha's Dharmakāya and the Buddha's wisdom—
in future ages, you shall certainly attain them.'
At that time, Dìshì, having heard the Buddha's teaching,
had his five signs of decline and demise immediately eliminated.
He rose and performed obeisance,
circled the Buddha three times,
and respectfully joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!
I am now dead and reborn,
having lost life and gained life.
Moreover, having heard the Buddha's prediction that I shall attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
this is truly being born anew and gaining life anew.
World-Honored One!
All humans and devas,
how do they gain increase?
And by what conditions
are they brought to loss and reduction?'
'Jiāoshījiā!
Through the causes and conditions of strife and conflict,
humans and devas suffer loss and reduction;
by cultivating harmony and respect well,
they gain increase.'
'World-Honored One!
If loss and reduction result from strife and conflict,
then from this day forward, I shall never again fight with the Asuras.'
The Buddha said:
'Excellent,
excellent!
Jiāoshījiā!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, teach the Dharma of patience and forbearance,
which is the cause for Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.'
Thereupon, Shìtí Huányīn
immediately came forward and paid homage to the Buddha,
and then departed.
Great King!
The Tathāgata is able to eliminate all evil signs;
for this reason, the Buddha is called inconceivable.
If the King goes,
all his grave offenses will certainly be eliminated.
Great King, listen further:
There was a Brāhmaṇa's son,
named Bùhài,
who, having killed countless sentient beings, was called Yāngjuémó.
He further wished to murder his mother.
When this evil thought arose,
his body moved accordingly.
The movement of the body and mind constitutes the cause of the Five Heinous Crimes.
Because of the cause of the Five Heinous Crimes, he was certain to fall into the hells.
Later, when he saw the Buddha, his body and mind moved together.
He again wished to murder him.
The movement of the body and mind constitutes the cause of the Five Heinous Crimes.
Because of the cause of the Five Heinous Crimes, he was due to enter the hells.
This person was able to meet the Tathāgata, the Great Teacher,
and immediately attained the cessation of the karmic causes for hell.
He generated the mind of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
For this reason, the Buddha is called the Supreme Physician,
not the Six Teachers.
'Great King!
Furthermore, there was Prince Xūpíluó.
His father, being enraged with him,
severed his hands and feet,
and pushed him into a deep well.
His mother, pitying him,
ordered people to pull him out
and brought him to the Buddha's location.
As soon as he saw the Buddha,
his hands and feet were restored,
and he immediately generated the mind of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Great King!
Because he saw the Buddha,
he obtained a visible reward.
For this reason, the Buddha is called the Supreme Physician,
not the Six Teachers.'
"Great King!
By the side of the Hénghé (Ganges) River there were numerous hungry ghosts (èguǐ),
five hundred in number.
For countless years,
they had never once seen water.
Although they reached the river,
they only saw flowing fire.
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, they cried out loudly.
At that time, the Rúlái,
was on the bank of that river,
in the Yùtánbō (Udumbara) Grove,
sitting under a tree.
Then these hungry ghosts came to the place of the Fó (Buddha),
and addressed the Fó, saying:
'Shìzūn (World-Honored One)!
We are hungry and thirsty;
our lives will soon end.'
The Fó said:
'The flowing water of the Hénghé,
why do you not drink it?'
The ghosts immediately replied:
'The Rúlái sees water,
but we see fire.'
The Fó said:
'The clear stream of the Hénghé
truly has no fire.
Due to your evil karma, your minds are deluded,
making you take it for fire.
I shall eliminate this delusion for you,
and enable you to see water.'
At that time, the Shìzūn,
extensively explained the faults of stinginess and greed to the ghosts.
The ghosts immediately said:
'We are now parched with thirst.
Although we hear the Dharma teachings,
they do not enter our minds at all.'
The Fó said:
'If you are thirsty,
you should first enter the river
and drink freely.'
These ghosts,
by the power of the Fó,
immediately managed to drink the water.
After they had drunk the water,
the Rúlái again preached various doctrines for them.
Having heard the Dharma,
they all generated the mind of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi),
abandoned the form of hungry ghosts,
and obtained celestial bodies.
Great King!
Therefore, the Fó is called the Supreme Physician,
not the six *Shī* (Masters)."
"Great King!
In the kingdom of Shèpótí (Śrāvastī), five hundred bandits,
were subjected by King Bōsīnì (Prasenajit)
to having their eyes gouged out.
Without guides,
they were unable to reach the Fó’s location.
Out of compassion, the Fó
immediately went to the bandits' location,
and comforted them, saying:
'Good men!
Carefully guard your body and speech,
and commit no further evil.'
The bandits, upon hearing the Rúlái's voice,
which was subtle and clear,
immediately recovered their sight.
They immediately joined their palms before the Fó and paid homage to the Fó,
and addressed the Fó, saying:
'Shìzūn!
We now know that the Fó's compassionate mind universally covers all sentient beings,
not just humans and devas.'
At that time, the Rúlái immediately preached the Dharma to them.
Having heard the Dharma,
they all generated the mind of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Therefore, the Rúlái is truly the Supreme Good Physician of the world,
not the six *Shī*."
"Great King!
In the kingdom of Shèpótí, there was a Caṇḍāla,
named Qìxū,
who had killed countless people.
Upon seeing the Fó's disciple, Dàmùjiànlián (Mahāmaudgalyāyana),
he immediately managed to destroy the causes for rebirth in hell,
and attained rebirth in the Thirty-Three Heavens (Sānshísān Tiān).
Because of having such holy disciples,
the Fó Rúlái is called the Supreme Physician,
not the six *Shī*."
"Great King!
In Bōluónà (Vārāṇasī) City,
there was the son of an elder,
named Āyìduō (Ajita).
He committed adultery with his mother,
and because of this cause,
he slaughtered his father.
His mother then had relations with an outsider;
when the son learned this,
he again killed her.
An Āluóhàn (Arhat) was his acquaintance;
toward this acquaintance, he again felt shame,
and promptly killed him.
After killing, he immediately went to the Qíhuán Jīngshè (Jetavana Vihāra),
seeking ordination.
The Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū) at that time fully knew that this person had committed the three cardinal sins (sān nì zuì),
and none dared to grant permission.
Because permission was not granted,
he became doubly enraged,
and that very night, he started a massive, fierce fire,
burning down the monasteries (sēngfáng),
and killing many innocent people.
Afterward, he went to Wángshě Chéng (Rājagṛha),
and went to the Rúlái's location, begging tearfully to be ordained.
The Rúlái immediately granted permission,
and preached the essentials of the Dharma to him,
causing his heavy sins to gradually diminish,
and enabling him to generate the mind of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Therefore, the Fó is called the Good Physician of the world,
not the six *Shī*."
"Great King!
Your Majesty was originally violent and evil,
and trusted the wicked man Típódádūo (Devadatta).
You released a greatly intoxicated elephant, intending it to trample the Fó.
When the elephant saw the Fó,
it immediately became sober and awakened.
The Fó then extended his hand and stroked its crown,
and again preached the Dharma to it,
enabling it entirely to generate the mind of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Great King!
If even animals see the Fó
and thereby destroy the karmic retribution of the animal realm,
how much more so humans?
Great King, you must know:
If one sees the Fó,
all heavy sins will certainly be extinguished."
"Great King!
When the Shìzūn had not yet attained Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
Mó (Māra) came to the Bódàsà (Bodhisattva)'s place with countless, boundless retinues.
The Bódàsà at that time, by the power of forbearance, destroyed Mó's wicked mind,
causing Mó to accept the Dharma,
and immediately generate the mind of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
The Fó possesses such great virtuous power."
"Great King!
There was a wilderness ghost,
who harmed many sentient beings.
The Rúlái at that time was known as Shànxián Zhǎngzhě (Good and Virtuous Elder).
He went to the wilderness village and preached the Dharma for the ghost.
The wilderness ghost, hearing the Dharma, was joyful,
and immediately dedicated the Elder to the Rúlái,
and then generated the mind of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí."
"Great King!
In the kingdom of Bōluónà, there was a butcher,
named Guǎng'é,
who, day after day,
killed countless sheep.
He saw Shèlìfú (Śāriputra),
and immediately accepted the Eight Precepts (bā jiè) for one day and one night.
Due to this cause,
when his life ended, he managed to become the son of the Northern Heavenly King, Píshāmén (Vaiśravaṇa).
If the Rúlái's disciples already have such great virtuous rewards,
how much more so the Fó?"
"Great King!
In Northern Tiānzhú (India) there was a city,
named Xìshí,
and in that city there was a king,
named Lóngyìn.
Coveting the kingdom and the important position,
he killed his father.
After having killed his father,
regret arose in his mind,
so he immediately abandoned state affairs,
came to the Fó's location,
and tearfully begged to be ordained.
The Fó said:
'Welcome.'
He immediately became a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū),
his heavy sins were extinguished,
and he generated the mind of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Great King, you must know:
The Fó possesses such measureless and boundless great virtuous rewards."
"Great King!
The Rúlái's cousin, Típódádūo (Devadatta),
fractured the Sangha (Sēng),
caused the Fó to bleed,
and killed the Bhikṣuṇī Liánhuā (Padma).
He committed the three cardinal sins.
The Rúlái preached various essentials of the Dharma for him,
causing his heavy sins to immediately become light.
Therefore, the Rúlái is the Great Good Physician,
not the six *Shī*."
“Great King!
If you can trust the words of your servant,
I only wish you would quickly go to the place of the Tàrúlái.
If you do not believe me,
I wish you would contemplate this carefully.
Great King!
The Fó Shìzūn (Buddhas, World-Honored Ones) cover all beings with great compassion,
not restricting it to a single person.
The Zhengfǎ (Right Dharma) is vast and widespread,
encompassing all things.
They treat enemies and kin equally, without hatred or attachment in their hearts.
They absolutely do not partially favor one person, enabling them to attain Ànòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
while others are denied.
The Tàrúlái is not merely the teacher of the Four Assemblies;
He is universally the teacher of all heavenly beings,
dragons,
ghosts,
hell beings,
animals,
and starving ghosts, etc.
All sentient beings should also regard the Fó as their parents.
Great King, you should know that
the Tàrúlái not only preaches the Dharma for noble persons like King Bàtíjiā,
but also for the lowly Ūpōlí, etc.
He does not exclusively accept the food offered by Sūdáduō Ānàbīnzhǐ,
but also accepts the food of the poor person Sūdáduō.
He not only preaches the Dharma for those with sharp faculties like Shèlifú, etc.,
but also for those with dull faculties like Zhōu Lí Pántè.
He not only permits those with the nature of non-greed, like Dàjiāshè, etc., to leave home and seek the Way,
but also permits the greatly greedy Nánduó to leave home.
He not only permits those with thin afflictions, like Yōulóupínluó Jiāyè, etc., to leave home and seek the Way,
but also permits those with deep and thick afflictions who committed grave crimes, like King Bōsīní's brother Yōutuóyē, to leave home and seek the Way.
He did not remove the root of hatred by respectfully offering the Shācǎo (sedge grass);
but when Āngujú Mólúo wished to harm him with evil intent, he did not abandon him and fail to save him.
He not only preaches the Dharma for intelligent men,
but also preaches the Dharma for extremely foolish women, who are intellectually dull (Pànhézhìzhě).
He not only enables those who leave home to attain the Four Fruits of the Way,
but also enables laypeople to attain the Three Fruits of the Way.
He not only preaches the essentials of the Dharma for Fùduōluó, etc., who abandoned all busy tasks and meditate in solitude,
but also preaches the essentials of the Dharma for King Pínpósuōluó, etc., who govern the state and manage royal affairs.
He not only preaches for those who have given up alcohol,
but also preaches for the intoxicated Ùjiā Zhǎngzhě, who is addicted to alcohol.
He not only preaches for those who have entered samādhi, like Líbōduō, etc.,
but also preaches for the Brāhman woman Pósīzhà, whose mind was distraught from losing her son.
He not only preaches for his own disciples,
but also preaches for the externalists, Ní Gānzǐ.
He not only preaches for those in their prime, twenty-five years old,
but also preaches for those who are old and infirm, eighty years old.
He not only preaches for those whose faculties are ripe,
but also preaches for those whose roots of goodness are not yet ripe.
He not only preaches for Mòlì Fūrén,
but also preaches for the courtesan Liánhuā Nǚ.
He not only accepts the supreme, sweet delicacies from King Bōsīní,
but also accepts the poisoned food mixed with toxins from the Elder Shīlì Jūduō.
Great King, you should know that
Shīlì Jūduō also created the cause for heinous crime in the past,
but upon meeting the Fó and hearing the Dharma,
he immediately generated the mind of Ànòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
“Great King!
Suppose that for one month, one constantly makes offerings of clothing and food to all sentient beings and reveres them;
this is not equal to one-sixteenth of the merit gained
by a person who remembers the Fó for a single instant.
Great King!
Suppose one casts gold into people, carriages, and horses carrying treasures,
a hundred of each, and uses them for giving (Dàna);
this is still not equal to a person generating the mind towards the Fó and taking one step.
Great King!
Suppose further one uses a hundred elephant carriages loaded with various treasures from the Kingdom of Dàqín,
along with women, each wearing a hundred strands of necklaces,
and uses them for giving (Dàna);
this is still not equal to generating the mind towards the Fó and taking one step.
Setting this aside again,
if one uses the four kinds of offerings to supply all sentient beings in the Three-Thousand Great-Thousand Worlds,
this is still not equal to generating the mind towards the Fó and taking one step.
Setting this aside again,
if the Great King offers to and reveres sentient beings equal to the sands of the Gangā River,
this is not equal to going once to the place of the Tàrúlái under the Twin Sāluó Trees and sincerely listening to the Dharma.
Thereupon, the Great King replied,
“Jīpó!
The Tàrúlái Shìzūn (World-Honored One) is inherently gentle and compliant,
and thus has gentle and compliant ones as his retinue.
It is like a Chándán (sandalwood) forest,
which is purely surrounded by Chándán trees.
The Tàrúlái is pure,
and his entire retinue is also pure.
It is like a Great Dragon,
whose retinue consists purely of dragons.
The Tàrúlái is tranquil,
and his entire retinue is also tranquil.
The Tàrúlái is free of greed,
and his entire retinue is also free of greed.
The Fó is without afflictions,
and his entire retinue is also without afflictions.
Since I am now an extremely wicked person,
wrapped up by wicked karma,
my body is foul and impure,
bound for Diyù (hell).
How can I go to the place of the Tàrúlái?
Even if I were to go,
I fear he would not regard me or exchange words with me.
Although you urge me to go to the Fó’s place,
I deeply despise and mourn myself today,
and have no intention of going.”
At that moment, a voice immediately emerged from the empty sky, saying:
“The Unsurpassed Buddha Dharma,
is about to decline and cease.
The deep river of Dharma is about to dry up.
The great bright lamp of Dharma will soon be extinguished.
The mountain of Dharma is about to collapse, and the boat of Dharma is about to sink.
The bridge of Dharma is about to break, and the palace of Dharma is about to crumble.
The banner of Dharma is about to fall, and the tree of Dharma is about to snap.
Good friends are about to depart.
Great terror is approaching.
Sentient beings starving for the Dharma will arrive soon.
The epidemic disease of afflictions is about to become widespread.
The time of great darkness has arrived; the time of thirst for the Dharma has come.
Máwáng (King of Māra) is rejoicing and loosening his armor.
The sun of the Fó is about to set behind the mountain of Great Nièpán.
Great King!
If the Fó enters Nirvāṇa,
there will be no one else to cure your grave wickedness.
Great King!
You have already created the extremely grave karma for Ābǐ Dìyù,
and you will inevitably receive the consequences of this karma without doubt.
Great King!
Ā means ‘without,’
and Bǐ is named ‘interval.’
There is no temporary pleasure in that interval,
hence it is named ‘Uninterrupted’ (Wújiàn).
Great King!
Suppose one person alone falls into this hell.
His body grows vast, eighty thousand Yóuyán (yojanas) in height,
filling the space completely without any gaps.
His body suffers various kinds of pain all around.
Even if there are many people, their bodies also fill the space completely without hindering each other.
Great King!
In the cold hells, temporarily encountering a warm wind is considered pleasure.
In the hot hells, temporarily encountering a cold wind is also named pleasure.
In the hell of Repeated Revival (Huó Dìyù),
even after death,
if one hears the word ‘Revive!’
one immediately comes back to life.
In Ābǐ Dìyù, none of these things happen.
Great King!
Ābǐ Dìyù has gates on its four sides.
Outside each gate, there are raging fires.
They cross and penetrate through east, west, south, and north for eighty thousand Yóuyán.
It is surrounded by iron walls,
completely covered by an iron net.
The ground is also iron.
The fire above penetrates downward,
and the fire below penetrates upward.
Great King!
If a fish is in a pan,
its fat and oil burn up.
The sinners within
are also like this.
Great King!
One who commits one heinous crime
fully receives one such punishment.
If one commits two heinous crimes, the punishment is doubled.
If one fully commits the Five Heinous Crimes, the punishment is quintupled.
Great King!
I now know for certain that your wicked karma is inescapable.
I only wish, Great King, that you quickly go to the Fó’s place.
Apart from the Fó Shìzūn,
there is no one else who can save you.
I pity you now,
and therefore urge you.”
Thereupon, the Great King heard these words,
and his heart was filled with terror.
His entire body trembled,
and his five limbs shook like a bājiāo (banana) tree.
He looked up and replied,
“Who are you?
You do not show your form,
but only have a voice.”
“Great King!
I am your father, Pínpósuōluó.
You should now follow what Jīpó says,
and do not follow the words of the six evil-view ministers.”
When the King heard this,
he fainted and collapsed to the ground.
His sores worsened,
becoming twice as foul as before.
Although cold medicine was applied to treat them,
the sores steamed with toxic heat,
only increasing, not diminishing.
At that time, the Shìzūn,
between the twin trees, saw Āshéshì fainting and collapsing to the ground,
