and immediately told the great assembly,
“I shall now remain in the world for this king for immeasurable kalpas,
and not enter Nirvāṇa.”
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Fó,
“Shìzūn!
The Tàrúlái should remain in the world for countless sentient beings and not enter Nirvāṇa.
Why do you only do so for King Āshéshì?”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
Among this great assembly,
there is not one person who says I will definitively enter Nirvāṇa.
King Āshìshì definitively says I am about to finally perish forever;
therefore, he fainted [from grief]
and threw himself upon the ground.
Good man!
As I have said,
it is for Āshìshì that I do not enter Nirvāṇa.
Such profound secret meaning,
you have not yet been able to understand.
Why is that?
The ones I spoke of as ‘for’
are all common mortals (fánfū).
The term Āshìshì
universally includes all those who commit the Five Heinous Crimes (Wǔnì).
Furthermore, the ones I spoke of as ‘for’
are precisely all conditioned sentient beings (yǒuwéi zhòngshēng).
I certainly do not remain in the world for unconditioned sentient beings (wúwéi zhòngshēng).
Why is that?
Indeed, the unconditioned
are not sentient beings.
The term Āshìshì
is precisely those who are fully burdened by afflictions (fánnǎo) and the like.
Furthermore, the ones I spoke of as ‘for’
are precisely sentient beings who do not see the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
If they see the Buddha Nature,
I certainly do not remain long in the world for them.
Why is that?
Those who see the Buddha Nature
are not sentient beings.
The term Āshìshì
is precisely all those who have not yet generated the mind of Anouduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Furthermore, the ones I spoke of as ‘for’
are precisely the two assemblies of Ānán
and Jiāshè.
The term Āshìshì
is precisely King Āshìshì,
the empresses and consorts of the inner palace,
and all the women of Wángshěchéng.
Furthermore, the ones I spoke of as ‘for’
are called the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
The word Āshé
means ‘not arising’;
Shì means ‘enemy’.
Because the Buddha Nature does not arise (is not recognized),
then the enemy of affliction arises.
Because the enemy of affliction arises,
one does not see the Buddha Nature.
Because afflictions do not arise,
then one sees the Buddha Nature.
Because one sees the Buddha Nature,
then one gains permanent dwelling in the Mahāpārinirvāṇa (Dàbō Nièpán).
This is called 'not arising';
therefore it is called 'for Āshìshì'.
Good man!
Āshé means ‘not arising’;
‘not arising’ means Nirvāṇa.
Shì means worldly dharmas (shìfǎ).
Wèi (for) means ‘not defiled’.
Because [he is] not defiled by the Eight Worldly Dharmas,
for immeasurable, boundless Asamkhyeya kalpas (ē-sēngqí jié) he does not enter Nirvāṇa.
Therefore I said,
for Āshìshì,
I will not enter Nirvāṇa for innumerable hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Good man!
The Tathāgata’s secret words are inconceivable (bù kě sīyì);
the Buddha,
the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha are also inconceivable;
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas are also inconceivable;
the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra is also inconceivable.”
At that time, the World-Honored One (Shìzūn),
the Greatly Compassionate Guide,
for the sake of King Āshìshì,
entered the Yuè’ài Sānmèi (Moon-Love Samādhi).
Having entered the Samādhi,
he emitted a great bright light.
That light was cool and refreshing,
and went to illuminate the king’s body.
The sores on his body immediately healed,
and the oppressive heat vanished.
The king, realizing his sores had healed
and his body felt cool and refreshed,
said to Qízhī (Jīvaka):
“I have previously heard people say
that when a kalpa is about to end, three moons appear simultaneously.
At that time, the suffering and distress of all sentient beings are entirely removed.
Since that time has not yet arrived,
where did this light come from that illuminates and touches my body,
removing and healing my painful sores,
and allowing my body to attain peace and joy?”
Qízhī replied:
“This is not the simultaneous illumination of three moons at the end of a kalpa,
nor is it the light of a fiery sun,
nor of constellations,
medicinal herbs,
precious jewels, or heavenly radiance.”
The king asked again:
“If this light is neither the simultaneous illumination of three moons
nor the brightness of precious jewels,
whose light is it?”
“Great King, you should know
this is the bright light emitted by the God among Gods (Tiānzhōngtiān).
This light is without origin and without boundary.
It is neither hot nor cold,
neither permanent nor perishable,
neither material (sè) nor immaterial (wú sè),
neither marked (xiàng) nor unmarked (wú xiàng),
neither blue nor yellow,
neither red nor white.
Wishing to save sentient beings,
it is therefore made visible,
possessing marks that can be spoken of,
having an origin,
having boundaries,
having heat and cold,
blue, yellow, red, and white.
Great King!
Although this light is like that,
in reality, it cannot be spoken of,
cannot be perceived,
and does not even possess blue, yellow, red, or white.”
The king said:
“Qízhī!
By what cause or condition
did that God among Gods emit this bright light?”
“Great King!
This auspicious sign now appears specifically for the Great King.
Because the King previously said
that there is no good doctor in the world who can treat the body and mind,
therefore this light was emitted,
first treating the King's body,
and then treating his mind.”
The king said:
“Qízhī!
Does the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, also remember (think of) me?”
Qízhī replied:
“For example, a person has seven children.
If one of these seven children contracts an illness,
the parents’ hearts are not unequal [in love],
but their attention to the sick child is particularly strong.
Great King!
The Tathāgata is also like this.
Towards all sentient beings, he is not unequal [in love],
but towards the sinful, his mind is particularly weighty [with compassion].
Towards those who are negligent (fàngyì), the Buddha has compassionate remembrance;
towards those who are not negligent, his mind lets go.
Who are called those who are not negligent?
They are the Bodhisattvas of the Six Stations (Liù Zhù Púsà).
Great King!
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, towards all sentient beings,
do not regard lineage,
old, young, or middle-aged,
poor or wealthy,
seasons,
the sun, moon, or stars,
craftsmanship,
lowly status,
or male and female servants.
They only regard those sentient beings who have a virtuous mind.
If there is a virtuous mind, they then hold compassionate remembrance.
Great King, you should know,
this auspicious sign
is precisely the bright light emitted by the Tathāgata when he entered the Yuè’ài Sānmèi.”
The king immediately asked:
“What is called the Yuè’ài Sānmèi?”
answered:
"For example, just as moonlight
enables all utpala flowers (yōubōluó huā) to bloom brightly;
the Yuè'ài Sānmèi (Moon-Loving Samādhi) is also like this,
it enables the wholesome minds of sentient beings to blossom,
therefore it is named the Yuè'ài Sānmèi.
Great King!
For example, just as moonlight enables the hearts of all travelers to generate joy;
the Yuè'ài Sānmèi is also like this,
it enables those who cultivate the path to Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) to generate joy,
therefore it is further named the Yuè'ài Sānmèi.
Great King!
For example, just as the moon,
from the first day to the fifteenth day,
its form, color, and brightness
gradually increase;
the Yuè'ài Sānmèi is also like this,
it causes the fundamental virtues of those who first arouse the mind [of enlightenment] to gradually increase,
until they are perfected in Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Bān Nièpán),
therefore it is further named the Yuè'ài Sānmèi.
Great King!
For example, just as moonlight,
from the sixteenth day to the thirtieth day,
its form, color, and brightness gradually decrease;
the Yuè'ài Sānmèi is also like this,
in the places illuminated by its light,
it enables all afflictions (fánnǎo) to gradually cease,
therefore it is further named the Yuè'ài Sānmèi.
Great King!
For example, during times of intense heat,
all sentient beings constantly long for moonlight;
when the moonlight shines upon them,
the stifling heat is immediately removed;
the Yuè'ài Sānmèi is also like this,
it can enable sentient beings to remove the heat of desire and affliction (tānnǎo).
Great King!
For example, just as the full moon,
the king among all stars,
is the taste of amṛta (gānlù),
and is cherished and enjoyed by all sentient beings;
the Yuè'ài Sānmèi is also like this,
the king among all wholesome roots, it is the taste of amṛta,
cherished and enjoyed by all sentient beings,
therefore it is further named the Yuè'ài Sānmèi."
The King said:
"I have heard that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) does not reside, sit, or rise together with wicked people,
nor does he speak or discuss with them,
just as the great ocean does not harbor corpses,
just as the Mandarin Duck (yuānyāng) does not dwell in a latrine,
just as Śakra Devānām Indra (Shìtíhuányīn) does not live with ghosts,
just as the Kūzhìluó bird does not perch on a dead tree;
the Tathāgata is also like this.
How then can I go and see him?
If I were to see him,
would my body not sink into the ground?
I observe that the Tathāgata
would rather approach a drunken elephant,
a lion, a tiger, or a wolf,
or fierce, raging flames,
than approach a person of grave wickedness.
Therefore, having considered this now,
what state of mind should I have to go and see the Tathāgata?"
Qípó answered:
"Great King!
For example, a thirsty person
quickly rushes to a clear spring,
a hungry person seeks food,
a frightened person seeks rescue,
a sick person seeks a good doctor,
one suffering heat seeks shade and coolness,
and a cold person seeks fire.
The King seeking the Buddha (Fó) should also be like this.
Great King!
The Tathāgata still expounds the essentials of the Dharma for those like the icchantika (yīchǎntí),
how much more so the Great King, who is not an icchantika,
should not fail to receive his compassionate rescue and aid?"
The King said:
"Qípó!
I once heard in the past
that the icchantika does not believe, does not listen,
cannot observe or contemplate,
and cannot obtain the true meaning.
Why then does the Tathāgata preach the Dharma for them?"
Jīvō answered,
“Great King!
It is like a person
whose body is afflicted with a serious illness.
This person dreams at night of ascending a pillar-hall,
consuming ghee and oil and smearing them on his body,
lying in ash and eating ash,
climbing up a withered tree,
or roaming, sitting, and lying down with macaques,
sinking in water and submerging in mud,
falling and tumbling from towers and halls,
high mountains,
and trees,
elephants, horses, cattle, and sheep.
He wears clothing of blue, yellow, red, black, or white,
and laughs, sings, and dances joyfully.
He might see crows, vultures, foxes, and the like,
his teeth and hair falling out,
lying naked, pillowing a dog, and sleeping among filth and excrement.
Furthermore, he walks, stays, sits, and rises with the deceased,
holding hands and eating and chewing.
Poisonous snakes fill the road, and he passes through them.
Or he dreams of embracing a woman with disheveled hair,
using tāluō leaves as clothing,
and traveling directly southward in a broken donkey cart.
After this person has had the dream,
his heart becomes distressed and troubled.
Because of this distress and trouble,
his bodily illness increases even more.
Because the illness increases,
his family and relatives send a messenger to summon a physician.
The messenger who is sent
is physically short and deficient,
his senses are not complete,
his head is covered with dust,
he wears worn-out, ruined clothes,
and rides in an old, broken cart.
He says to the physician,
‘Quickly get in the cart.’
At that time, the skilled physician immediately reflects:
‘Now that I see this messenger,
his appearance is inauspicious.
I should know that the patient will be difficult to cure.’
He further thinks:
‘Although the messenger is inauspicious,
I should consult the day
to see if he can be treated or not.
If it is the fourth day,
sixth day,
eighth day,
twelfth day,
or fourteenth day,
on such days,
the illness is also difficult to cure.’
He further thinks:
‘Although the day is inauspicious,
I should consult the constellations
to see if he can be treated or not.
If it is the Mars (Huǒxīng),
Venus (Jīnxīng),
Pleiades (Mǎoxīng),
Yánluówáng Star,
Moist Star (Shīxīng),
or Full Star (Mǎnxīng),
when such constellations rule,
the illness is also difficult to cure.’
He further thinks:
‘Although the constellations are inauspicious,
I should also observe the time.
If it is autumn time,
winter time,
or the time of sunset,
midnight time,
or moonset time,
it should be known that this illness is also difficult to cure.’
He further says:
‘Although these various signs
may be inauspicious—whether fixed or unfixed—
I should observe the patient.
If they have merit and virtue, they can all be treated.
If they lack merit and virtue,
what benefit is there, even if the signs are auspicious?’
Having reflected on this,
he immediately travels with the messenger.
On the road, he further thinks:
‘If that patient
has the signs of longevity, then they can be treated.
If they have the signs of short life, then they cannot be treated.’
Immediately ahead on the road, he sees two young children
pulling and fighting with each other,
grabbing heads and pulling hair,
and hitting each other with tiles, stones, knives, and sticks.
He sees someone holding fire that naturally extinguishes.
Or he sees someone chopping down trees,
or he sees someone dragging leather by hand and walking along the road,
or he sees lost objects on the road,
or he sees someone holding empty vessels,
or he sees a śrāmaṇa walking alone without companions,
and he further sees tigers, wolves, crows, vultures, and wild foxes.
Having seen these things,
he further thinks:
‘The messenger sent,
and even the signs seen on the road,
are all inauspicious.
I should know that the patient is definitely difficult to cure.’
He further thinks:
‘If I do not go,
then I am not a skilled master (physician).
If I go,
he cannot be saved and cured.’
He thinks again,
‘Although these various signs
are inauspicious,
I should set them aside for now
and go to the patient’s place.’
Having reflected on this,
he further hears such sounds
ahead on the road,
namely: lost,
dead,
crumbled,
broken,
stripped off,
fallen,
burnt,
not coming,
cannot be cured,
and cannot be saved or rescued.
He further hears the sound of flying birds from the south,
namely the sounds of crows and vultures (Wūjiù),
the Shèlì bird (Śārī),
or dogs (gǒu),
or rats (shǔ),
wild foxes (yěhú),
rabbits (tù), and pigs (zhū).
Having heard these sounds,
he further thinks:
‘I should know that the patient
is difficult to cure.’"
"At that time, [the physician] immediately entered the patient's dwelling,
saw that the patient frequently had chills and frequent fevers,
aching bones and joints,
red eyes and flowing tears,
auditory sensations coming from outside [the body],
a constricted and aching throat,
the surface of the tongue fissured and broken,
the complexion utterly black,
the head unable to support itself,
the body dry and without sweat,
urination and defecation blocked and not flowing,
the body suddenly becoming huge and swollen,
abnormally red,
speech uneven, sometimes coarse, sometimes faint,
the whole body mottled and patchy,
strangely colored blue and yellow,
the belly distended and full,
unable to speak clearly.
When the physician saw this,
he asked the attendant:
'What has been the patient's will and disposition since yesterday?'
He replied:
'Great Master (Dàshī)!
This person originally respected and believed in the Three Jewels and all the various deities,
but now there is a change,
and the feeling of reverence and faith has ceased.
Formerly fond of giving charity, now miserly and grasping;
originally naturally eating little, now eating excessively;
originally naturally depraved and wicked, now harmonious and good;
originally naturally compassionate and filial, revering parents, now having no respectful heart toward parents.'
When the physician heard this,
he immediately went forward and smelled [the patient].
The fragrance of *Upalaka* (Yōubōluó),
the mixed fragrance of *Chenshuǐ* (agarwood),
the fragrance of *Bìjiāduō*,
the fragrance of *Duōgēluó*,
the fragrance of *Duōmóluóbá*,
the fragrance of turmeric,
the fragrance of sandalwood (Zhāntán),
the smell of roasted meat,
the smell of grape wine,
the smell of burning sinews and bones,
the smell of fish,
the smell of feces.
Having perceived the odors and smells,
he immediately went forward and touched the body,
feeling the body to be delicate and soft,
like silk floss or cotton,
or the flower of *jiébèisuō*,
or hard like stone,
or cold like ice,
or hot like fire,
or rough like sand.
At that time, the excellent physician, having seen these various signs,
definitely knew that the patient would certainly die without doubt,
but did not state definitively that this person would die,
saying to the attendant:
'I have urgent duties now.
I shall return tomorrow.
Whatever he needs,
let him indulge freely, do not hinder him.'
He then returned home.
The next day, a messenger arrived,
and [the physician] spoke to the messenger again, saying:
'My work is not yet finished,
and I have not yet compounded the medicine.'
The wise should know
that such a patient
will certainly die without doubt.
"O Great King (Dàwáng)!
The World-Honored One (Shìzūn) is also like this.
For the *icchantika* (yīchǎntí) class,
He skillfully discerns their fundamental nature and preaches the Dharma to them.
Why is this?
If He does not preach to them,
all ordinary beings will say that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) has no great loving-kindness and compassion.
If one possesses loving-kindness and compassion, one is called All-Knowing.
If there is no loving-kindness and compassion,
how can one say that He is the All-Knowing Person?
Therefore, the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma for the *yīchǎntí*.
O Dàwáng!
The Tathāgata, the Shìzūn, seeing all sick beings,
constantly bestows the medicine of the Dharma.
If the sick do not take it,
the fault is not the Tathāgata's.
O Dàwáng!
The *yīchǎntí* class is divided into two types:
first, those who obtain roots of goodness in the present life,
second, those who obtain roots of goodness in a future life.
The Tathāgata skillfully knows the *yīchǎntí* class: for those able to obtain roots of goodness in the present life,
He preaches the Dharma;
for those who will obtain them in a future life,
He also preaches the Dharma.
Although there is no immediate benefit now,
it serves as a cause for a future life.
Therefore, the Tathāgata expounds the essentials of the Dharma for the *yīchǎntí*.
The *yīchǎntí* are furthermore of two kinds:
first, those of sharp faculty (lìgēn),
second, those of mediocre faculty (zhōnggēn).
Persons of *lìgēn* are able to obtain roots of goodness in the present world;
persons of *zhōnggēn* obtain them in a future life.
The Buddhas, the Shìzūn, do not preach the Dharma in vain.
O Dàwáng!
For example, a pure person
falls into a privy.
A good friend (shànzhīshi) sees him and pities him,
immediately going forward, grabbing his hair, and pulling him out.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are also like this.
Seeing all sentient beings fall into the Three Evil Paths,
they employ skillful means (fāngbiàn) to rescue them and enable them to escape.
Therefore, the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma for the *yīchǎntí*.
The King said to [Jīvaka] Qípó:
"If the Tathāgata is indeed as you say,
I shall select an auspicious day and lucky constellation tomorrow,
and only then shall I go."
Qípó replied to the King:
"O Dàwáng!
In the Dharma of the Tathāgata,
there is no selection of auspicious days or lucky constellations.
O Dàwáng!
Just as a gravely ill person does not consider days,
seasons,
or good or ill omens,
but only seeks an excellent physician.
Your Majesty is now gravely ill.
Seeking the Buddha, the excellent physician,
you should not select auspicious times or good days.
O Dàwáng!
Just as sandalwood fire (Zhāntán huǒ) and wormwood fire,
both have the characteristic of burning,
and there is no difference between them.
Auspicious days and inauspicious days
are also like this.
If you go to the Buddha's abode,
you will equally achieve the cessation of transgressions.
I only wish that Your Majesty would quickly go today."
At that time, the Dàwáng immediately ordered a minister named Jíxiáng,
and told him:
"Minister, you should know
that I now wish to go to the Buddha, the Shìzūn,
quickly prepare the necessary items for offerings."
The minister replied:
"O Dàwáng!
Excellent,
excellent!
All the necessary items for the offering are already prepared."
King Ājiāshì (Ajātaśatru), together with his consorts,
magnificently prepared twelve thousand chariots and carriages,
fifty thousand strong and handsome elephants.
On each elephant, three people were mounted,
carrying banners and canopies,
flowers and incense,
music and instruments,
various kinds of offerings,
nothing was unprepared or lacking.
The accompanying cavalry numbered one hundred and eighty thousand.
All the people of the country of Mójiātuó (Magadha) who followed the King,
fully numbered five hundred and eighty thousand.
At that time, all the great multitude in the city of Jūshīnà (Kuśinagara), filling twelve *yóuxún* (yojanas),
all saw King Ājiāshì and his retinue approaching along the road from afar.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying:
"For all sentient beings seeking the proximate cause for *Anuòduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí* (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi),
nothing comes before a good friend (*shànyǒu*).
Why is this?
If King Ājiāshì had not complied with Qípó's words,
on the seventh day of the coming month, he would certainly have died and fallen into Ābí Yù (Avīci Hell).
Therefore, regarding the proximate cause, nothing is better than a *shànyǒu*.
Further along the road, King Ājiāshì heard that King Píliúlí (Virūḍhaka) of Shèpótí (Śrāvastī) had entered the sea by boat and died, having encountered fire,
that the Bhikṣu Qúgālǐ (Kokālika) had entered the earth alive and reached Ābí Yù,
and that Sūnàchàduō (Sunakṣatra), having committed various evils, went to the Buddha's abode and had all his transgressions extinguished.
Having heard these statements, [Ājiāshì] said to Qípó:
"Although I have now heard these two kinds of statements,
I am still not completely sure.
You, Qípó, come!
I wish to ride on the same elephant with you.
If I should fall into Ābí Dìyù (Avīci Hell),
I hope you will grab hold of me and prevent me from falling.
Why is this?
I once heard that a person who has attained the Way does not enter hell."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the great assembly, saying:
"King Ājiāshì still possesses a doubtful mind.
I must now establish a resolved mind for him."
At that time, there was a Bodhisattva (Púsà) in the assembly
named Chí Yīqiè (Holding All),
who said to the Buddha:
"Shìzūn!
As the Buddha previously taught,
all phenomena (zhūfǎ) are without fixed characteristics (dìngxiàng).
That is to say, form (sè) is without fixed characteristics,
and even Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) is without fixed characteristics.
How then does the Tathāgata now say
that He will establish a resolved mind for Ājiāshì?"
The Fó said:
“Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
I shall now certainly establish a resolute conviction for Āshéshì Wáng.
Why is this?
If the King’s doubtful mind can be destroyed,
you should know that all phenomena have no fixed characteristics (no definitive nature).
Therefore, I shall establish a resolute conviction for Āshéshì Wáng,
and you should know that this mind is without resolution (undetermined).
Good man!
If that King’s mind were resolute (determined),
how could the King’s heinous offense be destroyed?
Because there are no fixed characteristics,
his offense can be destroyed.
Therefore, I shall establish a resolute conviction for Āshéshì Wáng.”
At that time, the Great King immediately went to the grove of the Suōluó Shuāngshù,
arriving where the Fó was.
He looked up upon the Rúlái’s thirty-two marks
and eighty secondary characteristics,
who resembled a subtle mountain of pure gold.
At that time, the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) spoke with eight types of sound and announced:
“Great King.”
Then, Āshéshì looked left and right,
saying, “Among this great assembly, who is the Great King?
Since I am sinful and wicked,
and also lack merit and virtue,
the Rúlái ought not to call me the Great King.”
At that time, the Rúlái immediately called out again:
“Āshéshì Dà Wáng.”
When the King heard this,
his heart was greatly joyful,
and he immediately spoke thus:
“That the Rúlái today addresses and speaks to me,
truly shows that the Rúlái, regarding all sentient beings,
possesses great compassion and pity,
treating them equally without discrimination.”
He addressed the Fó, saying:
“Shìzūn!
My doubtful mind is now eternally gone without remainder;
I know for certain that the Rúlái is truly the unsurpassed great master of sentient beings.”
At that time, Jiāshè Púsà spoke to all the Bodhisattvas who were present, saying:
“The Rúlái has already established a resolute conviction for Āshéshì Wáng.”
At that time, Āshéshì Wáng immediately addressed the Fó, saying:
“Shìzūn!
Even if I were now to sit, rise, and eat with the Fàn Wáng and Shìtíhuányīn,
I would still not be joyful;
but having received a single word of address from the Rúlái,
I am profoundly happy and celebratory.”
At that time, Āshéshì Wáng,
immediately presented the banners, canopies,
incense, flowers,
and musical offerings that he carried.
He advanced and prostrated at the Fó’s feet,
circumambulated three times to the right,
and having finished his respectful salutations,
he withdrew and sat down to one side.
At that time, the Fó spoke to Āshéshì Wáng, saying:
“Great King!
I shall now expound to you the essentials of the Right Dharma (Zhèng Fǎ);
you must concentrate your mind,
listen carefully!
Listen carefully!
Ordinary beings should constantly focus their minds on contemplating the body,
concerning twenty matters:
First,
namely the self (I),
that this body is void within,
and is without non-outflow (āsrava-free) qualities;
Second,
that it lacks the roots of all goodness;
Third,
that my cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra) has not yet attained harmonization;
Fourth,
that it falls and plunges into a deep pit, with nowhere free from fear;
Fifth,
by what means can I perceive the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng);
Sixth,
how can I cultivate concentration (dhyāna) to perceive the Fóxìng;
Seventh,
that saṃsāra is constantly suffering, impermanent, without self, and impure;
Eighth,
that the difficulties of the eight calamities (Bā Nán) are hard to escape;
Ninth,
that I am constantly pursued by enemies;
Tenth,
that there is no single dharma that can block all existence (bhāva);
Eleventh,
that I have not yet achieved liberation from the three evil realms (Sān È Qù);
Twelfth,
that I possess all kinds of evil and heterodox views;
Thirteenth,
that I have not yet established the ferry (means of passage) to cross over the five heinous offenses (Wǔ Nì);
Fourteenth,
that saṃsāra is limitless and I have not reached its end;
Fifteenth,
that without performing deeds (karma), one does not receive retribution;
Sixteenth,
that there is no case where I act and others receive the fruit;
Seventeenth,
that without performing the cause of happiness, there will ultimately be no fruit of happiness;
Eighteenth,
that if one creates karma, the fruit will ultimately not be lost;
Nineteenth,
that I am born due to ignorance (avidyā) and also die due to it;
Twentieth,
that in the past, present, and future, I constantly act with negligence (pramāda).
Great King!
Ordinary individuals must constantly contemplate this body
by performing these twenty kinds of contemplation.
Having performed this contemplation, they will not delight in saṃsāra;
not delighting in saṃsāra, they achieve Right View (Zhèng Guān).
At that time, they successively contemplate the characteristics of the mind’s arising (shēng xiāng),
abiding (zhù xiāng),
and cessation (miè xiāng);
Successively contemplating the characteristics of the mind’s arising, abiding, and cessation,
Concentration (Dìng),
Wisdom (Huì),
Diligence (Jìn),
and Precepts (Jiè),
are also contemplated in the same way.
Having contemplated arising, abiding, and cessation,
and having understood the characteristics of the mind up to the characteristics of the precepts,
one will ultimately not commit evil,
will have no fear of death,
or fear of the Sān È Dào.
If one does not focus the mind on observing these twenty matters,
the mind becomes negligent,
and there is no evil that is not committed.”
Āshéshì said:
“As I understand the meaning of what the Fó has explained,
since times past,
I have never contemplated these twenty matters;
thus, I created many evils.
Because I created many evils,
I naturally have fear of death
and fear of the Sān È Dào.
Shìzūn!
I brought calamity upon myself,
having committed this grave evil;
my father, the King, was innocent,
yet I unjustly inflicted the heinous harm upon him.
Whether these twenty matters are contemplated or not,
I am certainly destined to fall into Ābí Dìyù.”
The Fó informed the Great King:
“The inherent nature and characteristics of all phenomena are impermanent
and are without determination (fixed nature).
How can the King say
that he is certainly destined to fall into Ābí Dìyù?”
Āshéshì Wáng addressed the Fó, saying:
“Shìzūn!
If all phenomena are without fixed characteristics,
then my sin of patricide should also be undetermined (unfixed).
If the killing were determined (fixed),
then all phenomena would not be undetermined.”
The Buddha said:
“Great King!
Excellent,
excellent!
The Buddhas, Bhagāvats, preach that all phenomena are entirely without fixed characteristics.
You further know that killing is also unfixed;
therefore, you should understand that killing has no fixed characteristic.
Great King!
Regarding what you said,
that your former father was innocent and unjustly inflicted with violence,
who exactly is this father?
He is merely the five aggregates (Panca-Skandha) of a conventionally named sentient being.
You mistakenly generate the concept of 'father' concerning them.
Among the twelve entrances (Dvādaśāyatana)
and the eighteen realms (Aṣṭādaśadhātu),
which one is the father?
If form (rūpa) is the father,
then the other four aggregates should not be;
if the four aggregates are the father,
then form also should not be.
If form and non-form combine to be the father,
there is no such possibility.
Why is this?
Because form and non-form
are inherently incapable of combining.
Great King!
Ordinary sentient beings mistakenly generate the concept of 'father' concerning this aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha).
Yet, this aggregate of form cannot be harmed either.
Why is this?
Form has ten categories.
Among these ten categories,
only one category of form
is visible, graspable,
weighable, measurable,
pullable, and bindable.
Although it can be seen and bound,
its nature does not abide;
because it does not abide, it cannot be seen,
cannot be grasped,
cannot be weighed or measured,
cannot be pulled or bound.
The characteristic of form is thus;
how can it be killed?
If form is the father,
and can be killed, harmed,
and thus accrue sinful retribution;
then the other nine categories should not be.
If the nine categories are not (the father),
then there should be no sin.
Great King!
Form has three types:
past,
future,
and present.
The past
and the present cannot be harmed.
Why is this?
The past is past,
and the present perishes moment by moment;
the obstruction of the future is what is called killing.
In this way, this single form
is sometimes killable,
and sometimes unkillable.
Since there is killing and non-killing,
form is then unfixed.
If form is unfixed, then killing is also unfixed.
Since killing is unfixed, retribution is also unfixed.
How can you say that you are certainly entering the hells (Narakas)?
“Great King!
The sinful actions performed by all sentient beings generally have two types:
one is light,
the other is heavy.
If they are committed by mind and speech,
they are called light;
if committed by body, speech, and mind,
they are called heavy.
Great King!
If one merely thinks with the mind and speaks with the mouth,
but does not act with the body,
the resulting retribution is light.
Great King!
In the past, you did not explicitly order the killing,
but only spoke of ‘scraping off the feet.’
Great King!
If you had ordered a minister to immediately execute the king’s head,
and the execution only occurred when he was seated, even that would not incur sin.
How much less so when the King did not issue the order—how can you incur sin?
If the King incurs sin,
then the Buddhas, Bhagāvats, should also incur sin.
Why is this?
Your father, the former king Bimbisāra,
frequently planted good roots through the Buddhas,
which is why he holds the royal position today.
If the Buddhas had not accepted his offerings, he would not have become king.
If he had not become king,
then you would not have inflicted harm upon the country.
If your killing of your father means you must incur sin,
then we, the Buddhas, should also have sin.
If the Buddhas, Bhagāvats,
do not have sin, how can you alone incur sin?
Great King!
Bimbisāra previously harbored evil intentions.
He was hunting deer on Mount Vipuḷa,
traversing the wilderness without any gain,
when he saw a single immortal (rṣi) who possessed the five spiritual powers (pañcābhijñā).
Seeing him, he immediately generated anger and evil intent:
‘The reason I am hunting now and getting nothing
is precisely due to this person.
Drive him out and make him leave.’
He then ordered his attendants to kill him.
When that person was near death,
he generated anger and evil intent,
lost his spiritual powers,
and made a vow:
‘I am truly innocent.
You, through mind and speech,
unjustly inflict killing and harm upon me.
In future lives, I shall likewise,
through mind and speech, harm you.’
When the King heard this,
he immediately repented
and made offerings to the corpse.
Since that King, having acted thus, still received light retribution
and did not fall into the hells;
how can you, who did not act thus,
be certain to enter the hells to receive the retribution?
The former king performed the action himself and received the consequences himself.
How could this make the King incur the sin of killing?
Regarding what you said,
that the royal father was innocent.
Great King!
How can you say ‘innocent’?
Whoever has committed sin must receive sinful retribution;
whoever has committed no evil deeds receives no sinful retribution.
If your father, the former king, was without fault or sin,
how could he have received retribution?
Bimbisāra, in his present life,
received both good consequences and evil consequences.
Therefore, the former king was also unfixed (in destiny).
Because he was unfixed, the killing is also unfixed.
Since the killing is unfixed,
how can you say that you are certainly entering the hells?”
"Great King (Dàwáng)!
Living beings commonly become deluded (or mad/frenzied) in four ways:
The first is the frenzy of greed (tānkuáng);
The second is the frenzy of drugs (yàokuáng);
The third is the frenzy of spells (zhòukuáng);
The fourth is the frenzy due to the conditioning of past karma (běnyè yuánkuáng).
Great King (Dàwáng)!
Among my disciples, if there are those affected by these four frenzies,
although they commit many wicked deeds,
I ultimately do not count that person as having violated the precepts (fànjiè).
The actions performed by such a person
do not lead to the three evil paths (sān’è),
and if they regain their proper mind,
they are also not said to have transgressed.
You, the King (Wáng), originally coveted the kingdom,
and acted treasonously, harming your royal father (fùwáng);
these acts were committed by the frenzied mind of greed (tānkuáng xīn).
How, then, can you be found guilty?
Great King (Dàwáng)!
For instance, if a person is intoxicated by alcohol (jiǔzuì),
and commits the rebellious act of harming his mother,
but once sober and awakened,
his mind generates deep remorse,
you should know that this karma also does not receive retribution.
You, the King (Wáng), were now intoxicated by greed (tānzuì);
the act was not done by your fundamental mind.
If it was not your fundamental mind,
how can you be found guilty?
Great King (Dàwáng)!
For example, a magician (huànshī),
at the head of a crossroads (sìqúdàotóu),
conjures various illusions of men and women,
elephants and horses,
necklaces (yīngluò),
and clothing.
The foolish people consider these things to be real,
but the wise know they do not truly exist.
Killing (shā) is also like this:
common mortals (fánfū) consider it real,
but all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones (Zhūfó Shìzūn), know it is not true.
Great King (Dàwáng)!
For example, the echo (xiǎngshēng) between mountains;
foolish people consider it a real sound,
but the wise know it is not true.
Killing is also like this:
common mortals consider it real,
but all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones (Zhūfó Shìzūn), know it is not true.
Great King (Dàwáng)!
For example, if a person has an enemy (yuàn),
who falsely comes to them seeking closeness,
foolish people consider them truly intimate,
but the wise, upon understanding (liǎodá), know the deceit.
Killing is also like this:
common mortals consider it real,
but all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones (Zhūfó Shìzūn), know it is not true.
Great King (Dàwáng)!
For example, a person holding a mirror (zhíjìng),
sees their own face reflection (miànxiàng).
Foolish people consider it the true face,
but the wise, upon understanding, know it is not true.
Killing is also like this:
common mortals consider it real,
but all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones (Zhūfó Shìzūn), know it is not true.
Great King (Dàwáng)!
For example, the shimmering heat (yán) during hot weather;
foolish people consider it water,
but the wise, upon understanding, know it is not water.
Killing is also like this:
common mortals consider it real,
but all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones (Zhūfó Shìzūn), know it is not true.
Great King (Dàwáng)!
For example, a Gandharva city (Qiántàpóchéng),
foolish people consider it real,
but the wise, upon understanding, know it is not true.
Killing is also like this:
common mortals consider it real,
but all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones (Zhūfó Shìzūn), know it is not true.
Great King (Dàwáng)!
For example, a person enjoying the pleasures of the five desires (wǔyù lè) in a dream;
foolish people consider them real,
but the wise, upon understanding, know they are not true.
Killing is also like this:
common mortals consider it real,
but all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones (Zhūfó Shìzūn), know it is not true."
"Great King (Dàwáng)!
The principle of killing (shāfǎ),
the karma of killing (shāyè),
the killer (shāzhě),
the consequence of killing (shāguǒ), and liberation (jiětuō)—
I comprehend all of them,
and thus I have no guilt.
Though you, the King (Wáng), know killing,
how can you be guilty?
Great King (Dàwáng)!
For example, there is a person
whose duty is to manage and know about alcohol (diǎnjiǔ);
if he does not drink it,
then he also does not become intoxicated.
Although one knows about fire (huǒ),
one is also not burnt by it.
You, the King (Wáng), are also like this:
although you know killing,
how can you be guilty?
Great King (Dàwáng)!
There are living beings
who commit various sins at the time of sunrise (rìchū shí),
and again commit robbery at the time of moonrise (yuèchū shí).
If the sun and moon do not appear, they do not commit sins;
although they are caused by the sun and moon to commit sins,
yet the sun and moon are truly not guilty.
Killing is also like this:
although it was due to you, the King (Wáng),
you, the King (Wáng), are truly without guilt.
Great King (Dàwáng)!
In the royal palace,
sheep are often commanded to be slaughtered (túyáng),
and there is initially no fear in your mind.
Why is it that regarding your father (fù),
you alone generate a fearful mind?
Although there is a difference in rank (zūnbēi chābié) between humans and animals,
valuing life and fearing death,
are the same for both.
Why is it that toward the sheep,
your mind is light and without fear?
But toward your father, the former king (xiānwáng),
you generate heavy sorrow and suffering?
Great King (Dàwáng)!
People in the world are the servants (tóngpú) of craving (ài),
unable to be independent (zìzài),
they are employed by craving,
and commit killing and harm.
If there is retribution (guǒbào), it is truly the sin of craving (àizuì).
Since you, the King (Wáng), were not independent (bù zìzài),
what fault can you bear?
Great King (Dàwáng)!
For example, Nirvāṇa (Nièpán):
it is neither existent (yǒu) nor non-existent (wú),
yet it is also considered existent.
Killing (shā) is also like this:
although it is neither existent nor non-existent,
yet it is also considered existent.
For a person possessing shame (cánkuì zhī rén), it is regarded as non-existent;
for one without shame, it is regarded as not non-existent.
For those who receive retribution, it is named existent;
for a person holding the view of emptiness (kōngjiàn zhī rén), it is regarded as non-existent.
For a person holding the view of existence (yǒujiàn zhī rén), it is regarded as not non-existent;
for those who have the view of existence, it is also named existent.
Why is this?
Because those who have the view of existence receive retribution (guǒbào);
those without the view of existence have no retribution.
For a person holding the view of permanence (chángjiàn zhī rén), it is regarded as non-existent;
for one who is without the view of permanence, it is regarded as not non-existent.
One who constantly holds the view of permanence cannot be considered non-existent.
Why is this?
Because one who constantly holds the view of permanence
possesses the fruition of evil karma (èyè guǒ).
Therefore, one who constantly holds the view of permanence
cannot be considered non-existent.
For this reason,
although it is neither existent nor non-existent,
yet it is also considered existent.
"Great King (Dàwáng)!
Living beings (zhòngshēng)
are defined by the name ‘exhalation and inhalation’ (chūrùxī).
To cut off exhalation and inhalation,
is therefore named killing (shā).
All Buddhas (Zhūfó), following convention,
also speak of it as killing.
Great King (Dàwáng)!
Form (sè) is impermanent (wúcháng);
the causes and conditions (yīnyuán) of form are also impermanent.
Born from impermanent causes,
how can form be permanent?
Similarly, consciousness (shì) is impermanent;
the causes and conditions of consciousness are also impermanent.
Born from impermanent causes,
how can consciousness be permanent?
Because of impermanence, there is suffering (kǔ);
because of suffering, there is emptiness (kōng);
because of emptiness, there is no self (wúwǒ).
If that which is impermanent,
suffering,
empty,
and selfless,
what is there to be killed?
To kill impermanence is to attain permanent Nirvāṇa (cháng Nièpán);
to kill suffering is to attain joy (lè);
to kill emptiness is to attain reality (shí);
to kill the no-self is to attain the true self (zhēnwǒ).
Great King (Dàwáng)!
If you kill impermanence,
suffering,
emptiness,
and no-self,
then you are the same as me.
I also kill impermanence,
suffering,
emptiness, and no-self,
and I do not enter Avīci Hell (Dìyù).
How can you enter it?"
At that time, [Āshèshì Wáng],
following what the Buddha taught regarding contemplating form (rūpa) up to contemplating consciousness (vijñāna),
after completing this contemplation,
immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"[Shìzūn]!
I now first realize that form is impermanent, up to consciousness is impermanent;
if I had been able to know this earlier,
I would not have committed sins.
[Shìzūn]!
I once heard in the past,
that all Buddhas, the [Shìzūn]s, constantly act as parents for sentient beings.
Although I heard this saying,
I still had not fully confirmed it,
but now I know it definitively.
[Shìzūn]!
I also once heard,
that [Xūmí Shān Wáng] (Mount Sumeru) is formed of four treasures,
namely, gold,
silver,
lapis lazuli,
and crystal;
if flocks of birds gather upon it,
they take on its color.
Although I heard this analogy,
I also had not fully confirmed it.
Now that I have come to the Buddha, who is like [Xūmí Shān],
I have taken on the same color.
To take on the same color means
to know that all phenomena are impermanent,
suffering,
empty,
and non-self.
[Shìzūn]!
I see in the world,
that the Eranda seed gives rise to the Eranda tree,
but I do not see Eranda giving rise to the [Zhāntán] tree (sandalwood tree).
Now, for the first time, I see the Eranda seed giving rise to the [Zhāntán] tree.
The Eranda seed is my body;
the [Zhāntán] tree is my mind,
which is rootless,
but faithful.
Regarding 'rootless,'
it means that initially I did not know how to venerate the Tathāgata,
did not believe in the Dharma,
or the Saṅgha.
This is called 'rootless.'
[Shìzūn]!
If I had not met the Tathāgata, the [Shìzūn],
I would have had to endure immeasurable suffering in the Great Hells for countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
now that I have seen the Buddha,
by the merit obtained through seeing the Buddha,
I have destroyed all the afflictions and evil thoughts belonging to sentient beings."
The Buddha said:
"Great King!
Excellent,
excellent!
I now know that you will surely be able to destroy the evil thoughts of sentient beings."
"[Shìzūn]!
If I can truly destroy all the evil thoughts of sentient beings,
may I perpetually remain in [Ābí Dìyù],
undergoing great suffering and distress for sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas,
and not count it as suffering."
At that time, countless people in the [Mójiātuó Guó] all generated the mind of [Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí],
because of such countless people generating this great mind,
all the heavy sins belonging to [Āshèshì Wáng] immediately became attenuated.
The King, his Queen,
and the palace ladies,
all together generated the mind of [Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí].
At that time, [Āshèshì Wáng] spoke to [Qíjípó], saying:
"[Qíjípó]!
I have obtained a celestial body even before death.
I have cast aside short life and obtained long life.
I have cast aside the impermanent body and obtained the permanent body.
To cause all sentient beings to generate the mind of [Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí],
is itself the celestial body,
long life,
and permanent body.
This is what it means to be a disciple of all the Buddhas."
Having spoken these words,
he immediately offered various jeweled banners,
pennants, canopies,
incense, flowers, necklaces,
and subtle music to make offerings to the Buddha.
Furthermore, he used verses (gāthās) to praise him, saying:
At that time, the [Shìzūn] praised [Āshèshì Wáng]:
"Excellent,
excellent!
If there is a person who can generate the Bodhi-mind,
you should know that this person adorns the great assembly of the Buddhas.
Great King!
In the past, you first generated the mind of [Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí] under [Pípóshī Fó] (Vipaśyin Buddha).
From that time until my appearance in the world,
during that entire period, you never fell into the hells to endure suffering.
Great King, you should know,
the Bodhi-mind truly possesses such immeasurable rewards.
Great King!
From now on, you must constantly diligently cultivate the Bodhi-mind.
Why is that?
Because through this condition,
you will be able to eradicate immeasurable evils."
At that time, [Āshèshì Wáng],
and the people of the entire kingdom of [Mójiātuó], rose from their seats,
circled the Buddha three times,
bade farewell, and returned to the palace.
The Chapter on [Tiānxíng Pǐn] is described in the *Záhuā* Sūtra.
"O good man!
What is called the Infant Practice (Yīng'ér Xíng)?
O good man!
Inability to arise, to abide,
to come, to go,
or to speak—
this is called an infant.
The Rúlái is also like this.
Regarding the inability to arise:
the Rúlái ultimately does not give rise to the characteristics of various phenomena.
Regarding the inability to abide:
the Rúlái does not cling to any phenomena.
Regarding the inability to come:
the bodily actions of the Rúlái have no movement or shaking.
Regarding the inability to go:
the Rúlái has already reached Dàbān Nièpán.
Regarding the inability to speak:
although the Rúlái expounds various phenomena for all sentient beings,
there is truly nothing spoken.
Why is this?
That which is spoken
is called conditioned dharma (yǒuwéi fá).
The Rúlái Shìzūn is not conditioned;
therefore, there is no speaking.
Furthermore, regarding "no speech,"
it is like an infant
whose speech is incomplete (not understood).
Although there is speech,
in reality, there is also no speech.
The Rúlái is also like this.
That which is incomplete speech
is the secret language of the Buddhas.
Although there is speaking,
sentient beings do not understand;
thus it is called "no speech."
Furthermore, regarding an infant:
names and objects do not match,
and they do not yet know correct speech.
Although names and objects do not match,
and they do not yet know correct speech,
they are not unable to recognize objects based on this.
The Rúlái is also like this.
All sentient beings belong to different categories and classes,
and their languages differ.
The Rúlái employs skillful means (fāngbiàn) to speak accordingly,
and likewise enables all beings to gain understanding through it.
Furthermore, an infant
can speak great characters.
The Rúlái is also like this,
speaking the great characters,
namely Pó Hé.
Hé means conditioned (yǒuwéi),
and Pó means unconditioned (wúwéi).
This is called the infant.
Hé is named impermanence (wúcháng),
Pó is named permanence (yǒucháng).
The Rúlái speaks of permanence.
Sentient beings, having heard this,
because of the permanent dharma,
cut off impermanence.
This is called the Infant Practice (Yīng'ér Xíng).
Furthermore, an infant
knows neither suffering nor joy,
nor day and night,
nor parents.
A Púsà Móhèsà is also like this.
For the sake of sentient beings,
they know neither suffering nor joy;
they have no concept of day and night;
towards all sentient beings, their minds are equal;
thus, there is no distinguishing characteristic of proximity or distance, such as parents.
Furthermore, an infant
cannot create great or small matters.
A Púsà Móhèsà is also like this.
A Púsà does not create the karma of cyclic existence (shēngsǐ),
this is called "non-creation."
Great matters are the five heinous crimes (wǔnì).
A Púsà Móhèsà ultimately never commits the heavy offenses of the five heinous crimes.
Small matters are the minds of the two vehicles (èrcheng).
A Púsà ultimately does not retreat from the Bodhi-mind (Pútí Xīn),
and pursue the Śràvaka (Shēngwén) or Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó) vehicles.
Furthermore, regarding the Infant Practice (Yīng'ér Xíng):
just as when an infant cries,
the parents immediately take a yellow leaf from a poplar tree,
and say to the child:
'Stop crying, stop crying.
I will give you gold.'
The infant, having seen it, develops the concept of real gold,
and stops crying.
However, this poplar leaf is truly not gold.
Wooden oxen, wooden horses,
wooden men, wooden women—
the infant, having seen them,
likewise develops the concept of men and women,
and immediately stops crying.
They are truly not men and women.
Because they form such concepts of men and women,
they are called infants.
The Rúlái is also like this.
If there are sentient beings who wish to commit various evils,
the Rúlái speaks to them of the permanence, bliss, self, and purity (cháng lè wǒ jìng) of the thirty-three heavens (Sānshísān Tiān),
of perfect form and self-indulgence,
receiving the pleasures of the five desires (wǔ yù) in marvelous palaces,
where everything encountered by the six faculties is joy.
Because sentient beings hear of such joy,
their minds generate longing for joy,
and they cease committing evil,
diligently performing the wholesome karma leading to Sānshísān Tiān.
In reality, cyclic existence (shēngsǐ) is impermanent (wúcháng),
without bliss,
without self,
and impure (wú jìng).
In order to save sentient beings,
skillful means (fāngbiàn) are used to speak of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Furthermore, regarding the infant:
when there are sentient beings weary of cyclic existence (shēngsǐ),
the Rúlái then speaks to them of the two vehicles (èrcheng).
However, in reality, there is no inherent reality of the two vehicles.
By means of the two vehicles, they recognize the fault of cyclic existence,
and perceive the bliss of Nièpán.
Because of this perception,
they are able to know for themselves:
what is cessation,
and non-cessation;
what is truth,
and non-truth;
what is practice,
and non-practice;
what is attainment,
and non-attainment.
"O good man!
Just as that infant develops the concept of gold regarding what is not gold,
the Rúlái is also like this.
Regarding what is impure (bújìng), he speaks of purity (jìng).
Because the Rúlái has attained the highest truth (Dìyī Yì), there is no falsehood.
Just as that infant,
regarding what are not oxen or horses, develops the concept of oxen or horses,
if there are sentient beings who develop the concept of the true path (zhēndào) regarding what is not the path,
the Rúlái likewise speaks of the non-path as the path.
In the midst of the non-path, there is truly no path.
However, because of the subtle causes and conditions that enable the path to arise,
he speaks of the non-path as the path.
Just as that infant develops the concept of men and women regarding wooden figures,
the Rúlái is also like this.
Knowing that there are no sentient beings (zhòngshēng), he speaks of the concept of sentient beings,
yet truly there are no characteristics of sentient beings.
If the Fó Rúlái were to say there are no sentient beings,
all sentient beings would fall into false views (xiéjiàn).
Therefore, the Rúlái speaks of the existence of sentient beings.
Those who form the concept of sentient beings among sentient beings
cannot destroy the characteristics of sentient beings.
But those who destroy the characteristics of sentient beings among sentient beings,
they are then able to attain Dàbān Nièpán.
Because they attain such Great Nièpán,
they cease crying.
This is called the Infant Practice (Yīng'ér Xíng).
O good man!
If there are men or women who accept, uphold, read, and recite,
copy, and explain these five practices,
you should know that these people will certainly attain these five practices."
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Fó:
"Shìzūn!
According to the meaning of the Fó's teaching as I understand it,
I will also certainly attain these five practices."
The Fó said:
"O good man!
Not only you will attain these five practices.
The nine hundred thirty thousand people currently in this assembly are also like you;
they will attain these five practices."
At that time, the Bhagavān addressed Guāngmíng Piānzhào Gāoguì Dé Wáng Púsà Mòhēsà, saying:
“Good man!
If there is a Púsà Mòhēsà who practices this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
they obtain ten kinds of merit and virtue,
which are not shared with Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas,
which are inconceivable,
which astonish those who hear them,
which are neither internal,
nor external,
neither difficult,
nor easy,
neither characteristic,
nor non-characteristic,
which are not worldly dharmas,
which are without appearance or form,
and are nonexistent in the world.
What are these ten?
The first item consists of five [sub-points].
What are these five?
First, they can hear what they have never heard before.
Second, having heard it, they can achieve benefit.
Third, they can sever the mind of doubt and confusion.
Fourth, the wisdom-mind is upright and without distortion.
Fifth, they can know the Tathāgata’s secret store.
These are the five matters.
What is it that is unheard of yet can be heard?
It is the extremely profound and subtle store,
namely, that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature,
that the Buddha,
the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha are without distinction,
that the nature and characteristics of the Three Jewels are permanence (cháng), bliss (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng),
that no Buddhas ultimately enter Nirvāṇa,
but abide permanently without change.
The Tathāgata’s Nirvāṇa,
is neither existence nor non-existence,
neither conditioned (samskṛta) nor unconditioned (asaṃskṛta),
neither defiled (sāsrava) nor undefiled (anāsrava),
neither form nor non-form,
neither name nor non-name,
neither characteristic nor non-characteristic,
neither possession nor non-possession,
neither substance nor non-substance,
neither cause nor effect,
neither dependent nor non-dependent,
neither light nor darkness,
neither arising nor non-arising,
neither permanent nor impermanent,
neither cut off nor not cut off,
neither beginning nor end,
neither past,
nor future,
nor present,
neither skandha nor non-skandha,
neither āyatana nor non-āyatana,
neither dhātu nor non-dhātu,
neither the twelve links of dependent origination nor not the twelve links of dependent origination.
Dharmas such as these are extremely profound and subtle;
what was previously unheard of can now be heard.
Furthermore, there are [things] unheard of,
namely, all the scriptures and books of external paths (heretics),
the four Védas (Sì Pítuó Lùn),
the Vyākaraṇa śāstra (Píjiāluó Lùn),
the Vaiśeṣika śāstra (Wèishì Shī Lùn),
the Sāṃkhya śāstra (Jiāpíluó Lùn),
all spells and incantations,
medical prescriptions,
arts and skills,
eclipses of the sun and moon,
the movements and changes of constellations,
charts, documents, prophecies, and records.
Regarding scriptures such as these, the secret meanings which were never previously heard,
are now known through this sūtra.
Furthermore, there are eleven types of scriptures,
excluding Vaipulya (Pífúlüè),
which also lack such profound and secret meaning,
but are now known because of this sūtra.
Good man!
This is called hearing what was unheard of yet being able to hear it.
“Regarding the benefit gained from having heard it:
If one is able to listen to and receive this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
they can fully know the extremely profound meaning and flavor of all Vaipulya Mahāyāna scriptures.
Just as a man or woman,
looking in a bright, clean mirror,
sees their color and form
clearly and distinctly.
The mirror of the Great Nirvāṇa is also like this;
when a Púsà holds it,
they clearly see the extremely profound meanings of the Mahāyāna scriptures.
It is also like someone in a dark room holding a great torch,
and seeing all objects clearly.
The torch of the Great Nirvāṇa is also like this;
when a Púsà holds it,
they can see the profound and mysterious meaning of the Mahāyāna.
It is also like the rising sun,
with a thousand rays of light,
which illuminates the deep darkness of all mountains
allowing everyone to see objects from afar.
The sun of pure wisdom of this Mahāparinirvāṇa is also like this;
it illuminates the deep and profound places of the Mahāyāna,
allowing people of the Two Vehicles to see the path of the Buddha from afar.
Why is this so?
Because they are able to listen to and receive this subtle and wonderful scripture, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
Good man!
If there is a Púsà Mòhēsà who listens to and receives this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
they come to know the names of all dharmas.
If they can copy it,
read, recite, and become skillful in it,
explain it widely for others,
and contemplate its meaning,
they will then know the meaning and principle of all dharmas.
Good man!
Those who listen to and receive it
only know the names,
but do not know the meaning.
If they can copy it,
uphold, read, and recite it,
explain it widely for others,
and contemplate its meaning,
they are then able to know the meaning.
Furthermore, good man!
Those who listen to this sūtra,
hear that the Buddha-nature exists,
but have not yet been able to see it.
If they copy it, read, and recite it,
explain it widely for others,
and contemplate its meaning,
they will then see it.
Those who listen to this sūtra,
hear the name Dāna,
but have not yet been able to see Dānapāramitā.
If they copy it, read, and recite it,
explain it widely for others,
and contemplate its meaning,
they will then be able to see Dānapāramitā.
This holds true even up to Prajñāpāramitā.
Good man!
If a Púsà Mòhēsà is able to listen to this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
they know the Dharma and know the meaning,
and possess the two unobstructed [knowledges].
Among all Śramaṇas
and Brāhmaṇas,
among the Devas,
Māras,
and Brahmās,
throughout all the worlds,
they attain fearlessness,
openly display and differentiate the twelve divisions of scripture (Dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana),
and expound their meanings
without error or disparity,
not having heard it from others,
but being able to know it themselves,
thus drawing near to Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Good man!
This is called having heard it,
and being able to achieve benefit.
"Regarding cutting off the doubting mind:
Doubt has two types:
First, doubting the name (terminology);
Second, doubting the meaning (principle).
Those who listen to this *jīng* [sūtra]
cut off the mind that doubts the name;
Those who contemplate the meaning
cut off the mind that doubts the meaning.
Furthermore, *Shànnánzǐ* (Good Man)!
Doubt has five types:
First, doubting whether the *Fó* (Buddha) definitely entered *Nièpán* or not?
Second, doubting whether the *Fó* is eternal and abiding (*chángzhù*) or not?
Third, doubting whether the *Fó* is true bliss (*zhēnlè*) or not?
Fourth, doubting whether the *Fó* is true purity (*zhēnjìng*) or not?
Fifth, doubting whether the *Fó* is the true Self (*shíwǒ*) or not?
Those who listen to this *jīng*,
the doubt concerning the *Fó*'s *Nièpán* will be eternally severed;
If they copy, read, and recite it,
extensively preach it to others,
and contemplate its meaning,
the four remaining doubts will be eternally severed.
Furthermore, *Shànnánzǐ*!
Doubt has three types:
First, doubting whether the *Shēngwén* (Hearers) exist
or not?
Second, doubting whether the *Yuánjué* (Pratyekabuddhas) exist
or not?
Third, doubting whether the *Fóchéng* (Buddha Vehicle) exists
or not?
Those who listen to this *jīng*,
these three doubts will be eternally extinguished without remainder;
If they copy, read, and recite it,
extensively preach it to others,
and contemplate its meaning,
they will then clearly know that all sentient beings completely possess the *Fóxìng* (Buddha Nature).
Furthermore, *Shànnánzǐ*!
If there are sentient beings who have not heard such a great *Nièpán Jīng*,
their minds are full of doubts,
namely, whether there is permanence (*cháng*)
or impermanence (*wúcháng*);
whether there is bliss (*lè*)
or non-bliss;
whether there is purity (*jìng*)
or impurity;
whether there is self (*wǒ*)
or non-self (*wúwǒ*);
whether there is life (*mìng*)
or non-life;
whether there are sentient beings (*zhòngshēng*)
or non-sentient beings;
whether there is ultimacy (*bìjìng*)
or non-ultimacy;
whether there is the next world (*tāshì*)
or the past world;
whether there is existence (*yǒu*)
or non-existence (*wú*);
whether there is suffering (*kǔ*)
or non-suffering;
whether there is accumulation (*jí*)
or non-accumulation;
whether there is the path (*dào*)
or non-path;
whether there is extinction (*miè*)
or non-extinction;
whether there is dharma (*fǎ*)
or non-dharma;
whether there is good (*shàn*)
or non-good;
whether there is emptiness (*kōng*)
or non-emptiness.
Those who listen to this *jīng*,
all such doubts will be eternally severed.
Furthermore, *Shànnánzǐ*!
If there are those who have not heard this *jīng*,
they will also have various numerous doubts,
namely, is form (*sè*) the Self?
Are sensation (*shòu*), perception (*xiǎng*), volition (*xíng*), and consciousness (*shì*) the Self?
Can the eye see?
Can the Self see?
Likewise, can consciousness know?
Can the Self know?
Does form receive retribution?
Does the Self receive retribution?
Likewise, does consciousness receive retribution?
Does the Self receive retribution?
Does form go to the next world?
Does the Self go to the next world?
Likewise, consciousness is also the same.
Do the laws of transmigration (*shēngsǐ*) have a beginning and an end?
Or do they have neither a beginning nor an end?
Those who listen to this *jīng*,
such doubts will also be eternally severed.
Furthermore, some people doubt whether
*Icchanti* people,
who violate the four major prohibitions (*sìzhòngjìn*),
commit the five heinous crimes (*wǔnìzuì*),
and slander the *Fāngděng Jīng* [Vaipulya Sūtras]—
do such groups possess the *Fóxìng*?
Or do they lack the *Fóxìng*?
Those who listen to this *jīng*,
such doubts will all be eternally severed.
Furthermore, some people doubt:
Does the world have limits?
Is the world limitless?
Are there worlds in the ten directions?
Are there no worlds in the ten directions?
Those who listen to this *jīng*,
such doubts will also be eternally severed.
This is called the mind capable of cutting off confusion and doubt.
"Regarding the mind of wisdom that is upright and without perversity:
If the mind has doubt,
then its views are not correct.
If all common people (*fánfū*) do not hear this great and subtle *Nièpán* classic,
their views are perverse and distorted,
extending even to the *Shēngwén* and *Pìzhīfó* (Pratyekabuddha) persons,
whose views are also distorted.
How are the views of all common people called perverse and distorted?
They see permanence (*cháng*), bliss (*lè*), self (*wǒ*), and purity (*jìng*) in that which is defiled (*yǒulòu*);
And regarding the *Rúlái* (Tathāgata),
they see impermanence,
suffering,
impurity,
and non-self;
They see existence of sentient beings,
life span,
knowledge and views;
They take the state of neither perception nor non-perception (*fēi yǒuxiǎng fēi wúxiǎng chù*)
to be *Nièpán*;
They see the eight noble paths (*bāshèngdào*) in *Zìzàitiān* (Īśvara/Maheśvara);
They hold the view of existence (*yǒujiàn*)
and the view of annihilation (*duànjiàn*).
Views such as these
are called perverse and distorted.
If the *Púsà Móhēsà* (Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas) hear this great *Nièpán Jīng*,
and practice the sacred conduct (*shèngxíng*),
they will then be able to cut off such perversities and distortions.
How are the distorted views of the *Shēngwén* and *Yuánjué* called perverse?
They see the *Púsà* descending from *Dōushuài* (Tuṣita Heaven),
transforming and riding a white elephant,
casting his spirit into his mother's womb.
The father's name was *Jìngfàn* (Śuddhodana),
and the mother was called *Móyé* (Māyā).
He was born in *Jiāpíluó* City (Kapilavastu) after fully abiding in the womb for ten months.
Before the newborn reached the ground,
*Dìshì* (Śakra) received him by holding him up.
*Nántuó Lóngwáng* (Nanda Dragon King) and *Pónántuó* (Upananda) spat water to bathe him.
*Móníbátuó* (Maṇibhadra), the great spirit king (*guǐshén wáng*), held a precious canopy
and stood waiting behind him.
The Earth Spirit materialized flowers to support his feet.
He walked seven full steps in each of the four directions.
Upon arriving at the Celestial Temple,
he caused all the celestial statues to rise up and receive him.
*Āsītuó Xiān* (Asita the hermit) embraced and examined his characteristics.
After examining the characteristics,
he gave rise to great sorrow and pain,
lamenting that he would die and not witness the flourishing of the *Fó*.
He went to a teacher to study writing,
reckoning and calculation,
archery and charioteering (*shèyù*),
divination charts (*túchèn*),
and arts and crafts.
He dwelled in the inner palace,
enjoying pleasures entertained by sixty thousand concubines (*cǎinǚ*).
He left the city to stroll and observe, reaching the *Jiāpíluó* Garden.
On the road, he saw an old man, and eventually, a *shāmén* (śramaṇa) walking in religious robes.
Returning to the palace, he saw the physical appearance and forms of the concubines
resembling withered bones,
and all the palaces were no different from graves.
Disgusted, he renounced home life (*chūjiā*) and leaped over the city wall at midnight,
reaching the great hermits, such as *Yùtuógā* (Udraka Rāmaputra)
and *Āluólà* (Āḷāra Kālāma).
He heard them speak of the realm of consciousness (*shíchù*) and the realm of neither perception nor non-perception (*fēi yǒuxiǎng fēi wúxiǎng chù*).
After hearing this,
he carefully observed these realms,
[realizing] they were impermanent,
suffering,
impure,
and non-self.
Abandoning them, he went beneath a tree
and fully practiced asceticism (*kǔxíng*) for six years.
Knowing that this ascetic practice could not lead to the attainment of *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí* (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi),
he then went again to bathe in the *Ālìbátí* River (Nairaňjanā),
and accepted the milk porridge (*rǔméi*) offered by the cowherd woman.
Having accepted it, he proceeded to the *Pútíshù* (Bodhi Tree),
defeated *Mó Bōxún* (Māra Papiyas), and attained *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*.
In *Bōluónài* (Vārāṇasī), he first turned the Wheel of Dharma for the five *Bǐqiū* (bhikṣus),
and finally, in this *Jūshīnà* City (Kuśinagara), he entered *Bōnièpán* (Parinirvāṇa).
Views such as these
are called the distorted views of the *Shēngwén* and *Yuánjué*.
*Shànnánzǐ*!
The *Púsà Móhēsà* who listen to and accept this great *Nièpán Jīng*
will completely cut off views such as these;
If they are capable of copying,
reading, reciting, and mastering it,
explaining it to others,
and contemplating its meaning,
they will attain correct and upright views without perversity or distortion.
"Shànnánzǐ!
When the Púsà Móhēsà cultivates this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
knowing truly that the Púsà, for immeasurable kalpas,
did not descend from Dōulǜ to enter a mother's womb,
nor did he enter parinirvāṇa in the city of Jūshīnà,
this is called the correct view of the Púsà Móhēsà.
That which can know the profound secret meaning of the Rúlái
is what is called the Great Parinirvāṇa:
all sentient beings universally possess the Buddha nature (Fóxìng);
repenting the Four Grave Prohibitions (Sìzhòngjìn),
eliminating the mind that slanders the Dharma (Bàngfǎxīn),
exhausting the Five Heinous Sins (Wǔnìzuì),
and annihilating the Icchantika (Yīchǎntí),
after which one attains Anouduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
This is called the meaning of the extremely profound secret.
Furthermore, Shànnánzǐ!
What is again called the meaning of the extremely profound?
Although one knows that sentient beings truly possess no self (wúwǒ),
yet in the future they do not lose the fruit of karma (yèguǒ);
although one knows that the Five Skandhas (Wǔyīn) are extinguished here,
good and evil karma never perishes or disappears;
although there is karma (yè), there is no agent (zuòzhě);
although there is a destination, there is no one who goes (qùzhě);
although there is bondage (xìfù), there is no one who receives the bondage;
although there is Nièpán, there is no one who is extinguished.
This is called the meaning of the extremely profound secret.
At that time, Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng Púsà Móhēsà said to the Buddha:
"Shìzūn!
As I understand the meaning of 'hearing the unheard'
that the Buddha spoke of,
this meaning is incorrect.
Why is that?
If a phenomenon (fǎ) exists, then it must definitely exist;
if a phenomenon does not exist, then it must definitely not exist.
Non-existence should not arise,
and existence should not cease.
If something is heard, it is hearing;
if something is not heard, it is not hearing.
How can one say 'to hear the unheard'?
Shìzūn!
If something is unable to be heard, it is the unheard;
if one has already heard something, then one does not hear it again.
Why is that?
Because it has already been heard.
How can one say 'to hear the unheard'?
It is like one who goes:
having arrived, one does not go;
if one goes, one has not arrived.
It is also like: having arisen, it does not arise;
not arisen, it does not arise.
Having attained, one does not attain;
not attaining, one does not attain.
Having heard, one does not hear;
not hearing, one does not hear—it is also like this.
Shìzūn!
If 'the unheard' is heard,
all sentient beings who have not yet attained Bodhi (Pútí) should possess it immediately;
those who have not attained Nièpán should also attain it;
those who have not seen the Fóxìng should see the Fóxìng.
How can it be said again that the Púsà of the Ten Stages (Shízhù Púsà), although they see the Fóxìng, have not attained clarity?
Shìzūn!
If 'the unheard' is heard,
from whom did the Rúlái hear it in the past?
If you say he did hear it,
why did the Rúlái again say he had no teacher (wúshī) in the Āhán (Āgamas)?
If ‘not hearing’ is ‘not hearing,’
and the Rúlái attained Anouduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
then all sentient beings who 'not hear' should
also be able to attain Anouduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
If the Rúlái, by not hearing this Great Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, saw the Fóxìng,
then all sentient beings who do not hear this sūtra should also be able to see it.
Shìzūn!
Generally, concerning form (sè),
sometimes it is visible,
and sometimes it is invisible.
Sound (shēng) is also like this:
sometimes it is audible,
and sometimes it is inaudible.
This Great Nièpán is neither form nor sound.
How can it be said that it can be seen or heard?
Shìzūn!
The past, having ceased, cannot be heard.
The future, not having arrived, also cannot be heard.
The present, while listening, is not yet called 'heard' (Wén);
once heard, the sound ceases and cannot be heard again.
This Great Nièpán is also neither past,
future,
nor present.
If it is not the Three Times (Sānshì),
then it cannot be spoken of;
if it cannot be spoken of, then it cannot be heard.
How can it be said that the Púsà, cultivating this Great Nièpán Sūtra,
hears the unheard?"
At that time, the Shìzūn praised Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng Púsà Móhēsà, saying:
"Excellent!
Excellent!
Shànnánzǐ!
You now correctly know that all phenomena (zhūfǎ)
are like illusions (rǔhuàn), like mirages (rǔyàn),
like a city of the Gandharvas (Qiántàpóchéng),
like traces drawn on water,
and also like foam
or a plantain tree: empty and without substance.
They are neither life (mìng) nor self (wǒ),
and are without suffering or joy,
just as the Púsà of the Ten Stages knows and perceives."
Suddenly, in the great assembly, there was a great light:
not blue, yet seeing blue;
not yellow, yet seeing yellow;
not red, yet seeing red;
not white, yet seeing white;
not color, yet seeing color;
not brightness, yet seeing brightness;
not seeing, yet seeing.
At that time, when the great assembly encountered this light,
their bodies and minds were happy,
like a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) entering the Lion King Samādhi (Shīzǐwáng Dìng).
At that time, Wénshūshīlì Púsà Móhēsà said to the Buddha:
"Shìzūn!
Who emitted this current light?"
At that time, the Rúlái remained silent and did not speak.
Jiāshè Púsà again asked Wénshūshīlì:
"For what reason
is there this light shining upon the great assembly?"
Wénshūshīlì remained silent and did not answer.
At that time, Wúbiānshēn Púsà again asked Jiāshè Púsà:
"Whose possession is this current light?"
Jiāshè Púsà remained silent and did not speak.
Jìngzhù Wángzǐ Púsà again asked Wúbiānshēn Púsà:
"For what reason
is this light present in the great assembly?"
Wúbiānshēn Púsà remained silent and did not speak.
Likewise, five hundred Púsàs were all like this:
although they questioned each other, none answered.
At that time, the Shìzūn asked Wénshūshīlì, saying:
"Wénshūshīlì!
For what reason
is this light present in the great assembly?"
Wénshūshīlì said:
"Shìzūn!
This light is called Wisdom (Zhìhuì).
Wisdom is Eternal Abidance (Chángzhù).
The Dharma of Eternal Abidance has no cause or condition (yīnyuán).
How can the Buddha ask for what cause or condition this light exists?
This light is called Great Nièpán.
Great Nièpán is called Eternal Abidance.
The Dharma of Eternal Abidance does not come from causes or conditions.
How can the Buddha ask for what cause or condition this light exists?
This light is the Rúlái.
The Rúlái is Eternal Abidance.
The Dharma of Eternal Abidance does not come from causes or conditions.
How can the Rúlái ask about causes or conditions?
Light is called Great Loving-Kindness and Great Compassion (Dàcí Dàbēi).
Great Loving-Kindness and Great Compassion is called Eternal Abidance.
The Dharma of Eternal Abidance does not come from causes or conditions.
How can the Rúlái ask about causes or conditions?
Light is the recollection of the Buddha (Niànfó).
The recollection of the Buddha is called Eternal Abidance.
The Dharma of Eternal Abidance does not come from causes or conditions.
How can the Rúlái ask about causes or conditions?
Light is the non-common path of all Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué).
The non-common path of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is called Eternal Abidance.
The Dharma of Eternal Abidance does not come from causes or conditions.
How can the Rúlái ask about causes or conditions?
Shìzūn!
There are also causes and conditions.
Because of extinguishing ignorance (wúmíng), one gains the brightly burning lamp of Anouduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí."
The Buddha said:
"Wénshūshīlì!
You should not now enter the extremely profound Ultimate Truth (Dìyī Yìdì) of all phenomena.
You should explain it using Conventional Truth (Shìdì)."
Wénshūshīlì said:
"World-Honored One!
Passing eastward from here through worlds equal in number to twenty times the sands of the Ganges,
there is a Buddha-world named Búdòng,
the dwelling place of that Buddha,
whose length and width are exactly twelve thousand Yóuxún,
its ground is made of the seven treasures,
without earth or stones,
level, smooth, and soft, without any ditches or pits,
its trees are formed of four treasures:
gold,
silver,
lapis lazuli (liúlí), and crystal (pōlí).
Flowers and fruits flourish and are present at all times.
If any sentient being smells their fragrance,
their body and mind become peaceful and blissful,
just like a Bhikṣu entering the third Dhyāna.
Moreover, there are three thousand great rivers surrounding it,
their water is subtle and wondrous,
possessing the eight excellent qualities (flavors).
If any sentient being bathes in them,
the joy and pleasure obtained,
is like a Bhikṣu entering the second Dhyāna.
Those rivers contain numerous kinds of flowers:
Utpala flowers (yōubōluóhuā),
Padmas flowers (bōtóumóhuā),
Kumudas flowers (jūwùtóuhuā),
Puṇḍarīka flowers (fēntuólìhuā),
fragrant flowers,
great fragrant flowers,
subtle fragrant flowers,
constant flowers,
and flowers which shield and protect all sentient beings.
The two banks of the rivers also have various flowers,
namely, Atimuktaka flowers (ātímùduōgāhuā),
Campaka flowers (zhànbōhuā),
Pāṭala flowers (bōzhàluóhuā),
Vāśirā flowers (póshīluóhuā),
Mallikā flowers (mólìgāhuā),
great Mallikā flowers (dà mólìgāhuā),
new Mallikā flowers (xīn mólìgāhuā),
Sumanaka flowers (xūmónàgāhuā),
Yūthikā flowers (yóutígāhuā),
Dhānukarī flowers (tánnǔgālìhuā),
constant flowers,
and flowers which shield and protect all sentient beings.
Golden sand covers the bottom.
There are four flights of steps (tījié),
made of gold,
silver,
lapis lazuli (liúlí),
and variegated crystal (pōlí).
Numerous flocks of birds gather and play above them.
Moreover, countless tigers, wolves,
lions (shīzǐ),
and various evil birds and beasts,
look upon each other in their hearts,
just like newborn infants.
In that world, there is absolutely no one who commits grievous transgressions,
slanders the Right Dharma, or commits sins like Icchantikas (yīchǎntí) or the five heinous crimes (wǔnì).
That land is harmonious,
without cold or heat,
hunger or thirst,
or suffering and distress.
There is no greed (tān),
desire (yù),
hatred (huì),
negligence (fàngyì),
or jealousy (jídù).
There is no sun or moon,
day or night,
or seasonal changes,
just like the second heaven of Trāyastriṃśa (Dāolì Tiānshàng).
The people of that land equally possess radiance,
and none of them possess an arrogant mind.
All of them are Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas (Púsà Dàshì),
all having attained spiritual powers and great merit and virtue.
