Their hearts all deeply revere the Right Dharma,
relying on the Mahāyāna (Dàchéng),
loving and cherishing the Mahāyāna,
craving pleasure in the Mahāyāna,
guarding and valuing the Mahāyāna.
They have achieved great wisdom and attained great Dhāraṇī (zǒngchí),
and their minds constantly feel compassion for all sentient beings.
That Buddha is named Mǎnyuè Guāngmíng Rúlái (Full Moon Bright Radiance Tathāgata),
Worthy of Offerings (Yìnggōng),
Perfectly and Universally Knowing (Zhèngbiànzhī),
Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct (Míngxíngzú),
Well Gone (Shànshì),
Knower of the World (Shìjiānjiě),
Unsurpassed One (Wúshàngshì),
Tamer of Men (Diàoyù Zhàngfu),
Teacher of Gods and Humans (Tiānrénshī),
Buddha (Fó),
World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
Wherever he dwells,
and whatever he expounds,
the sentient beings in that land,
all are able to hear him expound the Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán Jīng) for Liúlí Guāng Púsà Móhēsà.
The Buddha said:
"Good men!
If Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas are able to practice the Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa,
everything they have not yet heard, they shall now hear.
That Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Liúlí Guāng asked Mǎnyuè Guāngmíng Fó,
just as Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Dé Wáng Púsà Móhēsà here has asked,
equally, without difference.
That Mǎnyuè Guāngmíng Fó immediately addressed Bodhisattva Liúlí Guāng, saying:
'Good man!
Westward from here, past twenty times the sands of the Ganges of Buddha-lands,
there is a world named Suōpó (Sahā),
that land has many mountains, hills,
mounds,
dirt, sand, gravel, and stones,
and is fully covered with thorny bushes and poisonous spines.
[This is continuation]
There is constant hunger, thirst,
cold, heat, suffering, and distress.
The people of that land
are unable to respect Śramaṇas (Shāmén),
Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén),
parents, teachers, or elders.
They cling greedily to unrighteousness,
desire unrighteousness,
practice evil dharma,
and do not believe the Right Dharma.
Their lifespans are short.
They are ruled by kings who engage in treachery and deceit.
Although the kings possess the kingdom, they know no satisfaction,
giving rise to thoughts of greed for gain regarding the possessions of others.
They raise armies to attack each other, and the wrongfully deceased are numerous.
Since the kings practice such unrighteous dharmas,
the benevolent gods of the four heavens feel no joy in their hearts,
thus they send down calamities and droughts.
Grain and rice do not ripen,
the people suffer from many illnesses,
and their suffering and distress are immeasurable.
There is a Buddha dwelling there,
named Shìjiāmóuní Rúlái (Śākyamuni Tathāgata),
Worthy of Offerings (Yìnggōng),
Perfectly and Universally Knowing (Zhèngbiànzhī),
Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct (Míngxíngzú),
Well Gone (Shànshì),
Knower of the World (Shìjiānjiě),
Unsurpassed One (Wúshàngshì),
Tamer of Men (Diàoyù Zhàngfu),
Teacher of Gods and Humans (Tiānrénshī),
Buddha (Fó),
World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
His great compassion is pure and profound,
and for the sake of pitying sentient beings,
in Kūshīna Chéng (Kuśinagara City), between the twin Śāla trees,
he is expounding this great Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa for the great assembly.
There is a Bodhisattva there,
named Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Dé Wáng,
who has already asked about this matter,
exactly as you have.
The Buddha is now answering him,
you should go quickly,
and you will surely be able to hear it.'
"World-Honored One!
When that Bodhisattva Liúlí Guāng heard this matter,
wishing to come here with eighty-four thousand Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas,
he therefore first manifested an auspicious sign.
Due to this cause and condition,
there is this bright radiance.
This is called the cause and condition,
and also the non-cause and non-condition."
At that time, Bodhisattva Liúlí Guāng, accompanied by eighty-four thousand Bodhisattvas,
carrying various banners and canopies,
fragrant flowers and necklaces (yīngluò),
and all kinds of musical instruments,
far superior to what was previously seen,
came together to Kūshīna Chéng (Kuśinagara City), between the twin Śāla trees.
Using the implements of offering they carried, they made offerings to the Buddha.
They bowed their heads to his feet,
pressed their palms together in reverence,
circumambulated three times clockwise.
Having completed their respectful rites,
they withdrew and sat down on one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked that Bodhisattva:
"Good man!
Have you arrived,
or have you not arrived?"
Líulíguāng Púsà said:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
Reached, yet not coming;
unreached, yet also not coming.
I observe this principle: there is entirely no coming.
Shìzūn!
If all conditioned phenomena (zhū xíng) are permanent (cháng),
they likewise do not come;
if they are impermanent (wúcháng), there is also no coming.
If a person sees that living beings possess inherent nature,
there is coming
and non-coming;
I now do not perceive the fixed nature of living beings,
how then can one speak of coming
and non-coming?
Those who possess arrogance (jiāomàn) see going and coming;
those without arrogance see no going and coming.
Those who possess attachment/clinging (qǔ xíng) see going and coming;
those without attachment see no going and coming.
If one sees the Tathāgata (Rúlái) in final Nirvāṇa (nièpán), then there is going and coming;
if one does not see the Rúlái in final Nièpán, then there is no going and coming.
If one has not heard of the Buddha-nature (fóxìng), then there is going and coming;
if one has heard of the Fóxìng, then there is no going and coming.
If one sees Śrāvakas (shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (pìzhīfó rén) as having attained Nièpán, then there is going and coming;
if one does not see Śēngwén and Pìzhīfó rén as having attained Nièpán, then there is no going and coming.
If one sees Śēngwén and Pìzhīfó rén as possessing permanence, bliss, self, and purity (cháng lè wǒ jìng), then there is going and coming;
if one does not see this, then there is no going and coming.
If one sees the Rúlái as lacking permanence, bliss, self, and purity (wúcháng lè wǒ jìng), then there is going and coming;
if one sees the Rúlái as possessing permanence, bliss, self, and purity (cháng lè wǒ jìng), then there is no going and coming.
Shìzūn!
Let us set aside this matter for now;
I have something I wish to ask.
I only beg you to bestow compassion (āimǐn),
and grant me permission for a little while."
The Buddha said:
“Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Ask whatever you wish.
Now is precisely the time.
I shall fully explain and expound upon it for you.
Why is this?
Buddhas (Zhū Fó) are hard to encounter,
like the Udumbara flower (Yōután Huā).
The Dharma (Fǎ) is also difficult to hear, just like this.
Among the Twelve Categories of Scriptures (shí'èr bù jīng), the Vaipulya (fāngděng) teachings are even harder [to encounter].
Therefore, you should listen and receive with single-minded attention.”
At that time, Líulíguāng Púsà Mahāsattva (Móhēsà),
having received both permission and exhortation,
immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Shìzūn!
How can a Púsà Móhēsà practice the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Nièpán Jīng) by hearing what has not been heard?”
Thereupon, the Rúlái praised him, saying:
“Excellent!
Excellent!
Shànnánzǐ!
You now wish to penetrate this great ocean of the Mahāyāna (Dàshèng) and Dà Nièpán.
You happen to have met me, who can skillfully explain it.
All the nets of doubt (yí wǎng) you now possess,
and poisoned arrows (dú zú),
I, being the great physician,
can skillfully extract them.
Since you are still unclear about the Fóxìng,
I possess the torch of wisdom (huì jù)
and can illuminate it for you.
You now wish to cross the great river of Saṃsāra (shēngsǐ),
I can be the great boatman for you.
You generate the thought of father and mother towards me;
I likewise generate the heart of a newborn child towards you.
Your heart now seeks the treasure of the True Dharma (Zhèngfǎ Bǎo).
Having met me, I am able to bestow it upon you abundantly.
Listen closely!
Listen closely!
Ponder it carefully!
I shall expound and explain it specifically for you.
Shànnánzǐ!
If you wish to hear the Dharma,
now is precisely the time.
Once you have heard the Dharma,
you should generate reverence and faith (jìngxìn),
listen and receive it with utmost sincerity, and regard it with respect and veneration.
Do not seek fault in the True Dharma.
Do not dwell on covetousness (tānyù),
anger (chēnhuì),
or ignorance (yúchī).
Do not observe the lineage or the good or bad qualities of the Dharma Master (Fǎshī).
Having heard the Dharma, do not give rise to arrogance.
Do not act for the sake of reverence,
fame,
or material gain (lìyǎng).
You should act for the sake of the benefit of the ambrosial Dharma (gānlù fǎ lì) that saves the world.
Furthermore, do not generate the thought:
'After I have heard the Dharma, I shall first save myself and then save others;
first liberate myself and then liberate others;
first bring peace to myself and then bring peace to others;
first attain Nièpán myself and then enable others to attain Nièpán.'
Regarding the Buddha (Fó),
the Dharma (Fǎ),
and the Saṅgha (Sēng),
you should generate the thought of equality.
Regarding Saṃsāra, generate the thought of great suffering.
Regarding Dà Nièpán, you should generate the thought of permanence, bliss, self, and purity (cháng lè wǒ jìng).
Act first for others,
and only then for yourself.
You should act for the Dàshèng, and not for the Two Vehicles (Èrshèng).
You should abide nowhere in all dharmas (yīqiè fǎ).
Also, do not exclusively cling to the marks (xiāng) of all yīqiè fǎ.
Among all phenomena, do not generate the mark of craving (tān xiāng).
Always generate the mark of knowing the Dharma
and seeing the Dharma.
Shànnánzǐ!
If you can listen to the Dharma with utmost sincerity in this manner,
this is then called 'hearing what has not been heard.'
“Shànnánzǐ!
There is the un-heard hearing;
there is the un-heard un-hearing;
there is the heard un-hearing;
there is the heard hearing.
Shànnánzǐ!
It is like the un-born birth;
the un-born un-birth;
the born un-birth;
and the born birth.
It is like the un-reached reaching;
the un-reached un-reaching;
the reached un-reaching;
and the reached reaching.”
“Shìzūn!
What is the un-born birth?”
“Shànnánzǐ!
Abiding in conventional truth (shìdì),
the moment one first exits the womb,
this is called the un-born birth.
What is the un-born un-birth?
Shànnánzǐ!
The Great Nièpán has no mark of birth;
this is called the un-born un-birth.
What is the born un-birth?
Shànnánzǐ!
In conventional truth, the moment of death is called the born un-birth.
What is the born birth?
Shànnánzǐ!
All ordinary beings (fánfū) are called the born birth.
Why is this?
Because birth after birth is not interrupted.
Because all defiled phenomena (yǒulòu) are born moment by moment,
this is called the born birth.
Púsàs in the Four Abodes (Sì Zhù Púsà) are called the born un-birth.
Why is this?
Because their birth is sovereign/autonomous (zìzài).
This is called the born un-birth.
Shànnánzǐ!
This is called the Internal Dharma (Nèifǎ).
What is the External Dharma (Wàifǎ)?
The un-born birth;
the un-born un-birth;
the born un-birth;
and the born birth.
Shànnánzǐ!
For example, a seed:
when it has not yet produced a sprout,
and obtains the harmonious union of the Four Great Elements (sì dà héhé),
and the effort of human action,
only then does it come into being.
This is called the un-born birth.
What is the un-born un-birth?
For example, a rotten seed or one that has not met the conditions (yuán).
Those of this kind
are called the un-born un-birth.
What is the born un-birth?
It is like a sprout that has been born but does not grow.
This is called the born un-birth.
What is the born birth?
It is like the growth of the sprout.
If there were the born un-birth, there would be no growth.
In this manner, all yǒulòu phenomena
are called the External Dharma born birth.”
Líulíguāng Púsà Móhēsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Shìzūn!
If defiled phenomena (yǒulòu zhī fǎ) possess birth,
is this birth permanent (cháng)?
Or is it impermanent (wúcháng)?
If birth is permanent,
then the yǒulòu zhī fǎ cannot have birth.
If birth is impermanent,
then the yǒulòu [phenomena] would be permanent.
Shìzūn!
If birth is capable of giving rise to itself,
then birth has no inherent nature (zìxìng).
If it is capable of giving rise to others,
then for what cause and condition (yīnyuán) does it not give rise to undefiled phenomena (wúlòu)?
Shìzūn!
If birth exists when [the object] is not yet born,
how is it that only now is it called birth?
If birth does not exist when [the object] is not yet born,
why do we not say that empty space (xūkōng) is birth?”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent,
excellent!
O good man!
Birth of the unborn cannot be spoken of,
birth of the born also cannot be spoken of,
unbirth of the born also cannot be spoken of,
unbirth of the unborn also cannot be spoken of,
birth also cannot be spoken of,
unbirth also cannot be spoken of.
But because there are causal conditions (yīnyuán),
they can also be spoken of.
How is it that the birth of the unborn cannot be spoken of?
The unborn is named 'birth'—
how can it be spoken of?
Why?
Because of its inherent birth.
How is it that the birth of the born cannot be spoken of?
The born is born because of birth,
the born is unborn because of birth,
therefore it also cannot be spoken of.
How is it that the unbirth of the born cannot be spoken of?
Birth is immediately named 'birth',
but birth does not give birth to itself,
thus it cannot be spoken of.
How is it that the unbirth of the unborn cannot be spoken of?
That which is unborn is named Nièpán,
Nièpán does not give birth, thus it cannot be spoken of!
Why?
Because it is obtained through cultivation of the path (dào).
How is it that birth also cannot be spoken of?
Because birth is nonexistent.
How is it that unbirth cannot be spoken of?
Because it is something attained.
How is it that because there are causal conditions (yīnyuán) it can also be spoken of?
The Dharma of the Ten Causal Conditions (shí yīnyuán fă) acts as the cause for birth.
Based on this meaning,
it also can be spoken of.
O good man!
Do not now enter into the extremely deep emptiness concentration (kōngdìng).
Why?
Because the great assembly is dull.
O good man!
For conditioned phenomena (yǒuwéi zhī fă), birth is also permanent,
but because dwelling is impermanent,
birth is also impermanent;
dwelling is also permanent,
but because of the arising of birth,
dwelling is also impermanent;
alteration is also permanent,
but because the Dharma is impermanent,
alteration is also impermanent;
destruction is also permanent,
but because it was originally non-existent and is now existent,
destruction is also impermanent.
O good man!
Based on nature (xìng), birth,
dwelling,
alteration,
and destruction are all certainly permanent,
but because they are annihilated moment by moment, they cannot be called permanent.
Because this great Nièpán can cut off and extinguish them,
therefore it is named 'impermanent.'
O good man!
When defiled phenomena (yǒulòu zhī fă) have not yet arisen,
they already possess the nature of arising (shēngxìng),
thus birth is able to produce them.
Undefiled phenomena (wúlòu zhī fă) originally lack the nature of arising,
therefore birth is unable to produce them.
Just as fire has an inherent nature,
when it meets conditions, it ignites.
The eye has the nature of seeing;
because of form (sè),
because of light (míng),
and because of mind (xīn), it sees.
The arising of sentient beings
is also like this:
due to an inherent nature,
meeting the causal conditions of karma (yè yīnyuán),
and the union of parents,
then there is birth.
At that time, Liúlíguāng Púsà Móhēsà, together with eighty-four thousand Púsà Móhēsàs,
having heard this Dharma,
leaped into the void,
seven tàluó trees high,
respectfully joined their palms,
and spoke to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
Having received the Tathāgata's (Rúlái) diligent instruction,
through the Great Nièpán, we have finally attained enlightenment and understanding,
hearing what was previously unheard.
It has also allowed eighty-four thousand Púsàs to deeply understand all dharmas,
such as the birth of the unborn, and so forth.
World-Honored One!
We have now understood,
cutting off the net of all doubts.
However, among this assembly, there is one Púsà
named Wúwèi,
who further wishes to consult and petition;
we humbly request your kind permission to listen."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Wúwèi Púsà:
"O good man!
Question me freely,
and I will explain and distinguish the meaning for you."
At that time, Wúwèi Púsà, along with sixty-four thousand Púsàs,
rose together from their seats,
rearranged their robes,
knelt down with joined palms, and spoke to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What karma (yè) must the sentient beings of this land perform
to be born in that Immovable World (Búdòng Shìjiè)?
How do the Púsàs in that land attain the perfection of wisdom,
become Elephant Kings among men,
possess great majesty and virtue (wēidé),
completely cultivate all practices (xíng),
have sharp, quick intelligence,
and understand as soon as they hear?
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately spoke a verse (jì), saying:
At that time, Wúwèi Púsà Móhēsà spoke to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I now know the karmic conditions (yè yuán) that must be created to be born in that land.
This Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng Púsà Móhēsà,
universally pitying all sentient beings,
had previously made an inquiry.
If the Tathāgata (Rúlái) speaks on it,
it will benefit
and bring peace and joy to
humans (rén),
devas (tiān),
Asúluó,
Gāntàpó,
Jiālóuluó,
Jǐnnàluó,
Móhóuluójiā, and others."
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately addressed the Bodhisattva Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng:
“Excellent,
excellent!
O good man!
You should now listen attentively to this;
I will analyze and explain it for you.
There are causes and conditions why
that which has not arrived does not arrive.
There are causes and conditions why
that which has not arrived arrives.
There are causes and conditions why
that which has arrived does not arrive.
There are causes and conditions why
that which has arrived arrives.
What causes and conditions lead to that which has not arrived not arriving?
O good man!
That which does not arrive is Great Nirvāṇa.
Common mortals have not arrived
because they possess greed,
anger,
and ignorance;
because their bodily actions
and verbal actions are impure;
and because they accept all impure things;
because they violate the four major prohibitions (sìchóng);
because they slander the Vaipulya (fāngděng) teachings;
because they are Icchantika (yīchǎntí);
because they commit the five heinous sins (wǔnì zuì).
For these reasons,
that which has not arrived does not arrive.
O good man!
What causes and conditions lead to that which has not arrived arriving?
That which has not arrived is named Great Nirvāṇa.
For what reason does it arrive?
Because they eternally cease greed, anger, ignorance, and evil bodily and verbal actions;
because they do not accept all impure things;
because they do not violate the four major prohibitions;
because they do not slander the Vaipulya sūtras;
because they do not act as Icchantika;
because they do not commit the five heinous sins.
For these reasons,
it is named that which has not arrived arriving.
A Śrotāpanna (Sūtuóhuán) arrives after eighty thousand kalpas;
a Sakṛdāgāmin (Sītuóhán) arrives after sixty thousand kalpas;
an Anāgāmin (Ānàhán) arrives after forty thousand kalpas;
an Arhat (Āluóhàn) arrives after twenty thousand kalpas;
a Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó) arrives after ten thousand kalpas.
For these reasons,
it is named that which has not arrived arriving.
O good man!
What causes and conditions lead to it being named that which has arrived not arriving?
That which has arrived is named the Twenty-five Realms of Existence (èrshíwǔ yǒu).
All sentient beings are constantly covered and concealed by immeasurable afflictions and fetters,
coming and going without separation,
like a turning wheel.
This is named arriving.
The Śrāvakas (Shēngwén),
Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué), and all Bodhisattvas have already permanently departed
—hence it is named not arriving.
To transform and guide sentient beings,
they manifest their presence within these realms;
this is also named arriving.
O good man!
What causes and conditions lead to it being named that which has arrived arriving?
That which has arrived is the Twenty-five Realms of Existence.
All common mortals,
from Śrotāpannas up to Anāgāmins,
because of the causes and conditions of afflictions,
are named that which has arrived arriving.
O good man!
The unheard hearing is also like this:
There is the unheard hearing,
there is the unheard not-hearing,
there is the heard not-hearing,
and there is the heard hearing.
What is the unheard hearing?
O good man!
The unheard is named Great Nirvāṇa.
Why is it unheard?
Because it is not conditioned (yǒuwéi),
because it is not sound,
because it cannot be spoken.
Why is it also heard?
Because it obtains a name that can be heard,
namely, permanence (cháng), joy (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng).
For these reasons,
it is named the unheard hearing.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has stated, Great Nirvāṇa is unobtainable by hearing;
how can you then say that permanence, joy, self, and purity can be obtained by hearing?
Why is that?
World-Honored One!
The ceasing of afflictions is named the attainment of Nirvāṇa.
If they are not ceased, it is named non-attainment.
For this reason, the nature of Nirvāṇa originally did not exist, but now exists.
If worldly phenomena originally did not exist but now exist, then they are named impermanent (wúcháng).
For instance, a jar, etc.,
originally did not exist but now exists,
and having existed, it returns to non-existence;
therefore, it is named impermanent.
Nirvāṇa is also like this;
how can it be said to possess permanence, joy, self, and purity?
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
All things that are established through ornamentation based on causes
are entirely named impermanent.
If Nirvāṇa is like that,
it ought to be impermanent.
What causes are these?
Namely, the Thirty-seven Aids to Enlightenment (sānshíqī pǐn),
the Six Pāramitās (liù bōluómì),
the Four Immeasurable Minds (sì wúliàng xīn),
the contemplation of bone appearance (gǔxiàng), Ānāpānā,
the Six Recollections (liù niànchù),
the analysis and breakdown of the six great elements (liù dà);
such teachings
are all causes and conditions for the realization of Nirvāṇa,
hence it is named impermanent.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
That which has names is impermanent.
If Nirvāṇa exists,
it should also be impermanent.
As the Buddha formerly stated in the Āgamas (Āhán),
Śrāvakas,
Pratyekabuddhas,
and all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, all possess Nirvāṇa;
for this reason, it is named impermanent.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
Phenomena that can be seen are named impermanent.
As the Buddha previously stated,
one who sees Nirvāṇa can then eliminate all afflictions.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
For instance, empty space,
which provides equal non-obstruction to all sentient beings,
is therefore named permanent.
If Nirvāṇa were permanent and equal,
why do some sentient beings attain it and others not?
If Nirvāṇa were like this,
not being equal toward all sentient beings,
then it would not be named permanent.
World-Honored One!
For instance, if one hundred people share a common enemy,
by killing this enemy,
many people experience joy.
If Nirvāṇa is an equal phenomenon,
when one person attains it, many people should attain it;
when one person breaks the fetters, many people should also break them.
If it is not like this,
how is it named permanent?
For instance, if someone reverently
offers,
respects,
and praises a king,
a prince,
parents,
or teachers,
they obtain benefits;
this is not named permanent.
Nirvāṇa is also like this;
it is not named permanent.
Why?
As the Buddha formerly told Ānánda in the Āgama sūtras:
‘If a person can revere Nirvāṇa,
they will break the fetters
and receive immeasurable joy.’
For this reason,
it is not named permanent.
World-Honored One!
If Nirvāṇa contains the names permanence, joy, self, and purity,
it is not named permanent.
If it does not contain them,
how can it be spoken of?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Dé Wáng Púsà Móhēsà, saying:
“The substance of Nièpán is not that it was originally nonexistent but now exists.
If the substance of Nièpán were originally nonexistent but now existed,
then it would not be the non-defiled ( wú lòu )
and permanent (constant dwelling) Dharma.
Whether there is a Buddha or there is no Buddha,
its nature and characteristics constantly abide.
Because all sentient beings are covered by afflictions ( fánnǎo ),
they do not see Nièpán,
and thus claim it to be nonexistent.
Púsà Móhēsàs use discipline ( jiè ),
concentration ( dìng ),
and wisdom ( huì )
to diligently cultivate their minds;
having severed their afflictions,
they then attain to seeing it.
You ought to know that Nièpán is the constantly abiding Dharma,
not something that was originally nonexistent but now exists;
for this reason, it is constant.
Good man!
It is like a well in a dark room,
with various kinds of seven treasures.
People also know they exist,
but because of the darkness, they cannot see them.
A person of wisdom,
who skillfully understands means ( fāngbiàn ),
lights a great bright lamp,
takes it there, and illuminates the place,
and is entirely able to see them.
This person ultimately does not produce the thought concerning this,
that the water and the seven treasures were originally nonexistent but now exist.
Nièpán is also like this;
it has existed inherently from the beginning;
it is not only recent.
Because of the darkness of afflictions,
sentient beings do not see it.
The Tathāgata ( Rúlái ) of great wisdom, using skillful means, lights the lamp of wisdom,
enabling all Púsàs to see the constancy ( cháng ), bliss ( lè ), self ( wǒ ), and purity ( jìng ) of Nièpán.
For this reason, the wise, regarding this Nièpán,
should not say that it was originally nonexistent but now exists.
“Good man!
Your saying that because of adornment ( zhuāngyán ) Nièpán is accomplished and therefore ought to be impermanent ( wú cháng )—
this is also incorrect.
Why is this?
Good man!
The substance of Nièpán
is neither born nor produced;
neither real nor empty;
it is not produced by action ( zuò yè );
it is not a conditioned ( yǒu wéi ) Dharma that is defiled ( yǒu lòu );
neither heard nor seen;
neither falling nor dying;
it is not the characteristic of difference;
nor is it the characteristic of sameness;
neither going nor returning;
it is neither past, coming (future), nor present;
neither singular nor multiple;
neither long nor short;
neither round nor square;
neither pointed nor slanted;
neither characterized nor uncharacterized;
neither name nor form;
neither cause nor effect;
neither self ( wǒ ) nor mine ( wǒ suǒ ).
Because of this meaning,
Nièpán is constant,
eternally unchanging.
Therefore, one must cultivate and accumulate good Dharmas for immeasurable Asàṅkhyeya ( Āsēngqí ) Kalpas,
in order to adorn oneself,
and then one is able to see it.
Good man!
For example, beneath the earth there is water of the Eight Flavors ( Bā Wèi Shuǐ ),
which all sentient beings cannot obtain.
A person of wisdom applies effort to pierce and dig,
and then immediately obtains it;
Nièpán is also like this.
For example, a blind person does not see the sun and moon,
but a good physician treats them and they immediately gain sight,
yet the sun and moon were not originally nonexistent but now exist;
Nièpán is also like this;
it has existed inherently from before, and is not only recent.
Good man!
Just as a person who has committed a crime
is bound and imprisoned,
and after a long time is finally released,
and upon returning home is able to see his parents, brothers,
wife, and dependents;
Nièpán is also like this.
“Good man!
Your saying that because of causal conditions ( yīnyuán ),
the Dharma of Nièpán ought to be impermanent—
this is also incorrect.
Why is this?
Good man,
there are five types of causes ( yīn ).
What are these five?
First is the generative cause ( shēng yīn );
second is the composite cause ( héhé yīn );
third is the abiding cause ( zhù yīn );
fourth is the augmenting cause ( zēngzhǎng yīn );
fifth is the remote cause ( yuǎn yīn ).
What is the generative cause?
The generative cause is Karma ( yè ), afflictions ( fánnǎo ), etc.,
as well as the seeds of outer grasses and trees;
this is called the generative cause.
What is the composite cause?
It is like the compounding of good with good mind,
the compounding of unwholesome with unwholesome mind,
the compounding of indeterminate with indeterminate mind;
this is called the composite cause.
What is the abiding cause?
It is like when there are pillars underneath,
the house does not fall;
mountains, rivers, and trees,
because of the great earth, are able to stand firm;
internally, because of the Four Great Elements ( sì dà )
and immeasurable afflictions,
sentient beings are able to abide;
this is called the abiding cause.
What is the augmenting cause?
Because of clothes, food, drink, etc.,
sentient beings are enabled to grow;
just as external seeds,
if not burned by fire
or eaten by birds,
are able to grow;
similarly, various Śramaṇas ( Shāmén )
and Brāhmaṇas ( Póluómén ),
by relying on their Upādhyāya ( Héshang )
and good teachers ( shàn zhīshí ), are enabled to grow;
just as relying on parents,
a child grows;
this is called the augmenting cause.
What is the remote cause?
For example, by relying on an incantation ( zhòu ),
ghosts cannot cause harm,
and poison cannot take effect;
by relying upon the king,
there are no thieves;
just as sprouts rely on the causal factors of earth,
water,
fire,
and wind, etc.;
just as water, churning, and humans
are the remote causes for cream ( sū );
just as luminosity ( míng ) and form ( sè ), etc.,
are the remote causes for consciousness ( shí );
the vital essence and blood of parents
are the remote causes for sentient beings;
seasonal conditions ( shí jié ), etc., are entirely called remote causes.
Good man!
The substance of Nièpán is not accomplished by these five types of causes.
How, then, can you say it is a cause for impermanence?
“Furthermore, good man!
There are two additional causes:
First is the operative cause ( zuò yīn );
second is the clarifying cause ( liǎo yīn ).
Like the potter's wheel and rope,
this is called the operative cause.
Like a lamp or candle illuminating objects in darkness,
this is called the clarifying cause.
Good man!
Mahāpārinirvāṇa ( Dà Nièpán )
does not come into existence from an operative cause,
but only has a clarifying cause.
The clarifying cause
refers to the Thirty-Seven Factors of Enlightenment ( Sānshíqī Zhù Dào Fǎ )
and the Six Pāramitās ( Liù Bōluómì );
these are called the clarifying cause.
Good man!
Giving ( bù shī ) is a cause for Nièpán,
but not a cause for Dà Nièpán.
Only Dānapāramitā ( Tán Bōluómì ) can be called the cause for Dà Nièpán.
The Thirty-Seven Components ( Sānshíqī Pǐn ) are causes for Nièpán,
but not causes for Dà Nièpán.
Only immeasurable Āsēngqí Dharma Factors supporting Bodhi ( Pútí )
can be called the cause for Dà Nièpán.
At that time, Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Dé Wáng Púsà Móhēsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One ( Shìzūn )!
How is it that giving ( bù shī ) cannot be called Dānapāramitā ( Tán Bōluómì )?
How is it that giving ( bù shī ) can be called Dānapāramitā ( Tán Bōluómì )?
Similarly, how is it that Prajñā ( Bōrě ) cannot be called Prajñāpāramitā ( Bōrě Bōluómì )?
How is it that Prajñā ( Bōrě ) can be called Prajñāpāramitā ( Bōrě Bōluómì )?
What is called Nièpán?
What is called Dà Nièpán?”
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
A Bódhisattvà Móhāsàtva, practicing the Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa (Fāngděng Dà Bān Nièpán),
does not hear of giving (bùshī),
does not see giving,
does not hear of the perfection of giving (Dān Bōluómì),
does not see the perfection of giving,
and so forth, does not hear of wisdom (Bōrě),
does not see wisdom,
does not hear of the perfection of wisdom (Bōrě Bōluómì),
does not see the perfection of wisdom,
does not hear of Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
does not see Nirvāṇa,
does not hear of Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán),
does not see Mahāparinirvāṇa.
The Bódhisattvà Móhāsàtva, practicing the Dà Nièpán,
knows and perceives the Dharma Realm (Fǎjiè),
understands the true form (shíxiàng) as empty and nonexistent,
without characteristics of compounded perception and consciousness,
achieving the characteristic of the unconditioned (wúlòu xiàng),
the characteristic of non-action (wú suǒ zuò xiàng),
the characteristic of illusion and transformation (huàn huà xiàng),
the characteristic of a mirage in the heat (rè shí yán xiàng),
the characteristic of a Gandhárva City (Gāntàpó Chéng),
and the characteristic of empty space (xūkōng zhī xiàng).
When the Bódhisattvà attains these characteristics,
being without greed, hatred, or delusion (tān huì chī),
neither hearing nor seeing,
this is called the true characteristic of the Bódhisattvà Móhāsàtva,
dwelling in the true form.
The Bódhisattvà Móhāsàtva knows for himself, 'This is giving (dàn),'
'This is the perfection of giving (Dān Bōluómì),'
and so forth, 'This is wisdom (bōrě),'
'This is the perfection of wisdom (Bōrě Bōluómì),'
'This is Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),'
'This is Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).'
"Good man!
How is it giving (shī)
but not a perfection (Bōluómì)?
Seeing that there is a beggar,
and then only giving,
this is called giving,
not a perfection.
If there is no beggar,
but one opens his mind and gives spontaneously (zì shī),
this is called the perfection of giving (Dān Bōluómì).
If one gives only sometimes,
this is called giving,
not a perfection.
If one practices constant giving,
this is called the perfection of giving (Dān Bōluómì).
If, after giving to others,
one subsequently generates regret,
this is called giving,
not a perfection.
Giving without subsequent regret
is called the perfection of giving (Dān Bōluómì).
If a Bódhisattvà Móhāsàtva, regarding his wealth, generates the four fears—
the king,
thieves,
water,
and fire—
and joyfully gives it away,
this is called the perfection of giving (Dān Bōluómì).
If one gives hoping for return,
this is called giving,
not a perfection.
Giving without hoping for return
is called the perfection of giving (Dān Bōluómì).
If one gives due to fear,
for reputation,
for profit and support,
for the continuity of family custom,
or for the five desires of the heavens,
because of arrogance,
in order to surpass others,
because of acquaintances,
or hoping for a future reward,
it is like the law of the market exchange.
Good man!
Just as a person plants a tree
in order to obtain shade,
or to obtain flowers, fruit, and timber.
If a person practices giving of this nature,
this is called giving,
not a perfection (Bōluómì).
A Bódhisattvà Móhāsàtva who practices such Dà Nièpán
does not perceive the giver,
the recipient,
or the wealth,
does not perceive the time,
does not perceive the field of merit (fútián) or non-field of merit,
does not perceive the cause (yīn),
does not perceive the condition (yuán),
does not perceive the retribution (guǒ bào),
does not perceive the doer,
does not perceive the receiver,
does not perceive much,
does not perceive little,
does not perceive purity,
does not perceive impurity,
does not disparage the recipient,
his own self,
or the wealth,
does not perceive the perceiver,
does not perceive the non-perceiver,
does not reckon self
or others;
he practices giving solely for the sake of the eternal Dharma (cháng zhù fǎ) of the Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa (Fāngděng Dà Bān Nièpán),
performs giving for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings (zhòngshēng),
performs giving for the sake of eliminating the afflictions (fánnǎo) of all sentient beings,
and performs giving so that sentient beings do not perceive the recipient, the giver, or the wealth.
Good man!
For example, if a person
falls into the great ocean water,
and by embracing a corpse
is able to cross over and escape;
when the Bódhisattvà Móhāsàtva practices Dà Nièpán and performs giving,
it is likewise
like that corpse.
Good man!
For example, if a person
is confined in a deep prison,
where the doors are secure and sturdy,
and there is only a latrine hole,
he then escapes from it to a place of freedom (wú ài chù);
when the Bódhisattvà Móhāsàtva practices Dà Nièpán and performs giving,
it is likewise so.
Good man!
For example, if a noble person, frightened by distress and difficulty,
having no other reliance,
depends on a Caṇḍāla (Zhāntuóluó);
when the Bódhisattvà Móhāsàtva practices Dà Nièpán
and performs giving, it is likewise so.
Good man!
For example, a sick person consumes impure substances (bù jìng) in order to remove the suffering of illness and attain peace and happiness;
when the Bódhisattvà Móhāsàtva practices Dà Nièpán and performs giving, it is likewise so.
Good man!
Just as a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén), encountering a time when grain is exceedingly expensive,
eats dog meat in order to preserve his life;
when the Bódhisattvà Móhāsàtva practices Dà Nièpán and performs giving, it is likewise so.
Good man!
Such matters within the Dà Nièpán,
never before heard throughout countless kalpas (wú liàng jié), now are heard;
morality (shīluó),
the perfection of morality (Shīluó Bōluómì),
and so forth, wisdom (bōrě),
the perfection of wisdom (Bōrě Bōluómì),
are extensively explained, as in the Buddhas' Mixed Flower Sūtra (Fó Zá Huā Jīng).
"Good man!
How does the Bódhisattvà Móhāsàtva practice Dà Nièpán, hearing what was previously unheard?
The profound meaning of the twelve divisions of the scriptures (shí'èr bù jīng),
which was never heard before,
is now, based on this Sūtra,
fully heard.
Although they were heard before,
only the names were heard;
but now, within this Dà Nièpán Jīng,
the meaning is finally heard.
Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué) only heard the names of the twelve divisions of the scriptures,
but did not hear their meaning;
now, in this Sūtra, they fully hear it,
which is called hearing what was previously unheard.
Good man!
In all the sūtras of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
they have never heard that the Buddha possesses permanence (cháng), joy (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng),
that He is not ultimately annihilated,
or that the Three Jewels (sānbǎo) and the Buddha Nature (fóxìng) are without distinction in characteristic,
or that those who commit the four grave offenses (sì chóng zuì),
slander the Vaipulya Sūtras (Fāngděng Jīng),
commit the five heinous crimes (wǔ nì zuì), and the Icchántika (Yīchǎntí) all possess the Buddha Nature (fóxìng);
now, in this Sūtra, they are able to hear this,
which is called hearing what was previously unheard."
Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng Púsà Móhēsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If those who transgress the serious prohibitions,
slander the Vaipulya Sūtras (Fāngděng jīng),
commit the five heinous sins (Wǔ Nì zuì),
or are Icchantikas (Yīchǎntí), and so forth—
since they possess the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng)—
how is it that they still fall into the hells?
World-Honored One!
If these beings possess the Buddha-nature,
why is it also said that they lack permanence (cháng), joy (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng)?
World-Honored One!
If severing the roots of goodness (shàngēn) is what defines an Icchantika,
when the roots of goodness are severed, why is the Buddha-nature they possess not also severed?
If the Buddha-nature were severed,
how could it still be called permanent, joyful, self, and pure?
If indeed it is not severed,
why then are they called Icchantikas?
World-Honored One!
Those who transgress the four serious prohibitions (sì chóng jìn) are called indeterminate (bùdìng).
Slandering the Vaipulya Sūtras,
committing the five heinous sins, and being an Icchantika are all called indeterminate.
If such beings were determined [to be utterly evil],
how could they attain Anuttarasamyaksambodhi (Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí)?
Attaining Srotaāpanna (Xūtuóhuán) up to Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó) is also called indeterminate.
If Srotaāpanna up to Pratyekabuddha were determined [to be final states],
they also ought not to attain Anuttarasamyaksambodhi.
World-Honored One!
If those who transgress the four serious prohibitions are indeterminate,
then Srotaāpanna up to Pratyekabuddha are also indeterminate.
If they are indeterminate in this manner,
then all Tathāgatas (Rúlái) are also indeterminate;
if the Buddhas are indeterminate,
then the essential nature of Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) is also indeterminate,
and consequently all phenomena are also indeterminate.
How is this indeterminacy manifested?
If an Icchantika ceases to be an Icchantika,
they attain the Buddha Way.
All Tathāgatas should also be like this:
having entered Nirvāṇa,
they should also exit again,
not remaining in Nirvāṇa.
If this is the case,
then the nature of Nirvāṇa is indeterminate.
Since it is indeterminate, we should know that there is no permanence, joy, self, or purity.
How then can it be said that Icchantikas, and others, shall attain Nirvāṇa?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng Púsà Móhēsà, saying:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
Wishing to benefit immeasurable sentient beings and allow them to attain peace and happiness,
out of compassion and loving concern for all the worlds,
and desiring to advance those Bodhisattvas (Púsà) who have aroused the resolve for Bodhi (Pútí xīn),
you have posed this question.
Good man!
You have already attended upon immeasurable Buddhas and World-Honored Ones in the past,
planting various roots of goodness in the presence of those Buddhas.
You have long ago perfected the merits and virtues of Bodhi,
subdued all the Māras (Mó) and caused them to disperse,
and already instructed countless, boundless sentient beings,
enabling them all to reach Anuttarasamyaksambodhi.
You have long penetrated the supremely profound and secret storehouse possessed by all Tathāgatas.
You have already inquired of countless, boundless Buddhas and World-Honored Ones, numerous as the sands of the Ganges, regarding such supremely profound and subtle meanings.
I do not see anyone,
throughout all the worlds,
whether human or celestial,
Śramaṇa (Shāmén),
Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén),
whether Māra or Brahmā (Fàn),
who is able to inquire of the Tathāgata concerning this meaning.
Now, listen sincerely and carefully,
listen carefully!
I shall explain and distinguish [this doctrine] for you.
Good man!
Icchantikas are also indeterminate.
If they were determined [to be fixed in evil],
then that Icchantika would ultimately be unable to attain Anuttarasamyaksambodhi;
because they are indeterminate,
they are therefore able to attain it.
As you have said,
the Buddha-nature is not severed,
but how can an Icchantika be one who severs the roots of goodness?
Good man!
The roots of goodness are of two kinds:
first, internal;
second, external.
The Buddha-nature is neither internal nor external.
Because of this meaning,
the Buddha-nature is not severed.
Furthermore, there are two kinds [of roots of goodness]:
first, defiled (yǒulòu);
second, undefiled (wúlòu).
The Buddha-nature is neither defiled
nor undefiled.
Therefore, it is not severed.
Furthermore, there are two kinds [of phenomena]:
first, permanent (cháng);
second, impermanent (wúcháng).
The Buddha-nature is neither permanent
nor impermanent.
Therefore, it is not severed.
If [the root of goodness] were severed,
then it should be regained later.
If it cannot be regained,
then it is called 'not severed.'
If [the root of goodness] is severed but later attained,
this is called the Icchantika.
Those who transgress the four serious prohibitions are also indeterminate.
If they were determined,
those who transgress the four serious prohibitions would ultimately be unable to attain Anuttarasamyaksambodhi.
Slandering the Vaipulya Sūtras is also indeterminate.
If they were determined,
those who slander the true Dharma would ultimately be unable to attain Anuttarasamyaksambodhi.
Committing the five heinous sins is also indeterminate.
If they were determined,
those who commit the five heinous sins would ultimately be unable to attain Anuttarasamyaksambodhi.
Form (sè) and the characteristic of form (sè xiàng) are both indeterminate.
Scent,
taste,
and the characteristic of touch,
the characteristic of origination (shēng xiàng),
up to the characteristic of ignorance (wúmíng xiàng),
the characteristics of the Skandhas (yīn), Āyatanas (rù), and Dhātus (jiè),
the characteristics of the twenty-five realms of existence (èrshíwǔ yǒu),
the four kinds of birth (sì shēng),
and even all phenomena,
are also all indeterminate."
"Shànnánzǐ!
For example, a magician (huànshī),
in a large crowd, conjures up four kinds of troops:
chariots,
infantry,
elephants,
and horses.
He creates various jewels and ornaments (yīngluò) for adorning the body,
cities, towns, and villages,
mountains, forests, trees,
springs, ponds, rivers, and wells.
However, among that audience,
there are some small children,
who lack wisdom.
When they observe these things,
they all take them to be real.
But the wise people among them know they are false and deceptive,
because the power of illusion (huànlì)
confuses people's sight.
Shànnánzǐ!
All ordinary beings (fánfū), up to and including Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Pìzhīfó),
regarding all dharmas (fǎ),
similarly see fixed characteristics (dìngxiàng).
All Buddhas (Fó) and Bodhisattvas (Púsà) do not see fixed characteristics in all dharmas.
Shànnánzǐ!
For example, when small children, during the height of the summer month,
see the summer heat shimmer (mirage),
they call it water.
A wise person,
regarding this heat shimmer,
never gives rise to the thought that it is actual water.
It is merely an illusory shimmer deceiving people's sight;
it is not actually water.
All ordinary beings, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué) who see all dharmas,
are also like this;
they all take them to be real.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not see fixed characteristics in all dharmas.
Shànnánzǐ!
For example, when a sound occurs in a mountain stream, it produces an echo (xiǎng).
Small children, hearing it, take it to be an actual sound.
A wise person understands that there is no fixed reality (dìngshí);
there is only the appearance of sound,
deceiving the ear consciousness (ěrshì).
Shànnánzǐ!
All ordinary beings, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, regarding all dharmas,
are also like this;
they see fixed characteristics.
But all Bodhisattvas understand all dharmas
completely lack fixed characteristics.
They see the characteristic of impermanence (wúcháng xiàng),
the characteristic of emptiness and tranquility (kōngjí xiàng),
and the characteristic of no arising or cessation (wú shēng miè xiàng).
Due to this meaning,
Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) see all dharmas as the characteristic of impermanence.
Shànnánzǐ!
There are also fixed characteristics.
What is considered fixed?
Permanence (cháng), Bliss (lè), Self (wǒ), and Purity (jìng).
Where are these found?
Namely, Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
Shànnánzǐ!
The fruit of Śrotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán guǒ) is also unfixed (bùdìng).
Because it is unfixed,
after passing eighty thousand kalpas (jié),
they attain the mind of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānbú tí xīn).
The fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin (Sītuóhán guǒ) is also unfixed.
Because it is unfixed,
after passing sixty thousand kalpas, they attain the mind of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānbú tí xīn.
The fruit of Anāgāmin (Ānàhán guǒ) is also unfixed.
Because it is unfixed,
after passing forty thousand kalpas, they attain the mind of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānbú tí xīn.
The fruit of Arhat (Āluóhàn guǒ) is also unfixed.
Because it is unfixed,
after passing twenty thousand kalpas, they attain the mind of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānbú tí xīn.
The path of Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó dào) is also unfixed.
Because it is unfixed,
after passing ten thousand kalpas, they attain the mind of Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānbú tí xīn.
"Shànnánzǐ!
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is now, in the city of Kuīshīnàchéng, between the twin Sāluó trees,
manifesting lying down on the lion's couch (shīzǐ zhī chuáng),
desiring to enter Nirvāṇa.
This causes all the assembled disciples who have not yet attained the fruit of Arhat,
and all the strong men (lìshì),
to feel great sorrow and distress.
It also causes the devas (tiān),
humans (rén),
Asuras (Āxiūluó),
Gandharvas (Gāntàpó),
Garuḍas (Jiālóuluó),
Kiṃnaras (Jǐnnàluó),
and Mahoragas (Móhóuluójiā), among others, to make great offerings.
They want people to wrap his body with one thousand lengths of fine cloth,
place him in a coffin made of seven treasures (qībǎo) filled with fragrant oil,
pile up fragrant wood, and burn it with fire.
Only two lengths of cloth will not be consumed by the fire:
the first is the length next to the body (cènshēn),
and the second is the outermost length.
For the sake of all sentient beings (zhòngshēng), the relics (shèlì) will be divided,
into eight portions.
All the Śrāvaka disciples present
uniformly say that the Tathāgata has entered Nirvāṇa.
You should know that the Tathāgata has not necessarily entered Nirvāṇa permanently.
Why is that?
Because the Tathāgata dwells eternally and does not change (chángzhù bù biànyì).
For this reason,
the Tathāgata's Nirvāṇa is also unfixed.
Shànnánzǐ!
You should know that the Tathāgata is also unfixed.
The Tathāgata is not a Deva (Tiān).
Why is that?
There are four kinds of Devas:
first, Mundane Devas (Shìjiān Tiān);
second, Generative Devas (Shēng Tiān);
third, Pure Devas (Jìng Tiān);
fourth, Meaning Devas (Yì Tiān).
Mundane Devas are like the various kings of countries.
Generative Devas are those from the Four Heavenly Kings (Sì Tiānwáng) up to the Heaven of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception (Fēi Yǒu Xiǎng Fēi Wú Xiǎng Tiān).
Pure Devas are those from Śrotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán) up to Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó).
Meaning Devas are the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) of the Ten Stages (Shí Zhù), and so forth.
For what reason,
are the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages called Meaning Devas?
Because they are able to skillfully understand the meaning of all dharmas.
What is that meaning?
It is the meaning of emptiness (kōng yì) by seeing that all dharmas are empty.
Shànnánzǐ!
The Tathāgata is not a king;
nor is he one of the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception,
or one from Śrotāpanna up to Pratyekabuddha,
or a Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages.
For this reason,
the Tathāgata is not a Deva.
Nevertheless, all sentient beings also call the Buddha the Deva of Devas (Tiān Zhōng Tiān).
Therefore, the Tathāgata is neither Deva
nor non-Deva;
neither human (rén)
nor non-human;
neither hungry ghost (guǐ)
nor non-hungry ghost;
neither hell-dweller (dìyù), animal (chùshēng), or hungry ghost (èguǐ),
nor non-hell-dweller, non-animal, or non-hungry ghost;
neither sentient being (zhòngshēng)
nor non-sentient being;
neither dharma (fǎ)
nor non-dharma;
neither form (sè)
nor non-form;
neither long (cháng)
nor non-long;
neither short (duǎn)
nor non-short;
neither characteristic (xiàng)
nor non-characteristic;
neither mind (xīn)
nor non-mind;
neither defiled (yǒulòu)
nor undefiled (wúlòu);
neither conditioned (yǒuwéi)
nor unconditioned (wúwéi);
neither permanent (cháng)
nor impermanent (wúcháng);
neither illusion (huàn)
nor non-illusion;
neither name (míng)
nor non-name;
neither fixed (dìng)
nor non-fixed;
neither existence (yǒu)
nor non-existence (wú);
neither expressed (shuō)
nor non-expressed;
neither Tathāgata (Rúlái)
nor non-Tathāgata.
For this reason,
the Tathāgata is unfixed (bùdìng)."
"O good man!
Why is the Tathāgata (Rúlái) not named a Worldly Deva (Shìtiān)?
A Worldly Deva is just all kings.
The Tathāgata long ago, throughout immeasurable kalpas (jié), already renounced the royal throne.
Therefore, he is not a king.
He is not a non-non-king.
The Tathāgata was born in Kapilavastu (Jiāpílúo Chéng), in the house of King Śuddhodana (Jìngfàn Wáng).
Therefore, he is not a non-non-king.
He is not one born in heaven (shēng tiān).
This is because the Tathāgata long ago departed from all forms of existence.
Therefore, he is not one born in heaven.
He is not a non-non-born-in-heaven.
Why is this?
[Because he] ascended to Tuṣita Heaven (Dōushuài Tiān),
and descended to Jambudvīpa (Yánfú Tí).
Therefore, the Tathāgata is not a non-non-born-in-heaven.
Nor is he a Pure Deva (Jìngtiān).
Why is this?
The Tathāgata is not a Srotaāpanna (Sūtuóhuán) nor even a Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhī Fó).
Therefore, the Tathāgata is not a Pure Deva.
He is not a non-non-Pure Deva.
Why is this?
Because he cannot be stained by the Eight Worldly Dharmas (Bā Fǎ),
just as a lotus flower does not receive dust or water.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is not a non-non-Pure Deva.
Nor is he a Righteous Deva (Yìtiān).
Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata is not a Bodhisattva (Púsà) of the Ten Stages (shí zhù).
Therefore, the Tathāgata is not a Righteous Deva.
He is not a non-non-Righteous Deva.
Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata constantly cultivates the meaning of the Eighteen Kinds of Emptiness (Shíbā Kōng Yì).
Therefore, the Tathāgata is not a non-non-Righteous Deva.
The Tathāgata is not a human (rén).
Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata long ago, throughout immeasurable kalpas, departed from human existence.
Therefore, he is not a human.
Nor is he a non-human (fēi rén).
Why is this?
Because he was born in Kapilavastu (Jiāpílúo Chéng).
Therefore, he is not a non-non-human.
The Tathāgata is not a ghost (guǐ).
Why is this?
Because he does not harm all sentient beings.
Therefore, he is not a ghost.
Nor is he a non-non-ghost.
Why is this?
Also because he transforms sentient beings through manifesting the form of a ghost.
Therefore, he is not a non-non-ghost.
The Tathāgata is also not a hell-dweller, an animal, or a hungry ghost.
Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata long ago departed from all evil karma.
Therefore, he is not a hell-dweller, an animal, or a hungry ghost.
Nor is he a non-non-hell-dweller, animal, or hungry ghost.
Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata also manifests receiving bodies in the Three Evil Paths
in order to transform sentient beings.
Therefore, he is not a non-non-hell-dweller, animal, or hungry ghost.
Nor is he a sentient being (zhòngshēng).
Why is this?
Because he long ago abandoned the nature of sentient beings.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is not a sentient being.
Nor is he a non-non-sentient being.
Why is this?
Because sometimes he expounds the characteristics of sentient beings.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is not a non-non-sentient being.
"The Tathāgata is not a dharma (fǎ).
Why is this?
All dharmas each have separate and distinct characteristics.
The Tathāgata is not so;
there is only one characteristic.
Therefore, he is not a dharma.
Nor is he a non-dharma.
Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata is the Dharma Realm (Fǎ Jiè).
Therefore, he is not a non-dharma.
The Tathāgata is not form (sè).
Why is this?
Because he is not contained within the Ten Forms of Input.
Therefore, he is not form.
Nor is he a non-non-form.
Why is this?
Because his body possesses the Thirty-two Marks,
and the Eighty Minor Characteristics.
Therefore, he is not a non-non-form.
The Tathāgata is not long.
Why is this?
Because he has severed all forms.
Therefore, he is not long.
Nor is he a non-non-long.
Why is this?
Because no one in the entire world can see the characteristic of his uṣṇīṣa.
Therefore, he is not a non-non-long.
The Tathāgata is not short.
Why is this?
Because he long ago abandoned the fetter of arrogance.
Therefore, he is not short.
Nor is he a non-non-short.
Why is this?
Because he manifested a three-foot body for the Elder Gūshīluó (Qúshīluó Zhǎngzhě).
Therefore, he is not a non-non-short.
The Tathāgata is not a characteristic.
Why is this?
Because he long ago abandoned the characteristics of all characteristics.
Therefore, he is not a characteristic.
Nor is he a non-non-characteristic.
Why is this?
Because he skillfully knows all characteristics.
Therefore, he is not a non-non-characteristic.
The Tathāgata is not mind (xīn).
Why is this?
Because [his nature is] like the characteristic of empty space.
Therefore, he is not mind.
Nor is he a non-non-mind.
Why is this?
Because he possesses the Dharma of the Mind of the Ten Powers,
and is also able to know the minds of other sentient beings.
Therefore, he is not a non-non-mind.
The Tathāgata is not compounded (yǒuwéi).
Why is this?
Because he is permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Therefore, he is not compounded.
Nor is he uncompounded (wúwéi).
Why is this?
Because he has coming, going, sitting, and lying down, and manifests entry into Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
Therefore, he is not uncompounded.
The Tathāgata is not permanent (cháng).
Why is this?
Because his body has divisions.
Therefore, he is not permanent.
How is he not permanent?
Because he possesses knowledge.
A permanent dharma is without knowledge,
just like empty space.
The Tathāgata possesses knowledge,
therefore, he is not permanent.
How is he not permanent?
Because he has speech.
A permanent dharma has no speech,
likewise like empty space.
The Tathāgata has speech,
therefore, he is impermanent.
Possessing a clan name means he is called impermanent.
A dharma without a clan name is called permanent.
Empty space is permanent, thus it has no clan name.
The Tathāgata has a clan name;
the name is Gautama (Qú tán shì).
Therefore, he is impermanent.
Having parents means he is called impermanent.
That which has no parents is called permanent.
Empty space is permanent, thus it has no parents.
The Buddha (Fó) has parents, therefore he is impermanent.
Possessing the Four Dignified Postures (Sì Wēiyí) means he is called impermanent.
That which is without the Four Dignified Postures is called permanent.
Empty space is permanent, thus it is without the Four Dignified Postures.
The Buddha possesses the Four Dignified Postures,
therefore, he is impermanent.
A permanent and abiding dharma has no location.
Empty space is permanent, thus it has no location.
The Tathāgata appeared in the land of Central India (Zhōng Tiānzhú Dì),
residing in Śrāvastī (Shěpótí) or Rājagṛha (Wángshě Chéng).
Therefore, he is impermanent.
Because of these meanings,
the Tathāgata is not permanent."
“Nor is it non-eternal.
Why is this?
Because birth is eternally severed.
A phenomenon that involves birth is called impermanent (wúcháng),
a phenomenon that involves no birth is then called eternal (cháng).
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) has no birth, therefore he is eternal.
An eternal phenomenon is without intrinsic nature (wú xìng);
a phenomenon that has intrinsic nature is called impermanent.
The Tathāgata has no birth
and no intrinsic nature.
Being without birth and without intrinsic nature, he is eternal.
An eternal phenomenon pervades all places,
like the empty sky (xūkōng) which is nowhere absent.
The Tathāgata is also like this,
pervading all places,
therefore he is eternal.
An impermanent phenomenon
is sometimes said to exist here,
or sometimes said not to exist there.
The Tathāgata is not like this;
it cannot be said that he exists in this place
and does not exist in that place,
therefore he is eternal.
An impermanent phenomenon
sometimes is existent,
and sometimes is nonexistent.
The Tathāgata is not like this—sometimes existent and sometimes nonexistent;
therefore he is eternal.
The constant and abiding phenomenon is without name and without form.
Since the empty sky is constant, it is without name and without form.
The Tathāgata is also like this, without name and without form,
therefore he is eternal.
The constant and abiding phenomenon is without cause and without effect.
Since the empty sky is constant, it is without cause and without effect.
The Tathāgata is also like this, without cause and without effect,
therefore he is eternal.
The constant and abiding phenomenon is not encompassed by the three times.
The Tathāgata is also like this, not encompassed by the three times,
therefore he is eternal.
“The Tathāgata is not illusory (huàn).
Why is this?
Because he has eternally severed all false and deceptive minds,
therefore he is not illusory.
Nor is he non-illusory.
Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata sometimes divides this single body into immeasurable bodies,
and the immeasurable bodies return to a single body;
he passes straight through mountains and walls without obstruction;
he walks on water as if it were land;
he enters the earth as if it were water;
he walks in the sky as if it were land;
his body emits smoke and flames like a great heap of fire;
he causes clouds and thunder to rumble, their sounds terrifying;
sometimes he appears as cities and towns,
villages, dwellings, and houses,
mountains, rivers, trees, and forests;
sometimes he makes a large body or makes a small body,
a male body or a female body,
a body of a boy or a body of a girl.
Therefore, the Tathāgata is also not non-illusory.
The Tathāgata is not indeterminate (dìng).
Why is this?
Because, in this Kūshīnāchéng, between the twin Sāluó trees,
he manifested entering Pari-nirvāṇa (bānnipán),
therefore he is not indeterminate.
Nor is he non-indeterminate.
Why is this?
Because he is Constant (cháng), Joyful (lè), Self (wǒ), and Pure (jìng),
therefore the Tathāgata is also not non-indeterminate.
The Tathāgata is not afflicted (yǒulòu).
Why is this?
Because he has severed the three afflictions (sān lòu),
therefore he is not afflicted.
Regarding the three afflictions:
All afflictions (fánnǎo) of the Desire Realm (yùjiè),
excluding ignorance (wúmíng),
are named the affliction of desire (yù lòu).
All afflictions of the Form Realm (sè)
and Formless Realm (wú sèjiè),
excluding ignorance,
are named the affliction of existence (yǒulòu).
The ignorance of the three realms
is named the affliction of ignorance (wúmíng lòu).
The Tathāgata has eternally severed these,
therefore he is not afflicted.
“Furthermore,
all ordinary beings (fánfū) do not see the afflictions.
How is it that ordinary beings do not see the afflictions?
All ordinary beings harbor doubt concerning the future life:
Will they obtain a body in the future life?
Or will they not obtain a body?
Concerning the past life:
Did the body originally exist?
Or was it originally non-existent?
Concerning the present life:
Does this body exist?
Is this body non-existent?
If I exist,
am I material (sè)?
Am I non-material (fēisè)?
Am I material and non-material?
Am I neither non-material nor not-non-material?
Am I conceived (xiǎng)?
Am I unconceived (fēixiǎng)?
Am I conceived and unconceived?
Am I neither unconceived nor not-unconceived?
Does this body belong to another?
Does it not belong to another?
Does it belong and not belong?
Does it neither belong nor not belong?
Is there life without body?
Is there body without life?
Is there body and life?
Is there neither body nor life?
Are the body and life eternal?
Are they impermanent?
Are they eternal and impermanent?
Are they neither eternal nor impermanent?
Are the body and life made by self-mastery (zìzài)?
Are they made by time (shíjié)?
Are they made without cause (wúyīn)?
Are they made by inherent world nature (shìxìng)?
Are they made by subtle dust (wéichén)?
Are they made by Dharma and non-Dharma (fǎ fēifǎ)?
Are they made by the individual (shìfū)?
Are they made by affliction?
Are they made by parents?
Does the self reside in the mind?
Does it reside in the eye?
Does it pervade the entire body?
From where does it come?
To where does it go?
Who is born?
Who dies?
Was I of the Brahmin (Póluómén) caste in the past?
Was I of the Kshatriya (Chàlì) caste?
Was I of the Vaishya (Píshè) caste?
Was I of the Shūdra (Shǒutuóluó) caste?
What caste shall I obtain in the future?
Concerning this body of mine,
in the past,
was it a male body?
Was it a female body?
Was it an animal body?
If I take a life,
will there be guilt?
Will there be no guilt?
Even down to drinking alcohol, will there be guilt?
Will there be no guilt?
Did I do it myself?
Was it done by another?
Do I receive the retribution?
Does the body receive the retribution?
Such doubtful views
and immeasurable afflictions
obscure the minds of sentient beings.
Due to these doubtful views,
six types of mind arise:
‘There is definitively a Self’;
‘There is definitively no Self’;
‘The Self sees the Self’;
‘The Self sees the non-Self’;
‘The non-Self sees the Self’;
‘I act, I receive, I know.’
These are named perverse views (xiéjiàn).
The Tathāgata has eternally eradicated the root of such immeasurable afflictions of views (jiàn lòu),
therefore he is not afflicted.”
"Good man!
The Púsà Mòhēsà who cultivates the noble path (āryacaryā) concerning the Dà Nièpán
can also permanently sever these outflows (āśravas).
All Buddhas and Rúlái constantly cultivate the noble path,
therefore they are without outflows (nirāśrava).
Good man!
Ordinary people (fanfú rén) cannot properly govern the five roots (wǔ gēn),
thus they have the three outflows,
and are dragged by evil to unwholesome states.
Good man!
For example, a wicked horse,
whose nature is stubborn and intractable,
can make the rider reach dangerous and dreadful places.
Those who cannot properly govern these wǔ gēn
are also like this,
causing people to stray far from the wholesome path of Nièpán
and reach all sorts of evil destinations.
For example, a vicious elephant,
whose mind has not been trained and tamed—
if someone rides it,
it does not go where desired,
but leaves the city and suburbs
and reaches desolate places.
Those who cannot properly govern these wǔ gēn
are also like this,
leading people away from the city and suburbs of Nièpán
to the wilderness of Saṅsāra (shēngsǐ).
Good man!
For example, a fawning minister
teaches the king to do evil;
the wǔ gēn are fawning ministers,
and they are also like this,
constantly teaching sentient beings to commit immeasurable evils.
Good man!
For example, a wicked child
who refuses the instructions
of teachers, elders, and parents,
then commits every evil;
failing to restrain the wǔ gēn
is also like this,
refusing the good words and instructions of teachers and elders,
committing every evil.
Good man!
Ordinary people who do not govern the wǔ gēn
are constantly harmed and damaged by Dìyù, Chùshēng, and Èguǐ,
just as enemies and bandits harm good people.
Good man!
Ordinary people who do not govern the wǔ gēn
rush forth upon the five dusts (wǔ chén),
just like a cowherd
who does not properly watch over the cattle,
allowing them to spoil others' crops.
Ordinary people who do not govern the wǔ gēn
constantly remain in various existences (bhāvas) suffering affliction.
Good man!
The Púsà Mòhēsà cultivating Dà Nièpán,
when practicing the noble path,
is constantly able to properly restrain
and guard the wǔ gēn,
fearing greed (tānyù),
anger (chēnhuì),
ignorance (yúchī),
arrogance (jiāomàn),
and jealousy (jídù),
in order to obtain all wholesome doctrines (dharma).
"Good man!
If one can properly guard these wǔ gēn,
then one can restrain the mind.
If one can restrain the mind,
then one restrains the wǔ gēn.
For example, if someone protects the king,
then they protect the country;
those who protect the country then protect the king.
The Púsà Mòhēsà is also like this:
if they hear this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Nièpán Jīng),
they gain wisdom (zhìhuì);
having gained wisdom, they gain concentrated mindfulness (zhuān niàn);
if the wǔ gēn scatter,
mindfulness can stop them.
Why is this?
Because this is mindfulness and wisdom (niàn huì).
Good man!
Just as a skillful cowherd,
if the cattle graze here and there, devouring others' crops,
immediately stops them and prevents damage.
The Púsà Mòhēsà is also like this:
due to the cause of mindfulness and wisdom,
they guard and restrain the wǔ gēn,
not allowing them to run wild and scatter.
The Púsà Mòhēsà who possesses mindfulness and wisdom
does not perceive the mark of self (wǒ xiāng),
does not perceive the mark of mine (wǒ suǒ xiāng),
does not perceive sentient beings or what they use and enjoy,
but sees that all phenomena share the mark of Dharmatā (fǎxìng xiāng),
arising from the marks of earth, stone, tile, and rubble,
like a house,
which arises from many causes and conditions,
having no fixed nature.
They see that all sentient beings are established by the four great elements (sì dà) and the five aggregates (wǔ yīn),
concluding that they have no fixed nature.
Because there is no fixed nature,
the Púsà does not give rise to greed or attachment toward them.
All ordinary people perceive the existence of sentient beings
and give rise to affliction (fánnǎo).
The Púsà Mòhēsà cultivates Dà Nièpán,
and because they possess mindfulness and wisdom,
they do not give rise to greed or attachment toward sentient beings.
"Furthermore, the Púsà Mòhēsà who cultivates the Dà Nièpán Jīng
is not attached to the mark of sentient beings,
but creates the marks of various phenomena.
Good man!
For example, a painter,
using various mixed colors,
paints various images,
whether men or women,
whether cattle or horses.
Ordinary people, being ignorant,
upon seeing them, give rise to the marks of men, women, and so forth,
but the painter clearly knows that there are no men or women present.
The Púsà Mòhēsà is also like this:
viewing the single mark within the different marks of phenomena,
they ultimately do not give rise to the mark of sentient beings.
Why is this?
Because they possess mindfulness and wisdom.
The Púsà Mòhēsà cultivating Dà Nièpán,
even if they happen to see a beautiful woman,
ultimately does not give rise to the mark of greed or attachment.
Why is this?
Because they skillfully contemplate marks.
Good man!
The Púsà Mòhēsà knows that the five desired objects (wǔ yù) offer no joy,
and cannot be retained for long,
like a dog gnawing on a dry bone,
like a person holding a torch and walking against the wind,
like a poisonous snake in a basket, or something obtained in a dream,
like a fruit tree on a roadside that is struck by many people,
also like a piece of meat pursued competitively by many birds,
like a bubble on water, or the trace made by drawing on water,
like the end of weaving the warp,
like a prisoner being led to execution (the marketplace),
just like borrowed power that cannot last long.
Contemplating desire thus reveals its many faults and evils."
"Furthermore, good man!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva observes all sentient beings
that, due to the conditions of form (rùpa),
smell (gandhā),
taste (rasā),
and touch (spraṣṭavyā),
have been enduring suffering
continuously since countless and measureless kalpas past.
The accumulated bones of every single sentient being
throughout one kalpa
would be like Mount Bǐfùluó (Vipula) in Rājagṛha (Wángshěchéng);
the milk they have drunk would be like the four great oceans (sāgara);
the blood shed from their bodies would be more than the four great oceans;
the tears wept at the passing of parents, brothers, wives, children, and dependents would be more than the four great oceans;
if all the grass and wood on Earth were used as four-inch counting sticks to count the number of parents, they could not be exhausted.
The practical suffering (karmic suffering) they have endured in hells, as animals (tiryagyoni), or as hungry ghosts (pretas) throughout measureless kalpas is incalculable.
Even kneading this great Earth, it is as easily exhausted as a date (fruit),
but saṃsāra (cycle of birth and death) is difficult to exhaust.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva profoundly observes all sentient beings in this manner,
that because of these desires (rāga) they endure measureless suffering.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva does not lose mindfulness (smṛti) and wisdom (prajñā) due to this suffering in the cycle of saṃsāra.
Good man!
The king commands a minister:
'Carry a bowl of oil and pass through the middle, taking care not to spill it.
If you drop even one drop,
your life will be severed.'
He also sends another person,
drawing a sword, to follow behind,
constantly intimidating him.
The minister receives the king's command,
holds the bowl with utmost care,
and passes through such a great multitude.
Although he sees the agreeable five false desires (pañca mithyā kāmāḥ),
he constantly thinks:
'If I become negligent
and attach myself to those false desires,
I will drop what I am carrying,
and my life will not be spared.'
Because of this fear,
this person does not spill even a single drop of oil.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this:
in saṃsāra, he does not lose mindfulness and wisdom.
Because he does not lose them,
though he sees the five desires, his mind is not greedy or attached.
If he sees pure form,
he does not generate the perception (saṃjñā) of form,
but only observes the characteristic of suffering (duḥkha-lakṣaṇa).
Even up to the characteristic of consciousness (vijñāna-lakṣaṇa), it is also like this:
he does not generate the characteristic of arising,
does not generate the characteristic of ceasing,
does not generate the characteristic of cause,
but observes the characteristic of combination (saṃskāra-lakṣaṇa).
At that time, the five faculties (pañcendriya) of the Bodhisattva are pure;
because the faculties are pure, the precepts of guarding the faculties are complete.
The five faculties of all ordinary people (pṛthagjana) are impure
and they are unable to guard them well;
this is called the outflow of the faculties (indriya-āsrava).
The Bodhisattva has permanently severed this, and thus is without outflow (anāsrava).
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) has uprooted it and permanently severed the root;
thus, it is not an outflow.
"Furthermore, good man!
There is also the separation from outflow (viraha-āsrava).
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, desiring the unsurpassed immortal fruit of Buddhahood (Bùfóguǒ),
separates himself from evil outflows.
What is separation?
If one is able to cultivate the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dànièpán Jīng),
copy it, receive and uphold it,
read, recite, and explain it,
and contemplate its meaning—this is called separation.
Why is that?
Good man!
I do not see any of the twelve divisions of the sūtras (dvādaśāṅga-pravacana) that can separate one from evil outflows like this Vaipulya (Fāngděng) Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
Good man!
For example, a good teacher instructs his disciples.
Among the disciples, those who accept the instruction
do not commit evil in their minds.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who cultivates the subtle and wonderful Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra
is also like this, not committing evil in his mind.
Good man!
For example, there is a benevolent incantation (mantra) in the world.
If someone hears it once,
for seven years thereafter,
they will not be poisoned by any venom,
nor can snakes sting them.
If someone recites it,
until the end of their life,
they will suffer no calamities.
Good man!
This Mahāparinirvāṇa
is also like this:
if any sentient being hears it even once,
for seven kalpas thereafter,
they will not fall into the evil paths.
If someone copies it,
reads, recites, explains it,
and contemplates its meaning,
they will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
purely perceive the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng),
just as that sacred king (cakravartin) obtains the taste of amṛta (gānlù).
Good man!
This Mahāparinirvāṇa possesses measureless merits such as these.
Good man!
If there is anyone who can copy this sūtra,
read, recite, explain it, and expound it to others,
and contemplate its meaning,
you should know that this person is truly my disciple,
having well received my instruction,
seen by me,
and remembered by me.
This person truly knows that I do not enter Nirvāṇa.
Wherever such a person resides,
whether in a city, town, village,
mountain forest, wilderness,
house, field, dwelling,
multi-story building, or palace hall,
I am also there, constantly dwelling without moving.
I constantly act to receive offerings from this person,
sometimes appearing as a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū),
Bhikṣuṇī (Bǐqiūní),
Upāsaka (Yōupósāi),
Upāsikā (Yōupóyí),
Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén),
Brahmacārins (Fànzhì),
or a poor beggar.
How can this person know
that the Tathāgata receives the objects of their offering?
Good man!
This person, when sleeping at night, may dream
of the image of the Buddha,
or the image of a god (deva),
the image of a Śramaṇa (Shā mén),
a king,
a sacred king,
the image of a lion king (Sīziwáng),
the image of a lotus flower (liánhuā),
the image of an Udumbara flower (Yōután huā),
or may see a great mountain,
or the great ocean water,
or may see the sun and moon,
or the image of a white elephant or a white horse,
or may see their parents,
or obtain flowers or fruits,
or treasures such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli (liúlí), or crystal (pōlí),
or the five flavors of cow products (pañca gavya).
At that time, one should know
that the Tathāgata is receiving their offering.
Upon waking, they feel joy and delight,
and immediately obtain the various things they need.
Their mind does not contemplate evil,
and they enjoy cultivating good dharmas.
Good man!
This Mahāparinirvāṇa is able to accomplish such measureless, asaṃkhyeya (āsēngzhī), inconceivable, boundless merits.
"Good man,
you should now believe and accept my words.
If there is any good man
or good woman who wishes to see me,
wishes to revere me,
wishes to see me by means of the inherent nature of the Dharma (fǎxìng),
wishes to attain the emptiness concentration (śūnyatā samādhi),
wishes to see the true characteristic (satya-lakṣaṇa),
wishes to attain and cultivate the Śūraṅgama Samādhi (Shǒuléngyán Dìng),
or the Lion King Samādhi (Shīziwáng Dìng),
wishes to destroy the eight Māras—the eight Māras
being the four Māras (catvāri mārāḥ), impermanence (anityatā, wúcháng), suffering (duḥkha, wúlè), non-self (anātman, wúwǒ), and impurity (aśubha, wújìng)—
and wishes to attain happiness among humans and gods,
when they see someone upholding the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra by copying it, reading, and reciting it,
explaining it to others,
and contemplating its meaning,
they should approach, rely upon, consult, and receive instruction from them.
They should make offerings, revere, respect, and praise them,
wash their hands and feet, arrange their couch and seating, and supply them with the four necessities (cātuḥpratyaya),
ensuring they lack nothing.
If they come from far away,
they should travel ten yojana
along the road to welcome them.
For the sake of this sūtra,
they should present their most treasured possessions as offerings.
If they have none, they should even sell their own bodies.
Why is that?
This sūtra is harder to encounter than the Udumbara flower."
“Shànnánzǐ!
I recall measureless, boundless, nayuta kalpas ago,
the world at that time was named Suōpó,
where there was a Fó Shìzūn,
titled Shìjiāmóuní Rúlái,
Yìng,
Zhèngbiànzhī,
Míngxíngzú,
Shànshì,
Shìjiānjiě,
Wúshàngshì,
Tiáoyù Zhàngfū,
Tiānrénshī,
Fó,
Shìzūn,
who preached this great Dà Nièpán Jīng to the great assembly.
At that time, I heard from a good friend
that that Fó was about to speak the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán) for the assembly.
When I heard this,
my heart was joyful.
I wished to offer gifts,
but being poor, I had nothing.
I wanted to sell my own body,
but due to meager merit, I found no buyer.
I immediately decided to return home.
On the road, I met a man,
and immediately said to him:
‘I wish to sell my body,
can you buy it?’
The man replied:
‘The task in my household,
no one can perform.
If you are able to do it,
I will buy you.’
I immediately asked:
‘What task is there
that no one can perform?’
The man answered:
‘I have a serious illness.
A skillful physician has prescribed medicine,
which requires consuming three liǎng of human flesh daily.
If you can daily provide three liǎng of your body’s flesh,
