I will then give you five pieces of gold money.’
When I heard this,
my heart was delighted.
I then said:
‘You give me the money,
and lend me seven days.
After my affairs are concluded,
I will return to you.’
The man replied:
‘Seven days is not permissible.
If you are truly able to do this,
I can allow one day.’
Shànnánzǐ!
At that time,
I immediately took the money,
and returned to where the Fó was,
bowed my head and face to his feet,
offered all that I possessed,
and presented it as an offering.
Then, with sincere mind, I listened to and received this Sūtra.
I was dull-witted at the time;
although I was able to hear the Sūtra,
I was only able to receive and memorize the text of one verse (jì):
Having received this verse,
I immediately returned to that sick man's house.
Shànnánzǐ!
Although I subsequently gave three liǎng of my flesh daily,
because of the reason of reciting the verse,
I did not feel pain,
and did not stop daily,
until a full month was complete.
Shànnánzǐ!
Because of this cause and condition,
his illness was cured,
and my body was restored without any wounds or scars.
When I saw my body perfectly intact,
I immediately generated the heart of Anòu duōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
The power of one verse could achieve this;
how much more so for one who completely receives, retains, studies, and recites [the Sūtra]?
Seeing the benefit of this Sūtra,
I redoubled my aspiration,
vowing in the future to achieve the path of a Fó,
bearing the name Shìjiāmóuní.
Shànnánzǐ!
Because of the power derived from this one verse,
I am today enabled to fully proclaim this teaching among the great assembly for the sake of the devas and humans.
Shànnánzǐ!
For this reason,
this Dà Nièpán is inconceivable;
it accomplishes immeasurable and boundless merit.
It is truly the deeply profound and secret treasury of all Fó Rúlái.
For this reason,
those who can receive and uphold it
sever and depart from wicked outflows (è lòu).
What are these wicked [things]?
Vicious elephants,
wicked horses,
evil oxen,
fierce dogs,
places where poisonous snakes dwell,
lands full of wicked thorns,
steep cliffs and perilous banks,
fierce whirlpools and torrents,
wicked people and wicked nations,
wicked cities and wicked dwellings,
and wicked associates (è zhīshi), etc.
Such types of beings,
if they cause outflows,
the Púsà immediately departs from them.
If they do not cause [outflows], then the Púsà does not distance himself from them.
If they increase existing outflows, then he departs from them;
if they do not increase [outflows], then he does not distance himself from them.
If they engage in evil practices, he departs from them;
if they can engage in goodness, then he does not distance himself from them.
How is this departure accomplished?
Not by holding knives or staves,
but by constantly employing right wisdom and skillful means to keep distant.
Therefore, this is called distance through right wisdom.
In order to generate good practices, one departs from evil practices.
The Púsà Móhēsà observes his own body
as sickness,
as a sore,
as a tumor,
as an enemy,
like an arrow entering the body.
It is a great mass of suffering,
and is entirely the root source of all evils.
Although this body is thus impure,
the Púsà still observes it and carefully sustains it.
Why is this?
It is not out of greed for the body,
but for the sake of good practices;
for the sake of Nirvāṇa, not for the sake of saṃsāra;
for the sake of permanence, joy, self, and purity,
not for the sake of impermanence, non-joy, non-self, and impurity.
It is for the sake of the Bodhi path, not for the sake of the path of existence;
for the sake of the One Vehicle, not for the sake of the Three Vehicles;
for the sake of the subtle and wondrous body possessing the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, not even for the state of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception.
It is for the sake of being a Fǎlúnwáng, not a Zhuǎnlúnwáng.
“Shànnánzǐ!
The Púsà Móhēsà must constantly protect his body.
Why is this?
If he does not protect his life and body,
his life will not be complete.
If it is not complete, he will be unable to write out this Sūtra, receive, retain, study, or recite it,
or widely expound it for others and contemplate its meaning.
Therefore, the Púsà should diligently protect his body.
For this reason,
the Púsà achieves separation from all wicked outflows.
Shànnánzǐ!
Just as one who wishes to cross [a river] should carefully guard his raft,
a traveler on the road should carefully guard his good horse,
a farmer planting crops should carefully guard the dung and filth,
just as one seeking to cure poison carefully guards the poisonous snake,
just as a man protects the Zhāntuóluó for the sake of wealth,
or protects the brave youth in order to defeat robbers,
and just as a cold person cherishes the fire,
or a leper seeks poisonous medicine.
The Púsà Móhēsà is also like this:
although he sees that this body is fully filled with measureless impurity,
because he wishes to receive and uphold the Dà Nièpán Jīng,
he still carefully sustains and protects it, not allowing it to fail or diminish.
The Púsà Móhēsà regards the vicious elephant and the wicked associate
as being equally non-dual.
Why is this?
Because both destroy the body.
The Púsà Móhēsà feels no fear towards the vicious elephant, etc.,
but generates a heart of dread towards wicked associates.
Why is this?
The vicious elephant, etc., can only destroy the body but cannot destroy the mind;
the wicked associate destroys both.
The vicious elephant, etc., only destroys one body;
the wicked associate destroys countless virtuous bodies
and countless virtuous minds.
The vicious elephant, etc., can only destroy the impure and foul body;
the wicked associate can destroy the pure body and the pure mind.
The vicious elephant, etc., can destroy the physical body;
the wicked associate destroys the Dharma Body.
Being killed by a vicious elephant does not lead to the Three Evil Paths,
but being killed by a wicked friend certainly leads to the Three Evil Paths.
The vicious elephant, etc., is merely an enemy to the body;
the wicked associate is an enemy to the good Dharma.
Therefore, the Púsà must constantly distance himself from all wicked associates.
Ordinary beings do not distance themselves from such outflows,
therefore outflows are generated.
The Púsà departs from them and thus does not generate outflows.
If a Púsà is thus without outflows,
how much more so the Rúlái?
Therefore, he is non-outflow.”
"How does one draw near to the outflow (Lòu)?
All common people (Fánfū),
receiving clothing and food,
bedding and medicine,
for the pleasure of body and mind,
seek such things,
committing various evils,
without knowing their faults,
and cycle through the three paths (sān qù).
Therefore, this is called the outflow (Lòu).
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà), seeing such faults,
thereupon keeps far away from them.
If clothing is needed, he receives it immediately,
not for the sake of the body, but solely for the sake of the Dharma (Fǎ).
He does not cultivate arrogance,
his mind is always humble,
not for adornment,
but merely for covering shame,
guarding against cold and heat,
fierce winds and torrential rains,
noxious insects, mosquitoes, and gadflies,
flies, fleas, vipers, and stings.
Although he receives food and drink,
his mind is without attachment,
not for the sake of the body,
but always for the Correct Dharma (Zhèngfǎ),
not for the flesh,
but only for sentient beings,
not for arrogance,
but for the strength of the body,
not for harm or spite,
but for treating the wound of hunger.
Although he receives delicacies,
his mind is without attachment.
Receiving dwellings is also like this.
He does not allow the fetters of greed and arrogance (tān màn zhī jié) to dwell in his mind.
He uses the dwelling of Bodhi (Pútí shě) to ward off the thieves of the fetters,
and receives shelter for the sake of guarding against fierce winds and rain.
When seeking medicine, his mind is without greed or arrogance,
but solely for the Correct Dharma (Zhèngfǎ),
not for longevity,
but for eternal life.
Good man (Shàn Nánzǐ)!
Just as a person with a diseased wound
applies ointment,
and wraps it with cloth.
To draw out the pus and blood,
ointment is applied and smoothed over,
medicine powder is sprinkled on for the wound to heal,
and he stays in a deep house because of the fierce winds.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) is also like this:
Observing the body as a wound, he covers it with clothing.
He seeks food and drink for the pus (exuding) from the nine orifices.
He takes a dwelling to protect against fierce winds and rain.
He seeks medicine for the stirring of the four poisons.
The Bodhisattva (Púsà) receives the four types of offerings,
for the path of Bodhi (Pútí Dào),
not for longevity.
Why is this?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) contemplates thus:
'If I do not receive these four offerings,
the body will wither away and not attain firmness;
if it is not firm, I cannot endure suffering.
If I cannot endure suffering, I cannot cultivate good practices (shànfǎ).
If I can endure suffering, I will be able to cultivate immeasurable good practices.
If I cannot bear and endure all sufferings,
then I will generate hatred (chēnhuì) toward painful sensations,
and generate attachment toward pleasurable sensations.
If pleasure is sought but not obtained, then ignorance (wúmíng) arises.
Therefore, common people (Fánfū) give rise to outflows (yǒulòu) regarding the four offerings,
but the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) observes profoundly and does not generate outflows.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva (Púsà) is named "Without Outflows" (Wúlòu).
How could the Tathāgata (Rúlái) be named "Having Outflows" (Yǒulòu)?
Therefore, the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is not named "Having Outflows."
"Furthermore, good man (Shàn Nánzǐ)!
Although all common people (Fánfū) carefully protect their bodies,
their minds still generate three kinds of evil awarenesses (è jué).
For this reason,
even if they sever the afflictions (fánnǎo),
and are born in the sphere of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception (Fēixiǎng Fēifēixiǎng Chù),
they still fall back into the three evil paths (sān è dào) ultimately.
Good man (Shàn Nánzǐ)!
For example, if a person crosses a great ocean,
and is about to reach the far shore,
but drowns and dies in the water.
Common people (Fánfū) are also like this:
they are about to exhaust the three realms of existence (sān yǒu),
but fall back into the three evil paths (sān tú).
Why is this?
Because they lack virtuous awarenesses (shàn jué).
What are the virtuous awarenesses?
They are the six mindfulnesses (liù niàn chù).
The virtuous mind of common people (Fánfū) is weak,
and the non-virtuous mind is blazing.
Because the virtuous mind is weak, the mind of wisdom (huì xīn) is slight and meager.
Because the mind of wisdom is slight, it increases all outflows (zhū lòu).
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà), with his purified eye of wisdom, sees the faults of the three awarenesses (sān jué),
knowing that these three awarenesses possess various calamities,
and constantly act as enemies of the Three Vehicles (Sān Chéng) for sentient beings.
Due to the conditions of the three awarenesses (sān jué),
immeasurable common sentient beings (Fánfū zhòngshēng) fail to see the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
generating inverted thoughts (diāndǎo xīn) throughout immeasurable kalpas,
asserting that the World-Honored Buddha (Fó Shìzūn)
is impermanent, without bliss, and without self,
possessing only purity (yī jìng),
and that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) ultimately enters Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
(They believe) all sentient beings are impermanent,
without bliss,
without self,
and without purity.
Because of inverted thoughts,
they say there is permanence, bliss, self, and purity (cháng lè wǒ jìng).
In reality, there is no Three Vehicles (Sān Chéng),
but because of inverted thoughts, they say there are Three Vehicles.
The path of One Reality (Yī Shí zhī Dào) is true and non-illusory,
but because of inverted thoughts, they say there is no One Reality.
These three evil awarenesses are constantly rebuked by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas (Púsà).
These three evil awarenesses constantly harm me,
and sometimes harm others.
If one possesses these three awarenesses,
all evils constantly follow along.
These three awarenesses are precisely the three bonds (sān fù),
tying sentient beings to endless cycles of birth and death (shēngsǐ).
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) constantly observes the three awarenesses in this manner.
If the Bodhisattva (Púsà), for some reason,
ought to generate the awareness of desire (yù jué), he silently refrains from accepting it.
Just as an upright and pure person
does not accept any filth or impurity;
like a hot iron ball,
which no one accepts;
like a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) nature,
that does not accept beef;
like a satiated person,
that does not accept poor food;
like a Wheel-Turning King (Zhuǎnlún Wáng),
who does not sit on the same couch as any Chaṇḍāla (Zhāntuóluó) or the like.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) despises and loathes the three awarenesses (sān jué),
and does not accept or savor them; it is also like this.
Why is this?
The Bodhisattva (Púsà) contemplates:
'Sentient beings know me as an excellent field of merit (fú tián).
How can I accept these evil practices?
If I accept the evil awarenesses (è jué), I am unfit to be a field of merit for sentient beings.
Although I myself do not claim to be an excellent field of merit,
sentient beings see the appearance and immediately say I am one.
If I now arouse such evil awarenesses,
I would be deceiving all sentient beings.
Because of deception in my past,
I have cycled through birth and death (shēngsǐ) and fallen into the three evil paths (sān è dào) throughout immeasurable kalpas.
If I receive offerings given in faith (xìn shī) with an evil mind,
all devas (tiānrén) and the five-powered immortals (wǔ tōng xiān) will bear witness and know it,
and they will rebuke me.
If, with evil awarenesses (è jué), I receive offerings given in faith (xìn shī) from others,
I might cause the reward (guǒ bào) of the donor (shī zhǔ) to diminish or become entirely void.
If I receive the donation (shī) of the Dānapati (Tányuè) with an evil mind,
I become an enemy (yuānchóu) to the donor.
All donors constantly treat me with the thought of a young child (chì zǐ xiǎng).
How can I deceive them,
and generate enmity toward them?
Why is this?
Because I cause the donor either to not receive karmic recompense (guǒ bào) or to receive little recompense.
I always refer to myself as one who has left home (chūjiā rén).
A person who has left home should not arouse evil.
If one arouses evil, one is not truly one who has left home.
For one who has left home, body and speech correspond (xiāngyìng).
If they do not correspond, one is not truly one who has left home.
I abandoned my parents, siblings, wife, children, relatives, and friends,
left home, and cultivated the Way (Xiūdào).
Now is precisely the time to cultivate the virtuous awarenesses (shàn jué),
it is not the time to cultivate unvirtuous awarenesses.
For example, if a person enters the sea seeking jewels,
but does not take the true treasure,
instead taking rock crystal.
It is also like a person who abandons marvelous music,
to play in filth.
Like abandoning a jeweled woman,
and consorting with a slave girl.
Like abandoning a gold vessel,
and using a clay bowl.
Like abandoning sweet dew (gānlù, amṛta),
and consuming poisonous medicine.
Like forsaking a kind, familiar, and virtuous physician,
and following an evil, hostile physician,
seeking medicine and taking it.'
“‘I am also like this:
abandoning the Great Teacher,
the sweet nectar of the Dharma flavor of the Rúlái Shìzūn,
and instead taking up the various evil thoughts of the demonic enemy.
The human body is as difficult to obtain as the Udumbara flower,
but I have now obtained it;
the Rúlái is harder to encounter than the Udumbara flower,
but I have now encountered him;
the pure Dharma treasure is difficult to see and hear,
but I have now heard it.
[I am] like a blind turtle encountering a floating log with a hole.
Human life is more fleeting than mountain streams;
though existing today,
one cannot guarantee tomorrow.
How can I indulge my mind and allow it to dwell in evil dharmas?
Youthful vigor is impermanent, like a galloping horse;
how can I rely upon it and give rise to arrogance?
Just as evil ghosts watch for human faults,
the four great evil ghosts (elements) are also like this,
constantly watching for my shortcomings.
How can I let evil thoughts arise?
It is like a decaying house,
a collapsing dwelling;
my life is also like this.
How can I give rise to evil?
My name is Shāméng (śramaṇa);
a Shāméng is called one who awakens to wholesome thoughts.
Yet I now give rise to unwholesome thoughts;
how can I be worthy of the name Shāméng?
My name is Chūjiā (one who has left home);
a Chūjiā person is called one who cultivates the wholesome path.
Yet I now act wickedly;
how can I be worthy of the name Chūjiā?
My name is now true Póluómén (Brahman);
a Póluómén is called one who cultivates pure conduct.
Yet I now engage in impure, evil thoughts;
how can I be worthy of the name Póluómén?
I am now also called Kuntì Dàxìng (great Kṣatriya lineage);
those of the Kuntì lineage are able to eliminate enemies.
Yet I now cannot eliminate my evil enemies;
how can I be worthy of the name Kuntì lineage?
My name is Bǐqiū (bhikṣu);
a Bǐqiū is called one who destroys afflictions.
Yet I now do not destroy the afflictions of evil thoughts;
how can I be worthy of the name Bǐqiū?
There are six circumstances in the world
that are difficult to encounter,
which I have now obtained.
How can I allow evil thoughts to reside in my mind?
What are the six?
First, the appearance of a Buddha in the world is difficult to encounter;
second, the true Dharma is difficult to hear;
third, the fearful mind is difficult to generate;
fourth, it is difficult to be born in the central kingdom (a place where the Dharma flourishes);
fifth, it is difficult to obtain a human body;
sixth, it is difficult for the faculties to be complete.
These six matters,
though difficult to obtain, have been obtained.
Therefore, I should not give rise to evil thoughts.’
At that time, the Púsà (Bodhisattva), practicing this Dà Nièpán Jīng (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra),
constantly and diligently observes these evil minds.
All ordinary beings do not see the faults and dangers of such evil minds, and thus suffer the three thoughts,
which are called 'receiving outflows' (suffering the leakage of defilements).
The Púsà, having seen them, does not accept them,
does not attach to them,
releases and does not protect them.
Relying on the Eight Noble Paths,
they push them away and cause them to depart,
and cut them off and cause them to be severed.
Therefore, the Púsà has no receiving of outflows.
How, then, can it be said that the Rúlái has outflows?
For this reason,
the Rúlái Shìzūn is not affected by outflows.
“Furthermore, good man!
When ordinary beings encounter physical and mental suffering, they give rise to various evils.
If they contract physical illness,
or mental illness,
they cause the body,
mouth,
and mind
to commit various evils.
Because they commit evil, they revolve through the three realms (of existence) and fully suffer all pains.
Why is this?
Because ordinary beings lack mindfulness and wisdom,
they thus produce various outflows (defilements).
This is called the 'outflow of mindfulness' (Niàn Lòu).
The Púsà Móhēsà constantly reflects:
‘I, since countless kalpas in the past,
have created various evils for the sake of this body and mind.
Due to these causes and conditions,
I have wandered through transmigration and death in the three evil paths,
fully suffering all pains,
thereby causing me to be far from the correct path of the Three Vehicles.’
Due to these evil causes and conditions, the Púsà
generates great fear regarding his own body and mind,
abandons all evils,
and turns toward the wholesome path.
Good man!
For example, there was a king
who placed four poisonous snakes into a basket
and ordered a person to look after them,
feed them, attend to their sleeping and rising,
and rub and wash their bodies.
If he allowed one snake to become enraged,
‘I shall execute him in the city according to the law.’
At that time, the man, hearing the king’s strict order,
became fearful in his heart
and abandoned the basket and fled.
The king then dispatched five Caṇḍālas, following after him with drawn knives.
The man looked back and saw the five people behind him,
and quickly fled further.
At that time, the five people, using evil tactics,
concealed the knives they carried
and secretly sent one person, who falsely pretended to be friendly,
and said to him:
‘You may return.’
The man did not believe him
and threw himself into a village
intending to conceal himself.
After entering the village,
he peered into the houses but saw no one.
The vessels and containers he grasped were all empty, without anything inside.
Since he saw no people
and could find no objects,
he immediately sat down on the ground
and heard a voice from the air:
‘Alas,
man!
This village is desolate
and has no inhabitants.
Tonight six great bandits will come.
If you encounter them, your life will not be spared.
How can you escape them?’
At that time, the man’s terror increased,
and he abandoned the spot and left again.
On the road, he encountered a river.
The river was swift and surging;
there were no boats or rafts.
Because of his fear,
he immediately gathered various grasses and wood to make a raft.
He reflected further:
‘If I stay here,
I will be harmed by the poisonous snakes,
the five Caṇḍālas,
the one who falsely claimed friendship,
and the six great bandits.
If I cross this river,
the raft cannot be relied upon,
and I will drown.
I would rather drown
than be harmed by those snakes and bandits.’
He immediately pushed the grass raft
into the water,
laid his body upon it,
held it with his hands and pushed with his feet,
and crossed against the current.
Having reached the other shore,
he was safe and without misfortune,
his mind was tranquil,
and his terror vanished.
"The Bódhisattva Móhēsàttva who obtains, hears, and upholds the Dà Nièpán Jīng (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra),
views the body as a basket,
and Earth, Water, Fire, and Wind as four poisonous snakes—the poison of sight,
the poison of touch,
the poison of odor,
and the poison of biting—all sentient beings perish because they encounter these four poisons.
The Four Great Elements (Sì Dà) in sentient beings are also like this:
sometimes perceived as evil,
sometimes touched as evil,
sometimes sensed as evil,
sometimes attacked (bitten) as evil.
Due to these causes and conditions, they abandon all virtues.
Furthermore, virtuous man (shàn nánzǐ)!
The Bódhisattva Móhēsàttva views the four poisonous snakes as having four castes (zhǒng xìng):
namely, Kṣatriya (Chàlì),
Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén),
Vaiśya (Píshè),
and Śūdra (Shǒutuó).
These Four Great Elements snakes are likewise
possessed of four natures:
the nature of solidity,
the nature of moisture,
the nature of heat,
and the nature of motion.
Therefore, the Bódhisattva views these Four Great Elements as sharing the same caste nature as the four poisonous snakes.
Furthermore, virtuous man!
The Bódhisattva Móhēsàttva views these Four Great Elements as four poisonous snakes.
How is this viewing performed?
These four poisonous snakes constantly watch for an opportunity to harm people:
When should they employ sight?
When should they employ touch?
When should they employ scent?
When should they employ biting?
The Four Great Elements poisonous snakes are also like this:
they constantly watch sentient beings, seeking their deficiencies.
If one is killed by the four snakes,
one will ultimately not reach the Three Evil Paths (Sān È Dào);
but if one is killed by the harm of the Four Great Elements,
one will certainly reach the Three Evil Paths,
definitely without doubt.
Although these four poisonous snakes are watched over and nourished,
they still wish to kill people;
the Four Great Elements are likewise,
although constantly supplied and nourished,
they constantly drag people into committing all kinds of evil.
If even one of these four poisonous snakes becomes angry, it can kill a person;
the nature of the Four Great Elements is also like this:
if one of the Great Elements flares up, it can also harm people.
Although these four poisonous snakes are in the same place,
their four intentions are distinct;
the Four Great Elements poisonous snakes are also like this:
although in the same place,
their natures are separately distinct.
Although these four poisonous snakes are treated respectfully,
they are difficult to approach intimately;
the Four Great Elements poisonous snakes are also like this:
although treated respectfully, they are also difficult to approach intimately.
When these four poisonous snakes harm people,
there may be Śrāmaṇas (Shāméng)
or Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén), etc.,
who, using incantations (zhòu) and medicine, can heal and treat the victim;
but when the Four Great Elements kill people,
even if there are Śrāmaṇas
or Brāhmaṇas, etc., with divine incantations and fine medicine,
they cannot cure them.
Just as a self-satisfied person hears the foul, repulsive stench of the four poisonous snakes' breath,
and immediately keeps far away;
all Buddhas and Bódhisattvas are also like this:
when they smell the foulness of the Four Great Elements,
they immediately keep far away.
At that time, the Bódhisattva further contemplates the Four Great Elements poisonous snakes,
gives rise to great fear,
turns his back and runs away,
cultivating the Eightfold Noble Path (Bā Shèng Dào).
"The Five Caṇḍālas (Wǔ Zhāntuóluó) are the Five Aggregates (Wǔ Yīn).
How does the Bódhisattva view the Five Aggregates as Caṇḍālas?
Caṇḍālas
are those who constantly cause others to separate from those they love
and gather with those they resent and hate.
The Five Aggregates are also like this:
they cause people to greedily approach unwholesome dharmas,
and keep far away from all purely wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, virtuous man!
Just as a Caṇḍāla
adorns himself with various weapons and armor:
whether knife,
shield,
bow,
arrow,
armor,
or spear—
they are able to harm people.
The Five Aggregates are also like this:
they firmly adorn themselves with various afflictions (fánnǎo),
harming all ignorant people
and causing them to fall into all realms of existence.
Virtuous man!
Just as a Caṇḍāla,
upon finding faults in a person, seizes the opportunity to harm them;
the Five Aggregates are also like this:
when there are faults (defilements),
they are constantly able to harm people.
For this reason,
the Bódhisattva profoundly views the Five Aggregates as Caṇḍālas.
Furthermore, the Bódhisattva observes the Five Aggregates as Caṇḍālas:
Caṇḍāla people lack a mind of compassion,
harming both enemies and relatives alike;
the Five Aggregates are also like this:
lacking a mind of compassion,
they harm both the virtuous and the evil alike.
Just as Caṇḍālas vex all people;
the Five Aggregates are also like this:
through various afflictions,
they constantly vex all sentient beings trapped in saṃsāra.
Therefore, the Bódhisattva views the Five Aggregates as Caṇḍālas.
Furthermore, the Bódhisattva observes the Five Aggregates as Caṇḍālas:
Caṇḍāla people constantly harbor a mind of malice;
the Five Aggregates are also like this:
they constantly harbor the mind of defilements, vexation, and malice.
Just as a person without feet, knife, staff, or attendants,
one should know, will certainly be killed by a Caṇḍāla person;
sentient beings are also like this:
without feet,
without a knife,
and without attendants,
they are harmed by the Five Aggregates.
'Feet' refers to precepts,
'knife' refers to wisdom,
and 'attendants' refers to virtuous friends (shàn zhīshì).
Lacking these three things,
they are harmed by the Five Aggregates.
Therefore, the Bódhisattva views the Five Aggregates as Caṇḍālas."
Furthermore, virtuous man!
The *Púsà Móhēsà* observes that the Five *Yīn* (Skandhas) surpass the *Zhāntuóluó* (Caṇḍālas) [in harm].
Why is this?
If sentient beings are slain by the five *Zhāntuóluó*,
they do not fall into *Dìyù* (hells);
but those slain by the *Yīn* fall into *Dìyù*.
Due to this meaning,
the *Púsà* observes that the *Yīn* surpass the *Zhāntuóluó*.
Having made this observation, they make a vow, saying:
'I would rather spend my entire life near *Zhāntuóluó*,
than approach the Five *Yīn* for a moment.
The *Zhāntuóluó*,
can only harm foolish people in the Desire Realm (*Yùjiè*);
but these five *Yīn* thieves,
harm ordinary sentient beings throughout the Three Realms (*Sānjiè*).
The *Zhāntuóluó* can only slaughter those who are guilty;
but these five *Yīn* thieves do not question whether sentient beings are guilty or innocent,
they are capable of harming all of them.
The *Zhāntuóluó* do not harm the aged,
women,
or the young;
but these five *Yīn* thieves do not question whether sentient beings are old or young,
or women,
they harm absolutely everyone.
Therefore, the *Púsà* deeply observes that these *Yīn* surpass the *Zhāntuóluó*,
and thus makes a vow,
saying they would rather approach the *Zhāntuóluó* for life,
than draw near to the Five *Yīn* for a moment.
Furthermore, virtuous man!
The *Zhāntuóluó* harm only others,
they never harm themselves;
but the thieves of the Five *Yīn* harm themselves
and harm others,
thus surpassing the *Zhāntuóluó*.
The *Zhāntuóluó* can be sought out and escaped from through kind words,
money,
or treasures and goods;
the Five *Yīn* are not like this.
They cannot be forcefully sought out and escaped from through kind words of persuasion,
or money, treasures, and goods.
The *Zhāntuóluó* do not necessarily kill constantly throughout the four seasons;
the Five *Yīn* are not like this.
They constantly harm sentient beings moment by moment.
The *Zhāntuóluó* can be escaped by fleeing to a single place;
the Five *Yīn* are not like this.
They are present everywhere,
and there is nowhere to flee.
Although the *Zhāntuóluó* harm people,
they do not follow them after causing harm;
the Five *Yīn* are not like this.
After slaying sentient beings, they follow them without separation.
Therefore, the *Púsà* would rather approach the *Zhāntuóluó* for life,
than approach the Five *Yīn* for a moment.
The wise person achieves liberation from the Five *Yīn* through skillful means.
These skillful means
are the Eight Noble Paths (*Bā Shèng Dào*),
the Six *Bōluómì* (Pāramitās),
and the Four Immeasurable Minds (*Sì Wúliàng Xīn*).
By these means, they achieve liberation,
and their body and mind are not harmed by the Five *Yīn*.
Why is this?
Their body is like a diamond (*Jīngāng*),
and their mind is like empty space (*Xūkōng*).
Therefore, the body and mind are difficult to destroy or corrupt.
Due to this meaning,
the *Púsà* observes that the *Yīn* accomplish various unwholesome *Dharma* (dharmas),
gives rise to great fear,
and practices the Eight Noble Paths.
It is also like a person who fears four poisonous snakes,
and five *Zhāntuóluó*,
traveling along the road,
without looking back or staying behind.
The 'false friend pretending kindness'
is called greedy craving (*tān ài*).
The *Púsà Móhēsà* deeply observes the bond of craving (*ài jié*),
as an enemy pretending to be a friend.
If the truth is known, it cannot prevail;
if it is not known, one will certainly be harmed by it.
Greedy craving is also like this.
If its nature is known,
it cannot cause sentient beings to cycle through the suffering of transmigration (*shēngsǐ kǔ zhōng*);
but if it is not known,
they revolve through the Six Destinies (*Liù Qù*) and undergo all forms of suffering.
Why is this?
Because craving, as a disease,
is difficult to renounce and abandon.
Like an enemy pretending to be a friend is difficult to avoid,
the enemy pretending to be a friend
constantly watches for opportunities,
causing beloved ones to separate,
and hateful enemies to congregate.
Craving is also like this.
It causes people to distance themselves from all wholesome *Dharma* (dharmas),
and approach all unwholesome *Dharma* (dharmas).
Due to this meaning,
the *Púsà Móhēsà* deeply observes greedy craving,
as an enemy pretending to be a friend.
Because they see and yet do not see,
and hear and yet do not hear,
it is like an ordinary person who sees the faults of transmigration (*shēngsǐ*),
but although possessing wisdom, because it is obscured by delusion (*chī*),
later they do not see it again.
The *Shēngwén* and *Yuánjué* are also like this.
Though they see, they do not see;
though they hear, they do not hear.
Why is this?
Because of the mind of craving.
Why is this so?
(If they) see the faults of transmigration,
they cannot quickly reach *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí* (Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi).
Due to this meaning,
the *Púsà Móhēsà* observes this bond of craving as an enemy pretending to be a friend.
What is meant by the appearance of an enemy pretending to be a friend?
Like an enemy who is unreal but falsely presents reality,
who cannot be approached but falsely presents the appearance of approachability,
who is truly unwholesome but falsely presents the appearance of wholesomeness,
who is truly unlovable but falsely creates the appearance of love.
Why is this?
Because they constantly watch for opportunities
and seek to cause harm.
Craving is also like this.
It constantly appears to sentient beings as non-real yet falsely real,
non-approachable yet falsely approachable,
non-wholesome yet falsely wholesome,
non-lovable yet falsely lovable,
constantly deceiving all
and causing them to revolve in transmigration.
Due to this meaning,
the *Púsà* observes craving as an enemy pretending to be a friend.
The enemy pretending to be a friend
only shows their body and mouth,
but their mind is not seen,
and thus they are able to deceive.
Craving is also like this.
It is only false deception,
truly unobtainable,
and thus it is able to confuse all sentient beings.
The enemy pretending to be a friend
has a beginning and an end,
and is easy to avoid.
Craving is not like this.
It is beginningless and endless,
and difficult to avoid.
The enemy pretending to be a friend
is hard to recognize from afar,
but easy to recognize up close;
craving is not like this.
It is difficult to recognize even when near,
how much more so when far away?
Due to this meaning,
the *Púsà* observes that craving surpasses the false friend [in danger].
All sentient beings, due to the bond of craving,
are distant from Great *Nièpán* (Nirvāṇa),
and close to transmigration (*shēngsǐ*);
distant from permanence, joy, self, and purity (*cháng lè wǒ jìng*),
and close to impermanence (*wúcháng*),
suffering (*kǔ*),
non-self (*wúwǒ*),
and impurity (*bú jìng*).
Therefore, in various *Jīng* (sūtras), I have spoken of them as the Three Defilements.
Regarding present affairs,
because of ignorance (*wúmíng*),
one does not see the faults and dangers,
and cannot renounce and abandon the enemy of craving pretending to be a friend.
[This enemy] ultimately cannot harm the wise person.
Therefore, the *Púsà* deeply observes this craving,
gives rise to great fear,
and practices the Eight Noble Paths,
just like that person who fears four poisonous snakes,
five *Zhāntuóluó*, and one false friend,
traveling the road without turning back.
"The empty village refers to the six sense entrances (liù rù).
The Púsà Móhēsà observes that the internal six entrances (liù rù) are empty and non-existent,
just like an empty village.
Just like that frightened person, having entered the village,
does not see even a single resident,
searching everywhere and seizing vessels,
but obtaining nothing.
The Púsà is also like this:
carefully observing the six entrances (liù rù) as empty and non-existent,
seeing no reality in any single thing belonging to sentient beings.
Therefore, the Púsà observes the internal six entrances (liù rù) as empty and non-existent,
like that empty village.
Shànnánzǐ!
That empty village,
when the group of robbers observes it from afar,
they never conceive the thought of emptiness.
Ordinary people are also like this:
regarding the cluster of six entrances (liù rù), they do not conceive the thought of emptiness.
Because they are unable to conceive the thought of emptiness,
they revolve in Saṃsāra, receiving immeasurable suffering.
Shànnánzǐ!
When the group of robbers arrives, they then conceive the thought of emptiness.
The Púsà is also like this:
observing these six entrances (liù rù), they constantly conceive the thought of emptiness.
Because they conceive the thought of emptiness,
they do not revolve in Saṃsāra, receiving suffering.
The Púsà Móhēsà is constantly free from delusion regarding these six entrances (liù rù).
Because they are free from delusion,
therefore, they no longer revolve in Saṃsāra.
Furthermore, Shànnánzǐ!
Just as a group of robbers, upon entering this empty village, finds peace and pleasure,
the robbers of affliction (fánnǎo) are also like this:
entering these six entrances (liù rù), they find peace and pleasure.
Just as robbers dwelling in an empty village
have no fear in their hearts,
the group of robbers of affliction (fánnǎo) are also like this:
dwelling in these six entrances (liù rù),
they also have no fear.
Just as that empty village
is the dwelling place of lions,
tigers, wolves,
and various fierce beasts,
these internal six entrances (liù rù) are also like this:
the dwelling place of all evil afflictions (fánnǎo) and running beasts.
Therefore, the Púsà observes deeply that the six entrances (liù rù) are empty and non-existent,
purely being the dwelling place of all that is unwholesome.
"Furthermore, Shànnánzǐ!
The Púsà Móhēsà observes the internal six entrances (liù rù) as empty and non-existent,
like that empty village.
Why is this?
Because they are illusory, deceitful, and unreal.
Although empty and non-existent, they give rise to the perception of existence.
Although truly without pleasure, they give rise to the perception of pleasure.
Although truly without a person, they give rise to the perception of a person.
These internal six entrances (liù rù) are also like this:
although empty and non-existent, one creates the perception of existence;
although truly without pleasure, one creates the perception of pleasure;
although truly without a person, one creates the perception of a person.
Only a wise person is able to know this and obtain the reality.
Furthermore, Shànnánzǐ!
Just as in an empty village,
sometimes there are people,
and sometimes there are no people;
the six entrances (liù rù) are not like this:
they are consistently without a person.
Why is this?
Because their nature is always empty.
This is known by the wise, not seen by the eye.
Therefore, the Púsà observes the internal six entrances (liù rù)
as having many enemies and harms,
and cultivates the Bā Shèngdào without rest or cessation,
just like that person who, fearing the Four Poisonous Snakes,
the Wǔ Zhāntuóluó,
the One False Friend, and the Six Great Robbers,
fearfully flees onto the Right Path.
"The Six Great Robbers are the external six sense objects (liù chén).
The Púsà Móhēsà observes these six sense objects (liù chén) as the Six Great Robbers.
Why is this?
Because they are able to plunder all wholesome dharmas.
Just as the Six Great Robbers can plunder all the property and wealth of the people,
these robbers of the six sense objects (liù chén) are also like this:
they can plunder the wholesome wealth of all sentient beings.
Just as the Six Great Robbers,
if they enter a person’s house, can steal all that the present household possesses,
without discriminating between good or bad,
suddenly rendering the extremely wealthy poor,
these robbers of the six sense objects (liù chén) are also like this:
if they enter a person’s faculties (roots), they can plunder all wholesome dharmas.
Once wholesome dharmas are exhausted,
poor and exposed,
one becomes an Yīchǎntí.
Therefore, the Púsà carefully observes the six sense objects (liù chén) as the Six Great Robbers.
Furthermore, Shànnánzǐ!
Just as the Six Great Robbers,
when they wish to plunder a person,
must rely on someone inside;
if there is no one inside,
they will turn back halfway.
These robbers of the six sense objects (liù chén) are also like this:
to plunder wholesome dharmas, they must rely on the internal existence of
sentient beings’ views and perceptions,
the marks of Eternity, Joy, Self, and Purity (Cháng Lè Wǒ Jìng),
and the mark of non-emptiness.
If internally these marks do not exist,
the evil robbers of the six sense objects (liù chén)
are unable to plunder all wholesome dharmas.
A wise person internally lacks these marks,
but ordinary people possess them.
Therefore, the six sense objects (liù chén) constantly come to encroach upon and plunder the wealth of wholesome dharmas.
Because it is not well-protected,
it is plundered by them.
The protector is named Wisdom.
A wise person is able to skillfully guard and protect,
and thus is not robbed.
Therefore, the Púsà observes these six sense objects (liù chén) as being no different from the Six Great Robbers.
"Furthermore, Shànnánzǐ!
Just as the Six Great Robbers can cause people suffering and distress in body and mind,
these robbers of the six sense objects (liù chén) are also like this:
they constantly cause sentient beings suffering and distress in body and mind.
The Six Great Robbers can only plunder people's current wealth;
these robbers of the six sense objects (liù chén) constantly plunder the wholesome wealth of sentient beings in the three times (past, present, future).
The Six Great Robbers find enjoyment at night;
the evil robbers of the six sense objects (liù chén) are also like this:
they find enjoyment when residing in the darkness of ignorance.
The Six Great Robbers can only be stopped by kings;
the evil robbers of the six sense objects (liù chén) are also like this:
they can only be stopped by Fó Púsà.
The Six Great Robbers, whenever they wish to plunder, do not discriminate based on whether the person is beautiful,
of high caste,
intelligent,
widely learned,
powerful, noble, or poor;
the evil robbers of the six sense objects (liù chén) are also like this:
when they wish to plunder wholesome dharmas, they do not discriminate from the beautiful up to the poor.
Even if kings cut off the hands and feet of the Six Great Robbers,
they still cannot make their minds cease;
the evil robbers of the six sense objects (liù chén) are also like this:
even though Xūtuóyuán,
Sītuóhán,
and Ānàhán cut off their hands and feet,
they still cannot prevent them from plundering wholesome dharmas.
Just as a brave and vigorous person is able to subdue these Six Great Robbers,
the Fó Púsà are also like this:
they are able to subdue the evil robbers of the six sense objects (liù chén).
For example, if a person has many relatives
and their clan power is flourishing,
they will not be plundered by those six robbers.
Sentient beings are also like this:
if they have good friends (shàn zhīshì),
they will not be plundered by the evil robbers of the six sense objects (liù chén).
These Six Great Robbers, if they see objects,
are then able to steal and plunder them.
The six sense objects (liù chén) are not like this:
whether seen or known,
heard or smelled,
touched or felt,
they can entirely plunder.
The Six Great Robbers can only plunder the wealth of people in the Desire Realm (Yùjiè);
they cannot plunder the Form and Formless Realms (Sè Wúsè Jiè).
The evil robbers of the six sense objects (liù chén) are not like this:
they are able to plunder all wholesome treasures across the Three Realms (Sānjiè).
Therefore, the Púsà carefully observes that the six sense objects (liù chén) surpass those six robbers [in severity].
Having made this observation,
they cultivate the Bā Shèngdào,
going straight forward without turning back.
Just like that frightened person,
fearing the Four Poisonous Snakes,
the Wǔ Zhāntuóluó,
the One False Friend, and the Six Great Robbers,
abandoned the empty village and proceeded upon the road.
"The road encountering a river is suffering (Fánnǎo).
How does a Bódìsà contemplate this suffering as being like a great river?
Just like that swift river,
which can wash away fragrant elephants;
the swift river of suffering is also like this,
able to wash away Yuánjué.
Therefore, the Bódìsà deeply contemplates suffering as being like a swift river.
It is deep and difficult to find the bottom,
hence it is named a river;
the banks cannot be found,
hence it is named great.
Within it are many kinds of evil fish,
the great river of suffering is also like this.
Only the Fó and Bódìsà are able to reach the bottom,
hence it is named extremely deep.
Only the Fó and Bódìsà obtain its banks,
hence it is named vast and great.
Because they constantly harm all foolish sentient beings,
they are named evil fish.
Therefore, the Bódìsà contemplates this suffering as being like a great river.
Just as the water of a great river can nourish all grass, trees, thickets, and forests;
the great river of suffering is also like this,
capable of nurturing sentient beings through the Twenty-Five Existences (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu).
Therefore, the Bódìsà contemplates this suffering as being like a great river.
For example, there is a person,
who falls into the great river water without shame or repentance (Cánkuì);
sentient beings are also like this,
falling into the river of suffering without shame or repentance (Cánkuì).
Just as one who falls into the river dies before reaching the bottom;
falling into the river of suffering is also like this:
not yet reaching the bottom,
one constantly revolves in transmigration through the Twenty-Five Existences (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu).
What is referred to as the bottom is named the sign of emptiness (Kōngxiàng).
If there is someone who does not cultivate this sign of emptiness (Kōngxiàng),
you should know that this person cannot escape the Twenty-Five Existences (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu).
Because all sentient beings cannot skillfully cultivate emptiness and non-signs (Kōngwú Xiàng),
they are constantly washed away by the swift river of suffering.
Just as that great river can only destroy the body,
and cannot wash away all good dharmas;
the great river of suffering is not like this,
it can destroy all good dharmas (shànfǎ) of body and mind.
That great fierce river,
can only wash away people within the Desire Realm (Yùjiè);
the great river of suffering, however, can wash away people and gods within the Three Realms (Sānjiè).
In worldly great rivers,
by holding on with hands and pushing with feet,
one reaches the other shore (Bǐ'àn);
in the great river of suffering,
only the Bódìsà, relying on the Six Pāramitā (Liù Bōluómì), can cross it.
Just as the water of a great river is difficult to cross;
the great river of suffering is also like this, difficult to cross.
What is meant by "difficult to cross"?
Even the great Bódìsàs of the Ten Stages (Shí Zhù),
are still unable to ultimately cross it,
only the various Fó can ultimately cross it,
hence it is named "difficult to cross."
For example, if a person is carried away by a river,
they cannot cultivate even an ounce of good dharma (shànfǎ);
sentient beings are also like this,
those who are washed away and submerged by the river of suffering,
are also unable to cultivate good dharma (shànfǎ).
Just as a person falling into a river and being washed away by the water,
others who are strong can rescue and save them;
those who fall into the river of suffering and become Icchantikas (Yīchǎntí),
even Shēngwén, Yuánjué, and the various Fó cannot rescue and save them.
When the great rivers of the world reach the end of the kalpa (jié),
and seven suns shine together,
they can cause them to dry up;
the great river of suffering is not like this.
Although Shēngwén and Yuánjué cultivate the Seven Awakenings (Qī Jué),
they still cannot dry it up.
Therefore, the Bódìsà contemplates all sufferings as being like a fierce river.
"For example, that person,
fearing the Four Poisonous Snakes (Sì Dúshé),
the Five Caṇḍālas (Wǔ Zhāntuóluó),
one who falsely feigns kinship and friendship (Yī Zhà Qīnshàn), and the Six Great Thieves (Liù Dà Zéi),
abandons the empty village,
and follows the road away.
Having arrived at the river, he takes grass to make a raft.
The Bódìsà is also like this,
fearing the Four Great Snakes (Sì Dà Shé),
the Five Skandhas (Wǔ Yīn) Caṇḍālas,
craving (Ài) which falsely feigns kinship and friendship,
the Six Entrances (Liù Rù) empty village,
and the Six Dusts (Liù Chén) evil thieves.
Arriving at the river of suffering,
they cultivate precepts (jiè),
concentration (dìng),
wisdom (huì),
liberation (jiětuō),
the knowledge and view of liberation (jiětuō zhījiàn),
the Six Pāramitā (Liù Bōluómì),
and the Thirty-Seven Factors of Enlightenment (Sānshíqī Pǐn),
taking them as a boat and a raft.
Relying upon and riding this raft,
they cross the river of suffering,
reach the other shore (Bǐ'àn),
and abide in constant bliss (chánglè) Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
The Bódìsà cultivating the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán) thinks thus:
'If I cannot endure and accept such suffering of body and mind,
then I cannot enable all sentient beings to cross the river of suffering.'
Due to this thought,
although there is such suffering and distress of body and mind,
they silently endure it.
Because of enduring it, outflows (lòu/āsravas) do not arise.
Since such a Bódìsà does not have any outflows,
how much less would the Fó Rúlái have outflows?
Therefore, the various Fó are not called "having outflows" (yǒulòu).
"Why is the Rúlái not without outflows (wúlòu)?
Because the Rúlái constantly practices within that which has outflows.
That which has outflows (yǒulòu) is precisely the Twenty-Five Existences (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu).
Therefore, Shēngwén
and ordinary persons (fánfū) say the Fó has outflows,
but the various Fó Rúlái are truly without outflows (wúlòu).
Good son!
Due to this cause and condition (yīnyuán),
the various Fó Rúlái do not possess a fixed characteristic (dìngxiàng).
Good son!
Therefore, those who commit the Four Cardinal Prohibitions (Sì Chóng Jìn),
slander the Vaipulya Sūtras (Fāngděng Jīng), and the Icchantikas (Yīchǎntí),
are all unfixed (bù dìng).
At that time, Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng Púsà Móhēsà spoke:
"Thus,
thus.
Truly, as the sage teachings state,
all dharmas (zhūfǎ) are entirely unfixed.
Because they are unfixed,
you should know that the Rúlái does not ultimately enter into Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
As the Fó previously taught,
the Púsà Móhēsà cultivates Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
Among that which is heard and that which is not heard, is there Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
and Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán)?
What is Nirvāṇa (Nièpán)?
What is Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán)?
At that time, the Buddha praised the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng, saying:
“Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
If there is a Bodhisattva who attains recollection and comprehensive retention (dhāraṇī),
then they are able to inquire as you have.
Good man!
Just as worldly people speak of a sea
and a great sea,
a river
and a great river,
a mountain
and a great mountain,
land
and great land,
a city
and a great city,
a sentient being
and a great sentient being,
a king
and a great king,
a person
and a great person,
a deity
and a deity among deities,
a path
and a great path;
Nièpán is likewise:
there is Nièpán
and there is Great Nièpán.
What is Nièpán?
Good man!
Just as when a person is hungry,
obtaining a little food is called peace and bliss,
such peace and bliss is also called Nièpán.
Just as recovering from illness is called peace and bliss,
such peace and bliss is also called Nièpán.
Just as a fearful person obtaining a refuge attains peace and bliss,
such peace and bliss is also called Nièpán.
Just as a poor person acquiring seven treasures attains peace and bliss,
such peace and bliss is also called Nièpán.
Just as a person contemplating bones (skeletons) and not giving rise to greed attains peace and bliss,
such peace and bliss is also called Nièpán.
Such Nièpán cannot be called Great Nièpán.
Why is that?
Because of hunger and thirst,
because of sickness,
because of fear,
because of poverty,
and because of giving rise to grasping (attachment).
This is called Nièpán,
not Great Nièpán.
Good man!
If ordinary people and those of the Shēngwén path,
either due to worldly matters
or due to the Noble Path,
sever the fetters of the desire realm, they attain peace and bliss;
such peace and bliss is also called Nièpán,
but it cannot be called Great Nièpán.
If they are able to sever the first jhāna,
and even able to sever the fetters of the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception,
they attain peace and bliss;
such peace and bliss is also called Nièpán,
but it cannot be called Great Nièpán.
Why is that?
Because defilements can return,
and because of the residual traces (vāsanā).
What are called the residual traces of defilement?
The Shēngwén and Yuánjué paths have the traces of defilement,
namely 'my body,'
'my clothes,'
'I go,'
'I come,'
'I speak,'
'I listen.'
When all Buddhas and Tathāgatas enter Nièpán,
the nature of Nièpán is without self
and without bliss,
only having permanence and purity.
This is then called the residual traces of defilement.
The Buddha,
the Dharma,
and the Sangha have distinct characteristics,
while the Tathāgata ultimately enters Nièpán.
The Nièpán attained by the Shēngwén,
Yuánjué, and all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is equally without distinction.
For this reason,
what the Two Vehicles attain is not Great Nièpán.
Why is that?
Because they lack permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Only permanence, bliss, self, and purity can be called Great Nièpán.
Good man!
For example, a place that can receive all waters
is called a great sea.
Similarly, the realm entered by Shēngwén,
Yuánjué,
Bodhisattvas,
and all Buddhas and Tathāgatas
is called Great Nièpán.
The Four Jhānas,
the Three Samādhis,
the Eight Vimokṣas (deliverances),
the Eight Abhibhāyatanas (mastery bases),
and the Ten Kṛtsnas (all-bases)—
whoever is able to encompass and absorb such measureless good dharmas
is called Great Nièpán.
“Good man!
For example, there is a river
whose bottom the foremost fragrant elephant cannot reach;
it is then called great.
If Shēngwén, Yuánjué, and Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (Daśa-bhūmi) do not perceive the Buddha nature,
it is called Nièpán,
but not Great Nièpán.
If one can clearly and distinctly perceive the Buddha nature,
then it is called Great Nièpán.
This Great Nièpán,
only the Great Elephant King can reach its depths;
the Great Elephant Kings are the Buddhas.
Good man!
If the Móhē Nàjiā (great nāgas) and Bōjiāntuó,
and great powerful beings spend much time
yet cannot ascend it,
then it is called a great mountain.
Shēngwén,
Yuánjué, and all Bodhisattvas Móhē Nàjiā,
and great powerful beings cannot perceive it;
only in this way is it called Great Nièpán.
Furthermore, good man!
Wherever a lesser king resides
is called a small city;
where the holy king Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng resides is then called a great city.
The residences of the Shēngwén
and Yuánjué,
eighty thousand,
sixty thousand,
forty thousand,
twenty thousand,
or ten thousand stages of abiding,
are called Nièpán.
The residence of the Supreme Dharma Master
and Holy King
is then called Great Parinirvāṇa;
it is for this reason that it is called Great Parinirvāṇa.
Good man!
For example, if a person sees the four kinds of troops yet does not give rise to fear,
you should know that this person is called a great sentient being.
If a sentient being, regarding the three evil realms
and the evil karma of defilement, does not give rise to fear,
but is able to extensively save sentient beings within them,
you should know that this person has attained Great Nièpán.
If there is a person who can support their parents,
respect Śramaṇas and Brāhmaṇas,
cultivate and implement good dharmas, whose speech is sincere and without deceit,
who can endure all evils,
and who gives generously to the poor and needy, they are called a great man (Mahāsattva).
A Bodhisattva is likewise:
having great compassion and pity for all,
treating all sentient beings as their parents,
able to ferry sentient beings across the river of life and death,
and universally showing all sentient beings the path of ultimate reality.
This, then, is called Great Parinirvāṇa.
“Good man!
The name ‘Great’ means inconceivable.
If it is inconceivable,
it is something that all sentient beings cannot believe;
this is then called Great Parinirvāṇa.
Because it is perceived only by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it is called Great Nièpán.
By what causes and conditions is it again called Great?
Because it is attained only after measureless causes and conditions,
therefore it is called Great.
Good man!
Just as worldly people
call something obtained through many causes and conditions
Great.
Nièpán is likewise;
because it is obtained through many causes and conditions,
therefore it is called Great.
Why is it again called Great Nièpán?
Because it possesses the Great Self (Mahātman),
it is called Great Nièpán.
The selflessness of Nièpán,
due to its Great Sovereignty (Mahā-aiśvarya),
is called the Great Self.
What is called Great Sovereignty?
The possession of the Eight Freedoms
is then called the Self.
What are the Eight?
First,
being able to manifest one body as many bodies,
the size and number of the bodies being like dust particles,
filling the measureless worlds of the ten directions.
The body of the Tathāgata is truly not a dust particle,
but through sovereignty, it manifests a dust-particle body;
such sovereignty is the Great Self.
“‘Secondly,
[the Tathāgata] demonstrates a body as small as a speck of dust filling the Three-Thousand Great-Thousand Worlds,
but the Tathāgata’s (Rúlái) body does not actually fill the Three-Thousand Great-Thousand Worlds.
Why is this?
Because of unimpededness (wú ài),
simply because of self-mastery (zìzài),
[He] fills the Three-Thousand Great-Thousand Worlds.
Such self-mastery
is called the Great Self (Dàwǒ).
“‘Thirdly,
[He] can lightly lift the body that fills this Three-Thousand Great-Thousand Worlds and fly through the air,
passing beyond worlds of Buddhas (Fó) equal to twenty Gánghéshā (Ganges sand grains) without impediment.
The Tathāgata’s body
is truly without lightness or heaviness;
because of self-mastery, it can become light or heavy.
Such self-mastery is called the Great Self.
“‘Fourthly,
because of self-mastery, [He] attains self-mastery.
What is this self-mastery?
The Tathāgata’s mind abides steadfastly in concentration (yīxīn ānlù bùdòng),
yet He can manifest and transform into measureless forms and kinds,
each with its own mind.
Sometimes the Tathāgata performs a single deed,
yet enables sentient beings (zhòngshēng) to accomplish it variously.
The Tathāgata’s body constantly abides in one land (tǔ),
yet allows all [beings] in other lands to see Him.
Such self-mastery is called the Great Self.
“‘Fifthly,
[it is called this] because of mastery over the faculties (gēn zìzài).
How is this mastery over the faculties named?
The Tathāgata’s single faculty
can also see forms (sè),
hear sounds (shēng),
smell scents (xiāng),
discern tastes (wèi),
perceive touches (chù),
and know phenomena (fǎ).
The Tathāgata’s six faculties
also do not see forms,
hear sounds,
smell scents,
discern tastes,
perceive touches,
or know phenomena.
Because of self-mastery,
He makes the faculties self-mastered.
Such self-mastery is called the Great Self.
“‘Sixthly,
because of self-mastery, [He] attains all phenomena,
yet the Tathāgata’s mind has no thought of attainment.
Why is this?
Because there is nothing to attain.
If there were existence, it could be called attainment;
since there is truly nothing existent, how can it be called attainment?
If the Tathāgata held the concept (jì) of having attained,
then the Buddhas would not attain Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
Because there is no attainment, it is named the attainment of Nirvāṇa.
Because of self-mastery, [He] attains all phenomena;
because of attaining the phenomena, [He] is called the Great Self.
“‘Seventhly,
[it is called this] because of mastery in speaking (shuō zìzài).
The Tathāgata expounds the meaning of a single verse (jì)
for measureless eons (jié),
and the meaning is still not exhausted—
that is to say, regarding precepts (jiè),
regarding concentration (dìng),
regarding giving (shī),
regarding wisdom (huì).
At that time, the Tathāgata does not give rise to the thought,
“I speak and others listen”;
nor does He give rise to the concept of a single verse.
People of the world (shìjiān zhī rén) take four lines to be a verse;
following worldly convention, it is said to be a verse.
The nature of all phenomena (fǎ xìng) is also without speech;
because of self-mastery, the Tathāgata expounds.
Because of expounding, [He] is called the Great Self.
“‘Eighthly,
the Tathāgata pervades all places,
just like empty space (xūkōng).
The nature of empty space cannot be seen;
the Tathāgata is also like this, truly unseen.
Because of self-mastery, [He] allows all [beings] to see Him.
Such self-mastery is called the Great Self.
Such a Great Self is named Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
Because of this meaning (yì), it is named Great Nirvāṇa.
“‘Furthermore, good man (shàn nánzǐ)!
For example, a treasure vault (bǎozàng)
contains many rare and precious things,
fully equipped in a hundred ways;
thus, it is called a Great Vault (Dàzàng).
The profound and hidden vault of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas is also like this:
rich in many wonders and rarities,
fully complete and lacking nothing;
it is named Great Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, good man!
A boundless thing is called Great.
Nirvāṇa is boundless, thus it is named Great.
“‘Furthermore, good man!
Because it possesses Great Joy (Dà Lè), it is named Great Nirvāṇa.
Nirvāṇa is without joy;
but because of the Four Joys,
it is named Great Nirvāṇa.
What are the four?
First,
it severs all joys (lè).
That which does not sever joy is called suffering (kǔ).
If there is suffering, it is not named Great Joy.
Because joy is severed, there is no suffering.
Where there is neither suffering nor joy, it is named Great Joy.
The nature of Nirvāṇa is without suffering and without joy.
Therefore, Nirvāṇa is named Great Joy.
Because of this meaning, it is named Great Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, good man!
Joy is of two kinds:
first, that of ordinary beings (fánfū);
second, that of the Buddhas.
The joy of ordinary beings
is impermanent (wúcháng) and subject to ruin;
therefore, it is not [true] joy.
The constant joy of the Buddhas is without change or variation;
thus, it is named Great Joy.
Furthermore, good man!
There are three kinds of feelings (shòu):
first, painful feeling (kǔ shòu);
second, pleasurable feeling (lè shòu);
third, neither-painful-nor-pleasurable feeling (bù kǔ bù lè shòu).
Neither-painful-nor-pleasurable is also suffering.
Although Nirvāṇa is similar to neither-painful-nor-pleasurable,
yet it is named Great Joy.
Because of Great Joy,
it is named Great Nirvāṇa.
“‘Secondly,
because of Great Tranquility (Dà Jìngjìng), it is named Great Joy.
The nature of Nirvāṇa is Great Tranquility.
Why is this?
Because it is far removed from all clamorous phenomena.
Because of Great Tranquility, it is named Great Nirvāṇa.
“‘Thirdly,
because of Omniscience (Yīqiè Zhī),
it is named Great Joy.
That which is not omniscient is not named Great Joy.
Because the Buddhas and Tathāgatas are omniscient, they are named Great Joy.
Because of Great Joy,
it is named Great Nirvāṇa.
“‘Fourthly,
because the body (shēn) is indestructible,
it is named Great Joy.
If the body were destructible, it would not be named Joy.
The Tathāgata’s body is adamantine (jīngāng) and indestructible.
It is not a body of affliction (fánnǎo shēn),
nor a body of impermanence;
thus, it is named Great Joy.
Because of Great Joy,
it is named Great Nirvāṇa.’”
"Good men!
Worldly names sometimes have causes (yīnyuán),
and sometimes have no causes.
Those with causes
are like Shèlìfú:
his mother was named Shèlì;
the name was established because of his mother,
thus he is named Shèlìfú.
Such as the ascetic Mótiūluó Rén,
who was born in the Mótiūluó kingdom;
the name was established because of the kingdom,
thus he is named the ascetic Mótiūluó Rén.
Such as Mùjiānlián;
Mùjiānlián is his surname,
the name was established because of his surname,
thus he is named Mùjiānlián.
Such as myself, born into the Qú tán lineage;
based on the lineage, the name Qú tán was established.
Such as the ascetic Píshèqū Rén.
Píshèqū
is the name of a star;
the name was established because of the star,
named Píshèqū.
Such as a person having six fingers;
because of the six fingers,
he is named the six-fingered person.
Such as Fónú (Buddha's Slave),
and Tiānnú (Deva's Slave);
based on the Buddha,
and based on the Deva,
thus they are named Fónú
and Tiānnú.
Because they are born from moisture,
they are named moisture-born.
Such as those named based on sound:
named Jiājiāluó,
named Jiūjiūluó,
or Tàtàluó.
Names such as these
are names based on cause (yīnyuán).
Those without cause (yīnyuán)
are like the lotus flower,
earth,
water,
fire,
wind,
and space.
Such as Mántuó pó,
where one name covers two realities:
one is a palace hall,
and the second is a juice-drinking hall.
Even if no juice is drunk, it is still named Mántuó pó.
Such as Sàpó chēduō, which is named "Snake Canopy,"
but in reality, it is not a snake canopy.
This is called being without cause,
a name forcefully established.
Such as Dǐluó póyí,
named "Oil Eater,"
but in reality, he does not eat oil.
The name was forcefully established for him,
named "Oil Eater."
This is called being without cause,
a name forcefully established.
Good men!
This Great Nièpán (Dà Nièpán) is also like this:
it has no cause (yīnyuán),
the name is forcefully established for it.
Good men!
For example, space:
it is not named Great Space because of Small Space.
Nièpán is also like this;
it is not named Dà Nièpán because of a small characteristic.
Good men!
For example, if there is a Dharma (teaching/phenomenon)
that cannot be measured
and cannot be conceived (is inconceivable),
then it is named Great.
Nièpán is also like this;
it cannot be measured
and cannot be conceived,
thus it obtains the name Great Parinirvāṇa (Dà Bō Nièpán).
Because of its complete purity, it is named Dà Nièpán.
What is complete purity?
Purity has four types.
What are these four?
First:
The Twenty-Five Existences are called impure;
because these can be permanently severed, it obtains the name Purity (Jìng);
Purity is Nièpán.
Such Nièpán
is also called "existent,"
but this Nièpán
is truly not existent.
The Buddhas and Tathāgatas, following worldly convention,
speak of Nièpán as existent.
Just like worldly people,
speak of someone who is not a father as a father,
and someone who is not a mother as a mother;
although they are truly not parents,
they are called parents.
Nièpán is also like this;
following worldly convention, it is said that the Buddhas possess Dà Nièpán.
Second:
Purity of Karma (Yè qīngjìng).
The karma of all common mortals is not pure,
thus they do not possess Nièpán.
The karma of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas is pure,
thus it is named Great Purity (Dà Jìng);
because of Great Purity, it is named Dà Nièpán.
Third:
Purity of Body (Shēn qīngjìng).
If the body is impermanent,
then it is named impure;
the body of the Tathāgata is permanent, thus it is named Great Purity;
because of Great Purity, it is named Dà Nièpán.
Fourth:
Purity of Mind (Xīn qīngjìng).
If the mind has outflows (āsravas),
it is called impure;
the Buddha's mind is without outflows,
thus it is named Great Purity;
because of Great Purity, it is named Dà Nièpán.
Good men!
This is what is called the good men
and good women who practice this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Nièpán Jīng),
fully accomplishing the merits of the first section.
"Furthermore, good men!
How does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) cultivate Dà Nièpán,
and fully accomplish the merits of the second section?
Good men!
When a Púsà Móhēsà cultivates Dà Nièpán,
what he previously did not obtain, he now obtains;
what he previously did not see, he now sees;
what he previously did not hear, he now hears;
where he previously did not arrive, he now arrives;
what he previously did not know, he now knows.
What is meant by ‘what he previously did not obtain, he now obtains’?
It refers to divine powers (shéntōng),
which he previously did not obtain but now obtains.
Shéntōng has two types:
first, internal;
second, external.
What is called external is shared with external practitioners (wàidào).
Internal, furthermore, has two types:
first, the Two Vehicles (Èr Chéng);
second, the Bodhisattvas (Púsà).
The divine powers obtained by the Púsà practicing the Dà Nièpán Jīng
are not shared with the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Pìzhīfó).
What is meant by ‘not shared with the Shēngwén and Pìzhīfó’?
The divine transformations performed by the Two Vehicles
manifest one (form) in a single thought;
they cannot manifest many.
The Púsà is not like this;
in a single thought,
they are fully able to manifest the bodies of the Five Destinies.
Why is this?
Because of the power and strength obtained from this Dà Nièpán Jīng.
This is what is meant by ‘what he previously did not obtain, he now obtains.’
Furthermore, what else is meant by ‘what he previously did not obtain, he now obtains’?
It refers to obtaining mastery over the body (shēn dé zìzài),
and obtaining mastery over the mind (xīn dé zìzài).
Why?
The bodies and minds of all common mortals do not obtain mastery (zìzài);
sometimes the mind follows the body,
and sometimes the body follows the mind.
"What is meant by the mind following the body?
For example, a drunken person:
the alcohol is in the body;
when the body moves,
the mind also moves accordingly.
Also, if the body is sluggish,
the mind is also sluggish accordingly.
This is what is meant by the mind following the body.
Furthermore, like an infant,
whose body is young and small,
the mind is also small accordingly.
An adult's body is large,
the mind is also large accordingly.
Also, like a person
whose body is coarse and rough,
the mind constantly thinks
of wanting to obtain ointment or oil to moisturize and soften it.
This is what is meant by the mind following the body.
"How is it named 'the body following the mind'?
It refers to going,
coming,
sitting and lying down,
practicing austerities (cultivation),
giving,
observing precepts,
patient endurance,
and vigorous effort.
When a person is distressed and troubled, their body is thin and withered.
When a person is joyful, their body is robust and radiant.
When a person is terrified, their body trembles.
When listening to the Dharma with concentrated mind, the body is pleased and joyful.
When a person is weeping sorrowfully, tears flow horizontally.
This is named 'the body following the mind.'
A Púsà is not like this.
They attain mastery over both body and mind.
This is named 'that which was not attained in the past is now attained.'
"Furthermore, O Shànnánzǐ!
The body form manifested by the Púsà Móhēsà
is like a fine dust particle.
With this tiny body,
they are entirely able to pervade and reach the worlds of all Buddhas, numerous as the sands of the immeasurable, boundless Ganges River,
without hindrance,
while the mind remains constantly stable
and never moves.
This is named 'the mind not following the body.'
"This is also named 'that which was not reached in the past is now able to be reached.'
Why is it again named 'that which was not reached in the past is now able to be reached'?
Because all Shēngwén and Pìzhīfó cannot reach it,
but the Púsà can reach it.
Therefore, it is named 'that which was not reached in the past is now able to be reached.'
All Shēngwén and Pìzhīfó,
although possessing spiritual powers, cannot transform their bodies to be like fine dust,
and pervade the worlds of all Buddhas numerous as the sands of the immeasurable Ganges.
When the bodies of the Shēngwén and Yuánjué move, their minds also move accordingly.
A Púsà is not like this.
Although the mind does not move,
the body reaches everywhere.
This is named 'the Púsà's mind not following the body.'
Furthermore, O Shànnánzǐ!
A Huàshēn of the Púsà is like a Sānqiān Dàqiān Shìjiè.
Taking this massive body and entering a body the size of a dust particle,
their mind does not become small at that time either.
Although Shēngwén and Yuánjué can transform their bodies to be like the Sānqiān Dàqiān Shìjiè,
they cannot take such a massive body and enter a body the size of a dust particle.
Since they are unable to accomplish this matter themselves,
how much less can they keep their mind from moving accordingly?
This is named 'the Púsà's mind not following the body.'
Furthermore, O Shànnánzǐ!
The Púsà Móhēsà, with a single sound,
can cause all sentient beings in the Sānqiān Dàqiān Shìjiè to hear it entirely.
The mind never holds the thought of causing this sound to pervade all worlds,
causing all sentient beings who had not heard it before to now be able to hear it.
Furthermore, this Púsà never says,
"I cause sentient beings who had not heard it before to now be able to hear it."
If a Púsà says,
"Because of my teaching the Dharma, sentient beings who had not heard it now hear it,"
you should know that this person will ultimately not attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Why is this?
The mind that thinks,
"Sentient beings did not hear, and I spoke for them,"
such a mind is the mind of shēngsǐ.
All Púsàs have exhausted this mind.
Because of this meaning,
the bodies and minds of Púsà Móhēsàs do not follow each other.
O Shànnánzǐ!
The bodies and minds of all Fánfū follow each other.
A Púsà is not like this.
In order to transform sentient beings,
although they manifest a small body,
the mind is not small either.
Why is this?
Because the essential nature of the minds of all Púsàs is constantly vast and great.
Although they manifest a great body,
the mind is also not great.
What is a great body?
A body like the Sānqiān Dàqiān Shìjiè.
What is a small body?
Acting the behavior of a child.
Because of this meaning,
the mind does not follow the body.
The Púsà Móhēsà, having passed through immeasurable Āsēngqí kalpas,
may refrain from drinking alcohol yet manifest mental movement (agitation),
may have no sorrow or distress in the mind yet the body sheds tears,
may truly have no fear yet the body trembles.
Because of this meaning,
you should know that the Púsà's body and mind are self-mastered
and do not follow each other.
The Púsà Móhēsà manifests only one body,
yet all sentient beings see it differently.
"Furthermore, O Shànnánzǐ!
How is it that the Púsà Móhēsà cultivates Dànièpán,
so that what was not heard in the past is now able to be heard?
The Púsà Móhēsà first takes hold of the Xiàng of sound,
namely, the sound of elephants, the sound of horses,
the sound of chariots, the sound of people,
the sound of conch shells, the sound of drums,
the sound of pipes and flutes,
the sound of singing, and the sound of crying, and practices concentration upon them.
Due to this cultivation,
they are able to hear the sounds of all hells within the immeasurable Sānqiān Dàqiān Shìjiè.
Furthermore, through further cultivation, they attain a unique sense of hearing (ear organ),
different from the Tiān'ěr of the Shēngwén and Yuánjué.
Why is this?
The purified hearing penetration attained by the Èrchéng,
if based on the pure and subtle four great elements of the Chūchán,
hears only the Chūchán and does not hear the Second Dhyāna.
Up to the Sìchán, it is also like this.
Although they can simultaneously hear all sounds of the Sānqiān Dàqiān Shìjiè,
they cannot hear the sounds of worlds numerous as the immeasurable, boundless sands of the Ganges.
Because of this meaning,
what the Púsà attains is different from the hearing faculty of the Shēngwén and Yuánjué.
Because of this difference,
what was not heard in the past is now able to be heard.
Although they hear sounds,
the mind initially has no Xiàng of hearing sound.
They do not create the mark of existence,
the mark of permanence,
the mark of pleasure,
the mark of self,
the mark of purity,
the mark of mastery and the mark of reliance,
the mark of acting and the mark of cause,
the mark of certainty and the mark of effect.
Because of this meaning,
all Púsàs are able to hear what was not heard in the past.
At that time, the Púsà Móhēsà Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng said:
"If what the Buddha speaks
does not produce the mark of certainty
and does not produce the mark of effect,
this principle is incorrect.
Why is this?
The Rúlái previously stated,
'If a person hears one phrase or one character of this Dànièpán Jīng,
they will definitely attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.'
How can the Rúlái now
again say there is no certainty
and no effect?
Attaining Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí
is precisely the mark of certainty
and precisely the mark of effect.
How can you say there is no certainty
and no effect?
Hearing evil sounds gives rise to evil minds;
giving rise to evil minds leads to the Sāntú.
If one reaches the Sāntú, that is a certain effect.
How can you say there is no certainty
and no effect?"
At that time, the Rúlái praised him, saying:
"Excellent!
Excellent!
O Shànnánzǐ!
You are able to ask this question.
If the sounds spoken by the Buddhas had the mark of certain effect,
then that would not be the mark of the Buddhas, the Shìzūn;
it would be the mark of the Mówáng,
the mark of shēngsǐ,
and the mark of being far from Nièpán.
Why is this?
Everything that all Buddhas speak and expound has no mark of certain effect.
O Shànnánzǐ!
For example, when one sees the image of a person's face in a sword (blade),
if it is held vertically, the face appears long;
if it is held horizontally, the face appears wide.
If there were a mark of certainty,
how could it be that when held vertically it appears long
and when held horizontally it appears wide?
Because of this meaning,
everything that the Buddhas, the Shìzūn, speak and expound has no mark of certain effect.
O Shànnánzǐ!
Nièpán is truly not the effect of sound.
If Nièpán were the effect of sound,
then you should know that Nièpán would not be an eternal Chángfǎ.
O Shànnánzǐ!
Consider how worldly *dharmas* arise from causes:
if there is a cause, there is an effect;
if there is no cause, there is no effect.
Because the cause is Wúcháng,
the effect is also Wúcháng.
Why is this?
The cause also produces the effect,
and the effect also functions as the cause.
Because of this meaning,
all *dharmas* have no fixed characteristic mark.
If Nièpán arose from a cause,
then because the cause is Wúcháng,
the effect would also be Wúcháng.
But Nièpán does not arise from a cause;
its essence is not an effect.
Therefore, it is eternal.
O Shànnánzǐ!
Because of this meaning,
the essence of Nièpán has neither certainty nor effect.
"Good man!
Indeed, Nièpán
can be called concentration (samādhi),
and it can be called the fruition (phala).
Why is it called concentration?
Because the Nièpán possessed by all Buddhas is permanent (cháng), joyful (lè), self (wǒ), and pure (jìng),
therefore it is concentration.
Because it is without birth, aging, or destruction, therefore it is concentration.
Because even Yīchǎntí,
those who violate the four cardinal prohibitions,
slander the Vaipulya (Fāngděng) scriptures,
or commit the five heinous sins,
upon renouncing their former intentions,
will definitely attain it,
therefore it is concentration.
"Good man!
Regarding what you said:
'If a person hears one word or one phrase of the Great Nièpán spoken by me,
they attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.'
You
still do not thoroughly understand this meaning.
You should listen carefully;
I shall explain it to you further.
Good man!
If there are good men
or good women
who hear one word or one phrase of the Great Nièpán,
