and do not grasp the characteristic of the word,
do not grasp the characteristic of the phrase,
do not grasp the characteristic of hearing,
do not grasp the characteristic of the Buddha,
and do not grasp the characteristic of the teaching;
this meaning is called the characteristic of non-characteristics.
Because of the characteristic of non-characteristics,
they attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Good man!
Regarding what you said,
that hearing bad sound leads to the three miserable realms (sāntú),
this meaning is not so.
Why is this?
One does not reach the sāntú because of bad sound;
you should know that this fruition comes from bad intention.
Why is this?
There are good men
and good women
who, although they hear bad sound, do not generate evil in their minds.
Therefore, you should know
that birth in the sāntú is not caused by bad sound.
Rather, all sentient beings, due to the bonds of afflictions (fánnǎo jié),
multiply their evil intentions
and are born in the three evil destinies (sān'è qù),
not because of bad sound.
If sound had a fixed characteristic,
then all who heard it would universally generate evil intentions.
But some generate it,
and some do not generate it.
Therefore, you should know that sound has no fixed characteristic.
Because there is no fixedness,
although one encounters the sound,
one does not generate evil intentions."
"Shìzūn!
If sound is not fixed,
how is it that a Púsà is able now to hear what he formerly did not hear?"
"Good man!
Sound has no fixed characteristic.
What was formerly unheard
is now heard by the Púsàs.
Because of this principle,
I make this statement:
'What was formerly unheard is now heard.'
"Good man!
How is it that what was formerly unseen is now seen?
Good man!
When the Púsà Mōhēsà cultivates the subtle and wonderful scriptures of the Great Nièpán,
he first grasps the characteristic of brightness,
namely, the light of the sun, moon, stars, and constellations,
of torches, lamps, and candles,
the brightness of jewels and fire,
and the light of medicinal herbs, and so forth.
Through this cultivation, he obtains a different faculty of vision (eye-root),
which is different from that attained by Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué).
How is it different?
The pure Heavenly Eye (divine vision) attained by the Two Vehicles
relies on the four great elements (sìdà) of the eye-root in the desire realm (yùjiè),
and therefore does not see the first Dhyāna.
If it relies on the first Dhyāna, it does not see the higher realms,
and even fails to see its own eye.
If they wish to see extensively,
the limit is three thousand great thousand worlds (sānqiān dàqiān shìjiè).
The Púsà Mōhēsà, without cultivating the Heavenly Eye [in the manner of the Two Vehicles],
sees all subtle material forms (sèshēn) as merely skeletal characteristics.
Although he sees the material forms of worlds equal to the sands of the Hénghé Shā in other directions,
he does not grasp the characteristic of material form,
does not grasp the characteristic of permanence,
of existence,
of substance,
or of names, and so forth.
He grasps the characteristic of cause and condition (yīnyuán),
and does not grasp the characteristic of seeing.
He does not say that this eye is a subtle and pure characteristic;
he only sees the characteristic of cause and condition,
and the characteristic of non-cause-and-condition.
What is cause and condition?
Material form (sè) is the condition for the eye.
If this material form were not a cause and condition,
then all ordinary beings (fánfū) would not generate the characteristic of seeing form.
Because of this principle,
form is named cause and condition.
As for non-cause-and-condition,
although the Púsà Mōhēsà sees it,
he does not generate the characteristic of form;
therefore, it is non-condition.
Because of this principle,
the pure Heavenly Eye attained by the Púsà
differs from that attained by the Śrāvaka (Shēngwén) and the Pratyekabuddha (Yuánjué).
Because of this difference,
he simultaneously sees all present Buddhas in the worlds of the ten directions.
This is called the Púsà now seeing what he formerly did not see.
Because of this difference,
he can see minute particles (wéichén),
which the Śrāvaka (Shēngwén) and the Pratyekabuddha (Yuánjué) cannot see.
Because of this difference,
although he sees his own eye,
he initially has no characteristic of seeing [the subject/doer],
but sees the characteristic of impermanence.
He sees the bodies of ordinary beings [fánfū shēn] full of thirty-six impure substances,
just as one observes an Ēmólè Guǒ in the palm of the hand.
Because of this principle,
he now sees what he formerly did not see.
If he sees the material form characteristics of sentient beings,
he then knows whether that person has the capacity for the Mahāyāna (Dàshèng) or Hīnayāna (Xiǎoshèng) roots.
Simply by touching their clothing,
he also knows the distinguishing characteristics of that person's wholesome or unwholesome faculties.
Because of this principle,
he now knows what he formerly did not know.
Because of one seeing,
he now knows what he formerly did not know;
and because of this knowing,
he now sees what he formerly did not see.
"Furthermore, good man!
How is it that a *Púsà* (Bodhisattva) knows now what he did not know before?
Although the *Púsà Móhēsà* (Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva) knows the greedy, hateful, and ignorant minds of ordinary beings,
he initially does not perceive the characteristics of mind or mental factors,
nor does he perceive the characteristics of sentient beings or material objects.
He cultivates the characteristic of ultimate, complete emptiness (*bìjìng kōng xiàng*), which is the foremost truth (*dìyī yì*).
Why is this?
Because all *Púsà* constantly and skillfully cultivate the characteristics of emptiness (*kōngxìng*).
By cultivating emptiness,
he now knows what he did not know before.
What is this knowledge?
It is knowing that there is no self (*wú yǒu wǒ*),
and no self-possession (*wú yǒu wǒ suǒ*).
It is knowing that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature (*fóxìng*).
Because of the Buddha-nature,
those like the *yīchǎntí* (Icchantikas) relinquish their fundamental minds,
and shall all achieve *Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí* (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi).
All these things are unknowable by *Shēngwén* (Śrāvakas) and *Yuánjué* (Pratyekabuddhas),
but the *Púsà* can know them.
For this reason,
he now knows what he did not know before.
Furthermore, good man!
How is it that he knows now what he did not know before?
The *Púsà Móhēsà*, cultivating the profound and subtle *Dà Nièpán* (Mahāparinirvāṇa) Sūtra,
recalls the past existences of all sentient beings—the *zhǒngxìng* (lineages) in which they were born,
their fathers, mothers, and brothers,
their wives, children, and relatives,
their friends, and those whom they hated or resented.
In a single moment, he attains unique knowledge,
which is different from the wisdom of *Shēngwén* and *Yuánjué*.
How is it different?
The wisdom possessed by *Shēngwén* and *Yuánjué*,
when recalling the past existences of all sentient beings, their *zhǒngxìng*,
fathers, mothers, and so forth, up to those whom they hated or resented,
perceives the characteristics of these *zhǒngxìng* up to those whom they hated or resented.
The *Púsà* is not like this.
Although he recalls the past *zhǒngxìng*,
fathers, mothers, and so forth, up to those whom they hated or resented,
he never gives rise to the characteristics of *zhǒngxìng*, fathers, mothers, resentment, and so forth.
He always perceives the characteristics of the Dharma (*fǎ xiàng*)
and the characteristic of empty stillness (*kōngjí zhī xiàng*).
This is called the *Púsà* now knowing what he did not know before.
Furthermore, good man!
How is it that he knows now what he did not know before?
The *Púsà Móhēsà*, cultivating the profound and subtle *Dà Nièpán* Sūtra,
attains the knowledge of others' minds (*tāxīn zhì*),
which differs from that attained by *Shēngwén* and *Yuánjué*.
How is it different?
When *Shēngwén* and *Yuánjué*, with the knowledge of a single instant,
know the minds of humans,
they cannot know the minds of those in *dìyù* (hell),
animals (*chùshēng*),
hungry ghosts (*èguǐ*),
or *tiān* (heavenly beings).
The *Púsà* is not like this.
In a single instant, he universally knows the minds of sentient beings in the six realms (*liù qù*).
This is called the *Púsà* now knowing what he did not know before.
Furthermore, good man!
There is another kind of knowledge:
The *Púsà Móhēsà*, in a single mind-instant,
knows the initial mind of a *Xūtuóhuán* (Sotāpanna),
and sequentially up to the sixteenth mind-instant.
For this reason,
he now knows what he did not know before.
This is how the *Púsà* cultivating the *Dà Nièpán* perfectly achieves the second merit (*gōngdé*).
"Furthermore, good man!
How does the *Púsà Móhēsà* cultivating the *Dà Nièpán* achieve the third merit?
Good man!
The *Púsà Móhēsà*, cultivating the *Dà Nièpán*,
relinquishes compassion (*cí*) and attains compassion (*cí*).
When he attains compassion,
it does not arise from causes and conditions.
What is meant by relinquishing compassion and attaining compassion?
Good man!
Compassion (*cí*) refers to conventional truth (*shìdì*).
The *Púsà Móhēsà* relinquishes the compassion of conventional truth,
and attains the compassion of the foremost truth (*dìyī yì cí*).
The compassion of the foremost truth is not attained through conditions.
Furthermore, how is it relinquishing compassion and attaining compassion?
If compassion can be relinquished,
it is called the compassion of ordinary beings (*fánfū cí*).
If compassion can be attained,
it is called the *Púsà*'s compassion without conditions (*wúyuán zhī cí*).
He relinquishes the compassion toward *yīchǎntí*,
the compassion toward those who violate the four weighty prohibitions (*sì chóng jìn*),
the compassion toward those who slander the *Fāngděng* (Vaipulya) teachings,
and the compassion toward those who commit the five grave offenses (*wǔ nì*).
He attains pitying compassion (*liánmǐn cí*),
he attains *Rúlái* (Tathāgata) compassion,
the compassion of the World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*),
and compassion without cause or condition.
Furthermore, how is it called relinquishing compassion and attaining compassion?
He relinquishes the compassion toward *huángmén* (eunuchs),
toward those without roots (asexuality/defective sexuality),
toward those with dual roots (intersex),
and toward women;
toward butchers (*tú*),
those who mince meat (*kuài*),
hunters (*lièshī*),
and those who raise chickens and pigs—compassion toward such beings.
He also relinquishes the compassion of *Shēngwén* and *Yuánjué*,
and attains the unconditional compassion of the *Púsà*s.
He does not perceive his own compassion,
nor does he perceive the compassion of others.
He does not perceive those who uphold the precepts,
nor does he perceive those who violate the precepts.
Although he perceives his own pity (*bēi*),
he does not perceive sentient beings.
Although there is suffering reception,
he does not perceive the recipient.
Why is this?
Because he cultivates the foremost true meaning (*dìyī zhēnshí yì*).
This is called the *Púsà* cultivating the *Dà Nièpán* achieving the third merit.
"Furthermore, good man!
How does the *Púsà Móhēsà* cultivating the *Dà Nièpán* achieve the fourth merit?
Good man!
The *Púsà Móhēsà* cultivating the *Dà Nièpán* achieves the fourth merit,
which consists of ten matters.
What are these ten?
First, the roots are deep and difficult to overthrow.
Second, generating the concept of certainty in one's own self.
Third, not viewing fields of merit (*fútián*) or non-fields of merit.
Fourth, cultivating pure Buddha-lands (*Fó tǔ*).
Fifth, eliminating remaining defilements (*yǒuyú*).
Sixth, cutting off the conditions of karma (*yèyuán*).
Seventh, cultivating the pure body.
Eighth, fully knowing all conditions.
Ninth, separating from all enemies.
Tenth, cutting off the two extremes (*èrbīan*).
How are the roots deep and difficult to overthrow?
The roots referred to
are called non-negligence (*bù fàngyì*).
What root is this non-negligence?
It is the root of *Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*.
Good man!
The root of all goodness for all Buddhas
is entirely non-negligence.
Because of non-negligence,
all other roots of goodness increasingly grow.
Because it can increase all roots of goodness,
it is the most outstanding among all good qualities.
Good man!
Just as among all footprints, the elephant's footprint is supreme;
the Dharma of non-negligence is also like this,
it is the most outstanding among all good Dharmas.
Good man!
Just as among all illuminations,
sunlight is the highest;
the Dharma of non-negligence is also like this,
it is the most outstanding among all good Dharmas.
Good man!
Just as among all kings, the *Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng* (Cakravartin) is the foremost;
the Dharma of non-negligence is also like this,
it is the foremost among all good Dharmas.
Good man!
Just as among all streams, the four rivers are the greatest;
the Dharma of non-negligence is also like this,
it is the highest and greatest among all good Dharmas.
Good man!
Just as among all mountains,
Mount *Xūmíshān* (Sumeru) is the foremost;
the Dharma of non-negligence is also like this,
it is the foremost among all good Dharmas.
Good man!
Just as among flowers born in water,
the blue lotus (*qīng liánhuā*) is the highest;
the Dharma of non-negligence is also like this,
it is the greatest and highest among all good Dharmas.
Good man!
Just as among flowers born on land,
the *pólìshī* flower (Vārṣika) is the greatest and highest;
the Dharma of non-negligence is also like this,
it is the greatest and highest among all good Dharmas.
Good man!
Just as among all beasts,
the lion (*shīzi*) is the greatest;
the Dharma of non-negligence is also like this,
it is the greatest and highest among all good Dharmas.
Good man!
Just as among flying birds,
the *Jīnchìniǎo Wáng* (King Garuḍa) is the greatest and highest;
the Dharma of non-negligence is also like this,
it is the greatest and highest among all good Dharmas."
“O good man!
Just as among great bodies,
the Asura King Rāhóu is the foremost and supreme;
the Dharma of Non-Negligence (Apromāda) is also like this,
it is the foremost and supreme among all wholesome Dharmas.
O good man!
Just as among all sentient beings,
whether two-footed,
four-footed,
many-footed,
or footless,
the Tathāgata is the most supreme;
the Dharma of Non-Negligence is also like this,
it is the foremost and supreme among wholesome Dharmas.
O good man!
Just as among assemblies,
the Buddha
and the Saṅgha are supreme;
the Dharma of Non-Negligence is also like this,
it is the foremost and supreme among wholesome Dharmas.
O good man!
Just as in the Buddha’s Dharma,
the Dharma of Mahāparinirvāṇa is the foremost and supreme;
the Dharma of Non-Negligence is also like this,
it is the foremost and supreme among all wholesome Dharmas.
O good man!
For this reason,
the root of Non-Negligence
is deep, firm, and difficult to uproot.
How is it that, by means of Non-Negligence,
the faith root (Śraddhā-indriya),
the discipline root (Śīla-indriya),
the giving root (Dāna-indriya),
the wisdom root (Prajñā-indriya),
the patience root (Kṣānti-indriya),
the hearing root (Śruta-indriya),
the diligence root (Vīrya-indriya),
the mindfulness root (Smṛti-indriya),
the concentration root (Samādhi-indriya),
and the good spiritual friend root (Kalyāṇamitra-indriya)
— how is it that these roots
are able to increase through Non-Negligence,
and because they increase, become deep, firm, and difficult to uproot?
For this reason,
it is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivating the deep and difficult-to-uproot root of Mahāparinirvāṇa.
“How does one form a definitive conception concerning the body?
A definitive mind is produced concerning one’s own body:
‘This present body of mine, in future lifetimes,
will definitely become a vessel for Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.’
The mind is also like this;
it does not become narrow,
it does not undergo alteration,
it does not become the mind of a Śrāváka
or a Pratyekabuddha,
it does not become a demon’s mind or a self-contented mind,
nor a mind that delights in Saṃsāra;
it constantly seeks the mind of compassion for sentient beings.
This is called the Bodhisattva producing a definitive mind concerning his own body:
‘In the future, I shall become a vessel for Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.’
For this reason,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates Mahāparinirvāṇa
by producing a definitive conception concerning his own body.
“How is it that the Bodhisattva does not observe fields of merit (Puṇyakṣetra) and non-fields of merit?
What are fields of merit?
Heretics,
those who uphold discipline,
up to and including the Buddhas—
these are called fields of merit.
If there are those who think:
‘Such persons are true fields of merit,’
know that this mind is then narrow and inferior.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva regards all infinite sentient beings without exception as fields of merit.
Why is this?
Because of the skillful cultivation of the different objects of mindfulness (Dharmas).
When there are different objects of mindfulness,
and they are skillfully cultivated,
one regards sentient beings as having neither upheld discipline nor violated discipline.
One constantly observes what the Buddhas, the Bhagavāts, have taught:
although giving is of four types,
a pure reward is obtained in all cases.
What are these four?
First, the donor is pure,
but the recipient is impure;
second, the donor is impure,
but the recipient is pure;
third, both the donor
and the recipient are pure;
fourth, both the donor
and the recipient are impure.
“What is meant by the donor being pure
and the recipient being impure?
The donor possesses discipline,
much hearing,
and wisdom;
he knows that giving with wisdom and
its retribution exist. The recipient violates discipline,
is firmly attached to wrong views,
and holds that there is no retribution for giving;
this is called the donor being pure and the recipient being impure.
“What is meant by the recipient being pure
and the donor being impure?
The donor violates discipline,
is firmly attached to wrong views,
and says that giving with wisdom and its retribution do not exist.
The recipient upholds discipline,
has much hearing and wisdom,
and knows that giving with wisdom and the retribution of giving exist;
this is called the donor being impure
and the recipient being pure.
“What is meant by both the donor
and the recipient being pure?
Both the donor and the recipient
possess discipline,
much hearing,
and wisdom,
and know that giving with wisdom and the retribution of giving exist;
this is called both the donor and the recipient being pure.
“What is meant by both being impure?
The donor and the recipient violate discipline,
hold wrong views,
and say that giving and the retribution of giving do not exist.
If this is the case,
how can it be said that a pure retribution is still obtained?
It is called pure because there is neither giving nor retribution.
O good man!
If a person does not perceive giving and the retribution of giving,
know that this person is not called one who violates discipline
and is firmly attached to wrong views.
If based on the Śrāváka doctrine,
one says that one does not perceive giving and the retribution of giving,
this is then called violating discipline and holding wrong views.
If based on this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
one does not perceive giving with wisdom and the retribution of giving,
this is then called upholding discipline and holding correct views.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva possesses different objects of mindfulness;
by cultivating them,
he does not perceive sentient beings, whether they uphold discipline
or violate discipline,
the donor,
the recipient, or the retribution of giving.
Therefore, he is called one who upholds discipline and holds correct views.
For this reason,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not observe fields of merit and non-fields of merit.
“How is the Buddha-field purified?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wonderful sūtra of Mahāparinirvāṇa
for the sake of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi
and the deliverance of sentient beings;
he separates himself from the intention to kill and harm.
With this root of wholesomeness,
he vows to share it with all sentient beings,
wishing that all sentient beings attain long life,
possess great power,
and acquire great supernormal powers (Abhijñā).
Because of the power of the causes and conditions of this solemn vow,
when he attains Buddhahood in the future,
all sentient beings in his Buddha-field
will attain long life,
possess great power,
and acquire great supernormal powers.
“Furthermore, O good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wonderful sūtra of Mahāparinirvāṇa
for the sake of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi
and the deliverance of sentient beings;
he separates himself from the intention to steal.
With this root of wholesomeness,
he vows to share it with all sentient beings,
wishing that the lands of all Buddha-fields consist purely of the seven treasures (Saptaratna),
that sentient beings be wealthy and content,
and freely indulge their desires.
Because of the power of the causes and conditions of this solemn vow,
when he attains Buddhahood in the future,
the land he obtains will consist purely of the seven treasures,
sentient beings will be wealthy and content,
and freely indulge their desires.
“Furthermore, O good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates the subtle and wonderful sūtra of Mahāparinirvāṇa
for the sake of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi
and the deliverance of sentient beings;
he separates himself from the intention of sexual misconduct.
With this root of wholesomeness,
he vows to share it with all sentient beings,
wishing that all sentient beings in the lands of the Buddhas
will not have minds of greed (Rāga), hatred (Dveṣa), or delusion (Moha),
and that none will suffer from hunger, thirst, or distress.
Because of the power of the causes and conditions of this solemn vow,
when he attains Buddhahood in the future,
the sentient beings in his Buddha-field will be far removed from minds of greedy lust,
hatred,
and delusion,
and none at all will suffer from hunger, thirst, or distress.”
"Furthermore, good man!
When a Púsà Móhēsà cultivates the subtle classic, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Nípián Wéimiào Jīngdiǎn),
for Anōuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi),
and for the sake of liberating sentient beings,
he distances himself from the mind of false speech (lying).
By means of these roots of goodness,
he vows to share them with all sentient beings,
wishing that all Buddhalands constantly possess flowering trees,
fruit trees,
and fragrant trees,
and that all sentient beings attain wondrous, beautiful voices.
Due to the power of the causes and conditions of this vow,
when he achieves Buddhahood in future ages,
all his lands will constantly possess flowering trees,
fruit trees,
and fragrant trees,
and the sentient beings within them will all attain pure, supreme, and wondrous voices.
"Furthermore, good man!
When a Púsà Móhēsà cultivates the subtle classic, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
for Anōuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
and for the sake of liberating sentient beings,
he distances himself from duplicity.
By means of these roots of goodness,
he vows to share them with all sentient beings,
wishing that all sentient beings in the Buddhalands,
constantly dwell in harmony and unity,
discussing and teaching the Correct Dharma (Zhèngfǎ).
Due to the power of the causes and conditions of this vow,
when he achieves Buddhahood,
all sentient beings in his land will entirely dwell in harmony and unity,
discussing the essential teachings of the Dharma.
"Furthermore, good man!
When a Púsà Móhēsà cultivates the subtle classic, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
for Anōuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
and for the sake of liberating sentient beings,
he distances himself from harsh speech.
By means of these roots of goodness,
he vows to share them with all sentient beings,
wishing that the grounds of all Buddhalands be flat like the palm of a hand,
free from the likes of sand, pebbles, tiles, or stones,
and thorny, harmful spines,
and that the minds of all sentient beings be equal and balanced.
Due to the power of the causes and conditions of this vow,
when he achieves Buddhahood in future ages,
all his lands,
will have ground flat like the palm of a hand,
free from sand and pebbles,
thorns and briars,
and harmful spines,
and the minds of all sentient beings will be equal and balanced.
"Furthermore, good man!
When a Púsà Móhēsà cultivates the subtle classic, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
for Anōuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
and for the sake of liberating sentient beings,
he distances himself from frivolous talk (useless speech).
By means of these roots of goodness,
he vows to share them with all sentient beings,
wishing that all sentient beings in the Buddhalands,
have no suffering or distress.
Due to the power of the causes and conditions of this vow,
when he achieves Buddhahood in future ages,
all sentient beings in his land,
will have no suffering or distress.
"Furthermore, good man!
When a Púsà Móhēsà cultivates the subtle classic, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
for Anōuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
and for the sake of liberating sentient beings,
he distances himself from avarice and jealousy (greed and envy).
By means of these roots of goodness, he vows to share them with all sentient beings,
wishing that all sentient beings in the Buddhalands have no avarice, jealousy,
vexation, harm,
or heterodox views (xiéjiàn).
Due to the power of the causes and conditions of this vow,
when he achieves Buddhahood in future ages,
all sentient beings in his land will entirely be free of avarice, jealousy,
vexation, harm,
and heterodox views.
"Furthermore, good man!
When a Púsà Móhēsà cultivates the subtle classic, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
for Anōuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
and for the sake of liberating sentient beings,
he distances himself from vexation and harm (cruelty).
By means of these roots of goodness,
he vows to share them with all sentient beings,
wishing that all sentient beings in the Buddhalands,
all cultivate great compassion (dàcí dàbēi) together,
and attain the stage of the Only Child (Yīzǐ Dì).
Due to the power of the causes and conditions of this vow,
when he achieves Buddhahood in future ages,
all sentient beings in the world (shìjiè),
will all cultivate great compassion (dàcí),
great pity (dàbēi),
and attain the stage of the Only Child.
"Furthermore, good man!
When a Púsà Móhēsà cultivates the subtle classic, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
for Anōuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
and for the sake of liberating sentient beings,
he distances himself from heterodox views (xiéjiàn).
By means of these roots of goodness,
he vows to share them with all sentient beings,
wishing that all sentient beings in the Buddhalands,
all attain Mahāprajñāpāramitā (Móhē Bōrě Bōluómì).
Due to the power of the causes and conditions of this vow,
when he achieves Buddhahood in future ages,
the sentient beings of his world will all attain and uphold Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
This is called the Púsà cultivating a pure Buddhaland.
"How does a Púsà Móhēsà destroy the remaining bonds (yǒuyú)?
There are three types of remaining bonds:
first, the residual retribution of afflictions (fánnǎo yúbào);
second, residual karma (yúyè);
third, residual existence (yúyǒu).
Good man!
What is called the residual retribution of afflictions?
If there are sentient beings who habitually approach greed and desire (tānyù),
when this retribution ripens,
they fall into the hells (dìyù).
After emerging from the hells,
they receive the bodies of animals (chùshēng),
namely, pigeons, sparrows,
mandarin ducks, parrots,
Jīpó Jīpó Shèlìgā (Jīvajīvaka Śārikā) birds,
blue sparrows, fish, turtles,
macaques, roebucks, and deer.
If they attain human bodies,
they receive the form of eunuchs (huángmén),
women,
those with dual sexual organs (èr gēn),
those without sexual organs (wú gēn),
or prostitutes (yínnǚ).
If they renounce home and violate the first major precept,
this is called residual retribution.
"Furthermore, good man!
If there are sentient beings who habitually approach hatred and anger (chēnhuì) with strong intent,
when this retribution ripens,
they fall into the hells.
After emerging from the hells,
they receive the bodies of animals,
namely, venomous snakes—possessing four types of poison:
sight poison,
touch poison,
bite poison,
and breath poison—lions (shīzǐ), tigers, wolves,
bears, panthers, wildcats, civet cats,
and the likes of eagles and falcons.
If they attain human bodies,
they are endowed with the sixteen evil rules of discipline (è lǜyí),
or if they renounce home and violate the second major precept,
this is called residual retribution.
"Furthermore, good man!
If there are people who cultivate ignorance and delusion (yúchī),
when this retribution ripens,
they fall into the hells.
After emerging from the hells,
they receive the bodies of animals,
namely, elephants, pigs,
cattle, sheep, water buffalo,
fleas, lice, mosquitoes, gadflies,
and the forms of ants and the like.
If they attain human bodies,
they are deaf,
blind,
mute,
crippled, mutilated, hunchbacked (bèilòu),
lacking complete sensory organs (zhū gēn bù jù),
and unable to accept the Dharma.
If they renounce home, their faculties are dark and dull,
they frequently violate major precepts, even for the sake of five coins.
This is called residual retribution.
"Furthermore, good man!
If there are people who cultivate arrogance and pride (jiāomàn),
when this retribution ripens,
they fall into the hells.
After emerging from the hells,
they receive the bodies of animals,
namely, dung beetles,
camels, donkeys, dogs, and horses.
If they are born among humans,
they receive the bodies of servants and slaves,
or are poor beggars (qǐgài).
Or, if they renounce home,
they are constantly scorned and belittled by sentient beings,
and violate the fourth precept.
This is called residual retribution.
These and similar cases are called the residual retribution of afflictions.
These residual retributions,
the Púsà Móhēsà, by being able to cultivate the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nípián),
is able to entirely destroy and eliminate.
"What is residual karma (yúyè)?
It refers to the karma of all common mortals (fánfū),
and the karma of all Śrāvakas (Shēngwén).
Sùtuóhuán (Sotāpanna) persons receive the karma of seven existences (qī yǒu yè).
Sītuóhán (Sakṛdāgāmin) persons receive the karma of two existences (èr yǒu yè).
Ānàhán (Anāgāmin) persons receive the karma of existence in the Form Realm (sè yǒu yè).
This is called residual karma.
This residual karma,
the Púsà Móhēsà, by being able to cultivate the Mahāparinirvāṇa,
is able to entirely cut off and eliminate."
"What is the remaining existence (Yúyǒu)?
An Arhat (Āluóhàn) attains the fruit of Arhatship (Āluóhànguǒ),
a Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó) attains the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood (Pìzhīfóguǒ),
and, without karma or defilements, they manifest these two fruits.
This is called remaining existence (Yúyǒu).
Such are these three types of conditioned phenomena with remainder (Yǒuyú zhī fǎ).
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) practices the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dàshèng Dà Nièpán Jīng),
and thus attains their eradication.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva eradicating the remainder (Mièchú Yǒuyú).
"How does a Bodhisattva cultivate the purified body (Qīngjìng Shēn)?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the precept of non-killing,
which has five types of mind states:
specifically, the lower (xià),
middle (zhōng),
upper (shàng),
upper-middle (shàng zhōng),
and supreme-upper (shàngshàng).
This applies similarly up to right view.
These fifty mind states
are called the initial arousal of the mind (Chū Fā Xīn);
when these fifty mind states are fully completed and perfected,
this is called perfection (Mǎnzú).
These hundred mind states
are called the hundred merits (Bǎi Fúdé).
Complete possession of a hundred merits constitutes one primary characteristic.
Progressing in this manner to fully accomplish the Thirty-Two Characteristics (Sānshí'èr Xiàng)
is called the purified body (Qīngjìng Shēn).
Furthermore, they cultivate the Eighty Subsidiary Characteristics (Bāshí Zhǒng Hǎo)
because sentient beings in the world serve the eighty divine beings (Bāshí Shén).
Which are the eighty?
The twelve Suns (Shí'èr Rì),
the twelve Great Devas (Shí'èr Dà Tiān),
the five Great Stars (Wǔ Dà Xīng),
the Great Deity of Běidǒu and the Horse Deity (Běidǒu Mǎ Tiān),
the Deities of the Paths (Xíngdào Tiān),
the Deities of Bhāradvāja (Póluó Duòbáshé Tiān),
the Merit Deity (Gōngdé Tiān),
the Twenty-Eight Constellations (Èrshíbā Xiù),
Earth Deity (Dì Tiān),
Wind Deity (Fēng Tiān),
Water Deity (Shuǐ Tiān),
Fire Deity (Huǒ Tiān),
Brahmā (Fàn Tiān),
Rudra (Lóutuó Tiān),
Indra (Yīndí Tiān),
Kumāra (Jūmóluó Tiān),
the Eight-Armed Deity (Bābì Tiān),
Maheśvara (Móxīshǒuluó Tiān),
the Pañcāla Deity (Bànshéluó Tiān),
Hārītī (Guǐzǐmǔ Tiān),
the Four Heavenly Kings (Sìtiānwáng Tiān),
the Scribe Deity (Zàoshū Tiān),
and the Vasu Deities (Póusǒu Tiān).
These are called the eighty.
For the sake of these sentient beings, they cultivate the Eighty Subsidiary Characteristics to adorn themselves.
This is called the Bodhisattva's purified body (Qīngjìng zhī Shēn).
Why is this?
Because these eighty deities
are revered and submitted to by all sentient beings.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva cultivates the Eighty Subsidiary Characteristics.
Though their body does not move,
they cause those sentient beings, according to their beliefs,
to see them differently.
Having seen them, they revere and respect them,
and each awakens the mind for Anuttarasamyaksambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí xīn).
For this reason,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates the pure body (Jìng Shēn).
"Good man!
For instance, if a person wishes to invite a great king,
they must first adorn their residence
and make it extremely pure;
they prepare various delicacies of a hundred flavors.
Only then will the king accept the invitation.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this.
Because they wish to invite the Dharma Wheel King of Anuttarasamyaksambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí Fǎlún Wáng),
they must first cultivate their body to be supremely pure.
Only then will the Supreme Dharma King dwell there.
For this reason,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva must cultivate the purified body (Qīngjìng zhī Shēn).
Good man!
For instance, if a person wishes to partake of sweet dew,
they must first purify their body.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this.
Wishing to partake of the supreme sweet dew, the flavor of Dharma, Prajñāpāramitā (Bānruò Bōluómì),
they must first purify their body using the Eighty Subsidiary Characteristics.
Good man!
For instance, an exquisite golden or silver vessel,
when filled with purified water,
is clean both inside and out.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva's body, being pure, is also like this:
containing the water of Anuttarasamyaksambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí Shuǐ),
it is clean both inside and out.
Good man!
Just as a plain white garment from Bōluónài (Vārāṇasī)
easily accepts dye.
Why is this?
Because its nature is white and pure.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this:
because their body is pure,
they swiftly attain Anuttarasamyaksambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).
For this reason,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates the pure body (Jìng Shēn).
"How does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva skillfully understand all conditions (zhū yuán)?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive the characteristic of form,
does not perceive the condition of form,
does not perceive the substance of form,
does not perceive the arising of form,
does not perceive the cessation of form,
does not perceive the characteristic of oneness,
does not perceive the characteristic of difference,
does not perceive the perceiver,
does not perceive the appearance,
and does not perceive the recipient.
Why is this?
Because they understand dependent origination (Yīnyuán).
Just like form,
all phenomena are also like this.
This is called the Bodhisattva understanding all conditions (Zhū Yuán).
"How does the Bodhisattva depart from all enemies?
All afflictions (fánnǎo) are the Bodhisattva's enemies.
Since the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva constantly keeps far away from them,
this is called the Bodhisattva destroying all enemies.
A Bodhisattva in the Fifth Abode (Wǔ Zhù Púsà) regards afflictions not as enemies.
Why is this?
Because of afflictions,
the Bodhisattva takes birth.
Because they take birth,
they are thus able to continuously transform and teach sentient beings.
For this reason,
they are not called enemies.
What, then, is an enemy?
It is those who slander the Vaipulya Sūtras (Fāngděng Jīng).
Wherever the Bodhisattva is born,
they do not fear the hells,
the animal realm,
or the realm of hungry ghosts;
they only fear those who thus slander the Vaipulya (Fāngděng).
All Bodhisattvas have eight types of Māras (bā zhǒng mó),
which are called enemies (yuānjiā).
Keeping far away from these eight Māras
is called departing from enemies (Lí Yuānjiā).
This is called the Bodhisattva departing from all enemies.
"How does the Bodhisattva keep far away from the two extremes (Èr Biān)?
The two extremes (Èr Biān) are meant to be
the Twenty-Five Existences (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu) and the affliction of craving (ài fánnǎo).
The Bodhisattva constantly departs from the Twenty-Five Existences and the affliction of craving.
This is called the Bodhisattva keeping far away from the two extremes (Yuǎnlí Èr Biān).
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivating the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán) and fully accomplishing the Fourth Merit (Dì Sì Gōngdé).
At that time, Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng Púsà Móhēsà (Bodhisattva Mahāsattva King of High Virtue Illumining Everywhere) said:
"As the Buddha has stated,
if a Bodhisattva cultivates the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán),
they must perform all ten such meritorious deeds.
Why does the Tathāgata (Rúlái) cultivate only nine deeds,
and not the Pure Land (Jìngtǔ)?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
I, too, in the past, constantly and completely cultivated these ten deeds.
There are no Bodhisattvas or Tathāgatas who do not cultivate these ten deeds.
If a world were entirely filled with impurity,
that the World-Honored Buddhas (Zhū Fó Shìzūn) should appear therein,
that is impossible.
Good man!
Do not now say that the Buddhas appear in an impure world.
You should know that this mind is unwholesome and narrow-minded.
You must now know that
I did not truly appear solely in the realm of Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí Jiè).
Just as if someone were to say that only this realm has the sun and moon,
and that other worlds have no sun or moon—
such a statement is baseless.
If a Bodhisattva makes such a statement,
saying, 'This Buddha world is filthy and impure,'
and 'The Buddha lands in other directions are pure and magnificent,'
it is likewise baseless.
Good man!
To the west, moving away from this Sahā World (Suōpó Shìjiè),
having passed thirty-two sand grains of the Ganges (Hénghé Shā) worth of Buddha lands,
there is a world named Wúshèng (Invincible).
Why is that land named Wúshèng?
All the magnificent adornments of that land
are entirely equal and without distinction,
just like the Western World of Sukhāvatī (Ānlè Shìjiè),
and also like the Eastern World of Mǎnyuè (Full Moon).
I appeared in the world in that land.
In order to transform sentient beings,
I here, in the realm of Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí), manifested the turning of the Dharma Wheel (zhuǎn Fǎlún).
It is not only my body that manifests the turning of the Dharma Wheel here;
all Buddhas also turn the Dharma Wheel here.
For this reason,
the World-Honored Buddhas (Zhū Fó Shìzūn) do not fail to practice these ten deeds.
Good man!
Maitreya Bodhisattva (Císhì Púsà), due to his vows,
will, in a future age,
cause this world to be pure and adorned.
For this reason,
all the worlds possessed by all Buddhas are adorned and pure."
"Furthermore, good man!
How does a Púsa Móhēsà cultivating the subtle and wonderful scripture of the Dà Nièpán
fully achieve the fifth merit?
Good man!
For the Púsa Móhēsà cultivating the Dà Nièpán to fully achieve the fifth merit,
there are five factors.
What are these five?
First, all faculties are complete;
second, not being born in borderlands;
third, being loved and cherished by all Devas (gods);
fourth, being constantly revered by Māras (demons),
Shāmén,
Chàlì,
Póluómén, and others;
fifth, obtaining the knowledge of past lives (Sùméng Zhì).
Due to the power of conditions related to this Dà Nièpán Sūtra, the Bodhisattva
fully achieves these five merits.
Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng Púsa said:
"As the Buddha has taught,
if good men
and good women practice giving (bùshī),
they attain the full achievement of five merits.
How is it now said that these five merits are obtained through the Dà Nièpán?
The Buddha said:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
The meaning of these matters differs;
I shall now explain and distinguish them for you.
The five factors obtained through giving
are not definite,
are not permanent,
are not pure,
are not supreme,
are not unique,
are not without outflow (anāsrava),
and cannot benefit, bring peace and happiness, or compassionately aid all sentient beings.
If the five factors are obtained by relying upon this Dà Nièpán Sūtra,
they are definite,
are permanent,
are pure,
are supreme,
are unique,
are without outflow (anāsrava),
and thus they can benefit, bring peace and happiness, and compassionately aid all sentient beings.
Good man!
Giving (Bùshī) allows one to depart from hunger and thirst,
but the Dà Nièpán Sūtra enables sentient beings to universally escape the affliction of thirsty desire regarding the twenty-five forms of existence.
The condition of giving causes the continuation of saṃsāra,
while the Dà Nièpán Sūtra enables saṃsāra to be severed and not continued.
Due to giving, one receives the dharmas of ordinary beings;
due to the Dà Nièpán, one becomes a Bodhisattva.
The condition of giving can sever all suffering arising from poverty and distress,
but the Dà Nièpán Sūtra can sever all those who are poor in wholesome dharmas.
The condition of giving has parts and has results;
through the Dà Nièpán, one attains Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
which has neither parts nor results.
This is called the Púsa Móhēsà cultivating the subtle and wonderful scripture of the Dà Nièpán,
fully achieving the fifth merit."
"Shànnánzǐ!
How does a Púsa cultivate the profound and subtle Sūtra of the Great Nièpán
to perfectly achieve the sixth merit?
The Púsa Mòhēsà cultivates the Great Nièpán,
obtains the Jīngāng Sānmèi,
abides within it,
and is thereby able to completely shatter all phenomena.
(He) sees that all phenomena are impermanent,
are manifestations of movement,
causes of fear,
suffering from illness and plunder,
instantly destroyed in every moment,
having no true reality,
all being the realm of Māra,
having no perceivable characteristics.
When the Púsa Mòhēsà abides in this Sānmèi,
although giving to sentient beings,
he does not even see a single sentient being.
Truly for the sake of sentient beings,
he diligently practices Shī Bōluómì,
and similarly
practices Bānruò Bōluómì.
If the Púsa sees any sentient being,
he cannot ultimately and perfectly achieve Dàn Bōluómì up to the perfect achievement of Bānruò Bōluómì.
Shànnánzǐ!
For instance, like a diamond (vajra):
wherever it is applied, nothing fails to be shattered,
yet the diamond suffers no damage or breaking.
The Jīngāng Sānmèi is also like this:
the phenomena to which it is applied are completely shattered,
yet the Sānmèi suffers no damage or breaking.
Shànnánzǐ!
Just as the diamond is supreme among all jewels,
the Jīngāng Sānmèi attained by the Púsa is also like this:
among all Sānmèis, it is the foremost.
Why is this?
When the Púsa Mòhēsà cultivates this Sānmèi,
all other Sānmèis naturally submit to it.
Shànnánzǐ!
Just as all minor kings submit to the Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng,
all Sānmèis are also like this;
they all submit to the Jīngāng Sānmèi.
Shànnánzǐ!
For example, if someone is an enemy of the state,
despised and loathed by the people,
and someone kills him,
all worldly people praise the merit of that person.
The Jīngāng Sānmèi is also like this;
when the Púsa cultivates it,
he can destroy all the enemies of sentient beings,
therefore, it is always honored and respected by all Sānmèis.
Shànnánzǐ!
For instance, if there is a person
whose strength is immense
and whom no one can match,
and then another person appears
whose strength can subdue him—
you should know that this person is lauded by the world.
The Jīngāng Sānmèi is also like this:
its power can vanquish phenomena that are difficult to subdue;
for this reason,
all Sānmèis submit to it.
Shànnánzǐ!
For example, if someone bathes in the great ocean,
you should know that this person has already used the waters of all rivers, springs, and pools.
The Púsa Mòhēsà is also like this:
by cultivating this Jīngāng Sānmèi,
you should know that he has already cultivated all other Sānmèis.
Shànnánzǐ!
Just as in Fragrant Mountain there is a spring
named Ānàpótàduō,
whose water possesses the eight tastes (qualities),
and anyone who drinks it is free from all suffering and illness.
The Jīngāng Sānmèi is also like this:
it possesses the Eightfold Noble Path;
when a Púsa cultivates it,
he severs all afflictions,
boils, and severe illnesses.
Shànnánzǐ!
If a person makes offerings to Móxīshǒuluó,
you should know that this person has already made offerings to all the heavenly beings.
The Jīngāng Sānmèi is also like this:
if someone cultivates it,
you should know that he has already cultivated all other Sānmèis.
Shànnánzǐ!
If a Púsa abides in this Jīngāng Sānmèi,
he sees all phenomena without obstruction,
like observing an Āmólè Guǒ in the palm of his hand.
Although the Púsa gains this vision,
he never forms the thought of seeing all phenomena.
Shànnánzǐ!
For instance, like a person
sitting at a crossroads,
who sees all sentient beings coming,
going,
sitting,
and lying down.
The Jīngāng Sānmèi is also like this:
(it) sees all phenomena arising and ceasing,
appearing and disappearing.
Shànnánzǐ!
For instance, like a high mountain:
if someone climbs it and looks far,
all directions become perfectly clear.
The Mountain of Jīngāng Concentration is also like this:
when the Púsa ascends it,
looking far, there is nothing among phenomena that is not perfectly clear.
Shànnánzǐ!
For example, in the spring month,
when Heaven sends down sweet rain,
the drops are so fine and close that there is no space between them,
and a person with clear sight sees them perfectly distinctly.
The Púsa is also like this:
having obtained the pure vision of Jīngāng Concentration,
he sees far into all worlds in the eastern direction,
including those lands that are forming or decaying;
he sees everything perfectly clearly without obstruction,
and the ten directions are likewise seen.
Shànnánzǐ!
Just as when seven suns rise simultaneously over Yóu Gāntuó Shān,
all the trees, groves, and forests on that mountain are completely burned up.
When the Púsa cultivates the Jīngāng Sānmèi, it is also like this:
all his forests of affliction are immediately extinguished.
Shànnánzǐ!
For example, although a diamond can shatter all physical objects,
it never produces the thought, "I am able to shatter them."
The Jīngāng Sānmèi is also like this:
when the Púsa has cultivated it, he can destroy afflictions,
but he never produces the thought, "I am able to destroy the fetters."
Shànnánzǐ!
For example, the great earth can support myriad things,
yet it never produces the thought, "My power is able to support."
Fire also does not think, "I am able to burn things."
Water also does not think, "I am able to moisten."
Wind also does not think, "I am able to move things."
Space also does not think, "I am able to contain."
Nièpán likewise does not produce the thought,
"I enable sentient beings to attain cessation and salvation."
The Jīngāng Sānmèi is also like this:
although it can eliminate all afflictions,
it originally has no mind that says, "I am able to eliminate them."
If a Púsa abides in this Jīngāng Sānmèi,
in a single moment, he can transform his body to be like the Buddha,
in countless numbers, filling the worlds of the Buddhas equal to the sands of the Hénghéshā in the ten directions.
But although this Púsa performs such transformations,
his mind originally has no thought of arrogance.
Why is this?
The Púsa constantly reflects:
'Who possesses such concentration
as to be able to perform such transformations?
Only the Púsa who abides in this Jīngāng Sānmèi can accomplish it.'
The Púsa Mòhēsà, abiding in this Jīngāng Sānmèi,
in a single moment, travels throughout the worlds of the Buddhas equal to the sands of the Hénghéshā in the ten directions
and returns to his original place.
Although possessing such power,
he does not think,
'I am able to do this.'
Why is this?
Because of the power derived from this Sānmèi.
The Púsa Mòhēsà, abiding in this Jīngāng Sānmèi,
in a single moment, can sever all the afflictions of sentient beings in worlds equal to the sands of the Hénghéshā in the ten directions,
yet his mind originally has no thought of severing the afflictions of sentient beings.
Why is this?
Because of the power derived from this Sānmèi.
When the Púsa abides in this Jīngāng Sānmèi,
and speaks using a single voice,
all sentient beings understand according to their respective kinds.
He displays a single color,
yet all sentient beings
see various colors and characteristics, each individually.
Abiding in one place,
his body does not move or change,
yet he is able to cause sentient beings to see him in their respective directions.
When he expounds a single Dharma,
whether in terms of dhātus (realms)
or āyatanas (entrances/bases),
all sentient beings hear it according to their foundational understanding."
"When the Púsà abides in such concentration (Sānmèi),
although he sees sentient beings,
his mind initially holds no characteristics (xiàng) of sentient beings.
Although he sees men and women, there are no characteristics of men and women.
Although he sees form phenomena, there are no characteristics of form.
Even if he sees consciousness, there are no characteristics of consciousness.
Although he sees day and night, there are no characteristics of day and night.
Although he sees all things, there are no characteristics of all things.
Although he sees all afflictions (fánnǎo) and bonds (jié), there are no characteristics of all afflictions.
Although he sees the Eight Noble Paths (Bā Shèng Dào), there are no characteristics of the Noble Paths.
Although he sees bodhi, there are no characteristics of bodhi.
Although he sees Nièpán, there are no characteristics of Nièpán.
Why is this?
Good man!
Because all phenomena are fundamentally without characteristics.
Due to the power of this concentration (Sānmèi),
the Púsà sees all phenomena as fundamentally without characteristics.
Why is it called Jīngāng Sānmèi (Diamond Concentration)?
Good man!
Just as a diamond (Jīngāng),
if placed in the sunlight, its color is unsettled.
Jīngāng Sānmèi is also like this;
when in the great assembly, its appearance is also unsettled.
Therefore, it is called Jīngāng Sānmèi.
Good man!
Just as a diamond (Jīngāng),
cannot be appraised by any worldly person.
Jīngāng Sānmèi is also like this;
its merits and virtues cannot be measured by all humans and devas.
Therefore, it is also called Jīngāng Sānmèi.
Good man!
Just as a poor person who obtains the diamond treasure (Jīngāng Bǎo),
immediately gains freedom from poverty, distress, and suffering,
and from evil spirits and malicious poisons.
The Púsà Móhēsà is also like this:
having attained this concentration (Sānmèi),
he is able to escape all suffering caused by afflictions (fánnǎo),
and all malicious poisons of the Māras.
Therefore, it is also called Jīngāng Sānmèi.
This is named the sixth merit completed and achieved by the Púsà who practices the Great Nièpán.
"Furthermore, good man!
How does the Púsà Móhēsà, practicing the profound scripture of the Great Nièpán,
fully achieve the seventh merit?
Good man!
The Púsà Móhēsà, practicing the profound scripture of the Great Nièpán,
contemplates thus:
'What Dharma can act as the direct cause for the Dà Bān Nièpán?'
The Púsà immediately knows that there are four kinds of Dharma
that act as the direct cause for the Great Nièpán.
If it is said that diligent practice of all asceticism (kǔxíng)
is the direct causal condition for the Great Nièpán,
this interpretation is incorrect.
Why is this?
That one could attain Nièpán apart from these four Dharmas
is impossible.
What are these four?
First, associating closely with good friends (shàn zhīshì).
Second, dedicating the mind to hearing the Dharma.
Third, focusing the mind on contemplation.
Fourth, practicing according to the Dharma.
Good man!
For example, if a person suffers from various illnesses—
whether fever or chills,
exhaustion, dysentery, or malaria,
or malicious ghosts and poisons—
and goes to a skilled physician,
the physician immediately prescribes medicine tailored to the disease.
That person sincerely and carefully accepts the doctor's instructions,
compounds the medicine according to the instructions,
and takes it according to the Dharma.
Having taken it, the illness is cured,
and the body attains peace and joy.
The sick person
is analogous to the Púsàs.
The great skilled physician is analogous to the good spiritual advisors (Shàn Zhīshì).
The physician's prescription is analogous to the Vaipulya Sūtras (Fāngděng Jīng).
Accepting the doctor's instructions carefully is analogous to carefully contemplating the meaning of the Vaipulya Sūtras.
Compounding the medicine according to the instructions is analogous to practicing the thirty-seven Dharmas conducive to enlightenment (zhù dào zhī fǎ) according to the Dharma.
The removal and cure of the illness is analogous to the cessation of afflictions (fánnǎo).
Attaining peace and joy is analogous to attaining Nièpán:
Permanence (Cháng),
Bliss (Lè),
Self (Wǒ),
Purity (Jìng).
Good man!
For example, there is a king
who wishes to rule according to the Dharma
so that his people may be peaceful and joyful.
He consults his wise ministers,
asking, "What is the method?"
The ministers then explain to him the old laws of the former kings.
When the king heard this,
he faithfully practiced it with utmost sincerity,
governing the country according to the Dharma.
There were no enemies or rivals,
and thus his people were peaceful, joyful, and free from calamities.
Good man!
The king is analogous to the Púsàs.
The wise ministers are analogous to the Shàn Zhīshì.
The laws of governance explained by the wise ministers to the king are analogous to the twelve categories of scripture (shí'èr bù jīng).
The king, having heard this, sincerely believed and practiced it,
which is analogous to the Púsàs focusing their minds to contemplate the profound meanings contained within the twelve categories of scripture.
Governing the country according to the Dharma is analogous to the Púsàs practicing according to the Dharma,
namely, the Six Pāramitās (Liù Bōluómì).
Because they are able to cultivate and practice the Six Pāramitās, there are no enemies or rivals,
which is analogous to the Púsàs having abandoned all bonds (jié), afflictions (fánnǎo), and evil bandits.
Attaining peace and joy is analogous to the Púsàs attaining the Great Nièpán, which is Permanence, Bliss, Self, and Purity (Cháng, Lè, Wǒ, Jìng).
"Good man!
For example, if a person contracts a severe leprosy,
a Shàn Zhīshì tells him:
'If you can reach the foot of Mount Xūmí Shān,
your disease can be cured.
Why is this?
There is an excellent medicine there,
tasting like sweet dew (gānlù).
If you can take it,
no disease will fail to be cured.'
That person sincerely believed this matter,
immediately went to that mountain, gathered and took the sweet dew.
His disease was eliminated and cured,
and his body attained peace and joy.
The severe leprosy is analogous to ordinary mortals (fánfū).
The Shàn Zhīshì are analogous to the Púsà Móhēsàs, and others.
Sincerely believing and accepting is analogous to the Four Immeasurable Minds (Sì Wúliàng Xīn).
Mount Xūmí Shān is analogous to the Eight Noble Paths (Bā Shèng Dào).
The taste of the sweet dew is analogous to the Fó Xìng (Buddha Nature).
The removal and cure of the leprosy is analogous to separation from afflictions (fánnǎo).
Attaining peace and joy is analogous to attaining Nièpán, which is Permanence, Bliss, Self, and Purity (Cháng, Lè, Wǒ, Jìng).
Good man!
For example, if someone takes on disciples who are bright and greatly wise,
that person constantly teaches them day and night without tiring.
The Púsàs are also like this;
regardless of whether sentient beings believe or do not believe,
they constantly teach and transform them without weariness or aversion.
"Good man!
Good spiritual advisors (Shàn Zhīshì)
are namely the Púsàs,
the Fó,
the Pìzhīfó,
the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén),
and those among humans who believe in the Vaipulya teachings (Fāngděng).
Why are they called Shàn Zhīshì?
A Shàn Zhīshì is able to teach sentient beings to abandon the Ten Evils
and practice the Ten Virtues.
Based on this meaning,
they are called Shàn Zhīshì.
Furthermore, a Shàn Zhīshì
speaks according to the Dharma
and practices according to what is spoken.
How are "speaking according to the Dharma"
and "practicing according to what is spoken" defined?
They themselves do not kill life
and teach others not to kill,
and similarly, they practice right view (zhèngjiàn) themselves
and teach others right view.
If one can do this, they are called a true Shàn Zhīshì.
They cultivate bodhi themselves
and can also teach others to cultivate bodhi.
Based on this meaning,
they are called Shàn Zhīshì.
They themselves are able to cultivate faith (xìn),
precepts (jiè),
generosity (bùshī),
extensive listening (duōwén),
and wisdom (zhìhuì),
and can also teach others faith,
precepts,
generosity,
extensive listening,
and wisdom.
Based on this meaning again, they are called Shàn Zhīshì.
A Shàn Zhīshì
possesses wholesome Dharmas.
What are these wholesome Dharmas?
In their actions, they do not seek joy for themselves,
but constantly seek joy for sentient beings.
When they see the faults of others, they do not proclaim their shortcomings.
Their mouths constantly speak only of purely wholesome matters.
Based on this meaning,
they are called Shàn Zhīshì.
"Good man!
Just like the moon in the sky,
from the first day to the fifteenth day, it gradually grows.
The `Shàn Zhīshì` (good spiritual advisor) is also like this,
causing all learners to gradually move far away from evil principles (dharma),
and increase good principles.
Good man!
If there are those who draw near to a `Shàn Zhīshì`,
and originally did not possess Precepts (`Jiè`),
Concentration (`Dìng`),
Wisdom (`Huì`),
Liberation (`Jiětuō`),
or the knowledge and view of liberation,
they immediately obtain them.
For those who have not fully realized them,
they will gain expansion and increase.
Why is this?
Because they draw near to a `Shàn Zhīshì`;
due to this closeness,
they furthermore attain realization of the extremely profound meaning of the Twelve Divisions of the `Jīng` (Sūtras).
If one is able to hear the extremely profound meaning of these Twelve Divisions of the `Jīng`,
this is called Hearing the Dharma (`Tīng Fǎ`).
Hearing the Dharma refers to the Vaipulya (Broad and Equal) `Jīngdiǎn` of the Great Vehicle (`Dàshèng Fāngdĕng Jīngdiǎn`).
Hearing the `Fāngdĕng Jīng` is called True Hearing of the Dharma (`Zhēn Tīng Fǎ`).
True Hearing of the Dharma is specifically hearing and receiving the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (`Dà Nièpán Jīng`).
To hear within the `Dà Nièpán` of the Buddha Nature (`Fóxìng`),
and that the Tathāgata (`Rúlái`) ultimately does not enter parinirvāṇa,
therefore this is called Single-mindedly Hearing the Dharma (`Zhuānxīn Tīng Fǎ`).
Single-mindedly Hearing the Dharma is called the Eightfold Noble Path (`Bā Shèng Dào`).
Because the Eightfold Noble Path can cut off greed,
hatred, and ignorance,
therefore it is called Hearing the Dharma.
Furthermore, Hearing the Dharma
is called the Eleven Kinds of Emptiness (`Shíyī Kōng`).
By means of these types of Emptiness,
one does not engage in form or characteristics regarding all phenomena (dharma).
Furthermore, Hearing the Dharma is called the Initial Aspiration (`Chū Fā Xīn`),
up to the ultimate mind of `Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí`.
It is by means of the Initial Aspiration that one attains the Great Nirvāṇa (`Dà Nièpán`),
not by means of merely hearing that one attains the Great Nirvāṇa,
but by means of cultivation and practice that one attains the Great Nirvāṇa.
"Good man!
For example, a sick person,
although hearing the doctor's instructions and the names of the medicines, cannot cure the illness;
it is by taking and eating the medicine that they can recover from the illness.
Although hearing the profound Dharma of the Twelvefold Chain of Dependent Origination (`Shí'èr Shēn Yīnyuán Fǎ`),
one cannot thereby sever all afflictions (`Fánnǎo`).
It is essential to bind the mind (concentrate `Xì Niàn`),
and through proper contemplation (`Shàn Sīwéi`),
one is able to eliminate and sever them.
This is called the Third Binding of Mind and Contemplation.
Furthermore, based on what meaning
is it called Binding of Mind and Contemplation?
It is referring to the Three Samādhis (`Sān Sānmèi`):
Emptiness Samādhi (`Kōng Sānmèi`),
Signlessness Samādhi (`Wú Xiàng Sānmèi`),
and Wishlessness Samādhi (`Wú Zuò Sānmèi`).
Emptiness means not seeing a single reality in the Twenty-five Realms of Existence (`Èrshíwŭ Yǒu`).
Wishlessness means not making wishes or seeking anything within the Twenty-five Realms of Existence.
Signlessness means being without the Ten Signs,
namely, the sign of form (`Sè Xiàng`),
the sign of sound (`Shēng Xiàng`),
the sign of smell (`Xiāng Xiàng`),
the sign of taste (`Wèi Xiàng`),
the sign of touch (`Chù Xiàng`),
the sign of arising (`Shēng Xiàng`),
the sign of abiding (`Zhù Xiàng`),
the sign of cessation (`Miè Xiàng`),
the sign of male (`Nán Xiàng`),
and the sign of female (`Nǚ Xiàng`).
One who cultivates and practices these Three Samādhis,
is called a Bodhisattva's Binding of Mind and Contemplation (`Púsà Xì Niàn Sīwéi`).
What is called Cultivation According to the Dharma (`Rú Fǎ Xiūxíng`)?
Cultivation According to the Dharma means cultivating the `Dàn Bōluómì` (Dāna Pāramitā) up to the `Bānruò Bōluómì` (Prajñā Pāramitā),
knowing the true characteristics of the Skandhas (`Yīn`), the Āyatanas (`Rù`), and the Dhātus (`Jiè`).
Furthermore, just like the `Shēngwén` (Hearers),
the `Yuánjué` (Pratyekabuddhas),
and all Buddhas,
they enter parinirvāṇa (`Bān Nièpán`) through the same single path.
The Dharma is specifically permanence, joy, self, and purity (`Cháng Lè Wǒ Jìng`),
not arising and not aging,
not being sick and not dying,
not being hungry and not being thirsty,
not suffering and not being afflicted,
not regressing and not sinking.
Good man!
One who understands the extremely profound meaning of the Great Nirvāṇa (`Dà Nièpán`),
then knows that the Buddhas ultimately never enter Nirvāṇa.
"Good man!
The foremost True `Shàn Zhīshì`
are the Bodhisattvas (`Púsà`),
and all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones (`Fó Shìzūn`).
Why is this?
Because they constantly employ three skillful methods of guidance and control.
What are the three?
First, ultimately soft words.
Second, ultimately harsh rebuke.
Third, soft words followed by harsh rebuke.
Due to these meanings,
the Bodhisattvas and all Buddhas are the True `Shàn Zhīshì`.
Furthermore, good man!
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas
are called `Shàn Zhīshì` because they are Great Physicians.
Why is this?
They know the illness,
they know the medicine,
and they prescribe the medicine according to the illness.
For example, a good physician,
skilled in the eight types of medical arts,
first observes the characteristics of the disease.
The characteristics are of three types.
What are the three?
Namely, wind (`Fēng`),
heat (`Rè`),
and water (`Shuǐ`).
For those who have a wind illness,
they are given clarified butter (`Sū Yóu`).
For people with a heat illness,
they are given rock candy (`Shí Mì`).
For people with a water illness,
they are given ginger decoction (`Jiāng Tāng`).
Since the root of the illness is known,
administering the medicine results in recovery;
therefore, they are called good physicians.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are also like this;
they know that the illnesses of all common beings (`Fánfū`) are of three kinds:
First, greed (`Tānyù`),
second, hatred (`Chēnhuì`),
and third, ignorance (`Yúchī`).
Those afflicted by the illness of greed are taught to contemplate the characteristic of the bones (`Guān Gǔ Xiàng`).
Those afflicted by the illness of hatred contemplate the characteristic of loving-kindness and compassion (`Cíbēi Xiàng`).
Those afflicted by the illness of ignorance contemplate the characteristic of the Twelvefold Chain of Dependent Origination (`Shí'èr Yuán Xiàng`).
Due to these meanings,
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called `Shàn Zhīshì`.
Good man!
Just as a Great Helmsman (`Dà Chuánshī`),
is called a Great Helmsman because he skillfully ferries people across.
(Marker placement adjustment for fluidity.)
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are also like this;
they ferry all sentient beings across the great ocean of transmigration (samsara, `Shēngsǐ Dàhǎi`).
Due to these meanings,
they are called `Shàn Zhīshì`.
Furthermore, good man!
Through the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
all sentient beings are enabled to fully cultivate and attain the root of good dharmas.
Good man!
For example, Mount Snow (`Xuěshān`),
is truly the fundamental source of various subtle and superior medicines.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are also like this;
they are entirely the source (fundamental root place) of all goodness.
Due to these meanings,
they are called `Shàn Zhīshì`.
Good man!
Within Mount `Xuěshān` there is a superior fragrant medicine,
named `Suōhē`.
If a person sees it,
they gain immeasurable longevity,
and are without the suffering of illness.
Although there may be the Four Poisons, they cannot harm them.
If one touches it, longevity increases to a full one hundred and twenty [years].
If one thinks of it, they gain the knowledge of past lives (`Sùmìng Zhì`).
Why is this?
Because of the power of the medicine.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are also like this;
if one sees them,
one immediately severs and eliminates all afflictions (`Fánnǎo`).
Although there may be the Four Māras, they cannot disrupt one.
If one touches them, life cannot be cut short,
there is no birth and no death,
no regression and no sinking.
What is called touching them
is being near the Buddha and hearing and receiving the subtle Dharma.
If one thinks of them,
one attains `Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí`.
Due to these meanings,
all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called `Shàn Zhīshì`.
Good man!
Just as in Fragrant Mountain (`Xiāngshān`),
there is the water of the `Ānàpó Tàduō` (Anavatapta) Pond.
Due to this pond,
there are the Four Great Rivers,
namely, the `Hénghé` (Ganges River),
the `Xīntóu` (Sindhu River),
the `Sītuó` (Sītā River),
and the `Bóshā` (Vakṣu River).
Worldly beings constantly make this statement:
'If there are those who are sinful,
by bathing in these four rivers,
all their sins will be extinguished.'
You should know that this statement is false and unreal.
Apart from this, what is truly real?
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—they are truly real.
Why is this?
If a person draws near to them,
they will extinguish and eliminate all sins.
Due to these meanings,
they are called `Shàn Zhīshì`."
"Furthermore, good man!
For example, the great earth,
all the medicinal trees and herbs,
all the forests,
the hundred grains and sugarcane,
and things like flowers and fruits,
when they meet a great drought in heaven and are about to wither and die,
Nántuó Lóngwáng (Nānda Dragon King) and Pó Nántuó (Upananda),
out of compassion for sentient beings,
emerge from the great sea
and pour down sweet rain.
All the forests,
the hundred grains, grasses, and trees are moistened and revive.
All sentient beings are also like this;
when their good roots are about to perish,
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas give rise to great compassion,
and pour down the rain of sweet dew from the sea of wisdom,
enabling all sentient beings to fully regain the Dharma of the Ten Virtues.
For this reason,
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called Good Friends (Kalyāṇamitra).
Good man!
For example, an excellent physician, skilled in the eight types of treatment,
when seeing various patients, does not regard their background or caste (zhǒngxìng),
whether they are upright (duānzhèng), beautiful or ugly,
or their money, wealth, or treasures,
but treats them all.
Therefore, the world calls him a Great Excellent Physician.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are also like this;
seeing that sentient beings have the sickness of afflictions (fánnǎo),
they do not regard their background or caste (zhǒngxìng),
whether they are upright (duānzhèng), beautiful or ugly,
or their money, wealth, or treasures.
They generate a heart of compassion,
and proclaim the Dharma for them all.
When sentient beings hear it, the sickness of their afflictions is eliminated.
For this reason,
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are called Good Friends.
By means of this cause—drawing near to Good Friends—
one thereby draws near to the Great Parinirvāṇa.
"How is it that Bodhisattvas draw near to the Great Parinirvāṇa through the cause of listening to the Dharma?
All sentient beings, by listening to the Dharma,
thereby complete the root of faith (xìnggēn).
Having obtained the root of faith,
they are happy to practice giving (bùshī),
keeping precepts (chíjiè),
forbearance (rěnrǔ),
diligence (jīngjìn),
meditative concentration (chándìng),
and wisdom (zhìhuì).
They attain the fruit of Srotāpanna up to the fruit of Buddhahood.
Therefore, one should know that obtaining all good dharmas
is entirely due to the power of the cause of listening to the Dharma.
Good man!
For example, a wealthy householder (zhǎngzhě) had only one son;
he sent him to another country to trade for necessary goods,
and showed him the roads, indicating the open and obstructed places.
He further cautioned him:
'If you meet an adulterous woman (yínnǚ),
take great care not to be intimate with her,
for if you are intimate with her,
you will lose your body, forfeit your life, and lose your wealth and treasures.
Also, do not associate
with wicked and malicious people (bì'è zhī rén).'
The son respectfully obeyed his father's instruction and command,
found peace and happiness (ānlè) in body and mind,
and acquired many precious goods.
The Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas expounding the essential Dharma for sentient beings are also like this:
they show all sentient beings and the four assemblies the open and obstructed paths of the various ways.
These sentient beings, by hearing the Dharma,
distance themselves from all evils
and complete good dharmas.
For this reason,
the cause of listening to the Dharma thereby draws one near to the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Good man!
For example, a bright mirror illuminates a person's face
with nothing unclear.
The bright mirror of listening to the Dharma is also like this:
when a person reflects upon it,
they see good and evil clearly, without obscuration (yì).
For this reason,
the cause of listening to the Dharma thereby draws one near to the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Good man!
For example, a merchant (gūkè),
wishing to reach the Isle of Treasures (bǎozhǔ),
but not knowing the way,
is shown by someone else.
That person follows the instructions
and immediately reaches the Isle of Treasures,
acquiring countless precious things.
All sentient beings are also like this:
wishing to reach a good destination (shànchù) to gather the treasures of the Way,
but not knowing the way, whether it is open or obstructed.
When a Bodhisattva shows them,
the sentient beings follow and manage to reach the good destination,
obtaining the supreme treasure of the Great Nirvāṇa.
For this reason,
the cause of listening to the Dharma thereby draws one near to the Great Parinirvāṇa.
"Good man!
For example, a drunken elephant
is frenzied, stupid, cruel, and wicked,
and greatly desires to kill.
An elephant trainer,
with a large iron hook,
pierces and chops its head.
Immediately, it becomes disciplined and docile,
and its wicked mind is completely extinguished.
All sentient beings are also like this:
because they are drunk on greed (tānyù),
hatred (chēnhuì),
and delusion (yúchī),
they desire to commit many evils.
The Bodhisattvas,
with the hook of listening to the Dharma,
chop at them, making them stop,
so that they can no longer give rise to evil intentions and commit evil deeds.
For this reason,
the cause of listening to the Dharma thereby draws one near to the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, in various Sūtras, I have said:
'My disciples focus their minds on listening to and receiving the twelve divisions of scriptures,
thereby leaving the Five Hindrances (wǔgài)
and cultivating the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (qījuéfēn).
By means of this cultivation of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment,
they thereby draw near to the Great Parinirvāṇa.
By listening to the Dharma, the Srotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán) person departs from all terrors.
Why is this?
The householder Sudatta (Sūdá Zhǎngzhě) encountered a severe illness in his body,
and his heart was greatly sorrowful and fearful.
He heard Shèlìfú (Śāriputra) speak of the Srotāpanna's four merits
and ten kinds of consolation.
Having heard this,
his terror was immediately dispelled.
For this reason,
the cause of listening to the Dharma thereby draws one near to the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Why is this?
Because it opens the Dharma eye.
There are three types of people in the world:
the first is blind (wúmù),
the second has one eye (yīmù),
and the third has two eyes (èrmù).
The one called blind is he who never hears the Dharma.
The one-eyed person is he who, although temporarily hearing the Dharma, his mind does not dwell on it.
The two-eyed person is he who focuses his mind on listening to and receiving it, and practices as he hears.
By listening to the Dharma,
one is able to know these three types of people in the world.
For this reason,
the cause of listening to the Dharma thereby draws one near to the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Good man!
As I was formerly in Kušinagara (Jūshīnàchéng),
at that time Shèlìfú's body encountered sickness and pain.
I then commanded the Bhikṣu Ānán (Ānanda) to extensively speak the Dharma for him.
Shèlìfú heard this
and told his four disciples:
'You carry my bed and go to where the Buddha is;
I wish to listen to the Dharma.'
At that time, the four disciples carried him together and went there.
As soon as he heard the Dharma,
due to the power of hearing the Dharma,
his suffering was eliminated and cured,
and his body attained peace and safety (ānyǐn).
For this reason,
the cause of listening to the Dharma thereby draws one near to the Great Parinirvāṇa."
(Bodhisattva), by contemplating conditions, draw near to the Mahāpārinirvāṇa (Dàbān Nièpán)?
Because of this contemplation,
the mind attains liberation.
Why is this?
All sentient beings are constantly bound by the five desires (wǔ yù),
but because of contemplation, they all attain liberation.
For this reason,
contemplating conditions enables one to draw near to the Mahāpārinirvāṇa (Dàbān Nièpán).
Furthermore, O virtuous man (shànnánzǐ)!
All sentient beings are constantly subject to the upside-down views (diāndǎo) of the four principles: permanence (cháng),
joy (lè),
self (wǒ),
and purity (jìng). Because of contemplation,
they gain insight that all phenomena (zhū fǎ) are impermanent (wúcháng),
non-joy (wúlè),
non-self (wúwǒ),
and impure (wújìng). Having this insight, the four upside-down views (sì dǎo) are immediately severed.
For this reason,
contemplating conditions enables one to draw near to the Mahāpārinirvāṇa (Dàbān Nièpán).
Furthermore, O virtuous man (shànnánzǐ)!
All phenomena (zhū fǎ) have four characteristics (sì zhǒng xiàng).
What are the four?
First, the characteristic of arising (shēng xiàng);
second, the characteristic of aging (lǎo xiàng);
third, the characteristic of sickness (bìng xiàng);
fourth, the characteristic of perishing (miè xiàng).
Because of these four characteristics,
all ordinary beings (fánfū zhòngshēng), up to those who have reached the stream-enterer (Xūtuóhuán) stage, give rise to great suffering (kǔnǎo);
but if one is able to focus the mind and contemplate well,
although encountering these four,
suffering does not arise.
For this reason,
contemplating conditions enables one to draw near to the Mahāpārinirvāṇa (Dàbān Nièpán).
Furthermore, O virtuous man (shànnánzǐ)!
All wholesome principles (shàn fǎ) are obtained only through contemplation.
Why is this?
Though someone may wholeheartedly listen to the Dharma (fǎ) throughout measureless and boundless asaṃkhyeya kalpas (ā-sēng-qí jié),
if they do not contemplate,
they ultimately cannot attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).
For this reason,
contemplating conditions enables one to draw near to the Mahāpārinirvāṇa (Dàbān Nièpán).
Furthermore, O virtuous man (shànnánzǐ)!
If there are sentient beings who have faith in the Buddha (Fó),
the Dharma (fǎ),
and the Saṅgha (sēng),
without change or alteration,
and give rise to reverence,
you should know that this is entirely due to the power of focusing the mind and contemplating conditions,
and thereby they are able to sever all afflictions (fánnǎo).
For this reason,
contemplating conditions enables one to draw near to the Mahāpārinirvāṇa (Dàbān Nièpán)."
"How does a Púsà (Bodhisattva) practice according to the Dharma (rú fǎ xiūxíng)?
O virtuous man (shànnánzǐ)!
Severing all evil principles (è fǎ)
and cultivating wholesome principles (shàn fǎ)
is called a Púsà practicing according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, what is practicing according to the Dharma?
Seeing that all phenomena (yīqiè fǎ) are empty (kōng) and nonexistent,
impermanent (wúcháng),
non-joy (wúlè),
non-self (wúwǒ),
and impure (wújìng);
because of this insight,
preferring to abandon one’s body and life
rather than violate the precepts (jìnjiè) —
this is called a Púsà practicing according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, what is practicing according to the Dharma?
Practice (xiū) has two kinds:
first, genuine (zhēnshí);
second, non-genuine (bù shí).
The non-genuine refers to
not knowing the characteristics (xiàng) of Nièpán (Nirvāṇa),
Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
the Dharma (fǎ),
the Saṅgha (sēng),
Ultimate Reality (shíxiàng),
and space (xūkōng), and so on.
This is called non-genuine.
What is genuine?
Being able to know the characteristics of Nièpán,
Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
the Dharma (fǎ),
the Saṅgha (sēng),
Ultimate Reality (shíxiàng),
and space (xūkōng), and so on.
This is called genuine.
What is called knowing the characteristic of Nièpán?
The characteristics of Nièpán generally involve eight items.
What are the eight?
First, exhaustion (jìn);
second, wholesome nature (shànxìng);
third, reality (shí);
fourth, truth (zhēn);
fifth, permanence (cháng);
sixth, joy (lè);
seventh, self (wǒ);
eighth, purity (jìng).
This is called Nièpán.
There are also eight other items.
What are the eight?
First, liberation (jiětuō);
second, wholesome nature (shànxìng);
third, non-reality (bù shí);
fourth, untruth (bù zhēn);
fifth, impermanence (wúcháng);
sixth, non-joy (wúlè);
seventh, non-self (wúwǒ);
eighth, impurity (wújìng).
Furthermore, there are six characteristics:
first, liberation (jiětuō);
second, wholesome nature (shànxìng);
third, non-reality (bù shí);
fourth, untruth (bù zhēn);
fifth, peaceful joy (ānlè);
sixth, purity (qīngjìng).
