If there are sentient beings who rely on the mundane path (shìsú dào)
to sever afflictions (fánnǎo),
such Nièpán
includes eight items: liberation (jiětuō) and non-reality (bù shí).
Why is this?
Because it is not permanent (bù cháng).
Since it is impermanent (wúcháng), there is no reality (shí);
since there is no reality, there is no truth (zhēn).
Although afflictions are severed,
because they can arise again,
there is impermanence (wúcháng),
non-self (wúwǒ),
non-joy (wúlè),
and impurity (wújìng).
This is called the eight items of Nièpán liberation (jiětuō).
What are the six characteristics?
The Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué), having severed afflictions (fánnǎo),
are called liberated (jiětuō),
yet they have not attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí);
thus it is called non-reality (bù shí).
Because it is non-reality,
it is called untruth (bù zhēn).
Since they will attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí) in a future age,
it is called impermanence (wúcháng).
Since they have attained the eight noble paths (bā shèng dào) free from outflow (wúlòu),
it is called purity and joy (jìng lè).
O virtuous man (shànnánzǐ)!
If one knows this way,
this is knowing Nièpán.
It is not called Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
the Dharma (fǎ),
the Saṅgha (sēng),
Ultimate Reality (shíxiàng),
or space (xūkōng)."
"How does a Púsà (Bodhisattva) know Buddha Nature (Fóxìng)?
Buddha Nature has six points.
What are the six?
First, permanence (cháng);
second, purity (jìng);
third, reality (shí);
fourth, wholesomeness (shàn);
fifth, subsequent sight/to be seen (dāng jiàn);
sixth, truth (zhēn).
Furthermore, there are seven items:
first, verifiable (kě zhèng);
the remaining six are as above.
This is called a Púsà knowing Buddha Nature (Fóxìng)."
"How does a Púsà (Bodhisattva) know the characteristics of the Tathāgata (Rúlái)?
The Tathāgata is immediately the characteristic of enlightenment (jué xiàng) and the wholesome characteristic (shàn xiàng):
permanence (cháng), joy (lè), self (wǒ), purity (jìng),
liberation (jiětuō),
reality/truth (zhēnshí),
demonstrating the path and being visible.
This is called a Púsà knowing the characteristics of the Tathāgata (Rúlái)."
"How does a Púsà (Bodhisattva) know the characteristics of the Dharma (fǎ)?
The Dharma refers to whether it is wholesome (shàn) or
unwholesome (bù shàn);
whether it is permanent (cháng) or
impermanent (bù cháng);
whether it is joyful (lè) or
not joyful (bù lè);
whether it is self (wǒ) or
non-self (wúwǒ);
whether it is pure (jìng) or
impure (bù jìng);
whether it is knowable (zhī) or
unknowable (bù zhī);
whether it is understandable (jiě) or
ununderstandable (bù jiě);
whether it is true (zhēn) or
untrue (bù zhēn);
whether it is cultivable (xiū) or
uncultivable (bù xiū);
whether it is a master (shī) or
not a master (fēi shī);
whether it is real (shí) or
unreal (bù shí) —
this is called a Púsà knowing the characteristics of the Dharma (fǎ)."
Bodhisattva know the characteristic of the Saṅgha (Sēng)?
If the Saṅgha is permanent, joyful, self-possessing, and pure,
these are the characteristics of disciples;
characteristics that are visible,
good,
true,
but not ultimate reality.
Why is this?
Because all Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) attain the Buddhahood (Fódào).
Why is it called true (zhēn)?
Because they awaken to the Dharma-nature (Fǎxìng).
This is called the Bodhisattva knowing the characteristic of the Saṅgha.
"How does a Bodhisattva know the characteristic of Ultimate Reality (Shíxiàng)?
Ultimate Reality (Shíxiàng) is:
whether permanent,
or impermanent;
whether joyful,
or joyless;
whether self-possessing,
or selfless;
whether pure,
or impure;
whether good,
or not good;
whether existing,
or non-existing;
whether Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
or not Nirvāṇa;
whether liberation (jiětuō),
or not liberation;
whether knowing,
or not knowing;
whether severed,
or not severed;
whether realized,
or not realized;
whether cultivated,
or not cultivated;
whether seen,
or not seen.
This is called Ultimate Reality (Shíxiàng).
It is neither Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
nor Buddha-nature (Fóxìng),
nor Tathāgata (Rúlái),
nor Dharma (Fǎ),
nor Saṅgha (Sēng),
nor emptiness (xūkōng).
This is called the Bodhisattva, because of cultivating this Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán),
knowing the distinguishing characteristics
of Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
Buddha-nature (Fóxìng),
Tathāgata (Rúlái),
Dharma (Fǎ),
Saṅgha (Sēng),
Ultimate Reality (Shíxiàng),
emptiness (xūkōng), and other such Dharmas.
"Good man!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) cultivates the subtle Sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán),
they do not see emptiness (xūkōng).
Why is this?
Because even the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas, though possessing the Five Eyes, cannot see it.
Only the Eye of Wisdom (Huìyǎn) is able to see it,
but what the Eye of Wisdom sees is that there is nothing visible;
hence, it is called seeing.
If that which is without substance is called emptiness (xūkōng),
then such emptiness is called reality (shí),
and because it is reality, it is called permanent non-existence (chángwú).
Because it is permanent non-existence,
it is without joy,
self,
or purity.
Good man!
Emptiness (kōng) means non-Dharma (wúfǎ);
non-Dharma means emptiness (kōng).
It is like in the world where the absence of substance is called empty.
The nature of emptiness (xūkōng) is also like this;
because it possesses nothing, it is called emptiness (xūkōng).
Good man!
The nature of sentient beings and the nature of emptiness (xūkōng) both lack ultimate reality (shíxìng).
Why is this?
It is like when people say
that by eliminating existing substance, emptiness is then created,
but this emptiness (xūkōng) cannot actually be created.
Why is this?
Because it possesses nothing.
Since there is nothing,
know that there is no emptiness (kōng).
If this nature of emptiness (xūkōng)
were something that could be created, it would be called impermanent,
and if it were impermanent, it would not be called emptiness (xūkōng).
Good man!
Just as worldly people say that emptiness (xūkōng) is without form,
unobstructed,
permanent, and unchanging;
therefore, the world calls the Dharma of emptiness (xūkōng)
the fifth great element (Dà).
Good man!
However, this emptiness (xūkōng) truly has no nature (xìng);
because of luminosity/radiance (guāngmíng),
it is called emptiness (xūkōng);
in reality, there is no emptiness (xūkōng).
Just like Worldly Truth (Shìdì),
which truly has no nature,
yet for the sake of sentient beings,
it is taught that Worldly Truth exists.
Good man!
The essence of Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) is also like this:
it has no dwelling place;
it is simply the place where all Buddhas sever afflictions (fánnǎo),
hence it is called Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
Nirvāṇa is permanence,
joy,
self,
and purity.
Although Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) is joy (lè),
it is not experienced joy;
rather, it is the supreme and subtle joy of quiescence (jìmie).
All Buddhas Tathāgata (Rúlái) possess two kinds of joy:
first, the joy of quiescence (jìmielè);
second, the joy of awakening (juézhīlè).
The essence of Ultimate Reality (Shíxiàng) possesses three kinds of joy:
first, experienced joy (shòulè);
second, the joy of quiescence (jìmielè);
third, the joy of awakening (juézhīlè).
Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) has one joy,
because it must be seen.
When one attains Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
it is called the joy of Bodhi (Pútílè).
At that time, Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng Púsà Móhēsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If the place where afflictions (fánnǎo) are severed is Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
this statement is incorrect.
Why is this?
When the Tathāgata (Rúlái) first attained Buddhahood (Fódào) in the past, arriving at the banks of the Níliánchán River,
at that time, the Demon King (Mówáng) and his retinues came to the Buddha's presence
and spoke these words:
'World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
The time for Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) has arrived, why do you not enter it?'
The Buddha told the Demon King (Mówáng):
'I do not yet have many disciples who are widely learned,
who skillfully uphold the precepts (jìnjiè),
who are wise and sharp-witted,
and who are capable of transforming sentient beings.
Therefore, I do not enter.'
If it is said that the place where afflictions (fánnǎo) are completely severed is Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
then all Bodhisattvas (Púsà) have already severed afflictions over immeasurable kalpas;
why can they not be called Nirvāṇa?
Since both are places where severance occurs,
why is it said only that all Buddhas possess it,
and that Bodhisattvas (Púsà) do not?
If the severance of afflictions (fánnǎo) is not Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
why did the Tathāgata (Rúlái) once tell the Brahmin whose name was Shēng (Shēngmíng Póluómén):
'My present body is precisely Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).'
When the Tathāgata (Rúlái) was previously in the country of Píshèlǐ,
the Demon King (Mówáng) again petitioned:
'In the past, the Tathāgata (Rúlái) did not enter Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) because he lacked disciples who were widely learned,
upholds of the precepts (chíjiè),
wise,
sharp-witted,
and capable of transforming sentient beings.
Now these are complete.
Why do you not enter?'
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) then told the Demon King:
'You should not harbor thoughts of vexation or delay now.
After three months, I shall enter Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).'
World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If entering extinction (mièdù) were not Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
why did the Tathāgata (Rúlái) himself appoint a time, saying that after three months he would enter Pari-Nirvāṇa (Bān Nièpán)?
World-Honored One!
If the severance of afflictions (fánnǎo) is Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
then in the past, when the Tathāgata (Rúlái)
first severed afflictions beneath the Bodhi Tree (Pútíshù) at the place of awakening (Dàochǎng),
that was already Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
Why then did he later say that after three months he would enter Pari-Nirvāṇa (Bān Nièpán)?
World-Honored One!
If that time were Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
why did he then tell the Mallas (lìshì) of the city of Jūshīnà
that he would enter Pari-Nirvāṇa (Bān Nièpán) during the last watch of the night?
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is truly honest;
how could he utter such deceitful words?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng Púsà Móhēsà, saying:
"Good man!
If it is said that the Tathāgata possesses the broad and long tongue,
you should know that the Tathāgata, throughout immeasurable kalpas, has already abandoned false speech.
All Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas,
whatever they utter,
is sincere, true, and without falsehood.
Good man!
Regarding what you said,
that Pāxún (Māra) formerly requested me to enter Nirvāṇa—
Good man!
This Demon King truly does not know the fixed characteristics of Nirvāṇa.
Why is this?
Pāxún assumes
that not transforming sentient beings,
remaining silently and still,
is Nirvāṇa.
Good man!
Just as worldly people,
seeing a person not speaking,
doing nothing,
immediately assume that this person
is no different from the dead.
The Demon King Pāxún is also like this;
he assumes the Tathāgata, not transforming sentient beings,
silently saying nothing,
has entered Parinirvāṇa.
Good man!
The Tathāgata does not teach that the Buddha,
the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha are without distinguishing characteristics,
but only teaches that the two Dharmas of permanence and purity are without distinguishing characteristics.
Good man!
The Buddha also does not teach that the Buddha, the Buddha nature,
and Nirvāṇa are without distinguishing characteristics,
but only teaches that permanence, constancy, and immutability are without distinguishing characteristics.
Good man!
The Buddha also does not teach that Nirvāṇa
and Ultimate Reality are without distinguishing characteristics,
but only teaches that permanence, reality, and immutability are without distinguishing characteristics.
Good man!
At that time, my Śrāvaka disciples
gave rise to disputes,
like the evil Bhikṣus of Jūshǎnmí,
who defied my teaching, frequently violated the disciplinary rules,
accepted impure goods,
and greedily sought profit and support.
They praised themselves before the lay followers, claiming to have attained outflows-ending (āsrava-kṣaya),
saying they attained the fruit of Sutāyuán (Sotāpanna) or even the fruit of Āluóhàn (Arhat),
while disparaging others,
and showing no reverence
the Dharma,
the Saṅgha,
the Precepts,
or the Upādhyāya (teacher).
toward the Buddha,
Publicly before me, they said that certain things were permitted by the Buddha to be kept,
and that certain other things were not permitted by the Buddha to be kept.
I also told them that I truly did not permit these things,
but they retorted against me, saying that these things were truly permitted by the Buddha.
Since such evil people did not believe my words,
because of these individuals,
I announced to Pāxún,
'Do not delay in anxiety;
in three months, I shall enter Parinirvāṇa.'
Good man!
Because of such evil Bhikṣus,
the various Śrāvakas
and disciples who received the teachings,
not seeing my body,
and not hearing my Dharma,
therefore said that the Tathāgata had entered Nirvāṇa.
Only the Bodhisattvas are able to see my body
and constantly hear my Dharma;
therefore, they do not say that I have entered Nirvāṇa.
Although the Śrāvaka disciples uttered that the Tathāgata had attained Nirvāṇa,
I have truly not entered Nirvāṇa.
Good man!
If any of my Śrāvaka disciples say that the Tathāgata has entered Nirvāṇa,
you should know that this person is not my disciple,
but a companion of Māra's faction,
an evil person with wrong views,
and not one of right view.
If they say that the Tathāgata does not enter Nirvāṇa,
you should know that this person is truly my disciple,
not a companion of Māra's faction,
a person of right view,
and not one who is evil or heterodox.
"Good man,
I have never seen among my disciples
anyone who says that the Tathāgata, not transforming sentient beings
and remaining silently still,
is called Parinirvāṇa.
Good man!
For example, a householder,
who has many sons,
leaves for distant lands;
before he is able to return,
all the sons believe their father is dead.
But this householder is truly not dead;
the sons are confused
and perceive death and rebirth (saṃsāra).
The Śrāvaka disciples are also like this:
because they do not see me,
they assume the Tathāgata has entered Parinirvāṇa between the twin Sāla trees in Kūshīnàchéng (Kuśinagara);
yet I have truly not entered Parinirvāṇa.
The Śrāvaka disciples generate the perception of Nirvāṇa.
Good man!
Suppose a bright lamp
is covered by someone;
others who do not know
believe the lamp is extinguished,
but that bright flame
is truly not extinguished;
because of their ignorance, they generate the perception of extinction.
The Śrāvaka disciples are also like this:
although they possess the eye of wisdom,
it is covered by defilements (kleśa),
causing their minds to be confused,
so they do not see the True Body,
and therefore generate the perception of extinction and liberation,
yet I have truly not attained extinction and liberation.
"Good man!
Just as a person blind from birth does not see the sun and moon,
because they do not see them,
they do not know the characteristics of day and night, light and darkness.
Because they do not know them,
they claim that the reality of the sun and moon does not exist.
The sun and moon truly exist,
but the blind person does not see them.
Because they do not see them,
they generate a mistaken perception,
saying there is no sun and moon.
The Śrāvaka disciples are also like this:
like that person blind from birth,
they do not see the Tathāgata,
and thus assume the Tathāgata has entered Nirvāṇa.
The Tathāgata has truly not entered Nirvāṇa;
because of their mistaken perception,
they generate such a thought.
Good man!
Just as clouds and fog cover and conceal the sun and moon,
ignorant people then say there is no sun and moon.
The sun and moon truly exist;
simply because they are covered,
sentient beings do not see them.
The Śrāvaka disciples are also like this:
having their eye of wisdom covered by various defilements,
they do not see the Tathāgata,
and therefore say the Tathāgata has entered extinction and liberation.
Good man!
This is merely the Tathāgata manifesting the conduct of an infant;
it is not extinction and liberation.
Good man!
Just as in Yánfútí (Jambudvīpa),
when the sun sets,
sentient beings do not see it
because it is obstructed by the Black Mountains.
Yet the nature of the sun
truly does not sink;
sentient beings do not see it
and generate the perception of its sinking.
The Śrāvaka disciples are also like this:
because they are obstructed by the mountain of defilements,
they do not see my body.
Because they do not see it,
they generate the perception that the Tathāgata has attained extinction and liberation,
yet I have truly not proceeded toward extinction and liberation.
"Therefore, in the country of Píshèlǐ (Vaiśālī), I announced to Pāxún, saying,
'In three months, I shall enter Nirvāṇa.'
Good man!
The Tathāgata mystically foresaw that the roots of goodness of Jiāyè Púsà (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva) would ripen in three months,
and also foresaw that Xūbá tuóluó of Xiāngshān (Subhadra of Gandhamādana), having completed the rainy retreat, would come to me.
Therefore, I announced to the Demon King Pāxún,
'In three months, I shall enter Parinirvāṇa.'
Good man!
There are five hundred
strong men (Lìshì),
and when the three months are over,
they shall also attain the arising of the mind for Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi).
Because of this,
I announced to Pāxún, saying,
'In three months, I shall enter Parinirvāṇa.'
Good man!
For the sake of Chúntuó and others, as well as the five hundred Licchavis
and the mango-fruit girls (Ānluóguǒ Nǚ),
whose roots of goodness for the mind of the unsurpassable Way would ripen
after three months—
because of these individuals,
I announced to Pāxún,
'In three months, I shall enter Parinirvāṇa.'
Good man!
Xūnàchàduō (Sunakṣatra) associated closely with the externalists like Nígānzǐ (Nigaṇṭha) and others.
I preached the Dharma to him for a full twelve years,
but that person held wrong views
and neither believed nor accepted them.
I knew that the roots and seeds of this person's wrong views
could definitely be chopped down after three months.
Because of this, I announced to Pāxún, saying,
'In three months, I shall enter Parinirvāṇa.'
"O good man!
For what reason did I, in the past, tell Māra Pāxún (波旬) by the side of the Nílián Hé (尼連河),
'I do not yet have many wise disciples,
therefore I cannot yet enter Nirvāṇa (Nièpán)'?
At that time, I wished to act for the five Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū) and others,
turning the Wheel of Dharma (Fǎlún) in Bōluónài (波羅㮈).
Furthermore, I wished to act for five Bhikṣus and others,
namely, Yēshē (耶奢),
Fùnà (富那),
Pímóluóshé (毘摩羅闍),
Jiàofànbōtí (憍梵波提),
and Xūpóhóu (須婆睺).
Next, I wished to act for Yùgā (郁伽) the Elder and fifty other people.
Next, I wished to act for King Pínpósuōluó (頻婆娑羅) of the Magadhà (摩伽陀) kingdom and countless humans and devas.
Next, I wished to act for the five hundred Bhikṣus who were disciples of Yōulóupínluó Jiāyè (優樓頻螺迦葉).
Next, I wished to act for Nàtí Jiāyè (那提迦葉),
and Gāyē Jiāyè (伽耶迦葉), the two brothers, and their five hundred disciples.
Next, I wished to act for Shèlìfú (舍利弗),
Mùjiànlián (目犍連) and others, two hundred and fifty Bhikṣus, turning the wonderful Wheel of Dharma.
For this reason, I told Māra Pāxún that I would not yet enter parinirvāṇa (bānnirván).
"O good man!
There is Nirvāṇa that is not Great Nirvāṇa.
How is Nirvāṇa not Great Nirvāṇa?
To cut off afflictions (fánnǎo) without seeing the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng),
this is called Nirvāṇa that is not Great Nirvāṇa.
Because the Buddha-nature is not seen,
(it is deemed) impermanent (wúcháng),
without Self (wúwǒ),
having only bliss (lè)
and purity (jìng).
For this reason,
although afflictions are cut off,
it cannot be called Great Parinirvāṇa.
If one sees the Buddha-nature and can cut off afflictions,
this is then called Great Nirvāṇa.
Because the Buddha-nature is seen,
it is called Eternal (cháng), Blissful (lè), Self (wǒ), and Pure (jìng).
For this reason,
cutting off and removing afflictions,
also achieves the name of Great Parinirvāṇa.
"O good man!
*Niè* (涅) means 'not.'
*Pán* (槃) means 'to weave.'
The meaning of 'not weaving' is called Nirvāṇa.
*Pán* also means 'to cover.'
The meaning of 'not covering' is called Nirvāṇa.
*Pán* means 'going and coming.'
'Not going and not coming' is called Nirvāṇa.
*Pán* means 'to grasp.'
The meaning of 'not grasping' is called Nirvāṇa.
*Pán* means 'uncertainty.'
'Certainly without uncertainty' is called Nirvāṇa.
*Pán* means 'new and old.'
The meaning of 'without new and old' is called Nirvāṇa.
*Pán* means 'obstruction.'
The meaning of 'without obstruction' is called Nirvāṇa.
O good man!
Yōuluōjiā Jiāpíluó (憂羅迦迦毘羅)'s disciples and others say,
*Pán* means 'characteristics.'
The meaning of 'without characteristics' is called Nirvāṇa.
O good man,
*Pán* means 'existence.'
The meaning of 'non-existence' is called Nirvāṇa.
*Pán* is called 'harmony and combination.'
The meaning of 'without harmony and combination' is called Nirvāṇa.
*Pán* means 'suffering' (kǔ).
The meaning of 'without suffering' is called Nirvāṇa.
O good man!
That which cuts off afflictions is not called Nirvāṇa;
that which does not give rise to afflictions is called Nirvāṇa.
O good man!
For all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas (Rúlái), the non-arising of afflictions is called Nirvāṇa.
The wisdom they possess, which is unobstructed regarding the Dharma, is what constitutes the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is not an ordinary being (fánfū),
a Śrāvaka (Shēngwén),
a Pratyekabuddha (Yuánjué),
or a Bodhisattva (Púsà)—
this is called the Buddha-nature.
The Tathāgata's body, mind, and wisdom,
fill countless, boundless, Asaṃkhyeya (Āsēngqí) lands.
Without obstruction,
this is called the void (xūkōng).
The permanence of the Tathāgata, without change,
is called Reality (Shíxiàng).
For this reason,
the Tathāgata truly does not ultimately enter Nirvāṇa.
This is the subtle sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa cultivated by the Bodhisattvas,
completely fulfilling the seventh merit (gōngdé).
"Furthermore, O good man!
How do the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) cultivate the subtle sūtra of the Great Nirvāṇa,
completely fulfilling the eighth merit?
O good man!
The Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas cultivate the Great Nirvāṇa
by eliminating and cutting off five matters,
moving far away from five matters,
accomplishing six matters,
practicing five matters,
guarding one matter,
drawing near to four matters,
trusting and according with the One Reality (Yīshí),
having well-liberated minds,
and having well-liberated wisdom.
"O good man!
How does the Bodhisattva eliminate and cut off five matters?
These are the Five Aggregates (Wǔ Yīn):
form (sè), sensation (shòu), perception (xiǎng), volition (xíng), and consciousness (shí).
What is the meaning of the word 'Aggregate' (Yīn)?
It is that which causes sentient beings' cycle of birth and death to continue unbroken,
not separating from repeated coverings (or burdens),
dispersing and gathering, contained within the three times (past, present, future).
If one seeks their true nature, it is utterly unobtainable.
Due to these meanings,
they are called Aggregates.
Although the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas see the Aggregate of Form,
they do not see its characteristics.
Why is this?
If one seeks its nature among the ten kinds of form, it is entirely unobtainable.
They are said to be Aggregates for the sake of the world.
Sensations number one hundred and eight.
Although they see the Aggregate of Sensation,
initially, there are no characteristics of sensation.
Why is this?
Although sensations number one hundred and eight,
rationally they are not truly fixed.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva does not see the Aggregate of Sensation.
Perception, Volition, and Consciousness Aggregates are also like this.
The Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas deeply see the Five Aggregates
as the root cause of the arising of afflictions.
For this reason,
they employ skillful means (fāngbiàn) to cut them off.
"How does the Bodhisattva move far away from five matters?
These are the Five Views (Wǔ Jiàn).
Which are the five?
First is the View of Self (Shēnjiàn),
second is the View of Extremes (Biānjian),
third is Wrong View (Xiéjiàn),
fourth is Grasping at Precepts (Jièqǔ),
fifth is Grasping at Views (Jiànqǔ).
Based on these Five Views,
sixty-two views arise.
Based on these numerous views,
the cycle of birth and death does not cease.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva guards against them and does not approach them.
"How does the Bodhisattva accomplish six matters?
These are the Six Recollections (Liù Niànchù).
Which are the six?
First is recollection of the Buddha (Niàn Fó),
second is recollection of the Dharma (Niàn Fǎ),
third is recollection of the Saṅgha (Niàn Sēng),
fourth is recollection of the Devas (Niàn Tiān),
fifth is recollection of Giving (Niàn Shī),
sixth is recollection of Precepts (Niàn Jiè).
This is how the Bodhisattva accomplishes the six matters.
"How does the Bodhisattva practice five matters?
These are the Five Samādhis (Wǔ Dìng):
first is Samādhi of Knowing (Zhīdìng),
second is Samādhi of Stillness (Jídìng),
third is Samādhi of receiving bodily and mental bliss (Shēnxīn Shòu Kuàilèdìng),
fourth is Samādhi without bliss (Wú Lèdìng),
fifth is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi (Shǒuléngyán Dìng).
By practicing these five types of focused minds,
one can approach Great Parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva diligently practices them.
"How does the Bodhisattva guard one matter?
It is the Bodhi-mind (Pútí Xīn).
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva constantly and diligently guards this Bodhi-mind,
just as a person in the world guards their only child,
or like a blind person protecting their remaining single eye,
or like those traveling in a vast wilderness protecting their guide.
The Bodhisattva guards the Bodhi-mind
in the same way.
Because they guard this Bodhi-mind,
they attain Anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi (Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).
Because they attain Anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi,
Permanence,
Bliss,
Self,
and Purity are fully possessed and present.
This is the Unsurpassed Great Parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva guards this one Dharma.
"How does the Bodhisattva draw near to four matters?
These are the Four Immeasurables (Sì Wúliàng Xīn).
Which are the four?
First is Great Loving-Kindness (Dà Cí),
second is Great Compassion (Dà Bēi),
third is Great Joy (Dà Xǐ),
fourth is Great Equanimity (Dà Shě).
Through these four minds,
one can cause countless, boundless sentient beings to bring forth the Bodhi-mind.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva attaches their mind to them and draws near.
"How does the Bodhisattva trust and accord with the One Reality?
The Bodhisattva understands that all sentient beings return to the One Path.
The One Path is the Mahāyāna (Dàshèng).
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, for the sake of sentient beings,
divide it into three (paths).
Therefore, the Bodhisattva trusts and accords with it without reversal."
"How does a Bodhisattva's mind achieve excellent liberation?
Because
greed,
hatred, and delusion
are forever cut off and extinguished—this is called a Bodhisattva's mind achieving excellent liberation.
"How does a Bodhisattva's wisdom achieve excellent liberation?
When a Púsà Mōhēsà (Bodhisattva Mahāsattva) knows all phenomena without obstruction,
this is called a Bodhisattva's wisdom achieving excellent liberation.
Due to this wisdom liberation, what was previously unheard is now heard;
what was previously unseen is now seen;
what was previously unattainable is now attained.
At that time, Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng Púsà Mōhēsà (Bodhisattva Mahāsattva) said:
"Honored by the World!
The teaching you gave regarding the mind's liberation
is not correct.
Why is this?
The mind is fundamentally unbound.
What is the reason for this?
The inherent nature of the mind
is not bound by the fetters of
desire/greed,
anger/hatred, and ignorance/delusion.
If it is fundamentally unbound,
how can you speak of the mind achieving excellent liberation?
Honored by the World!
If the inherent nature of the mind is not bound by the fetter of greed,
then by what causes and conditions can it become bound?
It is like a person who tries to milk a horn:
fundamentally it has no quality of milk,
and although effort is applied,
milk has no means by which to emerge.
For one who milks,
it is not like this;
even if little effort is applied,
milk comes forth plentifully.
The mind is also like this:
if fundamentally there is no greed,
how can it exist now?
If fundamentally there is no greed,
but it can arise later,
then since all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas fundamentally possess no aspect of greed,
they should all possess it now.
Honored by the World!
For example, a barren woman,
fundamentally possesses no characteristic of having a child;
although effort and immeasurable causes and conditions are applied,
a child cannot be obtained.
The mind is also like this:
fundamentally possessing no characteristic of greed,
although all conditions are created,
greed has no means by which to arise.
Honored by the World!
Just as with drilling wet wood,
fire cannot be obtained.
The mind is also like this:
although one drills and seeks,
greed cannot be obtained.
How then can the fetter of greed bind the mind?
Honored by the World!
For example, when pressing sand,
oil cannot be obtained.
The mind is also like this:
although one presses it,
greed cannot be obtained.
One should know that greed
and mind
are two distinct principles.
Even if greed were to exist,
how could it stain the mind?
Honored by the World!
For example, if a person
places a stake in the empty space,
it ultimately cannot remain firm.
Placing greed upon the mind
is also like this;
various causes and conditions
cannot cause greed to bind the mind.
Honored by the World!
If the mind being without greed is called liberation,
why do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not pull out thorns in the empty space?
Honored by the World!
The mind of the past world
is not called liberation.
The mind of the future world
also has no liberation.
The mind of the present world
does not abide with the Path.
Which world-mind, then, is called attained liberation?
Honored by the World!
Just as a past lamp cannot extinguish darkness,
a future lamp also does not extinguish darkness,
and a present lamp also does not extinguish darkness.
Why?
Because light and darkness
do not coexist.
The mind is also like this.
How, then, can you speak of the mind attaining liberation?
Honored by the World!
Greed also truly exists.
If greed did not exist,
when one sees the form of a woman,
one should not give rise to greed.
If, due to the form of a woman,
it is able to arise,
one must know that this greed
truly exists.
Because greed exists,
one falls into the three evil paths.
Honored by the World!
For example, if a person
sees the image of a painted woman,
he also gives rise to greed.
Because greed arises,
he incurs various kinds of evil karma (sins).
If fundamentally there were no greed,
how could one see a painting and give rise to greed?
If the mind were without greed,
why would the Tathāgata speak of the Bodhisattva's mind attaining liberation?
If the mind possesses greed,
why does it only arise after seeing a form,
and not arise if a form is not seen?
I now clearly see bad retributions,
therefore one should know that greed exists;
hatred
and delusion are also like this.
Honored by the World!
For example, sentient beings
have bodies but no Self (ātman),
yet all ordinary beings
falsely conceptualize the thought of a Self.
Although the thought of a Self exists,
they do not fall into the three evil paths.
How is it that the greedy one,
regarding something without the form of a woman, gives rise to the thought of a woman,
and falls into the three evil paths?
Honored by the World!
For example, drilling wood gives rise to fire,
yet the nature of this fire does not exist within the aggregated conditions.
By what cause and condition can it arise?
Honored by the World!
Greed is also like this:
there is no greed within form,
and flavor, smell, touch, and phenomena are also without greed.
How is it that regarding form,
smell,
flavor,
touch,
and phenomena,
greed arises?
If greed does not exist at all among the aggregated conditions,
how is it that sentient beings alone give rise to greed?
And why do the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not give rise to it?
Honored by the World!
The mind is also impermanent (or unstable/undetermined).
If the mind were permanent,
there would be no desire/greed,
hatred,
or delusion.
If it is impermanent,
how can you speak of the mind attaining liberation?
Greed is also impermanent.
If it is impermanent,
how can it be the cause for birth in the three evil destinies?
Greed
and the object/realm (kjíngjiè)
are both impermanent.
Why?
Because both rely on the same form:
sometimes greed arises,
sometimes hatred arises,
and sometimes delusion arises.
Therefore, greed and the object are both impermanent.
If both are impermanent,
why does the Tathāgata speak of the Bodhisattva cultivating the Great Nirvāṇa (Nirpián) and the mind attaining liberation?"
At that time, the Shìzūn addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng:
“Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
The mind is neither bound by the fetters of craving,
nor is it unbound;
it is not liberated,
nor is it unliberated;
it is neither existent,
nor is it non-existent;
it is neither present,
nor is it past,
nor is it future.
Why is this?
Good man!
Because all phenomena are without inherent nature.
Good man!
There are certain externalists who speak thus:
‘When causes and conditions harmonize and assemble, then fruit (effect) is produced.
If the nature of production were originally absent among the various conditions, yet they could still produce,
then the void (space), which does not produce, should also produce fruit.
Since the void does not produce, it is not a cause.
Because the nature of the fruit is originally present within the various conditions,
therefore, when they assemble and gather, the fruit is produced.
Why is this?
Just as Típó Dá, desiring to construct a wall,
takes earth and clay,
and does not take colors.
Desiring to create a painting or image,
he gathers colors,
and does not take grasses and woods.
To make clothes, he takes thread,
and does not take clay or wood.
To build a dwelling, he takes clay,
and does not take thread or yarn.
Since people take (these specific things),
it should be known that each of these things can produce its corresponding fruit.
Because they are capable of producing fruit,
it must be known that the nature (of the fruit) is necessarily present beforehand in the cause.
If this nature were absent, then from a single material, all phenomena should be produced.
If something can be taken,
can be made,
or can be brought forth,
it must be known that the fruit is necessarily present therein beforehand.
If the fruit were not present,
people would not take it,
would not make it,
and would not bring it forth.
Only the void is without taking [the action of taking],
and without making [the action of making],
therefore it is able to produce all things.
Because there is a cause,
such as the Ní​gōutuó zǐ producing the Ní​gōutuó shù;
ghee is in the milk;
cloth is in the thread;
the jar is in the clay.
Good man,
all ordinary people, blinded by ignorance, make this determined assertion:
form has the meaning of attachment,
and mind has the nature of craving.
Furthermore, they say:
‘The mind of an ordinary person possesses the nature of craving,
and also the nature of liberation.
If it encounters the conditions for craving, the mind produces craving;
if it encounters liberation, the mind is liberated.’
Although they make this assertion,
this meaning is incorrect.
There are other ordinary people who further say:
‘In all causes,
there is entirely no fruit.
Causes are of two kinds:
one is subtle,
the second is gross.
The subtle is permanent,
the gross is impermanent.
From the subtle cause, it transforms and becomes the gross cause;
from this gross cause, it transforms again and achieves the fruit.
Because the gross is impermanent,
the fruit is also impermanent.
Good man!
There are other ordinary people who further say:
‘The mind is also without cause,
and craving is also without cause.
Because of timely seasons, the craving mind is produced.’
Those of this sort,
because they cannot understand the causes and conditions of the mind,
revolve through the Six Destinies,
enduring the full extent of birth and death.
“Good man!
For example, a dog chained,
tied to a pillar,
circles the pillar all day long,
and cannot get away.
All ordinary people are likewise thus:
bound by the chain (cangue) of ignorance to the pillar of birth and death,
circling the Twenty-Five Existences,
unable to get away.
Good man!
Just as a person who has fallen into a filthy latrine,
after having gotten out,
returns and enters again.
Just as a person whose illness is cured,
returns to the cause of the illness.
Just as a person traveling on a road,
encountering a vast, empty place,
having passed through it,
returns again.
Furthermore, just as one who is cleanly washed
smears oneself again with mud and clay.
All ordinary people are likewise thus:
they have already attained liberation (escape)
up to the Sphere of Nothingness,
yet they have not yet achieved complete escape from the Sphere of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception,
and they return again, arriving at the sān è qù.
Why is this?
All ordinary people observe only the fruit,
and do not observe the causes and conditions,
like a dog chasing a clod of earth,
not chasing the person.
Ordinary people are likewise thus:
they observe only the fruit,
and do not observe the causes and conditions.
Because they do not observe them,
they retreat from (the Sphere of) Neither-Perception and return to the sān è qù.
“Good man!
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas never definitively assert:
that fruit is present within the cause,
that fruit is absent within the cause,
or that fruit is both existent and non-existent,
or that fruit is neither existent nor non-existent.
If one asserts that the fruit is definitively present beforehand in the cause,
or definitively absent,
or definitively both existent and non-existent,
or definitively neither existent nor non-existent,
it must be known that these persons are all companions and partisans of Māra,
bound and belonging to Māra.
They are persons fond of attachment;
such persons fond of attachment
cannot permanently sever the bonds of birth and death,
and do not know the characteristics of the mind and the characteristics of craving.
Good man!
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas demonstrate the Middle Way.
Why is this?
Although they state that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent,
they do not assert it definitively.
Why is that?
Due to the eye,
due to form,
due to light,
due to the mind,
and due to attention,
consciousness is produced.
This consciousness is definitively not located in the eye,
in form,
in light,
in the mind,
or in attention;
nor is it in the space between;
it is neither existent,
nor non-existent.
Because it arises from conditions,
it is named ‘existent’;
because it is without inherent nature, it is named ‘non-existent’.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all phenomena are neither existent
nor non-existent.
Good man!
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas never definitively assert that the mind has a pure nature, or an impure nature,
or a pure-and-impure nature,
because the mind has no fixed dwelling place.
Craving arises from conditions;
therefore, it is said to be not non-existent.
Originally, it lacks the nature of craving;
therefore, it is said to be not existent.
Good man!
Because of causes and conditions, the mind produces craving;
because of causes and conditions, the mind is liberated.
Good man!
Causes and conditions are of two types:
the first follows birth and death,
the second follows Dà Nièpán.
“Good man!
Due to causes and conditions,
the mind arises together with craving and ceases together with craving.
There are (cases where it) arises together with craving but does not cease together with craving.
There are (cases where it) arises not together with craving but ceases together with craving.
There are (cases where it) arises not together with craving and ceases not together with craving.”
"How is it that the mind arises together with greed (tān) and ceases together with greed?
Śhànnánzǐ!
If there is an ordinary person (fánfū) who has not severed the mind of greed,
but practices the mind of greed,
such a person,
the mind arises together with greed, and the mind ceases together with greed.
All sentient beings (zhòngshēng) who do not sever the mind of greed,
the mind arises together with greed, and the mind ceases together with greed.
For example, the sentient beings in the Desire Realm (Yùjiè),
all possess the flavor of the first stage of meditative concentration (chūdì wèichán);
whether they practice it
or do not practice it,
they constantly attain accomplishment.
When they encounter the necessary condition (yīnyuán),
they immediately obtain it.
That which is called the necessary condition refers to the conflagration (huǒzāi).
All ordinary people (fánfū) are also like this;
whether they practice
or do not practice,
the mind arises together with greed,
the mind ceases together with greed.
Why is this?
Because they do not sever greed.
"How is it that the mind arises together with greed but does not cease together with greed?
A disciple of the Śhengwén (Hearer) lineage, having encountered a necessary condition (yīnyuán),
gives rise to the mind of greed.
Because he fears the mind of greed,
he practices the Contemplation of the White Bone (báigǔ guān).
This is called the mind arising together with greed but not ceasing together with greed.
Furthermore, there is the mind arising together with greed but not ceasing together with greed,
such as a Śhengwén person who has not yet realized the four fruits (sìguǒ).
Having encountered a necessary condition, he gives rise to the mind of greed,
but when he realizes the four fruits, the mind of greed ceases.
This is called the mind arising together with greed but not ceasing together with greed.
When a Púsà Móhēsà (Bodhisattva Mahāsattva) attains the Immovable Stage (Bùdòngdì),
the mind arises together with greed but does not cease together with greed.
"How is it that the mind does not arise together with greed but ceases together with greed?
If a Púsà Móhēsà has already severed the mind of greed,
but for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests the appearance of having greed.
By means of this manifestation,
he is able to cause countless and boundless sentient beings to seek and receive the virtuous Dharma (shànfǎ),
fully accomplishing it.
This is called the mind not arising together with greed but ceasing together with greed.
"How is it that the mind does not arise together with greed and does not cease together with greed?
This refers to the Āluóhàn (Arhats),
Yuánjué (Pratyekabuddhas),
and all Buddhas,
and Púsà other than those in the Immovable Stage (Bùdòngdì).
This is called the mind not arising together with greed and not ceasing together with greed.
Based on this meaning,
all Buddhas and Púsà do not definitively state that the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure
or fundamentally impure.
"Śhànnánzǐ,
this mind does not combine with the fetter of greed (tānjié),
nor does it combine with anger (chēn) or delusion (chī).
Śhànnánzǐ!
For example, the sun and the moon,
although they are covered and concealed by smoke, dust,
clouds, mist, and Rāhóuluó (Rāhula),
due to these conditions, sentient beings are unable to see them.
Although the essential nature of the sun and moon cannot be seen,
they ultimately do not combine with those five obscurations (yì).
The mind is also like this;
due to necessary conditions (yīnyuán),
the fetter of greed arises.
Although sentient beings say the mind unites with greed,
the essential nature of the mind truly does not unite with it.
If that mind were greed, then it would be the nature of greed;
if it is not greed, then it is the nature of non-greed.
The mind of non-greed cannot become greed,
and the mind of the fetter of greed cannot become non-greed.
Śhànnánzǐ!
For this reason,
the fetter of craving and desire (tānyù zhī jié) cannot defile the mind.
All Buddhas and Púsà eternally break the fetter of greed;
therefore, it is said that the mind attains liberation (jiětuō).
All sentient beings, because of necessary conditions,
give rise to the fetter of greed;
because of necessary conditions,
the mind attains liberation.
"Śhànnánzǐ!
For example, in a precipitous and rugged place on a snow mountain (Xuěshān),
humans and macaques (míhóu) both cannot walk.
Or there might be a place
where the macaque can walk,
but the human cannot walk.
Or there might be a place
where both the human and the macaque can walk.
Śhànnánzǐ!
Regarding the place where both the human and the macaque can walk,
it is like the various hunters (lièshī),
who apply pure sticky glue (chījiāo),
place it upon a board, and use it to catch the macaque.
Because the macaque is deluded (chī),
it goes and touches it with its hand.
Having touched it, the hand sticks.
Desiring to free its hand,
it stamps on it with its foot,
and the foot also sticks.
Desiring to free its foot,
it bites it with its mouth,
and the mouth also sticks fast.
In this way, none of the five parts can escape.
Thereupon, the hunter pierces it with a staff,
carries it on his back, and returns home.
The rugged place on the snow mountain symbolizes the Right Path (zhèngdào) attained by the Buddhas and Púsà.
The macaque symbolizes all ordinary people (fánfū).
The hunter symbolizes Mó Bōxún (Māra Papiyas).
The sticky glue symbolizes the fetter of craving and desire (tānyù jié).
The place where both humans and macaques cannot walk
symbolizes that both ordinary people (fánfū)
and Māwáng Bōxún (Māra the King) are unable to practice (that path).
The place where the macaque can walk
but the human cannot
symbolizes those wise persons among the Non-Buddhist Paths (wàidào),
whom the evil Māras (èmó) cannot bind, even with the five desires (wǔyù).
The place where both the human and the macaque can walk
signifies that all ordinary people (fánfū) and Mó Bōxún constantly abide in the cycle of birth and death (shēngsǐ) and cannot practice cultivation.
Ordinary people are bound by the five desires,
allowing Mó Bōxún to freely lead them away,
just like that hunter catches the macaque with sticky glue,
carries it on his shoulder, and returns home."
“O good man!
For example, a king dwells safely within his own territory,
his body and mind are peaceful and happy.
If he travels to another’s territory,
then he encounters various sufferings.
It is the same for all sentient beings.
If they are able to dwell within their own realm (Gōngjìng),
they obtain peace and happiness.
If they go to another’s realm, they encounter the evil Māra
and suffer various distresses.
‘One’s own realm’ refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (Sì Niànchù).
‘Another’s realm’ refers to the five desires (Wǔ Yù).
What is called being bound and belonging to Māra?
There are sentient beings who regard the impermanent as permanent,
and the permanent as impermanent;
who regard suffering as happiness,
and happiness as suffering;
who regard the impure as pure,
and the pure as impure;
who regard the non-self as self,
and the self as non-self;
who falsely regard that which is not true liberation as liberation,
and regard true liberation as non-liberation;
who regard that which is not the vehicle (Chéng) as the vehicle,
and regard the vehicle as not the vehicle.
Such people are called bound and belonging to Māra.
Those bound and belonging to Māra have an impure mind.
Furthermore, O good man!
If one sees that all phenomena truly exist,
with general and specific defined characteristics (Dìng Xiàng),
know that such a person,
when seeing form (Sè),
then creates the characteristic of form;
and likewise, when seeing consciousness (Shí), he creates the characteristic of consciousness;
seeing males, they create the male characteristic;
seeing females, they create the female characteristic;
seeing days, they create the day characteristic;
seeing months, they create the month characteristic;
seeing years, they create the year characteristic;
seeing aggregates (Yīn), they create the aggregate characteristic;
seeing entrances (Rù), they create the entrance characteristic;
seeing constituents (Jiè), they create the constituent characteristic.
One who sees thus
is called bound and belonging to Māra.
Those bound and belonging to Māra have an impure mind.
Furthermore, O good man!
If one sees that the self (Wǒ) is form,
or that the self is within form,
or that form is within the self,
or that form belongs to the self;
and likewise, if one sees that the self is consciousness,
or that the self is within consciousness,
or that consciousness is within the self,
or that consciousness belongs to the self;
one who sees thus
is bound and belongs to Māra,
and is not my disciple.
O good man!
My Śrāvakā disciples (Shēngwén Dìzǐ) distance themselves from the twelve divisions of sūtras (Shí'èr Bù Jīng) taught by the Tathāgata,
and cultivate various texts of non-Buddhist schools (Wàidào Diǎnjí).
They do not cultivate the Dharma
of going forth (Chūjiā) and stillness (Jìmìe),
but purely engage in worldly, household affairs.
What are called household affairs?
Accepting and hoarding all impure things:
slaves and maidservants,
fields and houses,
elephants and horses,
carriages,
camels, donkeys, chickens, and dogs,
monkeys, pigs, and sheep,
various grains and wheat.
They distance themselves from the teacher
and the monastic community (Sēng),
and become close to laypeople (Báiyī).
They violate the sacred teachings (Shèngjiào),
and speak to the laypeople, saying:
‘The Buddha permits bhikṣus to accept and hoard various impure things.’
This is called cultivating household affairs.
There are disciples who do not strive for Nirvāṇa,
but only for gain and profit.
They draw near to and listen to the twelve divisions of sūtras.
They wear and eat the properties belonging to the collective monastic community (Zhāotísēng Wù) and the properties for the needs of the monks (Sēngmán Wù),
as if they were their own.
They are stingy with the properties of other households,
and also flatter and praise;
they associate closely with kings and various princes;
they practice divination (Bǔshì) for fortune and misfortune, and calculate the waxing and waning (of heavenly bodies);
they play Weiqí, Liùbó, Chūpú, and Tóuhú;
they associate closely with bhikṣuṇīs and various unmarried women;
they keep two śrāmaṇeras;
they constantly roam around the houses of butchers and hunters,
and those who sell liquor,
as well as places where Caṇḍālas dwell;
they engage in various forms of trading;
they cook their own food by hand;
they serve as messengers to neighboring countries to convey letters and commands.
Know that such people are the retinue of Māra,
and are not my disciples.
Due to these causes and conditions,
the mind is born together with greed (Tān),
and the mind ceases together with greed.
Likewise, the mind rooted in delusion (Chīxīn),
is born together and ceases together.
“O good man!
Because of these causes and conditions,
the nature of the mind is impure,
and also not impure.
Therefore, I teach that the mind attains liberation.
If one does not accept or hoard all impure things,
but for the sake of the Great Nirvāṇa, receives and upholds,
reads and recites the twelve divisions of sūtras,
writes them down and explains them,
know that these persons
are truly my disciples.
They do not walk in the realm (Jìngjiè) of the evil Māra Pāpīyas (Bōxún).
This is cultivating the thirty-seven components of awakening (Sānshíqī Pǐn).
Because they cultivate this,
they are not born together with greed,
and do not cease together with greed.
This is called the Bodhisattva cultivating the subtle classic of the Great Nirvāṇa,
fully accomplishing the eighth merit (Gōngdé).
“Furthermore, O good man!
How does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivate the subtle classic of the Great Nirvāṇa
and fully accomplish the ninth merit?
O good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, cultivating the subtle classic of the Great Nirvāṇa,
initially achieves success in five matters.
What are these five?
First is faith (Xìn),
second is a straightforward mind (Zhí Xīn),
third is morality (Jiè),
fourth is close association with good friends (Shàn Yǒu),
fifth is extensive learning (Duō Wén).
“What is faith?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has faith in the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo),
that giving (Shī) yields fruition (Guǒbào),
and faith in the Two Truths (Èr Dì).
They believe in the path of the One Vehicle (Yī Chéng), with no other distinct paths.
In order that sentient beings may quickly attain liberation,
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas differentiate it into three.
They have faith in the Ultimate Truth (Dìyī Yì Dì),
and faith in skillful means (Shàn Fāngbiàn).
This is called faith.
Such faith,
whether by Śramaṇas,
or by Brāhmaṇas,
or by devas,
Māra,
or Brahmā,
or by any sentient being, cannot be destroyed.
Because of this faith,
one attains the nature of a saintly person (Shèng Rén Xìng).
When practicing giving,
whether much
or little,
one gets close to Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Bōnièpán),
and does not fall into saṃsāra (Shēngsǐ).
Morality,
learning,
and wisdom are also like this.
This is called faith.
Though one possesses this faith,
one does not cling to it.
This is the first matter achieved by the Bodhisattva cultivating the Great Nirvāṇa.
“What is a straightforward mind?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva adopts an honest and straightforward mind towards all sentient beings.
All sentient beings become flattering and crooked when they encounter causes and conditions,
but the Bodhisattva is not like that.
Why?
Because they clearly understand that all phenomena are based on causes and conditions.
Although the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sees various wicked faults in sentient beings,
they ultimately do not speak of them.
Why?
Lest afflictions (Fánnǎo) arise.
If afflictions arise, they will fall into evil destinies (È Qù).
If such a Bodhisattva sees even a small virtuous deed in sentient beings,
they praise it.
What is virtuous?
Namely, the Buddha-nature (Fó Xìng).
By praising the Buddha-nature,
they cause sentient beings to conceive the mind set on Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí Xīn).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Déwáng said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
The meaning that, as the Buddha has stated, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas praise the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
causing countless sentient beings to arouse the mind of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
is not correct.
Why is this?
When the Tathāgata (Rúlái) first opened the Nirvāṇa Sūtra (Nièpán Jīng),
He spoke of three types:
First, if a sick person receives medicine from a good doctor and nursing care,
the illness is easily cured;
if they do not receive these, then it cannot be healed.
Second, whether they receive [care]
or do not receive [care],
in all cases, they cannot be cured.
Third, whether they receive [care] or do not receive [care],
in all cases, they can be cured.
All sentient beings are also like this:
If they meet good friends
— the Buddhas (Fó) and Bodhisattvas (Púsà) —
and hear the subtle Dharma being preached,
then they can arouse the mind of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí;
if they do not meet them,
then they cannot arouse it.
These are called the Śrotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán),
Sakṛdāgāmin (Sītuóhán),
Anāgāmin (Ānàhán),
Arhat (Hēluóhàn),
and Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó).
“Second, although they meet good friends
— the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas —
and hear the subtle Dharma being preached,
they still cannot arouse [the Bodhi mind];
if they do not meet them, they also cannot arouse it.
These are called the Icchantika (Yīchǎntí).
“Third, whether they meet [them]
or do not meet [them],
they are all able to arouse the mind of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
These are called the Bodhisattvas.
If it is said that whether one meets [them]
or does not meet [them],
all arouse the mind of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
then how is it that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) now says
that due to praising the Buddha Nature,
He causes sentient beings to arouse the mind of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí?
World-Honored One!
If [a being], whether meeting good friends
— the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas —
and hearing the subtle Dharma preached,
or not meeting them,
still cannot arouse the mind of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
you should know that this principle is also incorrect.
Why is this?
Because such people will eventually attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Since those of the Icchantika group, due to possessing the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
whether they hear [the Dharma]
or do not hear [the Dharma], will also eventually attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
World-Honored One!
According to what the Buddha says,
what is called an Icchantika?
It is said to be the cutting off of good roots.
This principle,
is also incorrect.
Why is this?
Because the Buddha Nature is not cut off.
Since the principle of Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) cannot be severed,
how can the Buddha (Fó) say that all good roots are severed?
In the past, when the Buddha spoke the Twelve Divisions of the Scriptures,
He said good [roots] are of two types:
First, permanent;
second, impermanent.
That which is permanent is not severed;
that which is impermanent is severed.
The impermanent can be severed,
and thus leads one to fall into hell.
The permanent cannot be severed.
Why then is it not the case that,
if the Buddha Nature is not severed,
they are not Icchantika?
Why does the Tathāgata speak thus,
calling them Icchantika?
World-Honored One!
If the mind of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí is aroused due to the Buddha Nature,
why did the Tathāgata (Rúlái) extensively preach the Twelve Divisions of the Scriptures for sentient beings?
World-Honored One!
For example, the Four Rivers
issue forth from the Anavatapta (Ānàpó Tuòduō) Lake.
If any deity,
human,
or World-Honored Buddha (Fó) were to say
that these rivers will not enter the great ocean,
but will return to their source,
there is no such possibility.
The Mind of Bodhi (Pútí) is also like this.
Those who possess the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
whether hearing [the Dharma]
or not hearing [it],
whether observing precepts
or not observing precepts,
whether practicing giving
or not practicing giving,
whether cultivating
or not cultivating,
whether having wisdom
or not having wisdom,
should all attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
World-Honored One!
It is like Mount Udayana (Yōutuóyán Shān):
The sun rises from it
and travels until due south.
If the sun were to think,
“I will not go west
but return to the east,”
there is no such possibility.
The Buddha Nature is also like this.
If [one were] not to hear,
not observe precepts,
not practice giving,
not cultivate,
not have wisdom,
and yet not attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
there is no such possibility.
World-Honored One!
The meaning that the Buddhas and Tathāgatas state that the nature of cause and effect is neither existent nor nonexistent,
this principle,
is also incorrect.
Why is this?
If the nature of curds were absent in milk,
then there would be no curds.
If the seed of the Nyagrodha (Nígōutuó) tree lacked the potential for a fifty-foot nature,
then it could not produce a substance fifty feet high.
If within the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) there were no seed for the tree of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
how could it produce the tree of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí?
Therefore,
the statement that cause and effect
is neither existent nor nonexistent—
how can this principle
be coherent?”
At that time, the World-Honored One praised him, saying:
“Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
There are two kinds of people in the world
who are extremely rare,
like the Udumbara flower (Yōután Huā):
The first does not practice evil deeds;
the second, having committed a sin, is able to repent.
Such people are extremely rare.
Furthermore, there are two people:
The first grants kindness;
the second remembers kindness.
Furthermore, there are two people:
The first consults and receives new Dharma;
the second reviews the old and does not forget it.
Furthermore, there are two people:
The first creates the new;
the second repairs the old.
Furthermore, there are two people:
The first enjoys hearing the Dharma;
the second enjoys speaking the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are two people:
The first is skilled at posing difficulties [in questions];
the second is skilled at giving answers.
The one skilled at posing difficulties
is you yourself.
The one skilled at giving answers
is the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Good man!
Because of this excellent questioning,
the Supreme Wheel of Dharma is immediately turned,
it can dry up the great tree of the Twelve Nidānas (Causes and Conditions),
it can cross the boundless great river of Samsāra (birth and death),
it can battle with Māra Papiyas (Mówáng Bōxún),
and it can shatter the victorious banner raised by Papiyas.
Good man!
Regarding what I said earlier,
about the three types of sick people who, whether encountering a good doctor,
nursing care, and fine medicine,
or not encountering them,
are all completely cured—
what is the meaning of this?
Whether receiving [care]
or not receiving [care],
it refers to having a fixed lifespan.
Why is this?
Because this person has cultivated three kinds of good [deeds] through countless lifetimes,
namely, superior,
middling,
and inferior.
Because they cultivated these three kinds of good [deeds],
they obtained a fixed lifespan.
For example, the people of Uttarakuru (Yùdānyuè)
have a lifespan of a thousand years.
If they encounter sickness,
whether they receive a good doctor, fine medicine, and nursing care,
or do not receive them,
they are all cured.
Why is this?
Because they possess a fixed lifespan.”
"Shànnánzǐ!
According to what I have taught,
if a sick person meets a good doctor, good medicine, and nursing care,
the illness can be cured and removed.
If they do not meet these, they cannot be cured.
What is the meaning of this doctrine?
Shànnánzǐ!
The lifespan of such a person is indeterminate.
Although their life is not yet complete,
there are nine conditions (causal factors)
that can prematurely cut short their life.
What are these nine?
First, knowing that food is unsuitable,
yet eating it conversely.
Second, overeating.
Third, undigested previous food remaining,
yet eating again.
Fourth, large or small evacuations,
not following the proper timing.
Fifth, during illness, not following the doctor's instructions.
Sixth, not following the instructions of the nurse.
Seventh, forcing oneself to endure and not vomit.
Eighth, traveling at night.
Because of traveling at night,
malignant ghosts strike them.
Ninth, excessive sexual activity (fángshì guòdù).
Due to these conditions,
I say that if a sick person meets medical treatment, the illness can be cured,
and if they do not meet these, they cannot be healed.
Shànnánzǐ!
Regarding what I previously stated,
what is the meaning of the doctrine that whether they meet (treatment) or not, neither results in a cure?
What is the meaning of this doctrine?
There are people whose life is finished.
Whether they meet (treatment) or not, they certainly cannot be cured.
Why is this?
Because their life is finished.
For this reason,
I say that whether a sick person meets medical treatment or does not meet it, they certainly cannot be cured.
Sentient beings are also like this.
Those who generate the Bodhi mind (fā Pútí xīn),
whether they meet noble friends (shàn yǒu),
Buddhas (Fó) and Bodhisattvas (Púsà),
consulting them and receiving the profound Dharma (shēnfǎ),
or whether they do not meet them,
they will all certainly succeed.
Why is this?
Because they are capable of generating the Bodhi mind.
It is like the people of Ùdānyuè having a fixed lifespan.
According to what I have taught,
from Sūtuóhuán (Srotāpanna) up to Pìzhīfó (Pratyekabuddha),
if they hear the profound Dharma (shēnfǎ) preached by noble friends,
Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas,
they then generate the mind of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi).
If they do not happen to meet Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and hear the profound Dharma preached,
then they cannot generate the mind of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
This is like one whose life is indeterminate,
whose life is suddenly cut short
due to the nine conditions.
It is like the patient who happens to meet medical treatment and thus the illness is cured.
If they do not meet it, the illness is not cured.
Therefore, I say that encountering Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and hearing the profound Dharma enables them to generate the mind.
If they do not happen to meet them, they cannot generate it.
"Regarding what I previously stated,
whether they meet noble friends,
Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
hearing the profound Dharma preached,
or whether they do not happen to meet them,
neither results in generating (the Bodhi mind)—
what is the meaning of this doctrine?
Shànnánzǐ!
The Icchantikas (Yīchǎntí bèi),
whether they meet noble friends, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas and hear the profound Dharma preached,
or whether they do not meet them,
neither results in their abandoning the Icchantika mind (Yīchǎntí xīn).
Why is this?
Because they have severed the roots of goodness (duàn shànfǎ).
Icchantikas also attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Why is this so?
If they are capable of generating the mind of Pútí,
then they are no longer named Yīchǎntí.
Shànnánzǐ!
For what reason
is it said that Yīchǎntí attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí?
Icchantikas actually cannot attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
It is like one whose life is finished: although they meet a good doctor, good medicine, and nursing care, they cannot be cured.
Why is this?
Because their life is finished.
"Shànnánzǐ!
Yīchǎn means 'faith' (xìn),
tí means 'incomplete' (bù jù).
Because of incomplete faith, they are named Yīchǎntí.
The Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) is not faith.
Sentient beings are not 'incomplete'.
If they are not 'incomplete',
how can it be severed?
Yīchǎn means 'skillful means of goodness' (shàn fāngbiàn),
tí means 'incomplete'.
Because of the incomplete fulfillment of cultivating skillful means of goodness,
they are named Yīchǎntí.
The Buddha-nature is not the cultivation of skillful means of goodness.
Sentient beings are not 'incomplete'.
If they are not 'incomplete',
how can it be severed?
Yīchǎn means 'diligence' (jìn),
tí means 'incomplete'.
Because of incomplete diligence, they are named Yīchǎntí.
The Buddha-nature is not diligence.
Sentient beings are not 'incomplete'.
If they are not 'incomplete', how can it be severed?
Yīchǎn means 'mindfulness' (niàn),
tí means 'incomplete'.
Because of incomplete mindfulness, they are named Yīchǎntí.
The Buddha-nature is not mindfulness.
Sentient beings are not 'incomplete'.
If they are not 'incomplete', how can it be severed?
Yīchǎn means 'concentration' (dìng),
tí means 'incomplete'.
Because of incomplete concentration,
they are named Yīchǎntí.
The Buddha-nature is not concentration.
Sentient beings are not 'incomplete'.
If they are not 'incomplete', how can it be severed?
Yīchǎn means 'wisdom' (huì),
tí means 'incomplete'.
Because of incomplete wisdom,
they are named Yīchǎntí.
The Buddha-nature is not wisdom.
Sentient beings are not 'incomplete'.
If they are not 'incomplete',
how can it be severed?
Yīchǎn means 'impermanent goodness' (wúcháng shàn),
tí means 'incomplete'.
Because of the incomplete fulfillment of impermanent goodness,
they are named Yīchǎntí.
The Buddha-nature is permanent (cháng),
neither good (shàn) nor non-good (bù shàn).
Why is this?
Good dharmas must be attained through expedient means (fāngbiàn).
But the Buddha-nature,
is not attained through expedient means.
Therefore, it is not good.
Then why is it also named 'non-non-good'?
Because it is able to attain the good fruit.
The good fruit is precisely Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Furthermore, good dharmas are attained upon being generated.
But the Buddha-nature is not attained upon being generated.
Therefore, it is not good.
Since they have severed all good dharmas that are attained through generation,
they are named Yīchǎntí.
"Shànnánzǐ!
Regarding what you said,
if an Yīchǎntí possesses the Buddha-nature,
why does this not block the penalty of the hells (dìyù)?
Shànnánzǐ!
Among Icchantikas there is no Buddha-nature.
Shànnánzǐ!
For instance, there was a king
who heard the sound of the Kōnghóu (harp),
its sound being pure and marvelous.
His mind immediately indulged in attachment.
He felt joyful, delighted, loved, and remembered it, unable to let go of the feeling.
He immediately told his ministers:
'From where does this marvelous sound emerge?'
The minister replied:
'This marvelous sound emerges from the Kōnghóu.'
The king further commanded:
'Bring this sound here.'
At that time, the minister brought the Kōnghóu and placed it before the king,
and said this:
'Great King, you should know,
this is the sound itself.'
The king spoke to the Kōnghóu:
'Emit sound!
Emit sound!'
But the Kōnghóu did not emit any sound.
At that time, the Great King immediately cut its strings, but still no sound emerged.
He took its hide and wood and split them all apart,
but searching for the sound, he ultimately could not find it.
At that time, the Great King became angry at the minister:
'How could you tell such a lie?'
The minister reported to the king:
'The method of obtaining sound
is not like this.
It must be with various factors,
and skillful expedient means (shàn qiǎo fāngbiàn),
only then can sound emerge.'
The Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) of sentient beings is also like this.
It has no fixed dwelling place.
By means of good expedient means (shàn fāngbiàn),
it can thus become visible.
Because it becomes visible, one attains Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
The Icchantikas (Yīchǎntí bèi) do not perceive the Buddha-nature,
how can they block the penalties of the three evil paths (sān è dào)?
Shànnánzǐ!
If an Icchantika believes that the Buddha-nature exists,
you should know that this person will not fall into the three evil paths.
They would also not be named an Yīchǎntí.
Because they do not believe the Buddha-nature exists, they immediately fall into the three evil paths.
Falling into the three evil paths is why they are named Yīchǎntí."
“‘Good man!
As you have said,
if milk lacked the nature of curds,
curds should not emerge [from it].
If the seed of the Níguotuó lacked the nature of a fifty-foot tree,
then there should be no substance of a fifty-foot tree.
Ignorant people speak in this manner,
but the wise ultimately do not utter such words.
Why is this?
Because [curds] are without inherent nature.
Good man!
If milk contained the nature of curds,
it should not need to rely on the power of various auxiliary conditions.
Good man!
If water and milk are mixed,
and left lying for a month, they still do not become curds.
If one drop of the juice of the Pǒqiú tree is cast into it,
it immediately becomes curds.
If curds were originally present,
why wait for conditions?
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is also like this;
relying on various conditions, it can be seen;
relying on various conditions, one attains Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
If one waits for various conditions to attain it, then it is without inherent nature;
because it is without inherent nature, one can attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Good man!
For this reason,
Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas constantly praise the goodness of others
and do not litigate their faults;
this is called the honest mind (zhízhí xīn).
Furthermore, good man!
What is the Bodhisattva’s honest mind?
Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas constantly do not commit evil.
If they have faults, they immediately confess them,
never concealing them from their teachers or fellow practitioners.
Out of shame and self-reproach, they dare not commit them again,
regarding even minor offenses as extremely grave.
If a person questions them,
they answer that they genuinely committed the offense.
When further asked whether this offense is good or not good,
they answer, "Not good."
When further asked whether this offense is wholesome or unwholesome,
they answer, "Unwholesome."
When further asked whether this offense is a wholesome result or an unwholesome result,
they answer that this offense
is truly not a wholesome result.
Again asked who committed this offense,
"Surely not the Buddhas,
the Dharma,
or the Saṅgha?"
They answer, "It was not the Buddha,
the Dharma,
or the Saṅgha;
it was committed by me,
and it was constructed by the kleśas (fánnǎo).
Due to the honest mind, one believes in the Buddha-nature.
Believing in the Buddha-nature, one cannot be called an Icchantika (Yīchǎntí).
Due to the honest mind, one is called a disciple of the Buddha.
If one receives tens of millions of each type of clothing, food and drink,
bedding, and medicine from sentient beings,
it is not considered excessive.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s honest mind.
“How does a Bodhisattva cultivate and perfect the precepts?
Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas uphold the prohibitions
not for the sake of rebirth in heaven,
and not for the sake of fear.
Furthermore, they do not accept the dog precept,
the chicken precept,
the ox precept,
or the pheasant precept.
They do not commit broken precepts,
incomplete precepts,
blemished precepts,
mixed precepts,
or the Śrāvakayāna precepts.
They uphold the precepts of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva,
the precepts of Śīlapāramitā,
and attain the complete precepts.
They do not give rise to arrogance.
This is called the Bodhisattva cultivating the Great Nirvāṇa’s complete third precept.
“How does a Bodhisattva associate with good friends?
Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas constantly speak to sentient beings about the wholesome path
and do not speak about the unwholesome path,
saying that the unwholesome path is not a wholesome retribution.
Good man!
I myself am the true good spiritual friend (zhēn shàn zhīshi) of all sentient beings,
therefore I am able to cut off all the wrong views of the brāhmaṇa Pùjiāluó.
Good man!
If there are sentient beings who associate with me,
even if they have the causes for being born in hell,
they immediately attain birth in heaven.
For example, Sūnàchàduō and others were due to fall into hell,
but by seeing me,
they immediately cut off the causes for hell
and were born in the Realm of Form heaven.
Although there are Śèlifú
and Mùjiànlián,
they are not called the true good spiritual friends of sentient beings.
Why?
Because they are the causes for giving rise to the mind of an Icchantika.
Good man!
When I was formerly dwelling in the country of Bōluónài,
Śèlifú taught two disciples:
one to contemplate white bones,
and one to count the breath.
After many years, neither attained samādhi.
Because of this, they immediately gave rise to wrong views,
saying:
‘There is no Nirvāṇa
and no untainted Dharma.
If there were, I should have attained it.
Why?
Because I am capable of upholding well the precepts I received.’
At that time, I
saw that these bhikṣus were giving rise to this heretical mind.
I summoned Śèlifú and reproached him:
‘You do not teach well.
Why did you preach the Dharma erroneously to these two disciples?
Your two disciples have different natures:
one is a master launderer,
and one is a goldsmith.
The goldsmith’s son should have been taught to count the breath,
and the launderer should have been taught bone contemplation.
Because of your mistaken instruction,
these two persons gave rise to evil heresies.
At that time, I preached the Dharma to these two persons appropriately,
and upon hearing it, both attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Therefore, I am the true good spiritual friend of all sentient beings,
not Śèlifú
and Mùjiànlián.
If sentient beings have extremely heavy fetters
and happen to meet me,
I immediately cut them off using skillful means.
For instance, my younger brother Nánduó had extremely heavy lust,
which I eliminated using various clever skillful means.
Yāngjuémóluó had heavy hatred,
but upon seeing me, his hatred immediately ceased.
King Āshéshì had heavy ignorance,
but upon seeing me, his ignorant mind immediately ceased.
For example, the elder Púxīgā had cultivated and perfected extremely heavy kleśas over immeasurable kalpas,
but upon seeing me, they were immediately cut off and eliminated.
If there are evil, despicable, and base people who associate with me and become my disciples,
because of this reason,
all devas and humans respect and cherish them.
Shīlìjúduō’s wrong views were raging,
but due to seeing me,
his wrong views immediately vanished.
Due to seeing me,
the cause for hell was cut off,
and the condition for rebirth in heaven was created,
such as the caṇḍāla Qìxū.
When his life was about to end,
due to seeing me,
he recovered his lifespan,
such as Jiāoshījiā.
His frantic mind was deranged,
but due to seeing me,
he recovered his original mind,
such as the thin Gòutómí.
The butcher’s son,
who constantly practiced evil deeds,
upon seeing me,
immediately abandoned them,
such as the bhikṣu Chǎntí.
Due to seeing me,
he would rather abandon his body and life
than destroy his prohibitions and precepts,
such as the bhikṣu Cǎoxì.
For this reason,
the bhikṣu Ānán said that half of the pure conduct (Brahma-carya) is called a good spiritual friend,
but I say that is not so;
complete pure conduct is called a good spiritual friend.
This is called the Bodhisattva cultivating the Great Nirvāṇa,
complete with the fourth practice: associating with good spiritual friends.
"How does a Púsa fulfill Extensive Hearing (Duō Wén)?
A Púsamóhasà, for the sake of the Great Nirvāṇa,
copies the twelve divisions of the scriptures,
recites them,
distinguishes and explains them.
This is called a Púsa fulfilling Extensive Hearing.
Excluding eleven divisions,
only the Wéipífólǜe (Vaipulya Sūtra),
if he receives and retains it, reads and recites it,
copies and explains it,
is also called a Púsa fulfilling Extensive Hearing.
Excluding the twelve divisions of the scriptures,
if he is able to receive and retain this profound scripture of the Dà Nièpán,
copies it, reads and recites it,
distinguishes and explains it,
this is called a Púsa fulfilling Extensive Hearing.
Excluding the full body of this scripture,
if he is able to receive and retain one four-line stanza;
and further excluding this stanza,
if he is able to receive and retain the permanence of the Rúlái,
whose nature is without change or decay,
this is called a Púsa fulfilling Extensive Hearing.
Furthermore, excluding this matter,
if he knows that the Rúlái perpetually does not preach the Dharma,
he is also called a Púsa fulfilling Extensive Hearing.
Why is this?
Because the Dharma is without inherent nature.
Although the Rúlái speaks of all Dharmas,
he perpetually speaks nothing.
This is called the Púsa practicing the Dà Nièpán,
achieving the fifth fulfillment of Extensive Hearing.
"Good man!
If there is a good man or
good woman,
who, for the sake of the Great Nirvāṇa, completely achieves these five matters,
they can do what is difficult to do,
they can endure what is difficult to endure,
they can give what is difficult to give.
How does a Púsa do what is difficult to do?
If he hears that someone who eats one sesame seed attains Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
believing this teaching,
he continuously eats one sesame seed for measureless *asṃkhyeya* kalpas.
If he hears that entering fire attains Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
for measureless kalpas he enters the raging fiery mass in the Àbí hell.
This is called a Púsa doing what is difficult to do.
How does a Púsa endure what is difficult to endure?
If he hears that receiving suffering,
caused by being chopped or beaten by hands, staffs, knives, or stones,
