results in the attainment of Dà Nièpán,
he immediately endures it completely in his body for measureless *asṃkhyeya* kalpas,
not considering it suffering.
This is called a Púsa enduring what is difficult to endure.
How does a Púsa give what is difficult to give?
If he hears that being able to give away his kingdom, city,
wife, children,
head, eyes, marrow, and brain,
as charity to others,
results in the attainment of Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
he immediately, for measureless *asṃkhyeya* kalpas,
uses all that he possesses—his kingdom, city,
wife, children,
head, eyes, marrow, and brain—
as charity to people.
This is called a Púsa giving what is difficult to give.
Although the Púsa does what is difficult to do,
he ultimately does not think, 'This is done by me.'
Giving what is difficult to give,
is also like this.
Good man!
For example, a father and mother have only one son,
whom they love deeply.
They use fine clothing,
and excellent, delicious food,
raising him according to the season,
ensuring he lacks nothing.
If the son, toward these parents,
gives rise to disrespect and arrogance,
and abuses them with foul language,
the parents, out of love, do not generate resentment or hatred,
nor do they think, 'I provided this son with clothing and food.'
A Púsamóhasà is also like this.
They regard all sentient beings as their only son.
If the son encounters illness, the parents also feel ill.
They diligently seek medicine to cure him.
Once the illness is cured,
they ultimately do not generate the thought,
'I cured this child's suffering from illness.'
Púsas are also like this.
Seeing all sentient beings encounter the illness of affliction,
they generate a mind of affection and preach the Dharma for them.
Because they hear the Dharma, all afflictions are broken.
Once the afflictions are broken, they ultimately do not think,
'I broke the afflictions for sentient beings.'
If they generate this thought,
they will ultimately not attain Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
They only hold this thought:
There is not a single sentient being for whom I preach the Dharma,
enabling them to break afflictions.
A Púsamóhasà feels neither hatred nor joy toward sentient beings.
Why is this?
Because they are skilled at practicing *kōng sānmèi* (emptiness samādhi).
If a Púsa practices *kōng sānmèi*,
toward whom should they generate hatred or joy?
Good man!
For example, a mountain forest consumed by raging fire,
if people chop it down or if it is swept away by water,
toward whom should this forest wood generate hatred or joy?
A Púsamóhasà is also like this,
feeling neither hatred nor joy toward sentient beings.
Why is this?
Because they practice *kōng sānmèi*.
At that time, Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Dewáng Púsamóhasà addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Are all Dharmas
inherently empty?
Empty due to emptiness.
If their nature is inherently empty,
one should not need to practice emptiness,
and then see emptiness.
Why does the Rúlái say that by practicing emptiness one sees emptiness?
If their nature is inherently not empty,
even if one practices emptiness,
it cannot be made empty.
"Good man!
The nature of all Dharmas is fundamentally empty.
Why is this?
Because the nature of all phenomena cannot be obtained.
Good man!
The nature of form (rūpa) cannot be obtained.
What is the nature of form?
The nature of form
is not earth,
water,
fire,
or wind;
it is not separate from earth,
water,
fire,
or wind.
It is not blue, yellow, red, or white,
yet it is not separate from blue, yellow, red, or white.
It is neither existence nor non-existence.
How then can we say that form has its own nature?
Since its nature cannot be obtained,
therefore it is said to be empty.
All Dharmas are also like this.
Because of similar continuous sequences,
ordinary people, seeing them,
say that the nature of Dharmas is not empty and quiescent.
A Púsamóhasà fulfills the five matters,
and therefore sees that the nature of the Dharma is fundamentally empty and quiescent.
Good man!
If there are Shāmén and Póluómén,
who see that the nature of all Dharmas is not empty,
you should know that these people
are not Shāmén,
nor Póluómén.
They cannot practice Bānruò Bōluómì (Prajñāpāramitā),
they cannot enter the Dà Bān Nièpán,
they cannot directly see the Buddhas and Púsas;
they are dependents of Māra.
Good man!
The nature of all Dharmas
is fundamentally empty,
but also because the Púsa practices emptiness,
they see all Dharmas as empty.
Good man!
Just as because the nature of all Dharmas is impermanent,
annihilation can annihilate them.
If they were not impermanent,
annihilation could not annihilate them.
Conditioned phenomena have the characteristic of arising, so arising can cause them to arise;
they have the characteristic of annihilation, so annihilation can annihilate them.
All Dharmas have the characteristic of suffering, so
suffering can cause them to suffer.
Good man!
Just as salt is inherently salty and can make other things salty,
rock sugar is inherently sweet and can make other things sweet,
bitter vinegar is inherently sour and can make other things sour,
ginger is fundamentally pungent and can make other things pungent,
Hēlílè (Harītakī) is bitter and can make other things bitter,
the Ānluó fruit is astringent and can make other things astringent,
poison is inherently harmful and can cause other things to be harmed,
the nature of amṛta causes people not to die,
and if it is mixed with other things, it can also prevent death.
The Púsa’s practice of emptiness is also like this.
Because they practice emptiness,
they see that the nature of all Dharmas is entirely empty and quiescent.
Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Dewáng Púsa spoke again, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If salt can make what is not salty become salty,
and if practicing *kōng sānmèi* is like this,
then you should know that this *samādhi* is neither good
nor profound;
its nature is erroneous.
If *kōng sānmèi* only sees emptiness,
it must be non-existent Dharma.
What, then, is seen?"
"Good man!
This Sūn Kōng Sānmèi (Emptiness Samādhi) sees the non-empty Dharma,
enabling emptiness and tranquility,
yet it is not Diāndǎo (delusion/inversion).
Just as salt is not salty, but makes things salty,
this Sūn Kōng Sānmèi is also like this:
it makes the non-empty empty.
Good man!
Greed possesses nature,
it is not empty nature.
If greed were emptiness,
sentient beings should not fall into the hells because of this cause and condition;
if they fall into the hells,
how could the nature of greed be emptiness?
Good man!
The nature of form exists.
What is the nature of form?
It is called Diāndǎo.
Because of Diāndǎo,
sentient beings generate greed.
If the nature of form were not Diāndǎo,
how could it cause sentient beings to generate greed?
Because greed is generated,
one should know that the nature of form is not non-existent.
Because of this meaning,
cultivating Sūn Kōng Sānmèi is not Diāndǎo.
Good man!
All ordinary beings (*fánfū*),
if they see a woman, immediately generate the appearance of a woman.
A Bódhisàttva is not like this;
although they see a woman, they do not generate the appearance of a woman.
Since the appearance is not generated, greed is not generated;
since greed is not generated, it is not Diāndǎo.
Because worldly people see the appearance of a woman,
the Bódhisàttva speaks accordingly, saying there is a woman.
If one sees a man,
and says it is a woman,
that is Diāndǎo.
Therefore, I said to Shétí (Jāti):
'You Brahmāṇa,
if you take day to be night,
that is Diāndǎo.
Taking night to be day is also Diāndǎo.
Day is the appearance of day,
night is the appearance of night.
How is that Diāndǎo?
Good man!
All Bódhisàttvas residing in the Ninth Stage (Jiǔ Dì),
see that the Dharma has nature.
Because of this view,
they do not see the Buddha-nature (Fó Xìng);
if they saw the Buddha-nature,
then they would no longer see the nature of all Dharmas.
By cultivating such Sūn Kōng Sānmèi,
one does not see the nature of Dharmas;
because one does not see (Dharma nature),
one then sees the Buddha-nature.
Buddhas and Bódhisàttvas have two kinds of teachings:
one is having nature,
the second is having no nature.
For the sake of sentient beings, they speak of existing Dharma nature;
for the various worthy Sages, they speak of non-existent Dharma nature.
For those who are not empty who see the Dharma as empty,
they cultivate Sūn Kōng Sānmèi,
enabling them to attain the sight of emptiness.
Those who have non-existent Dharma nature also cultivate emptiness,
hence emptiness.
Because of this meaning,
cultivating emptiness is seeing emptiness.
Good man!
You say, 'seeing emptiness,'
yet emptiness is non-existence (Wú Fǎ),
what is it that is seen?"
Good man!
So it is,
so it is.
The Bódhisàttva Máhāsàttva truly sees nothing.
That which sees nothing is that which possesses nothing;
that which possesses nothing is all Dharmas.
The Bódhisàttva Máhāsàttva cultivates the Great Nírpán,
seeing nothing in all Dharmas.
If there is anything seen, one does not see the Buddha-nature,
cannot cultivate Bōrě Bōluómì,
and cannot enter the Great Bānà Nírpán.
Therefore, the Bódhisàttva sees that the nature of all Dharmas possesses nothing.
Good man!
The Bódhisàttva does not see emptiness solely because of the sight obtained through Sānmèi;
Bōrě Bōluómì is also empty,
Chán Bōluómì is also empty,
Pílíyē Bōluómì is also empty,
Chàntí Bōluómì is also empty,
Shī Bōluómì is also empty,
Tán Bōluómì is also empty,
form is also empty,
eye is also empty,
consciousness is also empty,
the Rúlái is also empty,
the Great Bānà Nírpán is also empty.
Therefore, the Bódhisàttva sees that all Dharmas are completely empty.
This is why I spoke to Ānán in the city of Jiāpílúo (Kapilavastu), saying:
'Do not grieve, worry, weep, or cry.'
Ānán then said:
'Tathāgata, World-Honored One!
Now all my relatives and dependents have perished.
How can I not grieve and weep?
The Rúlái and I were both born in this city,
both belonged to the Shì clan (Śākya),
and were close relatives and dependents.
Why is the Rúlái alone not grieving and worried,
but rather is shining even brighter?'
Good man!
I replied, saying:
'Ānán!
You see Jiāpí as truly existing;
I see emptiness and tranquility, completely possessing nothing.
You see the Shì clan members as all relatives;
because I cultivate emptiness, I see nothing.
Because of these causes and conditions, you generate sorrow and suffering,
while my body and appearance shine even brighter.
Because all Buddhas and Bódhisàttvas cultivate such Sūn Kōng Sānmèi,
they do not generate sorrow or worry.
This is called the subtle scripture of the Great Nírpán cultivated by the Bódhisàttva,
completing the ninth merit (Gōngdé)."
"Good man!
How does the Bódhisàttva cultivate the subtle scripture of the Great Nírpán,
completing the final tenth merit?
Good man!
The Bódhisàttva cultivates the Thirty-Seven Factors (Sānshíqī Pǐn),
entering the Great Nírpán,
[which is] permanence,
bliss,
self,
and purity,
explaining and teaching the Great Nírpán Jīng separately for the various sentient beings,
revealing the Buddha-nature.
If a Xūtuóhuán,
Sītuóhán,
Ānàhán,
Āluóhàn,
Pìzhīfó,
or Bódhisàttva,
believes these words,
all will attain entrance into the Great Bānà Nírpán.
If they do not believe,
they will transmigrate in the cycle of life and death.
At that time, Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Dé Wáng Púsà (The Bódhisàttva Luminous and Pervasive Illumination, Exalted, Noble, Virtuous King) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What kind of sentient beings will not generate reverence toward this Sūtra?"
“Shànnánzǐ!
After my Nirvāṇa,
there will be Śrāvaka disciples
who are foolish, violate the precepts,
and delight in inciting strife and disputes;
they will abandon the twelve divisions of the Sūtras
and instead recite various scriptures of external paths (heretics),
anthologies,
and handwritten texts;
they will receive and store all manner of impure objects,
claiming that the Buddha permitted them.
Such people
exchange fine sandalwood (zhāntán) for common wood,
exchange gold for brass,
silver for white lead (bái là),
silk for coarse woolen cloth,
and the taste of sweet dew (amṛta) for foul poison.
How is it that they exchange sandalwood for common wood?
It is when my disciples, for the sake of offerings,
preach the Sūtra Dharma to lay people (bái yī),
but the lay people are negligent in spirit
and do not like to listen;
the lay people sit in high places,
while the Bhikṣus sit below;
furthermore, they are supplied with various delicacies and foods,
yet they still refuse to listen.
This is called exchanging sandalwood for common wood.
How is it that they exchange gold for brass?
Brass is compared to form,
sound,
smell,
taste,
and touch,
while gold is compared to the precepts.
My disciples, due to the causes and conditions of form,
violate the precepts they have received.
This is called exchanging gold for brass.
How is it that they exchange silver for white lead?
Silver is compared to the Ten Virtues (shí shàn),
while lead is compared to the Ten Evils (shí è).
My disciples abandon the Ten Virtues
and practice the Ten Evil Dharmas.
This is called exchanging silver for white lead.
How is it that they exchange silk for coarse woolen cloth?
Coarse woolen cloth is compared to having no shame and no remorse,
while silk is compared to shame and remorse.
My disciples abandon shame and remorse
and practice shamelessness and lack of remorse.
This is called exchanging silk for coarse woolen cloth.
How is it that they exchange sweet dew for poison?
Poison is compared to various gains and support (lìyǎng),
while sweet dew is compared to all undefiled Dharmas (wú lòu fǎ).
My disciples, for the sake of gain and support,
praise themselves to the lay people,
claiming they have attained the undefiled state.
This is called exchanging sweet dew for poison.
“Because of these evil Bhikṣus,
this subtle Sūtra of the Dà Nièpán (Great Nirvāṇa) will be widely propagated throughout Yánfú Tí.
At that time,
there will be disciples
who uphold, recite, write down, widely explain, and propagate this Sūtra;
they will be persecuted and killed by these evil Bhikṣus.
At that time, the evil Bhikṣus will gather together
and establish strict rules:
‘If anyone upholds the Dà Nièpán Jīng,
writes it down, recites it, or explains it discriminately,
none shall live with them, sit with them,
or converse with them.
Why?
The Nirvāṇa Sūtra was not spoken by the Buddha;
it was created by heterodox views.
People of heterodox views are identical to the Liù Shī (Six Masters).
The scriptures of the Liù Shī are not the scriptures of the Buddha.
Why is this so?
All Buddhas teach that all Dharmas are impermanent,
without self,
without joy,
and impure.
If a text says that all Dharmas are permanent,
joyful,
possess self,
and pure,
how can this be a Sūtra spoken by the Buddha?
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas allow Bhikṣus to keep various possessions,
but the teachings of the Liù Shī do not permit their disciples to keep anything whatsoever.
Based on this meaning,
how can this text be the teaching of the Buddha?
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not forbid their disciples from refraining from the five tastes derived from the cow (milk products) or from eating meat.
The Liù Shī do not permit the eating of five types of salt,
five types of bovine tastes, or fat and blood.
If this is what the text prohibits,
how can it be the authentic canon of the Buddha?
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak of the Three Vehicles (Sān Chéng),
but this Sūtra purely speaks of the One Vehicle,
namely, the Dà Nièpán.
How can such a statement be the authentic canon of the Buddha?
All Buddhas ultimately enter Nirvāṇa,
but this Sūtra says the Buddha is permanent, joyful, possesses self, and is pure,
and does not enter Nirvāṇa.
This Sūtra is not counted among the twelve divisions
—thus it is a discourse of Māra,
not spoken by the Buddha.’
Shànnánzǐ!
Such people, although they are my disciples,
cannot believe and follow this Nirvāṇa Sūtra.
Shànnánzǐ!
At that time, if there is any sentient being who believes this scripture, even half a sentence,
you should know that this person
is truly my disciple.
By means of such faith,
they shall immediately perceive the Buddha-nature
and enter Nirvāṇa.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Guāngmíng Biànzhào Gāoguì Dé Wáng addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Shìzūn!
Excellent,
excellent!
Today the Tathāgata has been able to skillfully illuminate the Dà Nièpán Jīng.
Shìzūn!
Because of this matter,
I have immediately awakened to and understood one sentence, or even half a sentence, of the Dà Nièpán Jīng.
Because I understand one sentence or half a sentence, I have perceived a small part of the Buddha-nature.
As the Buddha has taught,
I shall also attain entry into the Dà Nièpán.
“This is called the tenth merit of complete accomplishment
of the Bodhisattva who cultivates the subtle scripture of the Dà Nièpán.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the entire assembly:
“All Shànnánzǐ!
If you have any doubt
about the existence of the Buddha
or the non-existence of the Buddha;
the existence of the Dharma
or the non-existence of the Dharma;
the existence of the Saṅgha
or the non-existence of the Saṅgha;
the existence of suffering
or the non-existence of suffering;
the existence of accumulation
or the non-existence of accumulation;
the existence of cessation
or the non-existence of cessation;
the existence of the path
or the non-existence of the path;
the existence of the real
or the non-existence of the real;
the existence of the self
or the non-existence of the self;
the existence of joy
or the non-existence of joy;
the existence of purity
or the non-existence of purity;
the existence of permanence
or the non-existence of permanence;
the existence of the vehicle
or the non-existence of the vehicle;
the existence of nature
or the non-existence of nature;
the existence of sentient beings
or the non-existence of sentient beings;
the existence of being
or the non-existence of being;
the existence of the genuine
or the non-existence of the genuine;
the existence of cause
or the non-existence of cause;
the existence of effect
or the non-existence of effect;
the existence of action
or the non-existence of action;
the existence of karma
or the non-existence of karma;
the existence of retribution
or the non-existence of retribution—
you may now ask freely what you wish,
and I shall distinguish and explain it for you.
Shànnánzǐ!
I truly do not see
anyone, be they Devas,
humans,
Māra,
Brahmā,
Śramaṇas,
or Brāhmaṇas,
who might come to ask me a question that I cannot answer.”
At that time, there was a Bodhisattva in the assembly named Shīzǐ Hǒu,
who immediately rose from his seat,
composed his demeanor, adjusted his robes,
advanced and bowed to the Buddha’s feet,
knelt respectfully, clasped his hands,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Shìzūn!
I am just about to ask;
may the Tathāgata, in great compassion, again grant permission for me to speak?”
At that time, the Buddha told all the great assembly:
“O good men!
You should now hold
deep reverence,
respect, and praise
for this Bodhisattva,
and with various fragrant flowers, musical instruments,
necklaces, banners, and canopies,
clothing, food,
beds and furnishings, medicines,
houses, and halls,
make offerings to him,
receiving him when he comes and sending him off when he departs.
Why is this?
This person has already planted deep good roots in the presence of past Buddhas
and has perfected his blessings and virtues.
Therefore, he now wishes to perform a lion’s roar before me.
“Good men!
Just like the king of lions,
who knows his physical strength,
whose teeth and claws are sharp and pointed,
who stands firmly on all four feet,
dwells peacefully in a rock cave,
and shakes his tail and lets out a sound—
if there is one who can possess such characteristics,
know that he is able to perform the lion’s roar.
When the true Lion King
emerges from his cave in the morning,
stretches and yawns,
looks around in the four directions,
and issues his vibrating roar,
it is for eleven things.
What are these eleven?
First, it is to destroy those who are not truly lions but falsely pretend to be so;
second, it is to test his own strength;
third, it is to purify his dwelling place;
fourth, it is to let his cubs know their location;
fifth, it is to ensure that the herd has no fear;
sixth, it is to awaken those who are sleeping;
seventh, it is to prevent all wild beasts that are negligent from being negligent;
eighth, it is to make various beasts come and rely on him;
ninth, it is to tame the great fragrant elephants;
tenth, it is to instruct and notify his cubs;
eleventh, it is to adorn his own retinue.
When all birds and beasts hear the lion’s roar,
those belonging to the watery realm sink into the deep abyss,
those walking on land hide and lie low in caves,
the flying ones fall down,
and the great fragrant elephants flee in terror, losing their dung.
“O good men!
Just like the jackal, even if it follows the lion for a hundred years,
it is ultimately unable to perform the lion’s roar.
But if a lion cub
has just completed three years,
it can roar like the Lion King.
“Good men!
The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has wisdom as his teeth and claws,
the four bases of spiritual power (Rúyì Zú) and the six Pāramitās as his perfected body,
the ten powers as his masculine might,
great compassion as his tail.
He dwells peacefully in the pure cave-dwelling of the four Dhyānas,
and performs the lion’s roar for the sake of all sentient beings,
destroying the army of Māra.
He displays the ten powers to the assembly,
opens up the path of the Buddhas’ conduct,
becomes the refuge for those holding various incorrect views,
comforts the frightened multitudes caught in Saṃsāra,
awakens sentient beings sleeping in ignorance,
and causes those who practice evil Dharmas to develop a heart of repentance.
He reveals and demonstrates to all sentient beings with incorrect views
to let them know that the six teachers are not the lion’s roar;
to break the arrogant minds of Pūráṇa (Fùlánnà) and others;
to make the two vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) develop a heart of repentance;
to make the Bodhisattvas of the Five Abodes (Wǔ Zhù) develop a mighty heart;
to prevent the four groups of the righteous view from generating fear towards the four groups of followers holding incorrect views;
emerging from the cave-dwellings of the holy conduct (Shèng Xíng),
the pure conduct (Fàn Xíng),
and the heavenly conduct (Tiān Xíng),
he stretches
to cause those sentient beings to break their arrogance by yawning;
he looks around in the four directions to cause those sentient beings to generate wholesome Dharmas;
he stands firmly on all four feet to enable sentient beings to attain the four unrestrained capacities (Wú’ài);
he performs the lion’s roar
to enable sentient beings to fully dwell in the Śīlapāramitā.
The lion’s roar is named the definitive teaching (Juédìng Shuō),
that all sentient beings entirely possess the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
and that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding without change or alteration.
“Good men!
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, even though they follow the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas,
still cannot perform the lion’s roar.
If a Bodhisattva of the Ten Abodes (Shí Zhù) is able to cultivate these three conducts (Sān Xíng Chù),
know that he is then able to perform the lion’s roar.
O good men!
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, Shīzǐ Hǒu,
is now about to perform such a great lion’s roar.
Therefore, you should wholeheartedly make offerings, be reverent,
respectful, and praise him.”
At that time, the World-Honored One told the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, Shīzǐ Hǒu:
“Good man!
If you wish to ask, you may now do so as you please.”
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, Shīzǐ Hǒu, said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
What is Buddha Nature?
By what meaning is it named Buddha Nature?
Why is it also named the Permanent (Cháng), Blissful (Lè), Self (Wǒ), and Pure (Jìng)?
If all sentient beings possess Buddha Nature,
why is the Buddha Nature possessed by all sentient beings not seen?
By abiding in what Dharma
do the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes not see it clearly and distinctly?
By abiding in what Dharma
does the Buddha see it clearly and distinctly?
By what kind of eye
do the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes not see it clearly and distinctly?
By what kind of eye does the Buddha see it clearly and distinctly?”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
Excellent,
excellent!
If someone can inquire about the Dharma,
he is then endowed with two kinds of adornment:
first, wisdom (Zhìhuì),
second, blessings and virtues (Fúdél).
If a Bodhisattva is fully endowed with these two adornments,
he then knows the Buddha Nature,
and also understands the meaning of being named Buddha Nature,
and even knows by what eye the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes see,
and by what eye the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, see.”
The Bodhisattva, Shīzǐ Hǒu, said:
“World-Honored One!
What is named the Adornment of Wisdom?
What is named the Adornment of Blessings and Virtues?”
“Good man!
The Adornment of Wisdom (Huì Zhuāngyán)
refers to from the First Ground (Yī Dì) up to the Tenth Ground (Shí Dì).
This is named the Adornment of Wisdom.
The Adornment of Blessings and Virtues (Fúdé Zhuāngyán)
refers to Dānapāramitā up to Prajñā, excluding Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, good man!
The Adornment of Wisdom
refers to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The Adornment of Blessings and Virtues
refers to the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of the Nine Abodes (Jiǔ Zhù Púsà).
“Furthermore, good man!
The Adornment of Blessings and Virtues
is conditioned (Yǒuwéi),
is defiled (Yǒulòu),
has existence (Yǒuyǒu),
has fruition and retribution (Yǒu Guǒbào),
has obstruction (Yǒu'ài),
and is impermanent (Fēicháng);
this is the Dharma of ordinary people (Fánfū Fǎ).
The Adornment of Wisdom
is unconditioned (Wúwéi),
is undefiled (Wúlòu),
has no existence (Wúwú),
has no fruition and retribution (Wú Guǒbào),
has no obstruction (Wú'ài),
and is permanently abiding (Chángzhù).
Good man!
You are now fully endowed with these two adornments,
and are therefore able to ask about this profound and marvelous meaning,
and I am also fully endowed with these two adornments,
and am able to answer this meaning.”
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, Shīzǐ Hǒu, said:
“World-Honored One!
If a Bodhisattva is fully endowed with these two adornments,
he should not ask about ‘one kind’
or ‘two kinds.’
How can the World-Honored One say he is able to answer concerning ‘one kind’ and ‘two kinds’?
Why is this?
All Dharmas are without ‘one’
or ‘two kinds.’
‘One kind’
and ‘two kinds’
are the characteristics of ordinary people.”
The Buddha said:
"Good man (Shàn Nánzǐ)!
If there is a Bódhisàttva who lacks the two kinds of adornments (zhuāngyán),
then he cannot know the one kind
and the two kinds.
If there is a Bódhisàttva who possesses the two adornments,
then he can understand and know the one kind
and the two kinds.
If it is said that all phenomena (zhūfǎ) lack the one
and the two,
this meaning is incorrect.
Why is this?
If there is no one
and no two,
how can it be said that all phenomena lack the one
and lack the two?
Good man!
If it is said that the one
and the two are marks of ordinary beings (fánfū),
this refers to the Bódhisàttva of the Ten Abodes (Shí Zhù Bódhisàttva),
not ordinary beings.
Why is this?
The one is called Níèpán (Nirvāṇa);
the two are called Life and Death (shēngsǐ, Samsāra).
Why is the one called Níèpán?
Because of its permanence (cháng).
Why are the two called Life and Death?
Because of desire (ài)
and ignorance (wúmíng).
The permanent Níèpán
is not a mark of ordinary beings.
The two of Life and Death
are also not marks of ordinary beings.
Based on this meaning,
the one who possesses the two adornments can ask and can answer.
"Good man!
Regarding your question, 'What is the nature of the Buddha (Fóxìng)?'
Listen carefully,
listen carefully!
I shall explain it to you distinctly.
Good man!
Fóxìng is called the Emptiness of the Ultimate Truth (Dìyī Yì Kōng).
The Emptiness of the Ultimate Truth is called Wisdom (Zhìhuì).
Regarding what is meant by emptiness (kōng),
(it means) not seeing emptiness and non-emptiness.
The wise person sees emptiness and non-emptiness,
permanence and impermanence,
suffering and joy,
self and non-self.
Emptiness is all of Life and Death;
non-emptiness refers to the Great Níèpán.
Furthermore, non-self refers to Life and Death;
self (wǒ) refers to the Great Níèpán.
Seeing all emptiness
but not seeing non-emptiness
is not called the Middle Way (Zhōngdào).
Furthermore, seeing all non-self
but not seeing self
is not called the Middle Way.
The Middle Way is called Fóxìng.
Based on this meaning,
Fóxìng is eternally constant
and without change.
Because it is obscured by ignorance (wúmíng),
it causes sentient beings (zhòngshēng) not to be able to perceive it.
Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué) see all emptiness
but do not see non-emptiness;
furthermore, they see all non-self
but do not see the self.
Based on this meaning,
they do not attain the Emptiness of the Ultimate Truth.
Since they do not attain the Emptiness of the Ultimate Truth,
they do not practice the Middle Way.
Having no Middle Way,
they do not perceive Fóxìng.
Good man!
Those who do not perceive the Middle Way
are generally of three kinds:
The first is the fixed practice of joy (dìng lè xíng);
the second is the fixed practice of suffering (dìng kǔ xíng);
the third is the practice of suffering and joy (kǔ lè xíng).
The fixed practitioners of joy
are the Bódhisàttvas Mahāsattvas (Bódhisàttva Móhēsà) who, out of compassion for all sentient beings,
although dwelling in the Ābǐ Hell (Ābǐ Dìyù),
experience the joy of the Third Dhyāna (Sān Chán Lè).
The fixed practitioners of suffering
are the ordinary beings.
The practitioners of suffering and joy
are the Śrāvakas
and Pratyekabuddhas.
Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas practice suffering and joy,
thinking this to be the Middle Way.
Based on this meaning,
although they possess Fóxìng, they cannot perceive it.
Regarding your question,
for what reason is it called Fóxìng?
Good man!
Fóxìng
is the seed of the Middle Way of the Anuttarā Samyak Sambódhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmǐao Sānpútí) of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, good man!
The Way (Dào) has three kinds,
namely, the lower,
the higher,
and the middle.
The lower—Brahmā Heaven (Fàntiān) is impermanent,
yet they mistakenly view it as permanent.
The higher—Life and Death are impermanent,
yet they mistakenly view them as permanent;
the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo) are permanent,
yet they calculate them to be impermanent.
Why is it called higher?
Because it is able to attain the supreme Ānòu Duōluó Sānmǐao Sānpútí.
The middle is called the Emptiness of the Ultimate Truth.
It sees the impermanent as impermanent,
and it sees the permanent as permanent.
The Emptiness of the Ultimate Truth
is not called lower.
Why is this?
Because it is not attained by any ordinary being.
It is not called higher.
Why is this?
Because it includes the lower.
The Way cultivated by the Buddhas and Bódhisàttvas
is neither higher
nor lower.
Based on this meaning,
it is called the Middle Way.
"Furthermore, good man!
The fundamental limits (běnjì) of Life and Death
are generally of two kinds:
The first is ignorance (wúmíng),
the second is craving for existence (yǒu'ài).
Between these two,
there is the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, and death (shēng lǎo bìng sǐ).
This is called the Middle Way.
Such a Middle Way can break through Life and Death;
therefore, it is called the Middle.
Based on this meaning,
the Dharma of the Middle Way is called Fóxìng.
Therefore, Fóxìng is permanent (cháng), joyful (lè), self (wǒ), and pure (jìng).
Because sentient beings cannot perceive it,
(they experience) impermanence, no joy,
no self, and impurity.
Fóxìng is truly not impermanent, not without joy,
not without self, and not impure.
Good man!
For example, a poor person
has a treasure hidden in his house.
This person does not see it.
Because he does not see it,
(he experiences) impermanence, no joy,
no self, and impurity.
A good friend (shàn zhīshì) speaks to him, saying:
'In your dwelling,
there is a treasure of gold.
Why are you so poor and distressed,
experiencing impermanence, no joy,
no self, and impurity?'
He immediately uses skillful means (fāngbiàn) to enable the person to see it.
Having seen it,
that person immediately attains permanence, joy, self, and purity.
Fóxìng is also like this.
Sentient beings do not see it.
Because they do not see it,
(they experience) impermanence, no joy,
no self, and impurity.
The good friends, the Buddhas and Bódhisàttvas,
by the power of skillful means,
instruct and inform them in various ways,
enabling them to see it.
Having seen it,
sentient beings immediately attain permanence, joy, self, and purity."
"Furthermore, good man!
When sentient beings develop views,
there are generally two kinds:
first is the view of permanence (cháng jiàn),
second is the view of annihilation (duàn jiàn).
Such two views are not called the Middle Way (Zhōng Dào);
only neither permanence nor annihilation is called the Middle Way.
Neither permanence nor annihilation
is the wisdom (zhì) that contemplates the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yīnyuán);
such contemplative wisdom is called the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
Although people of the Two Vehicles (Èr Chéng) contemplate Dependent Origination,
they still cannot be called possessing the Buddha Nature.
Although the Buddha Nature is permanent,
because the ignorance (wúmíng) of all sentient beings covers it,
they cannot perceive it.
Furthermore, they have not yet crossed the river of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination,
like the hare or the horse.
Why is this?
Because they do not perceive the Buddha Nature.
Good man!
This wisdom of contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination
is the seed of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí;
for this reason,
the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are called the Buddha Nature.
Good man!
For example, the hūguā (melon/cucumber) is called 'fever illness.'
Why is this?
Because it can act as the condition (yīnyuán) for fever illness.
The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are also like this.
Good man!
Regarding the Buddha Nature,
there is a cause and a cause of the cause,
there is a result and a result of the result.
That which is the cause is the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;
that which is the cause of the cause is wisdom.
That which is the result is Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí;
that which is the result of the result is the supreme Great Parinirvāṇa (Wúshàng Dà Bān Nièpán).
Good man!
For example, take ignorance (wúmíng) as the cause,
and formations (xíng) as the result;
take formations as the cause and consciousness (shí) as the result.
For this reason,
that entity of ignorance is also the cause,
and also the cause of the cause;
consciousness is also the result,
and also the result of the result.
The Buddha Nature is also like this.
Good man!
For this reason,
the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination neither arise nor cease,
are neither permanent nor annihilated,
are neither one nor two,
neither come nor go,
and are neither cause nor result.
Good man!
That which is the cause but not the result is like the Buddha Nature;
that which is the result but not the cause is like the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
That which is both the cause and the result
is like the phenomena produced by the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
That which is neither cause nor result is called the Buddha Nature.
Because it is neither cause nor result,
it is perpetual, constant, and unchanging.
For this reason,
I have stated in the sūtras that the meaning of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination is extremely profound;
it is without apprehension and without perception,
incapable of being contemplated (sī wéi),
and is truly the realm (jìng jiè) of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
not attainable by Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué).
By what meaning is it extremely profound?
The karma and actions (yè xíng) of sentient beings, being neither permanent nor annihilated, nonetheless obtain retribution (guǒ bào).
Although they perish moment by moment, nothing is lost;
although there is no actor, there are actions performed;
although there is no experiencer, there is retribution;
although the experiencer perishes, the result does not decay or vanish;
it arises without premeditation, awareness, or combination.
Although all sentient beings proceed together with the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, they do not perceive or know them.
Because they do not perceive or know them, there is no beginning or end.
The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes (Shí Zhù Púsà) only see their end but do not see their beginning.
The World-Honored Buddhas (Fó Shìzūn) see both the beginning and the end.
For this reason,
all Buddhas clearly and fully perceive the Buddha Nature.
Good man!
All sentient beings are unable to perceive the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination,
thus they revolve (in samsara, lúnzhuǎn).
Good man!
Just as a silkworm spins a cocoon,
it generates its own life and death.
All sentient beings are also like this;
because they do not perceive the Buddha Nature,
they create binding karma (jié yè) themselves,
circulate through birth and death (shēngsǐ),
just like bouncing a ball.
Good man!
Therefore, I have stated in the various sūtras:
'If a person perceives the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination,
they are perceiving the Dharma.
One who perceives the Dharma
is perceiving the Buddha;
the Buddha is the Buddha Nature.
Why is this?
All Buddhas take this as their essential nature.'
"Good man!
The wisdom of contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination
generally has four kinds:
first is the lower (xià),
second is the middle (zhōng),
third is the upper (shàng),
fourth is the supreme upper (shàng shàng).
Those who contemplate with lower wisdom do not perceive the Buddha Nature;
because they do not perceive it, they attain the path of a Śrāvaka.
Those who contemplate with middle wisdom do not perceive the Buddha Nature;
because they do not perceive it, they attain the path of a Pratyekabuddha.
Those who contemplate with upper wisdom perceive it but not fully clearly;
because they do not perceive it fully clearly, they abide in the stage of the Ten Abodes.
Those who contemplate with supreme upper wisdom perceive it fully clearly,
and thus attain the path of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
For this reason,
the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are called the Buddha Nature.
The Buddha Nature is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (dìyī yì kōng);
the emptiness of the ultimate truth is called the Middle Way;
the Middle Way is called the Buddha;
the Buddha is called Nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Shīzǐhǒu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If the Buddha and the Buddha Nature are not different,
why do all sentient beings need to cultivate the path?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
That which you ask
is not so.
Although the Buddha and the Buddha Nature have no difference,
all sentient beings have not yet fully realized it.
Good man!
For example, a person with an evil mind harms his mother;
having harmed her, he generates remorse.
Although his three karmas (sān yè) are good [now],
this person is still called a person of the hells.
Why is this?
Because this person is certain to fall into the hells.
Although this person does not possess the skandhas, dhātus, and āyatanas (yīn jiè zhū rù) of the hells,
he is still named a person of the hells.
Good man!
Therefore, I state in the various sūtras:
'If one sees a person practicing goodness,
that is called seeing a celestial being (tiānrén).
If one practices evil,
that is called seeing the hells (dìyù).'
Why is this?
Because the retribution is certainly received.
Good man!
Because all sentient beings are certain to attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
therefore I say that all sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature;
all sentient beings do not truly yet possess the Thirty-Two Marks (sānshí'èr xiàng)
and the Eighty Minor Characteristics (bāshí zhǒng hǎo).
For this reason,
I speak this verse (gě) in this sūtra:
"Good man!
Being (yǒu) generally has three kinds:
first is future being,
second is present being,
third is past being.
All sentient beings in future ages
will possess Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí;
this is called the Buddha Nature.
All sentient beings presently possess vexations (fánnǎo) and various defilements (jié);
therefore, they presently lack the Thirty-Two Marks
and the Eighty Minor Characteristics.
Those among all sentient beings who, in past ages, severed vexations,
therefore now perceive the Buddha Nature.
For this reason,
I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature,
even those like the Icchantika (Yīchǎntí) also possess the Buddha Nature.
Those like the Icchantika have no virtuous qualities (shànfǎ);
the Buddha Nature is also a virtuous quality.
Because of future being,
those like the Icchantika all possess the Buddha Nature.
Why is this?
Because those like the Icchantika are certain to realize Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Good man!
For example, a person has curds (rǔ lào) at home;
someone asks him:
'Do you have clarified butter (sū)?'
He replies:
'I have curds,
which are truly not clarified butter,
but because by skillful means (qiǎo fāngbiàn) it will certainly be attained,
therefore I say I have clarified butter.'
Sentient beings are also like this;
they all possess mind (xīn).
All those who possess mind
are certain to realize Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
For this reason,
I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature."
"O good man!
There are ultimately two kinds:
First, the Ultimate Adornment (Zhuāngyán Bìjìng);
Second, the Ultimate Attainment (Jiūjìng Bìjìng).
First, the Worldly Ultimate (Shìjiān Bìjìng);
Second, the Transcendent Ultimate (Chūshì Bìjìng).
The Ultimate Adornment is
the Six Pāramitās (Liù Bōluómì).
The Ultimate Attainment is
the One Vehicle (Yī Chéng) attained by all sentient beings.
This One Vehicle is named the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
For this reason,
I state that all sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature.
All sentient beings possess the One Vehicle,
but cannot perceive it because it is covered by ignorance (wúmíng).
O good man!
Just like the Uttarakuru (Yùdān Yuè)
and the Heaven of the Thirty-three Gods (Sānshísān Tiān),
which are covered by karmic retribution (guǒbào),
the sentient beings here cannot perceive them.
The Buddha Nature is also like this;
covered by various afflictions (jié),
sentient beings do not perceive it.
Furthermore, O good man!
The Buddha Nature is the Śūrangama Samādhi (Shǒulèngyán Sānmèi).
Its nature is like clarified butter (tíhú);
it is the mother of all Buddhas.
By the power of the Śūrangama Samādhi,
the Buddhas are made to possess permanence (cháng), joy (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng).
All sentient beings possess the Śūrangama Samādhi,
but because they do not cultivate it, they cannot perceive it.
Therefore, they cannot attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).
O good man!
The Śūrangama Samādhi
has five names:
First, the Śūrangama Samādhi;
second, Prajñāpāramitā (Bānruò Bōluómì);
third, the Vajra Samādhi (Jīngāng Sānmèi);
fourth, the Lion’s Roar Samādhi (Shīzǐ Hǒu Sānmèi);
fifth, the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
According to the function it performs,
it acquires different names in different places.
O good man!
Just as one samādhi acquires various names—
like Dhāna (Chán), which is called the Four Dhānas (Sì Chán);
as a faculty (gēn), it is called the Faculty of Concentration (Dìng Gēn);
as a power (lì), it is called the Power of Concentration (Dìng Lì);
as an enlightenment (jué), it is called the Enlightenment of Concentration (Dìng Jué);
as rightness (zhèng), it is called Right Concentration (Zhèng Dìng).
The Eightfold Enlightenment of Great Beings (Bā Dàrén Jué) is named the Enlightenment of Concentration (Dìng Jué).
The Śūrangama Concentration (Shǒulèngyán Dìng) is also like this.
"O good man!
All sentient beings fully possess three concentrations (sān dìng),
namely, superior,
medium,
and inferior.
The superior concentration is the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
Therefore, it is said
that all sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature.
The medium concentration is that all sentient beings fully possess the First Dhāna (Chū Chán).
When the conditions (yīnyuán) arise, they can cultivate it;
if there are no conditions, they cannot cultivate it.
There are two kinds of conditions:
one is the conflagration (huǒzāi);
the second is the breaking of the afflictions of the Desire Realm (Yùjiè Jié).
Therefore, it is said that all sentient beings fully possess the medium concentration.
The inferior concentration
is the concentration pertaining to the ten great primary mental states (Shí Dàdì Xīn Shǔ Dìng).
Therefore, it is said
that all sentient beings fully possess the inferior concentration.
All sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature,
but because it is covered by defilements (fánnǎo), they cannot perceive it.
Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes (Shí Zhù Púsà), although they perceive the One Vehicle,
do not know that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is the eternally abiding Dharma (cháng zhù fǎ).
Therefore, it is said that Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (Shí Dì Púsà), although they perceive the Buddha Nature, do not understand it clearly.
O good man!
Shǒulèng (首楞) means the Ultimate of All Things (yīqiè bìjìng).
Yán (嚴) means firm or solid (jiān).
When the Ultimate of All Things achieves firmness, it is named Shǒulèngyán.
Therefore, it is said that the Śūrangama Concentration (Shǒulèngyán Dìng) is named the Buddha Nature.
"O good man!
On one occasion, I dwelt beside the Nīrañjanā River (Níliánchán Hé).
I told Ānán (Ānán),
'I wish to bathe now.
You may fetch the clothes and bathing powder.'
When I entered the water,
all flying birds and creatures of the land and water came to observe me.
At that time, there were also five hundred Brāhmaṇas (Fànzhì) who came to the riverbank.
They approached me and said to one another:
'How did he attain a Vajra Body (Jīngāng zhī Shēn)?
If Gautama (Qútán) did not preach the view of annihilation (duànjiàn),
we would request and receive the purification dharma (zhāifǎ) from him.'
O good man!
At that time, using the knowledge of others' minds (tāxīn zhì),
I knew what these Brāhmaṇas were thinking.
I addressed the Brāhmaṇas, saying:
'Why do you say that I preach the view of annihilation?'
Those Brāhmaṇas replied:
'Gautama has previously stated in various sūtras that all sentient beings are entirely without self (wú wǒ).
If you state there is no self,
how can it be said not to be the view of annihilation?
If there is no self,
who upholds the precepts?
And who violates the precepts?'
The Buddha said:
'I do not state that all sentient beings are entirely without self.
I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature.
Is the Buddha Nature not the self (wǒ)?
For this reason,
I do not preach the view of annihilation.
Since all sentient beings do not perceive the Buddha Nature,
[they perceive] impermanence (wúcháng),
non-self (wú wǒ),
suffering (wú lè),
and impurity (wú jìng).
To speak in this manner is then called preaching the view of annihilation.'
At that time, those Brāhmaṇas, hearing that the Buddha Nature is the self,
immediately aroused the resolve for Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).
Straightway they left home and cultivated the Bodhi path.
All flying birds and creatures of the land and water also aroused the mind of Unsurpassed Bodhi (Wúshàng Pútí).
Having aroused the resolve,
they immediately relinquished their bodies.
O good man!
This Buddha Nature is truly not a self (wǒ),
but for the sake of sentient beings, it is called the self.
"O good man!
The Tathāgata, due to conditions,
speaks of non-self as self.
Although fundamentally there is no self,
even though he speaks in this way,
there is no falsehood.
O good man!
Due to conditions,
he speaks of self as non-self,
yet fundamentally there is a self.
For the sake of the world,
although he speaks of non-self,
there is no falsehood.
The Buddha Nature is non-self (wú wǒ),
yet the Tathāgata speaks of it as self,
because of its permanence (cháng).
The Tathāgata is the self,
yet he speaks of non-self,
because he has attained mastery (zìzài).
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Lion's Roar (Shīzǐ Hǒu Púsà Móhēsà) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If all sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature,
like the Vajra Hercules (Jīngāng Lìshì),
for what reason
can all sentient beings not perceive it?"
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
It is like the forms (sèfǎ),
although there are differences in blue, yellow, red, and white,
and long, short, essential shapes,
blind people do not see them.
Although they do not see them,
one cannot say there are no blue, yellow, red, or white,
or long, short, essential shapes.
Why is this?
Although the blind do not see,
those with sight see them.
The Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) is also like this;
although all sentient beings cannot see it,
the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (Shí Zhù Púsà) see a small part of it,
and the Tathāgata (Rúlái) sees it completely.
The Fóxìng seen by the Shí Zhù Púsà is like seeing forms at night;
what the Rúlái sees is like seeing forms in the daytime.
Good man!
It is like a blind person who cannot see forms clearly,
but a good physician treats their eyes,
and due to the power of the medicine, they gain clear sight.
The Shí Zhù Púsà are also like this;
although they see the Fóxìng, they cannot see it clearly,
but due to the power of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi (Shǒuléngyán Sānmèi),
they are able to gain clarity.
Good man!
If there is a person who sees all phenomena (zhūfǎ) as impermanent (wúcháng),
without self (wúwǒ),
without happiness (wúlè),
and impure (wújìng),
and also sees the non-all phenomena as impermanent,
without self,
without happiness,
and impure,
such a person does not see the Fóxìng.
The term “all” refers to birth and death (shēngsǐ),
and the term “non-all” refers to the Three Jewels (Sān Bǎo).
The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas (Shēngwén Yuánjué) see all phenomena as impermanent,
without self,
without happiness,
and impure,
and they also see the non-all phenomena as impermanent,
without self,
without happiness,
and impure;
for this reason,
they do not see the Fóxìng.
The Shí Zhù Púsà see all phenomena as impermanent,
without self,
without happiness,
and impure,
but they partially see the non-all phenomena as permanent (cháng), happy (lè), endowed with self (wǒ), and pure (jìng);
for this reason,
they see one tenth out of ten parts.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, see all phenomena as impermanent,
without self,
without happiness,
and impure,
but they see the non-all phenomena as permanent, happy, endowed with self, and pure;
for this reason,
they see the Fóxìng,
just like observing an Amalaka fruit (Āmólè Guǒ) in the palm of their hand.
For this reason,
the Śūraṅgama Meditation (Shǒuléngyán Dìng) is named the Ultimate.
Good man!
It is like the new moon;
although it cannot be seen,
one cannot say that it does not exist.
The Fóxìng is also like this;
although all ordinary beings (fánfū) cannot see it,
one cannot say that the Fóxìng does not exist.
“Good man!
The Fóxìng
is what is called the Ten Powers (Shí Lì),
the Four Fearlessnesses (Sì Wúsuǒwèi),
Great Compassion (Dà Bēi),
and the Three Mindfulnesses (Sān Niànchù).
All sentient beings possess the three kinds of eradication of defilements (fánnǎo);
thereafter they can see the Icchantikas (Yīchǎntí), and so forth.
Upon eradicating the Yīchǎntí state,
they are then able to attain the Shí Lì,
Sì Wúsuǒwèi,
Dà Bēi,
and Sān Niànchù.
For this reason,
I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess the Fóxìng.
“Good man!
The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yīnyuán)
are equally shared by all sentient beings,
both internal and external.
Which are the twelve?
Past defilements are named Ignorance (Wúmíng);
past karmic actions (yè) are named Volitional Formations (Xíng).
In the present world,
the initial reception of the embryo
is named Consciousness (Shì).
The five divisions upon entering the womb,
where the four sense faculties are not yet complete,
are named Name-and-Form (Míngsè).
When the four sense faculties are complete,
but not yet called Contact,
this is named the Six Sense Bases (Liùrù).
When pain and pleasure are not yet differentiated,
this is named Contact (Chù).
Attachment to one desire
is named Feeling (Shòu).
Habitually approaching the five desires
is named Craving (Ài).
Seeking and desiring internally and externally
is named Grasping (Qǔ).
Performing internal and external activities,
generating karma through body, mouth, and mind,
this is named Existence (Yǒu).
The Consciousness of the present world
is named future Birth (Shēng).
The Name-and-Form,
Six Sense Bases,
Contact,
and Feeling of the present
are named future Old Age, Sickness, and Death (Lǎo Bìng Sǐ).
These are called the Shí'èr Yīnyuán.
Good man!
Although all sentient beings possess these Shí'èr Yīnyuán,
some may not have them complete.
For instance, if one dies during the Kalala (Gēluóluó) stage,
then the twelve are absent.
From birth up to old age and death,
one achieves the completion of the twelve.
Sentient beings in the Form Realm (Sèjiè) lack the three kinds of Feeling,
the three kinds of Contact,
and the three kinds of Craving,
and they have no old age or sickness,
yet they are also named as possessing the complete twelve.
Sentient beings in the Formless Realm (Wúsè) lack form, and likewise lack old age and sickness,
yet they are also named as possessing the complete twelve.
Because attainment is certain,
it is therefore said that sentient beings equally possess the Shí'èr Yīnyuán.
Good man!
The Fóxìng is also like this:
because all sentient beings will definitely attain Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
therefore, I say that all sentient beings possess the Fóxìng.”
“‘Good man!
On Xuěshān there is a grass named Rěnrǔ.
If cattle eat it, then creamed butter (tíhú) is produced.
There is another type of grass.
If cattle eat it,
then no creamed butter is produced.
Even though there is no creamed butter,
it cannot be said that there is no Rěnrǔ grass on Xuěshān.
The Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) is also like this.
Xuěshān is named Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Rěnrǔ grass is named Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
The other type of grass is the twelve sections (shí'èr bù jīng) of the scriptures.
If sentient beings are able to listen to and inquire about the Great Nirvāṇa,
then they see the Buddha-nature.
Although it is not heard within the twelve sections,
it cannot be said that the Buddha-nature does not exist.
Good man!
The Buddha-nature
is both form (sè) and not form,
neither form nor not form;
it is both characteristic (xiàng) and not characteristic,
neither characteristic nor not characteristic;
it is both one (yī) and not one,
neither one nor not one;
it is neither eternal (cháng) nor cut off (duàn),
neither not eternal nor not cut off;
it is both existent (yǒu) and non-existent (wú),
neither existent nor non-existent;
it is both exhaustive (jìn) and not exhaustive,
neither exhaustive nor not exhaustive;
it is both cause (yīn) and effect (guǒ),
neither cause nor effect;
it is both meaning (yì) and not meaning,
neither meaning nor not meaning;
it is both word (zì) and not word,
neither word nor not word.
How is it form?
Because of the Vajra (Jīngāng) body.
How is it not form?
Because the eighteen unshared (shíbā bù gòng) factors
are non-formal dharmas.
How is it neither form nor not form?
Because form and not form have no fixed characteristics.
How is it characteristic?
Because of the thirty-two characteristics.
How is it not characteristic?
Because the characteristics of all sentient beings are not manifested.
How is it neither characteristic nor not characteristic?
Because characteristic and not characteristic are not definite.
How is it one?
Because all sentient beings completely abide by the one vehicle (yī chéng).
How is it not one?
Because the three vehicles (sān chéng) are taught.
How is it neither one nor not one?
Because of countless dharmas.
How is it not eternal?
Because it is seen conditioned by causes.
How is it not cut off?
Because it departs from the view of cut off.
How is it neither not eternal nor not cut off?
Because it has no beginning or end.
How is it existent?
Because all sentient beings completely possess it.
How is it non-existent?
Because it is seen through skillful means.
How is it neither existent nor non-existent?
Because of the nature of empty space (xūkōng xìng).
How is it named exhaustive?
Because of attaining the Śūraṃgama Samādhi (Shǒulèngyán Sānmèi).
How is it not exhaustive?
Because of its eternality.
How is it neither exhaustive nor not exhaustive?
Because all characteristics of exhaustion are cut off.
How is it cause?
Because it is the illuminating cause (liǎo yīn).
How is it effect?
Because the effect is definite.
How is it neither cause nor effect?
Because of its eternality.
How is it meaning?
Because it is completely able to encompass meaning without obstruction.
How is it not meaning?
Because it is inexpressible.
How is it neither meaning nor not meaning?
Because it is ultimately empty.
How is it word?
Because it has names.
How is it not word?
Because names are nameless.
How is it neither word nor not word?
Because all words are cut off.
How is it neither suffering (kǔ) nor pleasure (lè)?
Because all feelings are cut off.
How is it not self (wǒ)?
Because the eight sovereign powers (bā zìzài) have not yet been fully attained.
How is it not not self?
Because of its eternality.
How is it neither self nor not self?
Because it neither makes nor receives.
How is it empty (kōng)?
Because of the ultimate truth of emptiness (dìyī yì kōng).
How is it not empty?
Because of its eternality.
How is it neither empty nor not empty?
Because it can act as a seed for wholesome dharmas.
“Good man!
If there is a person who can contemplate and understand such meaning in the Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Nièpán Jīng),
know that this person then sees the Buddha-nature.
The Buddha-nature is inconceivable;
it is the sphere of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas,
and not known by the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué).
Good man!
The Buddha-nature is neither the aggregates (yīn), elements (jiè), and sense-fields (rù);
it is neither fundamentally non-existent yet now existent,
nor previously existent yet returning to non-existence.
Sentient beings obtain sight of it through wholesome causes and conditions.
For example, black iron,
when put into fire, becomes red;
when taken out and cooled, it returns to black.
This blackness
is neither internal nor external,
but exists due to causes and conditions.
The Buddha-nature is also like this.
When the fire of afflictions (fánnǎo) of all sentient beings is extinguished,
then they obtain hearing and seeing.
Good man!
Just as when the seed is extinguished,
the sprout then obtains life.
The nature of this sprout
is neither internal nor external,
and even the flowers and fruits are also like this;
they exist due to causes.
Good man!
This Great Nirvāṇa, a subtle scripture,
is perfected and fully endowed with immeasurable merits (gōngdé).
The Buddha-nature is also like this,
completely accomplished by immeasurable and boundless merits.
At that time, Siizihǒu Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva said:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
How many dharmas must a Bodhisattva fully accomplish
to see the Buddha-nature but not clearly?
How many dharmas must the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, accomplish
to see it clearly?
“Good man!
A Bodhisattva fully accomplishes ten dharmas;
though they see the Buddha-nature,
they do not see it clearly.
What are the ten?
The first is having few desires (shǎo yù);
the second is contentment (zhī zú);
the third is tranquility (jí jìng);
the fourth is vigorous practice (jīng jìn);
the fifth is right mindfulness (zhèng niàn);
the sixth is right concentration (zhèng dìng);
the seventh is right wisdom (zhèng huì);
the eighth is liberation (jiě tuō);
the ninth is praising liberation;
the tenth is teaching and transforming sentient beings with the Great Nirvāṇa.
Siizihǒu Bodhisattva said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the difference between having few desires
and contentment?”
"Shànnánzǐ!
Those with little desire,
neither seek nor acquire;
those who are content,
when they obtain little, their minds have no regret or remorse.
Those with little desire
desire little;
those who are content
are only troubled or worried in mind concerning matters of the Dhamma (fǎ).
Shànnánzǐ!
There are three kinds of desire (yù):
First, evil desire (èyù);
second, great desire (dàyù);
third, desire for existence (yùyù).
Evil desire is this:
If there is a Bhikṣu (bǐqiū) whose mind produces greedy desire:
'I desire to be the chief among all the great assemblies,
causing the entire Saṃgha (sēng) to follow after me;
causing all four assemblies (sìbù) to completely offer, venerate, praise,
and respect me.
Cause me to first preach the Dhamma (shuōfǎ) for the four assemblies,
causing everyone to believe and accept my words.
Also cause kings (guówáng),
high ministers (dàchén),
and elders (zhǎngzhě),
all to venerate me,
causing me to greatly acquire robes, food, drink,
bedding, medicine,
and superior, marvelous dwellings.
[This is] desire related to saṃsāra (shēngsǐ),
and is called evil desire.
What is great desire?
If there is a Bhikṣu whose mind produces desire:
'How can I make the assembly of the four divisions
all know that I have attained the First Stage of Abiding (chūzhùdì) up to the Ten Stages of Abiding (shízhù)?
Attained Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi (Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí)?
Attained the fruit of Arhat (Āluóhàn guǒ) up to the fruit of Srotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán guǒ)?
I have attained the Four Dhyānas (Sìchán) up to the Four Unimpeded Knowledges (Sì wú hé zhì)?'
Done for the sake of benefit and gain (lìyǎng),
this is called great desire.
Desire for existence (yùyù) is this:
If there is a Bhikṣu
who desires to be born in Brahmā Heaven (Fàntiān),
Māra Heaven (Mótiān),
Sovereign Heaven (Zìzàitiān),
or as a Cakravartin Holy King (Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng),
or a Kṣatriya (chàlì),
or a householder (jūshì),
or a Brāhmaṇa (póluómén)—all attaining sovereignty.
Done for the sake of benefit and gain,
this is called desire for existence.
If one is not harmed by these three kinds of evil desire,
this is called little desire (shǎoyù).
Desire is named the Twenty-five Loves (èrshíwǔ ài).
One who does not have these Twenty-five Loves,
is called one with little desire.
Not seeking future desired matters,
this is called little desire;
obtaining things but not clinging to them is called contentment (zhīzú).
Not seeking veneration,
this is called little desire;
obtaining things but not accumulating them,
this is called contentment.
"Shànnánzǐ!
There are also those with little desire who are not called content,
there are those who are content who are not called having little desire,
there are those who both have little desire and are content,
and there are those who are neither content nor have little desire.
Those with little desire
are called Srotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán).
Those who are content
are called Pratyekabuddhas (Pìzhīfó).
Those with little desire and contentment
are called Arhats (Āluóhàn).
Those who are neither content nor have little desire
are called Bodhisattvas (Púsà).
Shànnánzǐ!
Little desire and contentment are furthermore of two kinds:
First, good (shàn);
second, not good (búshàn).
The not good are called ordinary beings (fánfū);
the good are the holy person (shèngrén) Bodhisattvas.
Although all holy persons have attained the fruit of the Way (dàoguǒ),
they do not proclaim it themselves;
because they do not proclaim it,
their minds have no vexation or hatred,
this is called contentment.
Shànnánzǐ!
The Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) cultivate the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dàchéng Dànièpán Jīng) desiring to see the Buddha Nature (fóxìng),
therefore they cultivate little desire and contentment.
"What is tranquility (jíjìng)?
There are two kinds of tranquility:
First, mental tranquility (xīnjìng);
second, physical tranquility (shēnjìng).
Those with physical tranquility
absolutely do not commit the three kinds of evil deeds of the body;
those with mental tranquility
likewise do not commit the three kinds of evil deeds of the mind;
this is then called physical and mental tranquility.
Those with physical tranquility
absolutely do not draw near to the four assemblies (sìzhòng),
nor participate in any of the affairs of the four assemblies;
those with mental tranquility
absolutely do not cultivate greed (tānyù),
hatred (chēnhuì),
or delusion (yúchī);
this is then called physical and mental tranquility.
There may be Bhikṣus whose bodies are tranquil,
but whose minds are not tranquil.
There are those whose minds are tranquil,
but whose bodies are not tranquil.
There are those whose bodies and minds are tranquil.
And there are those whose bodies and minds are both not tranquil.
Those whose bodies are tranquil but minds are not tranquil:
There may be Bhikṣus sitting in meditation in a quiet place,
distant from the four assemblies,
but whose minds constantly accumulate greed,
hatred, and delusion.
This is called physical tranquility but lack of mental tranquility.
Those whose minds are tranquil but bodies are not tranquil:
There may be Bhikṣus who draw near to the four assemblies,
kings (guówáng), and high ministers (dàchén),
but have cut off greed, hatred, and delusion.
This is called mental tranquility but lack of physical tranquility.
Those with physical and mental tranquility
are called the Buddhas (Fó) and Bodhisattvas (Púsà).
Those whose bodies and minds are not tranquil
are called the ordinary beings (fánfū).
Why?
Ordinary beings,
even if their bodies and minds are tranquil,
cannot deeply contemplate impermanence (wúcháng) and suffering (wúlè),
no-self (wúwǒ) and impurity (wújìng).
Because of this reason,
ordinary beings cannot tranquilize the karma of body, speech, and mind.
Icchantikas (Yīchǎntí),
those who violate the four major prohibitions (sìzhòng jìn),
and those who commit the five heinous crimes (wǔ nì zuì)—
such persons
also cannot be called having physical and mental tranquility.
"What is diligence (jīngjìn)?
If there is a Bhikṣu who desires to make the karma of body, speech, and mind pure,
departing from all non-wholesome karmas,
and cultivating all wholesome karmas,
this is called diligence.
Those who are earnest and diligent
fasten their mindfulness (niàn) to six places,
namely, the Buddha (Fó),
the Dhamma (Fǎ),
the Saṃgha (Sēng),
the precepts (jiè),
giving (shī),
and the heavens (tiān).
This is called right mindfulness (zhèngniàn).
Those who possess right mindfulness,
the Samādhi (sānmèi) they attain,
is called right concentration (zhèngdìng).
Those who possess right concentration,
observing that all phenomena (zhūfǎ) are like empty space (xūkōng),
this is called right wisdom (zhènghuì).
Those who possess right wisdom,
depart from all afflictions (fánnǎo) and fetters (zhūjié),
this is called liberation (jiětuō).
Those who attain liberation,
extol the excellence of liberation for all sentient beings (zhòngshēng),
saying that this liberation is constant, eternal, and unchanging.
This is called praising liberation.
Liberation is precisely the unsurpassed Mahāparinirvāṇa (Wúshàng Dà Bān Nièpán).
Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) is the extinguishing of the fire of afflictions and fetters.
Furthermore, Nirvāṇa
is called a dwelling (shìzhái).
Why?
Because it can block the evil winds and rains of affliction.
Furthermore, Nirvāṇa
is called a refuge (guīyī).
Why?
Because it can transcend all fears.
Furthermore, Nirvāṇa
is called an island or shoal (zhōuzhǔ).
Why?
Because the four fierce rivers (sìdà bàohé) cannot carry one away.
What are the four?
First, the fierce river of desire (yùbào);
second, the fierce river of existence (yǒubào);
third, the fierce river of views (jiànbào);
fourth, the fierce river of ignorance (wúmíng bào).
Therefore, Nirvāṇa is called an island or shoal.
Furthermore, Nirvāṇa
is called the ultimate return (bìjìng guī).
Why?
Because it can attain all ultimate bliss (bìjìng lè).
If there are Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) who accomplish and fully possess these ten attributes,
although they see the Buddha Nature (fóxìng), it is not yet clear."
"Furthermore, good man!
Those who leave home have four kinds of sicknesses,
therefore they do not attain the four Śrāmaṇa (Shāmén) fruits.
What are these four sicknesses?
They are the four evil desires (è yù):
First is the desire for robes (yī yù),
second is the desire for food (shí yù),
third is the desire for bedding and lodging (wò jù yù),
fourth is the desire for existence (yǒu yù).
These are called the four evil desires.
These sicknesses of the monastic life have four excellent medicines that can cure them:
namely, rags taken from a dust heap (fèn sǎo yī) can cure the Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) of the evil desire for robes,
begging for food (qǐ shí) can destroy the evil desire for food,
dwelling under a tree can destroy the evil desire for lodging,
physical and mental tranquility (jì jìng) can destroy the Bhikṣu’s (Bǐqiū) evil desire for existence.
When these four medicines remove these four sicknesses,
this is called the Holy Practice (Shèng Xíng).
Such Holy Practice,
is then called having few desires (shǎo yù) and knowing contentment (zhī zú).
The tranquil person has four kinds of happiness (lè).
What are these four?
First is the happiness of leaving home,
second is the happiness of tranquility,
third is the happiness of eternal extinction (yǒng miè),
fourth is the happiness of ultimate completeness (bì jìng).
Attaining these four happinesses,
is called tranquility (jì jìng);
possessing the four right efforts (jīng jìn),
is therefore called diligent effort;
possessing the four foundations of mindfulness (niàn chǔ),
is therefore called right mindfulness (zhèng niàn);
possessing the four Dhyānas (Chán),
is therefore called right concentration (zhèng dìng);
seeing the four Noble Truths (sì shèng shí),
is therefore called right wisdom (zhèng huì);
because one eternally cuts off all afflictions (fán nǎo) and fetters (jié),
is therefore called liberation (jiě tuō);
because one denounces and speaks of the faults of all afflictions,
is therefore called praising and extolling liberation (zàn tàn jiě tuō).
Good man!
Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) who abide in and fulfill such ten practices,
although they perceive the Buddha-nature (Fó xìng), it is not yet clear.
"Furthermore, good man!
When Púsà Móhēsà hear this Sūtra,
they draw near and practice it,
distancing themselves from all worldly affairs.
This is called having few desires (shǎo yù).
Having already left home, they do not give rise to regret.
This is called knowing contentment (zhī zú).
Having already attained contentment,
they approach quiet places and distance themselves from noise and clamor.
This is called tranquility (jì jìng).
Those who are not content do not delight in quietude,
but those who are content always delight in emptiness and tranquility (kōng jì),
and in that emptiness and tranquility they constantly think:
'All the world considers that I have attained the fruits of the Śrāmaṇa path (Shāmén Dào Guǒ),
yet in truth, I have not yet attained them.
How can I deceive and mislead people now?'
Having had this thought,
they diligently practice the fruits of the Śrāmaṇa path.
This is called diligent effort (jīng jìn).
Drawing near and practicing Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán),
this is called right mindfulness (zhèng niàn).
Conforming to celestial practice (tiān xíng),
this is called right concentration (zhèng dìng).
Abiding in this concentration,
with right view and right knowledge,
this is called right wisdom (zhèng huì).
Those who have right view and knowledge can attain separation from the bondage of afflictions and fetters.
This is called liberation (jiě tuō).
Púsà (Bodhisattvas) of the Ten Abodes (Shí Zhù Púsà) praise the beauty of Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) for the sake of sentient beings.
This is then called praising and extolling liberation (zàn tàn jiě tuō).
Good man!
Púsà Móhēsà who abide in and fulfill such ten practices,
although they perceive the Buddha-nature (Fó xìng), it is not yet clear.
"Furthermore, good man!
Regarding having few desires (shǎo yù):
If there is a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) who dwells in a place of emptiness and tranquility,
sitting upright and not lying down,
perhaps dwelling under a tree,
or in a charnel ground (zhǒng jiān),
or in an open space,
sitting upon whatever patch of grass is available,
eating food obtained by begging (qǐ shí),
being satisfied with whatever is obtained;
perhaps eating in one sitting,
not eating more than one meal;
keeping only the three robes (sān yī),
rags from a dust heap (fèn yī),
or coarse woolen cloth (cuì yī);
This is called having few desires.
Having already practiced these matters,
the mind does not give rise to regret.
This is called knowing contentment (zhī zú).
Practicing the contemplation (Sāmàiyì) of emptiness,
this is called tranquility (jì jìng).
Having attained the four fruits (sì guǒ),
their minds do not rest regarding Anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi (Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).
(Continuation of 98)
This is called diligent effort (jīng jìn).
Binding the mind to contemplate the permanent constancy (cháng héng) of the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
having no change or variation,
this is called right mindfulness (zhèng niàn).
Practicing the eight liberations (bā jiě tuō),
this is called right concentration (zhèng dìng).
Attaining the four unimpeded understandings (sì wú ài),
this is called right wisdom (zhèng huì).
Distancing oneself from the seven outflows (qī lòu),
this is called liberation (jiě tuō).
Praising the beauty of Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) which is without the ten marks (shí xiàng),
is called praising and extolling liberation (zàn tàn jiě tuō).
The ten marks are:
namely birth (shēng),
old age (lǎo),
sickness (bìng),
death (sǐ),
form (sè),
sound (shēng),
scent (xiāng),
taste (wèi),
touch (chù),
and impermanence (wú cháng).
That which is separated from these ten marks is called Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
Good man!
This is how Púsà Móhēsà abide in and fulfill such ten practices,
although they perceive the Buddha-nature (Fó xìng), it is not yet clear.
"Furthermore, good man!
Because of having many desires (duō yù),
one draws near to kings (guó wáng),
high ministers (dà chén),
elders (zhǎng zhě),
Kṣatriyas (Chàlì),
Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén),
Vaiśyas (Píshè),
and Śūdras (Shǒutuó),
claiming for oneself the attainment of the fruits from Srotāpanna (Sūtúohuán) up to Arhat (Āluóhàn);
for the sake of profit and gain (lì yǎng), one performs walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, and even defecating and urinating;
if one sees a donor (Dàn yuè),
one still shows respect and addresses them cordially.
One who destroys these evil desires is called having few desires (shǎo yù).
Although one has not yet been able to destroy all fetters (jié) and afflictions (fán nǎo),
one is able to be the same as the Tathāgata (Rúlái) in the places of practice.
This is called knowing contentment (zhī zú).
Good man!
These two dharmas (fǎ),
are the immediate cause and condition for mindfulness (niàn)
and concentration (dìng).
They are constantly praised by teachers, masters, and fellow practitioners.
I, too, constantly praise and extol these two dharmas
in various Sūtras.
If one can fulfill these two dharmas,
then one can approach the gate of Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán) and the five kinds of happiness.
This is called tranquility (jì jìng).
One who firmly upholds the precepts (jiè),
is called diligent effort (jīng jìn).
One who possesses shame and remorse (cán kuì),
is called right mindfulness (zhèng niàn).
Not perceiving the characteristics of the mind (xīn xiàng),
is called right concentration (zhèng dìng).
Not seeking the nature, characteristics, or causes and conditions of any phenomena (zhū fǎ),
this is called right wisdom (zhèng huì).
Because there are no characteristics (xiàng),
afflictions are therefore cut off.
This is called liberation (jiě tuō).
Praising the beauty of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Nièpán Jīng) in this way,
is called praising and extolling liberation (zàn tàn jiě tuō).
Good man!
This is how Púsà Móhēsà abide in the ten practices,
although they perceive the Buddha-nature (Fó xìng), it is not yet clear."
"Good man!
Regarding what you have said:
By what eye do the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (Shí Zhù Púsà),
though they see the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng), still not see it clearly?
By what eye do the World-Honored Buddhas
see the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) and attain clarity?
Good man!
Because they see with the Eye of Wisdom (Huìyǎn),
they do not attain clarity;
because they see with the Buddha Eye (Fóyǎn),
they therefore attain clarity.
Because of practicing the Bodhi deeds (Pútí xíng),
they are not yet clear;
if there are no [further] practices,
then they attain clarity.
Abiding in the Ten Stages (Shí Zhù), though they see, they are not clear;
abiding in non-abiding, they then attain clarity.
Because the Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) are still in the cause of wisdom,
their seeing is not clear;
because the World-Honored Buddhas have severed cause and effect,
their seeing is clear.
The fully awakened is named the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng).
Because the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (Shí Zhù Púsà) cannot be named the fully awakened,
therefore, though they see, they are not yet clear.
Good man!
There are two kinds of seeing:
first, seeing with the eye;
second, seeing through hearing.
The World-Honored Buddhas see the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) with the eye,
just like observing the Āmólè fruit (Āmólè Guǒ) in the palm of the hand.
The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (Shí Zhù Púsà) see the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) through hearing, and thus are not clear.
The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (Shí Zhù Púsà) are only able to know for themselves that they will definitely attain Ānuòduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi),
but they cannot know that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng).
"Good man!
Furthermore, there is seeing with the eye:
The Tathāgatas (Rúlái), the Buddhas,
and the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (Shí Zhù Púsà) see the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) with the eye.
Furthermore, there is seeing through hearing:
all sentient beings, up to the Ninth Stage (Jiǔ Dì), see the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) through hearing.
If a Bodhisattva hears that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng),
but faith does not arise in their heart,
this is not named seeing through hearing.
Good man!
If there are good men
and good women,
who wish to see the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
they ought to cultivate and practice the Twelve Divisions of the Canon (Shí'èr Bù Jīng),
receive, uphold, read, and recite them,
write and explain them."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Shīzǐhǒu (Lion's Roar) said:
"World-Honored One!
All sentient beings are unable to know the characteristic of the Tathāgata's (Rúlái) mind.
How should they observe this,
so that they may come to know it?"
"O good man!
All sentient beings truly cannot know the mental characteristics (mind-aspect) of the Rúlái,
If one desires to observe and thereby come to know them,
there are two conditions:
The first is seeing with the eye,
the second is seeing through hearing.
If one sees all the physical deeds (karma) of the Rúlái,
one should know that this is indeed the Rúlái,
this is called seeing with the eye;
If one observes all the verbal deeds (karma) of the Rúlái,
one should know that this is indeed the Rúlái,
this is called seeing through hearing.
If one sees a form and appearance which no sentient being can equal,
