one should know that this is indeed the Rúlái,
this is called seeing with the eye;
If one hears a sound that is subtle and supreme,
different from the sounds possessed by sentient beings,
one should know that this is indeed the Rúlái,
this is called seeing through hearing.
If one sees the supernatural powers performed by the Rúlái,
are they for the sake of sentient beings,
or for the sake of gain (material support)?
If they are for the sake of sentient beings,
and not for the sake of gain,
one should know that this is indeed the Rúlái,
this is called seeing with the eye;
If one observes the Rúlái when He perceives sentient beings using the knowledge of others' minds,
does He preach for gain?
Does He preach for sentient beings?
If He is for the sake of sentient beings,
and not for the sake of gain,
one should know that this is indeed the Rúlái,
this is called seeing through hearing.
How does the Rúlái assume this body?
For what reason does He assume a body?
For whom does He assume a body?
This is called seeing with the eye;
If one observes how the Rúlái preaches the Dharma?
For what reason does He preach the Dharma?
For whom does He preach the Dharma?
This is called seeing through hearing.
If He is met with physical evil deeds and does not become angry,
one should know that this is indeed the Rúlái,
this is called seeing with the eye;
If He is met with verbal evil deeds and does not become resentful,
one should know that this is indeed the Rúlái,
this is called seeing through hearing.
If one sees the moment the Bódìsà is first born,
walking seven steps in each of the ten directions,
Móluóbátuó
and Fùnàbátuó, the great generals of ghosts and spirits,
holding banners and canopies,
shaking measureless, boundless worlds,
golden light radiating and filling the void,
Nántuó Lóngwáng and Bánántuó use supernatural power to bathe the body of the Bódìsà,
the forms of all the gods receive and pay reverence,
Āsītuó Xiān joins his palms and reveres Him.
In the prime of life He renounces desires,
as if abandoning snot and spittle,
not being deluded by worldly pleasures,
He leaves home to cultivate the Dao, delighting in quiet solitude,
performing six years of painful ascetic practices to break down heterodox views,
treating all sentient beings with equality and non-duality,
His mind constantly abiding in concentration, never scattered,
the characteristics and features majestically adorning His body,
the hills and ruins in the places He travels are all leveled,
His clothing stays four inches away from His body and does not fall,
when walking, He looks straight ahead and does not glance left or right,
the food He eats leaves no residue,
the grass at the place where He sits down or gets up is not disturbed.
He goes to preach the Dharma to regulate sentient beings,
His mind free from arrogance,
this is called seeing with the eye.
If one hears that after the Bódìsà had walked seven steps,
He proclaimed these words:
'This body of mine is now the last.'
Āsītuó Xiān joined his palms and said:
'O Great King, you must know,
Sīddá Tàizǐ
will definitely attain Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
He will never stay at home and become a Cakravartin King.
Why is this?
Because His characteristics are manifest.
The characteristics of a sacred Cakravartin King are not manifest.
The bodily characteristics of Sīddá Tàizǐ are brilliant and obvious,
therefore He will certainly attain Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.'
Upon seeing old age, sickness, and death, He furthermore spoke these words:
'All sentient beings are greatly pitiful,
constantly accompanied and pursued by birth, old age, sickness, and death,
yet they are unable to observe the constant course of suffering,
I must sever this.'
He received the Non-Conceptual Concentration from the five-penetrating immortal Āluóluó,
and after achieving it,
He later spoke of its wrongness.
He received the Concentration of Neither Thought Nor Non-Thought from Yùtuógā Xiān,
and after achieving it,
He said it was not Niópán but the Dharma of Saṃsāra.
Having achieved nothing from six years of ascetic practice,
He then spoke these words:
'Cultivating this painful practice is empty and yields no gain.
If this were real, I ought to have obtained it,
because it is illusory, I obtained nothing,
this is called a heterodox art, not the proper path.'
After achieving the Way,
Fàntiān exhorted and requested:
'We only wish the Rúlái would broadly open the gate of sweet dew (amṛta) for sentient beings and preach the unsurpassed Dharma.'
The Fó said:
'O Fànwáng!
All sentient beings are constantly obscured and covered by afflictions,
and cannot receive the words of my correct Dharma.'
The Fànwáng spoke again:
'O Shìzūn!
There are generally three kinds of sentient beings:
namely, those with sharp faculties (Lìgēn),
medium faculties (Zhōnggēn),
and dull faculties (Dùngēn).
Those with sharp faculties can receive it;
we only wish you would preach for them.'
The Fó said:
'O Fànwáng!
Listen attentively,
listen attentively!
I shall now open the gate of sweet dew for all sentient beings.'
Immediately He turned the wheel of the correct Dharma in the country of Bōluónài,
proclaiming the Middle Way (Zhōngdào).
Sentient beings do not break all fetters,
yet it is not that they cannot break them,
neither breaking nor not breaking,
therefore it is called the Middle Way.
Not delivering sentient beings,
yet it is not that He cannot deliver them,
this is called the Middle Way.
Neither entirely accomplished,
nor entirely unaccomplished,
this is called the Middle Way.
In whatever He preaches,
He does not call Himself the teacher,
nor does He call them disciples,
this is called the Middle Way.
He preaches not for benefit,
yet it is not that He does not obtain results (the fruit),
this is called the Middle Way.
His speech is right speech and real speech,
timely speech and true speech,
His words are not uttered falsely,
subtle and supreme.
Dharma such as this,
is called seeing through hearing.
O good man!
The mental characteristics of the Rúlái are truly invisible.
If there is a good man,
or good woman,
who desires to see the Rúlái,
they should rely upon these two kinds of conditions.
At that time, Shīzihǒu Púsà Móhēsà addressed the Fó, saying:
"O Shìzūn!
According to what was previously preached,
concerning the simile of the mango (āmrā) fruit and the four kinds of people,
some people have refined conduct,
but their minds are not truly upright.
Some people have refined minds,
but their conduct is not truly upright.
Some people have refined minds,
and their conduct is also truly upright.
Some people have unrefined minds,
and their conduct is not truly upright.
Regarding the first two kinds,
how can they be known?
As the Fó has said,
although one relies on these two (methods of sight and hearing),
they cannot be known."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
The analogy of the Āmluó (Amra) fruit concerning the two types of people,
is truly hard to understand.
Because it is hard to understand,
I stated in my Sūtra,
you should live together with them;
if, living together, you still do not know,
you should associate with them for a long time;
if, associating for a long time, you still do not know,
you should use wisdom;
if, using wisdom, you still do not know,
you should observe deeply;
because of observation,
you will then know who upholds the precepts and who breaks them.
Good man!
By possessing these four items—
dwelling together,
associating for a long time,
wisdom,
and observation—
only then can you know who upholds the precepts and who breaks them.
Good man!
Precepts are of two kinds,
and the upholding of precepts is also two-fold:
one is ultimate precept (jìngjiūngjiè),
the second is non-ultimate.
Some people receive and uphold prohibitions due to conditional factors.
The wise should observe whether this person upholds the precepts,
is it for gain and support (lìyǎng)?
Or is it upheld ultimately?
Good man!
The Tathāgata's (Rúlái) precepts have no conditional factors (yīnyuán).
Therefore, they are named the ultimate precepts (jìngjiūngjiè).
Because of this meaning,
even if a Bodhisattva (Púsà) is harmed by all wicked sentient beings,
they do not give rise to resentment or obstruction.
Therefore, the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is named as one who has achieved completely finalized observance (bìjìng chíjiè),
ultimate observance (jìngjiūng chíjiè).
Good man!
Once, in the past,
together with Śèlìfó (Śāriputra) and five hundred disciples,
I was dwelling together in the great city of Zhānbō in the kingdom of Mójiātuó (Magadha).
At that time, there was a hunter pursuing a dove.
That dove, terrified,
flew toward Śèlìfó's (Śāriputra's) shadow,
yet it still trembled like a plantain tree.
When it reached my shadow, its body and mind became peaceful and stable,
and its terror was removed.
Therefore, you should know that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One (Rúlái Shìzūn), has achieved completely finalized observance (bìjìng chíjiè),
so much so that even his shadow possesses this power.
Good man!
Non-ultimate precepts,
are still unable to attain the fruit of Śèngwén (Śrāvaka) or Yuánjué (Pratyekabuddha),
how much less able are they to attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi)?
"Furthermore, there are two kinds:
one is for gain and support (lìyǎng),
the second is for the Right Dharma (Zhèngfǎ).
Those who, for the sake of gain and support (lìyǎng),
receive and uphold prohibitions,
know that these precepts cannot see the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) or the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Even though they hear the names of the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) and the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
they still cannot be truly called 'having heard and seen.'
If one receives and upholds prohibitions for the sake of the Right Dharma (Zhèngfǎ),
know that these precepts can see the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) and the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
This is named 'seeing with the eye,'
and also named 'having heard and seen.'
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
one is deep-rooted and hard to uproot,
the second is shallow-rooted and easily moved.
If one is able to cultivate emptiness (kōng), signlessness (wúxiàng), and wishlessness (yuàn),
this is named deep-rooted and hard to uproot.
If one does not cultivate these Three Samādhis (sān sānmèi),
even if one cultivates for the twenty-five realms of existence (èrshíwǔ yǒu),
this is named shallow-rooted and easily moved.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
one is for oneself,
the second is for sentient beings.
Those who act for sentient beings,
can see the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) and the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
People who uphold precepts are also of two kinds:
one is naturally able to uphold them (by intrinsic nature),
the second requires instruction from others.
If, having received the precepts,
through immeasurable ages they never initially leak or fail,
perhaps encountering a wicked country,
meeting evil companions (è zhīshi),
a wicked era,
or a wicked generation,
hearing perverse and wicked doctrines,
or dwelling with those of wrong views (xiéjiàn).
Even if at that time there is no method for receiving precepts,
they cultivate and uphold them as before,
without violating anything—
this is named naturally able to uphold them (xìng zì néng chí).
If one meets a Master (shī) or Sangha (sēng) and receives the four-part Karma ceremony (báisì jiémó),
and only then attains the precepts;
although the precepts have been attained,
they must rely on the Upādhyāya (Héshàng),
various teachers (zhū shī),
fellow students,
and virtuous friends (shànyǒu) for teaching and instruction,
only then knowing how to advance or halt;
listening to the Dharma, speaking the Dharma, and preparing all the dignified manners (wēiyí)—
this is named requiring instruction from others (xū tā jiàochì).
Good man!
Those who are naturally able to uphold them,
see the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) and the Tathāgata (Rúlái) with their own eyes,
and are also named 'having heard and seen.'
Precepts are furthermore of two kinds:
one is Śèngwén (Śrāvaka) precepts,
the second is Púsà (Bodhisattva) precepts.
From the initial arousal of the Bodhi-mind (fāxīn) until the attainment of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi),
this is named Púsà (Bodhisattva) precepts.
If one contemplates white bones until the attainment of the Āluóhàn (Arhat) fruit,
this is named Śèngwén (Śrāvaka) precepts.
If there is one who receives and upholds Śèngwén (Śrāvaka) precepts,
know that this person does not see the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) or the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
If there is one who receives and upholds Púsà (Bodhisattva) precepts,
know that this person attains Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi),
and is able to see the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng),
the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
and Nirvāṇa (Nièpán)."
The Bodhisattva Shīzǐhǒu (Simhanāda) said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
For what reason
does one receive and uphold prohibitions?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
It is for the sake of the mind having no regret (bùhuǐ).
Why no regret?
For the sake of experiencing joy (shòu lè).
Why experience joy?
For the sake of detachment (yuǎnlí).
Why detachment?
For the sake of peaceful stability (ānwěn).
Why peaceful stability?
For the sake of meditation (chándìng).
Why meditation?
For the sake of true knowledge and insight (shí zhījiàn).
Why true knowledge and insight?
For the sake of seeing all the faults and calamities of birth and death (shēngsǐ).
Why seeing the faults and calamities of birth and death?
For the sake of the mind having no greed or attachment (bù tānzhù).
Why the mind having no greed or attachment?
For the sake of attaining liberation (jiětuō).
Why attaining liberation?
For the sake of attaining the unsurpassed Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
Why attaining the Great Parinirvāṇa (Dà Bōnièpán)?
For the sake of attaining the doctrines of permanence (cháng), joy (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng).
Why attaining permanence, joy, self, and purity?
For the sake of attaining non-arising and non-ceasing (bù shēng bù miè).
Why attaining non-arising and non-ceasing?
For the sake of seeing the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng).
Therefore, the Bodhisattva (Púsà) is naturally able to uphold the ultimate pure precepts (jìngjiūng jìngjiè).
Good man!
A Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) who upholds the precepts, although not having made a vow seeking the mind of no regret (bùhuǐ xīn),
the mind of no regret is attained spontaneously.
Why is this?
Because the Dharma-nature (Fǎxìng) is thus.
Although he does not seek joy (lè),
detachment (yuǎnlí), peaceful stability (ānwěn),
true knowledge and insight (zhēnshí zhījiàn),
seeing the faults of birth and death (shēngsǐ),
and the mind having no greed or attachment (xīn bù tānzhù).
Liberation (jiětuō), Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
permanence, joy, self, purity,
non-arising and non-ceasing (bù shēng bù miè),
and seeing the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) are all attained spontaneously.
Why is this?
Because the Dharma-nature (Fǎxìng) is thus."
The Bodhisattva Shīzǐhǒu (Simhanāda) said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If upholding the precepts is the cause for attaining the fruit of no regret (bùhuǐ guǒ),
and if liberation (jiětuō) is the cause for attaining the fruit of Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
then the precepts would have no cause (wúyīn),
and Nirvāṇa would have no result (wúguǒ).
If the precepts have no cause,
then they are named permanent (cháng).
If Nirvāṇa has a cause,
then it is impermanent (wúcháng).
If this is the case,
then Nirvāṇa would be something that fundamentally did not exist but now exists.
If it fundamentally did not exist but now exists,
this is impermanent (wúcháng),
just like lighting a lamp.
If Nirvāṇa is like that,
how can it be named Self (wǒ), Joy (lè), and Purity (jìng)?"
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
Excellent,
excellent!
Because you have previously sown roots of goodness in the presence of countless Buddhas,
you are able to ask the Tathāgata (Rúlái) such a profound principle.
Good man!
You have not lost your fundamental aspiration,
and thus you ask this question.
I recall that in the past, countless kalpas ago,
in the city of Bōluónài, a Buddha appeared in the world,
named Shàndé.
At that time, that Buddha preached this Mahāpārinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dànièpán Jīng) for three hundred million years.
At that time, you and I
were both present in that assembly,
and I consulted that Buddha regarding this matter.
At that time, the Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings,
entered samādhi (sānmèi) and perfect concentration,
and did not answer this principle.
Excellent,
Great Being (Dàshì)!
You are indeed able to recall such a past event.
Listen carefully,
listen carefully.
I shall now speak it for you.
Precepts (jìe) also have a cause,
which is hearing the Proper Dharma (Zhèngfǎ).
Hearing the Proper Dharma also has a cause,
which is associating with a good friend (shàn yǒu).
Associating with a good friend also has a cause,
which is called faith (xìnxīn).
Faith also has a cause.
There are two kinds of cause:
First, hearing the Dharma (tīngfǎ);
second, reflecting upon its meaning (sīwéi yì).
Good man!
Faith is caused by hearing the Dharma,
and hearing the Dharma is caused by faith.
These two dharmas,
are both cause
and the cause of the cause,
and both effect
and the effect of the effect.
Good man!
Just as the Nirgrantha (Nígān), establishing a support, raises a jar,
they mutually act as cause and effect and cannot be separated.
Good man!
Just as ignorance (wúmíng) conditions volition (xíng),
volition conditions ignorance.
This ignorance and volition
are both cause
and the cause of the cause,
and both effect
and the effect of the effect.
And so forth, until birth conditions old age and death (lǎosǐ),
and old age and death conditions birth.
This birth, old age, and death
is both cause
and the cause of the cause,
and both effect
and the effect of the effect.
Good man!
Birth is the dharma that is capable of generating,
but it cannot generate itself.
Because it does not generate itself,
it is generated by generating birth;
the generated birth does not generate itself;
it must rely on birth to be generated.
Therefore, these two births
are both cause,
and the cause of the cause,
and both effect
and the effect of the effect.
Good man!
Faith
and hearing the Dharma
are also like this.
“Good man!
That which is an effect but not a cause is Mahāpārinirvāṇa (Dànièpán).
Why is it named an effect (guǒ)?
Because it is the supreme effect,
the effect of the Śramaṇa (Shā mén guǒ),
the effect of the Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén guǒ),
because it severs saṃsāra (shēngsǐ),
and because it destroys defilements (fánnǎo).
Therefore, it is named an effect.
It is denounced by all defilements.
Therefore, Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) is named the effect,
and defilement is named the transgression of transgression.
Good man!
Nirvāṇa is without cause,
but its essence is effect.
Why is this?
Because it is without arising and ceasing (shēngmiè),
because there is nothing produced,
because it is not conditioned (yǒuwéi),
because it is unconditioned (wúwéi),
because it is eternal and unchanging,
because it has no location,
and because it has no beginning or end.
Good man!
If Nirvāṇa had a cause,
it could not be called Nirvāṇa.
The word *pán* means cause (yīn).
The word *bōniè* means non-existence (wú).
Because there is no cause,
it is called Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
The Bodhisattva Shīzǐhǒu said:
“As the Buddha has said,
Nirvāṇa is without cause—
this principle is not so.
If you speak of ‘without’ (wú),
it conforms to six meanings:
First, because of ultimate non-existence,
it is named non-existence.
For example, in all dharmas there is no self (wú wǒ)
and no possessions of self.
Second, because of temporary non-existence,
it is named non-existence.
For example, when people say
that a river or pond has no water,
or that there is no sun or moon.
Third, because of scarcity,
it is named non-existence.
For example, when people say
that food has little salt,
they call it unsalted (wú xián);
when sweet liquid has little sweetness,
they call it unsweet (wú tián).
Fourth, because of incapacity to receive,
it is named non-existence.
For example, a Caṇḍāla (Zhāntuóluó) cannot receive and uphold the Dharma of a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén fǎ),
therefore it is named ‘without Brāhmaṇa.’
Fifth, because of receiving evil dharmas,
it is named non-existence.
For example, when people say
that those who receive evil dharmas are not named Śramaṇa (Shā mén) or Brāhmaṇa,
therefore it is named ‘without Śramaṇa and Brāhmaṇa.’
Sixth, because of contrast,
it is named non-existence.
For instance, the absence of white
is named black.
The absence of light
is named ignorance (wúmíng).
World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
Nirvāṇa is also like this.
It is sometimes ‘without cause’ (wú yīn),
and therefore is named Nirvāṇa.”
The *Fó* said:
"Good man!
Regarding these six meanings that you have just discussed,
why did you not use what is ultimately non-existent to illustrate *Nièpán*?
Instead, you took that which is temporarily non-existent, is that it?
Good man!
The essence of *Nièpán* is ultimately without cause,
just like the non-existence of self and the non-existence of what belongs to self.
Good man!
Worldly *dharmas*
and *Nièpán* are ultimately not relative (or mutually corresponding),
therefore, those six matters cannot serve as analogies.
Good man!
All *dharmas* are entirely without self,
but this *Nièpán* truly possesses the self.
For this reason,
*Nièpán* is without cause,
yet its essence is the effect (fruit/result).
That which is a cause but not an effect
is called the *Fóxìng*.
Because it is not produced by a cause,
it is a cause but not an effect.
It is not the fruit of a *Shāmén*,
therefore it is called 'not an effect.'
Why is it called a cause?
Because it is an illuminating cause (*liǎoyīn*).
Good man!
There are two kinds of cause:
The first is the generating cause (*shēngyīn*),
the second is the illuminating cause (*liǎoyīn*).
That which can produce *dharmas*
is called the generating cause;
a lamp can illuminate objects,
therefore it is called the illuminating cause.
Afflictions and various fetters
are called generating causes;
the parents of sentient beings
are called illuminating causes.
Things like grain seeds are called generating causes;
earth, water, manure, etc., are called illuminating causes.
Furthermore, there is a generating cause,
namely the Six *Pāramì*
and *Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*.
Furthermore, there is an illuminating cause,
namely the *Fóxìng*
and *Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*.
Furthermore, there is an illuminating cause,
namely the Six *Pāramì*
and the *Fóxìng*.
Furthermore, there is a generating cause,
namely the *Shǒuléngyán Sānmèi*
and *Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*.
Furthermore, there is an illuminating cause,
namely the *Bā Zhèngdào*
and *Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*.
Furthermore, there is a generating cause,
namely faith
and the Six *Pāramì*."
*Shīzǐhǒu Púsà* said:
"World-Honored One!
Regarding what the *Fó* has said,
'seeing the *Rúlái* and the *Fóxìng*,'
what does this meaning imply?
World-Honored One!
The body of the *Rúlái* has no characteristics,
it is neither long nor short,
neither white nor black,
it has no location,
it is not in the Three Realms,
it is not a conditioned phenomenon,
it is not recognized by eye-consciousness.
How, then, can it be seen?
The *Fóxìng* is also like this."
The *Fó* said:
"Good man!
The body of the *Fó* is of two kinds:
The first is permanent,
the second is impermanent.
The impermanent one
is manifested skillfully
for the sake of liberating all sentient beings;
this is called 'seeing with the eye.'
The permanent one,
the body of liberation of the *Rúlái Shìzūn*,
is also called 'seeing with the eye,'
and is also called 'seeing through hearing.'
The *Fóxìng* is also twofold:
The first is visible,
the second is invisible.
The visible one is
the *Shí Zhù Púsà* (Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages)
and all *Fó Shìzūn*.
The invisible one is
all sentient beings.
'Seeing with the eye' means
that the *Shí Zhù Púsà*
and all *Fó Rúlái*
see the *Fóxìng* possessed by sentient beings.
'Seeing through hearing' means
that all sentient beings
and the *Jiǔ Zhù Púsà* (Bodhisattvas of the Nine Stages)
hear about the existence of the *Fóxìng* and the body of the *Rúlái*.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
The first is form,
the second is non-form.
The form is
the liberation of the *Rúlái*;
the non-form is
because the *Rúlái* has eternally severed all characteristics of form.
The *Fóxìng* is of two kinds:
The first is form,
the second is non-form.
The form is
*Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*;
the non-form includes
ordinary people up to the *Shí Zhù Púsà*.
The *Shí Zhù Púsà* do not see it clearly,
therefore it is called non-form.
Good man!
Furthermore, the *Fóxìng* is of two kinds:
The first is form,
the second is non-form.
The form
refers to the *Fó* and *Púsà*;
the non-form
refers to all sentient beings.
The form
is called 'seeing with the eye';
the non-form
is called 'seeing through hearing.'
The *Fóxìng* is neither internal
nor external.
Although it is neither internal nor external,
yet it is not destroyed or lost,
therefore it is said that all sentient beings possess the *Fóxìng*."
*Shīzǐhǒu Púsà* said:
"World-Honored One!
As the *Fó* has taught,
all sentient beings possess the *Fóxìng*,
just as curd is present within milk.
The *Jīngāng Lìshì* (Vajra Warriors),
and the *Fóxìng* of all *Fó* are like pure clarified butter (*tíhú*).
Why, then, does the *Rúlái* say that the *Fóxìng* is neither internal nor external?"
The *Fó* said:
"Good man!
I also do not say that curd is present within milk.
Because curd is produced from milk, I speak of 'having curd.'
"World-Honored One!
All phenomena that are produced have their respective times."
"Good man!
When it is milk, there is no curd,
nor is there fresh butter,
cooked butter,
or clarified butter.
All sentient beings also call it milk;
therefore, I say there is no curd in milk.
If it truly were present,
why could it not be given two names?
Just as a person with two skills
is called a master of gold
and iron.
When it is curd, there is no milk,
fresh butter,
cooked butter, or clarified butter.
Sentient beings also call it curd,
not milk,
not fresh or cooked butter, or clarified butter;
it is also like this.
Good man!
There are two kinds of cause:
The first is the principal cause (*zhèngyīn*),
the second is the conditioning cause (*yuányīn*).
The principal cause
is like milk producing curd;
the conditioning cause
is like stirring and warming, etc.
Because it is produced from milk,
therefore it is said that the potentiality for curd is present within milk."
*Shīzǐhǒu Púsà* said:
"World-Honored One!
If milk does not possess the potentiality for curd,
then a horn also does not possess it.
Why is curd not produced from a horn?"
"Good man!
A horn can also produce curd.
Why is this?
I also stated that the conditioning cause is twofold:
first, stirring,
second, warming.
Since the nature of the horn is warm,
it can also produce curd."
*Shīzǐhǒu* said:
"World-Honored One!
If a horn can produce curd,
why do people seeking curd seek milk and not take the horn?"
The *Fó* said:
"Good man!
This is why I speak of the principal cause
and the conditioning cause.
The Bodhisattva Shīzǐhǒu said:
"If milk originally had no inherent characteristic (xìng) of curds (lào),
but only now possesses it,
then milk originally has no Āmóluó (mango) tree (xìng),
so why does it not grow?
Because both are originally absent.
"Good man!
Milk is also able to generate an Āmóluó tree.
If you irrigate it with milk,
it will grow five feet in a single night.
For this reason,
I speak of two causes.
Good man!
If all phenomena (fǎ) arose from a single cause,
then the difficulty (nàn) could be expressed,
'Why is milk unable to give birth to an Āmóluó tree?'
Good man!
Just as the Four Great Elements (sì dà),
serve as causal conditions (yīnyuán) for all form (sè),
yet the forms are individually different,
their distinctions varying.
For this reason,
the Āmóluó tree does not grow in milk.
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
As the Buddha has taught,
there are two types of causes:
the Direct Cause (zhèngyīn),
and the Conditioning Cause (yuányīn).
What kind of cause is the Buddha Nature (fóxìng) of sentient beings?
"Good man!
The Buddha Nature of sentient beings also has two types of causes:
one is the Direct Cause,
the second is the Conditioning Cause.
The Direct Cause is sentient beings themselves,
and the Conditioning Cause is the Six Pāramitās (liù bōluómì).
Shīzǐhǒu said:
"World-Honored One!
I now definitively know that milk possesses the characteristic of curds (lào xìng).
Why is this?
I see people in the world seeking curds
take only milk
and never take water.
Therefore, one ought to know that milk possesses the characteristic of curds.
"Good man!
What you have asked
is incorrect.
Why is this?
All sentient beings who wish to see their reflection (miàn xiàng),
immediately take a knife.
Shīzǐhǒu said:
"World-Honored One!
For this reason,
milk possesses the characteristic of curds.
If the knife lacked the reflection,
why would one take the knife?
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
If a reflection were definitely present within this knife,
why would it be inverted,
appearing tall when held vertically,
and wide when held horizontally?
If it were your own face,
why would you see it as tall?
If it were another's face,
how could you call it your own reflection?
If based on your own face,
you see another's face,
why do you not see the reflection of a donkey or a horse?
Shīzǐhǒu said:
"World-Honored One!
The visual ray (yǎnguāng) reaches it (the knife),
therefore the face appears long.
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
This visual ray, in reality, does not reach it.
Why is this?
Because the near and the far are seen simultaneously,
and the objects in between are not seen.
Good man!
If the light were to reach it and thereby allow seeing,
and since all sentient beings see fire,
why are they not burned?
If a person sees a white object from afar,
they should not have doubts: Is it a crane (hè)?
A flag (fān)?
A person?
A tree?
If the light reaches it,
how is it possible to see objects within rock crystal (shuǐjīng),
or fish and stones in deep water (yuān)?
If it does not reach,
why is it possible to see objects within rock crystal,
but not possible to see the colors beyond a wall?
Therefore, to say that the visual ray reaches it and thus causes it to appear long
is incorrect.
Good man!
Regarding your statement
that milk possesses curds (lào),
why does the person selling milk take only the price of milk
and not demand the value of the curds?
The person selling a pregnant mare (cǎomǎ)
takes only the price of the mare
and does not demand the value of the foal (jū).
Good man!
People in the world,
because they have no descendants (zǐxī),
seek to marry a wife (pìn fù).
If the wife becomes pregnant,
one cannot say it is a daughter (nǚ).
If you say it is a daughter,
and because she possesses the nature of a son (ér xìng),
she should therefore be married—
this reasoning is incorrect.
Why is this?
If the nature of a son is present, the nature of a grandson (sūn) should also be present.
If the nature of a grandson is present, then they are brothers.
Why is this?
Because they are born from the same womb (fù).
Therefore I say a daughter lacks the nature of a son.
If the nature of curds (lào xìng) is present in milk,
why are the five tastes not perceived simultaneously?
If within the seed of a tree there were the full five-zhang (fifteen-meter) substance (zhì) of a Nígōutuó (Nyagrodha) tree,
why are the differences in the sprouts and stems (yá jīng),
branches and leaves (zhī yè),
flowers and fruits (huā guǒ), shapes and colors not seen simultaneously?
Good man!
The color of milk changes over time,
the taste changes,
the resulting product changes,
and it is likewise even up to ghrita (tíhú, clarified butter).
How can it be said that milk possesses the characteristic of curds?
"Good man!
Suppose there is a person who is going to take (serve) sū (fresh butter) tomorrow,
but already complains of its odor today.
If you say that the characteristic of curds is definitely present in milk,
it is also like this.
Good man!
Suppose there is a person
who has a brush, paper, and ink,
and mixes these to form characters.
But in the paper itself, there are fundamentally no characters.
Because they are fundamentally absent, they are produced conditionally through causal factors (jiǎ yuán).
If they were fundamentally present,
why would various causal factors be necessary?
For example, blue (qīng) and yellow (huáng),
combine to form green (lǜ sè).
You ought to know that these two
fundamentally lack the characteristic of conditioned combination (yuán xìng).
If they were fundamentally present,
why would combination be necessary?
Good man!
For example, sentient beings gain life (mìng) through food (shí),
yet truly there is no life within this food.
If life were fundamentally present,
then before the food was eaten,
the food ought to be life itself.
Good man!
All phenomena fundamentally lack inherent characteristic (xìng).
For this reason, I speak this verse (jì):
"Good man!
All phenomena
arise due to causal conditions,
and cease due to causal conditions.
Good man!
If sentient beings inherently possessed Buddha Nature (fóxìng),
then all sentient beings ought to possess the Buddha Body (fó shēn),
just as I do now.
The Buddha Nature of sentient beings is neither damaged nor destroyed,
neither pulled nor grasped,
neither tied nor bound.
It is like the space (xūkōng) present within sentient beings.
All sentient beings completely possess space.
Because it is without hindrance (wú guà ài),
they each do not perceive this space within themselves.
If sentient beings lacked space,
then there would be no coming and going,
walking, standing, sitting, or lying down,
no birth and no growth.
For this reason,
I teach in the Sūtras (jīng) that all sentient beings possess the space element (xūkōng jiè).
The space element
is named space.
The Buddha Nature of sentient beings is also like this.
Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (shí zhù Púsà) are barely able to perceive it,
like a vajra gem (jīngāng zhū).
Good man!
The Buddha Nature of sentient beings is the sphere of the Buddhas (fó jìngjiè);
it is not known by Śrāvakas (shēngwén) or Pratyekabuddhas (yuánjué).
All sentient beings do not see the Buddha Nature,
therefore they are constantly tied down by afflictions (fánnǎo),
revolving in the cycle of birth and death (shēngsǐ).
Because they see the Buddha Nature,
they cannot be bound by various knots and afflictions (jié fánnǎo),
they are liberated from birth and death,
and attain Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán)."
Śīzihǒu
Púsà said: "
World-Honored One! All sentient beings possess the nature of Buddhahood [fóxìngxìng],
just as milk possesses the nature of ghee [làoxìng].
If milk were without the nature of ghee,
why would the Buddha speak of two types of causes:
first, the primary cause [zhèngyīn],
and second, the contributing cause [yuányīn]?
The contributing causes [yuányīn] are:
first, stirring [láo],
and second, heating [nuǎn].
The empty space [xūkōng] has no nature [wúxìng];
therefore, there are no contributing causes for it.
The Buddha said:
"Good
Man! If the nature of ghee were already definitively present in milk,
why would contributing causes be needed?"
Śīzihǒu
Púsà said: "
World-Honored One! Because the nature is present,
contributing causes are needed.
Why is this?
It is for the sake of making it clearly visible.
The contributing cause [yuányīn] is precisely the manifesting cause [liǎoyīn].
World-Honored One!
For instance, just as objects are already present in darkness,
but for the sake of seeing them,
a lamp is used to illuminate and manifest them.
If they were not fundamentally present,
what would the lamp illuminate?
Similarly,
a jar exists in the clay,
so people,
water,
wheels,
ropes,
sticks, and so forth are needed to act as the manifesting cause [liǎoyīn].
Similarly, for the seeds of the Banyan tree [Nígūtuó],
earth,
water,
and manure are needed to act as the manifesting cause [liǎoyīn].
The stirring and heating of milk
are also like this; they are needed to act as the manifesting cause.
Therefore, although the nature is present beforehand,
it must rely on the manifesting cause [liǎoyīn];
only then can it be seen.
Based on this meaning,
we can definitively know that the nature of ghee is already present in the milk.
"Good Man!
If the nature of ghee were definitively present in the milk,
then it would already be the manifesting cause.
If it were the manifesting cause,
what further manifestation would be needed?
Good Man!
If it were the manifesting cause [liǎoyīn],
and the nature itself were what manifests,
it should constantly manifest itself;
if it cannot manifest itself,
how can it manifest others?
If you say that the manifesting cause has two natures:
one that manifests itself [zìliǎo],
and one that manifests others [tāliǎo],
this idea is incorrect.
Why?
The manifesting cause is a single phenomenon [yīfǎ];
how can it have two?
If it has two,
then milk should also be two.
If milk does not possess two aspects,
how can the manifesting cause [liǎoyīn] alone possess two?
Śīzihǒu
said: "World-Honored One!
Just as common people say,
‘I am with eight people’ (including oneself),
the manifesting cause [liǎoyīn] is also like that—
it manifests itself [zìliǎo]
and manifests others [tāliǎo]."
The Buddha said:
"Good Man!
If the manifesting cause [liǎoyīn] were like that,
then it would not be the manifesting cause.
Why is this?
The counter [shù] is able to count its own color [zìsè]
and the color of others [tāsè];
hence, it can be said to be eight.
However, this nature of color [sèxìng]
itself has no aspect of manifestation [liǎoxiàng];
since it has no aspect of manifestation,
it must rely on the nature of wisdom [zhìxìng]
to count itself and others.
Therefore, the manifesting cause [liǎoyīn]
cannot manifest itself,
nor can it manifest others.
Good Man!
If all sentient beings possess the nature of Buddhahood,
why must they cultivate [xiūxí] immeasurable merits [gōngdé]?
If you say that cultivation is the manifesting cause [liǎoyīn],
this is already the same as the destruction of ghee [làohuài].
If you say that the fruit [guǒ] is definitively present within the cause [yīn],
then precepts [jiè],
concentration [dìng],
and wisdom [zhìhuì]
would have no growth or increase.
I see that worldly people fundamentally lack precepts,
meditation [chándìng],
and wisdom,
but after receiving instruction from a teacher,
they gradually increase and gain them.
If you say that the teacher's instruction is the manifesting cause [liǎoyīn],
at the time the teacher instructs,
the recipient has not yet acquired precepts,
concentration,
or wisdom.
If it is the manifestor [liǎo],
it should manifest what is not yet present;
how can it instead manifest precepts,
concentration,
and wisdom to cause them to grow?
Śīzihǒu
Púsà said: "
World-Honored One! If the manifesting cause [liǎoyīn] does not exist,
how can it be said that there is 'milk' and 'ghee'?
"Good Man!
There are generally three types of answers to difficulties [dánán] in the world:
First, the turning answer [zhuǎndá],
as previously explained:
Why are they called precepts [jiè]?
Because there is no regret,
and even for the attainment of great Nirvāṇa [Nièpán].
Second, the silent answer [mòrándá],
as when a Brāhmaṇa [Fànzhì] came and asked me,
‘Am I permanent [cháng]?’
At that time, I remained silent.
Third, the counter-question answer [yídá],
such as in this sūtra:
If the manifesting cause [liǎoyīn] has two,
why can't milk also have two?
Good Man!
I shall now give the turning answer [zhuǎndá].
Just as worldly people say
that 'there is milk and ghee' because attainment is definite [dìngdé],
therefore it is named 'having milk and having ghee.'
The nature of Buddhahood [Fóxìng] is also like this:
sentient beings possess the nature of Buddhahood [Fóxìng]
because they will see it in the future.
Śīzihǒu
said: "World-Honored One!
What the Buddha has said
is incorrect.
The past is already extinguished,
and the future has not yet arrived;
how can they be called existent?
If you say that 'will be present' [dāngyǒu] is called 'existent' [yǒu],
this idea is incorrect.
Just as people in the world,
seeing that someone has no children,
then say, 'He has no children.'
If all sentient beings lack the nature of Buddhahood,
how can it be said that all sentient beings completely possess the nature of Buddhahood?"
Fó said:
"Shànnánzǐ!
The past is named 'existent.'
For example, when planting an orange [seed],
the sprout grows and the seed perishes.
The sprout is also sweet,
and even when bearing fruit,
the taste is likewise [sweet],
but when ripe, it becomes sour.
Shànnánzǐ!
This sour taste
was entirely absent in the seed, the sprout, and even the developing fruit,
but following the time of its initial ripeness,
due to its form, color, and appearance, the sour taste arises.
This sour taste, originally non-existent, now exists.
Although originally non-existent now existent,
it is not without dependence on the origin.
In this way, the original seed,
though it has passed away,
is still called 'existent.'
Based on this meaning,
the past is named 'existent.'
Why is the future then named 'existent'?
For example, a person plants sesame (hú má).
Someone asks him,
'Why are you planting this?'
He replies,
'There is oil [in it].'
In reality, there is not yet any oil.
When the sesame is ripe,
the seeds are harvested, parched, and steamed,
pounded and pressed,
and then the oil is extracted.
Know that this person was not speaking falsely.
Based on this meaning,
it is named 'future existent.'
Why is the past again named 'existent'?
Shànnánzǐ!
For example, there is a person
who secretly insulted the king (wáng).
After years passed,
the king finally heard of it.
Having heard, he immediately asked:
'Why did you insult me?'
The person replied,
'Great King (Dàwáng),
I did not insult you.
Why?
The insulter has already perished.'
The king said:
'The one who was insulted,
I,
and your body both still exist;
how can you say [the insulter] perished?'
Due to this cause and condition, he lost his life.
Shànnánzǐ!
Although these two [the past action and the past self] were truly non-existent,
the consequence does not perish.
This is named 'past existent.'
Why is the future again named 'existent'?
For example, a person
goes to a potter (táoshī)
and asks, 'Is there a jar (píng)?'
He replies, 'There is a jar.'
In reality, the potter does not yet have a jar,
but because he has clay (ní),
he says there is a jar.
Know that this person was not speaking falsehoods.
That there is curds (là) in milk,
or the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) in sentient beings,
is likewise so.
If one desires to see the Fóxìng,
one should observe the season, form, and color.
Therefore, I say that all sentient beings completely possess the Fóxìng,
and this is truly not false.
The Lion's Roar (Shīzǐhǒu) said:
"If all sentient beings did not possess Fóxìng,
how could they attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi)?
It is due to the principal cause (zhèng yīn);
thus, sentient beings attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
What is the principal cause?
Namely, the Fóxìng.
World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If a Ní Jū Tuó (Nigrodha) seed
did not contain a Ní Jū Tuó tree,
why is it named a Ní Jū Tuó seed,
and not named a Qié Tuó Luó (Khadira) seed?
Shìzūn!
Just as the Gùtán (Gautama) lineage cannot be called the Āzhǐyē (Āditya) lineage,
and the Āzhǐyē lineage likewise cannot be called the Gùtán lineage,
the Ní Jū Tuó seed is also like this:
it cannot be called a Qié Tuó Luó seed,
and a Qié Tuó Luó seed cannot be called a Ní Jū Tuó seed.
Just as the Shìzūn cannot abandon the Gùtán clan lineage,
the Fóxìng of sentient beings is also like this.
Based on this meaning,
one must know that all sentient beings completely possess Fóxìng."
Fó said:
"Shànnánzǐ!
If you say that the Ní Jū Tuó [tree] exists inside the seed,
this reasoning is incorrect.
If it truly exists,
why is it not seen?
Shànnánzǐ!
Just like worldly objects,
there are causes and conditions for why they cannot be perceived.
What are these causes and conditions?
That which is distant cannot be seen,
like the tracks of a bird in the sky.
That which is too close cannot be seen,
like a person’s eyelashes.
Due to damage it cannot be seen,
like someone whose faculties (gēn) have failed.
Due to confused thought it cannot be seen,
like a mind that is not focused.
Due to being too minute it cannot be seen,
like tiny dust motes.
Due to obstruction it cannot be seen,
like a star behind the clouds.
Due to being too numerous it cannot be seen,
like sesame seeds (má) within a pile of grain (dào).
Due to being too similar it cannot be seen,
like a bean within a pile of beans.
The Ní Jū Tuó tree is not subject to these eight types of causes and conditions.
If it truly exists [in the seed],
why is it not seen?
If you say that it is not seen because it is minute (xì) or obstructed,
this reasoning is incorrect.
Why?
Because the characteristic form of a tree is coarse (cū).
If you say its nature is minute,
how can it increase and grow?
If you say it cannot be seen due to obstruction,
it should constantly remain unseen.
Originally, there was no coarse characteristic,
but now the coarse is seen.
You must know that this coarse [form] originally lacked its own nature (xìng).
Originally, the nature of visibility was absent, but now it is visible.
You must know that this visibility also originally lacked nature.
The seed is likewise:
originally there was no tree,
but now there is one.
What fault is there in this?
Shīzǐhǒu said:
"As the Fó has said,
there are two types of causes:
the first is the principal cause (zhèng yīn),
the second is the assisting cause (liǎo yīn).
The Ní Jū Tuó seed, using the earth (dì),
water (shuǐ),
and manure (fèn) as the liǎo yīn,
causes the minute [form] to attain the coarse [form]."
Fó said:
"Shànnánzǐ!
If it was inherently existent,
why would it need the liǎo yīn?
If it originally lacked nature,
what is there for the liǎo [yīn] to reveal/assist?
If the Ní Jū Tuó [seed] originally lacked the coarse characteristic,
and it only generated the coarse [form] due to the liǎo yīn,
why does it not produce a Qié Tuó Luó tree?
Because both [seeds] are without [the coarse nature originally].
Shànnánzǐ!
If the minute is not seen,
then the coarse ought to be seen.
For example, a single dust particle
cannot be seen,
but when many particles combine, they ought to be visible.
In this way, the coarse [nature] in the seed ought to be visible.
Why?
Because within it, there are already sprouts (yá),
stems (jīng),
flowers (huā),
and fruits (guǒ).
In every single fruit, there are countless seeds.
In every single seed, there are countless trees.
Therefore, this is named 'coarse.'
Because this coarse [nature] exists,
it ought to be visible.
Shànnánzǐ!
If the Ní Jū Tuó seed
possesses the Ní Jū Tuó nature
and then produces a tree,
one sees with one's own eyes that this seed is destroyed by fire.
This destructive nature (shāo xìng) ought also to be originally existent.
If it was originally existent,
the tree ought not to arise.
If all phenomena (fǎ) originally possessed existence (shēng) and perishing (miè),
why does existence occur first and perishing occur later, rather than simultaneously?
Based on this meaning,
one must know that [phenomena] are without inherent nature (wú xìng)."
The Bodhisattva Shīzǐhǒu said:
"Shìzūn!
If the Ní Jū Tuó seed,
which originally lacked the nature of a tree, can produce a tree,
why does this seed not produce oil?
Because both [oil and the tree, in this case] are absent [in the seed's original nature].
"Good man!
Oil can also be produced from such seeds;
although they intrinsically lack that nature,
they exist due to conditions (yīnyuán).
Shīzǐhǒu said:
'Why is it not called sesame oil (húmá yóu)?'
'Good man!
Because it is not sesame.
Good man!
Just as fire arises from conditions for fire,
water arises from conditions for water;
although both arise from conditions,
they cannot coexist in each other.
The seeds of the Nīgōutuó (Nyagrodha) tree and sesame oil (húmá yóu) are also like this;
although both arise from conditions,
they do not generate each other.
Nīgōutuó seeds
are effective in curing cold.
Sesame oil (húmá yóu),
is effective in curing wind (or wind disorders).
Good man!
For example, sugarcane
arises due to conditions (yīnyuán).
Rock candy (shímì),
dark molasses (hēimì),
although sharing the same condition,
have different appearances;
rock candy (shímì) cures heat,
dark molasses (hēimì) cures cold."
Shīzǐhǒu Púsà said:
"World-Honored One!
Just as milk intrinsically lacks the nature of curds (lào),
hemp lacks the nature of oil,
Nīgōutuó seeds lack the nature of the tree,
and mud lacks the nature of a jar;
if all sentient beings lack the nature of the Buddha (Fóxìng),
then the Buddha’s previous statement that all sentient beings universally possess the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
and should thus attain Ànòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi),
is incorrect.
Why is this?
Humans and gods (tiān) have no fixed nature (wúxìng).
Because they have no fixed nature,
a human can become a god,
and a god can become a human,
due to the conditions of karma (yè yīnyuán),
and not due to nature.
A Púsà Móhēsà attains
Ànòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí due to the conditions of karma (yè yīnyuán).
If all sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
for what reason
do the Ìchǎntíděng (Icchantikas) sever all roots of goodness
and fall into Avīci Hell?
If the Bodhi Mind (Pútíxīn) is the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
the Ìchǎntíděng should not be able to sever it;
if it can be severed,
how can it be said that the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) is permanent (cháng)?
If it is not permanent,
it cannot be called the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
If all sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
why is there mention of 'first arousing the mind' (chū fāxīn)?
How can we speak of the Bǐpózhì (Vipannacārī)
and the Ābǐpózhì (Avipannacārī)?
Know that the Bǐpózhì is a person who lacks the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
World-Honored One!
A Púsà Móhēsà single-mindedly aims toward Ànòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
possessing great compassion and great pity (dàcí dàbēi),
seeing the defects of affliction in birth, aging, sickness, and death,
observing that Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán) is free from the defects of birth, aging, sickness, death, and affliction;
having faith in the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo) and the retribution of karma;
upholding the precepts.
Such dharmas (fǎ) are called the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
If the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) exists apart from these dharmas,
why must these dharmas be relied upon as conditions (yīnyuán)?
World-Honored One!
Just as milk, without requiring conditions, will surely turn into curds (lào),
but producing ghee (shēngsū) is not so—it must await conditions (yīnyuán),
namely, human effort,
water, a jar,
and the churning rope.
Sentient beings are also like this;
if they possess the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
they should be able to attain Ànòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí without conditions (yīnyuán).
If it definitely exists,
why do practitioners, seeing the suffering of the Three Evil Paths (sān'è kǔ),
birth,
aging,
sickness,
death,
then produce a receding mind (tuìxīn)?
Nor would they need to cultivate the Six Pāramitās (liù bōluómì);
they should immediately attain Ànòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
just as milk turns into curds (lào) without conditions.
However, one does not attain Ànòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí without relying on the Six Pāramitās.
For this reason,
it should be known that sentient beings universally lack the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
Just as the Buddha previously said that the Saṅgha Jewel (Sēngbǎo) is permanent (cháng);
if it is permanent,
then it is not impermanent (wúcháng);
if it is not impermanent,
how can one attain Ànòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí?
If the Saṅgha is permanent,
why is it said again that all sentient beings universally possess the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng)?
World-Honored One!
If sentient beings originally lacked the Bodhi Mind (Pútíxīn),
and also lacked the mind of Ànòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
and only gained it later,
the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) of sentient beings should also be like this:
originally nonexistent, existing later.
For this reason,
all sentient beings should lack the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng)."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent!
Excellent!
Good man!
You have long understood the meaning of the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
and you ask this question for the sake of sentient beings.
All sentient beings truly possess the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
You said that if sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature,
there should not be a 'first arousing of the mind' (chū fāxīn).
Good man!
Mind is not the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
Why?
The mind is impermanent (wúcháng),
while the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) is permanent (cháng).
You asked why there are those who possess a receding mind (tuìxīn)?
There is truly no receding mind.
If the mind truly receded,
one could ultimately not attain Ànòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
but because attainment is slow, it is called recession.
This Bodhi Mind (Pútíxīn) is truly not the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
Why?
Because the Ìchǎntíděng sever the roots of goodness
and fall into Avīci Hell.
If the Bodhi Mind (Pútíxīn) were the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
the Ìchǎntíděng group could not be called Ìchǎntí.
The Bodhi Mind (Pútí zhī xīn)
also could not be called impermanent (wúcháng).
Therefore, it is definitely known that the Bodhi Mind (Pútí zhī xīn) is truly not the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
"Good man!
You said that if sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
they should not rely on conditions,
just as milk turns into curds (lào);
this reasoning is incorrect.
Why?
If it is said that five conditions produce ghee (shēngsū),
know that the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) is also like this.
For example, among stones,
there is gold (jīn),
silver (yín),
copper (tóng),
and iron (tiě);
though all partake of the Four Great Elements (sì dà),
they have one name and one reality,
yet what is extracted from them is different in each case.
They necessarily rely on various conditions,
the merit of sentient beings,
the furnace and the labor of humans,
before they are produced.
Therefore, one must know that originally there is no nature of gold (jīnxìng).
The Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) of sentient beings is not called the Buddha;
it is only when the conditions of various merits merge
that the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) is seen,
and then Buddhahood (Fó) is attained.
You said that if all sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
why is it not seen?
This reasoning is incorrect.
Why?
Because the various conditions (yīnyuán) have not yet merged.
Good man!
For this reason,
I speak of two causes (yīn):
the principal cause (zhèngyīn)
and the conditioned cause (yuányīn).
The principal cause (zhèngyīn) is called the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
and the conditioned cause (yuányīn) is the arousing of the Bodhi Mind (pútíxīn).
By means of these two conditions (yīnyuán),
one attains Ànòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
like gold extracted from stone.
"Good man!
You say the Saṅgha (Sēng) is permanent,
and that all sentient beings lack Buddha-nature (Fóxìng).
Good man!
Sēng means harmony and assembly (Héhé).
There are two kinds of Héhé:
first, worldly Héhé;
second, ultimate truth Héhé.
Worldly Héhé is called the Śrāvaka (Shēngwén) Sēng.
Ultimate truth Héhé is called the Bodhisattva (Púsà) Sēng.
The worldly Sēng is impermanent,
but the Fóxìng is permanent.
Just as the Fóxìng is permanent,
so too is the ultimate truth Sēng.
Furthermore, there is a Sēng referred to as the harmony of the Dharma (Fǎ Héhé).
Fǎ Héhé refers to the Twelve Divisions of the Scriptures (Shí'èr Bù Jīng).
The Shí'èr Bù Jīng are permanent;
therefore, I say that the Dharma
and the Sēng are permanent.
Good man!
Sēng means Héhé.
Héhé also refers to the Twelve Nidānas (Shí'èr Yīnyuán).
Within the Shí'èr Yīnyuán, there is also Fóxìng.
The Shí'èr Yīnyuán are permanent.
Fóxìng is also like this;
therefore, I say the Sēng possesses Fóxìng.
Furthermore, Sēng refers to the harmony of all Buddhas (Zhū Fó Héhé);
therefore, I say the Sēng possesses Fóxìng.
"Good man!
You say that if sentient beings possess Fóxìng,
why are there those who regress
and those who do not regress?
Listen carefully!
Listen carefully!
I shall clearly analyze and explain this for you.
Good man!
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà) have thirteen factors (Fǎ)
that cause them to regress (Tuìzhuǎn).
What are these thirteen?
First, a lack of faith in the mind;
second, a lack of resolve in the mind;
third, doubt in the mind;
fourth, being stingy with one's body and wealth;
fifth, generating great fear regarding Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
wondering how it can cause sentient beings to be eternally extinguished;
sixth, the mind being unable to endure;
seventh, the mind not being gentle or compliant;
eighth, worry and distress;
ninth, displeasure;
tenth, negligence (fàngyì);
eleventh, self-contempt for one's own body;
twelfth, seeing one's own afflictions (Fánnǎo) as incapable of being destroyed;
thirteenth, not delighting in the methods for advancing toward Bodhi (Pú tí).
Good man!
These are called the thirteen factors
that cause Bodhisattvas to regress from Bodhi.
Furthermore, there are six factors that destroy the Bodhi mind.
What are these six?
First, stinginess regarding the Dharma;
second, generating unwholesome thoughts toward sentient beings;
third, associating closely with bad friends (Èyǒu);
fourth, not diligently engaging in vigorous effort (Jīngjìn);
fifth, self-aggrandizement and arrogance (Jiāomàn);
sixth, being preoccupied with worldly affairs.
These six factors are thus able to destroy the Bodhi mind.
Good man!
There are people who, upon hearing that the World-Honored Buddhas (Fó Shìzūn) are the teachers of humans and gods,
are supreme and peerless among sentient beings,
and excel over Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Pìzhīfó), and so forth.
Their Dharma Eye (Fǎyǎn) is clear,
perceiving the Dharma without obstruction,
and they are able to ferry sentient beings across the great sea of suffering.
Having heard this, they immediately generate a great vow:
'Just as there are such people in the world,
I shall also attain this.'
Due to this cause and condition,
they generate the mind of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmǐao Sānpú tí).
Or perhaps they generate the Bodhi mind after being instructed and admonished by others.
Or perhaps they hear that Bodhisattvas practice asceticism for asaṃkhyeya kalpas,
and only then attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmǐao Sānpú tí.
Having heard this, they reflect:
'I am currently incapable of such ascetic practices.
How can I attain it?'
Therefore, there is regression.
"Good man!
Furthermore, there are five factors that cause the regression of the Bodhi mind.
What are these five?
First, delighting in leaving the household life in heterodox paths (Wàidào);
second, not cultivating the mind of Great Compassion (Dà Cí);
third, habitually seeking out the faults and transgressions of Dharma masters (Fǎshī);
fourth, always delighting in remaining within Saṃsāra (Shēngsǐ);
fifth, not liking to receive, uphold, recite, write, or explain the Shí'èr Bù Jīng.
These are called the five factors that cause the regression of the Bodhi mind.
Furthermore, there are two factors that cause the regression of the Bodhi mind.
What are these two?
First, greedily delighting in the five desires (Wǔ Yù);
second, being unable to revere and respect the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo).
Due to all such causes and conditions,
the Bodhi mind regresses."
"What, furthermore, is called the Mind of Non-Retrogression (Bùtuì zhī Xīn)?
If there is a person who, upon hearing that the Buddha is able to deliver sentient beings from birth, aging, sickness, and death,
without seeking counsel from a teacher,
naturally cultivates practice and attains Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi).
If the Bodhi Way (Pútí Dào) is attainable,
I ought to cultivate practice and surely attain it.
Because of this reason, one generates the Bodhi Mind (Pútí Xīn).
All merits created, whether great or small,
are all dedicated toward Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
One makes this solemn vow:
'May I always be able to draw near to all Buddhas and the Buddha's disciples,
always hear the profound Dharma, and possess complete Five Faculties (Wǔ Qíng),
and should I encounter suffering and hardship, never lose this mind.
Furthermore, I vow that all Buddhas and their disciples,
shall always generate a joyful mind toward me,
and possess the Five Roots of Goodness (Wǔ Shàngēn).
If sentient beings cut down my body,
sever my hands and feet,
or my head, eyes, or limbs,
I shall generate great compassionate loving-kindness (Dà Cí Xīn) toward these people,
deeply rejoice,
knowing that such persons are helping me increase the conditions for Bodhi (Pútí Yīnyuán),
for if these conditions did not exist,
how could I attain Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí?
Furthermore, I make this vow:
'May I not acquire the body of one who is rootless (Wú Gēn),
or bi-rooted (Èr Gēn),
or a woman's body.
May I not be bound to others,
not encounter evil masters,
not belong to evil kings,
and not be born in an evil country.
If I obtain a good body, with truly pure lineage (Zhǒngxìng),
and abundant wealth, may I not give rise to arrogance.
May I always hear the Twelve Divisions of the Sūtras (Shí'èr Bù Jīng),
accept, uphold, read, and recite them,
write them down, and explain them.
If I preach and explain anything for sentient beings,
may the listeners respect and believe without doubt,
and never generate ill will toward me.
I would rather hear little,
but understand the essence of the meaning thoroughly,
than hear much,
yet be unclear about the meaning.
I vow to be a master of the mind (Xīn Shī),
not mastered by the mind.
May my deeds of body, speech, and mind not associate with evil.
May I be able to bestow peace and joy upon all sentient beings.
May my body, precepts, mind, and wisdom be immovable like a mountain.
Desiring to receive and uphold the Supreme True Dharma (Wúshàng Zhèngfǎ),
I will generate no stinginess regarding my body, life, or wealth.
I will not use impure things for meritorious deeds.
I will live by right livelihood (Zhèng Mìng), and my mind will be free of deceit or flattery.
When receiving kindness, I will always be mindful of it;
a small kindness will be repaid with a great reward.
May I skillfully know all worldly arts and crafts,
and skillfully understand the local dialects and languages of sentient beings.
When reading, reciting, and writing the Twelve Divisions of the Sūtras,
I shall not give rise to a mind of slackness or laziness.
If sentient beings are unwilling to listen,
I will use skillful means (Fāngbiàn) to guide them,
causing them to be pleased to listen.
My words shall always be gentle,
and my mouth shall not speak evil.
I will make those who are disharmonious become harmonious.
I will cause those who have worries and fears to abandon them.
In times of famine, I will ensure they obtain abundance.
In times of sickness, I will act as a great king of physicians (Dà Yī Wáng),
controlling wealth and treasures needed for medicine and treatment,
causing the sick to be completely healed.
During the eon of warfare (Dāobīng zhī Jié),
I will possess great power and force to stop the violence and cruelty,
allowing none to remain.
I will be able to sever the various fears of sentient beings,
namely: death,
imprisonment,
beating,
water, fire, kings, or thieves,
poverty, breaking precepts,
evil reputation, and evil paths (È Dào).
Such fears as these,
I shall completely eliminate.
I will generate deep reverence toward my parents and teachers.
Amidst enemies and hated persons, I will generate great compassionate loving-kindness.
I will constantly cultivate the Six Remembrances (Liù Niàn),
the Gate of Emptiness Samādhi (Kōng Sānmèi Mén),
the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yīnyuán),
contemplation of birth and extinction (Shēngmiè),
in-breathing and out-breathing,
Heavenly Conduct (Tiān Xíng), Brahmā Conduct (Fàn Xíng), and Sagely Conduct (Shèng Xíng),
Vajra Samādhi (Jīngāng Sānmèi),
and Śūraṅgama Samādhi (Shǒuléngyán Dìng).
In places devoid of the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo), may I personally attain a tranquil mind.
If my body and mind endure great suffering,
may I not lose the mind of Supreme Bodhi (Wúshàng Pútí Xīn).
May I not become content with the mind of a Śrāvaka (Shēngwén) or a Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó).
In places devoid of the Three Jewels, I shall constantly renounce home life within the methods of external paths (Wàidào Fǎ),
in order to destroy wrong views (Xiéjiàn), but not practice their ways.
May I attain mastery over the Dharma (Fǎ Zìzài),
and attain mastery over the mind (Xīn Zìzài).
Regarding conditioned phenomena (Yǒuwéi Fǎ),
may I clearly see their faults.
Cause me to fear the realization of the Two Vehicles (Èr Chéng Dàoguǒ),
just as one who cherishes life fears abandoning the body.
For the sake of sentient beings, I joyfully dwell in the Three Evil Paths (Sān È),
just as sentient beings joyfully dwell in Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Dāolì Tiān).
For the sake of every single being, I will endure the suffering of the hells for measureless eons,
without my mind generating regret.
Seeing others gain benefit,
I will not generate jealousy,
but constantly generate joy,
as if I myself had attained happiness.
If I encounter the Three Jewels,
I shall make offerings of clothing,
food, bedding,
housing, medicine,
lamps, flowers, incense,
music, banners, canopies,
and the Seven Treasures (Qī Bǎo).
If I receive the Buddha's precepts,
I will firmly protect and uphold them,
and never generate the thought of transgression or breaking them.
If I hear of the difficult and painful ascetic practices (Kǔ Xíng) of the Bodhisattvas (Púsà),
my mind will rejoice and not give rise to regret.
May I spontaneously know the events of my past lives (Sùmìng zhī Shì),
and never commit the deeds motivated by greed (tān), hatred (chēn), and delusion (chī).
I will not accumulate causes and conditions (Yīnyuán) merely for the sake of future rewards (Guǒ Bào).
Regarding present joys, I will not generate grasping attachment.
Good man (Shàn Nánzǐ)!
If there is one who can generate such vows,
this is called a Bodhisattva who will ultimately not regress from the Bodhi Mind.
They are also called a Donor (Shī Zhǔ),
one who can see the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
clearly understand the Buddha Nature (Fó Xìng),
be able to discipline sentient beings and deliver them from saṃsāra (Shēngsǐ),
and skillfully protect and uphold the Supreme True Dharma.
They can fully attain the Six Pāramitās (Liù Bōluómì).
Good man!
For this reason,
the Mind of Non-Retrogression is not called the Buddha Nature.
“Shàn Nánzǐ!
You must not, because you possess a retreating mind,
say that all sentient beings lack Fóxìng (Buddha nature).
For example, two people both heard that in another region there was a mountain of seven treasures (Qībǎo Shān).
The mountain had a clear spring,
whose flavor was sweet and excellent.
Those who were able to reach it
would forever break the cycle of poverty.
Those who drank its water
would increase their lifespan by ten thousand years.
However, the road was extremely distant,
perilous, obstructed, and full of difficulties.
At that time, those two people
both desired to go together.
One person prepared various necessary supplies for the journey,
while the other went empty-handed, carrying nothing.
They proceeded onward together,
and on the road encountered a person
who carried many treasures and was fully equipped with the seven valuables (Qīzhēn).
The two people immediately stepped forward and asked:
‘Honorable Sir!
Does that land truly possess the Mountain of Seven Treasures (Qībǎo Shān)?’
That person replied:
‘It truly exists and is not false.
I have already acquired the treasures
and drunk its water.
I only suffered from the road being perilous and full of bandits.
It is sandy, saline, full of thorns and brambles, and lacks water and grass.
Ten million may go,
but those who reach it are very few.’
Having heard this,
one person immediately regretted [going],
and quickly made this statement:
‘The road is both extremely distant,
and the difficulties are numerous.
Innumerable people have gone,
but few have reached the destination.
How could I possibly be able to arrive there?
My current assets are just barely enough to sustain myself.
If I travel this road,
I might lose my body and life.
If my body and life are not complete,
where is the long life?’
The other person replied:
‘If someone else can pass,
I can also pass.
If I successfully reach the fruit (goal),
I will obtain my wish:
gathering precious treasures
and drinking the sweet water.
If I do not reach it,
I will take death as my limit.’
At this time, of the two people,
one regretted and returned,
and the other proceeded onward and arrived at the mountain.
He acquired many treasures,
drank the water as desired,
took many of his acquired possessions,
returned to his dwelling place,
provided for his parents,
and aided his clan relatives.
When the one who had regretted and returned saw this event,
a burning desire arose in his heart:
‘He went and has already returned.
Why am I staying here?’
He immediately prepared [supplies]
and traveled the road to depart.
The Mountain of Seven Treasures (Qībǎo Shān) symbolizes Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
The sweet and excellent water symbolizes Fóxìng (Buddha nature).
The two people symbolize two Púsà who first generate the resolve for the Way (Dàoxīn).
The perilous and evil road symbolizes Saṃsāra (Shēngsǐ).
The person they met symbolizes the Bhagavān Buddha (Fó Shìzūn).
The bandits symbolize the Four Māras (Sì Mó).
The sandy, saline, thorny brambles symbolize the various Kleśas (Fánnǎo).
The lack of water and grass symbolizes not cultivating the path of Bodhi (Pútí).
The one person who returned symbolizes the retreating Púsà (Tuìzhuǎn Púsà).
The one who went straight on symbolizes the non-retreating Púsà (Bútuì Púsà).
Shàn Nánzǐ!
The Fóxìng of sentient beings is constantly abiding and unchanging.
It is like that perilous road:
you cannot say that because a person regretted and returned,
it makes the road impermanent.
Fóxìng is likewise.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
In the path of Bodhi (Pútí Dào), there is ultimately no one who retreats.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
Just as the person who previously regretted [and returned],
when he saw his former companion return having acquired treasures,
mighty and at ease,
providing for his parents,
fully aiding his clan relatives,
and enjoying much peace and happiness.
Having seen this event,
a burning desire arose in his heart,
and he immediately prepared [supplies] and returned to the road to depart again,
not valuing his body and life,
enduring all difficulties.
Consequently, he reached the Mountain of Seven Treasures (Qībǎo Shān).
The retreating Púsà (Tuìzhuǎn Púsà) is also like this.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
All sentient beings are definitely going to achieve Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).
Because of this meaning,
I state in the Sūtras:
All sentient beings,
even those who commit the Five Heinous Crimes (Wǔ Nì),
violate the Four Grave Prohibitions (Sì Chóng Jìn), and Icchantikas (Yīchǎntí),
all possess Fóxìng."
Shīzǐhǒu said:
"Bhagavān (Shìzūn)!
How are Púsà classified as retreating (Yǒu Tuì)
and non-retreating (Bù Tuì)?"
“Shàn Nánzǐ!
If there is a Púsà who cultivates the karmic causes and conditions (yè yīnyuán) for the Thirty-Two Marks (Sānshí'èr Xiàng) of the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
they are named 'Non-retreating' (Bútuì).
They are named Púsà Móhēsà.
They are named 'Unmoving and Unchanging.'
They are named 'One who Compassionately Pities all Sentient Beings.'
They are named 'Victorious over all Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué).'
They are named Avaivartika (Āpíbázhì).
“Shàn Nánzǐ!
If a Púsà Móhēsà holds the precepts without wavering,
does not shift the mind of giving,
and abides in true speech like Mount Sumeru (Xūmí Shān),
by these karmic conditions,
they achieve the Flat Feet [Jī Píng Xiàng],
like the bottom of a lidded box.
“If a Púsà Móhēsà, towards their parents,
Upādhyāyas (Héshàng),
teachers, and even animals,
offers and provides sustenance with wealth acquired lawfully,
by these karmic conditions, they achieve the Mark of the Thousand-Spoked Wheel (Qiān Fú Lún Xiàng) on the soles of their feet.
“If a Púsà Móhēsà does not kill or steal,
and constantly generates joy towards their parents
and teachers,
by these karmic conditions, they achieve three marks:
First, the fingers are slender and long.
Second, the heel is long.
Third, the body is square and upright.
These three marks
share the same karmic condition.
“If a Púsà Móhēsà practices the Four Means of Embracing (Sì Shè Fǎ) to gather sentient beings,
by these karmic conditions,
they attain webbed fingers [Wǎngmàn Zhǐ],
like a king white goose.
“If a Púsà Móhēsà,
when their parents
or teachers are suffering from illness,
washes and cleans them with their own hands,
holding and massaging them,
by these karmic conditions,
they attain soft hands and feet.
“If a Púsà Móhēsà upholds the precepts, hears the Dharma,
and gives charity without weariness,
by these karmic conditions,
they attain full ankles and joints, and the hairs of the body curl upwards (Shēn Máo Shàng Mǐ).
“If a Púsà Móhēsà single-mindedly listens to the Dharma
and proclaims the correct teachings,
by these karmic conditions,
they attain the calves like a deer king (Lù Wáng Chǐ).
“If a Púsà Móhēsà does not generate the intention to harm towards any sentient being,
is content with food and drink, constantly joyful,
gives charity, looks after the sick, and provides medicine,
by these karmic conditions,
their body is perfectly round, like the Nyagrodha tree (Nígōutuó Shù).
When standing, the hands extend past the knees (Lì Shǒu Guò Xī).
There is a flesh protuberance (Ròujì) on the crown,
the Mark of the Invisible Crown (Wú Jiàn Dǐng Xiàng).
“If a Púsà Móhēsà rescues those whom they see are fearful,
and gives clothes to those whom they see are naked and barefoot,
by these karmic conditions, they attain the Mark of the Concealed Genitals (Yīn Zàng Xiàng).
“If a Púsà Móhēsà draws near to the wise,
keeps far from the foolish,
is skilled and delighted in questioning and answering,
and sweeps and clears the traveling paths,
by these karmic conditions,
the skin is fine and soft,
and the body hairs curl to the right (Shēn Máo Yòu Xuán).
“If a Púsà Móhēsà constantly offers clothes, food and drink,
bedding, medicine,
fragrant flowers, lamps, and light to others,
by these karmic conditions,
they attain a body of golden color (Shēn Jīnsè),
constantly radiating brightness.
“If a Púsà Móhēsà, when practicing generosity,
is able to renounce valuable possessions without reluctance,
and does not distinguish between a field of merit (fútián) and a non-field of merit,
by these karmic conditions,
they attain the Mark of the Seven Full Places (Qī Chù Mǎn Xiàng).
“If a Púsà Móhēsà, when practicing giving (Bùshī),
does not generate doubt in their mind,
by these karmic conditions,
they attain a soft and gentle voice.
“If a Púsà Móhēsà seeks wealth lawfully
and uses it for generosity (Bùshī),
by these karmic conditions,
they attain full shoulder bones (Quē Gǔ Chōngmǎn),
a lion-like upper body (Shīzǐ Shàng Shēn),
and arms and elbows that are beautifully rounded and slender.
"If a Bódìsà Mòhēsà avoids double-tongue (slander),
harsh speech,
and hateful thoughts,
due to the karma of these actions,
he obtains forty teeth that are white, pure, even, and close-set.
"If a Bódìsà Mòhēsà cultivates great loving-kindness and compassion towards all sentient beings,
due to the karma of these actions,
he obtains the mark of the two teeth (èr yá xiāng).
"If a Bódìsà Mòhēsà constantly makes this vow:
'To those who come seeking,
I shall give according to their wishes.'
Due to the karma of these actions,
he obtains the lion's cheeks.
"If a Bódìsà Mòhēsà gives all food and drink required by various sentient beings,
due to the karma of these actions, he obtains the supreme flavor among flavors.
"If a Bódìsà Mòhēsà personally cultivates the shí shàn (Ten Virtuous Deeds),
and also transforms others (to do the same),
due to the karma of these actions,
he obtains the broad and long tongue.
"If a Bódìsà Mòhēsà does not slander others' faults,
and does not malign the Right Dharma,
due to the karma of these actions,
he obtains the fàn yīn shēng (Brahmic voice).
"If a Bódìsà Mòhēsà, upon seeing those who harbor resentment and hatred,
gives rise to a joyful mind [towards them],
due to the karma of these actions,
he obtains indigo-colored eyelashes.
"If a Bódìsà Mòhēsà does not conceal the virtues of others,
but praises and exalts their goodness,
due to the karma of these actions,
he obtains the bái háo xiāng (white curl mark).
"Shànnánzǐ!
When a Bódìsà Mòhēsà cultivates the karmic causes and conditions for these sānshí'èr xiāng (Thirty-two Marks),
he then attains the non-regressing mind of Pútí.
"Shànnánzǐ,
all sentient beings are inconceivable,
the realm of all Buddhas,
the fruition of karma,
and Fóxìng (Buddha Nature),
are likewise inconceivable.
Why is this?
These four dharmas
are all eternal (constant).
Because they are eternal, they are inconceivable.
All sentient beings are covered and obstructed by afflictions,
thus they are called constant;
when the constant afflictions are severed,
they are called impermanent.
If one says that all sentient beings are constant,
why then cultivate the Bā Shèng Dào Fēn (Eightfold Noble Path) to cut off all suffering?
If suffering is cut off, then it is called impermanent,
and the joy that is received is then called constant.
Therefore I say,
all sentient beings are covered and obstructed by afflictions and do not see the Fóxìng;
because they do not see it, they do not attain Nièpán.
Shīzǐhǒu said:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has stated,
all dharmas have two kinds of causes:
first, the primary cause,
second, the conditioning cause.
Based on these two causes,
there should be neither bondage nor release.
These wǔ yīn (Five Aggregates)
arise and perish moment by moment.
If they thus arise and perish,
who is there to be bound or released?
World-Honored One!
Due to these wǔ yīn,
subsequent wǔ yīn arise.
This aggregate itself ceases;
it does not reach that aggregate.
Although it does not reach that [aggregate],
it is capable of generating that aggregate.
It is like a sprout arising from a seed—
the seed does not reach the sprout.
Although it does not reach the sprout,
it is still capable of generating the sprout.
Sentient beings are also like this.
How then can there be bondage and release?"
"Shànnánzǐ!
Listen carefully,
listen carefully!
I shall explain and differentiate it for you.
Shànnánzǐ!
For instance, when a person abandons life (dies),
and undergoes great suffering,
relatives surround him,
wailing and lamenting sorrowfully.
That person is terrified and fearful,
not knowing where to seek reliance or refuge.
Although he still has the five senses,
he lacks awareness and perception.
His limbs tremble and shake,
unable to support themselves.
The body is cold and weak,
the vital heat is about to be exhausted.
He sees the signs of retribution for the good and evil previously performed.
Shànnánzǐ!
Just as when the sun is setting,
the shadows cast by mountains, hills, and mounds appear to shift eastwards,
but in principle, they do not pass westward.
The karmic fruition of sentient beings is also like this:
when this aggregate ceases,
that aggregate immediately continues to arise.
Like a lamp arising and darkness ceasing,
when the lamp ceases, darkness arises.
Shànnánzǐ!
Just as a wax seal stamps clay,
the seal meets the clay.
The impression of the seal ceases (is removed) and the form (pattern) is completed.
But this wax seal
does not transform and remain in the clay.
The pattern did not originate from the clay,
nor did it come from elsewhere.
