Due to the conditioning cause of the seal,
this pattern arose.
When the present aggregate ceases,
the zhōng yīn (intermediate state) aggregate arises.
This present aggregate
definitely does not transform into the zhōng yīn wǔ yīn (Five Aggregates of the intermediate state).
The zhōng yīn wǔ yīn,
likewise, did not arise spontaneously,
nor did they come from elsewhere.
Due to the present aggregate,
the zhōng yīn aggregate arises,
just as the seal stamps the clay;
the seal is removed, and the pattern is completed.
Although the name [of the aggregates] is not different,
the time periods are distinct.
Therefore, I state that the zhōng yīn wǔ yīn
are not seen by the physical eye,
but are seen by the celestial eye.
In this intermediate state, there are three kinds of sustenance:
first, mental sustenance (sī shí),
second, contact sustenance (chù shí),
third, consciousness sustenance (yì shí).
The intermediate state has two types:
one is the fruition of good karma,
two is the fruition of evil karma.
Due to good karma,
one obtains good contemplation and observation.
Due to evil karma,
one obtains evil contemplation and observation.
At the time when the parents join and unite,
[the zhōng yīn] proceeds toward the place of rebirth according to the karmic cause and condition.
It generates affection towards the mother,
and generates hatred towards the father.
When the father’s semen is emitted, [the zhōng yīn] believes it belongs to itself;
having seen it, the mind is pleased,
and gives rise to joy.
Due to the conditioning cause of these three kinds of afflictions,
the zhōng yīn aggregate ceases,
and the subsequent wǔ yīn arise,
just like the seal stamping the clay;
the seal is removed, and the pattern is completed.
At the time of birth, the various faculties may be complete
or incomplete.
Those with complete faculties see forms (sights),
and consequently give rise to greed.
Because greed arises, this is named affection (craving).
Because of delusion, greed arises;
this is named ignorance (wú míng).
Due to the two causes of greed and affection,
and ignorance,
the objects perceived are all inverted:
seeing constancy in the impermanent,
seeing self in the non-self,
seeing pleasure in suffering,
seeing purity in the impure.
Due to these four inversions,
one performs good and evil deeds.
Afflictions create karma,
karma creates afflictions;
this is named bondage.
For this reason,
this is called the arising of the wǔ yīn.
If this person is able to approach and associate with the Buddha, the disciples of the Buddha,
and various Shàn Zhīshì (Spiritual Friends),
he immediately hears and accepts the shí'èr bù jīng (Twelve Divisions of the Canon).
Because he hears the Dharma, he contemplates good realms.
Because he contemplates good realms, he obtains great wisdom.
Great wisdom is named right knowledge and views (zhèng zhī jiàn).
Because he obtains knowledge and views, he gives rise to a sense of remorse regarding saṃsāra (birth and death).
Because he generates remorse, he does not generate joy [in saṃsāra].
Because he does not generate joy, he is able to break the mind of greed.
Because he breaks the mind of greed, he cultivates the Bā Shèng Dào (Eightfold Noble Path).
Because he cultivates the Bā Shèng Dào, he obtains cessation of birth and death (saṃsāra).
Cessation of birth and death is named the attainment of liberation (jiětuō).
Just as fire not meeting firewood
is named extinction (cessation),
cessation of birth and death
is named extinction [and] deliverance (mièdù).
For this reason,
this is called the cessation of the wǔ yīn.
Shīzǐhǒu said:
"There is no thorn in the sky,
how then can one speak of pulling it out?
If the aggregates have no one who is bound,
how can there be bondage?"
Fó says:
"Good man!
Using the chains of *fánnǎo* (afflictions),
binding the five *yīn* (aggregates).
Separate from the five *yīn*, there are no distinct *fánnǎo*;
separate from the *fánnǎo*, there are no distinct five *yīn*.
Good man!
Like a pillar supporting a house:
separate from the house, there is no pillar,
separate from the pillar, there is no house.
The five *yīn* of sentient beings are also like this:
when there are *fánnǎo*, it is called binding;
when there are no *fánnǎo*, it is called liberation (*jiětuō*).
Good man!
Like a fist,
palms joined,
and tying knots—these three;
gathering and scattering, arising and ceasing, there is no separate *fǎ* (dharma).
The five *yīn* of sentient beings are also like this:
when there are *fánnǎo*, it is called binding;
when there are no *fánnǎo*, it is called liberation.
Good man!
As when speaking of *míngsè* (name and form),
binding,
and sentient beings:
if *míngsè* ceases, then there are no sentient beings.
Separate from *míngsè*, there are no distinct sentient beings;
separate from sentient beings, there is no distinct *míngsè*.
It is also said that *míngsè* binds sentient beings,
and it is also said that sentient beings bind *míngsè*.
Shīzǐhǒu says:
"World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*)!
Just as the eye cannot see itself,
the finger cannot touch itself,
the knife cannot cut itself,
feeling cannot feel itself;
how then does the *Rúlái* say that *míngsè* binds *míngsè*?
Why do you say that *míngsè* is sentient beings?
And that sentient beings are *míngsè*?
If you say that *míngsè* binds sentient beings,
that means *míngsè* binds *míngsè*."
Fó says:
"Good man!
Just as when two hands join,
there is no distinct *fǎ* (thing) that comes to join them.
*Míng* (name) and *Sè* (form) are also like this.
For this reason,
I say that *míngsè* binds sentient beings.
If they are separated from *míngsè*, they attain liberation;
therefore, I say that sentient beings achieve liberation."
Shīzǐhǒu says:
"World-Honored One!
If *míngsè* constitutes binding,
then all the *Āluóhàn*
who have not yet abandoned *míngsè* should also be bound."
"Good man!
Liberation is of two types:
first, the severing of the seed;
second, the severing of the fruit.
Speaking of the severing of the seed:
it means severing the *fánnǎo*.
The *Āluóhàn* and others have already severed the *fánnǎo*,
and the host of bonds are spoiled and broken;
therefore, the bonds as seeds cannot bind them.
Because they have not severed the fruit,
it is called binding by the fruit.
All the *Āluóhàn* do not perceive the Buddha Nature (*Fóxìng*).
Because they do not perceive it,
they do not attain *Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí*.
For this reason,
it can be said they are bound by the fruit;
it cannot be said they are bound by *míngsè*.
Good man!
For example, when lighting a lamp:
when the oil is not yet exhausted,
the light does not cease.
If the oil is exhausted,
extinguishing is without doubt.
Good man!
What is called the oil symbolizes all *fánnǎo*;
the lamp symbolizes sentient beings.
All sentient beings,
because of the oil of *fánnǎo*,
do not enter *Nièpán* (Nirvāṇa).
If the oil is severed,
they then enter *Nièpán*."
Shīzǐhǒu says:
"World-Honored One!
The lamp and the oil,
their two natures are mutually distinct.
Sentient beings and *fánnǎo* are not like this.
Sentient beings are precisely *fánnǎo*;
*fánnǎo* are precisely sentient beings.
Sentient beings are called the five *yīn*;
the five *yīn* are called sentient beings.
The five *yīn* are called *fánnǎo*;
*fánnǎo* are called the five *yīn*.
How then does the *Rúlái* compare them to a lamp?"
Fó says:
"Good man!
Similes are of eight kinds:
first, sequential simile (*shùnyù*);
second, inverse simile (*nìyù*);
third, immediate simile (*xiànyù*);
fourth, non-simile (*fēiyù*);
fifth, preceding simile (*xiānyù*);
sixth, subsequent simile (*hòuyù*);
seventh, preceding-and-subsequent simile (*xiānhòuyù*);
eighth, pervasive simile (*biànyù*).
What is the sequential simile?
As it is said in the *Jīng* (Sūtra):
When the heavens send down great rain,
all the ditches and channels are filled.
Because the ditches and channels are filled, small pits are filled.
Because the small pits are filled, large pits are filled.
Because the large pits are filled, small springs are filled.
Because the small springs are filled, large springs are filled.
Because the large springs are filled, small pools are filled.
Because the small pools are filled, large pools are filled.
Because the large pools are filled, small rivers are filled.
Because the small rivers are filled, great rivers are filled.
Because the great rivers are filled, the great ocean is filled.
The *Rúlái*'s Dharma rain (*fǎyǔ*) is also like this:
sentient beings satisfy discipline (*jiè*).
Because discipline is satisfied, the non-regretting mind is satisfied.
Because the non-regretting mind is satisfied, joy (*huānxǐ*) is satisfied.
Because joy is satisfied, detachment (*yuǎnlí*) is satisfied.
Because detachment is satisfied, tranquility (*ānyǐn*) is satisfied.
Because tranquility is satisfied, *Sānmèi* (Samādhi) is satisfied.
Because *Sānmèi* is satisfied, right knowledge and view (*zhèngzhījiàn*) are satisfied.
Because right knowledge and view are satisfied, repulsion (*yànlí*) is satisfied.
Because repulsion is satisfied, censure (*hēzé*) is satisfied.
Because censure is satisfied, liberation is satisfied.
Because liberation is satisfied, *Nièpán* is satisfied.
This is called the sequential simile.
"What is the inverse simile?
The great ocean has its origin in the great rivers.
The great rivers have their origin in the small rivers.
The small rivers have their origin in the large pools.
The large pools have their origin in the small pools.
The small pools have their origin in the large springs.
The large springs have their origin in the small springs.
The small springs have their origin in the large pits.
The large pits have their origin in the small pits.
The small pits have their origin in the ditches and channels.
The ditches and channels have their origin in the great rain.
*Nièpán* has its origin in liberation.
Liberation has its origin in censure.
Censure has its origin in repulsion.
Repulsion has its origin in right knowledge and view.
Right knowledge and view have their origin in *Sānmèi*.
*Sānmèi* has its origin in tranquility.
Tranquility has its origin in detachment.
Detachment has its origin in the joyful mind.
The joyful mind has its origin in non-regret.
Non-regret has its origin in upholding discipline.
Upholding discipline has its origin in the Dharma rain.
This is called the inverse simile.
"What is the immediate simile?
As it is said in the *Jīng*:
The mind-nature of sentient beings is like a monkey.
The nature of a monkey is to abandon one thing and seize another.
The mind-nature of sentient beings is also like this,
clinging to form,
sound,
smell,
taste,
touch,
and *fǎ* (mental phenomena),
without dwelling for even a moment.
This is called the immediate simile.
"How is it a non-analogy (fēi yù)?
Just as I previously told King Bō Sī Nì (Pāsenadi):
'Great King!
There are trusted people coming from the four directions,
each making this statement:
"Great King!
There are four great mountains,
coming from the four directions,
wishing to harm the people.
If the King hears this, what plan should he devise?"
The King said:
'Shìzūn!
If this arrival were to happen,
there is no place to flee or hide.
We can only focus wholeheartedly on observing the precepts (chíjiè) and practicing giving (bùshī).'
I then praised him, saying:
'Excellent!
Great King!
The four mountains I spoke of
are precisely the birth (shēng), aging (lǎo), sickness (bìng), and death (sǐ) of sentient beings.
Birth, aging, sickness, and death constantly afflict people.
Why does the Great King not cultivate the precepts and giving?'
The King said:
'Shìzūn!
Observing the precepts
and practicing giving—what kind of results are attained?'
I said:
'Great King!
You will receive much happiness among humans and gods (rén tiān).'
The King said:
'Shìzūn!
If the Nígōutuó tree observed the precepts and practiced giving,
would it also receive peace and security among humans and gods?'
I said:
'Great King!
The Nígōutuó tree cannot observe the precepts and cultivate giving.
If it were able to do so, it would receive [reward] without difference.'
This is called a non-analogy (fēi yù).
"How is it a prior-analogy (xiān yù)?
I speak in the sūtra (jīng):
For example, if a person is attached to and covets beautiful flowers,
while gathering them, they are swept away by the water.
Sentient beings are also like this.
They greedily accept the five desires (wǔ yù),
and are swept away and drowned by the waters of Saṃsāra (shēng sǐ shuǐ).
This is called a prior-analogy (xiān yù).
"How is it a subsequent-analogy (hòu yù)?
As the Fǎjù (Dhammapada) states:
"This is called a subsequent-analogy (hòu yù).
"How is it a prior-and-subsequent-analogy (xiān hòu yù)?
For example, just as a plantain tree (bā jiāo) dies when it bears fruit,
the foolish person who obtains nourishment is also like this.
Just as a mule carrying a fetus does not preserve its life for long.
"How is it an overarching-analogy (biàn yù)?
As stated in the sūtra (jīng):
In the Thirty-three Heavens (sān shí sān tiān), there is the Bōlìzhìduō tree.
Its roots penetrate the ground five yóuyán (yojanas) deep,
it is one hundred yóuyán high,
its branches and leaves spread out fifty yóuyán in the four directions.
When the leaves mature, they turn yellow.
When the devas (zhū tiān) see this, joy arises in their hearts,
thinking: 'These leaves will certainly fall soon.'
When the leaves have fallen, joy arises again,
thinking: 'These branches will certainly change color soon.'
When the branches have changed color, joy arises again,
thinking: 'This coloration will certainly produce buds (pào) soon.'
Seeing this, joy arises again,
thinking: 'These buds will certainly produce beaks/calyxes (zuǐ) soon.'
Seeing this, joy arises again,
thinking: 'These beaks/calyxes will certainly open and split soon.'
When they open and split,
fragrance spreads throughout fifty yóuyán,
and light illuminates far into eighty yóuyán.
At that time, the devas enjoy pleasure beneath it during the three summer months.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
My disciples are also like this.
The leaves turning yellow
analogizes my disciples intending to leave home (chūjiā).
The falling of the leaves
analogizes my disciples shaving their beards and hair.
The change in coloration
analogizes my disciples receiving the complete precepts (jù zú jiè) through the White-Four Karma (bái sì jiémó).
The initial production of buds
analogizes my disciples generating the mind of Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Saṃbodhi).
The beaks/calyxes analogize the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes (shí zhù Púsà) attaining sight of the Buddha-nature (fó xìng).
The opening and splitting analogize the Bodhisattvas attaining Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
The fragrance analogizes the immeasurable sentient beings in the ten directions receiving and upholding the prohibitions and precepts (jìn jiè).
The light analogizes the Rúlái's (Tathāgata's) name and title pervading the ten directions without obstruction.
The three summer months analogize the three Samādhis (sān sānmèi).
The devas in the Thirty-three Heavens receiving pleasure
analogizes all the Buddhas attaining permanence, bliss, self, and purity (cháng lè wǒ jìng) in the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
This is called an overarching-analogy (biàn yù).
"Shàn Nánzǐ!
The analogies brought forth do not necessarily require taking the entire comparison.
Perhaps only a small part is taken,
or perhaps a large part,
or perhaps the entirety is taken.
For instance, saying the Rúlái's face is like the full moon.
This is called a small part [of the analogy].
Shàn Nánzǐ!
For example, if a person has never seen milk,
and he turns and asks others:
'What category is milk?'
That person replies:
'It is like water,
honey,
and a cowrie shell.'
Water represents the characteristic of wetness.
Honey represents the characteristic of sweetness.
The cowrie shell represents the characteristic of color.
Although three analogies are given, they do not immediately convey the reality of milk.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
My analogy of the lamp (dēng yù),
analogizing sentient beings,
is also like this.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
Separate from water, there is no river.
Sentient beings are also like this;
separate from the Five Aggregates (wǔ yīn), there is no separate sentient being.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
Just as separate from the carriage body, wheels, axles,
spokes, and rims (fú wǎng),
there is no separate chariot,
sentient beings are also like this.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
If you wish to match the parts of that lamp analogy,
listen carefully,
listen carefully!
I shall now speak.
The wick (zhù) analogizes the Twenty-five Existences (èr shí wǔ yǒu).
The oil (yóu) analogizes craving (ài).
The light (míng) analogizes wisdom (zhì huì).
Dispelling and breaking the darkness analogizes breaking ignorance (wú míng).
The heat (nuǎn) analogizes the Holy Path (shèng dào).
Just as when the lamp oil runs out,
the light and flame extinguish;
when the sentient being's craving ends,
they then perceive the Fó Xìng (Buddha-nature).
Although there are still name and form (míng sè), they cannot be bound.
Although they dwell in the Twenty-five Existences,
they are not polluted by those existences."
Shīzǐhǒu (Simhanāda) said:
"Shìzūn!
The Five Aggregates of sentient beings are empty and possess nothing.
Who receives the teaching,
and who cultivates the path?"
The Fó (Buddha) said:
"Shàn Nánzǐ!
All sentient beings
all possess the mind of mindfulness (niàn xīn),
the mind of wisdom (huì xīn),
the mind of aspiration (fā xīn),
the mind of diligence and vigor (qín jīng jìn xīn),
the mind of faith (xìn xīn),
and the mind of concentration (dìng xīn).
Although such dharmas arise and cease moment by moment,
they still continue uninterruptedly through similar succession.
Therefore, this is called cultivating the path (xiū dào)."
Shīzǐhǒu said:
"Shìzūn!
If such dharmas
all cease moment by moment,
and this momentary cessation
also continues through similar succession,
how can cultivation take place?"
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
Just as a lamp, although it vanishes moment by moment,
still has light to dispel and break the darkness,
all phenomena, including the moments of thought (niàn), are also like this.
Good man!
Just as the food eaten by sentient beings, although it vanishes moment by moment,
it still allows the hungry to become satisfied.
For example, the best medicine, although it vanishes moment by moment,
is still able to heal illness.
The light of the sun and moon, although it vanishes moment by moment,
is still able to grow forests, grasses, and trees.
Good man!
Regarding your statement that if things vanish moment by moment, how can they grow?
Because the mind (xīn) is not cut off,
it is called growth.
Good man!
Just as when a person recites texts,
the characters and sentences recited do not occur at the same time;
the preceding does not reach the middle,
the middle does not reach the subsequent.
The person and the characters, as well as the mental concepts (xīn xiăng),
all vanish moment by moment (niàn niàn miè),
but because of prolonged cultivation (jiŭ xiū), skill is attained.
Good man!
For example, a goldsmith (jīn shī),
from the beginning of practicing the craft until his hair is white,
although things vanish moment by moment and the preceding does not reach the subsequent,
because of accumulated practice, his creations become superb.
Therefore, he is entitled to be called a good and excellent goldsmith.
Reading and reciting scriptures (jīng shū) is also like this.
Good man!
For example, a seed:
The earth does not instruct, ‘You must produce a sprout,’
but because of its fundamental nature (fă xìng),
the sprout arises naturally.
Furthermore, the flower does not instruct, ‘You must become a fruit,’
but because of its fundamental nature, the fruit arises naturally.
Sentient beings cultivating the path (xiū dào) are also like this.
Good man!
For example, the method of counting (shŭ fă):
One does not reach two;
Two does not reach three.
Although things vanish moment by moment, counting reaches thousands and ten thousands.
Sentient beings cultivating the path are also like this.
Good man!
Just as a lamp vanishes moment by moment,
the initial vanishing flame
does not instruct the subsequent flame,
‘I vanish, you arise, and you must destroy all darkness.’
Good man!
For example, a calf is born seeking milk.
The knowledge of seeking milk is truly untaught by anyone.
Although it vanishes moment by moment,
it is initially hungry and later satisfied.
Therefore, you should know that they are not similar.
If they were similar, they should not arise differently.
Sentient beings cultivating the path are also like this.
Although initially there is no increase,
because of prolonged cultivation,
they are able to destroy all afflictions (fán năo).”
Shīzihŏu (Lion’s Roar) said:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
As the Buddha has said,
a Srotāpanna (Xūtúohuán) having attained the realization of the fruit,
although born in a bad realm (è guó),
still maintains the precepts (chí jiè),
not killing,
stealing,
sexual misconduct,
duplicity (liăng shé),
or drinking alcohol.
The skandhas (yīn) of the Srotāpanna vanish in this location,
they do not reach the bad realm.
Cultivating the path is also like this,
it does not reach the bad realm.
If they were similar,
why does one not arise in a pure and marvelous land (jìng miào guótŭ)?
If the skandhas of the bad realm are not the skandhas of the Srotāpanna,
how is it possible that he does not commit evil karma (è yè)?”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
Although a Srotāpanna is born in a bad realm,
he ultimately does not lose the designation of Srotāpanna.
The skandhas are not similar;
this is why I used the calf as a metaphor.
Although a Srotāpanna is born in a bad realm,
by the power of the path (dào lì) he does not commit evil karma.
Good man!
For example, on Fragrant Mountain (Xiāngshān) there is a Lion King (Shīziwáng);
therefore, all flying birds and running beasts vanish their tracks,
and no one dares approach this mountain.
Sometimes this King goes to Snowy Mountain (Xuěshān),
and all birds and beasts still do not remain there.
A Srotāpanna is also like this.
Although he does not cultivate the path,
by the power of the path he does not commit various evils.
Good man!
For example, someone takes and eats sweet dew (gānlù).
Although the sweet dew vanishes,
by its powerful efficacy (lì shì), it can cause this person to be neither born nor to die.
Good man!
On Mount Sumeru (Xūmíshān) there is a supreme and marvelous medicine called Léngqiélì.
If someone takes it,
although it vanishes moment by moment,
by the power of the medicine, he does not encounter sickness or suffering.
Good man!
Just as the place where a Cakravartin (Zhuǎnlúnwáng) sits:
Although the King is not present,
no one dares approach.
Why is this?
Because of the King’s majestic power (wēi lì).
A Srotāpanna is also like this.
Although he is born in a bad realm and does not cultivate the path,
by the power of the path he does not commit evil karma.
Good man!
The Srotāpanna skandha vanishes here,
and although a different skandha arises,
he still does not lose the Srotāpanna skandha.
Good man!
For example, sentient beings, for the sake of fruit,
perform many labors and tasks on the seeds—
fertilizing, tending, irrigating—
yet before the fruit is obtained, the seed vanishes again;
it is still said that the fruit is obtained because of the seed.
The Srotāpanna skandha is also like this.
Good man!
For example, someone has enormous wealth and assets.
He had only one son who had already died.
This son had a son (the grandson),
who was living in another land.
That man suddenly and abruptly passed away.
The grandson, hearing this, returned to collect the assets and property.
Although he knew the wealth was not created by himself,
yet when he collected it, there was no one to stop or protect against him.
Why is this?
Because the lineage (xìng) is one.
The Srotāpanna skandha is also like this.”
Shīzihŏu said:
“As the Buddha spoke in verses:
‘World-Honored One (Shìzūn),
how should we cultivate the precepts (xiū jiè)?
How should we cultivate concentration (xiū dìng)?
How should we cultivate wisdom (xiū huì)?’”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
If someone accepts and upholds the moral prohibitions (jìn jiè),
but only for their own benefit, enjoying pleasure among humans and devas,
not for the salvation and liberation of all sentient beings,
not for protecting the Supreme Right Dharma (Wúshàng Zhèngfă),
but only for material gain (lì yăng),
fearing the three evil paths (sān è dào),
for longevity (mìng),
beauty and strength (sè lì),
peace (ān),
unimpeded eloquence (wú ài biàn),
fearing the laws of the king (wáng fă),
bad reputation and foul titles,
or for worldly affairs,
such upholding of precepts cannot be called cultivating the precepts.
Good man!
What is truly called cultivating the precepts?
When upholding the precepts,
if it is for the salvation and liberation of all sentient beings and for protecting the Right Dharma (Zhèngfă)—
to save those who are unsaved,
to enlighten those who are unenlightened,
to give refuge to those without refuge,
to enable those who have not entered Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) to enter it—
when cultivating in this manner,
one does not perceive the precept,
does not perceive the characteristics of the precept,
does not perceive the upholder,
does not perceive the result (guŏ bào),
and does not observe the breaking of the precepts (huĭ fàn).
Good man!
If one can be like this,
that is called cultivating the precepts.”
"How is the cultivation (xiūxí) of Samādhi
further defined? If, when cultivating Samādhi, it is done for one's own liberation,
or for profit and sustenance,
not for sentient beings,
not for protecting the Dhárma,
(but) for seeing the faults of greed and desire,
of foul food and the like,
(or of) the faculties of men and women, the nine orifices, being impure,
(or) for fighting, quarreling, hitting, stabbing,
and mutual killing and harming—
if one cultivates Samādhi for these reasons,
this cannot be called the cultivation (xiūxí) of Samādhi.
Good man!
How, then, is true cultivation (xiū) of Samādhi defined?
If one cultivates (xiūxí) Samādhi for sentient beings,
attaining an equal mind regarding sentient beings,
in order to enable sentient beings to attain the non-regressing Dhárma,
in order to enable sentient beings to attain the Śānta heart,
in order to enable sentient beings to attain the Mahāyāna,
in order to protect and uphold the supreme Dhárma,
in order to prevent sentient beings from regressing from Pútí,
in order to enable sentient beings to attain the Shǒuléngyán Samādhi,
in order to enable sentient beings to attain the Jīngāng Samādhi,
in order to enable sentient beings to attain Dhāraṇī,
in order to enable sentient beings to attain the Four Unimpeded Knowledges,
in order to enable sentient beings to see the Fóxìng—
when performing such practices,
one does not perceive Samādhi,
does not perceive the characteristics of Samādhi,
does not perceive the cultivator,
does not perceive the retribution (or result).
Good man!
If one can do thus,
this is called the cultivation (xiūxí) of Samādhi.
"How, then, is the cultivation (xiū) of wisdom (zhìhuì) defined?
If a cultivator reflects thus:
'If I cultivate (xiūxí) this wisdom,
then I will attain liberation,
crossing over the Three Evil Paths.
Who is able to benefit all sentient beings?
Who is able to save people from the path of Saṃsāra (shēngsǐ)?
For a Fó to appear in the world is as rare as the Yōutánpō flower.
I am now able to cut off all bonds of affliction (fánnǎo),
and will certainly attain the fruit of liberation.
Therefore, I should diligently cultivate wisdom (zhìhuì),
quickly sever afflictions (fánnǎo),
and soon achieve deliverance.'
A cultivator who practices thus,
cannot be called one who cultivates (xiūxí) wisdom (zhìhuì).
How is a true cultivator (xiūxí) defined?
If a wise person observes birth,
aging,
death,
and suffering,
(and sees that) all sentient beings are obscured by ignorance (wúmíng),
and do not know how to cultivate (xiūxí) the supreme, true path.
'May this body of mine take the place of all sentient beings in enduring great suffering and distress.
May all the poverty,
lowliness,
the mindset of breaking precepts,
the greed, hatred, and ignorance (tānchēnchī) karma of sentient beings,
may all this come and gather upon my body.
May sentient beings not give rise to covetousness,
and not be bound by name and form (míngsè).
May sentient beings quickly cross over Saṃsāra (shēngsǐ).
Even if I alone dwell (in Saṃsāra), may I not be weary of it.
May all (sentient beings) attain Anòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.'
When cultivating thus,
one does not perceive wisdom (zhìhuì),
does not perceive the characteristics of wisdom,
does not perceive the cultivator,
does not perceive the retribution (or result),
this is called the cultivation (xiūxí) of wisdom (zhìhuì).
Good man!
To cultivate (xiūxí) precepts (jiè) thus,
concentration (dìng),
and wisdom (zhìhuì),
is called a Púsà.
If one cannot cultivate (xiū) precepts, concentration, and wisdom thus,
this is called a Shēngwén.
"Furthermore, good man!
How, then, is the cultivation (xiūxí) of precepts (jiè) further defined?
If one can destroy the sixteen evil livelihoods (è lǜyí) of all sentient beings.
What are these sixteen?
First, for profit,
raising lambs,
and selling them after fattening them.
Second, for profit,
buying them and then slaughtering them.
Third, for profit,
raising pigs,
and selling them after fattening them.
Fourth, for profit,
buying them and then slaughtering them.
Fifth, for profit,
raising calves,
and selling them after fattening them.
Sixth, for profit,
buying them and then slaughtering them.
Seventh, for profit,
raising chickens to fatten them,
and selling them after fattening them.
Eighth, for profit,
buying them and then slaughtering them.
Ninth, fishing.
Tenth, hunting.
Eleventh, robbery.
Twelfth, being an executioner (kuíkuài).
Thirteenth, trapping flying birds with nets.
Fourteenth, using a double-tongue (slander).
Fifteenth, being a jailer (yùzú).
Sixteenth, chanting spells against dragons (zhòulóng).
To be able to eternally sever these sixteen evil karmas (èyè) for sentient beings,
is called cultivating precepts (jiè).
How is concentration (dìng) cultivated?
To be able to sever all worldly Samādhis,
namely, the Samādhi of No Body (wúshēn sānmèi),
which causes sentient beings to generate a deluded mind and believe it is Nièpán;
the Samādhi of Boundless Mind (wúbiān xīn sānmèi),
the Samādhi of Pure Aggregates (jìng jù sānmèi),
the Samādhi of the End of the World (shì biān sānmèi),
the Samādhi of the Cessation of the World (shì duàn sānmèi),
the Samādhi of the Nature of the World (shì xìng sānmèi),
the Samādhi of the Worldly Great Man (shì zhàngfū sānmèi),
and the Samādhi of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception (fēixiǎng fēifēixiǎng sānmèi)—
such concentrations as these,
which cause sentient beings to generate a deluded mind and believe they are Nièpán—
if one can eternally sever such Samādhis,
this is called the cultivation (xiūxí) of Samādhi.
How, then, is the cultivation (xiūxí) of wisdom (zhìhuì) defined?
To be able to destroy all worldly evil views (èjiàn).
All sentient beings possess evil views,
namely, that form (sè) is the self, and is also what belongs to the self.
The self is within form;
form is within the self.
And even consciousness (shí) is also considered thus.
The eternal (cháng) is the self;
when form perishes, the self remains.
Form is the self;
when form perishes, the self perishes.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
'The agent (zuòzhě) is called the self;
the recipient (shòuzhě) is called form.'
Furthermore, there are those who say:
'The agent is called form;
the recipient is called the self.'
Furthermore, there are those who say:
'There is no agent, no recipient;
things spontaneously arise and spontaneously perish,
all without cause or condition (yīnyuán).'
Furthermore, there are those who say:
'There is no agent, no recipient,
all things are created by Īśvara (Zìzài).'
Furthermore, there are those who say:
'There is no agent,
no recipient,
everything is produced by time (shíjié).'
Furthermore, there are those who say:
'The agent and recipient are both nonexistent;
the Five Great Elements (wǔ dà), such as earth, are called sentient beings.'
Good man!
If one can destroy such evil views (èjiàn) held by all sentient beings,
this is called cultivating wisdom (zhìhuì).
"Good man!
The cultivation (xiūxí) of precepts (jiè)
is for the tranquility of the body.
The cultivation (xiūxí) of Samādhi
is for the tranquility of the mind.
The cultivation (xiūxí) of wisdom (zhìhuì)
is for destroying the doubting mind.
Destroying the doubting mind is for the cultivation (xiūxí) of the path (dào).
Cultivating (xiūxí) the path is for seeing the Fóxìng.
Seeing the Fóxìng is for the attainment of Anòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Attaining Anòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí is for the attainment of the supreme Great Nièpán.
Attaining Great Nièpán is for severing the Saṃsāra (shēngsǐ) of all sentient beings,
all afflictions (fánnǎo),
all forms of existence (zhū yǒu),
all realms (zhū jiè),
and all truths (zhū dì).
Severing Saṃsāra (shēngsǐ) and ultimately severing the truths
is for the attainment of the attributes of permanence (cháng),
bliss (lè),
self (wǒ),
and purity (jìng) Dhárma.
Shīzǐhǒu (Siṃhanāda) said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
As the Fó has said,
if that which is neither born nor extinguished is called Great Nièpán,
then birth (shēng) is also thus: neither born nor extinguished.
Why should it not also be called Nièpán?"
"Good man!
It is so,
it is so.
Just as you have said.
Although this birth (shēng) is indeed neither born nor extinguished,
yet it possesses a beginning and an end."
"Shìzūn!
This dharma of birth and death also has no beginning and no end.
If it has no beginning and no end, then it is named permanence (cháng).
Permanence is Nièpán.
Why, then, is birth and death not named Nièpán?
"Good man!
This dharma of birth and death entirely possesses cause and effect (yīnguǒ).
Because it has cause and effect,
it cannot be named Nièpán.
Why is this?
Because the essence (tǐ) of Nièpán is without cause and effect."
Shīzǐhǒu said:
"Shìzūn!
Now, Nièpán also has cause and effect.
Just as the Buddha said:
'Just as the Buddha previously instructed the various Bǐqiū:
"I shall now speak of the path-fruit (dàoguǒ) of the Shā mén.
Speaking of the Shā mén,
this means one who is able to fully cultivate the precepts (jiè),
concentration (dìng),
and wisdom (zhìhuì).
The path (dào) refers to the Eight Noble Paths (Bā Shèng Dào).
The fruit (guǒ) of the Shā mén is called Nièpán."
Shìzūn!
If Nièpán is like this,
how can it not be a fruit?
How can you say that the essence (tǐ) of Nièpán is without cause and without fruit?
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
What I proclaim as the cause (yīn) of Nièpán
is the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng).
The nature (xìng) of the Buddha-nature does not give rise to Nièpán;
therefore, I say Nièpán is without cause.
Because it can destroy afflictions (fánnǎo), it is named the great fruit (dàguǒ).
Because it does not arise from the Path (Dào), it is named without fruit (wúguǒ).
Therefore, Nièpán is without cause and without fruit.
Shīzǐhǒu said:
"Shìzūn!
Is the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) of sentient beings entirely shared?
Or does each possess their own?
If it is shared,
then when one person attains Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
all sentient beings should also attain it simultaneously.
Shìzūn!
Just as twenty people share one enemy,
if one person is able to eliminate him,
the remaining nineteen people are also freed simultaneously.
The Fóxìng is also like this;
when one person attains it,
the rest should also attain it.
If each possesses their own, then it is impermanent (wúcháng).
Why is this?
Because it can be calculated and counted.
However, the Buddha said that the Fóxìng of sentient beings is not one
and not two.
If each possesses their own,
it should not be said that all Buddhas are equal,
nor should it be said that the Fóxìng is like space (kōng)."
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
The Fóxìng of sentient beings
is not one and not two.
All Buddhas are equal, just like empty space (xūkōng);
all sentient beings share it in common.
If there is someone who can cultivate the Bā Shèng Dào,
you should know that this person will attain clear vision.
Good man!
On the Xuěshān there is a grass named Rěnrǔ.
If an ox eats it, it turns into tíhú.
The Fóxìng of sentient beings is also like this."
Shīzǐhǒu said:
"According to what the Buddha says,
is the Rěnrǔ grass
one [single plant]?
Or many?
If it were one,
the ox would eat it all up.
If it were many,
how can you say that the Fóxìng of sentient beings is also like this?
Furthermore, as the Buddha says,
if one cultivates the Bā Shèng Dào,
they will then see the Fóxìng.
This meaning is not acceptable.
Why is this?
If the Path (Dào) is one,
like the Rěnrǔ grass,
then it should be exhaustible.
If it is exhaustible,
then once one person has cultivated it,
the rest will have no share.
If the Path (Dào) is many,
how can it be said that cultivation is complete,
nor can it be named Sàpóruò Zhì?
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
It is like a flat, level road,
where all sentient beings travel without obstruction.
In the middle of the road is a tree whose shade is cool and refreshing.
Travelers stop their carriages beneath it and rest.
Yet the tree shade perpetually remains and does not shift,
nor does it wear away or perish,
nor can anyone take it away.
The road symbolizes the Noble Path (Shèng Dào),
and the shade symbolizes the Fóxìng.
Good man!
For example, a great city
has only one gate.
Although many people pass through it, entering and exiting,
there is absolutely no one who can create an obstruction,
nor is there anyone who can break it down, damage it, or carry it away.
Good man!
For example, a bridge that people pass over,
similarly, no one can block, obstruct, damage, or carry it away.
Good man!
For example, a good physician universally treats all diseases,
and there is no one who can prohibit this physician from treating one patient while abandoning another.
The Shèng Dào and the Fóxìng are also like this."
Shīzǐhǒu said:
"Shìzūn!
The analogies cited
do not correspond to this meaning.
Why is this?
The first traveler on the road
obstructs those who come later.
How can you say there are no obstructions?
The rest [of the analogies] are all the same.
If the Shèng Dào and Fóxìng are like this,
then when one person cultivates it,
they should obstruct the rest.
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
What you have said
does not accord with the meaning.
The path (dào) to which I drew an analogy
is a partial analogy,
not applicable to everything.
Good man!
Worldly paths (shìjiān dào) indeed have obstructions,
distinctions between 'this' and 'that,'
and lack equality.
The Unstained Path (Wú Lòu Dào) is not like this;
it enables sentient beings to be without obstruction,
equal and non-dual.
It has no distinctions of location, 'this place' or 'that place.'
This true path (zhèng dào),
is able to act as the manifesting cause (liǎoyīn) for the Fóxìng of all sentient beings,
but not the generating cause (shēngyīn).
It is like a bright lamp
illuminating objects.
Good man!
All sentient beings share the same ignorance (wúmíng),
which is the condition (yīnyuán) for action (xíng).
You cannot say that when one person's ignorance
has conditioned action,
the ignorance of the rest should cease to exist.
All sentient beings possess ignorance,
which conditions action.
Therefore, it is said that the Twelve Conditioned Originations (Shí'èr Yīnyuán) are all equal.
The Unstained True Path (Wú Lòu Zhèng Dào) cultivated by sentient beings
is also like this;
it equally severs the afflictions (fánnǎo) of sentient beings,
the four modes of birth (sì shēng),
the various realms (zhū jiè),
and the path of existence (yǒu dào).
Based on this meaning,
it is named equality.
For those who realize it,
their mutual knowledge and insight
are without obstruction;
therefore, it is named Sàpóruò Zhì."
Shīzǐhǒu said:
"The bodies of all sentient beings
are not the same kind.
Some have divine bodies (tiān shēn),
some have human bodies (rén shēn),
animal bodies (chùshēng),
hungry ghost bodies (èguǐ),
or hell bodies (dìyù).
Such numerous bodies are various and not singular.
How can you say that the Fóxìng is one?
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
For example, if a person puts poison into milk (rǔ),
even up to tíhú, it all contains poison.
Milk is not called curds (lào),
curds are not called milk,
and even up to tíhú it is also like this.
Although the name changes,
the nature of the poison is not lost.
Throughout the five flavors,
it is all like this.
If one takes the tíhú, it can also kill a person,
even though the poison was not actually placed in the tíhú itself.
The Fóxìng of sentient beings is also like this.
Although they dwell in the Five Paths (Wǔ Dào)
and receive different bodies,
this Fóxìng remains perpetually one and unchanged."
Shīzǐhǒu said:
“Shìzūn!
Among the Sixteen Great Kingdoms,
there are six great cities.
Namely, Shěpóntí Chéng,
Póqīduō Chéng,
Zhānpó Chéng,
Píshèlǐ Chéng,
Bōluónà Chéng,
and Wángshè Chéng.
These six cities are the greatest in the world.
Why does the Rúlái abandon them,
and here in this inferior and corrupt borderland,
the extremely shabby, narrow, and small Jūshīnà Chéng, enter Parinirvāṇa?
“Shànnánzǐ!
You should not say that Jūshīnà Chéng is an inferior and corrupt borderland
and the most shabby, narrow, and small.
You should say that this city
is adorned by subtle merits and virtues.
Why is that?
Because it is the place where all Buddhas and Púsàs travel.
Shànnánzǐ!
If a king passes by
the house of a low-caste person,
one should praise it, saying: 'This house is magnificent and complete with merits,
able to make the Great King turn his carriage and visit.'
Shànnánzǐ!
Just as a person seriously ill
takes foul and inferior medicine,
and after taking it the illness is cured,
he should immediately rejoice and praise it, saying,
'This medicine is supremely superior and subtle,
it was able to cure my illness.'
Shànnánzǐ!
Just as a person sailing on the ocean,
whose ship is suddenly destroyed and has nothing to rely upon,
and by leaning on a corpse manages to reach the other shore;
having reached the other shore,
he should greatly rejoice and praise it, saying,
'Because I relied on meeting this corpse, I obtained safety and peace.'
Jūshīnà Chéng is also like this;
it is truly the place where all Buddhas and Púsàs travel.
How can you call it an inferior, corrupt, shabby, narrow, and small city?
“Shànnánzǐ!
I recall that in the past, innumerable kalpas ago,
the kalpa was named Shànjué.
At that time there was a Holy King named Jiāoshījiā,
complete with the Seven Treasures
and fully having a thousand sons.
This king first established this city,
whose circumference and extent covered twelve Yóuyán,
adorned with the Seven Treasures.
The land had many rivers,
and their water was pure, soft, and sweet.
Namely, the Níliánchán Hé,
the Yīluóbátí Hé,
the Xīliánchán Hé,
the Yīsōumòduī Hé,
and the Pípóshěnà Hé.
There were five hundred such rivers.
The trees on both banks of the rivers were flourishing,
and the flowers and fruits were fresh and pure.
At that time, the people’s lifespan was immeasurable.
When the Zhuǎnlún Shèng Wáng had lived for more than a hundred years,
he made this proclamation:
‘As taught by the Buddha,
all phenomena are entirely impermanent.
If one can cultivate the Shíshàn Fǎ,
one can sever this great suffering caused by impermanence.’
When the people heard this,
they all jointly devoted themselves to cultivating the Shíshàn Fǎ.
I, at that time, heard the name of the Buddha,
accepted and upheld the Ten Good Deeds,
contemplated and cultivated them,
and first generated the Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí Xīn.
Having generated this mind,
I further used this Dharma
to pass the teaching on to immeasurable and boundless sentient beings,
saying that all phenomena are impermanent and subject to change and decay.
Therefore, I now continue in this place,
also teaching that all phenomena are impermanent and subject to change and decay,
but only saying that the Buddha's body is the eternal, abiding Dharma.
I recall the causes and conditions of my past actions,
and that is why I have now come here for Nièpán.
I also wish to repay the past kindness shown by this land.
For this reason,
I have said in the sūtras,
that my followers are those who receive kindness and are able to repay it.
“Furthermore, Shànnánzǐ!
In the past, when sentient beings had immeasurable lifespans,
this city was named Jūshěbátí.
Its circumference and extent covered fifty Yóuyán.
At that time, the residents of Yánfútí were so close together
that flying chickens could reach one another.
There was a Zhuǎnlún Wáng named Shànjiàn,
complete with the Seven Treasures,
fully having a thousand sons,
who ruled the Four Continents.
The eldest crown prince contemplated the True Dharma and attained Pìzhīfóhood.
When the Zhuǎnlún Wáng saw that his crown prince had attained Pìzhīfóhood,
with a dignified and orderly demeanor,
and rare spiritual powers.
Seeing this,
he immediately renounced the throne,
treating it like casting aside snot or spit,
and became a monastic here among the Suōluó trees.
For eighty thousand years, he cultivated the mind of Cí Xīn,
Bēi,
Xǐ,
and the mind of Shě Xīn, each for eighty thousand years.
Shànnánzǐ!
If you wish to know who the Holy King Shànjiàn was at that time,
he was myself.
Therefore, I constantly delight in dwelling in these Four Dharmas,
and these Four Dharmas are called Sānmèi.
For this reason,
the Rúlái's body possesses permanence, joy, self, and purity (Cháng Lè Wǒ Jìng).
Shànnánzǐ!
Due to these causes and conditions,
I have now come here to Jūshīnà Chéng among the Suōluó trees,
properly entering Sānmèi.
“Shànnánzǐ!
I recall that in the past, countless kalpas ago,
this city was then named Jiāpíluówèi.
There was a king in that city
named Báijìng.
The king’s queen consort was named Móyē.
The king had one son named Xīdáduō.
At that time, the prince, without being taught by a teacher,
naturally contemplated and attained Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
He had two disciples:
the first named Shèlìfú,
the second named Dà Mùjiànlián.
The attending disciple was named Ānán.
At that time, the Shìzūn,
between the twin trees, expounded this Dà Nièpán Jīng.
I was present in the assembly at that time,
was fortunate enough to participate in this event,
and heard that all sentient beings possess Fóxìng.
Having heard this,
I immediately attained Bù Tuìzhuǎn regarding Pútí,
and immediately generated a vow:
‘I vow that when I attain Buddhahood in a future age,
my parents, land,
named disciples,
and attendants who preach the Dharma and transform others
will be exactly the same as the current Shìzūn, without difference.’
For these causes and conditions,
I have now come here to widely expound and preach the Dà Nièpán Jīng.”
“Good man,
when I first left the household life and had not yet attained Ānòu-duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
King Bīnbōsuōluó sent an envoy who said:
‘If Prince Xīdá becomes a sage king,
I will be his vassal.
If he is not happy with the household life
and attains Ānòu-duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
I wish him to first come to this city of Wángshěchéng to preach the Dharma and save sentient beings,
and accept my offerings.’
I was silent then, having accepted his invitation.
Good man!
When I first attained Ānòu-duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
as I headed toward Jiéshé Guó,
there was a Brahmin of the surname Jiāyè at the Yīliánchán Hé [river],
who was on the bank of that river with five hundred disciples,
seeking the unsurpassed Way.
I went there to preach the Dharma for the sake of this person.
Jiāyè said:
‘Qútán!
I am now old, already one hundred and twenty,
and all the people of Mójiétuó Guó, including the Great King Bīnbōsuōluó,
all believe that I have already attained the fruition of Arhatship.
If I now sit before you to listen to and receive the Dharma,
all the people may develop incorrect views, thinking,
"Is the greatly virtuous Jiāyè not an Arhat?"
I sincerely wish that Qútán would quickly go elsewhere,
for if these people become certain that Qútán’s merit is superior to mine,
we will no longer be able to receive offerings.’
I replied then:
‘Jiāyè!
If you do not harbor intense respect and great hatred toward me,
allow me to stay for one night;
I will leave early tomorrow.’
Jiāyè said:
‘Qútán!
My heart has no other intention;
I deeply love and respect you.
But in my dwelling place, there is a venomous dragon,
whose nature is violent and swift,
and I fear it might harm you.’
I said:
‘Jiāyè!
The poison among poisons
is no more than the Three Poisons,
which I have now eradicated.
Worldly poisons
I do not fear.’
Jiāyè replied again:
‘If you are truly unafraid,
excellent!
I permit you to stay.’
Good man!
At that time, I manifested the eighteen transformations for Jiāyè’s sake,
as described in the sūtras.
At that time, Jiāyè and his dependents, the five hundred and others,
upon seeing and hearing this,
attained the fruition of Arhatship.
At that time, Jiāyè also had two younger brothers:
the first named Gāyé Jiāyè,
the second named Nàtí Jiāyè,
whose teachers, disciples, and dependents also numbered five hundred,
and they all likewise attained the fruition of Arhatship.
The followers of the Six Teachers in Wángshěchéng
heard about this matter
and immediately conceived great ill will toward me.
I then honored the promise, accepted the King’s invitation, and proceeded to Wángshěchéng.
Before reaching midway,
the King and countless hundreds of thousands of followers all came to welcome me,
and I preached the Dharma to them.
When they heard the Dharma at that time,
eighty-six thousand heavenly beings of the Desire Realm
developed the mind for Ānòu-duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
one hundred and twenty thousand people from the retinue led by King Bīnbōsuōluó attained the fruition of Sūtuóhuán,
Having entered the city,
I converted Shèlìfú
and countless sentient beings achieved the mind of forbearance.
I led them to abandon their original views and leave the household life to study the Way,
and I resided there, accepting the King’s offerings.
The Six Heretical Teachers gathered together
and went to Shèwèichéng.
"At that time, there was an elder (Zhàngzhě) in that city named Xūdáduō (Sudatta).
He went to Wángshěchéng (Rājagṛha) to arrange a marriage for his son.
Having reached that city,
he stayed at the house of the elder Shāntánnà (Sandhana).
At midnight, this elder arose and instructed his relatives:
'Good people (Rén), you must get up,
quickly prepare together,
sweep and clean the house,
and prepare the food and drink.'
Xūdá, having heard this,
immediately thought to himself:
'Is he perhaps planning to invite the King of Mógā (Magadha)?
Or is there a joyful wedding celebration?'
Having thought this,
he immediately went forward and asked:
'Great man (Dàshì)!
Are you planning to invite Pínpósuōluó (Bimbisāra), the King of Mógātuó (Magadha)?
Or is there a joyful wedding celebration?
Is the urgent preparation so intense that you are restless?'
The elder replied:
'No,
householder (Jūshì)!
Tomorrow I am inviting the Fó (Buddha), the unsurpassed Dharma King (Fǎwáng).'
When Elder Xūdá first heard the name of the Fó,
his hairs stood on end,
and he immediately asked again:
'What is called Fó?'
The elder replied:
'Have you not heard?
There is a son of the Śākya clan in Jiāpíluóchéng (Kapilavastu),
named Xīdáduō (Siddhārtha),
whose surname is Qútán (Gautama),
and whose father is named Báijìng (Śuddhodana).
Not long after he was born,
the physiognomists divined that
he was certain to become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng),
like the mango fruit already grasped in the hand.
His heart did not desire this, so he abandoned it and left home (Chūjiā),
and without a teacher, he awoke by himself,
attaining Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi),
extinguishing greed, hatred, and delusion.
He abides eternally and is unchanging,
neither born nor extinguished,
having no sorrow or fear.
Towards all sentient beings (Zhòngshēng),
his mind is impartial,
like parents regarding their single child equally.
His body and mind are the most excellent among all beings,
and though superior to all, he is without arrogance;
in the two matters of anointing and cutting (praise or harm), his mind is undifferentiated.
His wisdom penetrates all things (Fǎ) without obstruction,
possessing the Ten Powers (Shílì),
the Four Fearlessnesses (Sì Wúsuǒwèi),
the Five Wisdom Samādhis (Wǔzhì Sānmèi),
Great Compassion and Great Pity (Dàcí Dàbēi), and the Three Stations of Mindfulness (Sān Niànchǔ).
Therefore, he is called Fó.
Tomorrow he will accept my invitation,
thus I am busy and have not had time to look at you.'
Xūdáduō said:
'Excellent,
great man (Dàshì)!
This one you speak of, the Fó,
his merits (Gōngdé) are unsurpassed.
Where is he now?'
The elder replied:
'He is now here in the great city of Wángshě Dàchéng (Rājagṛha),
residing at the Jiālántuó Zhúlín Jīngshě (Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Vihāra).'
At that time, Xūdáduō wholeheartedly recalled all the merits of the Fó:
the Ten Powers (Shílì),
the Fearlessnesses (Wúwèi),
the Five Wisdom Samādhis (Wǔzhì Sānmèi),
Great Compassion and Great Pity (Dàcí Dàbēi), and the Three Stations of Mindfulness (Sān Niànchǔ).
While he was thinking this,
suddenly a great light appeared,
its brilliance was fierce and strong,
just like broad daylight.
He immediately followed the light out
and arrived beneath the city gate.
Due to the divine power (Shénlì) of the Fó,
the gate opened by itself.
Having gone out the gate,
there was a heavenly shrine (Tiāncí) on the road.
Xūdá passed by, paid homage and reverence,
and immediately the darkness returned.
Fear arose in his heart,
and he wished to turn back to the place where he was staying.
At that moment, there was a heaven-god (Tiānshén) at the city gate,
who told Xūdá:
'Benevolent one (Rénzhě), if you go to the place of the Rúlái (Tathāgata),
you will gain much good benefit.'
Xūdáduō asked:
'What kind of good benefit?'
He replied:
'Elder!
Suppose a person possesses genuine jewels and necklaces (Jiàoluò),
one hundred fine horses,
one hundred fragrant elephants,
one hundred jeweled carriages,
one hundred statues cast in gold,
beautiful women wearing necklaces
adorned with all kinds of treasures,
exquisite mansions,
halls, houses, and chambers,
carved and engraved,
golden plates filled with silver grain,
and silver plates filled with golden grain,
one hundred of each item,
and gives these in charity (Shī) to a single person.
If this is done repeatedly throughout the whole of Yánfú Tí (Jambudvīpa),
the merit (Gōngdé) obtained
is not equal to that gained by a person who sets his intention and takes one step
toward the place of the Rúlái.'
Xūdáduō said:
'Good man (Shàn Nánzǐ)!
Who are you?'
He replied:
'Elder!
I am the son of the Shèngxiàng (Victorious Marks) Brahmin (Póluómén),
and I was your good friend (Shàn Zhīshí) in times past.
Because I saw Shèlìfú (Śāriputra) and
Dà Mùjiànlián (Mahāmaudgalyāyana) previously,
joy arose in my heart,
and upon relinquishing my body, I became the son of Píshāmén (Vaiśravaṇa), the Northern Heaven King (Tiānwáng),
specifically tasked with guarding this Wángshěchéng.
Because I paid homage to Shèlìfú and the others,
and generated a joyous mind,
I was still able to obtain such a wonderful body.
How much more [benefit will be gained] by seeing the Great Master (Dàshī), the Rúlái,
and paying homage and making offerings?'
Elder Xūdá, having heard this,
immediately returned to the road and came to my place.
Having arrived, he paid reverence by touching his head to my feet,
and I immediately expounded the Dharma (Shuōfǎ) to him as was appropriate.
The elder, having heard it, attained the result of Suōtuóhuán Guǒ (Sotāpanna, Stream-Enterer).
Having attained this fruit of realization,
he further requested of me, saying:
'Rúlái, with your great compassion (Dàcí),
I only wish that you would graciously come to Shèwèichéng (Śrāvastī)
and accept my humble offering.'
I immediately asked him:
'In your country of Shèwèi,
are there vihāras (Jīngshě)
able to accommodate us?'
Xūdáduō replied:
'If the Fó shows pity,
and is certain to visit,
I will certainly exhaust my efforts to establish and prepare one.'
Good man (Shàn Nánzǐ)!
At that time, I silently accepted his invitation.
Elder Xūdá, having received permission,
immediately reported to me, saying:
'I have never done such a thing before;
I only wish that the Rúlái
would send Shèlìfú to instruct me on the procedures.'
I immediately looked at him, commanded and ordered him to assist in the construction."
“At that time, Shènglìfú and Sūdáduō were riding together in a cart,
heading toward Shèwèichéng.
Due to my divine power,
they arrived at their destination after only one day and night.
At that time, Sūdáduō said to Shènglìfú:
'Virtuous One!
Outside this great city,
where is there land neither too close nor too far,
abundant with springs and ponds,
having fine forests and trees,
flowers and fruits,
lush, clean, quiet, and pleasing?
I shall build a monastery there
for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the community of Bhikṣus.'
Shènglìfú said:
'The Jítuó Gardens are neither too close nor too far,
clean and secluded,
with many springs and ponds,
and trees, flowers, and fruits available in every season.
This place is the most excellent
for establishing a monastery.'
When Sūdáduō heard these words,
he immediately went to the great elder Jítuó,
and told Jítuó:
'I now wish to build a monastic residence for the Supreme King of the Dharma.
Only your garden land is suitable for building upon.
I wish to buy it now.
Are you able to sell it to me or not?'
Jítuó replied:
'Even if you were to cover the entire ground with pure gold,
I still would not give it to you.'
Sūdáduō said:
'Excellent,
Jítuó!
The garden land belongs to me,
so you may take the gold.'
Jítuó replied:
'My garden is not for sale;
why should I take the gold?'
Sūdáduō said:
'If your intention is unclear,
we should go together to the one who settles disputes.'
The two elders then went together to the dispute settler.
The dispute settler said:
'The garden belongs to Sūdá,
and Jítuó must take the gold.'
Elder Sūdá immediately commanded men to load wagons and horses with gold and pile it up to cover the ground.
In one day,
only five hundred paces
were covered completely with gold.
Jítuó said:
'Elder, if you regret this,
you may stop whenever you wish.'
Sūdáduō said:
'I do not regret it.
I am just thinking which vault I should take the remaining gold from to make it sufficient.'
Jítuó thought:
'The Tathāgata, the King of the Dharma,
is truly supreme and unsurpassed,
and the subtle Dharma he speaks
is pure and undefiled.
That is why this man treats wealth so lightly.'
He immediately said to Sūdá:
'For the part not yet covered,
I no longer need gold.
Please let me contribute it to you.
I shall personally build the gate tower for the Buddha,
so that the Tathāgata will always pass through it upon entering and exiting.'
Elder Jítuó built the gate tower himself,
and Elder Sūdá completed the main hall within seven days,
sufficient for three hundred people,
sixty-three rooms for meditation and seclusion,
with winter rooms and summer halls separately arranged.
Kitchens, bathrooms,
places for washing feet,
and both small and large latrines were all adequately prepared.
After everything was prepared,
he held an incense burner
and facing Rìwángshěchéng, he spoke from afar, saying:
'Everything I have arranged is complete.
May the Tathāgata, in his compassionate mercy,
accept this dwelling place for the sake of all sentient beings.'
“I divinely knew the elder's mind at that time,
and immediately departed from Wángshěchéng with the great assembly.
Just as a strong man can flex and extend his arm,
we arrived at the Jítuó Gardens, Sūdá's monastery, in Shèwèichéng.
After I had arrived,
Elder Sūdá offered everything he had prepared to me.
I accepted it at that time,
and dwelled therein.
“At that time, the six teachers [of other doctrines] felt jealousy in their hearts,
and they all gathered and went to King Bōsīní.
They spoke thus:
'Great King, you should know,
your realm
is peaceful, serene, and quiet,
truly a place for those who have left home to reside.
Therefore, we have come here for this reason.
Great King, you rule righteously according to the Dharma
and remove calamities for the people.
The Śramaṇa Qútán
is both young in age
and shallow in his study of the Dharma,
and his Way-practices offer no benefit;
this country already has long-established, senior, and virtuous practitioners
who rely on their royal lineage
and show no respect.
If he were of royal lineage,
he ought to govern the people according to the law;
if he has left home,
he should respect the established virtues.
Great King, listen carefully:
The Śramaṇa Qútán
was truly not born into the royal lineage.
If the Śramaṇa Qútán had parents,
how could he rob others of their parents?
Great King!
Our scripture states
that after a thousand years,
a monstrous phantom or illusion will appear;
this refers to the Śramaṇa Qútán.
Therefore, you should know
that the Śramaṇa Qútán has no father or mother.
If he had parents,
why would he speak of all phenomena as impermanent,
suffering,
empty,
without self,
without agent,
and without recipient?
He uses illusory tricks to deceive and bewilder sentient beings;
the ignorant believe and accept it, while the wise abandon it.
Great King!
A king
is the parent of the world,
like a scale,
like the earth,
like the wind,
like fire,
like a road,
like a river,
like a bridge,
like a lamp,
like the sun,
like the moon,
judging affairs according to the Dharma,
without distinction between enemy and friend.
The Śramaṇa Qútán does not allow us to live;
wherever we go,
he pursues and clings to us without giving up.
We sincerely wish, Great King,
that you would permit us
to compare our spiritual power
with that Qútán.
If he surpasses us,
we shall submit to him;
if we surpass him,
he shall submit to us.'
The King said:
'Virtuous Ones!
Each of you has your own practices and doctrines,
and your places of dwelling are also different.
I now clearly know
that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, poses no obstacle to you.'
The six teachers replied:
'How can there be no obstacle?
The Śramaṇa Qútán uses illusory magic
to entice and bewilder all people and Brāhmaṇas,
until they are completely subdued.
If the King allows us to compare our spiritual powers,
the King's good reputation will spread throughout the eight directions;
if not,
ill repute will fill the roads.'
The King said:
'Virtuous Ones!
You do not yet know the sublime, majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata,
which is why you seek a comparison.
If you truly knew it,
I fear you would be unable to do so.'
'Great King!
Have you now been captivated by Qútán's illusion?
We sincerely wish, Great King,
that you would reserve judgment and observe carefully,
and not slight us.
Fabricating false words
is not as good as verifying the truth.'
The King said:
'Excellent,
excellent.'
The followers of the six teachers departed joyfully.
“At that time, King Bōsīní immediately ordered his carriage prepared and came to my location,
bowed to me with his head to the ground in reverence,
circumambulated three times to the right,
withdrew and sat to one side,
and addressed me, saying:
'World-Honored One!
The six teachers just came seeking to compare spiritual powers,
and without fully considering the consequences,
I ventured to grant them permission.'
"The Fó said:
'Great Wáng!
Excellent,
excellent!
You should now further build monasteries (sēngfáng) everywhere throughout this country.
Why is this?
If I were to compare My spiritual power (shénlì) with theirs,
those among their followers who receive transformation would be numerous;
how could this small place accommodate them?
Good man (Shàn Nánzǐ)!
At that time, for the sake of the Liù Shī (Six Teachers),
from the first day to the fifteenth day,
I displayed great and rare spiritual transformations (shéntōng biànhuà).
At that time,
innumerable sentient beings generated the mind of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi),
innumerable sentient beings generated faith without doubt in the Sānbǎo (Three Jewels).
The followers of the Liù Shī were countless in number;
they destroyed their minds of erroneous views (xiéjiàn),
and left home according to the orthodox teaching (zhèngfǎ chūjiā).
Innumerable sentient beings attained the non-retreating mind (bùtuì xīn) in Pútí (Bodhi),
innumerable sentient beings attained the Dhāraṇī and various Sānmèi (Samādhi) gates,
innumerable sentient beings attained the fruit of Sūtuóhuán (Srotāpanna) up to the fruit of Āluóhàn (Arhat).
"At that time, the Liù Shī felt internal shame,
mutually surrounding each other, they went to the city of Pózhǐduō,
and taught the people there to believe in and accept the erroneous teachings (xiéfǎ),
saying that Qútán (Gautama) the Śrāmaṇa only speaks of emptiness.
Good man (Shàn Nánzǐ)!
I then, for the sake of My mother,
stayed in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven (Dāolì Tiān) under the Bōlìzhìduō (Pāricchattra) tree for the rainy retreat (ān jū) and preached the Dharma.
At this time, the Liù Shī were extremely joyful in their hearts and proclaimed:
'Excellent!
The magical arts (huànshù) of Qútán have now vanished and disappeared.'
They furthermore taught innumerable sentient beings, causing them to increase their erroneous views (xiéjiàn).
At that time, King Pínpósuōluó (Bimbisāra) and King Bōsīní (Prasenajit),
along with the four assemblies (sì bù zhòng),
said to Mùlián (Maudgalyāyana):
'Great Virtue (Dà Dé)!
In this Yánfútí (Jambudvīpa), erroneous views are growing stronger,
sentient beings are pitiful,
walking in great darkness.
We only wish, Great Virtue,
that you would go up to that heaven,
prostrate yourself before the Shìzūn (World-Honored One),
and speak as we say:
"Just as a calf,
newly born,
if it does not get milk,
will surely die without doubt.
We sentient beings are also like this.
We only wish that the Rúlái (Tathāgata),
out of compassion for sentient beings,
would return and dwell here."
At that time, Mùlián silently consented.
In the time it takes a strong man to flex and extend his arm,
he went to that heaven,
arriving at the place of the Shìzūn,
and addressed the Fó, saying:
'All four assemblies in Yánfútí thirstily long for the Rúlái,
desiring to see him and hear the Dharma.
King Pínpósuōluó and King Bōsīní and the four assemblies,
prostrate themselves at your feet.
All sentient beings in this Yánfútí have growing erroneous views,
walking in great darkness,
they are extremely pitiful.
Just as a calf newly born,
if it does not get milk, will surely die without doubt.
We are also like this.
We only wish that the Rúlái,
for the sake of sentient beings,
would return and be present here in Yánfútí.'
The Fó told Mùlián:
'You should now quickly return to Yánfútí,
and inform all the kings and the four assemblies,
that after seven days I shall descend and return.
For the sake of the Liù Shī,
I will once again go to that city of Pózhǐduō.'
After seven days had passed,
I, accompanied by Shì Tiān (Indra/Sakra),
Fàntiān (Brahmā),
Mó Tiān (Māra), and innumerable sons of heaven (tiānzǐ),
and all the celestial beings (tiān rén) of the Shǒutuóhuì (Śuddhāvāsa) heaven,
surrounded before and behind, went to the city of Pózhǐduō,
and made a great lion's roar (shīzǐ hǒu),
speaking thus:
'Only in My Dharma
are there truly Śrāmaṇas (Shāmén) and Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén),
where all phenomena (fǎ) are impermanent (wúcháng) and non-self (wúwǒ),
where Nièpán (Nirvāṇa) is tranquil and peaceful,
and free from all faults and evils.
If one says that other teachings also have Śrāmaṇas and Brāhmaṇas,
who possess permanence (yǒucháng), self (yǒuwǒ), and Nièpán,
there is no such possibility.'
At that time, innumerable and boundless sentient beings generated the mind of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
At this time, the Liù Shī said to each other:
'If in our teachings there are truly no Śrāmaṇas or Brāhmaṇas,
how can we obtain worldly offerings?'
Thereupon, the Liù Shī,
gathered together again and went to Píshèlǐ (Vaiśālī)."
"Good man!
Once, I dwelt in the Ānluó Grove in Píshèlǐ,
At that time, the Ānluó Nǚ knew I was there,
and wished to come to me.
At that time, I addressed the Bhikṣus:
'You should contemplate the foundations of mindfulness,
diligently cultivate wisdom,
and wherever you practice,
let your minds not be negligent.
What is meant by contemplating the foundations of mindfulness?
If a Bhikṣu observes the inner body,
seeing neither a self (ātman) nor anything belonging to a self.
Observing the outer body, and the inner and outer body,
seeing neither a self nor anything belonging to a self.
Observing feelings, mind, and dharmas is likewise done,
this is called the foundations of mindfulness.
What is meant by cultivating wisdom?
If a Bhikṣu truly sees suffering, accumulation, cessation, and the Path,
this is called a Bhikṣu cultivating wisdom.
What is meant by the mind not being negligent?
If a Bhikṣu recollects the Buddha,
recollects the Dharma,
recollects the Saṅgha,
recollects the precepts,
recollects renunciation,
recollects the heavens,
this is called a Bhikṣu whose mind is not negligent.
Then the Ānluó Nǚ immediately came to where I was,
bowed her head to the ground in reverence,
circumambulated three times to the right,
and having completed her respects,
sat down on one side.
Good man!
At that time, I preached the Dharma to the Ānluó Nǚ as was appropriate.
When this woman heard it,
she awakened the mind of Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
At that time, there were five hundred Líchēzǐ in that city who came to where I was,
bowed their heads to the ground in reverence,
circumambulated three times to the right,
and having completed their respects,
sat down on one side.
At that time, I again preached the Dharma to the Líchēzǐ as was appropriate:
'Good men,
negligence results in five consequences.
What are these five?
First, they do not gain wealth and benefits easily;
second, their bad reputation spreads externally;
third, they are unwilling to give charitable gifts and are intellectually poor;
fourth, they are unwilling to meet the Four Assemblies;
fifth, they do not obtain the body of the various devas.
Good men,
through non-negligence,
one can give rise to worldly dharmas
and supramundane dharmas.
If there is anyone who wishes to attain Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
they should diligently practice the Dharma of non-negligence.
Furthermore, negligence
has thirteen karmic results.
What are these thirteen?
First, delighting in performing worldly actions;
second, delighting in speaking useless words;
third, constantly delighting in long sleep;
fourth, delighting in speaking of worldly matters;
fifth, constantly delighting in associating with wicked friends;
sixth, being constantly sluggish and lazy;
seventh, being constantly looked down upon by others;
eighth, forgetting quickly what has been heard;
ninth, delighting in dwelling in remote areas;
tenth, being unable to subdue the various faculties;
eleventh, being discontented with food;
twelfth, not delighting in emptiness and solitude;
thirteenth, possessing incorrect views,
these are the thirteen.
Good man!
The negligent person,
even though they might be close to the Buddha and the Buddha's disciples,
is still considered distant.'
The Líchēzǐ said:
'We know ourselves to be negligent people.
Why?
If we were not negligent,
the Tathāgata, the King of Dharma, would have appeared in our land.'
At that time, there was a son of a Póluómén in the great assembly,
named Wúshèng,
who spoke to the Líchēzǐ:
'Excellent,
excellent!
As you have said,
Pínbōsuōluó Wáng has obtained great benefit.
The Tathāgata, the Shìzūn, appeared in his country,
just like a wondrous lotus flower growing in a great pond;
though born in the water,
the water cannot defile it.
Líchēzǐ!
The Buddha is also like this;
though born in that country,
he is not obstructed or affected by worldly dharmas.
The Buddhas, the Shìzūns, neither appear nor disappear;
they manifest in the world for the sake of sentient beings,
and are not obstructed or affected by worldly dharmas.
You yourselves are deluded, indulging in the five desires,
and you do not know to draw near and go to the Tathāgata;
therefore, you are called negligent people.
It is not that the Buddha appearing in Mójiātuó Guó makes you negligent.
Why?
The Tathāgata, the Shìzūn, is like the sun and moon;
he does not appear in the world for the sake of just one person
or two people.'
When the Líchē heard these words,
they immediately awakened the mind of Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
and further spoke these words:
'Excellent,
excellent!
Youth Wúshèng!
You have spoken such good and wonderful words.'
Then the Líchē
each removed one garment that they were wearing
and gave it as a gift to Wúshèng.
Wúshèng received it,
and in turn offered it to me,
further saying:
'Shìzūn!
I received these clothes from the Líchē;
I only wish that the Tathāgata,
pitying all sentient beings,
would accept my offering.'
At that time, I,
out of compassion for Wúshèng,
immediately accepted them.
Then the Líchē simultaneously joined their palms,
and spoke these words:
'We only wish that the Tathāgata
would dwell in this land for a time for the Ānjū,
and accept our small offering.'
At that time, I accepted the Líchē's invitation silently.
"When the Liù Shī heard about this matter,
these sectarian masters
went together to the city of Bōluónà.
At that time, I also went to Bōluónà and dwelt by the Bōluó River.
At that time, there was a householder's son in Bōluónà,
named Bǎochēng,
who was indulging in the five desires,
unaware of impermanence.
Because I had arrived,
he naturally attained the practice of meditating on white bones.
He saw his palaces, servants, and palace women all transformed into white bones.
Fear arose in his heart,
feeling as if he were facing a knife or a poisonous snake,
a thief or a fire.
He immediately left his dwelling
and came to where I was,
saying along the road:
'Qú tán Shāmén!
I am now as if being pursued by a thief,
greatly terrified,
I pray you rescue and save me.'
The Buddha said:
'Good man!
The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha,
grant safety and lack of fear.'
The householder's son said:
'If there is no fear within the Three Jewels,
then I should now also obtain freedom from fear.'
I immediately allowed him to leave home to follow the Way.
The householder's son
had fifty companions who were his friends.
When they heard from afar that Bǎochēng had become disgusted with desire and left home,
they immediately agreed and complied,
and together they left home.
When the Liù Shī heard this,
they moved on and went to the great city of Zhānbō."
"At that time, all the people of the great kingdom of Zhānpó entirely dedicated themselves to serving the followers of the Six Teachers (*Liù Shī*),
having never initially heard the name of the Buddha,
the Dharma,
or the Saṅgha,
and many people committed extremely wicked deeds.
I, at that time, for the sake of sentient beings,
went to the city of Zhānpó.
At that time, in that city, there was a great elder,
who had no heir.
He served the Six Teachers (*Liù Shī*)
in order to seek a son.
Not long after,
his wife became pregnant.
When the elder knew this,
he went to the place of the Six Teachers (*Liù Shī*),
and joyfully said:
'My wife is pregnant.
Is it a boy
or a girl?'
The Six Teachers replied:
'The birth will definitely be a daughter.'
When the elder heard this,
distress and anxiety arose in his heart.
Furthermore, an acquaintance came and addressed the elder, saying:
'Why is your distress and anxiety so great?'
The elder replied:
'My wife is pregnant, and the gender is unknown.
Therefore I asked the Six Teachers (*Liù Shī*).
The Six Teachers observed and told me,
according to their method of divination,
that the birth will definitely be a daughter.
Hearing this statement,
and considering myself old,
possessing immeasurable wealth,
if it is not a son,
there will be no one to whom I can entrust it.
Therefore, I am distressed.'
The acquaintance further said:
'You lack wisdom.
Have you not heard before:
Of whom were *Yōulóupínluó Jiāyè* and his brothers disciples?
The Buddha?
Or the Six Teachers (*Liù Shī*)?
If the Six Teachers were omniscient ones,
why did *Jiāyè* abandon them and not serve them,
becoming a disciple of the Buddha?
Furthermore, *Shèlìfú*,
*Mùjiànlián*, and others, as well as various kings such as *Pínpósuōluó*,
various queens,
such as *Mòlì Fūrén*,
and elders from various kingdoms such as *Xūdádūo*—
are these people not disciples of the Buddha?
The spirits and ghosts of the wilderness,
King *Āshéshì Wáng*,
the drunken elephant Protecting Wealth,
*Yāngjuémóluó*, whose evil intent burned fiercely when he tried to harm his mother—
such people as these,
were they not tamed and subdued by the Tathāgata?
Elder!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses unobstructed knowledge and insight regarding all phenomena,
hence he is called the Buddha.
His statements are without duality,
hence he is called the Tathāgata.
Because he has cut off the afflictions,
he is called an Arhat (*Āluóhē*).
What the World-Honored One speaks never has duality.
The Six Teachers (*Liù Shī*) are not like this.
How can they be trusted?
The Tathāgata now dwells nearby here.
If you truly wish to know,
you should go to the Buddha's place.'
At that time, the elder immediately went with that person and came to my place,
paid homage by bowing his head to the ground,
circumambulated three times clockwise,
joined his palms and knelt respectfully,
and spoke these words:
'World-Honored One, toward all sentient beings, you are impartial and non-dual,
treating enemies and relatives as one.
I am bound by the fetters of attachment,
and cannot yet treat enemies and relatives non-dually.
I now wish to ask the Tathāgata about a worldly matter,
but I feel deeply ashamed and fearful, and have not dared to speak.
World-Honored One!
My wife is pregnant,
and the Six Teachers (*Liù Shī*) have divined that the birth will definitely be a daughter.
What is the truth of this matter?'
The Buddha said:
'Elder!
Your wife's pregnancy
is undoubtedly a boy.
When this child is born,
his merit and virtue will be incomparable.'
At that time, when the elder heard my words,
great joy arose,
and he withdrew and returned home.
At that time, the Six Teachers (*Liù Shī*),
heard my profound prediction,
that the birth would certainly be a boy,
possessing great merit and virtue.
Jealousy arose in their hearts,
so they mixed poison into a mango fruit,
carried it to the elder's house,
and spoke to the elder, saying:
'Excellent!
*Qútán* (Gautama) skillfully explained the sign.
Your wife is approaching the time of birth; she should take this medicine.
After taking this medicine,
the child will be handsome
and the birth will be without trouble.'
The elder joyfully accepted the poisoned medicine,
gave it to his wife and made her take it.
Having taken it, she immediately died.
The Six Teachers (*Liù Shī*) rejoiced,
and went throughout the city, shouting loudly:
'The śramaṇa *Qútán* predicted that the elder's wife would give birth to a son,
and that his merit and virtue would be unmatched in the world.
But now, before the child is even born,
the mother has lost her life!'
At that time, the elder again developed lack of faith in me.
He immediately followed worldly custom,
prepared the body, placed it in a covered coffin, and sent it outside the city.
He piled up much dry firewood
and burned it with fire.
I, using the Eye of the Way,
clearly saw this matter.
I turned and instructed *Ānán* (Ānanda):
'Bring my robe. I wish to go there
to crush their wicked views."
"At that time, Píshāmóntiān (毘沙門天) addressed the great general Móníbátuó (摩尼跋陀) and spoke these words:
