'The Tathāgata (Rúlái) now wishes to go to that graveyard.
You must quickly go and level [the ground], sweep and cleanse it,
set up a lion throne,
seek fine flowers and incense,
and adorn that ground.'
At that time, the Six Teachers (Liù Shī) saw me approaching from afar,
and they said to each other:
'The śramaṇa Qútán (瞿曇) has come to this graveyard;
does he wish to eat meat?'
At that time, many Upāsakas (Yōupósāi) who had not yet attained the Dharma Eye,
each felt embarrassment and shame,
and they said to me:
'That woman is already dead.
We beg you not to go.'
At that time, Ānán (阿難) spoke to the assembly, saying:
'Wait a moment.
The Tathāgata will soon extensively open and reveal the realms of all Buddhas.'
When I arrived,
and sat upon the lion throne,
the elder questioned me, saying:
'Your words are non-dual (true),
and thus you can be named the World-Honored One (Shìzūn).
But the mother is already dead;
how can she give birth to a child?'
I said:
'Elder,
at that time,
you did not ask
whether the mother's life was long or short;
you only asked concerning what she carried—
was it a boy or a girl?
The words spoken by the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are non-dual (true).
Therefore, you should know
that a child will definitely be born.'
At that time, the corpse,
being burned by the fire, split open in the abdomen,
and the child emerged from within,
sitting upright in the middle of the fire,
just like a mandarin duck
situated upon a lotus pedestal.
When the Six Teachers saw this,
they again spoke, saying:
'What a sorcerer Qútán is!
He is skilled in illusionary arts.'
When the elder saw this,
his heart was filled with joy again,
and he rebuked the Six Teachers:
'If you say it is an illusion,
why don't you perform it?'
At that time, I immediately instructed Jīpó (耆婆):
'Go into the fire
and bring that child here.'
As Jīpó prepared to go,
the Six Teachers stepped forward and pulled him,
saying to Jīpó:
'The illusion performed by the śramaṇa Qútán
may not always succeed.
Perhaps he can, perhaps he cannot.
If he cannot,
you might be burned and harmed.
How can you believe and accept his words now?'
Jīpó answered, saying:
'If the Tathāgata sent me into Ābí Dìyù (阿鼻地獄),
the fierce fires there still could not burn me,
much less worldly fire?'
At that time, Jīpó went forward into the pile of fire,
as if entering the cool waters of a great river.
He embraced and held the child,
returned to my presence,
and handed the child to me.
When I received the child,
I told the elder:
'The lifespan of all sentient beings
is impermanent
like a bubble on water.
If a sentient being possesses heavy karmic retribution,
fire cannot burn them,
and poison cannot harm them.
This child's karmic retribution
was not created by me.'
The elder then said:
'Excellent!
Shìzūn!
If this child is able to fulfill his natural lifespan,
we only request that the Tathāgata bestow a name upon him.'
The Buddha said:
'Elder!
This child was born in the middle of fierce fire.
The name for fire is Shùtí (樹提).
He should be named Shùtí.'
At that time, upon seeing my divine transformation in the assembly,
immeasurable sentient beings generated the aspiration for Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (阿耨多羅三藐三菩提) (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi).
"At that time, the Six Teachers traveled throughout the six cities and could not find a place to stay.
Ashamed and lowering their heads,
they returned to this city, Jūshīnàchéng (拘尸那城) (Kuśinagara).
Having arrived here,
they proclaimed these words:
'Everyone should know
that the śramaṇa Qútán is a Great Illusionist,
deceiving and confusing the world,
throughout the six great cities.
For example, an illusionist creates the four types of soldiers by illusion—
namely, chariot soldiers,
cavalry,
elephant soldiers,
and infantry.
Furthermore, he creates various kinds of necklaces and ornaments,
city walls, palaces, and dwellings,
rivers, ponds, and trees.
The śramaṇa Qútán is also like this;
he creates the body of a king by illusion.
For the purpose of teaching the Dharma,
sometimes he assumes the body of a śramaṇa,
the body of a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén),
a male body,
a female body,
a small body,
a large body,
or the body of an animal (chùshēng),
or a ghost or spirit.
Sometimes he teaches impermanence (wúcháng),
sometimes he teaches permanence (yǒucháng).
Sometimes he speaks of suffering (kǔ),
sometimes he speaks of joy (lè).
Sometimes he speaks of a self (yǒuwǒ),
sometimes he speaks of no self (wúwǒ).
Sometimes he speaks of purity (yǒujìng),
sometimes he speaks of impurity (wújìng).
Sometimes he speaks of existence (yǒuhú),
sometimes he speaks of non-existence (wú).
His actions are false and deceptive,
therefore, he is called an illusionist.
For example, based on the son [as the cause],
the fruit is obtained from the son.
The śramaṇa Qútán
is also like this.
Since the mother, who gave birth to him (by Móyē, 摩耶), was an illusion,
the son cannot be otherwise.
The śramaṇa Qútán has no genuine knowledge or insight.
The Brāhmaṇas, who have practiced asceticism (kǔxíng) for years upon years,
and maintained prohibitive precepts,
still say they have not yet attained genuine knowledge and insight.
How much less Qútán, who is young and shallow in learning,
and does not practice asceticism?
How could he possess genuine knowledge and insight?
Even if one could fully complete seven years of ascetic practice,
the insight gained would still not be vast,
let alone his practice which was not fully six years?
Ignorant people lack wisdom
and believe and accept his teachings,
just as a great illusionist deceives the foolish.
The śramaṇa Qútán
is also like this.'
'Good son!
These Six Teachers
greatly fostered false views among sentient beings in this city.'
'Good son!
When I saw this matter, compassion arose in my heart,
and using my spiritual power,
I invited and summoned all the great Bodhisattvas (Púsà) from the ten directions,
to assemble like clouds in this grove,
surrounding and completely filling forty Yóuyán (由延) (Yojanas).
Now, in this very place, I proclaim the Great Lion's Roar (Dà Shīzǐ Hǒu).
Good son!
Although much may be spoken in an empty space,
it cannot be called the Lion's Roar.
It is within this great assembly of wise people
that it is truly named the Great Lion's Roar.
The Lion's Roar is
to declare that all phenomena (dharma)
are impermanent (wúcháng),
suffering (kǔ),
non-self (wúwǒ),
and impure (bùjìng),
except that the Tathāgata alone is permanent (cháng), joyful (lè), self (wǒ), and pure (jìng).'
“At that time, the Six Teachers again spoke these words:
‘If Qútán has a self (ātman),
I also have a self.
What is meant by the self?
That which sees is named the self.
Qútán!
For example, when a person looks toward a direction and sees an object,
I am also like this.
The direction is likened to the eye,
and that which sees is likened to the self.’
The Buddha told the Six Teachers:
‘To say that that which sees is named the self,
this meaning is incorrect.
Why?
In the analogy you cited,
seeing is dependent upon the direction.
The person is in one direction,
and the six sense faculties are used together.
If there were definitely a self,
and seeing were dependent on the eye,
why is it not able, like that [example], to simultaneously survey all objects of the senses within one faculty?
If it cannot hear and see the six objects of the senses simultaneously within one faculty,
you ought to know there is no self.
Regarding the analogy of the direction you cited,
even after a hundred years pass,
the things seen by the seer depending on it are no different.
If the eye faculty were like that,
then even as years advance and the faculty matures, there should likewise be no difference.
Because the direction a person faces is different, they see inside and they see outside.
If the eye faculty were like that,
it should also see inside and outside simultaneously.
If it does not see [simultaneously],
how can there be a self?’
The Six Teachers replied again:
‘Qútán!
If there is no self,
who is able to see?’
The Buddha said:
‘There is form (rūpa), there is illumination,
there is mind (citta), there is the eye—
the harmonization of these four
is therefore called seeing.
In this, there is truly no seer
or experiencer (saṃvedaka).
Sentient beings, due to delusion,
say that there is a seer
and an experiencer.
Due to this meaning,
what all sentient beings see is deluded,
while what all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas see is true reality.
Six Teachers!
If you say that form is the self,
this is also incorrect.
Why?
Form is truly not the self.
If form were the self,
one should not then acquire an ugly appearance and physical form.
Why then are there differences among the four castes,
not all being of the Brāhmaṇa caste?
Why are [some] subject to others
and unable to be autonomous?
Why are sense faculties deficient and flawed,
or why are they not born complete?
Why are [some] not made into the bodies of various deities,
but instead receive various bodies in the hells, among animals, and among hungry ghosts?
If one cannot
act according to one’s will,
then you ought to know that there is definitely no self.
Because there is no self, it is called impermanent (anitya).
Because it is impermanent, it is suffering (duḥkha).
Because it is suffering, it is empty (śūnya).
Because it is empty, there is delusion.
Due to delusion, all sentient beings revolve in saṃsāra,
and feeling (vedanā), conception (saṃjñā), volitional formation (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna) are also like this.
Six Teachers!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has eternally severed the bondage of form, and similarly up to the bondage of consciousness.
Therefore, [his nature] is called permanence (nitya), bliss (sukha), self (ātman), and purity (śubha).
Furthermore, form is fundamentally conditioned (hetu-pratyaya).
If it is conditioned, it is named non-self (anātman).
If it is non-self, it is named suffering and emptiness.
The body of the Tathāgata is not conditioned.
Because it is not conditioned, it is named having a self.
If it has a self, it is permanence, bliss, and purity.”
The Six Teachers spoke again:
‘Qútán!
Form is also not the self,
nor is consciousness the self.
The self pervades all places,
just like space.’
The Buddha said:
‘If the pervasive existence [of the self] were true,
then one should not say,
“I did not see [it] at first.”
If one did not see it at first,
then it is known that this seeing, originally absent, is now present.
If it was originally absent and is now present,
this is named impermanent.
If it is impermanent,
how can you say it is pervasive?
If it is pervadingly existent,
bodies should be present in all five paths (gati).
If there are bodies, they should each receive retribution.
If they each receive retribution,
how can you say that one transitions to receiving [birth] among humans and deities?
Regarding what you call pervasive,
is it one [self],
or many?
If the self were one,
then there would be no father and son,
or enemy, relative, and neutral person.
If the self were many,
then all sentient beings’ five sense faculties should all be equal,
and their karma and wisdom should also be like this.
If this were the case,
how can you speak of [some] sense faculties being complete
and others incomplete?
How can there be differences in good karma,
bad karma,
or foolishness and wisdom?
‘Qútán!
The self of sentient beings
has no boundaries.
The Law (dharma) and non-Law (adharma),
however, have divisions and limits.
Sentient beings who cultivate the Law attain good bodies,
and those who practice the non-Law attain bad bodies.
Due to this meaning,
the karmic retribution of sentient beings cannot be without difference.’
The Buddha said:
‘Shànnánzǐ!
If the Law and non-Law are like this,
then the self is not pervasive.
If the self were pervasive,
it should reach everywhere.
If it reaches everywhere,
then the person cultivating good should also have evil,
and the person practicing evil should also have good.
If it is not so, how can you say it is pervasive?
‘Qútán!
For example, in a single room,
when a hundred thousand lamps are lit,
each illuminates itself without hindering the others.
The self of sentient beings is also like this:
cultivating good and practicing evil do not mix together.’
‘Shànnánzǐ!
If you say that the self is like a lamp,
this meaning is incorrect.
Why?
The illumination of that lamp exists due to conditions.
As the lamp increases,
the illumination also increases.
The self of sentient beings is not like this.
Illumination issues from the lamp
and resides in a separate place.
The self of sentient beings cannot be like this,
issuing from the body
and residing in a separate place.
The light of that lamp coexists with darkness.
Why?
For example, when one lamp is lit in a dark room, the illumination is not distinct;
only when there are many lamps does it become clearly bright.
If the first lamp destroys the darkness,
then subsequent lamps are unnecessary.
If subsequent lamps are necessary,
you ought to know that the initial illumination coexists with darkness.
‘Qútán!
If there is no self,
who performs good and evil?’"
"The Buddha says:
'If the self (wǒ) were the creator/doer (zuòzhě),
how could it be called eternal (cháng)?
If it is eternal,
how can it sometimes perform good deeds (zuò shàn),
and sometimes perform evil deeds (zuò è)?
If it is said that it sometimes performs good and evil deeds,
how can one again say that the self (wǒ) is boundless (wúbiān)?
If the self (wǒ) is the creator/doer,
why then does it repeatedly practice evil dharmas (è fǎ)?
If the self (wǒ) is the creator/doer,
and the knower,
why does doubt arise that sentient beings (zhòngshēng) have no self (wú wǒ)?
For this reason,
among the teachings of the heterodox paths (wàidào fǎ),
there is definitely no self (wǒ).
If one speaks of the self (wǒ), it is the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Why?
Because the body is boundless (wúbiān),
because there is no net of doubt (wú yíwǎng),
not creating and not receiving,
therefore it is called eternal (cháng).
Not arising and not ceasing,
therefore it is called bliss (lè).
Without the defilement of afflictions (fánnǎo gòu),
therefore it is called purity (jìng).
Without the ten characteristics (shí xiàng),
therefore it is called emptiness (kōng).
Therefore, the Tathāgata (Rúlái) possesses permanence (cháng), bliss (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng),
empty of all characteristics (zhū xiàng).'
The various heterodox practitioners (zhū wàidào) said:
'If it is said that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) possesses permanence (cháng), bliss (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng),
and is empty (kōng) because there are no characteristics (wú xiàng).
It should be known that the Dharma (fǎ) spoken by Gotama (Qúntán) is then not empty (kōng),
therefore I shall now reverently receive and uphold it.'
At that time, the heterodox practitioners (wàidào), countless in number,
left home (chūjiā) with faith in the Buddha's Dharma (Fófǎ).
"Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Because of this reason and condition,
I uttered the Great Lion's Roar (Dà Shīzǐ Hǒu) among these Śālá Twin Trees (Suōluó Shuāngshù).
The Lion's Roar (Shīzǐ Hǒu)
is named the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The eastern twin (tree)
destroys impermanence (wúcháng),
and attains permanence (cháng).
And similarly, the northern twin (tree) destroys impurity (bú jìng),
and attains purity (jìng).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The sentient beings (zhòngshēng) here, for the sake of the Twin Trees (shuāngshù),
protect the Śālá forest (suōluó lín),
not allowing outsiders to take their branches and leaves,
or to chop, cut, or destroy them.
I am also like this:
for the sake of the Four Dharmas (sì fǎ),
I instruct all disciples (dìzǐ) to guard and uphold the Buddha Dharma (Fófǎ).
What are the Four?
Permanence (Cháng),
bliss (Lè),
self (Wǒ),
purity (Jìng).
These Four Twin Trees (sì shuāngshù)
are governed by the Four Kings (Sì Wáng),
and I, for the sake of the Four Kings (sì Wáng), guard and uphold my Dharma (fǎ);
therefore I enter Parinirvāṇa (Bānnirván) among them.
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The flowers and fruits of the Śālá Twin Trees (Suōluó Shuāngshù) are perpetually flourishing,
and constantly benefit countless sentient beings (wúliàng zhòngshēng).
I am also like this:
constantly benefiting the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué).
The flower symbolizes the self (wǒ),
the fruit symbolizes bliss (lè).
For this reason,
I entered the Great Tranquil Concentration (Dà Jìdìng) here among the Śālá Twin Trees (Suōluó Shuāngshù).
The Great Tranquil Concentration (Dà Jìdìng)
is named the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán)."
Shīzihǒu (Lion's Roar) said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
Why did the Tathāgata (Rúlái) enter Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) in the second month?"
"Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The second month is called spring (chūn).
In the month of spring warmth (chūnyáng),
the ten thousand things grow,
seeds are sown and roots are planted,
flowers and fruits blossom splendidly,
rivers and streams overflow,
and a hundred beasts nurture their young.
At this time, sentient beings (zhòngshēng) mostly develop the notion of permanence (cháng xiǎng).
In order to destroy this kind of notion of permanence (cháng xīn) in sentient beings,
I preach that all dharmas (yīqiè fǎ) are entirely impermanent (wúcháng),
speaking only that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) dwells eternally and is unchanging (chángzhù bú biàn).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Among the six seasons (liù shí),
early winter is withered and desolate,
which people do not love or enjoy.
The warmth of spring is gentle and mild,
which people covet and cherish.
In order to destroy the worldly bliss (shìjiān lè) held by sentient beings,
I expound eternal bliss (cháng lè).
Self (wǒ) and purity (jìng) are also like this.
The Tathāgata (Rúlái), in order to destroy the worldly self (shì wǒ)
and worldly purity (shì jìng),
proclaims the Tathāgata’s (Rúlái) true self (zhēnshí wǒ) and purity (jìng).
Speaking of the second month
symbolizes the Tathāgata's (Rúlái) two types of Dharma Body (Fǎshēn).
The displeasure associated with winter
symbolizes that the wise (zhìzhě) are displeased by the Tathāgata (Rúlái) entering Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) as impermanent (wúcháng).
The pleasure associated with the second month
symbolizes that the wise (zhìzhě) cherish and enjoy the Tathāgata's (Rúlái) permanence (cháng), bliss (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng).
Sowing seeds and planting
symbolizes all sentient beings (zhū zhòngshēng), who, hearing the Dharma (fǎ), are joyful,
and arouse the mind of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí xīn),
planting all wholesome roots (zhū shàngēn).
Rivers (hé)
symbolize the great Bodhisattvas (Dà Púsà) from the ten directions (shífāng) coming to my location,
consulting and receiving this Great Nirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Nièpán Diǎn).
A hundred beasts nurturing their young
symbolizes my disciples (dìzǐ) generating all wholesome roots (zhū shàngēn).
Flowers symbolize the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (Qī Jué).
Fruits symbolize the Four Fruits (Sì Guǒ).
For this reason,
I enter the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán) in the second month."
Shīzihǒu (Lion's Roar) said:
"The Tathāgata’s (Rúlái) initial birth,
leaving home (chūjiā),
attaining the Way (chéngdào),
and turning the marvelous Dharma Wheel (Miào Fǎlún),
all occurred on the eighth day.
Why does Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) alone occur on the fifteenth day?"
The Buddha said:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Just as the moon on the fifteenth day neither wanes nor waxes,
all Buddhas and Tathāgatas (Rúlái) are also like this:
when entering the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán), there is neither waning nor waxing.
For this reason,
I enter Parinirvāṇa (Bānnirván) on the fifteenth day.
Good man (Shànnánzǐ),
just as on the fifteenth day,
when the moon is in its full splendor,
there are eleven matters.
What are the eleven?
First, it can break the darkness (pò àn).
Second, it enables sentient beings (zhòngshēng) to see the path (dào)
and the non-path (fēi dào).
Third, it enables sentient beings (zhòngshēng) to see the crookedness (xié)
and straightness (zhèng) of the path.
Fourth, it removes heat and distress and grants the bliss of coolness (qīngliáng lè).
Fifth, it can destroy the lofty pride of fireflies (yínghuǒ gāoxīn).
Sixth, it halts all thoughts of robbery and theft.
Seventh, it removes the fear of ferocious beasts from sentient beings (zhòngshēng) hearts.
Eighth, it can open up Utpala flowers (Yōubōluó huā).
Ninth, it closes the lotus flowers (liánhuā).
Tenth, it leads and inspires travelers to advance on their way.
Eleventh, it causes all sentient beings (zhū zhòngshēng) to enjoy receiving the five desires (wǔ yù) and gain much pleasure.
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) as the full moon
is also like this.
First, destroying the great darkness of ignorance (wúmíng dà àn).
Second, expounding the straight path (zhèng dào) and the crooked path (xié dào).
Third, revealing the crooked danger of birth and death (shēngsǐ xié xiǎn)
and the level straightness of Nirvāṇa (Nièpán píng zhèng).
Fourth, enabling people to avoid craving (tānyù),
hatred (chēnhuì),
and the heat of delusion (chī rè).
Fifth, destroying the ignorance (wúmíng) of heterodox practitioners (wàidào).
Sixth, destroying the thieves of affliction and bondage (fánnǎo jié zéi).
Seventh, eliminating the fear of the five hindrances (wǔ gài) from the mind.
Eighth, opening up the minds of sentient beings (zhòngshēng) to plant wholesome roots (shàngēn).
Ninth, covering (or subduing) the minds of sentient beings (zhòngshēng) regarding the five desires (wǔ yù).
Tenth, rousing sentient beings (zhòngshēng) to diligently cultivate practices leading toward the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
Eleventh, causing all sentient beings (zhū zhòngshēng) to joyfully cultivate liberation (jiětuō).
For this reason,
I enter the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán) on the fifteenth day,
although in reality, I do not enter Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
The ignorant, foolish, and evil people among my disciples (dìzǐ)
definitely assume the Tathāgata (Rúlái) has entered Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
For example, a mother (mǔ rén)
who has many sons,
when the mother departs for another land
before she returns,
all the sons say,
'Our mother has died.'
Yet that mother (mǔ rén) has truly not died."
Bodhisattva Shīzihǒu (Shīzǐhǒu Púsà) said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
What kind of Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū)
is able to adorn these Śālá Twin Trees (Suōluó Shuāngshù)?"
"Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
If there is a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) who receives, upholds, reads, and recites the Twelve Divisions of the Sūtra Piṭaka (Shí'èr Bù Jīng),
correcting their sentences and phrases,
penetrating the profound meaning,
explaining to others the good of the beginning (chū),
middle (zhōng),
and end (hòu),
and expounding the Brahma-conduct (Fànxíng) in order to benefit countless sentient beings (wúliàng zhòngshēng)—
such a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) is able to adorn the Śālá Twin Trees (Suōluó Shuāngshù)."
Shīzǐhǒu Púsà said:
“World-Honored One!
According to my understanding of the meaning spoken by the Buddha,
the Bhikṣu Ānán is precisely that person.
Why is this?
The Bhikṣu Ānán received, upheld, read, and recited the twelve divisions of sūtras,
and for the benefit of others, opened and explained the right Dharma and right meaning,
just like pouring water
and placing it into a different vessel.
The Bhikṣu Ānán is also like this:
what he heard from the Buddha,
he transmits and speaks just as he heard it.
“Good man!
If there is a Bhikṣu who attains the pure divine eye,
and sees everything in the three thousand Great-Thousand Worlds in the ten directions,
just as if viewing an āmalaka fruit in his palm,
such a Bhikṣu can also adorn the twin Sālá trees.”
Shīzǐhǒu said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is like this,
the Bhikṣu Ānílóutuó is precisely that person.
Why is this?
Ānílóutuó,
with his divine eye, sees the three thousand Great-Thousand Worlds,
including everything even down to the intermediate state (antarābhava),
all clearly understood,
because there is no obstruction.
“Good man!
If there is a Bhikṣu who
has few desires and knows contentment,
whose mind delights in tranquility,
diligently practices vigor,
mindfulness and concentration,
and wisdom and liberation,
such a Bhikṣu can then adorn the twin Sālá trees.”
Shīzǐhǒu said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is like this,
the Bhikṣu Jiāyè is precisely that person.
Why is this?
The Bhikṣu Jiāyè skillfully cultivates the Dharma of having few desires and knowing contentment, and so forth.
“Good man!
If there is a Bhikṣu who,
for the sake of benefiting sentient beings,
and not for gain or sustenance,
cultivates and comprehends the Samādhi of Non-contention,
the Noble Practice,
and the Practice of Emptiness,
such a Bhikṣu can then adorn the twin Sālá trees.”
Shīzǐhǒu said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is like this,
the Bhikṣu Xūpútí is precisely that person.
Why is this?
Xūpútí
skillfully cultivates the Non-contention, Noble Practice, and Practice of Emptiness.
“Good man!
If there is a Bhikṣu who skillfully cultivates spiritual penetrations (siddhis),
and in a single instant can create various spiritual transformations,
and with one mind and one concentration can produce two opposing elements,
namely water and fire,
such a Bhikṣu can then adorn the twin Sālá trees.”
Shīzǐhǒu said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is like this,
the Bhikṣu Mùlián is precisely that person.
Why is this?
Mùjiànlián
skillfully cultivates spiritual penetrations and immeasurable transformations.
“Good man!
If there is a Bhikṣu who cultivates Great Wisdom,
Sharp Wisdom,
Swift Wisdom,
Liberation Wisdom,
Profound Wisdom,
Vast Wisdom,
Boundless Wisdom,
Unsurpassed Wisdom,
and True Wisdom,
fully perfecting such roots of wisdom,
and between enemies and loved ones,
his mind shows no differentiation.
If he hears that the Tathāgata enters Nirvāṇa and is impermanent, his mind is not distressed;
if he hears that He resides eternally and does not enter Nirvāṇa, he does not feel joyous celebration,
such a Bhikṣu can then adorn the twin Sālá trees.”
Shīzǐhǒu said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is like this,
the Bhikṣu Shèlìfú is precisely that person.
Why is this?
Shèlìfú
is skilled at perfecting and fully accomplishing such great wisdom.
“Good man!
If there is a Bhikṣu who can preach that all sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature,
attains a Vajra Body without boundary,
is Permanent, Joyful, Self, and Pure, and whose body and mind are unobstructed,
and attains the Eight Great Freedoms,
such a Bhikṣu can then adorn the twin Sālá trees.”
Shīzǐhǒu said:
“World-Honored One!
If it is like this,
only the Tathāgata is precisely that person.
Why is this?
The body of the Tathāgata is Vajra and boundless,
Permanent, Joyful, Self, and Pure,
His body and mind are unobstructed,
and He possesses the Eight Great Freedoms.
World-Honored One!
Only the Tathāgata is capable of adorning the twin Sālá trees;
if He is absent, they would not be beautifully adorned.
I only pray that Your great compassion
will, for the sake of adornment,
reside eternally in this Sālá grove.”
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
All phenomena
inherently abide in non-abiding.
How can you say,
'We wish the Tathāgata (Rúlái) to abide'?
Good man!
Generally speaking, that which abides
is called *sèfǎ* (form/matter),
which arises from causes and conditions (yīnyuán).
Therefore, it is called abiding.
Causes and conditions (Yīnyuán) have no fixed location;
thus, it is called Non-Abiding Abode.
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) has already cut off all fetters of form.
How can you then say that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) abides?
Sensation, conception, volition, and consciousness (shòu, xiǎng, xíng, shí) are also like this.
Good man!
Abiding is called arrogance (jiāomàn).
Because of arrogance, one does not attain liberation.
Because one does not attain liberation, it is called abiding.
Who possesses arrogance?
Where does it come from?
Therefore, it obtains the name of Non-Abiding Abode.
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) has eternally severed all arrogance.
How can you then say, 'We wish the Tathāgata (Rúlái) to abide'?
Abiding is called conditioned phenomena (yǒuwéi fǎ).
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) has already severed conditioned phenomena.
Therefore, he does not abide.
Abiding is called empty phenomena (kōngfǎ).
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) has already severed such empty phenomena.
Therefore, he obtains permanence, bliss, self, and purity (cháng, lè, wǒ, jìng).
How can you then say, 'We wish the Tathāgata (Rúlái) to abide'?
Abiding is called the twenty-five realms of existence (èrshíwǔ yǒu).
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) has already severed the twenty-five realms of existence.
How can you then say, 'We wish the Tathāgata (Rúlái) to abide'?
Abiding is precisely all common beings (fánfū).
All sages have no going,
no coming,
and no abiding.
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) has already severed the marks of going, coming, and abiding.
How can you speak of abiding?
Now, that which is non-abiding
is called the boundless body.
Since the body is boundless,
how can you say, 'We only wish the Tathāgata (Rúlái) to abide in the Sārandra Grove (Suōluó Lín)'?
If he were to abide in this grove,
then the body would have boundaries.
If it has boundaries, then it is impermanent.
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is permanent.
How can you speak of abiding?
Now, that which is non-abiding
is called empty space (xūkōng).
The nature of the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is the same as empty space.
How can you speak of abiding?
Furthermore, that which is non-abiding
is called the Adamantine Samādhi (Jīngāng Sānmèi).
The Adamantine Samādhi destroys all abiding.
The Adamantine Samādhi is precisely the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
How can you speak of abiding?
Furthermore, that which is non-abiding
is called illusion (huàn).
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is like illusion.
How can you speak of abiding?
Furthermore, that which is non-abiding
is called having no beginning or end.
The nature of the Tathāgata (Rúlái) has no beginning or end.
How can you speak of abiding?
Furthermore, that which is non-abiding
is called the boundless Dharma Realm (fǎjiè).
The boundless Dharma Realm is precisely the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
How can you speak of abiding?
Furthermore, that which is non-abiding is called the Śūrangama Samādhi (Shǒuléngyán Sānmèi).
The Śūrangama Samādhi knows all phenomena but is attached to nothing.
Because there is no attachment, it is named Śūrangama.
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is fully endowed with the Śūrangama concentration.
How can you speak of abiding?
Furthermore, that which is non-abiding
is called the power of knowing right and wrong (Chùfēichù Lì).
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) has perfected the power of knowing right and wrong.
How can you speak of abiding?
Furthermore, that which is non-abiding is called Dāna Pāramitā (Tánbōluómì).
If Dāna Pāramitā were to abide,
then it could not reach Śīla Pāramitā (Shībōluómì), nor even Prajñā Pāramitā (Bānruò Bōluómì).
Because of this meaning,
Dāna Pāramitā is called non-abiding.
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) does not even abide in Prajñā Pāramitā (Bānruò Bōluómì).
How can you wish, saying that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) permanently abides in the Sārandra Tree Grove (Suōluó Shùlín)?
Furthermore, that which is non-abiding is called the cultivation of the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Sì Niànchù).
If the Tathāgata (Rúlái) were to abide in the Four Foundations of Mindfulness,
he would not be able to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).
This is called non-abiding abode.
Furthermore, that which is non-abiding
is called the boundless realm of sentient beings.
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) reaches all boundless divisions of sentient beings,
yet abides nowhere.
Furthermore, that which is non-abiding
is called having no dwelling.
Having no dwelling is called having no existence.
Having no existence is called having no birth.
Having no birth is called having no death.
Having no death is called having no marks.
Having no marks is called having no bondage.
Having no bondage is called having no attachment.
Having no attachment is called having no defilements (wúlòu).
Having no defilements is goodness.
Goodness is unconditioned (wúwéi).
Unconditioned is Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
Great Nirvāṇa is permanence.
Permanence is the self.
The self is purity.
Purity is bliss.
Permanence, bliss, self, and purity (cháng, lè, wǒ, jìng) are precisely the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
"Good man!
Just like empty space,
it does not abide in the East,
South, West, or North,
nor in the four intermediary directions, above, or below.
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is also like this;
he does not abide in the East,
South, West, or North,
nor in the four intermediary directions, above, or below.
Good man!
If someone says that evil of body,
speech,
and mind
results in good fruit,
there is no such possibility.
That goodness of body,
speech,
and mind
results in evil fruit,
there is also no such possibility.
If one says that common beings (fánfū) can see the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
while Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes (Shí Zhù Púsà) cannot see it,
there is also no such possibility.
That those of the *Icchantika* (Yīchǎntí) rank,
who commit the Five Heinous Crimes (Wǔ Nì Zuì),
slander the Vaipulya Sūtras (Fāngděng Jīng),
and violate the Four Cardinal Prohibitions (Sì Zhòng Jìn),
attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
there is also no such possibility.
That a Bodhisattva of the Sixth Abode (Liù Zhù Púsà),
due to afflictions (fánnǎo),
falls into the three evil paths,
there is also no such possibility.
That a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà), using a body that is truly female,
attains Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
there is also no such possibility.
That an *Icchantika* (Yīchǎntí) is permanent,
and the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo) are impermanent,
there is also no such possibility.
That the Tathāgata (Rúlái) abides in Kuśinagara (Jūshīnà Chéng),
there is also no such possibility.
Good man!
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is now in this city of Kuśinagara (Jūshīnà Chéng),
entering the deep cavern of great concentration (sānmèi shēn chándìng kū).
Because the assembly does not see him,
it is called entering Nirvāṇa (Nièpán)."
Shīzǐ Hǒu (Lion's Roar) said:
"Why does the Tathāgata (Rúlái) enter the cavern of concentration?
Good man:
"It is because he desires to ferry across and liberate sentient beings.
For those who have not yet planted wholesome roots, he enables them to plant them;
for those who have already planted wholesome roots, he enables them to grow;
for those whose wholesome fruit is not yet ripe, he enables it to ripen;
for those who are already ripe, he speaks of the path leading to Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí);
For those who slight wholesome Dharma,
he causes them to develop reverence;
for those who indulge in heedlessness,
he causes them to abandon heedlessness;
It is to discuss the Dharma with the great fragrance-elephants, such as Mañjuśrī (Wénshūshīlì);
It is to teach and transform those who delight in recitation to deeply love concentration (chándìng);
It is to teach and transform sentient beings through the noble conduct (shèng xíng), pure conduct (fàn xíng), and heavenly conduct;
It is to observe the uncommon profound Dharma treasury;
It is to criticize heedless disciples;
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is eternally quiescent,
yet still delights in concentration.
How much more so should you all,
whose afflictions (fánnǎo) are not yet exhausted,
indulge in heedlessness?
It is to criticize those evil *bhikṣus* (bǐqiū) who accept and store eight kinds of impure substances,
and those who are not content with little,
nor know satisfaction;
It is to cause sentient beings to revere the Dharma of concentration they have heard.
Because of these causes and conditions,
he enters the cavern of concentration."
Shīzǐ Hǒu (Lion's Roar) said:
"World-Honored One!
That concentration which is without marks
is called Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
Therefore, Nirvāṇa (Nièpán)
is named 'without marks.'
By what cause and condition
is it named 'without marks'?"
“‘Good man
because there are no ten marks.
What are the ten?
Namely, the mark of form (sè xiàng),
the mark of sound (shēng xiàng),
the mark of smell (xiāng xiàng),
the mark of taste (wèi xiàng),
the mark of touch (chù xiàng),
the marks of arising, dwelling, and ceasing (shēng zhù huài xiàng),
the male mark (nán xiàng),
the female mark (nǚ xiàng).
These are called the ten marks.
Having no such marks
is therefore called markless (wú xiàng).
Good man!
Those who cling to marks
can then give rise to delusion (chī).
Because of delusion, love (ài) arises.
Because of love, bondage (xì fù) arises.
Because of bondage, birth (shòu shēng) is received.
Because birth is received, there is death.
Because of death, there is impermanence (wú cháng).
Those who do not cling to marks then do not give rise to delusion.
Because delusion does not arise, there is no love.
Because there is no love, there is no bondage.
Because there is no bondage, birth is not received.
Because birth is not received, there is no death.
Because there is no death, it is called permanence (cháng).
For this reason, Nirvāṇa is called permanence.’
Shīzǐ Hǒu said:
‘World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
What kind of Bhikṣu can sever the ten marks?’
The Buddha said:
‘Good man!
If there is a Bhikṣu who frequently cultivates the three kinds of marks,
then the ten marks are severed.
Frequently cultivating the mark of Samādhi and concentration (sānmèi dìng xiàng),
frequently cultivating the mark of wisdom (zhìhuì zhī xiàng),
frequently cultivating the mark of relinquishment (shě xiàng).
These are called the three marks.’
Shīzǐ Hǒu said:
‘World-Honored One!
What are called the marks of concentration,
wisdom,
and relinquishment?
Concentration is Samādhi.
All sentient beings possess Samādhi.
Why then do you say they should cultivate Samādhi?
If the mind is fixed on one object (yī jìng), it is called Samādhi.
If it shifts to other conditions (yú yuán), it is not called Samādhi.
If it is not fixed, it is not omniscient (yīqiè zhì).
If it is not omniscient, how can it be called concentration?
If attainment of Samādhi is achieved through a single practice (yī xíng),
the remaining practices are also not Samādhi.
If they are not Samādhi, then they are not omniscience.
If they are not omniscience, how can they be called Samādhi?
The two marks of wisdom and relinquishment are also like this.’
The Buddha said:
‘Good man!
What you say,
that Samādhi is attained by conditioning upon a single object,
and that conditioning upon other objects is not called Samādhi,
this meaning is incorrect.
Why?
Because those other objects are also single objects.
Practices are also like this.
Furthermore, your saying that sentient beings already possess Samādhi and do not need to cultivate it,
this is also incorrect.
Why is this?
What is meant by Samādhi is good Samādhi (shàn sānmèi).
All sentient beings truly do not yet possess it.
How can you say that cultivation is not needed?
By abiding in such good Samādhi,
observing all phenomena is called the mark of good wisdom (shàn huì xiàng).
Not seeing any difference between Samādhi and wisdom is
called the mark of relinquishment.
Furthermore, good man!
If one clings to the mark of form,
and cannot observe the marks of form’s permanence
or impermanence,
this is called Samādhi.
If one can observe the marks of form’s permanence
or impermanence,
this is called the mark of wisdom.
When Samādhi
and wisdom are equal in observing all phenomena,
this is called the mark of relinquishment.
Good man!
Just like a good charioteer driving a team of four horses,
who achieves appropriateness whether going slowly or quickly.
Achieving appropriateness whether going slowly or quickly is called the mark of relinquishment.
It is also like this for the Bodhisattva.
If Samādhi is dominant, then wisdom is cultivated.
If wisdom is dominant, then Samādhi is cultivated.
When Samādhi
and wisdom are equal,
it is called relinquishment.
Good man!
The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes (shí zhù),
have great power of wisdom
and little power of Samādhi.
For this reason, they cannot clearly see the Buddha Nature (fó xìng).
Śrāvakas (shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (yuánjué),
have great power of Samādhi
and little power of wisdom.
For this reason, they do not see the Buddha Nature.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,
because concentration and wisdom are equal,
clearly see the Buddha Nature,
distinctly and without hindrance,
just like observing the Āmalaka fruit in the palm of the hand.
Seeing the Buddha Nature is called the mark of relinquishment.
Śamatha (shē mó tuō) is called the capacity to extinguish,
because it can extinguish all defilements and bonds (fánnǎo jié);
furthermore, Śamatha is called the capacity to harmonize,
because it can harmonize the bad and unwholesome nature of the various sense faculties (zhū gēn);
furthermore, Śamatha is called calmness and stillness (jìjìng),
because it can cause the three karmic operations (sān yè) to become calm and still;
furthermore, Śamatha is called detachment (yuǎnlí),
because it can enable sentient beings to detach from the five desires (wǔ yù);
furthermore, Śamatha is called the capacity to purify,
because it can purify the three impurities of covetousness (tān yù), anger (chēnhuì), and delusion (yú chī).
Based on these meanings,
it is therefore called the mark of concentration.
Vipaśyanā (pí pó shě nà)
is called right view (zhèng jiàn),
also called complete view (liǎo jiàn),
called the capacity to see (néng jiàn),
called thorough view (biàn jiàn),
called sequential view (cìdì jiàn),
called distinct characteristic view (bié xiàng jiàn).
This is called wisdom.
Upekṣā (yōu bì chā)
is called equality (píngděng),
also called non-contention (bù zhēng),
also called non-observation (bù guān),
also called non-action (bù xíng).
This is called relinquishment.’
“Good man!
Shē-mó-tuō (Śamatha) has two kinds:
The first is mundane (worldly),
the second is supramundane (world-transcending).
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
The first is achievement (accomplishment),
the second is non-achievement.
Those who achieve [it]
are called the various Buddhas (Fó) and Bodhisattvas (Pú-sà).
Those who do not achieve [it]
are called Śrāvakas (Shēngwén)
and Pratyekabuddhas (Pìzhīfó), etc.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
Namely low,
middle,
and high.
The low are the various ordinary beings (fánfū),
the middle are the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén) and Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué),
the high are the various Buddhas (Fó) and Bodhisattvas (Pú-sà).
Furthermore, there are four kinds:
The first is regression (tuì),
the second is remaining (zhù),
the third is progress (jìn),
the fourth is great beneficial ability (neng dà lìyì).
Furthermore, there are five kinds:
Called the five wisdom samādhis (wǔ zhì sānmèi).
What are these five?
The first is the Samādhi of Non-Sustenance (Wúshí Sānmèi),
the second is the Samādhi of Non-Transgression (Wúguò Sānmèi),
the third is the Samādhi of Pure Body and Mind with Single Focus (Shēnyì Qīngjìng Yīxīn Sānmèi),
the fourth is the Samādhi of Joy in Cause and Effect Together (Yīnguǒ Jùlè Sānmèi),
the fifth is the Samādhi of Constant Mindfulness (Chángniàn Sānmèi).
Furthermore, there are six kinds:
The first is the Samādhi of Contemplation of the Bones (Guāngǔ Sānmèi),
the second is the Samādhi of Loving-Kindness (Cí Sānmèi),
the third is the Samādhi of Contemplation of the Twelve Nidānas (Guān shí’èr yīnyuán Sānmèi),
the fourth is the Samādhi of Ānāpānā (Ānàpónà Sānmèi),
the fifth is the Samādhi of Right Mindfulness, Awareness, and Investigation (Zhèngniàn Juéguān Sānmèi),
the sixth is the Samādhi of Contemplation of Production, Destruction, Persistence, and Alteration (Guān Shēngmiè Zhùyì Sānmèi).
Furthermore, there are seven kinds,
called the seven factors of enlightenment (qī juéfèn):
The first is the Factor of Mindfulness (Niànchù Juéfèn),
the second is the Factor of Investigation of Phenomena (Zéfǎ Juéfèn),
the third is the Factor of Effort/Energy (Jīngjìn Juéfèn),
the fourth is the Factor of Joy (Xǐ Juéfèn),
the fifth is the Factor of Tranquility/Purity (Chú Juéfèn),
the sixth is the Factor of Concentration (Dìng Juéfèn),
the seventh is the Factor of Equanimity (Shě Juéfèn).
Furthermore, there are seven kinds:
The first is the Sū-tuó-huán (Sotāpanna) Samādhi,
the second is the Sī-tuó-hán (Sakṛdāgāmin) Samādhi,
the third is the Ā-nà-hán (Anāgāmin) Samādhi,
the fourth is the Ā-luó-hàn (Arhat) Samādhi,
the fifth is the Pìzhīfó (Pratyekabuddha) Samādhi,
the sixth is the Pú-sà (Bodhisattva) Samādhi,
the seventh is the Rúlái (Tathāgata) Awareness Samādhi.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds,
called the Samādhi of the Eight Liberations (bā jiětuō sānmèi):
The first is the Samādhi of Liberation where, internally having form, one externally contemplates form;
the second is the Samādhi of Liberation where, internally having no form, one externally contemplates form;
the third is the Samādhi of Liberation of Purity Realized in the Body (Jìng Jiětuō Shēn Zhèng Sānmèi);
the fourth is the Samādhi of Liberation of the Sphere of Infinite Space (Kōngchù Jiětuō Sānmèi);
the fifth is the Samādhi of Liberation of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (Shíchù Jiětuō Sānmèi);
the sixth is the Samādhi of Liberation of the Sphere of Nothingness (Wúsuǒyǒu Chù Jiětuō Sānmèi);
the seventh is the Samādhi of Liberation of the Sphere of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception (Fēi Yǒuxiǎng Fēi Wúxiǎng Chù Jiětuō Sānmèi);
the eighth is the Samādhi of Liberation of the Sphere of Cessation (Mièjǐng Dìngchù Jiětuō Sānmèi).
Furthermore, there are nine kinds,
called the nine stages of concentration (jiǔ cìdì dìng):
The four Dhyānas (Sì Chán),
the four Immaterial Realms (Sì Kōng), and the Samādhi of the Concentration of Cessation (Mièjǐng Dìng Sānmèi).
Furthermore, there are ten kinds,
called the Samādhi of the Ten Totalities (shí yīqiè chù sānmèi).
What are these ten?
The first is the Samādhi of Earth Totality (Dì Yīqièchù Sānmèi),
the second is the Samādhi of Water Totality (Shuǐ Yīqièchù Sānmèi),
the third is the Samādhi of Wind Totality (Fēng Yīqièchù Sānmèi),
the fourth is the Samādhi of Blue Totality (Qīng Yīqièchù Sānmèi),
the fifth is the Samādhi of Yellow Totality (Huáng Yīqièchù Sānmèi),
the sixth is the Samādhi of Red Totality (Chì Yīqièchù Sānmèi),
the seventh is the Samādhi of White Totality (Bái Yīqièchù Sānmèi),
the eighth is the Samādhi of Space Totality (Kōng Yīqièchù Sānmèi),
the ninth is the Samādhi of Consciousness Totality (Shí Yīqièchù Sānmèi),
the tenth is the Samādhi of Nothingness Totality (Wúsuǒyǒu Yīqièchù Sānmèi).
Furthermore, there are countless kinds,
namely, those [practiced by] the various Buddhas (Fó) and Bodhisattvas (Pú-sà).
Good man,
these are the characteristics of Samādhi.
“Good man!
Wisdom (huì) has two kinds:
The first is mundane,
the second is supramundane.
Furthermore, there are three kinds:
The first is Bōrě (Prajñā),
the second is Pí-pó-shě-nà (Vipaśyanā),
the third is Shé-nà (Jñāna).
Bōrě refers to all sentient beings,
Pí-pó-shě-nà refers to all sages (shèngrén),
Shé-nà refers to the various Buddhas (Fó) and Bodhisattvas (Pú-sà).
Furthermore, Bōrě is called the distinct characteristic (biéxiàng),
Pí-pó-shě-nà is called the general characteristic (zǒngxiàng),
and Shé-nà is called the characteristic of breaking/destruction (pòxiàng).
Furthermore, there are four kinds,
namely the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths (sì zhēndì).
“Good man!
Shē-mó-tuō is cultivated for three reasons.
What are these three?
First, for the sake of non-negligence (bú fàngyì);
second, for the sake of adorning great wisdom (zhuāngyán dà zhì);
third, for the sake of attaining self-mastery/freedom (dé zìzài).
Next, Pí-pó-shě-nà is cultivated for three reasons.
What are these three?
First, for the sake of contemplating the evil retribution (guǒ bào) of saṃsāra (shēngsǐ);
second, for the sake of desiring to increase all wholesome roots (shàngēn);
third, for the sake of destroying all vexations (fánnǎo).
Śī-zǐ-hǒu (Simhanāda) said:
“Honored by the World (Shìzūn)!
As stated in the Sūtras,
if Pí-pó-shě-nà is able to destroy vexations,
why should Shē-mó-tuō be cultivated again?”
The Buddha (Fó) said:
“Good man!
That which you call Pí-pó-shě-nà destroying vexations—
this meaning is incorrect.
Why is that?
When there is wisdom, there are no vexations;
when there are vexations, there is no wisdom.
How then can you say that Pí-pó-shě-nà is able to destroy vexations?
Good man!
It is like when there is light, there is no darkness;
when there is darkness, there is no light.
If someone says
that light is able to destroy darkness,
there is no such principle.
Good man!
Who possesses wisdom?
Who possesses vexations?
To say that wisdom is able to destroy vexations;
if there is none [of the latter], then there is nothing to be destroyed.
Good man!
If you say that wisdom is able to destroy vexations,
does it destroy by reaching [them]?
Or does it destroy without reaching [them]?
If it destroys without reaching [them],
then ordinary beings (fánfū zhòngshēng) should also be able to destroy [them].
If it destroys by reaching [them],
it should be destroyed in the first instant of thought (chūniàn).
If it is not destroyed in the first instant of thought,
it will also not be destroyed afterward.
If it is destroyed upon the first arrival,
this means it does not arrive;
how then can you say that wisdom is able to destroy?
The meaning that [wisdom] can destroy by both reaching and not reaching [the vexations]
is also incorrect.
Furthermore, regarding Pí-pó-shě-nà destroying vexations,
does it destroy them alone?
Or does it destroy them by relying on a partner?
If it destroys them alone,
why do Bodhisattvas (Pú-sà) cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path (Bā Zhèng Dào)?
If it destroys them by relying on a partner,
one should know that alone it is not capable of destruction.
If alone it is incapable,
and with a partner it is also incapable,
it is like a blind person who cannot see form.
Even if accompanied by a multitude of blind persons,
they still cannot see.
Pí-pó-shě-nà is likewise so.”
"O good man!
Just as the earth has the nature of firmness,
fire has the nature of heat,
water has the nature of moisture,
and wind has the nature of movement.
Although the nature of earth's firmness, extending to the nature of wind's movement,
is not created by causes and conditions,
its nature is intrinsically so.
Like the nature of the Four Great Elements,
afflictions (fánnǎo) are also thus;
their nature is intrinsically cessation.
If they are intrinsically ceased,
why is it said that wisdom (zhìhuì) can sever them?
For this reason,
Vipassanā (Pí Pó Shě Nà) definitely cannot destroy all afflictions.
O good man!
Just as salt is intrinsically salty,
and makes other substances salty;
honey is intrinsically sweet,
and makes other substances sweet;
water is intrinsically moist,
and makes other substances moist;
if wisdom's nature is extinction,
it would cause phenomena (fǎ) to become extinct.
This principle is incorrect.
Why?
If a phenomenon does not have extinction,
how can wisdom forcibly cause it to become extinct?
If you say that just as salt's saltiness makes other substances salty,
wisdom's extinction is likewise,
and can cause other phenomena to become extinct,
this is also incorrect.
Why?
Because the nature of wisdom
ceases moment by moment.
If it ceases moment by moment,
how can it be said to extinguish other phenomena?
For this reason,
the nature of wisdom does not destroy afflictions.
"O good man!
All phenomena have two types of extinction:
first, intrinsic extinction (xìng miè),
second, ultimate extinction (bìjìng miè).
If they possess intrinsic extinction,
how can it be said that wisdom can extinguish them?
If you say that wisdom can burn afflictions,
like fire burning objects,
this principle is incorrect.
Why?
If fire burns an object,
there are remaining embers;
if wisdom were like this,
there should be remaining embers.
Like an axe cutting down a tree,
the place of chopping is visible;
if wisdom were like this,
what would be visible?
If wisdom can cause afflictions to depart,
these afflictions should appear elsewhere,
just as various externalists (wàidào) left the six great cities (Liù Dà Chéng)
and appeared at Kūshīnà;
if these afflictions do not appear elsewhere,
then it is known that wisdom cannot cause them to depart.
O good man!
If the nature of all phenomena is intrinsically empty,
who can cause them to arise?
Who can cause them to cease?
Arising and ceasing are different; there is no agent who creates them.
O good man!
If one practices concentration (dìng),
then one obtains such correct knowledge (zhèng zhī)
and correct view (zhèng jiàn).
For this reason,
I have said in the sūtras:
'If there is a bhikṣu (bǐqiū) who practices concentration,
he can see the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the Five Aggregates (Wǔ Yīn).'
O good man!
If one does not practice concentration,
one cannot even understand worldly matters,
much less transcendent matters?
If one lacks concentration,
one stumbles and falls on level ground,
the mind focuses on different phenomena,
the mouth proclaims different words,
the ears hear different speech,
the mind understands different meanings,
wishing to write one character,
the hand writes a different script,
wishing to walk one road,
the body enters a different path.
If one practices samādhi (sānmèi) and concentration,
then great benefit is obtained,
even up to Anuttarasamyaksaṃbodhi (Ānòu Duō Luó Sān Miǎo Sān Pútí).
"O good man!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) who possesses two dharmas can obtain great benefit:
first, concentration (dìng),
second, wisdom (zhì).
O good man!
Just like cutting sharp reeds;
if held firmly, they are severed.
When a Púsà Móhēsà practices these two dharmas,
it is also like this.
O good man!
Just like pulling out a firm stake;
first moving it by hand makes it easy to pull out later.
The Púsà's concentration and wisdom are also like this:
first using concentration to loosen,
then using wisdom to pull out.
O good man!
Just like washing dirty clothes:
first using lye/ash solution,
then using clear water,
the clothes become fresh and clean.
The Púsà's concentration and wisdom
are also like this.
O good man!
Just as first reading and reciting,
and later understanding the meaning;
the Púsà's concentration and wisdom are also like this.
O good man!
For instance, a brave man
first firmly adorns himself with armor and weapons,
and only then confronts the battle array,
able to destroy the hostile bandits.
The Púsà's concentration and wisdom are also like this.
O good man!
For instance, a skilled craftsman
puts gold in tongs,
freely stirring, mixing, melting, and dissolving it as desired.
The Púsà's concentration and wisdom are also like this.
O good man!
For instance, a bright mirror illuminating a facial image;
the Púsà's concentration and wisdom are also like this.
O good man!
Just as first leveling the ground,
and then planting seeds,
first receiving teaching from the master,
and later reflecting upon the meaning;
the Púsà's concentration and wisdom are also like this.
For this reason,
a Púsà Móhēsà who practices these two dharmas can obtain great benefit.
"O good man!
A Púsà Móhēsà who practices these two dharmas
controls and restrains the Five Faculties,
and can endure all sufferings,
namely hunger, thirst, cold, heat,
beating, throwing, scolding, and insults,
being bitten by vicious beasts,
or stung by mosquitoes and gadflies.
He constantly controls his mind and does not allow laxity,
and does not practice non-dharma for the sake of profit and sustenance.
He cannot be stained by extraneous defilements,
nor confused by various evil and deviant views.
He is always able to keep far away from all evil thought constructions,
and soon achieves Ānòu Duō Luó Sān Miǎo Sān Pútí,
for the sake of accomplishing benefit for sentient beings.
O good man!
When a Púsà Móhēsà practices these two dharmas,
the strong winds of the Four Inversions cannot shake him.
Just like Mount Sumeru (Xūmíshān), even though struck and blasted by the four winds, it cannot be moved.
He cannot be uprooted by externalists and wicked teachers,
just like the banner of Śakra (Dìshì), which cannot be moved.
Various evil and deviant arts cannot deceive or confuse him.
He constantly receives subtle, supreme peace and joy (ānlè),
and can understand the deep, secret meaning of the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Experiencing joy, he is not elated;
encountering suffering, he is not distressed.
He is respected and praised by all devas and worldly people,
clearly sees Saṃsāra (shēngsǐ) and the non-Saṃsāra,
is skilled at understanding the Dharma Realm (Fǎ Jiè) and the Dharma Nature (Fǎ Xìng).
His body possesses the dharmas of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
This is called the joy of Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
"O good man!
The characteristic of concentration is called the Samādhi of Emptiness (Kōng Sānmèi).
The characteristic of wisdom is called the Samādhi of Desirelessness (Wú Yuàn Sānmèi).
The characteristic of relinquishing is called the Samādhi of Signlessness (Wú Xiàng Sānmèi).
O good man!
If there is a Púsà Móhēsà who is skilled at knowing the time for concentration,
the time for wisdom,
the time for relinquishing, and also knowing the inappropriate time,
this is called a Púsà Móhēsà practicing the Bodhi path.
Shīzǐ Hǒu said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
How does a Púsà know the appropriate time and the inappropriate time?"
"Good man!
When a Púsà Móhēsà gives rise to great arrogance due to receiving pleasure,
or gives rise to arrogance due to expounding the Dharma,
or gives rise to arrogance due to diligence and effort,
or gives rise to arrogance due to understanding meaning and engaging in good questioning and answering,
or gives rise to arrogance due to proximity to evil associates (è zhīshi),
or gives rise to arrogance due to giving heavily valued items in Dāna (bùshī),
or gives rise to arrogance due to mundane wholesome Dharma merits (gōngdé),
or gives rise to arrogance due to being respected by powerful and noble people of the world—
know that at such a time,
it is not appropriate to cultivate wisdom (zhì),
it is appropriate to cultivate concentration (dìng).
This is called the Púsà knowing the time and the non-time.
If there is a Púsà diligently practicing effort,
but has not yet attained the benefit and pleasure of Nirvāṇa (nièpán),
and because of this non-attainment gives rise to regret,
and because of dull faculties (dùn gēn) cannot tame the five emotions and various senses,
and because the power of defilements (gòu) and afflictions (fánnǎo) is strong,
and because they doubt that their Vinaya (jièlǜ) has been weakened or damaged—
know that at such a time,
it is not appropriate to cultivate concentration (dìng),
it is appropriate to cultivate wisdom (zhì).
This is called the Púsà knowing the time and the non-time.
Good man!
If a Púsà's concentration (dìng)
and wisdom (huì)—these two Dharmas—are unequal,
know that at such a time it is not appropriate to cultivate relinquishment (shě).
If the two Dharmas are equal, then it is appropriate to cultivate it.
This is called the Púsà knowing the time and the non-time.
Good man!
If a Púsà cultivating concentration and wisdom gives rise to afflictions,
know that at such a time it is not appropriate to cultivate relinquishment (shě).
It is appropriate to recite,
copy, and explain the twelve categories of Sūtras (jīng).
Mindfulness of the Buddha (niàn Fó),
mindfulness of the Dharma (niàn Fǎ),
mindfulness of the Saṅgha (niàn Sēng),
mindfulness of the precepts (niàn jiè),
mindfulness of the devas (niàn tiān),
mindfulness of relinquishment (niàn shě).
This is called the cultivation of relinquishment.
Good man!
If a Púsà cultivates the marks of these three Dharmas,
by means of these causes and conditions, they attain markless Nirvāṇa (wú xiàng Nièpán)."
Shīzihǒu said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
Because there are no ten marks,
it is called the Great Nirvāṇa (Dà Nièpán).
If it is markless,
then by what reason,
is it called the Unarisen (wú shēng),
the Unmanifested (wú chū),
the Uncreated (wú zuò),
the Dwelling (wū zhái),
the Isle (zhōu),
the Refuge (guī),
the Security (ān yǐn),
the Extinction and Crossing Over (miè dù),
Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
the Tranquil Silence (jí jìng),
free from all sickness and suffering,
the Non-Possession (wú suǒ yǒu)?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Because there are no causes and conditions,
thus it is called the Unarisen (wú shēng).
Because it is unconditioned (wú wéi),
thus it is called the Unmanifested (wú chū).
Because there is no creation of karma (yè),
thus it is called the Uncreated (wú zuò).
It does not enter the five wrong views (wǔ jiàn),
thus it is called the Dwelling (wū zhái).
It is separated from the four torrents (sì pù shuǐ),
thus it is called the Isle (zhōu).
Because it tames sentient beings,
thus it is called the Refuge (guī yī).
Because it destroys the thieves of bondage (jié zéi),
thus it is called the Security (ān yǐn).
The fire of all bondages is extinguished,
thus it is called the Extinction and Crossing Over (miè dù).
Because it is separated from initial thought (jué) and sustained thought (guān),
it is called Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
Because it is far removed from confusion and clamor,
it is called the Tranquil Silence (jí jìng).
Because it eternally severs certain death,
thus it is called the Non-Sickness (wú bìng).
Because everything is nonexistent,
it is called Non-Possession (wú suǒ yǒu).
Good man!
When a Púsà Móhēsà makes this observation,
they immediately attain a clear view of the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng)."
Shīzihǒu said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
How many Dharmas must a Púsà Móhēsà fulfill,
to be able to clearly see such markless Nirvāṇa, extending to Non-Possession (wú suǒ yǒu)?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
A Púsà Móhēsà fulfills ten Dharmas,
and is then able to clearly see markless Nirvāṇa, extending to Non-Possession.
What are these ten?
First is the fulfillment of faith (xìnxīn).
What is meant by the fulfillment of faith?
Deep faith that the Buddha (Fó),
the Dharma (Fǎ),
and the Saṅgha (zhòng Sēng) are eternal;
that the Buddhas of the ten directions appear expediently;
and that all sentient beings and even Icchantikas (yīchǎntí) universally possess Buddha-nature (Fóxìng).
Not believing that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) truly underwent birth, old age, sickness, and death, or cultivated ascetic practices,
or that Devadatta (Típó dáduō) truly broke up the Saṅgha (pò Sēng) and drew the Buddha's blood,
or that the Tathāgata ultimately entered Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) and the Right Dharma (zhèng fǎ) was fully extinguished.
This is called the Púsà's fulfillment of faith.
"Second is the fulfillment of pure precepts (jìng jiè).
What is meant by the fulfillment of pure precepts?
Good man!
If a Púsà claims their precepts are pure,
yet even though they do not unite with a woman,
when they see a woman,
they sometimes engage in mockery, flirting language, or jesting laughter.
Such a Púsà fulfills the dharma of desire (yù fǎ),
destroys the pure precepts,
defiles the Brahma practice (fàn xíng),
making the precepts impure and defiled.
This cannot be called the fulfillment of pure precepts.
Furthermore, if a Púsà claims their precepts are pure,
even though they do not physically unite with a woman,
nor engage in mockery or jesting laughter,
but from beyond a wall or barrier,
they hear from afar the various sounds of women's jewelry (yīngluò huán chuàn),
and their mind gives rise to attachment and clinging.
Such a Púsà fulfills the dharma of desire,
destroys the pure precepts,
defiles the Brahma practice,
making the precepts impure and defiled.
This cannot be called the fulfillment of pure precepts.
Furthermore, if a Púsà claims their precepts are pure,
even though they do not unite with a woman,
use mocking language,
or listen to their sounds,
yet when they see a man following after a woman,
or see a woman following after a man,
they immediately give rise to greed and attachment (tān zhuó).
Such a Púsà fulfills the dharma of desire,
destroys the pure precepts,
defiles the Brahma practice,
making the precepts impure and defiled.
This cannot be called the fulfillment of pure precepts.
Furthermore, if a Púsà claims their precepts are pure,
even though they do not unite with a woman,
use mocking language,
listen to their sounds,
or observe men and women following one another,
but rather, they hold the precepts in order to be reborn in heaven (shēng tiān) and experience the pleasures of the five desires (wǔ yù lè).
Such a Púsà fulfills the dharma of desire,
destroys the pure precepts,
defiles the Brahma practice,
making the precepts impure and defiled.
This cannot be called the fulfillment of pure precepts.
Good man!
If a Púsà purely maintains the precepts,
but not for the sake of the precepts (jiè),
not for the sake of Śīla Pāramitā (Shīluó Bōluómì),
not for the sake of sentient beings,
not for the sake of benefit and offering (lì yǎng),
not for the sake of Bodhi (pútí),
not for the sake of Nirvāṇa (nièpán),
and not for the sake of Śrāvakas (shēngwén) or Pratyekabuddhas (pìzhīfó)—
but solely for the sake of the Supreme First Principle (Dìyī Yì),
maintaining the prohibitions and precepts—
Good man!
This is called the Púsà's fulfillment of pure precepts.
"Third is proximity to good spiritual friends (shàn zhīshi).
A good spiritual friend
is one who is able to speak about faith (xìn),
precepts (jiè),
extensive learning (duō wén),
Dāna (bùshī),
and wisdom (zhìhuì),
leading people to receive and practice them.
This is called the Púsà's good spiritual friend.
"Fourth is delight in tranquil silence (jí jìng).
Tranquil silence
refers to the tranquil silence of body and mind.
Observing all Dharmas and the exceedingly deep Dharma Realm (fǎ jiè),
this is called tranquil silence.
"Fifth is diligence (jīngjìn).
Diligence
refers to focusing the mind on observing the Four Noble Truths (Sì Zhēndì).
Even if their head were ablaze,
they would ultimately not relinquish this focus.
This is called diligence.
"Sixth is the fulfillment of mindfulness (niàn jùzú).
The fulfillment of mindfulness
refers to mindfulness of the Buddha (niàn Fó),
mindfulness of the Dharma (niàn Fǎ),
mindfulness of the Saṅgha (niàn Sēng),
mindfulness of the precepts (niàn jiè),
mindfulness of the devas (niàn tiān),
and mindfulness of relinquishment (niàn shě).
This is called the fulfillment of mindfulness."
"Seventh, gentle speech.
Gentle speech
refers to true speech,
wonderful speech,
inquiring about the well-being of others beforehand,
timely speech,
and genuine speech.
This is called gentle speech.
"Eighth, protecting the Dharma (Hùfǎ).
Protecting the Dharma
refers to loving and rejoicing in the Correct Dharma (Zhèngfǎ),
constantly delighting in expounding it,
reciting, chanting, and writing it,
contemplating its meaning,
widely proclaiming and spreading it so that it circulates.
If one sees someone writing, explaining,
reciting, praising,
or contemplating its meaning,
they should provide offerings for their livelihood,
such as clothing, food and drink,
bedding, and medicine.
For the sake of protecting the Dharma, they spare neither body nor life.
This is called protecting the Dharma.
"Ninth, if a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva (Púsà Mōhēsà) sees
classmates or those sharing the precepts lacking something,
they should beg it from others,
such as their censer, bowl, or dyed robes,
necessities for attending the sick,
clothing, food and drink,
bedding, or dwellings, and supply them.
"Tenth, being fully equipped with wisdom (Zhìhuì).
Wisdom
refers to observing that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is Eternal (Cháng), Blissful (Lè), Self (Wǒ), and Pure (Jìng),
and that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-Nature (Fóxìng).
One contemplates the two aspects of phenomena:
namely emptiness (kōng)
and non-emptiness (bùkōng);
permanence (cháng)
and impermanence (wúcháng);
bliss (lè)
and lack of bliss (wúlè);
self (wǒ)
and non-self (wúwǒ);
purity (jìng)
and impurity (bùjìng);
that one type of phenomenon can be eradicated,
and another type of phenomenon cannot be eradicated;
that one type of phenomenon arises from conditions,
another type of phenomenon is seen through conditions,
another type of phenomenon is the fruit of conditions,
and another type of phenomenon is not the fruit of conditions.
This is called being fully equipped with wisdom.
Good sons!
These are the ten practices that a Bodhisattva (Púsà) is fully equipped with,
enabling them to clearly perceive the signlessness of Nirvāṇa (Nièpán Wúxiàng).
Śīzǐhǒu said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
As the Buddha previously informed Chúntuó (Cunda),
'You have now attained the sight of the Buddha-Nature (Fóxìng),
attained Great Nirvāṇa,
and achieved Anuttarā-samyak-sambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).'
What does this statement mean?
World-Honored One!
As stated in the Sūtras:
If one gives charity to an animal, they receive a hundredfold reward;
giving charity to an Icchantika (Yīchǎntí) receives a thousandfold reward;
giving charity to one upholding the precepts receives a hundred thousandfold reward;
if one gives charity to a non-Buddhist (wàidào) who has eliminated defilements (fánnǎo), they receive immeasurable reward;
making offerings to the Four Paths (Sìxiàng) and the Four Fruits (Sìguǒ) up to a Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó) receives immeasurable reward;
giving charity to Non-Retrogressing Bodhisattvas (Bùtuì Púsà), those Great Bodhisattvas in their final lifetime,
and the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One (Rúlái Shìzūn),
the resulting blessed rewards (fúbào) are measureless, boundless, incalculable, and inconceivable.
If the great being Chúntuó receives such immeasurable rewards,
and if these rewards are inexhaustible,
when will he attain Anuttarā-samyak-sambodhi?
World-Honored One!
The Sūtras also state
that if a person commits good or evil karma (yè) with a focused mind, they will certainly receive the fruit of the karma,
whether received in this life,
in the next life,
or in later lives.
Chúntuó performed his wholesome karma with utmost focus and diligence,
therefore, we know that this karma will definitely result in a retribution (shòubào).
If he must definitely receive retribution,
how can he achieve Anuttarā-samyak-sambodhi?
How can he, furthermore, attain the sight of the Buddha-Nature?
World-Honored One!
The Sūtras also state
that the fruit of giving to three types of people is inexhaustible:
first, the sick;
second, one's parents (fùmǔ);
third, the Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!
The Sūtras also state:
'The Buddha told Ānán (Ānanda):
"If any sentient being possesses no karma of the desire realm (Yùjiè Yè),
they immediately attain Anuttarā-samyak-sambodhi.
The karma of the form realm (Sè)
and the formless realm (Wúsè Yè)
are also like this."'
World-Honored One!
As stated in the verse of the *Fǎjù* (Dharmapada):
'Neither in the sky nor in the ocean,
nor by entering the crevices of mountains and rocks—
there is no place
where one can escape from karmic retribution (yè).'
Moreover, Ānílóutuó (Aniruddha) said:
'World-Honored One!
I recall in the past, by giving just one meal as charity,
I did not fall into the Three Evil Paths for eighty thousand kalpas.
World-Honored One!
If the charity of a single meal still yields such a reward,
how much more so for Chúntuó, who gave charity to the Buddha with faith
and fully accomplished the Dānapāramitā (Tánbōluómì)?
World-Honored One!
If wholesome karmic rewards (guǒbào) cannot be exhausted,
how can the offenses of slandering Vaipulya Sūtras (Fāngděng Jīng),
committing the Five Heinous Crimes (Wǔ Nì Zuì),
violating the Four Cardinal Precepts (Sì Chóng Jìn),
or the offenses of an Icchantika (Yīchǎntí Zuì) ever be exhausted?
If they cannot be exhausted,
how can one attain the sight of the Buddha-Nature,
and achieve Anuttarā-samyak-sambodhi?
The Buddha said:
"Excellent!
Excellent!
Good sons!
There are only two types of people who can attain measureless and boundless merit and virtue (gōngdé),
which is incalculable and inexpressible,
who can dry up the swift river of saṃsāra,
subdue Māra's (Mó) enemies and crush Māra's victory banner,
and turn the Tathāgata's Supreme Dharma Wheel (Fǎlún):
First, those who ask well;
second, those who answer well.
Good sons!
Among the Buddha's Ten Powers (Shí Lì),
the power of karma (yèlì) is the deepest.
Good sons!
There are certain sentient beings
who, regarding the causes and conditions of karma (yèyuán),
are frivolous in mind and lack faith.
In order to save them, I speak thus.
Good sons!
All karma created has light and heavy aspects,
and these two types of light and heavy karma each have two sub-types:
first, determinate;
second, indeterminate.
Good sons!
Some people might say:
'Evil karma produces no fruit.'
If one asserts that evil karma must definitely produce fruit,
how is it that Qìxū Zhāntuóluó (Kṣemendra Cāṇḍāla) attained birth in heaven?
How did Yāngjué Móluó (Aṅgulimāla) attain the fruit of liberation?
For this reason,
you should know that created karma has definite results
and indefinite results.
I speak the words
in the Sūtras,
'All created karma receives a result,' in order to eliminate such heterodox views (xiéjiàn).
"Good sons!
There may be heavy karma that can be made light,
and there may be light karma that can be made heavy.
This is not true for all people,
only for the foolish
and the wise.
Therefore, you should know
that not all karma definitely produces a result.
Although it may not definitely be received,
it is also not the case that it is never received.
Good sons!
All sentient beings are generally of two types:
first, the wise person (zhìrén);
second, the ignorant person (yúchī).
The wise person,
by the power of wisdom,
is able to cause extremely heavy karma that would lead to hell (dìyù)
to be lightly received in this current life.
The ignorant person, whose karma is light in this current life,
receives heavy retribution in hell.
Śīzǐhǒu said:
"World-Honored One!
If this is the case,
then one should not seek pure Brahma practice (Fànhéng) and the fruit of liberation."
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
If all karma (yè) were certain to yield its result,
then one should not seek pure conduct (fànxíng) and liberation (jiětuō).
Because it is not certain,
then one cultivates pure conduct (fànxíng) and the fruit of liberation (jiětuō guǒ).
Good man!
If one is able to distance oneself from all evil karma (è yè),
then one obtains good results.
If one distances oneself from good karma (shàn yè),
then one obtains evil results.
If all karma (yè) were certain to yield its result,
then one should not seek to cultivate the Noble Path (Shèngdào).
If the Path (dào) is not cultivated, then there is no liberation (jiětuō).
The reason all noble ones (shèngrén) cultivate the Path (dào),
is to counteract certain karma (dìng yè),
and obtain a lighter retribution (qīng bào);
uncertain karma (bùdìng zhī yè) yields no fruit or retribution.
If all karma (yè) were certain to yield its result,
then one should not seek to cultivate the Noble Path (Shèngdào).
If a person achieves liberation (jiětuō) while avoiding the cultivation of the Noble Path (Shèngdào),
there is no such possibility.
Achieving Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) without obtaining liberation (jiětuō),
is also impossible.
Good man!
If all karma (yè) were certain to yield its result,
the purely good karma (chún shàn zhī yè) performed in one lifetime
should result in permanent and everlasting peace and joy.
The extremely heavy evil karma (jí zhòng è yè) performed in one lifetime
should also result in permanent and everlasting suffering and distress.
If karmic results (yè guǒ) were like that,
then there would be no cultivation of the Path (xiū dào), liberation (jiětuō), or Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
If a human performs it, a human receives it;
if a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) performs it, a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) receives it.
If this were the case,
then there should be no lower castes (xià xìng) or lower class people.
A human should always remain human,
and a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) should always remain a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén).
Karma (yè) performed in youth should be received in youth,
it should not be received in middle age or old age.
If evil is committed in old age and one is born in hell (dìyù),
the first body in hell (dìyù) should not receive the retribution immediately;
one should wait until old age before receiving it.
If one did not kill in old age,
one should not obtain longevity in prime age.
If there is no longevity in prime age,
how does one reach old age?
Yet, karma (yè) is never lost.
If karma (yè) is never lost,
how can there be the cultivation of the Path (xiū dào) and Nirvāṇa (Nièpán)?
Good man!
Karma (yè) has two types:
certain (dìng) and uncertain (bùdìng).
Certain karma (dìng yè) has two aspects:
first, the retribution (bào) is certain;
second, the time (shí) is certain.
Sometimes the retribution (bào) is certain,
but the time (shí) is uncertain;
one receives it when the conditions (yuán) align.
Or it is received in three times,
namely, received in the present (xiàn shòu),
received in the next life (shēng shòu),
or received in subsequent lives (hòu shòu).
Good man!
If one creates good or evil karma (yè) with a resolute mind (dìng xīn),
and having performed it, deeply generates faith and joy,
or if one makes a vow and offers alms to the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo),
this is called certain karma (dìng yè).
“Good man!
The virtuous roots (shàngēn) of the wise are deep, firm, and difficult to shake,
therefore they are able to transform heavy karma (zhòng yè) into light retribution.
The non-virtuous nature of the foolish is deep and thick,
able to transform light karma (qīng yè) into heavy retribution (zhòng bào).
For this reason,
all karma (yè) is not designated as certain (juédìng).
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) has no hell (dìyù) karma (yè),
but for the sake of sentient beings (zhòngshēng),
they make a great vow to be born in hell (dìyù).
Good man!
In the past, when sentient beings (zhòngshēng) lived for a hundred years,
sentient beings numerous as the sands of the Ganges (Héngshā) received hell (dìyù) retribution.
When I saw this,
I immediately made a great vow to receive a hell (dìyù) body.
The Bodhisattva (Púsà) at that time truly had no such karma (yè);
for the sake of sentient beings (zhòngshēng), they received the hell (dìyù) result.
At that time, I stayed in hell (dìyù) for immeasurable years,
extensively revealing and explaining the Twelve Divisions of the Sūtras (shí'èr bù jīng) for those sinners.
Having heard this, those people
destroyed their evil karmic retribution (è guǒ bào),
emptying the hell (dìyù),
except for the Icchantika (Yīchǎntí).
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) receiving this evil karma (è yè) not in the present, subsequent, or future lives.
“Furthermore, good man!
In this Bhadrakalpa (Xián Jié),
immeasurable sentient beings (zhòngshēng) fell into the animal realm (chùshēng) and received evil karmic results (è yè guǒ).
When I saw this,
I again made a vow,
in order to teach the Dharma and guide sentient beings (zhòngshēng):
sometimes becoming the body of a deer or elk,
a bear, a macaque, or a monkey,
a Nāga (Lóng), a snake, or a Garuda (Jīnchì),
a bird, a pigeon, a fish, or a turtle,
a rabbit, an elephant, an ox, or a horse.
Good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) truly had no such evil karma (è yè) of the animal realm (chùshēng);
by the power of their great vow, and for the sake of sentient beings (zhòngshēng),
they manifested and received these bodies.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) receiving this evil karma (è yè) not in the present, subsequent, or future lives.
“Furthermore, good man!
In this Bhadrakalpa (Xián Jié),
there were also immeasurable, boundless sentient beings (zhòngshēng) born into the hungry ghost realm (èguǐ zhōng).
They might eat spit,
fatty meat, pus, or blood,
excrement, urine, snot, or saliva.
Their lifespan was immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years,
they had never even heard the name of water or liquid refreshment,
much less seen it with their eyes and been able to drink it.
