Even if they saw water from afar and intended to approach it,
upon arrival it would transform into raging fire or pus and blood.
Or sometimes it did not change,
but many people holding spears and pikes would guard it, seize them, and hold them back,
not allowing them to advance.
Or when rain fell from the sky, it turned into fire upon touching their bodies.
This is called the retribution (guǒ bào) for evil karma (è yè).
Good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) truly had no such results of evil karma (è yè guǒ);
in order to transform sentient beings (zhòngshēng) and enable them to obtain liberation (jiětuō),
they made a vow and received such bodies.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) receiving this evil karma (è yè) not in the present, subsequent, or future lives.
“Good man!
In the Bhadrakalpa (Xián Jié), I was born into the family of a butcher and cook,
raising chickens, pigs,
cattle, and sheep,
hunting, netting, and trapping them;
and living in the house of a Caṇḍāla (Zhāntuóluó), committing theft and robbery.
The Bodhisattva (Púsà) truly had no such evil karma (è yè),
but in order to guide sentient beings (zhòngshēng) and enable them to obtain liberation (jiětuō),
they received such bodies by the power of their great vow.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) receiving this evil karma (è yè) not in the present, subsequent, or future lives.
“Good man!
In this Bhadrakalpa (Xián Jié), I was also born in remote lands (biāndì),
frequently engaging in greed (tānyù),
anger (chēnhuì),
and delusion (yúchī),
habitually practicing non-Dharma (fēifǎ),
not believing in the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo) or the retribution (guǒ bào) of future generations,
and unable to respect parents, relatives, or elders,
or long-time veterans and seniors.
Good man!
The Bodhisattva (Púsà) at that time truly had no such karma (yè);
in order to enable sentient beings (zhòngshēng) to obtain liberation (jiětuō),
they were born there by the power of their great vow.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) receiving this evil karma (è yè) not in the present, subsequent, or future lives.
“Good man!
In this Bhadrakalpa (Xián Jié), I also received the body of a woman (nǚ shēn),
an evil body (è shēn),
a greedy body (tān shēn),
an angry body (chēn shēn),
a deluded body (chī shēn),
an envious body (dù shēn),
a stingy body (qiān shēn),
an illusory body (huàn shēn),
a deceitful body (kuáng shēn),
and a body afflicted by fetters and coverings (chán gài zhī shēn).
Good man!
The Bodhisattva (Púsà) at that time also had no such karma (yè);
but solely to enable sentient beings (zhòngshēng) to obtain liberation (jiětuō),
they vowed to be born there by the power of their great vow.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) receiving this evil karma (è yè) not in the present, subsequent, or future lives.
“Good man!
In the Bhadrakalpa (Xián Jié), I received the body of a eunuch (huángmén shēn),
one without faculties (wú gēn), with dual faculties (èr gēn), or with indeterminate faculties (bùdìng gēn).
Good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) truly had no such evil bodily karma (è shēn yè);
in order to enable sentient beings (zhòngshēng) to obtain liberation (jiětuō),
they vowed to be born there by the power of their great vow.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) receiving this evil karma (è yè) not in the present, subsequent, or future lives.
“Good man!
In the Bhadrakalpa (Xián Jié), I also practiced the teachings of the heterodox Nigaṇṭha (Wàidào Nígānzǐ fǎ),
believing and accepting their doctrines:
that there is no giving (shī),
no sacrifice (cí),
no retribution for giving or sacrifice (shī cí bào),
no good or evil karma (shàn è yè),
no retribution for good or evil karma (shàn è yè bào),
no present world or future world,
no this shore and no other shore,
no noble ones (shèngrén),
no transformation bodies (biànhuà shēn),
and no Path (Dào) or Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
Good man!
The Bodhisattva (Púsà) truly had no such evil karma (è yè),
but solely to enable sentient beings (zhòngshēng) to obtain liberation (jiětuō),
they accepted these heterodox teachings (xié fǎ) by the power of their great vow.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà) receiving this evil karma (è yè) not in the present, subsequent, or future lives.”
"Good man!
I recall in the past, Dìpó Dáduō and I were both merchant leaders,
each of us having five hundred merchants,
and for the sake of profit,
we went into the great sea to gather rare treasures.
Due to the circumstances of evil karma,
we encountered a violent storm on the way,
which smashed our ships and boats,
and all our companions died completely.
At that time, Dìpó Dáduō and I,
due to the retribution of not killing (i.e., having preserved life),
and consequently having long life,
were blown by the wind
and both reached land.
Dìpó Dáduō then clung greedily to the precious goods,
generating great sorrow and distress,
and cried aloud.
I spoke to him then:
'Dìpó Dáduō!
There is no need to cry.'
Dìpó Dáduō immediately replied to me, saying:
'Listen carefully,
listen carefully!
Suppose there is a person who is poor and distressed,
who goes to a graveyard,
takes hold of a corpse,
and says this:
"I wish you would now grant me the joy of death,
and I will grant you my poor and lengthy life."
At that time, the corpse immediately sat up and spoke to the poor man, saying:
"Good man!
That poor and lengthy life, you should take it yourself.
I am now very happy;
such is the joy of death.
I truly do not desire your poverty and life.
However, today I neither have the joy of death
nor am I free from poverty,
how can I not cry?'
I then consoled him:
'Do not worry for now.
I currently have two pearls,
whose value is countless.
I shall divide one
and bestow it upon you as a gift.'
I immediately divided one and gave it to him,
and further spoke to him, saying:
'Only a living person can obtain this treasure;
if one has no life,
who can obtain it?'
I was weary then,
and went beneath a tree,
rested and slept.
Dìpó Dáduō's greedy mind became blazing hot,
and for the sake of the remaining pearl, he immediately generated ill will,
pierced and damaged my eyes,
and robbed me of my pearl.
I then suffered from the injury and groaned aloud.
At that time, a woman
came to where I was
and asked me:
'Honorable Sir!
Why do you groan like this?'
I then thoroughly recounted the entire incident to her.
When the woman heard this,
she asked me again:
'What is your name?'
I immediately answered:
'My name is Shíyǔ (True Speech).'
The woman said:
'How can I know you are truly Shíyǔ?'
I immediately made an oath:
'If I currently harbor ill will toward Dìpó Dáduō,
my eyes shall remain thus perpetually blind;
if I do not, then I shall regain my sight.'
Having spoken, his eyes were restored to their former state.
Good man!
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva speaking of present-life retribution.
"Good man!
I recall in the past,
I was born in Southern Tiānzhú (India),
in Fùdānnà City,
into a Brahmāṇa family.
At that time there was a king
named Jiāluófù.
His nature was violent and wicked,
arrogant and self-important.
He was in his prime and handsome in appearance,
addicted to the five desires.
At that time, I, for the purpose of saving sentient beings,
resided outside that city in silent meditation (Chán sī).
At that time, when the spring trees and flowers bloomed,
that king, with his retinue,
palace attendants, and ladies-in-waiting,
left the city to tour and observe.
Beneath the trees in the forest,
he amused himself with the five desires.
His various ladies-in-waiting,
leaving the king to amuse themselves,
consequently came to where I was.
At that time, wishing to help them break their attachment to greed,
I taught the Dharma to them.
The king soon arrived.
As soon as he saw me,
he immediately generated ill will,
and asked me, saying:
'Have you now attained the fruit of Arhat?'
I said:
'I have not attained it.'
He asked again:
'Have you attained the fruit of Anāgāmin (Non-Returner)?'
I said:
'I have not attained it.'
He then said this:
'If you have not attained these two fruits,
then you are fully afflicted by the vexations of greed and desire.
How dare you freely look upon my women?'
I immediately replied:
'Great King!
You should know that although I have not yet cut off the fetters of greed,
my inner mind is truly free from attachment.'
The king said:
'Foolish person!
There are various Immortals in the world
who breathe air and eat fruit,
yet still crave colors and forms.
How much more so you, in the prime of your life,
who have not cut off greedy desire?
How can you see form and not crave it?'
I said:
'Great King!
Non-attachment upon seeing form
truly does not depend on breathing air or eating fruit,
but entirely on fixing the mind upon impermanence and impurity.'
The king said:
'If one belittles others and generates slander,
how can one be called a practitioner who observes pure precepts (Jìng Jiè)?'
I said:
'Great King!
If one has a jealous mind,
then there is slander.
I have no jealous mind;
how can I be said to slander?'
The king said:
'Great Virtue!
What is meant by precept (Jiè)?'
'Great King!
Forbearance is called precept.'
The king said:
'If forbearance is the precept,
then I shall cut off your ears.
If you can endure it,
then I will know you uphold the precepts.'
He immediately cut off his ears.
At that time, when I was mutilated,
my countenance did not change.
The king's assembled ministers,
having seen this event,
immediately admonished the king, saying:
'Such a great being (Dàshì) should not be harmed.'
The king informed the ministers:
'How do you know he is a Dàshì?'
The ministers replied:
'We see that when he endured suffering, his countenance did not change.'
The king spoke to them again:
'I shall test him further,
to see whether he changes or not.'
He immediately cut off his nose
and chopped off his hands and feet.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, having cultivated compassion (Cí Bēi) and pity for suffering sentient beings
throughout countless and boundless lifetimes;
the Four Heavenly Kings (Sì Tiān Wáng) held wrath and indignation in their hearts
and rained down sand and gravel stones.
When the king saw this,
he was greatly terrified in his heart,
and again came to where I was,
knelt down for a long time and said:
'I only beg for your compassionate pity;
please allow me to repent.'
I said:
'Great King!
My mind is without anger,
just as it is without greed.'
The king said:
'Great Virtue!
How can one know that your mind is without hatred?'
I immediately made an oath:
'If I truly have no hatred,
let this body of mine be restored to its former state.'
Having made this vow,
his body was immediately restored.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva speaking of present-life retribution.
"Good man!
The retribution of good karma, received in this birth (shēng bào) or the next (hòu bào),
and that of unwholesome karma,
are likewise so.
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains Ānòu-duōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
all his various karmas immediately receive retribution (xiànbào).
Regarding unwholesome and wicked karma receiving immediate retribution,
it is like a king committing evil,
and Heaven sending down harmful rain.
It is also like a person
who points out the location of a bēi (bear) and a precious colored deer to a hunter,
and whose hand falls off.
This is called the immediate receipt of retribution for wicked karma.
Retribution received in this birth (shēng bào) is
like an Īchàntí,
committing the four pārājika offenses (sìzhòng jìn) and the five heinous crimes (wǔnì zuì).
Retribution received in the next life (hòu bào) is
like a person upholding the precepts who makes a profound vow,
wishing that in future existences they may always attain such a body of pure precepts.
If a sentient being has a lifespan of one hundred years,
they shall be a Cakravartin (zhuǎnlún shèngwáng) for eighty years within that period,
teaching and transforming sentient beings.
Good man!
If karma is fixed to receive retribution in this current life,
then it cannot receive the retribution of this birth (shēng bào),
or the retribution of the next life (hòu bào).
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who cultivates the karma for the Thirty-two Marks of a Great Man (Sānshí-èr Dàrén Xiàng),
then cannot receive immediate retribution in this current life.
If karma does not fall under these three types of retribution,
it is called Indeterminate (búdìng).
Good man!
If one says that all karma must inevitably receive retribution,
then there cannot be the cultivation of pure conduct (fànháng),
liberation, or Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
You should know that such a person is not my disciple,
but belongs to Māra's (Mó's) retinue.
If one says that karma has both fixed (dìng)
and indeterminate (búdìng) aspects;
the fixed type being immediate retribution (xiànbào),
retribution of this birth (shēng bào),
and retribution of the next life (hòu bào).
The indeterminate type,
is received if the conditions combine,
and not received if they do not combine.
For this reason,
there ought to be pure conduct (fànháng),
liberation,
and Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
You should know that such a person is truly my disciple,
not belonging to Māra's (Mó's) retinue.
Good man!
Among all sentient beings, indeterminate karma (búdìng yè) is abundant,
and fixed karma (juédìng yè) is scarce.
For this reason,
there is the cultivation of the Way.
Because the Way is cultivated,
heavy fixed karma can be caused to be received lightly,
and indeterminate karma is not received in this birth (shēng bào).
"Good man!
There are two kinds of people:
First, those who turn indeterminate retribution into fixed retribution,
immediate retribution into retribution of this birth (shēng bào),
light retribution into heavy retribution,
and what should be received in the human realm
is received in the hells (dìyù).
Second, those who turn fixed retribution into indeterminate,
what should be received in this birth (shēng bào) is turned into immediate retribution (xiànbào),
heavy retribution into light,
and what should be received in the hells (dìyù) is received lightly in the human realm.
These two kinds of people are one foolish and one wise;
the wise person makes it light,
the foolish person makes it heavy.
Good man!
For example, two people
have committed a crime against the king.
The one with many followers
has his crime lessened,
while the one with few followers
finds his crime, which should be light, made heavy.
The foolish and the wise person
are also like this.
Because the wise person has abundant good karma, he receives heavy retribution lightly,
whereas the foolish person, having little good karma, receives light retribution heavily.
Good man!
For example, two people,
one robust and strong,
and the other frail and thin,
both fall into deep mud.
The robust one can get out,
while the frail one sinks.
Good man!
For example, two people
both ingest poison.
One has the power of a dhāraṇī (zhòulì) and Agada (Ājiātuó) medicine,
and the other has none.
The one relying on the dhāraṇī and the medicine
is unharmed by the poison,
while the one without the dhāraṇī and medicine
dies immediately upon ingesting it.
Good man!
For example, two people both drink a great deal of liquid.
One has a vigorous digestive fire (huǒlì),
and the other has a weak one.
The one with the strong digestive fire can digest it,
while the one with the weak digestive fire suffers harm from it.
Good man!
For example, two people are imprisoned by the king.
One is wise,
and the other is foolish.
The wise one can gain release,
but the foolish person has no fixed time for release.
Good man!
For example, two people both travel a dangerous path.
One has eyes,
and the other is blind.
The one with eyes
passes straight through without mishap,
while the blind one falls and plunges into a deep, dangerous pit.
Good man!
For example, two people both drink wine.
One has eaten much,
and the other has eaten little.
The one who has eaten much,
drinks without mishap,
while the one who has eaten little,
suffers harm from drinking.
Good man!
For example, two people
both confront an enemy formation.
One is fully adorned and equipped with armor and weapons (kǎi zhàng),
and the other is bare (báishēn).
The one with weapons
can defeat the enemy,
while the one who is bare
cannot save himself.
Furthermore, there are two people whose clothes are soiled with excrement and filth.
One, upon noticing, immediately washes them;
the other, upon noticing, does not wash them.
The one who immediately washes them
has clean and pure clothes,
while the one who does not wash them
finds the filth increasing daily.
Furthermore, there are two people both riding in a carriage.
One has a spare axle,
and the other has none.
The one with the spare axle can proceed as desired,
while the one without a spare axle cannot move from the spot.
Furthermore, there are two people both traveling a desolate road.
One has provisions,
and the other goes empty-handed.
The one with provisions can cross the dangers,
while the one who goes empty-handed cannot pass.
Furthermore, there are two people who are robbed by thieves.
One has hidden treasures (bǎozàng),
and the other has no treasures.
The one with hidden treasures
has no sorrow or anxiety in his heart,
while the one without treasures
is distressed and worried in his heart.
The foolish and the wise person are also like this:
The one who has accumulated good (shàn zàng)
receives heavy karma lightly;
the one without accumulated good
receives light karma heavily.
The Bodhisattva Shīzǐhǒu (Lion's Roar) said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
As the Buddha has stated,
not all karma invariably yields a fixed result,
nor is it invariably received by all sentient beings.
World-Honored One!
How can sentient beings
cause light immediate retribution (xiànbào) to be received heavily in the hells (dìyù)?
Or heavy retribution from the hells (dìyù) to be received lightly in the current life?"
The Fo said:
"All sentient beings (zhòngshēng)
generally fall into two categories:
The first possesses wisdom (zhì),
the second is foolish (yúchī).
If one is able to cultivate the body (shēn),
precepts (jiè),
mind (xīn),
and wisdom (huì),
this is called the wise person (zhìzhě);
if one is unable to cultivate the shēn,
jiè,
xīn,
and huì,
this is called the foolish person (yúzhě).
How is the failure to cultivate the shēn defined?
If one cannot control the five faculties (wǔqíng) and various roots (zhūgēn),
it is called failing to cultivate the shēn.
Failure to accept and uphold the seven kinds of pure precepts (jìngjiè),
is called failing to cultivate the jiè.
Due to the failure to regulate the mind,
it is called failing to cultivate the xīn.
Failure to practice noble conduct (shèngxíng),
is called failing to cultivate the huì.
Furthermore, one who fails to cultivate the shēn
cannot fully possess the essence of pure precepts (qīngjìng jiètǐ).
One who fails to cultivate the jiè
accepts and stores eight kinds of impure things (bùjìng zhī wù).
One who fails to cultivate the xīn
is unable to cultivate the three characteristics (sānzhǒng xiāng).
One who fails to cultivate the huì
is due to not practicing brahmacārya (fànxíng).
Furthermore, one who fails to cultivate the shēn
cannot contemplate the body (guānshēn),
cannot contemplate form (guānsè) or contemplate the characteristics of form (sèxiāng),
does not contemplate the characteristics of the body (shēnxiāng),
does not know the number of bodies (shēnshù),
does not know that this body passes from here to there,
produces the appearance of a body (shēn xiāng) in that which is not a body,
and creates the appearance of form (sèxiāng) in that which is not form.
Therefore, being greedy and attached to the number of bodies belonging to oneself (wǒshēn shēnshù),
is called failing to cultivate the shēn.
One who fails to cultivate the jiè
if they accept inferior precepts (xiàjiè),
is not called cultivating the jiè.
Accepting and upholding marginal precepts (biānjiè),
precepts for self-benefit (zìlì jiè),
or precepts for self-regulation (zìtiáo jiè);
inability to universally bring peace and joy to sentient beings (zhòngshēng),
not for the sake of protecting and upholding the supreme Right Dharma (wúshàng zhèngfǎ),
but for the purpose of being born in heaven to enjoy the pleasures of the five desires (wǔyù lè),
is not called cultivating the jiè.
One who fails to cultivate the xīn
is one whose mind is scattered and confused (xīn sǎnluàn),
unable to focus solely on guarding one's own domain (zì jìngjiè),
one's own domain
refers to the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Sì Niànchù),
the domain of others (tā jìngjiè)
refers to the five desires (wǔyù).
If one cannot cultivate the Sì Niànchù,
it is called failing to cultivate the xīn.
Failure to skillfully guard the mind against evil karma (èyè),
is called failing to cultivate the huì.
"Furthermore, one who fails to cultivate the shēn
cannot deeply contemplate that this body is impermanent (wúcháng),
without abiding (wúzhù),
perilous and fragile (wēicuì),
is destroyed in every thought-moment (niànniàn mièhuài),
and is the domain of Māra (Mó jìngjiè).
One who fails to cultivate the jiè
cannot fully possess Sī Pō Luó Mì (Śīla Pāramitā).
One who fails to cultivate the xīn
cannot fully possess Chán Pō Luó Mì (Dhyāna Pāramitā).
One who fails to cultivate the huì
cannot fully possess Bōrě Pō Luó Mì (Prajñā Pāramitā).
Furthermore, one who fails to cultivate the shēn
is greedy and attached to the self (wǒshēn) and that which belongs to the self (wǒ suǒ shēn),
believing the self is constant and enduring (chánghéng),
and experiences no change (wú yǒu biànyì).
One who fails to cultivate the jiè
for the sake of their own body,
performs the Ten Evil Deeds (Shí Èyè).
One who fails to cultivate the xīn
is unable to restrain the mind
amidst evil karma.
One who fails to cultivate the huì
because the mind is unrestrained,
cannot distinguish between good, evil, and other dharmas (fǎ).
Furthermore, one who fails to cultivate the shēn
does not sever the view of self (wǒjiàn).
One who fails to cultivate the jiè
does not sever attachment to precepts (jièqǔ).
One who fails to cultivate the xīn
performs the karma of greed (tān) and anger (chēn),
heading towards the hell realms (dìyù).
One who fails to cultivate the huì
does not sever the mind of delusion (chīxīn).
Furthermore, one who fails to cultivate the shēn
cannot contemplate that although the body has no blame or fault,
it is constantly an enemy.
"Shànnánzǐ!
For example, a man
has an enemy constantly pursuing him,
seeking to take advantage;
a wise person, realizing this, fixes their mind and guards diligently.
If they do not guard diligently, they will suffer harm.
The body of all sentient beings is also like this:
it is constantly nourished
with food and drink,
and maintained by
adjusting cold and warmth.
If it is not thus nourished, protected, and guarded diligently,
it will immediately disintegrate.
Shànnánzǐ!
Like a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) who serves the Fire Deva (Huǒtiān),
constantly using fragrant flowers,
praising and paying homage,
offering service and attendance for a full hundred years,
yet if one touches it,
it immediately burns the person's hand.
Although this fire receives such offerings,
it never holds a single thought
of repaying the kindness of the servant.
The body of all sentient beings is also like this:
although for many years
it is supplied
with fine fragrant flowers, necklaces, clothing,
food, sleeping equipment,
and medicine for illness and weakness,
if it encounters internal or external evil causes and conditions,
it is immediately destroyed,
and never recalls the past kindness of the clothing and food supplied.
Shànnánzǐ!
For example, there is a king
who keeps four venomous snakes,
places them in a basket,
and entrusts them to a man,
ordering him to look after them.
Among these four snakes,
if even one becomes angry,
it can harm the man.
This man, in terror,
constantly seeks food and drink,
and guards them diligently according to the season.
The Four Great Elements (Sìdà) of all sentient beings are also
like these venomous snakes;
if one great element becomes unbalanced,
it can destroy the body.
Shànnánzǐ!
If a person has been ill for a long time,
they should earnestly seek medical treatment and cure.
If they do not diligently seek rescue,
death is certain and without doubt.
The body of all sentient beings is also like this:
one should constantly restrain the mind
and not allow negligence.
If one is negligent,
one immediately perishes and is destroyed.
Shànnánzǐ!
For example, an earthenware jar
cannot endure wind and rain,
or being struck, thrown, beaten, or pressed.
The body of all sentient beings is also like this:
it cannot endure hunger and thirst,
cold, heat, wind, and rain,
or being beaten, bound, or verbally abused.
Shànnánzǐ!
Just as an abscess that is not yet mature
must always be carefully guarded,
and not allowed to be touched by people;
if it is touched,
it causes great pain.
The body of all sentient beings is also like this.
Shànnánzǐ!
Just as a mule (luó) when pregnant
harms its own body,
the body of all sentient beings is also like this:
if there is internal coldness or wind,
the body immediately suffers harm.
Shànnánzǐ,
for example, the plantain (bājiāo),
when it bears fruit, it withers;
the body of all sentient beings is also like this.
Shànnánzǐ!
Also, like the plantain (bājiāo),
it has no solid core inside;
the body of all sentient beings is also like this.
Shànnánzǐ!
Just as snakes, rats, and wolves (shè shǔ láng),
mutually regard each other with constant enmity;
the Four Great Elements (Sìdà) of sentient beings are also like this.
Shànnánzǐ!
For example, the King of Geese (éwáng),
does not delight in burial grounds;
Bodhisattvas (Púsà) are likewise,
in regards to the body, which is a burial ground,
they do not greedily delight.
Shànnánzǐ!
Just as a Caṇḍāla (Zhāntuóluó),
seven generations in succession,
does not abandon their occupation,
and is therefore despised and scorned by people;
the seed of this body is also like this:
the seed (semen) and blood are ultimately impure.
Because of this impurity,
they are scorned and reprimanded by all Buddhas (Fó) and Bodhisattvas (Púsà).
“Shànnánzǐ!
This body cannot, like Mount Malaya (Móluóyé Shān), produce sandalwood (zhāntán).
Nor can it produce Utpala flowers (Yōubōluó Huā),
Puṇḍarīka flowers (Fēntuólì Huā),
Campaka flowers (Zhānpó Huā),
Mālikā flowers (Mólìjiā Huā),
or Vārṣikī flowers (Póshījiā Huā).
The nine apertures constantly flow with pus and blood, which is impure;
the place where it is produced is smelly and filthy,
ugly and repulsive,
and it constantly shares a dwelling with various insects.
Shànnánzǐ!
For example, in the world,
although there are superb, wonderful, and pure gardens and forests,
when a corpse arrives there, it becomes impure,
and everyone abandons it,
not generating affection or attachment.
The form realm (Sèjiè) is also like this:
although it is pure and wonderful,
because the body exists,
all Buddhas (Fó) and Bodhisattvas (Púsà) jointly abandon it.
“ Shànnánzǐ!
If there are those who cannot make this observation,
they are called those who do not cultivate the body
and do not cultivate the precepts (jiè).
Shànnánzǐ!
If one cannot observe that the precepts (jiè) are the ladder for all good Dharmas (shànfǎ),
and also the foundation of all good Dharmas,
just as the earth is the foundation from which all trees are produced;
The precepts are the primary guide for all virtuous roots (shàngēn),
like the merchant leader guiding the multitude of merchants.
The precepts are the victorious banner of all good Dharmas,
like the victorious banner raised by Śakra, the King of Devas (Tiāndìshì).
The precepts can permanently cut off all evil karma (èyè) and the three evil paths (sān èdào);
they can cure evil diseases, just like a medicinal tree.
The precepts are the provisions for the perilous path of transmigration (shēngsǐ).
The precepts are the armor and weapons that destroy afflictions (jié) and defeat bandits.
The precepts are the excellent mantra that eliminates the venomous snake of afflictions.
The precepts are the bridge for crossing over actions leading to evil karma (èyè).
If there are those who cannot observe thus,
they are called those who do not cultivate the precepts.
“Those who do not cultivate the mind
cannot observe the mind,
which is light, restless, and constantly changing,
difficult to grasp and difficult to tame,
racing and running loose,
like a great ferocious elephant.
Momentarily swift,
like lightning flash;
restless and unstable,
like a monkey;
like an illusion, like a mirage,
it is indeed the root of all evils.
The five desires (wǔ yù) are difficult to satisfy,
like fire receiving firewood;
also like the great ocean,
swallowing and receiving all streams;
like Mount Mandara (Mántuó Shān),
where grass and trees abundantly flourish.
If one cannot observe the emptiness and falsity of transmigration (shēngsǐ),
indulgence and delusion lead to calamity,
like a fish swallowing a hook.
The mind constantly leads first, with all karma following,
just like the mother-of-pearl (bèimǔ) leading its many shells (sons).
It greedily attaches to the five desires,
and does not delight in Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
like a camel eating honey even unto death;
it disregards fodder and deeply attaches to immediate pleasure,
not considering future faults,
like an ox greedy for seedlings
that fears no whipping.
It races and roams throughout the Twenty-Five Realms of Existence (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu),
just like a strong wind
blowing kapok catkins (dōuluó kòu).
What should not be sought,
is sought without satiety,
like an ignorant person
seeking fire that generates no heat.
It constantly delights in transmigration (shēngsǐ),
and does not delight in liberation;
like the Kiṃpāka insect (rènpó chóng)
that delights in the Kiṃpāka tree (rènpó shù).
It is confused, deluded, and attached to the stench and filth of transmigration (shēngsǐ);
just like a prisoner
who delights in the jailer's daughter;
or like a toilet pig (cè zhū)
that delights in being in filth.
If there are those who cannot observe thus,
they are called those who do not cultivate the mind."
"Those who do not cultivate wisdom,
do not contemplate the great power of wisdom.
It is like the Jīnchìniǎo,
capable of destroying evil karma;
destroying the darkness of ignorance,
it is like the light of the sun;
capable of uprooting the trees of defilement,
it is like water floating away objects;
burning wrong views,
it is like a fierce fire.
Wisdom is the root of all good *dharmas*,
and the seed of the mother of the Fó and Púsà.
If there are those who cannot contemplate thus,
they are not called cultivators of wisdom.
"Good man!
Regarding the ultimate truth (Dìyī Yì),
if one perceives the body,
the characteristics of the body,
the cause of the body,
the result of the body,
the aggregation of the body,
the oneness of the body,
the duality of the body,
this body,
that body,
the extinction of the body,
the equality of bodies,
the cultivation of the body,
or the cultivator (of the body)—
if one has such perceptions,
one is called a non-cultivator of the body.
"Good man!
If one perceives precepts,
the characteristics of precepts,
the cause of precepts,
the result of precepts,
higher precepts,
lower precepts,
the aggregation of precepts,
the oneness of precepts,
the duality of precepts,
these precepts,
those precepts,
the extinction of precepts,
the equality of precepts,
the cultivation of precepts,
the cultivator (of precepts),
or *Jiè Bōluómì*—
if one has such perceptions,
one is called a non-cultivator of precepts.
"If one perceives mind,
the characteristics of mind,
the cause of mind,
the result of mind,
the aggregation of mind,
mind and mental factors,
the oneness of mind,
the duality of mind,
this mind,
that mind,
the extinction of mind,
the equality of minds,
the cultivation of mind,
or the cultivator (of mind),
high, middle, or low minds,
good mind,
or evil mind—
if one has such perceptions,
one is called a non-cultivator of mind.
"Good man,
if one perceives wisdom,
the characteristics of wisdom,
the cause of wisdom,
the result of wisdom,
the aggregation of wisdom,
the oneness of wisdom,
the duality of wisdom,
this wisdom,
that wisdom,
the extinction of wisdom,
the equality of wisdom,
high, middle, or low wisdom,
dull wisdom or sharp wisdom,
the cultivation of wisdom,
or the cultivator (of wisdom)—
if one has such perceptions,
one is called a non-cultivator of wisdom.
"Good man,
a person who does not cultivate the body,
precepts,
mind,
and wisdom in this manner,
achieves great evil retribution
from minor evil karma.
Due to terror, they constantly generate this thought:
'I belong to the hells (Dìyù),
and I perform the actions of the hells.'
Although they hear the wise speak of the suffering of the hells,
they constantly generate this thought:
'Just as iron strikes iron,
stone strikes stone,
wood strikes wood,
and fire insects delight in fire,
the body in hells will resemble the hells.
If it resembles hell,
what suffering can there be?'
For example, a common fly,
stuck by saliva,
cannot get out.
This person is likewise
unable to extricate himself
from minor sins.
Initially, the mind has no remorse,
they cannot cultivate goodness,
and they conceal their faults.
Although they possess all past good karma,
it is entirely tainted and defiled by these sins.
All the minor retributions this person receives in the present life
transform into extremely heavy evil results in the hells (Dìyù).
Good man!
Just as a small vessel of water,
if a *shēng* of salt is placed in it,
its taste is salty and bitter,
and it is difficult to drink—
the karmic sins of this person are also like this.
Good man!
For example, if a person
owes another one coin
and cannot repay the debt,
their body is bound
and they suffer many hardships—
the karmic sins of this person are also like this."
The Púsà Shīzǐhǒu said:
"Shìzūn!
Why does this person cause a light retribution received currently to transform into a suffering in the hells (Dìyù)?"
The Fó said:
"Good man!
If any sentient being possesses five things,
they cause a light retribution received currently to transform into a suffering in the hells (Dìyù).
What are these five?
First, due to ignorance;
second, due to having very few roots of goodness;
third, due to deeply heavy evil karma;
fourth, due to not repenting;
fifth, due to not cultivating fundamental good karma.
Furthermore, there are five things:
First, due to constantly practicing evil karma;
second, due to lacking the wealth of precepts;
third, due to keeping away from all roots of goodness;
fourth, due to not cultivating body, precepts, mind, and wisdom;
fifth, due to associating closely with evil companions.
Good man!
This is why they cause the light retribution in the present world to transform into heavy suffering in the hells (Dìyù)."
Shīzǐhǒu said:
"Shìzūn!
What kind of person is able to transform the retribution of the hells (Dìyù) into light suffering in the present world?"
"Good man!
If there is one who cultivates body,
precepts,
mind,
and wisdom,
as previously stated,
and can view all phenomena as identical to empty space,
who does not perceive wisdom (zhìhuì),
does not perceive the wise person (zhìzhě),
does not perceive ignorance (yúchī),
does not perceive the foolish person (yúzhě),
does not perceive cultivation (xiūxí) or the cultivator,
this is called the wise person (zhìzhě).
Such a person is then able to cultivate body, precepts, mind, and wisdom.
This person is able to cause the karmic retribution (guǒbào) of the hells (dìyù) to be experienced lightly in the present life.
Even if this person performs extremely heavy evil deeds (èyè),
reflection and observation can make them slight,
and they make this thought, saying:
'Although my karma (yè) is heavy,
it is not equal to good karma (shànyè).
For example, like kapok fiber,
though it be a hundred catties (jīn),
it ultimately cannot match one ounce (liǎng) of pure gold.
Just as throwing one sheng of salt into the Gaṅgā River (Hénghé),
the water has no salty taste,
and the drinker does not notice.
Just as a greatly wealthy person (jùfùzhě),
even if they owe people millions of precious things,
none are able to bind them and make them suffer,
just as a great perfumed elephant can break iron chains,
and go freely.
The person of wisdom (zhìhuì zhī rén) is also like this.
They constantly reflect and say:
'The power of my good deeds (shàn lì) is great,
and evil karma is weak.
I am able to reveal and repent,
eliminating sinful and evil karma (zuì'è yè),
and I can cultivate wisdom.
The power of wisdom is great,
and the power of ignorance (wúmíng) is small.'
Having thought thus,
they draw near to virtuous friends (shànyǒu),
cultivate right view (zhèngjiàn),
receive, uphold, read aloud, and recite,
write down and explain the Twelve Divisions of the Sūtras (Shí'èr Bù Jīng).
When seeing those who receive, uphold, read aloud,
write down and explain them,
their hearts give rise to reverence.
Furthermore, using clothing, food,
dwellings, bedding,
medicine for illness, flowers, and incense, they make offerings to them.
They praise and respect them,
wherever they go, they speak of their goodness,
and do not dispute their shortcomings.
They make offerings to the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo),
reverence and believe in the Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Fāngděng Dà Nièpán Jīng),
believing that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is eternal and constant, without change,
and that all sentient beings (yīqiè zhòngshēng) universally possess the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
This person is able to cause the heavy retribution of the hells to be experienced lightly in the present life.
Good man!
For this reason,
not all karma universally has a fixed result (dìng guǒ),
nor do all sentient beings necessarily receive it.
The Bodhisattva Shīzǐhǒu (Lion's Roar) said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If all karma does not necessarily yield a result,
and all sentient beings universally possess the Buddha Nature,
then why should those who ought to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path (Bā Shèngdào),
for what reason,
do all sentient beings not obtain the Great Parinirvāṇa (Dà Bō Nièpán)?
World-Honored One!
If all sentient beings possess the Buddha Nature,
they ought certainly to attain Anuttarasamyaksambodhi (Ānòu duō luó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).
Why then is it necessary to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path?
World-Honored One!
Just as this Sūtra says there are sick people,
if they obtain medical treatment and attendants,
and food appropriate to the illness,
or even if they do not obtain these,
they are all cured.
All sentient beings are also like this.
If they encounter a Śrāvaka (Shēngwén) or a Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhī Fó),
all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas (Púsà),
or various virtuous friends (shàn zhīshì),
if they hear the Dharma taught,
and cultivate the Noble Path.
If they do not encounter them,
do not hear,
and do not cultivate the Path,
they all ought to attain Anuttarasamyaksambodhi.
Why is that?
Because of the Buddha Nature.
World-Honored One!
For example, the sun and moon,
nothing can obstruct them,
preventing them from reaching the side of the Adda Mountain (Èduō Shān),
preventing the water of the Four Great Rivers from reaching the Great Ocean,
preventing the Icchantika (Yīchǎntí), and others like them, from reaching the hells.
All sentient beings are also like this.
Nothing can obstruct them and prevent them from reaching Anuttarasamyaksambodhi.
Why is that?
Because of the Buddha Nature.
World-Honored One!
For this reason,
all sentient beings do not need to cultivate the Path,
because of the power of the Buddha Nature,
they ought to attain Anuttarasamyaksambodhi,
and not because of the power of cultivating the Noble Path.
World-Honored One!
If the Icchantika,
those who commit the Four Heavy Prohibitions (Sì Chóng Jìn),
and the Five Heinous Crimes (Wǔ Nì Zuì), and others like them,
cannot attain Anuttarasamyaksambodhi,
then cultivation would be necessary.
Because attainment is certain due to the inherent Buddha Nature,
it is not due to cultivation,
after which it is attained.
World-Honored One!
For example, just like a lodestone (císhí),
even though iron is far away,
because of its power,
the iron follows it.
The Buddha Nature of sentient beings is also like this.
Therefore, there is no need to diligently cultivate the Path."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
By the bank of the Gaṅgā River there are seven types of people.
They enter the river, either for bathing,
or fearing bandits,
or in order to gather flowers.
They thus enter the river.
The first person sinks immediately upon entering the water.
Why is that?
Because they are weak and powerless,
and are unaccustomed to floating.
The second person, though sinking, returns to the surface,
but having surfaced, sinks again.
Why is that?
Because their body's strength is great, they are able to return to the surface,
but being unaccustomed to floating, having surfaced, they sink again.
The third person, having sunk, surfaces immediately,
and having surfaced, does not sink again.
Why is that?
Because their body is heavy, they sink,
because their strength is great, they surface,
and because they were previously accustomed to floating,
having surfaced, they immediately stabilize.
The fourth person, having entered, sinks,
having sunk, returns to the surface,
having surfaced, immediately stabilizes,
and gazes everywhere in the four directions.
Why is that?
Because they are heavy, they sink,
because their strength is great, they return to the surface,
being accustomed to floating, they stabilize,
but not knowing where to exit,
they therefore gaze in the four directions.
The fifth person, having entered, sinks immediately,
having sunk, surfaces right away,
having surfaced, immediately stabilizes,
having stabilized, gazes in the directions,
and having gazed, departs immediately.
Why is that?
Because of fear.
The sixth person, having entered, immediately departs,
stabilizing in the shallow area.
Why is that?
Because they are observing the proximity or distance of the bandits.
The seventh person, having already reached the other shore (bǐ'àn),
ascends the great mountain,
having no more fear,
separated from all enemies and bandits,
and experiences great bliss."
"O good man!
The great river of life and death is also like this.
There are seven types of people who, fearing the thieves of *fánnǎo* (afflictions),
resolve to cross the great river of life and death.
They leave home and shave their heads,
their bodies clad in dharma robes.
After leaving home,
they associate closely with evil companions,
following their teachings,
and listen to and accept perverse doctrines.
They claim that the bodies of sentient beings are simply the Five *Yǐn* (Skandhas);
these Five *Yǐn* are named the Five Great Elements (*Wǔdà*).
If a sentient being dies, the Five Great Elements are eternally cut off.
Since the Five Great Elements are cut off,
why should one practice good and evil *yè* (karma)?
Therefore, one ought to know that there is no good or evil, nor any retribution for good or evil.
Such a person is then called an *Yīchǎntí*.
An *Yīchǎntí* is defined as one who severs the roots of goodness.
Because the roots of goodness are severed, they sink into the river of life and death,
unable to emerge.
Why is this?
Because their evil *yè* is heavy,
and they lack the power of faith.
This is like the first person by the side of the Hánghé (Ganges) River.
O good man,
the multitude of *Yīchǎntí* have six causes
for sinking into the Three Evil Paths (*Sān Èdào*) and being unable to emerge.
What are these six?
First, because their evil minds are blazing;
second, because they do not perceive the future life;
third, because they enjoy practicing *fánnǎo*;
fourth, because they are far removed from the roots of goodness;
fifth, because evil *yè* obstructs and separates them;
sixth, because they associate closely with evil companions.
Furthermore, there are five things
that cause sinking into the Three Evil Paths.
What are these five?
First, because they commit unlawful acts against *Bǐqiū* (monks);
second, because they commit unlawful acts against *Bǐqiūní* (nuns);
third, because they freely use property belonging to the *Sēngmán* (the monastic assembly's property);
fourth, because they commit unlawful acts against their mother;
fifth, because they cause quarrels and dispute right and wrong within the Five Sections of the *Sēng* (monastic community).
Furthermore, there are five things
that cause sinking into the Three Evil Paths.
What are these five?
First, because they constantly assert that there are no results (retributions) for good and evil;
second, because they kill sentient beings who have aroused the *Pútí* (Bodhi) mind;
third, because they enjoy speaking of the faults of Dharma Masters (*Fǎshī*);
fourth, because they speak of the Dharma as non-Dharma, and non-Dharma as Dharma;
fifth, because they listen to and accept the Dharma solely to seek out its faults.
Furthermore, there are three things
that cause sinking into the Three Evil Paths.
What are these three?
First, claiming that the *Rúlái* (Tathāgata) is impermanent and eternally annihilated;
second, claiming that the True Dharma (*Zhèngfǎ*) is impermanent and subject to change;
third, claiming that the *Sēng* (Saṅgha) jewel can be destroyed and ruined.
For this reason, they are constantly sinking in the Three Evil Paths.
"The second person,
resolves to cross the great river of life and death,
but because their roots of goodness are severed,
they sink and cannot emerge.
What is meant by ‘emerging’?
By associating closely with good friends, they gain faith.
This faith is
faith in giving,
and the result of giving;
faith in goodness,
and the result of goodness;
faith in evil,
and the result of evil;
faith in birth,
death,
suffering,
impermanence,
and destruction.
This is called faith.
Having gained faith, they practice pure precepts,
accept and uphold them, read and recite them, write and explain them.
They constantly delight in giving,
and skillfully cultivate wisdom.
Because of dull faculties,
they again encounter evil companions,
and cannot cultivate the body,
precepts,
mind,
or wisdom.
They listen to and accept perverse doctrines;
or perhaps they encounter evil times,
dwell in evil lands,
and sever all roots of goodness.
Because the roots of goodness are severed,
they are constantly sinking in life and death.
This is like the second person by the side of the Hánghé River.
"The third person,
resolves to cross the great river of life and death,
but because their roots of goodness are severed, they sink therein.
Associating closely with good friends is called emerging.
They believe that the *Rúlái* is the Omniscient One,
constant, eternal, and unchanging,
who speaks the unsurpassed path for the sake of sentient beings.
All sentient beings possess the *Fóxìng* (Buddha-nature).
The *Rúlái* is not annihilated;
the Dharma
and the *Sēng* are likewise,
without destruction or ruin.
If *Yīchǎntí* and others do not sever their doctrines,
they will ultimately not be able to attain *Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí* (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi);
they must distance themselves from them before they can attain it.
Due to their faith, they practice pure precepts.
Having practiced the precepts,
they accept and uphold, read, recite, write, and explain the Twelve Divisions of the Sūtras (*Shí'èr Bù Jīng*).
For the sake of various sentient beings, they widely propagate and spread them.
They delight in giving,
and cultivate wisdom.
Because of sharp faculties,
they dwell firmly in faith and wisdom,
and their minds do not regress.
This is like the third person by the side of the Hánghé River.
"The fourth person,
resolves to cross the great river of life and death,
but because their roots of goodness are severed, they sink therein.
By associating closely with good friends, they gain faith,
which is called emerging.
Having gained faith,
they accept and uphold, read, recite, write, and explain the Twelve Divisions of the Sūtras.
For the sake of sentient beings, they widely propagate and spread them.
They delight in giving,
and cultivate wisdom.
Because of sharp faculties, they dwell firmly in faith and wisdom,
and their minds do not regress.
They universally contemplate the four directions;
contemplating the four directions refers to the Four Fruits of the *Shāmén* (Ascetic).
This is like the fourth person by the side of the Hánghé River.
"The fifth person,
resolves to cross the great river of life and death,
but because their roots of goodness are severed, they sink therein.
By associating closely with good friends, they gain faith,
which is called emerging.
Due to their faith,
they accept and uphold, read, recite, write, and explain the Twelve Divisions of the Sūtras.
For the sake of sentient beings, they widely propagate and spread them.
They delight in giving and cultivate wisdom.
Because of sharp faculties,
they dwell firmly in faith and wisdom,
and their minds do not regress.
Having become non-regressing,
they then advance forward.
Advancing forward refers to the *Pìzhīfó* (Pratyekabuddha).
Although they are able to cross over themselves,
they do not reach sentient beings (i.e., they do not teach others extensively).
This is called ‘going away’.
This is like the fifth person by the side of the Hánghé River.
"The sixth person,
resolves to cross the great river of life and death,
but because their roots of goodness are severed, they sink therein.
They associate closely with good friends and obtain faith.
Obtaining faith is called emerging.
Due to their faith,
they accept and uphold, read, recite, write, and explain the Twelve Divisions of the Sūtras.
For the sake of sentient beings, they widely propagate and spread them.
They delight in giving,
and cultivate wisdom.
Because of sharp faculties,
they dwell firmly in faith and wisdom,
and their minds do not regress.
Having become non-regressing, they then advance forward and consequently reach the shallow area.
Having reached the shallow area, they stop and do not proceed further.
Those who stop and do not proceed further are called *Púsà* (Bodhisattvas).
They remain because they wish to deliver and save all sentient beings,
dwelling there to observe *fánnǎo*.
This is like the sixth person by the side of the Hánghé River.
"The seventh person,
resolves to cross the great river of life and death,
but because their roots of goodness are severed, they sink therein.
They associate closely with good friends and obtain faith.
Obtaining faith is called emerging.
Due to their faith,
they accept and uphold, read, recite, write, and explain the Twelve Divisions of the Sūtras.
For the sake of sentient beings, they widely propagate and spread them.
They delight in giving,
and cultivate wisdom.
Because of sharp faculties,
they dwell firmly in faith and wisdom,
and their minds do not regress.
Having become non-regressing, they immediately advance forward.
Having advanced forward, they reach the opposite shore,
ascend the great high mountain,
depart from all fears,
and receive abundant peace and joy.
O good man!
That mountain on the opposite shore symbolizes the *Rúlái*.
Receiving peace and joy symbolizes the eternal abiding of the Buddha.
The great high mountain symbolizes the Great *Nièpán* (Nirvāṇa)."
"Good man!
These people by the bank of the Héng Hé (Ganges River),
all possess hands and feet yet cannot cross.
All sentient beings are also like this:
they truly possess the Fóbǎo (Buddha Jewel),
the Fǎbǎo (Dharma Jewel),
and the Sēngbǎo (Saṅgha Jewel).
The Rúlái (Tathāgata) constantly speaks the essential meaning of the various Dharma teachings,
there is the Bā Shèng Dào (Eightfold Noble Path) and the Great Pānirvána (Nirvāṇa),
yet all sentient beings cannot attain it.
This is not my fault,
nor is it the fault of the Noble Path,
or the fault of sentient beings (themselves).
You should know that it is entirely the fault and evil of Fánnǎo (afflictions).
For this reason,
all sentient beings cannot attain Nièpán.
Good man!
For example, a skilled physician knows the illness and prescribes medicine,
if the sick person does not take it,
it is not the physician's fault.
Good man!
If there is a benefactor (Shīzhǔ),
who gives all that he has to everyone,
if there are those who do not accept, it is not the benefactor's fault.
Good man!
For example, when the sun rises,
all darkness becomes light,
if blind people do not see the road,
it is not the sun's fault.
Good man!
Just as the water of the Héng Hé (Ganges River) can remove thirst,
if the thirsty person does not drink,
it is not the water's fault.
Good man!
For example, the great earth,
universally produces fruits,
equally and without difference,
if the farmer does not plant,
it is not the earth's fault.
Good man!
The Rúlái universally and extensively opens up and explains the Twelve Divisions of Scripture (Shí'èr Bù Jīng) for all sentient beings,
if sentient beings do not accept,
it is not the Rúlái's fault.
Good man!
If one cultivates the path,
one immediately attains Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi).
"Good man!
You said that all sentient beings possess Fóxìng (Buddha Nature),
and thus ought to attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí,
just like a lodestone.
Excellent,
excellent!
Due to the power of the causal condition of possessing Fóxìng,
they attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí;
but if you say that there is no need to cultivate the Noble Path (Shèng Dào),
that meaning is incorrect.
Good man!
For example, if a person travels across a wilderness,
suffering from thirst, and encounters a well,
the well is deep and dark.
Although he does not see the water,
he should know that it must be there.
This person uses appropriate means (fāngbiàn),
seeks out a bucket and rope,
draws water, and then sees it.
Fóxìng is also like this:
although all sentient beings possess it,
they must cultivate the stainless Noble Path (Wúlòu Shèng Dào),
and only then can they see it.
Good man!
Just as one can obtain oil from sesame seeds (hú má),
but without various skillful means (fāngbiàn), one cannot see it.
Sugarcane (gānzhè) is also like this.
Good man!
Just as with the Thirty-Three Heavens (Sānshísān Tiān),
and the Northern Continent of Ùdānyuè (Uttarakuru),
although they are existing realities (yǒu fǎ),
if one lacks wholesome karma (shànyè),
and the power of divine penetration (shéntōng),
one cannot see them.
The roots of grass in the earth and the water beneath the ground,
because they are covered by the earth,
sentient beings do not see them.
Fóxìng is also like this:
if one does not cultivate the Noble Path (Shèng Dào),
therefore one cannot see it.
"Good man!
As you have said,
if there are sick people in the world,
whether they encounter medical care (zhānbìng),
skilled doctors, good medicine,
and appropriate dietary management (suí bìng yǐnshí),
or whether they do not encounter them,
(if you believe) all are cured—
Good man!
I speak such a meaning for the Bodhisattvas of the Six Stations (Liù Zhù Zhū Púsà) and those of similar rank.
Good man!
For example, empty space (xūkōng),
for all sentient beings,
is neither internal nor external,
and because it is neither internal nor external, it is also without obstruction (guà'ài).
The Fóxìng of sentient beings is also like this.
Good man!
For example, if there is a person
whose wealth is in a distant place.
Although it is not immediately present, he can enjoy it at will.
If someone asks him about it,
he says, 'It is mine.'
Why?
Because it definitely exists.
The Fóxìng of sentient beings is also like this:
it is neither here nor there,
because attainment is certain,
we say that all possess it.
Good man!
For example, when sentient beings
perform various deeds (yè/karma),
whether wholesome or unwholesome,
they are neither internal nor external.
The nature of such karma,
is neither existent nor non-existent,
nor is it originally non-existent and now existent,
nor does it arise without cause.
It is not that this person performs and this person receives (the consequence),
or that this person performs and that person receives,
or that that person performs and that person receives;
(rather) there is no performer and no receiver,
but when the time and conditions harmonize, the retribution (guǒbào) is obtained.
The Fóxìng of sentient beings is also like this:
it is also not originally non-existent and now existent,
neither internal nor external,
neither existent nor non-existent,
neither here nor there,
nor does it come from elsewhere,
nor is it without causes and conditions (yīnyuán),
nor is it unseen by all sentient beings.
There are certain Púsàs (Bodhisattvas) who, when the time, conditions, and causal conditions harmonize, are able to see it.
'Time and conditions' refers to the Púsà Móhēsàs (Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas) of the Ten Stations (Shí Zhù) cultivating the Bā Shèng Dào (Eightfold Noble Path).
They attain the mind of equality (píngděng xīn) toward all sentient beings;
at that time, they are able to see it.
This is not called 'creating.' "
"Good man!
The comparison you make to a lodestone
is incorrect.
Why is this?
The stone does not attract iron.
Why is that so?
Because it has no mind and no [intentional] action (yè).
Good man!
Because one factor (yì fǎ) exists, another factor arises;
because one factor ceases, another factor is destroyed.
There is no creator and no destroyer.
Good man!
It is like a fierce fire that cannot burn firewood;
the fire arises, and the firewood is destroyed,
which is called 'burning the firewood'.
Good man!
For example, the sunflower (kuí huò) turns following the sun,
but this sunflower also has no reverence,
no consciousness (shí),
and no [intentional] action (yè).
Due to the nature (xìng) of factors, it naturally revolves.
Good man!
Like the plantain tree (bā jiāo shù),
it grows due to thunder.
This tree has no ears,
no mind (xīn),
intention (yì),
or consciousness (shí).
Because one factor exists, another factor grows;
because one factor ceases, another factor is destroyed.
Good man!
Like the Aśoka tree (ā shú jiā shù):
when a woman touches it, flowers bloom from it.
This tree has no mind (xīn) and no sensation of touch (jué chù).
Because one factor exists, another factor arises;
because one factor ceases, another factor is destroyed.
Good man!
Like the orange (jú) getting a corpse (shī):
the fruit becomes greatly abundant.
But this orange tree has no mind (xīn) and no sensation of touch (chù).
Because one factor exists, another factor becomes greatly abundant;
because one factor ceases, another factor is destroyed.
Good man!
Like the pomegranate (ān shí liú), due to bone-ash (gǔ fèn) mixed with brick (zhuān),
the fruit proliferates profusely.
The pomegranate tree (ān shí liú shù) also has no mind (xīn) or sensation of touch (chù).
Because one factor exists, another factor arises;
because one factor ceases, another factor is destroyed.
Good man!
The lodestone attracting iron is also like this:
because one factor exists, another factor arises;
because one factor ceases, another factor is destroyed.
The Buddha-nature (fó xìng) of sentient beings is also like this;
it cannot attract and attain Anuttarā-samyak-sambodhi (Ānòu duōluó sānmiǎo sānpútí).
Good man!
Ignorance (wú míng) cannot attract the formations (zhū xíng);
nor can the formations attract consciousness (shí).
Yet, it is called 'ignorance conditions the formations' (wú míng yuán xíng)
and 'formations condition consciousness' (xíng yuán yú shí).
Whether there is a Buddha or not,
the Dharma-realm (fǎ jiè) abides eternally.
"Good man!
If you say that the Buddha-nature (fó xìng) resides within sentient beings—
Good man!
An eternal Dharma (cháng fǎ) has no fixed abode (wú zhù).
If there were a place of residence, it would be impermanent (wú cháng).
Good man!
Just as the twelve links of dependent origination (shí èr yīn yuán) have no fixed place of residence:
if there were a place of residence,
the twelve links of dependent origination could not be called eternal.
The Tathāgata's Dharma-body (rú lái fǎ shēn) also has no place of residence.
The Dharma-realm (fǎ jiè),
the Dharma-sphere (fǎ rù),
the Dharma-aggregate (fǎ yīn),
and space (xū kōng)
all have no place of residence.
The Buddha-nature (fó xìng) is also like this:
it has entirely no place of residence.
Good man!
For example, the Four Great Elements (sì dà):
although their powers are equal,
there is firmness (jiān),
heat (rè),
moisture (shī),
and motion (dòng);
there is heaviness (zhòng),
lightness (qīng),
red (chì),
white (bái),
yellow (huáng),
and black.
Yet, the Four Great Elements also have no [intentional] action (yè).
Because of the different Dharma-realms (fǎ jiè), they are dissimilar to one another.
The Buddha-nature (fó xìng) is also like this;
because of the different Dharma-realms,
when the time arrives, it manifests.
Good man!
Because all sentient beings do not retreat from the Buddha-nature (fó xìng),
it is said to exist.
Because they are Āvaivartika (Āpíbázhì),
because they will have it in the future,
because they are certain to attain it,
and because they are definitely going to see it,
for these reasons, it is said that all sentient beings completely possess the Buddha-nature (fó xìng).
"Good man!
Suppose there was a king who commanded a great minister,
'You must lead an elephant and show it to the blind.'
At that time, the great minister, having received the king's command,
gathered many blind people
and showed them the elephant.
Then those blind people each touched it with their hands.
The minister immediately returned and reported to the king:
'I have finished showing it.'
At that time, the great king summoned the blind people and asked each of them:
'Did you see the elephant?'
The blind people all replied:
'We have already seen it.'
The king asked:
'What kind of thing is the elephant?'
The one who touched the tusk
immediately said, 'The shape of the elephant is like a turnip root (lú bó gēn).'
The one who touched the ear
said, 'The elephant is like a winnowing basket (jī).'
The one who touched the head
said, 'The elephant is like a stone.'
The one who touched the trunk (bí)
said, 'The elephant is like a pestle (chǔ).'
The one who touched the leg (jiǎo)
said, 'The elephant is like a wooden mortar (mù jiǔ).'
The one who touched the spine (jí)
said, 'The elephant is like a bed (chuáng).'
The one who touched the belly (fù)
said, 'The elephant is like an urn (wèng).'
The one who touched the tail (wěi)
said, 'The elephant is like a rope.'
Good man!
Those blind people
did not describe the entire substance of the elephant,
yet they did not fail to describe it.
If these various characteristics
were all not the elephant,
then apart from these,
there would be no other elephant.
Good man!
The King is likened to the Tathāgata, the Fully Awakened One (Rúlái Zhèngbiànzhī).
The Minister is likened to the Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Fāngděng Dà Nièpán Jīng).
The Elephant is likened to the Buddha-nature (fó xìng).
The Blind [people] are likened to all ignorant (wú míng) sentient beings."
"When these sentient beings heard the Fó speak,
some said:
'Form (Rūpa) is the Fóxìng.
Why is this?
Although this form perishes,
it successively continues;
therefore, one attains the thirty-two marks of the supreme Rúlái.
The Rúlái's form is permanent.
Because the Rúlái's form is permanent and never ceases,
therefore, form is called Fóxìng.
For example, true gold:
although its substance changes,
its color remains constant and unchanged.
Sometimes it is made into a bangle (chuàn),
made into a hairpin (bī),
made into a plate (pán);
yet, its yellow color is fundamentally never altered.
The Fóxìng of sentient beings is also like this:
although the substance is impermanent,
the color is permanent.
Due to this, it is said
that form is Fóxìng.
Others say:
'Sensation (Vedanā) is the Fóxìng.
Why is this?
Because of the conditions of sensation,
one attains the true bliss of the Rúlái.
The Rúlái's sensation is the ultimate sensation,
the sensation of the foremost meaning.
Although the nature of sentient beings' sensation is impermanent,
yet its succession continues ceaselessly,
thereby attaining the Rúlái's permanent sensation.
For example, there is a person whose family name is Jiāoshījiā.
Although the person is impermanent,
the family name is permanent;
it is never altered throughout ten million generations.
The Fóxìng of sentient beings is also like this.
Due to this, it is said that sensation is Fóxìng.
Still others say:
'Perception (Saṃjñā) is the Fóxìng.
Why is this?
Because of the conditions of perception,
one attains the Rúlái's true perception.
The Rúlái's perception is called thoughtless perception.
Thoughtless perception is not the perception of sentient beings,
nor the perception of male or female,
nor the perception of form, sensation, perception, volition, or consciousness (Skandhas),
nor the perception of broken thoughts.
Although the perception of sentient beings is impermanent,
since the perceptions successively continue ceaselessly,
one attains the constant and eternal perception of the Rúlái.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
For example, the twelve links of dependent origination of sentient beings:
although sentient beings perish, the links of dependent origination are permanent.
The Fóxìng of sentient beings is also like this.
Due to this, it is said that perception is Fóxìng.
Still others say:
'Volition (Saṃskāra) is the Fóxìng.
Why is this?
Volition is called lifespan.
Because of the conditions of lifespan,
one attains the Rúlái's permanent lifespan.
Although the lifespan of sentient beings is impermanent,
since the lifespan successively continues ceaselessly,
one attains the Rúlái's true and permanent lifespan.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
For example, the twelve divisions of the scriptures:
although those who listen
and those who speak are impermanent,
these scriptures remain constant and unchanged.
The Fóxìng of sentient beings is also like this.
Due to this, it is said
that volition is Fóxìng.
Still others say:
'Consciousness (Vijñāna) is the Fóxìng.
Because of the conditions of consciousness,
one attains the Rúlái's mind of equality.
Although the consciousness of sentient beings is impermanent,
since the consciousness successively continues ceaselessly,
one attains the Rúlái's true and permanent mind.
Just like the hot nature of fire:
although the fire is impermanent,
the heat is not impermanent.
The Fóxìng of sentient beings is also like this.
Due to this, it is said that consciousness is Fóxìng.
"Still others say:
'Apart from the aggregates there is the Self,
and this Self is the Fóxìng.
Why is this?
Because of the conditions of the Self,
one attains the eight sovereign Selves of the Rúlái.
There are various external practitioners who say that going and coming,
seeing and hearing,
sorrow and joy,
and verbal expression are the Self.
Although such aspects of the Self are impermanent,
the Rúlái's Self is truly permanent.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
Although the aggregates, sense fields (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) are impermanent,
their names are permanent.
The Fóxìng of sentient beings is also like this.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
Just like those blind men who each describe the elephant,
although they do not grasp the reality,
it is not that they are not describing the elephant.
Those who speak of Fóxìng are also like this:
it is neither identical to the six principles (dharma),
nor separate from the six principles.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
Therefore, I say that the Fóxìng of sentient beings
is neither form nor separate from form,
and so forth, down to: neither the Self,
nor separate from the Self.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
There are various external practitioners who, although they speak of a Self,
in reality, have no Self.
The Self of sentient beings
is precisely the five aggregates.
Apart from the aggregates, there is no separate Self.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
For example, the stem, leaves,
filaments, and receptacle combine to form a lotus flower.
Apart from these, there is no separate flower.
The Self of sentient beings is also like this.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
For example, walls,
and grass and wood combine
and are called a dwelling.
Apart from these,
there is no separate dwelling.
Just as the Quètuóluó shù,
Bōluóshē shù,
Nígōutuó shù,
and Yùtánbō shù combine to form a forest.
Apart from these, there is no separate forest.
For example, chariots, soldiers,
elephants, horses, and foot soldiers combine to form an army.
Apart from these, there is no separate army.
For example, five colors of interwoven threads combine
and are called brocade.
Apart from these, there is no separate brocade.
Just as the four castes combine and are called the great assembly.
Apart from these, there is no separate assembly.
The Self of sentient beings is also like this:
apart from the five aggregates, there is no separate Self.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
The permanence of the Rúlái
is then called the Self.
The Rúlái's Dharma Body is boundless and unimpeded,
neither arising nor perishing,
having attained the eight great powers (Vibhuta).
This is called the Self.
Sentient beings fundamentally possess neither such a Self nor that which belongs to the Self,
but because they are certain to attain the ultimate foremost emptiness (Śūnyatā),
it is called Fóxìng.
"Shàn Nánzǐ!
Great loving-kindness (mahā-maitrī) and great compassion (mahā-karuṇā) are called Fóxìng.
Why is this?
Great loving-kindness and great compassion always follow the Púsà,
like a shadow following the form.
All sentient beings are certain to attain great loving-kindness and great compassion;
therefore, it is said that all sentient beings possess Fóxìng.
Great loving-kindness and great compassion are called Fóxìng.
Fóxìng is called the Rúlái.
Great joy (mahā-muditā) and great equanimity (mahā-upekṣā) are called Fóxìng.
Why is this?
If a Púsà Móhēsà cannot relinquish the twenty-five realms of existence (bhavas),
then he cannot attain Ānòu duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Because all sentient beings are certain to attain it,
therefore, it is said that all sentient beings possess Fóxìng.
Great joy and great equanimity are Fóxìng.
Fóxìng is the Rúlái.
"Fóxìng is called Great Faith.
Why is this?
Because of faith,
the Púsà Móhēsà is able to fulfill Dán Bōluómì, up to and including Bōrě Bōluómì.
Because all sentient beings are certain to attain Great Faith,
therefore, it is said that all sentient beings possess Fóxìng.
Great Faith is Fóxìng.
Fóxìng is the Rúlái.
Fóxìng is called the Stage of the Only Son (Ekaputra-bhūmi).
Why is this?
Because of the conditions of the Stage of the Only Son,
the Púsà attains a mind of equality toward all sentient beings.
Because all sentient beings are certain to attain the Stage of the Only Son,
therefore, it is said that all sentient beings possess Fóxìng.
The Stage of the Only Son is Fóxìng.
Fóxìng is the Rúlái.
"Fóxìng is called the Fourth Power.
Why is this?
Because of the conditions of the Fourth Power,
the Púsà is able to teach and transform sentient beings.
Because all sentient beings are certain to attain the Fourth Power,
therefore, it is said that all sentient beings possess Fóxìng.
The Fourth Power is Fóxìng.
Fóxìng is the Rúlái."
"Fóxìng is called the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
Why is this?
Because of dependent origination,
the Rúlái is eternal and abiding.
All sentient beings definitely possess these Twelve Links of Dependent Origination,
thus it is said that all sentient beings completely possess Fóxìng.
The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are precisely Fóxìng,
and Fóxìng is precisely the Rúlái.
"Fóxìng is called the Four Kinds of Unhindered Wisdom.
Because of the Four Kinds of Unhindered Wisdom, it is said that there is unhindered understanding of words and meaning,
and because of the unhindered understanding of words and meaning, one is able to transform sentient beings.
The Four Kinds of Unhindered Wisdom are precisely Fóxìng,
and Fóxìng is precisely the Rúlái.
"Fóxìng is called the Summit Samādhi.
By cultivating such Summit Samādhi,
one is able to completely encompass all Buddhadharma.
Therefore, it is said that the Summit Samādhi is named Fóxìng.
The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes cultivate this samādhi but have not yet fully realized it;
although they see Fóxìng, it is not yet clear.
Because all sentient beings will definitely attain it,
therefore it is said that all sentient beings completely possess Fóxìng.
"O virtuous man,
concerning the various Dharmas described above,
because all sentient beings will definitely attain them,
therefore it is said that all sentient beings completely possess Fóxìng.
"O virtuous man!
If I were to say that form is Fóxìng,
sentient beings, upon hearing this, would develop wrong views and inversion,
and because of these wrong views and inversion, they would be born in Avīci Hell upon the end of their lives.
The Rúlái preaches the Dharma in order to cut off the Hells.
For this reason, I do not say that form is Fóxìng;
likewise, even speaking of consciousness is the same.
"O virtuous man!
If there were sentient beings who clearly understood Fóxìng,
then they would not need to cultivate the Path.
The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes cultivate the Eight Noble Paths,
and only partially see Fóxìng.
How much less can those who do not cultivate see it?
O virtuous man!
Bodhisattvas like Wénshū Shīlì,
have for measureless ages cultivated the Noble Path and understood Fóxìng.
How then can Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas understand Fóxìng?
If sentient beings wish to clearly and completely understand Fóxìng,
they should single-mindedly accept, uphold, read, and recite;
copy, explain;
make offerings, venerate;
respect and praise this Nièpán Jīng.
When they see those who accept, uphold, or even praise this Sūtra,
they should provide them with good dwellings, clothing, food, bedding, medicine for the sick,
and moreover praise them, make obeisance, and inquire about their well-being.
O virtuous man,
if there are those who, in measureless and boundless ages past,
have drawn near and made offerings to measureless Buddhas and deeply planted roots of virtue,
only then can they hear the name of this Sūtra.
O virtuous man!
Fóxìng is inconceivable.
The Buddha,
the Dharma,
and the Jewel of the Saṅgha are also inconceivable.
That all sentient beings completely possess Fóxìng yet are unable to know it,
this, too, is inconceivable.
The Dharma of the Rúlái's eternity, joy, self, and purity is also inconceivable.
That all sentient beings can believe in this Great Nièpán Jīng is also inconceivable.
Shīzǐhǒu Púsà said:
"World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has stated,
it is inconceivable that all sentient beings can believe in this Great Nièpán Jīng.
World-Honored One!
Among this great assembly, there are eighty-five thousand million people
who do not generate faith in this Sūtra.
Therefore, the existence of those who can believe in this Sūtra
is called inconceivable."
"O virtuous man!
These people, in future ages, will also definitely gain faith in this scripture,
perceive Fóxìng,
and attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí."
Shīzǐhǒu said:
"World-Honored One!
How does a non-regressing Bodhisattva know for certain that they have a non-regressing mind?"
The Buddha said:
"O virtuous man!
A Púsà Móhēsà should test his mind through ascetic practices:
eating one sesame seed per day,
lasting for seven days.
Sticky rice,
mung beans,
hemp seeds,
millet husks, and white beans—
he shall also practice this, each for seven days.
When consuming only one sesame seed,
he should reflect thus:
'Such ascetic practice
brings absolutely no benefit.
If I can perform a deed that brings no benefit,
how much more
will I perform a deed that does bring benefit?
If the mind can endure and neither regress nor turn away from that which is non-beneficial,
thus it is certain that one will attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.'
During the days he cultivates such ascetic practices,
all his skin and flesh waste away and thin out,
becoming wrinkled and shrunken,
like a freshly cut gourd
placed in the sun.
His eyes sink in
like stars at the bottom of a well.
The flesh vanishes and the ribs stick out,
like a dilapidated grass hut.
His spine appears continuously like strung-up tiles.
The place where he sits is like the imprint of a horse's hoof.
When he wishes to sit, he collapses;
when he wishes to rise, he lies stretched out.
Although he undergoes such non-beneficial suffering,
yet his mind of Bodhi does not regress.
"Furthermore, O virtuous man!
A Púsà Móhēsà, in order to overcome the suffering of beings
and bestow peace and happiness,
is even able to give up external and internal wealth, as well as his body and life,
like discarding withered grass.
If one is able to not begrudge this body and life,
such a Bodhisattva knows for himself that he definitely possesses the non-regressing mind,
'I shall certainly attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.'
"Furthermore, a Bodhisattva, for the sake of the Dharma,
cuts his own body to serve as a lamp;
wrapping cotton cloth around his skin and flesh,
pouring ghee and oil over it,
and burning it as a wick.
The Bodhisattva, undergoing this great suffering at that time,
reproaches his heart, saying:
'This suffering,
compared to the suffering of the Hells,
is not even one part in a hundred thousand myriad parts.
You have endured great torment for measureless hundreds of thousands of kalpas, all without benefit.
If you cannot endure this minor suffering,
how will you be able to save suffering sentient beings in the Hells?'
When the Púsà Móhēsà makes this contemplation,
his body does not feel the suffering,
and his mind does not regress, is not moved, and does not turn away.
The Bodhisattva at that time should deeply know for himself,
'I shall certainly attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.'
O virtuous man!
Although the Bodhisattva at that time possesses all afflictions and has not yet severed them,
yet for the sake of the Dharma,
he can use his head, eyes,
marrow, brain,
hands, feet,
blood, and flesh to give to sentient beings.
He allows nails to be driven into his body,
throws himself off cliffs, and rushes into fire.
Although the Bodhisattva at that time endures such measureless suffering,
if his mind does not regress, is not moved, and does not turn away,
the Bodhisattva should know: 'I definitely possess the non-regressing mind now,
and I shall attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.'
"O virtuous man!
A Púsà Móhēsà, in order to destroy the suffering and distress of all sentient beings,
vows to take on the body of a coarse and great animal,
giving his body, blood, and flesh to sentient beings.
When sentient beings take it, he generates compassion again,
and the Bodhisattva at that time closes his breath and does not inhale,
showing the appearance of death,
so that those who take the body do not generate the thought of committing murder or doubt.
Although the Bodhisattva accepts the body of an animal,
he never creates the karma of an animal.
Why is this?
O virtuous man!
Once the Bodhisattva has attained the non-regressing mind,
he never creates the karma of the three evil paths.
If a Púsà Móhēsà has not yet definitely received the karmic retribution for evil deeds, even those as slight as a mote of dust, in future ages,
he accepts all of it by the power of his great vow, for the sake of sentient beings.
Just like a sick person
possessed by a ghost,
hidden within the body,
through the power of a mantra,
the form immediately appears—
perhaps speaking or rejoicing,
perhaps angered or cursing,
perhaps weeping or wailing.
The Púsà Móhēsà's karma of the three evil paths in future ages is also like this.
When a Púsà Móhēsà takes the body of a bear,
he constantly preaches the Right Dharma for sentient beings.
Or, taking the body of the Jiābīnshéluó Niǎo,
he preaches the Right Dharma for all sentient beings.
Therefore, whether taking the body of a Qútuó,
the body of a deer,
the body of a rabbit,
the body of an elephant,
the body of a ram,
a monkey,
a white pigeon,
