a golden-winged bird,
or the body of a dragon or snake—
when taking on such animal bodies,
he never creates the evil karma of an animal.
He constantly preaches the Right Dharma
for the rest of the animals and sentient beings,
so that, upon hearing the Dharma,
they may quickly turn away and leave the animal body.
When the Bodhisattva at that time accepts an animal body but commits no evil karma,
you should know that he definitely possesses the non-regressing mind.
"The Bódhisattvà Móhāsà, in an age of famine, sees starving sentient beings,
and transforms into the body of a turtle or fish, immeasurable in Yóuyán (Yojanas),
and furthermore makes this vow:
'May all sentient beings, when they take my flesh,
find that as much as they take, that much regenerates,
and by eating my flesh, they are freed from the suffering of hunger and thirst,
and all completely generate the heart of Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi).'
The Bódhisattvà makes the vow:
'If there is anyone who, because of me, is freed from hunger and thirst,
then in future ages,
they will quickly become distant from the calamities of hunger and thirst in the Twenty-Five Yǒu (Existences).'
The Bódhisattvà Móhāsà endures suffering such as this,
and if his mind does not regress,
you should know that he will certainly attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
"Furthermore, the Bódhisattvà, in an age of pestilence, sees those afflicted by sickness,
and reflects thus:
'Just like the King of Medicine Trees (Yàoshùwáng),
if there are sick people,
and they take the root, take the stem,
take the branches, take the leaves,
take the flowers, take the fruit,
take the bark, or take the skin, they are all cured of their illness.
May this body of mine be likewise;
if there are sick people,
hearing my voice,
touching my body,
consuming my flesh, blood, or even bone marrow,
their illness will all be removed and healed;
may all sentient beings, when they eat my flesh,
not generate evil intentions, like eating the flesh of their own child.
Once I have healed their sickness,
I will constantly speak the Dharma for them.
May they believe and accept it,
contemplate it, and spread the teaching.'
Furthermore, good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The Bódhisattvà, although afflicted by Fánnǎo (defilements) and enduring bodily suffering,
his mind does not regress, does not waver, and does not turn away.
You should know that he will certainly attain the non-regressing mind,
and achieve Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
"Furthermore, good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
If there are sentient beings who are afflicted by ghosts,
the Bódhisattvà, having seen this, immediately says:
'May I become the body of a ghost,
a great body,
a healthy body,
a body with many attendants,
so that they, upon hearing or seeing me, may have their sickness removed and healed.'
The Bódhisattvà Móhāsà diligently cultivates painful austerities for the sake of sentient beings;
although defilements (Fánnǎo) exist,
they do not pollute his mind.
"Furthermore, good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Although the Bódhisattvà Móhāsà practices the Six Pāluómì (Pāramitās),
he does not seek the fruit of the Six Pāramitās.
When practicing the supreme Six Pāramitās,
he makes this vow, saying:
'I now bestow these Six Pāramitās upon all sentient beings;
after each and every sentient being receives my gift,
I cause them all to attain Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
I myself also diligently cultivate painful austerities for the sake of the Six Pāramitās,
and endure all sufferings and afflictions.
When enduring suffering,
may I not regress from the mind of Pútí (Bodhi).'
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
When the Bódhisattvà Móhāsà makes such a vow,
this is called the sign of non-regression from Pútí.
"Furthermore, good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The Bódhisattvà Móhāsà is inconceivable (Bùkě Sīyì).
Why is this?
The Bódhisattvà Móhāsà profoundly knows that Sáñgsǐ (Samsāra/the cycle of birth and death) has many faults and transgressions,
and observes that great Nièpán (Nirvana) possesses great merit and virtue.
Yet, for the sake of all sentient beings, he dwells in Sáñgsǐ,
enduring various sufferings,
and his mind has no regression or turning away.
This is called the Bódhisattvà's inconceivability.
Furthermore, good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The Bódhisattvà Móhāsà generates compassion without relying on any specific cause or condition,
truly does not receive favor yet constantly bestows favor,
and although he bestows favor, he does not seek recompense.
Therefore, this is also called inconceivability.
Furthermore, good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Some sentient beings cultivate various painful austerities for their own benefit;
the Bódhisattvà Móhāsà practices painful austerities for the benefit of others.
(In doing so,) this is called self-benefit,
therefore, this is also called inconceivability.
"Furthermore, the Bódhisattvà, being endowed with defilements (Fánnǎo),
yet for the purpose of destroying the sufferings derived from [distinctions between] enemies and relatives,
cultivates the mind of equanimity (Píngděng Xīn).
Therefore, this is also called inconceivability.
Furthermore, if the Bódhisattvà sees various evil and unwholesome sentient beings,
whether he reproves them severely,
or speaks soft words,
or drives them out,
or abandons them,
for those of evil nature, he appears to speak soft words;
for those who are arrogant, he appears to display great arrogance,
yet internally his heart truly has no arrogance.
This is called the Bódhisattvà's inconceivable skillful means (Fāngbiàn).
Furthermore, the Bódhisattvà, being endowed with defilements (Fánnǎo), when he possesses few material goods,
yet those seeking help are many,
his mind is not distressed or narrowed.
This is called the Bódhisattvà's inconceivability.
Furthermore, the Bódhisattvà, during the time when a Fó (Buddha) appears in the world,
knowing the merits and virtues of the Fó,
yet for the sake of sentient beings,
accepts a body in remote lands where there is no Fó,
such as being blind, being deaf,
being lame, or being crippled.
This is called the Bódhisattvà's inconceivability.
Furthermore, the Bódhisattvà profoundly knows all the faults and transgressions that sentient beings possess,
yet for the purpose of delivering them, he constantly journeys with them.
Although he follows their intentions, the stain of their transgression does not pollute him.
Therefore, this is also called inconceivability.
"Furthermore, the Bódhisattvà clearly knows and sees
that there is no mark of a sentient being (Zhòngshēng Xiāng),
no pollution by defilements (Fánnǎo),
nor any practitioner who has attained separation from defilements through cultivation of the path.
Although striving for Pútí, there is no Pútí practice,
nor is there anyone who achieves Pútí practice.
There is no one who endures suffering, nor anyone who breaks suffering,
yet he is still able to destroy suffering and practice the Pútí path for sentient beings.
Therefore, this is also called inconceivability.
Furthermore, the Bódhisattvà, upon receiving his final life body,
dwells in the Dōushuài Tiān (Tushita Heaven).
This is also called inconceivability.
Why is this?
Dōushuàituó Tiān,
is superior among the desire realms (Yùjiè).
Those in the lower heavens have minds that are unrestrained,
and those in the upper heavens have faculties (gēn) that are dull and obscured.
Therefore, [Dōushuài] is called superior.
Cultivating charity (shī) and cultivating precepts (jiè),
one attains bodies in the lower and upper heavens;
cultivating charity, precepts, and concentration (dìng),
one attains a Dōushuài body.
All Bódhisattvás denigrate all existences (Zhū Yǒu),
destroying all existences.
They ultimately do not create the karma for Dōushuài Heaven,
nor receive the body of that heaven.
Why is this?
If the Bódhisattvà dwells in other existences,
he is also able to teach, transform, and perfect sentient beings.
Truly lacking a desirous mind, yet being born in the Desire Realm (Yùjiè),
therefore, this is also called inconceivability.
The Bódhisattvà Móhāsà is born in Dōushuài Tiān,
and there are three things about him that are superior:
first, life span (mìng);
second, physical form (sè);
third, reputation (míng).
The Bódhisattvà Móhāsà truly does not seek life span,
form,
or fame (míngchēng);
although he has no mind of seeking, what he obtains is superior.
The Bódhisattvà Móhāsà profoundly delights in Nièpán,
yet because of conditions (yīnyuán), he is also superior.
Therefore, this is also called inconceivability.
Although the Bódhisattvà Móhāsà is superior to all the Tiān (Devas/gods) in these three aspects,
the gods, towards the Bódhisattvà,
never generate a mind of hatred (chēnxīn),
a mind of jealousy (dùxīn),
or a mind of arrogance (jiāomàn zhī xīn).
They constantly generate a mind of joy.
The Bódhisattvà is also not arrogant toward the gods.
Therefore, this is also called inconceivability.
The Bódhisattvà Móhāsà does not create the karma for life span (mìng yè),
yet he completes his full life span in that heaven.
This is called superiority of life span (Mìng Shèng).
He also has no karma for physical form (sè yè),
yet his wondrous physical form (Miàosè Shēn) is completely filled with brilliance.
This is called superiority of form (Sè Shèng).
The Bódhisattvà Móhāsà dwells in that heavenly palace,
not delighting in the Five Desires (Wǔ Yù),
only engaging in matters of the Dharma (Fǎshì).
Therefore, his reputation (míngchēng) fills the ten directions.
This is called superiority of reputation (Míng Shèng).
Therefore, this is also called inconceivability.
"When the Bódhisattvà Móhāsà descends from Dōushuài Tiān,
at that time, the Great Earth shakes in six ways (Liùzhǒng Zhèndòng).
Therefore, this is also called inconceivability.
Why is this?
When the Bódhisattvà descends,
the gods of the Desire Realm (Yù) and Form Realm (Sè) all come to wait upon and escort him.
They emit a great sound, praising the Bódhisattvà,
and it is because of the breath and air from their mouths that the earth shakes.
Furthermore, the Bódhisattvà is the King of Elephants among men (Rén Zhōng Xiàngwáng).
The King of Elephants among men is called the King of Dragons (Lóngwáng).
When the King of Dragons first enters the womb,
there are various Dragon Kings beneath this earth who are either terrified
or joyful.
Therefore, the Great Earth shakes in six ways.
Therefore, this is also called inconceivability.
"The Bódhisattvà Móhāsà knows the time of entering the womb,
the time of dwelling [there],
and the time of exiting [the womb].
He knows his father,
and knows his mother.
He is neither impure nor defiled,
like the sapphire jewel in Dìshì's (Śakra's/Indra's) topknot.
Therefore, this is also called inconceivability."
"Good man!
The *Dà Nièpán Jīng* (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra) is also like this,
inconceivable.
Good man!
For example, the great ocean
has eight inconceivables.
What are the eight?
First, it gradually becomes deeper;
second, it is so deep that the bottom is hard to reach;
third, it has a single salty taste;
fourth, the tide does not exceed its limit;
fifth, it contains various treasures;
sixth, great-bodied sentient beings dwell therein;
seventh, it does not hold dead bodies overnight;
eighth, all ten thousand streams and great rains poured into it neither increase nor decrease it.
Good man!
That it gradually becomes deeper depends on three factors.
What are the three?
First, the power of merit of sentient beings;
second, traveling with the wind;
third, because river water flows in.
Furthermore, even regarding neither increase nor decrease, there are three factors for each.
"This subtle scripture of the Great Nirvāṇa (*Dà Nièpán*) is also like this,
having eight inconceivables:
First, it gradually deepens.
Namely, the precepts of the *Yōupósè* (Upāsaka),
the precepts of the *Shāmí* (Śrāmaṇera),
the precepts of the *Bǐqiū* (Bhikṣu),
the precepts of the *Púsà* (Bodhisattva);
the fruit of the *Xūtuóhuán* (Srotāpanna),
the fruit of the *Sītuóhán* (Sakṛdāgāmin),
the fruit of the *Anāhán* (Anāgāmin),
the fruit of the *Āluóhàn* (Arhat),
the fruit of the *Pìzhīfó* (Pratyekabuddha),
the fruit of the *Púsà* (Bodhisattva),
the fruit of *Ānòuduōluósānmiǎosānpútí* (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi).
This *Nièpán Jīng* speaks of such Dharma teachings;
this is called gradually deepening,
therefore this scripture is named gradually deepening.
"Second, it is so deep that the bottom is hard to reach.
The *Rúlái Shìzūn* (Tathāgata, World-Honored One) is neither born nor destroyed,
does not attain *Ānòuduōluósānmiǎosānpútí*,
does not turn the Dharma wheel,
does not eat and does not receive (offerings),
does not practice generosity.
Therefore, it is named permanence (*cháng*), bliss (*lè*), self (*wǒ*), and purity (*jìng*).
All sentient beings completely possess the Buddha Nature (*Fóxìng*);
the *Fóxìng* is not material form, yet it does not depart from material form;
it is not sensation, conception, volition, or consciousness, yet it does not depart from consciousness;
it is constantly visible,
it is an illuminating cause, not an originating cause.
From *Xūtuóhuán* up to *Pìzhīfó* will attain *Ānòuduōluósānmiǎosānpútí*;
they also have no afflictions,
and no dwelling place.
Although they have no afflictions, they are not named permanence;
therefore, it is named deep.
Furthermore, there is profound depth:
In this scripture, sometimes the self is spoken of,
sometimes the non-self is spoken of;
sometimes permanence is spoken of,
sometimes impermanence is spoken of;
sometimes purity is spoken of,
sometimes impurity is spoken of;
sometimes bliss is spoken of,
sometimes suffering is spoken of;
sometimes emptiness is spoken of,
sometimes non-emptiness is spoken of;
sometimes the existence of everything is spoken of,
sometimes the non-existence of everything is spoken of;
sometimes the Three Vehicles (*Sānshèng*) are spoken of,
sometimes the One Vehicle (*Yīshèng*) is spoken of.
Or, it is said that the Five Aggregates are precisely the *Fóxìng*,
and the *Jīngāng sānmèi* (Vajra Samādhi), and the Middle Way (*Zhōngdào*),
the *Shǒuléngyán sānmèi* (Śūraṅgama Samādhi),
the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (*Shí'èr Yīnyuán*),
Emptiness in the Ultimate Sense (*Dìyīyì Kōng*),
great compassion and equanimity,
wisdom atop confidence regarding sentient beings,
knowing all faculties and powers,
unimpeded wisdom in all dharmas.
Although there is *Fóxìng*, it is not spoken of as definitive;
therefore, it is named deep.
"Third, a single taste.
All sentient beings equally possess the *Fóxìng*,
all share the One Vehicle,
share a single liberation,
a single cause,
a single fruit,
share the same nectar.
All shall attain permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
This is named a single taste.
"Fourth, the tide does not exceed its limit.
In this scripture, *Bǐqiū* are regulated
not to receive and accumulate the eight impure things.
If my disciples are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, explain, and discriminate this subtle scripture of the Great Nirvāṇa,
they would rather lose their body and life than violate these rules.
This is named the tide does not exceed its limit.
"Fifth, it contains various treasures.
This scripture is precisely the immeasurable treasury of treasures.
As for what is called treasure:
It refers to the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (*Sì Niànchù*),
the Four Right Efforts (*Sì Zhèngqín*),
the Four Bases of Supernatural Power (*Sì Rúyì Fēn*),
the Five Roots (*Wǔ Gēn*),
the Five Powers (*Wǔ Lì*),
the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (*Qī Juéfēn*),
the Eightfold Noble Path (*Bā Shèngdào Fēn*);
the Conduct of an Infant (*Yīng'ér Xíng*),
the Conduct of a Sage (*Shèng Xíng*),
the Brahmā Conduct (*Fàn Xíng*),
the Heavenly Conduct (*Tiān Xíng*);
various skillful means of goodness,
the *Fóxìng* of sentient beings,
the merits of *Púsà* (Bodhisattvas),
the merits of the *Rúlái* (Tathāgata),
the merits of *Shēngwén* (Śrāvakas),
the merits of *Yuánjué* (Pratyekabuddhas),
the Six Pāramitās (*Liù Bōluómì*),
immeasurable Samādhis,
immeasurable wisdom.
This is named the treasury of treasures.
"Sixth, the dwelling place of great-bodied sentient beings.
The great-bodied sentient beings refer to the Buddha and *Púsà*.
They are called great sentient beings because of their great wisdom,
because of their great bodies,
because of their great minds,
because of their great adornment,
because of their great subjugation (of desires),
because of their great skillful means,
because of their great teaching of the Dharma,
because of their great power,
because of their great assembly (of disciples),
because of their great spiritual powers,
because of their great compassion,
because they are constant and unchanging,
because they are unimpeded regarding all sentient beings,
and because they accept and accommodate all sentient beings.
This is named the dwelling place of great-bodied sentient beings.
"Seventh, it does not hold dead bodies overnight.
Dead bodies refer to
the *Yīchǎntí* (Icchantikas),
those who violate the Four Major Prohibitions,
the Five Immeasurable Crimes (*Wǔ Wújiān Zuì*),
those who slander the *Fāngděng* (Vaipulya) scriptures,
speaking non-Dharma as Dharma,
and speaking Dharma as non-Dharma,
receiving and accumulating the eight types of impure things,
using Buddha property,
or *Sēng* (Saṅgha) property according to one's whim,
or performing unlawful deeds toward a *Bǐqiū*
or *Bǐqiūní* (Bhikṣuṇī).
This is named a dead body.
This *Nièpán Jīng* is separated from such beings;
therefore, it is named not holding dead bodies overnight.
"Eighth, neither increase nor decrease.
Because it is without boundary,
because it is without beginning or end,
because it is not form,
because it is not fabricated,
because it is permanent and abiding,
because it is neither born nor destroyed,
because all sentient beings are completely equal,
because the nature of all dharmas is a single nature.
This is named without increase or decrease,
therefore this scripture, like that great ocean, has eight inconceivables."
*Shīzǐ Hǒu* (Simhanāda) said:
"World-Honored One (*Shìzūn*)!
If it is said that the *Rúlái* (Tathāgata) being neither born nor destroyed is named deep,
all sentient beings have four kinds of birth:
egg-born (*Luǎnshēng*),
womb-born (*Tāishēng*),
moisture-born (*Shīshēng*),
and transformation-born (*Huàshēng*).
These four kinds of birth
are fully present among humans.
Such as *Shīpóluó Bǐqiū* (Śibala Bhikṣu),
*Yōupó Shīpóluó Bǐqiū* (Upashibala Bhikṣu),
the mother of the Elder *Míjiāluó* (Migara),
the mother of the Elder *Nígōutuó* (Nigrodha),
and the mother of the Elder *Bànzhēluó* (Pañjala)—
each having five hundred sons born through egg-birth.
It should be known that egg-birth exists among humans.
As for moisture-birth, as the Buddha stated,
'When I was a *Púsà* in past lives,
I was born as King *Dǐngshēng Wáng* (born from the crown) and King *Shǒushēng Wáng* (born from the hand);'
and as is currently said,
the Maiden of the *Ānluó* Tree (Amra),
and the Maiden of the *Jiābùduō* Tree (Kapitā).
It should be known that moisture-birth exists among humans.
At the beginning of the kalpa,
all sentient beings were transformation-born.
The *Rúlái Shìzūn* has attained the Eight Forms of Sovereignty;
for what reason was he not transformation-born?"
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"Good man!
All sentient beings are born through the four modes of birth.
Having attained the sagely Dharma (Shèngfǎ),
they cannot return to their original form of being born from eggs (luǎnshēng)
or being born from moisture (shīshēng).
Good man!
The beings at the beginning of the kalpa were all spontaneously generated (huàshēng).
At that time, the Buddha did not appear in the world.
Good man!
If there are sentient beings who encounter the suffering of sickness,
they require a doctor and medicine.
At the beginning of the kalpa,
sentient beings were spontaneously generated (huàshēng).
Although they had afflictions (fánnǎo),
their sicknesses had not yet manifested.
Therefore, the Tathāgata (Rúlái) did not appear in that world.
The bodies and minds of beings at the beginning of the kalpa were not suitable vessels,
therefore, the Tathāgata did not appear in that world.
Good man!
All the characteristics of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One (Shìzūn), surpass those of all sentient beings,
namely their lineage (zhǒngxìng),
relatives,
and parents.
Because of this excellence,
all people trust and accept the Dharma (Fǎ) He speaks.
Therefore, the Tathāgata does not accept spontaneous generation.
Good man!
Among all sentient beings, the father carries out the karma (yè) of the son,
and the son carries out the karma of the father.
If the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, were to take a spontaneously generated body (huàshēn), He would have no parents.
If He had no parents,
how could He cause all sentient beings to perform various good deeds (shànyè)?
Therefore, the Tathāgata does not accept a spontaneously generated body.
Good man!
Within the Buddha's Right Dharma (Zhèngfǎ), there are two kinds of protection:
the first is internal,
the second is external.
Internal protection refers to the precepts and prohibitions (jièjìn).
External protection refers to family, relatives, and dependents.
If the Buddha Tathāgata were to accept a spontaneously generated body,
then there would be no external protection.
Therefore, the Tathāgata does not accept a spontaneously generated body.
Good man!
Some people rely on their lineage (xìng) and give rise to arrogance (jiāomàn).
The Tathāgata, wishing to break such arrogance,
was born into a noble lineage,
and did not accept a spontaneously generated body.
Good man!
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, had true parents;
the father was named Jìngfàn,
and the mother was named Móyé.
Yet, all sentient beings still say this was an illusion.
How could He then accept a spontaneously generated body?
If He accepted a spontaneously generated body,
how could there be the shattered relics (shèlì) of His body?
The Tathāgata, in order to benefit the blessings and virtue (fúdé) of sentient beings,
shattered His body to allow them to make offerings.
Therefore, the Tathāgata does not accept a spontaneously generated body.
None of the Buddhas are spontaneously generated.
How could I alone be spontaneously generated?"
At that time, Shīzihǒu Púsà pressed his palms together and knelt for a long time,
placing his right knee on the ground,
and praised the Buddha with verses.
Jiāyè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata shows compassion for all sentient beings.
He tames the untamed,
He purifies the impure.
For those without refuge, He acts as refuge.
For those not yet liberated, He enables liberation.
He attains the Eight Liberations (bā zìzài),
acts as the great physician,
and is the great King of Medicine.
Shànxīng Bǐqiū was a son of the Buddha when the Buddha was a Bodhisattva (Púsà).
After leaving home (chūjiā),
he received, maintained, read, and recited,
analyzed, and explained the twelve divisions of the Sūtras.
He destroyed the bonds of the desire realm (yùjiè jié),
and attained the Four Dhyānas (sì chán).
Why does the Tathāgata then proclaim that Shànxīng
is an Yīchǎntí,
a contemptible person,
destined to abide in hell for a kalpa,
a person beyond remedy?
Why did the Tathāgata not first preach the Right Dharma for him,
and later for the Púsàs?
If the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, cannot save Shànxīng Bǐqiū,
how can He be named as possessing great loving-kindness and compassion (dà címǐn),
and great skill-in-means (dà fāngbiàn)?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Imagine parents
who have only three sons.
The first son has a mind of faith and obedience,
respects his parents,
has keen faculties and wisdom,
and can quickly understand worldly affairs.
The second son does not respect his parents,
has no mind of faith and obedience,
but has keen faculties and wisdom,
and can quickly understand worldly affairs.
The third son does not respect his parents,
has no mind of faith and obedience,
has dull faculties, and is unwise.
When the parents wish to instruct them,
whom should they teach first?
Whom should they love and cherish first?
Whom should they teach first to understand worldly affairs?"
Jiāyè Púsà replied to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
One should first instruct the one who has faith and obedience,
respects the parents,
and has keen faculties and wisdom to understand worldly matters;
followed by the second, and then the third.
As for those two sons,
although they lack faith
and respect,
out of compassion,
they are subsequently taught."
"Good man!
The Tathāgata is also like this.
The three sons
represent the Púsàs first,
the Shēngwén (Hearers) in the middle,
and the Yīchǎntí (Iccantikas) last.
The subtle meanings within the twelve divisions of the Xiūduōluó (Sūtras)
I have already preached first for the various Púsàs;
the shallow and accessible meanings I preach for the Shēngwén;
the worldly meanings I preach for the Yīchǎntí
and those who commit the Five Heinous Crimes (wǔ nì zuì).
Although there is no benefit in the present life,
out of compassion,
I sow seeds of various goodnesses for their future lives.
Good man!
Consider three kinds of fields.
The first has easy irrigation and flow,
is free of sand and gravel (shā pí),
tiles, stones, and thorns,
and yields a hundredfold for every seed planted.
The second, although free of sand and gravel,
tiles, stones, and thorns,
has difficult and treacherous irrigation,
and the harvest is halved.
The third has difficult and treacherous irrigation,
many sand deposits and gravel,
tiles, stones, and thorns,
and yields only one for every seed planted,
due to the poor soil (gǎocǎo).
Good man!
In the spring month,
which field does the farmer plant first?"
"World-Honored One!
He plants the first field first,
followed by the second field,
and finally the third."
"The first represents the Púsàs,
the second represents the Shēngwén,
and the third represents the Yīchǎntí.
Good man!
Imagine three jars (yīng).
The first is intact,
the second leaks,
and the third is broken.
If one wishes to store curds,
water,
or ghee (sū),
which one should be used first?"
"World-Honored One!
The intact one should be used first,
followed by the leaking one,
and lastly the broken one."
"The intact and pure one
represents the Púsàs
and the Saṅgha (Sēng).
The leaking one represents the Shēngwén.
The broken one represents the Yīchǎntí.
Good man!
Imagine three sick people who all arrive at the doctor's place.
The first is easy to treat,
the second is difficult to treat,
and the third is incurable.
Good man!
If the doctor treats them,
whom should he treat first?"
"World-Honored One!
He should treat the easy one first,
followed by the second,
and lastly the third.
Why is this?
Because of compassion for relatives."
"Those who are easily cured are compared to the community of Púsa;
those who are difficult to cure are compared to the community of Shēngwén;
those who cannot be cured are compared to the Yīchǎntí,
although they bear no good fruit in the present world,
out of compassion,
[I teach them] in order to sow the seeds of all good things for future lives.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
For example, a great king
has three kinds of horses.
The first is trained, robust,
and powerful.
The second is untrained,
mature in years, robust, and powerful.
The third is untrained,
weak, old, and powerless.
If the king were to ride, which one should he ride first?"
"Shìzūn!
He should first ride the trained, robust, and powerful one,
next use the second,
and finally use the third.
"Shàn Nánzǐ!
The trained, robust, and powerful one is compared to the community of Púsa;
the second is compared to the community of Shēngwén;
the third is compared to the Yīchǎntí,
who, although having no immediate benefit in the present world,
out of compassion, I sow in them the seeds of all good things for future lives.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
Just as when a great donation is made, three people come:
the first is a noble, intelligent, and morality-holding person;
the second is of middling birth, dull-rooted, and morality-holding;
the third is of low birth, dull-rooted, and morality-breaking.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
This great benefactor
should first give to whom?"
"Shìzūn!
The benefactor should first give to the noble-born, sharp-rooted, and morality-holding person,
next reaching the second,
and finally reaching the third.
"The first is compared to the community of Púsa,
the second is compared to the community of Shēngwén,
the third is compared to the Yīchǎntí.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
Just as when a great lion kills a Xiāngxiàng,
it uses all its strength;
when it kills a rabbit, it does likewise,
showing no thought of slightness.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are also like this:
when teaching the Dharma
for the Púsa and the Yīchǎntí,
their effort and exertion are without difference.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
Once upon a time, I was dwelling in Wángshè Chéng,
and Shànxīng Bǐqiū was my attendant.
During the first watch of the night,
I expounded the essentials of the Dharma for Tiāndì Shì.
It is the rule for disciples to sleep after the teacher has retired,
but at that time, because I had sat for a long time, Shànxīng produced evil thoughts in his mind.
At that time, if the small boys
and girls of Wángshè Chéng cried and did not stop,
their parents would say:
'If you don't stop,
we will hand you over to the Báoqūluó Guǐ.'
At that moment, Shànxīng felt seized [by fear]
and said to me:
'Quickly enter the meditation chamber!
The Báoqūluó has come.'
I said:
'Foolish person,
have you never heard that the Tathāgata, the Shìzūn, is without fear?'
At that moment, Tiāndì Shì immediately said to me:
'Shìzūn!
Can people such as this
also enter into the Buddha Dharma?'
I immediately replied:
'Jiāoshīkā!
Such people
can enter the Buddha Dharma,
also possess the Buddha Nature,
and shall attain Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Although I taught the Dharma for this Shànxīng,
he had absolutely no intention of believing or accepting it.
"Shàn Nánzǐ!
Once upon a time, I was in Shīpófùluó Chéng, Jiāshī Guó,
and Shànxīng Bǐqiū was my attendant.
At that time, I wished to enter that city for alms,
and countless beings,
with open hearts and fervent longing,
wished to see my footprints.
Shànxīng Bǐqiū immediately followed behind me
and tried to destroy them [the footprints];
since he could not destroy them,
he caused the sentient beings to develop unwholesome thoughts.
After I had entered the city,
in a wineshop,
I saw a Nígān,
crouched down with a hunched back,
eating fermented wine lees.
Shànxīng Bǐqiū saw this and said:
'Shìzūn!
If there is an Āluóhàn in the world,
this person is the supreme one.
Why is this?
Because this person teaches that there is neither cause nor effect.'
I said:
'Foolish person,
have you never heard that an Āluóhàn
does not drink alcohol,
does not harm others,
does not deceive,
does not steal,
and is not promiscuous?
This man killed his father and mother,
and is consuming wine lees.
How can you say he is an Āluóhàn?
When this person abandons his body,
he will certainly fall into the Ābí Dìyù.
An Āluóhàn forever cuts off the three evil [paths of existence].
How can you say he is an Āluóhàn?'
Shànxīng immediately replied:
'The nature of the four great elements
may still be changed.
To claim that this person
must fall into Ābí [Dìyù]
is impossible.'
I said:
'Foolish person, have you never heard that the true words of the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are without duality?
Although I taught the Dharma for this Shànxīng,
he utterly lacked the intention to believe or accept it."
"Good men (Shàn Nánzǐ),
at one time I was staying with the monk Shànxīng Bǐqiū in Wángshěchéng (Rājagṛha).
At that time, there was a Nirgrantha (Nígān) in the city,
named Kǔdé.
He constantly spoke thus:
'The afflictions (fánnǎo) of sentient beings have neither cause nor condition,
and the liberation of sentient beings likewise has neither cause nor condition.'
The monk Shànxīng Bǐqiū, moreover, spoke thus:
'World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If there are Arhats (Āluóhàn) in the world,
Kǔdé is the foremost.'
I said:
'O deluded person (chīrén),
the Nirgrantha Kǔdé
is truly not an Arhat;
he cannot understand the path of the Arhat (Āluóhàn Dào).'
Shànxīng replied again:
'For what cause or condition
does an Arhat (Āluóhàn Rén) harbor jealousy toward another Arhat?'
I said:
'O deluded person,
I bear no jealousy toward Arhats,
but you yourself generate evil heterodox views (è xiéjiàn).
If you say Kǔdé is an Arhat,
then after seven days,
he will suffer from indigestion (sùshí), die of a stomachache,
and having died, be reborn among the Vomit-Eating Ghosts (Shítǔ Guǐ Zhōng);
his fellow students
will carry his corpse
and place it in the Cold Forest (Hánlín).'
At that time, Shànxīng
immediately went to the dwelling of the Nirgrantha Kǔdé and spoke to him:
'Elder!
Do you know now?
The Śramaṇa Qúťán (Gautama)
prophesies that in seven days you will suffer from indigestion, die of a stomachache,
and having died, be reborn among the Vomit-Eating Ghosts;
your fellow students and shared teacher
will carry your corpse
and place it in the Cold Forest.
Elder!
You must reflect well,
use various skillful means,
and ensure that Qúťán falls into the sin of false speech (wàngyǔ).'
When Kǔdé heard these words,
he immediately ceased eating.
From the first day until the sixth day,
when the seventh day was complete,
he then ate black honey.
Having eaten the black honey,
he then drank cold water.
Having drunk the cold water,
he died of a stomachache.
After he died, his fellow students carried his remains
and placed them in the Cold Forest.
He immediately assumed the form of a Vomit-Eating Hungry Ghost (Shítǔ Èguǐ Zhī Xíng),
staying by his corpse.
The monk Shànxīng Bǐqiū heard of this matter,
went to the Cold Forest,
saw Kǔdé's body,
who had assumed the form of a Vomit-Eater,
standing by his corpse,
hunched over and crouching on the ground.
Shànxīng said to him:
'Venerable one (Dàdé), are you dead?'
Kǔdé replied:
'I am dead.'
'How did you die?'
He replied:
'I died due to a stomachache.'
'Who carried out your corpse?'
He replied:
'My fellow students.'
'Where did they take it?'
He replied:
'O deluded person,
do you not recognize this as the Cold Forest?'
'What kind of body did you obtain?'
He replied:
'I obtained the body of a Vomit-Eating Ghost (Shítǔ Guǐ Shēn).
Shànxīng!
Listen carefully to the Tathāgata's (Rúlái) good words,
true words,
timely words,
meaningful words,
and Dharma words.
Shànxīng!
The Tathāgata spoke these truthful words,
why did you not believe them at that time?
If there are sentient beings who do not believe the true words of the Tathāgata,
they shall likewise receive a body such as mine.'
At that time, Shànxīng immediately returned to my place
and spoke thus:
'World-Honored One!
After the Nirgrantha Kǔdé died, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Sānshí Sān Tiān).'
I said:
'O deluded person,
Arhats have no place of rebirth;
how can you say
that Kǔdé was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven?'
'World-Honored One!
It is truly as you said:
the Nirgrantha Kǔdé
was truly not reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
he is now receiving the body of a Vomit-Eating Hungry Ghost.'
I said:
'O deluded person,
the truthful words of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas are never contradictory (wú èr);
to say that the Tathāgata has two sayings
is utterly impossible.'
Shànxīng then said:
'Although the Tathāgata spoke thus at that time,
I truly did not generate faith regarding this matter.'
Good men (Shàn Nánzǐ),
I constantly spoke the true Dharma to the monk Shànxīng Bǐqiū,
yet he never had a heart willing to believe and accept it.
"Good men!
Although the monk Shànxīng Bǐqiū recited the twelve divisions of the scriptures (shí'èr bù jīng)
and attained the Four Dhyānas (Sì Chán),
he did not understand the meaning of even one verse (jì),
one phrase (jù),
or one character (zì).
He associated closely with evil friends
and lost the Four Dhyānas.
Having lost the Four Dhyānas,
he gave rise to evil heterodox views,
speaking thus:
'There is no Buddha (Fó),
no Dharma,
and no Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
The Śramaṇa Qúťán is only skilled in the art of physiognomy (xiàngfǎ),
which is why he is able to know the minds of others.'
I, at that time, informed Shànxīng:
'The Dharma that I preach
is good at the beginning,
in the middle,
and at the end.
Its words are skillful and subtle,
the meaning of its characters is genuine and correct,
what is spoken is unmixed,
perfectly accomplished,
and constitutes pure Brahma-practice (Fànxíng).'
The monk Shànxīng Bǐqiū again spoke thus:
'Although the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma to me,
I truly maintain that there is no cause and effect (yīn guǒ).'
Good men!
If you do not believe these matters,
the monk Shànxīng Bǐqiū is currently near the Níliánchán River (Nairañjanā River);
we can go and ask him together."
At that time, the Tathāgata went immediately with Jiāshè (Kāśyapa) to Shànxīng's place.
The monk Shànxīng Bǐqiū saw the Tathāgata from afar,
and upon seeing him, immediately generated a heart of evil heterodoxy.
Due to his evil mind, his living body sank into the ground and fell into the Ābǐ Hell (Ābǐ Yù).
“‘O good son!
Although the Bhikṣu Shànxīng entered the immeasurable treasure accumulation of the Buddha Dharma,
he obtained nothing,
not even gaining the benefit of a single dharma,
due to his negligence (pàngyì),
and due to having evil companions (è zhīshi).
This is like a person who, though entering the great sea,
sees many treasures,
but gains nothing,
due to negligence.
Furthermore, it is like entering the sea,
and although seeing heaps of treasures,
committing suicide and dying,
or being killed by Ràchà (Rākṣasa) evil spirits.
The Bhikṣu Shànxīng is also like this:
having entered the Buddha Dharma,
he was killed and destroyed
by evil companions and Ràchà great spirits.
O good son!
Therefore, the Tathāgata, out of compassion,
always says that Shànxīng is full of negligence.
O good son!
If someone was originally poor,
and one feels compassion for that person,
that compassion is slight;
but if someone was originally immensely wealthy and later lost their possessions,
when one feels compassion for that person,
that compassion is profound.
The Bhikṣu Shànxīng is also like this:
he received, upheld, read, and recited the twelve divisions of the Sūtras (shí'èr bù jīng),
and attained the four dhyānas (sì chán),
and then his subsequent downfall is greatly lamentable.
Therefore, I say that the Bhikṣu Shànxīng is full of negligence,
and because of much negligence, he severed all good roots (shàn gēn).
Among my disciples who saw or heard about this,
there was no one
who did not feel profound compassion for this person,
like someone who was initially immensely wealthy
and later lost their wealth.
For many years, I
constantly traveled and stayed with Shànxīng,
but he generated an evil and heterodox mind,
and because of that evil heterodoxy, he did not abandon his evil view.
O good son!
Since ancient times, I
have observed this Shànxīng;
if he had possessed even a slight amount of good roots,
like a hair's breadth,
I would never have predicted that he
would sever his good roots,
become an Icchantika (Yīchǎntí),
a base person (sīxià zhī rén),
who dwells in hell for an eon.
It was because he declared that there is no cause, no effect (wú yīn wú guǒ),
and no operation of karma (wú yǒu zuòyè),
that I then predicted that he would eternally sever his good roots,
become an Icchantika,
a base person,
who dwells in hell for an eon.
O good son!
It is like a person
submerged in a latrine pit.
If a good friend (shàn zhīshi)
reaches out a hand to stir,
and if he catches hold of the hair on the head,
he intends to pull him out,
but after seeking for a long time without success,
he then abandons the effort.
I am also like this:
I sought for the slightest good roots in Shànxīng,
intending to pull him out and save him,
but I sought all day long,
and failed to find even a hair's breadth;
therefore, I cannot pull him out of hell.
The Bodhisattva Jiāshè said:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
Why did the Tathāgata predict that he would fall into the Àbí Hell (Àbí Dìyù)?”
“O good son!
The Bhikṣu Shànxīng had many attendants and relatives,
all of whom believed that Shànxīng was an Āluóhàn (Arhat),
and had attained the fruition of the Way.
In order to destroy their evil heterodox minds,
I predicted that Shànxīng, due to negligence, would fall into hell.
O good son!
You should now know
that what the Tathāgata speaks is true and without duality.
Why is this?
If the Buddha predicts that someone will fall into hell,
it is impossible
that they would not fall.
The predictions given by Shēngwén (Śrāvaka) and Yuánjué (Pratyekabuddha)
are of two kinds:
they may be false
or true.
For example, when Mùjiànlián was in the country of Mójiātuó (Magadha),
he announced everywhere to the people
that rain would fall seven days later,
but when the time came, it did not rain;
he also predicted that a cow would give birth to a white calf,
but when it gave birth,
it produced a spotted calf;
he predicted the birth of a boy,
but later a girl was born.
“O good son!
The Bhikṣu Shànxīng constantly preached to immeasurable sentient beings
that there is no fruition of good or evil (wú shàn è guǒ) in anything.
At that time, he eternally severed all good roots,
not even having a hair's breadth remaining.
O good son!
I have long known that this Bhikṣu Shànxīng would sever his good roots,
yet I continued to live with him for twenty years,
providing for him and accompanying him.
If I had abandoned him and gone far away,
not keeping him close to me,
this person would have taught immeasurable sentient beings to commit evil deeds.
This is called the Tathāgata’s fifth power of liberation (dì wǔ jiě lì).
“World-Honored One!
By what cause or condition do the Icchantikas
possess no good dharmas?”
“O good son!
The Icchantikas
are so called because they sever their good roots.
Sentient beings all possess the five roots (wǔ gēn), such as faith,
but the Icchantikas eternally destroy and extinguish them.
Due to this meaning,
killing an ant still incurs the sin of killing,
but killing an Icchantika incurs no sin of killing.
“World-Honored One!
Is it because the Icchantika ultimately possesses no good dharmas
that he is called an Icchantika?”
The Buddha said:
“It is so,
it is so.”
“World-Honored One!
All sentient beings possess three kinds of good:
namely, past,
future,
and present.
Icchantikas cannot sever even the good dharmas of the future.
How can it be said that by severing all good dharmas
they are called Icchantikas?”
“O good son!
Severance is of two kinds:
first, the present extinguishment;
second, the present obstruction of the future.
Icchantikas possess both kinds of severance completely;
therefore, I say they sever all good roots.
O good son!
It is like a person submerged in a latrine pit,
with only one hair tip not yet submerged.
Although that one hair tip is not yet submerged,
that single hair tip cannot lift the body.
Icchantikas are also like this:
although in the future they will possess good roots,
they cannot rescue themselves from the suffering of hell.
Although they can be rescued in the future,
there is nothing that can be done in the present time;
therefore, they are called ‘not capable of being rescued.’
Due to the condition of the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng), they can be rescued.
The Buddha-nature is neither past,
nor future,
nor present;
therefore, the Buddha-nature cannot be severed.
Just as a rotten seed cannot sprout,
the Icchantikas are also like this.”
“World-Honored One!
If the Icchantikas do not sever the Buddha-nature,
and the Buddha-nature is also good,
how can it be said that they sever all good?”
“O good son!
If sentient beings possessed the Buddha-nature in the present world,
they would not be called Icchantikas.
As for the self-nature (wǒ xìng)
and the Buddha-nature
of sentient beings in the world, they are eternal (cháng),
and not contained within the three times (sānshì).
If they were contained within the three times,
they would be called impermanent (wúcháng).
The Buddha-nature is future because it will be seen later;
thus it is said that sentient beings all possess the Buddha-nature.
Due to this meaning,
a Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages (shí zhù Púsà), fully adorned, can only see a little of it.
The Bodhisattva Jiāshè said:
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha-nature is eternal,
like empty space.
Why does the Tathāgata say it is future?
If the Tathāgata says that the Icchantikas are without good dharmas,
then when the Icchantikas face their schoolmates (tóngxué),
their teachers (tóng shī),
their parents,
their relatives, wives, and children,
do they really not generate feelings of love and remembrance (ài niàn xīn)?
If they do generate them,
is that not good?”
The Buddha said:
“Excellent,
excellent!
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
You have swiftly raised this question.
The Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) is like empty space (xūkōng);
it is neither past,
nor future,
nor present.
All sentient beings (zhòngshēng) possess three types of bodies,
namely the past,
the future,
and the present.
When sentient beings in the future attain the fully adorned and pure body,
they will perceive the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
Therefore, I say that the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) is future.
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Sometimes, for the sake of sentient beings, I speak of the cause (yīn) as the result (guǒ),
and sometimes I speak of the result (guǒ) as the cause (yīn).
This is why the sūtras state that life is food,
and seeing form is contact.
The future body is pure,
thus, I speak of the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If the meaning of what the Buddha says
is thus,
why do you say that all sentient beings completely possess the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng)?
“Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Although the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) of sentient beings is not present now,
one cannot say it is non-existent.
Just like the nature of empty space (xūkōng),
although it has no present existence,
one cannot say it is non-existent.
Although all sentient beings are impermanent,
the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) is permanently abiding and unchanging.
Therefore, I say in this sūtra that
the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) of sentient beings is neither internal
nor external,
just like empty space (xūkōng),
which is neither internal nor external.
If empty space (xūkōng) had internal and external aspects,
empty space (xūkōng) would not be called single
or permanent,
nor could it be said to exist everywhere.
Although empty space (xūkōng) is neither internal nor external,
all sentient beings entirely possess it;
the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) of sentient beings is also like this.
As for what you said,
that the Īcchantikas (Yīchǎntí) possess good dharmas (shànfǎ),
this meaning is incorrect.
Why is this?
For the Īcchantikas (Yīchǎntí),
whether they have bodily karma,
verbal karma,
or mental karma;
the karma of grasping,
the karma of seeking,
the karma of giving,
or the karma of understanding—
all such karmas are deviant karmas (xiéyè).
Why is this?
Because they do not seek cause (yīn) and effect (guǒ).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Just like the Harītakī fruit (hēlìlè guǒ),
whose roots, stems, leaves,
flowers, and fruit are all bitter,
the karma of the Īcchantikas (Yīchǎntí) is also like this.
“Good man (Shànnánzǐ),
the Tathāgata (Rúlái) fully knows the power of all roots (gēnlì).
Therefore, he is skillfully able to distinguish between the superior,
middle,
and inferior roots (gēn) of sentient beings.
He can know when a person turns inferior roots into middle roots;
he can know when a person turns middle roots into superior roots;
he can know when a person turns superior roots into middle roots;
he can know when a person turns middle roots into inferior roots.
Therefore, you should know that the innate nature of sentient beings’ roots (gēnxìng) is not fixed.
Because they are not fixed,
they may sever their roots of goodness (shàngēn),
but after severing them, they can be reborn.
If the innate nature of sentient beings’ roots (gēnxìng) were fixed,
they would never be severed in the first place,
nor, after being severed, would they be reborn.
Nor should it be said that the Īcchantikas (Yīchǎntí) fall into the hells and have a lifespan of one kalpa (jié).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Therefore, the Tathāgata (Rúlái) says that all dharmas (fǎ) have no fixed characteristics.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa (Jiāyè Púsà) said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) fully knows the power of all roots (gēnlì),
and surely knew that Śānxīng (Shànxīng) would sever his roots of goodness (shàngēn).
For what reason,
did you allow him to leave home (chūjiā)?
The Buddha said:
“Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
When I first left home (chūjiā) in the past,
My younger brother Nánduó,
my cousin Ānán,
Diàopódádūo,
and my son Luóhóuluó,
such people and their like,
all followed me to leave home (chūjiā) and cultivate the Way (dào).
If I had not permitted Śānxīng (Shànxīng) to leave home (chūjiā),
that person would have subsequently inherited the throne.
With his power and freedom,
he would have destroyed the Buddhadharma (Fófǎ).
Due to this cause and condition (yīnyuán),
I then allowed him to leave home (chūjiā) and cultivate the Way (dào).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
If the Bhikṣu Śānxīng (Shànxīng Bǐqiū) had not left home (chūjiā),
he still would have severed his roots of goodness (shàngēn),
and for immeasurable lifetimes, there would have been no benefit whatsoever.
Now that he has left home (chūjiā),
although he severed his roots of goodness (shàngēn),
he is able to accept and uphold the precepts,
and to make offerings to, venerate, and respect the elderly, the long-standing,
and virtuous people.
He practices the First Dhyāna (Chūchán)
up to the Fourth Dhyāna (Sìchán)—
this is called a good cause (shànyīn).
Such a good cause (shànyīn) can generate good dharmas (shànfǎ).
Since good dharmas (shànfǎ) are generated, he is able to cultivate the Way (dào).
Since he cultivates the Way (dào),
he will attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (Ānòuduōluósānmiǎosānpútí).
This is why I allowed Śānxīng (Shànxīng) to leave home (chūjiā).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
If I had not permitted the Bhikṣu Śānxīng (Shànxīng Bǐqiū) to leave home (chūjiā) and receive the precepts,
I would not be rightly called the Tathāgata (Rúlái), possessed of the Ten Powers (Shílì).
“Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The Buddha observes sentient beings who possess both good dharmas (shànfǎ) and unwholesome dharmas.
Although this person possesses these two dharmas,
before long, he will be able to sever all roots of goodness (shàngēn),
and possess only unwholesome roots.
Why is this?
Such a sentient being
does not associate with good friends (shànyǒu),
does not listen to the True Dharma (Zhèngfǎ),
does not wisely contemplate,
and does not practice according to the Dharma (fǎ).
Due to these causes and conditions (yīnyuán),
he is able to sever the roots of goodness (shàngēn),
and possess only unwholesome roots.
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) further knows that this person, whether in the present life,
or in a future life,
in youth, maturity, or old age,
will approach a good friend (shànyǒu),
listen to and receive the True Dharma (Zhèngfǎ):
Suffering (Kǔ),
Origin (Jí),
Cessation (Miè),
and the Path (Dào).
At that time, he will then be able to regenerate the roots of goodness (shàngēn).
Good man (Shànnánzǐ)!
Suppose there is a spring,
not far from a village,
whose water is sweet and delicious,
possessing eight merits (gōngdé).
There is a person who is hot and thirsty
and wishes to go to the spring.
A wise person standing nearby observes this thirsty person
and knows that he will definitely, without doubt, reach the water.
Why is this?
Because there is no other path.
The Tathāgata (Rúlái), the World-Honored One (Shìzūn),
observes all sentient beings in the same way.
Therefore, the Tathāgata (Rúlái)
is called the one who fully knows the power of all roots (gēnlì).
At that time, the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) took a little earth from the ground,
placed it upon his fingernail,
and addressed Kāśyapa (Jiāyè):
“Is this amount of earth great,
or is the earth in the worlds of the ten directions greater?”
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa (Jiāyè Púsà) said to the Buddha:
“The earth upon the World-Honored One’s (Shìzūn) fingernail
cannot compare to all the earth existing in the ten directions.”
"Shànnánzǐ!
Some people, having abandoned their bodies,
return to obtain human bodies;
having abandoned bodies in the three evil realms,
they obtain and receive human bodies.
Their faculties are complete and perfect,
they are born in the central kingdom (*Zhōngguó*),
possessing complete right faith,
able to cultivate the Way (*Dào*).
Having cultivated the Way, they are able to achieve liberation (*Jiětuō*);
having achieved liberation, they are able to enter Nirvāṇa (*Nièpán*).
This is like the soil upon a fingernail.
Having abandoned human bodies,
they obtain bodies in the three evil realms;
having abandoned bodies in the three evil realms, they obtain bodies in the three evil realms.
Their faculties are incomplete,
they are born in remote borderlands,
believing in heterodox and perverse views,
cultivating false paths,
unable to attain liberation,
permanence,
bliss,
or Nirvāṇa.
This is like all the soil existing in the worlds of the ten directions.
Shànnánzǐ!
Those who uphold and maintain the precepts,
are diligent and unremitting,
do not violate the four cardinal offenses (*sìchóng*),
do not commit the five heinous sins (*wǔnì*),
do not utilize property belonging to the monastic community (*sēngmán wù*),
do not become an icchantika (*yīchǎntí*),
do not sever the roots of goodness,
and believe in Nirvāṇa sūtras such as these—
are like the soil upon a fingernail.
Those who destroy the precepts, are negligent,
violate the four cardinal prohibitions,
commit the five heinous sins,
utilize property belonging to the monastic community,
become an icchantika,
sever all roots of goodness,
and do not believe this Sūtra—
are like all the soil existing in the worlds of the ten directions.
Shànnánzǐ!
The Tathāgata (*Rúlái*) knows well the superior,
middling,
and inferior faculties (*gēn*) of sentient beings like these.
Therefore, the Buddha (*Fó*) is called one who completely possesses the power of knowing faculties (*zhī gēnlì*).
Kāshè (*Jiāshè*) Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān (*Shìzūn*)!
The Tathāgata completely possesses this power of knowing faculties;
therefore, you are able to know the superior,
middling,
and inferior faculties of all sentient beings,
and their differences in sharpness and dullness.
You know the faculties of sentient beings in the present age,
and also know the faculties of sentient beings in the future.
When sentient beings such as these, after the Buddha's passing,
make statements like the following:
‘The Tathāgata ultimately enters Nirvāṇa,’
or, ‘He does not ultimately enter Nirvāṇa;’
or, ‘There is a self,’
or, ‘There is no self;’
or, ‘There is an intermediate state (*zhōngyīn*),’
or, ‘There is no intermediate state;’
or, ‘There is backsliding,’
or, ‘There is no backsliding;’
or, ‘The Tathāgata’s body is conditioned (*yǒuwéi*),’
or, ‘The Tathāgata’s body is unconditioned (*wúwéi*);’
or, some say, ‘The twelve links of dependent origination (*shí'èr yīnyuán*) are conditioned dharmas,’
or, some say, ‘Dependent origination is an unconditioned dharma;’
or, some say, ‘Mind is permanent,’
or, some say, ‘Mind is impermanent;’
or, some say, ‘Enjoying the pleasure of the five desires obstructs the Noble Path (*Shèngdào*),’
or, some say, ‘It does not obstruct;’
or, some say, ‘The ultimate mundane dharma belongs only to the desire realm (*yùjiè*),’
or, some say, ‘It belongs to the three realms (*sānjiè*);’
or, some say, ‘Giving is only mental karma,’
or, some say, ‘It is the five skandhas (*wǔyīn*);’
or, some say, ‘There are three unconditioned dharmas,’
or, some say, ‘There are no three unconditioned dharmas;’
Furthermore, some say, ‘There are generated forms,’
and furthermore, some say, ‘There are no generated forms;’
or, some say, ‘There are unproduced forms,’
or, some say, ‘There are no unproduced forms;’
or, some say, ‘There are mental adjunct dharmas,’
or, some say, ‘There are no mental adjunct dharmas;’
or, some say, ‘There are five types of existence,’
or, some say, ‘There are six types of existence;’
or, some say, ‘The eight precepts of purity are fully received by a male lay devotee (*Yōupósè*),’
or, some say, ‘They are not fully received;’
or, some say, ‘If a Bhikṣu (*Bǐqiū*) violates the four cardinal offenses, the Bhikṣu precepts remain,’
or, some say, ‘They do not remain;’
or, some say, ‘A Srotāpanna (*Xūtuóhuán rén*), a Sakṛdāgāmin (*Sītuóhán rén*), an Anāgāmin (*Ānàhán rén*), and an Arhat (*Āluóhàn rén*) all attain the path of the Buddha,
or, some say, ‘They do not attain it;’
or, some say, ‘The Buddha Nature (*Fóxìng*) is immediately present in sentient beings,’
or, some say, ‘The Buddha Nature exists separately from sentient beings;’
or, some say, ‘Those who violate the four cardinal prohibitions, commit the five heinous sins, are icchantikas, etc., all possess Buddha Nature,’
or, some say, ‘They do not possess it;’
or, some say, ‘There are Buddhas in the ten directions,’
or, some say, ‘There are no Buddhas in the ten directions.’
If the Tathāgata completely possesses and achieves the power of knowing faculties,
why does he not make definitive statements today?"
The Buddha replied to Kāshè Bodhisattva:
"Shànnánzǐ!
Such meanings are not known by eye consciousness,
nor are they known even by mind consciousness.
Rather, they can only be known by wisdom.
If there is one who is wise,
regarding that person,
I never speak in two ways.
That person also recognizes that I do not make dualistic statements.
For the unwise, I make indefinite statements,
and these unwise people also suppose that I make indefinite statements.
Shànnánzǐ!
All good practices possessed by the Tathāgata
are entirely for the sake of taming and subduing all sentient beings.
It is like the prescriptions possessed by the King of Physicians:
they are all for the purpose of treating and healing all suffering from illness.
Shànnánzǐ!
The Tathāgata, the Bhagavān, for the sake of the country,
for the sake of the time period,
for the sake of the language of others,
for the sake of various people,
and for the sake of the faculties of the assembly,
speaks of a single dharma in two ways.
Regarding a single named dharma, he speaks countless names;
regarding a single meaning, he speaks countless names;
regarding countless meanings, he speaks countless names.
How does he speak countless names regarding a single named dharma?
It is like Nirvāṇa.
It is also called Nirvāṇa,
also called Non-arising (*Wúshēng*),
also called Non-emergence (*Wúchū*),
also called Non-action (*Wúzuò*),
also called Unconditioned (*Wúwéi*),
also called Refuge (*Guīyī*),
also called Dwelling Cave,
also called Liberation,
also called Bright Light,
also called Lamp Light,
also called The Other Shore,
also called Fearlessness,
also called Non-backsliding,
also called Peaceful Abode,
also called Calm Repose,
also called Formlessness,
also called Non-duality,
also called Single Practice,
also called Purity and Coolness,
also called Absence of Darkness,
also called Unobstructedness,
also called Non-contention,
also called Absence of Defilement,
also called Vastness,
also called Amṛta (*Gānlù*),
also called Auspiciousness.
This is called speaking countless names regarding a single named dharma.
"How does he speak countless names regarding a single meaning?
It is like Śakra (*Dìshì*).
He is also called Dìshì,
also called Kauśika (*Jiāoshījiā*),
also called Vāsava (*Pócuōpó*),
also called Purandara (*Fùlántuóluó*),
also called Maghavan (*Móqiépó*),
also called Indra (*Yīntuóluó*),
also called Thousand Eyes,
also called Śacīpati (*Shèzhīfū*),
also called Vajra (*Jīngāng*),
also called Jewel Peak,
also called Jewel Banner.
This is called speaking countless names regarding a single meaning.
"How is it that for boundless meaning (wú liàng yì), boundless names (wú liàng míng) are spoken?
For example, the Buddha, the Rú Lái (Tathāgata),
is also named Rú Lái,
where the meaning is different, and the name is different.
He is also named À Luó Hē (Arhat),
where the meaning is different, and the name is different.
He is also named Sān Miǎo Sān Fú Tuó (Samyaksambuddha),
where the meaning is different, and the name is different.
He is also named the Boat Master,
he is also named the Guide (Dǎo Shī),
he is also named the Rightly Enlightened One (Zhèng Jué),
he is also named Possessor of Perfect Knowledge and Conduct (Míng Xíng Zú),
he is also named the Great Lion King (Dà Shī Zǐ Wáng),
he is also named Śāman (Shā Mén),
he is also named Brāhmaṇa (Pó Luó Mén),
he is also named the Tranquil One (Jì Jìng),
he is also named the Donor (Shī Zhǔ),
he is also named the One Who Has Reached the Other Shore (Dào Bǐ Àn),
he is also named the Great King of Physicians (Dà Yī Wáng),
he is also named the Great Elephant King (Dà Xiàng Wáng),
he is also named the Great Dragon King (Dà Lóng Wáng),
he is also named the Giver of Eyes (Shī Yǎn),
he is also named the Great Hero (Dà Lì Shì),
he is also named the Great Fearless One (Dà Wú Wèi),
he is also named the Jewel Heap (Bǎo Jù),
he is also named the Chief Merchant (Shāng Zhǔ),
he is also named the Liberated One (Dé Tuō),
he is also named the Great Man (Dà Zhàng Fū),
he is also named the Teacher of Gods and Men (Tiān Rén Shī),
he is also named the Great Puṇḍarīka (Dà Fēn Tuó Lì),
he is also named the Peerless and Unequaled Companion (Dú Wú Děng Lǚ),
he is also named the Great Field of Merit (Dà Fú Tián),
he is also named the Great Ocean of Wisdom (Dà Zhì Huì Hǎi),
he is also named the Signless One (Wú Xiàng),
he is also named the Possessor of the Eightfold Wisdom (Jù Zú Bā Zhì).
In all such cases,
the meaning is different, and the name is different.
Good men!
This is called speaking boundless names (wú liàng míng) regarding boundless meaning (wú liàng yì).
"Furthermore, there is a single meaning for which boundless names are spoken,
namely, like the Skandhas (Yīn),
it is also named the Skandhas (Yīn),
it is also named Perversion (Diān Dǎo),
it is also named Truth (Dì),
it is also named the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Sì Niàn Chù),
it is also named the Four Foods (Sì Shí),
it is also named the Four Stations of Consciousness (Sì Shí Zhù Chù),
it is also named Existence (Yǒu),
it is also named the Path (Dào),
it is also named Time (Shí),
it is also named Sentient Beings (Zhòng Shēng),
it is also named the World (Shì),
it is also named the Ultimate Truth (Dì Yī Yì),
it is also named the Three Cultivations: body, precepts, and mind,
it is also named Cause and Effect (Yīn Guǒ),
it is also named Afflictions (Fán Nǎo),
it is also named Liberation (Jiě Tuō),
it is also named the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí Èr Yīn Yuán),
it is also named Śrāvaka (Shēng Wén) and Pratyekabuddha (Pì Zhī Fó),
it is also named Hell, Hungry Ghosts, Animals, Humans, and Heavenly Beings (Dì Yù, È Guǐ, Chù Shēng, Rén, Tiān),
it is also named the Past, Present, and Future.
This is called speaking boundless names for a single meaning.
"Good men!
The Rú Lái, the World-Honored One (Shì Zūn), for the sake of sentient beings,
speaks briefly within the extensive,
and speaks extensively within the brief.
He speaks of the Ultimate Truth (Dì Yī Yì Dì) as the Conventional Truth (Shì Dì),
and speaks of the doctrine of Conventional Truth as the Ultimate Truth.
How is it called speaking briefly within the extensive?
For example, when he told the Bhikṣus,
'I shall now explain the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí Èr Yīn Yuán).'
What is called the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination?
It is merely cause and effect (yīn guǒ).
How is it called speaking extensively within the brief?
For example, when he told the Bhikṣus,
'I shall now explain Suffering (Kǔ),
Accumulation (Jí),
Extinction (Miè),
and the Path (Dào).'
Suffering (Kǔ) refers to boundless kinds of suffering;
Accumulation (Jí) refers to boundless afflictions (fán nǎo);
Extinction (Miè) refers to boundless liberations (jiě tuō);
and the Path (Dào) refers to boundless skillful means (fāng biàn).
How is it called speaking of the Ultimate Truth as the Conventional Truth?
For example, when he told the Bhikṣus,
'This body of mine now has old age, sickness, and death.'
How is it called speaking of the Conventional Truth as the Ultimate Truth?
For example, when he told Jiāo Chén Rú (Kaundinya),
'Because you have attained the Dharma,
you are named Ā Ruò Jiāo Chén Rú (Aññāta Kaundinya).'
Therefore, according to the person,
according to the intention,
and according to the time,
the Rú Lái is thus named as knowing the powers of the faculties (gēn lì).
Good men,
if I were to deliver a fixed discourse regarding meanings such as these,
I could not be called the Rú Lái who completely knows the powers of the faculties.
"Good men,
the wise person should know that what the fragrant elephant carries,
is not manageable by a donkey.
The practices of all sentient beings are boundless.
Therefore, the Rú Lái speaks various boundless doctrines (fǎ) for them.
Why is this?
Because sentient beings have numerous afflictions (fán nǎo).
If the Rú Lái were only to teach a single practice,
he would not be called the Rú Lái who perfectly accomplishes knowing the powers of the faculties.
Therefore, in other Sūtras, I have said that
for five types of sentient beings, one should refrain from speaking five types of Dharma:
for the unbelieving, do not praise right faith (zhèng xìn);
for those who violate precepts, do not praise upholding the precepts (chí jiè);
for the greedy and stingy, do not praise giving (bù shī);
for the lazy, do not praise extensive hearing (duō wén);
for the ignorant and foolish, do not praise wisdom (zhì huì).
Why is this?
If a wise person speaks these five matters to these five types of people,
know that the speaker has not completely attained knowledge of the powers of the faculties,
nor can he be named as pitying sentient beings.
Why is this?
When these five types of people hear these matters,
they generate lack of faith,
evil intent,
and angry intent.
Due to these causes and conditions, they will receive painful results (kǔ guǒ bào) throughout boundless ages.
Therefore, he is not named as pitying sentient beings and completely knowing the powers of the faculties.
Therefore, I previously instructed Shè Lì Fú (Śāriputra) in another Sūtra:
'Be careful not to extensively preach the Dharma to people of sharp faculties,
while preaching briefly to people of dull faculties.'
Shè Lì Fú said:
'World-Honored One (Shì Zūn)!
I spoke merely out of compassion,
not because I completely possessed the powers of the faculties when I spoke.'
Good men!
Speaking the Dharma extensively or briefly is the sphere of the Buddha (Fó Jìng Jiè),
it is not what Śrāvakas (Shēng Wén) or Pratyekabuddhas (Yuán Jué) can know.
"Good men!
Regarding what you said,
that after the Buddha entered Nirvāṇa (Niè Pán),
the disciples, etc.,
each spoke differently:
these people, all due to causes and conditions of perversion (diān dǎo),
did not obtain right view (zhèng jiàn),
and therefore could not benefit themselves or benefit others.
Good men!
These sentient beings are not of a single nature,
a single practice,
a single faculty,
a single kind of land,
or a single good friend (Shàn Zhī Shì).
Therefore, the Rú Lái variously preaches the essentials of the Dharma for them.
Due to these causes and conditions,
the Buddhas and Rú Lái in the ten directions and the three periods of time, for the sake of sentient beings,
revealed, displayed, and expounded the Twelve Divisions of the Canon (Shí Èr Bù Jīng).
Good men!
The Rú Lái speaks these Twelve Divisions of the Canon,
not for self-benefit,
but solely for the benefit of others.
Therefore, the fifth power (lì) of the Rú Lái is named the Power of Discernment (Jiě Lì).
Because of these two powers,
the Rú Lái profoundly knows which people can now cut off the roots of goodness (shàn gēn),
which people can cut off the roots of goodness in a future life,
which people can now attain liberation,
which people can attain liberation in a future life.
Therefore, the Rú Lái is named the Unsurpassed Hero (Wú Shàng Lì Shì).
"Good men!
If someone says that the Rú Lái fundamentally enters Nirvāṇa (Bì Jìng Niè Pán),
or does not fundamentally enter Nirvāṇa,
this person speaks thus because he does not understand the Rú Lái's intent.
Good men!
On Xiāng Shān (Fragrant Mountain), there were fifty-three thousand Immortals (xiān rén).
All of them, in the presence of Jiā Yè Fó (Kāśyapa Buddha) in the past,
cultivated various merits but had not yet attained the right path (zhèng dào).
They had attended various Buddhas to hear and receive the true Dharma.
Because the Rú Lái desired to benefit such people,
he told Ā Nán (Ānanda):
'After three months have passed,
I shall enter Nirvāṇa.'
When the various heavenly beings heard this,
the sound spread until it reached Xiāng Shān.
When the Immortals heard this,
they immediately generated regretful thoughts,
and spoke thus:
'How is it that we were born among humans,
yet did not attend the Buddha?
The Rú Lái Buddhas appear in the world extremely rarely,
like the Udumbara (Yōu Tán Huā) flower.
We must now go to the place of the World-Honored One (Shì Zūn) to hear and receive the true Dharma.'
Good men!
At that time, the fifty-three thousand Immortals immediately came to my location.
At that moment, I immediately preached the Dharma appropriately for them:
'O great beings (dà shì)!
Form (sè) is impermanent (wú cháng).
Why?
Because the causes and conditions of form are impermanent.
Born from impermanent causes,
how can form be permanent?
Even consciousness (shì) is like this.'
At that time, when the Immortals heard this Dharma,
they immediately attained the fruit of À Luó Hàn (Arhatship).
"Good man!
In Kūshīnàjié, there were 300,000 strongmen (Likṣi),
who were unrestrained and undisciplined,
relying on themselves, proud and arrogant,
[relying on their] appearance, strength, longevity, and wealth,
intoxicated and confused in mind.
Good man!
In order to subdue those strongmen,
I informed Mùlián, saying:
'You must subdue strongmen such as these.'
Then Mùjiānlián respectfully followed my instruction,
and taught them in various ways for five years,
yet he could not cause even one strongman to accept the Dharma and be subdued.
Therefore, I again informed Ānán for the sake of those strongmen, saying:
'After three months have passed,
I shall enter Nièpán.'
Good man!
When those strongmen heard this news,
they gathered together
and leveled the roads.
After three months had passed,
I then went from Píshèlǐ Guó
to Kūshīnà Chéng,
and while on the road, I saw those strongmen far off.
I immediately transformed myself into the image of a Shāmén,
and went to the place of the strongmen, saying this:
'O youths!
What work are you doing?'
When the strongmen heard this,
they all became angry and resentful,
and spoke thus:
'Shāmén!
Why do you now call people like us youths?'
I then said to them:
'All 300,000 of you,
exerting all your bodily strength,
cannot move this tiny, insignificant stone.
How can you not be called youths?'
The strongmen said:
'If you call us youths,
then you must be acknowledged as a Great Man.'
Good man!
At that time, I used two toes
to dig out the stone.
When those strongmen saw this matter,
they immediately felt themselves to be insignificant and inferior,
and said again:
'Shāmén!
Can you also move this stone
so that it is off the path?'
I said, 'O youths:
'For what reason
are you diligently repairing this path?'
The strongmen said:
'Shāmén!
Do you not know?
Shìjiā Rúlái will travel this path to the Suōluó Lín
to enter Nièpán.
For this reason,
we are leveling [the path].'
I then praised them, saying:
'Excellent,
excellent!
O youths!
Since you have generated such good intentions,
I shall remove this stone for you.'
I then lifted the large stone with my hand and threw it,
up to Ājiānízhà.
When the strongmen saw the stone in the air,
they all became astonished and fearful,
and immediately wanted to scatter.
I then told them:
'O strongmen,
you should not now generate feelings of terror
and try to scatter.'
The strongmen said:
'Shāmén!
If you can save and protect us,
we will remain calm.'
At that moment, I again caught the stone with my hand
and placed it on my right palm.
When the strongmen saw this,
joy arose in their hearts,
and they spoke again, saying:
'Shāmén!
Is this stone permanent?
Or is it impermanent?'
At that moment,
I blew upon it with my mouth,
and the stone immediately disintegrated
just like fine dust.
The strongmen saw this and cried out, saying:
'Shāmén!
This stone is impermanent.'
Immediately feeling shame, they reproached themselves:
'How is it that we,
relying freely on our appearance, strength, longevity, and wealth,
generated such arrogance?'
Knowing their minds,
I immediately relinquished the manifested body
and returned to my original form, preaching the Dharma for them.
When the strongmen saw this,
they all generated the mind of Pútí.
"Good man!
In Kūshīnàjié, there was an artisan
named Chúntuó.
This person had previously, in the presence of Jiāyè Fó,
made a great vow:
'When Shìjiā Rúlái enters Nièpán,
I shall be the last to offer him food and drink.'
Therefore, while I was in Píshèlǐ Guó,
I commanded the Bhikṣu Yōupōmónà:
'Good man!
After three months have passed,
I shall enter Bān Nièpán
beneath the twin Sāla trees in Kūshīnàjié.
You should go and inform Chúntuó so that he knows.'
Good man!
In Wángshě Chéng, there was an immortal possessing the Five Supernatural Powers,
named Xūbátuó,
aged 120.
He constantly claimed to be an Omniscient One,
generating great arrogance.
He had already planted various good roots
under countless Buddhas in the past.
I also, wishing to subdue him,
informed Ānán, saying:
'After three months have passed,
I shall enter Nièpán.'
When Xūbátuó hears this,
he will come to my location
and generate a mind of faith and reverence.
I shall then preach various Dharmas to him,
and after he has heard them,
that person will attain the exhaustion of defilements (Asravas)."
"Good men!
King Bǐmbashāluó, the sovereign of Rólèqí,
had a crown prince named Shànjiàn.
Due to the conditioning of past karma,
he developed an evil, rebellious mind,
desiring to kill his father,
but he could not find the opportunity.
At that time, the wicked man Dípódáduō,
also due to the conditioning of past karma,
furthermore developed an unwholesome mind toward me,
wishing to harm me.
He immediately cultivated the Five Supernormal Powers (Wǔtōng),
which he soon acquired.
He became close and intimate with Crown Prince Shànjiàn.
For the sake of the crown prince,
he displayed various miraculous powers,
emerging through non-doors,
entering through doors,
emerging through doors,
and entering through non-doors.
Sometimes, he manifested as the bodies of elephants, horses, cattle, sheep,
men, or women.
When Crown Prince Shànjiàn saw this,
he immediately developed a mind of affection,
a mind of joy,
and a mind of reverence and faith.
Because of this,
he prepared various implements of offerings and made offerings to him.
He also addressed him, saying:
'Great Master,
Saint!
I now wish to see a Màntuóluó flower.'
Then Dípódáduō immediately went up to the Thirty-three Heavens (Sānshísāitiān),
and requested the flower from the gods there.
Since his merit was exhausted,
no one gave it to him at all.
Since he could not obtain the flower,
he reflected, saying:
'The Màntuóluó tree
has no self
and no belongings (wǒsuǒ).
If I take it myself,
what offense could there be?'
He immediately stepped forward intending to take it,
but instantly lost his supernormal powers
and found himself
back in Rúlèchéng.
Feeling shame and remorse,
he could not bring himself to see Crown Prince Shànjiàn again.
He reflected further, saying:
'I should now go to the Tathāgata's (Rúlái) place
and request the assembly of monks (dàzhòng).'
'If the Buddha agrees,
I shall instruct, command, and deploy Shèlìfú and the others as I please.'
At that time, Dípódáduō came to my place
and spoke thus:
'I only wish that the Tathāgata
would entrust this great assembly to me.
I shall preach the Dharma and teach them in various ways,
causing them to be disciplined.'
I said, 'O foolish man!
Shèlìfú and the others are intelligent and possessed of great wisdom,
trusted and revered by the world.
I do not even entrust the great assembly to them,
much less to a foolish man like you,
a devourer of spittle?'
Then Dípódáduō
felt doubly malicious toward me
and spoke thus:
'Qútán!
Although you discipline the great assembly now,
your power will not last long;
you will soon be destroyed.'
As soon as he finished speaking,
the great earth immediately shook six times.
Dípódáduō instantly collapsed to the ground,
and beside him,
a great fierce wind arose, blowing up dust and dirt,
fouling and contaminating him.
When Dípódáduō saw this ominous sign,
he spoke again:
'If this body of mine is certain to enter the Ābǐ Hell (Ābǐ Dìyù) in this lifetime,
I must surely avenge this great enmity.'
Then Dípódáduō
immediately rose and went to the place of Crown Prince Shànjiàn.
When Shànjiàn saw him, he immediately asked:
'Saint!
Why is your countenance haggard
and filled with sorrow?'
Dípódáduō said:
'I am always like this.
Do you not know?'
Shànjiàn replied:
'Please explain why this is so.'
Dípódáduō said:
'You and I are now extremely close and affectionate.
Outsiders speak ill of you, deeming it unreasonable,
how can I not be worried when I hear this?'
Crown Prince Shànjiàn replied:
'In what way do the people of the kingdom insult me?'
Dípódáduō said:
'The people of the kingdom call you Wèishēngyuàn (Enmity Not Yet Born).'
Shànjiàn asked again:
'Why am I named Wèishēngyuàn?
Who gave me this name?'
Dípódáduō said:
'Before you were born,
all the physiognomists said,
"When this child is born, he will kill his father."
That is why outsiders all refer to you as Wèishēngyuàn.
All the insiders,
to protect your feelings,
call you Shànjiàn.
When Lady Wéidí heard these words,
after giving birth to you on a high tower,
she cast you down to the ground,
damaging one of your fingers.
Due to this circumstance,
people also call you Póluóliúzhī.
When I heard this,
my heart became distressed with sorrow,
yet I could not bring myself to tell you.'
Dípódáduō used these and other various evil matters
to instruct him to kill his father:
'If you kill your father,
I will also be able to kill the monk Qútán.'
Crown Prince Shànjiàn asked a great minister
named Yǔxíng:
'Why did the Great King name me Wèishēngyuàn?'
The minister immediately recounted the whole story to him,
which was no different from what Dípódáduō had said.
When Shànjiàn heard this,
he and the minister immediately apprehended his royal father,
imprisoned him outside the city,
and guarded him with four types of troops.
When Lady Wéidí heard of this matter,
she went to the King's location,
but the guards
blocked her and would not let her enter.
At that moment, the Lady grew angry
and scolded them.
Then the guards reported to the Crown Prince:
'Great King!
The Lady wishes to go and see the Royal Father.
May we permit it?'
When Shànjiàn heard this,
he again became resentful and angry,
and immediately went to his mother's location,
grabbed his mother's hair,
and drew his sword intending to strike.
At that time, Jíphó addressed him, saying:
'Great King!
Since the founding of the kingdom,
no matter how heavy the crime,
it has never reached women,
let alone one's own mother!'
When Crown Prince Shànjiàn heard this,
for Jíphó's sake,
he immediately let her go.
He cut off the Royal Father's clothing, bedding,
food, drink, and medicine.
After seven days had passed,
the King's life ended.
When Crown Prince Shànjiàn saw his father's death,
