he finally gave rise to a mind of remorse.
Minister Yǔxíng then used various evil and heterodox doctrines to explain to him:
'Great King!
All karmic actions are utterly without sin.
Why are you now giving rise to a mind of remorse?'
Jíphó replied:
'Great King!
You should know that such karma
involves a double offense:
one, killing the royal father,
and two, killing a Sūtuóhuán (Stream-Enterer).
Such a transgression,
no one but the Buddha can eliminate.'
King Shànjiàn said:
'The Tathāgata is pure
and without defilement.
How can sinners like us
be worthy to see him?'
Good men!
Knowing this matter,
I therefore informed Ānán:
'After three months,
I shall enter Nirvāṇa.'
When Shànjiàn heard this,
he immediately came to my place.
I preached the Dharma for him,
and his heavy offenses were lightened,
and he gained unshakeable faith.
Good men!
When my disciples heard this saying,
they did not understand my intention,
and thus said:
'The Tathāgata has definitively declared that he will enter ultimate Nirvāṇa.'
“O good man!
Bodhisattvas are of two kinds:
the first are those of actual meaning (Śūnyatā),
the second are those of provisional designation.
Bodhisattvas of provisional designation,
hearing that I shall enter Nirvāṇa in three months,
all give rise to retreating minds,
and say this:
‘If the Tathāgata is impermanent and does not abide,
why have we, for this matter,
endured great suffering through measureless generations?
The Bhagavān Tathāgata, having fully accomplished measureless merits,
still cannot destroy the Māra of death,
how much less can people like us destroy it?’
O good man!
Therefore, I speak this to such Bodhisattvas:
‘The Tathāgata is permanent and has no variation.’
O good man!
When my disciples hear this teaching,
they do not understand my intention,
and definitively say that the Tathāgata ultimately will never enter Nirvāṇa.
“O good man!
There are various sentient beings
who hold the view of annihilation (Ucchedadiṭṭhi),
and say this:
‘After the body of any sentient being perishes,
there is no receiver of the karmic results of good and evil deeds.’
For these people, I
say this:
‘The fruits of good and evil retribution
truly have a receiver.
How do we know they exist?’
O good man!
In a past age, in Kuśināgata,
there was a king named Shànjiàn,
who, when he was a boy, spent eighty-four thousand years;
when he was a crown prince, eighty-four thousand years;
and after ascending the throne, also eighty-four thousand years.
While sitting in solitude,
he reflected thus:
‘Sentient beings are of meager fortune,
their lifespans are short and abrupt,
and four enemies constantly
follow them,
yet they are unaware of it,
and still remain negligent.
Therefore, I ought to leave home and cultivate the Way,
severing the four enemies:
birth,
old age,
sickness,
and death.’
Immediately, he commanded his officials
to build a hall of seven treasures
outside the city.
After it was built, he announced to his ministers,
all officials,
the consorts and queens in the palace,
and his sons and relatives:
‘You should know
that I wish to leave home;
can you allow me?’
Thereupon, the ministers and their relatives each said this:
‘Excellent,
O great king!
Now is precisely the time.’
Then King Shànjiàn,
taking one attendant,
resided alone in the hall,
and again spent eighty-four thousand years
cultivating the mind of loving-kindness (Maitrī).
Due to the cause of this loving-kindness,
in eighty-four thousand subsequent generations, he successively attained the state of a Cakravarti-rāja (Wheel-Turning Sage King),
served as Shìtíhuányīn (Śakra, Lord of the Gods) for thirty generations,
and served as various lesser kings for measureless generations.
O good man!
Was that King Shànjiàn someone else?
Do not hold this view;
he was precisely my own self.
O good man!
When my disciples hear this teaching,
they do not understand my intention,
and proclaim that the Tathāgata definitively preaches the existence of self (ātman) and what belongs to the self (ātmaniya).
“Also, at one time, I spoke to sentient beings, saying:
‘The self is precisely the nature (Xìng)
— namely, internal and external causes and conditions,
the twelve Nidānas (causes and conditions),
sentient beings,
the five Skandhas (aggregates),
the mind realms,
the world,
merits,
karmic actions,
Īśvara (the sovereign god),
and time
— all these are called the self.’
When my disciples hear this teaching,
they do not understand my intention,
and proclaim that the Tathāgata definitively preaches the existence of self.
“O good man!
Furthermore, at a different time,
there was a Bhikṣu
who came to my place
and said this:
‘Bhagavān!
What is called the self?
Who is the self?
For what reason is there a self?’
At that time, I immediately said to the Bhikṣu:
‘Bhikṣu!
There is no self,
nor what belongs to the self.
The eye is fundamentally non-existent but now exists;
having existed, it returns to non-existence.
When it is born,
it comes from nowhere,
and when it perishes,
it goes nowhere.
Although there are karmic results,
there is no agent (karta),
no one who abandons the Skandhas nor one who receives the Skandhas.
Regarding what you asked,
“What is the self?”
I say it is expectation (Kī).
“Who is the self?”
I say it is karma.
“For what reason is there a self?”
I say it is craving (Tṛṣṇā).
Bhikṣu!
Just as two hands clap together,
and a sound comes forth from them,
the self is also like this:
because of the three conditions—sentient beings,
karma,
and craving—
it is designated as the self.
Bhikṣu!
For all sentient beings,
form is not the self,
there is no form within the self,
and there is no self within form;
perception, up to consciousness, is also like this.
Bhikṣu!
Although the adherents of external paths preach the existence of a self,
they never depart from the Skandhas;
if they preach that there is a self separate from the Skandhas,
there is no such possibility.
All sentient beings’
actions are like magic and illusion,
like the shimmering heat haze in summer.
Bhikṣu!
The five Skandhas are all impermanent,
non-blissful,
non-self,
and non-pure.
O good man!
At that time, there were immeasurable Bhikṣus
who observed these five Skandhas
as non-self
and non-self-belonging,
and attained the fruit of an Arhat.
O good man!
When my disciples hear this teaching,
they do not understand my intention,
and proclaim that the Tathāgata definitively preaches the non-existence of self (anātman).
“O good man!
I also spoke in the Sūtras, saying:
‘Three elements must combine
for one to receive this body:
first, the father;
second, the mother;
third, the intermediate state (Antarābhava);
the combination of these three
leads to receiving this body.’
Sometimes I also said:
‘An Ānāgāmin enters Parinirvāṇa in the present life,
or enters Parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.’
I also said:
‘The sensory faculties of the intermediate state body
are complete and clear,
all due to past karma,
like pure Ti hú (cream/clarified butter).’
O good man!
I sometimes said:
‘The intermediate state received by evil and bad sentient beings
is
like the coarse, rough, woolen cloth of the world.
The intermediate state received by purely good sentient beings
is like the white cotton cloth produced in Bōluónài (Vārāṇasī).’
When my disciples hear this teaching,
they do not understand my intention,
and proclaim that the Tathāgata preaches the existence of the intermediate state.”
"Good man!
I moreover spoke to those sentient beings who committed heinous sins,
and said this:
'Those who commit the Five Heinous Sins (Wǔnì),
upon abandoning their body, immediately enter the Ābǐ Hell (Ābǐ Dìyù).
I moreover said:
'The Bhikṣu Tánmóliúzhī,
upon abandoning his body, immediately entered the Ābǐ Hell,
without any stopping point in between.'
I moreover spoke to that Brahmanist Dúzǐ and said:
'Brahmanist!
If there is an intermediate existence (zhōngyīn),
then there are Six Existences (Liùyǒu).'
I moreover said:
'Formless sentient beings,
do not have an intermediate existence.'
Good man,
when my various disciples heard this teaching,
they did not understand my true meaning,
and proclaimed that the Buddha definitively taught there is no intermediate existence.
"Good man!
In the Sūtras,
I moreover taught that regression (tuì) exists.
Why is this?
Because of countless lazy,
and sluggish Bhikṣus who do not cultivate the Way,
I spoke of five types of regression:
first, enjoying being busy with many things;
second, enjoying talking about worldly affairs;
third, enjoying sleeping;
fourth, enjoying closeness to laypeople;
fifth, enjoying traveling frequently.
Due to these causes and conditions, the Bhikṣus regress.
The causes and conditions for regression are moreover of two types:
one internal (nèi),
and the other external (wài).
An Arhat (Āluóhàn) person, although separated from internal causes,
is not separated from external causes.
Because of external causes and conditions, vexations (fánnǎo) arise;
because vexations arise,
they then regress and lose (their attainment).
There was moreover a Bhikṣu,
named Qúchǐ,
who regressed and lost six times.
After regressing, he felt ashamed,
and then advanced in cultivation again.
On the seventh attempt, he attained it.
Having attained it, he feared losing it,
and harmed himself with a knife.
I moreover sometimes spoke of 'timely liberation' (shí jiětuō),
or spoke of the Six Types of Arhats (Āluóhàn), and so forth.
When my various disciples heard this teaching,
they did not understand my true meaning,
and proclaimed that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) definitively taught that regression exists.
"Good man!
In the Sūtras, I moreover said,
for example, scorched charcoal,
does not revert back to wood.
Likewise, when a vase is broken,
it is no longer usable as a vase.
Vexations are also like this;
when severed by an Arhat (Āluóhàn),
they will ultimately not arise again.
I also said that the causes for sentient beings to generate vexations,
are generally three types:
first, not having severed vexations;
second, not severing the causal conditions;
third, improper reflection (bù shàn sīwéi).
However, Arhats (Āluóhàn) are without two of these causes and conditions:
namely, severing vexations and being free from improper reflection.
Good man!
When my various disciples heard this teaching,
they did not understand my true meaning,
and proclaimed that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) definitively taught that there is no regression.
"Good man!
In the Sūtras, I taught that the Tathāgata's body,
is generally of two types:
first, the generated body (shēngshēn);
second, the Dharma body (fǎshēn).
Regarding the generated body,
this is the body of expedient transformation (fāngbiàn yìnghuà).
A body such as this,
can be said to be subject to birth, aging, sickness, death,
long and short, black and white,
is this, is that,
is learner (xué), is non-learner (wúxué).
When my various disciples heard this teaching,
they did not understand my true meaning,
and proclaimed that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) definitively taught that the Buddha's body is a conditioned phenomenon (yǒuwéi fǎ).
The Dharma body (Fǎshēn) is eternal, blissful, endowed with self, and pure (cháng lè wǒ jìng),
eternally departed from all birth, aging, sickness, and death,
neither white nor black,
neither long nor short,
neither this nor that,
neither learner (xué) nor non-learner (wúxué).
Whether the Buddha appears in the world or does not appear,
it constantly abides immovably,
without change or alteration.
Good man!
When my various disciples heard this teaching,
they did not understand my true meaning,
and proclaimed that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) definitively taught that the Buddha's body is an unconditioned phenomenon (wúwéi fǎ).
"Good man!
In my Sūtras, I said:
'What is called the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yīnyuán)?
From ignorance (wúmíng) arises action (xíng);
from action arises consciousness (shí);
from consciousness arises name-and-form (míngsè);
from name-and-form arises the six sense bases (liùrù);
from the six sense bases arises contact (chù);
from contact arises sensation (shòu);
from sensation arises craving (ài);
from craving arises clinging (qǔ);
from clinging arises existence (yǒu);
from existence arises birth (shēng);
and from birth then arise aging, death, sorrow, and suffering.'
Good man!
When my various disciples heard this teaching,
they did not understand my true meaning,
and proclaimed that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) definitively taught that the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yuán) are conditioned (yǒuwéi).
At another time, I warned and instructed the Bhikṣus,
and said this:
'The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yīnyuán), whether a Buddha appears or does not appear,
their inherent nature and characteristics abide eternally.'
Good man!
There are Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yuán) that do not arise from causes and conditions (yuán shēng);
there are those that arise from causes and conditions.
There are things that arise from causes and conditions yet are not the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination;

there are also the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination that do not arise from causes and conditions, and things that are neither the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination nor arise from causes and conditions.
Those Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yuán) that do not arise from causes and conditions,
refer to the Twelve Members (Shí'èr Zhī) of the future existence.
Those that arise from causes and conditions yet are not the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination,
refer to the Five Aggregates (Wǔyīn) possessed by an Arhat (Āluóhàn).
Those that arise from causes and conditions and are also the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination,
refer to the Five Aggregates (Wǔyīn) possessed by an ordinary person (fánfū).
Those that are neither the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yīnyuán) nor arise from causes and conditions,
refer to space (xūkōng) and Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
Good man!
When my various disciples heard this teaching,
they did not understand my true meaning,
and proclaimed that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) definitively taught that the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yuán),
are unconditioned (wúwéi).
"Good man!
In my Sūtras, I said:
'When all sentient beings perform good or evil karma (yè),
at the moment they abandon their body,
the Four Great Elements (Sìdà) immediately dissolve and break up.
For those who commit purely good karma, the mind immediately rises;
for those who commit purely evil karma, the mind immediately descends.'
Good man!
When my various disciples heard this teaching,
they did not understand my true meaning,
and proclaimed that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) definitively taught that the mind is permanent.
Good man!
At one time, I spoke to King Bīmbashāluó and said this:
'Great King!
You should know that form (sè) is impermanent.
Why is this?
Because it arises from an impermanent cause.
If this form arises from an impermanent cause,
how can a wise person say that it is permanent?
If form were permanent,
it should not break down or perish,
nor cause various sufferings.
Now we see this form dispersing, perishing, and breaking down;
therefore, you should know that form is impermanent,
and consciousness (shí) is also like this.'
Good man!
When my various disciples heard this teaching,
they did not understand my true meaning,
and proclaimed that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) definitively taught that the mind is annihilated.
"Good man!
In my Sūtras, I said:
'My various disciples may accept various fragrances and flowers,
gold, silver, and precious objects,
wives and children, male and female slaves,
and the eight impure things (Bā Bùjìng Wù).
They attain the Right Way (Zhèng Dào),
and having attained the Right Way,
they still do not abandon them.'
When my various disciples heard this teaching,
they did not understand my true meaning,
and definitively claimed that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) taught that accepting the Five Desires (Wǔyù),
does not hinder the Noble Path (Shèng Dào).
Furthermore, at one time, I also spoke thus:
'For a householder (jiā zhī rén) to attain the Right Way (Zhèng Dào),
there is no such possibility.'
Good man!
When my various disciples heard this teaching,
they did not understand my true meaning,
and proclaimed that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) taught that accepting the Five Desires (Wǔyù),
definitively blocks the Right Way (Zhèng Dào).
“‘Good man!
In my sūtras, I have said:
“One who is far removed from the afflictions (kleshas) and has not yet attained liberation
is like one cultivating the Worldly Foremost Dharma (Shìjiān Dìyī Fǎ) in the Desire Realm (Yùjiè).”
Good man!
When my disciples heard this statement,
they did not understand my meaning,
and they proclaimed that the Tathāgata only spoke of the Foremost Dharma as being in the Desire Realm.
Furthermore, I said:
“The Warmth Dharma (Nuǎnfǎ),
the Summit Dharma (Dǐngfǎ),
the Forbearance Dharma (Rěnfǎ),
and the Worldly Foremost Dharma (Shìjiān Dìyī Fǎ)
exist in the First Jhāna up to the Fourth Jhāna.”
When my disciples heard this statement,
they did not understand my meaning,
and they proclaimed that the Tathāgata spoke of such dharmas as being in the Form Realm (Sèjiè).
Furthermore, I said:
“All non-Buddhist practitioners (wàidào),
having already eliminated the afflictions of the Four Jhānas,
cultivate the Warmth Dharma,
the Summit Dharma,
the Forbearance Dharma,
and the Worldly Foremost Dharma.
Contemplating the Four Noble Truths (Sì Zhēndì),
they attain the fruit of Anāgāmin (Ānàhán).”
When my disciples heard this statement,
they did not understand my meaning,
and they proclaimed that the Tathāgata spoke of the Foremost Dharma as being in the Formless Realm (Wúsèjiè).
“‘Good man,
in my sūtras, I have said:
“Among the four types of giving (shī),
there are three types that are pure (jìng):
The first is when the donor (shīzhǔ) believes in the cause (yīn),
believes in the effect (guǒ),
and believes in the giving,
but the recipient (shòuzhě) does not believe in the cause,
the effect,
or the giving;
The second is when the recipient believes in the cause,
the effect,
and the giving,
but the donor does not believe in the cause,
the effect, or the giving;
The third is when the donor and the recipient
both possess belief;
The fourth is when the donor and the recipient both lack belief.”
Of these four types of giving,
the first three are pure.”
When my disciples heard this statement,
they did not understand my meaning,
and they proclaimed that the Tathāgata taught that giving is only mental (yì).
Good man,
on one occasion, I further said:
“When a donor gives, they give with five matters.”
What are these five?
First, giving color/form (sè);
second, giving strength (lì);
third, giving tranquility (ān);
fourth, giving life (mìng);
fifth, giving eloquence (biàn).
Due to these causes and conditions,
the donor subsequently receives the retribution of five matters.”
When my disciples heard this statement,
they did not understand my meaning,
and they proclaimed that the Buddha taught that giving is identical to the Five Aggregates (Wǔ Yīn).
“‘Good man!
On one occasion, I proclaimed:
“Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) is detachment;
the afflictions are eternally exhausted,
extinguished without any remainder.
Just like the extinguishing of a lamp,
no further dharma arises—
Nirvāṇa is also like this.
That which is called ‘space’ (xūkōng)
is simply non-existence (wú suǒyǒu).
For example, because there is nothing existent in the world,
it is called ‘space.’
The extinction not caused by wisdom (fēi zhì yuán miè)
is simply non-existence.
If it were existent,
it should have causes and conditions.
Because it has causes and conditions,
it should have exhaustion and extinction.
Because it is non-existent,
there is no exhaustion and extinction.”
When my disciples heard this statement,
they did not understand my meaning,
and they proclaimed that the Buddha taught the non-existence of the Three Unconditioned Dharmas (sān wúwéi).
“‘Good man,
on one occasion,
I spoke to Mùlián (Maudgalyāyana), saying:
“Mùlián!
That which is Nirvāṇa
is the sentence/phrase (zhāngjù),
it is the footprint (zújì),
it is the ultimate state (bìjìng chù),
it is the fearless state (wú suǒwèi),
it is the Great Master (Dàshī),
it is the Great Fruit (Dàguǒ),
it is the ultimate wisdom (bìjìng zhì),
it is the Great Forbearance Unhindered Samādhi (Dà Rěnwú'ài Sānmèi),
it is the Great Dharma Realm (Dà Fǎjiè),
it is the taste of sweet dew (gānlù wèi),
it is the difficult-to-see.”
Mùlián!
If one were to say there is no Nirvāṇa,
how is it that those who give rise to slander fall into the hells?”
Good man!
When my disciples heard this statement,
they did not understand my meaning,
and they proclaimed that the Tathāgata taught the existence of Nirvāṇa.
“‘On another occasion,
I spoke to Mùlián, saying:
“Mùlián!
The eye is not firm/solid (láogù),
and likewise, the body up to the body is also not firm/solid.
Because it is not firm/solid,
it is called ‘space.’
The turning/circulation (huízhuǎn) of ingested food
and the place where it is digested,
all sounds,
are all called ‘space.’”
When my disciples heard this statement,
they did not understand my meaning,
and they proclaimed that the Tathāgata definitively taught the existence of the unconditioned dharma of space (xūkōng wúwéi).
“‘On another occasion, I spoke to Mùlián, saying:
“Mùlián!
When a person who has not yet attained the fruit of Srotāpanna (Suìtuóhuán Guǒ) abides in the Forbearance Dharma,
they cut off immeasurable retributions of the three evil paths.
You should know that this is not extinguished through causes conditioned by wisdom (zhì yuán).”
When my disciples heard this statement,
they did not understand my meaning,
and they proclaimed that the Tathāgata definitively taught the existence of the extinction not caused by wisdom (fēi zhì yuán miè).
“‘Good man!
On another occasion, I spoke to the bhikṣu Bápō (Vappa), saying:
“Bápō!
If a bhikṣu contemplates form (sè),
whether past,
future,
or present,
whether near
or far,
whether coarse
or subtle—
these kinds of form,
are not me,
nor mine.”
If a bhikṣu, having contemplated thus,
is able to cut off attachment to form (sè'ài).”
Bápō then asked:
“What is called ‘form’ (sè)?”
I replied:
“The Four Great Elements (Sì Dà) are called ‘form,’
and the Four Aggregates (Sì Yīn) are called ‘name’ (míng).”
When my disciples heard this statement,
they did not understand my meaning,
and they proclaimed that the Tathāgata definitively taught that
form is the Four Great Elements.
“‘Good man,
I further said:
“For example, based on a mirror,
an image appears.
Form (sè) is also like this,
manufactured based on the Four Great Elements.
That is, coarse and subtle,
rough and smooth,
blue, yellow, red, and white,
long, short, square, and round,
slanted, cornered, light, and heavy,
cold, hot, hunger, and thirst,
smoke, clouds, dust, and mist—
these are called manufactured form (zàosè),
like an echo or an image.”
When my disciples heard this statement,
they did not understand my meaning,
and they proclaimed that the Tathāgata taught that where there are Four Great Elements, there is manufactured form,
or that there are Four Great Elements without manufactured form.
“‘Good man!
In the past, on one occasion,
the prince Pútí (Bodhi) spoke thus:
“If a bhikṣu observes and maintains the prohibitions and precepts (jìnjiè),
but then generates an evil thought,
you should know that at that time, he loses the bhikṣu precepts.”
I then told him:
“Prince Pútí!
Precepts have seven kinds,
arising from body and mouth,
possessing unmanifested form (wúzuòsè).”
Due to the causes and conditions of this unmanifested form,
although his mind may be in an evil or indeterminate (wújì) state,
he is not said to have lost the precepts;
he is still said to maintain the precepts.
For what cause and condition is it called ‘unmanifested form’?
It is not the cause of different form,
nor does it create the cause and effect of different form.”
Good man!
When my disciples heard this statement,
they did not understand my meaning,
and they proclaimed that the Buddha taught the existence of unmanifested form.’"
"Good man!
I speak thus in other sūtras:
'Precepts (Jiè) are the restraint and inhibition of evil dharmas.
Not committing evil is called upholding the precepts (Chíjiè).'
When my disciples hear this saying,
they do not understand my intent,
and proclaim that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) definitively stated
that there is no unmanifested form (Wúzuò Sè)."
"Good man,
I speak thus in the sūtras:
'From the aggregate of form (Sè Yīn) to the aggregate of consciousness (Shí Yīn) of the noble ones (Shèngrén),
all arise from the causal condition of ignorance (Wúmíng).
All ordinary beings (Fánfū) are also like this;
from ignorance arises craving (Ài).
You should know that this craving is ignorance.
From craving arises grasping (Qǔ).
You should know that this grasping is ignorance and craving.
From grasping arises existence (Yǒu).
This existence is ignorance, craving, and grasping.
From existence arises feeling (Shòu).
You should know that this feeling is formation (Xíng) and existence (Yǒu).
Due to the causal condition of feeling, name and form (Míng Sè) arise,
as well as ignorance (Wúmíng),
craving and grasping (Ài Qǔ),
existence and formation (Yǒu Xíng),
feeling (Shòu),
contact (Chù),
consciousness (Shí),
the six sense bases (Liù Rù), and so forth.
Therefore, feeling (Shòu) is the Twelve Links (Shí'èr Zhī)."
"Good man!
When my disciples hear this saying,
they do not understand my intent,
and proclaim that the Tathāgata stated there are no mental factors (Xīn Shù)."
"Good man,
I speak thus in the sūtras:
'From the four elements—the eye (Yǎn),
form (Sè),
light (Míng),
and wicked desire (È Yù),
eye-consciousness (Yǎnshí) is born.
What is meant by wicked desire
is ignorance (Wúmíng).
When the nature of desire seeks,
it is called craving (Ài).
Craving is the causal condition for grasping (Qǔ).
Grasping is called karma (Yè).
Karma is the causal condition for consciousness (Shí).
Consciousness is the condition for name and form (Míng Sè).
Name and form are the condition for the six sense bases (Liù Rù).
The six sense bases are the condition for contact (Chù).
Contact is the condition for conception (Xiǎng),
feeling (Shòu),
craving (Ài),
faith (Xìn),
exertion (Jīngjìn),
concentration (Dìng), and wisdom (Huì).
Dharmas such as these
arise dependent on contact,
yet they are not contact itself.'
"Good man!
When my disciples hear this saying,
they do not understand my intent,
and proclaim that the Tathāgata stated there are mental factors (Xīn Shù)."
"Good man!
Sometimes I speak of
only one existence (Yǒu);
sometimes I speak of two,
three,
four,
five, six, seven, eight, nine,
up to twenty-five.
When my disciples hear this saying,
they do not understand my intent,
and proclaim that the Tathāgata spoke of five existences (Wǔ Yǒu),
or perhaps six existences (Liù Yǒu)."
"Good man,
once when I was residing in the Nígòutuó Grove (Nígòutuó Lín) in Kāpíluó Wèi (Kāpíluó Wèi),
Śì Mónán (Shì Mónán) came to my location
and spoke thus:
'What is called an Upāsaka (Yōupósāi)?'
I immediately explained to him:
'If there is a good man
or a good woman
whose faculties are complete
and who receives the Three Refuges (Sān Guīyī),
then he is called an Upāsaka (Yōupósāi).'
Śì Mónán said:
'World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
What is called a Partial Upāsaka (Yīfēn Yōupósāi)?'
I said:
'Mónán!
If one receives the Three Refuges (Sān Guī) and receives one precept,
he is called a Partial Upāsaka (Yīfēn Yōupósāi).'
When my disciples heard this saying,
they did not understand my intent,
and proclaimed that the Tathāgata stated that the Upāsaka precepts (Yōupósāi Jiè) cannot be fully received."
"Good man!
Once when I was residing by the Hénghé River (Hénghé Biān),
at that time Jiāzhānyán (Jiāzhānyán) came to my location
and spoke thus:
'World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
I instruct sentient beings to receive the fasting Dharma (Zhāifǎ),
whether for one day,
or one night,
or one time period,
or one thought moment.
Do such people
fulfill the fast or not?'
I said:
'Bhikkhu (Bǐqiū)!
This person obtains merit (Shàn),
but is not called having obtained the fast (Zhāi).'
When my disciples heard this saying,
they did not understand my intent,
and proclaimed that the Tathāgata stated that the eight precepts and fast (Bā Jiè Zhāi) must be fully received to be attained."
"Good man!
I speak thus in the sūtras:
'If a Bhikkhu (Bǐqiū) commits the Four Cardinal Sins (Sì Zhòng),
he is not called a Bhikkhu;
he is called a broken Bhikkhu,
a lost Bhikkhu,
and is no longer able to generate the seeds of wholesome sprouts (Shàn Yá Zhǒngzǐ).
Just as a burnt seed does not produce fruit,
and just as a tāla tree (Duōluó Shù),
if its crown is severed,
will not bear fruit,
a Bhikkhu who commits a heavy offense is also like this.'
When my disciples heard this saying,
they did not understand my intent,
and proclaimed that the Tathāgata stated
that all Bhikkhus who commit heavy prohibitions
lose the Bhikkhu precepts (Bǐqiū Jiè)."
"Good man!
In the sūtras, I spoke to Chúntuó (Chúntuó), saying:
'There are four kinds of Bhikkhus:
First, the one who reaches the path definitively (Bìjìng Dào Dào);
second, the one who shows the path (Shì Dào);
third, the one who accepts the path (Shòu Dào);
fourth, the one who defiles the path (Wū Dào).
The one who commits the Four Cardinal Sins (Sì Zhòng) is the defiler of the path.'
When my disciples heard this saying,
they did not understand my intent,
and proclaimed that the Tathāgata stated that all Bhikkhus who commit the Four Cardinal Sins
do not lose the prohibitive precepts (Jìn Jiè)."
"Good man!
In the sūtras, I told the Bhikkhus:
'The One Vehicle (Yī Chéng),
the One Path,
the One Practice,
the One Condition.
This One Vehicle up to the One Condition
can bring great tranquility to sentient beings,
forever severing all bonds,
sorrow and suffering,
suffering and the cause of suffering,
allowing all sentient beings to reach the One Existence.'
When my disciples heard this saying,
they did not understand my intent,
and proclaimed that the Tathāgata stated that persons from Śūdāhuán (Xūdàhuán) up to Āluóhàn (Āluóhàn) all attain the Buddha Path (Fódào)."
"Good man!
In the sūtras, I stated:
'A Śūdāhuán person
returns to the human and heavenly realms seven times,
and then attains Parinirvāṇa (Bān Nièpán).
A Sītuóhán (Sītuóhán) person
receives human and heavenly existence once,
and then attains Parinirvāṇa.
An Ānàhán (Ānàhán) person
generally has five types,
including those who attain Parinirvāṇa midway [in the cycle],
up to those who attain Parinirvāṇa in the upper stream.
An Āluóhàn (Āluóhàn) person generally has two types:
first, those in the present,
and second, those in the future.
Those in the present also sever defilements (Fánnǎo) and the five aggregates (Wǔ Yīn);
those in the future also sever defilements and the five aggregates.'
When my disciples heard this saying,
they did not understand my intent,
and proclaimed that the Tathāgata stated that Śūdāhuán up to Āluóhàn do not attain the Buddha Path."
"Good man!
In this sūtra, I state:
'The Buddha Nature (Fó Xìng) possesses six characteristics:
First, permanence (Cháng);
second, reality (Shí);
third, truth (Zhēn);
fourth, goodness (Shàn);
fifth, purity (Jìng);
sixth, visibility (Kě Jiàn).'
When my disciples hear this saying,
they do not understand my intent,
and proclaim that the Buddha stated
that the Buddha Nature of sentient beings exists apart from sentient beings."
"Good man!
I have also spoken thus:
'The Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) of sentient beings is like empty space (Xūkōng).
Empty space is neither past,
nor future,
nor present,
nor internal,
nor external.
It is not included in form (Sè),
sound (Shēng),
smell (Xiāng),
taste (Wèi),
or touch (Chù).
The Buddha-nature is also like this.'
My disciples, having heard this teaching,
did not understand my intention,
and proclaimed that the Buddha taught
that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings exists apart from sentient beings.
"Good man!
I have also spoken again:
'The Buddha-nature of sentient beings
is like the treasure concealed in the house of a poor woman,
the diamond jewel (Jīngāng Bǎozhū) on the forehead of a strong man (Lìshì),
or the sweet dew spring (Gānlù Zhī Quán) of the Cakravartin King (Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng).'
My disciples, having heard this teaching,
did not understand my intention,
and proclaimed that the Buddha taught
that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings exists apart from sentient beings.
"Good man!
I have also spoken again:
'Those who violate the four major prohibitions (Sì Chóng Jìn),
the Icchantikas (Yīchǎntí Rén),
those who slander the Vaipulya Sūtras (Fāngděng Jīng),
and those who commit the five heinous crimes (Wǔ Nì Zuì),
all possess Buddha-nature.
Such sentient beings possess no wholesome dharmas,
yet the Buddha-nature is wholesome.'
My disciples, having heard this teaching,
did not understand my intention,
and proclaimed that the Buddha taught
that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings exists apart from sentient beings.
"Good man!
I have also spoken again:
'Sentient beings are precisely the Buddha-nature.
Why is this?
If separated from sentient beings,
one cannot attain Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).'
Therefore, I spoke the simile of the elephant to King Prasenajit (Bōsīní Wáng).
It is like the blind speaking of the elephant;
although they do not attain the elephant,
they are not separate from the elephant.
When sentient beings speak of form (sè) up to consciousness (shì) as being the Buddha-nature,
it is also like this:
although it is not the Buddha-nature,
it is not non-Buddha-nature.
Just as I spoke the simile of the Konghou (Kōnghóu) to the King,
the Buddha-nature is also like this.
Good man!
My disciples, having heard this teaching,
did not understand my intention,
and offered various explanations.
It is like the blind asking about milk;
the Buddha-nature is also like this.
Because of this reason,
some say that those who violate the four major prohibitions (sì chóng jìn),
slander the Vaipulya Sūtras (fāngděng jīng),
commit the five heinous crimes (wǔ nì zuì),
or are Icchantikas (yīchǎntí), etc.,
all possess Buddha-nature,
while others say they do not.
"Good man,
I have stated in various Sūtras:
'One person appearing in the world benefits many people.
That there should be two Cakravartin Kings (zhuǎnlún wáng) in one country,
or two Buddhas appearing in one world,
there is no such possibility.'
That there should be eight Cāturmahārājika Devas (sì tiān wáng) or even two Paranirmitavaśavartin Devas (tāhuà zìzài tiān) in one Jambudvīpa (sì tiānxià),
there is also no such possibility.
Yet I have also spoken:
'From Jambudvīpa (Yánfútí),
to the Avīci Hell (Ābí Dìyù),
up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven (Ājiā Nìzhà Tiān).'
My disciples, having heard this teaching,
did not understand my intention,
and proclaimed that the Buddha taught
that there are no Buddhas in the ten directions.
I also stated in various Mahāyāna Sūtras (Dàchéng Jīng) that there are Buddhas in the ten directions.
"Good man!
Such debates and disputes are the realm of the Buddha,
and are not understood by the Śrāvakas (Shēngwén)
or Pratyekabuddhas (Yuánjué).
If a person gives rise to doubt concerning this,
they can still destroy countless afflictions (Fánnǎo) like Mount Sumeru (Xūmí Shān).
If, regarding this, they give rise to certainty,
this is called attachment (Zhízhuó).
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa (Jiāshè Púsà) addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
What is attachment (zhízhuó)?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Such a person,
whether hearing from others,
or searching the Sūtras themselves,
or being taught by others,
is unable to abandon the object of their attachment,
this is called attachment (zhízhuó)."
Kāśyapa (Jiāshè) spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
Is such attachment (zhízhuó)
wholesome,
or unwholesome?"
"Good man!
Such attachment (zhízhuó)
is not called wholesome.
Why is this?
Because it cannot destroy the net of doubts."
Kāśyapa (Jiāshè) spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
Such a person
inherently has no doubt,
how can it be said that they do not destroy the net of doubts?"
"Good man!
That which is called having no doubt
is precisely doubt."
"World-Honored One!
If a person states that a Sotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán Rén) will not fall into the three evil paths (Sān È),
should this person also be called attached
or called doubtful?"
"Good man!
This may be called certainty,
and should not be called doubt.
Why is this?
Good man!
Suppose a person first sees a person
and a tree.
Later, traveling at night,
they see a stump root from afar,
and immediately give rise to the thought of doubt:
'Is it a person?
Is it a tree?'
Good man!
Suppose a person first sees a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) and a Brahmin (Fànzhì).
Later, seeing a Bhikṣu (bǐqiū) from afar on the road,
they immediately give rise to the thought of doubt:
'Is this a Śramaṇa (Shāmén)?
Is this a Brahmin (fànzhì)?'
Good man!
Suppose a person first sees a cow and a water buffalo (shuǐ niú).
Later, seeing a cow from afar,
they immediately give rise to the thought of doubt:
'Is that a cow?
Is it a water buffalo (shuǐ niú)?'
Good man!
All sentient beings first see two objects,
and only later give rise to doubt.
Why is this?
Because the mind is not clear.
I do not say that the Sotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán Rén) will fall into the three evil paths
or not fall into the three evil paths.
For what reason does this person give rise to a doubtful mind?"
Kāśyapa (Jiāshè) said:
"World-Honored One!
According to what the Buddha has said,
doubt arises only after [the two objects] have been seen first.
Yet there are people who give rise to doubt
even when they have not seen the two kinds of objects.
What is this?
Namely, Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
World-Honored One!
For example, a person encounters turbid water on the road,
and although they have never seen it before, they still give rise to doubt:
'Is this water deep?
Or shallow?'
If this person has not seen it,
how does doubt arise?"
“O good man!
Nirvāṇa
is the cessation of suffering.
That which is not Nirvāṇa
is suffering.
All sentient beings perceive two kinds of things:
suffering,
and non-suffering.
That which is suffering and non-suffering
is hunger and thirst,
cold and heat,
anger and joy,
sickness and thinness versus safety and well-being,
old age and strength versus birth and death,
binding and liberation,
kindness and affection versus separation,
and resentment and hatred versus gathering.
When sentient beings perceive this, they immediately generate doubt,
wondering whether there will ultimately be an event that permanently removes such suffering and distress.
It is for this reason that sentient beings generate doubt regarding Nirvāṇa.
If you think that this person has previously never seen turbid water,
how can they doubt?
This reasoning is incorrect.
Why is that?
Because this person has seen it previously in other places,
thus, even concerning this place they have never reached,
they still generate doubt.
“O Bhagavat!
When this person previously saw deep and shallow places,
they did not generate doubt;
why do they now generate doubt again?”
The Buddha said:
“O good man!
Because they have not yet traversed it,
they therefore generate doubt.
This is why I say,
doubt arises from misunderstanding.”
Kāśyapa Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
“O Bhagavat!
As the Buddha has said,
doubt is attachment,
and attachment is doubt.
Who is it that possesses this?”
“O good man!
It is those who sever the roots of goodness.”
Kāśyapa said:
“O Bhagavat!
What kind of people
can sever the roots of goodness?”
“O good man!
If there is one who is clever, shrewd, and sharp-witted,
capable of skillful differentiation,
but who avoids good friends,
does not listen to the correct Dharma,
does not reflect skillfully,
and does not dwell in accordance with the Dharma—
such a person
can sever the roots of goodness.
Separated from these four things,
the mind reflects by itself:
‘There is no object given in generosity.
Why?
The giver is simply the discarder of wealth and possessions.
If generosity has a retribution,
one should know that the donor ought always to be poor.
Why?
Because the fruit resembles the seed.
Therefore, it is said that there is no cause and no effect.
If one speaks like this—that there is no cause and no effect—
this is called severing the roots of goodness.
“Furthermore, they generate this thought:
‘The donor,
the recipient, and the property,
these three things are impermanent
and have no fixed permanence.
If there is no fixed permanence,
how can one say,
“This is the donor,”
“the recipient,”
or “the property”?
If there is no recipient,
how can a result be attained?
Based on this reasoning,
there is no cause and no effect.’
If one speaks like this—that there is no cause and no effect—
one should know that this person can sever the roots of goodness.
“Furthermore, they generate this thought:
‘When the giver gives, there are five kinds of giving.
After the recipient receives,
they sometimes perform good deeds,
and sometimes perform unwholesome deeds.
Yet, the donor does not receive
the fruit of good or unwholesome deeds.
Just like the worldly principle:
from a seed, a fruit is born,
and the fruit reverts to being a seed.
The cause is the donor, and the fruit is the recipient.
However, the recipient cannot, through these good
or unwholesome Dharmas,
cause the donor to attain anything.
Based on this reasoning,
there is no cause and no effect.’
If one speaks like this—that there is no cause and no effect—
one should know that this person can sever the roots of goodness.
“Furthermore, they generate this thought:
‘There is no object given in generosity.
Why?
The object of giving is indeterminate (avyākrta).
If it is indeterminate,
how can one attain a wholesome retribution?
Having no wholesome or unwholesome result
is precisely what is meant by indeterminate.
If the wealth is indeterminate,
one should know that there is no wholesome or unwholesome retribution;
therefore, there is no giving,
no cause,
and no effect.’
If one speaks like this—that there is no cause and no effect—
one should know that this person can sever the roots of goodness.
“Furthermore, they generate this thought:
‘The donor is intention (manas).
If it is intention,
it is invisible and non-confronting;
it is not a physical form (rūpa).
If it is not physical form,
how can it be given?
Therefore, there is no giving,
no cause,
and no effect.’
If one speaks like this—that there is no cause and no effect—
one should know that this person can sever the roots of goodness.
“Furthermore, they generate this thought:
‘If the donor performs generosity for a Buddha image,
a celestial image,
or deceased parents,
there is no recipient.
If there is no recipient,
there should be no retribution.
If there is no retribution,
this means there is no cause;
if there is no cause, this means there is no effect.’
If one speaks like this—that there is no cause and no effect—
one should know that this person can sever the roots of goodness.
“Furthermore, they generate this thought:
‘There are no fathers and no mothers.
If one says that parents are the cause of sentient beings
and produce sentient beings,
then conceptually, they should produce continuously
without cessation.
Why?
Because the cause is always existent.
However, production is not continuous;
therefore, one should know there are no parents.’
“Furthermore, they generate this thought:
‘There are no fathers and no mothers.
Why?
If the body of sentient beings exists due to parents,
then one person ought to possess both male and female faculties,
yet there is no one who possesses both.
Therefore, one should know that sentient beings are not due to parents.’
“Furthermore, they generate this thought:
‘Sentient beings are not born due to parents.
Why?
The sentient beings seen by the eye
do not resemble their parents,
whether in body,
color,
mind,
deportment,
or movement and cessation.
Therefore, parents are not the cause of sentient beings.’
“Furthermore, they generate this thought:
‘In the entire world, there are four kinds of non-existence:
First, non-existence before birth,
such as when a lump of clay
does not yet have the function of a jar.
Second, non-existence after destruction,
such as when a jar has been broken—
this is called non-existence.
Third, reciprocal non-existence (mutual distinction),
such as there being no horse in a cow,
and no cow in a horse.
Fourth, ultimate non-existence,
such as the horns of a rabbit
and the hair of a turtle.
The parents of sentient beings are also like this,
sharing these four kinds of non-existence.
If one says that parents are the cause of sentient beings,
when the parents die,
the children do not necessarily die.
Therefore, parents are not the cause of sentient beings.’
“Furthermore, they generate this thought:
‘If one says that parents are the cause of sentient beings,
sentient beings should always be born through parents.
However, there are also spontaneously generated beings
and moisture-born beings.
Therefore, one should know
that sentient beings are not born through parents.”
"Again, one generates this thought:
'There are sentient beings
that grow and develop without the cause of parents.
For example, the peacock,
upon hearing the sound of thunder,
immediately becomes pregnant.
Also, like the green finch,
which drinks the urine of the male finch,
and immediately becomes pregnant.
Like the Mìngmìngniǎo,
seeing the male dance,
immediately becomes pregnant.'
When generating this thought,
if one does not meet a virtuous spiritual advisor (Shàn zhīshi),
you should know that this person is capable of severing their roots of goodness.
"Again, one generates this thought:
'In the entire world, there are no results of good or evil.
Why is this?
There are sentient beings who embody the Ten Virtuous Deeds (shí shàn fǎ),
delight in generosity and giving,
and diligently cultivate merit and virtue.
These people are nevertheless afflicted by diseases that gather in their bodies,
die prematurely in middle age,
suffer financial loss,
and have many sorrows and hardships.
There are those who practice the Ten Evil Deeds (shí è),
are stingy, greedy, and jealous,
are lazy and negligent,
and do not cultivate any goodness;
yet their bodies are at ease and free from sickness,
they complete their natural lifespan (nián shòu),
possess great wealth and treasures,
and are free from all worries and suffering.
Therefore, you should know that there are no results of good or evil.'
"Again, one generates this thought:
'I have also heard the various holy persons (Shèng rén) say that
some people cultivate goodness,
but when their life ends, they often fall into the three evil paths (sān'èdào);
some people practice evil,
but when their life ends, they are born among humans and devas.
Therefore, you should know that there are no results of good or evil.'
"Again, one generates this thought:
'All holy persons have two kinds of teachings:
some say that killing life brings a good retribution,
and some say that killing life brings an evil retribution.
Therefore, you should know that the holy teaching (shèng shuō) is not fixed.
If the holy teaching is not fixed,
how can I be fixed (certain)?
Therefore, you should know that there are no results of good or evil.'
"Again, one generates this thought:
'In the entire world, there are no holy persons (Shèng rén).
Why is this?
If you say that a holy person should attain the true path (Zhèngdào),
and if sentient beings cultivate the true path (Zhèngdào) while still possessing defilements (Fánnǎo),
you should know that for such a person, the true path
and defilements (Fánnǎo) exist simultaneously.
If they exist simultaneously,
you should know that the true path cannot break the fetters (jié).
If one cultivates the path without defilements,
then what is the purpose of such a true path?
Therefore, for those who possess defilements,
the path cannot destroy them;
for those who do not possess defilements,
the path is useless.
Therefore, you should know
that in the entire world, there are no holy persons.'
"Again, one generates this thought:
'Ignorance conditions action (wúmíng yuán xíng),
extending to birth conditioning old age and death—
these twelve links of dependent origination (Shí'èr Yīnyuán)—
are equally possessed by all sentient beings.
The Eightfold Noble Path (Bā Shèng Dào),
being equal in nature,
should also be such that when one person attains it,
all should attain it;
when one person cultivates it,
the suffering of all should be extinguished.
Why is this?
Because defilements (Fánnǎo) are equal.
Since this does not happen now,
therefore, you should know that there is no true path.'
"Again, one generates this thought:
'Holy persons (Shèng rén) all share the same characteristics as ordinary beings (Fánfū),
namely eating and drinking,
walking and abiding,
sitting and lying down,
sleeping,
rejoicing and laughing,
hunger and thirst,
cold and heat,
worry and sorrow,
and fear.
If they share these characteristics with ordinary beings,
then you should know that holy persons have not attained the holy path (Shèngdào);
if they had attained the holy path,
they ought to have eternally severed such matters.
If such matters are not severed,
then you should know there is no path.'
"Again, one generates this thought:
'Holy persons possess a body,
enjoy the pleasures of the five desires (wǔ yù),
and furthermore curse, insult, and strike others,
feeling jealousy, envy, and arrogance toward people,
undergoing suffering and happiness,
and performing good and evil actions (yè).
Due to these conditions,
we know there are no holy persons.
If there were a path,
these matters should be severed,
but since these matters are not severed,
you should know there is no path.'
"Again, one generates this thought:
'One who possesses great compassion
is called a holy person.
For what reason
are they called a holy person?
Because of the path,
they are called a holy person.
If the nature of the path is compassion,
then it should be compassionate toward all sentient beings,
not waiting until cultivation is complete before it is attained.
If it lacks compassion,
why then, after holy persons attain the holy path (Shèngdào),
are they able to be compassionate?
Therefore, you should know that in the world there is no holy path.'
"Again, one generates this thought:
'All Four Great Elements (Sìdà)
are not born from causes.
Sentient beings equally possess the nature of these Four Great Elements,
not distinguishing which sentient being should attain this shore
and which should not attain that one.
If there were a holy path (Shèngdào),
its nature should be like this.
But currently, it is not so.
Therefore, you should know
that in the world there are no holy persons.'
"Again, one generates this thought:
'If the various holy persons share a single Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
you should know that in that case, there are no holy persons.
Why is this?
Because it is unobtainable.
A permanent (chángzhù) phenomenon
is logically unobtainable
and cannot be taken or abandoned.
If the Nirvāṇa of the various holy persons were manifold,
then it would be impermanent (wúcháng).
Why is this?
Because it would be a countable phenomenon.
If Nirvāṇa is single,
then when one person attains it,
all should attain it.
If Nirvāṇa is manifold,
then it has boundaries (yǒu biān),
and if it has boundaries,
how can it be called permanent?
If someone says that the essence of Nirvāṇa is one
but liberation (jiětuō) is manifold,
like a cover (gài) is one
but the prongs or teeth (yá shé) are manifold,
this meaning is incorrect.
Why?
That which is attained individually
is not attained universally.
Because it has boundaries,
it must be impermanent.
If it is impermanent,
how can it be named Nirvāṇa?
If Nirvāṇa does not exist,
who then are the holy persons?
Therefore, you should know there are no holy persons.'
"Again, one generates this thought:
'The path of the holy person (Shèng rén zhī dào)
is not attained through conditioning causes (Yīnyuán).
If the holy person’s path
is not attained through conditioning causes,
why doesn't everyone become a holy person?
If not everyone is a holy person,
then you should know that there are neither holy persons
nor the holy path (Shèngdào).'
"Again, one generates this thought:
'The true view (Zhèngjiàn) spoken of by the holy ones
has two conditioning causes:
first, hearing the Dharma from others;
second, internal self-reflection.
If these two conditioning causes (Yīnyuán)
are born from conditions,
and that from which they are born
is also born from conditions,
then this transmission,
extending indefinitely, leads to the flaw of infinite regress (wú qióng guò).
If these two things
are not born from conditions,
why do all sentient beings not attain them?'
When one makes this observation, they are capable of severing the roots of goodness.
"Good man!
If there are sentient beings who deeply hold such views of no cause and no effect,
these people can sever the five faculties, such as faith (xìn).
Good man!
Those who sever the roots of goodness (shàn gēn)
are not people who are low, inferior, foolish, or dull,
nor are they among the Devas (tiān) or the three evil paths (sān è dào).
It is also true for those who cause schisms in the Saṅgha (pò sēng).
Kèyè Púsà (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva) said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
When will such people
be able to revive the roots of goodness?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
These people revive the roots of goodness at two times:
when they first enter the hells (dìyù),
and when they leave the hells.
Good man!
Goodness (shàn) has three types:
past (guòqù),
present (xiànzài),
and future (wèilái).
Regarding that which is past,
its nature is inherently extinguished.
Although the cause (yīn) is extinguished, the fruition (guǒ bào) has not yet ripened.
Therefore, it is not called severing the past fruition.
Severing the causes of the three times (sān shì yīn)
is why it is called severance (duàn).
Kèyè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"Shìzūn!
If severing the causes of the three times
is called severing the roots of goodness,
then the person who severs the roots of goodness
possesses the Buddha-nature (fóxìng).
Is this Fóxìng
past,
present,
or future?
Or does it pervade the three times?
If it is past,
how can it be called permanent (cháng)?
Fóxìng is also permanent,
therefore it must be known that it is not past.
If it is future,
how can it be called permanent?
Why does the Buddha say that all sentient beings must definitely attain it?
If it must definitely be attained,
how can it be said to be severed?
If it is present,
how again is it permanent?
Why is it further said that it can definitely be seen?
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) also stated that
Fóxìng has six characteristics:
one, permanent (cháng);
two, true (zhēn);
three, real (shí);
four, good (shàn);
five, pure (jìng);
six, visible (kě jiàn).
If a person who severs the roots of goodness possesses Fóxìng,
then he should not be called one who severs the roots of goodness.
If he does not possess Fóxìng,
how can it be said that all sentient beings possess Fóxìng?
If it is said that Fóxìng is both present
and severed,
how did the Rúlái then say it is permanent?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
The Rúlái Shìzūn, for the sake of sentient beings,
employs four types of answers:
one, the definitive answer (dìng dá);
two, the analytical answer (fēnbíedá);
three, the counter-question answer (suí wèn dá);
four, the silence answer (zhì dá).
"Good man!
What is the definitive answer?
If one asks whether evil karma (è yè) yields good fruition
or non-good fruition,
one should definitively answer that it yields non-good fruition.
Goodness (shàn) is also like this.
If one asks whether the Rúlái is omniscient (yīqiè zhì),
one should definitively answer that he is omniscient.
If one asks whether the Buddha Dharma (Fófǎ) is pure,
one should definitively answer that it is certainly pure.
If one asks whether the Rúlái's disciples abide according to the Dharma (rú fǎ zhù),
one should definitively answer that there are those who abide according to the Dharma.
This is called the definitive answer.
"What is the analytical answer?
Like the four Noble Truths (sì zhēndì fǎ) that I have taught.
What are the four?
Suffering (kǔ),
accumulation (jí),
cessation (miè),
and the path (dào).
What is the Truth of Suffering (Kǔ Dì)?
Because there are eight sufferings (bā kǔ),
it is called the Kǔ Dì.
What is the Truth of Accumulation (Jí Dì)?
Because it is the cause of the five aggregates (wǔ yīn),
it is called the Jí Dì.
What is the Truth of Cessation (Miè Dì)?
Because craving (tānyù),
hatred (chēn), and delusion (chī) are utterly exhausted,
it is called the Miè Dì.
What is the Truth of the Path (Dào Dì)?
Because of the thirty-seven factors contributing to enlightenment (sānshíqī zhù dào fǎ),
it is called the Dào Dì.
This is called the analytical answer.
"What is the counter-question answer?
For example, when I say,
'All dharmas (yīqiè fǎ) are impermanent (wúcháng).'
And someone asks:
'For the sake of which dharma does the Rúlái Shìzūn speak of impermanence?'
The answer is:
'The Rúlái speaks of impermanence for the sake of conditioned dharmas (yǒuwéi fǎ).'
Therefore, wúcháng is taught.
Non-self (wú wǒ) is also like this.
For example, when I say, 'All dharmas burn.'
And someone asks:
'For the sake of which dharma does the Rúlái Shìzūn say that all things burn?'
The answer is:
'The Rúlái says all things burn for the sake of greed (tān), hatred (chēn), and delusion (chī).'
"Good man!
The Rúlái's ten powers (shílì),
four fearlessnesses (sì wú suǒ wèi),
great compassion (dà cí dà bēi),
three mindfulness stations (sān niàn chù),
the 80 billion doors of concentration (sānmèi mén) such as the Śūraṅgama (Shǒu léng yán),
the thirty-two marks (sānshí'èr xiàng),
the eighty minor characteristics (bāshí zhǒng hǎo),
the 35,000 doors of concentration such as the Five Seals of Wisdom (wǔ zhì yìn) and the Vajra Concentration (jīngāng dìng),
the 4,200 doors of concentration, the immeasurable and boundless expedient concentrations (fāngbiàn sānmèi)—
all such dharmas constitute the Buddha
and the Fóxìng.
This Fóxìng thus has seven attributes:
one, permanent;
two, self (wǒ);
three, bliss (lè);
four, pure;
five, true;
six, real;
seven, good.
This is called the analytical answer.
"Good man!
The Fóxìng of the Bodhisattva of the Last Life (hòushēn púsà) has six attributes:
one, permanent;
two, pure;
three, true;
four, real;
five, good;
six, rarely seen.
This is called the analytical answer.
"As you asked previously:
Regarding the person who severs the roots of goodness—if he possesses Fóxìng,
this person also possesses the Fóxìng of the Rúlái;
he also possesses the Fóxìng of the Hòushēn Púsà.
These two Fóxìng,
because they are hindered in the future,
are designated as 'non-existent.'
Because they are ultimately attained,
they are designated as 'existent.'
This is called the analytical answer.
"The Fóxìng of the Rúlái is neither past,
nor present,
nor future.
The Fóxìng of the Hòushēn Púsà is present
because it is slightly visible in the future,
thus it is designated as 'present.'
Because it is not fully visible,
it is called 'future.'
When the Rúlái had not yet attained Anōuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi),
the Fóxìng, being the cause,
was also past,
present,
and future.
The fruition, however, is not like that;
sometimes it belongs to the three times,
sometimes it does not belong to the three times.
The Fóxìng of the Hòushēn Púsà, being the cause,
is also past,
present,
and future.
The fruition is also like this.
This is called the analytical answer.
"The Fóxìng of the Bodhisattva of the Nine Abodes (jiǔ zhù púsà) has six attributes:
one, permanent;
two, good;
three, true;
four, real;
five, pure;
six, visible.
The Fóxìng, being the cause,
is also past,
present,
and future.
The fruition is also like this.
This is called the analytical answer."
"For Bodhisattvas from the Eighth Abode down to the Sixth Abode,
the five aspects of the Fóxìng are:
First, reality (zhēn);
second, substance (shí);
third, purity (jìng);
fourth, goodness (shàn);
fifth, visibility (kějiàn).
Because the Fóxìng is the cause (yīn),
it is also the past,
present,
and future.
The result (guǒ) is likewise.
This is called the Differentiated Answer (Fēnbié Dá).
"For Bodhisattvas from the Fifth Abode down to the First Abode,
the five aspects of the Fóxìng are:
First, reality (zhēn);
second, substance (shí);
third, purity (jìng);
fourth, visibility (kějiàn);
fifth, good and not-good (shàn bù shàn).
Good man!
These five types of Fóxìng,
six types of Fóxìng,
and seven types of Fóxìng
must be attained by those who have cut off the roots of goodness (duàn shàngēn rén);
therefore, it can be said to exist.
This is called the Differentiated Answer (Fēnbié Dá).
"If someone were to say that
those who have cut off the roots of goodness definitely possess the Fóxìng,
or definitely do not possess the Fóxìng,
this is called the Evasive Answer (Zhì Dá).
Kǎyè Púsà said:
"World-Honored One!
When I hear something, not answering
is called the Evasive Answer.
For what reason does the Tathāgata now,
answer yet call it the Evasive Answer?"
"Good man!
I also did not say that evading and not answering is called the Evasive Answer.
Good man!
This Evasive Answer,
further has two kinds:
The first is prohibition (zhēzhǐ);
the second is non-attachment (mò zhuó).
Because of these meanings,
it is given the name Evasive Answer (Zhì Dá).
Kǎyè Púsà spoke to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
According to what the Buddha has said,
how is it that the cause (yīn) is also the past,
present,
and future?
And the result (guǒ) is also the past,
present,
and future,
but is not the past,
present,
and future?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
The five skandhas are of two types:
The first is the cause (yīn);
the second is the result (guǒ).
The causal five skandhas
are the past,
present,
and future.
The resulting five skandhas
are also the past,
present,
and future,
but are also not the past,
present,
and future.
Good man!
All afflictions (fánnǎo) and bonds (jié) such as ignorance (wúmíng),
are entirely the Fóxìng.
Why is that?
Because they are the cause of the Fóxìng.
To obtain the good five skandhas from the formation resulting from ignorance (wúmíng xíng) and various afflictions,
this is called the Fóxìng.
From the good five skandhas,
one eventually obtains Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Therefore, I previously said in the sūtra
that the Fóxìng of sentient beings
is like blood mixed with milk;
the blood is precisely all afflictions such as the formation resulting from ignorance,
and the milk is precisely the good five skandhas.
Therefore, I say that
from all afflictions and the good five skandhas,
one obtains Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí.
Just as the body of a sentient being
is formed entirely from semen and blood,
the Fóxìng is also like this.
For a Sūtuóhuán person,
and a Sītuóhán person,
who have cut off few afflictions,
the Fóxìng is like milk.
For an Ānàhán person,
the Fóxìng is like curds (lào).
For an Āluóhàn person,
it is like fresh ghee (shēng sū).
From Pratyekabuddhas (Pìzhīfó) up to Bodhisattvas of the Tenth Abode,
it is like refined ghee (shú sū).
The Tathāgata's Fóxìng
is like clarified butter (tíhú).
Good man!
Because present afflictions act as obstacles,
they prevent sentient beings from being able to perceive it.
Just as there is the patience herb (rěnrǔ cǎo) on Mount Xiāngshān,
not all cows are able to eat it;
the Fóxìng is also like this.
This is called the Differentiated Answer (Fēnbié Dá).
Kǎyè Púsà spoke to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If the five,
six,
or seven types of Fóxìng exist in the future,
how can it be said that those who have cut off the roots of goodness possess the Fóxìng?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Just as sentient beings possess past karma (yè),
and based on this karma,
sentient beings now receive their retribution (guǒbào).
There is future karma,
which, because it has not yet arisen,
will definitely not produce a result. There are present afflictions.
If there were no afflictions,
all sentient beings should clearly and manifestly see the Fóxìng.
Therefore, those who have cut off the roots of goodness,
due to the causality of present afflictions,
are able to cut off the roots of goodness.
Due to the power and causality of the future Fóxìng,
the roots of goodness are recovered.
Kǎyè said:
"World-Honored One!
How can the future be capable of generating the roots of goodness?"
"Good man!
Just like a lamp or the sun,
although they have not yet arisen,
they are also able to break the darkness.
The arising of the future
is able to generate the future Fóxìng of sentient beings;
it is also like this.
This is called the Differentiated Answer (Fēnbié Dá).
Kǎyè Púsà spoke to the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If it is said that the five skandhas are the Fóxìng,
how can it be said that the Fóxìng of sentient beings is neither internal
nor external?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
For what reason are you so confused?
Did I not previously say that the Fóxìng of sentient beings is the Middle Way (Zhōngdào)?
Kǎyè said:
"World-Honored One!
I am truly not confused;
I merely raise this question because sentient beings are unable to comprehend this Middle Way."
"Good man!
Sentient beings' incomprehension
is precisely the Middle Way.
Sometimes there is comprehension,
and sometimes there is no comprehension.
Good man!
To enable sentient beings to gain comprehension,
I speak of the Fóxìng as neither internal nor external.
Why is that?
Ordinary sentient beings (fánfū zhòngshēng) sometimes say that the Fóxìng resides within the five skandhas,
like a fruit in a vessel;
or they say it exists separate from the skandhas,
like empty space.
Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of the Middle Way.
The Fóxìng of sentient beings is neither the internal six entrances (nèi liù rù),
nor the external six entrances (wài liù rù);
the combination of internal and external
is called the Middle Way.
Therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims that the Fóxìng is precisely the Middle Way,
neither internal
nor external,
hence it is named the Middle Way.
This is called the Differentiated Answer (Fēnbié Dá)."
“Furthermore, good man!
What is meant by ‘neither internal nor external’?
Good man!
Some say that the Buddha nature (Fóxìng) is precisely the external path (wàidào).
Why is this?
Because Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà), over immeasurable kalpas, while amidst the external paths,
eradicated all afflictions (fánnǎo),
disciplined their minds,
and taught and transformed sentient beings,
and only then attained Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí).
Therefore, the Buddha nature is precisely the external path.
Others say that the Buddha nature is precisely the internal path (nèidào).
Why is this?
Although Bodhisattvas cultivate the external path over immeasurable kalpas,
if they depart from the internal path,
they cannot attain Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.
Therefore, the Buddha nature is precisely the internal path.
For this reason, the Tathāgata (Rúlái) precludes these two extremes
and declares that the Buddha nature is neither internal
nor external,
and is also called both internal and external.
This is called the Middle Way (Zhōngdào).
This is the answer given through differentiation.
“Furthermore, good man!
Some say that the Buddha nature is precisely the Vajra (Jīngāng) body of the Tathāgata,
the thirty-two marks,
and the eighty subsidiary characteristics.
Why is this?
Because they are not false or deceptive.
Others say that the Buddha nature is precisely the ten powers (shílì),
the four kinds of fearlessness (sì wúsuǒwèi),
great compassion (dàcí dàbēi), the three stations of mindfulness (sān niànchù),
the Śūraṅgama (Shǒuléngyán) and all other samādhis.
Why is this?
Because through these samādhis,
the Vajra body,
the thirty-two marks,
and the eighty subsidiary characteristics are generated.
For this reason, the Tathāgata precludes these two extremes
and declares that the Buddha nature is neither internal nor external,
and is also called both internal and external.
This is called the Middle Way.
This is the answer given through differentiation.
“Furthermore, good man!
Some say that the Buddha nature is precisely internal virtuous contemplation (shàn sīwéi).
Why is this?
Because without virtuous contemplation,
one cannot attain Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.
Therefore, the Buddha nature is precisely internal virtuous contemplation.
Others say that the Buddha nature is precisely hearing the Dharma (Fǎ) from others.
Why is this?
By hearing the Dharma from others,
one is then able to contemplate internally with virtue.
If one does not hear the Dharma, there is no contemplation.
Therefore, the Buddha nature is precisely hearing the Dharma from others.
For this reason, the Tathāgata precludes these two extremes
and declares that the Buddha nature is neither internal nor external,
and is also called both internal and external.
This is called the Middle Way.
“Furthermore, good man!
Again, some say the Buddha nature is external,
namely Dānapāramitā (Dànbōluómì).
By means of Dānapāramitā, one attains Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.
Therefore, it is said that Dānapāramitā is precisely the Buddha nature.
Others say the Buddha nature is internal,
namely the five Pāramitās (bōluómì).
Why is this?
Know that apart from these five things,
there is no cause or effect of the Buddha nature.
Therefore, it is said that the five Pāramitās are precisely the Buddha nature.
For this reason, the Tathāgata precludes these two extremes
and declares that the Buddha nature is neither internal nor external,
and is both internal and external.
This is called the Middle Way.
“Furthermore, good man!
Some say that the Buddha nature is internal,
likened to a precious pearl on the forehead of a strong man (lìshì).
Why is this?
Because it is permanent (cháng), blissful (lè), self (wǒ), and pure (jìng), just like a precious pearl.
Therefore, it is said that the Buddha nature is internal.
Others say that the Buddha nature is external,
like a treasure hidden from a poor person.
Why is this?
Because it is seen by means of skillful means (fāngbiàn).
The Buddha nature is also like this;
it is external to sentient beings,
and is seen by means of skillful means.
For this reason, the Tathāgata precludes these two extremes
and declares that the Buddha nature is neither internal nor external,
and is both internal and external.
This is called the Middle Way.
“Good man!
The Buddha nature of sentient beings is neither existent
nor nonexistent.
Why is this?
Although the Buddha nature exists,
it is not like empty space.
Why is this?
Although worldly empty space
cannot be seen by immeasurable skillful means,
the Buddha nature can be seen.
Therefore, although it exists, it is not like empty space.
Although the Buddha nature is nonexistent, it is not like a rabbit’s horn.
Why is this?
Turtle hair
and a rabbit’s horn
cannot be produced even by immeasurable skillful means;
the Buddha nature can be produced.
Therefore, although it is nonexistent, it is not like a rabbit’s horn.
Therefore, the Buddha nature
is neither existent nor nonexistent,
and is both existent and nonexistent.
What is meant by existent?
Everything possesses it;
it is the constant and unextinguished nature of sentient beings,
like the flame of a lamp,
until the attainment of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi.
Therefore, it is called existent.
What is meant by nonexistent?
All sentient beings do not currently possess all the qualities of the Buddha Dharma—
permanent,
blissful,
self,
and pure.
Therefore, it is called nonexistent.
The combination of existence and nonexistence
is precisely the Middle Way.
Therefore, the Buddha says that the Buddha nature of sentient beings is neither existent nor nonexistent.
“Good man!
If someone asks whether a seed
possesses fruit or not,
one should definitively answer:
both existent and nonexistent.
Why is this?
Apart from the seed, the fruit cannot be produced,
therefore it is called existent.
The seed has not yet sprouted,
therefore it is called nonexistent.
Because of this meaning,
it is both existent and nonexistent.
Why is this?
The time periods are different,
but the essence is one.
The Buddha nature of sentient beings is also like this.
If one were to say that there is a separate Buddha nature within sentient beings,
this statement is incorrect.
Why is this?
Sentient beings are precisely the Buddha nature,
and the Buddha nature is precisely sentient beings.
It is merely due to the difference in time
that there is purity and impurity.
Good man!
If someone asks whether the seed can produce fruit,
or whether the fruit can produce the seed,
one should definitively answer:
both produced and not produced.
“World Honored One (Shìzūn)!
Regarding what people commonly say,
that butter (là) is present in milk (rǔ)—
what is the meaning of this statement?
"Good man!
If someone says that curds are present inside milk,
this is called adherence (zhízhuó).
If one says there are no curds,
this is called falsehood (xūwàng).
Separated from these two extremes,
one should definitively say,
there is both existence and non-existence.
Why is it called existence?
Curds are produced from milk.
The cause is precisely milk,
and the effect is precisely curds.
This is called existence.
How is it called non-existence?
The color and flavor are mutually distinct;
the usage (consumption) is dissimilar.
Milk is consumed for heat illnesses,
and curds are consumed for cold illnesses.
Milk produces cold illnesses,
and curds produce heat illnesses.
Good man!
If one says that the nature of curds (làoxìng) is present inside milk,
then milk would be identical to curds,
and curds would be identical to milk,
because their nature is one.
For what reason,
does milk appear first,
and curds not appear first?
If there is a reason,
why do all worldly people not speak of it?
If there is no reason,
why do curds not appear first?
If curds do not appear first,
who established the sequence—milk,
curds,
fresh butter (shēngsū),
cooked butter (shúsū),
and clarified butter (tíhú)?
Therefore, one knows that curds,
were previously non-existent but now exist.
If they were previously non-existent but now exist,
this is the Dharma of impermanence (wúcháng fă).
Good man!
If someone says,
milk possesses the nature of curds (làoxìng),
and is thus able to produce curds,
but water lacks the nature of curds (làoxìng),
and therefore does not produce curds,
this assertion is incorrect.
Why is this?
Water and grass also possess the nature of milk and curds.
What is the reason for this?
Due to water and grass,
milk and curds are produced.
If one says that inside milk,
the nature of curds (làoxìng) is definitively present,
but water and grass lack it,
this is called falsehood (xūwàng).
Why is this?
Because the mind is not equal (or consistent/impartial),
therefore it is called falsehood.
Good man!
If one says that curds are definitively present in milk,
then milk nature (rǔxìng) should also be definitively present in curds.
For what reason,
do curds emerge from milk,
but milk does not emerge from curds?
If there is no reason,
you should know that these curds were originally non-existent but now exist.
Therefore, the wise person should say that inside milk there is neither the nature of curds (làoxìng)
nor the non-existence of the nature of curds (làoxìng).
Good man!
Therefore, the Tathāgata (Rúlái) speaks thus in this Sūtra (jīng):
'All sentient beings definitively possess Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),'
this is called adherence (clinging).
'If they lack Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),'
this is called falsehood (xūwàng).
The wise person should say that the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) of sentient beings is both existent and non-existent.
"Good man!
The harmonization of four conditions,
produces visual consciousness (yǎnshì).
What are the four?
The eye (yǎn),
the form (sè),
the light (míng),
and the desire (yù).
The nature of this visual consciousness (yǎnshìxìng),
is neither the eye (yǎn),
nor the form (sè),
nor the light (míng),
nor the desire (yù).
Because it arises from harmonization,
it consequently comes into being.
Such visual consciousness,
was originally non-existent but now exists,
and having existed, returns to non-existence.
Therefore, you should know that there is no fundamental nature (běnxìng).
The nature of curds (làoxìng) in milk is also like this.
If someone says,
water lacks the nature of curds (làoxìng),
and therefore does not produce curds,
thus the nature of curds (làoxìng) is definitively present in milk.
This assertion is incorrect.
Why is this?
Good man!
All dharmas (zhūfă) have distinct causes,
and distinct effects.
Also, it is not the case that a single cause produces all effects,
nor that all effects arise from a single cause.
Good man!
Just as visual consciousness (yǎnshì) is produced
from the four conditions,
it cannot furthermore be said that auditory consciousness (ěrshì) should be produced from these four conditions.
Good man!
Separated from skillful means (fāngbiàn),
the production of curds (lào) from milk,
or the production of fresh butter (shēngsū) from curds,
cannot occur.
Skillful means (fāngbiàn) are essential.
Good man!
The wise person must not see that curds (lào) are obtained from milk without skillful means (fāngbiàn),
and thus presume that fresh butter (shēngsū) must also be obtained without skillful means (fāngbiàn).
Good man!
Therefore, I speak in this Sūtra (jīng),
'Dharmas exist because of production (yīnshēng),
and dharmas are non-existent because of cessation (yīnmiè).'
Good man!
Just as salt, which is inherently salty (xián),
is able to make things that are not salty become salty.
If non-salty things initially possessed a salty nature (xiánxìng),
why would worldly people still seek salt?
If it was previously non-existent,
then you should know it was previously non-existent but now exists.
It becomes salty due to other conditions (yuán),
and thus obtains saltiness.
If one says that all non-salty things entirely possess a salty nature (xiánxìng),
but it is subtle and therefore unknown,
and that due to this subtle nature,
salt is able to make it salty.
If it fundamentally lacked that nature (xìng),
even if there were salt,
it could not make it salty.
For example, a seed inherently possesses the Four Great Elements (sìdà),
which rely on external Four Great Elements (sìdà),
in order to grow into a sprout (yá),
stem (jīng),
branch (zhī),
and leaf (yè).
If the nature of salt (yánxìng) is also like this,
this assertion is incorrect.
Why is this?
If non-salty objects
initially possess a salty nature (xiánxìng),
then salt should also possess a subtle non-salty nature (bùxiánxìng).
If this salt possessed these two natures,
for what reason,
when separated from non-salty objects,
cannot it be used alone?
Therefore, know that salt fundamentally lacks these two natures.
Like salt,
all non-salty objects are also like this.
If one says that the power of the external Four Great Elements (sì dà zhǒng) can increase the internal Four Great Elements (sìdà),
this assertion is incorrect.
Why is this?
Because it follows the order of instruction (or succession).
Curds (lào) cannot be obtained from milk without skillful means (fāngbiàn),
nor fresh butter (shēngsū) [from curds],
and similarly, all dharmas (zhūfă),
are not obtained without skillful means (fāngbiàn).
The Four Great Elements (sìdà) are also like this.
If one speaks of the external Four Great Elements (sìdà) increasing the internal Four Great Elements (sìdà),
we do not see the internal Four Great Elements (sìdà) increasing the external Four Great Elements (sìdà).
For example, the Shīlìshā (尸利沙) fruit initially lacks form and substance,
but when the Mǎo Xīng (昴星) constellation is seen, the fruit is produced,
and reaches a length of five inches.
Such a fruit,
truly does not increase due to external Four Great Elements (sìdà) [alone].
"Shàn Nánzǐ,
