regarding the Twelvefold Canon (*Shí'èr Bù Jīng*) that I preach,
sometimes it is preached according to my own intent,
sometimes it is preached according to the intent of others,
and sometimes it is preached according to the intent of both myself and others.
What is called preaching according to my own intent?
For example, five hundred Bhikṣus asked Shèlìfú:
'Great Virtuous One!
The cause of the body preached by the Buddha—
what is it?'
Shèlìfú said:
'Venerable Ones!
You have all attained genuine liberation,
and should know this yourselves.
Why do you ask such a question now?'
A Bhikṣu said:
'Great Virtuous One!
Before I attained genuine liberation,
I intended that ignorance (*wúmíng*) was the cause of the body,
and contemplating this, I attained the Arhat status (*Āluóhànguǒ*).'
Another said:
'Great Virtuous One!
Before I attained genuine liberation,
I believed that craving (*ài*) and ignorance were the cause of the body,
and contemplating this, I attained the Arhat status (*Āluóhànguǒ*).'
Still others said:
'Formations (*xíng*),
consciousness (*shì*),
name (*míng*),
form (*sè*),
six entrances (*liùrù*),
contact (*chù*),
feeling (*shòu*),
craving (*ài*),
grasping (*qǔ*),
existence (*yǒu*),
birth (*shēng*),
food, and the five desires,
are the cause of the body.'
Thereupon, the five hundred Bhikṣus,
having each stated their own understanding,
went together to the Buddha's presence,
bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated three times to the right,
and after completing their respects,
sat down on one side,
and each reported to the Buddha
the meaning of their individual understanding as stated above.
Shèlìfú addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!
Among these various people,
whose preaching is correct?
Whose is incorrect?'
The Buddha told Shèlìfú:
'Excellent,
excellent!
Not one Bhikṣu has preached incorrectly.'
Shèlìfú said:
'World-Honored One!
What is the Buddha's meaning?'
The Buddha said:
'Shèlìfú!
When I preach for the sentient beings of the desire realm, I say
that parents are the cause of the body.
Scriptures such as these
are called preaching according to my own intent.
'What is called preaching according to the intent of others?
For example, when the Elder Bāzhàluó (*Bāzhàluó Zhǎngzhě*),
came to me
and spoke thus:
'Qú Tán!
Do you understand illusion (*huàn*) or not?
If you understand illusion,
then you are a great illusionist.
If you do not understand it,
then you are not Omniscient.'
I replied:
'Elder!
Is a person who knows illusion
called an illusionist?'
The Elder said:
'Excellent,
excellent!
A person who knows illusion is an illusionist.'
The Buddha said:
'Elder!
King Bōsīnì Wáng of the Shèwèi Kingdom
has a Caṇḍāla (*Zhāntuóluó*)
named Qì Xū.
Do you know him or not?'
The Elder replied:
'Qú Tán!
I have known him for a long time.'
The Buddha said:
'Since you have known him for a long time,
can you therefore be a Caṇḍāla (*Zhāntuóluó*)?'
The Elder said:
'Qú Tán!
Although I know that person is a Caṇḍāla,
yet my own body is not a Caṇḍāla.'
The Buddha said:
'Elder!
You have grasped this principle:
knowing a Caṇḍāla,
yet not being a Caṇḍāla.
Why then can I not know illusion and yet not be an illusionist?
Elder!
I truly know illusion,
know the illusionist,
know the retribution of illusion,
and know the techniques of illusion.
I know killing,
know the killer,
know the retribution of killing,
and know the liberation from killing.
Likewise, I know wrong views,
know the person with wrong views,
know the retribution of wrong views,
and know the liberation from wrong views.
Elder!
If one says that a person who is not an illusionist is an illusionist,
or says that a person without wrong views is a person with wrong views,
one incurs immeasurable sin.'
The Elder said:
'Qú Tán!
As you have said,
I have incurred a great sin.
Everything I currently possess
I will offer to you,
hoping that King Bōsīnì Wáng does not know of this matter concerning me.'
The Buddha said:
'Elder!
The cause of this sin
will not necessarily result in the loss of wealth,
but it will instead cause you to fall into the Three Evil Paths (*Sān Èdào*).'
At that moment, the Elder,
hearing the name of the evil paths,
felt great terror in his heart,
and addressed the Buddha, saying:
'Holy One!
I have now lost my mind and incurred a great sin.
As the Holy One is Omniscient now,
you ought to understand how one obtains liberation.
How shall I obtain release from hell,
hungry ghosts,
and beasts?'
Thereupon, I preached the Four Noble Truths (*Sì Zhēndì*) for him,
and having heard them, the Elder attained the Sotāpanna status (*Xūtuóhuánguǒ*).
He felt shame and remorse in his heart,
and confessed to the Buddha:
'I was originally foolish.
The Buddha is not an illusionist,
yet I called him one.
From this day forward,
I take refuge in the Three Jewels (*Sānbǎo*).'
The Buddha said:
'Excellent,
excellent!
Elder!
This is called preaching according to the intent of others.
'What is called preaching according to the intent of both myself and others?
For example, when I preach:
If all the wise people of the world say something exists,
I also say it exists;
if the wise say something does not exist,
I also say it does not exist.
If the wise people of the world say that the pleasure of the five desires exists and is
impermanent (*wúcháng*),
suffering (*kǔ*),
selfless (*wúwǒ*),
and can be severed,
I also say it exists.
If the wise people of the world say that the pleasure of the five desires exists and is
permanent (*cháng*),
self (*wǒ*),
and pure (*jìng*),
there is no such principle.
I also say that there is no such principle.
This is called preaching according to the intent of both myself and others.
'Shàn Nánzǐ!
As I have preached, Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages (*Shízhù Púsà*) have a limited view of Buddha-nature (*Fóxìng*).
This is called preaching according to the intent of others.
Why is it called a limited view?
Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages attain the Śūraṅgama (*Shǒuléngyán*) and three thousand other Dharma gates of Samādhi (*sānmèi*).
Therefore, they clearly
know for themselves that they will attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (*Ānòuduōluósānmiǎosānpútí*),
but they do not see that all sentient beings will definitely attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
For this reason, I say that Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages have a limited view of Buddha-nature.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
I constantly proclaim that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature (*Fóxìng*).
This is called preaching according to my own intent.
All sentient beings are neither cut off
nor extinguished until they attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
This is called preaching according to my own intent.
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature,
but because of the covering of afflictions (*fánnǎo*), they cannot see it.
I preach thus,
and you preach likewise.
This is called preaching according to the intent of both myself and others.'
"Shànnánzǐ!
The Rúlái sometimes, for the sake of one Dharma,
speaks of immeasurable Dharmas.
Just as it is said in the Sūtras:
All pure conduct (Fànxíng) depends on a good spiritual friend (shànzhīshí).
Although the causes
of all pure conduct
are immeasurable, speaking of the shànzhīshí
already encompasses them entirely.
Just as I have said:
All evil conduct
takes wrong views (xiéjiàn) as its cause.
Although the causes
of all evil conduct
are immeasurable, if wrong views (xiéjiàn) are mentioned,
they are already encompassed entirely.
Or, it is said that Anòu duō luó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí
takes faith (xìnxīn) as its cause;
although the causes of this Pútí
are also immeasurable,
if faith is mentioned,
they are already encompassed entirely.
Shànnánzǐ!
Although the Rúlái speaks of immeasurable Dharmas as Fóxìng (Buddha nature),
yet they do not depart from the aggregates (yīn), entrances (rù), and realms (jiè).
"Shànnánzǐ!
The Rúlái, when speaking the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings,
uses seven types of speech:
First, causal speech (yīnyǔ);
second, resultant speech (guǒyǔ);
third, causal-resultant speech (yīnguǒyǔ);
fourth, metaphorical speech (yùyǔ);
fifth, speech that should not be spoken (bù yìng shuō yǔ);
sixth, worldly conventional speech (shì liú bù yǔ);
seventh, intentional speech (rúyìyǔ).
"What is called causal speech?
It is speaking of the future result
based on the present cause,
just as I have said:
Shànnánzǐ!
If you see a sentient being
who delights in killing, or delights in practicing wrong views (xiéjiàn),
you should regard this person immediately as a denizen of hell (dìyù rén).
Shànnánzǐ!
If there is a sentient being
who does not delight in killing or in wrong views (xiéjiàn),
you should regard this person immediately as a celestial being (tiānrén).
This is called causal speech.
"What is resultant speech?
It is speaking of the past cause based on the present result,
just as it is said in the Sūtras:
Shànnánzǐ!
If you see a poor sentient being,
ugly in appearance,
and lacking autonomy,
you should know that this person definitely [in the past] had broken precepts (pòjiè),
a jealous mind (dùxīn),
a hateful mind (chēnxīn),
and a mind lacking shame and remorse (wú cánkuì xīn).
If you see a sentient being who is rich and wealthy,
whose faculties are complete,
and who is powerful and autonomous,
you should know that this person definitely [in the past] possessed precepts (jiè),
giving (shī),
diligence (jīngqín),
and shame and remorse (cánkuì),
without jealousy or hatred.
This is called resultant speech.
"What is causal-resultant speech?
Just as it is said in the Sūtras:
Shànnánzǐ!
The present sensory contacts (liù rù chù) of sentient beings are causes.
This is called the result of past karma (yè guǒ).
The Rúlái also calls this karma,
and based on this karma as cause and condition, the future result is obtained.
This is called causal-resultant speech.
"What is metaphorical speech?
For example, speaking of the Lion King
is a metaphor for my body.
The Great Elephant King,
the Great Dragon King,
the Bōlìzhìduōluó Tree,
the Heap of Seven Treasures,
the Great Ocean,
Mount Xūmí,
the Great Earth,
the Great Rain,
the Boatman,
the Guide,
the Tamer of Men (Tiáoyù Zhàngfū),
the Strongman (Lìshì),
the Ox King,
the Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén),
the Śramaṇa (Shāmén),
the Great City,
the Tāluó Tree —
Sūtras using such metaphors
are called metaphorical speech.
"What is speech that should not be spoken (Bù yìng yǔ)?
In my Sūtras, I have stated:
Heaven and Earth may merge,
but rivers will not flow into the ocean.
This is like speaking to King Bōsī nì about the mountains coming from the four directions.
Or like speaking to the female lay devotee Lùmǔ Yōupóyí, saying:
If the Shāluó Tree were able to receive the Eight Precepts,
it would receive the bliss of humans and heaven (rén tiān zhī lè).
For example, saying that the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes (shí zhù Púsà) have regressing minds (tuì zhuǎn xīn),
but not saying that the Rúlái has two types of speech.
I would rather say that a stream-enterer (Xūtuóhuán rén) falls into the three evil paths (sān è dào)
than say that the Ten Abodes (shí zhù) have regressing minds.
This is called speech that should not be spoken.
"What is worldly conventional speech (Shì liú bù yǔ)?
For example, what the Buddha speaks concerning
male and female,
large and small,
going and coming,
sitting and lying down,
carts and mounts,
houses and dwellings,
jars and clothes,
sentient beings,
permanence, joy, self, and purity (cháng lè wǒ jìng),
armies and forests,
cities and towns,
monastic illusions (sēng huàn),
assembly and dispersion.
This is called worldly conventional speech.
"What is intentional speech (Rúyìyǔ)?
For example, when I reprimand those who violate the precepts,
to make them reproach themselves
and guard and uphold the prohibitive precepts.
For example, when I praise the stream-enterers (Xūtuóhuán rén),
it is to make ordinary people (fánfū)
generate virtuous minds.
Praising the Púsà
is to cause sentient beings to arouse the Pútí mind (Pútíxīn).
Speaking of all the suffering and distress of the three evil paths (sān è dào)
is to cause them to cultivate various good Dharmas.
Speaking of all things burning
is only for the sake of all conditioned Dharmas (yǒuwéi fǎ),
and saying ‘no-self’ (wúwǒ) is also like this.
Saying that all sentient beings entirely possess Fóxìng (Buddha nature)
is to cause all to avoid negligence.
This is called intentional speech."
“‘Good man!
The Táthāgata further possesses the speech that follows his own intention (suízìyì yǔ).
The Táthāgata’s Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) can be of two kinds:
the first is existence (yǒu),
the second is non-existence (wú).
What is existence?
It is what is called the Thirty-two Marks (Sānshí’èr Xiàng),
the Eighty Excellent Characteristics (Bāshí Zhǒng Hǎo),
the Ten Powers (Shílì),
the Four Fearlessnesses (Sì Wúsuǒwèi),
the Three Stations of Mindfulness (Sān Niànchù),
Great Loving-kindness and Great Compassion (Dàcí Dàbēi),
immeasurable samādhis such as the Shǒuléngyán,
immeasurable samādhis such as the Jīngāng (Vajra),
immeasurable samādhis such as skillful means (fāngbiàn),
and immeasurable samādhis such as the seals of the Five Wisdoms (Wǔ Zhì Yìn).
This is called existence (yǒu).
What is non-existence (wú)?
It is what is called the Táthāgata’s
past good,
unwholesome,
and indeterminate karmic causes, results, and retributions,
afflictions (fánnǎo),
the Five Aggregates (Wǔ Yīn),
and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí’èr Yīnyuán).
This is called non-existence (wú).
Good man!
Just as there are existence
and non-existence,
wholesome
and unwholesome,
defiled (yǒulòu)
and undefiled (wúlòu),
mundane (shìjiān)
and non-mundane (fēishìjiān),
noble (shèng)
and non-noble (fēishèng),
conditioned (yǒuwéi)
and unconditioned (wúwéi),
real (shí)
and unreal (bùshí),
still (jíjìng)
and non-still (fēijíjìng),
contentious (zhēng)
and non-contentious (fēizhēng),
realm (jiè)
and non-realm (fēijiè),
affliction (fánnǎo)
and non-affliction (fēifánnǎo),
grasping (qǔ)
and non-grasping (fēiqǔ),
receiving prophecy (shòujì)
and not receiving prophecy (fēishòujì),
having
and not having,
the three periods of time (sānshì)
and non-three periods of time (fēisānshì),
time (shí)
and non-time (fēishí),
permanence (cháng)
and impermanence (wúcháng),
self (wǒ)
and non-self (wúwǒ),
pleasure (lè)
and non-pleasure (wúlè),
purity (jìng)
and non-purity (wújìng),
form, sensation, perception, volition, and consciousness (sè shòu xiǎng xíng shí)
and non-form, sensation, perception, volition, and consciousness (fēisè shòu xiǎng xíng shí),
inner sense-fields (nèirù)
and non-inner sense-fields (fēinèirù),
outer sense-fields (wàirù)
and non-outer sense-fields (fēiwàirù),
the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (shí’èr yīnyuán)
and non-Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (fēishí’èr yīnyuán)—
this is how the Táthāgata’s Buddha-nature is spoken of in terms of existence and non-existence.
Even regarding the existence and non-existence of the Buddha-nature in an Icchántika (Yīchǎntí),
it is also like this.
“Good man!
Although I say that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature,
sentient beings do not understand the Táthāgata’s speech that follows his own intention in such cases.
Good man!
Such speech
cannot be understood even by Bodhisattvas of a later incarnation,
much less by the Two Vehicles (Èr Chéng)
or other Bodhisattvas?
Good man!
Once, when I was on Mount Gīdhrakūṭa (Qíshéqū Shān),
I discussed mundane truth (shìdì) with the Bodhisattva Mílè.
Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) and five hundred listeners (shēngwén)
did not recognize or understand this matter at all,
how much less the ultimate truth (dìyīyì dì) that transcends the world?
“Good man!
Sometimes the Buddha-nature exists in an Icchántika,
but not in a person with wholesome roots (shàngēnrén).
Sometimes the Buddha-nature exists in a person with wholesome roots,
but not in an Icchántika.
Sometimes the Buddha-nature
exists in both types of people.
Sometimes the Buddha-nature
exists in neither type of person.
Good man!
If my disciples understand the meaning of these four statements (sìjù yì),
they should not contend, saying,
‘The Icchántika definitely possesses the Buddha-nature,’
or ‘definitely does not possess the Buddha-nature.’
To say that all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature
is called the Táthāgata’s speech that follows his own intention.
When the Táthāgata speaks such speech that follows his own intention,
how can sentient beings uniformly interpret it [as absolute]?
“Good man!
For example, in the Ganges River (Hénghé) there are seven kinds of beings:
The first constantly sinks;
the second briefly emerges and then sinks again;
the third emerges and then stays put;
the fourth emerges and surveys the four directions;
the fifth surveys and then proceeds;
the sixth proceeds and then stops again;
and the seventh travels both by water and by land.
Those referred to as constantly sinking
are the large fish (dàyú),
which, having received great evil karma,
are heavy and dwell deep,
and therefore constantly sink.
Those that briefly emerge and then sink again
are such large fish
who, due to receiving evil karma,
are heavy but dwell in shallow water.
They briefly see the light,
and because of the light, they emerge,
but due to their weight, they sink again.
Those that emerge and stay put
are the Dímí (Chímí) fish,
whose bodies are in shallow water
and who enjoy seeing the light,
so they emerge and stay put.
Those that survey the directions
are the Gě (E) fish,
which, in search of food,
survey the four directions,
and are therefore said to survey the directions.
Those that survey and then proceed
are the Gě fish
that see something far away,
deem it edible,
and swiftly proceed towards it,
thus they survey and then proceed.
Those that proceed and then stop again
are these fish who, having reached [the spot]
and obtained something edible,
then stop,
thus they proceed and then stop again.
Those that travel both by water and by land
are the turtles (guī).
"Good man!
This subtle and profound Great Nièpán River,
within it also has seven kinds of sentient beings,
from the first perpetually sinking even to the seventh,
sometimes entering, sometimes exiting.
Regarding what is meant by 'sinking' (mò):
Some people, upon hearing this Great Nièpán Sūtra,
that the Rúlái is eternal,
without change or alteration,
possessing permanence (cháng), bliss (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng),
and will ultimately not enter (annihilative) Nièpán;
that all sentient beings entirely possess the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng),
that an Icchantika (Yīchǎntí rén), who slanders the Fāngděng Sūtras, commits the Five Heinous Crimes (Wǔ Nì Zuì), and violates the Four Grave Prohibitions (Sì Zhòng Jìn),
will certainly achieve the Way of Pútí;
that a Xūtuóhuán rén (Śrotāpanna),
a Sītuóhán rén (Sakṛdāgāmin),
an Ānàhán rén (Anāgāmin),
an Āluóhàn rén (Arhat),
and a Pìzhīfó (Pratyekabuddha) will certainly achieve Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí (Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi).
Having heard these words,
they generate lack of faith,
and immediately conceive such thoughts,
having conceived such thoughts,
they then speak these words:
'This Nièpán text
is actually an external path (wàidào) writing,
it is not a Buddhist Sūtra.'
At that time, this person moves far away from good friends,
does not hear the True Dharma,
although they sometimes manage to hear it,
they cannot contemplate it,
although they contemplate it,
they do not contemplate what is good.
Because they do not contemplate the good,
they abide by evil dharmas.
Those who abide by evil dharmas
have six characteristics:
First, evil (è);
second, absence of good (wú shàn);
third, defiling the dharma (wū fǎ);
fourth, increasing existence (zēng yǒu);
fifth, affliction and heat (nǎo rè);
and sixth, receiving evil retribution (shòu è guǒ).
This is called sinking (mò).
Why is it called sinking?
Because there is no wholesome mind,
because they constantly practice evil,
and because they do not cultivate counteracting remedies.
This is called sinking.
Regarding what is meant by evil (è):
Because the holy ones rebuke it,
because the mind generates terror and dread,
because good people keep far away from it,
and because it does not benefit sentient beings.
This is called evil.
Regarding the absence of good (wú shàn):
Because it can give rise to immeasurable evil karmic retribution,
because it is constantly ensnared by ignorance,
because it delights in associating with wicked people as companions,
because there are no skillful means for cultivating good,
and because the mind is inverted and constantly mistaken.
This is called the absence of good.
Regarding defiling the dharma (wū fǎ):
Because one constantly defiles the body and mouth,
because one defiles pure sentient beings,
because one increases unwholesome karma,
and because one distances oneself from wholesome dharmas.
This is called defiling the dharma.
Regarding increasing existence (zēng yǒu):
The dharmas practiced by the three types of people mentioned above,
can increase the [realms of] earth hells (dìyù),
animals,
and hungry ghosts.
They cannot cultivate the dharma of liberation.
The karma of body,
mouth,
and mind
does not weary of the various existences.
This is called increasing existence.
Regarding affliction and heat (nǎo rè):
This person fully practices the four preceding matters,
which causes the two matters of body
and mind to become afflicted and heated.
To be far from stillness and tranquility
is called heat (rè).
Receiving the retribution of the hells is therefore called heat.
Burning all sentient beings is therefore called heat.
Burning all wholesome dharmas is therefore called heat.
Good man!
Faith
is coolness.
This person does not possess it;
therefore, it is called heat.
Regarding receiving evil retribution (shòu è guǒ):
This person fully practices the five preceding matters,
and after death falls into the hells,
hungry ghosts,
or animals.
Good man!
There are three evil matters that are also called evil retribution:
First, the evil of vexations (fánnǎo è);
second, the evil of karma (yè è);
third, the evil of recompense (bào è).
This is called receiving evil karmic retribution.
Good man!
This person fully possesses the six preceding matters,
is able to sever the roots of goodness,
commit the Five Heinous Crimes,
is able to violate the Four Grave Prohibitions,
is able to slander the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo),
misappropriate Sangha property,
and is able to commit various kinds of unlawful deeds.
Because of these causes and conditions,
they sink and drown in Ābǐ Dìyù (Avīci Hell).
The body they receive is eighty-four thousand yóuxún (yojanas) in extent and width.
Because the karma of this person's body,
mouth,
and mind is heavy,
they cannot escape.
Why is this?
Because their mind cannot give rise to wholesome dharmas.
Although immeasurable Buddhas appear in the world,
they neither hear nor see them.
Therefore, they are called perpetually sinking (cháng mò),
like a large fish in the Hénghé (Ganges) River.
"Good man!
Although I also state that Icchantikas (Yīchǎntí) and others
are called perpetually sinking.
There are further [cases of] perpetually sinking,
who are not Icchantikas.
Who are they?
For example, people who, for the sake of [future] existence,
cultivate giving (shī),
precepts (jiè),
and wholesomeness (shàn).
This is called perpetually sinking.
Good man!
There are four wholesome deeds that result in evil retribution.
What are these four?
First, reciting Sūtras solely to surpass others;
second, upholding prohibitions and precepts solely for the sake of profit and gain;
third, practicing giving (bùshī) solely to become subservient to others;
fourth, binding the mind and contemplating solely for the sake of the Realm of Neither Thought Nor Non-thought (Fēixiǎng Fēifēixiǎng Chǔ).
These four wholesome deeds attain evil karmic retribution.
If a person cultivates these four matters,
this is called sinking and then returning out,
exiting and then returning to sink.
Why is it called sinking?
Because they delight in the Three Realms of Existence (Sān Yǒu).
Why is it called exiting?
Because they see the light.
The light is hearing the precepts,
giving,
and concentration.
Why do they return to sinking?
Because they increase false views and generate arrogance.
Therefore, I have spoken a verse in the Sūtra:
"O good man!
Just like that great fish,
because it saw the light,
it was momentarily able to get out of the water.
Because its body was heavy,
it sank back down again.
The two people mentioned above are also like this.
O good man!
Furthermore, there are people who delight in and are attached to the Three Realms (Sānyǒu);
this is called sinking (mò).
When they hear the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dànièpán Jīng) and generate faith,
this is called rising (chū).
For what reason is it called rising?
Having heard this sūtra,
they move far away from evil *dharmas* (fǎ),
and cultivate good *dharmas* (shànfǎ);
this is called rising.
Although this person has faith,
it is also not complete (jùzú).
For what reason is the faith incomplete?
Although this person believes in the Mahāparinirvāṇa (Dàbān Nièpán),
that is, permanence (cháng), bliss (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng),
they say that the Tathāgata’s (Rúlái) body is impermanent (wúcháng),
non-self (wúwǒ),
non-bliss (wúlè),
and impure (wújìng).
The Tathāgata thus has two kinds of Nirvāṇa (Nièpán):
one is conditioned (yǒuwéi),
and the second is unconditioned (wúwéi).
The conditioned Nirvāṇa lacks permanence, bliss, self, and purity,
while the unconditioned Nirvāṇa possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Although they believe that the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) exists in sentient beings,
[they believe] it is not necessarily possessed by all of them;
therefore, this is called incomplete faith.
O good man!
There are two kinds of faith:
the first is believing (xìn),
and the second is seeking (qiú).
Although a person such as this has faith,
they cannot investigate and seek;
therefore, this is called incomplete faith.
Furthermore, there are two [other types] of faith:
one arises from hearing (wén),
and the second arises from deliberation (sī).
The faith of this person arises from hearing,
and does not arise from deliberation;
therefore, this is called incomplete faith.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
one is believing that the path (dào) exists,
and the second is believing in those who have attained it (dédào zhě).
The faith of this person only believes that the path exists,
but does not believe in the existence of people who have attained the path;
therefore, this is called incomplete faith.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
one is believing the orthodox (zhèng),
and the second is believing the heterodox (xié).
Saying that cause and effect (yīnguǒ) exist,
and that the Buddha (Fó), Dharma (Fǎ), and Saṅgha (Sēng) exist,
this is called believing the orthodox.
Saying that cause and effect do not exist,
that the nature of the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo) is different [from each other],
believing various heterodox teachings,
such as those of Pūránnà (Pūraṇa) and others,
this is called believing the heterodox.
Although this person believes in the Buddha,
the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha,
they do not believe that the Three Jewels share the same essence and characteristics (xìngxiàng).
Although they believe in cause and effect,
they do not believe in those who have attained [the path].
Therefore, this is called incomplete faith.
Since this person achieves incomplete faith,
the precepts (jìnjiè) they undertake are also incomplete.
For what reason is it called incomplete?
Because the cause (yīn) is incomplete,
the precepts obtained are also incomplete.
"Furthermore, for what reason is it called incomplete?
There are two kinds of precepts (jiè):
one is the precept of comportment (wēiyí jiè),
and the second is the precept following the precepts (cóngjiè jiè).
This person only possesses the precepts of comportment and the like,
but does not possess the precept following the precepts;
therefore, this is called incomplete precepts.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
one is positive precepts (zuò jiè),
and the second is non-positive precepts (wúzuò jiè).
This person only possesses positive precepts,
but does not possess non-positive precepts;
therefore, this is called incomplete precepts.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
one is obtaining right livelihood (zhèngmìng) through body and speech,
and the second is not obtaining right livelihood through body and speech.
Although this person [uses] body and speech,
they do not obtain right livelihood;
therefore, this is called incomplete precepts.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
one is seeking precepts (qiú jiè),
and the second is relinquishing precepts (shě jiè).
This person only possesses the precepts associated with seeking existence (qiúyǒu),
but does not attain the relinquishing precepts;
therefore, this is called incomplete precepts.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
one is following existence (suíyǒu),
and the second is following the path (suídào).
This person only possesses the precepts following existence,
but does not possess [the precepts] following the path;
therefore, this is called incomplete precepts.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
one is good precepts (shàn jiè),
and the second is evil precepts (è jiè).
Bodily, verbal, and mental goodness is called good precepts,
ox precepts (niú jiè) and dog precepts (gǒu jiè) are called evil precepts.
This person deeply believes that both these two kinds of precepts result in good fruit;
therefore, this is called incomplete precepts.
"Since this person does not possess these two matters—faith and precepts—
the much hearing (duōwén) they cultivate is also incomplete.
How is it called incomplete hearing?
Of the twelve divisions of sūtras (shí'èr bù jīng) spoken by the Tathāgata,
they only believe six divisions,
and do not believe the other six divisions;
therefore, this is called incomplete hearing.
Although they undertake and maintain these six divisions of sūtras,
they cannot read, recite, or explain them for others,
achieving no benefit;
therefore, this is called incomplete hearing.
Furthermore, having received these six divisions of sūtras,
they receive, read, recite, and explain them for the sake of debate (lùnyì),
for the sake of defeating others,
for the sake of profit and offerings (lìyǎng),
or for the sake of various existences (zhūyǒu);
[they] receive, maintain, read, recite, and explain,
therefore, this is called incomplete hearing.
O good man!
In the sūtras, I have spoken of complete hearing.
How is it complete?
If there is a *bhikṣu* (bǐqiū) whose body,
speech,
and mind are good,
and who can first make offerings to the *Upādhyāya* (Héshàng),
various masters (shī),
and virtuous people.
These masters and others,
towards this person,
generate a mind of affection and remembrance,
and for this reason,
instruct them in the Dharma (fǎ).
This person sincerely accepts, maintains, recites, and practices [it].
Having maintained, recited, and practiced [it], they obtain wisdom (zhìhuì).
Having obtained wisdom, they are able to reflect well and abide in accordance with the Dharma.
Having reflected well, they attain the correct meaning (zhèngyì).
Having attained the correct meaning, their body and mind become tranquil (jíjìng).
When the body and mind are tranquil, a joyful mind (xǐxīn) arises.
Due to the joyful mind, the mind obtains concentration (dìng).
Because they obtain concentration, they gain right knowledge and insight (zhèng zhījiàn).
Having gained right knowledge and insight, their mind generates revulsion and remorse regarding various existences.
Because of their remorse regarding existences, they are able to attain liberation (jiětuō).
This person does not possess such qualities;
therefore, this is called incomplete hearing.
"Since this person does not possess these three matters,
their generosity (shī) is also incomplete.
Generosity has two kinds:
one is material giving (cáishī),
and the second is Dharma giving (fǎshī).
Although this person performs material giving,
it is for the sake of seeking existence (qiú yǒu);
although they perform Dharma giving,
it is also incomplete.
Why is this?
They conceal and do not fully speak [the teachings],
because they fear being surpassed by others;
therefore, this is called incomplete generosity.
Both material giving and Dharma giving each have two kinds:
one is noble (shèng),
and the second is non-noble (fēi shèng).
When the noble give,
they do not seek resulting retribution (guǒbào).
When the non-noble give,
they seek resulting retribution.
The Dharma giving of the noble is for the growth of the Dharma;
the Dharma giving of the non-noble is for the increase of various existences.
A person such as this,
performs material giving for the sake of increasing wealth,
and performs Dharma giving for the sake of increasing existence;
therefore, this is called incomplete generosity.
Furthermore, this person receives the six divisions of sūtras,
and supplies those whom they see receiving the Dharma,
but those who do not receive the Dharma they do not supply;
therefore, this is called incomplete generosity."
"If this person does not possess the four matters mentioned above,
the wisdom cultivated is also incomplete.
The nature of wisdom,
the nature is to distinguish (or differentiate).
This person cannot distinguish whether the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is permanent
or impermanent.
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) says in this Nirvāṇa Sūtra (Nièpán Jīng):
'The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is liberation (jiětuō),
liberation is the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is Nirvāṇa (nièpán),
Nirvāṇa (nièpán) is liberation (jiětuō),'
but this person cannot distinguish these meanings.
Pure Conduct (Fànxíng) is the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity (cíbēi xǐshě),
loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity (cíbēi xǐshě) is liberation (jiětuō),
liberation (jiětuō) is Nirvāṇa (nièpán),
Nirvāṇa (nièpán) is loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity (cíbēi xǐshě),
but this person cannot distinguish these meanings,
therefore it is called incomplete wisdom (zhì bù jùzú).
Furthermore, this person cannot distinguish the Buddha Nature (Fóxìng).
The Buddha Nature (Fóxìng) is the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is all the unshared dharmas (bù gòng zhī fǎ),
the unshared dharmas (bù gòng zhī fǎ) are liberation (jiětuō),
liberation (jiětuō) is Nirvāṇa (nièpán),
Nirvāṇa (nièpán) is the unshared dharmas (bù gòng zhī fǎ),
but this person cannot distinguish these meanings,
therefore it is called incomplete wisdom (zhì bù jùzú).
Furthermore, this person cannot distinguish the Four Noble Truths (Sì Dì): suffering (kǔ), accumulation (jí), cessation (miè), and the Way (dào).
Because they cannot distinguish the Four True Truths (Sì Zhēndì), they do not know the Noble Practice (shèng xíng).
Because they do not know the Noble Practice (shèng xíng), they do not know the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Because they do not know the Tathāgata (Rúlái), they do not know liberation (jiětuō).
Because they do not know liberation (jiětuō), they do not know Nirvāṇa (nièpán).
Therefore it is called incomplete wisdom (zhì bù jùzú).
"If this person does not possess these five matters,
there are two types:
first, increasing virtuous dharmas (zēng shàn fǎ);
second, increasing evil dharmas (zēng è fǎ).
What is meant by increasing evil dharmas (zēngzhǎng è fǎ)?
This person does not see their own incompleteness,
claims to be complete,
and develops attachment.
Among peers, they consider themselves superior,
and therefore draw near to evil friends (èyǒu) similar to themselves;
having drawn near,
they again hear incomplete doctrines (fǎ).
Hearing them, their minds rejoice,
their minds become stained with attachment,
they give rise to arrogance,
frequently engaging in negligence (fàngyì).
Because of negligence (fàngyì),
they draw close to laypeople,
and also enjoy hearing discussions of household matters,
moving away from the pure dharmas of those who have left home (chūjiā).
Due to these causes and conditions, they increase evil dharmas (zēngzhǎng è fǎ).
Because they increase evil dharmas,
in body (shēn),
speech (kǒu),
and mind (yì),
they commit impure karma (yè).
Because the Three Karmas (Sān Yè) are impure,
they increase [the path to] the hells (dìyù), animals (chùshēng), and hungry ghosts (ègǔi).
This is called 'briefly emerging and then sinking again.'
Who, among those who briefly emerge and then sink again,
are they within my Buddha Dharma (Fó Fǎ)?
Namely, Devadatta (Típó Dádūo),
Bhikṣu Gūqílí (Qújiālí),
Bhikṣu Wǎnshǒu,
Bhikṣu Shànxīng,
Bhikṣu Dīshè,
Bhikṣu Mǎnsù,
Bhikṣuṇī Cídì,
Bhikṣuṇī Kuàngyě,
Bhikṣuṇī Fāng,
Bhikṣuṇī Màn,
Elder Jìngjié,
Upāsaka Qiúyǒu,
Śākya (Shì) clan member Shèlè,
Elder Xiàng,
Upāsikā Míngchēng,
Upāsikā Guāngmíng,
Upāsikā Nántuó,
Upāsikā Jūn,
Upāsikā Líng.
People such as these,
are called 'briefly emerging and then sinking again.'
Just like a large fish,
seeing the light, emerges,
but because its body is heavy, it sinks.
"The second type of person
deeply recognizes and sees that their practice is incomplete.
Because it is incomplete, they seek to draw near to good friends (shànyǒu).
Having drawn near to good friends (shànyǒu), they joyfully inquire about what they have not heard.
Having heard it, they joyfully accept it.
Having accepted it, they joyfully reflect upon it well.
Having reflected upon it well, they are able to abide according to the Dharma (Rú Fǎ Zhù).
Because they abide according to the Dharma (Rú Fǎ Zhù), they increase virtuous dharmas (zēngzhǎng shàn fǎ).
Because they increase virtuous dharmas, they never sink again.
This is called 'abiding' (zhù).
Who are they within my Buddha Dharma (Fó Fǎ)?
Namely, Śāriputra (Shèlìfú),
Mahāmaudgalyāyana (Dà Mùjiànlián),
the five bhikṣus led by Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya (Ārě Jiāochénrú),
the five bhikṣus led by Yaśa (Yēshě),
Aniruddha (Ānú Lóutuó),
Kumāra Kāśyapa (Tóngzǐ Jiāshè),
Mahākāśyapa (Móhē Jiāshè),
Śilākāśyapa (Shílì Jiāshè),
Bhikṣuṇī Kṛśā Gautamī (Shòu Qú Tánmí),
Bhikṣuṇī Pāṭalīpuṣpa (Bōzhàluó Huā),
Bhikṣuṇī Shèng,
Bhikṣuṇī Shíyì,
Bhikṣuṇī Yì,
Bhikṣuṇī Bádà,
Bhikṣuṇī Jìng,
Bhikṣuṇī Bù Tuìzhuǎn,
King Bimbisāra (Pínbó Suōluó Wáng),
Elder Yùjiā,
Elder Sudatta (Xūdáduō),
Śākya (Shì) clan member Mó Nán,
Poor Sudatta (Pín Xūdáduō),
Elder Mongoose’s Son (Shǔláng Zhǎngzhě Zǐ),
Elder Míngchēng,
Elder Jùzú,
General Sīzǐ,
Elder Upāli (Yōubōlí),
Elder Dāo,
Upāsikā Wúwèi,
Upāsikā Shànzhù,
Upāsikā Àifǎ,
Upāsikā Yǒngjiàn,
Upāsikā Tiāndé,
Upāsikā Shànshēng,
Upāsikā Jùshēn,
Upāsikā Niú Dé,
Upāsikā Kuàngyě,
Upāsikā Móhēsīnà.
Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū),
Bhikṣuṇīs (Bǐqiūní),
Upāsakas (Yōupósè),
and Upāsikās (Yōupóyí) such as these,
are called 'abiding' (zhù).
What is meant by abiding (zhù)?
They constantly rejoice in observing the light of virtue (shàn guāngmíng).
For this reason, whether a Buddha appears in the world
or does not appear in the world,
people such as these will never commit evil.
This is called 'abiding' (zhù).
Just as the Tīmi fish (Dīmí yú) enjoys seeing the light
and does not sink or drown,
so too are these multitudes.
Therefore, I speak this verse in the sūtra (jīng):
"Good man!
When wisdom is incomplete,
there are five general matters.
When this person knows them,
they seek to draw near to good friends (shànyǒu).
Such a good friend (shànyǒu)
should observe this person's greed (tānyù),
hatred (chēnhuì),
delusion (yúchī),
and conceptual thought (sījué) —
which one is predominant?
If they know that this person has much greed (tānyù),
they should immediately teach them the method of impurity contemplation (bù jìng guān fǎ).
If they have much hatred (chēnhuì), teach them loving-kindness and compassion (cíbēi).
If they have much conceptual thought (sījué), instruct them to count breaths (shǔ xī).
If they have much attachment to self (zhuó wǒ), they should analyze the eighteen dhātus (shíbā jiè) for them.
Having heard this, the person sincerely accepts and retains it.
Having accepted and retained it sincerely, they practice according to the Dharma (rú fǎ xíng).
Having practiced according to the Dharma (rú fǎ xíng), they sequentially attain the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Sì Niànchù) regarding body, feelings, mind, and dharmas (shēn shòu xīn fǎ).
Having attained this contemplation, they sequentially further contemplate the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yīnyuán).
Having contemplated in this way, they next attain the warmth dharma (nuǎnfǎ).
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa (Jiāshè Púsà) said to the Buddha (Fó):
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
All sentient beings (zhòngshēng) possess the warmth dharma (nuǎnfǎ).
Why is this?
As the Buddha (Fó) has said,
when three dharmas combine,
they are called a sentient being (zhòngshēng):
first, longevity (shòu);
second, warmth (nuǎn);
third, consciousness (shì).
If we follow this meaning,
all sentient beings (zhòngshēng) should already possess warmth (nuǎn).
Why, then, does the Tathāgata (Rúlái) say that the warmth dharma (nuǎnfǎ) arises due to good friends (shànyǒu)?"
Fó says:
“Good man!
Regarding what you have asked,
concerning those who possess the Warming Dharmas (Nuǎnfǎ),
all sentient beings, even up to the Icchantika (Yīchǎntí), universally possess them.
However, the Nuǎnfǎ
which I am currently speaking of,
must be acquired through skillful means (fāngbiàn);
only then can they be obtained.
They were originally absent but are now present.
For this reason,
not all sentient beings possess them inherently beforehand.
Therefore, you should not now argue that all sentient beings universally possess the Nuǎnfǎ.
Good man!
These Nuǎnfǎ belong to the Form Realm (Sèjiè) Dharma,
they do not exist in the Desire Realm (Yùjiè).
If you claim that all sentient beings possess them,
then sentient beings in the Yùjiè should also universally possess them;
since they are absent in the Yùjiè,
you should know that not all [beings] necessarily possess them universally.
Good man!
Although they exist in the Sèjiè,
not everyone possesses them.
Why?
My disciples possess them,
but external practitioners (wàidào) do not.
For this reason,
not all sentient beings necessarily possess them universally.
Good man!
All external practitioners contemplate only the six practices (liù xíng),
but my disciples fully possess the sixteen practices (shíliù),
these sixteen practices,
not all sentient beings necessarily possess them universally.”
Jiāyè Púsà addressed the Fó, saying:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
Regarding the Nuǎnfǎ you speak of,
how are they named 'Warming'?
Are they warming by nature (zìxìng),
or are they warming due to something else?”
The Fó said:
“Good man!
These Nuǎnfǎ,
their intrinsic nature is warming (nuǎn);
they are not warming due to something else.”
Jiāyè Púsà said:
“Shìzūn!
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) previously stated
that Mǎshī and Mǎnsù do not possess the Nuǎnfǎ.
Why is this?
Because they lacked faith (xìnxīn) in the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo).
Therefore, they lacked Nuǎn (warming).
It should be understood that faith is precisely the Nuǎnfǎ.”
“Good man!
Faith is not the Nuǎnfǎ.
Why?
Because through faith, one attains Nuǎn.
Good man!
The Nuǎnfǎ are precisely wisdom (zhìhuì).
Why?
Because they contemplate the Four Noble Truths (Sì Dì).
Therefore, they are named the Sixteen Practices (Shíliù Xíng);
the practice is precisely the wisdom.
Good man!
Regarding what you asked,
for what reason are they named 'Warming'?
Good man!
The Nuǎnfǎ
are the fiery aspect (huǒ xiàng) of the Eightfold Noble Path (Bā Shèng Dào).
Hence, they are named 'Warming'.
Good man!
For example, when rubbing wood to make fire (cuán huǒ),
first there is warmth (nuǎn qì),
next, fire is produced,
and finally, smoke emerges.
The Uncontaminated Path (Wúlòudào)
is also like this:
the warming is precisely the sixteen practices,
the fire is precisely the fruit of the Stream-Enterer (Xūtuóhuánguǒ),
and the smoke is precisely the severing of fetters through the Path of Cultivation (xiūdào duàn jié).”
Jiāyè Púsà again addressed the Fó, saying:
“Shìzūn!
These Nuǎnfǎ,
are both existent dharmas (yǒufǎ),
and composite (yǒuwéi).
These dharmas are the five aggregates (wǔ yīn) of the Sèjiè attained as recompense (bàodé).
Therefore, they are named 'existent.'
For this reason,
they are again named 'composite.'
If they are composite,
how can they serve as the characteristics (xiàng) of the Uncontaminated Path (Wúlòudào)?”
The Fó said:
“Good man!
It is so,
it is so,
just as you have stated.
Good man!
Although these Nuǎnfǎ
are composite and existent dharmas,
they are still able to destroy composite and existent dharmas.
Therefore, they can serve as the characteristics of the Wúlòudào.
Good man!
It is like a person riding a horse,
both cherishing it and urging it on.
The warming mind (nuǎn xīn) is also like this:
due to cherishing, one accepts existence (shēng);
due to aversion, one contemplates practices.
Therefore, although they are existent dharmas and composite,
they can serve as the characteristics for that Right Path (Zhèngdào).
There are seventy-three types
of persons who attain the Nuǎnfǎ,
ten types in the Yùjiè.
These persons fully possess all afflictions (fánnǎo),
ranging from having severed one part [of affliction] up to nine parts.
This applies likewise from the Yùjiè up to the first Dhyāna (Chūchán) and even to the Sphere of Nothingness (Wú Suǒyǒu Chù).
It is also like this;
these are called the seventy-three types.
When such people have attained the Nuǎnfǎ,
they are then unable to sever the roots of goodness (shàngēn),
commit the Five Heinous Crimes (wǔ nì zuì),
or violate the Four Parājika Prohibitions (sì chóng jìn).
These persons are of two types:
first, those who meet a good friend (shànyǒu);
second, those who meet a bad friend (èyǒu).
Those who meet an èyǒu momentarily emerge but then sink back.
Those who meet a shànyǒu universally contemplate the four directions (sì fāng).
Contemplating the four directions is precisely the Summit Dharma (Dǐngfǎ).
Although this Dharma, by nature, consists of the five aggregates,
it also relies upon the Sì Dì.
Therefore, it receives the name 'universally contemplating the four directions.'
Having attained the Dǐngfǎ,
one next attains the Endurance Dharma (Rěnfǎ).
This Endurance is also like this:
its nature is also the five aggregates,
and it also relies upon the Sì Dì.
This person next attains the Highest Dharma in the World (Shì Dìyī Fǎ).
Although this Dharma, by nature, consists of the five aggregates,
it also relies upon the Sì Dì.
This person sequentially attains the Endurance of the Dharma of Suffering (Kǔ Fǎ Rěn).
The nature of endurance is wisdom;
it relies upon one truth (yī dì).
When this Rěnfǎ has relied upon one truth,
it leads up to the severing of afflictions through seeing (jiàn duàn fánnǎo),
and attaining the Xūtuóhuánguǒ.
This is named the fourth stage: 'universally contemplating the four directions.'
The four directions are precisely the Sì Dì.”
Jiāyè Púsà addressed the Fó, saying:
“Shìzūn!
As the Fó previously stated,
the afflictions severed by a Stream-Enterer (Xūtuóhuán)
are like water covering an area forty *lǐ* (li) wide and long,
and the remainder are like a drop (dī) on a single strand of hair.
Given this, why is the Xūtuóhuán said to have severed only the Three Fetters (sān jié)?
First, the view of self (*wǒ jiàn*);
second, seeing cause in what is not the cause (*fēi yīn jiàn yīn*);
third, the net of doubt (*yí wǎng*).
Shìzūn!
For what reason
is the Xūtuóhuán named 'universally contemplating the four directions'?
Furthermore, for what reason is [the person] named Xūtuóhuán?
Furthermore, for what reason is the Xūtuóhuán compared to a *qī* fish?"
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
A Sūtuóhuán (Sotāpanna) person,
although able to sever immeasurable afflictions,
because of these three being heavy,
it also covers all the afflictions severed by a Sūtuóhuán person.
Good man!
Just as when a great king goes out on a tour,
though there are four kinds of troops,
people only say the king is coming
or the king is going.
Why is that?
Because the world considers the king heavy (important).
These three afflictions are also like this.
What is the reason they are called heavy?
Because all sentient beings constantly give rise to them,
and because they are subtle and difficult to discern;
therefore they are called heavy.
These three fetters,
being difficult to sever,
and being capable of causing all afflictions,
are the enemies of the three antagonists,
namely, precepts (jiè),
concentration (dìng),
and wisdom (huì).
Good man!
There are sentient beings who, upon hearing that a Sūtuóhuán can sever such immeasurable afflictions,
give rise to a retreating mind,
and immediately say:
‘How can sentient beings possibly sever such immeasurable afflictions?’
Therefore, the Rúlái (Tathāgata) conveniently spoke of the three (fetters).
Regarding what you asked,
what is the reason a Sūtuóhuán person is likened to viewing the four directions?
Good man!
A Sūtuóhuán person contemplates the Four Noble Truths
and obtains four matters:
First, dwelling in the firm path;
second, being able to universally observe;
third, being able to see according to reality;
fourth, being able to destroy the great enemy.
“Dwelling in the firm path”
means the five roots possessed by the Sūtuóhuán
cannot be shaken by anyone;
therefore it is called dwelling in the firm path.
“Being able to universally observe”
means being able to universally condemn internal and external afflictions.
“Seeing according to reality”
is forbearance and wisdom (rěn zhì).
“Destroying the great enemy”
refers to the four inversions (diāndǎo).
Regarding what you asked,
what is the reason for the name Sūtuóhuán?
Good man!
Sū means ‘untainted’ (wúlòu),
and tuóhuán means ‘cultivation’ (xiūxí);
cultivating the untainted is called Sūtuóhuán.
Good man!
Furthermore, sū is also named ‘stream’ (liú).
There are two kinds of streams:
one is flowing with the stream (shùn liú),
and the second is flowing against the stream (nì liú).
Due to flowing against the stream, the person is named Sūtuóhuán.”
Kāyè Púsà (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva) said:
“World-Honored One!
If based on this meaning,
what is the reason
a Sītuóhán (Sakṛdāgāmin) person,
an Ānàhán (Anāgāmin) person,
or an Āluóhàn (Arhat) person
cannot be named Sūtuóhuán?”
“Good man!
From Sūtuóhuán up to all Buddhas,
they can also be named Sūtuóhuán.
If Sītuóhán up to all Buddhas had no Sūtuóhuán stage,
how could they be named Sītuóhán up to Buddha?
The names of all sentient beings are of two kinds:
one is the old (jiù),
and the second is the temporary (kè).
During the time of the ordinary person (fánfū), there are worldly names;
once the path is attained, a new name is established for them,
named Sūtuóhuán.
Because it is attained first,
it is named Sūtuóhuán.
Because it is attained later, it is named
Sītuóhán.
This person is also named Sūtuóhuán,
and also named Sītuóhán,
and likewise up to the Buddha.
Good man!
There are two kinds of stream:
one is liberation (jiětuō),
and the second is Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
All saints possess these two,
and can also be named Sūtuóhuán,
and also named Sītuóhán,
and likewise up to the Buddha.
Good man!
The Sūtuóhuán is also named Púsà (Bodhisattva).
Why is that?
Púsà means the Wisdom of Exhaustion (jìn zhì) and the Wisdom of Non-arising (wú shēng zhì).
The Sūtuóhuán person also seeks these two kinds of wisdom;
therefore, one should know that the Sūtuóhuán person can be named Púsà.
The Sūtuóhuán person can also be named ‘Awakened’ (jué).
Why is that?
Because of realizing the path through right awakening,
because of severing afflictions,
because of rightly awakening to cause and effect (yīn guǒ),
and because of rightly awakening to the common path and the uncommon path.
Sītuóhán up to Āluóhàn are likewise so.
Good man!
There are generally two types of Sūtuóhuán:
the first is sharp-rooted (lìgēn),
and the second is dull-rooted (dùngēn).
The dull-rooted person
returns seven times to the realms of humans and heavens.
This dull-rooted person
further has five types—
some have six,
five,
four,
three,
or two kinds [of rebirths remaining].
The sharp-rooted person
attains the Sūtuóhuán fruit in the present, progressing up to the Āluóhàn fruit.
Good man!
Regarding what you asked,
what is the reason a Sūtuóhuán person is likened to the flying fish (fèiyú)?
Good man!
The flying fish has four features:
First, its bones are fine, thus it is light;
second, it has wings, thus it is light;
third, it enjoys seeing the bright light;
fourth, it holds things firmly in its mouth.
The Sūtuóhuán person also has four features.
‘Its bones are fine’ is likened to afflictions being subtle.
‘It has wings’ is likened to Shēmótuō (Śamatha)
and Pípóshěnà (Vipaśyanā).
‘Enjoying seeing the bright light’ is likened to the Path of Seeing (jiàndào).
‘Holding things firmly in its mouth’ is likened to hearing the Rúlái speak of impermanence (wúcháng),
suffering (kǔ),
non-self (wú wǒ),
and impurity (bùjìng),
and adhering to it firmly without relinquishing it.
Just like Mówáng (Māra) transformed into the appearance of the Buddha,
Shǒuluó (Śūra), the Elder, saw it and was startled in his mind.
Māra, seeing that the Elder's mind was moved,
immediately spoke to the Elder:
‘The Four Noble Truths I spoke of previously
were not true.
I should now speak for you of the Five Truths,
the Six Skandhas (yīn),
the Thirteen Āyatanas (rù),
and the Nineteen Dhātus (jiè).’
The Elder, upon hearing this,
immediately contemplated the nature of the Dharma (fǎ xiàng),
which contained none of these principles.
Therefore, he adhered firmly
and his mind was not moved.”
Kāyè Púsà said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
The Sūtuóhuán, because he first attained the path,
is named Sūtuóhuán.
Because it is the first fruit,
it is named Sūtuóhuán.
If attaining the path first means being named Sūtuóhuán,
why, upon attaining the Forbearance of the Truth of Suffering (kǔ fǎ rěn shí),
is the person not named Sūtuóhuán,
but is instead named 'approaching' (xiàng)?
If based on the first fruit being named Sūtuóhuán,
the externalists (wàidào rén) first sever afflictions up to the State of Nothing-Whatsoever (wú suǒ yǒu chù),
cultivate the untainted path, and attain the Ānàhán fruit;
why are they not named Sūtuóhuán?”
“Good man!
Because it is the first fruit, it is named Sūtuóhuán.
Regarding what you asked,
the externalists first sever afflictions up to the State of Nothing-Whatsoever,
cultivate the untainted path, and attain Ānàhán;
why are they not named Sūtuóhuán?
Good man!
Because it is the first fruit,
it is named Sūtuóhuán.
That person at that time completely possesses the Eight Wisdoms (bā zhì) and the Sixteen Aspects (shíliù xíng).”
Kāyè said:
“World-Honored One!
Attaining Ānàhán is also like this;
one also attains the Eight Wisdoms
and completely possesses the Sixteen Aspects.
Why is one not named Sūtuóhuán?”
“Shàn Nánzǐ!
The sixteen aspects of defiled (sā sravā) actions have two types:
first, common (sādhārana);
second, uncommon (asādhārana).
The sixteen aspects of undefiled (anāsravā) actions also have two types:
first, heading towards the result (phala);
second, having attained the result.
The eight kinds of wisdom (jñāna) also have two:
first, heading towards the result;
second, having attained the result.
A Sūtuóhuán person abandons the common sixteen aspects of action,
and attains the uncommon sixteen aspects of action;
abandons the eight kinds of wisdom heading towards the result,
and attains the eight kinds of wisdom that have attained the result.
An Ānàhán person is not like this.
Therefore, the first result is called Sūtuóhuán.
“Shàn Nánzǐ!
A Sūtuóhuán person is focused on the Four Noble Truths (Sì Dì).
An Ānàhán person is focused only on one Truth.
Therefore, the first result is called Sūtuóhuán.
Because of this connection, he is likened to the 䱜 yú (fish),
having universally observed his actions and then proceeding.
‘Proceeding’ refers to a Sītuóhán person,
who concentrates his mind on cultivating the Path,
in order to sever greed (tānyù),
anger (chēn), delusion (chī),
and arrogance (jiāomàn).
Just like that 䱜 yú,
after universally observing the directions,
it proceeds for the sake of food.
After proceeding, it stays again.
This is likened to an Ānàhán who, having obtained the food, stays.
These Ānàhán are generally of two types:
first, those who attain Ānàhán in the present existence,
and by further cultivation immediately attain the Arhat (Āluóhàn) result;
second, those who are attached to the calm samādhi within the Form Realm (Sè Jiè) and the Formless Realm (Wú Sè Jiè).
This person, because he does not receive a body in the Desire Realm (Yù Jiè), is called Ānàhán.
These Ānàhán are further of five types:
first, attaining Nirvāṇa (Bān Nièpán) in the interim state (zhōng);
second, attaining Nirvāṇa after receiving a body (shòushēn);
third, attaining Nirvāṇa with effort (xíng);
fourth, attaining Nirvāṇa without effort (wúxíng);
fifth, attaining Nirvāṇa by flowing upwards (shàngliú).
Furthermore, there are six types:
the five types mentioned above,
plus attaining Nirvāṇa in the present existence (xiànzài).
Furthermore, there are seven types:
the six types mentioned above,
plus attaining Nirvāṇa in the Formless Realm.
Attaining Nirvāṇa with effort is further of two types:
either receiving two bodies,
or receiving four bodies.
If they receive two bodies, they are called those of keen faculties (lìgēn).
If they receive four bodies, they are called those of dull faculties (dùngēn).
Furthermore, there are two types:
first, those who are diligent but lack self-mastery in concentration (zìzài dìng);
second, those who are negligent but have self-mastery in concentration.
Furthermore, there are two types:
first, those who possess both diligence and concentration;
second, those who lack both of these two.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
Sentient beings in the Desire and Form Realms have two types of karma (yè):
first, active karma (zuòyè);
second, birth-receiving karma (shòushēng yè).
Those who attain Nirvāṇa in the interim state
have only active karma,
and no birth-receiving karma.
Therefore, they attain Nirvāṇa in the interim state.
Abandoning the Desire Realm body,
but having not yet reached the Form Realm,
and due to their keen faculties,
they attain Nirvāṇa in the interim state—
this is the interim Nirvāṇa.
An Ānàhán person has four types of mind:
first, neither learner (xué) nor non-learner (wúxué);
second, learner;
third, non-learner;
fourth, neither learner nor non-learner, entering Nirvāṇa.
Why is it again called Nirvāṇa in the interim state?
Shàn Nánzǐ!
Among these four types of mind of the Ānàhán,
two are Nirvāṇa,
and two are not Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is called Nirvāṇa in the interim state.
Attaining Nirvāṇa after receiving a body is further of two types:
first, active karma;
second, birth karma.
This person abandons the Desire Realm body,
receives a Form Realm body,
diligently cultivates the Path,
and when his lifespan is exhausted,
enters Nirvāṇa.
Jiāshè Púsà said:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If it is said that he enters Nirvāṇa when his life is exhausted,
how can it be called Nirvāṇa after receiving a body?”
The Buddha (Fó) said:
“Shàn Nánzǐ!
This person receives a body,
and only afterwards severs the afflictions (fánnǎo) of the Three Realms (Sān Jiè).
Therefore, it is called Nirvāṇa after receiving a body.
Shàn Nánzǐ!
Those who attain Nirvāṇa with effort
constantly cultivate the Path.
Due to the power of conditioned phenomena (yǒuwéi)
and samādhi,
they are able to sever afflictions
and enter Nirvāṇa.
This is called Nirvāṇa with effort.
Those who attain Nirvāṇa without effort
know certainly that they will attain Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, they are negligent.
They also, due to conditioned phenomena
and the power of samādhi,
attain Nirvāṇa when their lifespan is exhausted.
This is called Nirvāṇa without effort.
Those who attain Nirvāṇa by flowing upwards:
If a person has attained the Fourth Dhyāna (Dì Sì Chán),
he develops an affection for the First Dhyāna (Chū Chán).
Due to this connection,
he retrogresses and is born in the First Dhyāna.
There are two streams (liú):
one, the stream of afflictions;
two, the stream of the Path.
Due to the stream of the Path,
when this person’s lifespan is exhausted,
he develops an affection for the Second Dhyāna (Èr Chán).
Due to the connection of affection, he is born in the Second Dhyāna.
It is also like this until the Fourth Dhyāna.
In these Four Dhyānas, there are further two types:
first, entering the Formless Realm;
second, entering the Five Pure Abodes (Wǔ Jìng Jū).
These two types of people:
one delights in samādhi,
two delights in wisdom (zhìhuì).
Those who delight in wisdom
enter the Five Pure Abodes.
Those who delight in samādhi
enter the Formless Realm.
These two types of people:
one cultivates the Fourth Dhyāna with five levels of difference (jiē chā),
two does not cultivate it.
What are the five?
Low (xià),
medium (zhōng),
high (shàng),
high-medium (shàngzhōng),
and high-high (shàngshàng).
Those who cultivate the high-high
dwell in the Ākāniṣṭha Heaven (Wú Xiǎotiān).
Those who cultivate the high-medium
dwell in the Sudarśana Heaven (Shàn Jiàn Tiān).
Those who cultivate the high grade (shàng pǐn)
dwell in the Sudṛśā Heaven (Shàn Kě Jiàn Tiān).
Those who cultivate the medium grade (zhōng pǐn)
dwell in the Atapa Heaven (Wú Rè Tiān).
Those who cultivate the low grade (xià pǐn)
dwell in the Śubhākṛtsna Heaven (Shǎo Guǎng Tiān).
These two types of people:
one delights in discussion (lùnyì),
two delights in tranquility (jíjìng).
Those who delight in tranquility enter the Formless Realm.
Those who delight in discussion dwell in the Five Pure Abodes.
Furthermore, there are two types:
one cultivates the fumigation dhyāna (xūn chán),
two does not cultivate the fumigation dhyāna.
Those who cultivate the fumigation dhyāna enter the Five Pure Abodes.
Those who do not cultivate the fumigation dhyāna are born in the Formless Realm.
When their lifespan is exhausted, they attain Nirvāṇa.
This is called Nirvāṇa by flowing upwards.
If one desires to enter the Formless Realm,
one cannot cultivate the five levels of difference of the Four Dhyānas.
If one cultivates the five levels of difference of the Four Dhyānas,
one is then able to criticize the concentration of the Formless Realm.
Jiāshè Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Interim Nirvāṇa refers to those with keen faculties.
If they have keen faculties, why do they not attain Nirvāṇa in the present existence?
Why is there interim Nirvāṇa in the Desire Realm,
but none in the Form Realm?"
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
This person’s four great elements are currently weak,
and he cannot cultivate the Way.
Although there are Bhikṣus whose four great elements are healthy,
if they lack housing,
food and drink,
clothing,
bedding,
and medicine,
with all the necessary conditions incomplete,
they therefore cannot attain Nirvāṇa in the present life.
Good man!
Once, in the past, I was in the country of Shèwèiguó [Śrāvastī], at the vihāra of Ānàbīndī [Anāthapiṇḍika].
A Bhikṣu came to where I was,
and spoke these words:
‘World-Honored One!
I constantly cultivate the Way,
but I cannot attain the fruit of Sūtuóhuán [Sotāpanna] up to the fruit of Āluóhàn [Arhat].’
I immediately told Ānán [Ānanda]:
‘You should now provide this Bhikṣu with everything he needs.’
Then Ānán led this Bhikṣu to the Qítuó Lín [Jetavana] grove,
and gave him fine lodging.
At that time, the Bhikṣu said to Ānán:
‘Great Virtuous One!
I only ask that you adorn my dwelling,
cleanse and repair it thoroughly,
decorate it beautifully with the seven treasures,
and hang silk banners and canopies.’
Ānán replied:
‘Those in the world who are poor
are called Śāmén [Śramaṇas].
How can I possibly arrange these things?’
The Bhikṣu said:
‘Great Virtuous One!
If you can do this for me,
excellent,
excellent!
If you cannot,
I shall return to the World-Honored One.’
Then Ānán immediately went to the Buddha,
and spoke these words:
‘World-Honored One!
The Bhikṣu just now
requested various decorations from me,
and banners and canopies made of the seven treasures.
I am uncertain how this matter should be handled.’
At that time, I again told Ānán:
‘You should go back now,
and follow the Bhikṣu’s wishes.
Whatever items he requires,
prepare and provide them for him.’
Then Ānán returned to the lodging,
and prepared every item for this Bhikṣu.
After the Bhikṣu received them,
he focused his mind on cultivating the Way,
and before long attained the fruit of Sūtuóhuán up to the fruit of Āluóhàn.
Good man!
Immeasurable sentient beings ought to enter Nirvāṇa,
but because of what they lack,
their minds are obstructed and troubled,
and thus they fail to attain it.
Good man!
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who enjoy instructing others excessively;
their minds are busy with external affairs,
and they cannot attain concentration,
and therefore cannot attain Nirvāṇa in the present life.
Good man!
Regarding what you asked,
by what cause and condition
when abandoning the body of the desire realm,
is there middle Nirvāṇa,
but not in the form realm?
Good man!
This person perceives two causes for the afflictions of the desire realm:
first, internal;
second, external.
However, in the form realm, there are no external causes.
The desire realm also has two kinds of loving attachment:
first, desire-love;
second, form-love.
By contemplating these two kinds of love and thoroughly reprimanding them,
having already reprimanded them, they can enter Nirvāṇa.
In this desire realm, one is able to reprimand all coarse afflictions,
namely stinginess,
greed,
anger, jealousy,
lack of shame and lack of remorse.
Because of these causes and conditions,
one is able to attain Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the path in the desire realm is inherently courageous and robust.
Why is this?
Because the four fruits are attained there.
Therefore, the desire realm has middle Nirvāṇa,
the form realm does not.
Good man!
Middle Nirvāṇa generally has three types,
namely superior,
middle,
and inferior.
The superior type:
Upon abandoning the body, they attain Nirvāṇa before leaving the desire realm.
The middle type:
They attain Nirvāṇa just as they leave the desire realm,
before reaching the form realm.
The inferior type:
Having left the desire realm,
they attain Nirvāṇa only when they reach the border of the form realm.
This is likened to the *fǔ* fish stopping after finding food;
these individuals are also like that.
How are they named ‘stopping’ or ‘abiding’ (Zhù)?
Because they dwell in the form realm and the formless realm
and are capable of receiving bodies,
therefore they are named Zhù.
They do not receive bodies in the desire realm, such as humans,
devas,
hell beings,
animals,
or hungry ghosts,
therefore they are named Zhù.
They have already severed immeasurable afflictions and fetters,
but a few remain;
therefore they are named Zhù.
Furthermore, by what cause and condition are they named Zhù?
They never create actions shared with ordinary beings;
therefore they are named Zhù.
They have no fear themselves and do not cause fear in others;
therefore they are named Zhù.
They are far removed from the two kinds of love, stinginess, greed, and hatred;
therefore they are named Zhù.
“Good man!
Those who have reached the Other Shore
are likened to Āluóhàn,
Pìzhīfó [Pratyekabuddhas],
Púsà [Bodhisattvas],
and Buddhas,
just like the divine tortoise that travels both on water and on land.
For what cause and condition
is it likened to a tortoise?
Because it skillfully hides the five faculties.
Āluóhàn up to the various Buddhas are also like this;
they skillfully cover the five faculties,
therefore they are likened to the tortoise.
As for the terms ‘water’ and ‘land’:
Water symbolizes the worldly realm,
and land symbolizes the supramundane realm.
These various Sages are also like this;
because they are able to contemplate all evil afflictions,
they arrive at the Other Shore,
therefore they are likened to traveling on both water and land.
“Good man!
Just as the seven kinds of sentient beings in the Hénghé [Ganges] River,
although they have the names of fish or tortoise,
they do not leave the water.
In the same way, within the subtle great Nirvāṇa,
from the Yīchǎntí [Icchantika] up to the various Buddhas, although they have different names,
they nevertheless do not depart from the water of the Buddha nature (Fóxìng).
Good man!
These seven types of sentient beings,
whether wholesome Dharma (Shànfǎ),
or unwholesome Dharma,
or skillful means (Fāngbiàndào),
or the path to liberation (Jiětuōdào),
or the progressive path (Cìdàidào),
whether cause,
or fruit,
all are the Buddha nature (Fóxìng).
This is called the Tathāgata’s statement according to his own intent.”
Jiāshè Púsà [Kāśyapa Bodhisattva] said:
“World-Honored One!
If there is a cause, there is a fruit;
if there is no cause, there is no fruit.
Nirvāṇa is named the fruit,
but because it is permanent, it has no cause.
If it has no cause, how can it be named the fruit?
Yet this Nirvāṇa
is also named Śāmén [Śramaṇa],
and named the fruit of Śāmén.
What is Śāmén?
What is the fruit of Śāmén?”
“O good man!
All worldly existence has seven kinds of fruits:
The first is the fruit of expedience (fāngbiàn guǒ),
the second is the fruit of repaying kindness (bào’ēn guǒ),
the third is the fruit of close association (qīnjìn guǒ),
the fourth is the residual fruit (yú cán guǒ),
the fifth is the fruit of equality (píngděng guǒ),
the sixth is the resultant fruit (guǒbào guǒ),
and the seventh is the fruit of detachment (yuǎnlí guǒ).
Regarding the fruit of expedience,
it is like worldly people gathering much grain in autumn;
they all say to one another that they have obtained the fruit of expedience.
The fruit of expedience
is called the fruit of karmic action (yè xíng guǒ).
Such a fruit has two kinds of causes:
the first is the proximate cause (jìn yīn),
and the second is the distant cause (yuǎn yīn).
The proximate cause
is what is called the seed.
The distant cause
refers to water,
fertilizer,
and human effort (rén gōng).
This is called the fruit of expedience.
“Regarding the fruit of repaying kindness,
it is like worldly people providing for their parents.
The parents all say:
‘We have now obtained the fruit of being nurtured and cared for.’
The child’s ability to repay kindness is called the fruit.
Such a fruit also has two kinds of causes:
the first is the proximate cause,
and the second is the distant cause.
The proximate cause
is the purely good karma of the parents in the past.
The distant cause
is the filial child who has been born.
This is called the fruit of repaying kindness.
“Regarding the fruit of close association,
it is like a person associating closely with good friends,
and thus obtaining the fruit of a Śrotāpanna (Sūtuóhuán) up to the fruit of an Arhat (Āluóhàn).
This person proclaims:
‘I have now obtained the retribution of close association.’
Such a fruit
has two kinds of causes:
the first is the proximate cause,
and the second is the distant cause.
The proximate cause is faith (xìnxīn),
the distant cause is the good friend (shànyǒu).
This is called the fruit of close association.
“Regarding the residual fruit,
it is like obtaining the third body due to non-killing,
extending the years and increasing longevity.
This is called the residual fruit.
Such a fruit has two kinds of causes:
the first is the proximate cause,
and the second is the distant cause.
The proximate cause
is the purity of body,
speech,
and mind.
The distant cause
is the extension of years and increase of longevity.
This is called the residual fruit.
“Regarding the fruit of equality,
it refers to the world-vessel (shìjiè qì).
Such a fruit also has two kinds of causes:
the first is the proximate cause,
and the second is the distant cause.
The proximate cause
is the practice of the ten good karmas (shí shànyè) by sentient beings.
The distant cause
is the three calamities (sān zāi).
This is called the fruit of equality.
“Regarding the resultant fruit,
it is like a person who, having obtained a pure body,
cultivates the three pure karmas of body,
speech,
and mind.
This person then says:
‘I have obtained the resultant fruit.’
Such a fruit has two kinds of causes:
the first is the proximate cause,
and the second is the distant cause.
The proximate cause
is the present purity of body,
speech,
and mind.
The distant cause
is the past purity of body,
speech,
and mind.
This is called the resultant fruit.
“Regarding the fruit of detachment,
it is Nirvāṇa (Nièpán),
being detached from all afflictions and all good karmas.
The causes for this Nirvāṇa are also two kinds:
the first is the proximate cause,
and the second is the distant cause.
The proximate cause
is the three gates to liberation (sān jiětuō mén).
The distant cause
is the wholesome dharmas cultivated throughout immeasurable eons.
“O good man!
In worldly dharmas,
sometimes the productive cause (shēng yīn) is mentioned,
and sometimes the manifesting cause (liǎo yīn) is mentioned;
the supra-mundane dharma is also like this,
it also mentions the productive cause
and also mentions the manifesting cause.
O good man!
The three gates to liberation
and the thirty-seven factors (sānshíqī pǐn)
can serve as the non-productive productive cause (bù shēng shēng yīn) for all afflictions,
and also serve as the manifesting cause for Nirvāṇa.
O good man!
When afflictions are detached,
one attains the clear vision of Nirvāṇa;
therefore, Nirvāṇa only has the manifesting cause,
it does not have the productive cause.
“O good man!
Regarding what you asked,
what is Śramaṇa (Shāmén)
and what is the fruit of a Śramaṇa (Shāmén guǒ)?
O good man!
Śramaṇa is the Eightfold Noble Path (Bā Zhèngdào),
the fruit of a Śramaṇa is the complete and eternal severance of all greed, hatred, ignorance, and so on, resulting from the Path.
This is called Śramaṇa
and the fruit of a Śramaṇa.
Kāśyapa (Jiāyè) Bodhisattva said:
“O World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
For what reason
is the Eightfold Noble Path called Śramaṇa?”
"O good man!
The world speaks of Śrāmaṇa (Shā mén),
naming it as want (fá),
but what is named the path (dào)?
This path,
cuts off all want (fá),
and cuts off all paths.
For this reason,
the Eightfold Noble Path (Bā Zhèng Dào) is named Śramaṇa-na (Shā mén nà).
From this path,
the fruit is obtained,
hence it is named the Fruit of Śramaṇa (Shā mén Guǒ).
O good man!
Furthermore, regarding Śramaṇa-na (Shā mén nà):
just as worldly people include those who enjoy stillness (jìng),
they are also called Śramaṇa (Shā mén).
This path
is also like this;
it enables the practitioner to distance themselves from evil livelihoods (xiémìng), etc., associated with body,
speech,
and mind,
and to attain joyous tranquility (jìjìng).
Therefore, it is named Śramaṇa-na (Shā mén nà).
O good man!
Just as in the world, a low person
can become a superior person,
this is called Śramaṇa (Shā mén).
This path is also like this;
because it can enable a low person to become a superior person,
therefore it gains the name Śramaṇa-na (Shā mén nà).
O good man!
An Ārhat (Āluóhàn) who cultivates this path,
obtains the Fruit of Śrāmaṇa (Shā mén Guǒ).
Therefore, they gain the name of Reaching the Other Shore (Dào Yú Bǐ'àn).
The Fruit of the Ārhat (Āluóhàn Guǒ) is the state of No More Learning (Wú Xué),
and the Fivefold Dharma-Body (Wǔ Fēn Fǎ Shēn)—Sīla (Jiè, morality),
Samādhi (Dìng, concentration),
Prajñā (Huì, wisdom),
Vimukti (Jiětuō, liberation),
and Vimuktijñānadarśana (Jiětuō Zhījiàn, knowledge and vision of liberation)—because of these five parts, one reaches the Other Shore (Bǐ'àn).
Therefore, it is named Reaching the Other Shore (Dào Yú Bǐ'àn).
Because they have reached the Other Shore (Bǐ'àn), they state:
'My birth is exhausted;
the pure conduct (Fàn Xíng) has been established;
what was to be done has been accomplished;
there will be no further rebirth.'
O good man!
This Ārhat (Āluóhàn) has eternally severed the causes and conditions for generation in the three periods of time (sānshì);
therefore they state,
'My birth is exhausted.'
They have also severed the fruits of the Five Aggregates (Wǔ Yīn Guǒ) across the Three Realms (Sān Jiè);
therefore they also say, 'My birth is exhausted.'
Because the pure conduct (Fàn Xíng) cultivated has been ultimately completed,
therefore they proclaim, 'The pure conduct (Fàn Xíng) has been established.'
Furthermore, having abandoned the Path of Learning (Xué Dào),
this is also called 'established.'
What was originally sought
has now been attained;
therefore they proclaim,
'What was to be done has been accomplished.'
Having cultivated the path and attained the fruit,
they also say, 'accomplished.'
Having obtained the Knowledge of Exhaustion (Jìn Zhì)
and the Knowledge of Non-arising (Wú Shēng Zhì),
they proclaim, 'My birth is exhausted,'
exhausting all bonds of existence.
For this reason,
the Ārhat (Āluóhàn) is named one who Reaches the Other Shore (Dào Bǐ'àn).
Like the Ārhat (Āluóhàn),
the Pratyekabuddha (Pìzhīfó) is also like this.
The Bodhisattva (Púsa) and the Buddha, having completely perfected the Six Pāramitās (Liù Bōluómì),
are named those who Reach the Other Shore (Dào Bǐ'àn).
These Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, having attained Anuttara-Samyak-Sambodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
are named those who have fully perfected the Six Pāramitās (Liù Bōluómì).
Why is this?
Because they have obtained the fruit of the Six Pāramitās (Liù Bōluómì);
since the fruit is attained,
they are named 'fully perfected.'
"O good man!
These seven types of beings do not cultivate the body,
do not cultivate morality (jiè),
do not cultivate the mind,
do not cultivate wisdom (huì),
and are unable to practice these four things.
They are thus able to commit the grave offenses (zhòng zuì) of the Five Unpardonable Sins (Wǔ Nì),
capable of cutting off wholesome roots (shàngēn),
violating the Four Cardinal Prohibitions (Sì Zhòng Jìn),
and slandering the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha (Fó Fǎ Sēng).
Therefore, they gain the name of 'perpetually sinking' (Cháng Chén Mò).
O good man!
Among these seven people,
those who are able to approach good spiritual advisors (shàn zhīshì),
sincerely listen to and receive the Tathāgata’s True Dharma (Rúlái Zhèng Fǎ),
contemplate skillfully internally,
abide in accordance with the Dharma,
diligently cultivate the body,
morality (jiè),
mind,
and wisdom (huì),
therefore gain the name of Crossing the River of Saṃsāra (Shēngsǐ Hé) to Reach the Other Shore (Dào Yú Bǐ'àn).
If anyone asserts that an Icchantika (Yīchǎntí) attains Anuttara-Samyak-Sambodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
this is called 'attachment' (rǎn zhuó);
if they say they do not attain it,
this is called 'delusion' or 'falsehood' (xū wàng).
"O good man!
Regarding these seven types of people:
perhaps one person possesses all seven characteristics,
or perhaps seven people each possess one.
O good man!
If someone, whose mind and mouth differ,
and whose thoughts differ,
says that an Icchantika (Yīchǎntí) attains Anuttara-Samyak-Sambodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
you should know that this person slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha (Fó Fǎ Sēng);
if a person, whose mind and mouth differ,
and whose thoughts differ,
says that an Icchantika (Yīchǎntí) does not attain Anuttara-Samyak-Sambodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
this person is also named one who slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha (Fó Fǎ Sēng).
O good man!
If anyone says that the constituents of the Eightfold Noble Path (Bā Shèng Dào Fēn)
are attained by ordinary beings (fánfū),
this person is also named one who slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha (Fó Fǎ Sēng);
if anyone says that the constituents of the Eightfold Noble Path (Bā Shèng Dào Fēn)
are not attained by ordinary beings (fánfū),
this person is also named one who slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha (Fó Fǎ Sēng).
O good man!
If anyone says that all sentient beings definitively possess the Buddha Nature (Fó Xìng),
or definitively lack the Buddha Nature (Fó Xìng),
this person is also named one who slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha (Fó Fǎ Sēng).
O good man!
