Therefore, I taught in the Sūtras (Qì Jīng)
that there are two types of people who slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha (Fó Fǎ Sēng):
first, those who do not believe due to a hateful mind (chēnhuì xīn),
and second, those who, though they believe, do not understand the meaning (yì).
O good man!
If a person has faith (xìnxīn)
but lacks wisdom (zhìhuì),
this person is able to increase ignorance (wúmíng).
If they have wisdom (zhìhuì)
but lack faith (xìnxīn),
this person is able to increase wrong views (xiéjiàn).
O good man!
The person without faith, due to a hateful mind (chēnhuì xīn),
says that there is no Buddha (Fó),
Dharma (Fǎ),
or Sangha (Sēng) Jewel.
The believer without wisdom (huì)
understands the meaning erroneously (diāndǎo jiě yì),
causing those who hear the Dharma to slander the Buddha (Fó),
Dharma (Fǎ),
and Sangha (Sēng).
O good man!
Therefore, I say that people without faith due to a hateful mind (chēnhuì xīn),
and people with faith who lack wisdom (zhìhuì),
are able to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha (Fó Fǎ Sēng) Jewel.
O good man!
If anyone says that an Icchantika (Yīchǎntí), before generating wholesome qualities (shàn fǎ),
immediately attains Anuttara-Samyak-Sambodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
this person is also named one who slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha (Fó Fǎ Sēng);
If, furthermore, someone says that an Icchantika (Yīchǎntí), having abandoned their state as an Icchantika,
attains Anuttara-Samyak-Sambodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí) in a different body,
this person is also named one who slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha (Fó Fǎ Sēng).
If, furthermore, someone says that an Icchantika (Yīchǎntí) is able to generate wholesome roots (shàngēn),
and having generated wholesome roots,
they continue unbrokenly [in practice],
and attain Anuttara-Samyak-Sambodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
and thus says that an Icchantika (Yīchǎntí) attains Anuttara-Samyak-Sambodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
know that this person does not slander the Three Jewels (Sān Bǎo).
O good man!
If anyone says that all sentient beings definitively possess the Buddha Nature (Fó Xìng)—which is eternal (cháng),
joyful (lè),
self (wǒ),
and pure (jìng)—
and that because it neither acts nor arises through the causes and conditions of defilement (fánnǎo),
it is therefore invisible,
know that this person slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha (Fó Fǎ Sēng);
if anyone says that all sentient beings entirely lack the Buddha Nature (Fó Xìng),
like a rabbit's horn (tù jiǎo),
and that it arises from skillful means (fāngbiàn),
originally non-existent but now existent,
and having existed, returns to non-existence,
know that this person slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha (Fó Fǎ Sēng);
if anyone says that the Buddha Nature (Fó Xìng) of sentient beings
is neither existent, like space (xūkōng),
nor non-existent, like a rabbit's horn (tù jiǎo).
Why is this?
Because space (xūkōng) is eternal,
and a rabbit's horn (tù jiǎo) is non-existent.
Therefore, it can be said to be both existent and non-existent.
Because it is existent, it refutes the rabbit's horn (tù jiǎo);
because it is non-existent, it refutes space (xūkōng).
One who speaks in this manner does not slander the Three Jewels (Sān Bǎo)."
"O good man!
Now, this Fóxìng
is not called one dharma,
is not called ten dharmas,
is not called a hundred dharmas,
is not called a thousand dharmas,
is not called ten thousand dharmas.
When one has not yet attained Ānòuduōluósānmiǎosānpútí,
all good,
bad,
and neutral [acts]
are entirely called Fóxìng.
The Rúlái sometimes speaks of the result within the cause,
and speaks of the cause within the result.
This is called the Rúlái's speech following his own intent (Suíyìyǔ).
Because of his speech following his intent, he is called Rúlái;
because of his speech following his intent, he is called Āluóhē;
because of his speech following his intent, he is called Sānmiǎosānfótuó.
Jiāshè Púsà said:
"Bhagavān!
As the Buddha has said,
the Fóxìng of sentient beings is like empty space (ākāśa).
How is it called 'like empty space'?"
"O good man!
The nature of empty space
is not past,
is not future,
and is not present.
Fóxìng is also like this.
O good man!
Empty space is not past.
Why?
Because there is no present.
If a dharma were present,
one could speak of the past.
Since there is no present,
there is neither past nor present.
Why?
Because there is no future.
If a dharma were future,
one could speak of the present.
Since there is no future,
there is neither present nor future.
Why?
Because there is no present or past.
If there were present and past,
then there would be future.
Since there is no present or past,
there is therefore no future.
Based on this meaning,
the nature of empty space is not encompassed by the three times.
O good man!
Because empty space is nonexistent,
there are no three times.
It is not nonexistent because of existence.
Like flowers in the sky (sky-flowers),
because they are not existent,
they do not have the three times.
Empty space is also like this;
because it is not existent,
it does not have the three times.
O good man!
That which has no thing
is empty space.
Fóxìng is also like this.
O good man!
Empty space is not encompassed by the three times
because it is nonexistent;
Fóxìng is not encompassed by the three times
because it is eternal.
O good man!
Having already attained Ānòuduōluósānmiǎosānpútí, the Rúlái
possesses Fóxìng and
all Buddhadharmas,
which are eternal and unchanging.
Based on this meaning,
they do not possess the three times,
just like empty space.
O good man!
Empty space, being nonexistent,
is neither internal
nor external.
Fóxìng, being eternal,
is neither internal
nor external.
Therefore, it is said that Fóxìng is like empty space.
O good man!
Just as in the world, a place without obstruction
is called empty space,
the Rúlái, having attained Ānòuduōluósānmiǎosānpútí,
is unobstructed by all Buddhadharmas.
Therefore, it is said that Fóxìng is like empty space.
Based on these causes and conditions,
I say Fóxìng is like empty space."
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"Bhagavān!
Rúlái,
Fóxìng, and
Nièpán
are not encompassed by the three times,
yet they are designated as existent.
Empty space is also not encompassed by the three times,
so why may it not be designated as existent?"
The Buddha said:
"O good man!
That which is not Nièpán is called Nièpán.
That which is not Rúlái is called Rúlái.
That which is not Fóxìng is called Fóxìng.
How is that which is not Nièpán defined?
It refers to all afflicted, conditioned dharmas.
To destroy such conditioned afflictions,
this is called Nièpán.
That which is not Rúlái
refers to the range from Yīchǎntí up to the Pìzhīfó.
To destroy such Yīchǎntí and others up to the Pìzhīfó,
this is called Rúlái.
That which is not Fóxìng
refers to all walls,
tiles and stones,
and inanimate things.
To be separate from such inanimate things
is called Fóxìng.
O good man!
In all the world,
there is nothing that is not empty space facing empty space.
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"Bhagavān!
In the world, there is also nothing that is not opposed to the Sìdà (Four Great Elements),
yet the Sìdà are still designated as existent.
Empty space has no opposition.
Why may it not be designated as existent?"
The Buddha said:
"O good man!
If you say that Nièpán is not encompassed by the three times,
and empty space is also like this,
this meaning is incorrect.
Why?
Nièpán is existent,
visible and capable of realization.
It is form,
footprint,
and phrasing;
it is existence,
it is characteristic,
it is condition,
it is a refuge.
It is tranquility,
light,
peace,
the other shore.
Therefore, it is permitted to be designated as not encompassed by the three times.
The nature of empty space lacks such dharmas.
Therefore, it is called nonexistent.
If there were a dharma existing beyond these dharmas,
it should be encompassed by the three times.
If empty space were the same as these existent dharmas,
it could not avoid being encompassed by the three times.
O good man!
Just as people in the world say:
Empty space is called formless,
without obstruction,
and invisible.
If it is formless,
without obstruction,
and invisible,
then it is a mental dharma (Cittasaṁprayukta-dharma).
If empty space were the same as a mental dharma,
it could not avoid being encompassed by the three times.
If it is encompassed by the three times, then it is the four aggregates (excluding form/matter).
Therefore, being separate from the four aggregates,
there is no empty space."
"Furthermore, good man!
All externalists (Tīrthikas) say,
that *xūkōng* (space/ether) is light,
and if it is light, then it is a *sèfǎ* (form/matter phenomenon).
If *xūkōng* is thus a *sèfǎ*,
then it is impermanent (*wúcháng*).
Because it is impermanent,
it is included in the three periods (*sānshì*).
How can the externalists say it is not included in the three periods?
If it is included in the three periods, then it is not *xūkōng*.
Or it might be said that *xūkōng* is permanent (*cháng*).
Good man!
Furthermore, some people say,
that *xūkōng* is location/dwelling (*zhùchù*).
If there is a location, then it is a *sèfǎ*.
Since all locations are impermanent and included in the three periods,
if *xūkōng* were also permanent and not included in the three periods,
then knowing what location is, we know there is no *xūkōng*.
Furthermore, some say,
that *xūkōng* is sequence/order (*cìdì*).
If it is sequence, then it is a countable phenomenon (*shùfǎ*).
If it is countable, it is included in the three periods.
If it is included in the three periods, how can it be called permanent?
Good man!
If furthermore it is said,
that *xūkōng* is inseparable from three dharmas (phenomena):
first, emptiness (*kōng*);
second, reality/substance (*shí*);
third, emptiness and reality (*kōngshí*).
If it is said to be emptiness,
then know that *xūkōng* is an impermanent *fǎ*.
Why?
Because the place of reality is non-existent.
If it is said to be reality,
then know that *xūkōng* is also impermanent.
Why?
Because the place of emptiness is non-existent.
If it is emptiness and reality,
then know that *xūkōng* is also impermanent.
Why?
Because both places are non-existent.
Therefore, *xūkōng* is called non-existent.
Good man!
As when it is said that *xūkōng* is a phenomenon that can be produced (*kězuòfǎ*):
such as saying that by removing a tree or removing a house, *xūkōng* is created;
leveling creates *xūkōng*;
covering *xūkōng*;
rising above *xūkōng*;
painting the color of *xūkōng*,
like the water of the great ocean.
Therefore, *xūkōng* is a phenomenon that can be produced.
All produced phenomena are impermanent,
just like an earthen jar.
If *xūkōng* is like that,
it ought to be impermanent.
"Good man!
Worldly people say,
that which, among all phenomena, is the place without obstruction (*wúguà'ài chù*), is called *xūkōng*.
This unobstructed place, relative to all phenomena,
does it exist completely?
Or does it exist partially?
If it exists completely,
then know that in other places there is no *xūkōng*.
If it exists partially,
then it is a countable phenomenon that has ‘this’ and ‘that’.
If it is countable, know that it is impermanent.
Good man!
If someone says that unobstructed *xūkōng* joins and merges with existence,
and furthermore says that *xūkōng* is contained within things, like fruit in a container,
neither statement is correct.
Why?
If you speak of joining and merging,
there are three types:
first, merging through separate actions (*yìyè hé*),
like flying birds gathering on a tree;
second, merging through shared action (*gòngyè hé*),
like two sheep butting each other;
third, joining of that which is already joined (*yǐhé gònghé*),
like two paired fingers joining in one place.
If you speak of merging through separate actions,
the separate things are two:
first, the action of the thing;
second, the action of *xūkōng*.
If the action of *xūkōng* joins with the thing,
*xūkōng* is then impermanent.
If the action of the thing joins with *xūkōng*,
the thing is then not pervasive.
If it is not pervasive, it is also impermanent.
If it is said that *xūkōng* is permanent,
and its nature is motionless, yet it joins with moving things,
this meaning is incorrect.
Why?
If *xūkōng* is permanent,
things ought to also be permanent.
If things are impermanent,
*xūkōng* is also impermanent.
If it is said that *xūkōng* is both permanent
and impermanent,
there is no such case.
If it is merging through shared action,
this meaning is incorrect.
Why?
*Xūkōng* is defined as pervasive.
If it joins with action,
action ought to also be pervasive.
If it is pervasive, it should pervade everything.
If it pervades everything, everything should be joined.
It should not be possible to speak of joining and not joining.
If it is said to be the joining of that which is already joined, like two paired fingers joining,
this meaning is incorrect.
Why?
Because previously there was no joining,
and only afterward was there joining.
To be non-existent previously and existent afterward,
is an impermanent *fǎ*.
Therefore, one cannot say that *xūkōng* is the joining of that which is already joined.
Just as worldly phenomena are first non-existent and later existent,
these things are impermanent.
If *xūkōng* is like that,
it also ought to be impermanent.
If it is said that *xūkōng* is contained within things,
like fruit in a container,
this meaning is incorrect.
Why?
If *xūkōng* is like this,
when there was previously no container,
where did it reside?
If there is a place of residence,
then there are many instances of *xūkōng*.
If there are many instances,
how can it be called permanent,
called single,
or called pervasive?
If *xūkōng* resides separately from emptiness,
existing things ought also to reside separately from *xūkōng*.
Therefore, you should know that *xūkōng* does not exist.
Good man!
If someone says,
that the place where a finger rests is called *xūkōng*,
then know that *xūkōng* is an impermanent *fǎ*.
Why?
The finger has four directions (sides).
If there are four directions,
then know that *xūkōng* also has four directions.
All permanent *fǎ*s,
absolutely lack location and direction.
Because it has direction,
*xūkōng* is impermanent.
If it is impermanent,
it is not separate from the Five *Yīn* (Skandhas).
It must be separate from the Five *Yīn*
to be non-existent.
"Good man!
If an existent *fǎ* resides due to causes and conditions (*yīnyuán*),
then know that this *fǎ* is called impermanent.
Good man!
For example, all living beings and trees reside dependent on the earth.
Because the earth is impermanent,
things dependent on the earth are sequentially impermanent.
Good man!
Just as the earth depends on water,
because water is impermanent,
the earth is also impermanent.
Just as water depends on wind,
because wind is impermanent,
water is also impermanent.
Wind relies on *xūkōng*.
If *xūkōng* is impermanent,
wind is also impermanent.
If it is impermanent,
how can it be said that *xūkōng* is permanent
and pervasive in all places?
Because *xūkōng* is non-existent,
it is not past,
future,
or present.
Just like a rabbit horn (which is non-existent), because it is not a thing,
it is not past,
future,
or present.
Therefore, I say that because the Buddha nature (*Fóxìng*) is permanent,
it is not included in the three periods.
Because *xūkōng* is non-existent,
it is not included in the three periods.
Good man!
I ultimately do not contend with the world.
Why?
If worldly wisdom says there is existence,
I also say there is existence.
If worldly wisdom says there is non-existence,
I also say there is non-existence."
The Bodhisattva Jiāshè said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
What phenomena must a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (*Púsà Móhēsà*) possess in full to not contend with the world,
and not be tainted by worldly phenomena?"
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, possessing the ten Dharmas,
does not dispute with the world
and is not contaminated by worldly Dharmas.
What are the ten?
First, confidence (Śraddhā);
second, having precepts (Śīla);
third, drawing near to good friends (Kalyāṇamitra);
fourth, proper internal contemplation;
fifth, possessing diligence (Vīrya);
sixth, possessing right mindfulness (Samyak-smṛti);
seventh, possessing wisdom (Prajñā);
eighth, possessing right speech (Samyak-vāc);
ninth, delighting in the right Dharma;
tenth, having compassion for living beings.
Good man!
A Bodhisattva, possessing these ten Dharmas,
does not dispute with the world
and is not contaminated by worldly Dharmas,
like the Utpala flower.”
Kāśyapa Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Buddha has said,
what the wise of the world say exists,
I also say exists;
what the wise of the world say does not exist,
I also say does not exist.
What is meant by the existence and non-existence stated by the wise of the world?”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
If the wise of the world say that form (Rūpa) is impermanent,
suffering (Duḥkha),
empty (Śūnya),
and non-self (Anātman),
and consciousness (Vijñāna) is also like this.
Good man!
This is what the wise of the world call ‘existence,’
and I also say it exists.
Good man!
If the wise of the world say that form is not permanent,
joy,
self,
or pure,
and feeling (Vedanā), perception (Saṃjñā), volitions (Saṃskāra), and consciousness (Vijñāna) are also like this.
Good man!
This is what the wise of the world call ‘non-existence,’
and I also say it does not exist.”
Kāśyapa Púsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The wise of the world
are namely the Fó,
the Púsà,
and all the holy ones.
If the holy ones say that
form is impermanent,
suffering,
empty,
and non-self,
how does the Tathāgata say that the Fó’s physical body (Rūpakāya) is eternal and unchanging?
The Dharmas that the wise of the world say do not exist,
how does the Tathāgata say they exist?
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, speaks in this way,
how can he then say that he ‘does not dispute with the world?’
or ‘is not contaminated by worldly Dharmas?’
The Tathāgata has already departed from the three kinds of erroneous views (Viparyāsa),
namely the perversion of perception (Saṃjñā-viparyāsa),
the perversion of thought (Citta-viparyāsa),
and the perversion of view (Dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa).
He should say that the Fó’s form is truly impermanent,
yet now he says it is permanent.
How can he be called one who has departed from erroneous views
and does not dispute with the world?”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
The form of ordinary beings (Fanfú) arises from afflictions (Kleśa),
therefore the wise say that form is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
The form of the Tathāgata is far removed from afflictions,
therefore it is said to be eternal and unchanging.”
Kāśyapa Púsà said:
“World-Honored One!
What does it mean for form to arise from afflictions?”
“Good man!
There are three kinds of afflictions (Kleśa),
namely the defilement of desire (Kāma-āsrava),
the defilement of existence (Bhava-āsrava),
and the defilement of ignorance (Avidyā-āsrava).
The wise ought to observe the faults associated with these three defilements.
Why is that?
Having known the faults, one is then able to keep far away from them.
For example, a physician first diagnoses the pulse of the illness,
knows where the illness is located,
and then prescribes medicine.
Good man!
It is like a person leading a blind man
to a thorn thicket,
abandoning him, and returning.
It is extremely difficult for the blind man to get out afterward;
even if he gets out,
his body is utterly damaged.
The ordinary beings of the world are also like this;
if they cannot know and see the perils of the three defilements,
they will follow after and practice them.
If they see them, they will be able to keep far away from them.
Having known the faults, although they receive the karmic recompense,
the recompense is slight.
Good man!
There are four kinds of people:
First, those who perform heavy acts but receive light recompense;
second, those who perform light acts but receive heavy recompense;
third, those whose performing of acts is heavy and whose receiving of recompense is also heavy;
fourth, those whose performing of acts is light and whose receiving of recompense is also light.
Good man!
If a person is able to observe the faults of afflictions,
that person’s performing of acts and receiving of consequences are both light.
Good man!
A wise person generates this thought:
‘I ought to keep far away from such defilements as these,
and furthermore, I ought not to perform such vile and evil deeds as these.
Why is this?
Because I have not yet achieved liberation from the recompenses of the hells (Niraya),
hungry ghosts (Preta),
animals (Tiryagyoni),
humans, and gods (Deva).
If I cultivate the Path,
I will rely on this power to destroy all sufferings.’
When this person observes this,
covetousness (Rāga),
anger (Dveṣa),
and ignorance (Moha) become weak.
Having seen that covetousness, anger, and ignorance are light,
his mind rejoices,
and he thinks further:
‘The way I am now,
it is all due to the power of cultivating the Path,
enabling me to be freed from unwholesome Dharmas
and draw near to wholesome Dharmas.
Therefore, currently seeing the Right Path,
I should diligently practice and cultivate it.’
This person, due to this power of diligently cultivating the Path,
departs from immeasurable evil afflictions,
and is freed from the karmic recompense of the hells,
hungry ghosts,
animals,
humans, and gods.
Therefore, I have stated in the Sūtras (Kèjīng)
that one should observe all defilements (Sāsrava) and the causes of defilements.
Why is this?
If a wise person only observes the defilements
but does not observe the causes of the defilements,
he will not be able to sever all afflictions.
Why is this?
The wise observe that defilements arise from causes;
if I now sever the cause,
the defilements will not arise.
Good man!
It is like that physician:
first cutting off the cause of the disease,
and then the disease does not arise.
The wise person who first cuts off the cause of afflictions
is also like this.
The wise person should first observe the cause,
then observe the karmic recompense,
knowing that good consequences arise from good causes,
and knowing that bad consequences arise from bad causes.
Having observed the karmic recompense,
he keeps far away from bad causes.
Having observed the karmic recompense,
he should further observe the lightness and heaviness of afflictions.
Having observed the lightness and heaviness,
he first departs from the heavy ones.
Once the heavy ones are departed from, the light ones depart naturally.”
"Good man!
If the wise person knows the afflictions (kleshas),
the cause of afflictions,
the retribution (karmic fruits) of afflictions,
and the severity or lightness of afflictions,
this person will then diligently cultivate the Path,
without pause and without regret,
drawing near to virtuous friends (kalyāṇa-mitra),
listening to the Dharma with utmost sincerity,
in order to extinguish all such afflictions.
Good man!
For example, a sick person
knows their illness is slight,
and can certainly be cured and made well.
Although they receive bitter medicine,
they take it without regret.
The person of wisdom is also like this:
diligently cultivating the Noble Path,
they are joyful and not sorrowful,
without pause and without regret.
Good man!
If a person can know the afflictions,
the cause of afflictions,
the retribution of afflictions,
and the severity or lightness of afflictions,
and diligently cultivates the Noble Path for the sake of eliminating afflictions,
this person does not arise from afflictions;
form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise.
If one cannot know the afflictions,
the cause of afflictions,
the retribution of afflictions,
and the severity or lightness of afflictions,
and does not diligently cultivate the Path,
this person arises from afflictions;
form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise.
Good man!
One who knows the afflictions,
the cause of afflictions,
the retribution of afflictions,
and the severity or lightness of afflictions,
and practices the Path to sever afflictions,
is precisely the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
For this reason, the form of the Tathāgata (Rúlái) is eternal, extending even to consciousness being eternal.
Good man!
One who does not know the afflictions,
the cause of afflictions,
the retribution of afflictions,
and the severity or lightness of afflictions,
and cannot cultivate the Path is precisely a common mortal (*fánfū*).
Therefore, the form of the common mortal (*fánfū*) is impermanent (*wúcháng*),
and sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all impermanent.
Good man!
The worldly wise,
all Noble Ones (Saints),
Bódìsàtuo (Púsà),
and all Buddhas (Fó) speak these two meanings;
I also speak these two meanings in this way.
Therefore, I preach,
not contending with the worldly wise,
nor being stained by worldly doctrines.
The Bódìsàtuo Jiāyè (Kāśyapa) then said again to the Buddha (Fó):
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
According to what the Buddha (Fó) has preached,
regarding the three defilements (*āsravas*) which contain outflows:
what are named the desire defilement (*yùlòu*),
the existence defilement (*yǒulòu*),
and the ignorance defilement (*wúmíng lòu*)?"
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"Good man!
The desire defilement
is internal evil consideration and contemplation (*vitarka* and *vicāra*),
which, conditioned by external circumstances,
gives rise to the desire defilement.
Therefore, I formerly instructed Ānán (Ānanda) when I was in Wángshě Chéng (Rājagṛha):
'Ānán (Ānanda)!
You should now accept the verses recited by this woman;
these verses were proclaimed by the Buddhas (Fó) of the past.'
Therefore, all internal evil consideration and contemplation,
and all external conditions,
are named Desire;
this is called the desire defilement.
The existence defilement
pertains to the Form (Sè)
and Formless (Wúsè) Realms;
the internal evil phenomena
and the external conditions,
excluding the external conditions
and internal consideration and contemplation in the Desire Realm (Yùjiè),
this is named the existence defilement.
The ignorance defilement
is the inability to fully know the self and what belongs to the self,
and the failure to distinguish between internal and external;
this is named the ignorance defilement.
Good man!
Ignorance (*wúmíng*) is the root of all defilements.
Why is this?
Because all sentient beings, due to the conditions of ignorance,
conceive and create characteristics based on the skandhas (*yīn*), āyatanas (*rù*), and dhātus (*jiè*),
and this is named a sentient being.
This is named inverted perception (*xiǎng dǎo*),
inverted thought (*xīn dǎo*),
and inverted view (*jiàn dǎo*).
Based on these conditions, all defilements arise.
Therefore, in the twelve divisions of the Sūtras (Qìjīng), I state that ignorance
is the cause of greed (*tān*),
the cause of hatred (*chēn*),
and the cause of delusion (*chī*)."
The Bódìsàtuo Jiāyè (Kāśyapa) said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) previously stated in the twelve divisions of the Sūtras (Qìjīng)
that non-virtuous reflection (improper mentation) is the condition
that gives rise to greed,
hatred, and delusion.
Why now, based on what condition, do you speak of ignorance?"
"Good man!
These two phenomena
are mutually cause and effect,
mutually promoting growth.
Non-virtuous reflection gives rise to ignorance,
and the conditions of ignorance give rise to non-virtuous reflection.
Good man!
Those things that can give rise to and increase afflictions
are all named the conditions for affliction.
Drawing near to such conditions for affliction
is named ignorance.
Non-virtuous reflection is like a seed sprouting a shoot:
the seed is the proximate cause,
and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the remote cause.
Afflictions are also like this."
The Bódìsàtuo Jiāyè (Kāśyapa) said to the Buddha (Fó):
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
According to what the Buddha (Fó) has preached,
ignorance is itself defilement;
how then can you also say
that due to ignorance, various defilements arise?"
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"Good man!
According to what I have taught,
the ignorance defilement
is internal ignorance.
That which, conditioned by ignorance,
gives rise to various defilements
is internal and external causation.
If I speak of the ignorance defilement,
this refers to internal inversion (error),
failing to recognize impermanence (*wúcháng*),
suffering (*kǔ*),
emptiness (*kōng*),
and non-self (*wúwǒ*).
If I speak of the conditions for all afflictions,
this refers to the lack of knowledge concerning external self
and what belongs to the self.
If I speak of the ignorance defilement,
this refers to beginninglessness and endlessness,
wherein the skandhas (*yīn*), āyatanas (*rù*), dhātus (*jiè*), etc., arise from ignorance.
The Bódìsàtuo Jiāyè (Kāśyapa) said to the Buddha (Fó):
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
According to what the Buddha (Fó) has preached,
the person of wisdom knows the cause of defilements.
What is meant by knowing the cause of defilements?"
"Good man!
The wise person should observe:
Due to what condition
do these afflictions arise?
What actions are created
that give rise to these afflictions?
During what time
do these afflictions arise?
While associating with whom
do these afflictions arise?
Dwelling in what location
do these afflictions arise?
Having observed what things
do afflictions arise?
Receiving whose housing,
bedding, food and drink,
clothing, or medicine
do afflictions arise?
Due to what condition
are lower [states] transformed into middle [states],
and middle [states] transformed into higher [states]?
Are lower deeds transformed into middle [deeds],
and middle deeds transformed into higher [deeds]?
When the Bódìsàtuo Móhēsà (Bodhisattva Mahāsattva) performs this observation,
he then gains separation from the conditions that give rise to defilements.
When observing in this manner,
afflictions that have not yet arisen are blocked and prevented from arising,
and afflictions that have already arisen are consequently eliminated.
Therefore, I state in the Canonical Scriptures (Qìjīng)
that the wise person should observe the causes that give rise to afflictions."
The Bódìsàtuo Jiāyè (Kāśyapa) said to the Buddha (Fó):
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
Since a sentient being has one body,
how can various kinds of afflictions arise?"
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
Just as in one vessel,
there are various kinds of seeds,
when they receive water and rain,
each one sprouts by itself.
Sentient beings are also like this;
although the vessel is one,
due to the causes and conditions of attachment (*ài*),
they are able to produce and grow various afflictions (*fánnǎo*).
Kāyè Púsà said:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
How do the wise contemplate retribution (*guǒbào*)?”
“Good man!
The wise should observe
that the causes and conditions of the outflows (*lòu*)
can produce hells (Dìyù),
hungry ghosts (Èguǐ),
and animals (Chùshēng).
These causes and conditions of outflows,
even when one obtains the body of a human or a deity (Rén Tiān shēn),
immediately entail impermanence (*wúcháng*),
suffering (*kǔ*),
emptiness (*kōng*),
and non-self (*wúwǒ*).
In this vessel of the body,
one obtains three kinds of suffering,
and three kinds of impermanence.
These causes and conditions of outflows
can cause sentient beings to commit the Five Heinous Crimes (Wǔ Nì Zuì),
to receive all kinds of evil retribution,
to sever the roots of goodness (*shàngēn*),
to violate the Four Gravest Prohibitions (Sì Chóng Jìn),
and to slander the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo).
The wise should observe:
‘Since I have already received such a body,
I ought not to give rise to such afflictions,
or suffer all kinds of evil consequences.’
Kāyè Púsà said:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
There is the fruit of no-outflows (*wúlòu guǒ*),
yet you say that the wise cut off all retribution.
Is the retribution of no-outflows included in what is cut off?
Do those who attain the Way possess the fruit of no-outflows?
If the wise seek the fruit of no-outflows,
how is it that the Buddha says that all the wise should cut off retribution?
If they cut it off,
how do the various Sages now possess it?”
“Good man!
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) sometimes speaks of the fruit based on the cause,
and sometimes speaks of the cause based on the fruit.
Just as worldly people say clay is the jar,
or thread is the cloth;
this is called speaking of the fruit based on the cause.
Speaking of the cause based on the fruit means
the cow is the water and grass,
and man is the food.
I also do the same.
Speaking of the fruit based on the cause:
I previously made this statement in the sūtras,
‘I proceed from the body of the mind up to the boundary of Brahmā-heaven (Fàntiān).’
This is called speaking of the fruit based on the cause.
Speaking of the cause based on the fruit:
these six sense bases (*liù rù*) are called past karma (*yè*);
this is called speaking of the cause based on the fruit.
Good man!
All Sages,
in reality, do not possess the retribution of no-outflows (*wúlòu guǒbào*).
The retribution arising from the cultivation of the Way by all Sages
does not give rise to outflows again;
therefore, it is called the retribution of no-outflows.
Good man!
When a wise person observes in this way,
they immediately attain the eternal cessation of the retribution of afflictions.
Good man!
Having observed, the wise person,
in order to cut off such retribution of afflictions,
practices the Noble Path (Shèng Dào).
The Noble Path consists of emptiness (*kōng*),
non-form (*wú xiàng*), and wishlessness (*wú yuàn*).
Having practiced this Way,
one can extinguish all retribution of afflictions.
Kāyè Púsà said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
All sentient beings obtain retribution from afflictions.
Afflictions are what are called evil.
The afflictions generated from evil afflictions
are also named evil.
Thus, afflictions have two types:
first, cause;
second, fruit.
Because the cause is evil, the fruit is evil;
because the fruit is evil, the seed (offspring) is evil.
Like the fruit of the *rènbó* tree,
because its seeds are bitter,
its flowers, fruits, stems, and leaves are all bitter.
It is like a poisonous tree:
because its seeds are poisonous,
its fruit is also poisonous.
The cause is also sentient beings,
the fruit is also sentient beings;
the cause is also affliction,
the fruit is also affliction.
The cause and fruit of affliction are sentient beings,
and sentient beings are the cause and fruit of affliction.
If this is the meaning,
how is it that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) previously used the analogy of the snowy mountains (Xuěshān) which contain both poisonous grasses
and the subtle medicinal king (*miào yàowáng*)?
If you say afflictions are sentient beings,
and sentient beings are afflictions,
how can you then say that within the body of a sentient being there is the subtle medicinal king?”
The Buddha said:
“Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
Innumerable sentient beings share this doubt.
Now you are able to bring it up and request resolution,
and I am able to resolve it.
Listen carefully,
listen carefully,
and reflect upon it well.
I shall now distinguish and explain it for you.
Good man!
The analogy of the snowy mountains (Xuěshān) is sentient beings;
what is called the poisonous grass is affliction (*fánnǎo*);
the subtle medicinal king is pure Brahmā-conduct (Jìng Fànhéng).
Good man!
If there are sentient beings
who can cultivate such pure Brahmā-conduct,
this is called having the subtle medicinal king within the body.
Kāyè Púsà said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
How do sentient beings possess pure Brahmā-conduct?”
“Good man!
Just as in the world a fruit is born from a seed,
this fruit sometimes can act as the cause for another seed,
and sometimes cannot.
If it is able to do so,
it is called a seed-fruit.
If it is unable to do so,
it can only be called a fruit,
and cannot be called a seed.
All sentient beings are also like this;
they all have two types:
First, those whose affliction-fruit is an affliction-cause;
second, those whose affliction-fruit is not an affliction-cause.
The affliction-fruit that is not an affliction-cause
is thus named pure Brahmā-conduct.
“Good man!
When sentient beings contemplate sensation (*shòu*),
they know it is the proximate cause of all outflows,
that is, internal and external outflows.
Due to the causes and conditions of sensation,
one cannot cut off all outflows,
nor can one escape the prison of the Three Realms (Sānjiè).
Sentient beings, because of sensation, cling to ‘I’
and ‘mine,’
giving rise to distorted views of mind (*xīndào*),
distorted views of perception (*xiǎngdào*),
and distorted views of insight (*jiàndào*).
Therefore, sentient beings must first contemplate sensation.
Such sensation
acts as the proximate cause for all attachment.
Therefore, the wise person who wishes to cut off attachment
must first contemplate sensation.
Good man!
The good and evil deeds performed by all sentient beings through the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (*Shí’èr Yīnyuán*),
are all due to the time of sensation.
Therefore, I spoke to Ānán, saying:
‘Ānán!
All good and evil deeds performed by sentient beings
occur at the time of sensation.’
Therefore, the wise person must first contemplate sensation.
Having contemplated sensation,
they must further contemplate:
‘By what cause and condition is this sensation born?
If it is born from causes and conditions,
where do these causes and conditions, in turn, arise?
If it is born without cause,
why, without a cause, is there not the birth of no-sensation?
One further observes that this sensation is not born from Īśvara (Zìzàitiān),
is not born from a creator god (Shìfū),
is not born from atoms (Wéichén),
is not born from time/seasons (Shíjié),
is not born from perception (*xiǎng*),
is not born from inherent nature (*xìng*),
it is not self-generated,
it is not generated by others,
it is not generated by both self and others,
and it is not generated without cause.
This sensation is entirely born from the combination of conditions.
The cause and condition is exactly attachment (*ài*).
In this combination,
there is neither sensation
nor non-sensation.
Therefore, I must cut off this combination;
when the combination is cut off, then sensation will not arise.”
"O good man!
The wise person, having contemplated the cause,
next contemplates the retribution.
Sentient beings, due to feeling,
receive (suffering) in the hells (dìyù),
hungry ghosts (èguǐ),
animals (chùshēng), and even the measureless suffering and vexations of the Three Realms (sānjiè).
Because of the condition of feeling,
they receive impermanent joy.
Because of the condition of feeling,
they sever wholesome roots (shàngēn).
Because of the condition of feeling,
they obtain liberation (jiětuō).
When making this contemplation,
they do not create the cause of feeling.
What is meant by 'not creating the cause of feeling'?
It means analyzing feeling.
What kind of feeling is able to create the cause of craving (ài)?
What kind of craving is able to create the cause of feeling?
O good man!
If sentient beings can deeply contemplate the cause of craving
and the cause of feeling in this way,
they will then be able to sever the self and that which belongs to the self.
O good man!
If a person can perform contemplations such as these,
they should then analyze where craving and feeling are extinguished.
They will immediately see that craving
and feeling have some places of extinction;
you should know that there must also be ultimate extinction.
At that time, confidence in liberation
arises immediately. Having generated this confidence,
by what means is this place of liberation obtained?
Knowing it is through the Eightfold Proper [Path] (Bāzhèng),
one immediately cultivates and practices it.
What is called the Eightfold Proper Path (Bāzhèngdào)?
This Path contemplates that feeling has three characteristics:
first, suffering (kǔ);
second, joy (lè);
third, neither suffering nor joy (bù kǔ bù lè).
These three types
are all capable of increasing the body and the mind.
By what condition are they able to increase?
The condition of contact (chù).
This contact is of three types:
first, contact based on ignorance (wúmíng chù);
second, contact based on clarity (míng chù);
third, contact based on neither clarity nor ignorance (fēi míng wúmíng chù).
That which is called contact based on clarity is the Eightfold Proper Path (Bāzhèngdào).
The remaining two types of contact increase the body, mind, and the three types of feeling.
Therefore, I should sever the conditional causes of those two types of contact.
When contact is severed, the three types of feeling do not arise.
O good man!
This feeling
is also called a cause
and is also called an effect (guǒ).
The wise person should contemplate it as both cause and effect.
How is it a cause?
Because craving arises from feeling,
it is called a cause.
How is it called an effect?
Because it arises from contact,
it is called an effect.
Therefore, this feeling is both cause and effect.
The wise person, having contemplated this feeling in this manner,
next contemplates craving (ài).
Because it receives retribution (as its consequence),
it is called craving.
The wise person contemplates that craving again has two types:
first, contaminated nourishment (záshí);
second, uncontaminated nourishment (wúshí).
Contaminated nourishment craving
is the cause of birth, aging, sickness, death, and all existences (yǒu).
Uncontaminated nourishment craving
severs birth, aging, sickness, death, and all existences;
and craves
the uncontaminated path (wúlòu dào).
The wise person should further generate this thought:
'If I generate this contaminated nourishment craving,
then I cannot sever birth, aging, sickness, and death.
Although I now crave the uncontaminated path,
if I do not sever the cause of feeling,
then I cannot attain the fruit of the uncontaminated path.
Therefore, I must first sever this contact (chù).
Once contact is severed,
feeling naturally ceases.
Once feeling is extinguished,
craving also ceases accordingly.
This is called the Eightfold Proper Path (Bāzhèngdào).'
O good man!
If there is a sentient being who can contemplate in this way,
although they possess a poisoned body,
within it there is also a subtle and wondrous King of Medicine (Yàowáng),
just like how in the Snow Mountains (Xuěshān), although there are poisonous herbs,
there are also wonderful medicines.
O good man!
Such a sentient being,
although receiving retribution stemming from defilement (fánnǎo),
that retribution will never again serve as a cause for defilement.
This is called pure Brahman practice (Qīngjìng Fànxíng)."
"Furthermore, O good man!
The wise person should contemplate: Feeling and craving—
by what condition do they arise?
They know they arise due to perception (xiǎng).
Why is this?
When sentient beings see form (sè), they do not necessarily generate greed,
and when contemplating feeling, they also do not generate greed,
but if they generate inverted perception (dǎoxiǎng) regarding form,
thinking that form is permanence, joy, self, and purity (cháng lè wǒ jìng),
or that feeling is constant and permanent without change,
due to this inverted perception, greed (tān), hatred (huì), and delusion (chī) arise.
Therefore, the wise person should contemplate perception.
How does one contemplate perception?
They should generate this thought:
All sentient beings who have not attained the Proper Path (Zhèngdào) possess inverted perception.
What is inverted perception?
Generating the perception of permanence regarding the non-permanent;
generating the perception of joy regarding the non-joyful;
generating the perception of purity regarding the non-pure;
generating the perception of self regarding empty phenomena.
Regarding things that are not male/female,
large/small,
day/night,
year/month,
clothing,
houses, or bedding,
generating perceptions from male/female up to bedding.
This perception has three types:
first, small (xiǎo);
second, great (dà);
third, boundless (wúbiān).
Due to small conditions, small perception arises.
Due to great conditions, great perception arises.
Due to measureless conditions, measureless perception arises.
Furthermore, there is small perception,
meaning before entering samādhi (dìng).
Furthermore, there is great perception,
meaning having already entered samādhi.
Furthermore, there is measureless perception,
meaning the Ten All-Bases (Shí Yīqiè Rù).
Furthermore, there is small perception,
meaning all perceptions of the desire realm (yùjiè), and so forth.
Furthermore, there is great perception,
meaning all perceptions of the form realm (sèjiè), and so forth.
Furthermore, there is measureless perception,
meaning all perceptions of the formless realm (wúsèjiè), and so forth.
When the three types of perception are extinguished,
feeling naturally ceases.
Since perception and feeling are extinguished, this is called liberation (jiětuō).
Bodhisattva Jiāshè (Kāśyapa) said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
The extinction of all phenomena (fǎ)
is called liberation.
How does the Tathāgata (Rúlái) say that the extinction of perception
and feeling
is called liberation?"
The Buddha said:
"O good man!
Sometimes the Tathāgata speaks by relying on (the needs of) sentient beings,
and the listeners understand the Dharma.
And sometimes He speaks about sentient beings by relying on the Dharma,
and the listeners also understand the speaking about sentient beings.
What is meant by 'speaking by relying on sentient beings,
where the listeners understand the Dharma'?
It is like when I previously spoke to Mahākāśyapa (Dà Jiāshè):
'O Jiāshè!
When sentient beings are extinguished,
wholesome phenomena are also extinguished.'
This is called speaking by relying on sentient beings,
where the listeners understand the Dharma.
What is meant by 'speaking about sentient beings by relying on the Dharma,
where the listeners also understand the speaking about sentient beings'?
It is like when I previously spoke to Ānán:
'I neither say to draw near to all phenomena,
nor do I say not to draw near to all phenomena.
If, having drawn near to a phenomenon,
wholesome phenomena decline and wane,
and unwholesome phenomena flourish,
such a phenomenon should not be drawn near to.
If, having drawn near to a phenomenon,
unwholesome phenomena diminish and cease,
and wholesome phenomena increase,
such a phenomenon should be drawn near to.
This is called speaking about sentient beings by relying on the Dharma,
where the listeners also understand the speaking about sentient beings."
"Shànnánzǐ!
Although the Rúlái speaks of the cessation of perception (xiǎng)
and sensation (shòu),
he has thereby comprehensively stated all that is severable.
When the wise person observes this perception,
he next observes the cause of perception.
How are these immeasurable perceptions born?
He knows they are born from contact (chù).
This contact is of two kinds:
The first is contact due to defilements (fánnǎo chù),
the second is contact due to liberation (jiětuō chù).
That which is born from ignorance (wúmíng) is called defiled contact;
that which is born from wisdom (míng) is called liberated contact.
From defiled contact arises inverted perception (dǎoxiǎng);
from liberated contact arises non-inverted perception (bù dǎoxiǎng).
Having observed the cause of perception,
he next observes the retribution (guǒbào).
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"Shìzūn!
If, because of this perception rooted in defilement,
inverted perception arises,
then all noble persons (shèngrén) truly have inverted perception but are free from defilement.
What does this meaning imply?"
The Buddha said:
"Shànnánzǐ!
How is it that a noble person possesses inverted perception?"
Jiāshè Púsà said:
"Shìzūn!
All noble persons perceive a cow as a cow,
and also say it is a cow.
They perceive a horse as a horse,
and also say it is a horse.
Men and women, large and small,
houses, vehicles,
coming and going, are all likewise perceived.
This is called inverted perception."
"Shànnánzǐ!
All ordinary beings (fánfū) possess two kinds of perception:
The first is worldly conventional perception (shìliúbù xiǎng),
the second is attachment perception (zhuó xiǎng).
All noble persons only have worldly conventional perception,
and do not have attachment perception.
Because all ordinary beings have evil reflection and examination (è juéguān),
they generate attachment perception regarding worldly conventions.
Because all noble persons have good reflection and examination (shàn juéguān),
they do not generate attachment perception regarding worldly conventions.
Therefore, ordinary beings are called [those with] inverted perception,
even though noble persons know [the conventions],
they are not called [those with] inverted perception.
The wise person, having thus observed the cause of perception,
next observes the retribution.
The retribution for this evil perception
is experienced in the hells (dìyù),
hungry ghosts (èguǐ),
animals (chùshēng),
or among humans and devas (rén tiān).
Just as I, by severing evil reflection and examination,
severed contact rooted in ignorance (wúmíng chù),
therefore perception is severed,
and because perception is severed,
the retribution is also severed.
The wise person, in order to sever the cause of this perception,
cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path (Bā Zhèng Dào).
Shànnánzǐ!
If someone is able to perform observations such as these,
he is then called one who practices pure asceticism (qīngjìng fànhéng).
Shànnánzǐ!
This is likened to the King of Wondrous Medicine residing within the poisonous bodies of sentient beings,
just as in the Snow Mountains (Xuěshān), although there are poisonous herbs, there are also wondrous medicines.
"Furthermore, Shànnánzǐ!
The wise person observes desire (yù).
Desire refers to form (sè),
sound (shēng),
fragrance (xiāng),
taste (wèi),
and touch (chù).
Shànnánzǐ!
This is the Rúlái speaking of the result based on the cause;
desire is merely generated from these five things,
but they are not truly desire themselves.
Shànnánzǐ!
Ignorant people crave and accept them.
They generate inverted perception regarding form,
and similarly generate inverted perception regarding touch.
Due to the condition of inverted perception, sensation (shòu) is then generated.
Therefore, the world speaks of the ten kinds of perception arising from inverted perception.
Due to the condition of desire,
one experiences evil retribution in the world,
inflicting evil upon one's parents,
Śrāmaṇas (shāmé),
Brāhmaṇas (póluómén), and others.
Things that ought not to be done are deliberately performed,
disregarding body and life.
Therefore, the wise person
observes that the mind of desire arises due to the condition of evil perception.
The wise person, having thus observed the cause of desire,
next observes the retribution.
This desire yields many kinds of evil retribution,
namely, the hells (dìyù),
hungry ghosts (èguǐ),
animals (chùshēng),
among humans,
and in the heavens (tiānshàng).
This is called the observation of retribution.
If this evil perception is eliminated,
then the mind of desire will never arise.
Without the mind of desire, one does not experience evil sensation.
Without evil sensation, there is no evil result.
Therefore, I should first sever evil perception,
and once evil perception is severed,
phenomena such as these will naturally cease.
Therefore, the wise person cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path (Bā Zhèng Dào) in order to eliminate evil perception.
This is then called practicing pure asceticism (qīngjìng fànhéng).
This is likened to the King of Wondrous Medicine residing within the poisonous bodies of sentient beings,
just as in the Snow Mountains (Xuěshān), although there are poisonous herbs, there are also wondrous medicines.
"Furthermore, Shànnánzǐ!
The wise person, having observed this desire thus,
should next observe karma (yè).
Why is this?
The wise person should have this thought:
Sensation (shòu),
perception (xiǎng),
contact, and desire (chù yù) are defilements (fánnǎo).
These defilements
can create the karma that leads to future birth (shēng yè),
but cannot create the karma that leads to retribution/experience (shòu yè).
When defilements such as these act in conjunction with karma,
there are two kinds:
First, the karma that creates future birth (shēng yè);
second, the karma that creates experience (shòu yè).
Therefore, the wise person should observe karma.
This karma is of three kinds:
namely, body (shēn),
speech (kǒu),
and mind (yì).
Shànnánzǐ!
The two karmas of body and speech
are called karma,
and are also called the fruits of karma (yè guǒ).
The mind is only called karma,
and is not called the fruit,
but because it is the cause of karma,
it is called karma.
Shànnánzǐ!
The two karmas of body
and speech are called external karma (wài yè),
and mental karma (yì yè) is called internal.
Since these three kinds of karma function together with defilements,
they produce two kinds of karma:
First, the karma that creates future birth (shēng yè);
second, the karma that creates experience (shòu yè).
Shànnánzǐ!
Principal karma (zhèng yè) is mental karma (yì yè),
subsidiary karma (qī yè) refers to bodily
and vocal karma (shēn kǒu yè).
Because the mind arises first, it is called mental karma.
That which arises from mental karma
is called bodily
and vocal karma.
Therefore, mental karma is designated as principal.
Having observed karma, the wise person
next observes the cause of karma.
The cause of karma is contact rooted in ignorance (wúmíng chù).
Due to contact rooted in ignorance, sentient beings seek existence (qiú yǒu).
The condition for seeking existence is craving (ài).
Due to the condition of craving, they create the three kinds of karma: body,
speech,
and mind.
Shànnánzǐ!
The wise person, having thus observed the cause of karma,
next observes the retribution.
There are four kinds of retribution:
The first is black karma leading to black retribution (hēi hēi guǒbào);
the second is white karma leading to white retribution (bái bái guǒbào);
the third is mixed karma leading to mixed retribution (zázá guǒbào);
the fourth is neither black nor white karma leading to neither black nor white retribution (bù hēi bù bái bù hēi bù bái guǒbào).
Regarding black karma leading to black retribution:
The action is defiled (gòu),
and the retribution is also defiled.
Regarding white karma leading to white retribution:
The action is pure (jìng),
and the retribution is also pure.
Regarding mixed karma leading to mixed retribution:
The action is mixed,
and the retribution is also mixed.
Regarding neither black nor white karma leading to neither black nor white retribution:
This is called undefiled karma (wúlòu yè).
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"Shìzūn!
Previously, it was said that the undefiled (wúlòu) does not have retribution.
Now, why do you speak of neither black nor white retribution?"
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
This meaning has two parts:
The first is both result (guǒ) and requital (bào);
The second is only result (guǒ) but not requital (bào).
The result and requital of dark-dark [karma] is also called the result (guǒ),
and is also called the requital (bào).
Because it arises from a dark cause, it is called the result (guǒ);
because it is able to act as a cause for others, it is also called the requital (bào).
The pure-mixed [karma] is also like this.
The result of wúlòu (taintless) [karma],
arises due to yǒulòu (tainted) [karma],
thus it is called the result (guǒ),
but because it does not act as a cause for others,
it is not called the requital (bào).
Therefore, it is called the result (guǒ) but not the requital (bào).
Jiāyè Púsà said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
This wúlòu karma is not a dark phenomenon (fǎ),
for what reason is it not called white?”
“Good man!
Because there is no requital (bào),
it is not called white.
Since it counteracts the dark [karma],
it is provisionally called white.
I now say that what receives result and requital is named white,
but since this wúlòu karma does not receive requital,
it is not called white,
but is named tranquil stillness (jíjìng).
Such types of karma have definite places where their requitals are received.
For example, the ten evil laws definitely result in hell (dìyù),
hungry ghosts (èguǐ),
and animals (chùshēng).
The karma of the ten virtues definitely results in humans (rén) and
heavenly beings (tiān).
The ten non-virtuous laws have superior,
medium,
and inferior grades.
Due to superior conditions, one receives a hell body;
due to medium conditions, one receives an animal body;
due to inferior conditions, one receives a hungry ghost body.
The human karma of the ten virtues further has four types:
First is inferior,
second is medium,
third is superior,
and fourth is superior-superior.
Due to inferior conditions, one is born in Yùdānyuè.
Due to medium conditions, one is born in Fúpo tí.
Due to superior conditions, one is born in Qútuóní.
Due to superior-superior conditions, one is born in Yánfú tí.
When an intelligent person has made this observation,
they immediately think this:
‘How shall I cut off this result and requital?’
They further think this:
‘This karma arises due to the conditions of ignorance (wúmíng) and contact (chù).
If I cut off ignorance and contact,
such karmic results will cease and not arise.’
Therefore, the wise person, in order to sever the conditions of ignorance and contact,
cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path (Bāzhèngdào).
This is then called pure Brahmā practice (fànxíng).
Good man!
This is called the king of wondrous medicines within the poisoned body of sentient beings,
just as in the Snowy Mountains (Xuěshān) there are both poisonous grasses and wondrous medicines.
“Furthermore, good man!
After the wise person has observed karma and observed afflictions (fánnǎo),
they next observe the result and requital obtained from these two.
These two results and requitals are suffering (kǔ).
Having known this suffering, one is then able to relinquish all reception of rebirth.
The wise person further observes:
Afflictions arise due to the conditions of afflictions;
Afflictions also arise due to the conditions of karma;
Karma arises again due to the conditions of afflictions;
Suffering arises due to the conditions of karma;
Afflictions arise due to the conditions of suffering;
Existence (yǒu) arises due to the conditions of afflictions;
Suffering arises due to the conditions of existence;
Existence arises due to the conditions of existence;
Karma arises due to the conditions of existence;
Afflictions arise due to the conditions of karma;
Suffering arises due to the conditions of afflictions;
Suffering arises due to the conditions of suffering.
Good man!
If a wise person can make observations like these,
you should know that this person is capable of observing the suffering of karma.
Why is that?
What has been observed above
is precisely the twelve links of dependent origination (shí'èr yīnyuán) of transmigration (shēngsǐ).
If a person is able to observe these twelve links of dependent origination of transmigration,
you should know that this person does not create new karma,
and is able to destroy old karma.
Good man!
The intelligent person observes the suffering of hell,
observing one hell up to one hundred and thirty-six places.
Each and every hell has various types of suffering,
all arising from the conditions of afflictions and karma.
Having observed the hells,
they next observe the suffering of hungry ghosts
and animals, and so forth.
Having made this observation,
they further observe all the suffering that exists among humans and heavenly beings.
All these sufferings,
all arise from the conditions of afflictions and karma.
Good man!
Although there are no great suffering matters in heaven,
yet when their bodies, which are soft and delicate,
see the five signs of decay (wǔ xiàng), they endure extreme suffering,
which is no different from the suffering of hell.
Good man!
The wise person profoundly observes that all sufferings in the Three Realms (Sānjiè),
all arise from the conditions of afflictions and karma.
Good man!
For example, a cracked vessel
is easily broken.
Sentient beings receiving a body are also like this;
once a body has been received, it is a vessel for all sufferings.
For example, although a large tree has flourishing flowers and fruits, many birds can damage it;
or like abundant dry grass that a small fire can consume.
Sentient beings receiving a body are destroyed by suffering,
and this is also true.
Good man!
If the wise person can observe the eight types of suffering (bā kǔ), as taught in the Noble Practice (Shèngxíng),
you should know that this person can sever all sufferings.
Good man!
When the wise person has profoundly observed these eight sufferings,
they next observe the cause of suffering.
The cause of suffering
is craving (ài) and ignorance (wúmíng).
This craving and ignorance then have two types:
The first is seeking the body,
the second is seeking wealth.
Seeking the body and seeking wealth,
both are suffering.
Therefore, you should know that craving and ignorance
are precisely the cause of suffering.
Good man!
This craving and ignorance
then have two types:
The first is internal (nèi),
the second is external (wài).
The internal is capable of creating karma,
the external is capable of augmenting it.
Furthermore, the internal is capable of creating karma,
the external is the result of that karma.
Once internal craving is severed,
karma is severed.
Once external craving is severed,
the result is severed.
Internal craving can give rise to the suffering of future existences,
external craving can give rise to the suffering of the present existence.
The wise person observes that craving
is precisely the cause of suffering.
Having observed the cause,
they next observe the result and requital.
The result and requital of suffering
is clinging (qǔ).
The result of craving is named clinging.
The conditions for this clinging are internal and external craving,
and thus there is the suffering of craving.
Good man!
The wise person should observe:
Clinging arises due to the conditions of craving,
and craving arises due to the conditions of clinging.
If I can sever craving
and clinging—these two matters—
then I will not create karma and receive all sufferings.
Therefore, the wise person, in order to sever the suffering of craving,
cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path (Bāzhèngdào).
Good man!
If a person can observe in this manner,
this is then called pure Brahmā practice (Qīngjìng Fànxíng).
This is called the king of wondrous medicines within the poisoned body of sentient beings,
just as in the Snowy Mountains (Xuěshān) there are both poisonous grasses and wondrous medicines.
Jiāyè Púsà said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
What is called pure Brahmā practice (Qīngjìng Fànxíng)?”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
It is all phenomena (yīqiè fǎ).”
Jiāyè Púsà said:
“World-Honored One!
As for all phenomena,
the meaning is not fixed.
Why is that?
The Tathāgata sometimes speaks of it as virtuous and non-virtuous;
sometimes speaks of it as the contemplation of the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Sì Niànchù Guān);
sometimes speaks of it as the Twelve Bases (Shí'èr Rù);
sometimes speaks of it as a spiritual friend (Shànzhīshi);
sometimes speaks of it as the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (Shí'èr Yīnyuán);
sometimes speaks of it as sentient beings;
sometimes speaks of it as right view and wrong view (Zhèngjiàn Xiéjiàn);
sometimes speaks of it as the Twelve Divisions of the Scriptures (Shí'èr Bù Jīng);
sometimes speaks of it as the Two Truths (Èr Dì).
But now the Tathāgata states
that all phenomena are the pure Brahmā practice (jìng fànxíng).
Which 'all phenomena' are these exactly?”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
This subtle and marvelous Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (Dà Nièpán Jīng)
is truly the treasury of all good dharmas.
Just as the great ocean is the repository of many treasures,
so too is this Nièpán Jīng;
it is the secret treasury of all characters and meanings.
Good man!
Just as Mount Xūmí is the foundation of all herbs,
this sūtra is also like that;
it is the root of the Púsà Precepts.
Good man!
Just as space is the abiding place for all things,
this sūtra is also like that;
it is the abiding place for all good dharmas.
Good man!
Just as a fierce wind cannot be bound by anything,
this sūtra is also like that:
it is not bound by any afflictions (fánnǎo) or evil dharmas.
Good man!
Just as a vajra (jīngāng) cannot be destroyed by anything,
this sūtra is also like that;
even if there are heterodox (wàidào) and wicked, perverse people,
they cannot destroy it.
Good man!
Just as the sands of the Hénghé River cannot be counted,
the meanings of this sūtra are also like that:
they cannot be counted.
Good man!
This classic serves as the Dharma banner for the Púsàs,
like the banner of Dìshì.
Good man!
This sūtra is the chief merchant (shāngzhǔ) leading the way to the city of Nièpán,
just as a great guide leads merchants toward the great ocean.
Good man!
This sūtra can serve as the Dharma light for the Púsàs,
just as the sun and moon of the world can break through all darkness.
Good man!
This sūtra can act as a great excellent medicine for sentient beings afflicted by illness,
just like the subtle and marvelous King of Medicines in Xiāng Shān (Fragrant Mountain) that can cure all diseases.
Good man!
This sūtra can act as a staff for the Yīchǎntí,
just as a feeble person is able to rise because of it.
Good man!
This sūtra can serve as a bridge for all wicked people,
just as a worldly bridge can carry everyone across.
Good man!
This sūtra can provide cool shade
for those traversing the twenty-five existences who encounter the heat of affliction (fánnǎo),
just like a worldly canopy
that shelters
against the scorching heat.
Good man!
This sūtra is the great King of Fearlessness,
able to destroy all demonic afflictions (fánnǎo èmó),
just as the Lion King subdues all beasts.
Good man!
This sūtra is the great divine spell master (dà shén zhòushī),
able to destroy all wicked ghosts of affliction,
just as a worldly spell master can expel specters.
Good man!
This sūtra is the unsurpassed frost and hail,
able to destroy all karmic retribution of life and death,
just as worldly hailstones ruin fruits.
Good man!
This sūtra can serve as a great excellent medicine for those whose sight of the precepts is damaged,
just as the worldly medicine Ānshénà skillfully heals eye pain.
Good man!
This sūtra is able to uphold all good dharmas,
just as the ground in the world can uphold all things.
Good man!
This sūtra is the clear mirror for sentient beings who have broken the precepts,
just as a clear worldly mirror reflects all forms.
Good man!
This sūtra can serve as clothing for those lacking shame and remorse,
just as worldly garments conceal the body.
Good man!
This sūtra can serve as great wealth and treasure for those poor in good dharmas,
just as Gōngdé Tiān benefits the poor.
Good man!
This sūtra can serve as the nectar beverage for sentient beings thirsty for Dharma,
just as water of eight merits satisfies the thirsty.
Good man!
This sūtra can serve as the Dharma bed for people afflicted by fánnǎo,
just as worldly people find a comfortable bed.
Good man!
For Púsàs from the First Bhūmi (Chū Dì) up to the Púsàs of the Ten Abodes (Shí Zhù),
this sūtra serves as necklaces and pendants (yīngluò),
fragrant flowers and ointments,
powdered incense and burnt incense,
and the vehicle that fulfills pure lineage and nature,
surpassing all places of marvelous joy attained through the Six Pāramitās (Liù Bōluómì),
like the Pārijāta tree in Dāolì Heaven.
"Good man!
This sūtra is the sharp and strong Axe of Wisdom that can fell all great trees of affliction;
it is the sharp knife that can sever habitual tendencies;
it is the heroic strength that can crush the enmity of Māra;
it is the Fire of Wisdom that burns the firewood of affliction;
it is the treasury of interdependent origination that produces the Bìzhī Fó;
it is the treasury of hearing that gives rise to the Shēngwén Rén;
it is the eye of all heavenly beings;
it is the correct path for all human beings;
it is the refuge for all animals;
it is the place of liberation for hungry ghosts;
it is the unsurpassed venerated one for those in the hells;
it is the unsurpassed vessel for all sentient beings in the ten directions;
it is the parent of all Buddhas, past, future, and present, in the ten directions.
Good man!
Therefore, this sūtra encompasses all dharmas.
As I stated earlier,
although this sūtra encompasses all dharmas,
I declare that pure conduct (fànxíng) is the Thirty-seven Aids to the Way (sānshíqī zhù dàofǎ).
Good man!
If one departs from these Thirty-seven Factors (Sānshíqī Pǐn),
one will ultimately be unable to attain the true fruit of the Śrāvaka, or even the fruit of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòuduōluō Sānmiǎo Sānpútí);
one will not see the Buddha-nature (Fóxìng) nor the fruit of Fóxìng.
For this reason, pure conduct is the Thirty-seven Factors.
Why is this?
The nature of the Thirty-seven Factors is non-perverse;
it can destroy perversity (diāndǎo);
its nature is not wicked view;
it can destroy wicked view;
its nature is not fear;
it can destroy fear;
its nature is pure practice;
it enables sentient beings ultimately to create and practice pure Fànxíng.
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
Defiled dharmas (yǒulòu zhī fǎ)
are also able to act as causes for undefiled dharmas (wúlòu fǎ).
Why does the Tathāgata not declare defiled dharmas to be pure Fànxíng?"
"Good man!
All defiled dharmas are perversity;
therefore, defiled dharmas cannot be called pure Fànxíng.
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
Is the World-Supremost Dharma (Shì Dìyī Fǎ)
defiled,
or undefiled?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
It is defiled.
"World-Honored One!
Although it is defiled,
its nature is not perverse.
Why is it not called pure Fànxíng?
"Good man!
The Shì Dìyī Fǎ,
because it is the cause of the undefiled, resembles the undefiled.
Because it approaches the undefiled, it is not called perversity.
Good man!
Pure Fànxíng requires the continuous and ultimate resolve of the mind.
The Shì Dìyī Fǎ is merely a single moment;
therefore, it cannot be called pure Fànxíng.
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
The five consciousnesses of sentient beings are also defiled,
but they are not perversity,
nor are they merely a single moment.
Why are they not called pure Fànxíng?
"Good man!
Although the five consciousnesses of sentient beings are not merely a single moment,
they are defiled,
and moreover, they are perversity.
Because they increase defilements,
they are called defiled.
Their essence is not reality;
attachment to conceptualization causes perversity.
How is it that their essence is not reality
and attachment to conceptualization causes perversity?
Conceptions of male and female arise where there is neither male nor female;
the same applies to houses, carriages, jars, and clothing.
This is called perversity.
Good man!
The nature of the Thirty-seven Factors is without perversity,
therefore they are rightly named pure Fànxíng.
Good man!
If a Púsà, regarding the Thirty-seven Factors,
knows the root,
knows the cause,
knows the comprehension,
knows the increase,
knows the master,
knows the guide,
knows the supremacy,
knows the reality,
and knows the ultimate end,
such a Púsà is then called one who possesses pure Fànxíng.
Jiāshè Púsà said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
How does one define knowing the root, up to knowing the ultimate end?"
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
Excellent,
excellent.
The *Pú sà* (Bodhisattva) asks questions concerning two matters:
First, for self-knowledge;
second, for the knowledge of others.
You now already know,
but because innumerable sentient beings have not yet understood,
you request this matter,
therefore I now again praise you.
Excellent,
excellent!
Good man!
The Thirty-Seven Components (*Sān shí qī pǐn*),
the root is desire (*yù*);
the cause is called luminosity/understanding (*míng*) and contact (*chù*);
gathering/inclusion is called feeling (*shòu*);
increase is called wholesome volition (*shàn sī*);
the master is called mindfulness (*niàn*);
the guide is called concentration (*dìng*);
the superior is called wisdom (*zhì huì*);
the real is called liberation (*jiě tuō*);
the ultimate is called Great *Bō bān Niè pán* (Mahāparinirvāṇa).
Good man!
Wholesome desire (*Shàn yù*) is precisely the first arousal of the mind for the Way (Dào),
extending even to the root of *Ā nòu duō luó Sān miǎo Sān pú tí* (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi),
therefore I say desire (*yù*) is the root.
Good man!
Just as it is said in the world,
all suffering and distress,
craving (*ài*) is the root;
all chronic diseases,
stagnant food is the basis;
all lawsuits,
contention is the basis.
All evil deeds,
falsehood is the basis.”
*Jiā shè Pú sà* (Kāśyapa Bodhisattva) said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One (*Shì zūn*)!
The *Rú lái* (Tathāgata) previously said in this scripture
that non-negligence (*bù fàng yì*) is the basis of all wholesome *dharmas*,
but now you speak of desire (*yù*).
What is the meaning of this?”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
If speaking of the generative cause,
it is wholesome desire (*shàn yù*);
if speaking of the manifestive cause,
it is non-negligence.
Just as it is said in the world,
for all fruits, the seed is the cause.
Or again, there are those who say,
the seed is the generative cause,
the earth is the manifestive cause,
the meaning here is also thus.”
*Jiā shè Pú sà* said:
“World-Honored One!
The *Rú lái* previously said in other scriptures
that the Buddha is the root of the Thirty-Seven Components.
What is the meaning of this?”
“Good man!
The *Rú lái* previously spoke
that when sentient beings first know the Thirty-Seven Components,
the Buddha is the root.
If one realizes it oneself,
desire (*yù*) is the root.”
“World-Honored One!
How is luminosity/understanding and contact (*míng chù*),
named as the cause?”
“Good man!
The *Rú lái* sometimes calls luminosity/understanding wisdom (*huì*),
or sometimes calls it faith (*xìn*).
Good man!
Because of faith,
one draws near to wholesome friends,
this is called contact (*chù*).
Because of drawing near,
one obtains hearing the correct Dharma,
this is called contact (*chù*).
Because of hearing the correct Dharma,
body, speech, and mind are purified,
this is called contact (*chù*).
Because of the purity of the three actions (karma),
one obtains right livelihood (*zhèng mìng*),
this is called contact (*chù*).
Because of right livelihood,
one obtains the precepts of pure faculties;
because of the precepts of pure faculties,
one delights in secluded dwelling places;
because of delighting in seclusion,
one is able to wisely contemplate;
because of wise contemplation,
one obtains dwelling in accordance with the Dharma;
because of dwelling in accordance with the Dharma,
one obtains the Thirty-Seven Components,
and is able to destroy innumerable evil afflictions (*fán nǎo*),
this is called contact (*chù*).
Good man!
Feeling (*Shòu*) is called gathering/inclusion (*shè qǔ*).
When sentient beings experience feeling, they can generate wholesome or unwholesome deeds,
therefore feeling (*shòu*) is named gathering/inclusion.
Good man!
Because of feeling, various afflictions arise.
The Thirty-Seven Components are able to destroy them,
therefore feeling (*shòu*) is taken as gathering/inclusion.
Because of wholesome contemplation, one can destroy afflictions,
therefore it is named increase.
Why is this?
Because of diligent cultivation and practice.
Having obtained these Thirty-Seven Components,
if one contemplates the ability to destroy all evil afflictions,
it relies necessarily on focused mindfulness (*zhuān niàn*),
therefore mindfulness (*niàn*) is taken as the master.
Just as in the world all four divisions of the army follow the intent of the main general,
the Thirty-Seven Components are also like this;
they all follow the master of mindfulness.
Good man!
Once one has entered concentration (*dìng*),
the Thirty-Seven Components are able to properly differentiate the characteristics of all *dharmas* (*fǎ xiàng*),
therefore concentration (*dìng*) is taken as the guide.
In these Thirty-Seven Components differentiating the characteristics of *dharmas*,
wisdom (*zhì*) is the most superior,
therefore insight (*huì*) is taken as superior.
When such wisdom knows the afflictions,
by the power of wisdom,
the afflictions perish,
just as in the world the four divisions of the army destroy the enemy,
or one
or two brave and strong individuals can do it.
The Thirty-Seven Components are also thus;
by the power of wisdom, they can destroy afflictions,
therefore insight (*huì*) is taken as superior.
Good man!
Although by cultivating and practicing the Thirty-Seven Components,
one obtains the bliss of the Four *Chán* (Dhyānas) and supernormal powers (*shén tōng*),
it is still not named the real.
Only when one destroys afflictions and realizes liberation (*jiě tuō*),
is it named the real.
These Thirty-Seven Components, when generating the mind and cultivating the Way (Dào),
though one attains worldly bliss and supramundane bliss,
the Four *Shā mén* (Śramaṇa) Fruits, and liberation,
it still cannot be named the ultimate (*bì jìng*).
If one can cut off and eliminate the actions performed by the Thirty-Seven Components,
this is named *Niè pán* (Nirvāṇa),
therefore I say that the ultimate is precisely Great *Niè pán*.
“Furthermore, good man!
The mind that lovingly remembers wholesomeness (*shàn ài niàn xīn*),
this is precisely desire (*yù*).
Because of loving remembrance of wholesomeness,
one draws near to wholesome friends,
thus it is named contact (*chù*),
this is named the cause.
Because of drawing near to wholesome friends,
thus it is named feeling (*shòu*),
this is named gathering/inclusion.
Because of drawing near to wholesome friends, one is able to wisely contemplate,
thus it is named increase.
Because of these four *dharmas*, the Way (Dào) can be grown,
namely desire (*yù*),
mindfulness (*niàn*),
concentration (*dìng*),
and wisdom (*zhì*).
These are named the master, guide, and superior.
Because of these three *dharmas*,
one obtains the two liberations:
by eliminating and cutting off craving (*ài*),
the mind obtains liberation (*xīn dé jiě tuō*);
by cutting off ignorance (*wú míng*),
insight obtains liberation (*huì dé jiě tuō*).
This is named the real.
These eight *dharmas*,
when ultimately attaining the fruit,
are named *Niè pán*,
thus it is named the ultimate.
“Furthermore, good man,
desire (*yù*) is precisely generating the mind and leaving home;
contact (*chù*) is precisely the four-part official motion (*bái sì jié mò*),
this is named the cause.
Inclusion (*shè*) is precisely receiving the two types of precepts:
first, the *Bō luó tí mù chā* (Prātimokṣa) precepts,
second, the precepts of pure faculties (*jìng gēn jiè*);
this is named feeling (*shòu*),
this is named gathering/inclusion.
Increase (*zēng*) is precisely cultivating and practicing the Four *Chán* (Dhyānas).
The master (*zhǔ*) is precisely the fruit of *Xū tuó huán* (Srotāpanna)
and the fruit of *Sī tuó hán* (Sakṛdāgāmin).
The guide (*dǎo*) is precisely the fruit of *Ā nà hán* (Anāgāmin).
The superior (*shèng*) is precisely the fruit of *Ā luó hàn* (Arhat).
The real (*shí*) is precisely the fruit of *Pì zhī fó* (Pratyekabuddha).
The ultimate (*bì jìng*) is precisely the fruit of *Ā nòu duō luó Sān miǎo Sān pú tí* (Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi).
"Furthermore, good man!
Desire (Yù) is named consciousness (Shì);
contact (Chù) is named the six sense bases (Liù Rù);
grasping (Shè) is named feeling (Shòu);
increase (Zēng) is named ignorance (Wúmíng);
foundation (Zhǔ) is named name and form (Míngsè);
