leading (Dǎo) is named craving (Ài);
triumph (Shèng) is named clinging (Qǔ);
reality (Shí) is named existence (Yǒu);
ultimate conclusion (Bìjìng zhě) is named birth, aging, sickness, and death (Shēng lǎo bìng sǐ)."
Kūshè Púsà said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
Fundamental root (gēnběn),
cause (yīn),
increase (zēng)—
how do these three Dharma differ?"
"Good man!
What is called the root (gēn) is the initial arising;
the cause (yīn) is the continuous similarity;
the increase (zēng) is that which, after destroying the similarity, is still able to produce similarity.
Furthermore, good man!
The root (gēn) is the action (zuò);
the cause (yīn) is the result (guǒ);
the increase (zēng) is the utility (kěyòng).
Good man!
Although there is retribution (guǒbào) in future ages,
because it has not yet been experienced,
it is named the cause (yīn).
When it is experienced,
this is named the increase (zēng).
Furthermore, good man!
The root (gēn) is seeking (qiú);
acquisition (dé) is the cause (yīn);
usage (yòng) is the increase (zēng).
Good man!
In this sūtra, the root (gēn) is the Path of Seeing (Jiàndào);
the cause (yīn) is the Path of Cultivation (Xiūdào);
the increase (zēng) is the Path of No More Learning (Wúxuédào).
Furthermore, good man!
The root (gēn) is the principal cause (zhèngyīn);
the cause (yīn) is the expedient cause (fāngbiàn yīn);
from these two causes,
the retribution (guǒbào) is obtained,
which is named proliferation (zēngzhǎng)."
Kūshè Púsà said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
As the Buddha (Fó) has stated,
the ultimate conclusion (bìjìng zhě) is Nirvāṇa (Nièpán);
how can such Nirvāṇa be attained?"
"Good man!
If a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva (Púsà Móhēsà),
Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū),
Bhikṣuṇī (Bǐqiūní),
Upāsaka (Yōupósè),
or Upāsikā (Yōupóyí) can cultivate the ten contemplations (shí xiǎng),
know that this person can attain Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
What are these ten?
First, the contemplation of impermanence (Wúcháng Xiǎng);
second, the contemplation of suffering (Kǔ Xiǎng);
third, the contemplation of non-self (Wúwǒ Xiǎng);
fourth, the contemplation of repulsion toward food (Yànlí Shí Xiǎng);
fifth, the contemplation of the undesirability of all worldly things (Yīqiè Shìjiān Bùkělè Xiǎng);
sixth, the contemplation of death (Sǐ Xiǎng);
seventh, the contemplation of great fault and defilement (Duō Guòzuì Xiǎng);
eighth, the contemplation of detachment (Lí Xiǎng);
ninth, the contemplation of cessation (Miè Xiǎng);
tenth, the contemplation of non-craving (Wú'ài Xiǎng).
Good man!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas (Púsà Móhēsà),
Bhikṣus (Bǐqiū),
Bhikṣuṇīs (Bǐqiūní),
Upāsakas (Yōupósè),
and Upāsikās (Yōupóyí),
who cultivate these ten types of contemplation,
these people will ultimately and certainly attain Nirvāṇa (Nièpán).
Not following the minds of others,
they can personally distinguish the wholesome (shàn)
and the unwholesome (bù shàn), etc.
This is named the true meaning that corresponds to a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū),
up to and including the meaning that corresponds to an Upāsikā (Yōupóyí)."
Kūshè Púsà said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
How is it named that a Bodhisattva (Púsà) down to an Upāsikā (Yōupóyí), etc., cultivates the contemplation of impermanence (Wúcháng Xiǎng)?"
"Good man!
There are two types of Bódhisàttva (Púsà):
first, those who initially generate the thought (of enlightenment);
second, those who have already practiced the Way.
The perception of impermanence (wúcháng xiǎng),
is also of two types:
first, coarse (cū);
second, subtle (xì).
When the beginner Bódhisàttva contemplates the perception of impermanence,
he makes this reflection:
'Worldly things are generally of two kinds:
first, internal;
second, external.
Such internal things,
are impermanent and changing.
I see the time of birth,
the time of childhood,
the time of growth,
the time of vigor,
the time of old age,
the time of death.
These various periods are all different;
therefore, one should know that internal things are impermanent.
Furthermore, he has this thought:
'I see sentient beings,
some are healthy and strong,
fully endowed with physical form and vigor,
coming, going, advancing, and stopping freely and unimpeded.
Others I see suffering illness,
their form and vigor wasted and withered,
their countenance emaciated and damaged,
unable to be free.
Others I see possessing wealth,
their treasuries overflowing.
Others I see poor,
lacking in every endeavor.
Others I see attaining immeasurable merit and virtue (gōngdé).
Others I see fully equipped with immeasurable evil dharmas (è fà).
Therefore, it is definitively known that internal dharmas (nèi fà) are impermanent.
Furthermore, contemplating external dharmas (wài fà):
the time of the seed,
the time of the sprout,
the time of the stalk,
the time of the leaf,
the time of the flower,
the time of the fruit.
These various periods are all different.
Such external dharmas
are sometimes fully complete, or sometimes not fully complete.
Therefore, one should know
that all external things are definitively impermanent.
Having contemplated the visible dharmas as impermanent,
he further contemplates the heard dharmas.
I have heard that all the devas (zhū tiān), fully achieving the most exquisite happiness
and supernatural powers (shéntōng) and freedom,
also exhibit the Five Signs (wǔ xiàng);
therefore, one should know that they are immediately impermanent.
I have also heard that in the beginning of the kalpa (jié), there were sentient beings,
each fully equipped with supreme and marvelous merit and virtue (gōngdé).
Their body light shone by itself, not relying on the sun or moon,
but due to the power of impermanence (wúcháng), the light faded and the virtue diminished.
I have also heard that in the past there were Wheel-Turning Sage Kings (Zhuǎnlún Shèngwáng) who governed the four continents (sì tiānxià),
achieved the Seven Treasures (qī bǎo),
and attained great sovereignty,
yet they could not destroy the characteristic of impermanence.
Furthermore, contemplating the Great Earth (dà dì):
in ancient times,
it accommodated and sustained immeasurable sentient beings,
with no empty space
even the size of a carriage wheel,
and fully gave rise to all wonderful herbs;
thickets,
trees,
and fruits flourished.
Because sentient beings possessed meager fortune,
this Great Earth lost its power,
and the things it produced consequently became scarce and withered.
Therefore, one should know
that internal and external dharmas are all impermanent.
This is called coarse impermanence (cū wúcháng).
Having contemplated the coarse,
next he contemplates the subtle.
What is called subtle?
The Bódhisàttva Màhāsàttva (Púsà Màhāsàttva) contemplates all internal and external things, down to a tiny particle (wēichén),
realizing that they are already impermanent even in the future time.
Why is this?
Because they are fully equipped with the characteristic of destruction and disintegration.
If future form were not impermanent,
it could not be said that form has the differentiation of ten periods.
What are these ten periods?
First, the time of the membrane;
second, the time of the bubble;
third, the time of the blister;
fourth, the time of the flesh lump;
fifth, the time of the limbs;
sixth, the time of the infant;
seventh, the time of the child;
eighth, the time of the youth;
ninth, the time of full vigor;
tenth, the time of decline and old age.
If the Bódhisàttva observes that the membrane were not impermanent,
it ought not progress to the bubble, nor even up to full vigor.
If it were not impermanent, it would ultimately not reach old age.
If these various periods
did not perish moment by moment (niàn niàn miè),
they would ultimately not grow gradually;
they ought to reach full growth and completeness all at once.
Since this is not the case,
therefore one should know
that there is definitively subtle impermanence (wēixì wúcháng) occurring moment by moment.
Furthermore, seeing a person
fully endowed with all faculties (zhū gēn),
whose appearance is radiant and brilliant,
but later seeing him withered and frail.
He makes this further reflection:
'This person definitively experiences moment-by-moment impermanence.'
Furthermore, he contemplates the four elements (sì dà) and the four postures (sì wēiyí).
Furthermore, he contemplates the internal and external
factors, and the two kinds of suffering,
hunger and thirst, cold and heat.
Furthermore, contemplating these four,
if there were no moment-by-moment subtle impermanence,
these four kinds of suffering could also not be spoken of.
If a Bódhisàttva is able to have this reflection,
this is called the Bódhisàttva contemplating subtle impermanence.
Just as with internal and external form, mental dharmas (xīn fà) are also like this.
Why?
Because they function in the six sense fields (liù chù).
When functioning in the six sense fields,
sometimes a joyful mind arises,
sometimes an angry mind arises,
sometimes a loving mind arises,
sometimes a mindful mind arises;
they arise successively and differently, and cannot remain as one type.
Therefore, one should know
that all dharmas of form (sè fà) and dharmas of non-form (fēi sè fà) are entirely impermanent.
Good man!
If a Bódhisàttva can, in a single moment of thought (yī niàn zhōng),
see the arising, ceasing, and impermanence of all dharmas,
this is called the Bódhisàttva possessing the perception of impermanence.
Good man!
When the wise person has cultivated the perception of impermanence,
he separates himself from the pride of permanence (cháng màn),
the delusion of permanence (cháng dǎo),
and the delusion of perception (xiǎng dǎo).
"Next, he cultivates the perception of suffering (kǔ xiǎng).
For what reason is there such suffering?
He deeply knows that this suffering originates from impermanence,
because of impermanence,
one undergoes birth, aging, sickness, and death.
Because of the condition of birth, aging, sickness, and death,
this is called impermanence.
Because of the condition of impermanence,
one undergoes internal and external suffering:
hunger and thirst,
cold and heat,
whipping and beating,
scolding and insult.
Such sufferings
all originate from impermanence.
Furthermore, the wise person deeply contemplates this body,
which is immediately the vessel of impermanence.
This vessel is immediately suffering.
Because the vessel is suffering,
the dharmas contained within it are also suffering.
Good man!
The wise person further contemplates:
arising is suffering,
ceasing is suffering.
Because suffering arises and ceases,
it is immediately impermanent,
not self (wǒ)
nor what belongs to self (wǒ suǒ)."
'Practice the notion of non-self (anātman).
The wise further observe that suffering is impermanent,
and the impermanent is suffering.
If suffering is impermanent,
why does the wise person speak of the existence of a self?
Suffering is not the self,
and impermanence is likewise not the self.
Since the five skandhas are also suffering
and impermanent,
why do sentient beings speak of the existence of a self?
Furthermore, observe that all phenomena arise from various combinations and assemblages;
they are not all phenomena arising from a single combination,
nor is a single phenomenon the result of all combinations.
All combinations lack inherent nature (svabhāva);
they lack singularity,
they lack diversity,
they lack substantiality, and they lack independent sovereignty.
If phenomena possess such characteristics,
why does the wise person speak of the existence of a self?
Furthermore, consider this thought:
Among all phenomena, there is not a single phenomenon that can be the agent (the doer).
If a single phenomenon cannot be the agent,
then the combination of phenomena also cannot act as the agent.
All phenomena,
by nature, cannot ultimately arise or cease alone.
They cease due to combination,
and they arise due to combination.
When these phenomena have arisen,
sentient beings hold inverted notions,
saying, "This is a combination."
Born from combination,
the inverted notions of sentient beings lack reality.
How then can there be a real self?
Therefore, the wise person contemplates non-self.
Furthermore, observe closely: for what reason do sentient beings speak of a self?
If this self exists,
it should be either single or multiple.
If the self were single,
how then could there be Shàlì,
Póluómén,
Píshè,
Shǒutuó,
humans,
heavens,
hells,
hungry ghosts,
animals,
small and great,
old and young?
Therefore, it is known that the self is not single.
If the self were multiple,
how could it be said that
the self of sentient beings is single,
ubiquitous,
and without boundaries?
Whether single
or multiple,
both lead to non-self.
"When the wise person has thus contemplated non-self,
they next contemplate the notion of revulsion toward food.
They consider:
If all phenomena are impermanent,
suffering,
empty,
and non-self,
how can one, for the sake of food,
generate the three kinds of evil karma:
of body,
speech, and mind?
If there are sentient beings who, due to greed for food,
generate the three kinds of evil karma:
of body,
speech, and mind,
the wealth they obtain is shared by all;
but when they later undergo the painful retribution, there is no one who shares in that portion.
Good man!
The wise person further observes that
all sentient beings, for the sake of food and drink,
endure physical and mental suffering.
If food is obtained through collective suffering,
how should I develop attachment and craving for this food?
Therefore, one does not generate a greedy mind toward food.
Furthermore, the wise person should observe:
the body grows due to food and drink.
I have now left home,
received the precepts, and cultivated the Way,
aiming to abandon this body.
If I now crave this food,
how can I achieve the abandonment of this body?
Having contemplated thus,
although one receives food,
it is like eating the flesh of one's own child in a desolate wilderness;
the mind is repulsed and disgusted,
and finds no joy in it at all.
Having deeply contemplated that materialized food possesses such faults,
next contemplate contact food,
which is like a flayed ox
being devoured by innumerable worms.
Next, contemplate volitional food,
which is like a great mass of fire.
Consciousness food is like three hundred stabbing spears.
Good man!
When the wise person has contemplated the four kinds of food thus,
they never generate the notion of craving or pleasure toward food.
If craving still arises,
one should contemplate impurity.
Why is that?
In order to abandon the love of food.
Regarding all food,
one should skillfully analyze the notion of impurity,
making it analogous to various impurities.
Having contemplated thus,
whether receiving good food or bad food,
when taking it, it is like applying medicine to a festering sore;
one never generates a heart of craving and attachment.
Good man!
If the wise person can contemplate in this manner,
this is called achieving the notion of revulsion toward food."
Jiāyè Púsà said:
"World-Honored One!
When the wise person contemplates food and generates the notion of impurity,
is this a real contemplation,
or is it contemplation based on illusory understanding?
If it is a real contemplation,
the food being contemplated is not actually impure.
If it is an illusory understanding,
how can this method be called a beneficial notion?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Such a notion
is both a real contemplation
and an illusory understanding.
Because it can destroy greed for food, it is called real;
because one sees impurity where no impurity (worm) exists, it is called illusory understanding.
Good man!
Everything conditioned (āsrava) is called illusory,
yet it can also lead to the attainment of the real.
Good man!
If there is a Bhikṣu who sets out to beg for food
and holds this preconceived thought:
'I should beg for food;
I wish to obtain good food, not coarse or bad food;
I wish to obtain plenty, not too little;
I also wish to obtain it quickly, not late,'
such a Bhikṣu is not said to have achieved the notion of revulsion toward food.
The virtuous practices they cultivate will decline day and night,
and unwholesome phenomena will gradually increase.
Good man!
If there is a Bhikṣu who is about to beg for food,
they should first make this vow:
'May all beggars obtain fullness and satisfaction,
and may those who give the food attain immeasurable merit.
If I obtain food, it is only to treat this poisonous body,
to cultivate virtuous practices, and to benefit the donor.'
When making this vow,
the virtuous practices they cultivate increase day and night,
and unwholesome phenomena gradually vanish.
Good man!
If there is a Bhikṣu who can cultivate in this manner,
you should know that this person does not eat the offerings of faith from the country in vain."
"Good man!
The wise person, fulfilling these four contemplations (xiǎng),
is able to cultivate the contemplation of the unenjoyability of the world (shìjiān bùkělè xiǎng),
and makes this thought, saying:
'In all the world, there is no place where birth, old age, sickness, and death are absent,
and this body of mine is subject to birth everywhere.
If, within the world, there is no place that can be free from birth, old age, sickness, and death,
how then should I enjoy the world?
In all the world, there is no gain or advancement that is not subject to loss or decline.
Therefore, the world is definitely impermanent (wúcháng).
If it is impermanent,
how can a wise person find enjoyment in the world?
Every single sentient being (zhòngshēng),
traverses everywhere and experiences all worlds,
fully enduring suffering and pleasure.
Although they may attain the body of a Fàntiān god, up to the heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (Fēixiǎng Fēifēixiǎng Tiān),
when their life ends, they still fall back into the Three Evil Paths (Sān È Dào).
Although they may be the Four Heavenly Kings (Sì Wáng), up to the gods of the Heaven of Transformation by Others' Enjoyment (Tāhuà Zìzài Tiān),
when their lives end, they are born into the path of animals (chùshēng dào)—
perhaps as a lion,
a tiger, leopard, jackal, or wolf,
or an elephant, horse, ox, or donkey.
Next, observe the body of the Wheel-Turning Sagely King (Zhuǎnlún Shèng Wáng),
ruling over the Four Continents (Sì Tiānxià),
rich, noble, and free;
yet when their merit (fú) is exhausted, they become poor and distressed,
lacking clothing and food.
The wise person, having deeply contemplated such matters,
gives rise to the contemplation of the unenjoyability of the world.
The wise person further contemplates the things that exist in the world,
namely, houses,
clothing and food and drink,
bedding and medicine,
incense, flowers, and necklaces (yīngluò),
various kinds of music and entertainment,
wealth, materials, and treasures (bǎohuò).
Such things are all meant to escape suffering;
but the substance of these very things is suffering.
How can one use suffering to escape suffering?
Good man!
The wise person, having contemplated thus,
regarding worldly things,
does not give rise to attachment, enjoyment, or the contemplation of pleasure.
Good man!
For instance, if a person suffers from a severe illness,
although there may be various kinds of music, singing, and entertainment,
and incense, flowers, and necklaces (yīngluò),
they will ultimately not generate greed, attachment, or enjoyment towards them.
The wise person, having contemplated this, is also like this.
Good man!
The wise person deeply contemplates that all worlds
are not a refuge (guīyī chù),
are not a place of liberation (jiětuō chù),
are not a place of tranquility (jìjìng chù),
are not a desirable place,
are not the Further Shore (bǐ'àn chù),
nor are they the teachings of permanence (cháng), bliss (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng).
If I were greedy for and enjoyed such a world,
how then could I escape these teachings?
It is like a person who dislikes being in darkness
and seeks light,
yet returns again to darkness.
Darkness is the world (shìjiān);
light is transcendence of the world (chūshì).
If I enjoy the world,
I increase the darkness
and move far from the light.
Darkness is ignorance (wúmíng);
light is wisdom and clarity (zhìmíng).
The cause of this wisdom and clarity is precisely the contemplation of the unenjoyability of the world.
Although all greedy attachments (tānjié) are fetters,
yet I now crave wisdom and clarity,
and do not crave the world.
The wise person, having deeply contemplated these teachings,
fulfills the contemplation of the unenjoyability of the world.
"Good man!
The intelligent person, having already cultivated the contemplation of the unenjoyability of the world,
next cultivates the contemplation of death (sǐ xiǎng guān).
This lifespan is constantly surrounded by countless enemies,
diminishing moment by moment,
and never increasing.
It is like mountain torrents that cannot stand still,
and like morning dew that cannot remain for long,
like a prisoner being led to the execution ground, drawing closer to death with every step,
or like leading cattle and sheep to the slaughterhouse.
Kānànyè Púsà said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
How does a wise person contemplate the momentary cessation (niànniàn miè)?"
"Good man!
For example, four people,
all skilled in archery,
gathered in one place,
each shooting toward one direction,
all think this:
'Our four arrows launch and fall simultaneously.'
Furthermore, there is a person who thinks:
'Before these four arrows have fallen,
I can catch them all at once with my hand.'
Good man!
Can such a person be called swift?"
Kānànyè Púsà said:
"Indeed.
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha (Fó) said:
"Good man!
The speed of a ground-dwelling ghost (dìxíng guǐ) is swifter than this person;
the flying ghost (fēixíng guǐ) is swifter than the ground-dwelling one;
the speed of the Four Heavenly Kings (Sì Tiānwáng) is swifter than the flying ghost;
the gods of the sun and moon (rìyuè shéntiān) are swifter than the Four Kings;
the speed of the gods of Swift and Strong Movement (xíng jiānjí tiān) is swifter than the sun and moon;
and the lifespan of sentient beings (zhòngshēng shòumìng) is swifter than the Swift and Strong Movement gods.
Good man!
In the time of a single breath (xī) or a single blink (shùn),
the lifespan of a sentient being undergoes four hundred births and cessations (shēng miè).
If a wise person can contemplate life in this way,
this is called being able to contemplate momentary cessation.
Good man!
The wise person contemplates that life is bound to the King of Death (Sǐ Wáng).
If I can depart from such a King of Death,
then I will attain the eternal severing of impermanent life.
Furthermore, the wise person contemplates this lifespan
as being like a great tree leaning over a steep riverbank,
or like a person who has committed a great treacherous crime and, when being executed, finds no one to pity them,
or like a great lion king when intensely starved,
or like a poisonous snake when drawing a deep breath of wind,
like a thirsty horse guarding and cherishing water,
or like a great evil ghost when its anger erupts—
the King of Death for sentient beings is also like this.
Good man!
If a wise person can practice such contemplation,
this is then called cultivating the contemplation of death.
"Good man!
The wise person further contemplates:
Even if I, having left home (chūjiā), were to gain a lifespan of seven days and seven nights,
during that time I would diligently cultivate the Way (dào),
guard and uphold the precepts (jìnjiè),
preach the Dharma (shuōfǎ), educate, and benefit sentient beings.
This is how the wise person cultivates the contemplation of death.
Furthermore, taking seven days and seven nights as long,
if I were to gain six days,
five days,
four days,
three days,
two days,
one day,
one hour,
or even just the time it takes for an exhalation
and an inhalation,
I would diligently cultivate the Way during that time,
guard and uphold the precepts,
preach the Dharma, educate, and benefit sentient beings.
This is how the wise person excellently cultivates the contemplation of death.
The wise person, fulfilling the six contemplations mentioned above,
possesses the cause for the Seven Contemplations (qī xiǎng).
What are the seven?
First, the contemplation of constant cultivation (chángxiū xiǎng);
second, the contemplation of joyful cultivation (lèxiū xiǎng);
third, the contemplation of non-anger (wúchēn xiǎng);
fourth, the contemplation of non-jealousy (wúdù xiǎng);
fifth, the contemplation of good vows (shànyuàn xiǎng);
sixth, the contemplation of non-arrogance (wúmàn xiǎng);
seventh, the contemplation of mastery over Samādhi (sānmèi zìzài xiǎng).
Good man!
If there is a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) who fulfills the Seven Contemplations,
he is called a Śramaṇa (Shāmén),
called a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén),
called Tranquil (Jìjìng),
called Pure (Jìngjié),
called Liberated (Jiětuō),
called Wise (Zhìzhě),
called Right View (Zhèngjiàn),
called Attained the Further Shore (Dào Bǐ'àn),
called the Great King of Physicians (Dà Yī Wáng),
called the Great Merchant Leader (Dà Shāng Zhǔ),
called one who excellently understands the Tathāgata’s (Rúlái) secrets,
and also knows the seven kinds of speech of all Buddhas (Fó),
and is called one who knows by Right View (Zhèngjiàn Zhī),
severing the net of doubts arising from the seven kinds of speech.
Good man!
If a person fulfills the six contemplations mentioned above,
you should know that this person can denounce the Three Realms (Sān Jiè),
distance themselves from the Three Realms,
eradicate the Three Realms,
and give rise to no attachment within the Three Realms.
This is called the wise person fulfilling the Ten Contemplations (Shí Xiǎng).
If there is a Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū) who possesses these Ten Contemplations,
he immediately earns the designation befitting a Śramaṇa (Shāmén).
At that time, Kānànyè Púsà,
immediately before the Buddha (Fó), praised the Buddha with a verse:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kǎochénrú:
"Form (Rūpa) is impermanent.
By extinguishing this form,
one attains liberated, permanently abiding form.
Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also impermanent.
By extinguishing this consciousness,
one attains liberated, permanently abiding consciousness.
Kǎochénrú!
Form is suffering (Duḥkha).
By extinguishing this form,
one attains liberated, blissful form.
Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also like this.
Kǎochénrú!
Form is emptiness (Śūnyatā).
By extinguishing empty form,
one attains liberated, non-empty form.
Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also like this.
Kǎochénrú!
Form is non-self (Anātman).
By extinguishing this form,
one attains liberated, true self form.
Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also like this.
Kǎochénrú!
Form is impurity.
By extinguishing this form,
one attains liberated, pure form.
Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also like this.
Kǎochénrú!
Form is the characteristic of birth, aging, sickness, and death.
By extinguishing this form,
one attains liberated form that is not characterized by birth, aging, sickness, and death.
Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also like this.
Kǎochénrú!
Form is the cause of ignorance (Avidyā).
By extinguishing this form,
one attains liberated form that is not the cause of ignorance.
Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also like this.
Kǎochénrú!
Furthermore, form is the cause of rebirth.
By extinguishing this form,
one attains liberated form that is not the cause of rebirth.
Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also like this.
Kǎochénrú!
Form is precisely the cause of the four inversions.
By extinguishing inverted form,
one attains liberated form that is not the cause of the four inversions.
Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also like this.
Kǎochénrú!
Form is the cause of immeasurable evil phenomena,
namely, the bodies of men and women,
attachment to food,
sensual desire,
greed and hatred,
jealousy and evil intentions,
avarice,
eating solid food, consciousness food, volitional food, and contact food (the four kinds of nourishment),
birth from eggs, birth from the womb, birth from moisture, and spontaneous birth,
the five desires and the five hindrances.
All such phenomena arise from form.
Therefore, by extinguishing form,
one attains liberated form without such immeasurable evils.
Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also like this.
Kǎochénrú!
Form is precisely bondage.
By extinguishing bound form,
one attains liberated, unbound form.
Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also like this.
Kǎochénrú!
Form is precisely an outflow.
By extinguishing outflow form,
one attains liberated, non-outflow form.
Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also like this.
Kǎochénrú!
Form is not a refuge.
By extinguishing this form,
one attains liberated, refuge form.
Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also like this.
Kǎochénrú!
Form is an ulcer or running sore.
By extinguishing this form,
one attains liberated form without ulcers or running sores.
Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also like this.
Kǎochénrú!
Form is not quiescent.
By extinguishing this form,
one attains the form of Nirvāṇa and quiescence.
Feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also like this.
Kǎochénrú!
If there is a person who can know in this way,
this one is called a Śràman,
called a Brāhman,
who is fully endowed with the Dharma of the Śràman
and the Brāhman.
Kǎochénrú!
If one departs from the Buddha Dharma,
there is no Śràman,
no Brāhman,
nor is there the Dharma of the Śràman
and the Brāhman.
All external paths,
falsely pretend and fraudulently claim;
they are completely without true practice.
Although they make an appearance
saying these two exist,
in reality, there is no such state.
Why is this?
If there is no Dharma of the Śràman
and the Brāhman,
how can one speak of there being a Śràman
or a Brāhman?
I constantly utter the lion's roar among this great assembly,
and you all should also utter the lion's roar in the great assembly."
At that time, immeasurable people of the external paths
heard these words
and developed anger and malice in their minds, saying:
"Qúntán (Gautama) now says that among our assembly, there are no Śràmans or Brāhmans,
nor is there the Dharma of the Śràman
and the Brāhman.
How should we widely devise means to speak to Qúntán, saying,
'Among our assembly there are also Śràmans,
there is the Dharma of the Śràman,
there are Brāhmans,
and there is the Dharma of the Brāhman?'"
At that time, there was a Brahmacārin in that assembly
who proclaimed thus:
"Gentlemen!
The words of Qúntán
are no different from those of a madman.
How can they be examined or regulated?
A madman in the world
sometimes sings,
sometimes dances,
sometimes cries,
sometimes laughs,
sometimes curses,
sometimes praises,
unable to distinguish between enemies and relatives.
Śràman Qúntán is also like this:
sometimes he says, 'I was born into the house of King Jìngfàn (Śuddhodana)';
sometimes he says he was not born.
Sometimes he says that after birth he walked seven steps;
sometimes he says he did not walk.
Sometimes he says that from childhood he learned worldly affairs;
sometimes he says, 'I am the omniscient one.'
Sometimes he dwells in the palace enjoying pleasures and begetting a son;
sometimes he feels loathing, blames, and despises those evils.
Sometimes he personally practices severe asceticism for six years;
sometimes he blames the severe asceticism of the external paths.
Sometimes he says he received doctrines previously unheard from Yùtóulánfú
and Āluólúo;
sometimes he says they knew nothing.
Sometimes he says that under the Bodhi tree he attained Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí;
sometimes he says, 'I did not go to the tree and attained nothing.'
Sometimes he says, 'My body right now is Nirvāṇa';
sometimes he says, 'The cessation of the body is Nirvāṇa.'
What Qúntán speaks is no different from that of a madman.
Why are you sad and worried because of this?"
The Brāhmans immediately replied, saying:
"Great Sir!
How can we now avoid being sad?
Śràman Qúntán, having previously left home,
preached impermanence,
suffering,
emptiness,
and non-self, and other such doctrines.
Our disciples heard this and developed fear,
asking, 'How can sentient beings be impermanent,
suffering,
empty,
non-self,
and impure?'
and they did not accept his words.
Now Qúntán has again come here to this Śāluólín (Sāla grove),
preaching to the great assembly the doctrines of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
When our disciples heard these words,
they all abandoned us and left,
accepting the words of Qúntán.
Due to this reason, we suffer great sorrow and misery."
At that time, there was again one Brāhmaṇa who spoke thus:
“Gentlemen!
Listen carefully,
listen carefully.
The claim that the śramaṇa Qú tán cultivates loving-kindness and compassion
is false
and not true.
If he possessed loving-kindness and compassion,
how could he instruct my disciples to individually receive his Dharma?
Loving-kindness and compassion surely involve following the wishes of others,
yet now he violates my desires;
how can it be said that he possesses them?
If someone says that the śramaṇa Qú tán is not tainted by the eight worldly dharmas,
this is also false.
If it is said that Qú tán has few desires and is content,
how is it that he now steals our profit?
If it is said that his lineage is of the highest clan,
this is also false.
Why?
From ancient times until now,
we have never seen or heard of a great lion king harming and killing a small mouse.
If Qú tán were of the highest lineage,
how could he now vex and trouble us?
If it is said that Qú tán possesses great power,
this is also false.
Why?
From ancient times until now, we have never seen or heard of the Golden-Winged Bird King contending with crows.
If his power is great,
for what reason does he fight with us?
If it is said that Qú tán possesses the knowledge of others’ minds,
this is also false.
Why?
If he possessed this knowledge,
for what reason would he not know my mind?
Gentlemen!
I once heard from former wise men who spoke of this matter:
After a hundred years passed,
there would appear in the world a bewitching phantom.
This is none other than Qú tán.
Such a mesmerizing illusion
will soon perish here in the Sā luó Grove,
so you should not be anxious or distressed now.”
At that time, there was again a Ní jiān zǐ who replied:
“Gentleman!
My present anxiety
is not due to the offerings received by my own disciples,
but rather for the sake of the world, which is ignorant, dark, and sightless,
unable to discern fields of merit from non-fields of merit.
They abandon the former wise Brāhmaṇas
and offer homage to a youth;
this is what causes my distress.
The śramaṇa Qú tán is greatly skilled in spells and incantations.
By the power of his spells,
he is able to transform one body into infinite bodies,
and make infinite bodies revert to one body,
or transform his own body into the appearance of men and women,
oxen, sheep, elephants, or horses.
My power can destroy such spells.
Once the spells of the śramaṇa Qú tán are destroyed,
you all will regain abundant offerings
and experience peace and comfort.”
At that time, there was again one Brāhmaṇa who spoke thus:
“Gentlemen!
The śramaṇa Qú tán possesses and fulfills immeasurable merits;
therefore, you should not dispute with him.”
The crowd replied:
“Idiot!
How can you say that the śramaṇa Qú tán possesses great merit?
Seven days after he was born,
his mother died.
Can this be called a sign of fortune and merit?
The Brāhmaṇa said:
“Not getting angry when cursed,
not retaliating when struck—
you should know that this is precisely the sign of great fortune and merit.
His body is complete with the thirty-two marks,
the eighty minor characteristics,
and immeasurable spiritual powers;
therefore, you should know these are signs of fortune and merit.
His mind is without arrogance,
he inquires after others with forethought,
his speech is gentle and soft,
never coarse or harsh.
Though his years and ambition are both flourishing, his mind is never rash or violent.
He possessed a kingdom and great wealth, yet had no attachment to them,
abandoning them to leave home life as if discarding snot or spit.
This is why I say that the śramaṇa Qú tán possesses and fulfills immeasurable merits.”
The crowd replied:
“Well said,
Gentleman!
The śramaṇa Qú tán is indeed as you have described,
having attained immeasurable spiritual powers and transformations.
We will not contest these matters with him.
The śramaṇa Qú tán has a gentle nature,
is unsuited for ascetic practices,
grew up deep within the palace,
and is inexperienced in external affairs.
He is only capable of gentle speech.
Since he is ignorant of crafts,
books,
and debate,
we request to thoroughly discuss the essentials of the True Dharma with him.
If he defeats us,
we will serve him.
If we defeat him,
he shall serve us.”
At that time, many immeasurable adherents of external paths,
in harmony, went together to the presence of King Ā shé shì of Mó jiā tuó.
The King saw them and asked:
“Gentlemen, why have you come?
You each cultivate your respective holy paths,
being renunciants
who have abandoned wealth and household affairs.
Yet my countrymen all offer you sustenance,
regard you with reverence,
and do not offend or disturb one another.
Why have you come here together in harmony?
Gentlemen,
you each uphold different doctrines
and different precepts,
and your methods of renunciation differ.
Moreover, you each follow your own precepts and paths as renunciants.
For what reason
are you now united in one mind and assembled together,
like fallen leaves
gathered in one place by a whirlwind?
Tell me the reason for your arrival here.
I constantly protect those who have left home life,
not even begrudging my body or life.”
At that time, all the various groups of externalists unanimously spoke these words:
"Great King!
Listen carefully.
The Great King is now a bridge of the great Dharma,
a grindstone of the great Dharma,
a balance scale of the great Dharma,
that is, the vessel of all merits,
the true nature of all merits,
the road of the Right Dharma,
that is, the fertile field for seeds,
the root of all kingdoms,
the great bright mirror of all kingdoms,
the image of all devas,
the father and mother of all people in the kingdom.
Great King!
The treasure of merit in the entire world is the King's body.
Why is it called the treasury of merit?
When the King judges state affairs,
he does not distinguish between enemy and friend,
his mind is impartial,
like earth, water, fire, and wind.
Therefore, the King is named the treasury of merit.
Great King!
Although the lifespan of present sentient beings is short,
the King’s merit is like the ancient kings of long life and peaceful happiness,
and like Dǐngshēng,
Shànjiàn,
Rěnrǔ,
King Nàhóushā,
King Yēyēdì,
King Shībǐ,
King Yīchājiū,
Such kings were complete in virtuous Dharma.
The Great King is now also like this.
Great King!
Due to the King's condition,
the kingdom is peaceful and happy,
the people flourish.
Therefore, all renunciates admire and enjoy this kingdom,
upholding the precepts with diligence and effort,
cultivating the Right Path.
Great King!
Our scriptures state,
if a renunciate, in whatever kingdom he resides,
upholds the precepts and is diligent,
striving to cultivate the Right Path,
that King also shares in the portion of good cultivation.
Great King!
All robbers,
the King has already regulated,
so all renunciates are without fear.
Now there is only one great wicked person, the śramana Qútán,
whom the King has not yet inspected and controlled,
and we are greatly afraid.
That person relies on his noble clan lineage,
his body and color are complete (perfect),
and further, due to the retribution of past generosity,
he receives many offerings.
Relying on these many things, he gives rise to great arrogance.
Or perhaps he gives rise to arrogance due to magical spells (mantras).
Because of these conditions, he cannot practice asceticism,
but accepts and uses fine, soft clothing and bedding.
Therefore, all wicked people of the world,
for the sake of profit and sustenance, gather at his place,
and becoming his retinue, they cannot practice asceticism.
By the power of his magical spells,
he subdued Jiāyè and Shèlìfú,
Mùjiànlián, and others.
Now he has come again to our place,
residing in the suōluó lín,
proclaiming that this body is Permanent, Joyful, Self, and Pure,
thus enticing our disciples.
Great King!
Qútán previously preached impermanence,
suffering (non-joy),
non-self,
and impurity.
We could endure that,
but now he proclaims Permanent, Joyful, Self, and Pure!
We truly cannot tolerate this.
We only beg the Great King,
to allow us to hold a discussion (debate) with that Qútán."
The King then replied:
"All great men!
Who now, among you,
instructed and guided you,
to make your minds so frantic and unstable,
like the surging waves of water,
the whirling wheel of fire,
or a monkey leaping among trees?
This matter is shameful.
If wise people hear it, they will immediately feel pity;
if foolish people hear it, they will immediately burst into mockery.
What you speak is not the demeanor of renunciates.
If you suffer from wind disease,
or yellow water disease,
I possess medicine capable of healing and treating it.
If it is a spirit disease,
my elder brother Jīpó,
is skilled at removing it.
You now wish to scrape Mount Xūmí with your fingernails,
and wish to gnaw and chew vajra (diamond) with your teeth.
All great men!
It is like a foolish person,
who sees the lion king sleeping while hungry,
and wishes to awaken him.
It is like a person placing a finger inside the mouth of a poisonous snake,
or wishing to touch fire covered by ash with his hand.
You are now also like this.
Good men!
It is like a wild fox trying to give the lion's roar,
or like a mosquito competing with the jìnchì niǎo in speed of flight,
or like a rabbit crossing the ocean trying to reach its bottom.
You are now also like this.
If you dream that you have overcome Qútán,
that dream is delusion born of madness,
and is not worthy of belief.
All great men!
Your current intent to bring this forth,
is like a moth flying into a great pile of fire.
Follow my words,
you do not need to speak further.
Although you praised me as impartial like a balance scale,
do not let outsiders hear these words again."
At that time, the externalists spoke again, saying:
"Great King!
Have the magical illusions made by the śramana Qútán reached your side?
How can the Great King be doubtful and disbelieve such sacred men as us?
Great King!
You should not slight such great beings.
Great King!
The waxing and waning of the moon,
the salty taste of the great ocean,
Mount Móluóyán—
who created such things?
Was it not we, the Bóluómén?
Great King!
Have you not heard that the immortal Ājiéduō, for twelve years,
contained the water of the Hénghé River in his ear?
Great King!
Did you hear that the great immortal Qútán manifested divine powers,
transforming the body of Shì for twelve years,
and further making Shì's body take the form of a ram,
and creating a thousand vulvae (female organs) upon Shì's body?
Great King!
Have you not heard that the immortal Jínú,
in a single day, drank the water of the four great oceans,
causing the great earth to dry up?
Great King!
Have you not heard that the immortal Pósu created three eyes for Zìzàitiān?
Great King!
Have you not heard that the immortal Āluólā transformed Jiāfùluó chéng into baked earth?
Great King!
Among the Bóluómén, there are such great and powerful immortals,
who are visible and subject to inspection and control.
How can the Great King slight and despise us?"
The King said:
"All benevolent ones!
If you are not believed and still wish to proceed,
the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is now nearby in the suōluó lín.
You may go and question and challenge him as you wish.
The Tathāgata will certainly provide distinctions for you,
and answer according to your desire."
At that time, King Āzhēshì, along with the externalists, their disciples, and retinue,
went to the place of the Buddha.
They prostrated their heads to the ground in reverence, circled him three times clockwise,
and having completed their acts of respect,
they stood back to one side.
They addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
These externalists wish to question and challenge you as they wish.
We only wish that the Tathāgata would answer them as he sees fit."
The Buddha said:
"Great King, stop for now.
I will know the right time Myself."
At that time, there was a Bóluómén in the assembly named Shétíshǒunà.
He spoke these words:
"Qútán!
Do you say that Nièpán is an eternal Dharma (principle)?"
"It is so,
it is so.
Great Bóluómén!"
Bóluómén said:
"Qúntán!
If you state that Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) is permanent,
this meaning is incorrect.
Why is this?
The phenomena of the world, producing fruit from their seeds, continue without interruption,
just as a jar comes from clay,
or clothing is obtained from thread.
Qúntán consistently teaches that cultivating the perception of impermanence
leads to the attainment of Nièpán.
If the cause is impermanent,
how can the result be permanent?
Qúntán also says that freedom from desire-craving is Nièpán,
freedom from form-craving and formless-craving is Nièpán,
and extinguishing ignorance (wúmíng) and all other defilements (fánnǎo) is Nièpán.
From desire up to ignorance,
[and] defilements are all impermanent;
thus, the Nièpán obtained from this impermanent cause should also be impermanent.
Qúntán also says that one is born in heaven due to a cause,
falls into hell due to a cause,
and obtains liberation due to a cause.
Therefore, all phenomena arise from causes.
If liberation is obtained due to a cause,
how can you say it is permanent?
Qúntán also says that form (sè) arises from conditions, and is therefore called impermanent;
feeling (shòu), perception (xiǎng), volition (xíng), and consciousness (shì) are likewise,
and liberation is like this [too].
If this is form, you should know it is impermanent;
feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are likewise.
If there is liberation apart from the Five Aggregates (wǔyīn),
then you should know that liberation is identical to space (xūkōng).
If it is space,
one cannot say it arises from causes and conditions (yīnyuán).
Why is this?
It is permanent, singular, and pervades all places.
Qúntán also says that what arises from causes is suffering (kǔ).
If it is suffering,
how can you, furthermore, say that liberation is joy (lè)?
Qúntán also says that impermanence is suffering,
suffering is non-self (wúwǒ).
If it is impermanent, suffering, and non-self,
it is then impure (bú jìng).
All phenomena that arise from causes,
are all impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure.
How can you, furthermore, say that Nièpán is permanence, joy, self, and purity (cháng lè wǒ jìng)?
If Qúntán says,
both permanent and impermanent,
both suffering and joy,
both self and non-self,
both pure and impure,
wouldn't this be speaking in two ways (a double meaning)?
I have also heard this saying from wise men of old,
that if a Fó appears in the world,
his teaching will have no double meaning.
Now Qúntán speaks in two ways,
yet claims that the Fó is his own self.
What is the meaning of this doctrine?"
Fó said:
"Bóluómén!
Concerning what you have stated,
I shall now ask you;
answer as you wish."
Bóluómén said:
"Excellent!
Qúntán!"
Fó said:
"Bóluómén!
Is your fundamental nature (xìng) permanent,
or is it impermanent?"
Bóluómén said:
"My nature is permanent."
"Bóluómén!
Is this nature capable of being the cause of all internal and external phenomena?"
"It is so,
Qúntán."
Fó said:
"Bóluómén!
How does it act as the cause?"
"Qúntán!
From the nature arises 'the Great' (dà);
from 'the Great' arises pride/ego (màn);
from pride arises the sixteen principles (shíliù fǎ),
namely, earth (dì),
water (shuǐ),
fire (huǒ),
wind (fēng),
space (kōng);
the five cognitive faculties (wǔ zhī gēn):
eyes,
ears,
nose,
tongue,
body;
the five active faculties (wǔ yè gēn):
hands,
feet,
mouth,
voice,
the two roots of male and female,
and the equalizing root of mind (xīn píngděng gēn);
these are the sixteen principles.
From five principles arise form (sè),
sound (shēng),
odor (xiāng),
taste (wèi),
and touch (chù);
these are the twenty-one principles.
There are three fundamentals:
first, defilement (rǎn);
second, coarseness (cū);
third, darkness (hēi).
Defilement is called craving (ài);
coarseness is called hatred (chēn);
darkness is named ignorance (wúmíng).
Qúntán!
These twenty-five principles all arise due to [our fundamental] nature."
"Bóluómén!
Are these principles, such as 'the Great,'
permanent,
or impermanent?"
"Qúntán!
The nature in our teaching is permanent,
but the various principles, such as 'the Great,' are all impermanent."
"Bóluómén!
In your doctrine,
the cause is permanent, and the result is impermanent.
But in my doctrine, although the cause is impermanent,
if the result is permanent,
what fault is there?
Bóluómén!
Are there two types of causes in your doctrine?"
He replied:
"There are."
Fó said:
"How are there [two]?"
Bóluómén said:
"The first is the generative cause (shēngyīn),
the second is the revealing cause (liǎoyīn)."
Fó said:
"What is the generative cause?
What is the revealing cause?"
Bóluómén said:
"The generative cause is like a jar coming out of clay;
the revealing cause is like a lamp illuminating an object."
Fó said:
"Are these two kinds of causes
one in fundamental nature?
If they are one,
can the generative cause be made into the revealing cause,
and can the revealing cause be made into the generative cause?"
"No,
Qúntán."
Fó said:
"If the generative cause cannot be made into the revealing cause,
and the revealing cause cannot be made into the generative cause,
can you then say that they possess the characteristic of a cause?"
Bóluómén said:
"Although they cannot be made into one another, they still possess the characteristic of a cause."
"Bóluómén!
Is that which is revealed by the revealing cause
identical to the revealing itself?"
"No,
Qúntán."
Fó said:
"Although my doctrine obtains Nièpán from the impermanent,
it is not itself impermanent.
Bóluómén!
Because it is attained through the revealing cause,
it is permanence, joy, self, and purity.
Because it is attained through the generative cause,
it is impermanent,
not joyful,
non-self,
and impure.
Therefore, the Rúlái speaks in two ways,
but these two ways of speaking do not constitute a double meaning;
therefore, the Rúlái is named 'He whose speech is non-dual.'
As you have said,
having heard from wise men of old,
that when a Fó appears in the world, his teaching has no double meaning—
that saying is excellent.
What all Fós of the ten directions and the three times teach is without discrepancy;
therefore, it is said that the Fó’s speech is non-dual.
How is it without discrepancy?
When something exists, they consistently say it exists;
when something is nonexistent, they consistently say it is nonexistent.
Thus, it is called a single meaning.
Bóluómén!
Although the World-Honored Rúlái speaks in two ways,
it is for the sake of realizing a single meaning.
How do the two ways of speaking realize a single meaning?
Just as the two ways of speaking—eye and form—generate the single meaning of consciousness (shì),
likewise are the mind (yì) and phenomena (fǎ)."
Bóluómén said:
"Qúntán!
[You] skillfully distinguish such meanings in speech,
but I do not yet understand
how the two ways of speaking you set forth realize a single meaning."
At that time, the Shìzūn immediately proclaimed the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths:
"Brāhmaṇa!
The Noble Truth of Suffering is both twofold and singular,
and so too is the Noble Truth of the Path both twofold and singular."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Shìzūn!
I already know."
The Buddha said:
"Shànnánzǐ!
How do you know already?"
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Shìzūn!
Regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering,
for all ordinary people (fánfū) it is twofold,
but for the noble ones (shèngrén) it is singular;
the Noble Truth of the Path is also like this."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent!
You have understood."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Shìzūn!
Having now heard the Dharma,
I have attained right view.
I should now take refuge in the Buddha,
the Dharma,
and the Sangha Jewel.
I only wish that out of great compassion you would permit me to leave home (become a monk)."
At that time, the Shìzūn addressed Jiāochénrú:
"You must shave the beard and hair for this Shétíshǒunà,
and permit him
to leave home."
Then Jiāochénrú immediately received the Buddha's command
and shaved his hair.
As soon as the shaving began, two kinds of falling occurred:
first, the beard and hair;
second, the afflictions (fánnǎo).
Right there in his seat, he attained the fruit of Āluóhàn.
Furthermore, there was a Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) whose surname was Pósītā,
who then spoke thus:
"Does Qú Tán say that Nirvāṇa is eternal (cháng)?"
"It is so,
Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì)."
Pósītā said:
"Does Qú Tán not say that the absence of afflictions (fánnǎo) is Nirvāṇa?"
"It is so,
Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì)."
Pósītā said:
"Qú Tán!
In the world, there are four kinds of things called 'non-existent' (wú):
First, a phenomenon that has not yet arisen is called non-existent,
just as when a vase has not yet come out of the clay, it is called a non-existent vase;
second, a phenomenon that has already perished is called non-existent,
just as when a vase is broken, it is called a non-existent vase;
third, things mutually absent from each other are called non-existent,
just as there is no horse in the cow,
and no cow in the horse;
fourth, something ultimately non-existent is called non-existent,
such as tortoise hair
and rabbit horns.
Qú Tán!
If Nirvāṇa is named after the removal of afflictions,
then Nirvāṇa is non-existent.
If it is non-existent,
how can you say that it possesses eternity (cháng), bliss (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng)?"
The Buddha said:
"Shànnánzǐ!
This Nirvāṇa
is not 'non-existent beforehand' like a vase still in the clay;
nor is it 'non-existent by perishing' like a broken vase;
nor is it 'ultimately non-existent' like tortoise hair or rabbit horns,
but is similar to 'mutually absent non-existence.'
Shànnánzǐ!
As you said,
although there is no horse in the cow,
one cannot say that the cow is also non-existent.
Although there is no cow in the horse,
one also cannot say that the horse is non-existent.
Nirvāṇa is likewise:
there is no Nirvāṇa in afflictions (fánnǎo),
and there are no afflictions (fánnǎo) in Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is called 'mutually absent non-existence'."
Pósītā said:
"Qú Tán!
If mutual absence is taken as Nirvāṇa,
then mutual absence
does not possess eternity (cháng), bliss (lè), self (wǒ), or purity (jìng).
Qú Tán!
How do you say that Nirvāṇa possesses eternity (cháng), bliss (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng)?"
The Buddha said:
"Shànnánzǐ!
As you mentioned,
this mutual absence (yì wú)
involves three kinds of non-existence:
The cow and the horse are both non-existent before and existent later—
this is called 'non-existent beforehand';
what has existed reverts to non-existence—
this is called 'non-existent by perishing';
and regarding mutually absent non-existence,
it is as you have said.
Shànnánzǐ!
These three kinds of non-existence
are absent in Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, Nirvāṇa possesses eternity (cháng), bliss (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng).
Just like worldly patients:
first, those with fever (heat disease);
second, those with wind disease;
third, those with cold disease.
These three kinds of diseases
can be cured by three medicines.
Fever patients are cured by clarified butter (sū);
wind patients are cured by oil;
cold patients are cured by honey.
These three kinds of medicines can cure these three kinds of severe diseases.
Shànnánzǐ!
There is no oil in the wind,
there is no wind in the oil,
and likewise there is no cold in the honey,
and no honey in the cold—
therefore they can cure.
All sentient beings are likewise;
they have three kinds of diseases:
first, greed (tān);
second, hatred (chēn);
third, delusion (chī).
Against these three diseases there are three kinds of medicines:
the meditation on impurity (bù jìng guān) serves as medicine for greed;
the meditation on loving-kindness (cí xīn guān) serves as medicine for hatred;
the contemplation of dependent origination (yīnyuán zhì) serves as medicine for delusion.
Shànnánzǐ!
In order to eliminate greed, one practices the non-greed contemplation.
In order to eliminate hatred, one practices the non-hatred contemplation.
In order to eliminate delusion, one practices the non-delusion contemplation.
In the three kinds of diseases there are no three kinds of medicines;
in the three kinds of medicines there are no three kinds of diseases.
Shànnánzǐ!
Because there are no three medicines in the three kinds of diseases,
they are impermanent (wúcháng),
without self (wúwǒ),
without bliss (wúlè),
and impure (wújìng).
Since there are no three diseases in the three kinds of medicines,
they are therefore described as possessing eternity (cháng), bliss (lè), self (wǒ), and purity (jìng)."
Pósītā said:
"Shìzūn!
The Tathāgata speaks to me of eternity (cháng)
and impermanence (wúcháng).
What is meant by eternity (cháng)?
What is meant by impermanence (wúcháng)?"
The Buddha said:
"Shànnánzǐ!
Form (sè) is impermanent (wúcháng);
the liberation from form is eternal (cháng).
Up to and including consciousness (shí) is impermanent (wúcháng);
the liberation from consciousness is eternal (cháng).
Shànnánzǐ!
If any shànnánzǐ
or good woman (shànnǚrén)
can observe form up to and including consciousness as impermanent,
you should know that this person has attained the eternal Dharma."
Pósītā said:
"Shìzūn!
I now know the Dharma of eternity (cháng)
and impermanence (wúcháng)."
The Buddha said:
"Shànnánzǐ!
How do you know the Dharma of eternity (cháng)
and impermanence (wúcháng)?"
Pósītā said:
"Shìzūn!
I now know that my form (sè) is impermanent (wúcháng),
and attaining liberation is eternal (cháng);
and consciousness (shí) is also like this."
The Buddha said:
"Shànnánzǐ!
It is excellent that you have now
repaid this body."
He addressed Jiāochénrú:
"This Pósītā
has already realized the fruit of Āluóhàn.
You may bestow upon him the three robes and bowl."
Then Jiāochénrú, according to the Buddha's command,
bestowed the robes and bowl upon him.
When Pósītā had received the robes and bowl,
he spoke thus:
"Venerable Jiāochénrú!
I have now, because of this corrupt and evil body, attained good fruition.
I only wish, Venerable Sir,
that you would condescend to approach the Shìzūn
and fully express my thoughts:
'I, being an evil person, offended the Tathāgata by mentioning the surname Qú Tán.
I only wish that you would confess this sin on my behalf.
I also cannot remain in this poisoned body much longer;
I now enter Nirvāṇa.'
At that time, Jiāochénrú immediately went to the place of the Fó and spoke thus:
"Shìzūn!
Póshīzhà Bǐqiū has given rise to a heart of shame and remorse.
He says to himself:
'I, being dull and foolish, offended the Nǐ Qúchán Xìng of the Rúlái.
I cannot long remain in this venomous serpent body.
Now I wish to destroy my body,
and I entrust my confession to you.'"
The Fó said:
"Jiāochénrú!
Póshīzhà Bǐqiū has already perfected virtuous roots in the presence of countless Fó in the past.
Now he accepts my words,
and dwells according to the Dharma (law).
Because he dwells according to the Dharma, he will obtain the true fruit (Arhatship).
You all should make offerings to his body."
At that time, Jiāochénrú, having heard this from the Fó,
returned to his place,
and made offerings.
When Póshīzhà burned his body,
he manifested various supernatural powers.
All the sects of externalists, having seen this matter,
cried out loudly, saying:
"This Póshīzhà has obtained the magic spells of the Qúchán Shāmén.
This man will soon surpass that Qúchán Shāmén."
At that time, there was also a Fànzhì in the assembly named Xiānní.
He further spoke thus:
"Does Gautama hold that there is a self (ātman)?"
The Rúlái remained silent.
"Does Gautama hold that there is no self?"
The Rúlái remained silent.
A second and a third time he asked the same question,
and the Fó remained silent throughout.
Xiānní said:
"Gautama!
If the self exists for all sentient beings—it is pervasive everywhere,
it is one,
and it is the agent (doer)—
why does Gautama remain silent and not answer?"
The Fó said:
"Xiānní!
Do you say that the self is pervasive everywhere?"
Xiānní replied:
"Gautama!
It is not only I who says so,
all wise men also say thus."
The Fó said:
"Good man!
If the self pervades everywhere,
then the retribution in the Five Paths (Gati) should be received simultaneously.
If the retribution in the Five Paths were received simultaneously,
you Fànzhì,
for what reason
do you refrain from committing all wicked deeds in order to avoid Dìyù (hell)?
And cultivate all virtuous Dharmas in order to receive a Tiānshēn (heavenly body)?"
Xiānní said:
"Gautama!
In my Dharma (doctrine), the self has two types:
One is the performing body self (temporary/active self),
the second is the permanent body self.
Because of the performing body self,
we cultivate separation from evil deeds so as not to enter Dìyù,
and cultivate all virtuous Dharmas to be born in heaven."
The Fó said:
"Good man!
As you say that the self is pervasive everywhere,
such a self,
if it is in the performing body, should be known as impermanent.
If the performing body ceases,
how can you say it is pervasive?
"Gautama!
The self I establish is also in the active state,
and it is also permanent.
Gautama!
Just as when a person loses his fire [in an accidental conflagration],
and the dwelling house is burned,
the owner goes out,
one cannot say that since the dwelling house was burned,
the owner was also burned.
My doctrine is also like this.
Although this performing body is impermanent,
when it becomes impermanent, the self exits.
Therefore, my self is both pervasive and permanent."
The Fó said:
"Good man!
That which you say—that the self is both pervasive and permanent—
this reasoning is incorrect.
Why?
Pervasiveness (being pervasive) has two kinds:
one is permanent,
the other is impermanent.
Furthermore, there are two kinds (of the pervasive self):
One is material (Rūpa),
the second is immaterial (Arūpa).
Therefore, if you say that existence is absolute,
it is both permanent and impermanent,
and both material and immaterial.
If you say that the owner of the house got out and therefore cannot be called impermanent,
this reasoning is incorrect.
Why?
The house is not named the owner,
the owner is not named the house.
The burning is separate, the exiting is separate,
therefore they obtain this result.
The self, however, is not like this.
Why?
The self is immediately matter (form),
and matter is immediately the self;
the immaterial is immediately the self,
and the self is immediately the immaterial.
How then can you say that when matter is impermanent,
the self can exit?
Good man!
If you mean that all sentient beings have the same self,
this immediately violates both worldly
and supramundane Dharma.
Why?
Worldly Dharma refers to father,
son,
mother,
and daughter.
If the self is one,
the father is immediately the son,
the son is immediately the father;
the mother is immediately the daughter,
the daughter is immediately the mother.
The enemy is immediately the relative,
the relative is immediately the enemy;
this is immediately that,
that is immediately this.
Therefore, if you say that all sentient beings have the same self,
this immediately violates
both worldly and supramundane Dharma."
Xiānní said:
"I also do not say that all sentient beings share one self,
rather, I say that each person has their own self."
The Fó said:
"Good man!
If you say that each person has their own self,
that would be multiple selves,
but this reasoning is incorrect.
Why?
According to what you said earlier,
the self pervades everything.
If it pervades everything,
the faculties (roots) of action (karma) of all sentient beings should be the same.
When a deva (celestial being) is able to see, the Fó should also be able to see.
When a deva is able to act, the Fó should also be able to act.
When a deva is able to hear, the Fó should also be able to hear.
All Dharmas should be likewise.
If the deva is able to see but the Fó is not able to see,
you should not say that the self pervades everywhere.
If it is not pervasive,
then it is impermanent."
Xiānní said:
"Gautama!
For all sentient beings,
the self pervades everything;
but Dharma (virtue) and non-Dharma (non-virtue) do not pervade everything.
Because of this reasoning,
the action of the Fó is different,
and the action of the deva is different.
Therefore, Gautama!
You should not say that when the Fó is able to see, the deva should also be able to see,
or when the Fó is able to hear, the deva should also be able to hear."
The Fó said:
"Good man!
Are Dharma and non-Dharma
not created by karma (action)?"
Xiānní said:
"Gautama!
They are created by karma."
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
If Dharma (法)
and non-Dharma (非法) are the creators of action (karma),
then they are the same Dharma (同法).
How can you say they are different?
Why is this?
If the Buddha’s attainment (佛得) is the field of action (業處), then there is a celestial being’s attainment of the self (天得我).
If the celestial being’s attainment (天得) is the field of action, then there is the Buddha’s attainment of the self (佛得我).
Therefore, when the Buddha’s attainment acts, the celestial being’s attainment also acts.
Dharma and non-Dharma should also be like this.
Good man!
Therefore, if all sentient beings,
Dharma, and non-Dharma
are like this,
the resulting retributions (果報) should also not be different.
Good man!
When a fruit comes forth from a seed,
that seed never contemplates or distinguishes, saying:
‘I will only produce the fruit of a Brāhmaṇa (婆羅門),
and not produce the fruit for a Kṣatriya (剎利),
Vaiśya (毘舍),
or Śūdra (首陀).’
Why is this?
The fruit that comes forth from the seed
never obstructs these four castes.
Dharma and non-Dharma are also like this;
they cannot distinguish, saying, ‘I will only produce fruit for the Buddha’s attainment (佛得),
and not produce fruit for the celestial being’s attainment (天得).
I will produce the celestial being’s fruit,
but not produce the Buddha’s fruit.’
Why is this?
Because action (karma) is equal (平等)
Sēnì (先尼) said:
“Gōután (瞿曇)!
For example, if there are hundreds or thousands of lamps in one room,
although the wicks (炷) are different,
the light (明) is without disparity.
The difference between the lamp wicks illustrates Dharma and non-Dharma,
and the light being without disparity illustrates the self of sentient beings (眾生我).”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
Your use of the lamp light to illustrate the self
is not correct.
Why is this?
The room is separate from the lamp.
The light of this lamp
is also near the wick
and also pervades the entire room.
If the self that you speak of were like this,
then the self should be
in the vicinity of both Dharma and non-Dharma (非法),
and Dharma
and non-Dharma should also be in the self.
If Dharma
and non-Dharma do not contain the self,
it cannot be said that the self pervades all places.
If they both contain it, how can you then use the wick and light as an illustration?
Good man!
If you truly believe that the wick and the light are fundamentally separate and different,
for what reason
does the light grow brighter when the wick increases,
and the light diminish when the wick dries up?
Therefore, you should not
use Dharma and non-Dharma to illustrate the lamp wick,
or the light being without disparity to illustrate the self.
Why is this?
Dharma,
non-Dharma,
and the self are three things that are instantly one (即一).”
Sēnì said:
“Gōután!
The lamp analogy you introduced
is inauspicious (不吉).
Why is this?
If the lamp analogy were auspicious,
I would have introduced it first.
If it is inauspicious,
why are you speaking of it again?
“Good man!
The analogy I introduced is neither auspicious nor inauspicious;
it is spoken according to your intention.
This analogy also speaks of light existing apart from the wick,
and light existing instantly in the wick.
Your mind is unequal (不等),
hence you said the lamp wick illustrates Dharma
and non-Dharma,
and the light illustrates the self.
Therefore, I challenge you:
the wick is instantly the light,
and light exists apart from the wick;
Dharma instantly contains the self,
and the self instantly contains Dharma;
non-Dharma instantly contains the self,
and the self instantly contains non-Dharma.
Why do you now only accept one side
and not accept the other side?
Such an analogy
is inauspicious for you.
Therefore, I now use it to refute you.
Good man!
Such an analogy is instantly a non-analogy (非喻);
because it is a non-analogy,
it is instantly auspicious for me
and inauspicious for you.
Good man!
If you believe that if it is inauspicious for me,
it is also inauspicious for you,
this idea is incorrect.
Why is this?
You see people in the world harming themselves with their own knives,
making something for others to use.
The analogy you introduced is also like this;
it is auspicious for me
and inauspicious for you.”
Sēnì said:
“Gōután!
You first accused me of having an unequal mind,
but what you are now saying is also unequal.
Why is this?
Gōután is now attributing the auspiciousness to yourself
and the inauspiciousness to me.
Based on this reasoning,
it is truly unequal.”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
Since my inequality can destroy your inequality,
this means that your equality
and my inequality are instantly auspicious.
My inequality destroys your inequality
and causes you to attain equality,
which is instantly my equality.
Why is this?
Because it is the same as the equality attained by all noble persons (聖人).”
Sēnì said:
“Gōután!
I am always equal;
how can you say you are destroying my inequality?
All sentient beings equally possess the self;
how can you say I am unequal?”
"Good man!
You also say that
[the self] is bound to receive Hells,
is bound to receive hungry ghosts,
is bound to receive animals,
is bound to receive humans and devas.
If the self first pervades the Five Paths (Wǔ Dào),
how can you then say it is bound to receive these various destinations?
You also say that
when parents unite, only then is a son born.
If the son already existed beforehand,
why do you again say that the union resulted in existence?
Therefore, one self possesses the bodies of the Five Destinations.
If the body already existed beforehand in those five places,
for what reason does it create karma for the body?
Therefore, this is illogical.
Good man!
If your intention is to assert that the self is the creator/doer,
this assertion is wrong.
Why?
If the self is the creator,
for what reason would it create suffering for itself?
However, sentient beings now truly experience suffering.
Therefore, you should know the self is not the creator.
If you say this suffering is not created by the self,
and does not arise from causes,
all phenomena would also be like this,
not arising from causes.
For what reason do you then claim the self creates things?
Good man!
The suffering and happiness of sentient beings truly arise from conditions and causes.
Such suffering and happiness can create sorrow and joy.
When there is sorrow, there is no joy;
when there is joy, there is no sorrow.
Sometimes joy,
sometimes sorrow.
How can a wise person say that this is permanent?
Good man!
You say the self is permanent.
If it is permanent,
how can you speak of ten distinct periods/stages?
A permanent entity should not have stages from the Gēluóluó stage up to the stage of old age.
The permanence of space (xūkōng),
still lacks even one stage,
let alone ten stages.
Good man!
The self is not the Gēluóluó stage up to the stage of old age.
How can you say there are ten distinct periods?
Good man!
If the self is the creator,
this self also has times of prosperity and times of decline;
sentient beings also have times of prosperity and times of decline.
If the self is thus,
how can it be permanent?
Good man!
If the self is the creator,
how can one person be sharp and another dull?
Good man!
If the self is the creator,
this self can perform bodily karma
and vocal karma.
If vocal karma is created by the self,
how can the mouth speak of there being no self?
How can it doubt itself, asking, "Does it exist
or not exist?"
Good man!
If your intention is to assert that seeing exists apart from the eye,
this assertion is wrong.
Why?
If seeing exists separately after being separated from the eye,
why would this eye be necessary?
This applies likewise up to the body faculty.
If your intention is to assert that although the self is capable of seeing,
it must rely on the eye to see,
this is also wrong.
Why?
It is like someone saying the Xūmànnà flower can burn down a large village.
How can it burn?
It burns due to fire.
Your establishing the view of the self
is likewise.
Xiānnì said:
"Qútán!
Just as a person holding a sickle can cut grass,
the self, relying on the five roots (faculties), sees, hears, and touches, which is likewise."
"Good man!
The person and the sickle are distinct;
therefore, holding the sickle enables the performance of work.
Outside of the faculties,
there is no separate self.
How can you say that the self, relying on the faculties, is capable of performing work?
Good man!
If your intention is to assert that holding a sickle enables cutting,
and the self is likewise.
Does this self have hands?
Or does it not have hands?
If it has hands,
why doesn't it hold [the faculties] itself?
If it has no hands,
how can you say that the self is the creator?
Good man!
That which is capable of cutting grass is the sickle,
not the self,
nor the person.
If the self or person were capable,
why rely on the sickle?
Good man!
A person performs two actions:
first, grasping the grass;
second, holding the sickle.
The sickle merely has the function of cutting.
Sentient beings viewing phenomena are likewise:
the eye can see forms,
arising from aggregation/union.
If seeing arises from the aggregation of conditions and causes,
how can a wise person say that there is a self?
Good man!
If your intention is to assert that the body acts, and the self receives [the result],
this assertion is wrong.
Why?
It is not seen in the world that a Deva performs the karma,
while a Buddha receives the fruit.
If you say that the body does not act,
and the self does not receive the effect of the cause,
then why do you seek liberation relying on causes and conditions?
If your former body did not arise from causes and conditions,
after attaining liberation,
it likewise should not arise again as a body without cause;
like the body,
all afflictions should also be like this.
Xiānnì said:
"Qútán!
The self has two types:
one that knows (conscious),
and one that is ignorant (unconscious).
The ignorant self is able to obtain a body,
the knowing self is able to abandon and depart from the body.
Just like a damaged vase,
once it has been fired,
it loses its original color and does not arise again.
The afflictions of the wise person are likewise;
once they are destroyed and ruined,
they will never arise again."
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Regarding what you call 'knowing,'
does wisdom know?
Or does the self know?
If wisdom knows,
why do you say that the self is the knowing agent?
If the self knows,
why is effort made to seek wisdom furthermore?
If your intention is to assert,
that the self knows relying on wisdom,
this destroys the analogy of the flower.
Good man!
For example, a thorn tree inherently has the capacity to pierce;
one must not say that the tree holds the thorn to pierce.
Wisdom is likewise:
wisdom itself can know;
how can you say that the self holds wisdom to know?
Good man!
According to your doctrine, when the self attains liberation,
is it the ignorant self that attains it?
Or is it the knowing self that attains it?
If the ignorant self attains it,
you should know it still fully possesses afflictions.
If the knowing self attains it,
you should know it already possesses the five emotions and faculties.
Why?
Apart from the faculties,
there is no separate knowing.
If it possesses all the faculties,
how can it still be called 'attaining liberation'?
If you say the self is inherently pure and separate from the five faculties,
how can you say it pervades and exists in the Five Paths?
For what reason does one cultivate various good dharmas for the sake of liberation?
Good man!
It is like a person plucking a thorn from space (xūkōng);
you are also like this.
If the self were pure,
why would you still speak of cutting off all afflictions?
If your intention is to assert that liberation is attained without relying on causes and conditions,
why can all animals not attain it?
Xiānnì said:
"Qútán!
If there is no self,
who is capable of recollection?
The Buddha told Xiānnì:
"If there is a self,
for what reason does it forget again?
Good man!
If recollection belongs to the self,
for what reason
does it recollect bad recollections,
recollect what should not be recollected,
and fail to recollect what should be recollected?"
Śiānní
fù yán:
Ruò wú wǒ zhě,
shuí jiàn shuí wén?”
Fó yán:
“Shàn nánzǐ!
Nèi yǒu liù rù,
wài yǒu liù chén,
nèi wài héhé,
shēng liù zhǒng shí,
shì liù zhǒng shí yīnyuán dé míng.
Shàn nánzǐ!
Pìrú yī huǒ,
yīn mù dé gù míng wéi mù huǒ,
yīn cǎo dé gù míng wéi cǎo huǒ,
yīn kāng dé gù míng wéi kāng huǒ,
yīn niúfèn dé míng niúfèn huǒ.
Zhòngshēng yìshí yì fù rúshì,
yīn yǎn,
yīn sè,
yīn míng,
yīn yù,
míng wéi yǎnshí.
Shàn nánzǐ!
Rúshì yǎnshí,
bù zài yǎn zhōng nǎizhì yù zhōng,
sì shì héhé gù shēng shì shí,
nǎizhì yìshí yì fù rúshì.
Ruò shì yīnyuán héhé gù shēng,
zhì bù yìng shuō jiàn jí shì wǒ,
nǎizhì chù jí shì wǒ.
Shàn nánzǐ!
Shì gù wǒ shuō yǎnshí nǎizhì yìshí,
yīqiè zhūfǎ jí shì huàn yě.
Yún hé rú huàn?
Běn wú jīn yǒu,
yǐ yǒu hái wú.
Shàn nánzǐ!
Pìrú sū,
miàn,
mì,
jiāng,
hújiāo,
bìbá,
pú táo,
hútáo,
shí liú,
ruǐzǐ,
rúshì héhé,
míng huānxǐ wán,
lí shì héhé wú huānxǐ wán.
Nèi wài liù rù shì míng zhòngshēng,
wǒ,
rén,
shìfū.
Lí nèi wài rù,
wú bié zhòngshēng,
wǒ,
rén,
shìfū.”
Śiānní
yán:
Ruò wú wǒ zhě,
yún hé shuō yán wǒ jiàn,
wǒ wén,
wǒ kǔ,
wǒ lè,
wǒ yōu,
wǒ xǐ?”
Fó yán:
“Shàn nánzǐ!
Ruò yán wǒ jiàn,
wǒ wén,
míng yǒu wǒ zhě,
hé yīnyuán gù,
shìjiān fù yán,
rǔ suǒ zuò zuì,
fēi wǒ jiàn wén?
Shàn nánzǐ!
Pìrú sì bīng héhé míng jūn,
rúshì sì bīng bù míng wéi yī,
ér yì shuō yán wǒ jūn yǒng jiàn,
wǒ jūn shèng bǐ.
Shì nèi wài rù héhé suǒ zuò,
yì fù rúshì,
suī bú shì yī yì dé shuō yán,
wǒ zuò,
wǒ shòu,
wǒ jiàn,
wǒ wén,
wǒ kǔ,
wǒ lè.”
Śiānní
yán:
Rú rǔ suǒ yán,
nèi wài héhé,
shuí chū shēng yán,
wǒ zuò wǒ shòu?”
Fó yán:
“Śiānní!
Cóng ài,
wúmíng yīnyuán shēng yè,
cóng yè shēng yǒu,
cóng yǒu chūshēng wúliàng xīnshù,
xīn shēng jué guān,
jué guān dòng fēng,
fēng suí xīn chù hóu,
shé,
chǐ,
chún.
Zhòngshēng xiǎng dǎo,
shēng chū shuō yán,
wǒ zuò,
wǒ shòu,
wǒ jiàn,
wǒ wén.
Shàn nánzǐ!
Rú chuáng tóu líng,
fēng yīnyuán gù,
biàn chū yīnshēng.
Fēng dà shēng dà,
fēng xiǎo shēng xiǎo,
wú yǒu zuò zhě.
Shàn nánzǐ!
Pìrú rè tiě tóu zhī shuǐ zhōng,
chū zhǒngzhǒng shēng,
shì zhōng zhēnshí wú yǒu zuò zhě.
Shàn nánzǐ!
Fánfū bù néng sīwéi fēnbǐe rúshì shì gù,
shuō yán yǒu wǒ jí yǒu wǒ suǒ,
wǒ zuò,
wǒ shòu.”
Śiānní
yán:
wú wǒ,
wǒ suǒ,
hé yuán fù shuō cháng lè wǒ jìng?”
Fó yán:
“Shàn nánzǐ!
Wǒ yì bù shuō nèi wài liù rù jí liù shí yì cháng lè wǒ jìng,
wǒ nǎi xuānshuō miè nèi wài rù suǒ shēng liù shí,
míng zhī wéi cháng.
Yǐ shì cháng gù,
míng zhī wéi wǒ,
yǒu cháng wǒ gù,
míng zhī wéi lè,
cháng wǒ lè gù,
míng zhī wéi jìng.
Shàn nánzǐ!
Zhòngshēng yàn kǔ,
duàn shì kǔ yīn,
zìzài yuǎnlí,
shì míng wéi wǒ.
Yǐ shì yīnyuán,
wǒ jīn xuānshuō cháng lè wǒ jìng.”
Śiānní
yán:
Wéiyuàn dà cí wèi wǒ xuānshuō,
wǒ dāng yúnhé huòdé rúshì cháng lè wǒ jìng?”
Fó yán:
“Shàn nánzǐ!
Yīqiè shìjiān cóng běn yǐ lái,
jùzú dà màn,
néng zēngzhǎng màn,
yì fù zàozuò màn yīn,
màn yè,
