shì gù jīnzhě shòu màn guǒbào,
bù néng yuǎnlí yīqiè fánnǎo,
dé cháng lè wǒ jìng.
Ruò zhū zhòngshēng yù dé yuǎnlí yīqiè fánnǎo,
xiān dāng lí màn.”
Śiānní
yán:
Rúshì,
rúshì,
chéng rú shèng jiào.
Wǒ xiān yǒu màn,
yīn màn yīnyuán gù,
chēng Rúlái Níqū tán xìng.
Wǒ jīn yǐ lí rúshì dà màn,
shì gù chéngxīn qǐngqiú fǎ,
yúnhé dāng dé cháng lè wǒ jìng?”
Fó yán:
“Shàn nánzǐ!
Dì tīng,
dì tīng!
Jīn dāng wèi rǔ fēnbǐe jiěshuō.
Shàn nánzǐ!
Ruò néng fēi zì,
fēi tā,
fēi zhòngshēng zhě,
yuǎnlí shì fǎ.”
Śiānní
yán:
Wǒ yǐ zhī jiě,
dé zhèngfǎ yǎn.”
Fó yán:
“Shàn nánzǐ!
Rǔ yúnhé yán zhī yǐ jiě yǐ,
dé zhèngfǎ yǎn?”
“World-Honored One!
That which is called form
is not self,
is not other,
is not the various sentient beings;
even consciousness is also like this.
I observe thus,
and have attained the Eye of the Right Dharma.
World-Honored One!
I am now extremely pleased to leave home and cultivate the Way.
I pray that you grant me permission.”
The Buddha said:
“Well come, Bhikṣu.”
Immediately, he perfectly cultivated the pure monastic practice
and attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Among the followers of external paths, there was another Brāhmaṇa surnamed Jiāshè [Kāśyapa],
who spoke again, saying:
“Qú tán [Gautama]!
The body is identical to life,
or the body is separate from life.”
The Tathāgata remained silent.
A second and a third time, it was also like this.
The Brāhmaṇa spoke again:
“Qú tán!
If a person relinquishes the current body
and has not yet obtained the subsequent body,
how can it not be called the body being separate from life during that interim period?
If they are separate,
Qú tán,
why do you remain silent and not answer?”
“Good man!
I say that the body and life
both arise from causes and conditions,
not without causes and conditions.
Like the body
and life,
all phenomena are also thus.”
The Brāhmaṇa spoke again:
“Qú tán!
I see that there are phenomena in the world that do not arise from causes and conditions.”
The Buddha said:
“Brāhmaṇa!
How do you see that there are phenomena in the world that do not arise from causes and conditions?”
The Brāhmaṇa said:
“I see a great fire burning brushwood and trees.
The wind blows a separated flame
and it falls elsewhere.
Is this not called being without causes and conditions?”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
I say this fire
also arises from causes,
not without causes.”
The Brāhmaṇa said:
“Qú tán!
When the separated flame departs,
it is not dependent on firewood or charcoal.
How can you say it is dependent on causes and conditions?”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
Although there is no firewood or charcoal,
it departs due to the wind.
Because of the wind as a condition,
its flame is not extinguished.”
“Qú tán!
If a person relinquishes the current body
and has not yet obtained the subsequent body,
during the lifespan of that interim period,
what serves as the cause and condition?”
The Buddha said:
“Brāhmaṇa!
Ignorance and craving
serve as the causes and conditions.
Because of these two causes and conditions, ignorance
and craving,
the lifespan can persist.
Good man!
When there are causes and conditions,
the body is identical to life,
and life is identical to the body;
when there are causes and conditions,
the body is separate from life.
A wise person should not assert unilaterally that the body is separate from life.”
The Brāhmaṇa said:
“World-Honored One!
I only wish that you would clearly explain and differentiate this for me,
so that I may fully understand the cause and effect.”
The Buddha said:
“Brāhmaṇa!
The cause is the Five Aggregates (Wǔ Yīn),
and the effect is also the Five Aggregates.
Good man!
If there are sentient beings who do not light a fire,
then there is no smoke.”
The Brāhmaṇa said:
“World-Honored One!
I already know this,
I already understand this.”
The Buddha said:
“Good man!
How do you know?
How do you understand?”
“World-Honored One!
The fire is the afflictions (fán nǎo),
which can burn
in the hells,
among hungry ghosts,
animals,
humans, and devas. The smoke is the retribution of the afflictions.
It is impermanent, impure, foul-smelling, and repulsive;
therefore, it is called smoke.
If there are sentient beings who do not create afflictions,
then that person will not have the retribution of afflictions.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that if one does not light the fire, there will be no smoke.
World-Honored One!
I have attained the Right View.
I only wish for your compassionate regard to allow me to leave home.”
At that time, the World-Honored One instructed Jiāo Chénrú [Kaundinya]:
“Allow this Brāhmaṇa to leave home and receive the precepts.”
Then Jiāo Chénrú, having received the Buddha’s command,
gathered the assembly of monks
and allowed him to leave home
and receive the complete precepts.
After five days had passed,
he attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Among the followers of external paths,
there was another Brāhmaṇa named Fù Nà [Pūrṇa],
who spoke again, saying:
“Qú tán!
Do you say the world is permanent, seeing it as a permanent phenomenon?
Is this doctrine
true
or false?
Is it permanent,
impermanent,
both permanent and impermanent,
neither permanent nor impermanent?
Is it finite (yǒu biān),
infinite (wú biān),
both finite and infinite,
neither finite nor infinite?
Is the body identical to life,
or is the body separate from life?
After the Tathāgata passes away, does he go (rú qù),
not go (bù rú qù),
both go and not go,
or neither go nor not go?”
The Buddha said:
“Fù Nà!
I do not say that the world is permanent,
false,
true,
impermanent,
both permanent
and impermanent,
neither permanent
nor impermanent,
finite,
infinite,
both finite and infinite,
neither finite nor infinite;
nor that the body is identical to life,
or that the body is separate from life;
nor that after the Tathāgata passes away, he goes,
does not go,
both goes and does not go,
or neither goes nor does not go.”
Fù Nà spoke again:
“Qú tán!
What fault or harm do you now see that prevents you from making such a statement?”
The Buddha said:
“Fù Nà!
If someone says that the world is permanent,
and that only this is true while the rest is false speech,
this is called a view (jiàn).
The object of perception of the view
is called the activity of the view,
is called the karma of the view,
is called the attachment of the view,
is called the bondage of the view,
is called the suffering of the view,
is called the grasping of the view,
is called the fear of the view,
is called the fever of the view,
is called the entanglement of the view.
Fù Nà!
Ordinary people are entangled by views
and cannot distance themselves from birth, old age, sickness, and death.
They revolve through the six destinies and endure immeasurable suffering.
Even up to the statement ‘neither goes nor does not go,’
it is also like this.
Fù Nà!
I see that this view
has such faults;
therefore, I am not attached to it
and do not speak of it to others.”
"Qú Tán!
If you perceive such flaws,
you do not attach to them and do not speak of them.
What does Qú Tán now perceive,
what does he attach to,
and what does he proclaim?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Attachment to perception
is named the Dharma of life and death (Shēng Sǐ Fǎ).
Since the Rúlái has already departed from the Dharma of life and death,
therefore he does not attach.
Good man!
The Rúlái is named 'able to perceive and able to speak';
he is not named 'attached.'
"Qú Tán!
How is it that you are able to perceive?
How is it that you are able to speak?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
I am clearly able to perceive Suffering (Kǔ), Accumulation (Jí), Cessation (Miè), and the Way (Dào),
and differentiate and proclaim these Four Noble Truths (Sì Dì).
Because I perceive this way,
I am therefore able to separate from all views,
all craving (ài),
all outflows (liú),
and all conceit (màn).
Therefore, I possess the pure Brahman practice (Qīng Jìng Fàn Xíng),
unsurpassed stillness,
and have attained the eternal body (Cháng Shēn).
This body is also not East,
West,
South,
or North."
Fù Nà said:
"Qú Tán!
For what reason
is the eternal body not East, West, South, or North?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
I will now ask you a question;
answer according to your thoughts.
What do you think?
Good man!
Suppose there is a great burning fire heap before you;
when it is burning,
do you know that it is burning or not?"
"It is so,
Qú Tán!"
"When this fire is extinguished,
do you know that it is extinguished or not?"
"It is so,
Qú Tán!"
"Fù Nà!
If someone were to ask about the fire heap before you,
where did the burning come from?
Where did the extinguishing go?
How would you answer?"
"Qú Tán!
If someone were to ask,
I would answer by saying:
When this fire arose, it relied on many conditions.
When the former conditions have been exhausted,
and new conditions have not arrived,
this fire is extinguished."
"If they further ask,
to which direction did this fire go after it was extinguished?
How would you answer then?"
"Qú Tán!
I would answer by saying,
it was extinguished because the conditions were exhausted;
it did not go to any direction or location."
"Good man!
The Rúlái is also like this.
If there were impermanent form (Wú Cháng Sè) up to impermanent consciousness (Wú Cháng Shí),
it burns because of craving (ài).
That burning is experiencing the Twenty-Five Existences (Èrshíwǔ Yǒu).
Therefore, when it burns, one might say that the fire is East, West, South, or North.
Now, craving is extinguished.
The karmic rewards of the Twenty-Five Existences do not burn.
Because they do not burn,
it cannot be said that there is East, West, South, or North.
Good man!
The Rúlái has already extinguished the impermanent form up to the impermanent consciousness.
Therefore, the body is eternal (cháng).
If the body is eternal,
it cannot be said to have East, West, South, or North."
Fù Nà said:
"Please allow me to offer one analogy;
I only ask that you heed it."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Speak as you wish."
"World-Honored One (Shì Zūn)!
Suppose outside a great village there is a Suō Luó Lín (Sāla Grove).
In it there is one tree
that grew fully one hundred years before the rest of the grove.
At that time, the owner of the grove
watered it and cared for it seasonally.
That tree became old and rotten;
its bark, branches, and leaves all fell away,
only the solid core remained.
The Rúlái is also like this:
all that is old and obsolete has been utterly removed,
only the truly real Dharma remains.
Shì Zūn!
I am now greatly pleased to leave home and practice the Way."
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu (Bǐ Qiū)."
Having spoken this,
he immediately left home (chūjiā).
Having exhausted the outflows, he attained the fruit of the Ā Luó Hàn.
There was also a Brāhmaṇa (Fàn Zhì) named Qīng Jìng,
who spoke thus:
"Qú Tán!
Because all sentient beings do not know what Dharma,
they view the world as eternal,
impermanent,
both eternal and impermanent,
neither eternal nor impermanent,
and even up to neither gone nor not gone (Fēi Rú Qù Fēi Bù Rú Qù)?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Because they do not know form (sè), and so forth up to not knowing consciousness (shí),
they view the world as eternal, and so forth up to neither gone nor not gone."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Qú Tán!
Because sentient beings know what Dharma,
they do not view the world as eternal, and so forth up to neither gone nor not gone?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Because they know form, and so forth up to knowing consciousness,
they do not view the world as eternal, and so forth up to neither gone nor not gone."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Shì Zūn!
I only wish that you would distinguish and explain for me the world's eternality
and impermanence."
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
If a person casts away the old (gù)
and does not create new karma (yè),
this person is able to know eternality and impermanence."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Shì Zūn!
I have already realized (this view)."
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
How do you perceive?
How do you know?"
"Shì Zūn!
The old is named ignorance (wú míng) and craving (ài).
The new is named grasping (qǔ)
and existence (yǒu).
If a person departs from this ignorance and craving,
and does not create grasping and existence,
this person truly knows eternality
and impermanence.
I have now attained the pure eye of the Righteous Dharma (Zhèng Fǎ),
and I take refuge in the Three Jewels (Sān Bǎo).
I only wish that the Rúlái would allow me to leave home."
The Buddha instructed Jiāo Chén Rú:
"Allow this Brāhmaṇa
to leave home and receive the precepts."
At that time, Jiāo Chén Rú, having received the Buddha's command,
brought him into the Saṅgha (sēng zhōng),
performed the karma process (jiémó) for him, allowing him to leave home.
Fifteen days later,
all outflows were eternally exhausted,
and he attained the fruit of the Ā Luó Hàn.
The Brāhmaṇa Dú Zǐ spoke again, saying:
"Qú Tán!
I now wish to ask a question.
Will you allow me to?"
The Rúlái remained silent.
The second
and third times were also like this.
Dú Zǐ spoke again:
"Qú Tán!
I have long been a close friend with you.
The principle between you and me is not dual.
I wish to inquire;
why are you silent?"
At that time, the World-Honored One thought thus:
"This Brāhmaṇa
is refined in nature,
purely good and honest.
He always comes to inquire and seek guidance for the sake of knowledge,
not for disturbance or confusion.
If he asks,
I should answer as he wishes."
The Buddha said:
"Dú Zǐ!
Excellent,
excellent!
Whatever you question,
I shall answer it."
Dú Zǐ said:
"Qú Tán!
Is there goodness (Shàn) in the world?
"It is so."
"Fànzhì!
"Is there the non-good (unwholesome)?"
"It is so."
"Fànzhì!
"Gòután!
Please speak for me,
so that I may know the good
and the non-good Dharmas."
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
I am able to analyze and broadly explain its meaning,
but now I shall briefly speak of it for you.
Good man!
Desire is called non-good;
the one liberated from desire
is called good.
Hatred and ignorance are also like this.
Killing is called non-good;
not killing is called good.
Down to wrong view, it is also like this.
Good man!
I have now spoken for you about the three types of good and non-good Dharmas,
and also spoken about the ten types of good and non-good Dharmas.
If my disciple is able to make such an analysis of the three types of good and non-good Dharmas,
and even the ten types of good and non-good Dharmas,
you should know that this person
is able to exhaust greed,
hatred,
ignorance,
all defilements (āsravas),
and cut off all existence (bhāva)."
The Fànzhì said:
"Gòután!
Among the Buddha's teachings, is there perhaps one Bhikṣu who can exhaust such craving, hatred, and ignorance,
all defilements,
and all existence?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Among the Buddha's teachings, not only one, two, three, or even five hundred,
but rather immeasurable Bhikṣus
are able to exhaust such craving, hatred, and ignorance,
all defilements,
and all existences."
"Gòután!
Setting aside one Bhikṣu,
among the Buddha's teachings, is there perhaps one Bhikṣuṇī who can exhaust such craving, hatred, and ignorance,
all defilements,
and all existence?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Among the Buddha's teachings, not only one, two, three, or even five hundred,
but rather immeasurable Bhikṣuṇīs
are able to cut off such craving, hatred, and ignorance,
all defilements,
and all existences."
Dúzǐ said:
"Gòután!
Setting aside one Bhikṣu,
and one Bhikṣuṇī,
among the Buddha's teachings, is there perhaps one Upāsaka (Yōupósāi),
who maintains the precepts diligently,
whose holy conduct is pure,
who crosses to the shore beyond doubt,
and cuts off the net of doubt?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Among my Buddha's teachings, not only one, two, three, or even five hundred,
but rather immeasurable Upāsakas
maintain the precepts diligently and whose holy conduct is pure,
who cut off the five lower fetters,
attain Anāgāmi (Ānàhán),
cross to the shore beyond doubt,
and cut off the net of doubt."
Dúzǐ said:
"Gòután!
Setting aside one Bhikṣu,
one Bhikṣuṇī,
and one Upāsaka,
among the Buddha's teachings, is there perhaps one Upāsikā (Yōupóyí),
who maintains the precepts diligently, whose holy conduct is pure, who crosses to the shore beyond doubt, and cuts off the net of doubt?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Among my Buddha's teachings, not only one, two, three, or even five hundred,
but rather immeasurable Upāsikās
maintain the precepts diligently, whose holy conduct is pure, who cut off the five lower fetters,
attain Ānàhán,
cross to the shore beyond doubt,
and cut off the net of doubt."
Dúzǐ said:
"Gòután!
Setting aside one Bhikṣu,
one Bhikṣuṇī who have exhausted all defilements,
and one Upāsaka,
and one Upāsikā who maintain the precepts diligently, whose holy conduct is pure, and who cut off the net of doubt—
among the Buddha's teachings, are there perhaps Upāsakas who experience the pleasures of the five desires,
yet whose minds are free from the net of doubt?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
Among the Buddha's teachings,
not only one, two, three, or even five hundred,
but rather immeasurable Upāsakas cut off the three fetters,
and attain Sotāpanna (Xūtuóhuán);
who weaken greed, hatred, and ignorance,
and attain Sakadāgāmi (Sītuóhán)."
Like the Upāsakas,
the Upāsikās are also like this.
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
I would now like to speak a metaphor."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent!
If you wish to speak, then speak."
"Shìzūn!
For example, just as Nántuó
and Pónántuó Dragon Kings pour down great rain,
the Tathāgata's (Rúlái's) Dharma Rain is also like this,
raining equally upon the Upāsakas
and Upāsikās."
"Shìzūn!
If various heterodox followers wish to come and leave home (become monastics),
I wonder how many months the Tathāgata tests them?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
They are all tested for four months,
but not necessarily in the same way."
"Shìzūn!
If they are not tested in the same way,
I humbly request that with your great compassion, you allow me to leave home."
At that time, the Shìzūn instructed Jiāochénrú:
"Allow this Dúzǐ to leave home and receive the precepts."
Then Jiāochénrú, having received the Buddha's command,
performed the karma (ceremony) for him among the assembly of monks.
After leaving home, having completed fifteen days,
he attained the fruition of Xūtuóhuán.
After having attained the fruition,
he then formed this thought:
"Any wisdom that can be attained through learning,
I have now attained.
I am worthy to see the Buddha."
He immediately went to the place of the Buddha,
bowed his head to the ground in reverence.
Having completed his respectful duties,
he stood back on one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Shìzūn!
All wisdom that is attained through learning,
I have now attained.
I humbly request that you again separately explain the Dharma for me,
so that I may attain the wisdom of the non-learner (Aśaikṣa)."
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
You must diligently cultivate and practice two Dharmas:
first, Śamatha (Shēmótuō),
second, Vipaśyanā (Pípóshěnà).
Good man!
If there is a Bhikṣu who wishes to attain the fruition of Xūtuóhuán,
he must also diligently cultivate these two Dharmas.
If he further wishes to attain the fruition of Sītuóhán,
the fruition of Ānàhán,
or the fruition of Arhat (Āluóhàn),
he must also cultivate and practice these two Dharmas.
Good man!
If there is a Bhikṣu who wishes to attain the four Dhyānas,
the four immeasurable minds,
the six supernormal powers,
the eight liberations,
the eight overcoming masters,
the knowledge of non-contention,
the summit knowledge,
the ultimate knowledge,
the four unobstructed knowledges,
the knowledge of the exhaustion of defilements through Vajra Samādhi (Jīngāng Sānmèi),
and the knowledge of non-arising,
he must also cultivate and practice these two Dharmas.
Good man!
If one wishes to attain the ten Bhūmis (dwelling places),
the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena,
the patience regarding the signless nature of phenomena,
the patience regarding the inconceivable nature of phenomena,
the noble conduct,
the holy conduct,
the divine conduct,
the Bodhisattva (Púsà) conduct,
the Void Samādhi,
the Wisdom Seal Samādhi,
the Samādhi of Voidness, Signlessness, and Non-striving,
the Earth Samādhi,
the Non-retreat Samādhi,
the Śūraṅgama Samādhi (Shǒuléngyán Sānmèi);
the Vajra Samādhi,
Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòuduōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
and the conduct of a Buddha,
one must also cultivate and practice these two Dharmas."
Dúzǐ, having heard this,
bowed and left.
In the Sāla Grove (Suōluólín), he cultivated these two Dharmas,
and soon thereafter attained the fruition of Āluóhàn.
At that time, there were again immeasurable Bhikṣus who wished to go to the Buddha's place.
Dúzǐ saw them and asked:
"Venerable Ones!
Where are you going?"
The Bhikṣus said:
"We wish to go to the place of the Fó."
Dúzǐ Fànzhì again said:
"Venerable Sirs!
If you reach the place of the Fó,
I request that you announce [this] for me:
Dúzǐ Fànzhì, having cultivated the Two Dharmas,
attained the wisdom of the non-learner (Arhat),
and now, repaying the grace of the Fó,
enters Bōnièpán."
At that time, the Bhikṣus, having reached the place of the Fó,
reported to the Fó, saying:
"Shìzūn!
Bhikṣu Dúzǐ
entrusted us with a message:
'Shìzūn!
Dúzǐ Fànzhì,
having cultivated the Two Dharmas and attained the wisdom of the non-learner,
now repays the grace of the Fó,
and enters Nièpán.'"
The Fó said:
"Good man!
Dúzǐ Fànzhì has attained the fruit of Āluóhànguǒ.
You should go and make offerings to his body."
At that time, the Bhikṣus, having received the Fó's command,
returned to his corpse,
and made great offerings.
Nàyī Fànzhì again spoke thus:
"Qúntán!
According to what Qúntán teaches, having performed good [deeds]
and non-good [deeds] throughout countless lifetimes,
one will in the future again receive a good or non-good body.
This principle is incorrect.
Why is that?
According to what Qúntán says,
due to defilements (kleśa),
one obtains this body.
If one obtains the body due to defilements,
is the body prior?
Or are the defilements prior?
If the defilements are prior,
by whom were they created?
Where do they reside?
If the body is prior,
why is it said that it is obtained due to defilements?
Therefore, if it is said that the defilements are prior,
this is also impossible;
if the body is prior,
this is also impossible;
if it is said they are simultaneous,
this is also impossible.
Prior,
posterior,
or simultaneous—
all these interpretations are impossible.
Therefore, I say that all dharmas possess their own nature (svabhāva),
and do not arise from causation (hetupratyaya).
"Furthermore, Qúntán!
Solidity is the nature of earth,
moisture is the nature of water,
heat is the nature of fire,
movement is the nature of wind,
and unhinderedness is the nature of space (ākāśa).
These Five Great Natures do not exist due to causation.
If there is one dharma-nature in the world that does not exist due to causation,
then the nature of all dharmas should likewise exist without causation.
If there is one dharma that arises from causation,
then for what reason
do the natures of the Five Great Elements not arise from causation?
Qúntán!
The good bodies and non-good bodies of sentient beings, and the attainment of liberation,
are all [due to] self-nature,
and do not arise from causation.
Therefore, I say that all dharmas exist due to their self-nature,
and are not born from causation.
"Furthermore, Qúntán!
The dharmas of the world have fixed applications.
For example, a craftsman
says that certain wood is fit to make carriages,
and certain wood is fit to make doors,
beds, and stools.
Also, like a goldsmith:
the objects he creates—
that which is worn on the forehead is called a headband,
that which is worn below the neck is called a necklace,
that which is worn on the arm is called a bracelet,
and that which is worn on the finger is called a ring.
Because their application is fixed, they are called fixed nature.
Qúntán!
All sentient beings are also like this:
Because they possess the natures of the Five Paths,
there are Dìyù,
Èguǐ,
Chùshēng,
Rén,
and Tiān.
If this is the case,
how can you say that they arise from causation?
"Furthermore, Qúntán!
All sentient beings have distinct natures;
therefore, this is called the self-nature of all things.
Qúntán!
For example, a turtle born on land
is naturally able to enter water.
A calf, once born,
is naturally able to drink milk.
A fish seeing the hook and bait
naturally swallows and eats it.
A poisonous snake, once born,
naturally eats dirt.
For such things,
who is there to teach them?
Like a thorn, once it grows,
its point is naturally sharp.
The feathers of flying birds naturally have distinct colors.
Sentient beings in the world are also like this:
some are sharp, some are dull;
some are rich, some are poor;
some are good-looking, some are ugly;
some attain liberation,
and some do not attain liberation.
Therefore, you should know that every single dharma possesses its own self-nature.
"Furthermore, Qúntán!
According to what Qúntán says,
greed, anger, and delusion arise from causation.
Such Three Poisons
are caused by the Five Objects (of sense).
This principle is incorrect.
Why is that?
When sentient beings are sleeping, they are far removed from the Five Objects,
yet greed, anger, and delusion still arise.
It is the same when they are in the womb.
When they first emerge from the womb, they cannot yet distinguish the Five Objects,
good or bad,
yet greed, anger, and delusion still arise.
Sages and Worthies,
dwelling in secluded places,
where there are no Five Objects,
are also able to give rise to greed, anger, and delusion.
There are also people who, using the Five Objects,
give rise to non-greed,
non-anger,
and non-delusion.
Therefore, it is not necessarily through causation
that all dharmas arise,
but due to self-nature.
"Furthermore, Qúntán!
I see people in the world whose Five Faculties are incomplete,
yet they possess abundant wealth
and attain great independence.
Others have complete faculties,
yet are poor and lowly,
attain no independence,
and serve as slaves to others.
If there were causation,
why would it be like this?
Therefore, all dharmas possess their own self-nature,
and are not dependent on causation.
Qúntán!
Infants in the world
are also unable to distinguish the Five Objects.
They might laugh
or they might cry.
When they laugh, we know they are happy;
when they cry, we know they are distressed.
Therefore, you should know that all dharmas possess their own self-nature.
Furthermore, Qúntán!
Worldly dharmas are of two types:
first, existence (yǒu);
second, non-existence (wú).
Existence is defined as empty space;
non-existence is defined as a rabbit's horn.
These two dharmas:
one exists, and thus does not arise from causation;
the second is non-existent, and thus is also not causation.
Therefore, because all dharmas possess self-nature,
they do not arise from causation."
The Fó said:
"Good man!
According to what you have said,
that all dharmas should be
like the nature of the Five Great Elements,
this principle is incorrect.
Why is that?
Good man!
In your doctrine, you hold that the Five Great Elements are permanent.
For what reason, then, are all other dharmas completely non-permanent?
If the things of the world are impermanent,
then for what reason
is the nature of these Five Great Elements not impermanent?
If the Five Great Elements are permanent,
then the things of the world should also be permanent.
Therefore, your assertion that the nature of the Five Great Elements
does not arise from causation because it possesses self-nature,
and that all dharmas should be made the same as the Five Great Elements,
is impossible.
"Good man!
Your assertion that things have intrinsic nature (zìxìng) because their function (yòngchù) is fixed
is incorrect.
Why is this?
Because all things derive their name from causal conditions (yīnyuán).
If they acquire the name from causes,
they also acquire the meaning from causes.
How are things said to acquire their name from causes?
For example, when something is on the forehead, it is called a máng (wreath);
when on the neck, it is called a yīng (necklace);
when on the arm, it is called a chuàn (bracelet);
when on a chariot, it is called a lún (wheel);
when fire is in grass and wood,
it is called grass-and-wood fire.
Good man!
When a tree first grows,
it does not possess the nature of an arrow (jiàn) or a spear (shuò).
Due to causal conditions,
a craftsman makes it into an arrow;
due to causal conditions,
a craftsman makes it into a spear.
Therefore, one should not say that all dharmas possess intrinsic nature.
Good man!
Your assertion that just as a turtle (guī) is born on land
but naturally enters water,
and that a calf (dúzǐ), once born,
naturally possesses the capacity to drink milk—
this assertion is incorrect.
Why is this?
If you say entering the water is not due to causal conditions,
then if both actions are without causal conditions,
why does it not enter fire?
If you say that a calf, once born,
naturally possesses the capacity to suckle milk,
and this does not arise from causal conditions,
then if both actions are without causal conditions,
why does it not suckle a horn (jiǎo)?
Good man!
If you say that all dharmas possess intrinsic nature,
then instruction and practice would not be needed,
and there would be no growth.
This assertion is incorrect.
Why is this?
We now see that there is instruction (jiào),
and things grow based on instruction.
Therefore, you should know that there is no intrinsic nature.
Good man!
If all dharmas possess intrinsic nature,
then none of the Brāhmaṇas (Póluómén) should sacrifice sheep (shāyáng císì) for the purification of the body (qīngjìng shēn).
If they do perform sacrifices for the body,
therefore, you should know that there is no intrinsic nature.
"Good man!
Generally, worldly discourse (shìjiān yǔfǎ) has three types:
First, intending to do (yù zuò);
second, while doing (zuò shí);
third, having done (zuò yǐ).
If all dharmas possess intrinsic nature,
why are these three discourses present in the world?
Since these three discourses exist,
therefore, we know that nothing possesses intrinsic nature.
Good man!
If you say that all dharmas possess intrinsic nature,
then you should know that all dharmas must have a fixed nature (dìngxìng).
If there is a fixed nature,
why should sugarcane (gānzhè), being a single substance,
give rise to juice (jiāng),
rock sugar (mì shí),
honey wine (mì jiǔ),
and sour vinegar (kǔ jiǔ), etc.?
If it has one fixed nature,
how can it produce such different tastes (wèi)?
If a single substance produces such various things,
you should know that dharmas cannot be absolutely fixed
and each possess a single nature.
Good man!
If all dharmas possess a fixed nature,
why do the Noble Ones (Shèngrén) drink sugarcane juice,
rock sugar,
and black honey,
but refrain from drinking it when it becomes wine,
yet drink it again later when it turns into sour vinegar?
Therefore, you should know that there is no fixed nature.
If there is no fixed nature,
how could things exist without relying on causal conditions?
Good man!
If you say that all dharmas possess intrinsic nature,
how can you use analogies (yù)?
If analogies exist,
you should know that dharmas do not possess intrinsic nature.
If intrinsic nature exists,
you should know that analogies cannot exist.
All wise people in the world (shìjiān zhìzhě) use metaphors and analogies (pìyù).
Therefore, you should know that all dharmas have no intrinsic nature
and no fixed unitary nature.
"Good man!
Your assertion regarding whether the body (shēn) came first
or the defilements (fánnǎo) came first
is incorrect.
Why is this?
If I were to say that the body came first,
you could raise the objection
that you agree with me that the body did not come first.
For what causal reason do you raise this objection?
Good man!
The body and defilements of all sentient beings (zhòngshēng)
have neither a prior
nor a later existence; they arise simultaneously.
Although they arise simultaneously,
the body must rely on defilements to exist,
but defilements never rely on the body to exist.
If you suppose that they are like a person’s two eyes,
which are obtained simultaneously
and do not rely upon each other—
the left does not rely on the right,
the right does not rely on the left—
and that defilements and the body
are also like this:
This assertion is incorrect.
Why is this?
Good man!
In the world, we see clearly the wick (zhù) and the light (míng).
Although they are simultaneous,
the light must rely on the wick,
but the wick never relies on the light to exist.
"Good man!
If you suppose that since the body did not come first,
therefore it has no cause (wú yīn):
This assertion is incorrect.
Why is this?
If you say that the body being not prior means it is designated as non-existent because it lacks causal conditions,
then you should not assert
that all dharmas have causal conditions.
If you say you do not assert it because it is not seen (bù jiàn),
we now see that things like jars (píng) arise from causal conditions.
Why do you not say that, like the jar,
the prior causal conditions of the body are also like this?
Good man!
Whether seen
or unseen, all dharmas
arise from causal conditions
and have no intrinsic nature.
Good man!
If you say that all dharmas entirely possess intrinsic nature,
and are without causal conditions,
then for what causal reason do you speak of the Five Great Elements (Wǔ Dà)?
The nature of these Five Great Elements is precisely causal condition.
Good man!
Although the causal conditions of the Five Great Elements are indeed like this,
you still should not say that all dharmas are identical to the causal conditions of the Five Great Elements.
For example, worldly people say that all those who have left home (chūjiā) diligently observe the precepts (chíjiè).
Candālas (Zhāntuóluó) and others should also diligently observe the precepts in the same way.
"Good man!
You say that the Five Great Elements have a fixed hard nature.
I observe that this nature is mutable, thus it is not fixed.
Good man!
Ghee (sū), wax (là), and foreign glue (hújiāo),
which in your doctrine are designated as Earth,
are not fixed as Earth.
They may sometimes resemble water,
or sometimes resemble earth.
Therefore, you cannot say that they are hard due to their intrinsic nature.
Good man!
Pewter (báilà), lead (qián), tin (xī),
copper (tóng), iron (tiě), gold (jīn), and silver (yín)—
in your doctrine, these are designated as Fire.
This Fire element has four natures:
When flowing, it is the nature of Water;
when moving, it is the nature of Wind;
when hot, it is the nature of Fire;
when hard, it is the nature of Earth.
How can you assert that it is fixedly designated as the nature of Fire?
Good man!
The nature of Water is designated as flowing.
If water freezes,
it is not designated as Earth.
Therefore, if it is designated as Water,
for what causal reason
is it not designated as Wind when it is surging?
If movement is not designated as Wind,
then when frozen, it should likewise not be designated as Water.
If these two meanings arise from causal conditions,
why do you say that all dharmas do not arise from causal conditions?
"O good man!
If you say that the five faculties (wǔ gēn) are inherently capable of seeing,
hearing,
perceiving,
knowing,
and touching,
and that they are all self-existent (zìxìng) and do not arise from conditioning factors (yīnyuán),
this is incorrect.
Why is that?
O good man!
The nature of self-existence (zìxìng) cannot be changed.
If you say that the nature of the eye is to see, it should constantly be able to see,
and there should not be times when it sees
and times when it does not see.
Therefore, you should know that seeing arises from conditioning factors,
not without conditioning factors.
O good man!
Your statement that craving (tān) and liberation (jiětuō) are produced not because of the five sensory objects (wǔ chén)
is incorrect.
Why is that?
O good man!
The production of craving and liberation,
although seemingly not depending on the conditioning factors of the five sensory objects,
occurs because evil reflective thought (è juéguān) gives rise to covetous desire (tānyù),
and good reflective thought (shàn juéguān) leads to liberation.
O good man!
Internal conditioning factors (nèi yīnyuán) produce craving and liberation;
external conditioning factors (wài yīnyuán) can cause them to grow.
Therefore, your statement that all phenomena (zhūfǎ) each have their own self-existence,
and that craving and liberation are not produced by the five sensory objects,
is impossible.
"O good man!
Your statement that those possessing all faculties but lacking wealth cannot be self-mastered (zìzài),
while those with incomplete or damaged faculties but possessing great wealth achieve great self-mastery,
and that this proves the existence of self-existence,
independent of conditioning factors—
this is incorrect.
Why is that?
O good man!
Sentient beings receive karmic retribution (guǒbào) based on their actions (yè).
This retribution falls into three types:
first, present retribution (xiànbào);
second, next-life retribution (shēngbào);
third, subsequent retribution (hòubào).
Poverty,
great wealth,
complete faculties,
incomplete faculties—
these retributions of action are distinct.
If there were self-existence, those who possess all faculties
should be wealthy,
and those who are wealthy should possess all faculties.
Now, this is not the case.
Therefore, it is definitely known that there is no self-existence,
but everything arises from conditioning factors.
As for your statement that
worldly infants cannot yet distinguish the conditioning factors of the five sensory objects,
yet they cry and laugh,
and therefore everything has self-existence—
this is incorrect.
Why is that?
If it were self-existence,
laughter should be perpetual laughter,
and crying should be perpetual crying.
They should not sometimes laugh
and sometimes cry.
If they sometimes laugh and sometimes cry, you should know that everything arises entirely from conditioning factors.
Therefore, you should not say that all phenomena have self-existence
and do not arise from conditioning factors."
The Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) said:
"World-Honored One (Shìzūn)!
If all phenomena arise from conditioning factors,
then this body, from what conditioning factors does it arise?"
The Buddha said:
"O good man!
The conditioning factors for this body
are the afflictions (fánnǎo) and karma (yè)."
The Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) said:
"Shìzūn!
Since this body arises from afflictions and karma,
can these afflictions and karma
be severed or not?"
The Buddha said:
"It is so,
it is so."
The Brāhmaṇa (Fànzhì) further said:
"Shìzūn!
I only wish that you would distinguish and explain for me,
so that upon hearing it,
I may sever them all without leaving this place."
The Buddha said:
"O good man!
If one knows the two extremes (èr biān),
and the middle path is unobstructed (wú ài),
that person will be able to sever afflictions and karma."
"Shìzūn!
I already understand;
I have obtained the Eye of the True Dharma (Zhèngfǎ Yǎn)."
The Buddha said:
"How do you know?"
"Shìzūn!
The two extremes are Form (sè) and the liberation from Form (sè jiětuō);
the middle path is the Eightfold Noble Path (Bāzhèngdào).
Feeling (shòu), conception (xiǎng), volition (xíng), and consciousness (shí) are also like this."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent,
excellent!
O good man!
You know the two extremes well
and have severed afflictions and karma."
"Shìzūn!
I only wish that you would allow me to leave home (chūjiā) and receive the precepts (shòujiè)."
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu (Bǐqiū)."
Immediately, he severed the afflictions of the Three Realms (Sānjiè fánnǎo)
and attained the fruition of Arhatship (Āluóhàn guǒ).
At that time, there was again a Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) named Hóngguǎng,
who again spoke thus:
"Gautama (Qútán)!
Do you know what I am currently thinking?"
The Buddha said:
"O good man!
Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) is permanent (cháng);
conditioned phenomena (yǒuwéi) are impermanent (wúcháng).
Crookedness is heterodox views (xiéjiàn);
straightness is the noble path (shèngdào)."
The Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) said:
"Qútán!
For what conditioning factor do you speak thus?"
"O good man!
Your mind always considers begging for food (qǐshí) to be permanent,
and being invited separately (biéqǐng) to be impermanent.
Crookedness is the door key (hùyào);
straightness is the Emperor's standard (dìzhuàng).
Therefore, I say that Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) is permanent,
conditioned phenomena are impermanent,
crookedness refers to heterodox views,
and straightness refers to the Eightfold Noble Path (Bāzhèng),
not as you previously thought."
The Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) said:
"Qútán truly knows my mind.
Does this Eightfold Noble Path (Bāzhèngdào)
enable all sentient beings to achieve complete cessation (jìnmiè)?"
Thereupon the World-Honored One remained silent and did not answer.
The Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) said:
"Qútán!
Since you know my mind,
regarding what I have now asked,
why do you remain silent and not give an answer?"
At that moment, Kaundinya (Jiāochénrú) immediately spoke thus:
"Great Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén)!
If someone asks whether the world has limits (yǒu biān)
or is limitless (wú biān),
the Tathāgata (Rúlái) always remains silent and does not answer.
The Eight Noble (Paths) (Bāshèng) are straight;
Nirvāṇa (Nièpán) is permanent.
If one cultivates the Eight Noble [Paths], one immediately achieves cessation (mièjìn);
if one does not cultivate them, one cannot achieve it.
Great Póluómén!
For example, imagine a great city.
The city walls on all four sides
have no openings or holes,
only one gate.
The gatekeeper is intelligent and wise, skilled at distinguishing:
those who should be let go are let go;
those who should be blocked are blocked.
Although he cannot know exactly how many enter or exit,
he definitely knows that everyone who enters or exits must pass through this gate.
O good man!
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is also like this.
The city symbolizes Nirvāṇa (Nièpán);
the gate symbolizes the Eightfold Noble Path (Bāzhèng);
the gatekeeper symbolizes the Tathāgata.
O good man!
Although the Tathāgata does not now answer whether [beings] achieve cessation or not,
those who do achieve cessation
must cultivate this Eightfold Noble Path (Bāzhèngdào)."
The Brāhmaṇa (Póluómén) said:
"Excellent,
excellent!
Great Virtuous Jiāochénrú!
The Tathāgata is well able to preach the subtle Dharma (fǎ).
I truly wish now to know the city and know the path,
and become the gatekeeper myself."
Jiāochénrú said:
"Excellent,
excellent!
You, Póluómén, are able to arouse the unsurpassed, vast, and great mind."
The Buddha said:
“Stop,
stop!
Kǒuchénrú!
This Brāhmaṇa did not just today conceive this intention.
Kǒuchénrú!
A long time ago, in the immeasurable past kalpas, there was a World-Honored Buddha,
named Pǔguāngmíng Rúlái,
Arhat,
Samyak-sambuddha,
Vidyā-caraṇa-sampanna,
Sugata,
Lokavid,
Anuttara,
Puruṣa-damya-sārathi,
Śāstā Devamanuṣyāṇām,
Buddha,
Bhagavān (World-Honored One).
This person had already conceived the mind of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi before that Buddha.
In this Bhadrakalpa (Wise Kalpa), he shall attain Buddhahood.
He has long ago attained profound realization and fully understood the characteristics of the Dharma,
and for the sake of sentient beings, he currently appears within the path of outer teachings (heretics),
feigning ignorance.
Due to this reason,
you, Kǒuchénrú, should not praise him by saying,
‘Excellent,
excellent,
you are now able to conceive such a great resolve (mind).’”
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing this, immediately addressed Kǒuchénrú, saying:
“Where is the Bhikṣu Ānán now?”
Kǒuchénrú replied:
“World-Honored One!
The Bhikṣu Ānán is outside the Sāluólín (Sāla forest),
twelve yóuxún away from this great assembly,
and he is being tormented and confused by sixty-four billion Māras (demons).
All these hosts of Māras have transformed themselves into the likeness of the Rúlái (Tathāgata).
Some preach that all dharmas arise from causation (causes and conditions);
some say that all dharmas do not arise from causes;
some say that all causes and conditions are permanent dharmas;
while those that arise from conditions are all impermanent.
Some say that the Five Aggregates (Wǔyīn) are real;
some say they are illusory and false. The Dhātus (Jìe, elements/realms) are also spoken of in this manner.
Some say there are Twelve Nidānas (Twelve Links of Dependent Origination);
some say there are only Four Conditions (Sìyuán).
Some say all dharmas are like illusions, like transformations, or like the shimmering of a heat haze.
Some say the Dharma is obtained through hearing;
some say the Dharma is obtained through reflection;
some say the Dharma is obtained through practice (cultivation).
Furthermore, some preach the contemplation of impurity (Bùjìng Guān Fǎ);
some preach the incoming and outgoing breath (Ānāpāna);
some preach the contemplation of the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Sì Niànchù Guān);
some preach the meaning of the Three Kinds of Contemplation and the Seven Expedients;

some preach the stages of Warmth Dharma (Nuǎn Fǎ), Summit Dharma (Dǐng Fǎ), Forbearance Dharma (Rěn Fǎ), World’s Supreme Dharma (Shìjiān Dìyī Fǎ), the grounds of learning and no-learning (Xué Wúxué Dì), and the initial abode (Zhù) of the Bodhisattva up to the Tenth Abode.
Some preach emptiness (Kōng), signlessness (Wúxiàng), and wishlessness (Wúzuò).
Furthermore, some preach Sūtra (Xiūduōluó),
Geya (Qíyè),
Vyākaraṇa (Píjiāluó),
Gāthā (Nàjiātuó),
Udāna (Yōutuónà),
Nidāna (Níduōnà),
Avadāna (Āpōtuónà),
Itivṛttaka (Yīdìmutuōjiā),
Jātaka (Shétuójiā),
Vaipulya (Pífúlüè),
Adbhutadharma (Āfútuódámó),
Upadeśa (Yōupōtíshě).
Some preach the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Sì Niànchù),
the Four Proper Exertions (Sì Zhèngqín),
the Four Bases of Supernatural Power (Sì Rúyì Zú),
the Five Faculties (Wǔ Gēn),
the Five Powers (Wǔ Lì),
the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (Qī Juéfēn),
and the Eightfold Noble Path (Bā Shèng Dào).
Some preach inner emptiness (Nèikōng),
outer emptiness (Wàikōng),
inner and outer emptiness (Nèiwài Kōng),
conditioned emptiness (Yǒuwéi Kōng),
unconditioned emptiness (Wúwéi Kōng),
beginningless emptiness (Wúshǐ Kōng),
nature emptiness (Xìng Kōng),
emptiness of separation (Yuǎnlí Kōng),
emptiness of dispersion (Sàn Kōng),
emptiness of self-characteristics (Zìxiàng Kōng),
emptiness of signlessness (Wúxiàng Kōng),
emptiness of aggregates (Yīn Kōng),
emptiness of sense bases (Rù Kōng),
emptiness of elements (Jiè Kōng),
emptiness of good (Shàn Kōng),
emptiness of bad (Bùshàn Kōng),
emptiness of neutral (Wújì Kōng),
emptiness of Bodhi (Pútí Kōng),
emptiness of the Path (Dào Kōng),
emptiness of Nirvāṇa (Nièpán Kōng),
emptiness of formations (Xíng Kōng),
emptiness of acquisition (Dé Kōng),
emptiness of ultimate truth (Dìyī Yì Kōng),
emptiness of emptiness (Kōng Kōng),
and great emptiness (Dà Kōng).
Some display supernatural powers and transformations: fire and water issuing from the body;
or water issuing from the upper part of the body and fire issuing from the lower part;
or water issuing from the lower part of the body and fire issuing from the upper part;
the left side being down and water issuing from the right side;
the right side being down and water issuing from the left side;
or thunder shaking from one side and rain pouring from the other side.
Some display the worlds of various Buddhas;
or display the Bodhisattva taking seven steps upon his initial birth;
his time in the deep palace enjoying the Five Desires;
his initial renunciation and practice of asceticism;
his time going to the Bodhi tree and sitting in Samādhi;
his time destroying the hosts of Māra and turning the Dharma Wheel;
and his time displaying great supernatural powers and entering Nirvāṇa.
World-Honored One!
The Bhikṣu Ānán, having seen these things,
thought thus:
‘Such supernatural transformations,
I have never seen before.
Who performed them?
Could it be the World-Honored Śìjiā (Śākya) performing them?’
He wanted to speak but could not express his thoughts.
Since the Bhikṣu Ānán has fallen into the Māra’s trap,
he further thought:
‘The teachings spoken by the various Buddhas are all different.
Whose words should I accept now?’
World-Honored One!
Ānán is currently suffering greatly.
Although he thinks of the Rúlái,
there is no one who can save him.
For this reason,
he has not come to this great assembly.”
At that time, Wénshūshīlì Púsà Móhēsà addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Among this great assembly are various Bodhisattvas,
who have conceived the mind of Anuttarā Samyak Sambodhi in one lifetime, or have conceived the Bodhi mind for immeasurable lifetimes.
They have been able to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas.
Their minds are firm and resolute.
They have perfectly practiced Dānapāramitā up to Prajñāpāramitā.
They have perfected meritorious virtues.
They have long since associated closely with immeasurable Buddhas.
They cultivate pure Brahma practice (celibacy).
They have attained the irreversible Bodhi mind.
They have attained irreversible forbearance.
They hold irreversible maintenance (Dhāraṇī).
They have attained the Forbearance of the True Dharma.
They have attained immeasurable Samādhis, such as Śūraṅgama (Shǒuléngyán).
Such individuals,
upon hearing the Mahāyāna Sūtras, will never give rise to doubt.
They are skilled at distinguishing and proclaiming that the Three Jewels share a single nature and characteristic,
eternal and unchanging.
Upon hearing of the inconceivable, they are not startled or surprised.
Upon hearing of the various kinds of emptiness, their minds are not terrified or frightened.
They clearly and fully penetrate the nature of all dharmas.
They are capable of upholding all the Twelve Divisions of the Canon and extensively explaining their meaning.
They are also capable of accepting and maintaining the Twelve Divisions of the Canon taught by immeasurable Buddhas.
How could they worry about not being able to accept and maintain such a great Mahāparinirvāṇa canon?
For what reason, then,
do you ask Kǒuchénrú where Ānán is?”
At that time, the World-Honored One (Shìzūn) addressed Mañjuśrī (Wénshū Shīlì):
"Listen carefully,
listen carefully,
good man!
After I attained Buddhahood,
I spent more than twenty years residing in Rājagṛha (Wángshě Chéng).
At that time, I spoke to the bhikṣus (bǐqiū), saying:
‘Bhikkhus!
Among this assembly now, who is able to uphold the Tathāgata's (Rúlái) twelve divisions of the scriptures for me,
provide the necessities required for service,
and also ensure that they do not lose their own merits and benefits?’
At that time, Kauṇḍinya (Jiǎochénrú), being in that assembly, came and addressed me, saying:
‘I am able to uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures,
provide the necessities for service,
and not lose the benefits derived from my own practice.’
I replied:
‘Kauṇḍinya (Jiǎochénrú)!
You are already old and decrepit;
you yourself require attendance.
How then can you desire to serve me?’
Then Śāriputra (Shèlìfú) spoke again, saying:
‘I am able to uphold all of the Buddha's (Fó) words,
provide all that is necessary,
and not lose the benefits derived from my own practice.’
I replied:
‘Śāriputra (Shèlìfú)!
You are already old and decrepit;
you yourself require attendance.
How then can you desire to serve me?’
Even five hundred Arhats (Āluóhàn) spoke thus,
but the Buddha (Fó) did not accept any of them.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana (Mùlián) thought within the great assembly:
‘Since the Tathāgata (Rúlái) now
does not accept service from the five hundred bhikṣus,
Buddha's (Fó) mind intends for whom to perform this task?’
Having thought this,
he immediately entered meditation,
and saw that the Tathāgata's (Rúlái) intention was for Ānanda (Ānán),
like the sun at dawn
shining its light upon the western wall.
Having seen this matter,
he immediately arose from meditation,
and spoke to Kauṇḍinya (Jiǎochénrú):
‘Great Virtuous One!
I perceive that the Tathāgata (Rúlái) wishes Ānanda (Ānán) to attend to his affairs.’
At that time, Kauṇḍinya (Jiǎochénrú), together with the five hundred Arhats (Āluóhàn),
went to the place where Ānanda (Ānán) was,
and spoke thus:
‘Ānanda (Ānán)!
You should now serve the Tathāgata (Rúlái);
we request you to accept this task.’
Ānanda (Ānán) replied:
‘O Great Virtuous Ones!
I am truly incapable of serving the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
Why is that?
The Tathāgata (Rúlái) is venerable and respected,
like a lion king,
like a Nāga (lóng),
like fire.
I am currently impure and weak;
how can I manage this task?’
The bhikṣus (bǐqiū) said:
‘Ānanda (Ānán)!
Accept our words,
and serve the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
You will obtain great benefit.’
A second time,
and a third time, they spoke similarly.
Ānanda (Ānán) replied:
‘O Great Virtuous Ones!
I do not seek great benefits;
I am truly unable to assume the task of serving as attendant.’
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana (Mùjiànlián) spoke again, saying:
‘Ānanda (Ānán)!
You do not yet know the circumstances.’
Ānanda (Ānán) replied:
‘Great Virtuous One!
I only wish that you would explain it.’
Mahāmaudgalyāyana (Mùjiànlián) said:
‘A few days ago, the Tathāgata (Rúlái) sought an attendant among the Sangha (sēng);
five hundred Arhats (Luóhàn) all requested to serve him,
but the Tathāgata (Rúlái) did not permit it.
I immediately entered meditation,
and I saw that the Tathāgata's (Rúlái) intention was to have you perform the service.
How can you now, on the contrary, refuse to accept?’
When Ānanda (Ānán) heard this,
he joined his palms and knelt respectfully,
and spoke thus:
‘O Great Virtuous Ones!
If this is truly the case,
if the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One (Rúlái Shìzūn), grants me three wishes,
I will comply with the Sangha’s (sēng) command
and serve as attendant.’
Mahāmaudgalyāyana (Mùjiànlián) asked:
‘What are these three wishes?’
Ānanda (Ānán) replied:
‘First, if the Tathāgata (Rúlái) should bestow an old robe upon me,
allow me not to accept it.
Second, if the Tathāgata (Rúlái) accepts a separate invitation from a donor (Tányuè),
allow me not to go.
Third, allow my coming and going
to be without fixed times.
If the Buddha (Fó) grants these three matters,
If the Buddha (Fó) grants these,
I will comply with the Sangha’s (sēng) command
and serve the Tathāgata (Rúlái).’
Then Kauṇḍinya (Jiǎochénrú) and the five hundred bhikṣus (bǐqiū),
returned to my location,
and spoke thus:
‘We have already persuaded the bhikṣu (bǐqiū) Ānanda (Ānán),
but he only requests three wishes.
If the Buddha (Fó) grants them,
he will comply with the Sangha’s (sēng) command.’
Mañjuśrī (Wénshū Shīlì)!
At that time, I praised Ānanda (Ānán), saying:
‘Excellent,
excellent!
The bhikṣu (bǐqiū) Ānanda (Ānán)
possesses complete wisdom,
foreseeing criticism and reproach.
Why is that?
People might say that you serve the Tathāgata (Rúlái) for the sake of robes and food,
thus, he first requested not to accept old robes
and not to follow separate invitations.
Kauṇḍinya (Jiǎochénrú)!
The bhikṣu (bǐqiū) Ānanda (Ānán) possesses complete wisdom;
if his coming and going were restricted by time,
he would be unable to widely benefit the four assemblies of disciples.
Therefore, he requested to be able to come and go without fixed times.
Kauṇḍinya (Jiǎochénrú)!
I granted Ānanda (Ānán) permission regarding these three matters,
in accordance with his wishes.’
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana (Mùjiànlián) returned to Ānanda (Ānán)’s location,
and spoke to Ānanda (Ānán), saying:
‘I have already appealed on your behalf for the three matters,
and the Tathāgata (Rúlái), in his great compassion, has already granted them all.’
Ānanda (Ānán) replied:
‘Great Virtuous One!
If the Buddha (Fó) has granted them,
I request to go and serve him."
"Wénshū Shīlì!
Ānán has served me for more than twenty years,
possessing eight kinds of inconceivable [qualities] in full.
What are these eight?
First, since serving me for more than twenty years, he has never followed me to receive a separate invited meal.
Second, since serving me, he has never received old or worn clothes from me.
Third, since serving me, whenever he came to my location, it was never at an improper time.
Fourth, since serving me,
though complete with afflictions (kleshas),
following me when entering and leaving the residences of various kings and Kshatriyas,
high officials, nobles, and great families,
seeing various women, as well as celestial and
Nāga women,
he did not give rise to desire (lust).
Fifth, since serving me,
he has retained the Twelve Divisions of the Scriptures (Sūtras) that I have preached; once heard by the ear, he never asked about them again,
like pouring water from one jar into another jar,
except for one question.
Good man!
When Prince Liúlí killed all the Śākyas (Shì shì),
destroying Kapilavastu (Jiāpíluó chéng),
Ānán at that time felt distress and sorrow in his heart,
crying aloud,
and came to me,
speaking thus:
'I and the Tathāgata were both born in this city, belonging to the same Śākya clan.
How is it that the Tathāgata's face and appearance are as normal,
whereas I am haggard?'
I then replied:
'Ānán!
I cultivate the concentration (samādhi) of Emptiness (Kōng dìng),
therefore I am not like you.'
After three years had passed,
he returned and asked me:
'Honored by the World (Shìzūn)!
I went to Kapilavastu (Jiāpíluó chéng),
and heard that the Tathāgata cultivated the Samādhi of Emptiness (Kōng Sānmèi).
Is this matter true or false?'
I said:
'Ānán!
It is so,
it is so,
exactly as you have said.'
Sixth, since serving me,
although he has not yet obtained the wisdom of knowing others' minds (Tāxīn zhì),
he constantly knows the concentrations (samādhis) the Tathāgata enters.
Seventh, since serving me,
although he has not attained the wisdom of vows (Yuàn zhì),
he is able to clearly know which sentient beings, when they come to the Tathāgata's presence,
can attain the Four Fruits of the Śramaṇa immediately,
which ones will attain them later,
which ones will attain a human body [in the next life],
and which ones will attain a celestial body.
Eighth, since serving me,
he is entirely able to know the Tathāgata's secret words.
Good man!
The Bhikṣu Ānán possesses these eight inconceivable [qualities] in full.
Therefore, I call the Bhikṣu Ānán the Storehouse of Extensive Listening (Duōwén Zàng).
Good man!
The Bhikṣu Ānán possesses eight qualities,
enabling him to fully retain the Twelve Divisions of the Scriptures.
What are these eight?
First, the root of faith (Xìn gēn) is firm;
second, his mind is honest and upright (Zhì zhí);
third, his body is free from illness and suffering;
fourth, he is constantly diligent in striving forward (Jīngjìn);
fifth, he possesses complete mindfulness (Niàn xīn);
sixth, his mind is without arrogance (Jiāomàn);
seventh, he achieves concentration (Dìng) and wisdom (Huì);
eighth, he possesses the wisdom derived from hearing (Cóng wén shēng zhì) in full.
Wénshū Shīlì!
The attending disciple of Vipasyin Buddha (Pí Pōshī Fó) was named Āshújiā;
he also fully possessed these eight qualities.
The attending disciple of Śikhin Tathāgata (Shīqì Rúlái) was named Chàmójiāluó;
the attending disciple of Viśvabhū Buddha (Pí Shèfú Fó) was named Yōupōshàntuó;
the attending disciple of Krakucchanda Buddha (Jiāluójiūcūntuó Fó) was named Bhàtí;
the attending disciple of Kanakamuni Buddha (Jiānàhánmóuní Fó) was named Sūzhǐ;
the attending disciple of Kāśyapa Buddha (Jiāyè Fó) was named Yèpómìduō;
all of them also fully possessed these eight qualities.
My current Ānán likewise fully possesses these eight qualities,
therefore, I call the Bhikṣu Ānán the Storehouse of Extensive Listening.
Good man!
As you have said,
although there are immeasurable and boundless Bodhisattvas in this great assembly,
these Bodhisattvas all have serious duties,
namely, Great Loving-kindness (Dà Cí) and Great Compassion (Dà Bēi).
Due to the karmic conditions of such Loving-kindness and Compassion,
each of them is busy taming their respective retinues and adorning themselves.
For this reason,
after my Nirvāṇa (Nièpán), they will not be able to propagate the Twelve Divisions of the Scriptures.
Even if some Bodhisattvas might occasionally preach them,
people will not believe or accept them.
Wénshū Shīlì!
The Bhikṣu Ānán is my cousin,
serving me for more than twenty years.
The Dharma he has heard, he fully accepts and retains,
analogous to pouring water from one vessel into another.
Therefore, I now inquire,
where is Ānán?
I want him to receive and uphold this Nirvāṇa Sūtra (Nièpán Jīng).
Good man!
After my Nirvāṇa, whatever the Bhikṣu Ānán has not yet heard,
Hóngguǎng Púsà will be able to spread widely,
and what Ānán has heard, he himself will be able to declare and convey.
Wénshū Shīlì!
The Bhikṣu Ānán is currently in another place,
twelve yojanas (Yóuyán) away from this assembly,
and is being tormented and disturbed by sixty-four thousand billion Māras.
You should go there and declare in a loud voice:
'All you Māras!
Listen closely,
listen closely.
The Tathāgata is now speaking the Great Dhāraṇī (Dà Tuóluóní),
which all Devas (Tiān),
Nāgas (Lóng),
Gandharvas (Gāntàpó),
Asuras (Āxiūluó),
Garuḍas (Jiālóuluó),
Kinnaras (Jǐnnàluó),
Mahoragas (Móhóuluójiā),
humans and non-humans,
mountain spirits,
tree spirits,
river spirits,
sea spirits,
and house spirits, and others,
when they hear this name,
none fail to respectfully accept and uphold it.
This Dhāraṇī has been jointly proclaimed by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones (Fó Shìzūn), equal to the sands of ten Ganges Rivers.
It is able to transform the female body,
and allow one to know one's own past lives (Sùmìng).
If one accepts five matters:
first, pure conduct (Fànhéng);
second, ceasing meat consumption;
third, ceasing alcohol consumption;
fourth, ceasing pungent foods (Xīn);
fifth, delighting in stillness and solitude (Jìjìng);
having accepted the five matters,
wholeheartedly believing and accepting,
and reading, reciting, or writing this Dhāraṇī,
one should know that this person will immediately transcend seventy-seven billion vile and evil bodies.'
Thereupon, the World-Honored One (Shìzūn)
immediately spoke it:
"Āmólī Bīmólī Nièmólī Mèngqiélī Hīmóluó Ruòjiéyǐ Sānmànduō Bátí Lī Suōpóluótuō Suōtánní Póluómótuō Suōtánní Mónàsī Ābùtí Bīluóshì Ānmólàidī Póluómí Póluómósuō Lī Fùluōní Fùluōnà Mónúlàitì"
Thereupon, Wénshū Shīlì, having received this Dhāraṇī from the Buddha,
went to Ānán’s location,
and amidst the hosts of Māras, spoke thus:
"Hosts of Māras, listen closely!
I shall recite the Dhāraṇī spell (Zhòu) that I received from the Buddha."
When the Māra King heard this Dhāraṇī,
he immediately gave rise to the mind of Anuttara Samyak Sambodhi (Ānòu Duōluó Sānmiǎo Sānpútí),
abandoned his Māra work,
and released Ānán.
Wénshū Shīlì and Ānán together came to the Buddha’s location.
Ānán saw the Buddha,
and paid sincere reverence and respect,
then stood aside.
The Buddha told Ānán:
"Outside this Śāla grove (Suōluó Lín),
there is a Brahmacārin (Fànzhì) named Subhadra (Xūbátuó).
He is extremely old,
already one hundred and twenty years old.
Although he has attained the Five Supernatural Powers (Wǔ Tōng),
he has not yet abandoned arrogance.
He has achieved the Concentration of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception (Fēixiǎng Fēifēi Xiǎng Dìng),
giving rise to the notion of Nirvāṇa based on All-Knowledge.
You may go to him,
and tell Subhadra (Xūbá):
'The Tathāgata's appearance in the world is like the Udumbara flower.
He will enter Parinirvāṇa (Bō Nièpán) this midnight.
If you have anything to do, you should do it in time,
lest you generate regret later.'
Ānán!
What you say,
he will definitely believe and accept.
Why is this?
In the past, throughout five hundred lifetimes,
you were Subhadra's (Xūbátuó's) son.
That man's habit of affection is still not exhausted.
Due to this karmic condition, he will believe and accept your words."
Thereupon, Ānán, having received the Buddha's command,
went to Subhadra (Xūbá),
and spoke thus:
"Worthy one!
You should know that the Tathāgata's appearance in the world is like the Udumbara flower.
He will enter Parinirvāṇa this midnight.
If you wish to do anything, you should do it in time,
lest you generate regret later."
Subhadra (Xūbá) said:
"Excellent!
Ānán!
I shall now go to the Tathāgata's location."
Thereupon, Ānán and Subhadra (Xūbátuó) returned to the Buddha's location.
When Subhadra arrived, he offered greetings and inquiries,
and spoke thus:
"Gautama (Qú tán)!
I now wish to ask a question;
please answer as I desire."
The Fó said:
“Xūbá!
Now is precisely the time.
Whatever you ask,
I shall skillfully answer according to your desire.”
“Qútán!
There are various Śrāmaṇas and Brāhmaṇas, etc., who speak thus:
‘All sentient beings receive the retribution of suffering and pleasure,
all depending on the causes and conditions of their original actions from past existences.
Therefore, if there is one who maintains the precepts and diligently strives,
and endures suffering of body and mind,
they can destroy their original actions.
Once the original actions are exhausted,
all sufferings are completely extinguished.
The complete extinction of all suffering is the immediate attainment of Nièpán.’
What does this doctrine mean?”
The Buddha said:
“Good men!
If there are Śràmàṇas,
Brāhmaṇas, or others who hold such views,
I, out of compassion,
will always go to the location of such people.
Once I have arrived there,
I will ask them:
‘Worthy one!
Do you truly maintain this assertion?’
If they reply:
‘I maintain this assertion.’
‘Why is this so?’
‘Gùtán!
I observe that sentient beings who practice various evils
possess abundant wealth
and achieve self-mastery (autonomy);
I also observe those who cultivate good
are poor and greatly lacking,
and do not achieve self-mastery;
I also observe people who exert much effort seeking things but cannot obtain them;
I also observe those who do not seek yet obtain things naturally;
I also observe people who possess loving-kindness and do not kill, yet they suffer premature death;
I also observe those who delight in killing, yet they maintain their full lifespan;
I also observe people who purely cultivate Bràhma-practices and diligently uphold the precepts,
some attaining liberation,
and some not attaining it;
Therefore, I state that all sentient beings receiving the retribution of suffering and pleasure
is entirely due to the karmic causes and conditions from past fundamental deeds.’
Xūbá!
I would further ask:
‘Worthy one!
Do you truly perceive past karma?
If this karma exists,
is it great or small?
How much of it can present ascetic practices destroy?
Can you know whether this karma is already exhausted
or not exhausted?
Once this karma is exhausted,
is everything exhausted?’
If they reply:
‘I truly do not know.’
I would then offer that person an analogy:
‘Suppose there is a person whose body has been struck by a poisoned arrow.
His family and relatives invite a physician to extract the arrow.
Once the arrow is extracted, the person's body achieves peace and comfort.
Ten years later, this person still recalls,
clearly and distinctly,
that this physician extracted the poisoned arrow for me,
applied medicine and salve,
allowed me to recover,
and enjoy peace and pleasure.
Since you do not know the past fundamental karma,
how can you know that present ascetic practice can definitely destroy past karma?’
If they should further say:
‘Gùtán!
You also have past fundamental karma now,
why do you exclusively criticize my view of past karma?
Your Sūtras also state this:
If one sees a person who is rich, noble, and autonomous,
one should know that this person was fond of giving in previous lives.
Is this not called past karma?’
I would reply again:
‘Worthy one!
This manner of knowing
is called knowledge through analogy (comparative knowledge),
not true knowledge.
In my Dharma,
there is knowledge of the effect from the cause,
and there is knowledge of the cause from the effect.
In my Dharma, there is past karma
and there is present karma.
Your view is not so;
you only have past karma,
and no present karma.
Your doctrine does not cut off karma through skillful means,
but my Dharma is not like that;
it is cut off through skillful means.
When your karma is exhausted,
then suffering is exhausted.
I, however, am not so;
when afflictions (kleshas) are exhausted,
karmic suffering is exhausted.
This is why I now criticize your view of past karma.’
If that person says:
‘Gùtán!
I truly do not know;
I received it from my teacher.
The teacher made this assertion,
so I am truly without fault.’
I would say:
‘Worthy one!
Who is your teacher?’
If they reply:
‘It is Pùlánnà (Pūraṇa).’
I would further say:
‘Why did you not previously inquire in detail,
“Does the great master truly know past karma?”
If your teacher said, “I do not know,”
how could you accept the teacher's words?
If he said, “I know,”
you should have further asked:
“Does a cause of minor suffering result in medium
or major
suffering?
Does a cause of medium suffering result in minor
or major suffering?
Does a cause of major suffering result in medium
or minor
suffering?”
If he says no,
you should have further asked:
“Master, how can you say that the retribution of suffering and pleasure
is only due to past karma
and not the present?
You should have further asked:
“Is this present suffering
found in the past?
If it is found in the past,
the karma of the past is all completely exhausted.
If it is completely exhausted,
how do you receive the body of today?
If it is not found in the past,
but only exists in the present,
how can you say that the suffering and pleasure of sentient beings are all due to past karma?
Worthy one!
If you know that present ascetic practice can destroy past karma,
by what is present ascetic practice itself destroyed?
If it is not destroyed,
then suffering is eternal;
if suffering is eternal,
how can you speak of attaining liberation from suffering?
If there is still another practice that destroys the ascetic practice,
and if the past is already exhausted,
how can there be suffering?
Worthy one!
Can such ascetic practices
cause pleasurable karma to receive a suffering retribution?
Or cause suffering karma to receive a pleasurable retribution?
Can it cause karma that is neither suffering nor pleasure to produce no retribution?
Can it cause present retribution (immediate effect) to become retribution in the next life (posthumous effect)?
Can it cause retribution in the next life to become present retribution?
Can it cause both of these retributions to become non-retribution?
Can it cause fixed retribution to become non-retribution?
Can it cause non-retribution to become fixed retribution?’
If they further say:
‘Gùtán!
No, it cannot.’
I would further say:
‘Worthy one!
If it cannot,
for what cause and condition do you undertake this ascetic practice?
Worthy one!
You should know that there is definitely past karma,
and present causes and conditions.
Therefore, I state that karma arises from afflictions,
and retribution is received because of karma.
Worthy one!
You should know that all sentient beings have past karma
and present causes.
Although sentient beings have the karmic determination of lifespan from the past,
they must rely on the present causes and conditions of food and drink.
Worthy one!
If you state that sentient beings receive suffering and pleasure
definitely due to the causes and conditions of past fundamental karma,
this matter is incorrect.
Why is this so?
Worthy one!
For example, if someone eliminates a foe for the king,
due to this cause and condition, he obtains much wealth.
Due to this wealth, he receives present pleasure.
Such a person presently creates the cause of pleasure,
and presently receives the retribution of pleasure.
For example, if someone kills the king’s beloved son,
due to this cause and condition, he loses his life.
Such a person presently creates the cause of suffering and presently receives the retribution of suffering.
Worthy one!
All sentient beings presently depend on the Four Great Elements,
time, seasons,
land,
and people
to receive suffering and pleasure.
Therefore, I state that all sentient beings do not necessarily receive suffering and pleasure entirely due to past fundamental karma.
Worthy one!
If attaining liberation were based on the power derived from the causes and conditions of eliminating karma,
then all Sages would not attain liberation.
Why?
Because the past fundamental karma of all sentient beings has no beginning and no end.
Therefore, I state that when cultivating the Noble Path,
this Path is able to obstruct karma that has no beginning and no end.
Worthy one!
If undertaking ascetic practice immediately leads to attaining the Path,
then all animals should attain the Path.
Therefore, one must first regulate and subdue the mind,
not regulate and subdue the body.
Due to this cause and condition,
I state in my Sūtras:
‘Cut down this forest,
do not cut down the trees.’
Why is this so?”
from the forest,
not from the trees.
If one wishes to subdue
the body, one must first subdue the mind.
The mind is likened to the forest,
the body is likened to the tree.
Xū Bátuó said:
"World-Honored One!
I have already first subdued my mind."
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
How have you been able to subdue your mind first?"
Xū Bátuó said:
"World-Honored One!
I first contemplated
that desire is impermanent,
without pleasure,
and impure.
I observed that form (rūpa) is permanent, joyous, and pure.
Having made this observation,
the fetters of the desire realm were severed,
and I attained the form realm.
Therefore, this is called first subduing the mind.
Next, I again observed form:
Form is impermanent,
like a boil,
like an ulcer,
like poison,
like an arrow.
I saw that formlessness is permanent,
pure,
and tranquil.
Having made this observation,
the fetters of the form realm were extinguished,
and I attained the formless realm.
Therefore, this is called first subduing the mind.
Next, I again observed perception (saṃjñā):
it is impermanent,
a boil/ulcer,
poison/arrow.
Having made this observation,
I attained the state of neither perception nor non-perception.
This state of neither perception nor non-perception
is All-Knowledge,
tranquility,
purity,
without falling or perishing,
constant, eternal, and unchanging.
Therefore, I was able to subdue my mind."
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
How can you say you have subdued your mind?
The samādhi of neither perception nor non-perception that you have attained
is still named 'perception.'
Nirvāṇa is without perception;
how can you say you have attained Nirvāṇa?
Good man!
You were previously able to denounce coarse perceptions;
why now do you cling to subtle perception
and fail to denounce it?
Such a state of neither perception nor non-perception
is still called perception—
like a boil,
like an ulcer,
like poison,
like an arrow.
Good man!
Your teacher, Yùtóulánfú, though sharp-witted and intelligent,
still could not sever the state of neither perception nor non-perception,
and underwent a wretched existence.
How much less can others do so?
"World-Honored One!
How can one sever all existences?"
The Buddha said:
"Good man!
If one contemplates the true mark,
that person can sever all existences."
Xū Bátuó said:
"World-Honored One!
What is called the true mark?"
"Good man!
The mark of no-mark
is called the true mark."
"World-Honored One!
What is called the mark of no-mark?"
"Good man!
All phenomena are without their own mark,
the mark of others, and the mark of self and others.
Without the mark of no cause,
without the mark of action,
without the mark of reception,
without the mark of the actor,
without the mark of the receiver.
Without the mark of phenomena or non-phenomena,
without the mark of male or female,
without the mark of a man of substance,
without the mark of an atom,
without the mark of time and duration.
Without the mark of becoming self,
without the mark of becoming others,
without the mark of becoming self and others.
Without the mark of existence,
without the mark of non-existence,
without the mark of arising,
without the mark of the riser.
Without the mark of cause,
without the mark of the cause of cause,
without the mark of effect,
without the mark of the effect of effect.
Without the mark of day and night,
without the mark of brightness and darkness,
without the mark of seeing,
without the mark of the seer.
Without the mark of hearing,
without the mark of the hearer,
without the mark of perceiving/knowing,
without the mark of the perceiver/knower.
Without the mark of Bodhi,
without the mark of the one who attains Bodhi,
without the mark of karma,
without the mark of the master of karma.
Without the mark of affliction,
without the mark of the master of affliction.
Good man!
Where such marks
are extinguished,
that is called the true mark.
Good man!
All phenomena are illusory and false.
Where they are extinguished,
that is called the real.
That is called the true mark,
that is called the Dharma Realm,
called the Ultimate Wisdom,
called the Ultimate Truth,
called the Ultimate Emptiness.
Good man!
This mark,
the Dharma Realm,
the Ultimate Wisdom,
the Ultimate Truth,
the Ultimate Emptiness,
when contemplated by lower wisdom,
results in the Bodhi of the Śrāvaka;
when contemplated by middle wisdom,
results in the Bodhi of the Pratyekabuddha;
when contemplated by highest wisdom,
results in Unsurpassed Bodhi.
When this Dharma was taught,
ten thousand Bodhisattvas attained the true mark of one lifetime.
Fifteen thousand Bodhisattvas attained the Dharma Realm of two lifetimes.
Twenty-five thousand Bodhisattvas attained the Ultimate Wisdom.
Thirty-five thousand Bodhisattvas realized the Ultimate Truth.
This Ultimate Truth is also called the Ultimate Emptiness,
and also called the Shǒuléngyán Samādhi.
Forty-five thousand Bodhisattvas attained the Void Samādhi.
This Void Samādhi is also called the Vast and Great Samādhi,
and also called the Wisdom Seal Samādhi.
Fifty-five thousand Bodhisattvas attained the Forbearance of Non-Retrogression.
This Forbearance of Non-Retrogression is also called the Forbearance According to Dharma,
and also called the Dharma Realm as it is.
Sixty-five thousand Bodhisattvas attained Dhāraṇī.
This Dhāraṇī is also called the Great Mind of Mindfulness,
and also called Unimpeded Wisdom.
Seventy-five thousand Bodhisattvas attained the Lion's Roar Samādhi.
This Lion's Roar Samādhi is also called the Vajra Samādhi,
and also called the Five Wisdom Seals Samādhi.
Eighty-five thousand Bodhisattvas attained the Samādhi of Equality.
This Samādhi of Equality is also called Great Compassion and Great Kindness.
Immeasurable beings equal to the sands of the Ganges Rivers generated the aspiration for Anuttarasamyaksambodhi.
Immeasurable beings equal to the sands of the Ganges Rivers generated the Pratyekabuddha mind.
Immeasurable beings equal to the sands of the Ganges Rivers generated the Śrāvaka mind.
Two hundred billion
human women and celestial women
instantly transformed their female bodies and obtained male bodies.
Xū Bátuóluó attained the fruit of Arhat.
Āmólì, Pímólì, Nièmólì, Měnggālì, Xīmóluóruòjiébǎi, Sānmànnàbátí, Suōpótuó, Shātuóní, Bōluómótā, Suōtuóní, Mónàsī, Āzhuōtí, Píluóqí, Ānmǒlài, Póluómí, Póluómó, Shālí Fùní Fùnà, Mónúlàitì.
